text: Matteo Renzi came to power in February 2014 with a promise of widespread reform, at the head of Italy's powerful centre-left Democratic Party (PD). Before moving into Rome's Chigi Palace at the age of 39, his primary political experience was as mayor of Florence. He had never been a member of parliament. Yet, barely two months after assuming leadership of his party in December 2013, he instigated the downfall of his Prime Minister and party rival Enrico Letta, subsequently taking office. His entry into national politics was seen as a much-needed generational shift in a nation long led by elderly men. Even before becoming prime minister, he was known as Il Rottamatore (The Scrapper), referring to his call to dismantle Italy's political establishment, widely viewed as discredited, corrupt, and having failed the nation for decades. Although he led the party to success in European elections shortly after becoming prime minister, his party's vote share in local elections in May 2015 fell below 24%, and he has yet to contest a general election. Mr Renzi honed his political skills as mayor of Florence, earning widespread praise for promoting the city and managing a significant pedestrianisation plan. However, he was not without critics. A former Florentine councillor complained he was more focused on Facebook updates than on the city's budget. Opposition councillor Ornella De Zordo criticised him for being better at making promises than keeping them. He's used the slogan 'Said, Done!' many times, she remarked. I would say 'Said, But Not Done!' because Matteo Renzi excels at communication and making announcements. But when you examine his record, it is quite different. He markets himself very well. Matteo Renzi assumed power believing politics could be conducted differently and once called for the removal of the old guard. People are weary and disillusioned, he stated. They don't believe anymore. I believe, and that's why I do politics—because I still believe. Some saw similarities to the early years of former British leader Tony Blair and his capture of the left-wing Labour Party in the mid-1990s. Like Mr Blair, the reformist Mr Renzi sought to move the PD to the centre ground and appeal to voters typically aligned with the right. In his own words hugely ambitious, he pledged all the courage, commitment, energy, and enthusiasm of which I am capable. Exuding boundless energy, he appears relaxed on television and in parliament, delivering his speeches quickly and fluently. While his success in power will likely be judged by the outcomes of his reform efforts, his tenure has been overshadowed by Italy's Mediterranean migrant crisis. An estimated 45,000 migrants have arrived in Italy since January, and more than 1,830 people attempting to cross the Mediterranean have died. Mr Renzi has accused other European nations of ignoring the crisis unfolding near Italy's shores, and the issue has benefited his right-wing anti-immigrant opponents, the Northern League. His cause has been supported by Federica Mogherini, a party ally appointed EU foreign affairs chief after the 2014 European elections. In his reform efforts, he angered the left of his party by holding a high-profile meeting at PD headquarters with Silvio Berlusconi, the former centre-right prime minister expelled from parliament but still leading the opposition Forza Italia (FI) movement. However, Mr Renzi remained defiant. It's a contradiction in terms to say 'You should have spoken to FI but not to Berlusconi'. Should I have spoken to [Berlusconi's fiancee's dog] Dudu? Within weeks, Mr Renzi had moved towards a party coup. After dining with President Giorgio Napolitano, the young contender was quoted as saying the government's batteries were running low and a decision had to be made on whether they needed recharging or changing. After visiting Mr Letta, he thanked the prime minister but stated the country was at a crossroads: there was an urgent need for a new phase with a new executive. Shortly thereafter, Mr Letta announced he would resign. However, running the beautiful Renaissance city of Florence and removing traffic from its central squares and streets is vastly different from leading Italy and reforming its politics. He has succeeded in overhauling the electoral system, introducing a form of proportional representation that ensures a large majority for the winning party, after a protracted struggle that alienated some of his own party's MPs. Yet, he faces further challenges as he attempts to implement changes aimed at improving standards in Italy's schools. He has already begun work on reforming the labour market to boost job creation, but he plans to do more and faces opposition from trade unions and within his own party.

text: Being in a wheelchair doesn't mean that I can't do it or anyone else can't do it - we're just as capable as any other models. Gemma Flanagan made her debut on the catwalk at a London fashion event on Wednesday. It was incredible to do it and not fall off. My greatest concern was I'd roll off the end or the side, she stated. Before an illness rendered her unable to walk, she was an air hostess and part-time model. I surprisingly felt just as confident as I have in the past, which, considering it was my first time in the chair, I was unsure how I would manage. When you're walking, you can have a little strut and do your thing. That was my concern - not being able to showcase the clothes as effectively. The designer was very pleased with how I presented their items, and ultimately that's what modelling is about. The fashion show was organised by Models of Diversity, a group advocating for the fashion and beauty industries to represent diversity, and took place at the Ideal Home Show in London's Olympia. Gemma, who is celebrating her 32nd birthday this week, desires that using disabled models becomes standard practice. The more people open to using models with disabilities, the more it will be seen as normal. We've all participated in campaigns that were one-offs for companies, and many of them were unpaid. It would be beneficial to use models with disabilities just as models, not as one-offs - we deserve better, she says. Regarding her future, she states: I have a hair show in May and a few shoots planned with local photographers. I want to do much more using my chair. I'm in it almost all the time now. Part of doing this show was to embrace myself and accept that the chair is no longer the enemy. It's about seeing beyond the metal and wheels and simply saying, 'that's a beautiful model' rather than 'a girl in a chair'. In 2011, Gemma was diagnosed with Guillain-Barré Syndrome, a serious condition affecting the nervous system. She spent seven months in rehabilitation learning to speak, write, and walk again. Recently, however, she has found it increasingly difficult to walk with crutches and has become more reliant on her wheelchair. When I became ill, they hoped I would make a full recovery, she said. But I've started deteriorating again, and the consultant believes this may be the best I will ever be. I've been a bit up and down, but now I mostly feel OK. I want to show others they don't need to be defined by their disabilities. Follow @BBCNewsbeat on Twitter, BBCNewsbeat on Instagram, and Radio1Newsbeat on YouTube.

text: Fireworks scratched colours into the slate grey sky after being unleashed from the top of Tower Bridge as the historic royal flotilla finished gliding along the Thames. This marked the conclusion of the Diamond Jubilee pageant in London, though other events succumbed to the inclement weather—specifically the confetti cannons and a helicopter flypast, which was cancelled due to poor visibility. The persistent, fine rain spared no mercy for the drenched singers who valiantly performed the national anthem during the closing moments. These events were the final remnants of a day filled with fun, food, celebrations, costumes, and multiple renditions of the national anthem, as well as a protest against the monarchy—all defiantly conducted despite the rain. At the day's outset, some revellers travelling to the capital faced disruptions due to overcrowding on the train network, with reports of passengers left behind on platforms due to full carriages. Others opted to celebrate at home, with nearly 9,500 roads closed across England and Wales for parties. Those in the capital enthusiastically joined the festivities, particularly those attending the Big Jubilee Lunch in Piccadilly, featuring a long line of tables in this usually traffic-congested street. The main events to commemorate the Queen's Diamond Jubilee include: Monday, Tuesday, and a guide to the weekend of events. Strolling down Piccadilly, adorned in tiaras and red, white, and blue outfits, were three friends—Jodie Merrylees, 27, from Cheltenham, Gloucestershire, Charlotte Symonds, 30, from Brighouse, West Yorkshire, and Jodie Cosgrove, 27, from Leeds. Ms Symonds stated: I really like the Royal Family and the tradition it represents. I was at the royal wedding too and that was brilliant. We wanted to dress up for the Jubilee and get involved with the atmosphere to feel part of the celebrations. The event became even grander when the Duke and Duchess of Cornwall arrived, walking down the line of tables and even pausing to sit on a potentially damp seat to converse with some of those enjoying their meals. Street parties were notably popular on the day, especially in Bristol, which received more applications for road closures than any other city outside London. Revellers there gathered in a red, white, and blue-adorned Millennium Square, which featured its own make your own corgi attraction. Inspired by the Thames pageant, Andrew Southerden, a landlord in Kibworth, Leicestershire, transformed his pub into HMS Coach & Horses, attaching portholes, liferafts, funnels, and a bow to the building. Party-goers in Richmond Park, Gainsborough, Lincolnshire, could purchase food at 1950s prices. Hot dogs were 7p, bacon sandwiches 9p, and a cup of tea just 2p. In Belfast, Samuel and Margaret Sloan, 80, celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary alongside the Jubilee at a tea party hosted by the city's Lord Mayor. It is a great honour, said Mr Sloan, a retired motor mechanic. She is a very gracious Queen and she does care for the people. More than 300 official street parties took place across Wales. Cardiff's St Mary's Street hosted a Big Lunch celebration while hundreds attended a similar event in Swansea. A beach party was rained off in Rhosneigr, near the Anglesey home of the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge, but the party proceeded regardless—a picnic was held in the village hall instead, attended by hundreds. Ten street parties occurred in Edinburgh, with the Scottish capital believed to have accounted for a third of all of Scotland's street party applications. However, not all participants supported the royal family's constitutional role. Abigail Burnyeat, who attended a street party in Edinburgh's Stockbridge, told the BBC she enjoyed herself but did not view the event as an endorsement of the monarchy. It's a celebration of community, she said, adding: I wouldn't examine it too closely. As the Diamond Jubilee pageant commenced, its 1,000 vessels were greeted along the route by 1.2 million spectators, according to the organisers. Crowds lined the banks of the Thames, some climbing onto window ledges of nearby buildings to gain a better view, all grateful that by then the skies withheld their raindrops. On Lambeth Bridge, a carefully controlled number of the public were permitted, each choosing a side to stand on, to either watch the pageant arrive or see it pass into the distance. As it approached, the smaller boats before the larger ones, great cheers arose, as did the crackling of plastic flags. That sound reached a crescendo when the royal barge approached, prompting many hands to raise mobile phones and cameras, like electronic meerkats eager for a view. Among those on the bridge was Marilyn Griffiths, 59, from Ledbury, Herefordshire, adorned in a union jack hat, earrings, and carrying a flag. She described the pageant as spectacular, adding: I just love the Royal Family and admire them all for what they do. They all work so hard. I wanted to come here to show my support. By the end of the pageant, the rain had become almost torrential, with everyone thoroughly soaked. Yet the crowd's good humour endured, with one man even enjoying a rather soggy ice cream. The last of the steam boats sailed by sounding their horns together and drawing cheers from the flag-wavers along Tower Bridge. I saw the Queen, shouted one small child to his mother. It was certainly an achievement for all. See all the latest Diamond Jubilee news and features at bbc.co.uk/diamondjubilee.

text: Labour MP Simon Danczuk has been suspended by the party after newspaper allegations about his private life. These are external links and will open in a new window. The Sun alleged he exchanged explicit messages with a 17-year-old girl. On Twitter, the Rochdale MP stated the story was not entirely accurate but referred to an extremely low point in his life. He expressed his unreserved apology for his inappropriate behaviour, adding: I was stupid [and] there's no fool like an old fool. A Labour Party spokesman stated: The general secretary of the Labour Party has today suspended Simon Danczuk's membership of the party, pending an investigation into allegations published in the media today. A full investigation will now take place under the authority of the National Executive Committee, which will be responsible for determining any further action. Mr Danczuk, who separated from his wife earlier this year, has been the MP for Rochdale since 2010. The backbencher has been a strong critic of Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and his predecessor Ed Miliband, and has conducted a high-profile campaign to expose historical child abuse. In his statement on Twitter, he added: I'm more saddened that this episode could overshadow the important work we're doing to help Rochdale [and] that's where my focus lies. The Rochdale MP is known as an outspoken backbencher. He has been a thorn in Jeremy Corbyn's side and has described his predecessor Ed Miliband as one of the worst Labour Party leaders in history. The 49-year-old is perhaps best known for his campaigning work on historical child sex abuse, having co-authored a book on alleged abuse by former Rochdale MP Cyril Smith and called for action over a missing 1980s dossier about alleged paedophiles at Westminster. In July, he stated he was stepping back from his child abuse campaigning work to seek help for depression, adding that he was in no doubt it had taken its toll on his marriage. As a consequence of his suspension, Mr Danczuk has had the Labour whip withdrawn, meaning he will sit as an independent MP. Although the girl featured in The Sun was over the age of consent, BBC political correspondent Chris Mason said the allegations were particularly embarrassing for an MP who had devoted much of his time in recent years to campaigning about child protection. In interviews, Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and shadow chancellor John McDonnell both emphasised the independence of the National Executive Committee (NEC) investigation. Corbyn ally and NEC member Ken Livingstone told the BBC people should not jump to conclusions based on Mr Danczuk's suspension. We won't be rushing to any judgement, he stated. The party clearly had to investigate the allegations, he said, adding: The simple fact is that it might not be illegal but a lot of people are going to disapprove of that sort of age gap and that sort of texting, particularly given this is an MP who made the exposure of child abuse a key part of his political career.

text: Manchester City earned their first Premier League home win in almost three months as they battled past Watford at Etihad Stadium. The fourth-placed Blues, aiming to avoid a third consecutive top-flight defeat, took the lead when an unmarked Pablo Zabaleta calmly side-footed in Kevin de Bruyne's deep cross. Raheem Sterling struck the Watford bar after the interval, before Odion Ighalo squandered the visitors' best opportunity by poking over. The Hornets, who fall to 11th, were punished when David Silva scored a late second on his 200th league appearance following a swift City counter-attack. However, a setback for Blues manager Pep Guardiola was Germany midfielder Ilkay Gundogan suffering a severe knee injury, which the Spaniard stated would sideline him for several months. Reflecting on late September, Manchester City had won their first 10 matches under Pep Guardiola, including their opening six Premier League games, establishing a four-point lead at the top of the table. Fast forward to mid-December, and the outlook is less promising. Guardiola's team has since slipped from the summit, losing ground on their title rivals after securing just four victories in their previous 15 matches leading up to Watford's visit. Questions have arisen regarding the renowned Spanish manager's methods, which previously brought him significant success at Barcelona and Bayern Munich. The Blues had not secured a top-flight victory in front of their home fans since that 10th successive win—a 4-0 triumph against Bournemouth on 17 September. While their performance lacked the vigour and flair of those early days under Guardiola, the Blues will likely be content with a determined display that maintains their fourth position. It has been a long time without a win at home, it has been strange, said Zabaleta. City remain seven points behind leaders Chelsea, now a point behind Liverpool and Arsenal—with the Gunners visiting the Etihad on Sunday. The source of City's recent issues is evident—their porous defence. The Blues had kept just one clean sheet in their previous 17 matches and, following Saturday's embarrassing 4-2 defeat at champions Leicester City, Guardiola altered his defence in both personnel and formation. England centre-back John Stones was notably benched as his manager switched from three centre-backs to a four-man defence. Consequently, they appeared more organised and resolute than at any time in the past two months. It was not the prettiest game tonight, but we had the determination to win. We achieved the clean sheet we've been discussing and were solid defensively, added Zabaleta. Nonetheless, they were nearly punished when striker Ighalo eluded Zabaleta but directed Norden Amrabat's right-wing cross over the bar. The Blues were also grateful to goalkeeper Claudio Bravo, who has faced criticism from City fans, for a smart save from Hornets midfielder Etienne Capoue. It is not easy to join a new club and a new country, said Guardiola about the Chile international, who arrived from Barcelona in the summer. I know what people say about him, but he has good experience. When moments arise, he must be brave. Today he was excellent. Media playback is not supported on this device. Watford have displayed two sides to their character under Italian manager Walter Mazzarri—one capable of defeating Manchester United and Everton to climb as high as seventh, and another that capitulated in a 6-1 thrashing by Liverpool earlier in the season and lost three of four before beating the Toffees at the weekend. This Hornets performance was somewhere in the middle. They demonstrated resilience in preventing City from breaking them down, but opportunities at the other end were scarce. Despite scoring three against Everton at the weekend, Mazzarri's side have struggled to find goals throughout the season. Captain Troy Deeney has not scored since 1 October after failing to net in his past eight appearances, eventually being relegated to the bench at the Etihad. Instead, Mazzarri formed a new-look strike partnership with last season's top scorer Ighalo and 20-year-old former Liverpool forward Jerome Sinclair. Sinclair, making his full debut following a £4m summer move, was a peripheral figure, while Ighalo worked diligently but missed his first genuine sight of goal in the final stages. The defeat, combined with points for West Brom and Southampton, resulted in Watford dropping to 11th. Watford manager Walter Mazzarri stated: We were unfortunate with Ighalo's chance. If he had scored, we would have drawn, and in my opinion, that would have been the fair result. Ighalo played a great game and deserved to score. But my entire team performed well, and they deserved more. I am very pleased with them. On midfielder Roberto Pererya's injury: He has a knee issue. We need to determine what it is. We will know in the coming days. We have not been fortunate with injuries. I am not pleased with this one. I don't know how severe it is. I also asked during the game if he felt a twist. He said it was a knock. I am not certain. On leaving Deeney out: We wanted to prepare Deeney for Sunderland. We have three games in a week, and he is on four yellow cards. They did not play at their fluent best but managed to score a couple of really good goals. It wasn't convincing; it was a bit of a nervous atmosphere at the Etihad today, but it was an important three points. text: A Carmarthen school at the centre of a police investigation into claims of historical abuse has been criticised by care inspectors in a new report. The Care and Social Services Inspectorate Wales stated that the residential unit at Rhydygors School, Carmarthen, was not meeting minimum standards. It was also criticised by school inspectors, Estyn, last September. Governors stated they were building on the progress already made in addressing concerns raised in the Estyn report. Earlier this month, Dyfed Powys Police announced they had arrested six former staff members as part of Operation Almond, which is investigating claims of abuse at the school between 1976 and 1986. Rhydygors School, located in Johnstown, provides special education for pupils with social, emotional, and behavioural difficulties. The CSSIW report stated: Overall, we found that young people and their representatives cannot be confident that due care and attention has been paid to the national minimum standards for residential special schools in the period since our last inspection, as the service has not fully met these standards. The school is now subject to monthly visits from Carmarthenshire Council to monitor the quality of care pupils receive. The report stated its acting head teacher, Margaret Davies, and governing body should be more aware of national minimum standards. It also stated 80% of care staff should hold a relevant qualification, but the residential unit had failed to meet that target. The service also failed to complete an annual review of the school's welfare provision for boarding pupils. Inspectors Estyn described the school's performance as adequate but said its prospects for improvement were unsatisfactory. It stated: The school's arrangements for safeguarding pupils generally meet requirements but a few areas give a cause for concern. The school's chair of governors, Matthew Harries, stated: Rhydygors was inspected by Estyn in September 2014 and, as the new chair of governors, I will be looking to build on the progress that has been made to address the recommendations of the report. Indeed, we are pleased that progress has been made in many of these areas as noted in the more recent CSSIW report. A CSSIW spokesperson stated: We do not have any significant concerns about Rhydygors School. Operation Almond is also investigating allegations of abuse at Cartref-y-Gelli children's home in Carmarthen between 1986 and 1990.

text: The spacecraft which made a spectacular landing on a comet last year has discovered a rich array of carbon compounds. A prominent scientist has even described the chemicals as a frozen primordial soup. This supports the hypothesis that comets may have delivered the ingredients for life to early Earth. The findings emerged after the lander, named Philae, landed on comet Churyumov-Gerasimenko 67P in November. It was released by the European Space Agency's Rosetta mothership during the climactic stage of a decade-long mission. Results from the lander's seven instruments are published in a special collection of papers in the journal Science. A team operating a device called COSAC identified no fewer than 16 organic compounds, four of which were previously unknown on comets. Professor Ian Wright of the Open University, who leads another instrument, Ptolemy, described the results as really interesting. I view this cometary material we are analysing as frozen primordial soup. It's the kind of substance that, if warmed and placed in the right environment with suitable conditions, could eventually lead to life forming. What we may be observing here is our abiological ancestral material—this is the substance that contributed to the creation of life. In many respects, it's quite humbling to work on this, as it represents life before life began. One of Ptolemy's most notable discoveries is a compound known as polyoxymethylene, a chain of relatively simple molecules forming a polymer of formaldehyde. Professor Wright stated: The simplest unit of this polymer consists of a single carbon, two hydrogens, and a single oxygen, which then repeats itself. That same ratio of elements occurs in carbohydrates and sugars, making it very interesting and relevant to the biological cycle on Earth. In a separate paper, Fred Goesmann and colleagues describe the 16 compounds found by their COSAC instrument and their potential significance for the development of life. Hydroxyethanal is an efficient initiator in the prebiotic formation of sugars, they write. Methanenitrile is a key molecule in the prebiotic synthesis of amino acids and nucleobases and even offers an elegant pathway to sugars. The authors conclude that the complexity of the comet's chemical composition and the presence of organics containing nitrogen imply that early solar system chemistry fosters the formation of prebiotic material in noticeable concentrations. None of the papers suggests the presence of more complex compounds such as amino acids, though further analysis of the findings may reveal that. Professor Charles Cockell, director of the UK Astrobiology Centre, was not involved in the mission but told the BBC the results were very significant. Finding simple organic compounds on a comet in space, showing us they could have been delivered to early Earth, early in our planet's history, is tremendously exciting. It provides us with better insights into how those building blocks of life may have formed and where they may have originated. It confirms there is organic chemistry throughout the universe, that carbon-containing compounds, some of which are very complex, could be forming on comets in our solar system. Professor Mark McCaughrean, the European Space Agency's senior science advisor, told BBC News: Imagine you want to build a house and you go to a forest, where there are trees, mud, and rocks. You could make a house from that, but it would be hard work. Well, we've now discovered the comet is more like a hardware shop—lots of pre-made building blocks, like door frames, bricks, etc. It gives you a head start. One of the big questions, though, is whether this material is made on the comet or first in space and then incorporated into the comet? We don't know the answer yet. The data published today was gathered during Philae's chaotic landing on the comet. Ptolemy had been programmed to activate ten minutes after touchdown. Professor Wright told the BBC: The idea was we'd just have time for a sniff of the air—there was no great reason to do it, it was to check the instrument had survived landing, an insurance policy to get some data as soon as possible. As events transpired, Philae did not anchor itself to its original landing zone but bounced back up, meaning Ptolemy's 'sniff' occurred while the spacecraft was airborne. Despite this, the instrument successfully obtained readings of whatever material had entered its vent pipe. We've just got a snapshot of some dust that was flying around as we landed, but we've got some very significant data, Professor Wright said. After a long silence, the Philae lander made contact last month, but the link has been intermittent, and the spacecraft's fate is unclear. One theory is that it may have been dislodged or tipped over by a jet of gas emerging from the rocks beneath it. Gas jets are becoming more intense as the comet approaches the Sun, with its closest approach, known as perihelion, occurring shortly on 13 August. Another idea is that because Philae is believed to be sitting at the foot of a cliff, it may have been struck by falling debris, dislodged as the surface warms. However, those involved in the mission are determined to remain optimistic that the lander has survived and will resume contact. Even if it does not, several loads of data, collected and sent back in Philae's first 60 hours on the comet, are still being analysed and have yet to be published.

text: Nigeria's main opposition party has condemned a weekend raid of its Lagos offices by state security agents. We call for an independent commission of inquiry to determine the reasons why armed officers raided our office, stated the All Progressive Congress (APC) deputy chairman Lawal Shuaibu to the BBC. The party reported that computers were destroyed and documents seized during the raid. The State Security Service announced it was investigating alleged voter card cloning ahead of the February elections. The petition alleged that those involved were cloning Inec [Independent Electoral Commission] permanent voter cards, intending to hack into [the] Inec database, corrupt it, and replace them with their own data, stated the SSS. Based on this information, the Service placed the building under surveillance and, convinced that some unwholesome activities were occurring, conducted a raid on the premises. It reported that its agents had confiscated a server, three hard drives, and 31 bags of documents on Saturday. However, the APC described the incident as another in the string of attacks and illegal actions of the administration. It claimed more than a dozen computers had been destroyed, a server vandalised, and 28 individuals arrested. Nigerians have been witnessing the manner in which the government has been using force to oppress us, Mr Shuaibu told the BBC Hausa service. This is to be condemned, and we have been restraining ourselves from taking actions based on the provocations by the government and the security personnel. APC spokesman Lai Mohammed likened the raid to the Watergate scandal in the United States, which resulted in President Richard Nixon's resignation in 1974. Just like the Watergate scandal in the USA, the state-sponsored security operatives, apparently acting at the behest of the ruling PDP [People's Democratic Party] government, turned the office upside down and vandalised everything in sight, he told the AFP news agency. The APC stated the office was functioning as a data centre to process party membership registrations and was a legitimate operation. The APC was established in a merger of four opposition parties in 2013. It asserted there was an urgent need to challenge President Goodluck Jonathan, whose party, the PDP, has won every election in Nigeria since the end of military rule in 1999. The International Crisis Group recently cautioned that February's election might be volatile and vicious. If this violent trend continues, and particularly if the vote is close, marred, or followed by widespread violence, it would deepen Nigeria's already grave security and governance crises, the think tank stated. The government, its agencies, and all other national figures must work urgently to ensure that the vote is not conducted in an explosive situation, as this could further destabilise the country.

text: Writer and humourist Shovon Chowdhury gives his perspective on a recent advert featuring lesbians in India, arguing that we shouldn't be surprised, given India's ancient liberal tradition, which accepted all forms of sexuality and sexual expression. They did an advertisement about lesbians! exclaimed a friend. I misheard librarians, so I was initially perplexed. It seemed positive, as I often worry about reading habits in this nation. However, he then showed me. It is an advertisement for a women's clothing brand, depicting two women in love. I found it well-directed and acted, and frustratingly difficult to ridicule. Was this a significant step forward? It appeared so until I recalled Parveen Babi. Parveen Babi was an actress who illuminated our youth and made the nation proud by appearing on the cover of Time magazine. This entire lesbian subject is not as novel as it is being portrayed. In the 1983 film Razia Sultan, she and Hema Malini recline on a luxurious boat in carefree abandon, with Hema Malini half-asleep and Parveen Babi gazing at her intently, singing a lullaby. At one point, Hema Malini awakens, and they kiss. The kiss is obscured by feathers, which was customary for any kiss at that time, with feathers, flowers, and dupattas being the preferred methods of concealment. This television commercial offers a more contemporary setting, with fewer feathers, making it more relatable. That girl could be my cousin, you think, or my best friend's sister. However, cinema was the pioneer. Generally, cinema has been a powerful force for social change in this country. Post-independence filmmakers felt the warmth of freedom and were unashamed to include positive social messages in their films, as part of nation-building. Until the 1990s, when we discovered a crucial fact about television: you do not have to leave the house. This led to a decline in cinema's importance. More television meant more advertising, where economics plays a role. Most television serial producers are notoriously frugal, resulting in slow dialogue, with an arrow fired in one episode reaching its target several episodes later. Television writers are poorly compensated, while advertising professionals are better paid. Consequently, advertisements often surpass programmes in quality. Some copywriters aspire to do good, and occasionally, clients support them. Thus, Indian advertising has featured numerous positive social messages. We have witnessed three broad phases. We are a very poor country, and some products have had to establish their markets from scratch. Initially, in the 1970s and 1980s, advertising taught us basic lessons, such as the benefits of bathing, the virtues of brushing teeth, and why one should be kind to one's wife. During this phase, I first saw a woman in a bikini in a Liril soap advertisement, leaving an indelible mark, and I still remember her name. As society evolved, so did the lessons. In the next phase, women continued to play a significant role. Advertising demonstrated that women could indeed do things, such as purchasing clothes, owning credit cards, and driving stylish convertibles. In the current phase, socially conscious advertisers address issues like stuttering, cancer survivors, and partition [the 1947 partition that created Pakistan]. And also lesbians. But why all the fuss about lesbians, you may ask. Is it a conspiracy against women? Is it forbidden in the Kama Sutra? Has Indian society traditionally frowned upon gay individuals? Not really. For instance, in the Laws of Manu, over 2,000 years old, the prescribed punishment for homosexuality is bathing with clothes on, after which one is purified. If this seems extreme, consider that the punishment for forcible intercourse was the immediate removal of two fingers. Kautilya's Artha Shastra, an economic and political treatise, suggests a small fine. The Kama Sutra provides detailed instructions for homosexual acts, as it does for everything else. The Sushruta Samhita, a medical treatise from around 600 BC by Sushruta, one of history's greatest medical figures, defines types of homosexual behaviour and states that sexual orientation is determined at birth. He distinguished between transgenders and homosexuals. Transgenders have not always had an easy time in India, but they have a place in society. They have hosted television shows and been elected to office, sometimes as a statement against other leaders. The Khajuraho temples, built around 1000 AD, depict a wide variety of people in intimate scenarios, including some implausible combinations. So what went wrong, you may ask? When did we become such prudes? The primary cause was a small, plumpish white woman. It would be unfair to place all the blame on Queen Victoria, though. We also played a part. Unable to see the benefits of British rule, we revolted in 1857. Once the revolt was suppressed, a new Indian Penal Code (IPC) was developed, coming into force in 1861. It was designed to ensure the natives would never rise again. The creators of this document also considered their sovereign's wishes. Queen Victoria disapproved of sex, and the IPC of 1861 acknowledges this, criminalising almost any sexual activity except the missionary position. Nearly 75 years after independence, it seems the natives still cannot be trusted, which is why the IPC remains in force. This means that this film, which millions have liked on YouTube, is more than just a film. It is an act of civil disobedience. It depicts a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison under Section 377. I am unsure of the punishment for directors, but if the police fulfil their duty, as mandated by her majesty, we should soon find out. Shovon Chowdhury is a Delhi-based amateur humourist and advertising professional. Murder with Bengali Characteristics is his second novel.

text: There has been a 65% increase in children recorded as home educated in the UK over six years. Parents cited reasons such as lifestyle, dissatisfaction or disagreements with local schools, special needs, bullying, and religion. Responses to Freedom of Information requests from 190 local authorities revealed 36,609 home-educated children. The government states it will continue to respect the rights of parents to home educate their children. There is no legal requirement for parents to send their children to school, although they must provide a suitable education at home. The figures indicate an increase of at least 10,399 pupils, reaching nearly 37,000, within a school population of approximately 9.5 million pupils. The home-educated figure may be underestimated. When parents withdraw a child from school, they are recorded as being home educated, but children who never start school may not be included in the statistics. Among 190 councils with figures for 2014-15, there were 178 with data for the past three years, showing a 26% increase. For 133 of the local authorities, data from 2009-10 to 2014-15 showed numbers had risen by almost two-thirds. Graham Stuart, chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group on Home Education, suggests councils may have improved in recording information, and any figures are almost certainly underestimated. Local authorities have created groups to share best practice, and we're seeing what I hope is an increasing trend to stop treating home education as a problem to be regulated, and instead see it as an opportunity to be facilitated and supported, said the Conservative MP and former chairman of the education select committee. Parents are not required to provide a reason for withdrawing a child from school, but in 41 council areas, there is information about the purpose, offering insight into variations among home-educating families. Top of the list is a difference of philosophy or lifestyle at 13.4%. However, this can be higher in some areas, such as Gloucestershire, where this accounts for 235 of the 641 children being home educated. This is followed by dissatisfaction with the local school or a conflict, accounting for 9.3% of families. In Hertfordshire, 240 out of a total of 724 parents cited this as their motivation. Cultural or religious reasons are mentioned in 6.2% of cases, with bullying at 4.8% and special needs or medical problems at 4.3%. With increasing pressure on school places due to rising pupil numbers, 3.4% of home-educating parents state they could not secure a place for their child in a preferred school. Dr Helen Lees, of Newman University Birmingham, has written extensively about alternative education. She believes some parents dislike the structured assessment and testing in schools. She says parents find online accounts of the success of home education and are saying: If they can do it why can't we do it. They're hearing from groups on Facebook or Yahoo that it's working well, the children are happy. The recording of parents' motivations is inconsistent, partly because parents are not obliged to explain themselves, resulting in no comprehensive information. The same applies to the limited data about the families themselves. In the very few local authorities where there is information on religion, about 31% of home educators belong to a faith group, although that may not be the reason they have chosen an alternative to school. Of those, half are listed as Christian and a third as Muslim. The areas with the highest growth in home education are very diverse, suggesting numerous factors behind the increase. In two counties where there are grammar schools, numbers have remained relatively high, reaching 1,429 in Kent and 1,191 in Essex. In Rhondda Cynon Taf, where there were five home-educated children recorded in 2009-10, there are now 65. Ofsted has recently expressed concern that a very small number of people may be misusing the right to home educate to place their children in unregistered and potentially illegal schools. That concern has been echoed by the Education Secretary Nicky Morgan, who has asked the Chief Inspector of Schools Sir Michael Wilshaw to gather evidence for potential prosecutions. The government is consulting on greater regulation of part-time education settings providing more than six to eight hours a week of tuition. text: A law has come into force in France which makes it an offence for a Muslim woman to conceal her face behind a veil when in public. It is the first nation in Europe to openly prohibit a form of attire some Muslims consider a religious obligation. BBC News website readers in France have been submitting their reactions to this story. Here is a selection of their comments. In my view, the law seems to infringe upon individual freedoms. I am a Muslim but do not wear a headscarf as I believe it does not align with my principles. Nevertheless, this ban will undoubtedly stigmatise Islam. This practice affects a small number of Muslim women in France and thus seems extreme and unjust, as these women will likely be confined at home most of the time. The consequences will be socially disastrous. Through this law, it is evident that Islam in France is perceived as a threat to French values and society. Sabrina, Lille, France. As a Muslim residing in Paris, I am pleased that this new law is enacted, as there has been a growing issue for some time now in Paris, with the radicalisation of young Muslims. Some of the more extreme Muslims have started to use attire as a symbol or statement against French society. I believe that the extreme example of the Muslim faith contradicts all that Muslims in France represent. That is, that we can coexist harmoniously with other religions and faiths. Jean Paul Baptiste, Paris, France. Finally, a law that safeguards the dignity and human rights of women. This is not a racist law; it is a courageous and progressive law that aims to end the scandalous persecution of women in the Muslim community. I am not Sarkozy's biggest supporter and wish someone else was leading my country, but I support this law entirely as the plight of women having to wear this garment worldwide deeply saddens me. Rachel Sword, Aix en Provence, France. I concur with this law. The women who walk around in public in the burqa evoke feelings of both fear and pity. I have often heard that these women complain of being completely ignored by those around them - hardly surprising, really. Concealing your identity causes others to become wary and suspicious. Fiona Ricard, Gailhan, France. Despite being a human rights lawyer, I have mixed feelings about the law. Freedom of religion dictates that people should be able to express their faith as they wish, though it can be limited by the state if there are strong reasons and it is proportionate. I think it should not be banned outright and that it is excessive, but it should perhaps be restricted in employment or other societal areas. While the state must respect the diverse values of its population, immigrants also have to respect the values of the society they have chosen to live in - and France is a secular state. Andy, Strasbourg, France. Enacting a law to ban face-covering veils in France is taking an approach that will polarise and entrench opinions. Very few Muslim women wish to wear face veils, but prohibiting them will make them want to do so to defend what they perceive as an attack on their identity. Why take a stance that will push Muslims (the majority of whom are not conservative) into a more polarised position (unless, of course, it's to win a few votes)? Naveen Webber, Gex, France. I have been living in France for about six months now and the relative lack of political correctness is a refreshing change from the UK. The veil ban is not a significant issue here, more like a gentle reaffirmation of French equality values. It definitely has nothing to do with a personal crusade by Sarkozy to win votes. Robin Marshall, Avignon, France.

text: The museum at Cuba's most famous beach, the Bay of Pigs, is under renovation. Inside, workers are actively installing new multimedia exhibits, while outside, a team of builders is laying the concrete patio and painting the museum entrance. The grand reopening is scheduled for April, marking the 55th anniversary of the landing at Playa Giron by hundreds of CIA-trained Cuban exiles in a failed attempt to overthrow Fidel Castro and his socialist revolution. The unsuccessful invasion marked a low point in US-Cuba relations, only surpassed by the Cuban Missile Crisis a year later, and remains a symbol of Washington's covert interventions in Latin America. Many of the original Cuban fighters, both militias and regular army troops, are still alive today. However, in Playa Giron itself, only a few remain, and several are in poor health. Dolores Vic Hernandez, aged 83, may not have fought the invading forces, but she vividly recalls escaping from them, fleeing her home in the small coastal town into the surrounding hills with her sister-in-law and their children. We only had the clothes we were wearing, and the babies were in nappies. We collected our friend who had six children and whose husband was in Havana, and we took her with us to the mountains. Dolores cannot move as freely as she once did, and her sight is failing, but it is not difficult to imagine how determined she must have been as a young mother trying to protect her family from the escalating conflict. I'm a person who's never been afraid of anything, she says defiantly as she describes entering an abandoned house to take a little coffee and sugar, some biscuits for the children for their journey. Eventually, of course, Fidel Castro took control of the revolutionary forces at Giron and orchestrated a famous victory, one which would embarrass Washington for decades. Obama-Castro summit caps thaw in US-Cuba relations. What is behind the US-Cuba thaw? How does Obama get along with Latin America? Scenes from a warming Cuba-US relationship. Since the thaw with the US was announced, Fidel Castro, the elder statesman of the Cuban Revolution, has only made brief pronouncements about the new relationship: I don't trust in the United States' policy nor have I exchanged a word with them, he wrote in an editorial in the state-run newspaper, Granma, published a little over a year ago. His lack of trust is unsurprising, considering he survived numerous assassination attempts by the CIA during his time in power. Their concerns for Cuba are as much social and cultural as economic and political, he argues. They worry about what will happen to their way of life. However, they may already be too late in that regard: Most people in Cuba are aware that in the 25 years since the collapse of the Soviet Union and the changes that already began in Cuba, that erosion began some time ago. text: A teachers' union is warning that schools are increasingly likely to use unqualified teaching staff. Parents no longer have the certainty when they send their child to school that they will be taught by qualified teachers, stated NASUWT leader Chris Keates. Labour's Tristram Hunt described the situation as nothing less than a scandal. However, the Conservatives assert there are fewer teachers in schools without qualified status than in 2010. The NASUWT teachers' union, convening its annual conference in Cardiff, will hear claims that an increasing number of teachers without qualified teacher status are being employed in schools. The union surveyed its members about their experiences. Among the 4,600 respondents, 61% reported working alongside unqualified staff, with 66% asserting the situation was deteriorating due to funding issues. This is jeopardising the educational progress of children, remarked Ms Keates, criticising the employment of unqualified staff as a crude cost-cutting measure. Teachers responding to the union's survey included comments such as: They lack any training in classroom management and discipline and I feel that parents are being misled by the quality of teaching within the school. The employment of unqualified teachers has become a general election issue. Labour has campaigned against allowing academies and free schools to employ teachers who do not possess qualified teacher status or who are in training to become qualified. The rising number of unqualified teachers in our schools shows yet again that the Tory plan is threatening standards and failing children and working families, stated shadow education secretary Tristram Hunt. David Cameron has removed the requirement for teachers to be qualified, and as a result over 400,000 children are now being taught by unqualified teachers without receiving training in skills vital to the profession such as classroom discipline, safeguarding and how to deliver effective teaching for all children. The Liberal Democrats also advocate for requiring teachers to have qualified status. However, both the Liberal Democrats and the Conservatives claim there were more unqualified teachers in schools when Labour was in power. They refute the suggestion that the use of unqualified teachers is increasing. A Conservative party spokesman said: The number of teachers without qualified status has decreased since 2010. And we need to keep this in perspective - only 3.7% of teachers are 'unqualified'. But most importantly, we've given head teachers more freedom over the teachers they employ because we trust them to know what is best for their schools. There are some brilliant teachers who have not got qualified teacher status - nuns, great linguists, computer scientists, engineers and other specialists that inspire their pupils. They may have worked in the independent sector or have experience in the outside world. A spokesman for the Liberal Democrats stated they would change the law to guarantee a qualified teacher in every classroom. Teaching must be recognised as the vitally important and high status profession that it is, able to attract and retain the very best people. It is good news that there are now fewer unqualified teachers working in schools than under the previous Labour government. However, every child deserves to be taught by a qualified teacher, regardless of what type of school they attend. The most recent Department for Education figures available, for 2013, show the number of unqualified teachers rose compared with the previous year, from 14,800 to 17,100, but is lower than in 2010, when there were 17,800 teachers without qualified teacher status. However, for academies, the proportion of unqualified teachers has increased each year since 2010, from 2,200 to 7,900.

And the most important thing is that we have given head teachers more freedom to choose the teachers they want because we trust them to know what is best for their school. The number of ‘unqualified’ teachers is only three-point-seven percent. A Liberal Democrat spokeswoman said that they would change the law to guarantee a qualified teacher in every classroom. There are many excellent teachers who do not have the title of certified teachers – nuns, outstanding linguists, engineers, and other specialists who inspire their pupils. They may have worked in the private sector or have had experiences from the outside world. It is good news that there are now fewer unqualified teachers working in schools than under the previous Labour government. Teaching must be recognized as the vitally important and high-ranking profession it is and be able to attract and retain the best people. The proportion of unqualified teachers has increased every year since 2010 in academies from 2,200 to 7,900. The most recent figures available from the Department for Education show that the number of unqualified teachers increased from 14,800 to 17,100, but is lower than in 2010, when there were 17,800 unqualified teachers.

text: Shaun Johnson scored a winning drop-goal as New Zealand beat England in a tense and physical Four Nations match at a sell-out Huddersfield. Media playback is not supported on this device. Man of the match Johnson, who scored a decisive try to defeat England in the 2013 World Cup semi-final, put the Kiwis ahead 17-16 with 14 minutes remaining. His team then held on for a crucial two points, significantly advancing them towards the final on 20 November. Gareth Widdop had kicked two penalties, and England consistently threatened the Kiwi line as the home team dominated the opening 20 minutes. However, New Zealand then took control, scoring a Jordan Kahu penalty and a try from Jordan Rapana in the right corner, giving David Kidwell's side a 6-4 lead at the break. They soon doubled their advantage when Johnson intercepted a Widdop pass for an 80-yard score that Kahu converted. England rallied, with Huddersfield Giants winger Jermaine McGillvary scoring in the corner, bringing the hosts within two points. Another try from winger Rapana, following a brilliant Manu Ma'u offload, was cancelled out by a converted Ryan Hall touchdown by the corner flag, created by a sublime flicked pass from Widdop. This left the score at 16-16 before Johnson struck from in front of the posts. Media playback is not supported on this device. New Zealand captain Jesse Bromwich stated before the match that the round-robin format of the Four Nations gave Saturday's Test the feel of a semi-final. With both teams yet to face favourites Australia and minnows Scotland, the importance of winning at Huddersfield was clear. England will play Scotland in Coventry next Saturday but are likely to need to defeat the Kangaroos in London on 13 November to reach the final at Anfield. This leaves Wayne Bennett's talented team with a challenging task as they aim to end their long wait for a major tournament victory, a sequence stretching back to Great Britain's World Cup win in 1972. The match marked forward Sam Burgess's first for England since returning from rugby union and his debut as captain, and it was also the first time Australian Wayne Bennett had coached England in a meaningful fixture after last Saturday's warm-up win over France in Avignon. It appeared very promising for them as England began with a purpose and intent that the Kiwis seemed unable to match. Canberra hooker Josh Hodgson marshalled the team superbly, and England were deserving of their 4-0 lead. However, they were unable to score a try and, by the break, had been forced to defend numerous repeat sets as the Kiwis took charge. Although England refused to give in after the influential Johnson's intercept try, they were always chasing the game during an increasingly scrappy second half as the Kiwis demonstrated why they are rated as the world's number one side in the way they closed out the game. The promise that this might be the start of a bright new era for an England team with a history of falling short in key contests was quickly extinguished, and many of the players slumped to the floor at the end of what was ultimately a very disappointing afternoon. England defeated New Zealand 2-1 in a Test series last year, and the Kiwis had won only two of their past 10 away games against Great Britain or England. It has not been easy for new coach Kidwell in 2016, with his team managing only two line breaks and one try in their previous two matches this year, both of which saw them comfortably beaten by Australia. But with a huge forward pack providing a platform for versatile, in-your-face hooker Issac Luke, as well as the mercurial Johnson, the Kiwis secured a much-needed victory ahead of their match against the Kangaroos in Coventry next weekend. They defended solidly early in the match and built pressure superbly as they wrestled the initiative away from their opponents, along with a valuable two points. text: George the Poet, a spoken word performer and rapper who wants to use his voice as a force for change in society, has come fifth on the BBC Sound Of 2015 list, which showcases emerging artists for the coming 12 months. These are external links and will open in a new window. George Mpanga draws inspiration from the injustices he witnessed growing up on the Stonebridge Park estate in north-west London. After studying politics, psychology, and sociology at Cambridge University and conducting poetry workshops for children in London, he is now set to release his debut album on Island Records and publish his first poetry collection. The 23-year-old expresses a desire to inspire others to achieve greater things. I want people to be aware of their power, he states. He is the first artist announced from the BBC Sound Of 2015 top five, with one act from the top five being revealed each day this week, culminating in the winner's announcement on Friday. The list was compiled by asking 139 DJs, critics, and broadcasters to name their favourite new acts. Are you a poet or a rapper first? Chronologically, I was initially a rapper, but currently, I am primarily a poet. When did you discover the power of words? I have always been interested in music, and my mother often discussed lyrics with me. I recall her explaining the Bob Marley song Buffalo Soldier to me. Dreadlock Rasta/Taken from Africa/Brought to America/Fighting on arrival/Fighting for survival. It left a significant impression. Simultaneously, I grew up attending church, and my mother read the Bible with me. Observing the pastor commanding an audience made me aspire to do the same. Watching the film of Malcolm X and witnessing his use of words further inspired me. When did you transition from rap to poetry? I consider rap a specialised form of poetry, specialised in its strict adherence to time metre, similar to traditional poetry forms. In William Blake's poem London, one finds regimented thought. I would argue that I began writing in a traditional poetry form, but performing them extended that. Without the music, the essence was akin to what William Blake offered. You mention drawing on your early life in the inner city. How does that influence your work? It had a profound impact on me. I was exposed to a wide range of life experiences. I witnessed people losing loved ones, amassing wealth, and effecting change. In year six, around age 10 or 11, I was fond of some kids in my primary school. They were delightful, always cheerful. I recall them casually mentioning that their father had beaten their mother the previous night, and their older sister had to fend him off with a baseball bat. They did not grasp the seriousness of their words, but it disturbed me. I remember trying to combat everything, attempting to save everyone from every calamity. Eventually, I realised I could not save everyone, but when given a platform, I would strive for structural change. Many of my frustrations arise from being unable to share my blessings with my family, friends, and community. Structural issues, such as family disintegration, financial disorganisation, and lack of political influence, hinder their progress. These factors make it challenging for me to advance professionally with those I grew up with. This needs to change. How can you effect change? I must exemplify what I believe needs to occur. For instance, I am self-employed and have an enterprising mindset. Demonstrating these qualities could benefit everyone if they possess some degree of enterprise. I need to set an example, but content is also crucial. My EP, The Chicken and the Egg, addresses premature parenthood. Discussing this issue raises awareness and provides catharsis for those who can relate. Do you write about yourself or create fictional characters? I draw partly from personal experience and also from observation. Did premature parenthood affect you personally? No, it did not happen to me. It occurred around me. Why pursue structural change through entertainment instead of politics? The political arena is overly regulated and exclusive. Entertainment is less exclusive. If I am known for creating appealing sounds, it is harder to justify hindering that process. Is structural change possible through music and poetry? Yes. Beyond the notion that anything is possible, it is evident. I speak, you listen, you attend my gig. We simply need to make decisions. That is all. Where do you see yourself in five years? I envision the realisation of everything I am discussing now. I foresee myself providing structures for people to demonstrate autonomy, take control, and own the entertainment space. If my words seem too ambitious, demonstration is the highest form of argument. First, I will show you how to do it, then I will invite you to participate.

text: Chelsea underlined their title credentials with a superb come-from-behind victory over Manchester City at the start of an engrossing weekend of Premier League action. Arsenal delivered an impressive performance in their victory at West Ham, while Bournemouth shocked Liverpool in a thrilling seven-goal encounter. Tottenham, Sunderland, Crystal Palace, Stoke, and West Brom also secured wins, whereas Manchester United and Everton ended in a draw at Goodison Park. My team of the week is displayed above. Do you concur with my selection, or would you choose differently? Why not select your own Team of the Week from the shortlist provided by BBC Sport journalists and share it with your friends? Choose your XI from our list and share it with your friends. The save over the bar from Sergio Aguero in the early stages appeared effortless. His subsequent save, slightly more crucial, was from Kevin de Bruyne, but his most remarkable save was from a second attempt by Aguero, who must have thought Courtois was unbeatable by then. It required an excellent finish to initially beat the Belgian international goalkeeper, but Courtois soon demonstrated he was not inclined to be beaten again. Part of Manchester City's frustration stemmed from missing numerous chances, with Courtois matching everything they attempted. What I admire about Courtois is his lack of drama and his consistent performance in significant matches. Making the save is his sole focus. He does not act like a star, insisting on being impeccably groomed with perfectly arranged attire. In fact, he appears somewhat awkward with his preppy hairstyle, but who cares? He is proving to be an exceptional goalkeeper. The tackle by Aguero on Brazilian international Luiz was laden with animosity from previous encounters. Neither man was willing to retreat from the challenge, but it is not the first time Luiz has prevailed against the Argentine. The rivalry between their two remarkable football nations is well-known, but the pursuit of the Premier League title would only have intensified the competition. I have previously mentioned Luiz's current excellent form, and he persistently provoked Aguero throughout the match, hoping the striker would falter—and indeed he did. What Luiz or Chelsea could not have anticipated was Aguero's severe reaction, leading to his dismissal and suspension for several games. Discuss Luiz performing his role. He was outstanding in multiple ways, leaving Manchester City to reassess their title strategy and without Aguero for at least a few matches. I observed Muniesa play in a successful Stoke team against an indifferent Watford. I thought then that he was a player worth closer observation, but his performance against a completely outclassed Burnley was so impressive that I deemed him worthy of mention. His composure on the ball for a defender was evident, reflecting his time at Barcelona as a youth. His goal, however, was reminiscent of Gerard Pique. To witness a central defender initiate a move in his own half, follow the ball into the opposition's penalty area, demand the ball from a goalscorer, receive it, and finish like Lionel Messi was entirely unexpected. It was sheer class, reminiscent of Barcelona from start to finish. West Brom in the top six? They were on Saturday night. I must be dreaming. I am uncertain what Tony Pulis has achieved at The Hawthorns, but he has them playing and believing simultaneously. Their defenders appear to be the current stars, with McAuley particularly proving to be a significant asset once more. McAuley consistently contributes goals, typically from set-pieces, rarely misses games, and is wholly committed to the cause. The block he made on Troy Deeney to prevent the Watford captain from scoring his 100th goal was a monumental intervention. Pulis is doing an excellent job, and he now needs to prevent James McClean from acting unpredictably. McClean is a very talented footballer, and engaging in altercations occasionally for no reason will not enhance his reputation or West Brom's chances of winning matches. The cross for Harry Kane's header early on was a statement of intent. What followed was hardly something Swansea could contest, as they had been warned about the mood Tottenham and Walker, in particular, were in. We have all seen what happens when Spurs are in form—they can be devastating. However, I would have preferred a draw against Chelsea last week and a comfortable 2-0 victory, rather than a swashbuckling win, against Swansea. My reasoning is this: I am weary of being repeatedly led into a false sense of optimism about the title by a Tottenham team that dominates lesser teams yet falters against bigger clubs. Walker is not one to falter on the big stage, but this 5-0 victory over Swansea is likely to merely cover the cracks. Last week's defeat at Chelsea was more than a mere blip—it was a clear indication that more needs to be done at White Hart Lane before they can be considered serious title contenders. It is all well and good defeating teams like Swansea, but they are not going to compete for the Premier League title anytime soon. This was an outstanding performance from McArthur, and Crystal Palace desperately needed the three points. The Scot appeared commanding throughout, and manager Alan Pardew needed it more than anyone. In fact, defeat was not an option. I am a big fan of Pardew, but let us be clear, despite their recent poor run of results, Palace are exceeding expectations. They have simply lost their way slightly. The result against Southampton was impressive, and as long as they have players like McArthur performing well in key areas, they should be fine. What they did last week, asking Christian Benteke to mark players in the box against Swansea, was like something out of a comic book. Defenders defend and attackers attack—why complicate it? text: Welsh cyclist Elinor Barker believes there is less pressure on GB's women's Olympic pursuit team in Rio because they are not clear favourites to win. Team GB secured gold in London 2012 but only achieved third place at the 2016 World Championships. The USA and Canada pose threats to the British team comprising Barker, Laura Trott, Ciara Horne, and Joanna Rowsell Shand. There's perhaps less pressure now because it's not necessarily ours to lose, stated the 21-year-old Barker. It's still ours to win, but there isn't a dominant force in women's team pursuit now as there had been for many years. I think it makes it much more exciting, but it also means no one is focusing on any single team. We're all observing each other, we're all interested in what everyone will do, and there are probably about five teams who could quite easily win if it goes well for them on the day, which makes it quite exciting. Barker was a 17-year-old watching on television when the GB team of Trott, Rowsell Shand, and Danielle King defeated the USA in the pursuit final at the 2012 Games. She expressed disbelief that four years later she would be competing in Rio. Probably a combination of luck and very hard work has brought me here, Barker added. I wouldn't be here if I hadn't worked very hard and been very specific in my training, but I've also been very fortunate with the opportunities I've received. Barker, from Cardiff, was part of the team that claimed a bronze medal in the World Championships this year, when a poor performance in an early round ended their chances of reaching the final. After years of dominating the event, the result attracted criticism, though Barker believes there is much that the GB team have learned from that setback. It just goes to show people make mistakes all the time, but it doesn't mean that we're not a good team, she added. We came back from it [to take bronze] with exactly the same line-up, so it shows it was that ride rather than us—it was a bad race and it doesn't define us as a team.

text: Jeremy Corbyn says he will ask his MPs to vote for the Article 50 Brexit process to begin, if the government is forced to seek Parliament's approval. He stated it was very clear his party accepted the referendum outcome. Some shadow cabinet members are reportedly contemplating voting against initiating the UK's EU exit negotiations. The Supreme Court will announce next Tuesday whether the government must seek Parliament's approval. Ministers assert they already possess sufficient powers under the Royal Prerogative to proceed with Brexit. However, campaigners contend that commencing Brexit in this manner would be undemocratic and unconstitutional. In June's referendum, 51.9% of voters supported leaving the EU, while 48.1% favoured remaining in the 28-nation bloc. Mr Corbyn stated: It's very clear the referendum made a decision that Britain is to leave the European Union. It was not to destroy jobs and living standards or communities, but it was to leave the European Union and have a different relationship in the future. I have made it very clear that the Labour Party accepts and respects the decision of the British people. We will not block Article 50. Asked if that meant he would impose a three-line whip—the strongest available sanction—on Labour MPs, requiring them to support Article 50, he said: It means that all Labour MPs will be asked to vote in that direction next week or whenever the vote arises. The Guardian reports that four shadow cabinet ministers and several junior Labour spokespeople were considering defying Mr Corbyn and voting against Article 50 being invoked. The Supreme Court's decision on whether a vote needs to occur follows a government appeal against a High Court ruling last autumn that MPs and peers should have to vote to give their approval. Following Mr Corbyn's comments, Green Party co-leader Caroline Lucas said he was trying to deny Labour MPs the chance to make their own principled choice on one of the most important decisions of the UK's recent history. And Liberal Democrat leader Tim Farron said Mr Corbyn was actively helping the government in its plans to leave the European single market, at a huge cost to jobs and prosperity.

text: An adventurer is to spend Christmas Day alone in the Antarctic as he bids to become the first Scot to undertake a solo, unassisted and unsupported expedition to the South Pole. Luke Robertson, aged 30, aspires to become the youngest Briton to accomplish the feat, in support of the charity Marie Curie. He is spending 40 days alone, hauling 130kg of equipment over 730 miles of ice. Mr Robertson hails from Aberdeenshire but currently resides in Edinburgh. He will expend more than 10,000 calories daily while enduring temperatures of -50C and winds reaching 100mph. He has already covered nearly 300 miles since departing from Hercules Inlet on the Antarctic edge on 5 December. The adventurer was motivated to undertake the challenge after overcoming numerous health issues, including surgery to remove a suspected brain tumour a year ago, which was actually a large and rare cyst. He also had a pacemaker implanted at 23 after experiencing a complete heart block. text: Mae arweinydd Cyngor Conwy, Gareth Jones, wedi cyhoeddi ei fod yn gadael grŵp Plaid Cymru. Share this on Email Facebook Messenger Messenger Twitter Copy this link These are external links and will open in a new window This follows a debate within party ranks after Mr Jones appointed a cabinet that included Conservatives. The national party had stated that they would not permit their councillors to collaborate with the Tories. Among those who have criticised him is Assembly Member Simon Thomas, who said that the Plaid Cymru group on Conwy Council did not want Mr Jones to accept the position initially. Mr Thomas also stated there would be implications regarding disciplining Mr Jones. The dispute has continued with Mr Jones, former AM for Aberconwy 1999-2003 and 2007-2011, stating on BBC Radio Cymru's Post Cyntaf programme that he did not understand the party's central strategy in refusing to endorse his cabinet, which includes Conservative councillors. What is the rule as far as working with Labour is concerned, which is as much a threat as the Conservatives? he asked. I fail to understand Plaid Cymru's strategy - there is nothing in the constitution that refers to any party... but suddenly there's this business... we don't work with the Conservatives but there is collaboration with the Conservatives in several places across Wales, including the National Assembly. He added that his intention in forming a coalition was to govern openly. Conwy's cabinet includes two Plaid Cymru members - including Mr Jones - five Conservatives, and one independent councillor. Labour councillors declined an invitation to join. There were two other Plaid Cymru members in Mr Jones's original plans, but they are not in the final cabinet. Mr Jones said the decision to leave was difficult, but there was no choice, of course, because I must respect the decision made by the national working group. There was a discussion, and the majority opposed supporting what we are trying to achieve in Conwy's cabinet, and what has become entirely clear from that decision is that Plaid would not be able to support any Plaid Cymru member as a member of this cabinet in Conwy. My intention is to remain a member of Plaid Cymru, but that is a matter between me and the central party. In a statement issued following the Tuesday evening meeting between Plaid Cymru leader Leanne Wood and the party's councillors in Conwy, a spokesperson said: Plaid Cymru is proud of being a party governed by the will of its membership. Gareth Jones's proposals were presented to the party's National Executive Committee and rejected in a democratic vote. Plaid Cymru will therefore not be part of the proposed coalition on Conwy Council.

text: Pokemon Go was released to most parts of the world this month, and in a matter of days has become a global phenomenon. The augmented reality game has been downloaded by millions of players, who are encouraged to explore real-world locations to capture virtual monsters. However, the game has sparked controversy, with some users ignoring safety warnings, resulting in car accidents, muggings, injuries, and even fatalities. Saudi Arabian clerics have labelled the game un-Islamic. Indonesia has prohibited its military from playing the game, and a Cossack leader has claimed it smacks of Satanism. Police globally have issued warnings to players in an effort to prevent further incidents. So what do we know about the incidents so far? On 20 July, Jerson Lopez de Leon, 18, and his cousin Daniel Moises Picen, 17, were ambushed while playing the game southeast of Guatemala City. Mr Lopez de Leon was killed, and his cousin was seriously injured. Police discovered nearly 20 bullet casings at the scene but remain uncertain of the motive behind the killing. On 18 July, a man crashed into a parked police car in Baltimore, US, continued driving, and finally stopped at the end of the road after police pursued him. Police report he admitted to playing Pokemon Go at the time. Baltimore Police state there were two other Pokemon Go-related incidents just this week. On 19 July, a group of 20 teenagers stole a boat in an attempt to catch Pokemon characters on a lake in Liverpool, UK. The group abandoned the boat in the middle of the lake after the coastguard was called to investigate. The rescue team advised users to exercise caution to avoid endangering themselves and rescue services. A woman in New Jersey, US, had to be rescued by firemen after becoming stuck in a cemetery tree while playing the game. The fire chief issued a public safety warning but spared the woman further embarrassment by withholding her name. On 14 July, two men in California, US, fell up to 33m (108 ft) off a cliff after disregarding no trespassing signs while playing Pokemon Go. Firefighters rescued the men and transported them to a nearby hospital. They have not been charged with trespassing.
