text: Tom Watson, who has been elected as Labour's deputy leader, has been an MP since 2001. The 48-year-old previously served as a minister in the Labour government and held the position of deputy chairman of the party, earning a reputation—which he disputes—as a formidable political figure. The MP for West Bromwich East is also recognised as a campaigner, notably on historical child abuse and a recent legal challenge to the government's surveillance laws. However, his most renowned campaign was against phone hacking. He played a prominent role in the questioning of Rupert and James Murdoch in 2011, as a member of the Commons culture select committee. His persistent investigation received acclaim, and he co-authored an account of his hacking experience—Dial M for Murdoch—becoming a familiar presence on continuous news channels. He has since advocated for stricter press regulation and for the full implementation of the Leveson Inquiry's recommendations. Following his select committee examination of the Murdochs, he was brought into Labour leader Ed Miliband's senior team, tasked with organising efforts to secure an overall majority at the next general election. Mr Watson's performance as campaign chief was mixed—the party famously lost the safe Bradford West seat to a resurgent George Galloway but achieved other by-election successes. His downfall followed a dispute over trade union influence in Labour candidate selection. After Labour's general election defeat, he stood for the position of deputy leader, promising to rebuild the party across the UK. A former trade union official himself, who once shared accommodation with Unite leader Len McCluskey, Mr Watson entered Parliament in 2001 as MP for West Bromwich. After an initial period in the whips' office, he was appointed to the Ministry of Defence, where he was credited with helping secure pardons for soldiers executed for cowardice during World War One. However, in 2006, he resigned as a defence minister, urging Tony Blair to step down in the interest of the Labour Party and the nation—a move that accelerated the then prime minister's departure from office. He was accused of conspiring against Mr Blair with Gordon Brown when it was revealed he had visited the then chancellor at his home in North Queensferry, Fife, shortly before resigning. Both men denied any conspiracy, but many—inside and outside Labour—remained sceptical. When Gordon Brown assumed leadership and the role of prime minister in 2007, Mr Watson was reinstated in government as a whip and was appointed minister for digital engagement in 2008. In that capacity, he found a niche. Known as an early adopter of social media, he was the first MP to have a blog and has described himself as an apprentice nerd due to his enthusiasm for technology. However, during this period, Mr Watson was accused of involvement in the scandal concerning a plot by Gordon Brown's spin doctor Damian McBride to spread smears about senior Tories. The Mail on Sunday accused him of encouraging Mr McBride, while the Sun published a cartoon of him under the headline Mad dog was trained to maul. Mr Watson subsequently won substantial libel damages from both newspapers in the High Court, which ruled the stories linking him to the plot were false. He resigned from his ministerial role following the McBride controversy for family reasons, he maintained—he wished to step back from front-line politics and focus on his wife and children. Aspiring for what he termed a productive life as a backbencher, he joined the culture select committee to pursue his interests in sport and the arts. People then started coming to me—whistleblowers and victims—and I felt I had a responsibility towards them. I couldn't walk away. A prolific Tweeter on politics, as well as his latest discoveries in music, film, and video games, he managed to include a mention of the little-known blues-rock band, Drenge, in his resignation letter from the role of general election co-ordinator in 2013. In the letter, Mr Watson, the son of a union official and a social worker, who has two children with his estranged wife Siobhan, stated it was better for the future unity of the Labour Party that he resigned. His resignation was prompted by a dispute over the Falkirk seat being vacated by Labour's Eric Joyce—the Unite union was accused of hijacking the process to select a new candidate to replace him, and Mr Watson's office manager was the union's preferred candidate. In his letter to Mr Miliband, Mr Watson stated he was not resigning due to unattributed shadow cabinet briefings around the mess in Falkirk... though they don't help. He said some within the party had still not forgiven him for resigning as defence minister in 2006, but added: I fully accept the consequences of that decision and genuinely hope my departure allows the party to move on. text: Police are too sensitive about asking victims of crime if they are disabled, an inspection has found. Disability hate crime is overlooked and under-reported, according to a joint inspectorate review into police, probation, and the Crown Prosecution Service in England and Wales. The review recommends a new common definition of the crime to ensure it is addressed effectively and swiftly. Senior police officers stated they had worked hard to improve its handling. More than 1,700 disability hate crimes were recorded by police in England and Wales in 2011-12. The joint review of disability hate crime was prompted by the case of Fiona Pilkington, who killed herself and her disabled daughter Francecca Hardwick in 2007 after repeated complaints to police about harassment by youths. The review warned a similar case could occur again if urgent changes were not implemented. Inspectors interviewed staff of varying seniority at six police forces and the associated CPS and probation trust offices based in Cleveland, Cumbria, Derbyshire, Hertfordshire, Greater Manchester, and West Midlands. They also observed seven court hearings and spoke to disabled victims, representatives from witness care units, the witness service, victim support, and several independent disability advocates. Disabled people informed inspectors that police officers and control-room operators had become too sensitive about causing offence, leading to reluctance in asking victims if they were disabled. text: A dog owner whose pet was the latest victim to die from from Alabama Rot says more needs to be done to inform owners of the risks. Steve Kirwan, from Lyndhurst, Hampshire, believes his Labrador-collie cross exhibited symptoms following a walk in the Whitefield Moor area of the New Forest. Bodhi, aged three, succumbed to kidney failure in February, two weeks after falling ill. The cause of the disease, which has claimed the lives of 24 dogs in the UK since 2012, remains unidentified. Between November 2012 and March last year, there were 12 confirmed cases—five in the New Forest—and two unconfirmed cases, according to the Forestry Commission. Since December last year, there have been an additional 12 cases, with six occurring in the New Forest. Tests are ongoing for a further 22 suspected cases of the disease. Also referred to as cutaneous and renal glomerular vasculopathy (CRGV). First recognised in the US in the 1980s. Initial symptoms can, but do not necessarily, include lesions or wounds on legs, paws, and faces. Within two to seven days, dogs develop clinical signs of kidney failure, which may include vomiting, reduced appetite, and lethargy. It does not seem to transmit from dog to dog. Source: Anderson Moores Veterinary Specialists. The cases outside Hampshire were in Northamptonshire, Yorkshire, Monmouthshire, Dorset, Shropshire, Surrey, Cornwall, Worcestershire, and County Durham. The Forestry Commission has initiated a poster campaign in 29 of the New Forest's car parks, urging dog owners to remain vigilant. However, Mr Kirwan stated: I don't think it's enough. There are numerous car parks in the New Forest, far more than 29. I believe the coverage needs to extend across the forest, as there is a significant concentration in the New Forest as part of the national picture. Mr Kirwan mentioned Bodhi never had any lesions but was dragging his back legs. From his other symptoms, vets suspected it was Alabama Rot, but he did not respond to treatment and had to be euthanised. The investigation into the precise cause is being led by Anderson Moores Veterinary Specialists, in Hursley, near Winchester, who are collaborating with the Forestry Commission, Environment Agency, Suffolk-based Animal Health Trust, and local vets. David Walker, from Anderson Moores, stated: There's a substantial amount of research ongoing, exploring multiple avenues, but at this stage, we are no closer to identifying the trigger. Research will continue, but there is the possibility that we could investigate this disease for five, ten years and not discover the underlying cause. However, that does not mean we will cease our efforts.

text: The family of a 20-year-old woman from Glasgow who has travelled to Syria and married an Islamic State (IS) fighter have said that she has betrayed them. Khalida Mahmood and Muzaffar Mahmood expressed their horror upon discovering their daughter Aqsa had been radicalised. They spoke following comments attributed to their daughter on Twitter urging people in Britain to replicate terrorist acts seen in Woolwich and the US. Mr and Mrs Mahmood stated they loved their daughter and wished for her return. In a statement, the couple said: We still love you, Aqsa, but we must prioritise your family, your brother and sisters as you have betrayed us, our community, and the people of Scotland with your actions. You have torn the heart out of our family and altered our lives forever. Please come home. They cautioned: If our daughter, who had every opportunity and freedom, could become a bedroom radical, then this could happen to any family. Privately-educated Aqsa is reported to have advocated terrorist acts via a Twitter account under the name Umm Layth, which has since been deleted. She travelled through Turkey to Aleppo in Syria in November and was reported missing to police. Before disappearing, she attended Craigholme School, then university, and was well integrated into society, her parents stated. They said she was raised with love and affection in a happy home. Mrs Mahmood wiped away tears as solicitor Aamer Anwar read a statement on her and her husband's behalf at a news conference in Glasgow. They said: She may believe that the jihadists of Isis are her new family but they are not and are simply using her. The parents, who remained silent during the conference, stated: Aqsa was always a very sweet, peaceful, intelligent child and inquisitive about everything. We had high hopes for her and would have loved for her to be a doctor and to save lives. We dreamed that one day we would see her married with children but sadly that no longer seems likely. As parents, we would have liked for her to listen to us but we gave her everything possible in terms of love, freedom, and education, and she chose a path we could never approve of. They added: All parents want to be proud of their children but sadly we now feel nothing but sorrow and shame for Aqsa. We are not in denial and do not make any excuses for her and absolutely condemn her involvement in Isis and recent comments. But she is our daughter and we still love her, fear for her life, and would urge her to return home while she still can. Aqsa contacted her parents after arriving in Syria and had maintained contact through social media until Tuesday, when newspapers reported her involvement with IS. Mr Anwar said: Because of yesterday, all contact appears to have ceased with their daughter. So, they are hoping that this plea will reach their daughter and that she will reconsider and return home. They want her to come home while she still can. They are telling her that she is wrong, that she is deluded if she thinks she is helping people in Syria. The solicitor stated Aqsa, a British national, had become concerned and upset by media and online reports of the killings in Syria and had informed her parents she wanted to help. Her parents, who are liaising with Police Scotland, said: IS are killing in the name of religion and claiming to defend the weak, but by joining them our daughter is brainwashed and deluded and aiding those engaged in genocide. There is no smoking gun, no family member, no fundamentalist preacher that can be blamed for her radicalisation. Aqsa, like many young people in our community, was naturally angry and frustrated at the loss of innocent life in the Middle East but this is not the way to help. They added: We are concerned that a growing climate of fear in this country means that children will not discuss how they feel with their family and friends, and this will only spell disaster for society. We know that in the days and months ahead we will be scouring social media for clues of whether our daughter is still alive. As we try to hold back the tears today, we feel we have lost our child.

text: Home Secretary Theresa May's internet monitoring plans need significant work, a committee has ruled. The draft Investigatory Powers Bill will compel internet service providers to retain all web activity for a year. It will also sanction the bulk collection of personal data and hacking of smartphones by Britain's intelligence services. Ministers assert the changes will aid in apprehending terrorists and addressing organised crime by updating laws to align with the new technology utilised by criminals. However, civil liberties advocates argue the measures constitute mass surveillance of UK citizens, and the committee's report suggests the home secretary must return to the drawing board. Shami Chakrabarti, director of Liberty, stated: This report highlights the extensive work the government must undertake on this landmark legislation. Labour's shadow home secretary Andy Burnham has written to Mrs May, expressing that while Labour supports the bill's overall aim—to empower police and security services—the government must now reconsider its plans to ensure they achieve the right balance for our security and privacy. Mrs May stated the government would carefully consider the findings of three committees that have reported on the Bill before presenting its final proposals. This is vital legislation, and we are absolutely determined to get it right. Our draft Bill followed three independent reports on investigatory powers, whose authors unanimously agreed a new law was necessary. We are clear we need to introduce legislation which responds to the threats we face in the digital age, protects both the privacy and security of the public, and provides world-leading oversight and safeguards. There is consensus that a new law governing surveillance powers is necessary, but the details are contentious, as illustrated by a series of parliamentary reports. The existing law is widely regarded as complex and lacking in transparency, but indications suggest the new one has not yet fully resolved this issue. The current concern is how far the Home Office will address some of the criticisms and whether there is sufficient time to do so—a final bill is expected to be introduced soon to allow for debate and passage by the end of the year. Read more from Gordon. The Joint Committee on the Draft Investigatory Powers Bill stated in a 194-page report it was convinced the value of so-called Internet Connection Records to law enforcement agencies could outweigh the intrusiveness involved in collecting and using them. However, it echoed concerns from tech firms about the feasibility of safeguarding users' privacy in the manner Mrs May has promised, by only collecting the names of websites visited, rather than individual web pages. The committee was informed this might not be technically feasible, but it noted the Home Office was collaborating with the industry to find a solution. Ministers must also clarify their plans on encryption to ensure they will not compel tech firms to provide a back door for intelligence services, the parliamentary committee stated. Additionally, the Home Office must provide greater justification for the collection of emails and other internet traffic passing through the UK by the security services, as revealed by US whistleblower Edward Snowden, and other so-called bulk data gathering exercises. Committee chairman Lord Murphy of Torfaen remarked the Home Office had a significant amount of further work to do before Parliament can be confident that the provisions have been fully thought through. The bill was criticised as a dragnet approach and disproportionate by former Deputy Prime Minister Nick Clegg, who blocked Mrs May's previous attempt to pass spying legislation, dubbed the snooper's charter by critics, during his time in government. The Lib Dem MP told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the Home Office sought to collect everything on everyone to locate the information on suspected terrorists or criminals they are pursuing. Implying that everyone may be guilty when millions of innocent people are just going about their everyday business free of any wrongdoing at all is... something which is not in keeping with long-standing British traditions, Mr Clegg said. He questioned whether it was proportionate in a liberal democracy to retain information on everything from the music you download on Spotify, to the app that you open, to the supermarket website that you visit, in order to go after the bad guys? He advocated for a narrower approach to data retention, noting that other countries focus on collecting data on those individuals who flicker on the radar screen of security services in the first place. Much of the extensive bill is dedicated to the activities of Britain's intelligence agencies and aims to clarify the legal basis under which they operate, following Edward Snowden's revelations. It proposes equipment interference warrants, allowing intelligence services to hack into suspects' smartphones and computers and download data from them, either within the UK or abroad. Other warrants will cover the downloading of bulk databases of personal data, which could include medical records, and the collection of internet traffic passing through the UK for future analysis by GCHQ. Some of these techniques were not known to the public until recently and were covered by disparate and obscure pieces of legislation, some of which predated the internet. The draft bill also proposes:

text: Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has said the inconclusive election result means no party can govern alone. His party, the AKP, is convening to attempt to form a government after losing its majority in a general election for the first time in 13 years. It secured 41%, a significant decline from 2011, and must establish a coalition or face entering a minority government. Mr Erdogan has urged all parties to preserve the atmosphere of stability in Turkey. I believe the results, which do not allow any party to form a single-party government, will be assessed healthily and realistically by every party, Mr Erdogan stated. The AKP is now likely to attempt to form a coalition, but no party has yet indicated a willingness to join forces with it. Opposition parties may still attempt to form a coalition against the AKP. However, Numan Kurtulmus, one of Turkey's four deputy prime ministers, stated there would be no government without representation by the AKP. Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoglu is meeting AKP cabinet members and officials to evaluate the election results in Ankara. After the official final result is declared, he will have 45 days to form a government. Mr Kurtulmus mentioned another election was possible. This is potentially a new political era in Turkey. The AKP still won this election, with over 40% of the vote—a share of the vote that parties in any democracy would desire. It still has a substantial power base, mainly of the more religious, conservative Turks, who feel liberated by the party and the president. However, the AKP's dominance, the one-man political show that has played out in Turkey for 13 years and polarised this nation, has just taken a significant hit. Turkey: Setback for Erdogan Profile: Recep Tayyip Erdogan The result is a setback to Mr Erdogan's plans to enhance his office's powers. He had been seeking a two-thirds majority to transform Turkey into a presidential republic. The pro-Kurdish HDP crossed the 10% threshold, securing seats in parliament for the first time. The discussion of executive presidency and dictatorship have come to an end in Turkey with these elections, said HDP leader Selahattin Demirtas. Kurds, women, gays put faith in upstart Turkish party On Monday morning, the Turkish currency fell to near-record lows against the dollar, and shares dropped by more than 8% soon after the Istanbul stock exchange opened. The central bank acted swiftly to support the lira by cutting the interest rate on foreign currency deposits. Are you in Turkey? What is your reaction to the election result? text: Overall crime in England and Wales fell by 15% in 2013, official figures show. The Crime Survey for England and Wales reported 7.5 million crimes against households and adults in that year, marking the lowest level since its inception in 1981. Separate police statistics indicated a 2% decline in crime for 2013, with increases in areas such as fraud (25%) and a 17% rise in reported sexual offences following the Jimmy Savile scandal. Ministers stated the figures were good news and demonstrated that reforms were effective. The CSEW report, published by the Office for National Statistics (ONS), estimates crime levels based on the number of people who report being victims of crime. The survey indicated that crimes against households and adults in the year ending December 2013 decreased by 15% compared to the previous year. By Danny Shaw, Home Affairs Correspondent, BBC News. These figures are unsurprising, as crime has been declining almost continuously since the mid-1990s. However, the size of the reduction is unexpected: the 15% fall is the largest percentage decline since the survey began 33 years ago. The 22% drop in violence is also significantly greater than in other years, reinforcing recent findings from Cardiff University's study of individuals treated for crime-related injuries. The only statistics that tell a different story are those compiled by police forces. However, these should be treated with caution—not only due to concerns that the figures may have been manipulated but also because they depend on whether victims report crimes to the police. Mark Easton: The truth behind the rise in sex crimes. The ONS stated that the reduction in crime measured was driven by a fall in offences, including household theft, which decreased by 25%, and overall violence, which fell by 22%. Reports of vandalism declined by 15% over the year. The figures also suggested there were 762,000 crimes experienced by children aged 10-15 in 2013, down 13% compared to 2012. BBC Home Affairs Correspondent Danny Shaw said the fall in crime was no surprise. However, he noted that the size of the reduction—the largest since the survey began—was unexpected. Meanwhile, police figures on reported crime for England and Wales showed a decline across most main categories, with 3.7 million offences recorded in the year ending December 2013, down 2% from the previous year. However, increases in some categories were recorded, with incidents of shoplifting up 6% and violence against a person rising by 1%. The latter is thought to reflect improvements in recording and possibly an increase in public reporting. The rise in fraud follows a move to centralise the recording of the crime. Allegations against high-profile figures, including those related to the late DJ Savile, were linked to a surge in recorded sexual offences. Crime Prevention Minister Norman Baker said: Under this coalition government, overall crime is down by more than 10% according to both the independent crime survey and police-recorded crime. Today's statistics are more good news, and the evidence is clear: police reform is working and crime is falling. Adam Pemberton, assistant chief executive at Victim Support, said the group welcomed the fall in crime. However, he added: It is important to remember that for many of the victims of the 7.5 million crimes committed last year, the impact will have been severe and long-lasting. Chief Constable Jeff Farrar, head of crime statistics for the Association of Chief Police Officers, said the figures confirmed the impact that prominent operations on sexual abuse and fraud were having. The figures do not cover Scotland and Northern Ireland. In June last year, the Scottish government reported a 13% drop in recorded crime in the year to March 2013. In Northern Ireland, crime fell by 2.9% in 2012/13 compared to the previous year, according to statistics.

At Hillsborough, where 96 Liverpool fans died in a crush at a semi-final in the FA Cup in 1989, Manchester United announced that it was not welcome. “Manchester United has always maintained that songs like this, which make reference to a historic tragedy, do not represent the values of the club,” the statement said. “There were members of the crowd who lost loved ones at Hillsborough and they find it difficult to accept this. We are talking to our supporters and we are seeking their support in preventing such behaviour in the future.” It must come out of our game,” he said. “This is unacceptable. This is something we don’t want to hear.” There was no doubt that the Munich Air Crash was the reason. That should have been a night to celebrate, because they had never met each other in the European Cup before. In February, ’58, eight Manchester United players and three members of the staff were killed in a plane crash in Munich, after a game in the European Cup. The Sun published a story four days after the disaster in which it criticized the behavior of Liverpool fans that day. The crowd should have been supporting their own team. “When you sink to their level, it's really remarkable,” said Houghton. When they sink as low as they did last night, it’s terrible. In the first half they were singing and chanting that the Sun was right about Hillsborough. The paper has been boycotted heavily in Merseyside ever since. They were not continuous, but clearly heard four or five times. They were drowned out by the noise. Juliette Ferrington, BBC correspondent at Anfield, said: Then, just after the final whistle, the deafening roar was replaced by the roar of “You will never walk alone” and “We won it five times” (a reference to Liverpool’s five European Cup wins). Former United striker Dion Dublin told BBC radio that these songs were disgusting. There was deafening noise in the stadium. “It leaves a bad taste in the mouth,” he said. “It is in bad taste, and the people who sing it ought to be ashamed of themselves.”

text: Northern Ireland sprinter Leon Reid says he has no idea when he is going to be able to represent Ireland in international competition. Reid, originally from England, who secured European junior and U23 medals for Britain, applied to change his international allegiance earlier this year. However, the IAAF's decision to suspend all nationality changes, pending a review, is jeopardising Reid's plans. I am uncertain about the current situation, Reid informed BBC Sport NI. Athletics Ireland have been advocating on my behalf, but at present, there seems to be no progress since the IAAF announcement by Sebastian Coe in February. At that time, IAAF President Coe stated that a working group was being formed to develop new rules following the backlash over the significant number of African athletes who have changed allegiance in recent years. Nations such as Bahrain and Qatar have attracted talented Kenyan and Ethiopian athletes to switch allegiance, while several European countries have also utilised IAAF regulations to incorporate African athletes into their teams. Reid, aged 22, achieved a sprint double at the Northern Ireland Championships in Belfast on Saturday. After recording 10.59 seconds to defeat Paralympic star Jason Smyth in the 100m final, Reid narrowly missed the Commonwealth Games consideration standard by 0.04 seconds in his 200m semi-final, finishing in 20.81. Less favourable wind conditions resulted in him posting a time of 21.12 in the 200m final. I am not experiencing much luck at present. My blocks slipped back in the 100m final, significantly affecting my start, Reid added. But I am confident I will achieve the Commonwealth standards (100m 10.26, 200m 20.77). It is just a matter of time. The 200m has always been my strongest event, but my 100m performance has been excellent this year. I have improved my personal best to 10.33 and also run several wind-assisted times under 10.30. Reid set his 200m personal best of 20.62 in 2015 and has clocked 20.79 for the distance this year. Meanwhile, Smyth was satisfied with his 100m performance at the Mary Peters Track as he prepares for the IPC World Championships in London next month. The five-time Paralympics gold medallist spent three weeks at his former training base in Florida last month, although he managed only one race during the warm-weather training. A date change prevented me from competing in one of the scheduled meetings, and the other meet was cancelled due to a thunderstorm, Smyth stated. So, to some extent, I am still assessing my form. I actually had a very productive winter. I have been able to put in the necessary work, which is very positive. Thus, a solid foundation has been established, and it should be a matter of executing the races. After being coached by Clarence Callendar in London, following a long and successful period with Stephen Maguire, Smyth is now collaborating with various individuals in Belfast. I have support from Athletics Northern Ireland when I am here, such as Tom Reynolds, who assists with timing and monitoring, Smyth explained. I am essentially returning to what has worked for me in the past. Smyth aims for a sprint double in London after the birth of his daughter Evie prevented him from defending his T13 200m title, following his 100m victory at the last championships two years ago in Doha.

text: Prosecutors in Austria say former Kazakh ambassador Rakhat Aliyev, found dead in a Vienna prison on Tuesday, appears to have killed himself. These are external links and will open in a new window. They referred to a post-mortem on Mr Aliyev's body, who was discovered hanging in prison while awaiting trial for the murder of two bankers in Kazakhstan. His lawyers are seeking an investigation. The man, formerly married to a daughter of Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev, was sentenced in absentia in Kazakhstan for attempting to overthrow the government. Austria had declined requests to extradite Mr Aliyev, who was dismissed as Kazakh ambassador to Vienna in 2007. On the day he was found deceased, he was scheduled to testify against two former cellmates accused of blackmailing him with threats of making his death appear as suicide. No examinations to date indicate any third-party involvement in Mr Aliyev's death, according to the Austrian authorities. The body was assessed by an experienced forensic expert, stated Vienna's deputy chief prosecutor Gerhard Jarosch. Neither the examination of his body and the prison cell where it was found nor the prison's CCTV footage revealed any signs of violence or other third-party involvement in his death, he stated. The results of a toxicological test, routinely performed as part of judicial post-mortems, were expected in a few days, the deputy chief prosecutor added. This would determine whether Mr Aliyev's blood contained traces of anything other than his regular heart medication at the time of his death. Mr Aliyev had been transferred to a single cell after the alleged threat against him became known and was not under suicide watch. One of his lawyers demanded a full investigation into his death. I have significant doubts, Klaus Ainedter told Austrian press agency APA. I visited him only [on Monday]. There was absolutely no indication of a danger of suicide. Mr Aliyev was initially charged in 2007, with Austria twice rejecting extradition requests on the grounds that he would not receive a fair trial in Kazakhstan. He had been in custody since June after surrendering once Austria had agreed to conduct the trial. He had denied the murder charges, claiming they were politically motivated. A businessman with extensive contacts among the Kazakh elite, he criticised President Nazarbayev after being dismissed as ambassador. He was previously married to Dariga Nazarbayeva, eldest daughter of Mr Nazarbayev. In power virtually unchallenged since Kazakhstan's independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, Nursultan Nazarbayev has concentrated on economic reform while resisting efforts to democratise the political system. Mr Aliyev's case attracted significant publicity in Austria, with prominent lawyers becoming involved in the proceedings and allegations that the Kazakh secret service had attempted to influence the judicial process.

text: Apple has just turned 40 years old - a timely reason to track down a man who helped start the firm and then walked away. Drive an hour out of Las Vegas into the Nevada desert. When you reach what seems like the end of civilisation, continue onwards. That is where you will find Pahrump. In Pahrump, you will encounter the co-founder of the most valuable, perhaps most powerful company on Earth. Ronald G Wayne is 81. At 41, he worked at Atari, where he met a young, impressionable Steve Jobs who frequently sought Wayne's advice. Jobs inquired if he should start a business making slot machines. Wayne advised against it. Jobs asked if he should go to India to find himself. Wayne replied, if you must, just be careful. One day, Jobs posed the question that altered history: Could you help me talk some sense into Steve Wozniak? Bring him over to the house, Wayne said. We'll sit down, and we'll chat. The charismatic, lovable Wozniak—known as Woz—had been collaborating with Jobs on transforming business computers into something more personal. The pair often attended the now infamous Homebrew Computer Club, a gathering of enthusiasts who would dismantle circuitry and rebuild it with the enthusiasm of an imaginative six-year-old with a box of Lego. Woz was the best. A circuit board he created became the foundation of the Apple 1, the company's first computer, which sold at auction in 2015 for $365,000 (£254,300). Jobs wanted Woz's intellect to be exclusive to Apple. Woz was not interested. Thus, they went to Wayne's flat in Mountain View, California, to discuss the details. Jobs thought I was somewhat more diplomatic than he was, Wayne recalls. He was very eager to proceed with Steve Wozniak to get this into production. But Wozniak, being the whimsical character he was, did everything for pure enjoyment. Woz had no concept of business or its rules. Over approximately 45 minutes, Wayne changed the situation. He bought into it. He understood, he says. It was at that moment Steve Jobs said: 'We're going to start a company. It will be the Apple Computer Company.' Wayne typed up the documents immediately on an IBM typewriter, much to Woz's amusement, who could not quite believe Wayne's ability to produce four pages of legalese from memory. Dividing the Apple pie was straightforward: Jobs and Wozniak received 45% each, and Wayne had 10%, with a mandate to be the voice of reason in any disputes. Twelve days later, Wayne withdrew from the contract. For very excellent reasons that are still sound to me today, he said, 40 years and a market cap of $600bn later. Jobs, ever the skilful salesman, had just secured Apple's first major deal. A small computer chain, the Byte Shop, wanted 50 machines. To obtain the cash, Apple had to borrow $15,000. However, Wayne had heard—from an unknown source—that the Byte Shop did not have a particularly good reputation for paying its bills. If the company goes poof, we are individually liable for the debts, Wayne explained. Jobs and Wozniak didn't have two nickels to rub together. I had a house, a bank account, and a car… I was reachable! Wayne informed the Steves that he wanted to assist where he could but could no longer officially be part of the company. One lasting contribution was to design the company's first logo—an ink drawing of Newton sitting under a tree, an apple poised above his head. Wayne signed the image, but Jobs noticed it. Take that out! Wayne recalls him saying. He complied. Months after severing formal ties with Apple, Wayne received a letter. The letter says all you gotta do is sign away every possible interest you could have in the Apple Computer Company, and the cheque is yours, he says. In return, he received $1,500. As far as I was concerned, it was 'found money'. So I went ahead and I signed. Pahrump is 500 miles (800km) and a whole universe away from Cupertino, where Apple is headquartered today. Wayne's home is as modest as it is cherished. Ornaments from the life of a curious engineer and collector are scattered throughout. By the door, an old silver slot machine. Against one wall, a still-functioning radio from the thirties, housed in beautiful mahogany. He recounted the time he made a scale replica, both interior and exterior, of the Nautilus—the colossal submarine featured in the film 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea. He had no blueprint to work with, instead studying freeze-frames from the film. When finished, he donated it to a museum. Today, a 10% share of Apple would be worth nearly $60bn. If Wayne regrets his decision, he conceals it well. I would've wound up heading a very large documentation department at the back of the building, shuffling papers for the next 20 years of my life. That was not the future that I saw for myself. If money was the only thing that I wanted, there are many ways I could've done that. But it was much more important to do what appealed to me. My advice to young people is always this—find something you enjoy doing so much that you'd be willing to do it for nothing… and you'll never work a day in your life. Wayne keeps all his fan mail in a small box in the corner of his study. It is filled with autograph requests, calls for advice, and general messages of admiration. One letter, from a fan named Jason, jokes about the notion of the infamously self-assured and combative Steve Jobs ever being able to take the constructive criticism Wayne was able to offer. He was a fascinating man, Wayne reflects. Who made Apple what it is? Obviously, Jobs. Was Jobs a nice guy? In many ways, no. But that doesn't matter. Wayne considered himself the adult supervision to the Jobs dream, even offering a supportive boost early on. Jobs says: 'You know, I'm having second thoughts about this. There are other things I want to do'. I said: 'Steve, whatever it is that you want to do, you can do it a lot more easily with money in your pocket. Go ahead and make the money, and do whatever you want to do. Just don't forget what you wanted the money for'. He forgot. I think he became so involved in the mechanics of running Apple that it was more like he was caught up to such an extent that nothing else mattered. While having no remorse about relinquishing his role in Apple, Wayne does have at least one regret: selling his copy of the original signed contract for $500. In 2011, that same document fetched $1.6m at auction. Just one more what if to add to the list. Looking around Wayne's home, there are no Apple products to be seen. He prefers to build and customise his own technology—it is more enjoyable that way, he said. In 2011, someone gifted him an iPad 2. Like much else in his life, Wayne gave it away. text: Hourly pay rates for Tesco store staff will rise by 10.5% over the next two years, the supermarket has said. These are external links and will open in a new window. However, pay remains lower than at Aldi and Lidl, and overtime pay on Sundays and Bank Holidays is being reduced. Currently, Tesco workers receive £7.62 per hour, which will increase to £8.42 per hour by November 2018. The pay rise will elevate Tesco workers' pay above the £7.90 level that the National Living Wage is projected to reach by 2018. The National Living Wage is the effective minimum wage for adults aged 25 and over, and is currently £7.50. Those under the age of 25 are entitled to a lower minimum wage rate. Statutory minimum pay rates will continue to rise until at least 2020, according to recent government Budgets, and companies are preparing for those changes, as well as striving to remain competitive with rivals to recruit and retain staff. Wage growth in the UK has been slow in recent years, but inflation has risen and other supermarkets have increased the wages they pay. Aldi recently announced an increase in hourly pay to £8.53 per hour; Lidl's website states it pays store staff £8.45 per hour. Tesco stated it would raise hourly pay in three stages: to £8.02 in November 2017, then to £8.18 in July 2018, and to £8.42 in November 2018. This reward package represents our biggest investment in store pay for a decade, and provides colleagues with a sustainable pay deal that rewards them for everything they do, while allowing us to also attract new talent, said Tesco UK chief executive, Matt Davies. The retailer stated maternity pay terms had also been improved. However, extra pay for Sundays and bank holidays will be reduced from time-and-a-half to time-and-a-quarter after July 2018. This is designed to meet the government legislative requirement regarding the minimum wage. As expected, most of the businesses who have had to face up to this rise have had to reduce premiums and other perks that employees benefitted from in order to meet the core wage rises, said retail analyst Steve Dresser.

text: With the #OscarsSoWhite controversy and calls for the Brit Awards to be more truly representative, there has never been more discussion about diversity in the arts. On stage, recent major productions of Hamlet and King Lear featured predominantly black, Asian and ethnic minority (BAME) casts, yet according to some in the industry, you can walk onto a building site and see more diversity than in the average theatre. Paapa Essiedu, currently the Royal Shakespeare Company's Hamlet, states theatre is caught between two worlds at the moment. There's a lot of positivity about how we see our present and future and that's all good, but I still don't see or feel that impact. What is required is for people to be more bold and more adventurous in what they back. In Manchester, the Royal Exchange's King Lear featured veteran actor Don Warrington in the lead, which he says should not be in any way startling. Yet many reviews highlighted his race, which Warrington says is an indictment of where we are. He notes while conditions have improved since he began his acting career almost 50 years ago, that anyone wants to discuss his casting shows there is still a problem. There's a higher visibility, but the question is about the quality of that visibility and the quality of the parts. I don't think that is where it should be. Hamida Ali, the acting union Equity's equalities and diversity organiser, shares Warrington's unease. One of the things we remain concerned about is how surprised we might be when we see a black actor in a lead role, not just in Shakespeare, but in general. It says something in itself that that remains something of note. She states there is definitely a consensus that there is a problem, but what the cause is, who is responsible and what the solutions are is perhaps more in debate. The production of Lear was staged with Talawa, a theatre company established in the 1980s in direct response to the lack of creative opportunities for actors from minority ethnic backgrounds. Artistic director Michael Buffong says three decades on, there is still a rapid need for change. What we need is different people to reflect different aspects of the same world, otherwise we have this very narrow viewpoint. Essiedu agrees theatre needs to be more diverse about the stories we're telling and the people that are telling them. By doing that, there will be more opportunity for a more diverse group of actors. We're in 2016 in an international, multicultural, integrated society and we've got a responsibility as artists to reflect that in the work that we create. Matthew Xia, an associate artistic director at the Royal Exchange, says far from improving, theatre has gone backwards in so many ways. It's not just about the art, it's also about the organisational structure. In the majority of organisations, the moment you get to the leadership, it drops right down with regards to proportionate representation of the cities that they are working in. It's beyond me, because you can walk onto a building site and see more diversity than you can see in what is meant to be the liberal end of the work spectrum. Buffong states, as a result, there is a need to change the gatekeepers, because that's where the power is. You can cast two black actors in a play and go 'wow, we've got two black actors' but that's not really the same as having a story from a particular point of view. Just because there is a black actor on the stage doesn't necessarily mean it's your story. Dawn Walton, the founder of Sheffield's Eclipse - which uses the Black British experience to create new work that will enrich the canon of British theatre - agrees. There is a belief in theatre that what is on stage is what needs to be diverse, so cross-casting is always where people go - casting a black whatever - but if that solved it, we'd have beaten this in the 1970s. She says theatre boards need to change because they're very much into doing the same thing over and over again... but the country has shifted. The institution is becoming less and less relevant because it doesn't represent what goes on right outside its doors. Xia says theatre is still at a place where actors of colour are expected to play peripheral characters unless the play is explicitly dealing with race, which is ridiculous. The human experience is so much broader than that. I've heard quite scary things said by directors which shows a lack of understanding about roles and who can play what. Ultimately, people are always going to represent their world on stage, so if their world has been monocultural, it's highly likely that's how the work will be rendered. The diversity of theatre generally is an issue, according to Arts Council England's director of theatre, Neil Darlison. I think theatres are aware of it and if they're not, they should be, because ultimately it's going to affect their business. However, he says there are some positive signs, particularly in metropolitan centres, where the diversity of people working in organisations and running them is better than it was. They're starting to reflect the stories of the inhabitants of the city. Warrington believes direct action is needed to effect change. We have to wake up our consciences and we can do that by having a deliberate policy, so that it becomes part of everyday life. It has to become something we do. Buffong adds that he is in favour of anything that gets an instant result. Targets, quotas, ringfencing money - I'm in favour of making it happen now. The idea of more initiatives and training is so over. There's a wealth of people who just need the opportunity to work. Ali says those opportunities may be hampered by the law, which in some ways supports equality, but also has grey areas. There are exemptions from the duty not to discriminate where appropriate and casting is one of those. If you are casting for realism purposes or because of the way a character is written, that is permitted, so you could argue that exemption has worked against progress. I understand that we're talking about an artistic process, but we must recognise it is an industrial one, and decisions made have an impact disproportionately on working opportunities. It's a difficult and thorny question because there are pros and cons on both sides. Essiedu believes the answer may be a simple one. We mimic what we see, so we need to put that in front of people to get that machine started. I'd never seen a black actor performing the lead in a Shakespeare play until I was 18 and I saw Chiwetel Ejiofor doing Othello in the Donmar Warehouse. Because I hadn't seen it, I didn't think it was possible and I didn't explore that avenue. People from whatever background are only going to be inspired to write or perform if they see it. If you've got an artistic director who is willing to try and fail, then you're going to get a wider palette of works. Some of it will probably be terrible, but some of it will be unbelievably brilliant. Hamlet is in cinemas from 8 June and at the Royal Shakespeare Theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon 13 August.

text: Edinburgh Capitals captain Jacob Johnston was delighted as his team ended their losing run of games - but was then left to rue another defeat. The Capitals ended a seven-game winless streak with a 3-2 home victory over Dundee Stars on Saturday, before suffering a 6-0 defeat on Tayside in Sunday's rematch. This left Johnston with mixed feelings after a weekend that had promised much following their success at Murrayfield. Saturday's win felt very satisfying, Johnston remarked. We've faced challenges and adversity in recent weeks, so it was excellent to break that losing streak. We were eager for those points on Sunday, but we did not secure them. It was a prime opportunity to achieve a four-point weekend, as they are close to us in the standings. We approached it with that mindset, but we must expect to win every game. We cannot anticipate victories over specific teams, and we must start winning if we wish to climb the standings. The mixed weekend left the Capitals still three points behind second-bottom Dundee after the two games, although they have two games in hand over Marc LeFebvre's side. That losing streak, during which they conceded a staggering 47 goals, ended as they defeated the Stars 3-2 at Murrayfield on Saturday. Ian Schultz and Matt Tipoff scored to bookend the first period as Edinburgh began the game in the best possible manner, with Mason Wilgosh adding a third early in the second period. Stars responded through Matt White and Kevin Bruijsten, but failed to find an equaliser, extending their poor form to 13 losses in their last 14 games. The game returned to Tayside on Sunday with Dundee hosting, and the Stars ended their own run of seven straight defeats with a 6-0 shutout victory over Michal Dobron's side. Dundee went four up during the second period when Mikael Lidhammar, Brett Switzer, and two from Matt White put them in a comfortable position. Two more from Justin Faryna in the third period completed what turned out to be a successful night for the Stars. Fife Flyers secured two excellent points on the road at Manchester Storm on Saturday to begin their double header, winning 4-2 in a match that remained goalless for the first 35 minutes. Ryan Dingle eventually broke the deadlock before Taylor Dickin equalised, with both teams entering the third period tied at 1-1. Dingle restored the lead, then Sebastien Thinel extended it before Matt Bissonnette pulled one back for the home team. Flyers debutant Bryan Cameron added a fourth to secure the win. In Sunday's return game in Kirkcaldy, they achieved two wins from two and four points with a 3-1 victory on home ice. Paul Phillips put the visitors ahead late in the first period, but the Flyers turned the game around as Brendan Brooks and Dingle each scored, with Justin Fox adding a late empty net goal. Braehead Clan began their weekend at in-form Nottingham Panthers, and despite missing five players, they still secured a point in a 4-3 overtime loss. Lee Baldwin opened the scoring for the Clan, but Panthers turned the game around through Brian McGrattan and Matt Carter before Mike Hammond equalised for the Glasgow side. Jeff Brown and Alex Leavitt exchanged goals for each team, taking the game into overtime where Robert Farmer secured victory with the overtime goal. Clan returned to Glasgow to host league leaders Cardiff Devils, and despite more heroics from the depleted team, finished with a penalty shots loss after a 2-2 draw. Daniel Åhsberg's opener was cancelled out by Joey Hadded, before Bari McKenzie put Braehead ahead in the second period, which was equalised by Andrew Hotham. The Devils prevailed in the penalty shootout, with their goalie Ben Bowns saving Åhsberg's crucial attempt to secure the points for the Welsh side. text: Sinn Féin has dismissed a proposal to stand independent anti-Brexit candidates as part of a general election pact in Northern Ireland. These are external links and will open in a new window. The SDLP proposed that parties supporting a Remain vote in last year's EU referendum should negotiate a deal on candidates for the 8 June election. The party's leader, Colum Eastwood, mentioned that presenting agreed candidates without party affiliation was an option. However, Sinn Féin's John O'Dowd stated this was not a credible offer. Some parties opposing Brexit have engaged in discussions about forming what Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill termed a progressive alliance in certain constituencies for the Westminster election. The goal was to secure seats from parties endorsing the UK's exit from the EU. The Democratic Unionist Party and the Ulster Unionists, both of which voted in the House of Commons to initiate the Brexit process, have also discussed the possibility of agreeing to present a single unionist unity candidate in some areas. It is understood that Mr Eastwood's proposal for independent anti-Brexit candidates was intended for the East Londonderry, Fermanagh and South Tyrone, and North Belfast constituencies. However, Mr O'Dowd stated it would not receive Sinn Féin's support, and any pact would focus on political party representation. We don't believe that's an acceptable way forward, said the Upper Bann MLA. It is political parties that will drive forward change in this society. We see that as a proposal from Colum to stymie Sinn Féin and bolster the SDLP - that's not what progressive political alliances should be about. He added that his party remained open to discussions with others about a potential agreement. Mr Eastwood admitted that there is probably no chance now of his proposal materialising. If Sinn Féin have ruled that out, I think it's very, very difficult, he said. We have always said that we would not do a pact with Sinn Féin alone. We wanted this to be broad; we wanted this to be non-nationalist; we wanted to go right across the political spectrum. On Tuesday, the Green Party stated it would not align with parties that did not share its vision for a progressive society. Its leader, Steven Agnew, said the SDLP's decision to select incumbent MP Alasdair McDonnell as its South Belfast candidate for the snap election ended chances of an agreement in the constituency.

text: Police Scotland has said that it does not collate or hold specific figures on child sexual exploitation. In a series of Freedom of Information requests, BBC Scotland inquired about the number of cases, concerns, and complaints of child exploitation and child sexual exploitation recorded over the past four years. However, the force stated that the figures were not maintained on a single system. Scotland's Children's Commissioner described the revelation as disturbing. This coincides with the launch of a new unit by officers to address the complex issue of child abuse and neglect across Scotland. The unit will offer expertise to enable local teams to thoroughly investigate cases, including child sexual exploitation, online offences, and other forms of abuse. In response to the BBC's FOI requests, Police Scotland stated: Child exploitation encompasses a broad range of criminal activities and does not correspond to a specific offence, but rather can involve a variety of different offences...The level of data you have requested is not held on a single system. This follows the publication last summer of the Jay report into sexual exploitation in Rotherham, South Yorkshire. It disclosed that over 1,400 children were subjected to appalling sexual abuse. Last year, Glasgow City Council reported that 97 children in the city were victims, or at risk, of sexual exploitation. The Association of Chief Police Officers stated that most forces in England and Wales now mark such offences in their records, but senior officers here say it is not straightforward to do so. Children's Commissioner Tam Baillie stated: I am disturbed that we do not yet collect police figures on children who are the subject of sexual exploitation. This was a recommendation of the Scottish Parliament and features in the Scottish government action plan on child sexual exploitation. The reason this is so important is that unless we know the scope of the problem we are trying to deal with, then we won't have the appropriate or proportionate response. Assistant Chief Constable Malcolm Graham, from Police Scotland, said the nature of child sexual exploitation made it highly unlikely that young people would come forward to report being abused. Our priority is to be focusing on identifying as many victims as we can and identifying perpetrators who have the intent to commit these devastating crimes so we can prevent the abuse from happening, he said. Scotland is at the forefront of approaches to child sexual exploitation. Sexual exploitation is a form of abuse and it is not a specific crime type recorded as such. Children and young people may be victims of repeated rapes, physical assaults, or grooming offences and we categorise all of these in crime recording. He added: But what is most important here is our focus on identifying who these victims are. Our focus is always on where there are child protection issues and on keeping children safe. Martin Crewe, director of Barnardo's Scotland, said: Rotherham was a real wake-up call and led to the Scottish government's national action plan last year but we could and should be doing more. Our concern is that we don't know the full extent of the problem. We welcome the work of the police. Since the publication of the Barnardo's Scotland petition in 2011 we have been pushing for a better understanding of child sexual exploitation in Scotland. In January 2013, Aileen Campbell, Minister for Children and Young People, responded to the Public Petitions Committee inquiry into Child Sexual Exploitation in Scotland and announced four points including, action to improve the way child sexual exploitation is identified by Scotland's new single police force to make this form of abuse more visible. However, sexual exploitation per se is still not recorded or centrally collated. The Scottish government stated figures are available on the wider problem of child abuse. A spokeswoman said: The safety of our children is a key priority for the government and an issue we take extremely seriously. The launch of the National Child Abuse Investigation Unit will help to target and bring to justice those who seek to harm our young people. The unit has been set up to tackle all forms of child abuse, and child sexual exploitation is one aspect of this. We have robust legislation in place to cover a wide range of these offences, including online abuse and are working to strengthen the law even further. She added: The extent of the problem is often difficult to assess because abuse by its very nature is concealed. That's why prevention and swift action to safeguard children are a big part of our strategy to tackle these terrible crimes. This includes robust National Child Protection guidance, action to tackle emerging forms of child abuse including child sexual exploitation, a national public awareness campaign and guidance for night-time workers such as taxi drivers and hotel staff who may come into contact with those at risk.

text: The range and quality of research at Scotland's universities has been praised in a new UK-wide survey. Most Scottish universities have either maintained or improved their positions in the league table. Overall, the University of Edinburgh secured 4th place, while the University of Glasgow was ranked 13th. Over 85% of university research in Scotland was deemed to have an outstanding or very significant impact on wider society and the economy. This percentage exceeded the UK average. The analysis, conducted by Research Fortnight, was based on the 2014 Research Excellence Framework (REF 2014) results. This was a comprehensive exercise reviewing research quality across various subjects at UK universities. Panels of experts evaluated the work of more than 52,000 academics from 154 UK universities. Both Edinburgh and Glasgow Universities advanced by one position compared to the previous table in 2008. St Andrews, Strathclyde, Aberdeen, Dundee, Heriot-Watt, and Stirling also ranked in the top 50. Strathclyde's physics department was named the best in the UK, surpassing Oxford, Cambridge, and Imperial College. Aberdeen and Dundee experienced slight declines in the overall rankings, while the others improved. Generally, the data indicated that Scottish universities have maintained or even enhanced their research rankings since the abolition of tuition fees for Scottish students. International rankings also suggest that the overall standing of Scottish universities is being maintained. All 18 of Scotland's higher education institutions conduct research judged to be of world-leading quality, with Scotland outperforming the UK average in terms of research impact. For the first time, REF 2014 also evaluated the research's impact on the economy, society, public policy, culture, and quality of life. Laurence Howells, chief executive of the Scottish Funding Council, stated: Today we have had confirmation that our universities' research is world-leading and impacts on almost every aspect of daily life, from the way we treat patients in hospital, to the way we communicate with smartphones. By making the most of our investments in research, Scotland's universities are rightly on the podium with the best in the world. text: The mother of an RAF airman who went missing more than three weeks ago has said she absolutely believes her son is still alive. Corrie Mckeague, aged 23, a gunner stationed at RAF Honington in Suffolk, disappeared following a night out in Bury St Edmunds early on the morning of 24 September. His mother, Nicola Urquhart, informed the BBC's Victoria Derbyshire programme: Nobody can just disappear. She stated it would be typical for Mr Mckeague to enter a stranger's vehicle. Mr Mckeague, originally from Dunfermline in Fife, was last seen on CCTV walking alone and consuming takeaway food in Bury St Edmunds at 03:20 BST. A trace on his mobile phone indicated it was in Bury St Edmunds early on 24 September but later moved to the Barton Mills area. For further updates on this story, visit BBC Suffolk Live. Ms Urquhart mentioned the phone data suggests this journey took 28 minutes, which is how long it would take to drive [between the two places]. It remains unknown whether the phone was in Mr Mckeague's possession during the journey, but Ms Urquhart remarked that entering a stranger's car was genuinely something Corrie would do. She noted he was the sort of person who, if he saw someone walking down the road and he was in a car, he would stop and give that complete stranger a lift. Police have located neither Mr Mckeague nor his phone. However, Ms Urquhart stated there were many possibilities as to why the phone's signal was no longer being detected - it could have run out of battery or been damaged. She mentioned that police - who are continuing the search for the missing airman - have got so much CCTV they've still not been able to watch it all. She added: They've widened the parameter to look further out. They've got [access to] private CCTV. But not a single [new] image of Corrie [has been discovered]. Ms Urquhart expressed her belief that somebody does know something about the circumstances surrounding her son's disappearance, but added that the public have been desperate to help. But nothing, not one person [has been able to] give us anything - and that just doesn't make sense, she added. If you possess any information which might be relevant, please contact the Suffolk Police incident room on 01473 782019. The Victoria Derbyshire programme is broadcast on weekdays between 09:00 and 11:00 on BBC Two and the BBC News Channel.

text: UN human rights chief Zeid Raad Al Hussein has described the Syrian city of Aleppo as a slaughterhouse. In a speech, he stated that the siege and bombardment of Aleppo's rebel-held east were among the crimes of historic proportions occurring in Syria. Nearly 500 individuals have been killed and 2,000 injured since government forces, supported by Russian air strikes, initiated an assault on the east a month ago. Syria's government has claimed civilians are suffering due to terrorists. Meanwhile, the UN reported that a lack of security guarantees had compelled it to delay plans for medical evacuations from Aleppo on Friday during the second 11-hour humanitarian pause declared unilaterally by the government and its ally, Russia. Russia announced it would also suspend air strikes between 08:00 and 19:00 local time (05:00-16:00 GMT) on Saturday to permit civilians and rebels to exit the city via safe corridors. However, very few individuals have reportedly utilised the offer, with rebel factions asserting that it would equate to forced displacement and surrender. Aleppo, once Syria's largest city and the nation's commercial and industrial hub, has been devastated by conflict since 2012. It has been left roughly divided in two, with President Bashar al-Assad's forces controlling the west and rebels the east. At the beginning of September, troops and Iranian-backed militiamen severed the rebels' last route into the east and placed its 275,000 residents under siege. Two weeks later, following the collapse of a nationwide truce brokered by the US and Russia, the government launched a ground offensive to seize full control of the city, accompanied by an aerial bombardment of unprecedented scale and intensity. At an emergency session of the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva on Friday, Mr Zeid warned that crimes of historic proportions were being committed in eastern Aleppo and elsewhere in Syria. The ancient city of Aleppo, a place of millennial civility and beauty, is today a slaughterhouse - a gruesome locus of pain and fear, where the lifeless bodies of small children are trapped under streets of rubble and pregnant women deliberately bombed, he said. Mr Zeid added that his staff had documented violations of international humanitarian law by all parties in Aleppo. Armed opposition groups continue to fire mortars and other projectiles into civilian neighbourhoods of western Aleppo, but indiscriminate air strikes across the eastern part of the city by government forces and their allies are responsible for the overwhelming majority of civilian casualties. These violations constitute war crimes. And if knowingly committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack directed against civilians, they constitute crimes against humanity. The commissioner stated the failure of the international community - particularly the UN Security Council - to protect civilians and halt the bloodshed should haunt every one of us. Syria's permanent representative to the UN, Hussam al-Din Ala, made a visibly angry statement afterwards, insisting that the Syrian government was waging a battle against terrorism. Later, the charity Save the Children warned that aid workers and medical professionals in eastern Aleppo were reporting the widespread use of cluster bombs, which are banned under international law. It cited the Violations Documentation Centre, an activist-run site, as recording 137 cluster-bomb attacks in Aleppo between 10 September and 10 October - a 791% increase on the average of the previous eight months.

text: Sipping from a cup of tea in the Hampden dressing room, surrounded by jubilant players and coaches, Roy MacGregor might have dwelled upon how far Ross County have come. The chairman of the county may have experienced a sense of reflection as he observed long-serving staff members, some of whose parents had also worked for the club, celebrating on the pitch at the national stadium following the team's 2-1 victory over Hibernian. Their Scottish League Cup success was a tale of numerous individuals, yet it all seemed to revolve around MacGregor himself. Jim McIntyre, the triumphant manager, referred to his chairman as Mr Ross County and expressed his joy at delivering a first major trophy for him. The two shared a lengthy embrace as the cup was paraded by the players. A symbolic moment occurred when MacGregor lifted his grandson, and both were loudly cheered and applauded by the County supporters. Media playback is not supported on this device. MacGregor was modest then, but he has long maintained that County should function as a community club with strong family values. This moment of glory, joy, and sheer exuberance belonged to all at County, but most fittingly to MacGregor. We've been on a journey together, he stated. This isn't the end of the journey. He appeared appreciative of the values McIntyre applies. The manager insisted that the dressing room celebrations would be curtailed, as training was scheduled for Monday and a crucial match against St Johnstone on Wednesday. A top-six finish is County's goal, so the celebrations would have to wait. Media playback is not supported on this device. MacGregor, a deeply religious man, built a global engineering business but strongly believed his focus should be on his local community. He joked that Dingwall, with its population of around 6,000, would have been emptied as over 9,000 Ross County fans descended on Hampden. If the game itself was challenging at times for County - Hibs dominated possession for long periods in the first half - the victory was filled with uplifting moments. Jackson Irvine was tireless in midfield, with his long legs covering the ground as he moved across the pitch, also sliding in to steal the ball from opponents. He had the acumen to create the opening goal for Michael Gardyne. Irvine's boots bore the name of his grandfather, who first introduced him to football and coached him for four years in Irvine's native Australia, and the player paid for his parents and sister to fly over from Melbourne for the final. The winning goal was symbolic as well. Brian Graham made a significant impact as a substitute, allowing County to become more competitive with his presence and movement up front. In the 90th minute, it was Graham who won the ball in the centre of the pitch, enabling Gardyne to dash down the left. Earlier in the half, it seemed an injury would force Gardyne off, but he persevered, driven by the desire to deliver his best in the final. His cross was cleared by Liam Fontaine, but only to Alex Schalk, who had been prone with cramp moments before. After tapping the ball over the line, Schalk sprinted towards the County fans to celebrate. County's players had suffered at times during the game, but they prevailed nonetheless. The winning goal was harsh on Fontaine. The Hibs defender had equalised in the first half and was desperate to atone for the second County goal, pushing upfield and seeing his overhead kick in added time pushed over the bar by Gary Woods. Fontaine looked distraught at the end, and several Hibs players appeared to be in tears. They had contributed much to the game - particularly Liam Henderson with his energy and running, John McGinn's scheming, and Darren McGregor's resolute defending - but they fell short. Alan Stubbs stated his side had been the better team. That was true for much of the first half, but it still has to be made to count. Hibs lacked composure in the final third, with Jason Cummings and Anthony Stokes often seeming disconnected up front rather than an effective partnership. The major decision had been made by McIntyre, as he sent his side out with a back three for the first time this season. It could have failed badly, and it might be said that County struggled as they tried to impose themselves on the game since the players were unaccustomed to the formation. Yet still, they won. MacGregor's financial and personal investment, combined with McIntyre's management, delivered a historic moment for County. In a sense, it is also a triumph for football in the Highlands, where on Saturday, Ross County face Inverness Caledonian Thistle in the Premiership. At present, it is these two clubs that hold the trophies for the two major cup competitions in Scotland. That thought would make MacGregor smile even more.

text: UK astronaut Tim Peake has begun his life in space with tea and a bacon sandwich. He arrived at the International Space Station on Tuesday after launching from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan aboard a Soyuz rocket. In tweets, he expressed that he was loving every minute of the initial days of his stay. Later on Friday, he will respond to questions from journalists in a live link-up with the European Astronaut Centre in Cologne, Germany. Mr Peake is one of six crew members residing and working in space. They include US station commander Scott Kelly, who is spending a year on board the ISS. In a tweet, referring to the Nasa astronaut, the 43-year-old from Chichester in Sussex remarked: What makes a good leader? @StationCDRKelly having a hot bacon sarnie waiting as my 1st meal on #ISS. Boy that tasted good! #Principia. He further added: 1st 48hrs on ISS - busy but incredible. Amazing how fast the body adapts to new environment. Found my tea ... life is good! The former Army aviator and helicopter test pilot also received messages of support from the Queen and Sir Elton John following the successful launch and docking on Tuesday. He tweeted singer Sir Elton John from space, quoting his famous song Rocket Man, in response to a good luck message. He also tweeted the Queen from space after Buckingham Palace's Twitter account posted a good luck letter from the monarch. Later on Friday, Mr Peake will address members of the press via a live link to the European Astronaut Centre near Cologne in Germany. The question and answer session will be streamed live on the European Space Agency website. It will serve as a brief respite from a busy schedule. According to the European Space Agency, he has several tasks to perform, including unpacking cargo, spending an hour on an exercise bike, and participating in an experiment examining the effects of microgravity on the bone marrow. text: The wife of Turkey's president has described the harem of the Ottoman era as an educational establishment that prepared women for life, reports say. Emine Erdogan addressed an official event on Ottoman sultans in Ankara, according to Turkish television stations. Her remarks followed a day after President Recep Tayyip Erdogan stated that a woman was above all a mother in a speech commemorating International Women's Day. Family members, servants, and concubines resided in the imperial harem. The sultans who governed the Ottoman Empire maintained a harem at Istanbul's Topkapi Palace, which has been a museum since 1924. The sultan conducted his domestic life in the harem, where his wives, female family members, and concubines, numbering in the hundreds, lived. Male staff members were eunuchs. Read more: Ottoman Empire 1302-1922. Mrs Erdogan described the harem as a school for members of the Ottoman dynasty. Traces left by harem women in the empire's six centuries of history could serve as an inspiration, she stated, according to Turkish media. Concubines in the harem received some training and were well fed, and not all were used for sex. However, they were not free to leave the palace if they wished. Some Turks swiftly criticised the first lady's remarks on social media. Receiving education in harem doesn't make it a school. This is nonsense, tweeted @GaziCaglar, asserting there would have been about 400 concubines in the sultan's harem. If the Ottoman harem was a scholarly institution then why were the men who worked there castrated? inquired @anlam75. Those who mention harem do not send their daughters to anything less than American universities, tweeted @kizmonot, referencing the fact that both the Erdogans' daughters studied at Indiana University. However, some, including pro-government journalist Ceren Kenar, noted that Mrs Erdogan is correct in stating that women were educated in the harem. Mr Erdogan provoked anger in 2014 when he said women and men are not equal. His comments on Tuesday regarding the role of women led to street protests in Istanbul.
