text: All living flowers ultimately derive from a single ancestor that lived about 140 million years ago, a study suggests. These are external links and will open in a new window. Scientists have combined models of flower evolution with the largest dataset of features from living flowers ever assembled. From this, the team was able to deduce the appearance of the ancestral flower. The flower possessed many concentric cycles of petal-like organs in sets of three, arranged in whorls, and was bisexual. Hervé Sauquet, from Université Paris-Sud, France, one of the authors of the paper published this week in Nature Communications, stated: There is no living flower that looks exactly like the ancestral one - and why should there be? This is a flower that existed at least 140 million years ago and has had considerable time to evolve into the incredible diversity of flowers that exist today. We are all familiar with the beauty of flowers - the reproductive structures produced by about 90% of all living land plants. However, their origin and early evolution remain a mystery. This is mainly due to the lack of fossil flowers from the period when the ancestor of living flowers is thought to have existed. Dr Jason Hilton from the University of Birmingham, UK, who was not involved in the study, remarked: The structure and organisation of the ancestral flower has remained enigmatic. For instance, we don't know if the oldest flowers were unisexual or bisexual, or if they were pollinated by wind or insects. To reconstruct the appearance of the first flower, the scientists recorded the features - such as the petals and sepals - of the flowers from 792 living species. They mapped the distribution of these features onto the evolutionary tree of flowering plants, enabling them to build a picture of what flowers looked like at key points in their history - including the last common ancestor of all living flowers. The first flower is reconstructed with petal-like structures arranged in a whorl, so each petal appears in the same plane, like a common lily (but with more whorls), rather than in a spiral, where petals overlap in a spiral arrangement around the stem, like a lotus. For some of the features we studied, the result was surprising, especially the fact that organs (such as sepals and petals and the stamens) were probably arranged in whorls instead of spirals, as commonly assumed for the ancestral flower, said Hervé Sauquet. The evolution of sex in flowers has been highly debated. Flowers can be unisexual or bisexual, and this study infers a bisexual early flower with both male and female organs. This study is important as it tells us how complicated the ancestral flower is likely to be - now the search is on to find it or something closely resembling it in the fossil record. That's if the model is correct - only time (and further study) will tell, said Jason Hilton.

text: The Solar Impulse plane has broken the record for the longest non-stop solo flight without refuelling. His jet-powered Virgin GlobalFlyer aircraft completed a full circumnavigation of the world in that time, covering more than 41,000km. In contrast, Mr Borschberg's Solar Impulse plane, which carries no fuel at all, had travelled only some 5,500km in its 76 hours of flight. text: A petition calling for jousting to be made an Olympic sport has been launched by English Heritage. The charity's jousting expert Dominic Sewell informed BBC Radio 5 live that the medieval pursuit was a worldwide phenomenon that should be recognised. Only approximately 20 individuals in the UK engage in competitive jousting, but the charity stated tournaments were held globally. The International Olympic Committee (IOC) stated it was unaware of any official request for its recognition. For a sport to be included in the Olympic Games programme, it must be governed by an international federation, practised widely worldwide, and meet other various criteria before being considered by the IOC's executive board. English Heritage stated it had made an initial approach to the IOC and the Fédération Equestre Internationale (FEI) - which governs all Olympic equestrian disciplines - as a first step on jousting's path to the Olympics. Jousting would need to be recognised by the FEI before it could be considered as an Olympic sport by the IOC, English Heritage stated. Mr Sewell, who jousts competitively, remarked: Just like the Olympic British equestrian team, we ride beautiful horses to an exceptional level. He said jousting required a huge amount of skill and a daily training regime, adding one had to be strong, not just physically but mentally, so you can sit fearlessly in your saddle, face your rival, and offer yourself as a target. Mr Sewell, a former furniture assembler in a factory, stated: This has gone from being a hobby to being a sport and a career. He informed BBC Radio 4's Today programme his interest had originally been fuelled by visiting historical re-enactments, but added: I'm a sportsman, I'm not an actor. Mr Sewell continued: As soon as I got on a horse everything changed and I thought: this is what I want to do, I want to be good at this. English Heritage admitted it could be a long road to get jousting recognised as an Olympic sport, but said there were encouraging signs. Tournaments were growing in popularity, the charity stated, and were now held in countries such as Belgium, Brazil and New Zealand. In the US, where jousting has been the official state sport of Maryland since 1962, competitors have launched a similar Olympic campaign. Jousting today is quite a safe sport to take part in, Mr Sewell says. The rules are essentially that you are in a single combat situation, in a designated area, in a pitch - or 'tilt-yard' - and in that yard is a tilt rail. The competitors charge down the rail towards each other with points awarded on the style and strength of their hit. Wearing a suit of armour weighing around 20kg, the athletes hold a 12ft lance in one hand and their horse's reins in the other, all while riding towards their opponents at a flat-out gallop - at speeds of up to 30mph. These days injuries are few and far between... but the odd un-horsing might result in a few bruises, Mr Sewell says. The IOC stated its programme was currently being addressed as part of the Olympic Agenda 2020, the group's strategy for the future of the Olympics. A spokesman said: One recommendation was to make the Olympic programme more flexible by moving from a sport-based to an event-based programme. Earlier this month, the IOC supported a bid to add karate, skateboarding, sports climbing, surfing and baseball/softball to the programme for Tokyo 2020. If approved, the inclusion would add 18 events and 474 athletes to the Olympic Games. Jousting, with its roots in Ancient Greece, where it was practised as part of preparations for war, emerged in England in the 10th Century as a sport for knights to hone their equine and lance skills. The first jousting tournament in England is said to have been organised by the Frenchman Godfrey de Preuilly in 1066. The tournaments became so popular that in the 12th Century, King Henry II banned the sport, as he considered it too dangerous to have a number of highly skilled knights in the same place at the same time. The ban was lifted under King Richard I and the sport remained popular, particularly during the Tudor era, until declining after the French King Henry II was killed during a joust in 1559. Jousting enjoyed a revival under 19th Century romanticism, with writers such as Lord Byron, Percy Shelley and Sir Walter Scott glamorising notions of chivalry with tales of knights and fair maidens.

text: Two 15-year-olds have been given life sentences with 20-year minimum terms for the murder of a mother and daughter in Lincolnshire in April. Dinner lady Elizabeth Edwards, aged 49, and Katie, 13, were smothered and stabbed while they slept at their home in Spalding. Sentencing them, the judge described it as a terrible crime which has few parallels in modern criminal history. The perpetrators were 14 at the time, apparently making them Britain's youngest double murderers. The judge at Nottingham Crown Court, Mr Justice Haddon-Cave, stated the case had defining and particularly chilling features, condemning the killers' actions as grotesque. Jurors heard that the killers went on to share a bath, engage in sexual activity, and watch four Twilight vampire films after the murders on Dawson Avenue, Spalding, on 13 April. For more on this and other Lincolnshire stories. Addressing the teenagers, the judge informed them: There is a clear intention to kill both victims - both defendants admitted wanting to murder them. There was remarkable premeditation and planning - it was, on any view, substantial, meticulous and repeated. He added: The killings were brutal in the form of executions, and both victims, particularly Elizabeth Edwards, must have suffered terribly in the last minutes of their lives. Mrs Edwards and her daughter were repeatedly stabbed by the couple, who were described in court as having a Bonnie and Clyde-style relationship. Mrs Edwards was stabbed by the boy eight times, twice in the throat, in a deliberate attempt to ensure her daughter was not woken by screams or cries for help. Katie was stabbed twice in the neck with severe force before being smothered by the boy. During his sentencing remarks, the judge said both teenagers were equally responsible for the murders and had revelled in what you achieved. I see no reason to distinguish between you in any way, he said. Had you been adults you may have been facing the whole of your lives in prison for this double murder. Outside court, Karen Thompson, deputy chief crown prosecutor for the East Midlands, stated: This is one of the most distressing and disturbing cases that I have ever encountered. Our deepest sympathies are now with the extended family and friends of Elizabeth and Katie Edwards as they attempt to come to terms with this horrific crime. Det Ch Insp Martin Holvey, of Lincolnshire Police, said it had been a rare and unprecedented case. The planning that went into these brutal murders of Elizabeth and Katie, as they slept in their own beds, was cold, ruthless and chilling - as was the lack of remorse shown by the two juveniles afterwards. In court, Peter Joyce QC, prosecuting, detailed for the first time the account given by the boy shortly after his arrest. He said the pair had met up and both agreed to kill Mrs Edwards and her daughter after the girl had asked him to kill both of the victims as she did not like the smell of blood. He went on to describe the killing of the mother, Elizabeth, and said that during the attack she had struggled and scratched his face, back and bum, Mr Joyce told the court. After about three minutes she had stopped struggling and had gone limp. He had got off the bed and taken off his trainers since they had made the floorboards creak. The boy then went into Katie's room, bent down and pushed the knife through her throat before using a pillow to smother her, the court heard. Defending the boy, Simon Myerson QC said the two children became trapped in a fantasy of their own devising. Andrew Stubbs QC, representing the girl, said the pair were in a toxic relationship and were almost playing chicken with each other as they spurred each other on to commit the killings. The pair pleaded guilty to manslaughter at a hearing in September but later the boy admitted to murder before the trial began. His girlfriend maintained her innocence to murder but was found guilty of two counts.

text: Steven Wilson is often dubbed the hardest working musician in the world of progressive rock. The versatile musician secured three awards at this month's Progressive Music Awards in London, including album of the year for Hand. Cannot. Erase. The Guardian's five-star review described it as a smart, soulful and immersive work of art. Since the 1980s, Wilson has been the leading figure in several musical projects, the most renowned being the rock band Porcupine Tree. Now, prior to two sold-out performances at the Royal Albert Hall, Wilson is releasing a vinyl-only double LP, Transience, to highlight the more accessible aspect of his solo work. He discusses with the BBC his passion for vinyl, his hectic schedule, and how comic actor Matt Berry became his support act. What does vinyl mean to you? I grew up at the very end of the vinyl era, and at the time, I recall, we eagerly awaited the arrival of CDs because vinyl was so frustrating. You would purchase the record, take it home, and it would have a scratch, necessitating a return. I appreciate CDs, and for certain types of music - classical, for instance - it is superior to vinyl. However, the issue with CDs and digital downloads is that there's nothing you can truly cherish or treasure. Owning vinyl is akin to having a beautiful painting in your living room. It's something you can hold, examine the lyrics, and immerse yourself in the artwork. I thought it was merely nostalgic, but it cannot be if youngsters too young to remember vinyl are enjoying that kind of experience. Do you have a piece of vinyl that you treasure? The truth is I disposed of all my vinyl in the 90s. All the vinyl I possess is repurchased. I initially aimed to recreate the collection I had at 15, but it has surpassed that. The first record I convinced my parents to buy for me was Electric Light Orchestra's Out of the Blue. If I still had my original copy, it would hold sentimental value, but, unfortunately, it's in a charity shop somewhere. Why release your new compilation Transience on vinyl? It was initially conceived as an idea for Record Store Day, but we missed that opportunity. My record company suggested I compile some of my shorter, more accessible songs. I became somewhat obsessed with the idea of creating an introduction to Steven Wilson, and I was determined it would be a vinyl-only release. Anyone who purchases the vinyl also receives a high-resolution download. Do you have a concern that the album won't reflect your work accurately? No - because although I do focus on more extended pieces of music, there is one thing I have always valued above all: melody. There is a lot of progressive rock that emphasises the technical complexity of the track rather than the melodic aspect. Pink Floyd, the most successful progressive rock band of all time, have endured because the emphasis was always on melody and atmosphere. What do you have planned for your Albert Hall shows? I don't wish to reveal too much. The repertoire will be entirely different each night. The first night will be a version of the Hand. Cannot. Erase. show I've been performing this year - but enhanced - with a few guests. The second night will delve more into my history, aimed at fans who have followed me for years. How did it happen that Matt Berry is the support act on the second night? Myself and everyone on the tour bus are huge fans of [Channel 4 comedy series] Toast of London to the extent that we quote it endlessly. I decided to explore Matt's music, so I acquired a copy of his Music for Insomniacs. I spoke with him about our shared love of Mike Oldfield and invited him to perform at the Royal Albert Hall. I'm going to be incredibly star-struck by my opening act. You've been remixing albums by the likes of XTC, Tears for Fears, and Yes. How much does that influence your own work? I don't consciously draw from that, but, inevitably, if you are deconstructing these classic albums, they truly get into your head. My last solo album, The Raven That Refused to Sing, was undoubtedly the most traditional progressive album I've ever created. I don't think it was a coincidence that I had been remixing King Crimson, Jethro Tull, and Yes almost exclusively for the previous year. The current album, Hand. Cannot. Erase., opened up much more because I'd been working on Tears for Fears and XTC. You are often described as progressive rock's busiest musician. Is that how it feels? You can remove the word progressive. I believe I am likely one of the most work-obsessed individuals in the music industry today, and I don't say that with any pride because, believe me, it's a curse. I think I inherited it from my father, who also had an incredibly strong work ethic. If I don't accomplish anything for a whole day, I start to feel this creeping guilt. That's why the remix work has been such a gift to me because it means I don't have to be creating my own music all the time. The music industry is a challenging place to make a living. I wouldn't recommend it to anyone as a profession now. I work every day, and I'm not wealthy, but I make a good living. I love what I do, it's a privilege, but if I were lazy about it, I don't think I'd be able to survive. Transience is released in the UK on 25 September. Steven Wilson performs at the Royal Albert Hall on 28 and 29 September as part of his 2015-16 European tour.

text: Food bank use in Scotland has increased to record levels, with more than 60,000 referrals over a six-month period, according to a charity. These are external links and will open in a new window. The Trussell Trust reported that, on average, individuals required 1.7 referrals, indicating that 35,000 people received assistance. From April to September, its food banks distributed 60,458 three-day emergency supplies, marking a 17% increase from the previous year. The most frequently cited reason for financial hardship was delays in receiving benefits. Approximately 28% of recipients attributed their difficulties to this reason, the same proportion as last year. The percentage of referrals due to benefit changes decreased from 18% to 16%. The proportion of those referred due to low income rose from 18% to 21%. Ewan Gurr, the trust's Scotland network manager, expressed concern that low income would become a more significant issue in the coming months. He stated: Difficulties related to welfare benefits are still driving the majority of people to our Scottish food banks, but now one in five of those referred is on a low income. Among that number is a growing body of people in low paid employment who are simply unable to make the pay cheque stretch far enough when crisis hits. The increasing instability of the oil, gas and steel industries has already led to significant numbers of people being made redundant, and figures revealed in the last week also show that unemployment has risen in Scotland while decreasing in the rest of the UK. The trust also expressed concern about a repeat of last year when low income referrals surged in December as fuel costs added an extra burden on household finances. Reacting to the figures, SNP MSP Kevin Stewart described them as alarming. He added: The figures also show that UK government benefit changes and delays continue to be the most common reason for people seeking emergency food aid. While Tory ministers have their head in the sand on the issue, the Scottish government recognises this link and is spending almost £300m over three years to mitigate Tory social security cuts. That any government would consider further cuts to the incomes of the poorest families in our society in the face of such clear evidence of rising poverty is appalling - yet George Osborne is set to plough ahead with £12bn more social security cuts. A UK government spokesman stated: Our reforms have secured record employment, a near record number of job vacancies and a growing economy. We maintain a strong social safety net and continue to spend around £80bn on working age benefits. We know that the reasons for food bank use are complex and overlapping and it is spurious to claim that it is driven by changes to welfare. Work remains the best route out of poverty and thanks to this government's long term economic plan thousands of people are experiencing the dignity of a job, the security of a wage and the peace of mind that comes from supporting your family, many for the first time. In terms of food donated, the figures showed Scotland was second only to the north west of England. When populations were compared, the statistics also indicated that a disproportionately high number of people were being referred to food banks in Scotland compared to other parts of the UK, the trust reported. Scottish Labour's equality spokesman Neil Findlay commented: In a country as wealthy as Scotland it is unacceptable that more than 60,000 people had to rely on food banks over the last six months. As winter approaches, the need for extra support is only going to increase. These figures should act as a wake-up call to both of Scotland's governments. After eight years of the SNP in office, and more than five years of the Tories, the gap between the richest and the rest in Scotland remains unacceptably high. The Trussell Trust describes itself as a charity motivated by Christian values. Its 50 Scottish food banks are part of a network of 425 across the UK. Everyone who visits its food banks is referred by a professional such as a social worker, health visitor or schools liaison officer.

text: Skier Dave Ryding matched Britain's best ever alpine World Cup result when he finished second in the Kitzbuhel slalom in Austria. He was leading after the first run but was surpassed by home favourite Marcel Hirscher, achieving the first podium of his career. It marked the best result in over 35 years, since Konrad Bartelski secured second place in a downhill event in Italy in 1981. The 30-year-old had already finished sixth and seventh this season. He informed BBC Sport: The first run was just insane. I knew I had skied it clean, but couldn't believe it when I crossed the finish line. Between runs, I tried to keep calm and not get stressed. I was trying to convince myself I wasn't the last to go, but it was challenging. It was a mental battle with myself, but I won it. Hirscher skied so well, so coming second almost felt like a victory. It's crazy. I'm just really proud of what I've achieved. The Lancastrian competes without UK Sport funding after it was withdrawn from the alpine programme in 2010 but does receive other sponsorship. Ryding, who learned to ski on a dry slope at Pendle Ski Club, has been a member of the British ski team since 2006 and competed in the 2010 and 2014 Winter Olympics, finishing 17th. He had a 0.29-second lead over Italy's Stefano Gross going into the second run, with Hirscher 1.02 seconds behind. However, the Austrian, who won the race in 2013 and has claimed the overall slalom title three times, had a remarkable second run to move from seventh to first, with Ryding finishing 0.76 seconds behind. More than 60,000 spectators were present, and Ryding remarked that the noise was deafening. Kitzbuhel is like the FA Cup final in England. The downhill race is the number one, but the slalom is also massive. The fans are incredible. The alpine ski World Cup was established in 1967, and in 50 years of racing, Ryding and Bartelski are the only British men to finish on the podium, while Gina Hathorn (1967) and Divina Galica (1968) achieved top-three finishes on the women's circuit. When Bartelski accomplished this in Val Gardena, Italy, it prompted a French commentator to exclaim: This is not possible, he is English! In the pre-World Cup era, Britain's Gordon Cleaver won the combined race on Kitzbuhel's Hahnenkamm course in 1931. While the alpine team no longer receives UK Sport funding, the Great British freestyle ski and snowboard team does. Following Jenny Jones' historic slopestyle bronze in Sochi, they will receive £4.9 million for the four-year cycle leading to the 2018 Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang, South Korea. They have achieved numerous World Cup successes, with Katie Ormerod becoming the first snowboarder to win a World Cup big air, while cousin Jamie Nicholls has triumphed in slopestyle, Lesley McKenna and Rowan Cheshire in halfpipe, and Zoe Gillings-Brier in snowboardcross. Skier James Woods has won three World Cup slopestyle events. Meanwhile, in cross-country skiing, Briton Andrew Musgrave recorded his best World Cup result, finishing sixth in a 15km race in Sweden on Saturday.

text: An archive of sketchbooks, drawings and letters belonging to artist Lucian Freud has been acquired by the nation through the acceptance in lieu scheme. The collection has been allocated to the National Portrait Gallery, which hosted a record-breaking Lucian Freud Portraits exhibition in 2012. Some of the items, never published or exhibited before, are expected to be displayed there next summer. The sketchbooks span his career from the mid-1940s until his death in 2011. This rare collection of Lucian Freud drawings and letters provides a fascinating glimpse into the work of one of our most pioneering artists, stated Culture Minister Ed Vaizey. Bringing these never seen before treasures into public collections means that everyone can enjoy and see the early beginnings that shaped his most celebrated work. The archive includes studies for many of the artist's major works as well as a collection of 162 childhood drawings depicting family life. They were created while Freud was living in Germany, before his family fled to England in 1933 as Hitler came to power, and were saved and dated by his mother. The National Portrait Gallery stated the archive would give added context to the two works housed in the gallery's collection—a self-portrait in oils and a charcoal drawing of Lord Goodman from 1985. Several drawings in the sketchbooks show the beginnings of portraits, including Lord Goodman's, starting with the nose and eyes and developing outwards. Also included are Freud's early designs of book covers, including one for his daughter, Esther Freud's 1992 novel Hideous Kinky and Nigel Dennis's Cards of Identity from 1955. Dr Nicholas Cullinan, director of the National Portrait Gallery in London, said the archive material was a very important, extensive and generous gift to the nation that would be a vital source of reference. The 47 sketchbooks together with drawings and letters settle a bill of £2,940,000 of inheritance tax from the Lucian Freud Estate, under the inheritance in lieu scheme. Sir Peter Bazalgette, chair of Arts Council England, added the collection offered a real insight into the life of one of Britain's most compelling and influential artists.

text: Three years ago thousands of Tunisians protested on the streets, demanding, among other things, more economic opportunity. The protests resulted in the ousting of the nation's former leader, President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, and ignited the broader Arab Spring throughout North Africa and the Middle East. However, despite President Ben Ali's removal, economic reforms in Tunisia since 2011 have stalled due to ongoing political unrest, which persisted until the end of last year. Yet, with a moderate interim government of independent figures appointed in December and the country's new constitution agreed upon in January, there is now renewed optimism that pro-business changes will be forthcoming to enable entrepreneurship and small businesses to thrive. Confidence has been bolstered by support from the World Bank, which last month awarded Tunisia loans totalling $1.2bn (£719m) to aid economic and political reform. The World Bank stated that this amount included $750m in support of government reforms to level the economic playing field and promote growth and job creation, and $100m to increase lending to small and medium-sized enterprises. For most Tunisian entrepreneurs, reforms to ease their work cannot come quickly enough. Ramzi el Fekih, 46, believes the key to aiding new businesses in Tunisia is an improved judicial system. Mr el Fekih is the chief executive of Viamobile, a mobile phone banking and payments app. He launched the business in Tunisia in 2009 after returning to the country following 25 years working abroad, including 20 years in the mobile phone technology sector in California. The biggest difference between working here and in California is the lack of trust, says Mr el Fekih. People try to protect themselves because they have been deceived before, but it becomes very constraining. There is so much control that we can't move, but what we need is a judicial system that punishes those who don't follow the law. Mr el Fekih says he would also like to see much less regulation and bureaucracy, complaining that it took him two years to get Viamobile approved by the country's central bank. But despite his frustrations, he says he has no regrets about returning to his homeland. I really believe that there is a huge potential in Tunisia and Tunisian entrepreneurs, he says. Mr el Fekih hopes that now, with the new constitution in place, the Tunisian state will move swiftly on reforms. His analogy is borrowed from the world of mobile technology. What politicians can do is design an easy and accessible operating system, so entrepreneurs can follow and create applications, he says. Now is the time. For fellow entrepreneur Zied Jallouli, 29, the major issue for start-ups in Tunisia is securing financial backing. Raising funds here for a big idea is really, really tough, says Mr Jallouli, shaking his head. He and his business partner have created a smartphone app called Disrupt CK, which they claim can help people buy clothes or other consumer goods similar to those they see in a film or TV show. Mr Jallouli says you simply point your smartphone at the television, press the app button, and it will produce a list of suggested items. While Mr Jallouli couldn't secure backing from a Tunisian bank or wealthy Tunisian investor, he ultimately obtained investment from a Swedish expatriate. The Swede in question is Thomas Adner, a former executive for Swedish packaging giant Tetra Pak, who had been working in North Africa for eight years. Mr Adner is so impressed with Mr Jallouli's product that he has even joined the company as its chief marketing officer. There are some great business opportunities in Tunisia, says Mr Adner, who highlights the low cost of hiring well-trained web developers and programmers. You can run quite a few miles with the cash that you have, he says. But Mr Adner still sees numerous hurdles to doing business in Tunisia that need removing. Back home [in Sweden] it takes about 30 minutes to register a new business, and in two days all the paperwork is done, he says. Tunisian authorities make it not only very difficult to start a company, it takes months if not longer. There is so much red tape here for anyone who wants to start a business. The government really needs to make it easier to start a company. Laurent Gonnet, the World Bank's financial sector specialist in Tunisia, also agrees that much work needs to be done in the country to assist businesses. He says the country's commercial banks are extremely cautious and risk averse, particularly when it comes to technology companies. He adds that Tunisia is also one of the last countries that lack a private credit rating system, making it even harder for entrepreneurs to convince banks to lend them money to back a business idea. Thankfully, the country's politicians now seem committed to pro-business reform, no doubt spurred on by the World Bank, and a challenging economic backdrop, with unemployment at 16%. The hope is that this commitment will not be curtailed by general elections due at the end of this year. We are reviewing the investment code in order to reduce red tape, says Dhamir Mannai, an assembly member from the CPR party of current President Moncef Marzouki. Meanwhile, Moncef Cheikhrouhou, a member of the opposition Democratic Alliance and the deputy chairman of the parliament's finance, planning and development committee, says that entrepreneurship is most needed to create wealth. We are treating this as an urgent matter and are looking for input from entrepreneurs as well, he says.

text: A former Labour chief whip has urged Jeremy Corbyn to reflect on Tony Blair's approach when party leader by ruling out the de-selection of MPs. These are external links and will open in a new window. Baroness Hilary Armstrong informed the BBC that Mr Corbyn was the greatest rebel ever as a backbencher, yet Mr Blair was reluctant to discipline him. She stated that the then prime minister believed Labour was a broad church. Amid claims that Mr Corbyn's opponents could be forced out, Baroness Armstrong remarked that he needed to demonstrate he is tolerant. Speaking to BBC Radio 4's The Westminster Hour, Baroness Armstrong expressed her satisfaction that Labour party chairman Ian Lavery had stated de-selection was not the way forward. However, she added: I know MPs where basically there is a process of harassment, where at every meeting they are criticised, they are challenged, they are told that they don't represent the people in the room. And all this is meant to do is grind them down, is wear them down, and get them to believe they shouldn't be in the Labour party any more. She remarked that sectarianism was ruling in certain areas. Baroness Armstrong added: Jeremy has the opportunity over the summer and at party conference to make it absolutely clear that he is not going to lead a narrow sectarian faction, he's going to lead a broad church that is tolerant. And the real test for Jeremy is, is he up to it? Mr Corbyn voted against his own government more than 500 times, and Baroness Armstrong said at the time there was upset among party members in his Islington North constituency. I had a couple of folk from Jeremy's constituency come to see me and say 'People are a bit upset with Jeremy always being against the Labour government, what if we try to de-select him?'. She advised them they would not be supported by the leadership. Baroness Armstrong stated: The prime minister was very clear about that when Jeremy was a backbench MP. And he was right, we shouldn't have worked to de-select him. But I hope that Jeremy will now reflect on that and I hope that he will be absolutely determined to make sure it doesn't happen under his watch.

text: Formula 1 is the most technologically advanced sport on the planet, and the latest radical rule changes have imposed a whole new set of challenges on the teams. Special Report: The Technology of Business Hey you, get on to my cloud Domain shift sends cyber world dotty How to cash in with off-the-peg apps Taj Mahal comes to your living room Sochi 2014: Hi-tech Winter Games The BBC visited the Lotus F1 Team in Enstone, Oxfordshire, to observe its preparations for the 2014 race season, set to commence in Melbourne, Australia, on 16 March. With a budget less than half that of the leading F1 teams and other challenges to address, Lotus requires all the technological assistance it can obtain. It is managing the recent departure of its team principal, Eric Boullier, to McLaren and a new leader attempting to resolve last year's £140m deficit in the company's finances, which resulted in the departure of star driver Kimi Raikkonen to Ferrari. As every tenth of a second is crucial in F1 racing, the optimisation of technology can ultimately make a difference of tens of millions of dollars to a team's annual revenue, states chief executive Matthew Carter, brought in by owners Genii Capital to stabilise the business. We are operating on half the budget of some of the big boys, so we have to think of different ways of making that work and being competitive, he says. This necessitates better utilisation of technology in every aspect of the business. The latest rule changes—featuring a smaller turbo-charged engine with a more powerful electric battery and energy recovery system, as well as a narrower front wing and lower chassis to reduce downforce—have required thousands of new drawings, parts, and tests. They're the biggest rule changes I've seen in 20 years of working in the sport, says Nick Chester, chief technical director for Lotus F1 Team. We had to start developing this car two and a half years ago. To enhance efficiency, the team has abandoned its fragmented approach to software—different packages performing different tasks—and entered into a £4m, four-year contract to implement Microsoft's Dynamics enterprise resource planning (ERP) software across the entire organisation, says Mr Chester. The nature of the Microsoft partnership—although not exclusive to Lotus—allows the team to customise the software to meet its needs and access the technology giant's research and development team in Redmond, Washington, he says. The ERP assists in planning and managing the highly complex process by which computer-aided designs, informed by computational fluid dynamics, eventually result in wind-tunnel-honed carbon-fibre speed machines racing around a track. It helped us cope with an increase from 12,000 to 14,000 drawings that the new car required, he says. It also enables us to run parallel design programmes and allocate resources accordingly. During a season, a car might receive 200 to 250 aerodynamic and mechanical upgrades, he says, necessitating an additional 6,000 drawings, all of which must be planned for, resourced, and delivered to the tracks on schedule. Development costs have been reduced by the introduction of laser 3D printing, which can transform designs into prototype parts far more quickly and cheaply than before. Enhanced technology also helps reduce time wasted on basic administration by automating common processes, according to IT director Michael Taylor. If you can free up an aerodynamicist's time by just one minute a day, over the course of the year that's a significant amount of time. And if you can extend the design lifecycle, in theory, you create a better design, he says. When a part fails, the team needs to identify exactly what caused the problem and at what stage the weakness occurred, from the moment the purchase order for the materials was placed right up to the second it broke. We need a single source of truth, says Mr Taylor. Data is a significant part of the sport—the car's on-board computer and the numerous sensors that wirelessly communicate with the team will generate up to 50 gigabytes of data per race, all of which must be analysed immediately. While the car is speeding around the track at up to 200mph in Abu Dhabi, for instance, the team back in Enstone is monitoring the real-time data flow remotely using VMware's virtual desktop technology. All this commercially sensitive data is stored in two concrete bunkers at the Oxfordshire site—external cloud storage services are not yet trusted enough, although Mr Taylor does foresee such a move in the future. Top-secret files are securely shared between partners, such as engine provider Renault, using EMC's Syncplicity software. It's like a commercial version of Dropbox, he says. IT enables everything inside this business. And the be-all and end-all of our IT strategy is to give us a competitive edge, says Mr Taylor. In-season testing on track, in wind tunnels, and simulators has been restricted by the sport's governing body, the FIA, in an effort to reduce costs and allow the smaller teams to survive. While these restrictions were absolutely essential, according to boss Matthew Carter, it places far more emphasis on IT to fill the gap. The lack of testing in F1 means we have to do an awful lot of work back here, ensuring there's a real good correlation between the information we get from the simulator and wind-tunnel testing and what happens on the track, so that we can continue punching above our weight, he says. If you stop investing in technology and stand still, others overtake you very rapidly in this sport.

text: A financial scam was committed once every 15 seconds in the first half of the year, prompting a new campaign to highlight the risks. These are external links and will open in a new window. More than one million cases of card, cheque, phone, or online fraud were recorded from January to June, according to Financial Fraud Action (FFA). This represents a 53% increase compared to the same period last year. The FFA, funded by banks and payment card companies, is promoting advice to help prevent fraud. Losses are often reimbursed by banks, but not in every instance. Many individuals feel too embarrassed to admit they have been deceived. The Take Five campaign, supported by police, the banking industry, and consumer groups, aims to ensure that busy lives do not make individuals easy targets. We are asking people to take five—to take that moment—to pause and think before they respond to any financial requests and share any personal or financial details, stated Katy Worobec, director of FFA. Home Office Security Minister Ben Wallace said: The impact of financial fraud can be devastating on victims, with fraudsters employing increasingly cunning and convincing tactics. They prey on people who are trying to get on with their lives but become vulnerable in moments when they are busy or distracted. At the same time, the government is working closely with law enforcement and the banking sector through the Joint Fraud Taskforce to take action to stop the organised criminals behind financial fraud. Banks assert they are preventing £7 of every £10 in potential fraud losses, yet millions of pounds are still being lost to fraudsters. Last year, financial fraud losses reached £755 million—a 26% rise on the previous year. You can likely add to that a significant sum that goes unreported annually. Email deception, along with phone and text-based scams, are now common tools in the modern-day bank robber's arsenal—reflected in official crime figures which now include fraud data. Fraud and cybercrime account for nearly half of all offences, according to the British Crime Survey. Police experts indicate that consumers are aware of the dangers of sharing personal details but can still be deceived. A survey by FFA suggested that this was most commonly because victims believed the caller was genuine, with nearly four in ten being caught out as they felt pressurised, and a similar proportion letting their guard down when they were busy. How to avoid falling victim to a scam. A separate survey commissioned by a comparison website suggested that more than four in ten people have needed to cancel credit or debit cards after falling victim to fraud in the past year. Jody Baker, head of money at comparethemarket.com, said: Most of the transactions we make now are digital and our research suggests that over a quarter of people carry as little as £10 in cash. text: Families of football fans who died in the Hillsborough disaster are pursuing High Court misconduct action against the South Yorkshire and West Midlands police forces, lawyers have said. The inquests jury determined that victims were unlawfully killed and identified police failings. Families have filed claims of misfeasance in public office, according to Saunders Law Solicitors. Legal proceedings commenced in 2015 but were paused pending the outcomes. Both police forces have been approached for comment. Following a 27-year campaign by victims' families, the inquests jury concluded that match commander Chief Superintendent David Duckenfield was responsible for manslaughter by gross negligence due to a breach of his duty of care. Police errors exacerbated a hazardous situation at the FA Cup semi-final where 96 fans perished, jurors concluded on Tuesday. Five myths rejected by the jury Hillsborough: What's next? Police chief's role in the disaster The 96 who died Misfeasance in public office is a civil action against a public office holder, alleging misuse or abuse of power. The action pertains to the events of 15 April 1989 and their aftermath. Families are pursuing the claim in an effort to secure accountability, lawyers stated. South Yorkshire Police was responsible for planning and operational duties on the disaster day. West Midlands Police was tasked with the original investigation into officers' conduct. A statement from Saunders Legal team claimed there was evidence of a systematic cover-up intended to shift the blame for what happened from South Yorkshire Police to the innocent, by spreading lies, doctoring evidence, pressurising witnesses and suppressing the truth. The evidence indicates abuse on an industrial scale by both South Yorkshire and West Midlands Police, beyond any one bad apple analysis, it added. It stated the evidence suggested institutional misfeasance by the two forces against fans. South Yorkshire Police's current chief constable David Crompton was suspended on Wednesday due to the force's approach to the inquest. In 2012, Mr Crompton acknowledged grave errors during the Hillsborough disaster and apologised profoundly. On Tuesday, after the inquests' conclusions were delivered, he admitted the policing of the match was catastrophically wrong and unequivocally accepted the findings. Hillsborough families have expressed anger after retired South Yorkshire police officers were encouraged to be proud of their work, despite the inquests' conclusions. A message on a website for the force's retired officers stated they had served dedicated and courageous careers. Families of the deceased have called for criminal prosecutions to follow the hearings. The CPS stated it would formally consider whether any criminal charges should be brought against any individual or corporate body based upon all the available evidence. Two ongoing investigations into the disaster and its aftermath could conclude by the end of this year. A police inquiry, Operation Resolve, is examining the lead-up to the crush on the match day, while a separate inquiry by the IPCC is investigating allegations of a cover-up.

text: The botched Renewable Heat Incentive (RHI) scheme was set up to encourage uptake of eco-friendly heat systems over the use of fossil fuels. These are external links and will open in a new window. However, its overly generous offer of fuel subsidies could cost taxpayers an additional £490 million. The fallout has now led to the collapse of the power-sharing Northern Ireland Executive. BBC News NI examines those who have found themselves in the spotlight over the scandal. Northern Ireland's former first minister, Arlene Foster, led the Department of Enterprise, Trade and Investment (Deti) when the RHI scheme was designed. Crucial controls to limit the scheme's cost were not implemented, which she has since described as her deepest political regret. However, the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader strongly disputed claims by Jonathan Bell—her party colleague and successor as enterprise minister—that she instructed him to keep the scheme open. Following his allegations, Mrs Foster faced calls to step aside to allow a judge-led public inquiry into the scheme. In January, Mrs Foster reiterated that she would not be resigning over the issue, adding that some calls for her to do so were misogynistic. Ultimately, her tenure as first minister ended abruptly when Deputy First Minister Martin McGuinness resigned, prompting an election. Jonathan Bell was the minister at Deti during the period when the RHI scheme inflicted the most damage on the public purse. A total of £485 million was committed when applications suddenly inundated the department in October and November 2015. However, in an explosive interview with the BBC's Stephen Nolan earlier this month, Mr Bell stated he attempted to close it down before that point, only to be blocked by DUP advisers. He also accused the advisers of attempting to alter documents without my knowledge, without my consent. The DUP MLA has called for a public inquiry into the scandal and has since been suspended by his party. Although he avoids the public eye, Timothy Johnston (above left, with former DUP leader Peter Robinson) has long been considered perhaps the most influential official behind the scenes at the DUP. In the days when the party opposed David Trimble's Ulster Unionists, Mr Johnston was its communications director, working particularly closely with Peter Robinson. He was involved in the negotiations around the St Andrews Agreement that led to the restoration of devolution in 2007 and has been an adviser at Stormont Castle for Ian Paisley, Peter Robinson, and now Arlene Foster. The Paisley family publicly blamed Mr Johnston for compiling a critical survey about Dr Paisley's leadership before the party founder resigned, a claim he said was regrettable and inaccurate. He is one of two DUP advisers that Jonathan Bell has claimed would not allow the RHI scheme to close in early autumn 2015, but he has rejected that allegation. As an adviser to Arlene Foster, he receives the maximum salary allowed for a special adviser—£91,809. A son of a farmer from Beragh in County Tyrone, Dr Andrew Crawford is a former employee of the Ulster Farmers' Union. He was an assistant to the former DUP MEP Jim Allister before the North Antrim politician left to form the Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV). Dr Crawford was an adviser to Arlene Foster when she was enterprise minister during the time the RHI scheme was created and followed her to the Department of Finance and Personnel last year. Jonathan Bell accused him of preventing the closure of the scheme, but Dr Crawford has denied that claim. He was also named by senior civil servant Andrew McCormick, in a PAC hearing, as the adviser who exerted influence to keep the scheme open—although Dr McCormick said he had no evidence for his claim. These days, he advises another DUP minister, Michelle McIlveen, in the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs. Dr Crawford's poultry-farmer brother is a claimant of the RHI scheme. Last year, he gave evidence to a Stormont committee about contacts between ministers and bidders involved in the controversial Nama property deal. In the more distant past, he was a junior barrister to Jim Allister and was involved in the DUP's decision to lure Mr Allister back from the legal world to replace Ian Paisley as an MEP. However, the DUP's leadership later regretted that move when Mr Allister rejected its deal with Sinn Féin and set up his own party, the TUV. He was an aide to the former social development minister Nelson McCausland, during which time he became entangled in the Red Sky housing maintenance scandal, and his treatment of then DUP councillor Jenny Palmer over that affair led to her whistleblowing on a BBC Spotlight programme. Mr Brimstone was later promoted to advise the first minister but resigned from his role in November. According to Jonathan Bell, Mr Brimstone was one of three advisers who witnessed a tense and angry exchange between him and Arlene Foster over the proposed closure of the scheme in early 2016, but he, like Mr Bullick, said that was not the case. He has confirmed that he is a claimant on the RHI scheme, but Arlene Foster has said his link to it was not a factor in his decision to quit his £91,809-a-year job. His brother, Aaron, is also a beneficiary of the green energy initiative, the Irish News reported in December. Timothy Cairns was Jonathan Bell's adviser at Deti and offered advice to the minister about the controversial RHI scheme. However, he has said that the ultimate decisions about it were for the minister to make. Mr Bell said his adviser told him that other DUP advisers were preventing the closure of the scheme. Timothy Cairns previously worked as an aide to Peter Robinson when he was first minister but is no longer employed as a DUP adviser. As the permanent secretary at the Department for the Economy, formerly Deti, Dr Andrew McCormick is the man who has to clear up much of the mess of the RHI scheme. He arrived at the department in 2014, long after the scheme was conceived, and drew Jonathan Bell's attention to major concerns over its operation in the summer of 2015. In an email in January 2016, Dr McCormick said there was some initial reluctance to limit the generous tariff offered by the scheme shortly before a crucial spike in applications that led to a spending commitment of almost half a billion pounds. And appearing before Stormont's Public Accounts Committee in November, he said a whistleblower flagged concerns with the scheme two years before its closure, but she was not believed by officials. The former minister said Mr Stewart was willing to back his claims in a public inquiry, but three days later the civil servant disputed Mr Bell's version of events. He did acknowledge that a DUP adviser changed wording of a Deti document, but added that Mr Bell later advised that he had dealt with the matter to his satisfaction. text: Developing post-Brexit trade with the Gulf region will be the focus of a two-day trip to Bahrain by Theresa May. Mrs May stated that some might argue the UK should not seek to strengthen ties with these states due to their controversial human rights records. The prime minister will attend a dinner with the leaders of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, and Oman on Tuesday evening, before addressing the plenary session on Wednesday morning. There is so much we can do together—whether it is helping one another to prevent terrorist attacks, Gulf investment regenerating cities across the UK or British businesses assisting Gulf countries to achieve their long-term vision of reform, Mrs May said. During a series of bilateral meetings, Downing Street stated it expected the situations in Syria and Yemen and relations with Iran to be discussed. However, he said he did not believe a threshold has been crossed requiring the suspension of British arms sales to Saudi Arabia. Mrs May will meet young people in Bahrain to discuss progress on political and social reforms since the widespread unrest in the Gulf nation in 2011, which prompted a much-criticised crackdown by the authorities. That is how Britain can be a force for good in the world as well as helping to keep our people safe and create new opportunities for business. text: There is a new class of planet out there that astronomers are calling the mega-Earth. It is an object with a hard surface similar to our own world but significantly larger. The necessity for the new designation follows the discovery of a planet with a mass approximately 17 times that of Earth. Known as Kepler-10c, it orbits a star about 560 light-years distant. Scientists described its properties at an American Astronomical Society meeting in Boston. They admit it is somewhat perplexing. Theorists had always believed that any planet of that size would attract so much hydrogen that it would resemble Neptune or Jupiter. The proper way to call it is something bigger than a 'super-Earth,' so how about 'mega-Earth,' stated Prof Dimitar Sasselov of the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics (CfA) to reporters. He also referred to it as the Godzilla of Earths! Kepler-10c, as the name implies, was detected by the US space agency's Kepler telescope. This instrument discovers new worlds by observing the slight dip in light as they transit in front of their parent stars. The technique provides a diameter—in this case, 29,000 km, or just over twice the width of Earth—but not a mass. For that, astronomers examined 10c with the Harps-North instrument on the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo in the Canary Islands. It derives a mass measurement by analysing the gravitational interaction between the planet and its host star. Combined with the diameter, the mass figure indicated that Kepler-10c cannot be a gaseous world but must consist of very dense material. It's 17—in fact, it's more than 17—Earth masses, and that brings the density to 7.5 grams per cubic centimetre, which is considerably more than what we know of rock here on Earth (5.5g/cm3), said Prof Sasselov. But remember, this is a very massive planet, which means those same minerals are highly compressed. So, what you see in the density is mostly due to compression rather than different composition. text: Terror attacks can be difficult for adults to understand - so how should we talk to children about terrorism? These are external links and will open in a new window. A report by the NSPCC last year revealed that children are increasingly anxious about global issues. Many who contacted Childline expressed concerns to counsellors about the EU referendum, the US presidential election, and conflicts in the Middle East. Is it feasible to discuss distressing news stories with children without exacerbating their worries? Psychologist Emma Kenny and Nicky Cox, editor of the children's newspaper First News, addressed the issue on BBC Radio Scotland. Even if children are shielded from distressing news stories at home, they are likely to hear about them from friends in the playground or on social media. Indeed, parents who believe they are protecting their children may be doing them a disservice, according to Nicky Cox. The editor stated: If you think as a parent you've done a really good job in shielding your child, you're doing them a disservice because they're going to go into school, they're going to be talking about it in the playground, in the lunch hall, and they're going to be getting information second, third and fourth hand. It is crucial that parents do not assume they control how their children access information because they do not. They need to ensure that children receive accurate information and are empowered to know the truth when conversing with their friends. As editor-in-chief of First News, Nicky Cox said her team of reporters are diligent in presenting facts to their readership. She emphasised the importance of teaching children to identify reliable news sources over so-called fake news. We tell the truth, she added. I believe there's absolutely no reason not to tell them the truth because they are going to hear all sorts of misinformation if they're on the internet or just talking at school. There is so much fake news and misinformation out there, and it is vital that they are educated to recognise where to find proper information. I think children are more savvy than most adults give them credit for. Psychologist Emma Kenny said very young children are likely to be comforted by reassurance from their parents. However, older children may not inform their parents if they have heard about a distressing news story or seen graphic images on social media. Ms Kenny said it is important for parents to initiate an open conversation. Ask them if they've heard the news and allow them to have that conversation, she said. That's how they can start to ask you the questions that really most people want to ask each other. Ms Kenny told BBC Radio Scotland that her eldest son expressed reluctance to return to London after the Westminster attack. I said to him, we're going to London in April because the reality is you're more likely to die by falling out of bed than in a terrorist attack, she said. She assured him that the few bad or sick people were in the minority and the UK is full of good people. When you look at what happened yesterday, it was full of people running towards that attack to help, not people running away to save themselves, she added. She advised parents to use their children's experiences as props for their conversation, then use statistical analysis to provide reassurance. Ask your child, in all the years you've been here, how many times has that occurred for you, how many times have you been involved in it?

text: London Underground office staff have voted for industrial action in a row over ticket office closures. Nearly 68% of Transport Salaried Staffs' Association members voted in favour of strikes, with a turnout of 44%. The Union stated its members have faced unprecedented levels of abuse since the closure of ticket offices. A TSSA survey revealed that most staff felt less safe since moving from offices to station concourses. Tom Edwards, BBC London Transport Correspondent The closure of ticket offices was one of the most significant changes on the Tube for generations. With the advent of automatic payment methods like the Oyster card and contactless, the aim was to move staff from behind glass screens to ticket gate lines. However, the unions have consistently opposed this, arguing that the redeployment has resulted in more lone working and staff shortages. The TSSA, representing station staff, announced it would decide, likely tomorrow, on the industrial action to take in the dispute. Strikes remain a possibility, although an overtime ban could also be considered. Other forms of industrial action received nine-to-one support. The union claimed staff were targeted by frustrated passengers when ticket machines malfunctioned. TSSA general secretary Manuel Cortes stated the vote was about our members being prepared to take part in a strike to let the world know that the Tube they are using is not fit for safe purpose. Our customer service assistants are overwhelmingly trying to warn the public that the Tube they use is not safe. We no longer have enough staff, he said. Steve Griffiths, London Underground's chief operating officer, commented: We urge the TSSA leadership to work with us constructively on the issues they have raised rather than threaten to disrupt our customers with strikes. The ticket offices were closed under the Fit for the Future programme initiated by former London mayor Boris Johnson. His successor Sadiq Khan has ordered a review of the project. Tube drivers are set to stage 24-hour strikes on 6 and 7 December, coinciding with a walkout by Southern Rail guards.

text: The new Harry Potter play in London has removed the use of live owls from the production. The decision follows an incident during Tuesday's initial show when an owl escaped into the auditorium. The bird did not return to its handler after a brief flight during a scene. Previews of the two-part play, Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, commenced this week. At Thursday's performance of part two, a sign at the Palace Theatre informed the audience that there were no real birds in the production. A statement issued on behalf of the producers said: The production of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child is currently in its preview stage, with the process designed to allow the creative team time to rehearse changes or explore specific scenes further before the play's official opening. As part of this process earlier this week the decision was made not to feature live owls in any aspect of the production moving forward. The owls associated with the production were expertly cared for by a team of certified trainers and an on-site specialist veterinary surgeon (Steve Smith, MRCVS) who ensured the owls' welfare and enrichment needs were safeguarded at all times. This was of utmost importance to the production. Fan excitement for JK Rowling. Animal charity Peta (People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals) welcomed the news. Peta commends the production team for coming to its senses and recognising that treating owls like props goes against every message of respect and kindness that JK Rowling's wonderful books taught us, director Mimi Bekhechi said. Harry Potter can now join the ranks of innovative stage productions like War Horse, The Lion King and Running Wild which prove that animals need not be exploited for the theatre - and that the possibilities of prop design are limited only by our own creativity. Shortly before the second half of Thursday's performance began, JK Rowling was spotted in a box stage right, causing screams of excitement from the audience with hundreds craning their necks trying to catch a glimpse of her. The show does not have its official opening until 30 July. Based on an original story by Rowling, writer Jack Thorne and director John Tiffany, the play is set 19 years after the events of the seventh and final book in the series, the Deathly Hallows. It portrays a grown-up Harry (Jamie Parker) as an employee at the Ministry of Magic, while his youngest son Albus (Sam Clemmett) has to deal with the heavy burden of the Potter family legacy. The show runs in the West End until May 2017.

text: Liam Neeson and Graham Norton have called for the introduction of same-sex marriage in Northern Ireland ahead of a planned protest in Belfast. These are external links and will open in a new window. Snow Patrol singer Gary Lightbody and The Fall star Bronagh Waugh have also lent their voices to the campaign. Northern Ireland remains the only part of the UK and Ireland where same-sex marriage is still prohibited. The issue is a significant stumbling block in the ongoing negotiations to restore power-sharing at Stormont. It has received considerable media attention recently after Northern Ireland's Democratic Unionist Party, which opposes same-sex marriage, entered into an agreement with UK Prime Minister Theresa May following her failure to secure a majority at Westminster in the general election. The DUP denies accusations of homophobia, asserting it is instead upholding the traditional definition of marriage. Several celebrities, including actor and writer Stephen Fry and singer Neil Hannon of The Divine Comedy, expressed their views with Amnesty International, a leading member of the Love Equality coalition organising the march in Belfast on Saturday 1 July. Ballymena-born actor Liam Neeson stated: We've had enough of a history in our society in Northern Ireland of discrimination, mistrust and hatred. Yet, we're also an open-hearted, welcoming and terrific people. Let us show that to the world by treating gay, lesbian and transgender peoples as our brothers and sisters and allowing them to marry, if they so wish. TV presenter Norton remarked the historic referendum that approved same-sex marriage in the Irish Republic was a proud gay day. My own mother was from Northern Ireland, so of course I have a huge affection for the place and its people, he said. I know it is hugely frustrating for gay people there that it is the last part of these islands still without marriage equality. Especially when there is such overwhelming support for it among the public. County Down-born singer Lightbody added: Two years ago, I marched with 20,000 fellow Northern Ireland citizens for marriage equality. It was a beautiful day of hope, joy and solidarity and I was so proud to be from 'Norn Iron'. Two years on and somehow - defying reason given it's the will of the people - we still do not have marriage equality in Northern Ireland. Coleraine-born actress Waugh, who will host the parade rally at Belfast City Hall, said: With the spotlight on Northern Ireland at the minute, now is our chance to really step up our campaigning a gear and give Northern Ireland what it so clearly wants and deserves, finally - equal marriage.

text: Chinese internet giant Tencent insists its profits won't take a hit from a decision to limit the time children can play one of its most popular games. These are external links and will open in a new window. Access to Honour of Kings is now limited to one hour daily for children under 12 and two hours for those aged 12 to 18. These restrictions were implemented after the government-owned People's Daily described the game as poison and advocated for increased regulations. Also known as Kings of Glory, Honour of Kings is a fantasy role-playing multiplayer online battle arena game. It closely resembles another Tencent game, League of Legends, which is the world's most popular PC game. There are some differences. Unlike League of Legends, it is based on Chinese historical figures. It is also specifically designed for mobile platforms. This is a significant reason for its popularity in China, where many gamers lack access to a games console or PC at home. The app is free to download, but players pay to enhance their characters or costumes to progress to the next level. Estimates of average player spending range from about $1.50 to $6 monthly. That may not seem substantial, but it accumulates in a game with over 50 million monthly active users. Parents and teachers are concerned that children are becoming addicted to the game. While concerns over gaming are not new, Honour of Kings has attracted particular criticism from the government-owned People's Daily newspaper, which labelled it poison and a drug harmful to teenagers. It also called for stricter regulatory controls on online games. Tencent's revenue model relies on encouraging existing gamers to spend more time on their products. Its last annual report states its strategy is to convert casual gamers into midcore or hardcore gamers. Tencent earned $7.2bn in the first quarter of this year, with more than half - approximately $3.9bn - derived from gaming. Two titles dominate its portfolio. League of Legends is its largest title globally, but in China, Honour of Kings is its top-grossing mobile game. Chinese gaming industry database CNG estimates the game generated about $810.5m in the first quarter of this year. That would represent about 11% of its total revenue. Tencent is a vast company. Besides gaming, it is involved in payment services, social media, and messaging apps (notably the phenomenally successful WeChat). The majority of Tencent's business is in China, making it susceptible to regulatory changes there. This could increase investor anxiety. After Tencent implemented the time limits, its shares dropped 4%, erasing $12bn from its market value. However, shares have slightly rebounded since then. Overall, the company has grown more than 40% over the past year, and it states the limits will not significantly impact the bottom line, as children under 12 comprise only a small portion of its user base.

text: I'm not a tech person. It is not what one would expect a tech millionaire to say. It is even stranger when one realises that the person saying it, Chad Mureta, is an archetypal tech millionaire. Mr Mureta amassed his wealth by designing apps. His creations, including the Emoji app, which assists users in annotating their messages with a wider variety of amusing images, and a phone security app, Fingerprint Scanner Pro, have been downloaded over fifty million times. His company, App Empire, generates between $3 million and $5 million (£1.9 million to £3.3 million) in revenue annually. However, in other respects, he is not your typical tech entrepreneur. It required a brush with death to guide him in the right direction. In 2009, he was driving back from a basketball game. Things were not going well for him. He had sold items on eBay, sold timeshares, and managed a nightclub. At that time, he was an estate agent and was deeply unhappy, with no clear idea of what he wanted to do with his life. As he drove down the motorway, a deer stepped onto the road ahead of him. He swerved to avoid it. His car collided with the central reservation barrier. The car flipped end over end, rolling four times before coming to a stop. Mr Mureta's left arm was severely injured. In hospital, the doctors nearly amputated it. What followed were six gruelling months in hospital, and another six months in rehabilitation, with nothing more than a $100,000 medical bill awaiting him at the end—the United States requires patients to pay for treatment, and his insurance policy would not cover the costs. I was at such a low point, he says. Very depressed, couldn't sleep, loads of medication—and actually very suicidal. I was in so much pain I didn't think I could continue. What happened next is the kind of scenario that Hollywood screenwriters would struggle to make believable—yet Mr Mureta insists it is true. One of the few things to survive the accident was his smartphone. It was brand new on the day of the accident, but unlike his torn clothing, it had somehow emerged relatively unscathed, retaining 12% of battery life. As he lay in his hospital bed, he observed doctors idly flicking through the phone; and he began to consider how it would be beneficial to have a way of enhancing security on one's phone. He was still on strong medication, and his mind drifted from the idea. However, a visiting friend brought him a magazine article about apps. This was during the early days of app development when individual coders were transforming the world single-handedly from their attics. I just had this 'A-ha' moment, where I said, 'holy cow, I'm going to do this', says Mr Mureta. I was sitting there, on all these IV drips, morphine, and I looked around and I finally saw the picture. I envisioned a different destiny. I'll never forget that emotion—I can't describe it in words. It was this transparent moment: here's your answer, and you're foolish if you look at anything else. It was easier said than done. The resources for developing apps were not as readily available as they are now, and Mr Mureta had no experience in coding. However, he did have one valuable asset as he recuperated: time. I just sat there, looking at all these apps, he says. I was asking: 'Why? Why does the customer like this app?' That gave me the competitive advantage to make this happen. Furthermore, one of the doctors had a cousin in India and mentioned to Mr Mureta that he was just getting into app development. Mr Mureta took a chance, borrowed $1,800 from his stepfather, and overcame language and technical barriers to shape his first product. Two months later, Fingerprint Security Pro was in the app store. Ultimately, the app did not actually offer any security—it was a gimmick that pretended to read someone's fingerprint and deny them access to the phone, with a hidden unlock button in its top corner. However, it did not matter. Users loved it. In its first month, it generated $12,000. Mr Mureta was on his way. In the years since the accident, Mr Mureta, now 34, has built and sold three app companies and developed over fifty apps. App Empire, his current company, earns its revenue from teaching others how to develop and release their own apps, both through bespoke tutoring and through publishing books on the process. One of the reasons the company has been so successful, Mr Mureta says, is that he ensured he only did what he was good at, and let others handle the rest. He keeps his company lean and fast, relying on a team of freelancers complemented by a small core of full-time staff. And he is not very hands-on himself. I work probably one or two hours a day on App Empire, he says. I just make sure things are running smoothly. This is why Mr Mureta says he is not a tech guy, although he is fascinated by technology. He cannot personally code an app. But he can advise you on getting one made, and how to launch it successfully. A traumatic accident like the one Mr Mureta experienced is often difficult to discuss, but he is happy to share details. Part of this, he says, is that he realised his recovery has inspired others in similar situations. And although it will never be fully functional, Mr Mureta retained his arm. I have titanium all the way up from my elbow, he says. It was groundbreaking and unbelievable surgery. Because I still have feeling in my arm, I can use it for the most part, and most people wouldn't even know—aside from the crazy, bear-like scar I have on there!
