text: If this secret left-wing plan to take over the Labour Party comes to pass, our electoral existence is in peril. These are external links and will open in a new window. Tom Watson did not hold back when he spoke to me on Monday morning. However, was he truly more concerned about his party's future or the future of his union, Unite, which now seems inappropriately named? Both are, indeed, currently inextricably linked. Mr Watson had been personally close to the union's general secretary, Len McCluskey, as they are former flatmates. However, relations soured when Labour's deputy leader failed to persuade Mr McCluskey to convince Jeremy Corbyn to agree on a date to step down as party leader last summer, after eight out of ten of his MPs declared no confidence in him. Thus, there is now political and personal animosity. Mr McCluskey faces re-election at the end of next month, and those close to Mr Watson see an opportunity to weaken both him and the current party leader. Mr McCluskey's main opponent is the West Midlands organiser, Gerard Coyne, who is politically to his right. Mr Watson supports the challenger partly because Unite, under its current leadership, has generously funded Mr Corbyn's two leadership campaigns, and a change at the top might halt funding to any aspiring left-wing replacement. Mr Coyne's initial argument was that the union was too focused on Westminster politics under Mr McCluskey and not enough on members' interests. However, some of Mr Corbyn's critics at Westminster argued that the Coyne campaign had too subtle a message to gain significant media coverage, and the contest should be recast as a proxy battle for Labour's future. Thus, this weekend Mr Watson was provided with strong ammunition to launch a campaign of shock and awe to get party and union members to take notice. Jon Lansman established Momentum to maintain the spirit of the first Corbyn leadership campaign, harnessing the energies of those who joined Labour to change both the party and the country. However, the recording of his remarks to a local group in Richmond, obtained by the Observer, suggested he was more interested in changing Labour than changing the government—he spoke of how an early election would disrupt our plans but what we need to do next is a number of things to change the nature of the Labour Party. Even more advantageous for Mr Watson was the suggestion that the link between the current Unite general secretary and Momentum was set to become stronger and tighter. Mr Lansman opined that assuming Len McCluskey wins the general secretaryship...Unite will affiliate to Momentum and will fully participate in Momentum. Mr Watson has suggested that Mr McCluskey would prefer to fund a left-wing faction inside Labour rather than the party itself. He believes this revelation might encourage more moderate members of Unite to vote to change their general secretary. The acting Unite leader, Gail Cartmail, told me there were no plans to affiliate with Momentum and Mr Watson had not verified his story before going public. However, with or without union funding, what exactly is the hard-left plot that Mr Watson believes will destroy Labour? Firstly, Momentum seeks to change Labour's leadership rules. Currently, a leadership candidate requires the support of 15% of MPs and MEPs before the wider, left-wing membership gets a chance to vote for them. Mr Corbyn only managed to get on the ballot in 2015 because some of those to his right 'lent' support to broaden the debate. Those MPs who viewed their actions as a significant mistake will not repeat it. Mr Lansman is heard emphasising how crucial it is that the 15% threshold is reduced should Mr Corbyn stand down. At this September's Labour conference, it is almost certain delegates will be given the option to reduce that threshold from 15% to only 5%—a much smaller hurdle for a left-wing candidate to overcome. Mr Lansman is recorded saying we really need to win that vote and we have to work to get delegates to that conference. However, internal groups such as Labour First and Progress—put simply, Brownites and Blairites and those once called modernisers—are collaborating in many local constituencies to select delegates sympathetic to them. Like Mr Watson, they believe that if Mr Corbyn were simply replaced by someone with similar politics, Labour would miss an opportunity to appeal to a broader electorate who believe the party is now too left-wing. The only way to stop the changes is to get more anti-Corbyn delegates to Labour's conference this autumn than those who support the leadership. Thus, Mr Watson's apocalyptic warnings are partly aimed at sounding a klaxon that the longer-standing but demoralised moderate party members will hear. Equally, perhaps the reason Mr Lansman was so candid about Momentum's intentions was to encourage left-wing, newer Labour members who would prefer to be on demonstrations to attend the rather tedious party meetings that nominate conference delegates. Secondly, Mr Watson believes that Momentum will seek to depose MPs and councillors it regards as hostile or right-wing or both. Momentum claims it is entitled to express its views, and it is up to local members to decide who they would like to represent them. Far from hatching secret plans, Mr Lansman made his remarks at a meeting open to the wider public. It is entirely possible, of course, that Mr McCluskey wins the union leadership contest and Momentum members fail to secure the leadership changes they desire. Thus, the armed impasse between Corbyn supporters and opponents could continue, possibly to the party's electoral detriment. Already, sources close to the leadership warn that Mr Watson's intervention means we are really worried about our local election prospects in the spring because he has highlighted divisions. They were going to be tough enough to begin with but this stuff from Watson put the elections in real jeopardy, they say. Thus, if there are poor results, the anti-Corbyn camp would use this as further evidence of the leadership's failures. However, leadership supporters are getting their retaliation in first by attempting to shift the blame to the deputy leader's door. At the end of a shadow cabinet away day on Monday afternoon, Messrs Corbyn and Watson issued a statement saying they had had robust and constructive discussions. However, there may have been more of the former—and a bit less of the latter.

text: The daily commute to work is something to be put up with rather than enjoyed, yet how we get there and how long it takes has an impact on how we feel. It is hardly surprising when considering that the average worker in Britain spends 54 minutes commuting daily. This significant and ever-growing portion of the working week incurs costs beyond the financial. According to the Office for National Statistics, feelings of happiness, life satisfaction, and the sense that one's activities are worthwhile all diminish with each additional minute of travel to work. This defines personal wellbeing, and generally, the longer the commute, the more it diminishes. Lengthy commutes, ranging from an hour to an hour-and-a-half, have the most detrimental effect on personal wellbeing, the ONS research found, while taking the bus to work on a journey exceeding 30 minutes was the commuting option most likely to cause dissatisfaction. I live in Porthcawl, Wales, and travel a minimum of five days a week to Watford. My alarm sounds at 03:30 each day, and my journey takes two-and-a-half to three hours. My day can last up to 12 hours. I then travel home when there is significantly more traffic than in the mornings, with an average of three to three-and-a-half hours being typical for this single journey. Readers' accounts of extreme commuting. The 2011 census indicates that 7.2% of working individuals in England and Wales travel by bus or coach to work, compared to 5% by train and 3.8% by underground or tram. The vast majority, 59%, drive or receive a lift in a car or van. Ideally, commuting should not affect psychological health because it is a choice. Commuting journeys increase as people move out of towns and cities to find better housing, more green space, and a higher standard of living. Professor Jenny Roberts, from the University of Sheffield, has researched how wellbeing is impacted by changes in commuting times by tracking 7,000 men and 7,000 women over 13 years. In contrast, the ONS report is based on a one-off survey of over 60,000 employed individuals between 2012 and 2013. She found, in her paper published in the Journal of Health Economics, that women were adversely affected by commuting, while men were not, despite women generally commuting less and working shorter hours. This was after accounting for income, job satisfaction, and housing quality. So why are women more sensitive to time spent commuting? The only reason we could propose was trip-chaining, Prof Roberts explains. Women tend to make more interim stops on their journey, via the nursery or the school or the shops, so they have less flexibility and engage in more multiple activities. This adds stress to commuting. Commuting affects wellbeing due to the well-established link between stress and mental health. The stress is caused by a lack of control during commuting, such as delayed trains, traffic jams, and unpredictable weather. Research also indicates that boredom and social isolation among commuters can lead to unhappiness. However, some commuters find positives in the daily commute as it provides time to work, read, or simply unwind. 'Extreme commuting' is becoming more common, and the ONS research suggests that a commute time of three hours or more is often a happier experience than shorter journeys. This may be because these extra-long journeys are a positive lifestyle choice for extreme commuters, who tend to have a higher average income and can use their travel time more productively as a result. Those who cycle or walk to work benefit from knowing that physical activity improves wellbeing, but the ONS research indicates that cycling to work can also be stressful. This is particularly true if commuters cycle due to a lack of other options or on a route through heavy traffic. Ultimately, the psychological health of commuters is important because everyone commutes, but we are often reluctant to analyse how we do it, says Prof Rogers. Do people really consider when moving to a suburban house how much time, how much income it's going to cost, and how it's going to affect their mental health?

text: In a football match, it is not usual to start 3-0 down. However, in economic terms, that is effectively the position the government finds itself in as it approaches the Autumn Statement at the month's end. The former Chancellor, George Osborne, established three rules for the government to follow, in an effort to demonstrate to a sceptical public that it was addressing the country's deficit (the difference between public spending and tax receipts) and managing the accumulation of debt (the total amount owed by the government). All three rules have been broken or abandoned—the cap on welfare spending, the commitment to reduce debt as a proportion of national income, and the promise to balance the books (eliminating the deficit) by 2020. The final target was discarded after the referendum result led to a series of economic downgrades for the UK economy, which—if realised—will reduce government income and make eliminating the deficit even more challenging without further tax increases and public sector cuts. This is the difficult situation in which the current Chancellor, Philip Hammond, finds himself ahead of his first major economic event, the Autumn Statement in two weeks. Today's report by the Institute for Fiscal Studies highlights the challenges ahead. It indicates that given the predicted economic slowdown, the chancellor will face a public finances outlook £25bn worse than anticipated in the Budget last March. Without policy changes—and that is a significant assumption given that Mr Hammond is (a) a new chancellor and (b) has already mentioned a fiscal reset—the IFS states tax revenues will be £31bn lower. This will be partially offset, the IFS notes, by the £6bn the government might recover by ceasing its contributions to the EU budget. However, that is also a significant assumption. Many government sources I have consulted believe that to facilitate the transition to a free trade deal with the EU (particularly if there is no agreement on freedom of movement), the government may need to maintain some budget payments. Of course, in terms of public finance, Brexit is not entirely negative. The Bank of England's decision to cut interest rates to 0.25% reduces the cost of servicing government debt. The depreciation of the pound (which raises import prices) also narrows Britain's trade deficit by enhancing export performance. Additionally, the increase in dollar earnings and profits for global companies based in the UK will benefit the government's tax receipts. These factors are somewhat marginal compared to the overall negative impact of the anticipated economic slowdown. Some believe those pessimistic forecasts will prove overly negative—just as the predictions of a possible recession this year did. If they are, all the public finance estimates will need to be revised again. Such is the difficulty and unpredictability of economic forecasting. This close to the Autumn Statement, the Office for Budget Responsibility—the official economic watchdog—will be providing the Treasury with weekly updates on its public finance forecasts. The OBR is expected to downgrade its growth forecasts for the UK economy, following the Bank of England's lead. This implies that government receipts will be projected to be lower. The government could respond by further cutting spending (unpalatable), raising taxes (unpalatable), or loosening the deficit reduction target (likely). If economic growth slows, Mr Hammond's options to recover some of those lost objectives will be limited.

text: Motorists trying to access a new system for hiring a car have been experiencing problems with the DVLA website. Several individuals stated that the system, which does not apply to Northern Ireland drivers, was malfunctioning, while some car hire firms had to manage queues. The changes, involving the abolition of the paper counterpart, take effect on Monday, 8 June. However, the DVLA reported that over 20,000 drivers had accessed the site without difficulty. Henceforth, motorists hiring a car may need to produce a special temporary code as proof of their convictions. The DVLA stated it had been developing the new system for months. As a result of abolishing the paper counterpart, all evidence of driving endorsements and convictions will be held exclusively online. Motorists are being asked to log on to the DVLA website and obtain a code, which they may be required to present when hiring a car, either in the UK or abroad. However, the code is only valid for three days, raising the possibility that holidaymakers may need to find internet access. Several customers complained to the BBC that they were unable to access parts of the website on Monday. A car hire firm in Bristol reported having a queue of 20 people waiting, as staff struggled to access details online. The DVLA system has crashed a dozen times this morning, said Richard Stock from U-drive. Another operator nearby had a queue of customers out of the door. The DVLA informed the BBC that there had been exceptionally high demand on its website, and it was urgently investigating the issue. The car hire industry has accused the DVLA of implementing the system too hastily. The project's being rushed through. It's not brilliant, said Gerry Keaney, chief executive of the British Vehicle Rental and Leasing Association (BVRLA). The RAC previously warned that many people were unaware of the new rules. A more recent survey by the website money.co.uk indicated that 73% of drivers were unaware they needed to produce a code when hiring a car. The AA has advised motorists to take their paper counterpart with them, even though it is no longer valid. However, the DVLA denied that the system is complicated. It's very easy to view and share your driving record. Just go to gov.uk and search for 'view driving licence', said Oliver Morley, the DVLA's chief executive. He stated that motorists could also save their driving records as a PDF file, which they could store on a mobile device. The DVLA has produced a step-by-step guide to assist motorists through the process. For those who forget to take a code, a phone number is available, but only between 8am and 7pm on weekdays, and 8am and 2pm on Saturdays. In many cases, motorists hiring a car are not asked for evidence of convictions. Nevertheless, drivers are advised to contact their hire company before travelling to determine which documents they need to bring. Smaller hire companies, especially those based abroad, may be unaware of the changes. Up to eight million old-style paper licences, which carry endorsements, will remain valid. However, endorsements will no longer be added to them by the courts. The government has defended the new system, claiming it will save millions of pounds and reduce red tape. Last year, the DVLA had to replace 445,000 paper counterparts. Motorists who lost them were charged £20 for replacements. However, the British Vehicle Rental and Leasing Association stated it would be preferable if there were an online IT system that hire companies could use to check convictions themselves. It has also produced advice for motorists. The new arrangements are valid in Britain only. Northern Ireland has a separate licence scheme.

text: The makers of the Raspberry Pi computer have created a version of its graphical front end that can run on ordinary desktop computers. These are external links and will open in a new window. The Pixel desktop has been redesigned to operate on PCs and Apple Mac machines, the Foundation stated. Users on a Raspberry Pi and other devices will now have the same familiar software on both. The Pi Foundation stated the release also supports its aim to deliver the best desktop computing experience. Raspberry Pi co-creator Eben Upton remarked that the software should assist schoolchildren who use the credit-card-sized Pi in class or for personal projects but need to continue their work on PCs or Macs. The Pi edition of Pixel and the version adapted for larger machines utilise exactly the same productivity software and programming tools, in exactly the same desktop environment, he wrote. There is no learning curve, and no need to adjust... schoolwork to operate on two subtly different operating systems, he stated. Additionally, he mentioned that creating such a version of Pixel kept the Raspberry Pi Foundation honest as it would assist the organisation's coders in identifying which parts of the user interface required improvement. Mr Upton noted that because the core software underlying Pixel was based on a relatively old computer architecture, it should function on vintage machines. He cautioned that the software was still experimental and might contain bugs or other minor issues that could prevent it from running well on some machines. Pixel was initially released in September this year and revamped the main graphical interface users see and use when working with their Pi. It is based on a version of the open-source Linux software known as Debian. The desktop version lacks two programs—Minecraft and Mathematica—because the Pi organisation has not licensed those applications on any machines other than its own. In April last year, the Raspberry Pi officially became the most popular British computer ever made. More than 10 million units have now been sold. The computer was first released in 2012 and is widely used as an educational tool for programming.

text: Doctor Who's Peter Capaldi has passed on his sonic screwdriver to Jodie Whittaker who becomes the 13th doctor and first woman to take on the role of television's famous Time Lord. These are external links and will open in a new window. She follows a distinguished line-up of male thespian talent that dates back to the sci-fi favourite's first episode in 1963. William Hartnell was the inaugural actor to portray the Doctor, appearing in the BBC show from 1963 to 1966. Hartnell, who passed away in 1975, had previously featured in TV's The Army Game and Carry On Sergeant, the first Carry On film, in 1958. When ill health compelled Hartnell to vacate the role, the Doctor regenerated for the first time into Patrick Troughton. Memorably scruffy and eccentric, Troughton spent three years traversing time and space before stepping down in 1969. When the raffish Jon Pertwee became the third Doctor, he also became the first to be seen on television in colour. His tenure, from 1970 to 1974, saw the Time Lord exiled to Earth and collaborating with Unit, also known as the United Nations Intelligence Taskforce. Pertwee's time with the show also introduced the first of the popular ensemble stories where previous Doctors appear alongside the current one. Broadcast over December 1972 and January 1973, The Three Doctors saw him joined by Patrick Troughton and William Hartnell in what would be the latter's final acting engagement. When Pertwee departed in 1974, Tom Baker took over and would become the longest-serving Doctor to date. Deep-voiced, curly-haired, and eternally long of scarf, his seven years in the Tardis earned him legions of fans who were delighted anew in 2013 when he appeared at the end of a 50th-anniversary special. When Baker finally stepped down from the role in 1981, his shoes were filled by the fresh-faced Peter Davison. The boyish actor spent three years as the Fifth Doctor before departing at the end of the show's 21st series. Davison's tenure coincided with Doctor Who's 20th anniversary, celebrated by a feature-length special that saw him joined by Jon Pertwee and Patrick Troughton. The First Doctor also made an appearance, with Richard Hurndall standing in for the late William Hartnell. Tom Baker opted not to return for The Five Doctors, which covered his absence by incorporating material from one of the actor's unbroadcast adventures. Similar subterfuge was required for this 1983 photo shoot, which saw Hurndall, Davison, Pertwee, and Troughton joined by an unconvincing Baker mannequin. Davison's departure opened the door for another Baker to take control of the Doctor's time-travelling police box in 1984. Colin Baker (no relation to Tom) spent less than three years in the role, with his appearances further limited by an 18-month production hiatus. Though Baker had limited time to enjoy the Tardis, he did get the chance to meet one of his predecessors when Patrick Troughton returned for the third time in 1985. The Two Doctors marked Troughton's final reprise of his signature role. Some years later, his sons David and Michael would both make Doctor Who appearances. Scottish actor Sylvester McCoy took over from Colin Baker in 1987 and played the Doctor until the show's cancellation in 1989. Michael Grade, the controller of BBC One at the time, was no fan of the programme, which appeared increasingly threadbare and cheap-looking compared to glossier cinema fare. Some feel, though, that this period in the show's evolution has been harshly judged. An attempt was made to revive Doctor Who in 1996 with a TV film that saw McCoy regenerate into Paul McGann on American soil. It was hoped the special would spawn a TV series, but it never materialised, making McGann's tenure the shortest of all the Doctors. In 2005, Doctor Who regenerated into the ambitious, well-financed property it is today. It also introduced a new Doctor in the form of Christopher Eccleston. To the disappointment of many, the Salford-born actor chose to make only one series of the rebooted show. His departure was confirmed only days after his debut episode was broadcast. Eccleston's exit saw David Tennant join the show, with his first full episode, The Christmas Invasion, shown on BBC One on Christmas Day 2005. Tennant's amiable style and enthusiasm made him a popular choice for the role, which he finally relinquished on the first day of 2010. The spate of junior Doctors continued with the casting of Matt Smith, who was just 27 when he made his debut as the Time Lord's 11th incarnation. His four years in the role, which coincided with Doctor Who's 50th anniversary, saw the programme both maintain and bolster its renewed popularity. Doctor Who's 50th anniversary in 2013 was marked by The Day of the Doctor, a feature-length special in which Matt Smith's Time Lord was joined by David Tennant's version of the character. The Day of the Doctor also introduced a previously unknown incarnation of the Doctor, known as The War Doctor, played by Sir John Hurt. Peter Capaldi was no stranger to the Doctor Who universe when he was cast as the Doctor in 2013. A lifelong fan of the show, he appeared in an episode of the programme in 2008 and also had a role in its spin-off Torchwood. His hawkish features brought a new intensity and maturity to the Tardis from the moment his first full episode was broadcast in August 2014. Capaldi's most recent adventure saw him briefly joined by the original Doctor, played on this occasion by David Bradley. Bradley will return in this year's Doctor Who Christmas special. Bradley's appearance was a pleasing one for Whovians after his role as William Hartnell in An Adventure in Space and Time, a 2013 dramatisation of the show's early years. Jodie Whittaker has been named as the 13th Doctor and the first-ever woman to play the role. She will make her debut on the sci-fi show this Christmas when Capaldi regenerates. text: Celtic reached an important milestone by beating Aberdeen in the League Cup final, says manager Brendan Rodgers. Media playback is not supported on this device. The 3-0 victory, courtesy of goals from Tom Rogic, James Forrest, and Moussa Dembele, secured Celtic's 100th major trophy and marked Rodgers' first as manager. The Northern Irishman stated his players had been really impressive, but they must now build on their success. It's a winning club; that's what the history of this club has been based on, said the former Liverpool manager. It marks a milestone, the century of trophies, and we've got to start off the next century of trophies. That will be important for us and the club. Celtic, unbeaten domestically this season, dominated most of the game, scoring twice in the first half through Rogic and Forrest. Aberdeen rallied just after the interval, but their challenge ended when Anthony O'Connor conceded a penalty that Dembele converted. It's a great night for the Celtic supporters to celebrate, and we push for the next one, said Rodgers. It's six months and a week since I came in, and we talked about what we wanted to achieve and how we wanted to do it, and we're well on our way to that. We're trying to improve standards on and off the field. We're shaping up the team to play in a certain style, and that's going very well. There are things we'll analyse, what can we do better, how can we improve. Ultimately, the goal was to win the cup, and thankfully we've won it. Rather than dwelling on his first trophy, Rodgers focused instead on the efforts of his players. He praised the performance and, in particular, the command of Scott Brown in midfield. I've a huge job to do here in terms of building on it and sustaining it, he said. It's a great achievement. For the players, it's something to show for the great work they've been doing. It's great for the confidence, and it sets us up for the rest of the season. If I'm to say anything on getting my own first trophy as Celtic manager, having Scott as the captain is a huge honour. He really dominated the game, and collectively he pulls the team together on the field. Counterpart Derek McInnes urged his Aberdeen players to use the disappointment of the defeat as motivation to reach another cup final this season. He felt some in his side did not perform to their full potential and insists that, although Celtic will grow stronger, they can still be defeated in a one-off match. There's a lot of pain and not feeling good about ourselves, McInnes said. We were beaten by a better team. The difference is that, when we take them on in a cup final, we need everyone to be at their maximum. It's important we try to pick ourselves up. We're a team that can get to another final this season. This isn't an end-of-season defeat. There's so much more to come this season. We expect more of ourselves, and people maybe expect more of us. It's important that we stick together and recognise there's plenty to play for. I don't mind putting ourselves up there to be shot down. We were huge underdogs, but I still expected us to win, and I still thought we would win the game.

In the second half, Aberdeen pressed hard but their momentum was cut short when Anthony O’Connor conceded a penalty, which Dembele put away. “It’s a great night for the Celtic supporters to celebrate and we look forward to the next game,” said Rodgers. “I’ve been here six months and a week now, and we’ve been talking about what we want to achieve and how, and we’re well on our way. The captaincy is a great honour. It’s a reward for the excellent work the players have done. It’s a good sign of confidence, and the rest of the season is within our sights. The game was completely dominated by the performance of the Celtic goalkeeper, the evergreen, John Ramsay, who was a real focal point for the team. The opposition coach, Derek MacInnes, told his players to take the defeat as a spur to another cup final this season. It is important that we stick together and recognize that we have a lot to play for. We expect more from ourselves and maybe others expect more from us. “I am not afraid to go up and be shot down.

text: A team of UK scientists hopes to shed light on the mysteries of bleeding canker, a disease that is threatening the nation's horse chestnut trees. The researchers have sequenced the genome of a strain of bacterium responsible for the virulent infection. A 2007 survey indicated that bleeding canker had spread rapidly, with nearly half of the two million horse chestnuts exhibiting symptoms of the disease. The findings have been published in the journal PLoS One. A visible symptom of the disease is a lesion on the bark, which exudes a resin onto the trunk or occasionally the branches. The bark beneath the canker is killed, and if cankers encircle the trunk, the horse chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum) will die as it severs the food supply. The researchers sequenced the genome of the bacterium Pseudomonas syringae pathovar aesuli (Pae) from three samples collected from different locations within the UK. They compared them with samples from the only other recorded case, taken from an Indian horse chestnut in India in the 1960s. What we found was that the three British samples were all identical, said co-author Dr David Studholme, currently at the University of Exeter but who was based at The Sainsbury Laboratory, Norwich, during the study. This means that they all probably descended from a single introduction, he told BBC News. However, he added that more work was needed before they could determine whether or not the bacterium originated from India, where the pathovar (a strain of bacterium that only affects certain plants, in this case horse chestnuts) was originally recorded. The Indian [specimen] has only ever been known to cause a leaf spot; there is no evidence of it causing cankers. Dr Studholme's fellow co-author was Sarah Green, a plant pathologist at Forest Research, the research wing of the UK Forestry Commission. She stated that Pae was very mobile, very aggressive and that it definitely required study. There were some interesting genes that we found that may well be helping it to be so aggressive, she explained. It affects the woody part of the trees, whereas other bacterial diseases attack the soft tissues (such as leaves). However, she added that much more work was needed before it would be possible to understand how the bacterial strain interacted with the trees and how it was spread. Since Pae was first recorded in 2002, it has become prevalent throughout the UK, and more than 70% of horse chestnuts in some areas are showing symptoms of infection. Roddie Burgess, head of plant health at the Forestry Commission, said he hoped the research would help develop a strategy to tackle the problem. It always takes you by surprise when you investigate a previously unknown disease and find out that almost half of your tree population may already be infected, he told BBC News. He said that a few thousand trees were known to have been cut down by local authorities amid fears that infected trees would pose a risk to the public. Quite a hefty number were felled before we realised that the trees sometimes go into remission and maybe recover. Our advice for now is not to go jumping in with a chainsaw. He added that further research was underway to determine if the disease had the potential to kill the trees in ways other than cutting off the supply of nutrients. These are the sorts of things we need to understand before we even begin to think about how best to manage infected trees.

text: Head teachers warning that they face financial meltdown are furious that the government has been pledging funds to create grammar schools in England. It was disclosed on Wednesday that ministers had invited grammar school leaders to apply for £150 million over three years for new selective school places. School leaders have also demanded the return of £384 million, initially promised to convert schools into academies. The Department for Education states that school funding is at record levels. School leaders have expressed anger that while they have been warning about a lack of basic funding, the government has been able to promise hundreds of millions for projects such as expanding grammars and converting schools to academy status. Head teachers in West Sussex have been campaigning against what they claim are serious budget shortfalls. They have written to local MPs to express their incredulity at the funding that appears to be available for grammars. They are also calling on political leaders to account for their spending decisions. The Grammar School Heads' Association had a private meeting with the education secretary and schools minister in which they discussed plans to expand selective places and to create new grammar schools for 2020. The notes of the meeting, published by the grammar heads, include details of how to contact the department for £50 million per year for new selective places. The heads in West Sussex have called for emergency funding of £20 million and have warned that without this schools might have to cut hours, increase class sizes or stop teaching some subjects. They have told MPs that throughout our campaign school leaders have sought to be 'relentlessly reasonable'; now we are simply furious. They describe local schools as scrabbling around for any form of cash like a desperate person checking down the side of their sofa for the odd pound coin or two. Earlier this week, finance directors and school business managers from Barnet wrote to the Department for Education warning of an impending financial crisis. They called on the government to return the £384 million promised to fund a plan to turn all of England's schools into academies. When that was overturned by a backbench rebellion, it was revealed that the funding was taken back by the Treasury. School leaders have argued that a redistribution of how schools are funded, in a new funding formula, could avoid having any losers if this money, once announced for schools, could be returned. Grammar school head teachers have also been complaining about funding shortages - and have warned that they might have to start asking parents for payments. The National Union of Teachers has attacked the government for pledging funds for new grammar places when schools are already crying out for sufficient funding. The union's general secretary Kevin Courtney accused the education secretary of fiddling around with secret plans for a return to a two-tier education system which would be of no benefit to 90% of children. A Department for Education spokeswoman said schools in West Sussex would gain from changes in the funding formula - with an extra £145 per pupil per year. We have protected the core schools budget in real terms since 2010, with school funding at its highest level on record at more than £40 billion in 2016-17, said the DFE spokeswoman.

The Yorkshireman secured triathlon gold at Rio 2016, successfully defending his title from London 2012. There's a possibility I may never attend an Olympic Games again, but to say I'll never do it is impossible, he stated. The Olympic Games are simply fantastic, and I'd certainly love to be there, but the course in Tokyo will significantly influence whether I believe I can go there and win. It will involve sitting down at the end of 2018 and considering it—am I enjoying the long-distance events? Am I still competitive enough to win a medal in Tokyo? Brownlee will defend his World Series title in Leeds on 11 June, but this is his only confirmed race this season, while his brother and Rio silver medallist Jonny will begin his campaign at the second race on the Gold Coast on 8 April. For the remainder of the year, Alistair Brownlee will combine standard Olympic-length events—1.5km swim, 40km cycling, and 10km running—with half Ironman distance competitions, also known as Ironman 70.3, referring to the total miles covered. He mentioned that the Ironman 70.3 World Championship in September is an obvious target as he progresses towards the full Ironman distance, which he says has always been on his bucket list. Ironman must be one of those events you always desire to do—it's akin to the London or Boston marathon of triathlon, he remarked. With Gomez, 33, returning from that injury, Brownlee anticipates the Spaniard will contend for the World Series title, alongside compatriot and current champion Mario Mola, 27. Alistair Brownlee admits he might have been bored returning to World Series racing, having experienced the same kind of racing against essentially the same individuals for the past 10 years. However, he states that he is driven by his new objectives, which could include competing in 10,000m running races and the marathon. I now have an opportunity to explore these other pursuits without jeopardising my chances if I decide to compete in four years in Tokyo, he said. I contemplated many things after Rio. The other obvious pursuit is cycling and attempting to make a wholehearted transition to being a professional cyclist, but although that's feasible, I'm very aware that in that field and in running, I can be good and reach a level where I could be professional, but never to a level where I can win titles. Subsequently: After three months of deliberations behind the closed doors of 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue, the president decisively aligned himself with those near the exits. Withdrawing from the Paris agreement, signed by nearly 200 countries, will take a few years but this is unmistakably a promise fulfilled. Previously: One of Mr Trump's signature rally pledges was to repeal and replace Obamacare—his predecessor's effort to extend healthcare to the estimated 15% of the country who are uninsured. It is widely disliked by Republicans, who argue the law imposes excessive costs on businesses, with many labelling it a job killer and criticising the reforms—officially the Affordable Care Act—as an unwarranted intrusion into the affairs of private businesses and individuals. Then the House Republicans proposed a plan, which the president fully supported, but it was criticised by doctors' groups, hospitals, and other sectors of the medical industry. The Democrats opposed it and several factions of the Republican party were uneasy. It was passed by the House of Representatives but the Senate has indicated it will rewrite the bill entirely. text: Five disabled social housing tenants have lost their Court of Appeal bid to have benefit cuts for those deemed to have spare bedrooms ruled unlawful. Judges stated that the court could not intervene in the government's controversial housing benefit changes, which critics have labelled a bedroom tax. Lawyers for the group contended that the regulations in England, Wales, and Scotland did not address the accommodation needs of disabled individuals. They expressed their intention to continue their legal battle. The court also ruled against two lone parents who argued that the government's cap on total benefits paid to families breached human rights laws and common law due to its effect on vulnerable families. Lord Dyson, Master of the Rolls, remarked that the legal challenges pertained to two of the government's most controversial measures concerning state benefits. He stated that the court could only intervene if the measures were manifestly without reasonable foundation, and he concluded that this stringent test was not met, resulting in the failure of both challenges. However, Ugo Hayter, representing two individuals contesting the changes, expressed confusion over the Court of Appeal's decision and considered taking the case to the Supreme Court. The court acknowledged that our clients and thousands of disabled people across the UK required accommodation not provided by the new housing benefit rules, yet decided that disabled tenants should not have their housing needs met on an equal basis to their able-bodied counterparts, solely because they are disabled, said Jayson Carmichael, Appellant. I hope we can appeal it in the Supreme Court. It must be the worst High Court decision ever made, and I am very angry about it. We will continue to fight for justice, as we do not truly have a spare bedroom due to my wife's severe disabilities, and asserting that disabled people are justifiably discriminated against cannot be right for Britain in 2014. We face numerous medical challenges; I am a 24/7 carer and provide overnight care for her, and this case has left me exhausted. We have received some discretionary housing payments but have been promised no more for this year, so we may fall behind on our rent like other disabled tenants now. We hope to stay. We do not have much space as it is; with medical equipment, there is not much room in a two-bedroom housing association flat. Instead, disabled tenants are forced to rely on short-term and discretionary payments. Anne McMurdie, whose firm represents three of the appellants, stated: Disabled tenants are not requesting extra funds; they are seeking housing benefit at a level that meets their needs - for the same rights as others. Discretionary payments are not the solution. Jayson Carmichael, from Southport, Merseyside, one of the appellants, said he was devastated by the ruling. He commented: It's ludicrous because human rights laws have been enforced by tribunal judges nationwide. I believe we are being made an example of due to our high profile in this group case. Richard Kramer, deputy chief executive of the national deaf-blind charity Sense, expressed being extremely disappointed with the outcome. Although this decision concerns the cases of five individuals, the policy's impact has been devastating for many disabled people, he stated. National Housing Federation head of policy Kevin Williamson remarked that the court action demonstrated how desperate people had become. He said: Disabled people across the country are being forced to cut back on food and heating to pay the bedroom tax. Richard Hawkes, chief executive of disability charity Scope, described the ruling as a setback for the campaigners and a major blow for the 400,000 disabled people affected by this policy. The Department for Work and Pensions, a defendant in both cases, welcomed the rulings. Reform of housing benefit in the social sector is essential to ensure the benefit's long-term sustainability. However, we have ensured extra discretionary housing support is available for vulnerable people, a spokesman stated. Referring to the benefit cap, the spokesman added: We are pleased that the courts have ruled again that the benefit cap complies with the European Convention on Human Rights. The benefit cap sets a fair limit to what people can expect from the welfare system - so that claimants cannot receive more than £500 a week, the average household earnings. Since April last year, individuals deemed to have one spare bedroom have had their housing benefit reduced by 14%, while those with two or more spare bedrooms have seen reductions of 25%. The challenge to the change initially involved 10 families, but five cases concerning disabled children are no longer pursued due to their exemption from the benefit cut. The group includes wheelchair user Richard Rourke, 46, from Bakestone Moor, Derbyshire, who claims he needs an additional bedroom to store mobility equipment. Among others involved in the case is Mr Carmichael's wife, Charlotte, who asserts that her spina bifida prevents her from sharing a bedroom with her husband, who is also her full-time carer.

text: Argentina's economy minister Axel Kicillof has returned to the negotiating table in a last-ditch attempt to prevent the country defaulting on its bonds. Mr Kicillof's discussions with hold-out investors concluded late on Tuesday night in New York without reaching an agreement. They are demanding a full payment of $1.3 billion (£766 million) on the bonds they possess. A US judge has ruled that the hold-outs must be paid by Wednesday night if no deal is reached. However, thousands of miles away in Buenos Aires, many remain sceptical about the possibility of any agreement. The government's rhetoric has been unequivocal. The hold-outs are US hedge funds that purchased debt at low prices during Argentina's most challenging times and never consented to restructuring. President Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner refers to them as vultures, accusing them of exploiting Argentina's debt issues for substantial profit. The situation is exacerbated by the fact that if the hold-outs succeed, other bondholders who agreed to reductions of up to 70% in their claims may also demand full repayment. When asked about their views on Argentina's debt troubles, most people admit it is too complex for them to comprehend. However, the two words they recognise are fondos buitres - vulture funds in Spanish. Despite the government's defiant tone, many people appear resigned. Argentina has defaulted before, and it may do so again. I met Carina Etchegaray, a mother of two children aged 14 and 16. When Argentina last defaulted at the end of 2001, she lost significant savings. She had intended to purchase a house for her young family. But at the end of 2001, the government implemented what was known as the corralito. It literally means a small enclosure in Spanish, but refers to when the government partially froze bank accounts, preventing people from withdrawing money. When we finally had the money, due to devaluation, we could only buy a car for the same amount we had for a house, she says. Yet she remains practical. We live with this shadow of crisis. You have to continue with your life because you have children and have to work. You have to adapt - in this country, it's the way of life. And that is what entrepreneur Federico Dumas is also doing - but not in the manner Argentina would prefer. He owns a software company but says he is not investing as he would like to. I'm afraid of everything, and my customers are not willing to invest, so that will affect my business, he says, adding that he hopes Argentina's issues will be resolved reasonably. But if the country defaults, I'm very afraid of what's going to happen to my business and my employees. Default or not, when I met Guillermo Nielsen, the man who led the negotiations when the country was restructuring its debts in 2005, he stated that what is happening in Argentina is something he had never anticipated. I never imagined this - not in my wildest dreams, he says. People, although they were unsatisfied and the negotiations were very tough, knew that Argentina was not able to pay, so that's a very big difference. Today, Argentina has the money - back then, we didn't have the money. In my own perception, I think the upcoming negotiations are going to be much tougher than the ones we had to go through. His concern is that if the country defaults, it could trigger what is known as an acceleration clause. It would mean creditors could demand Argentina repay bonds within a much shorter timeframe than previously agreed. That, he says, is a real concern. But all this remains speculative. With just a few hours remaining, no decisions have been made, and it is all still talk. The details of what has been discussed remain unclear. As people here say, the Argentine way of doing things will mean talks until the eleventh hour. The vultures will continue to circle until then.

text: Military landing craft have been suggested as a possible solution to a breakdown of Lochaber's Corran Ferry. These are external links and will open in a new window. A report to Highland councillors following an issue affecting the ferry last month indicated that seeking assistance from the Royal Navy has been proposed. However, council officers stated that due to the number of cars transported, more than one landing craft would be necessary. Additionally, the ferry's slipways are unsuitable for military craft. Last month, the Corran Ferry, operated by Highland Council on Loch Linnhe in Lochaber, was non-operational for several days due to a breakdown. The vessel had drifted and collided with rocks near a slipway. The usual backup ferry, the Maid of Glencoul, was unavailable as it was undergoing a refit. The Corran Ferry was able to resume service following repairs and an inspection. The council officers' report on the incident noted it cost the local authority £39,000 due to lost income and the expenses of repairs and inspection, which involved a remotely operated vehicle. The report to Tuesday's Lochaber Committee also commended the meticulous and diligent efforts of the ferry's staff in maintaining a low incidence of breakdowns. Highland Council faced criticism at the time for suspending the service. There were allegations of insufficient information on the service's status and contingency plans. At the time, Highland Council stated it had done everything possible to restore the service and had provided information on its website and Twitter. It also requested Traffic Scotland to alert people to the ferry issues with messages on its electronic signs on the A82 trunk road. However, road works and warnings of heavy rain had to take precedence. text: Housing is too expensive for would-be buyers to take advantage of the government's Help to Buy Isa (HTB Isa), savers have told the BBC. A BBC investigation discovered that in many regions, the average price of a starter home surpasses the maximum purchase cap allowed under the scheme. Here we present your stories. Claire Etheridge, from Greenwich, south-east London, works in the capital but cannot afford to purchase a home there. The 28-year-old solicitor believes the £250,000 cap should be increased for areas surrounding London. I am looking to buy in St Albans and commute in, she stated. However, this is outside of London, and therefore I will not be able to use what I have been saving in the Isa, as the properties I am considering are just over the £250,000 cap for outside London. It's a great scheme for outside London, but I really think the surrounding areas of London, such as Kent or Hertfordshire, should have some allowance for the fact that prices are still high and therefore the £250,000 cap does not help. Liane Reilly, from Hemel Hempstead in Hertfordshire, said she and her partner did not have enough money left to save after paying bills. The 30-year-old remarked: We are renting a one-bedroom flat at £900 per month. This consumes almost one of our salaries, and we will never be able to save enough to afford to buy. Our salaries go on bills and rent. The HTB Isa is the latest component of the overall Help to Buy scheme, where the government also provides equity loans to cover up to 20% of the cost of a newly built home. Borrowers are not charged fees on the loan for the first five years. Management consultant Matthew Taylor, aged 27, and his wife Anne, a research client manager, utilised the loan scheme to purchase a house in Dartford, Kent. Help to Buy genuinely works, he commented. Perhaps people need to consider the practical side of why this scheme was implemented. Find out about your area by tapping here. I'd love to live in central London in a house with a garden. Living and working in London involves a compromise; generally, you choose the perfect location with a compromise on the property or a great property with a compromise on the location. Catharina, who did not wish to disclose her surname, told BBC News she feared house prices would rise too quickly for her savings to make a difference. I am using the Help to Buy Isa but would struggle to purchase even a small one-bedroom flat with those savings in London. Even if properties were currently available within the cap, historical data suggests that by the time I fill up my Help to Buy Isa, they wouldn't be.

text: William Hague is standing down as an MP after an illustrious 25 year career in the House of Commons. These are external links and will open in a new window. Reflecting on his political career, in an interview with the BBC's Norman Smith, the former Foreign Secretary and Conservative Party leader expressed few regrets, aside from losing the 2001 general election. I'm not one for having a lot of regrets, but I do regret that we didn't get things back together again faster in the Conservative Party, he stated. However, Mr Hague is not alone in seeking a new role, away from the renowned green benches, following the general election on 7 May. A total of 86 MPs have declared their intention to stand down, according to BBC Analysis and Research. It might seem like a significant number, out of 650 MPs, but it falls short of the total in 2010, when 149 MPs departed in the largest Commons clear-out in history, following the expenses scandal. A total of 17 former cabinet ministers - 12 Labour and five Conservative - are stepping down at this election. The departure of Mr Hague, Sir George Young, and Stephen Dorrell reduces the number of John Major cabinet survivors to three: Ken Clarke, Peter Lilley (both of whom also served under Margaret Thatcher), and John Redwood. Three female Conservative MPs, all elected in 2010, have announced their retirement. This represents 6% of female Tory MPs. In total, seven of the 2010 Tory intake will stand down after a single term. High-profile Tory retirees include former Health Secretary Andrew Lansley, Sir George Young, and Sir Peter Tapsell, the Father of the House, first elected to the Commons in 1959. He has accumulated 54 years on the green benches, with a two-year break from the Commons in the mid-1960s, making him one of the longest-serving MPs in British history. Former Foreign Secretary Sir Malcolm Rifkind, who now sits as an independent after having the Tory whip withdrawn, is also standing down. The retirements on the Labour side leave only three members of Tony Blair's first cabinet - Nick Brown, Margaret Beckett, and Harriet Harman - in the Commons, assuming they retain their seats. High-profile Labour retirees include former Prime Minister Gordon Brown and ex-cabinet ministers Alistair Darling, David Blunkett, and Dame Tessa Jowell. text: The Irish government arranged for a doctor to visit Ibrahim Halawa in jail in Egypt following concerns about the health of the 21-year-old Dubliner. These are external links and will open in a new window. He has conducted a series of hunger strikes in protest against being imprisoned without trial for over three years. Last month, his lawyer stated he was so weak that prison staff used a wheelchair to transport him to family visits. On the doctor's advice, the Irish government urged Egypt to release him for further medical examinations. Before the visit, Taoiseach [Irish Prime Minister] Enda Kenny expressed he was disturbed by reports that Mr Halawa was using a wheelchair and wanted his health assessed from an Irish medical point of view. In a statement on Monday, Irish Minister for Foreign Affairs, Charlie Flanagan, confirmed that the prison assessment occurred last week, at his government's request. It has long been the government's stated desire to see Mr Halawa returned to Ireland, and we have made direct appeals to the Egyptian government on several occasions, Mr Flanagan added. He stated that after receiving the doctor's report, Mr Kenny wrote to the Egyptian president, requesting Mr Halawa's release to enable further tests. The foreign minister added that he discussed the case with the Secretary General of the League of Arab States, Abou El Gheit, on Monday. I also again raised the case with the EU's High Representative, Vice President Federica Mogherini, who has taken a personal interest in the case, Mr Flanagan added. He said the case was continuing to receive unprecedented attention and resources in Dublin and in Cairo. However, the Halawa family has stated that the Irish government must do more and have previously urged Mr Kenny to initiate international legal action against the Egyptian government. Mr Halawa is the son of the most senior Muslim cleric in the Republic of Ireland. He was 17 when he was arrested with three of his sisters during a siege at the Al-Fath mosque in Cairo in 2013. The women were released after three months, but their younger brother remained in jail, and his court case has been adjourned 20 times. For several years, Mr Halawa was informed he would face the death penalty if convicted at a mass trial. However, in January, the Egyptian president told a delegation of Irish politicians that he would offer a pardon to Mr Halawa once his trial concludes. The Egyptian parliament has previously opposed calls from the Irish parliament to release the Dubliner, stating the request would interfere in the affairs of the Egyptian judiciary.

text: A County Down couple, who foster five boys including two sets of siblings with a range of complex needs, have been named Northern Ireland's Foster Carers of the Year. Glen and Regina Mahon, who have been fostering for 15 years, were commended for their steadfastness, generosity and big-heartedness. The couple expressed their astonishment upon being announced as winners. Regina informed the BBC they were ecstatic. We were gobsmacked—I couldn't believe it when they announced our names. After hearing the other personal stories, we both felt many other carers deserved to win. Despite having five boys aged between seven and 17, their home remains an oasis of calm. The kitchen serves as the heart of the home, with football kits and boots visible in every corner. Regina attributes their success to a good routine. The boys all have chores. One takes the bin out in the morning, another sets the table—we have chores. That's what makes us work. The children arrived at the Mahons' home in Ballykinler when they were vulnerable and in desperate need of love and support. Among them, they face various health issues, including attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and epilepsy. The youngest boy is living with a hypoplastic heart. Despite being strangers, a bond developed not only between the adults and the children but also among the children themselves—all from three different families. I met with the Mahons following a weekend of celebrations with the children. In their kitchen, Regina expressed their gratitude. Every one of them is a character. There is no doubt about it, she stated. These are children who are traumatised for one reason or another, and they seek reassurance, compassion, patience, and someone to listen to them. Each one has complex needs—it is tough. But, you wouldn't be without them. So why did the Mahons stand out among the other finalists? One particular story is noteworthy. When one of the children was in Birmingham for major heart surgery, lasting 16 weeks, Glen took leave from work to be with him. Why did I do it? How could I not, he explained. If it was one of your own, you'd be there with them. I didn't mind at all. I had to be at his bedside 24 hours a day, before his operation and then in intensive care. All in all, 16 weeks. It was harder on him as he took longer to recover. So why open your home and lives to other people's children? You do it because these children need love and care. They need a family, Glen stated. They arrive cowering at the door. Then they come round and feel part of the natural environment. They call you mum and dad. It brings a lump to your throat. It feels good. Over 2,150 children reside with more than 2,000 foster families across Northern Ireland. While that may seem impressive, the Fostering Network estimates that at least 170 new foster families are required annually to meet demand. There is a particular need for foster carers for teenagers, disabled children, and sibling groups. Foster carers can provide children with a home for as long as they need it, said Kathleen Toner, director of the Fostering Network. The survey results clearly indicate that children and young people want and need stability. If you have room in your heart, and in your home, then 2016 could be the year you start to make a positive difference to a child—a positive difference that can last a lifetime. There has been a 14% increase in the past four years in the number of young people requiring foster care. According to Kathleen Toner, the increase is due to several reasons. People are more aware of child protection issues. text: The board of Rangers discussed putting the club into administration months before it was bought by businessman Craig Whyte. These are external links and will open in a new window. According to former financial director Donald McIntyre, the magnitude of the club's financial liabilities meant it would have been remiss not to proceed. Mr Whyte is accused of fraudulently acquiring Rangers. The 46-year-old denies two charges related to the purchase—one of fraud and another under the Companies Act. Speaking from the witness box, where he was giving evidence for a second day, Mr McIntyre discussed the financial obligations faced by Rangers in the months leading up to the club's sale to Mr Whyte in May 2011. He stated Rangers faced a potential bill from HMRC of about £50 million, which had been termed the Big Tax Case. Defence QC Donald Findlay referred to the debt as a nuclear missile targeting Rangers. He described it as like an exocet, nothing could be done to stop it. Mr McIntyre said Rangers board members had hoped to contest the amount owed and that counsel at the time had suggested they had a very good chance in the case. However, Mr Findlay suggested to the witness that the tax bill was a potentially terminal event for the club. The advocate inquired when Mr McIntyre first knew the board was discussing the possibility of administration for Rangers. Mr McIntyre said he could not be specific of a date but that the subject would have cropped up in 2010. The court proceeded to hear about a meeting of Rangers directors in March 2011. They discussed the money owed to HMRC and the possible impact on the club. Mr Findlay suggested to Mr McIntyre: Rangers could not contemplate paying up that size of debt? Mr McIntyre concurred. Later, the jury was informed that Rangers did enter administration much later but that it was nothing to do with the Big Tax Case. The trial also heard the claim that Rangers' former owner Sir David Murray, who purchased the club in 1988, had described Mr Whyte's bid for the club as the only show in town. Mr Findlay asked Mr McIntyre: Did it become abundantly clear that Murray would do virtually anything to secure the deal with Mr Whyte? Mr McIntyre replied: I would not put it like that. I don't think a deal would have been done under any circumstance. The defence advocate continued: A deal was done under any circumstance...Rangers was bought for a pound. Mr McIntyre added: With commitments and obligations. Mr Whyte is accused of pretending to former Rangers owner Sir David Murray, and others, that funds were available to make all required payments to acquire a controlling and majority stake in the club. The funds included clearing the £18 million bank debt, £2.8 million for the small tax case liability, a £1.7 million health-and-safety liability, and £5 million for the playing squad. The Crown alleges Mr Whyte had only £4 million available from two sources at the time but took out the £24 million loan from Ticketus which was held subject to an agreement or agreements being entered into between the club and Ticketus after said acquisition. The second charge under the Companies Act concerns the £18 million payment between Mr Whyte's Wavetower company and Rangers to clear a bank debt. The trial before eight men and seven women continues.

text: Huddersfield Giants climbed off the bottom of the Super League table to leave Hull Kingston Rovers as the only winless side in the top flight. The Giants led 12-0 at half-time after tries from on-loan debutant full-back Jordan Tansey and Michael Lawrence. Rovers then reduced the deficit with Thomas Minns' converted try. However, Aaron Murphy's try reinstated the 12-point lead, and the Giants extended their advantage through Jermaine McGillvary, Larne Patrick, and Ukuma Ta'ai. Danny Brough, who troubled the visitors with his tactical kicking, successfully landed all six conversions, including one after England winger McGillvary's 100th Super League try, as well as a penalty, achieving an individual 14-point total. Huddersfield had lost their first four matches in Super League, but this victory allowed them to surpass Rovers, who have secured only one point from their first six games, thanks to last month's draw with Castleford. In his first match as interim head coach until the season's end, former Rovers captain James Webster's team was outplayed throughout, despite being bolstered by the return from injury of former Huddersfield forwards Shaun Lunt and Graeme Horne, while James Green and John Boudebza returned from suspension. However, captain Terry Campese lasted only 42 minutes before leaving with a hamstring injury on his comeback from a nine-month absence following knee reconstruction. Giants coach Paul Anderson confirmed that prop Daniel Smith will not play again this season after undergoing foot surgery but expects fellow front-rower Craig Huby to be the next player to return from injury at Easter. Huddersfield coach Paul Anderson stated: Winning is definitely better than losing. It does relieve some pressure, the boys are happy in there. There was no real sense of panic but we can't rest on that. We have an opportunity to start knocking some points off. For 40 to 50 minutes you could tell both teams were a little bit nervous but we settled the quicker and created a lot of opportunities. We stayed patient and came up with some good sets. We just need to get people back on the field and training continuously. We've not lost anybody else today which is a positive. All the people who came back grew into the game and Jordan Tansey had an impact and is only going to get better as he gets to know our structures. Hull KR interim coach James Webster told BBC Radio Humberside: We weren't good enough with the ball at the start. We were second best at the ruck and they ran a bit harder than us. We did a really good job to stay within 12 points at half-time. We seemed to rectify a few of the things we spoke about at half-time but the fatigue factor really hurt us towards the end. It's going to be hard work but we're a confident club and we think we can turn it around. When Terry Campese was on the ground with his hand up in the air, you think 'has he done his knee?' but it's the hamstring in his other leg. While we're obviously disappointed, it's good that it's not his knee. Huddersfield: Tansey; McGillvary, Cudjoe, Connor, Murphy; Brough, K Wood; Crabtree, Hinchcliffe, Rapira, Wardle, Lawrence, Ta'ai. Replacements: Patrick, J Johnson, Leeming, Roberts. Hull KR: Cockayne; Shaw, Thornley, Minns, Sio; Blair, Marsh; Walker, Lunt, Tilse, Clarkson, Horne, Allgood. Replacements: Green, Greenwood, Campese, Boudebza. Referee: Robert Hicks.

text: The search for two climbers missing on Ben Nevis has been suspended because conditions were too dangerous. Tim Newton, aged 27, and Rachel Slater, aged 24, from Bradford, had been climbing the mountain over the weekend. The alarm was raised when they were reported overdue from their expedition on Monday. Lochaber Mountain Rescue Team stated that 36 individuals were involved in searches on Tuesday, with two members caught in an avalanche. It is believed the couple had been camping in a green tent behind the Charles Inglis Clark (CIC) memorial hut on the mountain's north side. A vehicle belonging to Ms Slater has also been recovered. Rescuers described the conditions as challenging, with winds gusting up to 80/90 mph. A statement on the Lochaber MRT Facebook page said: After five hours of searching, it was decided that conditions were too dangerous to continue the search, which was focused on Coire na Ciste and South Trident Buttress area following a possible sighting of two people matching their description climbing in this area early Sunday afternoon. It added: Two of the rescue team members were caught in an avalanche while traversing below No 3 Gully Buttress. Anyone with information about the missing couple has been asked to contact the police in Fort William. Police Scotland released a picture of the couple and stated they would have been wearing climbing gear similar to that seen in the photograph. Ms Slater is an experienced, well-travelled climber. In an online blog, she wrote: I've been around rocks my whole life as my parents are very keen climbers—most of my childhood was spent scrambling around at the bottom of the cliff with the occasional easy top rope. She is currently employed as a mineral, waste and environmental consultant near Bradford. Mr Newton, originally from Leicester, also resides in Bradford and has studied physics at the universities of Manchester and Leeds, according to his Facebook profile. Logbook entries for Ms Slater on UKClimbing.com suggest she has undertaken several climbs with Mr Newton. Numerous messages have been posted on social media from individuals sharing information and expressing hope that the couple will be found safe. On the Lochaber MRT Facebook page, Tony Walker wrote: The missing persons are Rachel Slater (my niece) and her partner Tim Newton. Both very experienced climbers. Most likely they are wearing the same clothing as in the photo. Any info greatly appreciated. On a climbing forum, Patrick Roman stated he saw the pair at the weekend. He said: I was outside the CIC on Saturday morning. There were two people matching the image in the photo. He was wearing a red jacket and she a green and turquoise jacket.

text: A 14-year-old boy who stabbed a supply teacher before bragging about the racially-motivated attack on Facebook has been handed an 11-year sentence. The boy stabbed Vincent Uzomah, 50, in a classroom at Dixons Kings Academy, Bradford, on 11 June. There was clear evidence he attacked Mr Uzomah because he was black, the city's crown court was informed. He received an 11-year extended sentence, comprising six years' detention and five years on licence. The boy, who admitted causing grievous bodily harm with intent but denied attempted murder, was informed he could serve half of the six years in custody. He racially abused Mr Uzomah before stabbing him in the stomach with a kitchen knife he had brought to school, the court heard. Jonathan Sharp, prosecuting, stated the boy had discussed the attack with a friend beforehand and later made sick boasts about his actions on Facebook. About 20 minutes after the attack, the boy, who was not arrested until six hours later, posted a status update containing the line I stick a blade straight in his tummy. The post received 69 likes, which the judge described as an appalling reflection of a small microcosm of our society. Mr Sharp informed the court the boy had taken a dislike to Mr Uzomah in the seven weeks he had worked at the school. The defendant disliked him, claiming he couldn't teach, and freely referred to him by the epithet beginning with the letter n, including saying it in anger just before he attacked him, he said. He stated the boy attacked Mr Uzomah after a row over his mobile phone. The teenager was described by witnesses as getting angry, red in the face, Mr Sharp said. He approached Mr Uzomah and reached into his pocket, but at that point he took out the knife and stabbed Mr Uzomah in the stomach. Mr Uzomah thought he was going to die. Sentencing the boy, who cannot be named because of his age, Judge Durham Hall QC described him as out of control and a bully who could not tolerate being told off. Speaking outside court, Mr Uzomah said: As a Christian, I have forgiven this boy who has inflicted this trauma and pain on to me and my family. It was, however, important for the law to run its course and for a strong message to be sent out, especially to kids of similar tendencies, that violence is never acceptable. Our prayer for him is that he will make use of the opportunities and support that will be provided to him, to become a changed person who will make a positive contribution to society. Det Supt Simon Atkinson, from West Yorkshire Police, said: This was a shocking and very serious attack on a man doing a job he loved, and he was lucky that the consequences were not more serious. His attacker showed no concern by fleeing the scene... he worryingly showed a further lack of remorse towards his victim by boasting about it on social media. Outside court, Mr Sharp said it was truly remarkable that Mr Uzomah had forgiven his attacker. He said: The victim has suffered serious physical and psychological injuries, has had to put his career plans on hold and is uncertain when, or if, he will feel able to return to teaching - a profession he loved. It was also profoundly distressing to Mr Uzomah - and shocking - that the youth posted a Facebook update boasting of what he had done. This subsequently received 69 'likes' from his circle of acquaintances. In the circumstances it is remarkable that Mr Uzomah has expressed his desire to forgive the attacker, whilst wishing to see justice done as a deterrent to others. In a statement posted on the Dixons Kings Academy website, the school said: This was a very shocking crime, and today a young man has had to face the consequences of his actions. We are pleased that Mr Uzomah is making a good recovery, and our school community will continue to do what we can to support Vincent and his family.

text: A leading Liverpool fans' group has warned members they need to discuss the issue of safe standing or risk the conversation happening around them. Media playback is not supported on this device. Spirit of Shankly (SOS) is set to vote on the matter on Saturday. Its chairman, Jay McKenna, stated the Hillsborough disaster's impact might have left fans behind the curve in the debate on reintroducing standing. The club expressed it would listen to fans' opinions if legislation mandating all-seater stadiums were ever altered. Liverpool noted their fans were in a uniquely complex and difficult position regarding safe standing, as the all-seater stadium requirement in England's top flight was a response to the Hillsborough disaster, where 96 fans perished in a crush at an FA Cup semi-final in 1989. SOS has engaged with members on the issue since September and will meet with disaster survivors and families of the deceased on Tuesday. It will conduct an open meeting in the city this weekend, followed by an online vote. The vote aims to establish an official stance on safe standing for the group's members, while a separate vote will gather non-members' views to form a supporter-wide consensus. We think it's important that everybody has a say, McKenna added. It can be a factual and emotional debate. We are fully aware of that. In the past, nobody has wanted to discuss it, perhaps for fear of causing upset. If we don't have this conversation, it will happen around us. We just want to know, are you in favour of it or not? Government legislation would need to change for safe standing to be implemented. The Premier League contacted its 20 clubs last month to gauge interest in trialling safe standing. The debate has intensified since Celtic introduced approximately 3,000 rail seats at Celtic Park at the start of last season. The Scottish club will be represented at Saturday's open SOS meeting, as will the Sports Ground Safety Authority, which oversaw regulations for the transition to all-seater stadiums. However, Margaret Aspinall, chair of the Hillsborough Family Support Group, which aids families of over 70 of those killed at Hillsborough, reiterated the group's opposition to safe standing. We have had a vote not so long ago with the families and they voted against any form of standing whatsoever, she stated. We don't call it safe standing; we call it unsafe standing. Another organisation, the Hillsborough Justice Campaign, stated it remains neutral on any move to safe standing, but chairman Kenny Derbyshire said it was now imperative for people to express their views. In April 2016, inquests concluded the 96 people who died due to Hillsborough were unlawfully killed. In June, it was announced six senior figures would face charges related to the disaster.
