text: Listening to new music is rewarding for the brain, a study suggests. Utilising MRI scans, a team of Canadian scientists discovered that areas in the brain's reward centre became active when individuals heard a song for the first time. The more the listener enjoyed the music, the stronger the connections were in the brain region known as the nucleus accumbens. The study is published in the journal Science. Dr Valorie Salimpoor, from the Rotman Research Institute in Toronto, informed the BBC's Science in Action programme: We know that the nucleus accumbens is involved with reward. But music is abstract: It's not like you are genuinely hungry and about to receive food, becoming excited because you will eat it - or similarly with sex or money - that's when you would typically observe activity in the nucleus accumbens. But what's intriguing is that you're anticipating and becoming excited over something entirely abstract - and that's the next sound that is forthcoming. New tunes To conduct the study, which occurred at the Montreal Neurological Institute at McGill University, the scientists played 19 volunteers 60 excerpts of new music, based on their musical preferences. While listening to the 30-second tracks, they had the opportunity to purchase the ones they liked in a simulated online music store. All of this was conducted while the participants were lying in an MRI machine. Test yourself with 'How Musical Are You?' Can the tone deaf learn to sing? By analysing the scans, the scientists observed that the nucleus accumbens was lighting up and, depending on the level of activity, the researchers could predict whether the participant was likely to purchase a song. Dr Salimpoor stated: As they are listening to this music, we can examine their brain activity and determine how they are appreciating or enjoying this music before they even tell us anything. And that's part of this new direction that neuroscience is pursuing - trying to understand what people are thinking, and inferring their thoughts and motivations and eventually their behaviour through their brain activity. The researchers discovered that the nucleus accumbens was also interacting with another brain region called the auditory cortical stores. This is an area that stores sound information based on music that individuals have previously encountered. This part of the brain will be unique for each individual, because we've all heard different music in the past, explained Dr Salimpoor. The researchers now aim to discover how this influences our music tastes, and whether our brain activity can explain why people are attracted to different music styles. text: Former soap-actress Tracy Brabin has been selected as Labour's candidate for the Batley and Spen by-election prompted by the killing of Jo Cox. The Coronation Street, EastEnders, and Emmerdale actress was selected as the party's candidate over fellow nominee Jane Thomas. Mrs Cox, who served as MP for Batley and Spen, was shot and stabbed in Birstall, West Yorkshire, on 16 June. The by-election is scheduled for 20 October. Ms Brabin, born in Batley, collaborated with Mrs Cox on her campaign to preserve the town's library. She portrayed Tricia Armstrong in Coronation Street during the 1990s, later appearing as Roxy Drake in EastEnders and Carole in Emmerdale, and has also contributed as a writer for programmes such as Family Affairs, Tracy Beaker, and Hollyoaks. Ms Brabin, chosen at a hustings event on Friday, expressed she was humbled and privileged to have the opportunity to succeed Mrs Cox. Jo was my inspiration. I intend to do her proud, she stated. Obviously no-one wanted this, but I'm the only person on the ballot paper that can stand up for everyone in Batley and Spen. I'm hoping people will put party politics aside and we can work together. Meanwhile, Mrs Cox's husband has met with US President Barack Obama at the White House in Washington DC. Brendan Cox, who brought his two children, tweeted that he and the president had talked about Jo and fighting extremism. He commended President Obama for being excellent with the kids, adding that the kids gave him their best drawings. Following the announcement of Ms Brabin's selection, Yorks&Humber Labour tweeted: Many congratulations to @Tracy4MP who has been selected as Labour's candidate for Batley and Spen. She'll be a strong voice for everyone. Her opponent Ms Thomas ran for Parliament as a Labour candidate in the 2010 general election but finished second to the Conservatives in Keighley, West Yorkshire. The Conservatives, Liberal Democrats, and UKIP have all announced they will not field a candidate in the by-election, as a gesture of respect. However, a ballot is anticipated as the English Democrats have declared their deputy chairman, Therese Hirst, will stand, while Jack Buckby will represent Liberty GB. Jo Cox's majority in Batley and Spen at the 2015 general election was 6,057. The Conservatives secured second place and UKIP came third.

text: Parents who restrict their children to a vegan diet could face a jail term if a controversial bill is passed by the Italian parliament. Such parents, the draft bill asserts, are enforcing a diet lacking essential elements for [children's] healthy and balanced growth. It has been introduced by Elvira Savino of the centre-right Forza Italia party. It follows several high-profile Italian cases where malnourished children have been taken into care. In four instances over the past 18 months, malnourished children were hospitalised in Italy after being fed a vegan diet. However, dieticians such as the American Dietetic Association state vegan diets are suitable for children but advise that care must be taken to ensure children receive the full range of required nutrients, particularly vitamin B12. Doctors speculated in some cases that the guardians of the hospitalised children may not have understood how to supplement a vegan diet to make it safe for children. A vegan diet excludes anything originating from animals: The rise of the part-time vegans Is it more difficult for vegans to push themselves to physical extremes? Ms Savino's proposed bill will be reviewed by parliamentary committees before proceeding to the chamber for debate, likely later this year, reports Reuters news agency. Meanwhile, three rival bills are on the table, all aiming to make vegan and vegetarian options more common in Italian canteens. In the preamble of Ms Savino's bill (in Italian), she highlights the growing belief in Italy of substantial health benefits provided by a vegetarian or vegan diet. There is no objection if the person making this choice is an informed adult. The problem arises when children are involved... The vegetarian or vegan diet is, in fact, deficient in zinc, iron, vitamin D, vitamin B12 and omega-3. Her draft bill aims to stigmatise the reckless and dangerous eating behaviour imposed by parents who pursue a vegan diet, to the detriment of minors. Offenders would face up to a year in jail, increasing to a maximum of four years where the child suffers illness or permanent injury and six years in the case of death. While some nutrition experts have challenged the validity of the bill, other commentators have warned that its vague wording means it could be used to penalise a much broader range of parents than vegans or vegetarians, for instance, the parents of obese children. Some suggest better public health education rather than punitive measures would be more effective at improving children's nutrition.

text: Is Facebook a media company? This abstract question may appear to be the domain of Palo Alto aspirants, Lower East Side podcasters, and local media analysts. In reality, the answer, though intricate, touches the core of democracy in our era. One cannot comprehend Thursday's announcement from the company about its crackdown on fake news without addressing the preceding question. The measures Facebook is implementing—ranging from simplifying the process to flag fake news to impacting the finances of fake news creators—are welcome but fall short of what some critics desire. The media revolution means platforms like Facebook increasingly perform the functions of publishers. As Tony Haile argued in a recent episode of the Wall Street Journal's excellent Media Mix podcast, Publishers do five things: they create, post, curate, distribute and monetise content. Facebook now does four of those five... [But] they don't create. I believe even this point is debatable. It is true that Facebook does not commission original content or journalism. However, the introduction of Facebook Live brings them very close to doing so. When Lavish Reynolds used that tool to produce an astonishing broadcast of the moments following her boyfriend Philando Castile being shot by a Minnesota Police officer, she was clearly broadcasting live news. Of course, Facebook did not request her to; but through Facebook Live, as through the social network's Instant Articles feature, Facebook facilitates original journalism, much like Amazon aided entrepreneurs with its Web Services technology. Funded by advertising; contributing to the creation of vast amounts of stories; the primary source of news for millions globally. That resembles a media company, does it not? Yet Facebook does not perceive it that way, in one crucial aspect. It does not wish to employ human judgement to arbitrate between truth and falsehood. On Wednesday, I had an extensive conversation with Adam Mosseri, Vice President of Product for News Feed at Facebook. He briefed me on Facebook's latest efforts to combat the fake news which, some argue, assisted Donald Trump in entering the White House. Mark Zuckerberg initially described such a claim as crazy, but has since endeavoured to show he takes the issue seriously. Hence the announcement that Facebook will undertake four actions: Together, these measures will make a difference. As Zuckerberg has argued, and Mosseri reiterated, fake news constitutes a very small fraction of the material shared by the Facebook community, and eradicating it completely is impracticable. However, there is one intriguing, vital aspect in which Facebook will not comply with its critics' demands. It will not instruct staff to determine what is true or false. In other words, it will not employ editors. As Mosseri stated to me regarding the above, this effort to combat fake news is algorithmic—Facebook will rely on algorithms and the judgement of its community of users to flag potential fake news. It will not make those decisions itself, using its own staff. Years ago, Zuckerberg described Facebook as a utility company. Then some astute individuals pointed out that utilities operate in a regulatory environment. Consequently, the emphasis shifted to it being a technology company. Just this August, Zuckerberg stated, we are a tech company, not a media company in Rome. However, Facebook's impact on the media industry has been revolutionary, consuming advertising and attracting vast new audiences. Every day there are numerous pieces lamenting the duopoly that Facebook and Google allegedly hold over the media industry. Those complaints unite the New York Times with The Sun. So while Facebook claims not to be a media company, the impact it has on other media companies, along with its role in disseminating false information, will ensure that publishers continue to criticise it. They argue that Facebook may be one of the world's greatest companies, but it is neglecting a crucial public duty—namely, to be arbiters of truth. The world's largest platform increasingly assumes the role once fulfilled by news publishers, without the legal restrictions and social obligations. In summary, Facebook is a media company—even though it does not wish to be.

text: The plays of William Shakespeare have endured for centuries, and so have many of the names he created for his characters. Some of these names are currently popular, and even a few of the more unusual ones still persist today. For the anniversary of the Bard's death, we interviewed a Hero, a Lysander, a Macbeth, and a William Shakespeare to discover how their Shakespearean names have influenced their lives. My parents never really explained why they chose to call me William, but I suspect it was because of my father. My father was also named William, but he was the first William I know of in the family. I have not continued that family tradition; my son is named Peter and my daughter Susan. I do not recall people commenting on my name during my childhood. It was during the War, so I assume people had other concerns. I have wanted to learn more about the name and whether our family is related to the other William Shakespeare. I researched the family tree and we believe there might be a connection, but we are uncertain of its legitimacy. I have been reading about William Shakespeare, but I have no other links to him. I did visit Stratford-upon-Avon once. I was in a bookshop there and offered to sit in a corner and sign some books for visiting tourists—I do not think the shop owner understood the joke. William Shakespeare, London I have always been surrounded by a multitude of cultures and histories, people and experiences, but the one constant, regardless of where I am, is that everyone remembers my Shakespearean middle name. My lecturers and fellow students seem to appreciate my name, likely because we study literature and it seems I was destined for this field. When I began studying for my bachelor's degree in England, there was no doubt I would study English (and German) literature—I am currently pursuing my master's in Sweden. I collect Shakespeare works in various editions and in both English and German because I am interested in how the works are translated and reissued. Shakespeare is a significant part of my studies, as his works are frequently referenced or alluded to in new works about post-colonialism and world literature. Overall, I cherish my name and it is very dear to me. I enjoy the amusing reactions I receive and the fact that I usually only need to introduce myself once. I have never had a truly negative reaction to it, unless you count being associated with bad luck because of your name. My two sisters and I all share the middle name Macbeth and are, therefore, often referred to as the three little witches by the rest of my family. My friends, however, tend to call me Lady Macbeth when I become angry or make a snobbish comment (usually about food). So, even if it has been on a light-hearted and fun level, my Shakespearean name has always followed me. Shuna Macbeth Blankenhaus, Sweden My parents clearly love Shakespeare. Ariel was my father's favourite name, and he was always fascinated by the shape-shifting sprite seeking freedom, while Ophelia was my great-grandmother's name. The Shakespearean connection was not lost on my mother, who was a theatre major at university. It is certainly an icebreaker, and I can instantly identify a Shakespeare fan when introduced if they say: Ariel, as in The Tempest? instead of: Ariel, as in The Little Mermaid? It does amuse people to discover I have a Shakespearean middle name as well, and I am quite sure it always put me in good stead with my English teachers and literature professors over the years. The name certainly gave me a connection to Shakespeare at an early age, and I have taken a keen interest in his work throughout my life. When I was very young, around the age of five, my parents took me to Shakespeare in the Park in Savannah, Georgia, US. I vividly remember A Midsummer Night's Dream—I enjoyed it so much that we attended several times. I recall being delighted by the fairies, the mischievous Puck, and the humour of it all. It was magical to me and remains one of my fondest childhood memories. Later in high school, I recited Ophelia's monologue from Hamlet for an English class. I still enjoy attending the occasional play or watching my favourite film adaptations. Naturally, I have reflected on these two characters. Both were constrained in life: Ariel a slave and Ophelia a young woman in a nobleman's world. Life overcame the latter, but she was loved by all and revered in death. Ariel was determined to succeed and ultimately won his freedom. Both characters have taught me something about strength and kindness. Ariel Ophelia Meadows, New Zealand My mother and father attended a performance of A Midsummer Night's Dream, and afterwards, my mother told my father she wished to name her next child after Lysander. There was no debate; they both adored the name. Occasionally, when people have only read my name without meeting me in person, they assume I am a girl, as my name resembles Lisanne, which is a common name in Belgium. Fortunately, this has not occurred too often. When I introduce myself to new people, I often have to repeat my name several times before they realise they have not heard it before. Although it is from A Midsummer Night's Dream, one of the better-known plays, it is not widely recognised among average Belgians. However, after I explain that it is from a Shakespeare play, they are impressed and tell me it is a great name to have. A distinctive name like this is always a good conversation starter, and I feel it sparked my interest in Shakespeare and other literary and cultural activities. Lysander Fockaert, Belgium My parents apparently named me partly after the character in Much Ado About Nothing and partly after the Greek myth of Hero and Leander. My mother loved Shakespeare. I used to be teased as a child, which was unpleasant; they would say things like: Why aren't you called Heroine as you're a girl? I did not like my name then, but I do appreciate it now. My name is a topic of conversation upon first meeting and is rarely forgotten, which can be embarrassing because I am terrible at remembering names. I have noticed that Hero is becoming more common as a name. When I was a child, it was extremely rare (I am in my mid-50s now). One of [radio presenter] Myleene Klass's children is named Hero, and I saw a writer from a newspaper mention she named her daughter Hero. Additionally, my niece is named Hero, and my brother's friend's daughter is named Hero. My job requires me to email many customers, and they are often surprised when we then speak on the phone and they discover I am a woman—a bit disconcerting but amusing. Hero Selwood, Cornwall When I was young, I disliked my name because I was frequently bullied by my classmates. The name Puck was very unusual at that time. Typically, dogs were named Puck. That is why I always thought I was named after an acquaintance's dog. As I grew older, I learned that my parents named me after one of Shakespeare's characters. I felt much better until I discovered that Puck was this mischievous, male goblin from Shakespeare's Midsummer Night's Dream. Personally, I do not have a particular interest in Shakespeare—but my parents do. My name has affected my life in both negative and positive ways. Children my age bullied me, but older people always told me they thought Puck was a great name to have. Despite not liking my name when I was younger, I have really grown to love it. I now appreciate the fact that I have a connection to Shakespeare, and I am honoured to have this unique yet famous name. Puck Creemer, Holland My name certainly attracts a lot of attention, but people mispronounce it frequently. I was named Portia after the heroine in The Merchant of Venice. However, most people are unaware of this and ask what it means. They assume I was named after the car when I first tell them my name. Additionally, they find it difficult to pronounce when they read it, so I often hear Pour-tia. My parents heard the name associated with [US talk show host] Ellen DeGeneres, whose wife is the actress Portia de Rossi. But they later learned more and thought it was classy. I know the story by Shakespeare, and I do like Portia's character—she stands up for what she believes in. I think it is a unique name. Portia Miller, Berkshire My husband is from Stratford-upon-Avon, and we live in Belfast. We lived in Stratford together for a while some years ago and resided on Arden Street in the centre of town. When we discovered we were expecting a baby girl, we wanted to name her something meaningful yet unique. We love visiting the Forest of Arden and generally love all things Shakespearean, so we thought Arden would be a perfect choice of name for our little girl. Fortunately, when she arrived, she suited the name and still does now. Everyone always comments on how beautiful a name it is, and we love it as it serves as a pleasant reminder of Stratford. Lynsey Richards (mother of Arden), Northern Ireland Compiled by Andree Massiah

text: A dog which went missing on a mountain, sparking a social media campaign by more than 6,000 people to find him, has been rescued. Border Collie Jasper disappeared while on a walk up Scafell Pike in the Lake District with his owner Adam Nolan. A mountain rescue team, helicopter, police, and dog enthusiasts searched for him, and he was found on Thursday. A JustGiving page established by Mr Nolan to raise funds for the rescue team had collected more than £25,000 by 19:00 GMT. Jasper was last seen at approximately 14:00 on Sunday at Cam Spout Crag below Scafell Pike. The outing was nothing out of the blue, and Jasper was accustomed to walking and running on the fells, his owner stated. Distressed by his disappearance, Mr Nolan, from Cleator Moor, turned to social media for assistance in finding his four-legged companion, with the #FindJasper campaign going viral. On Wednesday, following a possible sighting in Seascale, Mr Nolan pledged he would not cease searching until Jasper was home and in front of the fire. The local community supported the search for Jasper, and Wasdale Mountain Rescue located him in the early hours of Thursday. Mr Nolan stated on Facebook: I'm over the moon to announce the safe return of my best friend Jasper. This morning Geoff Horky [from the rescue team] ascended Scafell Pike in response to the information received yesterday regarding the sighting of Jasper near the Scafell Pike summit. Geoff found Jasper at 2:00 am in very good condition. The Wasdale Mountain Rescue Team were then alerted and began the rescue operation. Upon hearing the news, I followed the Wasdale Mountain Rescue team to Lingmell Col where I was united with Jasper. Naturally, there are numerous individuals whom I would like to thank, but at the moment I would say a huge thank you to Geoff and the Wasdale Mountain Rescue Team for their heroic efforts this morning. A spokesman for Wasdale Mountain Rescue said: The team are pleased to announce that we have been involved in the successful rescue of Jasper. The team responded and recovered Jasper back to the valley to meet Adam.

text: India's space agency has successfully launched its heaviest rocket. These are external links and will open in a new window. The 640-tonne rocket launched from a site off the Bay of Bengal in Sriharikota. As one website stated, it's been a big day for India. The rocket will decrease the Indian Space Research Organisation's (Isro) dependence on European vehicles for launching heavy satellites. The launch coverage has been euphoric and often colourful, with websites comparing the rocket to the weight of 200 elephants or five jumbo jets. Such comparisons emphasise the launch's significance for the country, which is aggressively competing for a larger share of the global commercial satellite launch market. India has so far depended on other countries to send heavy satellites into space, which is costly and a strain on Isro's budget. The GSLV Mark III can carry a payload weighing more than three tonnes into the high-altitude orbit occupied by spacecraft that relay TV, telephone calls, and broadband connections. However, it is far from being the world's heaviest rocket, as Nasa's Saturn V, used between 1967 and 1973, still holds that record, with a total mass at lift-off about four times that of India's GSLV Mark III. The NDTV website states the rocket is as heavy as five jumbo jets. And the weight is significant because communication satellites are quite heavy. Experts suggest the rocket provides India with more flexibility in launching different types of satellites. We were able to send [satellites weighing] up to two tonnes previously. This is a double quantum jump for India, Ajay Lele from the Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses told the AFP news agency. Isro hopes that the rocket, dubbed the monster by one newspaper, will be capable of carrying an astronaut to space by 2024. India aims to become the fourth country after the US, China, and Russia to send a person into space. Experts say the successful launch will boost India's indigenous space programme. The launch follows Isro's other recent achievements, including a mission to Mars and the launch of more than 100 satellites in a single mission earlier in the year. In the spirit of finding fun facts, the BBC also conducted research on the rocket's height and found it is taller than the Statue of Liberty. The rocket is 43m (141ft) tall, while the statue stands at 33.83m, excluding the pedestal foundation. Cartoons by the BBC's Kirtish Bhat.

text: Sprinter Sacre beat favourite Un De Sceaux to win the coveted Queen Mother Champion Chase for a second time at the Cheltenham Festival. With three former winners in the major race, Nicky Henderson's 10-year-old, a 5-1 contender ridden by Nico de Boinville, surged home by seven lengths. Ruby Walsh, aiming for his 50th Festival victory, finished second on the Willie Mullins-trained 4-6 favourite. Outsider Special Tiara (16-1) secured third place for trainer Henry de Bromhead. Sprinter Sacre had been a dominant winner by 19 lengths three years prior but did not compete in 2014 due to an irregular heartbeat. After two second-place finishes last year, he triumphed by 14 lengths at Cheltenham in November and subsequently won the Desert Orchid Chase at Kempton the following month, surpassing Sire De Grugy. Another former winner, the Gary Moore-trained 10-year-old Sire De Grugy, finished eighth this time. It's been a long, long journey - those were two very, very grim years, said Sprinter Sacre's trainer Henderson. That was unbelievable. That was about dreams, wasn't it? BBC racing correspondent Cornelius Lysaght commented: Nicky Henderson has long demonstrated his skill in handling more delicate horses, regardless of their ailments. In his early training days in the 1980s, he guided the fragile See You Then to three Champion Hurdle victories, and this week, despite two years off the track, My Tent Or Yours ran impressively to be runner-up to Annie Power. But Sprinter Sacre is exceptional. A dramatic fall from grace with heart problems after a brilliant 2013 seemed terminal, but Henderson never gave up, continued nurturing and maintaining faith, and today that was repaid in abundance. Walsh and Mullins continued their remarkable start to the Festival with a victory in the opening race on day two. Having secured three wins on the first day, Walsh rode the Mullins-trained six-year-old Yorkhill to another victory in the Novices' Hurdle. Walsh, who guided the Mullins-trained Annie Power to victory in day one's feature - the Champion Hurdle - directed Yorkhill on an inside path and turned for home to defeat favourite Yanworth by a length and three-quarters. Its'afreebee held on gamely for third, seven lengths further back. Walsh was in contention again on Roi Des Francs in the RSA Chase but eventually faded to sixth as the Nigel Twiston-Davies-trained Blaklion, (8-1) ridden by 22-year-old Ryan Hatch, triumphed in a gripping contest with Shaneshill to win by half a length. Favourite More Of That, ridden by Barry Geraghty, was third, another eight lengths behind. Gordon Elliott's eight-year-old Diamond King, (12-1) with Davy Russell aboard, surged through on the far side to claim victory by a length and a quarter. Long House Hall, ridden by Harry Skelton for his brother Dan, was second, with Ubak another neck away in third. The Mullins-Walsh combination Blood Cotil was pulled up. Veteran performer Any Currency (11-1) persevered to win for trainer Martin Keighley and jockey Aidan Coleman in the Glenfarclas Chase. Second in this race for the past two years, the 13-year-old took over from long-time leader Valadom in the final part of the cross-country test over three and three-quarter miles and was the clear leader from the third-last fence. Josies Orders, the 15-8 favourite, finished strongly up the hill to get within a length of the winner at the line. Bless The Wings (33-1) was another length and a quarter away in third. Trainer Paul Nicholls achieved his first success at this year's Festival when Diego Du Charmil (13-2) and Romain De Senam gave him a one-two in the Juvenile Handicap Hurdle. At the final flight, Voix De Reve and Campeador fell independently when well placed. This left Diego Du Charmil in front from long-time leader Coo Star Sivola, but he had to be driven out by Sam Twiston-Davies to fend off a late challenge from stablemate Romain De Senam (20-1) by a head. Coo Star Sivola was a head away in third. Ballyandy edged home by a nose in the final race of the day, the Champion Bumper, to give both trainer Nigel Twiston-Davies and his jockey son Sam doubles. In a gritty 23-runner race, Ballyandy (5-1) secured the verdict from the Mullins-trained Battleford (25-1). Mullins and Walsh were third with Bacardys (16-1).

text: Peterhead boss Jim McInally hailed his League Two side after they stunned Hearts in the League Cup. I thought we deserved it, McInally stated after Rory McAllister's late penalty secured a 2-1 victory over the Premiership side at Balmoor Stadium. For 70 minutes we were probably the better team and we got the break at the end, McInally told BBC's Sportsound. Hearts head coach Ian Cathro remarked: We're disappointed and we should be performing better in these situations. Jason Brown headed the League Two side into an early lead in their Group B match, with Kyle Lafferty equalising with his fourth goal in three games. As the League Cup match seemed destined for a penalty shoot-out and a fight for a bonus point, McAllister's penalty clinched a memorable win. Ironically, we scored or got our penalty when we had really tired in the last 10 minutes and were hanging on, said McInally. I'm so pleased for the players because they concentrated for the entire game and passed it well when necessary. [Playing] twice in four days is challenging for part-timers. Many of these players have just travelled up from Glasgow today. Willie Gibson and Greg Fleming, the goalkeeper, [have come] from Dumfries. Hearts were up here last night resting. So, it makes it even better and the significant thing is we have a chance of progressing now if we can win on Saturday [against Elgin City]. Cathro, while disappointed with the outcome, believes his players are still forming connections. We anticipated a challenging game, he said. And it's always the case, particularly at the start of these games when you play against teams from the lower leagues. We're disappointed and we should be doing better in these situations but we're at a stage where new players are here and we're progressing some things and things are a work in progress. We started to get ourselves in front in the game, we had some energy and played with a little more urgency as things progressed. But we didn't take our chances and maybe some of our decisions in the final third weren't quite right. We suffered because of that but, as I said, there are a lot of new relationships within the team and there's a lot of positive things building across all three [League Cup] games and we'll continue to work to get ourselves ready and improving. We're disappointed with the result and have expectations which are higher than that - we move forward very quickly and focus on Saturday [against Dunfermline at Tynecastle].

text: The EU's latest Earth observer has returned its first pictures. Sentinel-3a, launched two weeks ago, will focus particularly on the oceans, measuring the colour, temperature, and height of sea surfaces. The information will be invaluable to weather forecasters and marine biologists seeking to understand the health of global waters. The first images depict the Strait of Gibraltar, the Californian coast, and an ice-covered Svalbard archipelago. These were acquired by the spacecraft's Ocean and Land Colour Instrument (OLCI). As the name implies, this sensor is not solely dedicated to ocean work and will also collect data on land surfaces, such as monitoring global vegetation. We received the first images on 29 February, but we've had to spend some time working on them to get the calibration right, said Volker Liebig, director of Earth observation at the European Space Agency (ESA). We're not ready with everything onboard the satellite yet, that's clear; but we thought it important to get the pictures out there, he told BBC News. A few months of testing remain before the spacecraft begins routine observations. Sentinel-3a is part of a series of satellites procured for the European Union's Copernicus programme. The data from this multi-billion-euro project is expected to drive numerous applications, ranging from air quality updates to crop-performance monitoring, from water-resource management to transport infrastructure planning. ESA acts as the technical agent, designing the satellites and then commissioning industry to build them. For Sentinel-3, all follow-on models - b, c, and d - have already been contracted, ensuring operational continuity in orbit through at least 2030. In addition to OLCI, the new satellite has a radiometer to measure the temperature of ocean and land surfaces, and an altimeter to measure ocean height. Together, these instruments will be useful for tracking phenomena such as El Niño, which causes warm waters to bulge in the eastern Pacific every few years. The current event - one of the largest on record - has disrupted weather patterns worldwide. It is unsurprising that Europe's national meteorological agencies are eager to access Sentinel-3 data for their numerical forecasting models. Yes, Sentinel-3 is an ocean workhorse, but it's also a global workhorse, said ESA senior scientist Dr Craig Donlon. The vegetation products we'll get from OLCI in 21 bands will be really excellent, so there will be a huge amount we'll get out of it just looking at land surfaces. And then there's all the work it will do measuring ice surfaces, and rivers and lakes using its altimeter, he told BBC News. Sentinel-3a joins two other series satellites already in orbit. Sentinel-1a was launched in 2014 and is equipped with a radar to measure the shape of the Earth's surface; Sentinel-2a, launched last year, has a colour camera to record land use and changes over time. More Sentinels are forthcoming, and the European Commission and ESA have begun considering extending the initial suite of sensors. There is a desire for Europe to develop a space-borne carbon-monitoring capability - a tool to verify that countries are implementing policies to reduce emissions of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases. This would be a multi-satellite mission, said Prof Liebig. The idea would be to have a first prototype satellite by 2025, let's say; and then a full system around 2030. But if we want to achieve this we have to start in this (EU) financial perspective. The European-funded Sentinel series What is the Copernicus programme? text: It didn't much look like a protest. Numerous casually dressed, smiling, middle-class Germans—some accompanied by children, others with dogs—were conversing animatedly in picturesque parkland on the outskirts of Hamburg on a sunny Sunday afternoon. However, this was indeed a protest group, organising a petition to prevent the construction of a new refugee centre on the green. Participants were eager to stress that they were not anti-immigrant, asserting their primary goal was to protect an area of natural beauty. Yet, as discussions progressed, broader concerns emerged. Birgit remarked that securing housing was already challenging for Germans. Hamburg faces a severe housing shortage even in the best of times. With the influx of tens of thousands of immigrants, the port city seemed on the verge of being overwhelmed. In desperation, authorities have been converting shipping containers into refugee homes and repurposing vacant commercial properties and open spaces to establish new migrant centres. text: Former bouncer Levi Bellfield, 43, has been convicted of murdering three young women and trying to kill another in south-west London and Surrey. Here are profiles of the women targeted during his campaign of violence. Amanda Dowler, known as Milly, was a pretty, popular and intelligent 13-year-old girl. To all intents and purposes she was an ordinary girl who was developing into a fine young woman, prosecutor Brian Altman informed the Old Bailey. Milly resided in Walton with her parents Bob and Sally and older sister Gemma, to whom the court heard she was close. Gemma told the court: We would go to bed at the same time and lie in the room chatting about our day. Milly and I didn't have any secrets and she would tell me about boys at school she fancied. Milly admired Gareth Gates and had seen him at a Pop Idol concert a few days before her death. She had been anticipating an upcoming school event, where she was to see a boy she liked. However, the court also heard there was another side to her, as poems and a goodbye letter were found after her death, indicating she was unhappy. Milly was in Year 9 at Heathside School in Weybridge, where her mother Sally taught mathematics. It was only by chance that she took the route home which led her to cross Bellfield's path—she would normally have alighted at another station but had gone to a café with friends. She was one of the funniest people I had ever met. She was always trying to make people laugh and smile, her friend Danielle Sykes stated. Marsha McDonnell, 19, had completed her A-levels and was taking a gap year before starting university when she died. Described in court as an attractive blonde, she was attacked by Bellfield just yards from the Hampton home she shared with her parents, Phil and Ute, her two sisters and younger brother. Ms McDonnell, who was working in a gift shop in Kingston, had visited the cinema with friends on the night she was attacked. Her sister Nathalie said: She always thought of other people. She was a free spirit. Speaking after the verdict, her uncle, Shane McDonnell, said: Five years have passed since the night our beloved Marsha was so cruelly taken from this world, a girl that only had love in her heart, brutally slain by a man who only has hate in his. Her uncle described the family's loss as devastating. Marsha we miss you. Our world now is incomplete, like a rainbow with a colour missing. We thank you for the joy that you brought us in your short life. Your goodness, sense of fun, spirit and passion for life remain with us, he said. Ms McDonnell was passionate about music and a music room at the local children's hospice is dedicated to her memory. Her uncle said: For her family, life will never quite be the same ever again. The pain and hurt that we carry will always be there. It is a sentence with no remission. Amelie Delagrange, 22, had a passion for the English language and had moved to Britain to further her studies. Ms Delagrange, from Amiens in France, had passed her baccalaureate exams with ease, and spent six weeks living in Manchester as part of a language course. She enjoyed and wanted to return to the UK. She had been living in Twickenham for just three months when she was killed. Ms Delagrange was working at a patisserie in Richmond, had a close circle of both English and French friends and was happy, the court heard. Her parents Jean Francois and Dominique Delagrange travelled from France to the Old Bailey to hear details of their daughter's death. She was a good student, sensible, and never gave her parents any problems, her mother told the court. Her boyfriend, Olivier Lenfant, also described her as a sensible girl who thought she lived in a safe area. In a statement Ms Delagrange's parents Dominique and Jean-Francois said: It is nearly four years since our lives and our family's lives were so seriously disrupted, descending into a horror—a living nightmare. They added: We would like to have heard from Bellfield a confession of sorts, some evidence of remorse. In this we were disappointed. A memorial tree and a bench dedicated to her memory were placed on Twickenham Green by the local community and her family. Kate Sheedy, was 18 and the head girl at her convent school in Isleworth when she was attacked in 2004. She had spent the evening saying goodbye to friends after her last day at Gumley House School and was walking home when she was mown down by a car. She missed her A-levels because of the attack but was granted her predicted grades by the exam board and went on to study history and drama at York University. The trial heard she remains mentally and physically scarred by the attack. In a statement, Ms Sheedy said: On the day I was attacked I was celebrating about moving onto a new and exciting time in my life. All that hope and excitement was taken from me and I thought my life had changed for ever. The attack meant she attended university a year later than she had hoped. I will never be able to forget what happened to me, the scars on my body and the memories I have, are something I will never be rid of, but hopefully I can move on, she said. On top of the physical and mental ordeal, Ms Sheedy said she had also suffered additional trauma and stress from the police investigation.

text: Floyd Mayweather directed a homophobic slur at Conor McGregor after accusing him of making racist comments during the media tour to promote their Las Vegas fight. Former five-weight boxing world champion Mayweather will compete against UFC lightweight title-holder McGregor in a 12-round match under boxing rules in August. He referred to black people as 'monkeys', stated the American, aged 40, during a news conference at Wembley Arena on Friday. Subsequently, once the pair entered a boxing ring at the event for the official promotion, Mayweather addressed McGregor as: You punk. You faggot. You ho. The two men have held a series of news conferences in recent days to promote the fight, with stops in Los Angeles and Toronto before proceeding to New York and London. The 29-year-old Irishman has faced criticism for a series of remarks during those events and is alleged to have made racist comments during the third stop of the tour in New York on Thursday. He completely disrespected black women, added Mayweather. Then he spoke disrespectfully to my mother and he spoke disrespectfully to my daughter. The American further stated on Friday: Racism still exists. I'm not going to stoop that low and speak about his like or speak about his child. I'm glad that he just had a healthy child and he has a beautiful family. Responding to Mayweather at the New York press conference on Thursday, McGregor said: I'm a multicultural individual and I don't harbour any ill feelings towards anyone. I don't even see colour. Then, speaking to BBC Sport after the London event, he said: I know who I am, people around me know who I am. We know his history, but I didn't bring it up. The fight game is ruthless and it's what I expect. In 2010, Mayweather made racist and homophobic remarks towards Filipino boxer Manny Pacquiao in a video posted on the website Ustream. At the conclusion of the news conference, Mayweather and McGregor fielded several questions from the media. BBC boxing correspondent Mike Costello asked McGregor—who has never boxed as an amateur or professional—how he responds to pundits who claim he has no chance of defeating Mayweather. McGregor replied: I do what I say I'm going to do, by sleeping [Mayweather] inside of four rounds—the same way I silence them every time. Mayweather, who won all 49 of his bouts, was asked how he thought the McGregor fight would impact his legacy in boxing. In boxing, it's all about taking chances, he said. In contact sports, it's about taking risks, so if you're going to take a risk, take it against the top guys. BBC Radio 5 live sports news correspondent Richard Conway The four-night global promotional tour has concluded and will reconvene in Las Vegas in the lead-up to the contest on 26 August. Thousands of fans packed Wembley Arena, cheering and shouting McGregor's name. Chants of pay your taxes and sit down, shut up were repeatedly directed at Mayweather. This was more pantomime than press conference. However, troubling elements of this fight have emerged before the question of its sporting validity is even addressed. Sexist and homophobic language was used repeatedly. The hype and hoopla—what should have been a carnival of over-the-top bravado—sadly had a misogynistic and outdated overtone.

text: The doctor at the centre of the Nike Oregon Project (NOP) drugs investigation altered athletes' medical records before handing them to anti-doping authorities, according to new disclosures. Dr Jeffrey Brown, alongside the contentious NOP coach Alberto Salazar, has been under scrutiny by the US Anti-Doping Agency (Usada) since the BBC's Panorama programme and ProPublica accused NOP of doping and unethical practices in 2015. The elite endurance camp, funded by Nike and led by Salazar, has coached Britain's double Olympic champion Mo Farah since 2011. Both Salazar and Dr Brown firmly deny any misconduct. In February this year, an interim report by Usada investigators into the NOP allegations was leaked by the Russian hacking group Fancy Bears. Details of various alleged anti-doping rule violations outlined in the report were published by the Sunday Times, the BBC, and the New York Times. Usada has yet to formally charge anyone in connection with its investigation. Now, new disclosures seen by the BBC and ProPublica further implicate Dr Brown, a Texas-based endocrinologist who has treated many of Salazar's athletes and has previously been accused of prescribing thyroid medication (which is not banned under World Anti-Doping Agency rules) to athletes to enhance performance. Dr Brown denies this. Dr Brown, who is Salazar's personal physician, provided Usada with the medical records of certain athletes, including Steve Magness, then also Salazar's assistant coach. However, Magness, a key contributor to the BBC/ProPublica investigation in 2015, claims his medical notes have been altered by Dr Brown. He states he requested a copy of his notes in August 2015 before signing a release form to allow Usada to obtain them from his former physician. One note details an infusion of a controversial but legal supplement, L-carnitine, administered by Dr Brown in his Texas office, on Salazar's instructions, in 2011. The note on the left is, according to Magness, his copy of the infusion note, a medical procedure involving Dr Brown putting him on a drip for over four hours. In the same note later provided by Dr Brown's office to Usada, on the right, and seen in the Usada report, various additions appear to have been made. Several ticks seem to have been added under 'EXAM' options, including 'General,' 'Lungs,' 'Thyroid,' 'CV' (cardiovascular), and 'Neuro,' suggesting a full health check was conducted by Dr Brown on Magness. Magness, who left NOP in 2012 and is now a coach at the University of Houston, says those checks were never performed. He states: I do not recall these being done. I wasn't even in a patient room, but instead in his office during this visit. I do not recall him going through his normal checks of my thyroid or [anything else]. My only speculation is that [those boxes were ticked] to make it look like care for the patient had been given. He might have realised after the fact that when you have a patient, your doctoral duty is to the health of that individual. And that without the proper checks, it might look like he was prioritising a company, Nike, Salazar, that was paying him over the health of his patient. Dr Brown had been my physician since the age of 16. The Usada report alleges Dr Brown committed at least four anti-doping violations. Dr Brown strongly denies breaking anti-doping rules. The Texas Medical Board is also investigating Dr Brown, but it declined to comment. The supplement, L-carnitine, is legal, is produced naturally in the body, and helps convert fat to energy. Salazar had been excited by a study suggesting the benefits of L-carnitine and had been eager to try it on his athletes. After trialling it on Magness, Salazar wrote to Lance Armstrong, who was then training for a long-distance triathlon. He told the now disgraced former cyclist: Lance, call me asap! We have tested it and it's amazing. You are the only athlete I'm going to tell the actual numbers to other than Galen Rupp. It's too incredible. Magness says he had been a reluctant guinea pig. Wada rules stipulate that infusions of any kind must be less than 50ml every six hours - but according to the Usada report, infusions of this relatively small amount of L-carnitine would be largely ineffective for an athlete's performance. Analysing the available data from the notes, Usada experts have concluded the infusion levels must have been much greater than 50ml and therefore constitute a breach of doping rules. Usada believes similar protocols were used on up to six of Salazar's other US NOP athletes, including Dathan Ritzenhein. Usada also believes the medical notes relating to Ritzenhein provided by Dr Brown have also been altered surreptitiously to suggest the infusion was within the Wada limit of 50ml. In this case, an annotation of 40ml appears to have been added before submission to Usada. The Usada report concludes that Salazar and Dr Brown were aware that infusions given to NOP athletes, including Magness and Ritzenhein, were above the legal limits and broke Wada rules. The report concludes: Usada has found that these potential anti-doping rule violations appear to have wholly or largely occurred in the context of a larger conspiracy between Nike Oregon Project coach Alberto Salazar and Houston endocrinologist Dr Jeffrey Brown to collude in order to employ risky and untested alternative and unconventional [and sometimes potentially unlawful] uses of medical procedures and prescription medications [including both substances and methods prohibited under the rules of sport…] to attempt to increase the testosterone, energy and blood levels of Nike Oregon Project athletes in order to boost athletic performance. The Usada report credits Magness, who became aware that rules had been broken, for withdrawing from future competitions because he felt he had been given an unfair advantage. Though Magness has contributed significantly to the Usada investigation as a whistleblower, he may also face a ban for his part in the L-carnitine experiment. Dr Brown's lawyer told the BBC and ProPublica the allegations against him were false. In a letter, lawyer Joan Bain stated the Usada report leak was unlawful and accused it of fake news. Ms Bain said patient confidentiality prevented Dr Brown from responding to specific enquiries. Ms Bain was also highly critical of Usada and its investigation, stating: Notwithstanding its name, you should understand that Usada is not an official government entity, but rather a private corporation which stands to gain financially through publicity, essentially using the press to spread its own 'fake news'. She wrote that this was the latest attempt by Usada to bait Dr Brown into breaking the law by 'leaking' false information to journalists in the hope that Dr Brown will cross the line while trying to defend himself. In reference to the allegations notes were altered, she said: No-one at Dr Brown's office has inappropriately changed medical records. All medical records provided to Usada were accurate and provided with the patient's consent. She added: Dr Brown did not break any Wada rules and is unaware of any violation of Wada rules by Alberto Salazar… Dr Brown did not infuse any active athlete with more than 50ml of an L-carnitine solution. L-carnitine is an FDA approved amino acid supplement. It is not a banned substance. Following the response from Ms Bain, Magness wrote to her and Dr Brown waiving confidentiality on the specific notes the BBC and ProPublica were enquiring about, but Ms Bain did not provide further comment. Alberto Salazar has always strenuously denied breaking Wada rules or putting the health of his athletes at risk, and in response to the BBC and ProPublica's investigation, published a lengthy and detailed response. In 2014, Mo Farah received an injection of L-carnitine before a major race which UK Athletics (UKA) doctor Robin Chakraverty failed to record properly. Before the Culture, Media and Sport Select Committee in April, Dr Chakraverty said the injection was 13.5mls, well within the legal limit of 50ml, though UKA chairman Ed Warner called his failure to record the treatment properly inexcusable. The use of the substance by Farah remains under investigation by Usada, according to the leaked report, to determine whether rules were broken. Farah says he has never broken any rules and has vowed to stand by Salazar unless he is proven to have cheated anti-doping rules.

text: Southern rail commuters are facing more travel misery after drivers walked out for the third day this week following the failure of conciliation talks. Labour's transport spokesman has urged the government to intervene before another conductors' strike next week. Andy McDonald stated: What's needed is a pause. People to step back and let's have a thorough examination of this. The shadow transport secretary told Radio 4's Today programme: I'm absolutely furious at the intransigence and stupidity of Southern and the Department for Transport in perpetuating this. It's a hugely important issue around compromising safety and security... this issue has been trivialised and dismissed. He added: Let Chris Grayling intervene and agree a moratorium so that we can get people back on these trains immediately. It's what a Secretary of State should be doing right now. Angry passengers staged a protest at London Victoria station on Thursday evening before delivering a letter to the Department for Transport (DfT) to demand government action. The Association of British Commuters, which organised the protest, said it had received support for its campaign to persuade ministers to do more to resolve the industrial disputes and other problems at Southern. A spokesman said: We have suffered a year-long nightmare because of the collapse of Southern rail. We have desperately called for government action and have been repeatedly ignored - even while many of us have lost our jobs, or had to move house. The DfT has informed the BBC the dispute is between Southern and the unions and not something the government is involved in. A spokeswoman for the department declined to comment further. text: In our series of letters from African journalists, Nigerian writer and novelist Adaobi Tricia Nwaubani looks at the clamour for assistance that accompanies a politician's rise to office. These are external links and will open in a new window. The political party primaries in Nigeria have concluded, providing voters with a clearer understanding of whose turn it might be to share in the national wealth following the elections in February 2015. However, the victorious candidates will not be the only ones partaking in the nation's riches. In Nigeria, news of an individual's electoral success often spreads rapidly, crossing rivers and mountains, fields and forests, to reach relatives in all parts of the world. Those without employment believe their days of joblessness are ending; those lacking education think it will soon no longer hinder their ascent up the corporate ladder; those in distant lands begin planning their return home. Soon, these relatives commence their journey towards the successful candidate. They call his phone; they send text messages; they knock at his gate. They offer to assist his campaign in any possible way; they organise prayer sessions for his victory, typically late at night in his living room. A friend of mine residing in Lagos informed me last week that he was travelling to Benin City. His friend had just secured a position in the House of Assembly there. Another acquaintance was poised for another prominent role. He's a good friend of my elder brother in Florida, he stated. I've already told my brother: 'You'd better come down and connect with him and introduce us to him.' Another friend, whose husband is a close associate of a winning candidate in one of Nigeria's most desirable states, told me her phone did not cease ringing after his victory was announced. People had been calling to offer congratulations. Indeed, even I had called for that very reason. In Nigeria, the tradition has always been that anyone who attains power, who suddenly finds himself wielding a knife to cut the national cake, must invite his clan to both slice and partake in it with him. The most unforgivable sin a politician can commit is to forget his people after assuming office. He must remember his sisters, brothers, cousins, nieces, nephews, in-laws, friends, schoolmates, and so forth. Preferably through contracts, appointments, and jobs. Failure to do so will result in taunts and ostracism, and on the day his tenure concludes, he will find himself utterly alone. Long after his funeral, the bitter tongues will continue to wag. Local history will eternally record him as having denied his relatives their turn. I have heard numerous amusing stories about the influx of people from the Niger Delta region into Abuja, the Nigerian capital, after their kinsman, Goodluck Jonathan, was elected president in 2011. One of my favourite tales was recounted by my British-Nigerian friend who teaches in one of those Abuja schools where the children pay exorbitant fees in dollars and mock their teachers' inexpensive mobile phones. She was astonished when a particular pupil, during a science lesson, appeared to know more about crustaceans than one would expect of a child his age in the city. This child stood before the class and described in great detail how the creatures are caught, cleaned, and cooked. At the end, my friend called the boy aside and inquired how he knew so much about the topic. The child explained that he had grown up in the creeks, where his family engaged in petty trading of crustaceans for a living. That is why the news of a candidate's potential rise to political office brings such joy. In many parts of the world, it requires years of steady progress for one's economic circumstances to undergo a radical transformation. Here in Nigeria, all it takes is an election and a new political appointment. Suddenly, a child transitions from capturing crustaceans in the creeks to attending an exclusive school in Abuja. Voracious relatives are the primary force behind Nigeria's corruption issue. Imagine the thousands lined up with outstretched palms behind each political office holder. Try telling them that you intend to reform the system now that it is finally their turn to benefit. If you would like to comment on Adaobi Tricia Nwaubani's column, please do so below.

text: Nigeria's Ogoniland region could take 30 years to recover fully from the damage caused by years of oil spills, a long-awaited UN report says. The study indicates that complete restoration could involve the world's most wide-ranging and long-term oil clean-up. Communities faced a significant health risk, with some families consuming water containing high levels of carcinogens, it stated. Oil giant Shell has accepted responsibility for two spills and stated that all oil spills were detrimental to Nigeria and the company. We will continue collaborating with our partners in Nigeria, including the government, to address these issues and on the next steps to assist in cleaning up Ogoniland, Mutiu Sunmonu, managing director of the Shell Petroleum Development Company of Nigeria (SPDC), stated. The Bodo fishing community has announced it will seek hundreds of millions of dollars in compensation. Nigeria is one of the world's leading oil producers. The UN assessment of Ogoniland, located in the Niger Delta, stated that 50 years of oil operations in the region had penetrated further and deeper than many had supposed. By Peter Okwoche, BBC News. During a visit to a village in Ogoniland in 2007, I went to a small stream that provided people with water for all their daily needs. The effects of oil spillage were evident. On the water's surface, there was a thin film of oil. Villagers moved it with their hands before collecting water. Villagers informed me no fish had been seen in the stream for more than five years. They told me people had died from oil pipes exploding and others had developed health issues after inhaling fumes from burning oil well heads. When I revisited the village in 2011, oil spillage had worsened. Villagers no longer drank water from the stream. They walked for up to four hours to obtain water. Over the past two decades, successive Nigerian governments have failed the people of Ogoniland. I doubt this report will change anything. Meanwhile, the voices of secession in Ogoniland will grow louder. In at least 10 Ogoni communities where drinking water is contaminated with high levels of hydrocarbons, public health is seriously threatened, the UN Environmental Programme (Unep) stated. Some areas that appeared unaffected were actually severely contaminated underground, Unep reported. In one community, the report states, families were drinking from wells contaminated with benzene, a known carcinogen, at 900 times the recommended levels. It mentioned scientists at the site, which was near a Nigerian National Petroleum Company pipeline, found oil slicks eight centimetres thick floating on the water. This was reportedly due to an oil spill more than six years ago, it stated. The report, based on examinations of approximately 200 locations over 14 months, said Shell had created public health and safety issues by failing to apply its own procedures in the control and maintenance of oilfield infrastructure. However, it also mentioned that local people were sabotaging pipelines to steal oil. The report states that restoring the region could cost $1bn (£613m) and take 25-30 years to complete. The environmental restoration of Ogoniland could prove to be the world's most wide-ranging and long-term oil clean-up exercise ever undertaken if contaminated drinking water, land, creeks, and important ecosystems such as mangroves are to be brought back to full, productive health, Unep stated. The report, considered the most detailed study on any area in the oil-rich Niger Delta, was partially funded by Shell following a request by the Nigerian government. Amnesty International, which has campaigned on the issue, stated the report proved Shell was responsible for the pollution. This report proves Shell has had a terrible impact in Nigeria, but has got away with denying it for decades, falsely claiming they work to best international standards, said Audrey Gaughran, Amnesty's global issues director. However, earlier, Unep spokesman Nick Nuttal told the BBC's Network Africa that the study was not intended to blame any particular stakeholder operating in Ogoniland. He also emphasised that Shell's admission of liability for two spills was unrelated to the Unep report. Shell stated on Wednesday that it accepted responsibility for the spills, which occurred in 2008 and 2009, and would settle the case under Nigerian law. The Bodo fishing community had claimed that the leaks had destroyed their environment and livelihoods. In response to Thursday's report, Mr Sunmonu said it contributed towards improving understanding of the issue of oil spills in Ogoniland. All oil spills are bad - bad for local communities, bad for the environment, bad for Nigeria and bad for SPDC, he said. We clean up all spills from our facilities, whatever the cause, and restore the land to its original state, he said. The SPDC managing director also urged the authorities to do everything possible to curb illegal refining and the sabotaging of pipelines. Ogoni communities have long complained about the damage to their communities, but they say they have mostly been ignored. The issue was highlighted by the writer Ken Saro-Wiwa, who was executed in 1995 by Nigeria's military government, sparking international condemnation. The campaign forced Shell to stop pumping oil out of Ogoniland, but it continues to operate pipelines in the region and spills have persisted.

text: Learning a foreign language should be made compulsory in primary schools here, a new report has said. These are external links and will open in a new window. In Northern Ireland, learning a second language is not a statutory component of the primary school curriculum. In England and Scotland, conversely, primary school pupils are expected to learn a foreign language. The review of primary languages in Northern Ireland has been conducted by researchers from Stranmillis University College. The authors surveyed language learning at over 100 schools. They discovered that Spanish and French were the most popular in schools where languages were taught. Some pupils also learned German or Mandarin. However, not all primary schools offered an additional language. This led the authors to conclude that there was a lack of equity in provision for children across the country. They also found little consistency in how often languages were taught to pupils and when they began to learn a language. Some primary principals also expressed concerns about the level of support and resources available to their teachers and pupils. However, the majority of principals and teachers who participated in the study agreed that learning an additional language was important and valuable. But they also stated that teaching foreign languages was not a priority for schools as it was not assessed or measured. The report's authors stated that the development of language skills was vital for economic prosperity, social cohesion and the acceptance of diverse cultural identities. It is hoped that the findings of this study may encourage policymakers, business and educational providers to support the revision and improvement of current curriculum provision in additional language learning, the report said. It also stated that language learning was conducive to economic growth and that can enhance the lives and future employability of children and young people. Across the European Union (EU), more than 80% of primary pupils learn an additional language. The research was commissioned by the Northern Ireland Languages Council. It is a body established by the Department of Education, and over 20 organisations are represented on the council, from business, education and the community sector.

text: Lewis Hamilton collided with Mercedes team-mate Nico Rosberg on the last lap before passing him to win a thrilling Austrian Grand Prix. The German entered a corner late as Hamilton attempted to pass around the outside, damaging his front wing and finishing fourth. Rosberg received a 10-second penalty and two licence penalty points from stewards for causing a collision. This reduces Hamilton's deficit to Rosberg to 11 points in the championship race. He was pushed off the track, but the collision had damaged Rosberg's front wing, which sparked along the track as Hamilton passed the German, who then lost further positions to Red Bull's Max Verstappen and Ferrari's Kimi Raikkonen. After enduring a round of booing from the predominantly German-Austrian crowd, Hamilton remarked on the podium: He made a mistake into Turn One and I had an opportunity to go around the outside in Turn Two. I left a lot of room on the inside and I guess he locked up and crashed into me. Rosberg, who also received a reprimand for driving with a damaged car, had a different perspective, but BBC F1 analyst Allan McNish stated that any blame for the collision lay with Rosberg. Absolutely gutted, said Rosberg. We were battling and I was struggling a little with my brakes. I went a bit deep but that is fine because I am on the inside so I can dictate. So I was surprised Lewis turned in and caused a collision. It's unbelievable. Mercedes stated Rosberg experienced a brake-by-wire failure, affecting the rear axle, at the end of the penultimate lap. However, team boss Toto Wolff initially described the collision as brainless without specifying who he believed was at fault. The victory will be a relief to Hamilton, who might have thought pit errors and questionable strategy could cost him. The world champion will also want to understand how he ended up behind Rosberg initially, having started from pole and led the first 21 laps of the race as the second Mercedes advanced from sixth. Hamilton secured a brilliant pole position in the damp conditions on Saturday, beating Rosberg by more than half a second and appeared well-positioned for a win with his team-mate demoted to sixth on the grid due to a gearbox penalty. Hamilton led comfortably in the early stages of the race as Rosberg overtook Force India's Nico Hulkenberg and McLaren's Jenson Button to run third behind Hamilton and Ferrari's Kimi Raikkonen by lap 10. His engineer then decided to bring him in for his first pit stop, fitting the most durable soft tyres, while Hamilton remained out on the more fragile ultra-softs at the front. Although Hamilton was easily able to stay clear of Raikkonen, this allowed Rosberg to close in on Hamilton, leaving him 21 seconds behind and in fourth place behind Raikkonen and his team-mate Sebastian Vettel when Hamilton made his first stop on lap 21. That should have been just enough to ensure Hamilton retained the lead, but he was delayed in the pits by a problem with his left rear wheel and rejoined behind Rosberg. After a mid-race safety car, it initially appeared as if Rosberg might be on a two-stop strategy and Hamilton only one, and Mercedes confirmed that was indeed the initial plan. However, Mercedes realised the one-stop would not work for Hamilton, so in the end both stopped for tyres within a lap of each other, Hamilton first on lap 54. Hamilton was fitted with used soft tyres, while Rosberg was on new super-softs, a set of which the world champion did not have. Hamilton questioned the decision but was told by Bonnington they felt they were the best available tyres. He was proved right, leading to the dramatic climax. The safety car was triggered by Vettel's right rear tyre exploding on the pit straight on lap 27, within the predicted life of the tyre at the start of the race. Vettel was leading ahead of Rosberg at the time and will be furious about another lost opportunity in a season full of them for Ferrari. Out of nowhere the tyre decided to blow up, said Vettel, who was the last driver to suffer a tyre failure during the race with a 200mph blow-out at the Belgian Grand Prix last year. Behind Rosberg at the finish was Red Bull's Daniel Ricciardo and McLaren's Jenson Button, who drove a strong race to convert his remarkable third place on the grid to a solid points finish. If it were a three-game series at the same time, maybe it would have an effect, but for one game they'll be ready. But I don't think it's much of a gain for us." Manly will welcome back the Australian and Manly winger David Williams, who has been cleared after missing the Sea Eagles' grand final victory with a broken neck. Of the nine players still with the Manly club after their 28-20 victory over Leeds in the World Club Challenge in 2009, one is in the squad of twenty and will be playing for coach Geoff Toovey’s team this week. “We’ll go anywhere,” he said. 'I think it will be a very exciting experience for our players to play in front of hostile supporters. We have hardly any of our actors here.'

text: Thirteen schoolgirls have been on a hunger strike for six days to protest against daily sexual harassment in the northern Indian state of Haryana. These are external links and will open in a new window. The girls, aged between 16 and 18, informed the BBC that men frequently made sexual remarks when they travelled to school in a neighbouring village. The teenagers stated that local officials in Rewari district had failed to protect them. Police have now pledged to provide better security for the girls. The government has also vowed to upgrade the existing school in their village to higher-secondary level so they no longer need to commute to school. Views of sexual harassment in India. On patrol with India's anti-harassment squad. However, the students, who have been drinking water but refusing food, declared they would not end their strike until they received written orders. Some parents and students who are not on hunger strike have also joined the protest. Almost every day, we face eve teasing [a local term for sexual harassment], Sheetal, one of the 13 students, told BBC Hindi's Nitin Srivastava. Should we stop studying? Should we stop dreaming? Are only rich people and their children allowed to dream? The government should protect us or open a higher-secondary school in our village. Another student, Sujata, said men often try to touch us inappropriately. They write our phone numbers on walls, make nasty comments. Actually much worse happens, but not everything can be described, she said. It has been a harrowing week for these girls as they demand better schooling options and safety. Their parents have also been protesting, putting aside their farm work and daily jobs. Haryana is one of the most backward states in India in terms of gender ratio, and crimes against women are not uncommon. But this is likely the first time that young girls have decided to protest. They have found strong support from their community, including men who admit that women need to be treated equally. The mother of a protesting student said it was painful to see these girls suffer. These young girls face the kind of harassment that I can't even describe. When we complain to the police, they put pressure on us to take such cases back, she said. Rohtash Kumar, the father of a protesting girl, said the problem of harassment had existed for years. It's the first time that girls have taken the matter into their own hands. The men in our village support their struggle, he said. He wants to see concrete assurances that changes promised by police and local officials will be implemented. Such promises have not been fulfilled in the past. We want to be sure that our struggle doesn't go waste because of a false promise, Mr Kumar added.
