text: In our series of letters from African journalists, veteran Ghanaian journalist Elizabeth Ohene reflects on why in Ghana a person's age is not etched in stone. These are external links and will open in a new window. Ghanaians do not have a particular fondness for numbers. We tend to be rather relaxed, especially concerning figures related to age. A person's date of birth or age is not deemed significant and seldom features in any narrative about that individual. I understand that in many regions globally, once you are born and acquire a date of birth, it remains with you. It is immutable and accompanies you to the grave. In Ghana, it is not uncommon to see newspaper notices announcing a change in someone's date of birth. This frequently occurs when a working individual's retirement date is imminent. People then swear an affidavit to alter their profiles from being known as 59-year-olds to becoming 55-year-olds, enabling them to continue receiving a salary for a few additional years. According to the constitution, the retirement age for most public officers is 60. Seven years younger. Some individuals have been known to swear affidavits to alter their date of birth, placing them in Primary Class One before they were born. The most dramatic Notice of Change of Date of Birth I have witnessed reduced an official's age by seven years. I am addressing this topic due to a recent news item I found to be exceptionally extraordinary, even for Ghana. The news report indicated that approximately 800 teachers had applied to the Ghana Education Service to have their ages changed. Some sought to alter their dates of birth to appear younger, while a few wished to change them to appear older than what was documented. The news story was met with considerable outrage, and I thought: This must mean Ghana is finally aligning with the rest of the world in respecting dates of birth. How can people want their dates of birth to be changed? was the incredulous reaction I heard from many young people. However, the head of one of the teaching unions came forward to vigorously defend his members. The teachers wanted their dates of birth changed only because, according to him, errors had been made at the time of their employment by the payroll departments in entering the dates. This phenomenon has been possible because very few births are recorded. In the past, illiterate parents did not bother to record their children's births, and over time the date was lost in the mists of memory. A birth certificate is supposed to be provided before a child can be enrolled in school, yet somehow many people manage to enrol their children without birth certificates. Elizabeth Ohene: This total disregard for the sanctity of dates of birth manifests in other ways that sometimes undermine all official records in Ghana. When later in life you require a birth certificate, you would go before a commissioner of oaths and offer a date said to be based on the best guessestimate given by your parents or family member. Much later in life, when approaching the compulsory retirement age of 60 and desperately wanting to continue working a few more years because you cannot survive on your pension, you return to the commissioner of oaths and swear you have now discovered compelling evidence that the original date on your certificate was incorrect. For instance, you were told you were born in the year the village chief was enstooled (inaugurated), and you have discovered he was enstooled in 1968 and not 1965. There probably does not exist any official record of the date of the enstoolment of this chief anyway, so why make a fuss about a difference of three years? This total disregard for the sanctity of dates of birth manifests in other ways that sometimes undermine all official records in Ghana. I have seen school children who cannot be more than 14 years old possessing voter registration cards. The law states you must be 18 to register to vote. The consequences might follow you through life unless you are prepared to continue visiting the commissioner of oaths to acquire new dates of birth. Police recruitment advertisements have a cut-off age of 25 years. You are actually 21 but possess a voter registration card stating you are 26 because you passed yourself off as 18 when you were 14. Sometimes it has been football players attempting to reduce their ages to participate in age-restricted competitions. Nowadays, technology is being employed to ensure the integrity of such competitions, making it challenging for individuals in their 20s to participate in under-17 competitions. Numerous attempts have been made to enforce the registration of births and deaths, and so far all these attempts have failed spectacularly. There is already a regulation issued by the head of the civil service some years ago which states public officials are not permitted to change their dates of birth during their tenure in government employment. In other words, you are bound to the date of birth you enter the service with, and you cannot become younger or older by swearing an affidavit. It was always going to be challenging to enforce this directive because many people here believe their ages are confidential and should not be disclosed. You could ask someone how old they were and receive a reply: Is it my official or real age that you want? One of the firm promises made by the new government is that within its first year in office, a national identification system will be established. In other words, all Ghanaians will possess identification cards with their unchangeable biometric data, and none of us will be able to swear an affidavit to acquire a new date of birth. We are all holding our breath. And whilst I await this dramatic change, I have been pondering if there are any advantages in the current situation where a person's age is a changeable and confidential figure. My mind turned to a sentence I read in an online article in a British newspaper earlier this year. Those who follow tennis would recognise that this was part of a report during the Australian Open: A few hours after Serena Williams, 35, joined her 36-year-old sister, Venus, in the women's final by trouncing the 34-year-old Mirjana Lucic-Baroni, Federer, 35, somehow conjured some more retro magic to beat Stan Wawrinka, a mere 31, for the 19th time in 22 matches, the article in The Guardian stated. I fear that faced with the possibility of such prose in our newspapers, many people in Ghana are going to opt to keep dates of birth a changeable and private event. text: A chronology of key events: These are external links and will open in a new window. c. AD 250-900 - Classical Maya city-states thrive in the far south of present-day Mexico, as well as in neighbouring Guatemala and Belize, before experiencing a mysterious collapse. c. AD 0-500 - The major cultural and religious centre of Teotihuacan prospers. It is believed to have been one of the world's largest cities at the time, but little is known about its ethnic and political nature. Aztec-era traditions are still being preserved. Mexico City to teach the Aztec language. Festival highlights indigenous pride. 6th-7th century - Influx of new peoples into central Mexico from the north, including Nahuatl speakers. 800-1000 - The peak of Toltec culture, centred on the city of Tula, in present-day Hidalgo province. 10th-16th centuries - Revitalised Maya civilisation flourishes in the northern Yucatan peninsula, creating major cities such as Chichen Itza and Uxmal. 1428-1521 - The latest in a long line of indigenous civilisations, the Aztec Empire—an alliance of Nahuatl-speaking city-states led by Tenochtitlan (modern-day Mexico City)—establishes dominance over much of central Mexico. 1519 - A small Spanish army led by Hernan Cortes lands at Veracruz, marking the beginning of Spain's conquest of Mexico. 1521 - Allied with native anti-Aztec forces, Cortes' men capture the capital Tenochtitlan (modern-day Mexico City). The Spanish conquest took decades to complete. BBC History: Story of the Conquistadors. 1521-1820 - Mexico becomes part of the Viceroyalty of New Spain. Independence. 1810-21 - War of Independence concludes with the creation of the short-lived Mexican Empire, which includes Central America to the southern border of present-day Costa Rica, as well as what is now the southwestern US. 1824 - Mexico becomes a federal republic after the ousting and exile of Emperor Augustin de Iturbide. Central American provinces secede, becoming the countries of Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica. The new Mexican state is marked by tension between the conservative Spanish-origin landowning elite and the largely indigenous landless minority, resulting in instability and frequent armed conflict. 1836 - The former province of Texas, by now increasingly populated by English-speaking Americans, secedes after a war, later joining the United States nine years later. 1846-8 - Mexican-American War ends with Mexico being compelled to sell its northern provinces (including present-day California, Nevada, New Mexico, Arizona, and Utah) to the US. 1855-72 - La Reforma period, characterised by liberal reforms limiting the power and landholdings of the Catholic Church. 1864-7 - Archduke Maximilian Habsburg of Austria is installed as Mexican emperor with support from Napoleon III of France and conservative landowners, but is overthrown and executed by Republican rebels. 1876-1911 - Porfirio Diaz's 35-year-long dictatorship—known as the Porfiriato—brings a long period of stability, modernisation, and economic growth, but at the cost of political repression and stagnation. 1910-1920 - Mexican Revolution ends the Porfirio Diaz dictatorship and leads to the establishment of a constitutional republic. 1913-14 - Diaz's successor, the liberal Francisco Madero, introduces land reform and labour legislation before being assassinated. Victoriano Huerta seizes power. Political unrest continues with Zapata leading a peasant revolt in the south. Russian revolutionary Leon Trotsky (l) arrives in Mexico, where he was tracked down and killed. The ice pick assassination. 1914 - Victoriano Huerta—viewed with suspicion by the United States for alleged pro-German sympathies—resigns and is succeeded by Venustiano Carranza. 1916 - US forces cross the border in pursuit of the guerrilla leader Francisco Pancho Villa. 1917 - US forces withdraw, having failed to kill Villa. A new constitution is adopted, designed to ensure permanent democracy in Mexico. 1920 - President Venustiano Carranza is murdered. Civil war follows. 1929 - The National Revolutionary Party is formed. In 1946 it is renamed the Institutional Revolutionary Party, or PRI. 1934 - President Lazaro Cardenas begins a programme of oil nationalisation, land reform, and industrial expansion. 1940 - Leon Trotsky is murdered in Mexico. 1942 - Mexico declares war on Japan and Germany. 1960s - Unrest among peasants and labourers over unequal wealth distribution is suppressed. 1968 - Student demonstration in Tlatelolco, Mexico City, during the Olympic Games is fired upon by Mexican security forces. Hundreds of protesters are killed or wounded. The extent of the violence shocks the country. 1976 - Huge offshore oil reserves are discovered; the Cantarell field becomes the mainstay of Mexico's oil production. 1985 - Earthquake in Mexico City kills thousands and leaves many more homeless. 1993 - Mexican parliament ratifies the North American Free Trade Agreement (Nafta) with the US and Canada. 1994 - A guerrilla rebellion in Chiapas by the Zapatista National Liberation Army is brutally suppressed by government troops. The rebels oppose Nafta and want greater recognition for Indian rights. The government recognises the Zapatista National Liberation Front (EZLN). 1994 August - Presidential elections are won by PRI candidate Ernesto Zedillo Ponce de Leon, after the previous candidate, Luis Donaldo Colosio, was murdered. The stock market plunges in December, and the peso loses a third of its value. 1995 - Former President Carlos Salinas goes into exile after his brother Raul Salinas is connected with Colosio's murder. 1995 November - The government and the EZLN reach an agreement on greater autonomy for the indigenous Mayans of Chiapas. 1996 - The insurgency in the south escalates as the leftist Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) attacks government troops. 1997 - The PRI suffers heavy losses in elections and loses its overall majority in the lower house of parliament for the first time since 1929. 1997 December - 45 Indians are killed by paramilitary gunmen in a Chiapas village. The incident causes an international outcry, and President Zedillo starts an investigation. 1998 January - Governor of Chiapas resigns. Peace talks with the rebels are reactivated but break down at the end of the year. 2000 July - Vicente Fox of the opposition Alliance for Change wins presidential elections, the first opposition candidate ever to do so. Parliamentary elections see the Alliance for Change emerge as the strongest party, beating the PRI by just over 1%. 2000 December - Vicente Fox is sworn in as president. 2001 March - Zapatista guerrillas, led by Subcomandante Marcos, stage their Zapatour, a march from Chiapas to Mexico City to highlight their demands. 2001 April - Parliament passes a bill increasing the rights of indigenous people. A few days later, Subcomandante Marcos rejects the bill, saying it leaves the Indian population worse off than before. Marcos says the uprising in Chiapas will continue. 2001 November - President Fox appoints a prosecutor to investigate the disappearance of left-wing activists during the 1970s and 1980s. 2002 March - Roberto Madrazo wins the contest to lead the PRI, which governed for 71 years until 2000. 2002 June - Millions of secret security files are released, shedding light on the torture and killing by security forces of hundreds of political activists in the 1960s and 1970s. President Fox says his government is not afraid to pursue prosecutions. 2002 July - Former President Luis Echeverria is questioned about massacres of student protesters in 1968, when he was interior minister, and in 1971 when he was president. The ski-mask-wearing sub-commandante Marcos was the public face of the popular rebellion. In the footsteps of Zapata. Profile: Zapatista's mysterious leader. 2002 September - Three army officers are charged with first-degree murder over the killings of 134 leftists in the 1970s. 2004 July - Investigator deems 1971 shooting of student protesters by government forces to have been genocide; judge refuses to order arrest of former President Luis Echeverria on charges that he ordered the attack. 2005 January - Six prison officers are murdered and top-security jails are put on high alert amid escalating tension between the authorities and drug gangs. 2005 April - Political furore as Mexico City mayor and presidential favourite Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador is stripped of his immunity from prosecution by Congress in a land dispute. The government eventually abandons the prosecution. 2006 February - A federal post of special prosecutor is created to tackle violent crime against women. text: Comedian Bob Mortimer has revealed that he got married less than an hour before he went into hospital for a triple bypass operation. Mortimer's heart issues compelled him and comedy partner Vic Reeves to cancel the initial leg of their 25th anniversary UK tour last October. text: Stoke City boss Mark Hughes says Liverpool were incredibly fortunate to reach the League Cup final. The Potters exited on penalties after concluding 1-1 on aggregate in the two-leg semi-final, following their first victory at Anfield since March 1959. Stoke's goal in first-half injury time by forward Marko Arnautovic was largely due to good fortune. It was offside, but we deserved it. We got the goal that won us the game, but not the tie, Hughes told BBC Stoke. We always thought we had a chance even if others didn't, but we just couldn't get that second goal even though we appeared the likelier side to score. You can see by the reaction of their fans and their players that they have been incredibly fortunate to progress to the final. Obviously once it goes to penalties it can go either way and heartbreakingly for us it has gone their way. These sorts of things happen in sport, but that still doesn't make it any easier to accept. Stoke, who are ninth in the Premier League table, just a point behind Jurgen Klopp's seventh-placed Liverpool, faced a challenge after a disappointing performance in the first leg at the Britannia Stadium three weeks earlier. However, despite being without captain Ryan Shawcross at the back, with Marc Muniesa stepping in, the Potters prevented Liverpool from managing a single effort on target. And a return to old Tony Pulis tactics with the selection of big men Jon Walters and Peter Crouch up front made them more of an attacking threat than the home side. To a man I can't fault any of them, said Hughes. They all put in fantastic performances. I'd highlight Peter Crouch who, along with Marc Muniesa, hadn't played for a long time. We will hopefully get the credit we deserve. We came in difficult circumstances after losing the home leg, but were very positive and made a few changes, and on the night we were by far the better team. I'm really proud of what the players produced, but unfortunately we aren't the ones going to Wembley. Stoke manager Hughes now has concerns about Arnautovic and Charlie Adam ahead of Saturday's fourth round FA Cup tie at Crystal Palace. Arnautovic suffered a back injury after twice falling heavily following challenges from Liverpool defender Jon Flanagan, while second-half substitute Adam lasted barely half an hour before going off in the first half of extra time with calf trouble. Adam was one of three players on the pitch from the last time Liverpool won a trophy, the League Cup final, also on penalties, when he missed in the shootout against Cardiff City in 2012. Stoke right-back Glen Johnson was also in the Liverpool team that day, scoring one of their three penalties. The only survivor from Kenny Dalglish's Reds team from 2012 still present was Jordan Henderson, now the captain. Lucas Leiva, one of the Reds' penalty shootout heroes on Tuesday night, missed that Wembley final due to injury.

text: The debate over flying the Confederate flag has reignited in the US, but the American South isn't the only place in the world you'll see the emblem - it's also proudly displayed in the rural Brazilian town of Santa Barbara D'Oeste. Once annually, the descendants of approximately 10,000 Confederates who fled the United States to Brazil after the US Civil War gather for a type of family reunion. They all participate in stereotypically southern activities such as square dancing, eating fried chicken and biscuits, and listening to George Strait, states Asher Levine, a Sao Paulo-based correspondent for Reuters. And numerous Confederate flags are present everywhere. Despite being six or seven generations removed from their antebellum ancestry, many local Brazilians still uphold strong connections to Southern culture and proudly display the Confederate flag. However, for them, Levine notes, the flag serves more as an ethnic symbol than a political one. They perceive themselves as ethnically American to some extent, he remarks. At an Italian festival, you would observe people waving an Italian flag. Or on Saint Patrick's Day, you see people waving the Irish flag. They view it similarly. They have no political affiliation to it whatsoever. Over time, the Southern white population has intermingled with Brazilians, resulting in individuals with a variety of different skin tones waving the Confederate flag. Americans might find the resulting visual surprising. Many descendants of these Confederates also have African ancestry, so at the party, you will see people with dark skin waving the Confederate flag. Levine mentions he spoke to an American at the festival who was utterly astonished at witnessing a young girl singing Amazing Grace—often sung in black churches across the US—while standing atop a Confederate flag. The banner is ubiquitous—children wave mini-flags and women don Confederate flag dresses. You know, the symbolism is entirely lost on them, but for us, it's quite a contrast, Levine comments. Despite being a very mixed-race country, Levine notes that the killings in Charleston are perceived in Brazil more as a gun safety issue than a racial one. When they observe an event like what occurred in South Carolina last week, they question if it's truly safer in the United States. This story was originally broadcast on PRI's The World. Listen here. text: The Labour Party has made legal checks to ensure its leadership contest is complying with the law and try to avoid challenges to the result. New regulations permit members of the public to register to vote as a registered supporter for £3. The contest has been troubled by concerns that members of other parties have attempted to influence the outcome. A spokeswoman for acting leader Harriet Harman dismissed any suggestion of plans to halt or suspend the election. The spokeswoman stated: The party's focus is on ensuring that the 2014 rules are fully adhered to. We have sought legal advice to ensure that the rules are being followed and that all possible due diligence is being conducted. However, there are no plans to halt or suspend the contest. We monitor the process closely. A Labour spokeswoman reported that a Conservative activist who had paid £1 to join the Labour Party—under a discounted rate for former armed forces members—had been barred and would not receive a vote in the leadership contest. Alan Pearmain, a parish councillor and deputy chairman of the South Ribble Conservative Association, informed the BBC's Victoria Derbyshire programme he had joined as a form of mischief-making. Meanwhile, Scotland's Daily Record has endorsed left-winger Jeremy Corbyn in the leadership race. The newspaper's front-page endorsement follows a week after its sister paper—the Daily Mirror—endorsed Andy Burnham. • Everything you need to know about the four candidates aspiring to become the next Labour leader. Mr Corbyn expressed: I'm obviously pleased to have the backing of a paper with such a long tradition of support for the Labour Party. I'm sure that, at least in part, this endorsement will have been made with Labour's future in Scotland in mind, which is crucial as Labour needs to reconnect with communities in Scotland if we are to succeed across the UK. Meanwhile, former Home Secretary David Blunkett—who supports Andy Burnham for the leadership—has joined other senior Labour figures in warning about a Corbyn victory. He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: Jeremy Corbyn has not only been effective at opposing the Tories, he's also been profoundly effective at opposing my party. If you want to continue being in opposition, vote for someone who is good at opposition, he added. Mr Blunkett expressed his desire for someone who can actually address the world of tomorrow rather than taking us back to Old Labour or, for that matter, New Labour in the 90s, because we are addressing an entirely different world. Sarah Brown, the wife of former Prime Minister Gordon, has meanwhile endorsed Yvette Cooper for the leadership, with Andy Burnham as her second choice. Opinion polls indicate Ms Cooper is in a close contest with Mr Burnham to emerge as the main challenger to Mr Corbyn, with Liz Kendall trailing in fourth place. Mr Burnham, Yvette Cooper, and Liz Kendall are competing against Mr Corbyn in the contest. Former Labour leader Ed Miliband has faced calls to apologise for the voting system being used to elect his successor. The shift from an electoral college system, which gave equal weight to MPs, party members, and trade unionists, to one member, one vote, with the public allowed to join as registered supporters for £3, was overwhelmingly supported by a special Labour conference last year. However, critics, including backbench Labour MPs Simon Danczuk and Graham Stringer, argue that the new system is too open to abuse. The election result will be announced at a special conference on 12 September.

text: Nearly 15 years ago, successful Nigerian businessman Anselm Okoukoni was one of the desperate African migrants prepared to do anything to get to Europe. As the eldest son of his widowed mother, a farmer, custom dictated that the responsibility for his six siblings would transfer to him immediately upon his graduation from university. Long before obtaining his degree in statistics, he resolved not to join the ranks of unemployed university graduates in his country. However, the embassies of Italy, Germany, Spain, Austria, France, Belgium, the UK, and the US all denied him a visa. Nonetheless, his prospects improved when an acquaintance introduced him to someone who could facilitate a visa to Greece for approximately 400,000 naira, then equivalent to about $3,500 (£2,350). My uncle in America had already told me to inform him whenever I secured a visa, Mr Okoukoni stated. He soon received a total of $5,000 to cover the visa, airfare, and some travel allowance—a gift, not a loan—his uncle's contribution to his nephew's future. At 24, Mr Okoukoni departed Nigeria in December 2002, arriving in a country where he knew no one, and quickly proceeded to Italy where he had friends. Anselm Okoukoni: I felt I was doing something professional. I was paying taxes. I was sending money home to Nigeria. When his visa expired several weeks later, he followed the example of most of his friends and claimed asylum. I don't remember what story I told, he said, explaining that the thing to do was to choose a topical narrative. Over the next two years, he struggled to learn Italian and found it impossible to secure a decent job. He ended up street hawking, which is illegal in Italy, and was arrested several times with his goods seized. It wasn't the kind of life I wanted to live, he said, adding that his income was barely sufficient to pay for his siblings' school fees. Once again, fortune favoured Mr Okoukoni when someone introduced him to a man with a genuine passport from a European country who bore a strong resemblance to him. He agreed to let him use his passport to cross into the UK in the summer of 2004. Safe in London at last, Mr Okoukoni was both shocked and thrilled by his first impressions of the city. I saw Africans driving buses and cabs, and working in McDonald's and in hospitals, he said. In Italy, you could hardly see a black person doing those kinds of jobs. Most of the black people I saw were factory workers or farm workers or cleaners or prostitutes. His Nigerian friends in London assisted him with accommodation, found him a job as a parking attendant, and organised the necessary documentation. He would work under someone else's identity. Within one year, I had job satisfaction, he said. I felt I was doing something professional. I was paying taxes. I was sending money home to Nigeria. Mr Okoukoni recalls being delighted with his salary of £8.50 an hour, but after seeing an advert for a community college open day, he decided it was time to further his education. Of all the vocational courses available, he chose to study plumbing. I remembered that I'd never entered a house in Nigeria where the plumbing was done properly, he said. The one-day-a-week course was free for British citizens but not for foreigners, and he was required to show his passport proving his leave to remain in the UK when he paid his fee of £1,400. Fortunately, the woman who registered him believed his story that he had forgotten his passport at home. After a year of studying, he quit his job and, using his student ID card, secured a new job as an apprentice plumber with a construction company. The pay was even more than what I earned as a parking attendant—at £9.70 an hour, he said. Why visa rejections do not halt Nigerian migrants Over the next few years, Mr Okoukoni obtained another qualification in plumbing, one in heating and gas, and a certificate in building services engineering. I paid for all these courses myself. Everything cost me roughly £10,000. Long before completing his studies in 2012, he had decided to return to Nigeria, knowing his skills would be invaluable in his home country. In 2013, he purchased a van and loaded it with all manner of tools of his trade, then shipped it off to Nigeria. Shortly afterwards, he resigned from his £12-an-hour job in London for a property development company in Lagos. He proved so efficient his employer was reluctant to let him go at the end of it. But I wanted to go and build my own business, Mr Okoukoni said. His plans to immediately build a website and advertise aggressively did not materialise, as he was soon overwhelmed with contracts that came simply by referral from satisfied clients. As he had anticipated, the shortage of quality workmen in Nigeria made his plumbing, fire protection, air conditioning, and ventilation services highly sought after. Right now, I shuttle between Port Harcourt and Lagos doing jobs, he said. In Nigeria, it is common to enter a magnificent building only to find that the toilets do not flush properly, or that the wall sockets are misaligned, or that the door handles come off in your hand, or that the windows cannot shut, or that the interlocking tiles have gaps that can damage the Gucci or Jimmy Choo heels of the owners. Many developers aiming for high quality have resorted to importing artisans from nearby countries like Togo and Benin, reputed to be more skilled than their Nigerian counterparts. Mr Okoukoni attributes the poor quality of work by Nigerian artisans to their primary focus on money. The time it takes to learn a skill is time not earning an income. So, once they can hang one door, they go away and tell everyone that they are a carpenter. They stop coming to work. They don't wait to learn everything they should. His company, Ansko Building Services Ltd, currently employs 12 plumbers and two apprentices. His plumbers initially claimed to be experienced, but he had to train them anew. However, he paid them while they were learning and also pays his two apprentices a salary above the country's minimum wage. That way, they are motivated to stay. Since the beginning of this year I've not touched any tool. They now do all the work while I supervise. Mr Okoukoni's future plans include opening a training centre for people in the building services industry, to show them in particular the range of tools they could use. Nobody has ever taken the time to teach them, he said. He is ashamed of all the illegal steps he took during his journey to and through Europe, but he is pleased with how things have turned out. He is now able to provide employment for other young Nigerians, take care of the wife he married after returning to Nigeria, look after his mother, and pay for his brother's studies in the US. And his advice for those migrants in Europe or making their way there? When they get to Europe, they should obey the law and do the right thing. They should look for unique skills that they can develop and use to improve the society over there and also back home. If you go to Europe to simply look for money, you are wasting your time.

text: Planning permission for a controversial peace centre at Northern Ireland's former Maze prison has been granted. It follows years of political disagreement over the future of the site near Lisburn, which housed paramilitary prisoners during the Troubles from 1971 to 2000. Ten men perished at the prison during the 1981 republican hunger strikes. Unionists expressed concern that it should not become a republican shrine. Although there have been protests by some individuals opposing the new centre, it is understood that planners received only a single formal objection to the application for the new building. It has been designed by architect Daniel Libeskind, renowned for his involvement in the plan for building on the site of New York's Ground Zero. It is a standalone structure but is situated between two other sets of buildings that have also been retained and include parts of the former prison, such as a watchtower, prison hospital, compound, and H Block. There are also a pair of World War II hangars that were part of the old Long Kesh RAF airfield. Announcing the decision, Northern Ireland Environment Minister Alex Attwood stated: There is learning to be taken from the conflict here. The centre can contribute to sharing this learning and perhaps help inform the resolution of conflict in other places. I believe that good planning needs good design. That is certainly the case in the design of the centre created by Daniel Libeskind, a world leader in architecture and a friend of Northern Ireland. Most of the cost of the peace-building and conflict resolution centre will be covered by an £18m grant from the European Union. The 350-acre site of the former prison is being redeveloped at a cost of £300m. A large part of it has been designated for the Royal Ulster Agricultural Society (RUAS). Since the jail closed in 2000, there has been ongoing debate about how the site should be used. It was earmarked for a new national sports stadium, but the proposal was rejected after years of disagreement. In April, DUP MLA Edwin Poots stated his party had made a corporate decision to support the redevelopment of the former Maze Prison site. Speaking on BBC NI's The View, the Lagan Valley MLA said the sooner the site was redeveloped, the better, and asserted it would not become a republican shrine. Simultaneously, a senior republican ex-prisoner stated any new peace and reconciliation centre on the former prison site must reflect the stories of all involved. Seanna Walsh said this should include loyalists and the British Army.

text: Married couple Dilshad and Barinder Hothi are joint founders of the international training company, the Knowledge Academy, which they aim to turn into the Amazon of the education world. When a husband and wife team jointly manage a business, one might wonder: who truly holds the reins? With the Hothis, it is difficult to discern. In conversation, they enthusiastically overlap, interrupting and completing each other's sentences. She is eager to discuss what distinguishes their company in the already saturated market for professional training. The future is about blending, she states. Our online learning courses are traditional, computer-based courses, as expected, but we offer what we call walk-in clinics. So if someone wishes to discuss an issue, they can find a locally-based instructor, visit, ask questions, and receive human interaction. Dilshad is expansive about their grand vision. From the outset, he says, they observed how the internet was transforming the way people purchased books, groceries, and clothes, and thought: Why won't it do the same for training? I knew there was a phenomenal opportunity, he asserts. In the next 10 years, we'll be a global household name, I firmly believe that—similar to Google or Facebook—we will probably be as large, if not larger. That might sound like hubris, but the Knowledge Academy has expanded rapidly in its first six years and is one of the largest training companies globally, measured by the number of courses it offers—over 5,000—in numerous locations. By the end of this year, they claim they will provide training in 3,000 cities across 210 countries, from the US to Australia, Bhutan to Chile. It delivers courses in dozens of professional areas from project management and IT to social media, aviation, and animation. They have provided training to companies including Rolls Royce, HSBC, PwC, and Disney. However, while their operations are global, they themselves originate from a very specific cultural blend, a combination of Indian and English influences. Barinder's parents, immigrants to Britain from the Punjab, operated a restaurant in Harrow, London. Neither of them spoke any English, she says, which meant she and her siblings were involved in the business from an early age, assisting their parents at the bank and with customers. But as in many Asian immigrant families, the children's education was always a priority. I still can hear my mum now saying 'Study, because this is what is going to help you in life,' says Barinder. Yet if Barinder's life in Britain was imbued with Indian values, Dilshad's schooldays were a mirror image. I was born and raised in India itself, he says. His father was in the Indian air force, and his family chose for him the closest they could find to a British public school experience. They put me in Lawrence School, Sanawar, he says. It's the Eton equivalent of India. He became house captain, played cricket, and absorbed the very British atmosphere of the former colonial military school, at the foot of the Himalayas. I think my school background was very important, being a house captain. We were very competitive and sports-driven. We had a cricket competition and field hockey and athletics, and I used to build tactics and think how many medals I'd go after. When he arrived in the UK, at the age of 21, Dilshad met Barinder through his aunt. For several years he worked for a UK-based training company while she worked for Microsoft. They decided to launch their own company at what to many would have seemed an inauspicious moment—in 2009 as the global economy crashed. It was actually the best decision ever. Any other time would have been more challenging, says Barinder. The new business benefited from the large pool of people who had been made redundant and lacked formal qualifications to present to prospective employers. There were so few positions that you needed to have more badges on your CV to get a job, says Dilshad. Now, he says, sites like LinkedIn have made formal qualifications even more important by making them constantly visible to everyone. There is now one risk on the horizon, though. That for Dilshad and Barinder, the business will consume their life together entirely. Although they barely spend 10 minutes together during the working day from 8am to 6pm, once at home around the kitchen table or on walks at the weekend, they admit, the conversation almost always turns to work. Their daughter, aged nine, has already spent so many hours at their office she is a proficient operator of the franking machine and can recite the names of almost every member of staff. Quite often we have to tell each other to turn the iPads off, says Barinder. They have developed a pattern of working very hard for a few months then taking a luxury break, somewhere like Dubai, for a few days. Neither seems to resent the time and dedication required, though they do approach things differently. I'm more conservative, says Barinder. Typically British. And if she were not there to keep Dilshad in check? I'd try to do 10 things at once, he says, grinning. So who is in charge? Barinder's in charge of the people. I'm probably in charge of the strategy itself, he admits. Do they argue? Barinder has been very supportive, he says. If she's supportive, then is he really in charge? She laughs. But refuses to concede any ground at all.

text: Prestonpans' Josh Taylor feels the calming influence of stable-mate Carl Frampton is helping him focus before his debut in Las Vegas on Saturday. The undefeated Commonwealth super-lightweight champion will face Mexico's Alfonso Olvera on the undercard of Frampton's WBA featherweight world title defence against Leo Santa Cruz. He does not put any pressure on himself, he just remains calm, Taylor said of Belfast's Frampton. I am not getting too excited about it. Taylor, 26, secured Commonwealth Games gold as an amateur in 2014. He subsequently claimed the Commonwealth title in only his seventh professional fight, defeating Derby's Dave Ryan in five rounds at Meadowbank last October. He has achieved victories in Texas and New York since turning professional in July 2015, but the contest against Olvera marks his debut in the so-called fight capital of the world. I am dazzled, star-struck, being here, said Taylor, who progressed through Terry McCormack's Lochend club in Edinburgh. You dream of fighting in Vegas and the MGM Grand, where the likes of Floyd Mayweather and Manny Pacquiao compete, when you first turn professional. I just never imagined it would be at such an early stage in my career on such a significant undercard. I am pinching myself but at the same time I am relaxed and looking forward to the fight. Being in the same stable as Carl, seeing his face up on the MGM, provides me with massive motivation to be in his position one day, fighting for a world title. If I dedicate myself as he has done, there is no reason why I cannot. He believes in his own ability. Between training sessions and away from the gym he switches off. I think it is really important, it aids recovery and makes you feel sharper. Taylor admits to being amazed at the casinos and hotels and the madness of the non-stop city and jokes he plans to tackle a 10,000-calorie burger after the fight. Before then, he must overcome Arizona-based Olvera. He has had 11 fights, he has drawn one, lost two and they were against unbeaten opponents, Taylor said of his 27-year-old adversary. He can fight and he comes to win so I am taking it very seriously. I take every fight seriously, as if it could be my last fight. Many fighters underestimate opponents and they get beaten or get hurt. Taylor is being considered as a potential opponent for his compatriot Ricky Burns, the WBA world super-lightweight champion. I feel I am ready to go in with anybody, but it is just about being smart, he said. I need to earn the right to fight Ricky Burns. He is world champion and I have only had seven fights. I have to climb the ladder. If I were in against him I would be confident, but it is not my style to call fighters out. I have massive respect for Ricky Burns. He has put Scottish boxing back on the map. Interview by Mike Costello.

text: Pop stars have always been clothes horses for fashion designers - but more and more of them are turning to designing themselves. These are external links and will open in a new window. This year, Skepta has launched his debut fashion range, and Zayn Malik's Versace Versus collection has been revealed. They join a roster of musicians-turned-designers, including Victoria Beckham, Kanye West, and Rihanna. But how straightforward is it for a pop star to succeed as a designer in a world where traditionally one had to gain experience in the trade before their designs graced the catwalk? Bid farewell to the artist formerly known as Posh Spice and welcome top British fashion designer Victoria Beckham. The former Spice Girl introduced her first fashion range in 2008, and it is fair to say there was some sniggering and raised eyebrows. However, her initial collection—a modest offering of just 10 dresses—was a hit with critics. Nicole Phelps wrote in Vogue: The woman formerly known as Posh Spice has launched a dress collection, and, believe it or not, it's one of the hottest things going in New York this week. Since then, Mrs Beckham has continued to thrive. With Victoria Beckham, everyone wanted to criticise her, but she learned from the start how to do everything from scratch—now, she might not be able to pattern-cut, but does that really matter? says Glamour's fashion director Natalie Hartley. Beckham is gaining respect because she really took a risk from the beginning. I recall the early days when she would present her shows in New York, personally guiding you through the collections and becoming very friendly with the editors. It was a clever strategy. People felt they got to know her, and she would remember you each season... she was genuinely personable, and I think that won them over. VB has received several prestigious awards, including two best brand accolades at the British Fashion Awards in 2011 and 2014. In addition to her collections, she has collaborated with US high street brand Target, offering clothes in larger sizes and affordable for those who cannot afford designer prices. She once stated: I want a woman to look and feel like the best version of herself. Kanye is just one of many US music stars who have ventured into fashion—honourable mentions also go to Jay Z and Pharrell. Kim Kardashian's husband first entered the fashion world in 2009 with a Nike collaboration—introducing the Air Yeezys—followed by further shoe lines with designer labels, including Luis Vuitton. To demonstrate his commitment to fashion, West completed an internship with Fendi that same year. An original pair of 2009 Air Yeezys is currently listed on eBay for an astounding $1,349.99 (£1,055). In 2011, the rapper debuted DW Kanye West, his women's fashion label, at Paris Fashion Week. However, it is fair to say it did not receive a warm reception from the fashion community. The Daily Telegraph's Lisa Armstrong described it as a stupendously vacuous enterprise. And the New York Times' Suzy Menkes wrote: His collection of sexpot low-bodice dresses and skintight pants, adorned with heaps of ginger fur, did not inspire the fashion crowd to tell him to give up his day job. Ouch. On the positive side, Style.com did blog that it was a work in progress. Ever the optimist, Kanye quickly returned and his second line, launched in 2012, was largely well-received. He has since produced five seasons of his Yeezy clothing line, plus a trainer collaboration with Adidas. I am actually a fan of Kanye's Yeezy collections, Natalie Hartley says. I love sportswear and think he has done a great job making simple, modern sportswear. He has also worked hard to learn the ropes, he is passionate about fashion, and who can criticise that? The No Doubt singer first ventured into fashion with the launch of her label L.A.M.B in 2004. The name is an acronym of her debut solo album Love.Angel.Music.Baby. She has frequently showcased her collections during New York Fashion Week and has received largely positive reviews. On the label's Facebook page, L.A.M.B is described as a playful juxtaposition between classic Hollywood movie star glamour and more modern and casual street influences. L.A.M.B. is always a mixture of vintage inspiration mashed up with modern and futuristic elements. It has certainly been a commercial success for the singer, generating millions of dollars annually, allowing her to expand her fashion empire to include labels Harajuku Lovers (inspired by Japanese street style) and Design With Purpose (her eco-friendly line designed with Seven for all Mankind founder Michael Glasser). While Natalie Hartley says she's personally not hugely into [Gwen's] style, she credits her for adhering to her own instincts and her fan base are up for dressing just like her. Stefani took a break from New York Fashion Week some time ago, explaining that the only reason I haven't [been] lately is because it falls when my kids go back to school and I was like, 'Oh, I guess I will go to NYFW and miss my kid's first day of kindergarten.' No. But never fear fashion fans, Gwen has returned to showcasing her creations on the runway. Hoorah for childcare! RiRi has proven to be a designer's dream in recent years, gracing red carpets in the likes of Stella McCartney, Chanel, Prada, and Giambattista Valli. But she is not just a clothes horse—she has been designing clothing for several years now across various brands. Her fashion credits include underwear, denim, and T-shirts for Armani Jeans and Emporio Armani Underwear, plus a high street collection for River Island. Natalie explains that there's an authenticity about Rihanna's fashion credentials: Rihanna does stuff that's true to her. She wouldn't put anything together she would never wear herself. Being named creative director of Puma in 2014, which involves overseeing the direction of the womenswear collection, was a significant moment for the star. She has gone on to achieve great success with her Puma trainer line, including her creeper-style trainers and furry sliders. Other recent collaborations include an all-denim collection with shoe god Manolo Blahnik (including thigh-high boots) and a range of sunglasses for Dior. Not content with clothes and shoes, RiRi also has several perfumes to her name—including Kiss and Crush—and a jewellery line with Chopard. The south London rapper first gained fashion experience shortly after achieving his first number one with his debut single Pass Out in 2010. His label Disturbing London is very much based on his own style—street mixed with high fashion. Consistently listed as one of Britain's best-dressed men, Tinie launched his What We Wear line earlier this year. Natalie says: Tinie Tempah's whole stance is sustainability and recycling materials. He obviously has a passion for that and that's what he wants to promote. Speaking about his decision to enter fashion, the man himself told Reuters: To be honest I got a little bit bored of people just saying I was really stylish just for wearing other people's clothes. After a while I feel like people start to put more of the emphasis on the clothes than the actual person...I started to feel like I was a bit of a walking mannequin. He has also expressed interest in designing a women's collection at some point. Regardless of what you're wearing, confidence is key. You can pretty much wear anything as long as you're confident enough to wear it. Fashion and style are two different things—you can wear the same things, he once told GQ. Wise words indeed. text: The UK is to spend £25m on building a prison in Jamaica so that foreign criminals in the UK can be sent home to serve sentences in the Caribbean. Prime Minister David Cameron announced the agreement as he commenced a visit to Jamaica. The initiative has been established to resolve the impasse in negotiations over a prisoner transfer agreement between the two nations. Over 600 Jamaican nationals are in UK prisons but cannot be deported due to Jamaica's inadequate prison conditions. Officials state the foreign aid-funded agreement could save taxpayers £10 million annually when transfers commence in 2020. More than 300 current offenders are anticipated to be returned under the Jamaica prison scheme, which applies to those sentenced to at least four years with 18 months or more remaining in custody. Presently, they cannot be sent to Jamaica due to concerns that prison conditions in the country would permit a successful challenge under human rights law. Jamaica ranks third highest among foreign countries with nationals serving prison sentences in the UK. Nearly 70% of Jamaicans in British prisons are serving sentences for violence and drug offences. The UK is contributing approximately 40% of the cost of constructing the planned prison, which would accommodate 1,500 individuals. Mr Cameron, who had been at the United Nations in New York for discussions on combating the Islamic State group, stated: It is absolutely right that foreign criminals who break our laws are properly punished but this shouldn't be at the expense of the hard-working British taxpayer, he remarked. That's why this agreement is so important. It will mean Jamaican criminals are sent back home to serve their sentences, saving the British taxpayer millions of pounds but still ensuring justice is done. And it will help Jamaica by helping to provide a new prison, strengthening their criminal justice system. Mr Cameron, the first British prime minister to visit the island in 14 years, is also set to announce £300 million of aid funding for infrastructure projects across the Caribbean, including roads, bridges, and ports. He stated the regional infrastructure fund, which will be delivered in collaboration with the Caribbean Development Bank, would help support economic growth in the Caribbean. Mr Cameron was greeted upon his arrival at Kingston Airport by an honour guard and national anthems before he visited RFA Lyme Bay, the British ship currently on anti-drug smuggling and emergency relief duties in the Caribbean. He is scheduled to conclude the day by holding talks with Jamaican Prime Minister Portia Simpson-Miller and attending a reception. BBC political correspondent Carole Walker reports that the PM has expressed a desire to improve a neglected relationship between the UK and Jamaica.

text: Eye doctors are warning about bird-scaring explosives, called bangers, being modified and used as fireworks. Last year, these caused five serious eye injuries when thrown into a crowd at a Bonfire Night celebration in Sussex. They expressed their concerns in a letter to the British Medical Journal (BMJ). The bangers, also known as rookies and deer scarers, have a slow-burning rope fuse that ignites several explosives along the rope. When shortened, the fuse and explosive can be ignited and thrown. They are sold to scare birds and deer away from crops. Edward Pringle, retinal fellow at Sussex Eye Hospital and one of the letter's authors, stated: These banger fireworks are easy to throw into a crowd, people look at them, and debris shoots into the eye. It's like a hand grenade going off—a flash in front of the eye, and then the sensation of a blunt injury. Doctors typically see these types of injuries in a war zone. We were observing them in a small market town—those throwing them and the people attending public events do not realise how dangerous they can be. text: More than half of overseas students in the UK say they have felt less welcome because of policies on migration, a survey suggests. A survey of over 500 overseas students across 105 institutions indicated that 52% had a negative perception of efforts to reduce migration numbers. Nearly half of North American students in the UK expressed this concern. Universities have advocated for students to be counted separately from headline migration statistics. Business Secretary Vince Cable recently stated that the UK's torrid debate on immigration risked harming the economically valuable recruitment of overseas students. He cautioned about the public panic over migrant numbers and its potential negative impact on overseas students. The survey of overseas students' attitudes in the UK, commissioned by Regent's University in London, presents a contrasting view. While students feel that migration targets have made them feel less welcome, they report a positive experience in the UK. Approximately four in five students endorsed the quality of their courses and teaching, and nearly nine in 10 would recommend studying in the UK. There is also a distinction between the public drive to reduce migrant numbers and their private experience with people in the UK, with nearly nine in 10 stating they felt welcome. There was more uncertainty regarding overseas students' relationships with other students and the broader university community, with a quarter saying they did not feel part of the university community. The survey found that 40% of overseas students mainly spend time with other students from their country, and about one in five admitted feeling isolated. Almost a third of overseas students agreed with the suggestion that my university is only interested in the fees I pay. However, despite warnings that negative rhetoric about immigration could deter potential students, application figures for this year show rising rather than declining interest in UK universities. There have been decreases from individual countries, but overall figures from the admissions service Ucas, published last month, show that applications from overseas students are higher than last year. Aldwyn Cooper, vice-chancellor of Regent's University, a private college that gained university status this year, said: These findings show that UK higher education is unmatched in its global reputation. However, there are worrying signs that the government's migration policy risks alienating overseas students in the UK. This is being compounded by the tendency in some institutions for overseas students to be left in de facto ghettos, rarely mixing outside their national groups. A spokeswoman for the Department for Business, Innovation and Skills said that international students make a huge contribution to the UK and emphasised that there is no cap on the number of legitimate overseas students. But we need to ensure that the message gets through that they are fully welcome in the UK to study. Our universities are second only to the USA as the favoured destination for international students, and to maintain this strong appeal around the globe the government is developing an industrial strategy to ensure our universities stay ahead in the global race.

text: History is useful when trying to make sense of present tensions between Russia and the West. At the Defence Academy near Shrivenham, Oxfordshire, a warehouse houses library shelves filled with an extraordinary collection of military volumes. Many are in Russian and other languages of the former Soviet bloc, meticulously gathered over the past half-century to better understand the enemy. Now renamed the Russian Military Studies Archive, it serves as a valuable chronicle of the rise and fall of the USSR, the Cold War, and ongoing tensions between Russia and the West. Since the collapse of the USSR and the Warsaw Pact, and with the advent of digital records, maintaining archives like this has become more challenging. Some have argued that in this era of cost-cutting, libraries of physical books are luxuries we may not afford. Fortunately, this military archive has not ended up as landfill. In recent years, the notion of Russia as a security priority has regained prominence. Paying attention to recent history may be crucial as we attempt to understand developments in Moscow and predict future events. Some memorabilia recalls one of the most extraordinary moments of my career: the three days in Moscow in August 1991 when defence, KGB, and Communist chiefs attempted a coup d'état. Their goal was to halt and reverse Mikhail Gorbachev's perestroika reforms, which they believed were leading their great country towards ruin. I will never forget that moment. It felt as though history was on a knife-edge, and the world could have gone either way. I remember venturing out of our BBC office in Moscow to find a line of tanks parked along the inner ring road, with confused young soldiers poking their heads out of the turrets to determine their location. The tanks were menacing, but the young soldiers were not. Our cleaning lady, Masha, wearing her usual headscarf and apron, limped out to wag a finger at them. What do you think you are doing here? Your mothers would be ashamed of you, she scolded. Take yourselves back to the barracks where you belong. The attempted coup failed because Russia's new President, Boris Yeltsin, declared their actions illegal and urged the armed forces not to follow orders, appealing to the people of Moscow to join him in forcing the coup leaders to back down. The response was astonishing and humbling. Soviet citizens, who only a few years earlier had been so fearful of speaking out in public, now took to the streets to defy the Kremlin. Young women with pushchairs, civil servants with briefcases, musicians with guitars and violins, all flocked to the Russian parliament to demonstrate through sheer numbers that they would no longer be cowed and would not allow the clock to be turned back. Among the collection are leaflets from that time—some still muddy from being trampled underfoot—hastily printed and distributed throughout Moscow by Yeltsin's supporters to counter the coup leaders' broadcasts on state TV and radio. I remember them plastered all over the metro. The words are powerful and urgent. Over Russia storm clouds are gathering, clouds of dictatorship and terror… Soldiers! I believe at this tragic hour that you will make the right choice, says one appeal. And, my heartfelt thanks to you all for your courage, says another, addressed from Yeltsin to the citizens of Moscow. I have been reflecting a lot on 1991 recently, wondering if it is possible that many Russians might take to the streets again if the current economic downturn worsened, for instance, and desperation set in. Or would they keep their heads down and focus grimly on self-preservation? And do they feel completely differently about their country and their leader today, more supportive and more reluctant to risk turmoil? It is what Russian opposition leaders must endlessly ponder, as do Vladimir Putin and his inner circle. It is perhaps important to note that the political atmosphere in 1991 was very different from now. Then, Russians felt entitled to protest, given permission from above—both at Yeltsin's urging and because for six years they had been told by none other than the General Secretary of the Communist Party, Mikhail Gorbachev, that speaking out was their right. Arguably, this empowerment from above was also a factor in 2011, when middle-class Muscovites once again took to the streets in large numbers to protest against election fraud. Possibly they too were responding to the more relaxed atmosphere that prevailed when Dmitry Medvedev was president, before Mr Putin returned. Today, there is a different mood. The public space to speak out has narrowed. Grassroots movements, far from being encouraged, are often seen as a threat. New laws and the example of top opposition leaders being murdered all conspire to persuade critics they had better stay quiet or emigrate. The new wave of patriotism since the Russian takeover of Crimea in 2014 has reinforced a powerful message from the top: that Russia is under threat from without (both from NATO and jihadists) and facing difficult times at home. So, now more than ever, goes the message, the country needs a strong leader to hold it together, smoke out that fifth column of enemies, and keep Russia safe. If there is a lesson from history, it is what happened nearly 100 years ago when the Bolshevik revolution tore the country apart. The last thing Russia needs, say President Putin's supporters, is more revolution and bloodshed. However, if I look back over my personal experience of Russia in the past 30 or 40 years, I keep thinking that it is precisely when you think the giant is slumbering that it surprises you by waking up. I cannot help remembering those Moscow citizens, young and old, who thronged to the city centre in 1991 to stop the Communists from returning. No-one, not even the demonstrators themselves most probably, expected such a street revolt. So who is to say what destiny lies ahead for Russia? History offers many parallels, from which we all draw different lessons. Perhaps what is most likely is a new twist, which will catch us all unawares.

text: More than 60% of Australia's major organised crime figures now deal in crystal meth, a new report has found. The Australian Crime Commission (ACC) report stated that the drug known as ice posed the greatest risk to Australian communities of any illegal substance. It also determined that the drug's purity had increased over recent years, rendering it even more hazardous. Methylamphetamine is available in various forms, with the crystal ice variant being the most prevalent in Australia. The report found that the price of crystal meth in Australia ranks among the highest globally, prompting the country's organised crime gangs to increasingly trade in the drug. According to the report, gangs supplying the drug were also incorporating other illegal substances into crystal meth to heighten addiction levels. The ACC reported a considerable increase in the number and weight of detections at the Australian border without any reduction in domestic production. It stated that Mexican drug cartels were becoming increasingly involved in supplying the drug internationally, collaborating with distribution networks in countries such as Australia. The precursor chemicals used by Australia's domestic producers to manufacture the drug were increasingly being imported from India and China, the report found. Chris Dawson, chief executive of the ACC, stated that the availability and addictive nature of crystal meth had created new demand in urban, rural and disadvantaged communities. Ice is a devastating, insidious drug. It affects everyone from users, their families, and their communities, to the authorities who deal with the users, he said. In November last year, New South Wales police seized more than 800 kilograms of methylamphetamine, along with two tonnes of MDMA, with a combined estimated street value of A$1.5bn (£800m; $1.2m). Earlier this month, police discovered 230 kilograms of liquid methylamphetamine in a consignment of 20,000 bottles of flavoured water intended for a Sydney warehouse. The ACC report recommended a collective national response to address the drug's increasing prevalence. Everyone plays a role in the fight against illicit drugs - including governments, law enforcement, health, education, industry, non-government organisations and the community, Mr Dawson said.

text: Former Chancellor George Osborne is to become editor of the London Evening Standard newspaper, in a surprise move that has angered opposition MPs. These are external links and will open in a new window. The Conservative MP expressed he was thrilled to succeed Sarah Sands, who is departing to edit the BBC's Today programme. Mr Osborne, who will edit the paper four days a week, plans to remain as MP for Tatton, in Cheshire. However, he is facing calls to leave politics entirely, with Jeremy Corbyn labelling the appointment a joke. The Labour leader demanded an immediate by-election in Tatton, the seat Mr Osborne has represented since 2001 and is set to be abolished at the next election. The appointment makes a mockery of the independence of the media, Mr Corbyn stated. It takes multitasking to a new level and is an insult to the electors he is supposed to serve. The Standard's owner, Evgeny Lebedev, remarked Mr Osborne was London through and through and expressed confidence that the MP was the right person to build on the fantastic legacy of Sarah Sands. I am proud to have an editor of such substance, who reinforces The Standard's standing and influence in London and whose political viewpoint - socially liberal and economically pragmatic - closely matches that of many of our readers, tweeted Mr Lebedev. The newspaper stated Mr Osborne would work as editor an average of four days a week and its schedule would enable him to continue to fulfil his other commitments, including as an MP; giving him the time to vote and contribute in Parliament in the afternoon after the paper has gone to print, and be in his constituency. Mr Osborne, who earlier addressed Standard journalists in the paper's newsroom, said it was a great honour to be asked to take charge of one of the UK's most influential newspapers. The 45-year-old sought to downplay concerns about his political neutrality, stating he would be independent and fearless in advocating for Londoners' interests. Growing up as a Londoner, I've always known that the Evening Standard is an institution that plays a huge part in the life of the city and its people, he said. Mr Osborne added: I am proud to be a Conservative MP, but as editor and leader of a team of dedicated and independent journalists, our only interest will be to give a voice to all Londoners. We will judge what the government, London's politicians and the political parties do against this simple test: is it good for our readers and good for London? If it is, we'll support them; if it isn't we'll be quick to say so. He told the newspaper's journalists I've got to learn from you because I may have run the country but I haven't actually run a newspaper. I know there's a lot for me to learn. Amol Rajan, the BBC's media editor who is a former editor of The Independent, noted that as an afternoon paper, the Standard is sent to the printers at 11:00 GMT. Mr Osborne will arrive at the office around 05:00 GMT, work until midday, and then balance his other duties thereafter, he added. Most people who edit newspapers will have spent years crafting headlines, sub-editing copy, designing pages, planning stories, and above all reporting. Osborne has never done any of that, and will need to grasp some basic skills very quickly if he is to keep Standard staff on-side. Read Amol's full blog. Patti Goddard, president of the Tatton Conservative Association, said it fully supported the former chancellor on his exciting career move, insisting it would not affect his reputation as a hard-working constituency MP. Mr Osborne has been congratulated by London Mayor Sadiq Khan, who said he would be covering the world's greatest city. But Labour's John Mann said Mr Osborne was already invisible in Parliament and accepting a new job devalued democracy while fellow Labour MP Paul Flynn criticised what he said was the revolving door between government and the private sector. Green Party co-leader Caroline Lucas said she would be seeking assurances in Parliament that the Conservatives would not exert undue influence over the newspaper and called for Mr Osborne to be removed from the Privy Council so he would not have access to any confidential government briefings. Robert Barrington, director of campaign group Transparency International, said it was an astonishing conflict of interest that damaged democracy and smacks of greed and the accumulation of power. Former Tatton MP Martin Bell said his first reaction to the announcement was that it sounds like fake news to me, suggesting on BBC Radio 5 Live that the politician would have to be superman to combine his various roles. Former Labour leader Ed Miliband joked on Twitter that he would shortly be announced as editor of Heat magazine while Lib Dem leader Tim Farron suggested his next job would be as editor of the adult comic Viz. Since leaving frontline politics, the former chancellor has become a visiting fellow at a US university and an adviser to US fund manager BlackRock, for which he is being paid £650,000 for four days work a month. Mr Osborne, who was chancellor for six years, had ambitions to be a journalist as a young man. He failed to get a place on The Times' trainee scheme after graduating from Oxford University - at which he edited its Isis magazine - and was briefly a freelance reporter on the Daily Telegraph's diary column. Defending his new job, he told BBC News there are plenty of examples of MPs who've edited newspapers and magazines over the years. His Conservative colleague Boris Johnson edited The Spectator magazine while an MP but agreed to stand down as a condition of joining David Cameron's front bench team in 2005. The now foreign secretary - who was endorsed by the Standard when he ran for London mayor in 2008 and was re-elected in 2012 - said Mr Osborne's appointment was brilliant and good for the city. Most other examples of MP journalists, such as Labour's Michael Foot, who edited the Evening Standard, and Conservative Bill Deedes, who edited the Daily Telegraph, did not do both jobs at the same time. The National Union of Journalists said the appointment was a blatantly cynical political move at a time when staff were facing pay cuts and reduced hours. But it said it looked forward to receiving Mr Osborne's application to become a member of the union.

The Conservative MP expressed his delight at taking over from Sarah Sands, who is leaving to take over the programme Today on the BBC. Mr Osborne, who will be editor of the paper four days a week, plans to continue as an MP for Tatton in Cheshire. These are external links and will open in a new window. But the appointment is already being seen as a joke. Jeremy Corbyn described it as "simply a joke" and demanded a by-election in Tatton, which Osborne has held since 2001 and which is to be abolished at the next election. The owner of the Standard, Evgeny Lebedev, remarked that Osborne was London through and through and that he was the right person to continue the magnificent work of Sarah Sands. ‘I am proud to have an editor who will strengthen The Standard’s prestige and influence in London and whose political outlook – socially liberal and economically pragmatic – is in line with many of our readers’, Mr Lebedev said in a statement. ‘This takes multi-taskeding to a new level and is an insult to the voters he is supposed to serve.’ The 45-year-old Chancellor, who had already addressed journalists in the newspaper's newsroom, said that it was a great honor to be entrusted with one of the most influential newspapers in the country. As the newspaper said, Mr Osborne will work as an editor an average of four days a week, and that this arrangement would enable him to continue to perform his other functions, including as an MP, by giving him the time to vote and speak in Parliament in the afternoon, after the newspaper had gone to print, and then to be in his constituency in the evening. Mr Osborne added: “I’m proud to be a Conservative MP but as editor and leader of a team of dedicated and independent journalists, our only interest will be to give a voice to all Londoners. I’ve grown up in London and have always known that the Evening Standard is an institution that plays an important role in the life of the city and its people. What the government, its politicians and the political parties do, we will judge against this simple test: is it good for our readers and good for London?” He told the journalists of the newspaper: "I have to learn from you, because I may have governed the country, but I have not actually run a newspaper. I know there is a lot to learn. If it is, we support them, if it is not, we will be quick to say so." Most newspaper editors will have spent years preparing headlines, copy-editing, laying out the pages, planning stories and, above all, reporting. Amol Rajan, the BBC’s media editor and former editor of the Independent, said that as an afternoon paper the Standard is printed at 11:30. He added that Osborne will arrive at the office at five in the morning, work until noon, and then balance his other work. Patti Goddard, the chairman of the Tatton Conservative Association, said the association supported the former Chancellor’s exciting career move, despite insisting it would not affect his reputation as a hard-working constituency MP. Osborne has never done any of that, and will need to pick up a few basic skills very quickly if he wants to keep the staff on his side. Read Amol’s full blog here. The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, congratulated Osborne on covering the world's greatest city. But Labour MP John Mann said he was invisible in parliament and a new job devalued democracy, while fellow Labour MP Paul Flynn criticised the revolving door between government and the private sector. Green co-leader Caroline Lucas said she would seek assurances in parliament that the Conservatives would not exercise undue influence over the newspaper, and called for Mr Osborne to be removed from the privy council so that he would not have access to confidential government briefings. Former Tatton MP Martin Bell said his first reaction to the announcement was that it sounded like fake news to him, pointing out on BBC radio that the politician would need to be superman to cope with all his roles. Former Labour leader Ed Miliband joked on twitter that he would be announcing him as the new editor of Heat magazine, while Lib Dem leader Tim Farron suggested he would soon be appointed editor of Viz. Robert Barrington, executive director of Transparency International, said it was an astonishing example of how greed and the accumulation of power could undermine democracy. Former Chancellor Osborne, who had been chancellor for six years, had as a young man had the ambition of being a journalist; he had applied for a place in The Times, had failed to obtain it, and had worked for a while as a freelance on the diary page of the Daily Telegraph. Since leaving front-line politics, he has become a visiting fellow at a university in the United States and is now an adviser to the US investment bank BlackRock, where he earns £650,000 a month for working four days a month. Foreign Secretary William Hague, who in 2008 was endorsed by the Standard for the mayoral contest, and in 2012 was re-elected, praised Osborne’s appointment as a brilliant stroke and a triumph for London. Defending the new job, he told the BBC there were plenty of examples of MPs who had been editors of newspapers and magazines. His Conservative colleague Boris Johnson was editor of the Spectator magazine while an MP but resigned from it as a condition of being appointed to David Cameron’s front-bench team in 2005. The National Union of Journalists said the appointment was a blatant political maneuver at a time when its members were being subjected to pay cuts and reduced hours of work, but it said it looked forward to receiving Mr. Osborne's application for union membership. Most of the examples of MPs who were also journalists, such as the Labourist Michael Foot, who was editor of the Evening Standard, or the Conservative Bill Deedes, who was editor of the Daily Telegraph, did not have both positions at the same time.
