text: Video sites such as YouTube will be forced to pay more to musicians and record companies under plans to reform European copyright laws. The draft directive will also mandate publishers and producers to inform performers or authors about the profits their works have generated. The music industry has long criticised YouTube for insufficient payment for content such as music. News publishers will be recognised as rights holders for the first time. Under the directive, platforms such as Google News would be required to pay newspaper publishers a fee for using small extracts or snippets of news stories. Carlo Perrone, head of the European Newspaper Publishers' Association, stated that creating a copyright for news publishers in Europe was a significant and historic step. Jean-Claude Juncker, president of the European Commission, remarked: I want journalists, publishers and authors to be paid fairly for their work, whether it is made in studios or living rooms, whether it is disseminated offline or online, whether it is published via a copying machine or hyperlinked on the web. The Commission has not specified how it would compel sites such as YouTube to pay more to artists. The plans also propose easier access to online content across all EU countries and to reform copyright rules for research and education. Andrus Ansip, vice-president for the digital single market, said: Our proposal will ensure that more content will be available, transforming Europe's copyright rules in light of a new digital reality. The proposals, which are likely to face challenges from lobbyists, must be approved by the European Parliament and EU states, a process that could take years. A Google spokesperson said: We believe there's a better way. Innovation and partnership - not subsidies and onerous restrictions - are the key to a successful, diverse and sustainable news sector in the EU. More than 1,000 artists, including Lady Gaga and Coldplay, signed a letter earlier this year urging the Commission to address the value gap. It stated that sites such as YouTube were unfairly siphoning value away from the music community and its artists and songwriters. YouTube, which hosts videos as well as audio-only content, generates revenue by selling advertising and then divides profits among rights owners. Its business model differs from music streaming sites such as Spotify and Apple Music, which pay record companies a small amount each time a song is played. The body representing the UK recorded music business, the BPI, welcomed Brussels' recognition of the need for a level playing field for digital music. Geoff Taylor, BPI chief executive, said it was unfair that platforms such as YouTube are building huge businesses using music and other content while paying only a fraction of the royalties paid to artists and labels by services such as Spotify and Apple Music. PRS for Music, which represents the rights of almost 120,000 songwriters, composers and music publishers in the UK, said it welcomed the move to ensure that searchable sites such as YouTube require a licence from the rights holders. The European Commission's proposed new copyright directive provides the framework for this essential legal clarity, said chief executive Robert Ashcroft. IFPI, which represents the international recording industry worldwide, said the proposals were a good first step towards better and fairer licensing for content in Europe. Chief executive Frances Moore said: Importantly, it confirms that user uploaded content services such as YouTube, which are the largest source of on-demand music, should not be able to operate outside normal licensing rules. However, there is a lot more to do to make this a workable proposal. UK Music, which represents the British music industry, said this week that YouTube was still not paying artists enough for their music. UK Music said the Google-owned site was yet to deliver fair financial returns for rights owners and creators, artists, composers, songwriters and publishers. The band Two Door Cinema Club said: I don't think things at the minute are fair. YouTube don't pay a fair royalty. Google claims it has paid the music industry more than $3bn (£2.3bn) since 2007. However, the Commission's proposals did not go far enough to prevent geo-blocking of online content, the European Consumer Organisation, BEUC, said. It also criticised plans to force websites to automatically detect and remove videos containing parts of copyrighted works. This would punish millions of consumers who share a self-made remix of a song, family videos or holiday pictures which contain parts of a music tune or video clip, BEUC said. The Commission has also proposed an overhaul of EU telecoms rules to ensure much faster internet access across Europe. It aims for schools, universities, hospitals, transport hubs and companies that rely on digital technologies to have extremely fast connectivity in excess of 1 gigabit a second. All homes - both rural and urban - should have broadband speed of at least 100 megabits a second. Finally, the Commission calls for all urban areas, as well as major roads and railways, to have 5G wireless mobile data coverage. Each EU country should have 5G in at least one major city by 2020.

text: Back in the heady days of May 2010, when the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats united in government, they set out a detailed set of policy proposals called the Coalition Agreement. One paragraph stated: We will... pursue a detailed agreement on limiting donations and reforming party funding in order to remove big money from politics. Following disagreement between the parties after the cash-for-honours scandal, this seemed rather promising. A few weeks later, the independent Committee on Standards in Public Life deemed the issue worthy of investigation and initiated an inquiry. The chairman, Sir Christopher Kelly, acknowledged that significant difficulties remain but was optimistic enough to assert that there is sufficient will to reform the system to give us some hope that it ought to be possible to find a solution. In the language of Whitehall, that is bold, optimistic rhetoric. Sir Christopher's outlook was not just half full; it was positively overflowing with hope. Now, after a delay of many months, we have discovered the results of Sir Christopher's efforts. He is proposing a £10,000 cap on individual donations to political parties. He also suggested that union members should decide individually whether they wish to donate to the Labour Party. Currently, they must opt out if they do not want their money to end up in Ed Miliband's coffers. In exchange for these two measures, which would significantly reduce the income of the three largest parties, Sir Christopher recommends that the public should contribute to the funding of political parties themselves. Parties with MPs - or representation in the Scottish Parliament or Welsh and Northern Ireland assemblies - would receive approximately £3 for each vote cast in their favour. At the last general election, about 30 million of us voted. Thus, the plan would theoretically provide a substantial £90m to be distributed among the parties over a five-year parliament. That is quite a significant amount. The public would also be able to donate a large sum to a party without paying tax. The issue is that no one seems to agree with this. The Conservative member of the committee, Oliver Heald, has written a dissenting opinion opposing a £10,000 cap. The Tories would prefer £50,000. They also wish for union members to have the option to donate part of their fee to parties other than Labour. The Labour member, Margaret Beckett, has expressed her opposition to the union reforms. Additionally, Deputy Prime Minister Nick Clegg - whose party could benefit from some state funding - has ruled out any immediate move towards increased taxpayer support for parties. Only last week, he informed MPs: It would not be right to ask our hard-pressed taxpayers to pay more to political parties at a time when they are having to deal with so many cuts and savings elsewhere. And there are many others in government who do not disagree. Sir Christopher Kelly contends that the public are concerned about party funding, are suspicious of big donors, and notes that the three largest parties all made manifesto commitments to reform. The Conservatives, Labour and the Liberal Democrats all agree that the only way forward is through consensus. Yet, for now, that is the sole point on which there is consensus. The coalition agreement promised that the government would pursue reform. However, it did not promise to achieve it.

text: Ahead of Kenya's elections in August, we asked you what issues you want us to report on. These are external links and will open in a new window. We will be updating this page with further questions: Kenya lacks an election campaign funding law. An attempt by the electoral commission to introduce one last year was defeated by MPs. The commission had proposed caps for different seats. The absence of the law means candidates are currently free to spend as much as they wish. According to the privately owned Daily Nation, most of the money is spent on logistics and advertisements but many candidates and parties also bribe voters. It reports that in the 2013 election, the then opposition coalition Cord spent in excess of $50m (£40m) while the governing Jubilee Party spent more than $100m to run its presidential campaign. Politicians raise money from businessmen and some hold fundraisers. Opposition parties, however, accuse the ruling party of using state resources in its campaigns. text: New rules for moving livestock will be disastrous for small agricultural shows, the Farmers Union of Wales said. These are external links and will open in a new window. Farmers have stated that the Welsh Government's new regulations on livestock movement are excessively strict and costly. From 10 June, farmers must register a quarantine unit (QU) on their farm to move livestock on and off, thereby avoiding six-day standstill rules. The Welsh Government stated the system was developed in collaboration with the farming industry. Currently, if farmers introduce new stock to their farm, the entire farm undergoes a six-day lockdown, during which no animals can be moved off. However, there are exemptions for seasonal events such as agricultural shows. A field or shed separated from other livestock, known as an approved isolation unit, can be utilised to circumvent the rules. Yet, these isolation units cannot be used after 10 June, and farmers must apply and pay for the new quarantine units. There are 61 rules within the new system, including the installation of double gates and double fences, as well as the wearing of specialised clothing. The fee is £172.80 for one QU and £244.80 for two. Farmer Gwilym Jones, from Blaenau Ffestiniog, remarked: It makes no sense to show, it's not worth it. The rules are going backwards instead of forwards. Geraint Jones, from Ystrad Meurig, stated: I will break the law, and if they want to put me in jail, they can - I've got nothing to lose. If they want to kill the countryside, they're doing the right thing. Sian Davies, who exhibits her texel sheep nationwide, said the new changes cost money, they're a nuisance and they increase paperwork. She mentioned the Welsh Government don't know what's going on. I called the office in Aberystwyth and they didn't know what I was referring to. Geraint Jones reported a similar experience with the offices in Cardiff and Carmarthen. The Welsh Government has not confirmed any delays in the registration process. Brian Walters, vice-president of Farmers Union of Wales, commented: This is disastrous for smaller agricultural shows. We don't feel there is enough evidence to indicate that diseases are passed between livestock at agricultural shows to justify such draconian measures. In England, the changes to the rules have been postponed until the autumn, avoiding the show season. In a statement, the Welsh Government said: The new QU system was designed to simplify the standstill regime and provide extra flexibility whilst maintaining disease movement curbs. It was developed in partnership with the farming industry. Although QUs can be used to manage movements to and from shows, it is important to note they are intended for all types of animal movement, not just for shows. The alternative arrangements to the six-day standstill were developed at the industry's request (through the Working Smarter review) and in close collaboration with the industry through the LIDAG (Livestock Identification Advisory Group) over the past few years - not rushed, worked through systematically, and collaboratively, with the support of Independent Veterinary Risk Assessments. It stated the recommendations were published in January 2012, and the Welsh Government had written to everyone in the industry twice, in April and May 2017, alongside an extensive communications campaign.

text: Supermarkets and other big businesses could face higher business rates under a Welsh Conservative government, with a tax cut for smaller companies. The Conservatives propose altering the calculation of rates as part of a commitment to prioritise the needs of small businesses at the heart of the Welsh government. Welsh Conservative leader Andrew RT Davies stated that small firms are crucial to Wales and require assistance to develop and grow. Retailers cautioned against creating winners or losers or more complexity. The Conservatives would also establish a team of officials within the Welsh government dedicated to small businesses and accountable to the assembly, should they gain power in May's assembly election. Other measures, some previously announced, include removing the age limit on a job creation scheme and promising to facilitate business loans from the Welsh government. Mr Davies remarked: Wales is a nation of shopkeepers, and those small firms are the lifeblood of the Welsh economy; which is why they need support to develop and grow. Business rates are paid to local councils and are based on property values. There are already discounts available to small businesses from the Welsh government, known as rate relief. For instance, businesses with property valued up to £6,000 pay no rates. The Conservatives claim they would extend rate relief to more businesses. However, they would also implement different rates for large and small businesses, so that larger businesses pay more. England and Scotland already have separate rates, but Wales does not. The Welsh Retail Consortium, representing shop owners, called for fundamental reform of business rates for all, whether that be small, medium-sized or larger businesses. A spokeswoman stated: The proposed small firms' relief is a welcome acknowledgement of the need to keep down costs, however many high street retailers won't benefit and we would be alarmed if this new rate for medium and larger sized commercial premises simply opened the door to even higher taxes, as has been proposed in Scotland.

text: A Chinese authority has banned the importation of brown crabs from Anglesey after claiming they contain a metallic contaminant. The Hong Kong-based Centre for Food Safety (CFS) announced a ban on the sea creatures and advised people on Wednesday not to consume them. The CFS reported that samples it had collected from the island contained excessive cadmium. Defra stated that all crabs sold in the UK must adhere to EU regulations regarding the permissible level of cadmium. It further mentioned it was collaborating with the Hong Kong authorities to find a workable solution so trade could resume as soon as possible. Two crab samples prepared for export to China contained the metal at 15 and 22 parts per million (ppm) - surpassing a limit of 2ppm, according to the CFS. Over 220kg of meat from one of the exporters has been retained by Hong Kong officials, but 160kg has already been distributed, the CFS reported. Officials cautioned that, while occasional consumption of crabs with cadmium will not cause significant harm, prolonged intake may adversely affect people's kidneys. The CFS has informed the relevant authorities of the United Kingdom and the local trade and will continue to closely follow up the incident and take appropriate actions, including enhanced surveillance of aquatic products imported from the United Kingdom, the announcement stated. Anglesey council said it had not received communication from the Chinese authority but added it was aware of the situation and was making inquiries. Brown crab is known to accumulate cadmium in the hepatopancreas (a component of the brown meat) due to the detoxifying function of this organ, a spokesperson stated. The authority has not issued export certificates for brown crab destined for China for some months, following advice from Defra that the Chinese had placed restrictions on the import of live crabs from the entire UK, due to excessive cadmium levels found on testing. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) in Wales said cadmium concentrations in brown meat from crabs - as opposed to white crab meat, which comes from the legs and claws - vary widely. It stated the NHS advises regular fish-eaters to avoid consuming brown crab meat too frequently. The FSA is continuing to work with the crab industry to explore ways of reducing cadmium levels in brown crab meat through different processing methods, an FSA spokesperson stated.

text: The BBC's Children in Need appeal has raised more than £32.6m on the night, with acts including One Direction, S Club 7 and Susan Boyle taking part. Sir Terry Wogan hosted the BBC One event on Friday alongside Tess Daly, Fearne Cotton, and Radio 1's Nick Grimshaw. The annual telethon featured Boyzone on stage, while Sir Bruce Forsyth returned to Strictly Come Dancing to assist in finding a young ballroom champion. By the conclusion of the show at 02:00 GMT on Saturday, £32,620,469 had been raised. This surpasses the £31.1m raised on the night of the 2013 gala, with the final total expected to increase once all donations are received. text: Australian Justine Damond was killed by US police who were responding to her call at an upscale Minneapolis neighbourhood on Saturday night. These are external links and will open in a new window. Few details have been disclosed by the city, Minneapolis police, or the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension (BCA), which is leading the inquiry. The BCA investigation could take up to four months, according to the Hennepin County Attorney, who will decide whether to charge the officers after investigators present their findings. So what do we know? Just before 23:30 local time, officers Matthew Harrity and Mohamed Noor responded to Damond's 911 emergency call reporting a suspected assault in an alleyway behind her home. She resided at the property with her American fiancé, whom she had planned to marry in August. Clad in her pyjamas, Damond approached the squad car, which had its lights turned off. A conversation ensued, and Officer Noor, seated in the passenger's seat, shot her through the driver's open window, Officer Harrity informed officials. Harrity indicated that he was startled by a loud sound near the car, according to the preliminary BCA report released on Tuesday. A police radio recording from the incident mentions they also heard a loud noise, suspected to be fireworks. The 40-year-old yoga teacher was struck in the abdomen and died at the scene at 23:51 local time, despite the officers' attempts to save her. No weapons were discovered at the scene. Damond's mobile phone was found near her body. Officer Noor has declined to speak to investigators, as is his legal right, and officials do not know if he will ever provide a statement. Neither officer had activated their bodycams, and the vehicle's dashboard camera did not capture the incident, investigators state. For the past six months, every police officer in Minneapolis has been equipped with body-worn cameras, but officers are required to activate them only during certain encounters. Unlike in Los Angeles or Washington DC, where cameras must be activated for any response to a call for service, Minneapolis officers have more discretion to turn them off - for instance, when interviewing a confidential source. Instead, there are more than a dozen situations in which cameras should be used, according to the police manual, which adds that failure to use the camera could result in job termination. Without any video evidence, investigators are hopeful that a cyclist who was seen observing police perform CPR on Damond will come forward to provide his account. Australian media has extensively covered the story, and Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull stated that he wants answers from the US. It is a shocking killing, and yes, we are demanding answers on behalf of her family, he told Australian TV on Wednesday. Her fiancé, Don Damond, said the family is desperate for information, adding that piecing together Justine's last moments before the homicide would be a small comfort as we grieve this tragedy. Minneapolis officials have described the death as a tragedy and have demanded a transparent and swift investigation. Officer Noor, described by local media as a Somali-American, was portrayed as a caring person with a family he loves and he empathised with the loss others are experiencing. On Wednesday morning, hundreds of people gathered for a dawn vigil at a Sydney beach to honour Ms Damond.

text: Almost four million children in the UK do not own a book, according to a report by the National Literacy Trust. These are external links and will open in a new window. The proportion of children without books is rising, the charity reported. It is now one in three, compared with one in 10 in 2005. Children with their own books were more likely to be above-average readers and perform better at school, the study of 18,000 children indicated. Poorer children and boys were less likely to possess books, it noted. The survey was conducted in September with school-aged children from 111 schools across the UK. It indicated that a third (33.2%) did not own books. That equates to 3.8 million children UK-wide. More affluent children and young people were more likely to report having their own books, compared with those receiving free school meals. Trust director Jonathan Douglas expressed particular concern over the sharp increase in the number of children without their own books. He stated: We know there is a direct correlation between book ownership and children's reading abilities. With one in six in the UK struggling with literacy, it is very worrying that many children could be missing out on opportunities to develop these essential skills. The trust stated that children who owned books were more likely than others to read daily, and that book ownership had a clear link with reading ability. Of the children and young people with their own books, more than half read above the level expected for their age, with fewer than one in 10 reading below the level. In contrast, among those without their own books, nearly a fifth were failing to meet the expected reading level, with only a third reading above that level. The trust launched the survey to coincide with an appeal for public donations towards books and reading support for disadvantaged children. Several children's book illustrators have designed cards to support the trust's Christmas Gift of Reading campaign. The survey also uncovered links between reading ability and receiving books as gifts. About a fifth of children said they had never visited a bookshop or a library. However, the survey also showed that reading any type of material, such as magazines, outside class at least once a month was also associated with greater reading attainment.

text: Conservative backbenchers are demanding radical changes to school funding in England within months. Ministers are reportedly facing a campaign from numerous MPs within their own party unless they commit to prompt reform. Without action, teachers will face redundancy and class sizes will increase, it is claimed. Backbencher Daniel Kawczynski stated that huge numbers of Conservatives in the Commons are demanding change. He informed BBC Radio 4's The World at One: I think you would be fascinated by how strong the feelings are on this issue and the type of campaign that will be pursued this year. Conservative former chairman of the education select committee, Graham Stuart, expressed that he believed dozens of Tories would desire the earliest possible announcement, ideally in July's Budget. He remarked: Schools are facing the prospect of deficits unless they take significant action to reduce headcount. We may potentially be looking at redundancies to cope with the funding pressures. Backbenchers assert that the method by which government money is allocated to local authorities for school funding must change from next April. There are significant variations nationwide, with the best-funded areas receiving up to £7,000 per pupil, while the worst-off receive just over £4,000. Ministers have intended to change the system since 2010, promised reform in 2013, and reiterated the commitment in the Conservative manifesto. They provided an additional £390 million to the worst-funded authorities at the end of the last Parliament but have not revised the funding formula. The change would likely result in well-funded inner-city authorities losing money, while some rural areas would benefit. A Department for Education spokeswoman stated: The last government made considerable progress in reforming the school funding system. In 2014, an additional £390 million was allocated to boost 69 of the least fairly funded areas in the country in 2015-16—the biggest step toward fairer schools funding in 10 years. But we recognise there is still work to be done, which is why we have committed to examining what more needs to be done to ensure all local areas are funded justly.

text: Brightly coloured murals adorn the walls of the 'Little Hands' nursery. The classroom walls are made of concrete, with a roof of plastic tenting. Outside, a group of four- and five-year-olds are engaged in singing and dancing. Disregard the dusty roads beyond the chicken wire fence, and it could resemble any kindergarten worldwide. However, this is the Zaatari camp in Jordan, where thousands of Syrians escaping their homeland now reside. Many of the children we are seeing here now were born in the camp. They've known no other existence, states Neil Mathers, the head of Save the Children in Scotland. The charity operates three nurseries in Zaatari, catering to 52% of the camp's children. Mr Mathers comments: There are 40,000 children who need this kind of support in Zaatari camp alone. Our kindergartens reach around 2,000 children, so much more is needed to handle just the children in this camp. Zaatari refugee camp is one of the locations from which refugees granted admission to the UK will be selected. A few miles south of Jordan's border with Syria, the camp extends across 8 sq km (3 sq miles) of barren stony desert. It has grown from nothing to effectively become Jordan's fourth largest city. With a population exceeding 80,000, it is the world's second largest refugee camp. A combination of tents, tin shacks, and makeshift huts are what the refugees now call home. In summer, temperatures here exceed 50C, and in winter, nights can drop below freezing. It's tough, remarks Dominic Graham, Jordan country director for the Edinburgh-based charity Mercy Corps. Life in the camps is tough. Mercy Corps is one of numerous non-governmental organisations that have been active in Zaatari since it was established four years ago when refugees first began fleeing Syria's increasingly brutal civil war. Water, sanitation, and shelter are all available in Zaatari. Rudimentary commerce has developed—there's a market and small shacks selling everyday items. Zaatari is gradually developing an unwanted permanence. But it remains a bleak existence. Lives on hold, going nowhere. When the Syrian refugees first arrived, most believed they would soon return to Syria. They thought President Assad's regime was about to collapse. The government and aid agencies thought so too. A crisis of months rather than years. No-one believes that now. Hassan arrived in Zaatari last year. Like many here, he is reluctant to disclose his full name for fear of repercussions for relatives who remain in Syria. He and his family have no savings and now wish to return to Syria. He stated: I will go back as soon as it is safe. However, he does not believe that will be soon. Mr Graham, from Mercy Corps, says most refugees are desperate to return to their former lives in Syria, but the prospects of that are getting thinner and thinner. Zaatari is merely the tip of the refugee iceberg. Inside Syria, it is estimated there are nearly eight million internally displaced people. Those who escape to camps such as Zaatari are those who are able to. Some had geography on their side, living just over the border. Others reached here because they could afford to pay smugglers to help them cross into Syria's neighbouring countries. Those left inside are often the most vulnerable, the poorest. Delivering aid to them is crucial, according to Steve Gordon, from Glasgow, who is Mercy Corps' security manager for the region. If you are assisting inside Syria and people are staying there and not coming out, they are not becoming a burden on the surrounding countries. The challenges are immense. Front lines are constantly shifting. Russia's intervention has altered the dynamics. Mercy Corps reports seeing massive changes with populations shifting. Gordon says even as the situation becomes more dangerous, the need to keep supplies flowing increases. If an area is going to be cut off, you have to pre-position supplies in those areas to sustain those communities through what could be very hard times. In Zaatari, children play in the spray of water being hosed from a tanker to dampen the dusty streets of the camp. In the distance, the hills of Syria are just visible through the haze. Whether these children will ever return to their homeland is impossible to know. But what the future holds increasingly drives the thinking of the refugees here. Should they stay or should they go? A battered silver bus waits near the camp's security checkpoint. Its destination is the Syrian border. For some, life in the refugee camps offers so little hope they are choosing to return. It's only a trickle, but memories of the dangers that drove people here fade. For some, Europe and the prospect of a new life there has become their goal. Individuals and small family groups undertake the arduous and dangerous journey. If they succeed and successfully settle in Germany, France, or Britain, perhaps the rest of the family can follow. Billions of pounds are being spent trying to address the Syrian refugee crisis. The UK alone has spent just over £1bn across the region, with £330m in Jordan alone, since the start of the war in Syria. Jeff Tudor is head of the UK government's international development programme in Jordan. As a veteran of the humanitarian and development aid sector, he knows there is no easy or quick answer to the refugee crisis. He says: We're hanging on in there, but ultimately we will need a political solution to what is happening in Syria. Even if we get a political solution tomorrow, we are looking at at least a decade. The refugees won't go back overnight; the situation in Syria won't allow it.

text: Asian stocks opened higher after turmoil on financial markets saw European and US indexes tumble following another oil price fall. Thursday's gains, however, did not recover the losses financial markets have experienced in recent days. Investors remain concerned about declining oil prices and slowing growth in China. On Wednesday, stocks had plummeted to their lowest levels since May 2009, with UK, French, and Japanese shares falling more than 20% below their 2015 highs. Wall Street was not exempt either. The Dow Jones closed 1.6% lower after a volatile trading day saw stocks fall as much as 3%. Overnight markets in Europe and the US had a terrible day, where sentiments around a 'drunk' Asia spilled over, market strategist Bernard Aw of IG explained in a note. Mainland China's main market in Shanghai was slightly lower by 0.3%, confirming international concerns over the world's second-largest economy. Hong Kong, however, managed to recover slightly from the previous day's record loss. The Hang Seng index rose 1.3% after losing nearly 4% on Wednesday. Traders say there is not much conviction behind the latest rally, the BBC's Juliana Liu in Hong Kong reported. In fact, the gains are rather modest and vulnerable to any hint of bad news. They think this could even be a so-called dead cat bounce, a term coined in the 1980s to describe a brief recovery in an otherwise declining market. Earlier in the day, Australia was the first to buck the share market downturn, with the ASX/200 gaining 1.1%. The rise occurred despite Australia being particularly dependent on China's economic performance, as most of the commodities driving the economy down under are exported to China. Japan and South Korea also saw increases, with the Nikkei up by 1.4% while the Kospi rose by 0.5%. Markets are just very uncertain about the slowdown in the Chinese economy, Stephen Koukoulas, chief strategist at TD Securities, told the BBC. We saw the official numbers, but frankly not many people put a lot of weight on the reliability of them and instead look at commodity prices as a barometer for how the Chinese economy is going. Oil prices have fallen below $28 a barrel, while coal, iron ore, and other metals are also in a prolonged slump. Many analysts have reduced their 2016 oil price forecasts, with Morgan Stanley analysts stating that oil in the $20s is possible if China devalues its currency further. Economists at the Royal Bank of Scotland suggest that oil could fall to $16, while Standard Chartered predicts prices could hit just $10 a barrel. So, investors are particularly nervous about the loss of momentum in China, Mr Koukoulas said. The question is: Is it just an adjustment to some of the previous excesses or is this the start of something a little more nasty that will drag the economy to a much weaker growth path? Some observers believe that many markets were set for a fall. Asset prices were inflated by ultra-low interest rates in the developed world and also by central banks that have engaged in quantitative easing, buying financial assets with newly created money. That occurred with shares, bonds, and commodities. For commodities, the boom is well and truly over, partly due to the slowdown in China and in the case of oil mainly due to plentiful supplies. Clearly, there are some troublesome developments and the IMF has issued a warning: If these key challenges are not successfully managed, global growth could be derailed. That, fundamentally, is what the markets are worried about. Read more from Andrew here. Just how low can oil prices go? China economic slowdown: Can it avoid a crash? What markets are really worried about.

text: Scotland's largest council has said the greater Glasgow area will suffer unless there is specific government action to mitigate the effects of Brexit. A new report from Glasgow City Council outlines the challenges the area will face following the referendum result favouring the UK's departure from the European Union. It states that specific policy decisions are required from the UK and Scottish governments to support the city region. Among these is the need for both governments to take over EU-funded projects. Glasgow City Council leader Frank McAveety stated that action from both governments is necessary to prevent a potential crisis. I believe that Brexit will present Glasgow with significant economic challenges, he said. I also believe these can be overcome if special measures are taken by the Scottish and UK governments. If that occurs, the problems associated with Brexit can become an opportunity for economic growth rather than a crisis threat. The report, Brexit and the Glasgow Economy: Impacts, Actions and Asks, was produced by the council, Glasgow Chamber of Commerce, and the Glasgow Economic Leadership board—a partnership group including the council, chamber of commerce, Scottish Enterprise, and Skills Development Scotland. The council stated the report was compiled with input from over 100 senior business, local government, and academic leaders. It will now be submitted to the first minister's Standing Committee on Europe, led by Professor Anton Muscatelli, Principal of Glasgow University. The report makes six main asks of the Scottish and UK governments to mitigate Brexit's effects. Professor Sir Jim McDonald, chair of the Glasgow Economic Leadership board and Principal of Strathclyde University, said: There is no doubt that Brexit is a fundamental system shock and one that poses challenges to us all. We will now position our city to meet the challenges of Brexit and exploit longer-term opportunities to grow our economy. Only by working together can we enhance our economic fundamentals: our skills, innovation, and entrepreneurship. It is on these foundations that our future will and must be based. Stuart Patrick, chief executive of Glasgow Chamber of Commerce, said swift action is needed to address the challenges ahead. He stated: To take advantage of the new world as it exists post-Brexit vote and to seize the opportunities that will be presented to us, a clear, collective, coherent, and forward-looking approach from the City of Glasgow and from the Scottish and UK governments is required. We cannot do this alone, and while uncertainty persists around our future trading relationship with the EU, we must combine all our efforts now to secure investment and jobs and to boost trade.

text: The UK's home secretary has expressed concerns about plans to make it easier for Chinese tourists to get visas. Culture Secretary Jeremy Hunt had advocated for the system to be simplified to help turbocharge tourism following the London 2012 Olympics. However, a letter seen by the Daily Telegraph indicates Theresa May considers it a security risk. The letter, authored by Mrs May's private secretary, states she finds the proposal unacceptable. On Tuesday, Mr Hunt outlined a strategy to boost UK tourism after London's Games, mentioning that ministers were considering simplifying visa applications for non-EU nationals. The strategy aimed to attract visitors from China, where the government believes there is potential to triple tourist numbers, generating over £500m in additional spending and creating more than 14,000 jobs. Currently, visitors can apply for a single visa to visit much of Europe, but a separate one is needed for the UK. Countries like France and Germany are more successful in attracting Chinese visitors, and the UK could improve if obtaining a visa were easier, Mr Hunt suggested. However, a letter from Mrs May's private secretary to the prime minister's private secretary stated the current rules were a key tool in protecting the public against significant harm. It noted there are already 400 Chinese criminals awaiting deportation and 1,000 asylum applications from Chinese citizens last year. The proposal... is not acceptable to the home secretary for national security reasons, the letter stated. We also face significant challenges with foreign national offenders and organised crime, including drugs, money laundering, fraud, criminal finances, intellectual property, immigration and cyber crime. Yet Mark Tanzer, chief executive of the Association of British Travel Agents (Abta), remarked: In the absence of concrete data about visa abuse, it is impossible to determine whether the right balance is being struck between the UK's commercial interests and its security needs. He contended that proper visa monitoring and reporting processes were necessary, and any system abuses could be addressed as they occurred. We must not forget that visas are only one of the factors that deter Chinese tourists from visiting us - lack of air routes and high aviation taxes also depress demand, he added. Mr Tanzer has previously stated his organisation welcomed Mr Hunt's stance as a step in the right direction. Meanwhile, Immigration Minister Damian Green stated that a visa scheme had failed to attract as many of the most talented artists, musicians, and scientists to work in the UK as the government had hoped. We offer a thousand visas a year for the exceptionally talented, Mr Green said. In its first year in operation it came nowhere near using them all. That tells me we need to fine-tune the system to ensure that globally, if you are a bright young artist or a gifted young scientist, you know there is this route to come and work in Britain. We need to do better on that. The minister added: If you are a current Nobel Prize winner, you won't find it very difficult to get into this country. But we want the next generation of Nobel Prize winners, so we have carved out a specific route in the immigration system.

He cited an Islamic teaching regarding jihad: We are the ones who pledged loyalty to [the Prophet] Muhammad to fight jihad as long as we live. He also exclaimed Allahu Akbar, meaning God is great. Switching to fluent Turkish, he then stated: Do not forget about Syria, do not forget about Aleppo. All those who participate in this tyranny will be held accountable. He was identified by Interior Minister Suleyman Soylu as a 22-year-old policeman. Soylu stated Altintas was born on 24 June 1994 in the town of Soke in the quiet, conservative Aydin province in western Turkey, and attended police college in the coastal city of Izmir to the north. He had been employed in Ankara's riot police department for two-and-a-half years but was reportedly on leave at the time of his attack. Investigators must determine whether he was motivated by the destruction of eastern Aleppo or was part of a broader plot to disrupt relations with Russia. Unconfirmed reports suggested he had been suspended for several weeks until mid-November due to suspected links to the plotters behind Turkey's failed July coup. Pro-government media presented a document indicating he had also taken three days' leave immediately after the coup. He triggered a metal detector upon entering the exhibition but was allowed through after presenting his official police ID. After shooting the ambassador and terrifying onlookers, he refused to surrender and exchanged gunfire with police for about 15 minutes before they fatally shot him. Family members, including his father, mother, and sister, were then immediately detained for questioning at their homes in Soke. Outspoken Ankara mayor Melih Gokcek stated on his Twitter account that Altintas may have had connections to the movement of US-based Islamic cleric Fethullah Gulen. However, the Gulenists have denounced the attack on the Russian ambassador and denied any links to the attacker. text: Lufthansa pilots have begun their eighth strike this year, forcing the cancellation of 1,511 flights over Monday and Tuesday. The strike initially targeted primarily European flights but will extend to international routes on Tuesday, affecting 200,000 passengers. Lufthansa stated that the strike, concerning changes to retirement and pension terms, would impact profits and its reputation. However, the Vereinigung Cockpit (VC) union expressed its intention to deliver a clear message. Last week, VC called for a 12-hour stoppage by its members at Lufthansa's budget airline, Germanwings. The union, representing approximately 5,400 Lufthansa pilots, is urging the airline to reconsider its decision to raise the retirement age from 55. The company has proposed maintaining the scheme for current members but not extending it to new recruits. VC accused Lufthansa of stonewalling negotiations. Union board member Markus Wahl stated: We are extending the strike to send a clearer signal. Perhaps now, Lufthansa will finally come round. However, Simone Menne, Lufthansa's chief financial officer, remarked in a statement: The strikes are not only causing significant financial damage but are also damaging our image, the consequences of which are significant and not yet clear. The airline expressed hope to operate a third of its flights over the two days. The Lufthansa strike follows a weekend walk-out by railway drivers. The train drivers' strike concerned demands by the GDL for a 5% pay increase for 20,000 drivers and a shorter working week. The head of the GDL union, Claus Weselsky, announced a week-long break before any further strikes. The German Industry Federation business lobby criticised the strikes, stating they harmed the entire economy by affecting logistics, tourism, and business travel. Germany's economy has been slowing recently. However, the Economy Ministry stated that although the strikes would certainly impact some sectors of the economy, there was no reason to alter the 2014 growth forecast, which was lowered this month to 1.2%. Germany's government is expected to draft a law later this year aimed at preventing small numbers of employees from paralysing large parts of the country's infrastructure through strike action.

text: AMs have agreed that the National Assembly for Wales should change its name. These are external links and will open in a new window. The assembly's presiding officer, Elin Jones, has informed AMs of several potential options. Welsh Parliament has been suggested previously, but one AM stated the name Senedd should be considered. However, UKIP AM Gareth Bennett remarked that some organisations with Welsh-only names were recognised only in the Welsh-speaking colony of Pontcanna in Cardiff. First Minister Carwyn Jones stated that some might find his comments offensive. No new name was decided at an assembly debate on Tuesday, but the presiding officer and assembly commission will now assess the implications of such a change. AMs unanimously endorsed, without a vote, a motion stating the assembly should change its name to reflect its constitutional status as a national parliament. The assembly will soon acquire the power under the Wales Bill, currently progressing through the UK parliament, to rename the National Assembly of Wales with the agreement of two-thirds of the chamber, with calls for the name change to reflect its expanding powers. The Welsh Government had planned a vote advocating for the assembly to be known as the Welsh Parliament unofficially before a legal change could be enacted, but the vote was withdrawn. Ms Jones stated the next step will be to consult soon on what the name should be. There are several possibilities and many associated terms which would stem from that choice, she stated. The name should continue to inspire confidence and pride among the people of Wales. She added she will inform the assembly of the next steps at the outset of the autumn term. Bethan Jenkins, Plaid Cymru AM for South Wales West, has proposed that the Welsh word Senedd, which is used to refer to the assembly building, be used to refer to the institution itself. Let us be self-confident enough to discard our mental baggage and take this opportunity to be unique by adopting an official Welsh name for our Senedd, she told the debate. She stated some AMs wish to retain the name National Assembly, but added Senedd is already widely used on the ground. Welsh Conservative leader Andrew RT Davies, who suggested the Assembly be renamed the Welsh Parliament back in 2012, said: I couldn't see why we couldn't have Senedd and Parliament, because obviously for people there is a complete understanding of the word Parliament, in the way UK democracy works. Over time I think the word Senedd could be readily taken on board, he added. UKIP group leader Neil Hamilton questioned whether the public at large would regard the debate as pretentious navel gazing. As and when the Wales Bill passes and tax raising powers are devolved to this institution there is, of course, a serious argument for calling ourselves a Parliament, he said. He said he was personally attracted to the idea of the Senedd as a name. I wonder whether that would make us Senators, he added. But Gareth Bennett, UKIP AM for South Wales Central, called for the term Senedd to be kicked into the long grass and said it would distance the assembly from the majority of the people of Wales. Bethan is from a Welsh speaking background, or a bilingual background, and in her social circle Senedd may be a well-used term, Mr Bennett said, to laughter and derision from Ms Jenkins. In the Wetherspoons pub in Canton few people would know what I was talking about if I started talking about the Senedd, and I can tell you that from experience. Referring to a list of organisations with Welsh-only names, including the Urdd and Chwarae Teg, that Ms Jenkins had read out, Mr Bennett said: The problem is most people outside the Welsh speaking colony of Pontcanna, most people in Cardiff don't know what these things are. First Minister Carwyn Jones said: If someone stood up in this chamber and described people in Ceredigion or in Gwynedd who are English speakers as a colony there would be uproar. It makes it sound as if people in Wales who speak a certain language don't belong in our capital city, and that is a wholly wrong remark, he said, adding it would be highly offensive to a number of people although he wasn't sure Mr Bennett meant it that way.

text: The stories of those visiting and working at the Royal Welsh Show are being told on social media by a PhD student for his thesis. I did not want the thesis to be really dull, stated Mr Thomas, who is due to submit his work in October. I did not want it to be read by merely five bearded academics—I wanted it to be useful and for everyone to gain something from it. So, what about examining the individuals behind the statistics? It's 100,000 words—but with so much happening here and the show meaning so much to so many, is that even sufficient? Mr Thomas decided to enrich his doctorate—which explores the interaction between farmers and non-farmers, Welsh identity, and politics—with photographs and quotes from farmers, visitors, stewards, and organisers. In other words, the humans of the Royal Welsh Show. Drawing inspiration from the Humans of New York social media phenomenon, Mr Thomas arranged interviews during the show and also approached people he encountered who might have intriguing stories to share. Although Mr Thomas noted that his most popular posts typically feature real people rather than celebrities or politicians, rugby referee Nigel Owens was an exception. But over the last few years, I've been president of Wales Young Farmers clubs, and most of the time I've been coming here to compete with the Young Farmers when I was a member and then to assist in the YFC office during the competitions. The last four or five years, I've been coming here to referee the final of the sevens tournament. A voice frequently resonating across the showground belongs to chief announcer and commentator Nicola Davies. Mr Thomas wanted to attribute a name to that familiar voice, so he interviewed Ms Davies for his Facebook page. I've been coming here as a child with my family, exhibited Welsh cobs here for many, many years, she said. But I was asked to commentate here on an equine display between 10 and 15 years ago, and I got the bug. I was part of the team, some say it was a promotion, some not. But I'm now chief commentator, so I'm in charge of the commentators at the main ring, horse ring, the sheep, the cattle, and the pig section. So I do not know much about pigs and cattle, but I try to find people who do. Wales UKIP leader Neil Hamilton and his wife, author and media personality Christine Hamilton, joked they were attending the show purely for Mr Thomas's doctorate. We're Neil and Christine Hamilton, and we are basically here to provide you with a couple of extra paragraphs for your thesis, Mr Hamilton said. But apart from that, it is, of course, the largest agricultural show in northern Europe, and I believe this brings in £20m a year to the mid Wales economy. It is a vitally important event in the year. Mr Thomas stated that people he approaches rarely refuse interviews—he actually has more success than when conducting simple surveys. I'm quite excited about it, but I'm also very nervous. However, there is still one man who has never featured as a Human of the Royal Welsh Show. So how about giving Mr Thomas a taste of his own medicine? I'm Greg Thomas, a PhD student in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University. The young gentleman, Mr. Thomas, has decided to enrich his dissertation—which deals with the relationship between the peasantry and the non-peasants, with national identity and politics—with photographs and quotations from the peasants, visitors, bailiffs, and bailiffesses. He wished to make it useful to everyone. But what if one could see the people behind the figures? The human beings of New York were his inspiration. Mr. Thomas arranged for himself to be interviewed on the air, and he sought out people whom he met who might have an interesting story to tell. It runs to a hundred thousand words, but is that enough? And does it represent the whole? Basically, the people at the Royal Welsh Show. He said that most of the posts he received were ordinary people rather than celebrities or politicians, but Nigel Owens, the referee of the game, was an exception. He explained that he had attended the Royal Welsh for many years, coming from a farming background and having worked on a farm. For the last four or five years he had been coming to referee the final of the sevens tournament. However, he has been President of the Young Farmers’ Club of Wales for several years now, and has come here most often to represent the YFC when he was a member, and then to help out in the office during the competitions. The voice of Nicola Davies, chief announcer and commentator, is often heard in the ring. “I’ve been coming here with my family since I was a child, showing the Welsh cobs for many years,” she said. Mr. Thomas wanted to put a name to this familiar voice, so he interviewed Ms. Davies for his Facebook page. But then I was asked to make a commentary about the horses some ten or fifteen years ago, and I caught the fever. Now I am the chief commentator, and I have control of the commentators of the main ring, the horse ring, the cattle, the sheep, and the pigs. I was part of the team, but some say it was promotion, others not. “We are, of course, the husband and wife team of the leader of the UKIP in Wales, Neil and Christine Hamilton, and we are here mainly to give you a few more paragraphs for your thesis. He told me that people rarely refuse to be interviewed and indeed find this a more successful method than a simple questionnaire. I don’t know very much about pigs and cattle, but I’ll try and find someone who does,” said Mr. Neil. A police officer from the Dyfed Powys force was among those who consented to be interviewed. It is, besides, the greatest agricultural show in North Europe, and I understand it brings into the Mid-Wales economy £20 million a year. It is an important event in the calendar. I have been an officer with the Dyfed-Powys police, and I have been at the show three days this week. Barbara Green, wife of the steward, is showing a barren mare in the main ring. I am from a farming background, so I am interested in the animals. I showed a horse here for the first time when I was sixteen, and since then quite a few years have gone by. I’m rather excited, but also very nervous. I’d have come anyway, so I have a little extra work and I’m also going to help my partner show a horse tomorrow,” she said. I’m Greg Thomas, a postgrad geography student at the University of Wales, Aberystwyth. I’ve been collecting stories for the Humans of the Royal Welsh project this week, and it’s been great to meet so many of the people who work so hard to make the show the best in Europe. I’ve been looking forward to it, but also a bit anxious. Now, shall we give Mr Thomas a taste of his own medicine? As I am myself from the parish of Builth Wells and of a farming background, I am in the position of privileged student of the events of my home country, Wales. It is my privilege to study an event that means so much to so many.

text: The final leaders' debate gave the opposition parties what they wanted in throwing the focus of the campaign well and truly onto the NHS. The initial half hour was emotionally charged, filled with policy and vigorous exchanges. Compelling content. Carwyn Jones himself established the tone in his opening statement by concentrating entirely on health services and inevitably mentioning the absence of a junior doctors' strike in Wales. The ongoing dispute in England has provided Labour with a useful point of contrast when addressing criticisms of the NHS, and the strike this week could not have been better timed for them as polling day approaches next week. There was a notable difference compared to last week's leaders' debate, when the opposition parties spent much of their time uniting against Carwyn Jones. This debate felt fragmented, with various disputes erupting among different leaders at different times. Nathan Gill and Kirsty Williams clashed over EU steel dumping, and Andrew RT Davies criticised Kirsty Williams and Leanne Wood for making deals with the Labour administration. An intriguing theme was the consistent attacks by Carwyn Jones on Leanne Wood regarding Plaid's plans to reorganise the NHS and their proposal to only pay off the debt of students who return to Wales. This occurred despite Labour repeatedly stating that this election is a contest between them and the Conservatives. Ultimately, a clearly frustrated Leanne Wood had enough and accused him of misrepresenting her policies. Subsequently, Plaid stated they took the criticism as a compliment, asserting it clearly indicated Labour were unsettled by a Plaid threat. Labour, for their part, believe there are soft Plaid votes available in marginal seats like the Vale of Glamorgan and the Vale of Clwyd, where they face the Tories. Elsewhere, Nathan Gill adopted a different tone. Thus far in the assembly campaign, he has been eager to distance himself from any discussion of the EU as the party attempts to demonstrate its serious commitment to devolution. That seemed to conclude with repeated references to the EU during the debate. This appeared to me as an appeal to mobilise their core voters. A significant question is whether UKIP voters, who are clearly energised by the EU referendum, will be sufficiently motivated to turn out next week. There is no precedent to rely on, so we will all have to wait and see, but the impact of the UKIP numbers, particularly in the marginal seats, could be substantial. One party insider described a strong UKIP vote in a tight marginal as like a bomb going off due to the effect it could have on the votes of the other parties and, consequently, the final outcome in many counts.

text: Timing is everything in politics if you want to have a chance of being heard. The outspoken Chief Inspector of Schools, Sir Michael Wilshaw, has carefully chosen his moment to deliver a verdict on serious weaknesses at seven of the poorest performing chains of academy schools in a hard-hitting letter to the education secretary. He does not hold back on what he describes as worrying findings. Just a few days ago, the government took a further step towards removing local councils from the management of schools. Draft plans for a national funding formula will result in the vast bulk of government education funds going directly to schools by 2020. This will allow the distribution to be altered, but it is also a preparatory measure for another significant government ambition—to render councils running schools in England a thing of the past. It is understood that the Treasury was eager for the funding formula announcement to be made this week, which suggests we may hear more in the Budget next week about the push for more schools to become academies. Many parents in England scarcely notice whether their local school is run by the council or by an academy trust. They are preoccupied with other essentials like a sense of order and community and, of course, exam results. However, generally, people do care whether their taxes, their public money, is well spent. Therefore, it is unsurprising that Sir Michael focuses some of his criticism not only on poor results but also on high salaries and large bank reserves. Essentially, he is questioning if these particular seven trusts offer value for money for the pupils, the parents, and taxpayers. Is it a partial and skewed assessment as the government suggests? Certainly, there are many excellent academy schools too, which he acknowledges. Regarding council-run schools, only yesterday, schools minister Nick Gibb highlighted some of the worst-performing local authorities in terms of GCSE results. Thus, it cuts both ways. Labour wants the government to press the pause button to review the system of holding academy trusts accountable and ensure it is robust. That is not going to happen. Instead, the government will continue to point to its network of eight regional schools commissioners whose role it is to do just that. If anything, all indications are that the momentum will increase towards all schools in England becoming academies.

text: Sheffield United got their first win of the season as goals from Billy Sharp and James Wilson cancelled out a Kane Hemmings opener to give them victory over Oxford United. Oxford took the lead through Hemmings in the 16th minute after United goalkeeper Simon Moore could only parry a long-range effort from Liam Sercombe into the path of the advancing striker. United sought a response, and Kieron Freeman was unfortunate to see his attempt deflect over the bar following a mazy run and pass by Mark Duffy. Matt Done then had a low drive from inside the area pushed away by a strong hand from Simon Eastwood. In the 52nd minute, a first-time shot from John Lundstram at the edge of the box was parried away by Moore after a clever free-kick routine by the visitors. United equalised in the 65th minute as Sharp converted a Matt Done cross from close range. The home side then took the lead as an in-swinging free-kick by Duffy was headed in by Wilson with 17 minutes remaining. Report supplied by the Press Association. text: Joe Rowley scored his first goal to give Chesterfield a victory over Port Vale that keeps their slender League One survival hopes alive for another week. The 17-year-old capitalised in the second half, leaving Chesterfield nine points from safety with four matches remaining and condemning Vale to another fruitless away day, placing them in relegation danger. Although Thorsten Stuckmann saved a low shot from JJ Hooper in the 27th minute, the first half reflected the teams' league positions, but the match gained momentum after the interval. Vale nearly scored in the 52nd minute when Chris Eagles' close-range shot was superbly saved by Stuckmann, before Chesterfield countered two minutes later, with Rowley scoring after Deniz Mehmet could only parry Kristian Dennis' shot. Vale struggled to create chances, and Chesterfield nearly scored again in the 81st minute when a 25-yard shot from Dan Gardner was tipped over by Mehmet. Chesterfield had to defend desperately in stoppage time as Vale, one point from safety with a game in hand, pressed for an equaliser but held on for a victory that leaves both clubs facing League Two football next season. text: Sri Lanka's Kumar Sangakkara became the first player to score four successive one-day international centuries as his side beat Scotland at the World Cup. The 37-year-old scored 124 in a total of 363-9 in Hobart, adding to his previous centuries in the tournament against Bangladesh, England, and Australia. Sangakkara surpassed 500 ODI dismissals as Scotland were bowled out for 215. Captain Preston Mommsen and Freddie Coleman scored half-centuries, but Sri Lanka concluded with four victories in Pool A. They appear set to face South Africa in the first quarter-final in Sydney on Wednesday. Despite posting their best-ever total batting second against a Test-playing nation, a fifth defeat means Scotland remain winless. They will play co-hosts Australia in their final match on Saturday in Hobart. On a day of records at Bellerive Oval, left-hander Sangakkara recorded his fifth World Cup century and is now one behind the record of six held by India's Sachin Tendulkar. He has now amassed 14,189 ODI runs, with only Tendulkar (18,426), who retired in 2013, having more runs for their country in the 50-over format. Sangakkara, who became the first player to score four centuries at a World Cup, has previously indicated he will retire from ODI cricket at the end of the tournament. I've been batting and keeping for a long time, it's getting harder and the joints are creaking and aching, but I consider myself lucky to be part of a great team, he said. Davey's figures of 3-63 moved him to the top of the World Cup wicket-takers with 14, one ahead of New Zealand pair Trent Boult and Tim Southee. A 20-ball half-century from Sri Lanka captain Angelo Mathews, which included four successive sixes off the bowling of Matt Machan, had set them on course for a score of more than 400. However, a flurry of late wickets and some impressive catching meant Scotland restricted their tail-enders. text: Too many patients are locked into mental health rehabilitation wards far from home, a review of England's psychiatric services suggests. These are external links and will open in a new window. The Care Quality Commission reported there were 3,500 beds in locked facilities nationwide, but it believes more individuals could and should receive care in residential settings near their homes. The report highlighted safety on mental health wards as another significant concern. NHS England stated progress was being made with increased funding for care. Claire Murdoch, head of mental health for NHS England, noted that while there were reasons for optimism, improvements were needed in line with the priorities set out by the NHS five-year plan. The Care Quality Commission (CQC) examined all specialist mental health services across England, inspecting NHS care and NHS services provided by the independent sector. It reported that almost all services were rated as good or outstanding for having caring and compassionate staff, with many examples of excellent care. However, the report identified several areas of concern. CQC leaders specifically stated that locked rehabilitation wards (of which two-thirds are managed by independent providers) did not offer the appropriate model of care for the 21st Century. They indicated some patients spent excessive time on these wards, with an average stay of 341 days. This situation leaves patients at risk of becoming institutionalised, with the ultimate goal of rehabilitation back into the community being overlooked, the report warns. Dr Paul Lelliott, lead for mental health at the CQC, stated: We weren't expecting to find this many [locked rehabilitation beds]. We can't specify exactly how many individuals on these wards don't need to be in locked facilities, but we suspect that a substantial proportion of people in these services could, and should be, relocated closer to home and cared for in residential settings that offer greater independence, supported by community services rather than being in hospital. Inspectors also reported that about a third of services required improvement in terms of safety. One in 20 were deemed inadequate for safety, indicating real and sometimes immediate concerns for patient safety, according to CQC leaders. Inspectors highlighted old and unsuitable buildings—for example, buildings with blind spots in corridors where patients at risk of self-harm could not be observed. Adding to safety concerns were nurse shortages, with a 12% decline in mental health nursing staff between January 2010 and 2017. Commenting on the report, Brian Dow, from the charity Rethink Mental Illness, said there was a significant level of commitment from individuals in the sector to deliver high-quality care but that there was an awful long way to go. He added: There is a fairly large number of services that the CQC says need improvement, raising big questions about what is happening in this system. Is there sufficient funding? Do we have the right personnel to deliver the care? Are individuals involved in their own care, and are people supported and trained to deliver the care? Meanwhile, Ms Murdoch told the BBC she believed the report was a really fair assessment of the state of the nation's mental health services. She added: It highlights that most providers of mental health care are now either moving towards the good category or are good and moving towards outstanding—so it is showing improvement. But quite rightly, it also addresses what needs to improve next.

text: Safety inspections will be carried out at schools across Scotland following the collapse of a wall at an Edinburgh primary, BBC Scotland has learned. Four buildings in the capital were temporarily closed after defects were found in schools constructed by Miller Construction a decade ago. The new surveys focus on schools built by the same company in Glasgow, Fife, and Inverclyde. The contractor stated that inspections were a precautionary measure. Hundreds of bricks were dislodged from the wall of Oxgangs Primary School during Storm Gertrude in January. A safety inspection identified issues with the construction of the external wall when the school was built in 2005, as part of the Public Private Partnership 1 project. Oxgangs was part of a broader programme that included 17 schools built or refurbished following an agreement between the council and a private finance consortium. When the wall collapsed, further inspections uncovered similar problems at three other schools in Edinburgh - St Peter's RC Primary, Firrhill High, and Braidburn Special Schools. All were constructed around the same time by Miller Construction, which was acquired by Galliford Try in 2014. The four schools were deemed unsafe for pupils and temporarily closed. They are scheduled to reopen after the Easter holidays. A spokesperson for Galliford Try said: The four schools temporarily closed in Edinburgh comprised the second phase of the PPP1 programme, which was completed by Miller Construction in 2005. We have already commenced remedial work at Oxgangs Primary School and are assessing the requirement for work on the further three schools. Any remedial work required will be carried out as quickly as possible, allowing the children to return to their studies with the minimum disruption. While we are not aware of any defects, as a precautionary measure, we have contacted the clients of the PPP school projects Miller Construction undertook in Glasgow, Fife, and Inverclyde. Further investigations will be carried out as appropriate. Signed in 2001, Edinburgh's Public Private Partnership deal for schools was valued at £360m. In return for 30 years of fixed payments from the council, a private consortium designed, built, and managed the schools. Miller Construction was part of that consortium and part of others building schools elsewhere in Scotland. A PPP1 deal signed in Glasgow a year earlier was valued at three times as much as Edinburgh's and involved 29 secondaries and one primary school across the country. Glasgow City Council stated its PPP contract would now conduct surveys on the handful of schools built by Miller Construction. Galliford Try said it had also contacted the clients of schools built by the company in Inverclyde, and inspections are also being conducted by the council in Fife. Shelagh McLean, head of education and children's services (equity and system improvement), said: Fife Council has contacted both of our PPP Contractors, who are monitoring the situation in Edinburgh. They will be carrying out inspections in Fife during the school Easter holidays. Both contractors also carry out annual inspections of the building fabric and free-standing walls as part of their ongoing maintenance. Oxgangs Primary School and St Peter's are scheduled to reopen on 11 April.

text: Police have said the number of people caught drink-driving during the annual Christmas crackdown increased significantly on the previous year. In total, 396 arrests were made between 27 November last year and 2 January, marking a 42% increase from the 282 arrests in 2014-15. Among those arrested was a police officer, and one individual was stopped while their children were in the vehicle. One driver was found to be four times over the drink-drive limit, while another was caught drink-driving on two separate occasions. Assistant Chief Constable Alan Todd, of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI), stated that drink-drivers were disregarding the safety of themselves and others with this shameful and incredibly dangerous practice. He mentioned that those caught would face losing their driving licence for at least a year, and many risked losing their jobs or going to jail. Every year across Northern Ireland, drinking and driving kills, maims and wrecks families, he stated. We detected a driver, with their children in the car, at three o'clock in the afternoon having been drinking. Think about the consequences to yourself and your family of being involved in a serious collision. How would you feel if your actions resulted in you or one of your family being paralysed? How would you feel if some innocent person was killed? ACC Todd noted that the police officer who was arrested could expect to face court as well as disciplinary proceedings within the PSNI, where suspension or dismissal was possible. The signal is clear - it is unacceptable in today's society to drink and drive. Mr Durkan added that the Road Traffic Amendment Bill, which was passed in the Northern Ireland Assembly this week, will lower drink-drive limits.

text: The amount of nursery and pre-school provision for children in special schools is to be reduced. The change will be implemented in September and will impact all 39 special schools in Northern Ireland. It will result in pre-school children with moderate to severe learning difficulties attending school for 2.5 hours instead of at least 4.5 hours daily. The reduction was disclosed by the Education Authority (EA) in a letter to a parent. It confirms that from September 2016 all pre-school children will receive 2.5 hours in pre-school per day. The EA stated the change is designed to increase the opportunity for children to access special school places, and will ensure greater regional consistency. However, an organisation representing special school principals and governors expressed that the reduction will hold back and restrict the development of children with complex needs. In a submission to the Northern Ireland Assembly, the Strategic Leadership Forum for Special Schools (SLFSS) stated they totally disagree with the change. They indicated it will have a range of impacts including: Francine Wilson's three-year-old son Aodhan, is set to begin pre-school at a special school in September. Aodhan has Down's Syndrome and we were hoping in September 2016 he would get five hours of nursery placement, she stated. Receiving two and a half hours will, I believe, result in delayed development in Aodhan, both educationally and socially. However, a spokesperson for the EA said the reduction was in line with the Department of Education's 'Learning to Learn' policy. There has been a progressive move towards part-time places in all sectors, the spokesperson stated. This policy recognises the research evidence that there is no discernible difference in children's development at the start of primary school between those who received part-time and full-time pre-school provision. This move is designed to increase the opportunity for children to access special school places, preferably nearer to their homes. The provision of increased access and greater regional consistency is a priority, they added.

He seems to have misspoken, as the research actually indicated pensioners would lose £817 over five years. Responding to a question from Angus Robertson, the SNP's leader in Westminster, she pledged that pensioners' incomes would continue to rise but did not specify by how much. The government is currently committed to maintaining the pension triple-lock until 2020, meaning it will increase the basic state pension by average earnings, inflation, or 2.5%, whichever is higher. Labour, the Liberal Democrats, and the SNP are all committed to maintaining the triple-lock. However, the Work and Pensions Committee has stated it should be scrapped, arguing it is unsustainable and unfair on younger families. It suggested that pensions should rise with earnings and be protected against inflation exceeding earnings, but with no minimum annual increase. John Cridland, who published a report on the future of state pensions last month, suggested that the triple-lock would also eventually need to be abandoned in favour of an earnings link. Speaking on BBC Newsnight, Mr Blackford cited research from the House of Commons Library, which found that over a five-year period, pensioners would be £872 worse off if the triple-lock were removed. Providing more detail, the library was asked to take Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts for the next five years of inflation and average earnings figures. It then compared what would happen to pensions under different scenarios. It turned out that protecting it in line with earnings would make almost no difference, as average earnings are expected to exceed 2.5% throughout the period. Protecting only in line with inflation would cost a total of £642 over five years for a pensioner on the basic state pension and £817 over five years for someone on the new state pension. Mr Blackford presumably remembered that figure incorrectly when he said it would cost £872. Clearly, these figures are based on forecasts for future events, which are uncertain.
