text: Chris Coleman says the 2018 World Cup campaign will be his last as Wales manager. Having led Wales to a historic semi-final at Euro 2016, Coleman's reputation is at an all-time high. The 46-year-old is under contract until the end of the next World Cup, with his team playing their first qualifier at home against Moldova on 5 September. I am sure this will be my last campaign whether we qualify or not, said Coleman. That will be six or seven years in the job, which is a long time. So I think this will be my last attempt, so I will give it my best shot, but I would not consider going elsewhere. I want to see this through. There's success in this team, I think, because they're at a good age. But I'll certainly give everything I've got in this next campaign. I'll make sure they do. Coleman has overseen a remarkable transformation in Wales' - and his own - fortunes since his appointment in January 2012. Five months earlier, Wales had fallen to their lowest world ranking of 117th and, despite making the worst start of any Wales manager with four defeats from his first four games, Coleman is now guiding his country through its most successful era. Euro 2016 was Wales' first appearance at a major tournament for 58 years, and their progress to the semi-finals saw them surpass the previous best performance at a major tournament - reaching the last eight at the 1958 World Cup. If they [FAW] wanted to talk to me about another contract I would be cashing in a bit, wouldn't I? Same as if I jumped ship and went somewhere else because we had done well at a tournament. Wales have been the underdogs for much of their history, though that could change following their achievements at Euro 2016. The biggest challenge for us is that we will be a target now in this campaign because of what we've just done, said Coleman. I'll never make that mistake again.

text: Rafael Nadal beat world number one Novak Djokovic in a pulsating four-set final to claim his second US Open title in New York. The 27-year-old Spaniard held on superbly in the third set to win a thrilling contest 6-2 3-6 6-4 6-1 in three hours and 21 minutes. An extraordinary 54-shot rally—the longest in the tournament by 20 shots—epitomised a battle that captivated the 23,000 spectators in Arthur Ashe Stadium. Nadal has now secured 13 Grand Slam singles titles and moves within one of Pete Sampras on the all-time list, with Roger Federer leading on 17. After missing last year's US Open due to a seven-month absence with a knee injury, Nadal is poised to regain the number one ranking. Having this success is amazing, he stated. I never expected it. That's life, and I'm fortunate to have what I have. If he remains healthy, he can easily win four or five more Slams. No question about it. To me, he's better than ever. It's amazing how much he desires it. I've never seen anything like it. Let's hope he stays healthy because it will be great for our sport. I truly love the competition, I truly love the sport. All my career, I dreamed of being involved in matches like today. I enjoy every moment. These things are not forever. In a few years, I won't have this chance. I try my best, I have passion, and that's all I can do. Monday's final was predictably electrifying and punishing as the pair met for the 37th time, surpassing the rivalry of John McEnroe and Ivan Lendl to set a new record since the Open era began in 1968. It was their sixth Grand Slam final and third at Flushing Meadows, after the Spaniard won in 2010 and Djokovic avenged in 2011. Nadal, seeded second, had a 21-0 record on hard courts this year heading into the final and had dropped serve just once while advancing through the draw in New York. He began as many people's favourite and set about proving them right as he dominated for the first hour, accelerating through his forehand to find a gear that Djokovic simply could not contain. Two breaks earned Nadal the first set in a relatively swift 42 minutes, but for the next 80 minutes it was all Djokovic as his forehand began to dictate, while his returning ability increased the pressure. Nadal's seemingly impregnable serve was broken three times in succession, the first due to that lung-busting 54-shot rally that explored every inch of the court, and Djokovic raced through six of seven games to take a 2-0 lead in the third. Nadal was reeling, fending off another break point to avoid falling a double break behind, and it proved significant when the Djokovic storm subsided and the errors crept back in game six. After two hours and 17 minutes, the world's top two players were level at 3-3 in the third set, and it appeared Djokovic had made the decisive move when he earned three break points at 4-4. Nadal was knocked off his feet by the force of one strike that clipped his baseline, but the indomitable Majorcan refused to yield, coming back to hold and then launching into a return game at 5-4 to earn set point. A trademark hammer of a forehand was too much for even the elastic Djokovic to return, and a jubilant Nadal crouched at the baseline, punching his fist, as he took a lead that had seemed highly unlikely only minutes earlier. The belief appeared to drain from Djokovic and, after saving an early break point in the fourth set with a net cord, Nadal left no room for bad luck when he crunched another forehand on his next opportunity. A titanic struggle came to a tame end as Djokovic sprayed two backhands into the tramlines to fall 5-1 behind, but there were plenty of emotions on display after Nadal saw the Serb find the net on match point. The victorious Spaniard fell to the ground before tearfully celebrating with his supporters. All of my team knows how much this match today means to me, added Nadal. Playing against Novak is always a very special feeling and nobody brings my game to the limit like he does. Again, it was a huge privilege and an honour to fight for this trophy.

text: Yorkshire captain Andrew Gale and one-day skipper Alex Lees both made half-centuries to help their side avoid the follow-on against Lancashire. However, the home team remains in control as they head into the final day of the Roses match at Old Trafford. Lees (85) and Gale (83) contributed a 130-run third-wicket partnership as Yorkshire reached a total of 360, with Kyle Jarvis claiming 4-70. text: They call Lynton Crosby the Wizard of Oz - the political magician who has been hired by the Conservatives to mastermind their next election campaign. These are external links and will open in a new window. Like the wizard, Crosby is an enigmatic figure, and some assert he is not as impressive as believed—after all, the last time he managed a general election for the Tories, they were defeated. However, he has achieved notable successes, both in his native Australia and most recently by running a successful re-election campaign for the Mayor of London, Boris Johnson. Lynton Crosby was born 55 years ago on a farm in rural South Australia. His father was not a natural farmer—he was musical and artistic—and soon relocated the family to the nearby town of Kadina, where he established an arts and crafts shop. By all accounts, Crosby enjoyed a very happy—and somewhat indulged—childhood. Mum and Dad adored him. They did anything for him, says Robyn Hewett, one of his two elder sisters. At primary school, he loved debating. He was easy-going and friendly and enjoyed putting on plays and performing in the shed for other children. And very academic, I suppose you'd say. Nothing was too much when it came to caring for the young Lynton. When he was accepted into Adelaide University to study economics, his parents moved to the city to be near him. Although they were not particularly political, like most rural folk, they were instinctive supporters of the Liberals—Australia's conservative party. Perhaps it was unsurprising that after a period in the private sector, Crosby moved into Liberal politics—and fell in love with it. He was not particularly effective as a candidate, though. As he puts it, he managed to turn a marginal seat into a safe Labour one and later admitted, with hindsight, I wouldn't have voted for me. Instead, Lynton Crosby shifted to the backroom, eventually becoming campaign director for Australia's Liberal Prime Minister John Howard. I think he's a very professional political campaigner. He's just interested in ensuring that the party he supports wins, Mr Howard told BBC Radio 4's Profile. As a party leader of long-time standing, I can only say that's exactly the sort of mentality you want from somebody who is your principal campaign manager. Crosby managed to secure four consecutive election victories for John Howard, but critics claimed he employed some dubious tactics: so-called dog-whistle campaigns that appealed to people's basest instincts on crime and immigration, and wedge issues, which force the opposition to defend an unpopular policy. His company's website describes him, with a certain amount of pride, I think, as a 'master of the dark arts of politics,' says Cheryl Kernot, a former Australian Senator who has been on the receiving end of several of Crosby's campaigns. I remember most vividly the 10 years that he was masterminding conservative campaigns here, and the focus on refugees and asylum seekers, and the exploitation of basic instincts of fear of difference, and latent prejudice, Kernot recalls. There's nothing grubby about Lynton, counters John Howard. He's a tough campaigner. He's no more or less ruthless than any other effective campaigner. And this wedge nonsense [is] the bleating of people who didn't like the Liberal Party winning in Australia. However, similar criticisms were levelled at Crosby when he came to Britain to assist Michael Howard's Conservatives in the 2005 campaign. Daniel Finkelstein, now a Times columnist, then working for the Tory Party, was the man who first introduced Lynton Crosby to then Conservative leader Michael Howard. They immediately hit it off. Both of them are very obsessive about politics... I think Michael appreciated Lynton's ability to pick issues because that's the way that Michael thinks, Finkelstein says. Crosby certainly brought focus and discipline to the Conservative campaign and he raised morale among party workers by awarding prizes every day for the best press release. But slogans like: How would you feel if a bloke on early release attacked your daughter? were blamed for giving the Tories the reputation of the nasty party. Conservative ads also had dog-whistle messages like are you thinking what we're thinking? However, Crosby's admirers—and there are many—claim that while his ads may be brutal, the man is far from uncivilised. The one thing that I think would be a mistake is to think of Lynton Crosby as a sort of crude, ball-busting Australian outsider. He is not an intellectually unsophisticated, crude campaigning person at all. He's a pretty clever guy, says Daniel Finkelstein. When the Conservatives lost the 2005 election, Crosby said he had come in too late: You can't fatten a pig on market day, he said—but he left enough admirers here in Britain for Boris Johnson to recall him for the 2008 London mayoral campaign. London is naturally a Labour city, so it took some political acumen to persuade voters to elect a Tory mayor two terms in a row. Crosby imposed discipline on Johnson, demanding that he take himself more seriously, and concentrate not just on his pet projects, but on issues that voters actually cared about—and he did not shy from telling truth to power. I remember once, it was the end of a very long day, I was absolutely exhausted and I had to give a speech to a bunch of Conservative councillors—this was the 2007/2008 campaign, recalls Boris Johnson. I was at the end of my tether—barely knew what I was talking about and I thought I'd done more or less a good job with these guys and got through it in one piece. I tottered out of the room and my phone buzzed with a text. It said 'crap speech, mate'—and that was very much his approach to candidate management. Lynton Crosby is known for his earthy language, but his candid approach worked on Boris Johnson. Find out more about the people making the headlines on Radio 4's Profile. Download Radio 4's Profile. Listen to the profile of Lynton Crosby. Explore the best of Radio 4's Profile. But Ken Livingstone—Boris Johnson's Labour opponent in both 2008 and 2012—still feels aggrieved about what he says was the negative personal campaigning Crosby masterminded against him. There was almost never a time when Boris was launching some great new idea or anything else like that. It was just a pretty unremitting series of personal attacks and negative campaigning, says Livingstone. It certainly worked, though. When Boris Johnson won again in London earlier this year, he told David Cameron that Crosby was just the man to help the Tories fight the next general election campaign and that he should break the piggy bank to hire him. Although the recent appointment was not met with universal acclaim. Tory modernisers fear that Crosby will pander to the core vote, using issues like immigration and crime. Daniel Finkelstein, himself a moderniser, thinks this is too simplistic a reading: I don't think he'll take the party away from the strategy the leader of the party wants to follow, providing David Cameron is clear enough about what that is. I think he will turn that into a disciplined strategy. Labour and the Liberal Democrats will now be studying Crosby's techniques and working out their own defence against his dark arts. I had no doubt from the moment I lost to Boris this time round that Lynton Crosby would be brought in to run Cameron's re-election campaign, says Ken Livingstone. For Crosby to have been able to deliver a Tory victory in London when they were losing everything everywhere else is an endorsement, effectively. And I remember saying to Ed Miliband throughout our campaign, 'you know, really follow this one closely, because this is what you will be up against'. text: Matt Done's first-half goal clinched three points for Sheffield United over Peterborough and a fourth straight league win. The home team dominated the early stages of the match with Billy Sharp's first-time effort missing the target, Daniel Lafferty's drive deflected wide, and Done forcing Luke McGee into a superb reflex save. Done scored the match's only goal after 13 minutes, steering the ball past McGee at the near post following Kieron Freeman's low cross. Peterborough's Chris Forrester then had a long-range shot deflected wide, while Blades goalkeeper Simon Moore made a fine save to his right to deny Paul Taylor's shot on the turn. Substitute Stefan Scougall nearly scored a second goal for the hosts in the second half when his 20-yard effort was palmed wide by McGee. Moore preserved his team's lead with a great save to keep out Gwion Edwards' close-range shot and also stopped efforts from Forrester and Marcus Maddison. Reports provided by the Press Association. text: The gaming industry needs to get behind a centre dedicated to videogames or risk losing it forever, Games Workshop founder Ian Livingstone has said. Mr Livingstone, alongside other developers, has assisted in establishing The National Videogame Foundation to support Nottingham's National Videogame Arcade (NVA). He stated it should be to gaming what the National Gallery is to art. The NVA was on the brink of closure just one year after its opening. Mr Livingstone, who contributed to launching the Lara Croft franchise, stated it was his and the gaming industry's duty to support the NVA, the sole institute of its kind in the UK. He mentioned it was only when it nearly closed that its profile was elevated. There were people [in the industry] who were unaware of it, he remarked. They inquired 'what is it?', 'how can we assist?' Visitor feedback was favourable, with an average score of 4.5 out of 5 on Tripadvisor, but due to several reasons, including funding delays, the business exhausted its finances. The NVA's co-director, Iain Simons, stated the arcade's staff accepted deferred payment to keep it operational. He also sought assistance from videogame developers for investment, with Mr Livingstone being one of those who responded. It was unsurprising that Ian Livingstone, the co-founder of games company Games Workshop, intervened to assist the NVA. He has been a significant supporter and asserts the National Videogame Arcade should be to gaming what the National Gallery is to fine art. He was present at its launch in March 2015 and spoke of the ubiquity of gaming, noting that everywhere you go, individuals of all ages are playing games on smartphones and consoles. Mr Livingstone also likes to remind people of the games industry's worth, a substantial $100bn. However, he stated gaming was much more than entertainment; it is a genuine art form and should be acknowledged as such. He said the NVA should not merely be a museum but should explore the cultural impact of videogames. The National Videogame Foundation will focus primarily on education. Mr Livingstone described it as a call to action and a vital moment for videogames' cultural confidence. The foundation will organise the GameCity Festival, held every October, and manage the arcade. Richard Wilson, CEO of TIGA, which represents the UK's games industry, stated the NVA was a great project and suggested the largest videogame developers could have a bigger role to play there. However, he noted smaller companies were up against it and could not always allocate time and resources. National Videogame Arcade timeline.

text: China's economy is slowing down. We are aware of that, as is President Xi Jinping. It is one of the significant issues, or even shadows, looming over his visit to the United States. After an average annual growth rate of 10% for three decades, that pace has significantly slowed. Last year, it was 7.4%. Many economists are profoundly sceptical about China's official data, believing the true figure is considerably lower. For next year, the IMF forecasts 6.8%, and the slowdown was inevitable. The IMF described the transition underway in China as moving to a 'new normal', characterised by slower yet safer and more sustainable growth. A new normal is necessary because the forces behind China's previous dynamism are weakening. The ageing population limits the contribution a growing labour force can make to the economy. All that previous strong growth means the technological gap with the rest of the world has narrowed, limiting the scope for rapid gains from catching up. Investment is another growth source, adding to the economy's productive capacity. However, China's investment level is already extremely high. Indeed, IMF research suggested even in 2012 that it was excessive. Why excessive? Because it diverts resources from other sectors of the economy, including household spending, and if a country over-invests, an increasing number of projects are likely to be economically inefficient. The question troubling financial markets intermittently for the past few weeks has been whether the transition will be smooth or if China will suffer a hard landing, meaning an abrupt slowdown or even a recession. The answer is indeed significant for the rest of us. China is, by one measure, the largest economy on the planet. It accounts for 17% of global economic activity. The US economy is almost as large but is not growing as rapidly. This situation is likely to persist for years or even decades after China has settled to a more sustainable growth rate. This means China's impact on global growth is larger, as is the potential contribution it can make to increased demand for goods produced by other countries. Thus, whether a hard or soft landing occurs is indeed significant. What can we expect? Views among economists vary—as they often do. One influential voice has expressed a rather gloomy judgement: Willem Buiter, chief economist at the giant financial firm Citigroup, formerly of the Bank of England and the London School of Economics. He states: We believe that there is a high and rising likelihood of a Chinese, emerging market and global recession scenario playing out. There is a debate to be had about what the term recession means, especially when applied to emerging economies and even more so for the global economy. Mr Buiter's definition is based on an economy's potential to grow. He concludes that growth of less than 2% for at least a year constitutes a global recession. The threshold for China is 2.5%. He is among the sceptics regarding China's data, so he believes the Chinese economy is already closer to that than official figures suggest. For the world economy, he estimates a 40% chance of a moderate recession, with a 15% chance of a more severe downturn and a financial crisis. If it does occur, he says, it is most likely that the world will be dragged into a recession by slow growth in several key emerging economies, especially China: We consider China to be at high and rapidly rising risk of a cyclical hard landing. Why? Many classical warning signs are present, he says—excess capacity in an increasing number of industries, excessive borrowing and debt, and episodes of irrational exuberance in asset markets, recently in property and the stock market. He states: This is the classical recipe for a recession in capitalist market economies. If it does occur, it would surely affect many others. Moreover, other emerging economies are already in recession, including two large ones, Brazil and Russia. China is among the most important export destinations for many countries—number one for South Korea (more than a quarter of exports), Saudi Arabia, and Iran. For the largest economies, China ranks as the second-largest export market for Japan, fourth for the US, and for Germany, it is second among markets outside the European Union. Even countries with little direct trade with China could easily feel the effects of a hard landing if they supply countries that sell directly to China or if they export commodities whose price in international markets is affected by weakened Chinese demand. Consider two key industrial commodities, crude oil and copper. The price of crude oil has fallen by more than half since June last year. There are supply factors behind that—shale oil in the US and the unwillingness of Saudi Arabia and others to curtail production as they might have done in the past. However, weaker-than-expected growth in demand from China is another element in the price fall. Copper is a key raw material for the construction industry. It is used extensively in electrical installations, and China's building boom has been hungry for copper. Its price is also down by half, in this case from 2011. China's slowdown is the key factor. So that is the case for pessimism. However, some are more optimistic about the outlook. In a recent note to clients, the London consultancy Capital Economics wrote: In contrast to the widespread doom and gloom about China's immediate economic outlook, we think growth has already stabilised after a slowdown at the start of the year, and that there are good reasons to expect stronger growth in the months ahead. Ahead of his visit to the US, President Xi told the Wall Street Journal: The Chinese economy is still operating within the proper range. His host, President Barack Obama, must be hoping he is correct and that it remains that way. He is not alone in this hope.

text: An error with the Global Positioning System (GPS) network has been blamed for causing problems with digital radio broadcasts last week. The US Air Force reported that the removal of a satellite from service resulted in a software error. A BBC spokesperson confirmed that the decommissioning of a GPS satellite caused difficulties for listeners receiving digital radio signals. The BBC understands that several other satellites were also affected. I live on the Worksop side of Sheffield and for the past two days the reception of the BBC National Ensemble [BBC radio stations] has been virtually non-existent indoors, wrote Darcy72 on Digital Spy's online forums last week. In response to the reported issues, the BBC stated: The outages were caused by a rogue GPS satellite (SVN23), which was taken out of service in the evening of 26 January. The BBC has now learned that the issue arose after a decommissioned satellite caused software problems affecting several other satellites. DAB transmitters must broadcast at precisely the same frequencies and, to synchronise, they lock onto GPS satellite signals. The GPS signals themselves broadcast the time and are intended to be accurate to within a few nanoseconds. However, on 26 January, one of the GPS satellites—named SVN23—orbiting the Earth was decommissioned. This unexpectedly caused problems for the entire network. While the core navigation systems were working normally, the coordinated universal time timing signal was off by 13 microseconds, which exceeded the design specifications, stated the US Air Force. The issue was resolved at 06:10 MST, however, global users may have experienced GPS timing issues for several hours. In fact, due to the problem, some GPS positioning would have been thrown off by nearly 4km. The time discrepancy was detected by the Metsahovi Radio Observatory in Finland. It is not yet clear whether other systems worldwide, such as navigational tools, were affected. The BBC is still seeking further details about the incident from the US Air Force. They knew they were decommissioning it, so shouldn't they have been aware this would happen? questioned Prof Danielle George, a radio engineer at the University of Manchester. It was decommissioned after 25 years—actually it should have just had a seven-and-a-half-year lifespan, so it lasted much longer than it should have done. Prof George added that if there had only been a problem with one satellite, DAB transmitters would probably not have experienced difficulties. They shouldn't have seen an issue with that because, as far as I understand, the way they work is they need two frequencies to lock, and there are a number of GPS [signals] to look at, she told the BBC. This should be treated as a warning of what could go wrong, said Martyn Thomas, a fellow at the Royal Academy of Engineering who has criticised technological reliance on GPS. The world is dependent on GPS for a vast range of critical applications from navigation to financial trading, and precision docking of oil tankers to high-tech farming. In the future, Prof Thomas stated, it was essential that there was a back-up.

text: Councils have warned they may be charging more for services despite some already increasing such revenue by more than 100% in three years. Government data indicates councils generated over £11 billion in fees, charges, and sales in 2014/2015. The total increase in fees and charges income has been 3% since 2012/2013. The Local Government Association stated councils faced a challenging balancing act when determining fees and charges. The charges encompass various services, including car parking, adult social care, planning, and country parks. While some councils have seen their income from these sources rise by tens of millions of pounds, others have experienced a decline in their fees, charges, and sales revenue. Six English councils—Breckland, Devon, Hinckley and Bosworth, South Northamptonshire, and Sedgemoor—have seen their income from fees, sales, and charges increase by more than 100% in the past three years, while Derbyshire, Westminster, Bristol, and Shropshire were the largest risers in real terms, collecting tens of millions of pounds more each year. A spokeswoman for Derbyshire, which increased its fees, charges, and sales income by £33 million between 2013/2014 and 2015, stated: Like all councils, we are looking to increase our income where we can as we need to find savings of £157 million between 2013 and 2018. There are also many areas where we are charging more for our services than we were. These include increasing co-funding contributions for adult social care, charging for home to school transport for pupils who attend faith schools, and charging for parking at some of our countryside sites. Sharon Taylor, acting leader of the Local Government Association, commented: There is a law of diminishing returns with council charges. If you increase prices, it can result in a reduction in the use of services. It has to be a reasonable increase; it is a balancing act. Councils of whatever political persuasion are aware that family budgets are tight, and they don't want to put costs up. At the end of the day, fees and charges have to be balanced against council tax rises. Cambridge City Council, where fees and charges revenue has risen from £20.5 million to £23.1 million in the past three financial years, requires any department wishing to increase fees above the rate of inflation to justify the necessity of the rise first. Lewis Herbert, leader at the Labour-led council, said: We are trying to strike a balance between the costs of running services and not impacting our residents. We are not trying to cry wolf and are not in as bad a position as some councils, but it really is touch and go for many of us because we have to see what is in the detail of the government's plans for local government. We are more business-like than some councils, so we may build a café at the crematorium or sell flowers or rent out more space in the Guildhall building—thus stretching income by selling more rather than increasing charges. The Department for Communities and Local Government did not respond to a request for comment.

text: Brazil's President Michel Temer has nominated his justice minister to the Supreme Court as it prepares to rule on one the biggest corruption scandals in the country's history. The minister, Alexandre de Moraes, is among Mr Temer's closest allies. He succeeds Judge Teori Zavascki, who perished in a plane crash last month. There have been demands for a less politically sensitive appointment, as numerous senior politicians face charges in the corruption scandal. Mr Temer stated he selected Mr Moraes for his solid academic credentials. The 49-year-old lawyer is affiliated with the PSDB party, which is part of Mr Temer's ruling coalition. He joined the cabinet in May, when Mr Temer succeeded President Dilma Rousseff, who was undergoing impeachment proceedings. Earlier this year, Mr Moraes confronted his most severe crisis since assuming office, when over 100 prisoners were killed by fellow inmates in a series of prison riots. He announced a strategy to establish police intelligence units and enhance cooperation with neighbouring countries to diminish the influence of gangs controlling most Brazilian prisons. Mr Moraes's appointment requires ratification by the Senate. He requested a 30-day leave of absence to prepare for the ratification process. However, analysts indicate the government does not anticipate the nomination being rejected, as it holds a substantial majority in the Senate. Later this month, the Supreme Court is set to commence ruling on the extensive evidence collected during an investigation into corruption at the state oil company, Petrobras. Judge Zavascki had been supervising the investigation, known as Operation Car Wash. He had compiled a list containing the names of numerous politicians who allegedly accepted bribes from Brazilian construction giant Odebrecht to ensure the company secured lucrative contracts with Petrobras. Odebrecht has confessed to paying $1bn (£800m) in bribes to secure contracts in 12 different countries. Mr Zavascki was a highly respected judge, and the Car Wash investigation gained significant credibility when he was appointed to oversee it in the Supreme Court, reports the BBC's Daniel Gallas. The plane he was travelling on crashed into the sea amid heavy rain near the town of Paraty on 19 January. The opposition expressed suspicion of foul play and called for a comprehensive investigation. Since Judge Zavascki's death, the Supreme Court has been functioning with 10 judges. His role overseeing the corruption probe was assigned last week to Judge Edson Fachin. He was selected at random from a shortlist of five Supreme Court judges.

text: New Edinburgh centre Sasa Tofilau is primed for his Pro12 debut after a rapid switch from the 'jungle rugby' of the Scottish club game's third tier. The 22-year-old, born in Samoa, played for Kirkcaldy in Scottish National League Two last season. After being invited to trial for Edinburgh's A team, he excelled in their victory at the Melrose Sevens. A one-year contract offer ensued, and Tofilau is now poised for his Pro12 debut after participating in both pre-season matches. Tofilau stated: I had no contract back in New Zealand and Quintan Sanft [Kirkcaldy's head coach, who earned two caps for Samoa in 2000] called me and suggested 'why don't you come here and experience Edinburgh?' I heard Edinburgh was a fantastic city, so I decided to tick it off my bucket list, and that is how it all transpired. Tofilau is a former member of the Chiefs development squad in Waikato and has also played for Australia's Under-20s. However, the transition from the third division of Scottish club rugby in Fife to the professional game in recent months has been swift. Kirkcaldy was 'no structure' rugby, more 'jungle rugby', as I call it - everyone flying everywhere, Tofilau remarked. Coming to Edinburgh has certainly awakened me and added many more skills to my game. We have some excellent coaches and [backs coach] Duncan Hodge has mentored me. He has advised me that it takes time, be patient - I will learn gradually and there is no rush. It has been fantastic so far. It is probably the toughest training I have experienced in pre-season, but I have enjoyed it. I am very grateful for the opportunity I have been given. Coming from the outside, I definitely have something to prove so if I start this week against Cardiff Blues, I will cherish the moment. If the 16st 12lb Tofilau, who moved to New Zealand with his family at the age of five, remains true to his Samoan heritage, Edinburgh may discover a new dimension to their attacking play. I like the ball in hand and I also enjoy defence a lot, he said. But I think I bring a different kind of flair to the backline - I like to attack and offload and put my wingers in space. Our forwards are excellent at the set-piece so I just have to focus on my job of breaking the gain-line. Fortunately, I have Phil Burleigh and Duncan Weir to assist me. Phil has really supported me in terms of the midfield and his understanding of the game. It is not always about 'crash and bash', it is about playing smart and territory. Tofilau may be new to the squad, but he shares the pre-season optimism circulating around the capital club that the new season will yield more success than recent campaigns. The boys have said the last couple of seasons have been quite inconsistent but we have set a strong goal this year, he added. We have had a tough pre-season and we are ready to reap the benefits now. Top four is a definite positive target for us. I believe we can achieve it. We have a robust squad and a lot of depth, so I think we will have a lot of rotation this year.

text: Arkansas will become the first US state in 17 years to hold two executions on the same day, if two inmates are put to death as planned on Monday evening. These are external links and will open in a new window. Lawyers representing Jack Jones and Marcel Williams are requesting stays of execution due to poor health. Arkansas initially intended to execute eight inmates within 11 days before an execution drug expired. On Thursday, Ledell Lee was executed, marking the state's first execution since 2005. Another inmate, Kenneth Williams, is scheduled for execution on Thursday, though his lawyers claim he is intellectually disabled. The remaining four of the eight planned executions have been halted by court order. However, the state's chief prosecutor has pledged to surmount legal challenges and return the condemned to the death chamber. The last instance of a US state executing two inmates on the same day was in 2000 in Texas. Both inmates scheduled for execution on Monday have confessed to their crimes. Jones was convicted in 1996 for raping and strangling Mary Phillips and attempting to murder her 11-year-old daughter. He was also convicted of rape and murder in Florida. Williams was sentenced to death in 1997 for kidnapping, raping, and murdering Stacy Errickson. He also abducted and raped two other women. Jones is set to be executed at 19:00 local time (midnight GMT) at Cummins Unit prison, while Williams is scheduled for 20:15. They applied on Sunday for a stay of execution to the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals, which has not yet ruled. It is anticipated to be among a last-minute surge of legal motions. Jones and Williams contend that obesity and related conditions may render midazolam, a sedative in the three-drug lethal injection cocktail, ineffective on them. Jones's attorneys claim he could endure a torturous death due to potential resistance to midazolam. They state he is already on high doses of two other medications for various ailments, including diabetes, high blood pressure, and neuropathy. Williams's lawyers argue it may be challenging to locate a vein for the lethal injection due to his 400lb (180kg) weight. A federal judge in Little Rock, Arkansas, last Friday dismissed a health-based challenge from Williams and Jones. James Phillips, the husband of Jones's victim, told the BBC: It don't matter if they suffer a little bit as far as I'm concerned, because my wife suffered big time. She was sexually abused in every way possible and as she was suffering he took a cord off a coffee pot and strangled her. And I don't know how much meaner a man can get to do something like that. The state attorney general, Leslie Rutledge, asserts that the inmates' appeals are merely delaying tactics. A lawsuit from the manufacturer of one of the execution drugs has been part of a series of legal challenges to the state's unprecedented execution schedule. The Arkansas Supreme Court last week dismissed the manufacturer's lawsuit, which claimed the state did not disclose its intention to use the supplies for executions.

text: Saudi King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz has died, royal officials have announced, weeks after he was admitted to hospital. Abdullah, who had reigned since 2005 and was believed to be approximately 90 years old, had been suffering from a lung infection. His 79-year-old half-brother, Salman, has been confirmed as the new king. Within hours of ascending to the throne of the oil-rich kingdom, King Salman pledged to uphold the same policies as his predecessors. We will continue adhering to the correct policies which Saudi Arabia has followed since its establishment, he stated in a speech broadcast on state television. Abdullah had experienced frequent bouts of ill health in recent years, and King Salman had recently assumed the ailing monarch's responsibilities. Prior to announcing Abdullah's death, Saudi television aired Koranic verses, which often indicate the passing of a senior royal. A statement announced that Abdullah had died at 01:00 (22:00 GMT Thursday). In Saudi Arabia's second city, the streets were quiet this morning as many people gathered at mosques for Friday prayers. There is a subdued sadness in the air as Saudis absorb the loss of their king. People throughout the kingdom are mourning a man whom many regarded as a good monarch. A Jedawi I spoke to mentioned that although it was known Abdullah was ailing, waking up to the news of the king's death was distressing. Another Jedawi likened the loss to the passing of a family member. It is only after the king is later laid to rest that people here and across the kingdom can begin to adjust to his passing. Another of the late king's half-brothers, Muqrin, who is in his late 60s, has been named the new crown prince, according to an official statement. Abdullah, Salman, and Muqrin are all sons of the founder of modern Saudi Arabia, King Abdulaziz, commonly referred to as Ibn Saud, who died in 1953. King Salman called on the royal family's Allegiance Council to recognise Muqrin as his heir. He swiftly appointed Interior Minister Prince Mohammed bin Nayef as deputy crown prince, making him second in line to the throne, and named his own son, Mohammed bin Salman, as defence minister. Other ministers, including those for foreign affairs, oil, and finance, were retained, state TV reported. The new king's profile was updated on his official Twitter account, where he wrote: I ask God to help me succeed in my service of the dear [Saudi] people. In accordance with the traditions of Wahhabism - the ultra-conservative form of Sunni Islam followed by the kingdom - King Abdullah will be buried in an unmarked grave immediately after Friday prayers. The Saudi religious establishment views every aspect of life and death as a submission to God's supreme will, and protocol allows no official mourning period. Government offices remain open and flags stay at full mast. Saudi Arabia under King Salman faces several challenges. The first is ensuring the succession passes smoothly without any divisive jockeying for power within the ruling family. Then there is the ongoing threat from jihadists, both domestically and across its borders. Saudi Arabia is now positioned between an aggressive Islamic State (IS) to the north and al-Qaeda in Yemen to the south. Saudi warplanes have joined the US-led coalition in air strikes against IS, but this is deeply unpopular with many Saudis. The government has yet to find a way to address mild calls for reforms and is using anti-terror laws to silence reformers and punish its critics. In the longer term, it faces a growing unemployment problem. About half the population is under 25, and there are nowhere near enough meaningful jobs for young Saudis. However, the country does at least have oil in its favour. With prices below $45 a barrel, Saudi Arabia is one of the very few exporting countries to still make significant margins on production and exploration. That places it in a powerful position on the world stage. US President Barack Obama expressed his personal condolences, and those of the American people, on Abdullah's death. As a leader, he was always candid and had the courage of his convictions. One of those convictions was his steadfast and passionate belief in the importance of the US-Saudi relationship as a force for stability and security in the Middle East and beyond, he said. Vice-President Joe Biden tweeted that he would lead a delegation to Riyadh to pay respects. UK Prime Minister David Cameron said Abdullah would be remembered for his commitment to peace and for strengthening understanding between faiths. Jordan's King Abdullah II cut short a visit to Davos, Switzerland, to travel to Saudi Arabia, as Jordan's royal court declared 40 days of mourning. Israeli President Reuven Rivlin praised Abdullah's grounded, considered and responsible leadership, while Iran offered Saudi Arabia its condolences and stated its foreign minister would travel to Riyadh for an official ceremony on Saturday. King Abdullah was the 13th of the 45 sons of King Abdulaziz. He is believed to have been born in August 1924 in Riyadh, although there is some dispute about his actual birth date. When he ascended to the throne in 2005, he succeeded another half-brother, Fahd. However, he had already been Saudi Arabia's de-facto leader for 10 years because his predecessor had been debilitated by a stroke. In recent months, Abdullah's age and failing health had led to increasing focus on the issue of the Saudi royal succession. The crown has traditionally passed between Ibn Saud's sons, but few are still alive. King Salman's appointment of Mohammed bin Nayef - a grandson of Ibn Saud - as deputy crown prince effectively smooths the line of succession for years to come. Correspondents say Abdullah was seen as a reformer at home, albeit a slow and steady one. He allowed mild criticism of his government in the press and hinted that more women should be allowed to work. King Salman spent 48 years as governor of Riyadh Province before becoming crown prince and defence minister. BBC security correspondent Frank Gardner says it is thought unlikely that he will embark on any great changes. In a recent meeting with the BBC in Jeddah, he appeared alert and well-briefed but walked with the aid of a stick, our correspondent adds. Profile: King Salman

text: A doctor who misled other medics about Pauline Cafferkey - a nurse who developed the Ebola virus - has been suspended from practising for a month. These are external links and will open in a new window. Dr Hannah Ryan measured Ms Cafferkey's temperature at Heathrow Airport upon their return from West Africa, where they had volunteered. Despite a high temperature, which is a warning sign of the virus, Dr Ryan consented to a lower value being recorded. The Medical Practitioners Tribunal declared her guilty of serious misconduct. Dr Ryan stated she was in a state of disbelief, fear and panic at the time. Ms Cafferkey was subsequently permitted to travel home to Scotland, carrying the virus and putting others at unwarranted risk, the tribunal heard. The Scottish nurse fell ill the following day and endured a prolonged illness with Ebola and its complications. Dr Ryan and Ms Cafferkey had been working in Sierra Leone with other volunteers to treat Ebola victims in 2014. The outbreak of the highly contagious virus resulted in thousands of deaths in the region. Returning on 28 December, Dr Ryan and Ms Cafferkey arrived at Heathrow, keen to be home for the Christmas holiday period, the tribunal heard. They queued for clearance from Public Health England medics to be allowed to leave. In an attempt to assist PHE staff with the process, Dr Ryan and Ms Cafferkey agreed to take and record their own temperatures. Dr Ryan then measured Ms Cafferkey's temperature and obtained a reading of 38.2C, which was higher than normal. However, a lower temperature of 37.2C was actually recorded, and Ms Cafferkey was then allowed to board her connecting flight to Glasgow to return home. Later, when a consultant called to investigate the airport incident, Dr Ryan provided a dishonest response regarding her involvement, the tribunal was informed. The tribunal determined that while there were extenuating circumstances for her actions at Heathrow, her conduct five days later during the call was deeply deplorable. Dr Ryan told the hearing: Pauline Cafferkey was my friend and someone I cared about and was really worried she might die. Dr Bernard Herdan, chairman of the tribunal, stated: Since the tribunal is satisfied the risk of repetition of your misconduct is low, and there is no risk to patient safety, it has concluded that a one-month suspension will be sufficient to mark the seriousness of your misconduct and to send a message to the profession that dishonesty by a doctor cannot be tolerated under any circumstances. In September 2016, the Nursing and Midwifery Council cleared Ms Cafferkey of misconduct over claims she had concealed her infection, after a panel ruled that her judgement had been impaired by her illness. In November, another colleague, senior nurse Donna Wood, was suspended by the NMC for two months. The panel found Ms Wood suggested a lower temperature be recorded on Ms Cafferkey's screening form to expedite their passage through passport control checks.

text: St Johnstone extended their unbeaten streak against Hearts to six games as they held the hosts to a draw at Tynecastle. Media playback is not supported on this device. Prince Buaben gave the capital side a first-half lead with a header, but a refined finish from Danny Swanson equalised for Saints before the interval. Substitute Chris Kane nudged home a David Wotherspoon cross with five minutes remaining to put the visitors ahead. However, Callum Paterson headed in Don Cowie's corner to secure a point. Hearts move above Rangers—who play Ross County on Sunday—into third on goal difference, with Saints remaining fifth, level on points with the two teams directly above them. Both teams entered this match following inconsistent form; Hearts had conceded five goals in their last two, winless matches, while St Johnstone had only one victory in their last four. Recent history was intriguing. Saints had three wins and two draws in their last five encounters with Robbie Neilson's side. They were under pressure from the start, though. Hearts enjoyed more possession and more opportunities, but it was not until Buaben scored midway through the half that they took the lead. And it was peculiar. A shot from Don Cowie rebounded off the crossbar to Buaben, who directed his close-range header goalward until it seemed to be deflected by a St Johnstone hand. It was debatable whether the ball had crossed the line, but had it not, we would be discussing a penalty and a red card. The goal was awarded instead, and Tynecastle erupted. Shortly after his goal, Buaben tested Zander Clark in the Saints goal, and during these moments, Hearts were comfortable. They were caught off guard by a moment of brilliance when Swanson gained possession. Steven MacLean sent Swanson through one-on-one with John Souttar, and there was no contest. Swanson turned inside the centre-half, then placed a splendid shot past Jack Hamilton for his 10th goal of the season and his third against Hearts this campaign. Swanson is already two-thirds of the way to matching Saints' top scorer from last season, MacLean. In the early minutes of the second half, there were significant moments at both ends. David Wotherspoon forced a save from Hamilton, then Wotherspoon struck the inside of Hamilton's post with a superb free-kick. The rebound fell to Joe Shaughnessy, who tapped it home, but he was offside. Hearts had a significant chance of their own minutes later when Bjorn Johnsen's close-range shot was brilliantly blocked by Steven Anderson. The defender's awareness of the danger around him saved Saints. The match had become a tight contest between two sides who, for a while, seemed to lack the creativity to score again. They did. Both of them. Saints surely believed they had won it when Wotherspoon, who improved as the day progressed, found Kane, who slotted his shot past Hamilton. Hearts protested vehemently about the goal, claiming offside, but their objections were in vain. Five minutes remained, but the home team persevered, and Paterson secured them the point they undoubtedly deserved by heading home from a corner with two minutes left. It was the Scotland full-back's fifth goal of the season. For him, the next stop is Wembley. Hearts manager Robbie Neilson: It was a really tough match. We knew St Johnstone would make it difficult and it would be a very combative game, and it turned out that way. We managed to get ourselves in front, then conceded a poor goal, and then there was an offside goal for St Johnstone, and they took the lead. But we managed to fight back, show our quality, and equalise. Media playback is not supported on this device. We are disappointed not to take the three points, but the manner in which we fought back was really pleasing. Saints manager Tommy Wright: It maybe lacked quality at times, but I think it was end-to-end and entertaining, and I think we picked up a very good point. I've reviewed the first Hearts goal, and one thing I'll say is the referee's assistant had a clear view of it, in a very good position. Brian Easton doesn't think it's over, but the angle I've got on the video doesn't clarify it for me. For the disallowed goal, the referee's assistant seems to think Joe Shaughnessy was a couple of yards offside, but I have reviewed that, and he looks level to me. Ryan Bertrand tested Lee Grant with a powerful shot from the edge of the box in one of the few direct attempts by Southampton, but Rodriguez's miss was the pivotal moment. text: Oxfordshire could be voting for its first elected mayor by 2018, according to a council leader. These are external links and will open in a new window. Oxford City Council's Bob Price stated that a county mayor would enable Oxfordshire to reclaim powers back from Whitehall. He also asserted that a mayor would boost central government funding and offer greater control over housing and transport for the county's six council authorities. Authority leaders have confirmed they are considering elected-mayor proposals. It was disclosed in November that the Oxfordshire Local Enterprise Partnership (OxLEP) - responsible for enhancing the county's economy - had only provisionally received £15m of the £382m requested funding to complete infrastructure projects across the county. Mr Price, a member of OxLEP, remarked: We think that in the latest round of local growth fund allocations there was a strong bias in the allocations made by government to places which had elected mayors and combined authorities. There's no evidence to really prove that, but that seems to be the evidence in terms of allocations. Mr Price expressed his belief that there would be political consensus between the mayor and respective Labour and Conservative-run Oxfordshire authorities, as all authorities aimed to improve roads such as the A34 and address the county's housing crisis. Analysis: Bethan Phillips, BBC Oxford political reporter: The absence of an elected mayor in Oxfordshire is speculated to be the reason the county recently missed out on hundreds of millions of pounds for major projects from the government. Council leaders and Oxfordshire's Local Enterprise Partnership submitted a bid for £382m for projects like upgrading railway stations, constructing new junctions on the A34, and creating new roads. However, the county is only anticipated to receive a small portion of that funding. Oxford City Council leader Bob Price claims there was a bias in allocating funds to areas that have elected mayors or plans to introduce one. There is no consensus yet among our councils on whether having an elected mayor is a favourable idea - and they will all need to agree for the plan to proceed. But if potentially large sums of money are involved, the change will be very enticing for councils. The six councils - Oxfordshire County Council, Oxford City Council, and Cherwell, West Oxfordshire, South Oxfordshire, and Vale of White Horse district councils - are considering lobbying the government for an elected mayor, potentially as part of a devolution bid. A spokesperson for Oxfordshire County Council, which manages transport infrastructure, social care, and children and adult services in the county, stated: We cannot pass up the chance to secure infrastructure investment from the government, so we will work closely with the district and city councils on a devolution bid - which is likely to include an elected mayor and combined authority. But we still need to be convinced that adding another layer of council administration is right for Oxfordshire. OxLEP chief executive Nigel Tipple said: Ultimately, proposals will be submitted to central government for consideration and final decision. OxLEP will continue to work closely with all local authorities, universities, businesses, and other partner organisations to create the conditions that will best enable the county's already thriving economy to flourish and grow in future.

text: Sinn Féin and the SDLP have criticised the government's plan for Brexit, but a White Paper published on Thursday has been welcomed by unionists. The document outlines the government's 12 principles, recently detailed by Prime Minister Theresa May in a significant speech in London. Brexit Secretary David Davis presented the plan to the House of Commons. It emphasises a range of themes, including trade, immigration, devolution, and the Irish border. DUP Deputy Leader Nigel Dodds stated that the central stress of the plan was the opportunity the UK's departure from the EU provides to strengthen the union. This is why the DUP supported Brexit, and this is precisely what Brexit allows the UK to do, he added. I am pleased that the government reiterated the obvious - that Brexit would not affect the Common Travel Area or the unique relationship between British and Irish citizens. This long preceded EU membership and will happily outlast it. However, the White Paper received a less favourable response from Sinn Féin, which campaigned for the UK to remain in the EU. Michelle O'Neill, Sinn Féin's leader north of the border, said the government is acting in its own self-interest. It's clear the only credible approach is for the north to be designated a special status within, rather than outside of, the EU, she said. The SDLP's Mark Durkan was also heavily critical of what he perceived in it, saying it was padded out with platitudes and there was not a lot of solid content. The Foyle MP added that the government was heading in the wrong direction and had set a course to Brexit with no sat-nav, map or compass. Both Sinn Féin and the SDLP want Northern Ireland to have special status after Brexit, but such a move has been dismissed by Northern Ireland Secretary James Brokenshire, who believes it is the wrong approach. The Ulster Unionist MP Danny Kinahan welcomed the publication of the White Paper, stating that clarity is what constituents and businesses deserve in order to best plan for the future. He added: Now that we know the government's intentions, we will work tirelessly to hold them to their commitment to ensure a frictionless border, protect the rights of UK citizens in EU member states and secure the best trade deal possible for Northern Ireland and the rest of the UK. MPs backed the European Union Bill by 498 votes to 114 on Wednesday evening after two days of debate. The DUP and the Ulster Unionists supported the bill, while the SDLP and independent unionist Lady Sylvia Hermon voted against it. MPs will discuss the bill in more detail next week, when it reaches the committee stage in the Commons, and the Labour Party has vowed to push through amendments.

text: A study confirming a link between atmospheric pollution and heart-attack risk strengthens the EU case for tougher clean-air targets, experts say. Research published in the BMJ examining long-term data for 100,000 individuals in five European countries found evidence of harm, even at permissible concentrations. Experts emphasised that the risk to an individual remained relatively small. Some argued the findings were inconclusive as they did not account for previous exposure to higher levels. Other factors, such as smoking or having high blood pressure, contribute more to a person's risk of heart attack than pollution from traffic fumes and industry, they state. However, repeated, long-term exposure to air pollution—such as residing next to a busy road in a city—does take its toll, the research, involving a collaboration of European universities and institutes, reveals. The BMJ study found that for each 5 µg/m3 increase in annual exposure to fine-particulate (PM 2.5) air pollution—considered the most damaging type, as smaller particles can penetrate deep into the body—there is a 13% relative increase in the incidence of heart attacks, even after considering other risk factors such as smoking. Similarly, rising levels of larger-particulate air pollution (PM 10) were also linked to heart-attack risk. These associations persisted even when exposure concentrations were below the current European limits. Authors of the study—the largest ever examining the impact of pollution exposure in European individuals—state its results support the case for lowering EU limits for particulate matter air pollution. Current EU legislation sets the annual mean limit on PM 2.5 at twice that recommended by the World Health Organization. Jon Ayres, professor of environmental and respiratory medicine at the University of Birmingham, stated: There is no doubt that further reduction of PM levels would result in improvements in cardiac health in Europe. One can only hope that our European politicians will be persuaded of the importance of these findings and reassess their position on air pollution in Europe. Prof David Coggon, from the Department of Occupational and Environmental Medicine at the University of Southampton, was more cautious. This study adds to the evidence that particulate air pollution is a cause of heart disease, but it does not establish that there are important health risks from levels of exposure below current exposure limits, he said. This is because the differences in risk that were observed may have been a long-term effect of exposures in the past when levels of pollution were higher. UK estimates suggest nearly 30,000 people die prematurely each year as a direct result of exposure to air pollution, which has been linked to asthma and other lung diseases, including cancer, as well as heart problems. A recent report by Defra on the issue states evidence suggests that there is no safe limit for exposure to PM 2.5, and that this type of man-made pollution reduces the average life expectancy of people living in the UK by seven to eight months. A Defra spokeswoman said: Air quality has improved significantly in recent decades and the UK currently meets the EU limits for this type of pollution. We want to keep improving air quality and reduce the impact it can have on human health and the environment.

text: Restoration work has started on a World War I cemetery in Surrey built for Muslim soldiers killed in combat. Horsell Common Preservation Society aims to complete the project in time for the 100th anniversary of the outbreak of WWI, on 4 August next year. The Grade II listed structure in Woking has deteriorated over the years and suffered vandalism. It is anticipated that the first phase of work, partially funded by English Heritage, will be completed by November. The preservation society also plans to establish a memorial garden at the site. John Kingsbury, leader of Woking council, stated that the heritage site holds significance for local people and descendants of those who sacrificed their lives in the war. English Heritage senior designation adviser Paul Stamper remarked: Its architectural interest and unique status as a site of memory for Muslims who died fighting for Britain in two world wars is recognised in its national designation as a Grade II listed structure. David Robbins, chairman of Horsell Common Preservation Society, expressed hope that the town would take pride in the unique war memorial upon completion of the work. Over one million troops from pre-independence India served Great Britain during World War I. Wounded soldiers were transported to hospitals in the South East. Hindu and Sikh soldiers were taken to crematoriums, but Muslim soldiers lacked a burial ground until 1915. Woking's site was finished in 1917. According to the preservation society, there were 17 burials at the site in 1917, each marked with a round arched headstone facing west, in line with Islamic tradition. A cadet from the Sandhurst military academy was interred there in 1920, before the War Graves Commission assumed responsibility for the ground's maintenance in 1921. During World War II, an additional eight Muslim soldiers were buried at the site, including three from the Free French forces. In 1968, following a series of vandalism incidents, all the burials were relocated to Brookwood cemetery and the ground was de-consecrated. The structure remains a Registered War Memorial.

text: Coach Vern Cotter insisted Scotland can still secure a top-half finish in this year's Six Nations despite a record points defeat by England. The Scots aspired to secure their first victory at Twickenham since 1983 but suffered a record points tally in a 61-21 defeat, matching the margin of the 43-3 loss in 2001. Stuart Hogg, Mark Bennett, Tommy Seymour, and Ryan Wilson were all compelled to leave the field due to injuries, with three sustaining head knocks. We have had two away games and eight concussions, Cotter informed BBC Scotland. It isn't the sole reason, but we certainly had to make early substitutions. We concluded with (scrum-half) Ali [Price] on the wing and (replacement fly-half) Duncy [Weir] at full-back, so there were several changes. We accept it. Credit to England. I thought they performed well. We didn't play particularly well, although we scored three tries. We would have preferred to score four to secure something [a losing bonus point]. Media playback is not supported on this device. My priority at present is to assess the injuries and determine how many we have to prepare for Italy at home next week. If our feet weren't on the ground, they certainly are now. We will work diligently to deliver a strong performance next week. The fifth-placed Scots, who are level on points with Wales but a point behind Ireland and France, will host Italy in next Saturday's early match, with France hosting Wales in the afternoon and England away to Ireland in the evening. John Barclay captained Scotland once more in Greig Laidlaw's absence and remarked afterwards: It certainly wasn't a good day. It wasn't due to a lack of effort, just too many errors. We didn't play well. Credit to England. They played well, executing plays under pressure—perhaps not under sufficient pressure.

text: The first new design of an electricity pylon in almost 90 years has been erected at a site in Nottinghamshire. After nearly a century of service, the traditional steel lattice pylon has been modernised. The T-pylon is shorter, measuring approximately 120ft (36m), compared to the old steel structures, which are typically 165ft (50m). The National Grid states it will address the need to harness energy from an increasing number of lower-carbon energy sources. The new tower can be shorter yet still operate at 400,000 volts due to the manner in which the cables are secured. Instead of being attached to three arms, a diamond configuration is used to carry the cables off in one arm in a much smaller space. Each arm must support 60 tonnes. With only eight main structural components plus bolts, it is simpler to erect and install, taking a day rather than a week. According to the National Grid, new pylons are necessary to accommodate the shift away from coal towards other forms of generation such as wind, solar, and nuclear. These new low-carbon energy sources originate from different geographical locations compared to the traditional ring of coal-fired generation in central England. This test line will not be connected to the rest of the grid; it will be utilised to train staff and contractors. Specifically, it will be used for individuals to practise stringing the conductors (wires) onto the pylons, as a significantly different technique is required. The T-Pylon design was selected following an international competition held by the National Grid in 2011, won by Danish company Bystrup. It is claimed these pylons will be less obtrusive not only due to their shorter height but also because the design allows them to follow the contours of the land. According to project manager Alan Large, maintenance will be simpler as operators will not need to climb the tower; they will work from elevated platforms positioned alongside it. Their smooth, impenetrable surface will also make them more resistant to vandalism. It will not replace the 88,000 lattice pylons currently spanning the UK countryside. It will primarily be used in the construction of new power lines in England and Wales. The National Grid is applying to use them to connect the new Hinkley Point C nuclear power station to the UK's electricity transmission network. The UK's electricity transmission network began with the construction of the first pylon in 1928 near Edinburgh. Follow Claire on Twitter. text: The final of this year's Britain's Got Talent drew the lowest audience in the show's 10-year history, according to overnight figures. An average of eight million viewers tuned in to watch the finale as it was broadcast live, with an additional 500,000 watching on ITV+1. Viewing peaked at 9.7 million when Army bandsman and magician Richard Jones was announced the winner. The previous low was in 2014, when 10.7 million saw singing act Collabro win. Jones, a lance corporal of The Household Cavalry, impressed the judges and public with his military-themed act. I can't believe it, thank you so much to everyone that voted - it's been an incredible experience, it means the world to me, the 25-year-old said. The first magician to ever win the talent show, he wins a £250,000 prize and the opportunity to appear at the Royal Variety Performance. Live viewing represented a 39.7% share of all TV viewing, although final consolidated figures - where all on-demand and catch-up viewing is taken into account - will not be known for a week. An ITV spokeswoman said audiences peaked at 10.5 million viewers when ITV+1 figures were added. The finale was broadcast at the same time as the Uefa Champions League Final between Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, which was broadcast on subscription service BT Sport and YouTube free of charge. Last year's Britain's Got Talent final was watched by an average of 11.7 million viewers, accounting for a 46.6% audience share. More than 17 million viewers tuned in to watch the final at its peak in 2009, when dance act Diversity famously triumphed over Susan Boyle. The final usually counts itself as one of the most-watched programmes of the year. However, this year it is unlikely to feature in the top 10. 'Brilliantly British' Wearing his Household Cavalry uniform, Jones's act featured a card trick which told the story of Britain's oldest living magician, Fergus Anckorn, and how he used magic to help him cope with being a prisoner of war in Singapore. The act culminated in bringing the 97-year-old out on stage. Receiving a standing ovation from the judges, Alesha Dixon described the performance as poignant, noble and brilliantly British. Speaking on Britain's Got More Talent after the main show, head judge Simon Cowell said he thought the public voted Jones the winner not just because of his skill as a magician. I think people rooted for him as a person, he said. His presentation, his whole performance was immaculate - it was very patriotic and heart-warming and he deserved to win. Fellow judge Amanda Holden added: I'm absolutely delighted because when magic first started on Britain's Got Talent it was rubbish and after 10 years he has done such a great job. The Army tweeted its congratulations to Jones, as well as a picture of The Band of the Household Cavalry celebrating his win. Swing singer Wayne Woodward - who became the bookmakers' favourite late on Saturday afternoon - finished as the runner-up with his rendition of Nina Simone's Feeling Good. Boogie Storm, a group of disco dancing Star Wars stormtroopers, were voted third. Also among the 12 finalists was sword swallower Alex Magala, whose act had to be pre-recorded for safety reasons. It involved him sliding upside down a pole, while handcuffed, stopping centimetres above a powered chainsaw. Other finalists included schoolgirl singers Jasmine Elcock and Beau Dermott, mother and son duo Mel and Jaime, 100 Voices of Gospel, dancers Shannon and Peter and Balance Unity, impersonator Craig Ball and dancing dog Trip Hazard. To celebrate the show's 10 years, a number of past winners and memorable acts appeared on stage as part of a special performance. Choreographed by Diversity's Ashley Banjo, it featured six winning acts including 2008's George Sampson, 2010's Spelbound, 2012's dancing dog Pudsey and 2013 victors Attraction. Last year's runner-up, Jamie Raven, also appeared, although last year's winner, Jules Dwyer and her dog Matisse, were noticeably absent from the line-up. Dwyer became embroiled in controversy last year when it emerged a stunt dog was used in the final performance instead of Matisse. Ofcom ruled the public had been misled over the incident, but said it did not believe ITV intended to deceive viewers.

text: The BBC has argued the case for popular shows like Strictly Come Dancing and Sherlock in its response to the government's green paper on its future. The broadcaster stated that the public wants and expects the BBC to deliver entertainment, amid claims it is overly focused on ratings. It also defended the popular music stations Radio 1 and 2, asserting they offer a wider variety of music than their commercial competitors. The response has been published online. This occurs as the government concludes a public consultation on the renewal of the BBC's charter, which raised several key questions: When the green paper was launched in July, Culture Secretary John Whittingdale stated hard questions would be posed about the size and ambition of the BBC and said a decision had to be made on whether the corporation should attempt to do all things or become more precise. More than 80,000 people have responded to the public consultation, Mr Whittingdale informed the Conservative Party Conference earlier this week. The BBC's response, which exceeds 100 pages, concurs that the Government consultation is right to insist that the BBC should be distinctive. However, it adds: Distinctiveness does not equal... stepping back from popular content. The BBC makes good popular programmes - if we withdrew, audiences would have less choice. It refutes the suggestion that the BBC should retreat from crowd-pleasing shows, stating: Competition on a Saturday night has been part of the TV landscape for generations and drives up quality - with the viewer being the winner. The response states the debate about the BBC should start with what it is for and consider the sort of society we want. Access to culture, media and information should be a basic human right, ensured regardless of a person's ability to pay for it, says the report, adding that it is the BBC's role to inform, educate and entertain. The document also reveals that 49% of Radio 1's playlist consists of artists without a top 10 single, while for Capital FM it is just 12%; and that 27% of BBC One's primetime output is factual, compared to 12% on ITV. The corporation has also outlined plans for a radical programme of reform; including greater efficiency and a drive to increase profits from the BBC's commercial arm, BBC Worldwide. It argues for future-proofing the corporation by modernising it for the internet age, and requests policy-makers to help ensure public service broadcasting is easy to find on future as well as existing platforms. And it asks the government to wait 11 years, rather than 10, before debating the BBC's charter again - thus removing discussions from the election cycle. The issue of funding the BBC is addressed too, with the report calling the licence fee the best way. It states subscription funding - either alone or as a partial substitute to the licence fee - is the wrong model. It does agree that the licence fee needs to be modernised, however, including closing the current loophole which makes watching catch-up programmes on the iPlayer online exempt from the fee.

text: The final Anfield memorial service to remember 96 football fans who died at Hillsborough will take place in April. Memorial services have been held at Liverpool's stadium most years since the disaster on 15 April 1989. Hillsborough families have agreed that this year's service, marking the 27th anniversary, will be the final one. The coroner at the inquests into the fatal crush at the Sheffield stadium will begin summing up evidence later this month. The decision to conclude the Anfield services was made by the Hillsborough Family Support Group (HFSG) after consulting the relatives of those who died. On Tuesday, Coroner Lord Justice Goldring adjourned the inquests, being held in Warrington, Cheshire, until 25 January, when he expects to summarise evidence for the jury. Margaret Aspinall, chairwoman of the HFSG, stated: The 96 will never be forgotten. This final memorial service will provide the families with some closure. Mrs Aspinall, whose 18-year-old son James died in the disaster, added: The HFSG would like to thank everyone for all the support the families have received over the past 27 years and all those who have attended the service at Anfield each year. We hope that the public and fans respect the decision of the HFSG and will continue to remember the 96 in their own, perhaps more private, way. In the days following the disaster, Anfield became the focus of grief on Merseyside. A carpet of flowers was laid over the pitch, and a chain of football scarves stretched from the stadium, across the city's Stanley Park, to Goodison Park, home of local rivals Everton. On the first anniversary, the club unveiled its permanent memorial to those who died—a 10-tonne granite block inscribed with the names of the victims alongside an eternal flame. Since then, bereaved families, survivors, Liverpool players, and managers have attended the annual service at the ground. The service has been a very public show of remembrance, but also of the support shown to those affected by the disaster. More recently, it has also helped keep the bereaved families' campaign in the public eye. Mrs Aspinall has also requested people to stop pledging financial donations to HFSG. The families have received many donations over the years, including £96,000 pledged by former Liverpool manager Rafa Benitez. But Mrs Aspinall said: The families don't need the money now. I'd like to thank everybody, not just for their support, but the monetary side of it. BBC News: Profiles of all those who died.
