text: The SNP leader has hit back at claims that too much cash comes over Hadrian's wall during the ITV leaders' debate. UKIP leader Nigel Farage stated that taxpayers in England were cheesed off with the amount of public funds allocated to Scotland. However, Nicola Sturgeon countered that Scots had contributed more tax per capita every year for the past 34 years. The debate included leaders from seven parties across the UK. It was the sole occasion Prime Minister David Cameron and Labour leader Ed Miliband would appear together on television before the general election on 7 May. Mr Cameron asserted that the Conservatives' economic strategy was effective, adding: Let's not go back to square one, Britain can do so much better than that. Mr Miliband repeatedly outlined his plans if I am prime minister, including raising the minimum wage, banning exploitative zero-hours contracts, and rescuing our NHS. Liberal Democrat leader Nick Clegg also participated in Thursday evening's debate, alongside Plaid Cymru leader Leanne Wood and the Green Party's Natalie Bennett. A YouGov poll of 1,100 people showed a clear victory for Ms Sturgeon, with 28%, followed by Mr Farage on 20%, Mr Cameron on 18%, Mr Miliband on 15%, Mr Clegg on 10%, Ms Bennett on 5%, and Ms Wood on 4%. However, a ComRes poll for ITV resulted in a tie between Mr Cameron, Mr Miliband, Mr Farage, and Ms Sturgeon, although Mr Cameron was favoured as the most capable leader for the country. Mr Miliband was deemed the best performer in an ICM poll for the Guardian, receiving 25% support, just ahead of Mr Cameron on 24%. Nigel Farage received 19%, Nicola Sturgeon 17%, and Nick Clegg 9%. A Survation poll for the Daily Mirror also placed the Tory and Labour leaders neck and neck on 25%, with Mr Farage on 24%, Ms Sturgeon 15%, Mr Clegg 6%, Ms Bennett 3%, and Ms Wood 2%. When asked to rate leaders out of 10 by YouGov for the Times, the scores were: Ms Sturgeon 6.7, Mr Miliband and Mr Cameron 5.9, Mr Clegg and Mr Farage 5.5. Ms Sturgeon began by asserting that the SNP—predicted by polls to return a record number of MPs to Westminster—would always stand up for Scotland, but wished to extend friendship to the peoples of England, Wales, and Northern Ireland and would help to bring about change for you too. Mr Farage, however, claimed canny Scots had secured a better deal than other UK regions when the Barnett formula—determining public fund distribution—was established. He remarked: This all has to be rebalanced because frankly English taxpayers are a bit cheesed off with so much of their money going over Hadrian's wall, giving people no prescription charges and no university tuition. Ms Sturgeon informed him that Scots had paid more tax per head of population in every single year for the last 34 years. In the television debate, Ms Sturgeon also criticised the prime minister, arguing that the UK government could not cut its way out of a deficit, and insisted the NHS was the nation's most precious public service. In an apparent effort to frame the election as a direct choice between himself and Mr Miliband, the prime minister told the debate audience: The choice at this election is sticking with a plan that is working or going back to the debt, taxes, borrowing and spending that got us in this mess in the first place. I say let's not go back to square one. Britain can do so much better than that. Mr Cameron added: The problem—and the real choice—is with Ed Miliband, who still thinks the last government didn't tax too much and borrow too much. But Mr Miliband accused Mr Cameron of focusing on the past rather than the future and said: Some people will tell you that this is as good as it gets for Britain. I say Britain can do so much better than it has done over the last five years. There could have been no better image of the changing political landscape of Britain. While 50 years ago two parties took almost every vote between them, and just five years ago viewers of the TV debates might well have thought the era of three-party politics was permanent, this time there were seven politicians on stage. And three were women. The SNP's Nicola Sturgeon dressed boldly in red—perhaps to emphasise her determination to supplant Labour as the main party in Scotland. And she criticised the old boys' network in SW1. The prime minister was introduced last and appeared to find it challenging to maintain a smile while welcoming his six opponents. He seemed to grow in confidence but was perhaps initially questioning why he had insisted on broadening the field from the 2010 threesome. One could almost believe the women on the panel—Natalie Bennett from the Greens, and Leanne Wood from Plaid Cymru, as well as Ms Sturgeon—had coordinated an early attack on the austerity advocated by the main Westminster parties. Mr Miliband said Mr Cameron had marginalised Britain in Europe, and added: I don't think our place lies outside the EU. I think that would be a disaster for jobs, a disaster for families and business. The Labour leader also criticised his Liberal Democrat counterpart Mr Clegg for betraying young people over tuition fees. In response, Mr Clegg criticised the Labour leader's pious stance and challenged Mr Miliband to apologise to the British public for crashing the economy. Mr Clegg directly challenged Mr Cameron over his decision not to ask the wealthiest to contribute more towards deficit reduction, but instead to impose ideologically-driven cuts. Responding to Mr Cameron's portrayal of the election as a choice between competence and chaos, the Lib Dem leader urged him to imagine the chaos in people's lives caused by cuts in spending on health, schools, and childcare. The SNP later reported gaining 1,200 new members during the two-hour debate programme. The party's deputy leader, Stewart Hosie MP, also stated that an average of the YouGov, ComRes, and ICM polls released immediately after the debate suggested Ms Sturgeon had won, which Mr Hosie said demonstrated how strong and persuasive she had been. Scottish Labour leader Jim Murphy said the debate had made crystal clear the choice facing Scots at the general election. He said: In the debate there were seven passionate speakers but only two potential prime ministers. There are lots of ways to protest against David Cameron but only one way to replace him. UKIP's Scottish MEP David Coburn—in an interview with Radio Scotland's Good Morning Scotland programme—defended Mr Farage's comments from the television debate. He said: I think most reasonable Scots believe in the fair allocation of money. I think the SNP may make a big fuss about this but I think fair minded Scots like myself and everyone else believe we should give the English a reasonable deal too.

text: Restrictions put on terror suspects by the home secretary may be withering on the vine, a group of MPs and peers has warned. They stated that the forthcoming government in 2015 must urgently address the role and effectiveness of Terrorism Prevention and Investigation Measures (TPims). The Joint Committee on Human Rights' report emphasised the risk of individuals going missing while under TPims. The Home Office asserted the measures were the strongest the courts would permit. TPims involve restrictions such as overnight residence at a specified address, GPS tagging, reporting requirements, and limitations on travel, movement, association, communication, finances, work, and study. By Dominic Casciani, Home Affairs Correspondent, BBC News. By the end of this month, six TPim suspects will be free, leaving only one man still subject to the monitoring conditions. Given the secrecy surrounding the system, it is uncertain whether there is another suspect unknown to the public. Control orders, the more restrictive regime preceding TPims, had numerous opponents who argued that the house-arrest style conditions were unjust and oppressive. TPims inherited those critics and attracted additional ones, including security experts who claimed the new regime was too lenient. What appears to be effective now is a strategy to intervene earlier by charging suspects with preparing acts of terrorism. This group may include suspects who, at one time, would have been considered for a TPim due to police concerns that they had substantial intelligence but no concrete evidence to present to a jury. The measures were introduced in December 2011 as a replacement for the more restrictive regime of control orders, aimed at preventing suspects from engaging in terrorist-related activity. The report stated there were eight TPim notices in force as of November last year, all of which were for British citizens. However, seven of those will have expired by the end of this month, according to the report. The committee suggested TPims should be reviewed as part of a broader examination of counter-terrorism powers. Its report urged the government to engage more transparently and substantively with the recommendations of the independent reviewer of terrorism legislation. The report stated: We are left with the impression that in practice TPims may be withering on the vine as a counter-terrorism tool of practical utility. The committee concluded that the measures were not investigative in any real sense and suggested they should be known as Terrorism Prevention Orders or something similar. It agreed with the independent reviewer that the very nature of TPims carries an inherent risk of the subject absconding. It recommended that more information about an internal review of TPims, launched after two subjects went missing, be made public. Mohammed Ahmed Mohamed, linked to the Somali militant group al-Shabab, absconded in November after changing into a burka while visiting a west London mosque. His case followed that of Ibrahim Magag, who went missing in December 2012 in a black cab after removing his electronic tag. Committee chairman Hywel Francis said: There is no evidence that they serve any investigative function and even as preventive measures they seem to be going out of favour with the agencies. Very few TPims are in operation and almost all of these are due shortly to lapse after their two-year duration. Mr Francis stated there is insufficient information known about the individuals on whom these measures have been imposed to make a proper judgement about whether the power to impose them is no longer required. The next government will need to look again at these measures within the context of counter-terrorism powers more generally, he added. David Anderson, the independent reviewer of terror legislation, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme TPims were a necessary evil. One thing it shows is that police and prosecutors are doing their job, he said. We've had a lot of convictions over the last couple of years, a lot of guilty pleas and a lot of heavy sentences. TPims don't present a long-term solution, he added. Home Secretary Theresa May stated TPims would also assist the authorities in gathering material that would lead to prosecutions. However, the committee said it failed to find any evidence the measures had led to more suspects being charged. TPim restrictions have been or are about to be lifted from seven suspects, including men allegedly involved in planning terrorist attacks. The measures were imposed two years ago and cannot be renewed. A Home Office spokesman said: TPims were introduced because control orders were not working and their powers were being struck down by the courts. They now provide some of the strongest possible protections that the courts will allow.

text: The idea that party leaders are decisively important in the winning or losing of general elections is implicit in much political journalism and it is a belief that some political leaders themselves - Tony Blair, in particular - have been eager to propagate. It is very rarely true. It is only in an extremely close contest that the leader's personality and the gap between that leader's standing and the popularity of his or her main opponent can determine victory or defeat. It is not even particularly uncommon for the political party of the less popular leader of the two main parties to win the election. Thus, for instance, although journalists still refer to Margaret Thatcher's rout of James Callaghan, the Labour leader was about 20 points ahead of Mrs Thatcher on the eve of the Conservative victory in the 1979 election. It was not Thatcher who defeated Callaghan but the Conservative Party that defeated Labour. A serious study of post-World War Two UK elections found that the only leader who could have made the difference between his party forming a government or being in opposition was Harold Wilson, and on two occasions - in October 1964 and February 1974. That was because those elections were extremely close and Wilson was vastly more popular than the Conservative leader in each case - Sir Alec Douglas-Home in 1964 and Edward Heath in 1974. In between, the Conservatives had won the 1970 election, despite the fact that then, too, Wilson was more popular than Heath. Since all the available evidence suggests that the May 2015 election is likely to be a cliff-hanger, with a distinct possibility that once again no single party will have an overall majority, does this mean that journalists' excessive focus on the top leader might for once be justified? Probably not. The two main political parties would be well advised to give ample interview time to other front-benchers rather than over-expose David Cameron and Ed Miliband in what, due to the fixed election date, is going to be a very long campaign by British standards - four whole months. Nick Clegg might also cut his losses by sharing (with Vince Cable in the first instance) whatever diminished limelight the Liberal Democrats will secure. Mr Clegg is highly unlikely to replicate his 2010 campaign, when he was deemed the outstanding performer, especially in the televised debates, of the three party leaders. Even then, with unprecedented mass media exposure and Cleggmania rampant, the party's national vote rose by only 1%, and the Lib Dems ended up with five fewer MPs than in 2005. text: Swedish journalists Johan Persson and Martin Schibbye have been speaking to the BBC about their time in prison in Ethiopia. They were recently released after serving over 400 days of an 11-year sentence. The duo were convicted of entering the country illegally and supporting a rebel group, the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF). Their lengthy prison sentences brought international attention to the treatment of journalists in Ethiopia. Martin Schibbye and Johan Persson were captured with ONLF rebels in June 2011. They insisted they were merely performing their duties, and human rights organisation Amnesty International stated the journalists had been prosecuted for conducting legitimate work. However, Ethiopian government spokesman Bereket Simon previously justified the decision to imprison the pair, claiming the journalists were caught red handed collaborating with terrorist organisations. Former Prime Minister Meles Zenawi reportedly pardoned the journalists before his death in August, resulting in their release. Johan Persson informed the BBC World Service programme Newsday that conditions in the prison where they were held were poor. It was 200% overcrowded. It was very hot. There was a lack of water. It was dusty. There were rats, fleas, and many people were ill with HIV or tuberculosis, he stated. Yet he remarked that the conditions were less significant than the other inmates: What's interesting is who they put in there: journalists and the political opposition. Although the pair acknowledge entering Ethiopia illegally, they contend that their trial was unjust. The trial was a joke, said Mr Persson. Meles Zenawi was saying on national television, three or four weeks before the trial started, that we were guilty. They also believe the charge of moral support for terrorism, of which they were found guilty, has been misapplied against other journalists in Ethiopia. For the last few years Ethiopia has been using its anti-terror legislation to crack down on the media and to crack down on journalism, Mr Schibbye told Newsday. The freelance reporters had been in the Ogaden, an ethnic Somali region in eastern Ethiopia, for four days before their arrest. The Ethiopian army spotted us. Then they followed in our footsteps for three to four days. Then they ambushed us. We were attacked by about 150 Ethiopian army soldiers who opened fire on us. We got hit quite quickly. I got hit in the shoulder and Johan got hit in the arm. Somebody shouted, 'media, media, international press,' and we were arrested, said Martin Schibbye. Following their arrest, they claimed they were forced at gunpoint to participate in a film allegedly documenting their relationship with the Ogaden National Liberation Front. Two civilians, who we'd never seen before, were dressed up as rebels. The soldiers gave them guns and stood them in front of us, and they testified against us and said that we came with them from Somalia, says Mr Schibbye. The journalists allege that senior Ethiopian civilian officials were responsible for the filming. This was not being done by some crazy militia: the director was the vice president in the region, and in the evening the regional president called us and said, 'We are not satisfied by your performances in the film,' said Mr Schibbye. Eventually, the film was used against them in court. Ethiopia's eastern Ogaden region has been the focus of an insurgency by local ethnic Somalis. We were walking through villages where there had been people living till recently, but now they had fled, forced out by the conflict. There was heavy fighting and that was one of the reasons why we were detected and followed and ambushed by the Ethiopian army, Mr Persson said. Despite spending more than a year in prison, they say they have no regrets about their time in Ethiopia. For Martin Schibbye, the work of a foreign correspondent is one that requires taking risks and refusing to accept there are areas closed to journalists. His colleague concurs: As long as governments make laws to protect themselves against journalists, our job is to break those laws. I would do the same again today.

Over three and a half decades later, approximately 400 super-elite members of the party reconvened at the same venue. This alone generated expectations that historic events were imminent. The communique from the Third Plenum of the 18th Party Congress, issued on 12 November after the three-day meeting, should dispel the notion that this leadership is poised to undertake the same dramatic reversal achieved in 1978. Times have changed. The simple fact is that a misstep now would be far more costly than back then, when the country was emerging exhausted from late Maoism and needed to take radical action to energise its economy. Now, China is a global economy, with everything to play for in the coming decades. Its challenge this time is simply to, in the words of Premier Li Keqiang, unlock new sources of growth within itself. There is no question, at present at least, of needing to fundamentally change course. The mechanism to achieve growth will be improving and perfecting the market, and liberalising new areas where growth might arise. That is the most powerful message from this plenum. Challenging the fundamental principles of the Reform and Opening Up era was never going to occur. The primacy of the party is stated with crystal clarity in the plenum report. Its key role in society remains paramount. The need for internal unity and collective leadership remains as valued as it was in the Hu Jintao and Wen Jiabao era. The objective remains, through the ideological instruments of Deng Xiaoping theory and Socialism with Chinese characteristics, to achieve the primary state of socialism. That will take, in the words of the communique, many years. There are more explicit references to the creation of a national security coordination body. This appears to be the Hu and Wen fixation with pro-stability measures in another guise, with some attempt to finally coordinate and streamline decision-making in this area, particularly as there is no one on the Standing Committee of the current Politburo with specific responsibility for security issues as there was in the previous one. Q&A: China's Third Plenum Third Plenum: Key issues The premium this leadership places on stability remains high, and the car explosion in Tiananmen in early November along with the homemade bomb attack in Taiyuan at the same time will only emphasise to this leadership that relaxing on the issue is not an option. Politburo member Yu Zhengsheng mentioned before the plenum that deeper new reforms were on the horizon. It is clear now that this referred to introducing a more flexible system whereby rural residents can move to urban areas, find work there, settle there, have access to social welfare and, perhaps most critically of all, educate their children. The government in recent months has heavily referred to the need to accelerate urbanisation, and having a framework within which to enfranchise and incentivise rural dwellers to move is important. Implementation, however, remains key here, so while the statement of intent is strong enough, the question will be how to convince provincial governments across China that they can bear the costs of a new wave of citizens for whom they must provide social goods. There is no explicit mention of whether provinces will be granted wider tax-raising powers, though this would seem a natural corollary to having a new influx of residents. On economic reform, the strongest theme is that of developing a finance market. Here too we see the intellectual influence of Li Keqiang, the person most closely associated with the establishment in October of a Free Trade Zone in Shanghai, a place where China's capital account might be liberalised and the trading of Chinese yuan accelerated. Finance will be a critical sector for this leadership, one of the key means to delivering a high service component in the economy, and of creating a high value-added economy. This plenum provides a framework, confirming some of the themes that have already emerged from this leadership. No quick ideological or political change, a continuation of emphasising people's material well-being and striving for strong growth, with the key drive being to achieve a high level of urbanisation before 2020. If there is one bold feature of this plan, it is that almost everything is staked on an urban China being one where the current problems of achieving growth, addressing some of the sustainability issues, and tackling inequality will become more manageable. This is a significant gamble, as the rate at which China evidently plans to urbanise is faster than any other society has attempted. There are vast issues concerning how social cohesion will be achieved, and what sort of social and political structures might ultimately emerge to achieve the kind of harmonious society that the previous leadership frequently spoke about. Kerry Brown is a professor of Chinese politics at the University of Sydney, team leader of the Europe China Research and Advice Network (ECRAN) funded by the European Union, and an Associate Fellow of the Asia Programme at Chatham House.

text: Spain and Germany sought to reassure investors that Spain would not need a full international bailout, after its borrowing costs hit a record high. German Finance Minister Wolfgang Schaeuble and his Spanish counterpart Luis de Guindos issued a statement. They asserted that Tuesday's record 7.6% yield on 10-year Spanish bonds, which represents the government's implied borrowing costs, did not reflect economic fundamentals. Mr Guindos is scheduled to meet French Finance Minister Laurent Fabius on Wednesday. Spain's financial situation continues to concern investors, with borrowing costs rising and the Catalonia region indicating it will require government funds. On Tuesday, Spain claimed that Italy and France support a plan for the immediate implementation of measures agreed last month. These measures include aid directed at Spain's banks without increasing national debt. Spain stated there had been a worrying delay in executing the agreements reached at the eurozone leaders summit on 29 June. The main provision would allow the future European bailout fund, the ESM, to directly inject money into ailing banks such as those in Spain, bypassing national governments. The creation of the fund has been hindered by constitutional challenges in Germany, which mean Berlin will not be able to ratify the agreement before 12 September. Speed is an essential condition for the success of any European action, the statement released by the Spanish foreign ministry said. However, France's European Affairs Minister Bernard Cazeneuve denied any accord with Italy and Spain on immediate implementation. It makes no sense to say that. We are following the decisions taken at the European summit and are working on them, said Mr Cazeneuve. The Italian government also categorically denied being part of any joint initiative with Spain. The record high yield on the Spanish government's benchmark 10-year bond reflects market tension over the strain on its finances. Rating agency Moody's warned that Spain was more likely to require a full bailout, putting pressure on the euro's strongest economies, such as Germany. By Andrew Walker, BBC World Service Economics correspondent. Higher borrowing costs can make the difference between a debt situation that is problematic and one that is ultimately unsustainable. However, the impact on the interest bill is gradual, which is why a spike in bond yields does not immediately ruin the Spanish government's finances. It is akin to turning an oil tanker. When governments borrow, they generally do so by selling bonds, which are a promise to repay, and the effective interest rate that the borrower must pay is fixed for the lifetime of each batch of bonds. Each time Spain enters the market for new funds, the interest rate it pays then feeds into its total borrowing costs. The general trend is upwards, meaning the tanker is gradually turning towards the rocks. Moody's warned that Germany and other highly-rated countries might have to increase levels of support for countries such as Spain and Italy, who have not requested a Greek-style bailout but are struggling with high debt levels. It stated: Even if such an event [a Greek exit] is avoided, there is an increasing likelihood that greater collective support for other euro area sovereigns, most notably Spain and Italy, will be required. This burden will likely fall most heavily on more highly rated member states if the euro area is to be preserved in its current form. Moody's said there was an increased chance that Greece could leave the eurozone, which would set off a chain of financial sector shocks. It added that policymakers could only contain these shocks at a very high cost. text: Rangers have identified Southampton director of scouting and recruitment Ross Wilson as their number one target for their director of football role. BBC Scotland has discovered that discussions have occurred, but Wilson has much to contemplate before committing to the Ibrox club. Rangers state they wish to establish this new role, in addition to appointing a new head coach, to succeed Mark Warburton. The Englishman vacated his position as team manager over two weeks ago. Meanwhile, former Rangers captain Barry Ferguson would welcome a return to Ibrox following his resignation as Clyde manager on Sunday. However, there has been no contact between the former Scotland midfielder, whose team had endured 10 League Two games without a victory, and his former club. It is improbable that Rangers will make any appointment this week, meaning caretaker manager Graeme Murty will oversee Wednesday's match against St Johnstone in the Scottish Premiership. Murty, who has overseen one win and two losses, has supported the board's prerogative to deliberate over a long-term appointment. If we appoint quickly and get it wrong, it would be much more damaging, said the club's under-20s coach. So we must respect the board's wishes to conduct their process, perform due diligence, and secure the right individual. I've been informed the process is ongoing, interviews are occurring, and someone will be appointed. I do not know when it will be. Murty has admitted he is not enjoying being thrust into the hotseat, although he is relishing the opportunity to gain experience. It's not about me, it's about the football club and the players, he stated. I'm here to facilitate the players playing well, hopefully, and ensuring they know what they need to do on a match day. I'm here fulfilling the role I was asked to do. Rangers have fallen nine points behind second-placed Aberdeen after two consecutive league defeats, and Murty said he would step down if he did not believe he could benefit the team. I'm content to look in the mirror and say that the practices we implement, the work we're doing, is of a good standard, it's what the players need, he remarked. If I felt I wasn't being impactful to the players, I would feel more than comfortable approaching the board and saying: 'You need to replace me'. As it stands, the board have been fantastically supportive. All they are asking me again is: 'Can we help you?' But I think, if you look at the Inverness game from the Dundee game, there was a definite impact, the players responded really, really well, and there was an improvement in our performance levels. I reiterate, however, that we need to secure points to ensure that everyone sees this as a positive and a step forward for the football club. Following the midweek league match, Rangers host Hamilton Academical in a Scottish Cup quarter-final on Saturday, then face Premiership leaders Celtic on 12 March. Barry Ferguson is a guest on BBC Radio Scotland 810MW's Sportsound, starting at 18.30GMT on Monday 27 February.

He received a rock star's welcome in Boston, Massachusetts, yet the esteemed novelist had a mission: he aimed to halt the distribution of cheap, poorly made pirated editions of his work in the US. These circulated freely because the United States did not extend copyright protection to non-citizens. In a resentful letter to a friend, Dickens likened the situation to being robbed and then paraded in absurd attire through the streets. Is it tolerable that besides being robbed and rifled, he wrote, an author should be forced to appear in any form - in any vulgar dress - in any atrocious company? It was a striking and melodramatic metaphor. However, the truth is that the argument for what Dickens was demanding - legal protection for ideas that could otherwise be freely copied and adapted - has never been entirely straightforward. 50 Things That Made the Modern Economy highlights the inventions, ideas, and innovations that helped shape the economic world. Yet these potential large profits encourage new ideas. It took Dickens a considerable time to write Bleak House. If other British publishers could have exploited it like the Americans, perhaps he would not have bothered. Thus, intellectual property reflects an economic trade-off, a balancing act. If it is too generous to the creators, then good ideas will take too long to copy, adapt, and spread. If it is too stingy, then perhaps we will not see the good ideas at all. This trade-off has always been influenced by politics. The British legal system strongly protected the rights of British authors and British inventors in the 1800s because the UK was then - as now - a significant force in world culture and innovation. However, in Dickens's era, American literature and innovation were in their infancy. The US economy was in full-blown copying mode: they desired the cheapest possible access to the best ideas that Europe could offer. US newspapers filled their pages with blatant copying - alongside attacks on the interfering Mr Dickens. A few decades later, when American authors and inventors spoke with a more powerful voice, America's lawmakers began to adopt an increasingly favourable view of the idea of intellectual property. Newspapers, once opposed to copyright, now rely upon it. And we can expect to see a similar transition in developing countries today: the less they copy other ideas and the more they create their own, the more they protect ideas. There has been a lot of recent movement: China did not have a copyright system at all until 1991. The modern form of intellectual property originated, like so many things, in 15th Century Venice. Venetian patents were explicitly designed to encourage innovation. The inventor would automatically receive a patent if their invention was useful. The patent was temporary, but could be sold, transferred, or even inherited during its lifetime. It would be forfeited if it was not used, and invalidated if the invention proved to be closely based on a previous idea. These are all very modern ideas. And they soon created very modern problems. During the British industrial revolution, the great engineer James Watt developed a superior way to design a steam engine. He spent months developing a prototype, but then put even more effort into securing a patent. His influential business partner, Matthew Boulton, even got the patent extended by lobbying Parliament. Boulton and Watt used it to extract licensing fees and crush rivals - for example, Jonathan Hornblower, who made an even better steam engine yet found himself ruined and imprisoned. They redirected their attention from litigation towards the challenge of producing the best steam engines in the world. They kept their prices as high as ever, and their order books swelled. Far from incentivising improvements in the steam engine, the patent actually delayed them. Yet since the days of Boulton and Watt, intellectual property protection has grown more expansive, not less so. Copyright terms are growing ever longer. Patents have become broader and are being granted on vague ideas - for example, Amazon's one-click US patent protects the not-entirely-radical idea of buying a product on the internet by clicking only one button. The US intellectual property system now has a global reach, thanks to the inclusion of intellectual property rules in what tend to be described as trade agreements. These enlargements are hard to justify, but easy to explain. Why is gambling bad, but insurance good? Geeks vs. the government in the battle over encryption. As the first accountants of the world figured by cuneiform. Intellectual property is of great value to its owners, which makes it worth their while to employ expensive lawyers and lobbyists. And the costs of the restrictions are spread among so many people that they barely notice them. But there are other rewards for inventions: the advantage over competitors of being first to market, the brand power, the deeper understanding of what makes a product work. Matthew Boulton and Charles Dickens have strong incentives to demand even stricter intellectual property laws, and consumers of steam engines and Bleak House do not much organize themselves to protest. And the economists Boldrin and Levine offer a radical solution: abolish intellectual property. It is too far for most economists to do away with all rights of property in ideas. In 2014, the manufacturer of electric cars, Tesla, opened up its patents in order to promote the industry, and estimated that it would ultimately profit. They cite the vital example of the new drugs, where the cost of invention is immense, but the cost of copying is negligible. Twenty-five years after his first visit to America, Dickens returned there in search of his fortune. But those who still defend copyright still like to claim that, as things stand, it is a sufficient recompense for the creation of ideas. In the end, however, he found the monetary advantages of a weak copyright. Perhaps the intellectual property is more valuable when it is given away. He thought that so many people had read the cheap copies of his stories that he could make a fortune lecturing. And he was right: Charles Dickens made a fortune lecturing, millions in today's money. 50 Things That Made The Modern Economy is a program of the BBC World Service. Tim Harford is the author of the column Undercover Economist for the Financial Times. You can listen to the program on the BBC World Service or subscribe to the program as a podcast.

text: The gap between male and female life expectancy is closing and men could catch up by 2030, according to an adviser for the Office for National Statistics. Professor Les Mayhew stated that the disparity between the sexes peaked at nearly six years during the 1970s. Life expectancy is rising overall, but the rates for men are increasing more rapidly. Declining smoking rates among men are believed to account for much of the change. Professor Mayhew, a professor of statistics at Cass Business School, analysed life expectancy data in England and Wales. He was determining how long 30-year-olds could expect to live. His findings indicate men have lagged significantly behind for decades, but are now beginning to approach women. If current trends persist, Professor Mayhew forecasts, both sexes could, on average, live to the age of 87 by 2030. He remarked: What's interesting currently is that in the last 20 years or so, male life expectancy at 30 has increased by about six years and if it increases by the same amount in the next 20 years it will align with female life expectancy. The reason could be attributed to men adopting healthier lifestyles. One of the main reasons, I believe, is the trend in the prevalence of smoking. Smoking became prevalent after 1920 among the male population and at its peak about 80% of males smoked. This was reflected in greater divergence in life expectancy, so by around 1970 it was at its peak—the difference in life expectancy was about 5.7 years. Other factors are believed to be safer, more office-based jobs. Millions of men previously worked in hazardous occupations such as coal mining. Healthcare advancements have also contributed to men living longer. Individuals with heart disease, more common in men, can now expect to live much longer than a few decades ago. In contrast, women began smoking later than men. However, smoking rates are declining rapidly among men. A boy and a girl born on the same day will still not have identical life expectancies, as the study only considered individuals who had already reached 30. Boys are more likely to die in their first year of life and are more prone to engaging in dangerous sports or being involved in fatal accidents. This implies that women could maintain the advantage for some time. Professor David Leon, from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, stated: In virtually all countries in the world, women do have a slight advantage. However, he noted the gap is definitely closing in some countries. Countries with lower levels of life expectancy, such as those in sub-Saharan Africa, showed very little difference between the genders. This was due to the prevalence of infectious diseases which are not selective about men and women, he said. In countries that have overcome most infectious diseases, such as those in Eastern Europe, there is a much larger difference, mostly influenced by lifestyle factors. At one point in the 1990s, the gap between life expectancies in Russia reached 13 years. Professor Leon described it as an absolutely massive difference in a very gendered society. In his third category of countries, such as the UK, the gap in life expectancies is beginning to narrow. He commented: Men are becoming slightly better behaved and women are adopting male life expectancies.

text: How often do we really look into someone's eyes? We exchange fleeting glances with strangers on the street and gaze affectionately at friends and family, but how often do we maintain eye contact for more than a few seconds? Not often enough, according to Nuala McKeever, who describes herself as a happiness instructor. Nuala believes eye contact could enable us to reconnect with each other in a profound and spiritual manner, and the 40-year-old is well-versed in the human spirit. After departing a high-pressure role in the financial services sector, Nuala embarked on a journey of self-discovery, leading her to become a 'laughter-yoga' instructor. Originally from Londonderry, she now resides in Belfast and operates the Sunshine Project with her friend Michelle Major. As part of their mission to promote peace and love, the duo organised an event near Victoria Square, Belfast, on Thursday, encouraging the public to share 60 seconds of eye contact with a volunteer. I attended to experience the intimacy of such a moment with a stranger. The group set up at Belfast's Corn Market during lunchtime. Each volunteer gazer was stationed inside a hula hoop, on a cushion or chair, with an empty space before them. The public was invited to sit or stand before the volunteer and, without speaking, gaze into their eyes for 60 seconds. I was paired with Nuala, who instructed me to focus on each other's left eye to prevent breaking eye contact by shifting our gaze. As our 60 seconds commenced, I began to feel uneasy. Nuala, however, with her head slightly tilted, appeared perfectly calm. As the seconds passed, I wanted to look away or down, but our eyes remained locked. When I accepted this and gradually relaxed, I started to experience the practice's positive effects. I felt very calm, and everything in the background blurred. For a brief moment, it seemed as though we were the only two people in the bustling city centre. When the session concluded, Nuala embraced me, an act that would have felt more peculiar had I not spent the last 60 seconds staring at her. She expressed that I had made her feel emotional, though she was unsure why. She remarked: I often see myself when I stare into someone's eyes. Eye contact is our connection as human beings, and it varies each time, but it always reminds me that I am part of something much larger than myself. When we look into each other's eyes, we see beyond our differences; I can't think of anywhere this is more crucial than in Belfast. One participant, Marcela Vojacova, 44, explained her involvement in the project. I wanted to discover what could be achieved by staring into another person's eyes and what I might perceive, she said. When I participate, I feel a sense of fulfilment, love, and happiness—I hope others do too. Mark Graham, who visited the event to see if it would help him de-stress, was surprised by his experience. I have a job interview approaching, and sharing 60 seconds with Marcela truly helped me to relax, he said. During our shared experience, it felt as though no one else was present. I think many would laugh at the idea of participating in something like this, but it could be genuinely beneficial for some.

text: Free movement of workers in the EU has made life tougher for low paid workers in the UK, Andy Burnham has said. He was delivering a speech to regain Labour voters from UKIP in his inaugural major address as shadow home secretary. He stated it was not true that free movement had benefited everyone as Labour had previously asserted. UKIP described it as a welcome recognition of the blindingly obvious, but suggested if Mr Burnham wished to address it, he should campaign for the UK to leave the EU. Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, who defeated Mr Burnham for the Labour leadership by a significant margin, has meanwhile emphasised the positive contributions EU migrants have made to the UK. People who have migrated to this country over many years have made an enormous contribution to our society, supported our economic growth, assisted our health service and supported our social services and education services, so do not view immigration as necessarily a problem; it is often a very great opportunity, Mr Corbyn told BBC Radio 4's Today programme. He noted Mr Burnham had highlighted during the leadership campaign that the government needed to be far more focused on the shortage of doctors' surgeries, school places, and housing issues in certain areas. However, Mr Burnham stated in his speech that Labour had not faced up to some impacts of EU migration and consequently seemed out of touch. To win back the voters we lost to UKIP, I wish to reframe the debate about immigration and the way Labour approaches it, he told delegates in Brighton. For too long, we have argued that free movement across Europe benefits everyone and affects all areas equally. That is just not true. In some places, a free market in labour benefits private companies more than people and communities. Labour has not faced up to that, and that is why we appear out of touch. He remarked that David Cameron's renegotiation of Britain's relationship with the EU, ahead of a planned in/out referendum, offered an opportunity to protect workers. The truth is that free movement under the current rules is widening inequality. It has strengthened the economic power of the big cities, which is good. But it has made life harder for people in our poorest communities, where wages have been undercut and job security lost. The forthcoming referendum presents a chance to change that. Let us seize it as an opportunity to put Labour back on the front foot and back in touch. Let us propose a new vision for a social Europe. A Europe that prioritises people over profits and multinationals; a floor beneath all workers. The Tories and UKIP wish to remove those protections. Let us have the strength to challenge their scapegoating rhetoric, which will not pay anyone's bills, feed anyone's children, or protect anyone's job. We welcome people here to work, as we always have. But let us make it work for everyone with new EU rules to prevent undercutting, protecting the going rate for skilled workers. UKIP employment spokeswoman, MEP Jane Collins, stated Mr Burnham's words were the desperate attempts of a man who has ignored the plight of the working classes due to mass immigration for years.

text: Justin Timberlake has said he'll be performing at this year's Eurovision Song contest in Stockholm, Sweden. The 35-year-old will perform during the interval at the grand final on Saturday. Eurovision organisers clarified that his performance would be non-competitive. It is the first instance in the contest's history that an artist of global renown has performed independently on stage. In a statement, Sven Stojanovic, one of the show's producers, said: This is a fantastic opportunity, we are very happy and excited that Justin Timberlake will perform his new song together with his band in our show. It is particularly special that the Swedish songwriters Max Martin and Shellback have co-written and co-produced the song with Justin Timberlake. The nine-time Grammy award-winner will perform his new song, Can't Stop the Feeling, which he composed for the Dreamworks animation, Trolls. BBC Radio 1 presenter Scott Mills and The Great British Bake Off's Mel Giedroyc will co-host BBC Four's live coverage of the two semi-finals on 10 and 12 May. Graham Norton will once again provide commentary for BBC One's live broadcast of the final from the Globe Arena. Timberlake, who is on a promotional tour for his single, also presented the best drama series award at this year's Bafta TV awards, alongside actress Anna Kendrick. The award was given to BBC Two's Wolf Hall. Timberlake's performance announcement follows Eurovision's decision to expel Romania from the competition for failing to pay their fees. It also comes days after Eurovision organisers relaxed their flag rules, allowing the UK entry to fly a Welsh flag. It was initially included in a list of banned flags because its red dragon was deemed a political statement. Previously, only flags of contest members and UN states were permitted due to the event's non-political nature. The UK entry features Joe Woolford from Ruthin, Denbighshire, who will perform You're Not Alone with Jake Shakeshaft from Stoke-on-Trent. The Eurovision Song Contest will be broadcast on BBC One from 2000 BST.

text: Pupils have been so violent or disruptive that on eight occasions last year teachers held ballots to refuse to teach them in their classes. These votes, cast by members of the NASUWT teachers' union, included instances where pupils had assaulted teachers but were permitted to remain in school. In response to these ballots, pupils were either expelled or relocated. Schools Minister Nick Gibb stated that teachers had been provided with the backing they need to tackle poor behaviour. text: Is banning a person from contesting for public office if he or she does not have a toilet at home a good idea? India's western state of Gujarat certainly believes so. Earlier this week, the state's legislators passed a bill mandating that candidates must have toilets in their homes to qualify for contesting elections to local municipalities and village councils. Existing elected members will also be required to declare within six months that they have toilets at home, failing which they will face disqualification. Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who governed Gujarat for over a decade before ascending to power in Delhi in May, has prioritised the abolition of open defecation. It is a commendable aim, though critics argue it does not seem to connect what is largely an individual-driven campaign to the deplorable practice of manual scavenging. Clearly, legislators from Mr Modi's ruling BJP in Gujarat have enthusiastically supported their leader's initiative. Surely, there is nothing objectionable in that. Open defecation affects the lives of millions of Indians and poses a persistent health hazard. Nearly half of Indians continue to defecate in the open. Gujarat, one of India's most prosperous states, is eager to construct more toilets; the state has a patchy record in this area. Its new Chief Minister Anandi Patel states she wants the state to be open defecation free in two years. A recent report indicated more than 70,000 people defecate in the open in the main city of Ahmedabad alone. Good economics does not always lead to good sanitation. But is the latest move linking a democratic right to building a private utility such a wise idea? Approximately 40% of people in Gujarat reside in its 159 municipalities and eight municipal corporation areas in what is one of India's most urbanised states. There are about 13,500 village councils in its more than 18,500 villages. Elections to these bodies are crucial to the health of Gujarat's democracy and development. The freedom to contest the polls is also an inalienable right of every citizen living in their cities and villages. That is why critics like economist Hemant Shah believe that the bill is essentially undemocratic and discriminatory and should be contested in the courts. Tens of thousands of people in Gujarat's bustling cities live in sprawling chawls—densely packed buildings with more than a dozen tenements—where many families share a single toilet. Will a chawl resident be barred from contesting because he does not have his private toilet? What happens to the political aspirations of a resident of a squalid shantytown home so small that his living space is sometimes equal to the non-existent toilet? The government should first provide space and money to build toilets for the poor. The poor are most affected by urban planning because it has always excluded them. Now they can't dream of standing for public office just because they don't have the space or money to build their own toilets? asks Professor Shah. It's a valid question.

text: Scientists have discovered another eight pieces of genetic code linked to osteoarthritis, bringing the total number to 11. These are external links and will open in a new window. Inherited factors account for at least half of an individual's likelihood of developing this common joint condition, experts assert. Understanding these factors could lead to new treatments. The research in The Lancet compared the DNA of 7,400 UK osteoarthritis patients with that of 11,000 healthy volunteers. This enabled scientists to identify the most promising culprit regions of the genetic code for further study. They repeated their work with another group of 7,500 people with osteoarthritis and approximately 43,000 individuals without the condition from Iceland, Estonia, the Netherlands, and the UK. The results confirmed three previously reported gene variants and identified an additional eight linked to osteoarthritis. Further research is required to pinpoint the specific DNA changes within the genetic regions to determine precisely how these changes lead to osteoarthritis. The variant with the strongest effect was located in the region of the GNL3 gene, which produces a protein crucial for cell maintenance. Three others were in DNA regions involved in the regulation of cartilage, bone development, and body weight. One of the lead scientists, John Loughlin, a professor of musculoskeletal research at Newcastle University, stated: We know that osteoarthritis runs in families and that this is due to the genes that people pass on, rather than their shared environment. In this study, we were able to say with a high degree of confidence which genetic regions are the major risk factors for developing osteoarthritis: the first time that this has been possible for this common yet complex disease. It's an important first step. Prof Alan Silman, medical director of Arthritis Research UK, the charity that funded the work, said: Until we understand the cause of this complex disease, we cannot hope to find a cure. This is a major breakthrough in our understanding of osteoarthritis, which we hope will help us to unlock the genetic basis of the disease.

text: The number of young men using steroids in London is rising on a regular basis a drugs charity has warned. South Westminster Drug and Alcohol Service reported a rising number of young male clients seeking assistance for anabolic steroid use. Home Office statistics indicate 60,000 individuals used steroids in the UK in 2014. However, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence described this as the tip of the iceberg and recommended that gyms provide sharps bins for needles. Roy Jones, from the South Westminster service, stated: Our numbers are increasing on a regular basis. I've been working with steroid users for 16 years and initially, the individuals using them were bodybuilders in their 30s. Now the average age I see is 23. Professor Gillian Leng, deputy chief executive of the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), noted a concerning trend of young professionals resorting to the drugs. She remarked: It's fair to say it is becoming a much more normal thing to do among some groups of young men who are concerned about the way they look... injecting steroids has become a solution. Although government data suggests 60,000 people used steroids in 2014, professional organisations believe the actual figure is significantly higher, as only those detained by police are included in the statistics. What are anabolic steroids? Professor Leng commented: I think it is inevitable that the number is a lot higher. From the epidemiology (the data) we have about the kind of people who use steroids - it's a group that's not all going to appear in custody so that figure is bound to be the tip of the iceberg - it might be three times that number. A 25-year-old, employed in the City of London and wishing to remain anonymous, informed BBC London he had used steroids for two years. He stated he purchased them from a dealer at his local gym and knew many others who did the same. I started taking them because I felt I couldn't get any bigger training naturally, he said. It was the next step for me. There's immense pressure to look good - it's part of the culture we live in, we all want that big figure. Easygym has installed sharps bins in all their gyms, while Fitness First, Virgin Active and David Lloyd reported some of their clubs also have them. All the gyms stated they had a zero-tolerance policy towards steroids, and the bins were a health and safety measure for diabetic members and the disposal of razors. The Department of Health stated it had given local areas the power and the funding to tackle public health issues like this. Despite the increased awareness, Matthew Dear, 17, from Southend, died following an adverse reaction to steroids. His mother Tina, who runs the Matthew Dear Foundation, established to warn people about the dangers of steroid use, said: When we lost Matthew six years ago, people thought it was a problem that wasn't going to boil over. We are now at that point where it is boiling over and somebody needs to take ownership. Rolandas Malinauskas, from east London, is a natural bodybuilder - meaning strictly no steroids. The former British Champion stated many young men did not consider the dangers of the drugs. In the long term, you do not win with steroids - they create a mirage, he said. You can build muscle naturally but it takes time and dedication. It's all about precision, training and diet.

text: England seem set to end the series in South Africa with a defeat after a horrible start to their second innings. They quickly subsided to 18-3, and it seems something extraordinary must occur from the overnight score of 52-3 to avert a heavy defeat, with a victory target of 382 appearing purely academic. South Africa's pace attack exposed some familiar weaknesses while also highlighting the Centurion pitch's difficulty, particularly with the new ball. There was pressure; the light was poor; England could not win the game; they were batting to save the game—all the usual issues. One might think England should have performed slightly better, but the new ball is challenging. It is very awkward for a batsman when the ball lands in the same spot on separate occasions and behaves differently. Captain Alastair Cook faced one delivery that rolled along the ground and another that nearly hit his armpit, and with only half a second to react while wondering what the pitch will do, it creates uncertainty. Top batsmen must handle these situations, but it is easier said than done. Alex Hales received one that kept a bit low, resulting in another failure. He has played four games and scored 136 runs. My opinion remains unchanged: any opening bowler would consider Hales offers more chances than he should as an opening batsman. They might continue with him. They dropped Adam Lyth after seven matches, and they are running out of options, having tried eight opening batsmen since Andrew Strauss retired in 2012. They could promote Nick Compton, but he has hardly excelled, either opening or at number three, and he played a loose shot to become the third England wicket to fall within the first 10 overs. They must think carefully about it, but they must resolve the opening position. In early summer conditions, when England play three Tests against Sri Lanka, Hales might score some runs, and it might be one score that launches his Test career. text: Syrian forces are continuing their crackdown on protesters in the port city of Latakia for a third day, reportedly using tanks and gunboats. Activists report that at least 30 individuals have died since Saturday, and that residents attempting to escape the city's Ramel district have been fired upon by troops. The government in Damascus asserts it is addressing armed terrorist gangs. Over 1,700 people have reportedly perished in the six-month uprising against President Bashar al-Assad's rule. The Ramel quarter and adjacent areas are reportedly under constant heavy gunfire on Monday as tanks and troops advance through the streets. The assault commenced on Saturday, a day after mass anti-government protests in the city. By Jim Muir, BBC News, Beirut. Latakia was among the cities embroiled in the revolt shortly after it began in mid-March. Despite repeated attempts by the regime to suppress defiance, it continues to resurface. It is a sensitive city. Its population is approximately 600,000, with a Sunni Muslim majority, as does the country, but there are also areas dominated by President Assad's minority Alawite community. The current punishment is being inflicted on mainly Sunni areas, a fact that could further exacerbate sectarian tensions already heightened by the situation. On Sunday, activists claimed Syrian warships had joined the attack, firing shells on the city. A resident of Ramel told the Associated Press news agency: We are being targeted from the ground and the sea. The shooting is intense. We cannot go out. They are raiding and breaking into people's homes. He stated that at least three gunboats were involved and mosques had been targeted. A Syrian military official on Monday dismissed as absolutely baseless reports that gunboats had fired on Latakia, Syria's official Sana news agency reported. A UK-based Anglican priest visiting his family in Latakia described the atmosphere in the city as extremely tense. [On Sunday] you could hear a lot of shooting and bombing from different parts of the city, the Reverend Nadim Nassar told the BBC. The whole city is now shut... the fear is very high and people don't know what's going on and what is next, he said. The London-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported that at least one young child had been killed. State television denied any shelling had occurred. It stated the security forces were combating armed gangs who had erected barricades and were shooting from rooftops. The government reported three members of the security forces were killed and 40 wounded in clashes. It interviewed some of the city's residents in other locations who called on the army to clear out the terrorist gangs. Activists deny their movement is armed but said at least one officer and several soldiers had defected to join the uprising. International journalists face severe restrictions in operating in Syria, making it difficult to verify reports. Meanwhile, newspapers in the region have expressed anger over Arab states' failure to respond to events in that country. Latakia has witnessed numerous anti-government protests in the past six months. Syria has come under increased diplomatic pressure in the past week to halt its crackdown on dissent. The US has imposed sanctions on Damascus and stated these could be increased, while urging other countries to follow suit. Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, and Kuwait have all recalled their ambassadors, while Turkish Foreign Minister Ahmet Davutoglu has described the methods used by the Syrian security forces as unacceptable. Mr Assad has reiterated promises of political reform, while remaining adamant his government would continue to pursue the terrorist groups he has blamed for the unrest. Protests have been targeted in Homs, Hama, Damascus, Deir al-Zour in the east, Deraa in the south, and Aleppo and Idlib near Turkey's border. A doctor in Hama told the BBC that medical services there had been severely impacted by recent government attacks. He said two hospitals were closed and one had been stormed by troops, injuring many of the medical staff.

text: Young people who went through pre-school education are much more likely to do well in international Pisa tests when they are teenagers, says the OECD. These are external links and will open in a new window. However, the international think tank asserts that to maximise the benefits of early years education, places must be available for the poorest families. The OECD reports that the UK has low levels of hours in pre-school education. There are proposals in England to increase the amount of free childcare to 30 hours, but only for working families. The OECD study indicates there are significant economic and personal advantages from investing in early years education and endorses the initiative in England to expand access to pre-school places. Currently, the 15 hours of free childcare is among the lowest levels of provision in any OECD country, but it will increase to 30 hours in the autumn for families with a working parent. Andreas Schleicher, the OECD's education director, acknowledges the rationale for prioritising pre-school places for working families, enabling parents to afford employment. Yet, he suggests that this strategy might diminish the educational benefits of early years support, which are most significant for the most disadvantaged families. The OECD study reveals that by international standards, the UK has a high proportion of children in workless families, especially in lone-parent families. These families may miss out if access to early years places is concentrated on working families. Mr Schleicher emphasised the significance of pre-school education in providing children with a strong start. This extended beyond education, with the study highlighting connections between access to early years education and reduced obesity levels. However, the report cautioned that spending in this sector might be inconsistent and that staff could be less well-paid than in the school system. According to the OECD survey, pre-school staff in the UK have experienced a real-term pay decrease since 2010. Finding good quality pre-school places might also be considerably more challenging for parents compared to the amount of information available about schools. Mr Schleicher stated that the variety of early years places could be very fragmented and hard to navigate. Neil Leitch, chief executive of the Pre-school Learning Alliance, remarked: We have long argued that, given current limited resources, the government should focus its spending on where it is needed most. As such, we remain at a loss as to why there has been no attempt to rethink the current eligibility criteria for the 30-hour offer. A Department for Education spokeswoman stated: We are investing more than ever before into childcare - £6bn per year by 2020 - and doubling our existing offer of free childcare for all three and four year olds to 30 hours for working parents. We are also supporting the most disadvantaged families with 15 free hours per week for two year olds, our pupil premium which is worth over £300 a year per child and our new Disability Access Fund, providing £615 per eligible child.

text: A Spanish MP has provoked criticism by taking her baby into parliament and breastfeeding him during its first session since an inconclusive general election last month. These are external links and will open in a new window. All attention was on Carolina Bescansa, who was standing as a candidate for speaker. Pablo Iglesias, leader of the anti-austerity Podemos party, was among those photographed cuddling the young boy. Political leaders are still negotiating over the formation of a government following the 20 December election. The conservative People's Party (PP) secured the most seats in parliament but did not achieve a majority. Ms Bescansa, an MP with Podemos (We Can), which came third in the election, had pledged to breastfeed in parliament during her campaign, according to reports. Speaking on Wednesday, she defended the right of every parent to raise their child in whatever way they are able to or wish to, after some politicians suggested her actions were unnecessary, Spanish news agency Efe reported. She stated she had been privileged not to have been separated from her baby, Diego, since his birth. However, acting Interior Minister Jorge Fernandez Diaz, of the PP, criticised the move as lamentable, according to El Mundo. Socialist MP Carme Chacon described it as frankly unnecessary. Ms Bescansa reportedly requested photographers not to broadcast her baby's face. Yet some critics accused her of attention-seeking and highlighted the existence of a nursery in the parliament building, introduced in 2006 to assist MPs with childcare. She was unsuccessful in her attempt to become parliamentary speaker. Socialist MP Patxi Lopez won the vote to become the first-ever speaker from a party that did not win the most seats in an election. Ms Bescansa has previously brought her son into parliament for ceremonial events, including her swearing-in as an MP. Iolanda Pineda, of the Socialists' Party of Catalonia (PSC), also brought her baby into Spain's upper house of parliament in 2012. Italian politician Licia Ronziulli was first photographed with her baby in the European parliament in September 2010 when the child was six weeks old. Since then, photos of the MEP with her daughter have documented the little girl growing up. Last year, a group of MPs in the UK called for a ban on new mothers breastfeeding their babies in the House of Commons chamber to be overturned. Spanish MPs gathered for the first session of parliament on Wednesday, but deadlock persists over the formation of a government. Mariano Rajoy's Popular Party is advocating for a coalition with the Socialists (PSOE) and the centre-right Ciudadanos (Citizens) party, which came fourth in the election. However, the Socialists are pursuing a deal with Citizens and Podemos. So far, Podemos has refused to abandon a demand for a referendum on independence in Catalonia, which the two other parties reject. If the main parties fail to reach an agreement, King Felipe VI will ask a party leader to form a government and MPs will vote on his nomination. New elections might have to be conducted.

text: Newcastle Falcons survive a second-half fightback from Bristol at Kingston Park to earn their third win of the season. Juan Pablo Socino, Will Welch, and Joel Hodgson's first-half tries provided Newcastle with a 19-point advantage. However, Bristol—still seeking their first victory since rejoining the Premiership—responded with tries from John Fisher and Mitch Eadie, reducing the gap to five points. The Falcons managed to hold on to secure a win, handing Bristol their sixth consecutive defeat, leaving them at the bottom of the table. Both teams concluded the match with 14 players as Newcastle's Alex Rogers and Bristol's Gaston Cortez were both sent to the sin bin. The visitors made a late push in a tense conclusion but failed to complete an impressive comeback, although they did secure their second losing bonus point of the season, doubling their points tally. Joel Hodgson and Mike Delany both missed second-half penalties that could have extended the Falcons' lead in the final stages. Nonetheless, the hosts' dominant first-half performance was sufficient to secure victory, with Hodgson's slick score just before half-time proving decisive. Newcastle's director of rugby, Dean Richards, commented: If you'd asked me 15 minutes before kick-off would I take a 19-14 win, the answer would have been yes, but I'm sitting here now slightly frustrated, and so is the team. We're in the top half of the Premiership with three wins and a couple of losing bonus points, but we do have a lot of injuries to key players and are a little frustrated rather than happy. We played so well in the first half and could have scored two or three more tries, and we could have done with those in the second half because we took our foot off the gas. They had two chances and took them both, and our kicking went off a little, and that was probably the root cause of the problem. I never thought we would ever lose, but we could well have thrown it away. Bristol's director of rugby, Andy Robinson, stated: I thought we started reasonably well, but we lost our discipline, and it was a bit of an own goal when Newcastle scored their first try, giving them the momentum. In the second half, we started to get up off the line, made our tackles, and gained momentum. We scored two really good tries but unfortunately just could not keep that momentum going. That second half was pleasing in that it proved we do have the talent to succeed in the Premiership. We did some good things here today and in the opening game of the season, but we wanted at least one win from the first six games of the season, and we're frustrated we haven't done that.
