text: On a warm Saturday afternoon in March a group of campaigners heads to the Golden Lane estate in central London. These are external links and will open in a new window. Local council elections are imminent, yet these volunteers are not canvassing for councillors. Members of the campaign group We Can Win aim to ensure residents understand the unique electoral system of their local authority, which they oppose. The City of London Corporation governs the Square Mile, London's financial hub, distinct from the Greater London Authority, which encompasses the entire UK capital. The City has fewer than 8,000 residents, but approximately 450,000 people work there, and the City Corporation allows some of these workers to vote for councillors, raising the electorate to nearly 19,000. I believed democracy was simply one person, one vote, states campaign director Dan Firth. But in the City of London Corporation elections, businesses have nearly twice the votes of ordinary people, which seems unjust to me. We Can Win targets the City elections with two main objectives: opposing what it perceives as votes for big business and maximising resident voter turnout. The City is divided into 25 wards, with residents mainly in four: Portsoken, Queenhithe, Aldersgate, and Cripplegate, which includes Golden Lane. Each ward is represented by Common Councillors and an alderman. Common Councillor elections occur every four years, with the next on 23 March, while aldermen are elected at least every six years as their terms expire. Some residents I spoke to already knew how the voting system worked, says campaigner Georgia O'Brien. But those unaware were shocked. When I explained that workers had almost double the votes of residents, they appeared utterly defeated. Golden Lane resident Beverley Bytheway is active in the residents' association yet unaware that workers and residents both vote. The road straddles the border with the London Borough of Islington, and she thought both councils were elected similarly. She is not fond of the Corporation: If they could offload the residents, they would... they're really not interested. Despite some residents' apparent lack of awareness, the City of London Corporation is transparent about its election system, with its website providing information on how to register to vote as a resident or worker. The City is a democratic institution, insisted a spokesman. All of its councillors are elected. For residents, it is one person, one vote, but for businesses, the number of votes depends on the number of employees. Sole traders and businesses with up to nine employees get one vote, while organisations with up to 50 staff can appoint one voter for every five employees. Organisations with more than 50 staff can appoint 10 voters and then one voter per 50 employees thereafter. The City's spokesman added: As the local authority, we provide public services to both 7,400 residents and 450,000 City workers. Therefore, to reflect the needs of the workers who come to the City daily, businesses located in the City can appoint people to vote in our local elections. The votes allocated to a business are proportional to their number of employees—the first 50 staff entitles a business to appoint 10 voters, but every additional 50 members of staff only entitle it to appoint an extra one voter, so the largest firms do not dominate the voter list as they could if it was a simple proportional representation of their workforce size. In its advice to firms wanting to register staff as voters, the Corporation states: It is important that people nominated to vote reflect the organisation's overall make-up—from chief executive to entry-level employees and even regular contractors—so that the City Corporation represents the full range of the City's workforce. Voters nominated should reflect the whole diversity of an organisation's employees, including gender, ethnicity, and seniority. Professional services giant Deloitte employs over 10,000 staff and has 260 voters across two wards. A spokesperson said: We value the votes we have in the City of London. The City does have an unusual electoral system due to its high number of workers and small residential population, but there are many local issues that Deloitte people care greatly about. For example, a thousand Deloitte people cycle into work daily. Their safety and the safety of all road users in our neighbourhood is important to us. The councillors provide a valuable link between Deloitte and our neighbours—other businesses and local residents. Local government in the City of London can be traced back to medieval times. It is the oldest local authority in Britain and a contender for the oldest continuing authority worldwide. Non-residential votes in other council areas were abolished in 1969, but the system continued for the City Corporation. The current electoral system dates from a 2002 act of Parliament, which extended voting rights to companies limited by guarantee and increased the business vote. Boundary changes followed, reducing the number of councillors. The City is known for its financial institutions, but bodies qualifying for a vote include shops, bars, restaurants, charities, and even churches and hospital trusts. Tobacconist Mukesh Gaglani has been a registered voter in the City for 25 years. As a small business owner with two part-time employees, he gets one vote. You have a say in the progress of the City, he tells me, adding that he does not feel that big business dominates. As far as I'm concerned, my vote is the same as anyone else's. You don't feel like you are in a minority. What is his response to proposals that only residents should be allowed to vote? I don't think it's appropriate. The City gets most of its revenue from commercial properties. So how does being elected by workers and residents affect a councillor's job? Sophie Fernandes has served as one of four independent Common Councillors representing Coleman Street ward since 2009. I get queries about rubbish collection, I get queries about the ease with which people get to work, about infrastructure, she says, adding: The City of London is also a landlord. It owns a few buildings in my ward. I have complaints just like any other landlord has. When asked how many residents her ward has, she can think of just four, two of whom moved out temporarily due to work on London's Crossrail transport project. We try to break up the wards, depending on whether it's a business vote or a residential vote, so that we can concentrate on the needs of that particular ward because the needs of residents and businesses are very different, she says. It is workers who have a vote, it's not businesses who have a vote, she says. She adds: I don't think every worker should have a vote because it would completely outweigh residents, but in wards such as mine, it is heavily business-oriented without residents, so how would you represent this ward otherwise? What does she make of the allegation of Golden Lane resident Beverley that the City Corporation would rather be rid of its residential population? That's totally untrue. The residents bring diversity to the City. To stand as a councillor, you need to be a registered voter and a Freeman of the City of London. If you are a voter in the City, then you can get freedom without cost, so there is no barrier to standing, Ms Fernandes says. Like nearly all councillors at present, she sits as an independent and does not take a party whip. She is standing this time on a slate alongside fellow independents Michael Cassidy, Stuart Fraser, and Andrew McMurtie and argues that being independent helps the City work with both a Conservative government and a Labour mayor of London. We do not want party politics, she says. I fail to see the benefit that party politics will bring when you can still argue your point of view from an independent platform. That view is being challenged by the Labour Party, which first ran candidates in 2009 and is contesting wards in 2017. Paul O'Brien, who is contesting Coleman Street for the party, claims that there is an urban myth of independents in the City. He argues that many councillors list party memberships in their declarations of interests but only Labour openly fields candidates. A resident of the City himself, Mr O'Brien nevertheless agrees with Sophie Fernandes on the need for worker representation. Clearly there are wards with no, or virtually no residents, so there needs to be a different system, he says. Both opponents and supporters of the voting system agree that the City of London is an unusual organisation with a reach stretching well beyond the Square Mile. It owns and maintains housing estates and open spaces across Greater London and beyond, including Hampstead Heath and Epping Forest, and provides money to London boroughs through its City Bridge Trust. The elections for the City of London's Common Councillors take place on Thursday 23 March - A full list of candidates is available here.

text: All it takes to officially run for the Republican presidential nomination is a one-page form sent to the Federal Election Commission, the US government entity in charge of overseeing campaign laws. That is the straightforward part. Thus far this year, 213 aspiring commanders-in-chief have achieved precisely that. The challenging part is everything that follows. Announcing one's candidacy and formalising it with federal paperwork places a name on precisely zero ballots in the state-level primaries and caucuses, which are crucial for securing enough delegates to win the presidential nomination at the Republican National Convention in July. Qualifying for those ballots is a state-by-state endeavour, with varying rules and regulations for each. It requires time and money—and a substantial amount of both. Only the most organised, professional campaigns can accomplish this task. For example, there is a $1,000 (£600) fee for getting on the ballot in New Hampshire—the early-voting state that has made and broken many candidacies. However, this is insignificant compared to South Carolina, the third state in the nominee selection process and a battleground for Republican candidates seeking to build momentum as the Southern states hold their votes. To have a chance of winning there, Republicans by Wednesday had to write a cheque for $40,000 (£26,500) to the state's Republican Party—half of which is forwarded to the state government for administrative costs. The remaining $20,000 goes directly to the party's funds. It's extortion, says Richard Winger, editor of Ballot Access News. And it may not even be legal. In 1972, the US Supreme Court unanimously ruled that a fee of up to $8,900 to run for a local office in the Democratic Party primary was unconstitutional. Many potential office seekers lacking both personal wealth and affluent backers are, in every practical sense, precluded from seeking the nomination of their chosen party, no matter how qualified they might be and no matter how broad or enthusiastic their popular support, Chief Justice Warren Burger wrote. The case directly addresses fees like the one in South Carolina, says Winger. I think it's unconstitutional. If all these states started doing this, pretty soon it'd be up to a million dollars. And South Carolina and New Hampshire are merely the beginning. Eight other states have primaries with filing fees, mostly around the $1,000 mark. Arkansas, which holds a primary on 1 March, charges $25,000—payable by 9 November. Interested in the caucuses in Kansas or Kentucky? Those will cost $15,000 each. Complicating matters is the fact that filing fees must come directly from the candidates or their campaign funds—which have maximum contribution limits and strict reporting requirements—not from friends, relatives or the supposedly independent Super PAC entities that can raise unlimited amounts of money from wealthy donors to support candidates. South Carolina's prohibitive fee is said to have influenced former Texas Governor Rick Perry to end his financially strained presidential bid in mid-September. Wisconsin Governor Scott Walker paid the fee only to withdraw the following month. His campaign was reportedly more than $750,000 in debt by the time it concluded. Despite this high barrier, no one has come forward to contest the fee in court—and all 15 remaining Republican candidates paid up in South Carolina. Some, like New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, former New York Governor George Pataki, and the longest of long-shots, former Virginia Governor Jim Gilmore, filed within days—or even hours—of the afternoon deadline. Everyone, it appears, is content to simply sign the cheque and avoid causing political disruption. Democrats have their share of fees as well, of course, but they are generally much lower. In South Carolina, for instance, candidates like Hillary Clinton will have to pay $2,500 to the state party, which is then responsible for covering the remaining $20,000 to the state for election administration costs from its own funds. Money is not the only hurdle, either. Many states require candidates to gather up to 5,000 signatures from in-state registered voters—a task that demands a strong national organisation with a motivated volunteer base or the funds to pay professional signature-gatherers to canvass. In 2012, Virginia ballot-seekers had to submit petitions with at least 10,000 names—and only two, eventual winner Mitt Romney and libertarian Ron Paul, managed to qualify. Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich and former Senator Rick Santorum—each with earlier primary wins—failed to make the cut. For the 1 March 2016 balloting, Virginia has reduced the signature requirement to 5,000, due by 10 December, but at least 200 of those names must come from each of the state's 11 congressional districts. Many states have similar district-by-district requirements, where failing to gather enough signatures in even one district will keep a name off the ballot. Some states offer candidates a choice. To qualify for the 1 March primary in delegate-rich Texas, for instance, presidential aspirants must either pay a $5,000 filing fee or submit the signatures of 300 registered voters in at least 15 of the state's 36 congressional districts. Florida, unsurprisingly, is somewhat unique. Candidates can write a cheque for $25,000, gather at least 3,375 volunteer-obtained signatures from across Florida, or commit to attending the Sunshine Summit—a presidential forum hosted in Orlando by the state Republican Party in November. That summit could be a significant fundraiser for the party, which expects to sell 2,500 tickets to the event—and is charging $200 for a two-day pass and $1,000 for premium reserve seating (all major credit cards gladly accepted). Then there is first-in-the-nation Iowa, which has no petition requirements, filing fees or, for that matter, ballots. Voters can support whomever they wish in the caucuses, and if enough like-minded individuals show up to do the same, the candidate will be on their way to winning prized delegates. However, the state's caucus system presents challenges of its own. Encouraging Iowans to turn out on a cold February weekday and spend an evening advocating for their politician can be a logistical effort that makes South Carolina's $40,000 entry fee seem trivial. text: Venezuela has donated $500,000 to US President Donald Trump's inauguration, newly released records show. These are external links and will open in a new window. Citgo Petroleum, a US-based subsidiary of the Venezuelan state-owned oil company, is mentioned in documents filed with the Federal Election Commission. The disclosure comes as the Venezuelan economy appears to be debilitated by food shortages, violent crime, and inflation. Three individuals were killed in protests on Wednesday as tens of thousands took to the streets to demand new elections. Other major corporations listed in the documents include Pepsi and Walmart, which contributed $250,000 and $150,000 respectively, while owners of NFL teams or their companies contributed more than $5 million. Casino owner and billionaire Sheldon Adelson also contributed $5 million. Venezuela is experiencing a significant economic crisis, with the oil-rich nation on the brink of hyperinflation. This Wednesday, street protests demanding the resignation of President Nicolas Maduro resulted in at least two people being shot dead. In this turbulent context, it is perhaps less surprising that Venezuelan media did not seem to devote much time to cover the news that their government provided, through a state-owned oil company, a $500,000 contribution to Donald Trump's inauguration. Nonetheless, some analysts in Venezuela are expressing outrage at the news. We have been experiencing four consecutive years of recession, we have the highest inflation in the world and are facing shortages in many basic goods. It is scandalous that Venezuela, facing such a crisis, would make those donations to the inauguration of a US president, who at least in theory, is ideologically opposed to the revolution, Jose Manuel Puente, a professor of public policy at IESA university in Caracas, tells the BBC. The payment was reportedly made through Citgo, a US subsidiary of Venezuelan state-owned oil company PDVSA. It is not the first time Citgo has been involved in politically controversial activities in the US. President Maduro's predecessor, Hugo Chavez, used the company a few years ago to provide subsidised fuel to low-income citizens in several major US cities. His critics said then it was a propaganda tactic designed to irritate his ideological opponents at the White House. However, the Maduro administration now appears to be in a less confrontational stance towards Washington. The Venezuelan president has recently been quoted saying that Trump has been the target of a brutal hate campaign and added that he won't be worse than Obama. The (Bolivarian) revolution is pragmatic, Puente tells the BBC. Eighteen years after the beginning of the revolution, the US is still their main trading partner. It is business as usual.

text: Neil Gaiman's The Ocean at the End of the Lane has been voted 2013's Book of the Year, winning the public vote by a considerable margin. Gaiman's fantasy novel triumphed over fellow National Book Award winners, including Kate Atkinson and David Walliams. The story, about a man returning to his childhood home for a funeral, won the public vote from a shortlist of this year's 10 National Book Award winners. The graphic novelist expressed he was amazed and thrilled. I've never written a book before that was so close to my own heart—a story about memory and magic and the fear and danger of being a child, stated Gaiman. I wasn't sure that anyone else would appreciate it. I'm amazed and thrilled that so many others have read it, loved it, and encouraged their friends to read it too. Winning a National Book Award was thrilling; discovering that the public have made The Ocean at the End of the Lane their Book of the Year is somewhere out beyond wonderful. Thank you to everyone who voted. 'Dedication' Gaiman's novel had already triumphed in the Audiobook of the Year category. The book secured the public vote from a shortlist including Gillian Flynn's bestseller Gone Girl, David Jason's My Life, and schoolgirl Malala Yousafzai's I Am Malala to win the Book of the Year title. Online voting for the title, the only book award chosen by readers, concluded on 19 December. Last year's winner was EL James' raunchy blockbuster Fifty Shades of Grey, while Caitlin Moran's How To Be A Woman and David Nicholls' romantic novel One Day have also claimed the prize. Dame Mary Perkins, founder of the award's sponsors Specsavers, congratulated Gaiman on this fantastic award. The competition was tough but to be chosen by members of the public as well as your industry peers truly is a tribute to hard work, dedication and creativity, she remarked. Gaiman gained fame writing graphic novels including The Sandman series and Coraline. He has authored two recent Doctor Who episodes featuring Matt Smith and is currently writing a prequel to The Sandman. A TV series of his book American Gods is in development.

text: Italy produced a passionate and tactically superior display to end Spain's quest for a third consecutive European Championship title and secure a mouth-watering quarter-final tie against world champions Germany. Utilising wing-backs Mattia de Sciglio and Alessandro Florenzi to great effect, they were the more potent attacking side until they retreated to defend their lead in the final stages. Giorgio Chiellini netted the game's opening goal, bundling home from close range after David de Gea had parried an Eder free-kick in slippery conditions during the first half. Southampton striker Graziano Pelle secured victory in injury time, volleying home from eight yards after an attempted clearance from substitute Matteo Darmian's cross had looped up invitingly as Italy caught a tiring team on the break. The scoreline could have been significantly worse for Spain were it not for a series of outstanding saves by Manchester United goalkeeper De Gea. He made three in the first 45 minutes before smothering an effort from Eder in the second half after being put clean through by a sublime flick from Pelle. Italy played with an intensity and fierce determination that hinted at their ambition to avenge their 4-0 defeat in the 2012 final. It was only in the latter stages that they faced any threatening, sustained pressure - but Sergio Ramos headed wide and Gianluigi Buffon saved long-range efforts from Andres Iniesta and Gerard Pique. And with full-time approaching, Buffon made a brilliant dive to his right to save a close-range effort from Pique before Italy broke clear to score their decisive second. Spanish newspaper Marca ran the headline 'The End' after Spain were eliminated from the 2014 World Cup in Brazil after just two matches. If it was not true then, it certainly appears so now after La Roja's run as European champions was ended by a team that swarmed all over them and seemed to possess a hunger and desire no longer present in their opponents. Spain manager Vicente del Bosque is out of contract, and the side he has memorably coached since taking over from Luis Aragones after the 2008 European Championship seems in need of fresh impetus. The fact that they introduced a 35-year-old striker with just one previous international goal in Aritz Aduriz at the break perhaps suggests they are a team in need of a new direction. Former Spain international Xavi had stated in the build-up that this would be a troublesome match - and he was correct. Spain resembled a boxer with too many rounds in the legs, and only the imperious Iniesta offered any sense of attacking drive and craft. Sergio Busquets failed to exert much influence on the tie, and David Silva was another peripheral figure on a night when Italy seldom allowed their opponents any time on the ball. Indeed, if it were not for De Gea's brilliance, the tie would surely have been over by the break. He made three sensational saves - a Pelle header, a brilliant and acrobatic overhead kick from Emanuele Giaccherini that he tipped onto the post, and a one-handed effort at full stretch to thwart the same player after he drifted inside from the left. Chiellini - part of an all-Juventus back three with Leonardo Bonucci and Andrea Barzagli - said before the match that it would be settled by small details, and his side played like a team that left nothing to chance. From the intensity with which they sang the national anthem to the way they took the match to Spain as the heavens opened at the start, they played with incomparable determination. And all the while, coach Antonio Conte prowled his touchline. He must issue more than a thousand positional instructions during a match, and Chelsea fans can look forward to an electrifying presence in the dugout next season. The speed with which Italy - playing 3-5-2 - transitioned from defence to attack and exploited wide areas was something their opponents could not contend with. Spain could not pass their way through a superbly organised Italian side and lacked the speed to get around the edges. When Pelle scored the decisive second goal with seconds remaining, Conte leapt onto his team's dugout. He might have entered this tournament downplaying his team's chances - and said before the match on Monday that Spain were big favourites - but he exhibits the body language and drive of a man who believes his side can go a long way. text: Derby County climbed into the Championship play-off zone for the first time under new boss Paul Clement as they proved too good for Wolves. Chris Martin's two first-half goals—a 20-yard curler and a powerful header—came on either side of Benik Afobe's well-struck response for Wolves. Martin then had a penalty saved by Emiliano Martinez, but Bradley Johnson's soft strike made it 3-1 at the break. Johnny Russell scored a fourth before Adam Le Fondre made it 4-2. Le Fondre's looping volley, from substitute Sheyi Ojo's knockdown, sneaked in despite home keeper Scott Carson getting his fingertips to it. It compensated for the penalty shout Wolves did not receive before the break when his goalbound shot was blocked by former Wolves defender Jason Shackell's elbow. Additionally, the home side's second goal might have been disallowed as Martin levered himself into the air off Kortney Hause's shoulders. Johnson knew little about the third goal, which hit his outstretched left boot after Wolves failed to clear the Russell corner resulting from Martinez saving Martin's penalty, awarded for Danny Batth's foul on Tom Ince. Kenny Jackett's men executed a well-worked training ground move for their first goal when Afobe lashed in James Henry's corner to cancel out Martin's early strike. Media playback is not supported on this device. However, the visitors were generally second best, especially when sustained Derby pressure led to Russell toe-poking in from 12 yards for the Rams' fourth. Le Fondre's goal gave the scoreline a fairer reflection, but few would argue that Derby deserved all three points as they extended their current run to 16 points out of a possible 18 to climb to sixth. Wolves, who had won both their previous two games 3-0 before the international break, have dropped a place to 11th this weekend, now five points adrift of the play-off places. Derby head coach Paul Clement told BBC Sport: Our best performance of the season. We've had some good first halves and some good second halves, but this time we were solid throughout and were deserved victors. Chris Martin put in the best performance I've seen from a Championship centre forward from the games I've seen this season. A great finish for the first, a brave header for the second and he led the line well. It was a shame he didn't finish off the penalty for what would have been a first-half hat-trick. But he was a well-deserved man of the match. Against a good side, it was also a great response from the team to come back and score the way we did following the penalty miss. We could have gone in at half-time on a low. But to make it 3-1 was a big moment. Wolves head coach Kenny Jackett told BBC Sport: Derby were strong and take some stopping, but our defending was poor. text: A fund to raise money for the families of the five Birmingham wall collapse victims has passed £20,000. The men perished when a 15ft wall of concrete and scrap metal collapsed on them as they worked on Thursday at Hawkeswood Metal in Nechells. The editor of the Birmingham Mail, which initiated the fund, stated the response had been overwhelming. Police reported the site remains closed and post-mortem examinations would occur on Monday. Donations have been pouring in from across the nation for the men, who were Spanish citizens originally from Gambia. All the bodies were retrieved from the debris by Friday. Mr Reeves stated: No money can ever fill the void left by a loved one, especially in a tragedy of this sort. But at least if the families are relieved from the concerns of paying for funerals, travel for family members, and all the other immediate financial worries that hinder grieving, then it is worthwhile to raise some money to help. The response is overwhelming, and as well as the financial support, we hope this sends a message to the families that Birmingham cares about them and feels their pain. The men have been identified locally as Bangaly Dukureh, Ousman Jabbie, Alimamo Jammeh, Mohammed Jangana, and Saibo Sillah. All are believed to be married with children. Relatives have expressed they want the bodies recovered for burial as soon as possible, in accordance with Muslim custom. A sixth man, who escaped with a broken leg, is also a Spanish citizen of Gambian heritage. Detectives have stated they have a reasonable idea about what transpired. Hawkeswood Metal Recycling Ltd, which employs about 50 people, was established more than 40 years ago and claims it handles more than 500,000 tonnes of scrap metal each year at its Nechells site. In 2012 it was fined £50,000 when a worker got his arm trapped in machinery. It also pleaded guilty at Birmingham Crown Court to a breach of health and safety law. The plant was also the scene of a major fire in February this year, as 700 tonnes of scrap metal went up in flames.

Libby Chamberlain, the founder of Pantsuit Nation, is encouraging members to contribute. The page was named after Mrs Clinton's signature trouser suits, which she frequently wore during her campaign. In a piece for the feminist newsletter Lenny Letter, Ms Harris explained that the idea emerged as she dropped off her dry cleaning near her San Francisco residence. The former Facebook employee, educated at Stanford and Harvard, reflected on what an obvious privilege it is to even own a pantsuit, let alone to buy a new one for a special occasion. She remarked: In 2016, too many women still struggle to raise their families. text: Hosts France advanced to the Euro 2016 final with their first victory over Germany in a major tournament since 1958 on a night of high emotion in Marseille. Antoine Griezmann, the tournament's leading scorer, made crucial contributions in each half to secure a final against Portugal at the Stade de France on Sunday. Griezmann scored from the penalty spot just before half-time when Germany's Bastian Schweinsteiger was penalised for handball by Italian referee Nicola Rizzoli during an aerial challenge with Patrice Evra. France resisted German pressure before Griezmann determined the outcome of a thrilling semi-final with 18 minutes remaining, turning in from close range after goalkeeper Manuel Neuer could only partially clear Paul Pogba's cross. Joshua Kimmich then struck the woodwork for Germany and also had a header brilliantly saved by France goalkeeper Hugo Lloris, but there was no comeback for the World Cup holders. France began Euro 2016 slowly, but there was a palpable sense inside Marseille's vast Stade Velodrome that Didier Deschamps' team is now being propelled towards the finishing line in Paris on Sunday by a national wave of emotion. It was during a friendly between France and Germany at the Stade de France, which will host Sunday's Euro 2016 final, that the first explosions were heard on the night of the Paris attacks in November, in which 130 people died and hundreds were wounded. Fourteen players who started that night were in the line-ups that took to the field here in Marseille. The atmosphere inside the Stade Velodrome was electric after a day of intense heat, and the unity now felt between France's players and their supporters was encapsulated in one moment in the second half. Germany were exerting pressure in an attempt to recover from a 1-0 deficit when the entire stadium erupted into a rousing chorus of the national anthem, La Marseillaise, to encourage their team. One more task remains against Portugal on Sunday—the whole of France expects. Antoine Griezmann carried the hopes of a nation into Euro 2016, the diminutive Atletico Madrid forward regarded as their greatest threat and most significant asset. And how the 25-year-old has delivered, effortlessly handling the burden of expectation to emerge as a talisman and match-winner, bringing his tournament tally to six—the same number of European Championship goals as Thierry Henry, whose tally spanned three tournaments. Griezmann may not yet be in the league of Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo, and Luis Suarez, but every performance at this tournament brings him closer to that echelon. He made the difference with two goals when France were trailing the Republic of Ireland in the last 16, seizing the initiative from Martin O'Neill's side, and here, on an even grander stage, he was the game-changer once more. Griezmann had already tested Neuer with a low shot after a slick exchange with Blaise Matuidi, and even during a period of complete German dominance in the first half, he never allowed the World Cup holders to relax. He confidently converted his pressure penalty just before half-time, then reacted coolly when Neuer failed to handle Pogba's cross. Griezmann possesses a superb first touch, links play with quality, is an all-round team player, and scores crucial goals. He is the complete package. He is sometimes carrying France alone in attack as Olivier Giroud continues to struggle, with France supporters now increasing their criticism, but with Griezmann, there is always hope, and he will be their inspiration again in Paris on Sunday. Germany have failed to emulate France and Spain in achieving the double of holding the European Championship and World Cup simultaneously. They have been the scourge of host countries in the past, defeating six at the semi-final stage in major tournaments, including England at Euro 96 and, most memorably, thrashing hosts Brazil 7-1 at the 2014 World Cup. France managed to break the curse on this occasion and emerged victorious. Here, Joachim Low's side performed impressively for extended periods but either lacked the killer touch or found themselves thwarted by fiercely determined French defending or outstanding goalkeeping from Hugo Lloris. Germany have also developed a tendency to concede needless penalties, with Schweinsteiger once again inviting punishment with a raised arm while his team was dominant—in the same manner that Jerome Boateng gifted Italy a penalty in the quarter-final. Based on this evidence, Germany remain a European football superpower, but every weakness was exploited by France in front of an ecstatic home crowd. Former France striker Thierry Henry on BBC One: A sign of a great team is that you take advantage of mistakes. You punish a team. France did that. They were like an Italian or German side of old times. Two opportunities. Two goals. I am actually so emotional at the moment. It's nice to see that togetherness in the team, and with the fans. At the back they were great, Evra, Sagna, Umtiti. Everybody. The main man Griezmann, we all knew that he had to play this type of game. text: Another City shareholder has called on Sky's independent directors to explain why they have backed a takeover by Rupert Murdoch's 21st Century Fox. Last Friday, the US media giant announced it would offer £10.75 per share for the 61% of Sky it does not yet own. The independent directors of both companies have reached a provisional agreement on this price. However, Richard Marwood of Royal London Asset Management has requested more information. Those independent directors have taken advice, and we believe they should share that with shareholders, to actually allow the rest of us to see if £10.75 is the right price, so we are all acting from the same information, he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme. As it is part of the FTSE 100, the shares in Sky that 21st Century Fox aims to purchase are owned by numerous City investment firms. The shares were trading at 982p on Wednesday amid increasing calls for any bid to be referred by the government to the media regulator, Ofcom. Royal London is only the 68th largest investor in Sky with a stake of just 2.4 million shares, amounting to 0.14% of the total. Nevertheless, Royal London's comments add to a growing outcry from some shareholders that Sky's directors should explain their reasoning and hold out for a higher price. Standard Life and Jupiter Asset Management have already questioned the supposed independence of the Sky board, noting that Rupert Murdoch's son James is both chairman of Sky and chief executive of Fox. Chase Carey, a former chief executive of Fox Television and co-chief operating officer of Rupert Murdoch's newspaper group, News Corporation, is also on the Sky board. Another non-executive director at Sky, John Nallen, is also the chief financial officer of 21st Century Fox. Mr Marwood of Royal London stated there were a few question marks about the corporate governance of Sky. We had concerns when he [James Murdoch] was appointed to be the chairman of Sky, just for this situation, he said. We felt if there were ever to be a bid, there would be a conflict, and our fears have been realised with what's happened. Mr Marwood added: To some extent, Sky have tried to allay the fears of investors by having these independent directors opining on the bid. But I think more transparency to give us some confidence that there is some independence there would be very good.

text: Hungary has passed a law that critics say could undermine the independence of its central bank. The ruling Fidesz party, holding a two-thirds majority, has sanctioned the constitutional amendment in the final parliamentary session this year. Ratings agency Standard & Poor's downgraded Hungary's debt to junk status last week, partly due to the proposed constitutional amendments. EU and IMF officials have curtailed aid discussions with Hungary due to the law. Hungary had been seeking a standby credit line of 15-20bn euros (£12.6bn, $19.5bn) in case of difficulties in issuing new debt. However, the International Monetary Fund and the European Commission have both expressed doubts over aid due to the law. On Thursday, Hungary abandoned part of a planned bond auction when investors demanded a higher interest rate on the debt the country intended to issue. Hungary's central bank governor, Andras Simor, has stated the bill equates to a takeover of the central bank. The law has also been criticised by the European Central Bank, which said it raised concern as to whether [it] could be used to influence the decision-making process, to the detriment of central bank independence. International pressure The government aims to maintain low interest rates to stimulate growth, but last week, Hungary's central bank raised rates for the second consecutive month, to 7% from 6.5%. Consumer price inflation in Hungary is currently at 4.25%, significantly above the official 3% target. Some amendments have been made since the original draft was presented before the Christmas holiday, but concerns remain that the essence of the law has not changed, said the BBC's Eastern Europe reporter Nick Thorpe. The reform of the bank would introduce deputy governors and allow the government greater potential influence over key aspects of monetary policy, such as the level of interest rates. Hungary received a 20bn-euro standby loan from the IMF in 2008 to prevent a default on its debts. However, the newly-elected Prime Minister Viktor Orban chose not to renew the standby facility last year. Standard & Poor's has cited increased risks to the country's debt repayment ability due to the weakening domestic and global economic outlook. In our view, the predictability of Hungary's policy framework continues to weaken, harming Hungary's medium-term growth prospects, S&P stated. Last month, fellow ratings agency Moody's also downgraded Hungary to junk status, citing the economy's high debt levels and weak growth prospects.

text: The OFT has made a move to try to help people access discounts when booking online, after closing an investigation into competition practice between three companies. It examined online agents Booking.com, Expedia, and hotel group InterContinental Hotels (IHG). The investigation initially suspected the agreements violated competition law by restricting price competition. However, it has now permitted such agreements subject to specific conditions. The OFT has allowed online agents to reduce the hotel's room price to encourage more competitive pricing. Previously, the websites were unable to offer reductions. Under the conditions, the OFT stated consumers must first enrol in a membership scheme with a hotel, either of the agents, or another online agent. Customers must have also previously booked one room at the full rate with the online agent or hotel to qualify for future reductions, said the OFT. Booking.com and Expedia are two of the UK's largest online travel agents. The OFT initiated its investigation in 2010 to examine allegations of agreements and concerted practices resulting in fixed or minimum resale prices. Whether the move will enhance competition and reduce prices is a matter of debate. Gaucho Rasmussen, enforcement director at the OFT, stated he had examined the conditions very, very carefully. He said: We conducted consumer research and a significant number of people would shop around and use smaller websites and new entrants. Mr Rasmussen said the OFT had conducted two consultations and the decision was the best outcome. He stated that as the market continued to evolve, smaller websites could innovate and find ways to remain competitive. Dorian Harris, founder of discount booking website Skoosh, said he did not believe the move would open up the market and reduce prices. He said: I am baffled by the outcome. Smaller companies, such as Skoosh, could not afford to alter their marketing strategy and hotel contracts to meet the OFT's conditions, so would struggle to offer the reductions, he said. Mr Harris says the conditions would deter new consumers from using smaller, lesser-known websites rather than Booking.com or Expedia: The OFT have not understood the market. It is a huge failure in assessment. He said consumers would not want to pay for a full-rate room to qualify for the reduced rooms from a new website such as Skoosh. They would instead prefer to receive the reduction immediately from larger websites, such as Expedia, where customers would most likely have already purchased a premium-rate hotel room from, to qualify. He said the conditions would reinforce Booking.com or Expedia's dominance, adding the OFT had pandered to the interests of the two major companies. The OFT's Mr Rasmussen acknowledged there was a possibility the arrangement could lead to further monopoly, but he said the OFT would be monitoring developments in the market.

Unaware it was a 26-carat diamond, she wore it daily for decades. The cushion-shaped white diamond is believed to date from the 19th Century. Prior to the sale, the head of the auction house's London jewellery department, Jessica Wyndham, stated: The owner would wear it out shopping, wear it day-to-day. It's a good looking ring. No-one had any idea it had any intrinsic value at all. They enjoyed it all this time. Ms Wyndham mentioned the owner—who wishes to remain anonymous—assumed it was not a genuine gemstone because it was in a filthy mount and lacked the sparkle of a diamond. It was not until after 30 years of wearing the ring that the owners took it to Sotheby's, where a jeweller informed them it might be valuable. After purchasing a floral vase for £10 at a car boot sale, the Hampshire-based owner decided to sell it on eBay. When bids rose to £10,000, he withdrew it and sought professional assistance in identifying what he had bought. The £10 pot was, in fact, a rare enamel two quails vase, believed to have been crafted at Beijing's Imperial Palace at least 220 years ago. John Axford, Asian art expert at Woolley & Wallis auctioneers, confirmed the excellent investment bore the four-character mark of Qianlong—the sixth emperor of the Qing dynasty—and would have been made in the palace workshop between 1736 and 1795. text: Supporters and opponents of Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych are to hold rival protests in Kiev, amid fears of possible clashes. Activists and opposition parties anticipate that hundreds of thousands will participate in a Dignity Day rally at central Independence Square. Supporters of Mr Yanukovych will assemble in the nearby Mariinskyi Park. Protests commenced last month following the president's abrupt decision to withdraw from a significant EU agreement. Mr Yanukovych has expressed concerns that the association and trade agreement could jeopardise many businesses reliant on trade with Russia. The president, who asserts he still intends to sign the deal, has also acknowledged substantial pressure from Moscow, which prefers Kiev to join a Russian-led customs union. Several thousand pro-EU demonstrators stayed overnight in Independence Square before their rally, expected to begin at 12:00 local time (10:00 GMT) on Sunday. Barricades surrounding the main protest camp in the capital's centre have been reinforced after a special police attempt to dismantle them earlier this week. Opposition leaders have called on protesters to remain alert, fearing provocateurs might incite clashes between opposing demonstrators. The opposition has also accused authorities of transporting people to Kiev for the pro-government rally and providing them with money and food. The authorities officially deny this, but some rally participants have claimed they were coerced into attending. The two rival groups held demonstrations near each other on Saturday, with no reports of clashes. Separately, Mr Yanukovych suspended his deputy security chief and Kiev's mayor over police violence against pro-EU protesters on 30 November. Prosecutors are investigating Volodymyr Syvkovych and Olexander Popov, along with two other senior officials, on suspicion of office abuse in the crackdown. This has invigorated pro-EU protesters, who demand that all involved in the clampdown be dismissed and punished. They also seek the government's resignation. While pro-EU protests have dominated the capital and other cities in western and central Ukraine, President Yanukovych maintains support in the east and south. However, correspondents suggest that support may be waning, with pro-EU rallies already occurring in the south-east. Protesters claim Mr Yanukovych's reversal on the EU deal sparked the mass demonstration, but they now call for a complete reload of what they describe as a corrupt governance system. They believe signing the EU deal would eliminate corruption and make Ukraine's economy more open and transparent, citing Ukraine's western neighbours now in the EU as examples. However, the government and its supporters fear that economic liberalisation would harm the country's economy, particularly the industrial south-east dependent on Russian trade. Moscow has already exerted economic pressure on Ukraine, with customs delays and a ban on Ukrainian chocolates, and concerns persist that such measures could intensify if Kiev moved closer to Brussels.

text: Swiss pilot Andre Borschberg has begun his bid to cross the Pacific, from China to Hawaii, in the zero-fuel Solar Impulse aeroplane. The experimental aircraft, boasting a wingspan larger than a jumbo jet yet weighing only slightly more than a large car, departed Nanjing at 02:39 (18:39 GMT). It is expected to take Mr Borschberg five to six days of continuous flight to reach his central Pacific destination. He will endeavour to remain awake for most of that period, taking only brief catnaps. His progress will be constantly monitored from a control room in Monaco. Meteorologists and flight strategists will provide him with continuous updates on the optimal route to follow. The journey marks the seventh leg in the single-seat, propeller-driven aircraft's mission to circumnavigate the globe using solely solar energy. The project made steady progress after commencing from Abu Dhabi in March, but was delayed for over a month on China's east coast awaiting suitable weather conditions over the ocean. Solar Impulse requires not only favourable winds to aid its forward movement but also clear skies to allow its 17,000 wing-mounted photovoltaic cells to perform optimally. These cells must fully charge the vehicle's lithium-ion batteries by dusk to maintain flight until dawn the next day. Mr Borschberg is a highly experienced pilot and, as a trained engineer, is thoroughly familiar with the plane's systems. Nonetheless, he is fully aware of the mission's challenges. It's more in the end about myself; it's going to be an inner-voyage, he told the BBC before departure. It's going to be a discovery about how I feel and how I sustain myself during these five or six days in the air. Bertrand Piccard, who has piloted Solar Impulse on other legs of the journey, told the BBC: There's one pilot at a time, so the pilot needs to do everything on his own. And it's a very large aeroplane, big wingspans, sensitive to turbulence, flying quite slow. So sometimes it's difficult to handle when the air moves. But we have an auto-pilot, we have toilets on board, we have food for days, water reserves and everything, and we are well trained. The distance to Kalaeloa airport on Hawaii's O'ahu island exceeds 8,000km (5,000 miles). If, early in the flight, the weather deteriorates or he encounters a significant technical problem, Mr Borschberg can opt to return to China or Japan. However, there will be a point where that option is no longer available, and Mr Borschberg and his support team have had to prepare for the possibility of ditching in the Pacific if something goes seriously wrong. The pilot himself would not remain with the plane due to the risk of electrocution upon entering the water. Instead, he would bail out with a dinghy and await rescue by a ship. If he succeeds in reaching Kalaeloa airport, he will set several aviation records, including the longest-duration journey for a single-seater plane. The aim of the Solar Impulse project is not to showcase a specific future for aviation but rather to demonstrate the potential of clean technologies more broadly. LEG 1: 9 March. text: There is no obvious link between tough laws and levels of illegal drug use, a government report has found. Liberal Democrat Home Office Minister Norman Baker stated that the report, which compares the UK with other nations, should put an end to mindless rhetoric on drugs policy. He accused the Conservatives of suppressing the findings for several months. Prime Minister David Cameron remarked that the research did not provide specific conclusions and expressed his opposition to decriminalising drugs. Drugs policy was discussed in the House of Commons earlier, with Green MP Caroline Lucas urging the government to review failing drugs laws. Under current legislation, offenders can face up to seven years in prison for possessing Class A drugs and life imprisonment for producing or supplying drugs. The Home Office report compared the UK's approach to drug misuse with that of 13 other countries. Nine have sanctioned drug consumption rooms, including Canada, Denmark, and Switzerland. Eight are trialling the treatment of addicts with pure heroin rather than methadone, including Switzerland, the Netherlands, and the UK. Four have special drug courts, where individuals pleading guilty to drug offences can choose treatment over prison, including the US. One has established dissuasion commissions—Portugal. After examining a range of approaches, from zero-tolerance to decriminalisation, it concluded that drug use was influenced by factors more complex and nuanced than legislation and enforcement alone. However, it found a considerable improvement in the health of drug users in Portugal since the country reclassified drug possession as a health issue rather than a criminal one in 2001. The Home Office stated these outcomes could not be attributed solely to decriminalisation. Nonetheless, Mr Baker believes treating drug use as a health matter would be more effective, rather than presuming locking people up is the answer. Alex, a recovering heroin and crack addict from London, shared: The majority of my family either suffer from addiction or have died as a consequence of it. I have buried two friends this year. Addiction is a progressive illness. I started smoking cannabis when I was 18 or 19 at university. I was abstinent in the army but used alcohol in cross-addiction for about six years. I served in Iraq and was blown up in Basra. Post-Iraq, I worked in contract security and would use when I got back to the UK. I'm 38. I got clean at 30 and go to 12-step fellowship meetings nearly every day. I don't believe for one moment that the current laws deter any addict from using; to assume they do makes the assumption that addicts have control and choice. The views of the Home Office are out of touch and most probably based in ignorance of what addiction is. No-one I know chose to become an addict. The fact the Home Office is responsible for drug policy, including treatment, is alarming and probably why the UK is blighted with addiction. Lib Dem leader Nick Clegg accused the Conservatives of a totally misplaced, outdated, backward-looking view. While Mr Baker commented: We've had what I would call mindless rhetoric over the last 40 years, which has tended to say there is only one solution and anyone who offers any alternative must by definition be 'soft on drugs'. He claimed the Conservatives had suppressed the report's publication due to the inconvenient truths it contained. However, Tory MP Michael Ellis, a member of the Home Affairs Committee, stated the Lib Dems had hijacked it for political gain. Their frankly pro-drugs policy is dangerous and irresponsible, he added. Mr Cameron stated: Under this government, drug use is falling, and I think that's because we have followed an evidence-based approach. We have been focusing on education and prevention and treatment—that is the right approach to take. He described the report as interesting but added: It doesn't draw specific conclusions. I don't think anyone can read that report and say it definitely justifies this approach or that approach. Danny Shaw, BBC home affairs correspondent, noted that the divisions within the coalition could not be more sharply exposed. The official Home Office stance is that its drug strategy is effective. Norman Baker, the Liberal Democrat minister responsible for drugs, asserts that radical change is necessary. Mr Baker's claims have been fuelled by his department's own report, which finds no link between how tough a country is on drugs and how many people use them. It's an important finding, but the study also makes clear that drug policy is highly complex—approaches that may work abroad can't necessarily be implemented in the UK. The report stated it would be inappropriate to compare the success of drug policies in different countries because data collection and many other factors differ between each one. However, it said some observations can be made, and it was not clear decriminalisation has an impact on levels of drug use. Looking across different countries, there is no apparent correlation between the 'toughness' of a country's approach and the prevalence of adult drug use, it stated. Nick Barton, of charity Action on Addiction, said: Today's report once again highlights the need for addiction to be treated as a health condition, rather than a criminal justice one. He stated that imprisoning drug users was rarely a solution. Danny Kushlick, the founder of the group Transform, which has been campaigning for the legal regulation of drugs in the UK for almost 20 years, described the report as an important step. For the first time in over 40 years, the Home Office has admitted that enforcing tough drug laws doesn't necessarily reduce levels of drug use, he said. Matthew Price, Europe correspondent, BBC News, reported that back in the 1990s, Portugal was grappling with a heroin epidemic of almost epic proportions. One person in every 100 was a heroin addict. Not everyone agreed with the approach adopted to try and end the problem. In fact, many on the right wing of politics were appalled when prosecutions for people using drugs were ended. They didn't like the idea that addiction would be treated as a health issue, rather than a criminal one, and that addicts would be given treatment and healthcare to help them overcome their addiction. Those voices have been silenced now. Fifteen years later, the number of people addicted to heroin has been halved, and there have been positive results in terms of Aids infection, hepatitis infection, and the like. Back in the 1990s, we feared that Portugal could turn into a paradise for drug users, says Dr Jaoa Goulao, Portugal's national co-ordinator on drugs and drug addiction. Thanks to the policy, that didn't happen, he says. A separate Home Office report has called for a blanket ban on all brain-altering drugs in a bid to tackle legal highs. Currently, when a legal high is made illegal, manufacturers are avoiding the law by tweaking the chemical compound and creating a new substance. The government will consider legislation introduced in Ireland four years ago that bans the sale of all psychoactive substances but exempts some, such as alcohol and tobacco.

text: Vital health services in England including stop smoking, obesity and sexual health clinics are at risk, experts are warning. Earlier this year, the Chancellor revealed plans to reduce the £2.8 billion public health budget by £200 million starting in January. The funds are managed by councils and are not included in the government's pledge to safeguard the health service. However, doctors, nurses, and other senior health officials assert that the money is crucial for alleviating pressure on the broader NHS. A total of 11 organisations, including the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges, Royal College of Nursing, NHS Confederation, and Faculty of Public Health, have signed a letter to George Osborne urging him to reconsider the plans. The letter warned that cutting the funds would exacerbate ill-health and inequality within the population. It also highlighted that the argument made by NHS England chief executive Simon Stevens for additional funding before the election—requesting an extra £8 billion annually in exchange for £22 billion in efficiency savings by 2020—included achieving gains from improvements in public health. It added: We urge you to consider very seriously the position we have outlined, to reverse these cuts in your forthcoming spending review and give a clear commitment that no further cuts will be made to public health budgets in future years. The Chancellor is expected to announce his spending plans for this Parliament in November. Prof John Ashton, of the Faculty of Public Health, stated: The legacy of a decision to cut the public health grant will be major further burdens on the health service within the foreseeable future. Avoidable ill health, heart disease, sexual health problems, unplanned pregnancies—these are the kind of things which are being affected by this irrational cut to funding. The cost of being unhealthy. Read more from Nick. Follow Nick on Twitter. Rob Webster, chief executive of the NHS Confederation, concurred, stating: There is an unprecedented consensus that we can only address the problems facing the NHS if we invest in the future of our nation's health by helping people to stay well. Open any report from any director of public health in any part of the country and you can see health inequalities and poor health putting pressure on NHS services and blighting people's lives. We need the upcoming spending review to protect public health budgets. A government spokesman stated the NHS was a priority for investment—as would be demonstrated by the additional funds to be announced in the spending review. However, he added: Difficult decisions need to be made across government to reduce the deficit and ensure the sustainability of our public services.

text: In just a few years, Wonga has become one of the country's biggest, and certainly fastest growing, money lenders. Since its inception in autumn 2007, it has issued four million small, short-term loans, totalling over a billion pounds. The company has faced significant criticism, with some suggesting it is akin to a digital loan-shark, exploiting the financially vulnerable. In January, the firm was embroiled in controversy over advertisements encouraging employed students to take out loans for expenses like overseas trips. In March, supporters of certain football clubs demanded the removal of the company's adverts from their clubs' websites. This week, it drew further attention by launching a loan service for cash-strapped businesses. Errol Damelin, Wonga's founder, remains notably unfazed by the critics. At a press briefing this week, he expressed optimism about his business's prospects and the legitimacy of short-term lending. He likens Wonga to iTunes in the financial sector. Wonga is a platform for the future of financial services; the digital revolution in financial services has not yet begun, he stated. Comparing his firm to companies like Google, Amazon, PayPal, and Netflix, he argued that leveraging technology and customer data would be crucial to success. Wonga is on a multi-year and multi-decade journey to build the future of financial services, using data and technology to make objective and unbiased decisions, said Mr Damelin. Customers borrow from Wonga by applying on its website. This provides a quick decision and transfers the funds to a bank account within 15 minutes. The company employs over 100 staff to develop its technology and ensure the site functions properly. Its main feature is combining customer information in a vast in-house credit scoring operation. Errol Damelin stated that his computers use artificial-intelligence software to analyse up to 8,000 pieces of information about applicants to decide on loan offers. We have built the world's first completely straight-through processing system for credit, so when someone comes to Wonga as an individual or business owner and applies for a cash advance, the entire process is automated, he said. Thus, there is no need to dress formally and plead with a bank manager for a loan or overdraft extension, at least for short-term cashflow issues. Wonga's technology filters out applicants deemed too risky, with about 66% currently rejected for lacking creditworthiness. For example, applicants must have a regular income, a bank account, a working debit card, a mobile phone, and a good credit record. This filtering results in only about 7% of Wonga borrowers failing to repay, a lower default rate than the 10% bad debt rate on credit card lending, which has led banks to write off billions in recent years. The credit scoring process is more sophisticated than merely asking a few simple questions. The firm's technology measures how customers interact with the website, providing valuable insights. For instance, potential borrowers use online sliders to determine how much they wish to borrow and for how long. The firm has found that those who immediately push the slider to the maximum amount, currently £400 for 30 days for first-time personal loan applicants, are more likely to default. The great thing about that is our decisions are always objective; we are not subject to the same imperfections as traditional lenders, where different bank managers have varying preferences and prejudices affecting credit access, Damelin argued. What about the cost? Wonga is candid about its APR, a standard interest cost measure, which is an astonishing 4,214% annually. This is clearly stated on the front page. Borrowers are informed precisely how much they must repay and when. However, Errol Damelin said that for his target audience, price is not the issue, nor should it be. He emphasises speed, convenience, and transparency—alongside cash. We have dared to ask some hard questions, like how can we make loans instant, how can we get money to people 24/7, how can we be totally transparent? he said. So what we have built is a solution around speed and convenience, helping people by dealing with them when they want to deal with us. Wonga counters criticism by noting its users appear very satisfied. Using a customer satisfaction measure called the net-promoter score, it claims a score exceeding 90%. Essentially, most customers would recommend its services to friends and family. In contrast, most banks have negative scores, and even highly-rated banks like First Direct score below 50%. Nonetheless, the regulated money lending industry has a poor image and is under renewed scrutiny. The Office of Fair Trading (OFT) announced in February it would reassess the lending practices of many payday loan firms. Two years ago, it concluded that they and other high-cost credit businesses—like home-credit lenders and pawn brokers—should not have capped interest rates. Now, it is concerned again about poor selling practices, such as targeting loans at those who cannot afford them and allowing debts to roll over and grow. Wonga insists it is not associated with the less reputable end of the expanding payday lending market. For Errol Damelin, the current goal is to expand his business by lending to small companies facing sudden cash shortages. Financial services is a challenging place to innovate in, so we are responding where we can deliver a better service, he says. Businesses have been crying out for a solution available 24/7 to solve relatively small, short-term cashflow problems.

text: A senior Labour MP has called for its leadership contest to be paused over fears it has been infiltrated by supporters of other parties. Barry Sheerman stated that those registering to participate included members of the Socialist Workers Party, the Green Party, the Conservatives, and UKIP. Labour dismisses claims of hard left and Conservative supporters enrolling to support left-winger Jeremy Corbyn. A Labour spokeswoman also dismissed calls to suspend the leadership contest. She stated there was a very robust system in place to prevent fraudulent and malicious applications, with additional checks being conducted to ensure the rules are upheld. An exclusion list is being compiled of those who have previously stood against Labour or assisted others in opposing the party. The BBC understands that up to 1,000 applications have been rejected. One of Mr Corbyn's supporters labelled Mr Sheerman's suggestion as ridiculous. Backbench MP Diane Abbott stated it was coming from individuals who think their side will lose. She added: This election is being conducted under rules agreed by the entire party last year. Under the new rules, introduced by former leader Ed Miliband, individuals can register as supporters for £3 and participate in the vote. They are required to confirm they support the aims and values of the Labour Party. The popularity of Mr Corbyn's campaign has prompted warnings from other candidates, Andy Burnham, Yvette Cooper, and Liz Kendall, about the party shifting to the left. Mr Sheerman's remarks follow similar sentiments from two backbench MPs, Graham Stringer and John Mann, who called for the leadership contest to be halted. The Huddersfield MP and former select committee chairman, first elected in 1979, told the BBC there were large numbers of people joining Labour to vote for the new leader and some of their reasons were malign. Labour MPs were dumbfounded when they learned how the contest was to be conducted, and the process was now in real trouble, he stated. At-a-glance profiles of the four contenders. Labour's acting leader Harriet Harman has emailed the party's MPs with a list of new members in their constituencies, asking them to identify any suspicious names. Mr Sheerman stated that although he might be able to identify some usual suspects, many others would remain undetected. He denied his concerns were motivated by his support for Liz Kendall, stating he had previously fought against entryism and believed the current process was flawed. Labour states the verification process is ongoing, and ballot papers have not yet been distributed. Labour recently rejected an application from Conservative MP Tim Loughton, who claimed he attempted to become a registered supporter to highlight flaws in the system. Speaking on BBC Radio 4's The World at One, Ms Kendall said it was great that more people were signing up to Labour and stated she had not seen anything that concerned her. The important thing is that the checks are put in place, she added. The Trade Unionist and Socialist Coalition, which stood in 135 constituencies in May's general election and includes the Socialist Workers Party, stated reports of infiltration were due to Blairite manoeuvres against the Corbyn campaign. It stated one of its members, former councillor Chris Flood, had been wrongly named in a report in The Times as having signed up. Labour's former communications director, Alastair Campbell, stated the party could be finished if Mr Corbyn wins. On his blog, he warned of a car crash scenario and urged supporters to back anyone but Corbyn, warning it would not be easy to replace him if he won and Labour was struggling in the polls.

text: Chelsea moved six points clear at the top of the Premier League as Cesc Fabregas' first-half goal beat a stubborn Sunderland at the Stadium of Light. Fabregas directed the ball into the far corner from the edge of the box as the Blues secured a 10th consecutive league win. Sunderland goalkeeper Jordan Pickford made saves from former Black Cat Marcos Alonso and Willian to prevent Chelsea from achieving a larger victory. The hosts, who aimed to neutralise their opponents' attacking prowess, had limited opportunities, although they nearly secured a point in injury time, but Thibaut Courtois brilliantly denied Patrick van Aanholt. It was a crucial and hard-earned victory for Chelsea after Arsenal faltered against Everton on Tuesday, ensuring Antonio Conte's team will lead the table at Christmas. A significant factor in Chelsea's recent winning streak has been consistency, with Conte naming an unchanged side in eight of the nine matches before the trip to Sunderland. Liverpool manager Jurgen Klopp had recently suggested that Chelsea's successful run might stumble if either Eden Hazard or Diego Costa sustained an injury, and Wednesday's match offered a chance to test this theory. Hazard did not travel after sustaining a knock in Chelsea's 1-0 victory over West Brom at the weekend, so he was replaced by Willian. Conte also opted to rest Nemanja Matic, allowing Fabregas to make his first start since 3 December. Initially, Chelsea seemed to miss Hazard's creativity as they struggled to penetrate a crowded Sunderland defence, but Fabregas demonstrated the Blues' depth of talent. As Sunderland's seven-man defence frustrated the visitors, Fabregas managed to find a gap to slot a shot into the far corner, ultimately securing Chelsea's victory. Media playback is not supported on this device. Chelsea have maintained a clean sheet in five of their last seven matches, but their failure to put the game beyond Sunderland's reach was a concern for Conte. For the third time in four matches, they won by a single goal margin, and Conte is eager to see his team improve their finishing. When you have the chance to kill the game, you must kill the game, he stated. We had this chance but did not take it, and in the end, Courtois made a good save. I hope we can improve in the future. Three points for Sunderland would have lifted them off the bottom of the table, but facing the league's in-form side was always going to be a challenging task. While their own chances were scarce, the hosts displayed plenty of spirit and determination, and Diego Costa, the joint-top scorer in the Premier League, was largely subdued by a well-organised and disciplined defence. On the occasions Chelsea did manage to breach the Sunderland back line, Pickford once again demonstrated why he is one of the most promising young English goalkeepers. There is still a long way to go, but three wins from their last six matches, along with an encouraging performance against the league leaders, suggest they have every chance of clawing their way to safety. We don't have the quality of Chelsea, but we did a really good job. I thought we would get a goal, but Courtois made two great saves, and it would have been a really good point. Both teams do not have long to wait for their next match, as Sunderland host Watford at the Stadium of Light (15:00 GMT) on Saturday, while Chelsea return to London to face Crystal Palace on the same day (12:30). The mixed martial arts fighter from Craigneuk is set to face Brazilian Luis Henrique Da Silva at the 18,000-capacity Golden 1 Center in Sacramento, becoming only the fourth Scot to advance to the UFC. The 29-year-old has secured a four-fight contract with what he refers to as the Champions League of MMA, a significant departure from his days at Tynecastle. It is a platform he never aimed for until he realised he was making opponents cry. The truth was I wasn't good enough, Craig remarked about his attempts to pursue a football career. I knew that myself, so I transitioned into coaching football. I was competent, it was enjoyable, but I truly missed the competitive aspect, the sense of competition. I began experimenting with martial arts and discovered I excelled at it. It was never a case of 'I'm going to be in the UFC one day.' I travelled extensively across Britain, competing in various jiu-jitsu events. My coach mentioned 'there's an opportunity, do you fancy it?' and it was for a show in Sunderland. I distinctly remember the opponent was Gary Sivills, a top contender in that region. He had an impressive record and aimed to fight for a British title, using me as a mere stepping stone. He was expected to defeat me easily. I faced no pressure, entering as the underdog. I took four or five friends with me, and I defeated him in approximately a minute and 37 seconds. I spoke to him afterwards, and he was in tears, which puzzled me. It wasn't until I defeated Karl Moore as a professional in my first BAMMA (British Association of Mixed Martial Arts) fight. He was considered the next big prospect, and it lasted two rounds. I recall the same reaction, him crying. I reflected on all the opponents I've faced, all striving to reach this point. All these fighters aim for the UFC, and I've halted them. I understand the pressure they faced. By day, Craig teaches with Skillforce, an educational charity that aids pupils in engaging with school and maximising their potential. Now, with eight wins from eight fights, all within the distance, he has caught the attention of the UFC and is poised to compete on the same stage that elevated Irishman Conor McGregor to global stardom. Craig will not have an easy introduction to the UFC against the kickboxing prowess of Da Silva, but after sparring with Scottish boxers Stephen Simmons and Jay McFarlane, Craig is confident he can end the Brazilian's 12-fight unbeaten streak. The UFC is the pinnacle; everyone aspires to fight there, Craig told BBC Scotland. It's going to be a challenging opponent, and I wanted that. I wanted to demonstrate that I deserve to be in the UFC and to fight a top 20 opponent. As you can imagine, as an MMA fighter entering a boxing gym, I'm always the underdog, but I'm holding my own. I'm sparring with the best professional fighters in Scotland. It's advancing me because the stand-up was my weakness, and I now believe it's my strongest aspect. I believe I can knock him out in the first round. If not the first, certainly in the second round, and it will be over. I'm often seen as the submission fighter, but this is my opportunity to showcase my stand-up skills, and since he's a stand-up fighter, it will be an exciting match.

text: The UN special envoy for Syria, Staffan de Mistura, says he is appalled and shocked that rebels in Aleppo are targeting civilians in the city. The relentless and indiscriminate rocket attacks have resulted in the deaths of numerous civilians in western Aleppo over the past 48 hours, Mr de Mistura stated. He indicated that such attacks could constitute war crimes. On Friday, rebels launched an offensive to break the government siege of eastern Aleppo. Approximately 275,000 individuals have been besieged in the eastern part of the city for months. Russian and Syrian government aircraft commenced bombarding Aleppo in September. Over 2,700 people are reported to have been killed and injured since that time. Russia halted its air campaign on 18 October to permit the evacuation of sick and wounded individuals, but few have responded to the call to leave. On Sunday, Syrian state media reported that rebels had used chemical weapons against government-controlled districts of Aleppo. A spokesman for a rebel group refuted the claim, asserting that rebel groups did not possess such weapons, according to the Associated Press news agency. Sana news agency reported that 35 individuals in the districts of Dahiyet al-Assad and Hamdaniya experienced shortness of breath and numbness. More than 40 civilians are reported to have been killed in western Aleppo since the rebel attacks commenced, according to activists. The UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported that 16 of them were children. It also stated that 55 soldiers and 64 rebels had died. There is no confirmation of these casualties. Rebels from outside Aleppo are reported to be leading the new offensive, targeting Hamdaniya, which is currently held by troops loyal to Syrian President Bashar al-Assad. The rebel groups include Jabhat Fateh al-Sham, formerly the al-Qaeda-linked Nusra Front, along with fellow Islamists Ahrar al-Sham. This is the rebels' second attempt to break the Aleppo siege. In August, they temporarily opened a corridor between the east and west after the government completely encircled them for the first time in July. The city, once Syria's economic hub, has been divided between the two factions since 2012.
