text: Undercover journalist Mazher Mahmood plotted to change a witness statement in a case against pop singer Tulisa Contostavlos, the Old Bailey has heard. The journalist known as the Fake Sheikh and his driver Alan Smith both deny conspiring to pervert the course of justice. Miss Contostavlos had been accused of supplying cocaine, but the case against her collapsed in 2014. Prosecutors stated Mr Mahmood had a vested interest in her prosecution. The court was informed that Miss Contostavlos had been targeted by the self-proclaimed king of the sting, who posed as a film producer seeking the singer for a Hollywood film. The singer allegedly arranged for Mr Mahmood to purchase half an ounce of cocaine from one of her contacts for £800. The former N-Dubz star and X Factor judge was subsequently arrested and charged with involvement in the supply of a class A drug, after Mr Mahmood provided evidence to police. Mr Mahmood, 53, of Purley, south London, and Mr Smith, 67, from Dereham, Norfolk, are accused of arranging to alter a written statement Mr Smith had made to police because it was favourable to Miss Contostavlos's defence. Opening the trial against Mr Mahmood and Mr Smith, Sarah Forshaw QC informed the jury: In effect, the hearing in June 2014 put Mr Mahmood and his journalistic process on trial. He liked to call himself the king of sting, he boasted in a book he had written of the number of convictions that he personally was responsible for. He knew that if it could be shown that he had acted improperly as an agent provocateur, inducing Miss Contostavlos to do something she would not otherwise do, his own credibility and standing and the prospect of conviction in the case might both be severely damaged. Miss Forshaw added: Miss Contostavlos had expressed her disapproval of hard drugs to his own driver, that was the part of the statement that was altered. Mr Smith had told the police officer making the statement that he remembered that while driving Miss Contostavlos... that she had spoken about someone in her family being dependent on cocaine. Mr Smith had informed a police officer she seemed very negative about cocaine but, a day later, he told police he wished to retract that part of his statement, the court heard. It is alleged that in the intervening 24 hours Mr Smith had sent a copy of his interview to Mr Mahmood and they had exchanged several texts and calls. During a pre-trial hearing at Southwark Crown Court in June 2014, Mr Mahmood stated on oath that he had not spoken to Mr Smith about Miss Contostavlos's comments. He deliberately misled the court - not only had he discussed it but he had been sent a copy of the statement, Miss Forshaw said. When later giving evidence to the jury in the case, Mr Mahmood admitted he had seen a copy of Mr Smith's statement and Miss Contostavlos's trial subsequently collapsed, she added. Miss Forshaw told the jury: There is no doubt that Smith did change his statement... The change would undoubtedly have disadvantaged Miss Contostavlos's case. It would have deprived her of supporting evidence from Mahmood's own right-hand man that she made an anti-drugs comment at a time when untainted by any influence or pressure. She said the evidence in the case was overwhelming, adding: Mr Mahmood may be the master of subterfuge and deception. But on this occasion it is he, together with his employee, who are exposed. The jury also heard Miss Contostavlos describe how she was tricked by Mr Mahmood after meeting him at the Metropolitan Hotel in Park Lane, London, in May 2013. In a statement read to the court, she said she could not fully remember the events because she was drunk. Miss Contostavlos said Mr Smith had later driven her home and she had talked about an unnamed family member with a hard drug problem. Mr Mahmood and Mr Smith are charged with conspiring together to do an act, namely that Mr Smith would change a draft statement to police, with the intention to pervert the course of justice, between 22 June and 22 July 2014. Both deny the charges. The trial continues.

text: Bydd y rhestrau diweddara' o gategorïau ysgolion yng Nghymru yn cael eu cyhoeddi yn ddiweddarach heddiw. Share this on Email Facebook Messenger Messenger Twitter Copy this link These are external links and open in a new window Every school is placed in a colour category ranging from green, to yellow, orange, and red. This is the third year this grading system for schools has been used. Last year, 333 primary and secondary schools succeeded in reaching the top category, the green category—an increase of 41% from the previous year. The number of schools in the red category, those needing the most improvement, decreased from 81 to 58. The Welsh Government believes the categorisation system helps identify schools that require the most assistance and offers them support and advice. The 2016 results will be published on the My Local School website. The latest figures come a week after the inspection body Estyn released its annual report. The report stated that seven out of every ten primary schools are good or better, but this figure drops to four out of ten for secondary schools. Teachers' unions have generally given cautious approval to the system, provided it is used as part of a broader school evaluation framework. Rob Williams of the headteachers' union NAHT Cymru said: We still believe for the categorisation system to work best, it needs to be part of a broader system coordinated to improve schools. As Estyn highlighted in their recent report, performance variation still exists across Wales, and the additional focus on schools in the orange and red categories does not hide the funding disparity that exists between schools. We know the Welsh Government is listening to school leaders and their concerns about a system that uses such data in isolation, without recognising the progress individual pupils make while at school. The National School Categorisation System has been agreed jointly between the education authorities and the Welsh Government with the premise that the system's purpose is not to label or create bare league tables.

text: Nurses and midwives who complete their training in hospitals outside Europe will now face shorter tests to check they are fit to work in the UK. The Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) states its plans include a computer-based examination and tests in simulated clinical scenarios. The regulator indicates these will replace the current requirement of a minimum three months of supervised practice. However, nurse leaders caution they require more details to confirm the adequacy of the checks. Presently, nurses and midwives trained overseas constitute about 10% of the workforce registered to work in the UK. Approximately 1,000 nurses annually arrive to work in the UK from outside the European Economic Area, primarily from Australia, India, or the Philippines. The NMC asserts one reason for changing assessments is that the existing supervised placements, lasting between three months and one year, are insufficiently rapid to meet demand. The regulator claims the system is not agile enough for employers who need to recruit quickly. Experts report applicants have encountered difficulties securing places on the programme, as they are limited. The new tests, scheduled to commence in the autumn, comprise two parts. According to the NMC, similar checks have already been adopted by other healthcare regulators. The regulator states: This will ensure the hundreds of nurses and midwives who trained overseas and wish to practise in the UK are assessed in a proportionate and robust way, in order to protect the public. Jackie Smith, the NMC chief executive, remarked: The new system will not replace the need for employers to ensure that the staff they recruit display the behaviours, skills and knowledge necessary for the specific role to which they are recruited, and provide further support and development as required. Janet Davies, executive director of nursing at the Royal College of Nursing, commented: Healthcare in the UK relies on the hard work and dedication of many nurses who trained overseas. These proposals may well form part of a more robust and consistent mechanism for ensuring that nurses who work in the UK are equipped to practise in the UK. However, we need to know more about how nurses will be evaluated as part of this system before we can judge whether or not the system is adequate. Whether nurses come from the EU or the rest of the world, it is vital that employers are recruiting them for the right reasons and supporting them when they get there. Too often, nurses are recruited from overseas to fill short-term gaps and given inadequate support to care for patients well. Official figures suggest some 67,000 nurses and midwives who completed training outside Europe currently hold NMC registration. This adds to the current workforce of more than 600,000 nursing and midwifery staff who have trained within Europe and gained registration with the UK regulator.

text: Norwich City had to come from behind to beat League Two side Swindon Town in the opening round of the EFL Cup. text: Plans to help nearly 100,000 small businesses due to be hit by changes to rates next month are being considered by Communities Secretary Sajid Javid. Out of those, approximately 25,000 firms face a cliff edge under the new business rates revaluation, according to ratings agency CVS. It presented several proposals to Mr Javid during a meeting on Wednesday. The Treasury is attempting to devise additional support for small firms following an outcry from businesses. Ministers have stated that the revaluation—the first since 2010—will result in three-quarters of firms seeing their rates remain unchanged or decrease. However, Mr Javid and Chancellor Philip Hammond have faced pressure to assist businesses experiencing significant increases in areas where rental values have risen sharply. Critics argue the situation favours large retailers and online firms over high street shops. CVS held discussions with Mr Javid on Wednesday, and the firm proposed a package worth up to £150m. The government is anticipated to take action to mitigate the revaluation's impact in next week's Budget. CVS chief Mark Rigby stated: The Secretary of State was clearly in listening mode and it was evident to me that he was acutely aware of the potential impact that the revaluation will bring to some communities and the anger felt by small businesses, particularly the retail and leisure sectors. He was clear in his determination to find a meaningful, targeted solution to ease the financial burden for those most in need ahead of the April tax changes. Theresa May indicated at Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday that Mr Hammond would address the situation in the Budget. She said Mr Hammond and Mr Javid had been asked to make sure that the support that is provided is appropriate and is in place for the hardest cases, adding she would expect... the Chancellor to say more about this next week in the Budget. The government has already implemented a system of transitional relief, worth £3.6bn, to phase in the rises over five years. Additional potential mitigation measures could include introducing a package similar to the retail relief scheme, which was worth £1,500 to firms when it ended in April last year, and the threshold for tapered relief could also be raised.

text: The publisher of GQ magazine has been found guilty of contempt of court over its coverage of the News of the World (NoW) phone-hacking trial. GQ had created a substantial risk that the trial of Rebekah Brooks, Andy Coulson, and others would be seriously impeded or prejudiced, the High Court ruled. The court heard that a GQ article, published by Conde Nast Publications Ltd, could have suggested to jurors that the owners of NoW directed or knew about hacking. Mrs Brooks was acquitted of all charges. Mr Coulson was found guilty of conspiracy to hack phones and was sentenced to 18 months in prison. Lord Thomas, the Lord Chief Justice, stated that a future hearing would determine the penalty for Conde Nast. The GQ article, authored by Michael Wolff, was published in the men's magazine in April 2014, during the Old Bailey trial, which had been ongoing for more than three months. The case against Conde Nast was initiated by the Attorney General, represented by Andrew Caldecott QC. The thrust of the piece was that [Rupert] Murdoch, proprietor of News International, was, or probably was, implicated in voicemail interception and that he should have been prosecuted and in his absence the trial had an air of unreality about it, Mr Caldecott informed the court at a hearing in July. He stated that such suggestions had not been made by the prosecution in court. He also claimed the article implied defence lawyers had a hidden agenda of protecting Mr Murdoch's interests and concealing his involvement. Adrienne Page QC, representing Conde Nast, argued the article was a highly subjective, personal and impressionistic sketch based upon the experience of visiting the trial courtroom. However, Lord Thomas, sitting with Mrs Justice Nicola Davies, ruled that the article was seriously prejudicial. Following the ruling, Attorney General Jeremy Wright QC remarked: While it is rare to bring proceedings against publishers, the GQ article went against the most fundamental principle of our criminal justice system; namely that everyone is entitled to a fair trial and it is not for the press to decide who is deserving of this protection.

text: A major children's musical drama is being made in Northern Ireland by the Disney Channel. The 10-part series is titled The Lodge and will be broadcast on the channel in September. Nearly 100 cast and crew members are employed on the show, which is being filmed at locations in County Down. David Levine, the Disney Channel's head for the UK and Ireland, stated it was the first time a production of this scale had been brought to Northern Ireland. So far Northern Ireland's been mostly known for swords and dragons - Disney Channel is bringing songs and dancing, he remarked. We're investing quite a bit, and you have production, post-production, builders, sets, and filming in multiple locations here. Most of the filming is occurring at Montalto Lodge just outside Ballynahinch, but scenes are also being shot in Castlewellan and Tollymore Forest near Newcastle. The Lodge features a cast of 22 and 67 crew members, of whom 46 are from Northern Ireland, including local producer Raymond Lau. The series narrates the story of a 15-year-old girl named Skye who, along with her father, swaps city life to manage the family's country lodge. Skye discovers her father is planning to sell the business, so she has the summer to persuade him to change his mind. Sophie Simnett, who most recently appeared in the BBC series Dickensian, portrays Skye. There are a lot of sub-plots, all of which involve a lot of activity, she stated. So as well as the singing and dancing, I had to learn to rock climb as there is one scene where I go on a date and go rock-climbing. We also had to learn how to kayak as there is a scene where the whole group goes kayaking. Thomas Doherty, who has appeared in the TV series Dracula and the film Hercules, plays Sean. He is fun-loving, he's very sporty, and he has a love interest in Skye, he commented. I originally trained to do musical theatre, so it was amazing to get this. We've had choreography, we've had singing coaches, so we've had the best training and it's good fun. The Lodge will complete filming before the summer and will be shown first on the Disney Channel in the UK and the Republic of Ireland. It is then expected to be screened on the channel elsewhere in Europe.

text: On a small yet busy lane in central Bangalore is a three-storey white house with a bright orange gate. These are external links and will open in a new window. You might not notice the property as you walk past, but some of India's future leading companies may be conceived inside. The southern Indian city of Bangalore is India's start-up capital. Entrepreneurs from across the nation, and indeed some from around the globe, converge on the city—which is also the hub of India's computer industry—seeking ideas, investors, and office space. They also require accommodation, but when you immerse yourself in entrepreneurship 24 hours a day, returning to a mundane hotel room or dormitory at day's end is not appealing. This is where the white house with its orange gate has come to the rescue. Opening its doors in May this year, it claims to be India's first start-up hostel. Providing a home-from-home for aspiring entrepreneurs, the 20-bed property—the Construkt Start-up Hostel—enables them to live with like-minded individuals and exchange business ideas day and night. More than half of the bunk beds in the hostel are occupied during my visit. Besides a kitchen and a laundry machine, it offers those most essential services for aspiring entrepreneurs—wi-fi and a coffee-maker. One of the ground floor walls has been transformed into a blackboard. On it, a calendar grid is drawn in chalk, listing all the start-up and technology events in the city for the coming month. Among them is a boot camp for start-ups, where they can pitch to potential investors, and a conference on data analysis. The founders of Construkt say this exemplifies how they assist residents in connecting with the city's broader start-up ecosystem. Most of the hostel's occupants are men and women who have come to Bangalore to identify the company they wish to establish. Others know what business they want to start but are in the city assessing the market. Construkt resident Krishna Elakara is working on creating a fitness training product. The 42-year-old is of Indian origin but has lived abroad all his life, most recently in Australia. On the first floor of the hostel, in a cheerful small room serving as a mini-library, he explains why he has come to Bangalore. All the elements you need to put together a start-up, they're here, he says. I'm staying at this hostel because I want to build my network in the city. Other hostels or hotels usually have tourists, whereas here you meet people with a similar mindset. Downstairs in the semi-circular living room, an open hack session is about to commence. The hostel residents gather, and some entrepreneurs share their business ideas with the group. Krishna is the first to present. What's unique about your idea? and Who would you partner with? are some of the questions posed to him. Shashikiran Rao, 36, one of the hostel's founders, says with a smile: We take the idea and tear it apart, allowing everyone to jump in and critique it. We're very good at it. The idea is to help entrepreneurs develop their plans. Aashna Kaur is the next presenter at the session. The 24-year-old holds a degree in business administration and has been consulting with start-ups for over a year. But now she wants to establish her own company and is considering two ideas—technology that assists solo female travellers, or products encouraging more Indian women to join the workforce. Aashna has been at Construkt for over a week. At approximately $14 (£10.70) a night and $220 a month, I ask if low cost is why she chose to stay there. She says she could find a cheap hotel at the same rate, or perhaps even lower, but it is the networking opportunities that drew her to the hostel. Currently, apart from aspiring entrepreneurs, Construkt is also attracting individuals still exploring their career options. Prerna Gautam is still in university but has relocated from Mumbai to Bangalore for the summer to work as an intern at Microsoft Accelerator, a branch of the tech giant that assists entrepreneurs in bridging the gap from idea to execution. She is yet unsure of what she wants to do upon completing her degree, but says her time in Bangalore is drawing her towards a start-up life. text: Scottish rugby suffered two body blows this week and, rather like boxer Ricky Burns who drew with his opponent after getting one heck of a hiding from opponent Raymundo Beltran, it's a little battered, a little broken and in need of time off the canvas. It is difficult to determine which revelation was more unexpected: the first positive steroids test in Scottish rugby history or the criticism that many Scottish, Welsh, and Irish teams qualify for the Heineken Cup from a league without relegation. However, let us focus on the issue of using steroids to gain an advantage in rugby and leave the Heineken Cup discussion for another occasion. Sam Chalmers, son of esteemed player Craig Chalmers, publicly apologised, stating he obtained the substances online. This explanation resembles the convenient lone wolf theory. Was he the only player involved? Did he discuss it with others? Coaches in age-group rugby report that weight training and supplements are increasingly linked. I accept that players feel pressured to increase their size and weight. The rugby field has remained the same size for 150 years, while players have evolved. Rugby now emphasises power over agility. However, I do not accept that players are pressured to purchase steroids. It is cheating. Buying them constitutes cheating, as it is prohibited. Players hope to evade detection by drug testers. Some may have considered steroids but refrained. If you lack the size, choose another career. Rugby no longer accommodates all body types. Coaches in age-group rugby report that weight training and supplements are increasingly linked. Young players consume supplements before, during, and after gym sessions. Perhaps they are led to believe food alone is insufficient. Possibly, this leads to the belief that artificial aids are beneficial, with steroids being the ultimate illegal option. Is it possible to achieve the desired size through diet alone? The IRB's latest drug test figures are available online. It states: The IRB conducted 1,542 tests both in and out of competition in 2012, across all IRB tournaments and events, including the HSBC Sevens World Series, Rugby World Cup 2015 qualifiers, men's and women's Tests and Age Grade Rugby. The programme recorded 21 anti-doping rule violations, equating to 1.36% of the IRB's entire programme. This suggests about 1.4% of elite players use drugs and attempt to evade detection. Some, as indicated on the website, were caught using stanozolol, the steroid linked to both Sam Chalmers and disgraced Canadian sprinter Ben Johnson. The 2011 World Anti-Doping Agency figures, also on the IRB website, reveal 5,553 global rugby drug tests in 2011, with 61 violations—just over 1%. I suspect more players take risks at lower league levels or while trying to enter the system, but I am uncertain. During my coverage of the 1995 Rugby World Cup in South Africa, I reported that the most significant increase in GP requests in Cape Town nearly 20 years ago was from schoolboys seeking steroid prescriptions, often accompanied by parents. Could this occur here? Sam Chalmers belongs to the most vulnerable group: young men aspiring to professional or top-level rugby. It will be challenging for him. Life is not easy. It was not easy for those involved in the Bloodgate scandal, eye-gouging allegations, or the 60-plus rugby players caught by the IRB for drug use or sample tampering. This is a test. He serves his penalty and then returns to the sport. I leave you with this thought: I wager he was not alone. And I suspect there are younger players than Sam Chalmers who remain undetected. text: Donald Trump's plan to erect a huge sea wall at his Irish golf course has been withdrawn in the light of stiff opposition. The initial application identified rising sea levels due to climate change as a principal reason for the protective barrier. However, environmental campaigners opposed the two-mile-long development, claiming it endangered a rare species of snail. A revised plan featuring a smaller wall is anticipated to be submitted soon. The Trump International hotel and golf links at Doonbeg on the west coast of County Clare was purchased in 2014. Storms that year caused significant erosion of sand dunes at the course, prompting the Trump organisation to submit plans to Clare County Council to construct a two-mile (2.8km) limestone wall to mitigate the impact of the seas. Standing 4m high and 20m wide, the 200,000-tonne structure would have required approximately 200,000 tonnes of rock for its construction. The €10m wall was intended to protect against the erosive impacts of the seas, according to the original application. The documents further explained that the rising sea levels and increased storm frequency and wave energy associated with global warming can increase the rate of erosion. The wall would also benefit the community, the documents stated, through coastal protection works. While many local residents and businesses strongly supported the plan, there was significant opposition from environmental groups. Concerns were raised that the wall would affect the tiny, EU-protected whorl snail, Vertigo angustior. Six months ago, the local authority requested further information from the Trump group on how the structure would impact the Carrowmore dunes special area of conservation, but none was provided. We received notification from the applicant yesterday that they were withdrawing their application, a council spokesman informed BBC News. The Trump group indicated they had withdrawn their plans because the planning process would have taken excessively long. In a statement, they mentioned that the resort contributed approximately €6m annually to the local economy. Plans to expand the facilities are being closely considered, but protection from the relentless sea is necessary. The realisation of these plans, however, is fundamentally dependent on the provision of adequate protection from coastal erosion, the statement read. Since 2002, an estimated 15m to 20m of dune face has been eroded from the beach front and the golf course. All efforts at soft management of the coastline have failed. All efforts to readjust the course have also been expended. In a statement, the group announced plans for a scaled-down version of the wall, which would extend to 900 metres in two sections, incorporating metal sheet piles inserted into the ground on the golf course with limestone boulders placed around them. Some campaigners believe that the international attention on Donald Trump's promise to build a wall on the southern border of the US did not aid the plans for Doonbeg. You could tell that they were upset, because there were already analogies being made with the Mexican wall, said Tony Lowes from Friends of the Irish Environment, who met with the Trump camp. You could tell that they didn't like that because they could sense that this could turn into something more than a little planning battle in Ireland. Approximately 100,000 people from around the world signed a petition organised by the surfing group, Save the Waves, to oppose the original plans. Campaigners believe that the criticism the President-elect has faced regarding his perceived antipathy towards the environment and climate change did not significantly influence the opposition. In this case, I think the absurdity of the proposal, the outrage at what was about to be inflicted was so great, that no one could look at the proposal without being shocked, said Tony Lowes. I have very rarely seen an environmental case that looked so absolutely horrific. It is expected that the new proposal will be submitted before Christmas and could be decided by March next year. Analysts will be examining the new documents to determine if there are any further references to climate change and the impact of rising seas. Follow Matt on Twitter and on Facebook.

text: A new loan scheme is to be offered to Scottish farmers to prevent a repeat of the problems caused by delays to Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) payments. Rural Affairs Secretary Fergus Ewing announced that the IT system largely responsible for the delays was not there yet. Mr Ewing stated that next year's payments were therefore not-risk free. However, he mentioned that farmers and crofters would be able to apply for a loan worth 80% of their total entitlement. Farming union NFU Scotland welcomed the new scheme, stating it would provide clarity and certainty to farmers. Opposition parties claimed the scheme was an admission that issues with the CAP payment system might not yet be resolved. The CAP Futures programme in Scotland was intended to make the rural payment process more efficient. However, problems with a new Scottish government IT system caused delays for many farmers receiving the money. In May, public spending watchdog Audit Scotland reported that the lengthy delays had a significant impact on farmers, many of whom were already facing financial difficulties due to low milk prices and severe flooding. Mr Ewing informed MSPs at Holyrood that 17,744 out of 18,479 eligible businesses had now received their 2015 payments, with the majority of outstanding cases expected to be paid by the 15 October deadline. He also anticipated that the next round of payments for 2016 would be substantially completed by the deadline at the end of June next year. However, Mr Ewing stated that the new loan scheme would provide certainty for farmers and crofters over the winter and aimed to inject up to £300m into the rural economy, safeguarding jobs and local agricultural businesses. He told MSPs: Having learned lessons from the 2015 round of CAP payments, I am determined to provide as much certainty as we can, not just for farmers and crofters, but for the wider economy in our rural communities. I am therefore announcing today that farmers will not have to wait until 2017 to receive payment of their CAP entitlement. Letters will be issued before the end of the month to farmers inviting them to apply. Everyone who applies by the deadline of 12 October will receive a loan of 80% of their entitlement in November. Responding to the announcement, NFU Scotland president Allan Bowie said it would have a positive impact on the entire rural economy. Mr Bowie added: Knowing that up to 80% of your support package will be delivered in early November gives clarity and certainty to farm businesses. The bitter legacy of the flawed 2015 payment run continues and the cabinet secretary again apologised for the problems, some of which still remain. On behalf of our members, we will continue to keep pressure on the Scottish government until all outstanding payments for 2015 have been delivered. However, Peter Chapman, the Scottish Conservative rural affairs spokesman, said the loan scheme was effectively an admission by Mr Ewing that issues with the computer system had still not been resolved. Mr Chapman added: He can't deliver 100% payments in December as we should expect - instead he has to offer an 80% loan for November. These loans are an admission of failure. This is not good enough and it certainly won't win the trust of the farming community which has long run out of patience with the SNP on this issue. Mr Ewing should finally agree that we need a parliamentary inquiry into this issue. Mike Rumbles of the Scottish Liberal Democrats said Mr Ewing's claim that the loan scheme was injecting £300m into the rural economy was complete nonsense because farmers should already be receiving full payment anyway if the new system was working properly. He added: The statement today was a dreadful admission of the failure of the Scottish government. His 80% loan plan will be offered to all applicants but this still means that the average farm business will be over £6,000 out of pocket goodness knows how long.

text: European banking stocks have fallen sharply despite the victory of the pro-bailout New Democracy party in Greece's elections on Sunday. While the outcome raised hopes that Greece would adhere to austerity measures and remain in the euro, analysts indicated that considerable uncertainty persisted. The decline in bank shares was observed across Europe, with Germany's Commerzbank and France's BNP Paribas both down 4.4%. Spanish bond yields remained volatile, surpassing the 7% danger threshold. Broader share indexes were mixed. France's Cac 40 closed down 0.7%, while Germany's Dax was 0.3% higher, having both risen 1% earlier. London's FTSE 100 closed up 0.3% after an early decline, while in New York, the Dow Jones closed down 0.2%. Among other banking shares, Deutsche Bank fell 1.1%, while Credit Agricole dropped 3.4%. In the UK, Royal Bank of Scotland fell 5.0% and Lloyds Banking Group declined 3.6%, marking them as the biggest fallers on the FTSE 100. The interest rate on Spanish government bonds - the eurozone country considered most at risk of requiring a full international bailout in the future - reached another new high. The yield on Spain's 10-year bonds initially fell to 6.767% before rising to 7.144%. Italy's 10-year bond yield also increased, reaching 6.08%, after earlier falling to 5.85%. The main share indexes of Spain and Italy also declined. By Robert Peston Business editor Read Robert's blog in full Spain's Ibex closed down 3.0%, while Italy's FTSE MIB lost 2.9%. In the currency markets, the euro was slightly lower against the dollar, at $1.2579 from $1.2637 late on Friday. Asian shares had earlier posted strong gains, with Japan's Nikkei 225 index and South Korea's Kospi both closing up 1.8%, while Australia's ASX 200 added 1.9%. Antonis Samaras, leader of the New Democracy party, stated on Sunday that the Greek people voted today to stay on the European course and remain in the eurozone. There will be no more adventures. Greece's place in Europe will not be put in doubt. Adrian Slack, head of equities at Bastion Capital, remarked that the initial reaction to the Greek election result was too euphoric. He added: Fundamentally, the problems [in Greece and the eurozone] haven't changed. Peter Schiff, of the brokerage Euro Pacific Capital, added: How long is it going to take for people to worry about Spain again? Spain's borrowing costs have been reaching euro-era record levels, indicating that lenders were concerned about Madrid's ability to repay its debts. Last week, the ratings agency Moody's downgraded Spain's credit rating to one notch above junk. Yet other analysts were more optimistic. Masayuki Doshida, a senior market analyst at Rakuten Securities, said the victory of Greece's New Democracy party had allayed eurozone fears for now. There'll be a definite sense of relief spreading around today, said Masayuki Doshida, she said. Fellow analyst, David Lennox of Fat Prophets, told the BBC that the worst of the Greek crisis could now be over. We think that early punters are already taking the view that a floor has been put under the crisis for now, he said. The elections in Greece were being closely monitored, not just by eurozone leaders but also by investors worldwide. Greece, which is suffering from a sovereign debt crisis, has received two bailouts in the past two years. It was granted an initial package worth 110bn euros (£89bn; $138bn) in 2010, followed by another agreed last year worth 130bn euros. However, the EU and IMF have attached stringent austerity measures, including state spending cuts, as pre-conditions to those packages. There have been various demonstrations against these cuts in Greece, and the Syriza party had stated it would renegotiate the conditions if it came to power. This led to fears that if eurozone leaders and Athens did not agree on the existing terms, Greece might be forced to leave the eurozone. There were concerns that such a move might spread contagion to other eurozone countries and result in turmoil in the global economy. However, the BBC's business editor, Robert Peston, said the new Greek government still faced a significant challenge. He said that bankers had told him Greece needed eurozone governments and the European Central Bank to write off a big slug of what they are owed.

text: Researchers attempting to learn why people snack are to study the health and habits of more than 100 Scots. These are external links and will open in a new window. It is part of a Scottish government initiative to address the obesity issue. The team at Aberdeen's Rowett Institute of Nutrition and Health aims to recruit 120 volunteers who will be monitored over the span of a week. Researchers will document their heart rates, activity levels, and snacking habits using heart sensors, GPS devices, and an electronic diary. The scientists aim to identify a connection between so-called executive functions in the brain and snacking. Dr David McMinn, from the institute, who is leading the study, stated: We live in an environment where snack foods are readily available, and where desk jobs and labour-saving devices mean that we are less active than in previous generations. Because our environment makes it easy to consume high-calorie snack foods and spend long periods inactive, eating well and being active requires considerable self-regulation. It requires us to make an effort, such as deciding not to snack in order to maintain a healthy weight. He added: We are particularly interested in the way food choices and physical activity behaviours are linked to psychological processes in the brain called the 'executive functions'. We use executive functions to achieve goals, for example, planning actions in advance, solving problems, ignoring distractions, and resisting temptations. The executive functions can be depleted if used intensively, or due to particularly stressful situations. We are interested to know if reductions in executive functions are associated with behaviours such as snacking on unhealthy foods or sedentary behaviour. Researchers hope to recruit 120 individuals, over 18, who are not taking beta-blockers and who can attend the university's health sciences building on the Foresterhill campus to participate in psychological testing before the seven-day monitoring period. Information from the different monitoring devices will be used to identify where periods of snacking, activity, sedentary behaviour, and stress occur, Dr McMinn said. The aim is to try to understand why people snack, because we all know that sticking to a healthy diet is easier said than done.

text: There is one sentence in the press release announcing Nicholas Serota's departure from Tate that stands out. It is a direct quote from the man himself and reads: I leave an institution that has the potential to reach broad audiences across the UK and abroad, through its own programmes, partnerships and online. It is that word potential that stands out. What does he mean by potential? He refers to an institution that has evolved—under his leadership—from a well-respected but modestly visited gallery in Pimlico to an international art megabrand featuring the most visited museum of modern art in the world (Tate Modern), two highly popular regional galleries, a nationwide network of partnerships, and a lending programme that showcases Tate's collection of British art in major museums from Beijing to Boston. By most people's estimation, Nicholas Serota has already realised Tate's potential. However, he clearly does not see it that way, which is indicative of his character and provides insight into why he has been so successful during his tenure at Tate. He does not indulge in complacency. His remark about potential highlights three aspects of his character: a tendency not to boast, a relentless drive, and a challenging nature. He does not want the next incumbent to think he or she has an easy task: there is work to be done. Although he is leaving, he is setting the agenda before his departure. And who might that person be to come in and fulfil Tate's potential? The front-runner, I believe, is Maria Balshaw, who has performed excellently as the head of the Whitworth in Manchester, a position she has combined with leading the city's cultural programme. Then there is Iwona Blazwick, the long-serving director of the Whitechapel Gallery in east London, who helped shape Tate Modern's curatorial philosophy when she worked for the gallery in the late '90s. She has long been considered Serota's successor, and the path from Whitechapel to Tate is the one he followed. Among the internal candidates, the most obvious is Frances Morris, but she has only just assumed the role of director of Tate Modern. The recently departed Jessica Morgan could also be a contender, but again, she has barely settled into her position as the head of the DIA Art Foundation. The search team is likely to look further afield. Klaus Biesenbach from MoMA PS1 might receive a call, as could super-curator Carolyn Christov-Bakargiev, and quite possibly Michael Govan of the LA County Museum. Finally, Tim Marlow from the Royal Academy and Matthew Slotover, the co-founder of Frieze, are both notable figures who could bring something new to the table.

text: Gatwick Airport has been given approval to run six narrower flight paths to allow planes to fly in less airspace. The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) stated that aircraft departing from Gatwick would be more concentrated due to advancements in aviation navigation. It indicated that the objective was to lessen the environmental impact of flights, with fewer individuals affected by noise. Sally Pavey, from the Gatwick Area Conservation Campaign, remarked it would resemble a superhighway of planes. There are approximately 350 daily flights from Gatwick's single runway. The CAA's approval follows its review of the impact of a 2013 airspace change for departures. Advanced satellite navigation technology enables aircraft to avoid flying over ground-based beacons, allowing planes to fly closer together and use less airspace. New European legislation mandates the UK to optimise this technology, and the concentrated flight paths are Gatwick's response to this. Phil Roberts, the CAA's head of airspace, air traffic management and aerodromes, stated: We fully understand that aircraft noise disturbs many people and we have taken the necessary time to thoroughly assess the significant feedback we have received from local communities. As we have done throughout this review, we will continue to consider the environmental impact of all our airspace decisions. Opponents have claimed Gatwick is adversely affecting some areas of the south east. Tonbridge and Malling Conservative MP Tom Tugendhat said he would need to examine the changes in more detail but urged Gatwick to become a better neighbour. There are communities as far as Hildenborough and Tonbridge, running through Leigh and Penshurst, Chiddingstone, Edenbridge and even over my own home, just south of Edenbridge, who are very badly affected by the noise and it is absolutely unbearable. Gatwick Airport stated that over time the narrowing of the flight paths would allow it to switch some of them on and off, providing some respite for those facing a concentrated over-flight.

text: After two days of talks, Labour and Plaid Cymru have got a deal. These are external links and will open in a new window. Consequently, Carwyn Jones was reinstated as First Minister on Wednesday after Plaid withdrew Leanne Wood as a candidate. However, details of the agreement revealed it addresses several areas where the two groups align. It omits areas where the parties disagree, potentially fuelling future disputes. Labour and Plaid have committed to prioritising work on areas that enjoy support from across much of the assembly. These areas had some level of consensus in their respective manifestos. The parties have stated they would establish a new National Infrastructure Commission and a Welsh development bank. Three committees will also be established for joint work on financial, legislative, and constitutional matters. There was considerable consensus among several parties on various issues during the election. Plaid and Labour, in particular, have similar policies in their manifestos, including areas included in the agreement. The agreement has committed the Welsh Government to prioritise work on apprenticeships, and both parties stated they would create more positions. Plaid proposed creating 50,000 additional apprenticeships, while Labour proposed 100,000 all-age apprenticeships. Both parties have policies to increase the number of healthcare workers in Wales. A key Plaid policy is to create 1,000 extra doctors and 5,000 more nurses, while Labour has pledged to attract more GPs to Wales. A new treatment fund was also proposed by both parties. Plaid proposed a £50m New Medicines and Treatments Fund for Wales, while Labour proposed an £80m fund. Most parties have promised measures on childcare. Labour proposed providing 30 hours of free childcare a week for working parents of three and four-year-olds. Plaid proposed providing full-time early education of 30 hours a week by 2021. On the economy, both parties promised a new bank to provide finance to Welsh firms. Plaid supports a national bank of Wales, while Labour proposes a Welsh development bank. They have also pledged action on business rates. Labour promised a cut for all small firms, while Plaid also planned to support small firms by cutting business rates. The two parties have also made commitments regarding a possible smacking ban, although Labour has placed an important proviso on what many would consider a smacking ban. Plaid proposed introducing legislation to remove the defence of reasonable chastisement. Labour stated it would seek cross-party support to do the same. The party stated it has achieved agreement on five policies from its nine main manifesto pledges. Party figures highlight the National Infrastructure Commission—an arms-length body that would take a strategic approach to Wales' infrastructure and have access to new financial resources—as a significant achievement and something not in Labour's manifesto. However, on issues like apprenticeships and childcare, where there is significant overlap between the parties, Plaid stated it is ensuring Labour considers these issues a priority. Labour, for its part, managed to re-elect a First Minister without, it claimed, relinquishing any of its commitments for government. The agreement does not address two important issues for the last Welsh Government, where consensus proved elusive. One of these is the M4 Relief Road. Labour's preferred option is to build a black route six-lane motorway south of Newport. Plaid wants to upgrade existing roads along the lines of Professor Stuart Cole's proposed blue route. Both parties have had different approaches to local government reform. Labour proposed merging Wales' 22 councils to as few as eight or nine. Plaid suggested retaining the existing council structure and adding regional coordinating authorities. In its 2016 manifesto, Labour did not specify details of which M4 route it would build or how many councils would remain, despite its previous commitments on both. Elsewhere, demands for the single transferable vote at elections have long been on Plaid's agenda but were not included in the agreement. Ms Wood told the chamber on Wednesday there was insufficient time to consider and negotiate on the most difficult issues including the M4, detailed measures to save the steel industry, fair voting, or student finance. She stated Plaid would return to these and other matters through the budget and the other vehicles that are available to us.

text: Some businesses hit by malware in a cyber-attack that began on 27 June are still struggling to return operations to normal, the BBC has learned. These are external links and will open in a new window. Nuance Communications, which supplies transcription software for medical professionals, has gradually been restoring its products online. However, one IT worker informed the BBC that two US hospitals were still encountering issues. A security researcher described the situation as alarming but commended some companies for their transparency. The IT worker, who wished to remain anonymous, stated: We have been waiting for [Nuance Communications'] iChart [product] since they were initially affected by the ransomware and are still awaiting its return. We will probably have to switch to another product or even another vendor to obtain the same type of benefit. A spokesman for Nuance Communications declined to comment on the issue but referred the BBC to an update from 5 July. On Monday, logistics company FedEx reported that customers of its TNT Express division were still facing widespread service and invoicing delays. Shipping giant Maersk was also impacted by Petya. Some port terminals operated by its subsidiary APM Terminals had to be closed following the attack. Maersk had restored all of its major systems and customer interfaces, a spokesman informed the BBC. However, he added: There are some delays in certain processes due to manual workarounds or backlogs that needed to be cleared. In some cases, our turn time to customers might be longer than usual, but we are nevertheless providing them with the services they expect from us. There have been financial repercussions as well. Some affected companies, including Mondelez International - which owns chocolate-maker Cadbury - and consumer health manufacturer Reckitt Benckiser, stated that the impact of the attack would reduce their quarterly sales figures by a few percentage points. French construction giant Saint-Gobain, which recorded €39.1bn (£34.7bn) in sales in 2016, indicated that sales in the first half of the current financial year would likely decrease by about 1%. On one hand, it is alarming to see large multinational corporations still feeling the impact and attempting to recover systems, said security researcher Kevin Beaumont. On the other hand, it is good to see some of the businesses communicating so openly about the problems they are experiencing. Both Mr Beaumont and Mikko Hypponen, at cyber-security company F-Secure, have praised Maersk's openness. The wave of malware infections that unfolded during the Petya cyber-attack seemed to begin in Ukraine at the end of June. Since then, approximately £8,000 of ransom payments in Bitcoin have been transferred from a digital wallet - but it remains unknown who was behind the attack.

text: Levels of unconscious racist and sexist bias have been reduced by manipulating the way the brain learns during sleep. A team at Northwestern University, Chicago, utilised sounds during sleep to trigger and reinforce memories of an exercise conducted earlier in the day. The trial involving 40 participants, published in the journal Science, demonstrated that the changes persisted for at least a week. Experts stated the findings had potential in various contexts but also raised ethical concerns. Sexual and racial prejudice are prevalent but may often be unintentional, according to the Northwestern team. They reference studies in computer games where individuals chose to shoot black characters more frequently than white ones or favoured men over women despite identical job applications. Participants' prejudices were assessed using a series of publicly available tests at the study's outset. They subsequently underwent counter-bias training. During the session, images of faces were paired with words that opposed widely-held stereotypes. Thus, female faces were paired with words like maths or black faces with positive words like sunshine. Distinctive sounds were played during the counter-bias training and were replayed at low volume during a 90-minute afternoon nap. The outcome was a reduction in sexual and racial bias scores, which lasted for at least a week. So, could this genuinely make someone less sexist or racist? Prof Ken Paller, director of the cognitive neuroscience programme at Northwestern University, informed the BBC News website: We didn't have people interact with or make decisions about other people, so that sort of experiment is needed to know the full effects of the methods we used. But we suggest that modifying unconscious social bias is likely to influence the extent to which decisions are influenced by racist or sexist attitudes. He contends the technique may have potential in addressing addiction or unhealthy eating. In a commentary, Gordon Feld and Jan Born from the University of Tubingen commended the study, stating: This is the first to demonstrate that this method can be used to break long-lived, highly pervasive response habits deeply rooted in memory. However, they cautioned that sleep was a vulnerable state in which individuals lacked wilful consciousness. They added: However, Aldous Huxley's description of a dystopian 'brave new world' where young children are conditioned to certain values during sleep reminds us that this research also needs to be guided by ethical considerations. Prof Paller noted there were similarities to subliminal advertising and that an ethical discussion was necessary. However, he continued: More importantly, perhaps, is the question of whether people in positions of authority in society, such as judges and police officers, and perhaps people who make hiring decisions, should have their unconscious bias evaluated and perhaps trained to some standard.

text: A firm has been handed a record fine for nuisance calls after making more than six million automated calls in a solar panel marketing campaign. Glasgow-based Home Energy & Lifestyle Management Ltd has been fined £200,000 by the Information Commissioner. Complainants reported feeling powerless against the calls or finding that calls were filling up their answering machines. The company attributed the issue to another firm it hired to make calls and stated it was appealing the decision. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) reported that the company conducted a large-scale automated call marketing campaign offering free solar panels. One complainant informed the ICO that they had been awaiting news of a terminally ill family member and could not ignore the phone. The bottom line is companies trying to sell a product must adhere to the rules. Nuisance phone calls are a modern pest, said Information Commissioner Christopher Graham. People expect the Information Commissioner and other agencies to put an end to this, and we are now cracking down on these phone pests. The ICO stated that an organisation must have people's permission, specifically naming the company concerned, to make automated calls, but the company admitted it was unaware of the rules. To grant that permission, consumers must tick a box indicating they are interested in a particular product from a specific company. This company's ignorance of the law is beyond belief. It did not even bother to ascertain what the rules were, and its poorly conceived marketing campaign made people's lives a misery, said Steve Eckersley, head of enforcement at the ICO. The firm is also required to provide a means for consumers to stop receiving such calls, but in some instances, it failed to do so. The Telephone Preference Service, which allows people to opt out of unsolicited calls, only applies when there is a real person on the line. In this case, Home Energy & Lifestyle Management (Helms) used special software to send automated messages, which can be frequently repeated. The company, part of the government's Green Deal initiative, was also misleading people in the calls as the solar panels were not free, the ICO stated. However, Helms responded, claiming that the campaign had ceased before the ICO investigation began and blaming another company for the issues raised. Helms had significant difficulty in fully cooperating with the ICO, due to the failure of the third-party company to provide any information to verify and explain the extent of the calls made, the company said in a statement from its lawyer. It stated the ICO had seemingly disregarded its representations and vowed to appeal, as well as taking action against the other company.

text: This week three senior figures were appointed to oversee investigations into claims that a small group of hard-line Muslims had tried to take over schools in Birmingham. These are external links and will open in a new window. This followed revelations that the inquiry into the so-called Operation Trojan Horse plot was far more extensive than initially thought. Over 200 separate complaints have been lodged concerning 25 schools, all situated in areas of the city with Muslim populations of 90% or more. What exactly is the Operation Trojan Horse 'plot', is it genuine, and are we likely to uncover the truth? At the centre of the story is a document first sent to the city council at the start of last November. An accompanying letter from a concerned citizen urges the leader, Sir Albert Bore, to act immediately upon reading a document, which the sender claims was discovered in the office of their boss at a Birmingham school. The same letter was dispatched to four schools in early February. There are four pages, but the document must have been longer as it is evident that at least one page is missing at the beginning and at least one more at the end. Allegedly written in Birmingham with instructions to someone in Bradford, it outlines a five-point plan on how to take over schools, which the author terms Operation Trojan Horse. Many have questioned its authenticity because the document appears simply too convenient to be true. Conspiracies, where they exist, are rarely laid out in black and white so conveniently. However, some allegations about Adderley School had not previously been in the public domain. They are at the centre of an unfair dismissal claim to be heard at an industrial tribunal later this year, and documents related to the case are being investigated by the West Midlands Police economic crime unit. Four women have been arrested in connection with that case. It is therefore challenging to report those details at present. Allegedly written in Birmingham with instructions to someone in Bradford, it outlines a five-point plan on how to take over schools, which the author terms Operation Trojan Horse. It suggests targeting schools with predominantly Muslim populations, particularly in poorer areas, before selecting a group of parents, described as hard liners, to agitate at the school gate and in the playground and to raise questions about staff, the syllabus, and teaching methods. It continues to state that after infiltrating the governing body, a policy of disruption should be enacted from within until leadership is changed to one more sympathetic to the group's religious views. Trojan Horse, it states, is totally invisible to the naked eye and allows us to operate under the radar. I have detailed the plan we have in Birmingham and how well it has worked, and you will see how easy the whole process is to get the head teacher out and your own person in. It identifies four schools where it claims Operation Trojan Horse has been successfully implemented: Saltley School, Adderley School, Regents Park Community School, and Park View Academy. A Park View governor, Tahir Alam, is named in the document as someone involved in the plot, an accusation he has repeatedly and strenuously denied. Another school, Highfield, is mentioned as a potential target. Those arguing it is a hoax point to issues with the language used in the document and question the accuracy of some of its content. Much of what is referred to in the document had been widely reported locally before attracting national press attention. They argue it is too good to be true. If there were a genuine conspiracy, who would take the trouble to document it all and leave an incriminating paper trail? Those asserting its authenticity say some allegations had not previously been in the public domain. They claim the document has been with Birmingham City Council for six months and was scrutinised by detectives during the early stages of the investigation. If it had been proven fake, why has no one been able to categorically declare it so? When asked directly, officials have qualified their responses, saying it is probably a fake or likely to be spurious, but without a definitive answer. Unless the author of the letter or the Trojan Horse document is positively identified, it may be impossible to prove its provenance. Even if fabricated, it might have been a well-intentioned attempt by a whistleblower to alert authorities to genuine concerns about leadership and governance. Hoax or not, it has sparked a storm of allegations about bullying and intimidation at schools, as well as accusations that the Department of Education and the city council allowed a small clique to remove teachers, staff, and governors and introduce more Islamic teaching methods. Many of the schools have received good or outstanding Ofsted inspection reports and can point to strong exam achievements. In the seven weeks since the story became public, there have been repeated complaints that state-funded, secular institutions have been turned into faith schools by stealth. It has been alleged that girls and boys are forced to sit apart in class; female teaching staff are bullied or ignored by male Muslim counterparts; Arabic has replaced French or other European languages on the curriculum; ultra-conservative dress codes are strictly enforced and, most controversially, that on at least one occasion, a radical cleric and senior figure within al-Qaeda was praised in an assembly. Many of those making these accusations have refused to speak publicly, instead giving anonymous interviews to the media. They have been accused of being racist Islamophobes with personal grudges. The claims are being taken extremely seriously by all authorities and have prompted several inquiries. Ofsted is investigating the schools on behalf of the Department for Education. It is specifically examining allegations of wrongdoing within the schools. Questions will have been asked about leadership, the curriculum, teaching methods, the quality of teachers, and the education received by the children. Birmingham City Council has appointed Ian Kershaw, a former head teacher, to oversee its main inquiry into the Operation Trojan Horse allegations. This also involves Ofsted and the DfE, but includes West Midlands Police and the National Association of Head Teachers. The unions and the council believe the allegations reveal genuine problems with the system of school governance, especially within academies. The council has appointed Stephen Rimmer to head a second review group involving the education sector, councillors and MPs, faith groups, and community leaders. Mr Rimmer is a former Home Office director general, who also led the government's anti-radicalisation strategy Prevent. The most controversial appointment was that of the former head of the Met's counter-terrorism unit, Peter Clarke, as an education commissioner by the secretary of state Michael Gove. His background raised concerns in the predominantly Muslim areas at the heart of the Trojan Horse allegations. It is a community that already feels victimised and isolated. Even though several terror plots have been uncovered in the same streets, there is anger that the language used by the DfE, which included words like extremist and Islamist, has shifted the tone of the story from one about school governance to something darker and more sinister. There have also been murmurs that other government departments were unhappy about the timing of this particular announcement, despite an official statement insisting it was 100% supported. Another inquiry is quietly ongoing in the background. Accusations have also been made about financial wrongdoing at some schools, and the Education Funding Agency is investigating these. Ofsted is likely to publish its reports first. It has conducted inspections at 15 of the 25 schools being investigated by the authorities. They have all been what are commonly referred to as snap inspections under Section 8 of the 2005 Education Act, which allows for the re-inspection of schools causing concern. Most last two days and involve questioning staff, parents, governors, and pupils. The first school to be inspected was Park View Academy on 6 and 7 March. There was a further visit there a week later. That inspection report is overdue, but it is thought Ofsted will wait until reports into the other schools are ready before publishing them altogether. After the Easter break is all that we know for certain. The Kershaw and Rimmer reviews will publish their findings by the end of the school year in July, but interim reports are expected in early May. The Clarke inquiry is expected to run alongside both of these. As part of the Rimmer review, the Youth Parliament has been commissioned to produce two pieces of work to answer two questions: What does a good inclusive education in Birmingham look like? And what does a safe and resilient citizen of the future look like? This is likely to be published during the summer. There is no firm date for the publication of the EFA findings.

text: Female workers continue to face a rapid rise in pay inequality when they get into their 30s and 40s, according to the Resolution Foundation. Women born between 1981 and 2000 are expected to earn 9% less than men upon reaching their 30th birthday, it stated. This contrasts with a 5% pay disparity between men and women in their 20s. Consequently, having children imposes a sharp and long-lasting pay penalty, the think tank concluded. It reported that over a lifetime, women could lose hundreds of thousands of pounds. Young women today face relatively little disadvantage in terms of their pay packets compared to what their parents' and grandparents' generation faced, stated Laura Gardiner, senior policy analyst at the Resolution Foundation. But while many millennial women haven't experienced much of a pay gap yet, most probably will once they reach their 30s, when they start having children. What's more, this pay penalty is big and long-lasting, and remains for younger generations despite the progress in early careers. The gender pay gap for women in their 30s has altered very little over a generation, the research indicated. Last year, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) published similar research, concluding that men in their 30s tend to see their wages increase, while women's wages tend to plateau. Jo Swinson, a former member of the coalition government and now director of Equal Power Consulting, informed the BBC that sexism was still partly to blame. There is some occupational segregation, with more men going into science and engineering-type roles, but we also know there is discrimination at work. However, others argue the issue is not related to gender discrimination, but is due to more women of child-bearing age working in part-time jobs than men. On average, part-time jobs offer lower pay rates than full-time jobs. Four ways the gender pay gap isn't all it seems. The Resolution Foundation is urging policymakers and businesses to work harder to eliminate the pay gap altogether. But Jill Kirby, a former director of the Centre for Policy Studies think tank, stated change should not be imposed on women if they do not desire it. Women who are highly-qualified will choose to take less demanding jobs - more nine to five, and less nine to nine-type jobs - when they have a family, because they actually feel there are better things in life than spending all their time at the office, she told the BBC. From April 2018, companies with more than 250 employees will be required to publish detailed information about the size of the pay gap within their workforces. A government spokesperson said: The gender pay gap is at a record low, but we have to push further to eliminate it completely. Shining a light on organisations' pay gaps means employers can take action to tackle the causes and drive change.

text: Almost a third of dogs checked at random across the UK were found to be carrying a tick, researchers say. The discovery arises from the most extensive survey of ticks in dogs. Researchers also determined that the risk of an animal acquiring a tick is as significant in urban areas as in rural ones. Ticks can transmit various diseases, including Lyme disease, and a parasite identified in the UK for the first time earlier this year that is potentially lethal to dogs. Lyme disease can lead to severe health issues, such as meningitis and heart failure. In the most severe cases, it can be fatal. Nearly 15,000 dogs from across the UK were assessed in the study, conducted by Bristol University last year. Just under a third (31%) of these dogs, randomly checked during a visit to the vet, were found to be carrying a tick. The researchers discovered that the arachnids are present throughout the UK, with the highest risk areas being Scotland, East Anglia, and the South West. There can be as many in urban areas as in rural areas. Initiated in April 2015, the project requested participating vets to examine dogs in their practice weekly and complete a questionnaire regarding the clinical history of each dog. The species, life-cycle stage, sex, location of origin, and whether it was carrying any pathogens were recorded. Professor Richard Wall, who led the Big Tick Project team at the University of Bristol, stated: The work that we have conducted shows that ticks are extremely widely dispersed. The records we have appear to indicate an increase in tick numbers across the country. Our primary concern is the diseases that ticks carry. In the UK, we currently have relatively low rates of these pathogens, whereas, in continental Europe, they have much higher disease rates. As there seems to be a rise in tick numbers, we need to be vigilant and aware of the potential for increasing problems. Professor Wall advised pet owners to be aware of the risk in woodland or areas of long grass, but urban areas were also affected. Responding to the new data, conservationist Chris Packham said the good solid hard data from a tremendously significant project had revealed some very shocking and surprising things about the distribution, the population, and potential that ticks have to transmit diseases to our pets and ourselves. It was surprising that ticks were not just found in isolated parts of the UK, but throughout the UK, he said. Ticks do not jump or fly; they climb onto clothes if a person brushes against something the tick is holding onto. Typically, they can be found in woods, urban parks, heathland, and fields. They can also be found in gardens. Lyme disease is transmitted by the bite of a tick infected with Borrelia burgdorferi bacteria. The tick acts as a vector. In the same manner that a mosquito transmits malaria when it sucks blood from a person, the tick does the same to an animal or a person. According to Public Health England, it is estimated that there are 2,000 to 3,000 new confirmed cases of Lyme disease in England and Wales each year, although not all cases are confirmed by laboratory testing. About 15% of cases involve people who have returned from abroad. One initial symptom can be a red circular rash around the bite, known as a bullseye rash. However, this is not always present and cannot be relied upon as a warning signal. Victims may develop flu-like symptoms along with muscle and joint pain. Lyme disease can be treated with antibiotics. However, if left untreated, it can seriously damage a person's health, including affecting the nervous system, causing meningitis or heart failure. The threat of Lyme disease (Lyme borreliosis) in the UK is still considered small compared with other countries, with approximately 3% of ticks carrying the bacteria. However, given the results of this study showing the high numbers of ticks across the country and the serious potential consequences of Lyme disease, scientists are urging people to be aware of the risks and do their best to avoid being bitten. The Big Tick Project has launched an online tool that people can access to find out where ticks are most prevalent. Sarah Bignell was a very fit and active vet before she went on a walking holiday in Aberfeldy in Scotland in 2011. There was a small note in the cabin saying this was a Lyme disease hotspot, but I didn't think anything of it. I had no idea, she says. Six weeks later, she began experiencing pain in her bones, joints, and nerves. Doctors attributed her symptoms to other conditions, including multiple sclerosis or a brain tumour. However, Sarah's background meant she knew to push for a Lyme disease test. She had been bitten by a tick and was completely unaware of it. She also had no bullseye rash. It became agony virtually overnight for Sarah to cope with sound or light. She could not swallow, and when she could, it was agony. She had developed encephalitis. I spent eight-and-a-half months locked in a room, she explains. She required constant care and could no longer look after her dog and cat. Over the next four-and-a-half years, Sarah had many close calls. I was in danger of dying. I am very lucky, she says. The pain used to be so severe and my quality of life so awful, at that point I was living hour to hour. If I had been well enough, I would have ended up in Switzerland, and I wouldn't be here now—I am a vet, and I am used to ending suffering. With extremely strong treatment, Sarah says she now only has one or two really bad days a month. I still get bouts of extreme fatigue. Days when I think—having a shower or putting the washing out—which one should I do today? Again, I am lucky; there are many people not receiving the same treatment. So what does she think should be done about Lyme disease? It's not particularly about investment or research, Sarah says. It is a very cunning and specialised bacteria. It is so complicated and mimics so many other diseases, and each effect needs individual treatment. It's about being aware and not getting bitten, she explains. I'm not saying avoid the outdoors. The first thing I did again when I could get myself up on sticks was to go to the woods with my dog Matty. I walk him every day, but I wear wellies even in the sunshine. I also wear trousers and long-sleeved shirts if I'm walking in long grass. Always light-coloured so the ticks show up. I live in Kent, and one day this year when I got back to the car, I found five ticks. Sarah is working on her fitness and says she hopes to return to part-time work as a vet next year. text: The violence and murder of a protester in Charlottesville, Virginia, over the weekend has been attributed to far-right elements that descended on the city to demonstrate against the proposed removal of a statue of Confederate war hero Robert E Lee. These are external links and will open in a new window. President Donald Trump faced widespread criticism on Saturday after stating there was violence on many sides in Charlottesville and initially failing to explicitly condemn the white supremacists who organised the rally. On Monday, he succumbed to pressure to denounce the KKK, white supremacists, and neo-Nazis. However, many conservatives argue that blame should also be attributed to Antifa, a loosely affiliated group of far-left protesters. Critics contend that the media often excuses violence by Antifa militants simply because they oppose white supremacists and their reprehensible ideology. What precisely is Antifa? The social causes of Antifa (short for anti-fascist or Anti-Fascist action) are clearly identifiable as left-leaning. Most members oppose all forms of racism and sexism and strongly resist what they perceive as the nationalist, anti-immigration, and anti-Muslim policies enacted by Mr Trump. However, as their name suggests, Antifa concentrates more on combating far-right ideology than promoting pro-left policy. Unlike the mainstream left, they do not aim to gain power through traditional channels such as winning elections and passing legislation. Antifa is anti-government and anti-capitalist, and their methods are often seen as more closely aligned with anarchists than the mainstream left. Antifa does not avoid militant protest methods, including property destruction and sometimes physical violence. They were present at the 2017 Berkeley protests against far-right speaker Milo Yiannopoulos and at violent protests against Donald Trump's inauguration; they were also present at Charlottesville. Much like the far-right, Antifa members globally comprise a patchwork of groups, though the most active seem to be based in the US, the UK (under the name Anti-Fascist Action), and Germany (Antifaschistische Aktion). The German movement was founded in 1932 to provide a militant far-left group to counter the rapidly rising Nazi party. They were disbanded in 1933 after Hitler took control of parliament and revived in the 1980s as a response to neo-Nazism following the fall of the Berlin Wall. President Trump's election appears to have been something of a catalyst for the Antifa movement, which has connections with the Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement and various anarchist groups. According to James Anderson, one of a group of individuals who manage the popular anti-fascist and anarchist news site, It's Going Down, interest has surged since Mr Trump's election. The It's Going Down website, which received approximately 300 hits daily in 2015, now attracts between 10,000 and 20,000 hits a day. Since the events in Charlottesville on Saturday, the It's Going Down Twitter account has gained 2,000 new followers. While interest may have increased since Mr Trump's election, it is nearly impossible to quantify how many people are active members of Antifa. Much like the far-right, chapters of Antifa are loosely connected and highly secretive, organising mostly on message boards such as Reddit and over social networks like Twitter and Facebook. Antifa has become a popular topic for right-leaning websites and among conservative commentators. Fox News commentator and conservative speaker Erick Erickson states in The Resurgent, a conservative blog, that Antifa and the white supremacists are two sides of a common coin. The people dead in Charlottesville died because of one neo-Nazi, but there were dozens of people left bleeding in the streets because of Antifa. Meanwhile, a change.org petition urging Mr Trump to declare Antifa a domestic terror organisation has garnered nearly 100,000 supporters. While Antifa has received relatively little attention in the mainstream media, that may soon change. According to Mr Anderson, the events in Charlottesville over the weekend signify a sea change in how Antifa is perceived. This is a huge turning point and vindication for our movement, he said. We are working with Black Lives Matter, local clergy, this is not a movement that wants to be a lone group of militants, he said. This is about popular power. Sometimes that looks controversial - but this is a broad movement, and we are looking to engage a wide variety of people.
