text: There are few areas of life in which comic and actor Lenny Henry has not made an impact - working in theatre, television, film and charity. The star expressed he was very chuffed about his knighthood, first reported in the press last weekend. Throughout his five-decade career, he has endured occasional criticism without losing the affection of the British public. Born to Jamaican parents on 29 August 1958 in the West Midlands town of Dudley, Lenworth George Henry rose to fame in 1975 at the age of just 17 after appearing on the TV talent show New Faces. His winning performance led to the comedy series The Fosters and the anarchic children's show Tiswas, where he began to develop his own energetic and spontaneous comedy style. However, his subsequent career move was to haunt him for many years. He joined the Black and White Minstrel Show, in which blacked up white entertainers sang songs from the American South—a concept now much ridiculed and reviled. The comedian spent five years touring with the show, which he has since described as a grotesque parody of black people. I sort of wish it had never happened, but I don't regret that I did it, he told The Telegraph last year. Although it was a weird, reprehensible position to be in, I was working in huge venues and learning how to work a crowd. His escape route was the BBC sketch series Three of a Kind, which also starred Tracey Ullman and David Copperfield. First broadcast in 1981, it utilised state-of-the-art video effects and Ceefax-style graphics to deliver a fast-paced, gag-filled show—although many of its idiosyncrasies seem dated today. Simultaneously, the alternative comedy scene was heating up, and through TV producer Paul Jackson, Henry met the cutting-edge comedians of the Comic Strip team—one of whom was Dawn French. Initially, French was critical of the comedian's manner and the stand-up routines he still used to make a living, which had evolved in northern working men's clubs. He would wipe sweat from his forehead and say it tasted like chocolate—or threaten to move next door to hecklers if they did not quieten down. But, despite their first impressions, the couple warmed to each other, eventually marrying in 1984 at St Paul's Church in London's Covent Garden. Concurrently, Henry's political views began to mature. He refused to judge a Miss Blackpool beauty contest in 1984, stating it was degrading to women. His TV career progressed rapidly with BBC One's The Lenny Henry Show, and later The Delbert Wilkins Show. As a charity fundraiser, he also co-founded Comic Relief in 1985, which has raised more than £1bn over the past three decades. 1993's Chef! was another successful BBC One vehicle—but behind the scenes Henry was trying to nurture new black comedy talent, helping to set up BBC Two's The Real McCoy sketch show. He also began to take on more serious roles. Hope and Glory, in which Henry played an embattled head teacher, first aired on BBC One in 1999 while other projects included White Goods, Alive And Kicking and The Man. He also co-created, with Neil Gaiman, and produced the 1996 BBC drama serial Neverwhere. In 2009, he turned his attention to the stage, appearing in the title role of Northern Broadsides production of Othello at the West Yorkshire Playhouse in Leeds. It transferred to London and earned Sir Lenny the title of best newcomer at the London Evening Standard theatre awards. In 2010, the star's 25-year marriage ended in divorce. Soon after, his older brother Hylton lost his wife and two children, to cancer and TB. Sir Lenny said the cataclysmic deaths helped put his own life in perspective and reassert his love for his family. He immersed himself in work and, in 2011, followed up his Othello role with a debut at the Royal National Theatre in London, playing Antipholus of Ephesus in Shakespeare's The Comedy of Errors. His reputation as a serious actor was cemented in 2014, with a best actor title at the Critics' Circle Theatre Awards for his lead performance in Fences. In recent years, Sir Lenny has become an outspoken critic of British television's lack of ethnic diversity in its programming. I'm used to being the only black person wherever I go, he said. There was never a black or Asian director when I went to the BBC. Eventually I thought 'where are they all?' I spent a lot of time on my own. Things have changed a bit, but rarely at the BBC do I meet anyone of colour in a position of power. During a speech at Bafta in March 2014, he called the lack of minorities appalling, and he has continued to raise the issue publicly. On learning of his knighthood, the star said his mum would have absolutely been chuffed—and admitted to being bowled over himself. It was lovely, it was a lovely feeling, it was like being filled with lemonade for 10 or 15 minutes, he told BBC Radio 2.

text: Ukraine's defence minister says a new ceasefire has been holding in eastern Ukraine since midnight, despite a recent intensification of shelling. This morning, I am pleasantly surprised that at 09:00 (06:00 GMT), since midnight, not a single shot has been fired, stated Stepan Poltorak. It is the first instance of a true cessation of hostilities in 11 months, according to BBC correspondent Tom Burridge. The ceasefire was negotiated with pro-Russian rebels and international mediators. It coincides with the beginning of a new school year in Donetsk and Luhansk. Eastern Ukraine has experienced some of its most severe violence in recent weeks, with intense shelling last weekend. On Monday, international monitors from the OSCE security organisation reported nearly 1,000 explosions in the Donetsk region within just 24 hours - a significant surge in fighting along the front line. Most occurred in an area north of Donetsk airport and between the villages of Avdiivka and Yasynuvata. The neighbouring Luhansk region also experienced a substantial increase in explosions over the weekend. Ukraine asserts that extensive Russian military exercises near the border have heightened tensions. Meanwhile, the UK government has joined international calls for Russia to release Crimean Tatar leader Ilmi Umerov from a psychiatric unit and provide him with necessary medical care. He is reportedly suffering from diabetes and Parkinson's disease. Russia has prosecuted several prominent Crimean Tatar activists since its annexation of Crimea in March 2014. The Muslim Tatars, like the Ukrainian government, regard Russia's annexation as a blatant violation of international law. Crimean Tatars uneasy under Russian rule. Why are Russia-Ukraine tensions high over Crimea? On Wednesday, Ukraine's President Petro Poroshenko stated that France and Germany - the Western powers that facilitated a peace deal in Minsk in February 2015 - had supported Ukraine's call for a ceasefire commencing on 1 September. He mentioned he was awaiting a response from Russian President Vladimir Putin. Kiev and the West accuse Moscow of arming the rebels and deploying Russian regular troops to assist them. The Kremlin denies sending troops but acknowledges that Russian volunteers have been fighting alongside the rebels. A spokeswoman for Ukraine's delegation to the ceasefire talks, Darya Olifer, stated that more than 150,000 children were attending school in Ukrainian-held areas of Donbass, the industrial region that includes Donetsk and Luhansk. We insist that all children in the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, wherever they reside, have a right to care and security, she said. More than 9,500 people - including many civilians - have been killed in the two regions since the pro-Russian insurgents seized a large portion of territory in April 2014. Despite the ceasefire agreed in Minsk in February 2015, there have been violations by both sides almost daily.

text: Iran has confirmed some of its computer systems were infected with the Duqu trojan, but said it has found a way to control the malware. Security organisations had previously identified Iran as one of at least eight countries targeted by the code. The spyware is believed to have been designed to steal data to facilitate further cyber attacks. The sender remains unidentified, but researchers have discovered a reference to a US television programme in Duqu's code. The Iranian news agency, IRNA, reported that the country's cyber defence unit was taking measures to combat the infection. The software to control the virus has been developed and made available to organisations and corporations, Brigadier General Gholamreza Jalali, head of Iran's civil defence body, is quoted as saying. All the organisations and centres that could be susceptible to being contaminated are being controlled. Mr Jalali stated a final report into which organisations had been targeted was still being prepared. Last year the Iranian government accused the West of attempting to disrupt its nuclear facilities using the Stuxnet worm computer attack. Then in April 2011 officials announced the country's facilities had been targeted by a second piece of malware dubbed Stars. Officials now describe the Duqu attack as the third virus to strike Iran. The computer security specialist Kaspersky Lab stated it believed that Stars was a keylogging programme that may have been part of the same attack that installed Duqu. Keylogging programmes can collect information about a computer system, take screenshots, search for files and capture passwords. The firm also provided further details about how Duqu operated based on its analysis of other targets. It reported another unidentified company received an email from an individual identifying himself as Mr B Jason who proposed a joint business venture. The firm believed this was a reference to the Jason Bourne books and spy films. The recipient was asked to open a Microsoft Word attachment that referenced the targeted company's name in its title, and thus did not appear to be spam. It stated that for every victim a separate set of attack files was created using a different control server. The firm said this occurred at least 12 times. When the addressee opened the file the malware became active through a Truetype font exploit, but did nothing until it detected that there had been no keyboard or mouse activity for ten minutes. Kaspersky Lab said the font was called Dexter Regular and its creators were identified as Showtime Inc. This is another prank pulled by the Duqu authors, since Showtime Inc is the cable broadcasting company behind the TV series Dexter, about a CSI doctor who happens also to be a serial killer, the report stated. The firm said the exploit then loaded a driver onto the system. Analysis of the driver suggested it was compiled as long ago as August 2007. If this information is correct, then the authors of Duqu must have been working on this project for over four years, the report stated. The firm said the driver then initiated a process that led to the Duqu trojan being installed, allowing the attackers to introduce new modules, infect other networked computers, and collect information. The company said efforts to identify the attackers have been complicated by the fact that the suspects appear to have deactivated several of the control servers thought to have been involved in the attacks.

text: More than 150 beavers living in Tayside waterways have adapted well to life in Scotland, studies have found. The Scottish government is deliberating on the permanent reintroduction of the animals to the wild, with a trial programme currently in progress in Knapdale, Argyll. Studies have concluded that the Tayside beavers, which originated from escapes or illegal releases, have adapted well to the local environment. Proposals to trap or cull the rogue beavers have sparked controversy. The Scottish government agreed to monitor the situation for three years when the issue was last addressed in 2012, faced with the options of removing the animals or accepting their presence. The findings from the Tayside Beaver Study Group will assist in informing a government decision on the future of the animals in Scotland, alongside a trial reintroduction at Knapdale in Argyll. There were concerns that the beavers might damage ecosystems or spread diseases, but the study group established by Scottish Natural Heritage suggests they have settled in effectively, despite some land management challenges. The beavers, of the Eurasian species once native to Britain, have been found in rivers and lochs from Kinloch Rannoch, Kenmore, and Crieff in the west to Forfar, Perth, and Bridge of Earn in the east. They are likely of Bavarian or German descent. They are successfully reproducing and continue to spread through the Tayside area, and are free from diseases of concern to humans, domestic animals, and other wildlife. The most significant impact beavers could have is on agricultural land, such as building dams on the River Isla or the Tay and causing flooding on nearby arable land. Several methods of protecting trees from being gnawed and felled have been successful, preventing flooding, but the impact of the animals burrowing into flood banks and damming drainage ditches has been more challenging to manage. The study group stated this issue must be addressed if the beavers are to remain, as 70% of reported negative impacts due to beaver activity indicated a financial cost. David Bale, chairman of the study group and SNH's area manager for Tayside and Grampian, said the findings were very useful. He stated: The findings show there is no evident risk of diseases being transmitted from the Tayside beavers to other animals, or indeed to humans. The genetic tests indicate they would be suitable for permanent reintroduction to Scotland, as they are Eurasian rather than North American beavers. They are also genetically diverse enough to serve as a reasonable first step towards a full reintroduction if that was the decision of the Scottish Government. Our work documenting the impacts of beavers on land management interests has shown that in many situations, beavers are likely to cause few concerns. However, if they were to be permanently reintroduced, efficient, effective, and affordable ways of managing and reducing potentially significant impacts on intensively farmed land and other interests would need to be found. The reports from the study group will be submitted to the government, along with other beaver studies, in May. text: Babies born by Caesarean are at higher risk of becoming obese, especially compared with siblings born by vaginal delivery, a large study suggests. Writing in JAMA Pediatrics, the researchers suggested this might be because infants born vaginally are exposed to beneficial gut bacteria that play a crucial role in regulating diet. The study tracked more than 22,000 infants into adulthood. However, experts indicated that numerous factors were likely involved. These include the mother's diet, whether she had diabetes during pregnancy, and whether the infant was breastfed. Infants born via Caesarean are less likely to be breastfed, which has been shown to increase the risk of obesity. Children's diets also influence their future weight. In the UK, approximately 26% of infants are delivered by Caesarean section, an operation involving an incision in the abdomen and womb to deliver the baby. Rates have been steadily rising over recent years, according to the Royal College of Midwives. In this study, American researchers from Harvard Medical School and other institutions discovered that infants delivered by Caesarean were 15% more likely to become obese after adjusting for various factors, including the mother's weight and age. In families where children were born by different methods, those born by Caesarean were 64% more likely to be obese than their siblings born by vaginal delivery. However, the researchers could not confirm that Caesareans were the cause of obesity or explain the mechanisms behind the link. Their best hypothesis was that differences in gastrointestinal microbiota, or beneficial gut bacteria, between infants born by different methods could have an impact. Microbiota refers to the microbes that colonise our bodies and vary from person to person. They are associated with some diseases but can also be used to treat disease and promote health. A technique called vaginal seeding can be employed to transfer maternal vaginal fluid, which contains beneficial bacteria, to an infant born by Caesarean, but doctors warn there could be infection risks. Dr Simon Cork, research associate in the department of investigative medicine at Imperial College London, stated there were numerous factors to consider in children's risk of obesity, not just their mode of delivery at birth. Overall, the literature in this area suggests there may be a link between Caesarean section and obesity. However, this link is neither fully proven nor understood. Most often Caesarean births result from medical necessity rather than elective choice, and as such, this risk would outweigh any concerns mothers should have regarding the possibility of future weight issues. Prof Neena Modi, President of the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, stated more research was needed to determine whether birth by Caesarean was a cause of obesity. Caesarean section can be life-saving for women and their infants. However, many women are now considering Caesarean section where there is no medical indication. It is important that they are informed about the potential increased risk of obesity in their children, to help them make an informed birth choice. She added: It is also important for parents to focus on factors they can influence, which definitely impact their infant's health. This includes maintaining a healthy weight at the time of conception and throughout pregnancy.

text: Ian Bell has stepped down as captain of Warwickshire in all formats of the game to focus on batting. The 35-year-old captained the Bears to One-Day Cup victory in September 2016, but less than 12 months later the county is at the bottom of the Division One Championship table. Bell, who last represented England in November 2015, was recently excluded from the Bears' T20 team. This is the right time for me to stand down, Bell stated. As a senior player, I will support the team in all ways possible and I believe that our squad has very exciting times ahead. It has been an absolute honour to lead my home county over the last 18 months and my decision to stand down is something that I have thought long and hard about over a period of weeks. Bell will be succeeded by former England batsman Jonathan Trott as captain of Warwickshire's Championship team. The county's sports director Ashley Giles remarked that Bell made a brave decision to concentrate on batting. Having him focused solely on scoring runs for Warwickshire and Birmingham Bears is a huge asset to the club, Giles commented. Warwickshire, who secured limited-overs silverware in Bell's first season as captain, are facing Division One relegation issues, having lost five of their nine matches—four of them by an innings. Bell, the most capped international in Warwickshire history, having played 118 Tests, 161 one-day internationals and eight T20 matches, has accumulated 345 runs from 14 innings, at an average of 24.64. He has not scored a Championship century since April 2016. In the T20 Blast, he has amassed 251 runs in 12 matches at a strike rate of 117.29, but he was demoted in the order after a series of poor scores as opener. Having not batted at all in the Bears' penultimate game, he was entirely omitted for the final group game on Friday, which the Bears won against Lancashire at Old Trafford to secure a place in the quarter-finals. New Zealand international Grant Elliott captained the side and is expected to do so again for this Friday's last-eight match against Surrey at The Oval. Bell, who was part of the Birmingham Bears T20 Blast title-winning team in 2014, also won the Big Bash in Australia last winter with Perth Scorchers.

text: Heinz has been taken to court in Australia after a watchdog said it falsely marketed a children's food as healthy. These are external links and will open in a new window. The lawsuit pertains to Shredz, a snack made from fruit juice concentrate and pastes. Heinz, which refutes the allegations, asserts the bars have a similar nutrition profile to sultanas. However, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) argues they should be classified as confectionery. It alleges the snack, targeted at toddlers, contains over 60% sugar. The product is no longer available, but was offered in three flavours - peach apple and veg, berries apple and veg, and strawberry and apple with chia seeds. The packaging claimed it was 99% fruit and veg and prominently displayed a selection of fruits on the front. The ACCC's lawyer, Tom Duggan, informed the Federal Court in Adelaide that the berries, apple and veg Shredz contained up to 68.7 grams of sugar per 100 grams. Nutritionist Rosemary Stanton, who contributed to Australia's dietary guidelines, stated the bars resembled sweets more than fruit or vegetables. Confectionery with added vitamins is still confectionery, she remarked. She further noted that while the product did contain some dietary fibre and various vitamins, the same applies to many unhealthy foods. Indeed, there are some positive nutrients in there, just as there are positive nutrients in a Big Mac, she commented. The nutritionist suggested that Shredz, in her view, should be classified as an occasional treat. The food company vehemently denies the allegations of false marketing. In a statement, Heinz dismissed the ACCC's assertions regarding the bars' packaging. The Shredz products were snack foods available in small individually-packaged servings suitable for children aged one to three, it stated. The Shredz products had a similar nutrition profile to dried apple or sultanas. Heinz stands behind the Shredz products and their packaging. The legal action commenced in June 2016 following a complaint about toddlers' foodstuffs by campaign group the Obesity Policy Coalition. The ACCC is seeking financial penalties, corrective notices, and costs from Heinz.

text: Former US Open champions Roger Federer and Maria Sharapova enjoyed straight sets wins at Flushing Meadows on a day that brought some notable exits. Swiss second seed Federer defeated Australia's Sam Groth 6-4 6-4 6-4 to advance to the third round. Russia's fifth seed Sharapova also progressed, reaching the fourth round with a 6-2 6-4 victory over Sabine Lisicki. Two-time champion Venus Williams and second seed Simona Halep were eliminated in their third-round matches. Home favourite Venus Williams lost 6-0 0-6 7-6 (7-5) to Italy's Sara Errani. Errani will face Mirjana Lucic-Baroni next after the Croatian qualifier defeated Romania's Halep 7-6 (8-6) 6-2. Germany's sixth seed Angelique Kerber was also defeated 6-1 7-5 by Switzerland's Belinda Bencic. Federer, a five-time US Open champion, will play Spain's Marcel Granollers in the third round, while 2006 champion Sharapova faces Denmark's Caroline Wozniacki in the fourth round. Having twice come back from being down a break in the third set, Williams had a chance to serve out the match. However, Errani, who had not won more than three games in a set against Williams in three previous encounters, showed great determination to force a tie-break. Ultimately, Williams was undone by too many unforced errors—she had 52 in total—although with seeds falling all around her, Errani will fancy her chances of progressing far in the tournament. Lucic-Baroni, 32, reached the semi-finals at Wimbledon in 1999 but had not reached the fourth round of a Grand Slam tournament since. Off-court issues derailed her career, but she returned to the Grand Slam stage in 2010 after an eight-year hiatus and defeated future Wimbledon champion Marion Bartoli at SW12 in 2012. text: High street stores had a disappointing October, according to figures from the Scottish Retail Consortium (SRC). While total sales across the UK increased by 0.9% compared to the previous year, figures for Scotland indicated a decline of 2.4%. Like-for-like sales, which exclude factors such as new store openings, were 2.8% lower, according to the SRC/KPMG Scottish Retail Sales Monitor. Mild autumn weather may have reduced clothing sales, while consumers of electrical goods may be awaiting sales. David McCorquodale, head of retail at KPMG, remarked that the figures were a sobering reminder of the frailty of the economic recovery. He stated: There is no doubt the declines in Scottish retail sales in October, when measured against a relatively weak month last year, are disappointing for retailers when set against mainly dry weather and temperatures only marginally warmer than average. Mr McCorquodale noted the weather wasn't cold enough for sales of coats or boots to perform well, adding that with shoppers perhaps waiting for heavy promotions, retailers were left pushing themed products for Halloween. He mentioned the next few weeks would be crucial for retailers with the strategies around Black Friday and the lead-up to Christmas beginning to unfold. Total food sales decreased by 3.2% compared to October 2014, with stores unable to fully capitalise on the Rugby World Cup after Scotland exited the tournament. With Halloween occurring on a Saturday this year, some Scots chose guising over shopping, the SRC suggested. Although Scotland experienced the driest and sunniest October since 2003, sales of autumn and winter clothing were hindered, although Halloween fancy dress costumes reportedly sold well. Shoppers also delayed purchasing electrical products in anticipation of discounts in the Black Friday sales at the end of this month, and total non-food sales for October declined by 1.8% on last year. SRC director David Lonsdale said: This rather pallid set of results paints a disappointing October overall for Scotland's retailers, with total retail sales edging down again once falling shop prices are taken into account. It could be that shoppers are simply holding out for even better deals in the run-up to Christmas, perhaps with an eye towards potential online discounting at the end of this month, despite the fact that shop prices are already at record lows. With the spotlight on the Autumn Statement and the Scottish Budget over the next few weeks, retailers will be hoping for measures which put money in people's pockets and which encourage them to invest and grow.

As the song says, step by step, slowly and suavely, they [the critics] want to create a coup, he said, according to local media. text: A BBC sitcom has been criticised as Islamophobic during a Commons debate about whether the BBC's programmes and staff reflect UK diversity. Labour's Rupa Huq criticised Citizen Khan for portraying a quite backward Muslim family. The programme faced accusations of stereotyping Muslims upon its 2012 debut, and its creator, Adil Ray, informed the Radio Times he had received death threats. The BBC stated that the award-winning show had garnered significant positive feedback. However, Ms Huq, MP for Ealing Central and Acton, whose sister Konnie is a former Blue Peter presenter, remarked: I feel as if I didn't know what the year is... you would think it's an everyday tale of a Birmingham family of Muslims but they're really quite backward. Again, the Islamophobic point [Labour MP Chuka Umunna] made, it's a beardy weirdy chap and they're not quite cutting off people's hands but I can imagine that being in a future episode. Citizen Khan prompted complaints at its launch in 2012, and Mr Ray has previously stated he received abuse from those who believed it mocked Islam or stereotyped Muslims. Nevertheless, the show has secured various awards at the Royal Television Society and Asian Media Awards. A BBC spokesman commented: The fact that Citizen Khan returns for its fifth series this year is a sign of its popularity with all audiences - indeed the show has won several awards, including Best TV character at the Asian Media Awards. We've also had positive comments from members of the Muslim community for the show and for creator Adil Ray who, like the family portrayed, is a British Pakistani Muslim. As with all sitcoms the characters are comic creations and not meant to be representative of the community as a whole. Ms Huq expressed her views during a backbench debate initiated by former culture minister David Lammy. Mr Lammy accused the BBC of employing the same old faces from the same old schools to the same old jobs and mentioned he had been approached by black and Asian BBC staff who felt unable to speak up for fear of being labelled troublemakers. He further stated the Chinese community was totally invisible on the broadcaster and insisted the BBC's new charter must tackle the lack of progress in enhancing ethnic minority representation. He noted that although the BBC ran 29 schemes aimed at ethnic minorities between 1999 and 2014, the situation was not improving, with the proportion of ethnic minority staff declining from 13.1% in 2015 to 12.2% now. The Labour MP for Tottenham commended the diversity in children's television, BBC Three, and documentaries but questioned whether management diversity was adequate. He stated: We all go into Broadcasting House and see the security, see black staff at the junior ends, but walk into that newsroom, think about the editorial decisions that are being made, and ask yourself, is that really representative of our country as a whole? Conservative MP Helen Grant proposed the BBC could voluntarily disclose data on the recruitment, retention, promotion, and pay of staff from ethnic minorities. Labour Sunderland Central MP Julie Elliott asserted the BBC should reflect every region in the UK, adding that Salford - where MediaCity UK is a major BBC base - was not where the North ends. Earlier, Mr Umunna criticised the representation of our Muslim communities on TV. He claimed rising Islamophobia could partly be attributed to broadcasters' use of community leaders who purport to speak for that community but have no mandate whatsoever to do so. The BBC stated it was making good progress on becoming more diverse but pledged to continue developing new and innovative ideas to do even better and would soon outline its new diversity strategy. Almost half of our workforce is made up of women and the proportion of our workforce who are black, Asian and other ethnic minority is at an all-time high, the spokesman added.

text: Two Welsh councils are facing legal action over claims they continue to uphold motions alleged to be racist. Jewish Human Rights Watch, an organisation established to address an alleged increase in anti-Semitism in the UK, has secured the right to a judicial review hearing concerning motions passed by Swansea and Gwynedd councils. It is anticipated that the legal battle could cost both local authorities tens of thousands of pounds. Both councils have refuted the allegations. In 2010, Swansea council sought involvement in contracts with Veolia, a company also part of a consortium aiming to construct a railway system linking Israel to settlements in occupied East Jerusalem. The motion presented to the council stated the project not only contravenes UN demands but is in contravention of international law. It also mentioned that the United Nations has demanded that Israeli settlement activities and occupation should not be supported. Several councillors urged the council leader at the time and its chief executive to support the position of the UN in regards to the Israeli settlements in East Jerusalem, so long as to do so would not be in breach of any relevant legislation. They also urged the council to refrain from doing business with any company in breach of international law or UN obligations or demands, so long as to do so would not be in breach of any relevant legislation. The motion was approved in June 2010, yet it remains non-binding. In 2014, Gwynedd council passed a motion calling for a trade embargo with Israel, condemning the attacks by the Israeli state on the territory of the Palestinians living in the Gaza Strip. It also stated: It must be made clear that the proposal condemned the Israeli state and not the Jewish religion. However, a solicitor representing Jewish Human Rights Watch, Robert Festenstein, stated: We would like to see the motions quashed. I don't understand why they would pass it in the first place. I mean, they wouldn't pass a motion saying something derogatory about women, so why would they do that about Jews? Why would they pass a motion which has a detrimental impact upon the relationship with Jewish people in Swansea, particularly in Wales generally? It has absolutely nothing to do with Swansea. In a statement, a Swansea council spokesman said: On 10 March 2016, full council decided not to rescind the notice of motion that was passed on 17 June, 2010. The council has never boycotted Israeli goods and has no intention of doing so. For legal reasons, it would be inappropriate to comment further. A spokesman for Gwynedd council stated: It would not be appropriate for us to comment regarding this matter due to ongoing legal proceedings which the council is defending. JHRW will also be taking action against Leicester council. The judicial review hearing will commence on Wednesday and is expected to last for two days.

text: Roger Ailes revolutionised cable news in the US, creating the hyper-partisan, opinion-based environment that currently dominates the American media landscape. These are external links and will open in a new window. It is perhaps appropriate, then, that the reactions to the death of the founder of the conservative media giant Fox News have been starkly divided along partisan lines. He was described as a monster who corrupted American society and made people dumber and angrier. Alternatively, he was hailed as a great American patriot and a media genius. One individual, two distinctly different portrayals in a nation with two distinctly different perspectives on the world. Much has been written recently about the fragmentation of US culture; about how Americans are retreating into their own bubbles, where they receive news and entertainment that align with their political and social inclinations. Over the past two decades, Ailes developed Fox News into one of the largest bubbles of all. In 1996, when Ailes was appointed by Fox head Rupert Murdoch to launch his new network, CNN dominated the cable news landscape. Its style was not unlike the network evening news formats that had become a staple in America since the advent of television, from Walter Cronkite to Tom Brokaw. Authoritative, supposedly unbiased television presenters delivered the news and introduced stories, day and night, week after week. A few talk shows were scattered throughout the schedule. Crossfire and Capital Gang featured politicians and pundits exchanging jabs, and Larry King provided a safe platform for major public figures to convey their messages. CNN, however, presented itself as a neutral forum. Ailes infused cable news with a partisan slant. The long-time Republican operative, who worked for Richard Nixon, Ronald Reagan, and George HW Bush, transformed the television news format into an ideological instrument - a megaphone or a cudgel, depending on one's viewpoint. His network's nightly line-ups abandoned the guise of impartiality and offered conservative red meat - which audiences consumed in record numbers. Ailes astutely concluded that much of the American public did not seek information from their television news; they sought confirmation. It is impossible to separate Ailes, who for decades was arguably the most influential man in US media, from his dramatic downfall, of course. He was accused of being a serial sexual harasser who exploited his position of power to demean and degrade the women around him. More than 25 women came forward to accuse him of various predatory behaviours, and Fox Corporation had to pay millions of dollars in legal settlements. If Ailes constructed a news empire unlike any before it, like all empires, there is a peak followed by eventual decline. His network has been plagued by a series of crises. Many of its top talents have departed - including Megyn Kelly, who wrote a book detailing Ailes's misconduct. Bill O'Reilly, the highest-rated Fox News personality, was recently ousted in his own sexual harassment scandal. Beyond the allegations that it has become a toxic environment for some of its employees, Fox News has found itself adrift in the Donald Trump era. The optimistic portrayal it offers of the Republican president has often appeared woefully out of sync with the daily barrage of crises afflicting the White House. If the Trump presidency becomes a sinking ship, Fox News is poised to be the orchestra that plays Nearer My God to Thee until the bitter end. This week, when James Comey's memo-writing habits and the details of Mr Trump's conversations with Russians in the Oval Office were causing shockwaves through Washington, Fox evening hosts Tucker Carlson and Sean Hannity were focusing on Hillary Clinton's email server and a false conspiracy theory about a Democratic staffer who was murdered last year. Even viewership ratings, which Fox News once dominated, have recently shown signs of weakness, as left-leaning MSNBC has frequently posted better numbers during the evening hours over the past few weeks. With Ailes gone, Fox News' future is far from certain. Murdoch recently toured the network's New York headquarters and unveiled plans for a massive structural renovation. A similar programming overhaul could eventually reshape much of what Ailes built. His legacy, however - both the good and the bad - is secure.

text: A 15-year-old girl who was sentenced to 100 lashes for engaging in premarital sex has had her punishment overturned by a Maldives court. The High Court ruled on Wednesday that the girl, whose stepfather is on trial for raping her, had been wrongly convicted by a juvenile court of engaging in premarital sex with another man. Premarital sex is prohibited in the Maldives, a popular tourist destination. The case provoked outrage among rights groups who welcomed the recent ruling. We are relieved that the girl will be spared this inhumane 'punishment' based on an outrageous conviction, which we hope has also been quashed, stated Polly Truscott, Amnesty International's deputy Asia-Pacific director. No-one should ever be prosecuted for sex outside marriage in the first place. Ms Truscott remarked that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment. She urged the Maldivian government to annul all outstanding flogging sentences. In its ruling, the court stated that the sentence of the lower court was based on a confession the girl made while suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder. It noted that she had been unfit for trial following the alleged rape. The Maldivian government appealed on behalf of the teenager after international outrage in February over plans to punish her with 100 lashes when she reached the age of 18. The girl—who cannot be named for legal reasons—was only charged after police investigating the rape allegations discovered she had been having consensual sex with another man. President Mohamed Waheed expressed that he was overjoyed with the ruling, his spokesman Masood Imad informed the AFP news agency on Thursday. Mr Imad stated: It is the government's policy to protect victims, but we had to do it within the framework of the law. The case was forwarded for prosecution after police were summoned to investigate a dead baby buried on the island of Feydhoo in Shaviyani Atoll, in the north of the country. Her stepfather was accused of raping her and impregnating her, then killing the baby. The legal system of the Maldives, an Islamic archipelago with a population of approximately 400,000, incorporates elements of Islamic law (Sharia) as well as English common law.

text: The European Space Agency (Esa) has turned off one of its most successful ever missions. These are external links and will open in a new window. LISA Pathfinder was launched into orbit in 2015 to validate key technologies that could be utilised in a future project to detect gravitational waves—ripples that disturb space-time when black holes collide. The satellite exceeded its set objectives spectacularly. This success directly led to the selection of the LISA mission in June. This billion-euro venture, envisioned as a trio of satellites, is anticipated to launch between 2030 and 2034. It will incorporate many of Pathfinder's systems, including its crucial laser interferometer instrumentation, which has proven capable of detecting gravitational waves (GW) in space. LISA Pathfinder has demonstrated that LISA is feasible at full sensitivity, more than we could hope for, stated principal investigator Stefano Vitale. I believe it has been a stepping stone for GW astronomy and an incredibly rewarding experience for all the team involved. Thank you, and stay tuned on LISA! he told BBC News. Prof Vitale was invited to send the final kill commands to Pathfinder, which had been conducting its measurement demonstration 1.5 million km from Earth in the sunward direction. The commands, sent from Esa's mission control centre in Darmstadt, Germany, tricked Pathfinder into rebooting onto software that had already been corrupted. This meant the gravity probe was locked down, unable to operate its subsystems, including its transmitter. The only way you could recover the spacecraft would be to go up there and attach an umbilical and restart from another computer, explained Pathfinder's spacecraft operations manager, Ian Harrison. The kill procedure, more formally known as passivating the satellite, ensures there is no hazard to future missions through a collision or interference of radio communications. The Darmstadt team in April had already fired the thrusters on Pathfinder to move it away from its station—a popular location for many Sun-studying missions. It should now drift harmlessly around our star. There's a very, very small chance it could return to the Earth-Moon system; it's so remote but you can't actually say it's zero, said Ian Harrison. The mission analysis actually looked at the planetary positions 500 years into the future. Gravitational waves—Ripples in the fabric of space-time Gravitational waves are currently a major focus in science. Ground-based laboratories in the US have recently begun detecting them from coalescing objects that are 20-30 times the mass of our Sun. However, by sending an observatory into space, scientists expect to discover sources that are millions of times larger and to sense their activity all the way to the edge of the observable Universe. This should significantly advance our understanding of gravity and its workings, and perhaps even reveal some flaws in Einstein's so-far flawless equations. LISA will detect gravitational waves by bouncing laser light between three spacecraft flying in a triangular formation, with sides of the triangle 2.5 million km long. The light beams will measure the precise positions of small, free-floating blocks inside the satellites. When gravitational waves pass through the triangle, the distance between blocks of the different spacecraft should change by tiny amounts—just fractions of the width of an atom. Laser science: LISA Pathfinder's technology demonstration LISA Pathfinder's laser and gold-block monitoring system was reduced to fit inside a single satellite. As such, it could not itself detect gravitational waves, but the exquisite sensitivity of the instrumentation demonstrated that the metrology principles were sound. LISA Pathfinder did more than we ever asked for, said Paul McNamara, Esa's Pathfinder project scientist. It met its requirements on day one, the day we switched on its science. But we then met and surpassed the requirements of LISA. So, it's been a phenomenal mission. It's sad to turn Pathfinder off but at some point we have to look to the future, he told BBC News. text: Police investigating the murder of a man in a car shooting in Glasgow have issued a fresh appeal for witnesses. Euan Johnston, aged 26, was in the driver's seat of a black Audi RS4 estate when he was shot on Shields Road, near Scotland Street, at 23:45 on Tuesday. He later succumbed to his injuries in hospital. His 29-year-old male passenger was unharmed. The shots were fired by an occupant of a dark-coloured Audi Q5, which subsequently sped off into Scotland Street towards the M8 motorway and Kingston Bridge. Police reported that just before midnight on Tuesday, officers were alerted to a car on fire in Bracken Street, in the Parkhouse area, north of Glasgow. The vehicle is currently undergoing forensic examination to determine any connection to the murder on Shields Road. Detectives have appealed for anyone who witnessed a vehicle being driven at speed in the area to come forward. Detective Superintendent Jim Kerr, from Police Scotland's major investigations team, stated: Our priority remains tracing whoever is responsible, and a team of highly experienced detectives are working on this murder inquiry. Although we believe this was a targeted, planned attack and Euan Johnston was the intended target, the shooting was executed with complete disregard for public safety, and I fully understand that people will be concerned about this. I would stress that everything is being done to track down whoever is responsible for this shooting, including numerous officers examining CCTV footage from the area around the scene of the shooting. Police stated that forensic and search inquiries had been completed at the scene of the shooting on Shields Road, and the area had fully reopened. Superintendent Kerr added: We are doing everything we can to trace whoever is responsible for this murder, but we would appreciate any assistance the public can provide, as even the smallest piece of information could be vital to our investigation. We have support mechanisms in place should people feel vulnerable about contacting us, and I would urge people to do the right thing and report any information they have. Police have established an incident room at Baird Street Police Office in Glasgow to handle information. Superintendent Kerr disclosed on Wednesday that Mr Johnston, who was from the Maryhill area of Glasgow, was known to police but did not provide details. He stated the victim had been returning home after a meal when he was targeted. The 29-year-old man who was a passenger in Mr Johnston's car is being treated as a significant witness, the detective said. He also revealed that the shooting had been witnessed by members of the public.

text: UK scientists have successfully germinated seeds from the critically endangered Japanese Birch, a species that has just 21 known trees remaining. The seeds were collected last year during an expedition to a remote area in the mountains near Tokyo. Experts indicate that the remaining wild population of Betula chichibuensis is insufficient to sustain itself without assistance. The young trees will be distributed to other arboretums to aid in conserving the endangered species. The International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) predicts a grim future for the tree species in the wild. In its Red List of Threatened Species, it notes: The small population and restricted distribution... make it vulnerable to natural disaster or disease. The species is also self-incompatible, requiring two individuals to be close enough to cross-pollinate each other, rendering seed production uncertain in small subpopulations. It further states that there is evidence of deforestation and habitat degradation in the area where the remaining trees are located, posing a threat to the survival of this species. Growing hope In 2014, a team led by researchers from the University of Oxford Botanic Gardens, in collaboration with the University of Tokyo, embarked on an expedition to collect seed samples from the endangered birch trees. Among the team was Dan Luscombe, a dendrologist from the Forestry Commission's Bedgebury National Pinetum and Forest. He informed BBC News: I suppose we were somewhat fortunate to be there at the right time. It is located in a very, very remote area and is not easily accessible. It has very, very low viability, so we were fortunate to collect a substantial number of seeds... as birch seeds shatter and disperse everywhere, so once that occurs, you will never find them. Mr Luscombe estimated that the team managed to collect about 1,000 seeds, from which the team at Bedgebury Pinetum produced approximately 100 seedlings. Ideally, we always cultivate trees sourced from the wild to conserve the genetic resource, he explained. Ultimately, we have these exceptionally rare trees, and their habitats are severely threatened. If you wish to reintroduce them or place them elsewhere, you need to know how to cultivate them. The long-term goal of the project is also to plant Japanese birch saplings in arboretums nationwide, as well as collaborating closely with their Japanese colleagues to protect the species' survival in the wild. We will share the love so other arboretums can attempt to grow this species in different climates and soils, Mr Luscombe added. He also explained that planting samples of the trees in various parts of the UK would mitigate the risk of the species being lost to storm damage or disease. There are also plans to plant a grove of the trees, known as a seed orchard, to provide a continuous supply of seeds.

text: Almost 1,500 secondary pupils across Aberdeen have been given anti-weapons lessons in the wake of the killing of schoolboy Bailey Gwynne. Bailey, aged 16, was stabbed during an altercation with another student at Cults Academy. The schoolboy's assailant is serving a nine-year sentence for culpable homicide. An independent review into Bailey's death in October last year concluded that his death was potentially avoidable if teachers had been aware that his attacker carried a knife. The sessions will be introduced next year to Primary 7 pupils in Aberdeen. Critics have raised concerns about whether pupils would report their friends. PC Seb Cook, of Police Scotland, addressed one S1 class at Aberdeen's Hazlehead Academy: You will have heard about the tragic incident that occurred a year ago in Aberdeen. We never want anything like that to happen again. You will never need to bring anything sharp or dangerous into school. Hazlehead head teacher Jim Purdie stated: It's not just about carrying weapons or blades, it's about the legal aspect of that, and then the consequences for the pupils, for their families, for their friends. There's an expression we often use, which is if we don't know things are happening we can't do anything about them. We are constantly reminding our children to take responsibility. If there's something that is upsetting them, they know who to tell. One pupil, when asked what they would do if they knew someone had a weapon, told BBC Scotland: I would probably just go up to a teacher, maybe even up to the person and just say 'why are you doing that, think of the consequences'. Another commented: People say don't grass up a mate, but if it's serious I think you should. Police Scotland was queried about incidents involving weapons in schools. Supt Andy McKay, of Police Scotland Safer Communities, stated: Police Scotland relies on local authorities to report all incidents of weapon possession so that accurate figures can be collated. Following the report into Bailey Gwynne's death, Aberdeen City has been working closely with Police Scotland to ensure each and every incident of weapon possession is reported, however it will be up to other local authorities to consider this recommendation moving forward. As a result, the figures collated to date may not offer a true reflection of the national picture in relation to possession of weapons in schools due to inconsistent reporting and recording methods. text: When Wes Metcalfe bought a cucumber from a Tesco shop in Dinnington, South Yorkshire, he did not expect it to come with a dead worm. I excitedly called the children downstairs to meet our new pet. We decided to name him William. Our new pet appeared very unresponsive, we just attributed it to him being sleepy and decided to give him some time to revive. Twenty-four hours later and William still hasn't moved - upon closer inspection he seems quite flat (again, see picture) and I think he may be dead. Well... I'm no vet, but I think the tight shrink wrap on the cucumber may have squashed and killed William. I know Aldi's banana spiders were deadly, but at least they had some life in them. I now have three very upset children, a worm funeral to plan and to top it all off I've completely lost my taste for cucumber sandwiches, which as everyone knows are a favourite at any wake. So come on Tesco, wiggle your way out of this one. Tesco's equally humorous response began: I'll be heading to a muddy festival shortly, trawling through the fields of damp grass and dirt much like William would've during his happier times. This means I won't be able to make it on the day unfortunately, though I've decided to compose a poem, which I hope you can read out on the day. Would that be OK? Here goes: 'An ode to William. Although life takes funny turns, we can all learn from William the worm. Let us gather, light a candle to burn, and celebrate the life of William the worm. Lights shine bright, let's eat sponge cake through the night! Because there's many a lesson to learn. He wriggles many miles; he gave us many smiles, so we stand confident and firm... William will be back, very much like Arnie, though now we will all check before we make a sarnie!' #PoemsforWilliam. Wishing you the best, Rob - customer care. It's been an emotional day, but the funeral went without a hitch. Tesco Rob, we read out your poem, and there wasn't a dry eye amongst us. text: Mark Wigglesworth has resigned as musical director of the English National Opera. In an email, he stated he was departing because the ENO was evolving now into something I do not recognise. The company, which has experienced a period of turmoil, announced he would leave at the end of the current season. He will continue to fulfil his contractual commitments as a conductor and looks forward to continuing to work with the wonderful musicians of ENO. Wigglesworth was appointed as the company's new musical director in 2014. He remarked at the time that he considered his appointment a huge privilege. He later stated the company would continue to take risks and pursue adventurous work despite funding cuts. In the email, which he sent to colleagues, the 51-year-old mentioned the ENO's plan for the future is one that the board and chief executive have always known I cannot support. As hard as I have tried to argue to maintain what I believe to be the fundamental pillars of our identity, I have failed to persuade others of this necessity, he said. I believe in efficiencies that increase our value for money and do not lose the opportunity of performing the highest quality opera to the largest number of people. Wigglesworth has been a regular at the Proms since 1991, conducting works by composers including Olivier Messiaen and Richard Wagner. His departure follows a series of troubles at the English National Opera. In February last year, the Arts Council of England reduced the ENO's core funding to the company by £5m as it removed the company from its national portfolio of organisations for 2015-18. Two months later, the ENO announced it was reducing ticket prices in an effort to secure its financial future. Earlier this year, the company requested members of the chorus to shift from a 12-month to a nine-month contract. The proposal led to the ENO chorus voting to strike over the changes, which they claimed amounted to a cut in pay. The chorus stated it would not appear in part of a performance of Akhnaten at the London Coliseum as part of the strike action. The ENO argued at the time that it risked bankruptcy if the proposed changes were not implemented. The pay dispute was later resolved and the strike action was called off.

text: When Avi Yaron was 26 years old he had a motorbike accident - a day he describes as the luckiest of his life. As doctors conducted a scan of his head to assess for damage, they discovered a tumour deep within his brain that might otherwise have gone undetected. In 1993, the electronic engineering student from Israel was informed that the mass they had uncovered was situated close to areas of the brain essential for movement and thought. He was then faced with a decision: to undergo complex, invasive surgery with a risk of paralysis, or to seek an alternative solution. After a year of searching, Mr Yaron found a surgeon in New York who successfully removed part of the tumour, and tests revealed it was benign. The engineer was subsequently advised to wait until technological advancements made the next operation less risky. However, for Mr Yaron, this was not feasible. The potential remained for it to exert pressure on parts of the brain as it grew. He stated: I was young and considering starting a family. I could not remain passive with this sword hanging over my head. After five years of consulting key surgeons and technology experts, Mr Yaron had the remainder of the tumour removed through a conventional operation, with positive results. Yet, this extensive search for improved surgical options continued to occupy his thoughts. He persistently contemplated and experimented with methods to perform brain surgery in a less invasive manner. Over recent years, he perfected a technique to conduct surgery on the brain in 3D. In the past 25 years, minimally invasive surgery has become routine for relatively accessible areas of the body, such as keyhole surgery on the abdomen and womb. More recently, surgeons have also been able to utilise scopes (tube-like instruments) in brain surgery. During these procedures, a thin scope is inserted through a surgically-made or naturally-occurring port in the skin. A camera attached to the end of the scope transmits images to a screen for the surgeon to view. Surgical instruments are then passed through the scopes to collect tissue samples or remove masses. Early versions allowed surgeons to view 2D images in standard definition, evolving over the last decade into higher definition systems. Surgeons constantly convert these 2D images into 3D as they operate, similar to how we perceive 2D television screens. Recently, 3D technology has become available for certain types of operations. However, achieving 3D brain surgery has been significantly more challenging. In neurosurgery, the scopes must be very small in diameter to pass through narrow ports such as the nose. text: After leaders of the billion-euro Human Brain Project hit back at critics, six top neuroscientists have expressed dismay at their public response. These are external links and will open in a new window. Last week, an open message signed by over 600 researchers claimed the HBP was not on course and called for a review. An official response stated HBP members were saddened by the protest, while Prof Henry Markram, the project's chair, described it as a personal crusade. In a letter to Nature, the six authors urged a more open-minded attitude. They did not sign the original protest letter but are disappointed by the publicly reported stance of the HBP leadership. Instead of acknowledging that there is a problem and genuinely seeking to address scientists' concerns, the project leaders seem to be of the opinion that the letter's 580 signatories [now over 600] are misguided, wrote Prof Richard Morris, a prominent neuroscientist from the University of Edinburgh, and five colleagues. The six correspondents describe themselves as neuroscientists in Europe who care about the success of research projects large and small in our field. Prof Richard Frackowiak, a co-executive director of the HBP, told the BBC he strongly objects to the notion that the project leaders were dismissive. We've taken this extremely seriously, he said. The HBP is one of two flagship technology projects (the other being graphene research) announced in January 2013 by the European Commission (EC). In an open message to the EC, hundreds of neuroscientists last week expressed concern at the narrow scientific focus and closed management style of the project's leaders. They demanded an independent review and pledged to boycott HBP-related funding if not heeded. The HBP team issued a response, stating [Our members] are saddened by the open letter... as we feel that it divides rather than unifies our efforts to understand the brain. However, we recognise that the signatories have important concerns about the project. But in a subsequent email to the BBC, project figurehead Prof Henry Markram, from the EPFL (Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne) in Switzerland, questioned the motivation behind the letter. He suggested it was driven largely by one person - Dr Zachary Mainen, the Director of the Champalimaud Neuroscience Programme in Portugal. He pointed out that Dr Mainen was among a group of cognitive scientists who were repositioned outside the core of the project. We have issued a formal response to explain the project better, but we will no longer be taking his Open Letter seriously, Prof Markram wrote. Other signatories - and now, it seems, interested observers like the six neuroscientists who have written to Nature - disagree. You don't get the support of 600 people if it's a one man crusade, said Dr Alexandre Pouget from the University of Geneva, who helped Dr Mainen organise the open message. Dr Pouget was involved in the HBP before it received the flagship funding but withdrew, along with several colleagues, in 2012. It was originally supposed to have a big theory component, but many of us were worried about the increasing focus on simulations, he told BBC News. Prof Frackowiak conceded that perhaps communication within the project could have been more proactive, but said its leadership had been far from autocratic. We remain a project that is totally open and is building infrastructures for the use of the whole community, he said. We're going through a process of construction. Our governance procedures are evolving. The structure at the top of the project would soon change, Prof Frackowiak explained, with the appointment of a new chair whose role will be separate from Prof Markram, who will act as a CEO. A US politician has also stepped in to defend the project. Congressman Chaka Fattah, who is a supporter of the HBP's transatlantic counterpart the BRAIN Initiative, wrote in the Huffington Post, The Human Brain Project is large and ambitious, and as a result has the potential to be a disruptive force in a field that for far too long has been narrowly focused on an incremental approach. The EC has responded to the open message, thanking the authors for their feedback and pointing to a rigorous annual review scheduled for January 2015. Asked whether that review would be transparent and independent, as requested by the signatories, a spokesperson told the BBC it would take into account the requests contained in the open letter... while respecting the existing rules which are related to data protection. Dr Pouget said he and Dr Mainen had met with the head of the EC's FET (Future and Emerging Technologies) Flagships Unit, which funds both the HBP and the Graphene Flagship. It was very positive, said Dr Pouget. I'm still waiting to see what happens next. We certainly hope that the European Commission will take this crisis seriously. What happened last week is very unusual. Prof Frackowiak does not see the situation as a crisis. I think this has been good, because it's raised the issue in the public eye, he said. Our next scientific review will be in January and we're looking forward to it.

text: Six young voters from Wales who took part in an election debate geared around young people have described it as brilliant to a lot of hot air. More than 100 individuals aged 18-24 engaged with five politicians in the debate organised by BBC's Newsbeat. Trust was the primary issue, but tuition fees, gender equality, and the voting age were also prominent topics. Voters were accompanied by politicians from five major parties at Leeds City Museum on Tuesday evening. Sam Gyimah from the Conservatives, Sadiq Khan of Labour, Sal Brinton from the Liberal Democrats, Mhairi Black of the SNP, and Rhun ap Iorwerth from Plaid Cymru were all under scrutiny. BBC Wales followed six Welsh audience members to gather their opinions on the debate. Guto Gwilym, 21, Lampeter It was excellent to have that one hour focused solely on young people and our issues. It was very much an evening where politicians listened to us, and I sincerely hope they have been taking notes. For me, one urgent matter we need to address now is diversity among MPs. Aled Illtud, 20, Aberystwyth It was pleasant to witness a different kind of debate—it was much more dynamic. I did feel there were more questions than answers, but that perhaps reflects the passion of the audience members. We seemed to have a barrage of questions directed at the politicians. It was impressive to see, but I would have appreciated more answers from the politicians. Peter Gillibrand, 18, Carmarthen I believe the debate focused excessively on tuition fees. I would have preferred to hear more about what politicians would do for disabled individuals like my brother. He is severely autistic, but funding for many of the services he uses has been reduced. I am a Plaid Cymru voter, but I think the true winners of this debate were the SNP and Lib Dems. The SNP representative was truly inspirational, and the Lib Dem representative also made a good impression. She admitted, 'we made a mistake on tuition fees,' but you felt she genuinely cared about young people. Robyn Holley, 21, Cwmbran It was everything I anticipated it to be—people shouting, numerous opinions swirling around, and politicians just being politicians. I was not impressed by what they had to say—it was merely a lot of empty rhetoric. I have considered not voting, but I think I will probably participate if only to attempt to effect change. Gwion Dafydd, 20, Pembrokeshire I think a few politicians said the right things. I appreciated that Labour, Plaid Cymru, and the Lib Dems all supported lowering the voting age for 16 and 17-year-olds. It shows they care about what young people have to say. I have gained more respect for some of the parties now. Rhys Taylor, 21, Bangor I stood up and made a comment during the discussion on tuition fees. I think it's important that politicians admit when they've made a mistake and apologise if they cannot fulfil their promises. It's not often that we hear politicians apologising, but the more we can get them to acknowledge their mistakes, the more we will be able to trust them.

text: When BBC Alba was launched in 2008, as a collaboration between the BBC and the Gaelic TV body MG Alba, it was a huge achievement for supporters of the Gaelic language. They had long contended that a dedicated channel would offer a superior service for Gaelic speakers compared to individual Gaelic programmes on the major channels. They also maintained that a dedicated Gaelic channel could significantly contribute to safeguarding the future of the language itself. Uniquely for a BBC service within the UK, it is a joint venture. Some of the programmes are funded by the BBC, while others fall under the responsibility of MG Alba, which is financed by government funds. However, there was disappointment when it became evident that the channel would only be broadcast on satellite TV, which is viewed in 43% of Scottish homes, although programmes can also be accessed online via the BBC iPlayer. Supporters argued it was essential for the channel to also be broadcast on Freeview, like all other public service channels. BBC management devised a plan to make this feasible. The drawback was that it would necessitate the removal of the BBC's radio stations from Freeview whenever BBC Alba was on air. The BBC Trust postponed a decision earlier this year as it was also scheduled to conduct a broader review on how all BBC services should be broadcast. It has now endorsed the scheme following extensive research, although no date has been set for BBC Alba's appearance on Freeview. Some are hopeful it will appear on Freeview by the time the digital switchover occurs in central Scotland next May and June. In practice, BBC Alba will be available in almost every home in Scotland, and the challenge for the station will be to demonstrate that it can offer value to as many people as possible and appeal to viewers who do not speak Gaelic. Some newspaper commentators have claimed it is challenging for Alba to prove it is achieving this, as standard viewing figures are not available for the station. Instead, other forms of research have been utilised. It is understood one reason for this is that the sample used to compile standard ratings does not include viewers in the islands of Scotland. Although the BBC's radio stations will no longer be broadcast on Freeview once this occurs, it is possible they may return in the future due to technological advancements. Despite this, the main radio stations will still be broadcast on FM and medium wave as usual, while the digital stations—such as 1 Extra and BBC7—will still be available on satellite, cable, through digital radios, and online. Deciding between the merits of BBC Alba and the radio stations was a challenging decision. However, the alternative could have involved the BBC purchasing capacity on another part of the Freeview system at commercial rates—capacity which might not have been able to reach viewers served by relay transmitters. The BBC Trust has also ruled that Gaelic programmes should remain on BBC Two Scotland, although it will no longer be designated as the BBC's key channel for Gaelic. However, the scheduling of Gaelic on BBC Two Scotland is changing. Gaelic programmes were broadcast in a two-hour block on Thursday evenings until recently. Individual programmes are now appearing in various slots across the schedule, although the overall amount of Gaelic in peak viewing hours should remain the same.

text: Pirelli will be told to produce a tyre drivers can push to the limit in 2017 as Formula 1 bosses seek to make the sport more exciting. It has been granted 12 days for this purpose in 2016. The BBC has discovered that the FIA, which regulates F1, will direct Pirelli to create a tyre enabling drivers to maintain high speeds for longer durations. Pirelli chairman Marco Tronchetti Provera informed teams and drivers at a meeting earlier this month, where dissatisfaction with the current tyres was addressed, that it could produce whatever F1 desired, provided it received a clear mandate. Pirelli has received preliminary data regarding the expected performance of the cars in 2017 to commence tyre design work. The FIA intends to specify its tyre performance expectations and will supply all necessary information to the company by the end of March. Pirelli entered F1 in 2011 and was tasked with ensuring races featured multiple pit stops. It achieved this by creating tyres prone to thermal degradation. These tyres begin to lose performance above a certain temperature and do not regain it. Consequently, drivers often race below the limit throughout most races to manage the tyres and achieve optimal race times. Occasionally, they cannot even push to the limit during a qualifying lap due to the need to maintain the tyres below their temperature threshold. Drivers have consistently disliked this, but the issue escalated last season after two 200mph tyre failures at the Belgian Grand Prix. Alexander Wurz, chairman of the Grand Prix Drivers' Association, recently informed BBC Sport that drivers desire tyres fit for maximum-attack racing. Pirelli has altered the tyre characteristics for 2016 in an effort to make it less predictable when they lose grip. It hopes this development will allow drivers to push harder. However, world champion Lewis Hamilton is unimpressed with the new tyres after testing them this week in Barcelona. It's definitely not better, that's for sure, he stated. It just feels like a harder tyre and it's not providing me with any more grip. I think I preferred last year's. Plans to accelerate the cars for 2017 were briefly disrupted when Pirelli stated it would have to run its tyres at unusually high pressures to handle the planned increases in cornering forces. Teams and the FIA began working on a diluted set of changes, only for analysis to reveal these would not achieve performance targets. New rules agreed this week represent a compromise, based on a proposal from McLaren. The objective is to have a greater share of the aerodynamic downforce generated by the underfloor and to increase mechanical grip. The cars will be widened in both the lateral distance between the wheels and the bodywork, while tyres will be enlarged. The expectation is that cars will be four to five seconds per lap faster in 2017.

French fighter jets are already participating in strikes in Iraq, with Belgium and the Netherlands each committing six F-16 aircraft and Denmark deploying seven. Speaking at the Pentagon, General Dempsey remarked that this week's strikes in Syria had disrupted IS's command, control, and logistics capabilities. He noted that more than air power would be needed to reclaim lost territory in Syria and neighbouring Iraq, but a ground force need not involve US troops. In fact, ideally for the kind of issues we are confronting there, the only truly effective force that will actually be able to reject ISIL (IS) from within its own population is a force comprised of Iraqis and Kurds and moderate Syrian opposition, he stated. Approximately 40 countries, including several from the Middle East, have joined the US-led coalition against IS. European nations have thus far only agreed to strike targets in Iraq, where the government has requested assistance. text: An NHS trust has apologised unreservedly after a misdiagnosis resulted in a three-year-old boy having his legs and seven fingers amputated. Lou Harvey-Smith took her son Reuben to Ipswich Hospital in July 2015 after he sustained a burn. Two days later, she returned with him due to a fever and was informed he had tonsillitis. He was subsequently diagnosed with toxic shock syndrome and underwent amputations. The trust admitted full liability and settlement negotiations are ongoing. After being treated at the hospital for the burn, Reuben developed a fever and sore throat. Ms Harvey-Smith took him back and was prescribed antibiotics for tonsillitis. The next day, the child was critically ill. His mother contacted the burns unit at Chelsea and Westminster Hospital for a second opinion. Doctors suspected toxic shock, a life-threatening infection likely caused by bacteria entering the wound and releasing toxins into Reuben's blood. The boy was rushed back to Ipswich Hospital and then transferred to St Mary's Hospital in Paddington, London, where staff performed the amputations. Ms Harvey-Smith, 41, from Chelmondiston, near Ipswich, said: [Reuben] looked at his amputated legs and said 'poorly feet gone, get new ones.' He just accepts it and gets on with things. However, she pursued legal action against Ipswich Hospital NHS Trust, which admitted toxic shock was a significant possibility based on the child's symptoms at the time, and amputation could have been avoided with earlier diagnosis and treatment. Ms Harvey-Smith's solicitor, Tim Deeling, stated: It is extremely concerning they were aware of the link between burns and toxic shock, yet didn't consider this for Reuben's case. The trust has made an interim payment of £50,000. A spokesman said: In an ongoing legal case, the trust has admitted full liability for shortcomings in the A&E care provided to Reuben in July 2015 and have offered an unreserved apology. Further training has been provided to staff in recognising the warning signs of septic shock syndrome, he stated. The trust was committed to ensuring that Reuben is appropriately compensated so that he has the care, prostheses and equipment that he needs throughout his life, he added.

text: The maker of the EpiPen will start selling a generic version in the wake of criticism about steep price increases. text: Former England captain David Beckham is being cast away for the 75th birthday celebrations of BBC Radio 4's Desert Island Discs next weekend. More than 3,000 guests have appeared on the show since it first aired on 29 January 1942. Presenter Kirsty Young stated that having Beckham select his favourite tracks for the anniversary show was the perfect gift. Beckham, aged 41, remarked that music has been a huge part of his family's life. He is married to former Spice Girl singer turned fashion designer Victoria Beckham, and the couple's youngest son Cruz, aged 11, released a Christmas-themed single last month. It is not yet confirmed if he has chosen any of his wife's hits with the pop group, or any of her solo projects. What is Desert Island Discs? Beckham expressed: I'm delighted to join Desert Island Discs for its 75th anniversary celebrations. Music has been a huge part of my - and my family's - life and it is a real pleasure to highlight that on such an iconic programme. Young commented on her guest: His sporting legacy is of course extraordinary. And along with his charisma, cultural impact and humanitarian work, he is a modern man of many parts. He'll be a fascinating guest to welcome on to my little interview island. Desert Island Discs' anniversary will be commemorated with a three-hour programme on BBC Radio 4 Extra on 28 January, presented by Young, featuring some of the guests from past shows. They include Cilla Black, discussing her early career singing with The Beatles, and Richard Dimbleby, recounting taking a cutlery set from Hitler's bunker after being one of the first correspondents to visit it following the dictator's death. Extracts from recently rediscovered episodes that are being added to the show's online archive will also be featured. The show featuring Beckham will reintroduce the sound of the sea to the opening and closing of the programme for the first time since the 1960s. BBC Radio 4 and Radio 4 Extra controller Gwyneth Williams stated: A sure way to uncover an elusive British national identity is to listen to this programme week after week. The broad range of guests is a measure of contemporary talent and achievement, and the music opens up different eras and prompts emotional memory in all of us.
