text: India's Supreme Court has struck down a controversial law which allowed police to arrest people for comments on social networks and other internet sites. The court has declared the controversial Section 66A of the Information Technology Act unconstitutional. In recent years, numerous individuals have been arrested for their remarks on Facebook or Twitter, causing public outrage. The government defended the law, claiming it aimed to prevent the uploading of offensive material. Tuesday's ruling was issued by a two-judge bench of the Supreme Court on petitions from civil rights groups and a law student who argued that Section 66A infringed upon people's fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression. Section 66A is unconstitutional, and we have no hesitation in striking it down, news agency AFP quoted Justice RF Nariman as stating in court. The public's right to know is directly affected by Section 66A, he added. Section 66A was extensive in its powers, allowing for a three-year jail term for sending an email or electronic message that causes annoyance or inconvenience. The law was first contested by a law student after two young women were arrested in November 2012 in Mumbai for Facebook comments following politician Bal Thackeray's death. Shaheen Dhada was detained for criticising Mumbai's shutdown after Thackeray's death. Renu Srinivasan, who liked the comment, was also arrested. Both were later released on bail. The arrests provoked outrage in India, with many demanding the law be abolished. Since then, there have been several other arrests under the law, resulting in accusations of misuse. Within minutes of Tuesday's court ruling, #Sec66A was trending on Twitter, with many Indians praising the decision. Delhi's governing Aam Aadmi Party welcomed the ruling. Journalist Swati Vashishtha stated that the right to dissent was the most crucial right for citizens. Popular author Chetan Bhagat expressed he was super happy. Pankaj Pachauri, communications advisor to former prime minister Manmohan Singh, remarked good riddance to the law.

text: The issue of foreign prisoners in England's jails has long been a contentious one. It cost Charles Clarke his position as Home Secretary when it was revealed in 2006 that over 1,000 foreign prisoners who should have been deported had not been. It has also been the focus of several select committee inquiries. The issue continues to trouble the Conservative MP for Kettering, Philip Hollobone. Throughout his tenure as an MP, he has expressed concerns about the number of foreigners in British prisons and the failure to repatriate them to serve their sentences. Recently, a government minister not only commended him for his campaign but also admitted that he shares Mr Hollobone's frustration. Mike Penning, Minister for Policing and Criminal Justice, informed Parliament that during briefings with officials, he was very surprised... about some of the things that are being done and found it mind-bogglingly difficult to work out why, in many cases, things do not happen. He was responding to a debate initiated by Mr Hollobone, who presented new figures on the scale of the issue. He informed MPs that there are 10,837 foreign national offenders in British prisons, comprising 13% of the prison population. The highest number of offenders (938) are from Poland, followed by Ireland (779) and Jamaica (737). The cost of maintaining them, he stated, was north of £300m annually. Such individuals need to serve their sentences in secure detention in prisons in their own country, he stated. At a time of severe constraints on public expenditure, that is far too large a bill to ask British taxpayers to pay. Mr Hollobone is particularly incensed that many of these countries lack prisoner transfer agreements with the UK. A compulsory agreement with Jamaica is still pending ratification by the Jamaican government; there is only a voluntary agreement with Pakistan and India, and no agreement with Somalia or Bangladesh or several EU countries, including Poland. Poland, which is top of the list with almost 1,000 of its nationals in our prisons, has a specific derogation from accepting prisoner transfers under that EU agreement until the end of December 2016, said Mr Hollobone. That is an absolute outrage. Poland should be securing those people in secure detention back in Poland, at the expense of Polish taxpayers. He is also advocating for the British government to utilise the huge and increasing international aid budget to build suitable prisons in countries that provide us with a large number of prisoners. He has discovered that in 2012, the UK provided £973m in aid to Jamaica, Pakistan, Nigeria, Somalia, India, and Bangladesh, which have a total of 2,900 of their citizens in British jails. It costs this country more than £100m a year to incarcerate these people in our jails. It would be a good idea to spend some of that £973m on building prisons in those six countries, he argued. Mr Penning admitted that he had been advised by his officials to ensure that I stuck to the line and read the speech, which I will not do. He further admitted that he agreed with nearly everything Mr Hollobone had stated: The frustration that he can hear in my voice was in his voice. I share his frustration. The minister expressed his desire for as many foreign nationals as possible to serve their sentences in their country of origin and added that it was important that our friends in Europe fulfil their commitments. I agree that we have to work much harder because this matter has been ignored for too many years, he said. Eight years, in fact, since Charles Clarke was compelled to resign, and it appears it could be the same again until any resolution is found.

Mr Hollobone was particularly indignant that many of these countries had no prisoner-transfer agreements with the United Kingdom. The irritation that he had heard in my voice he heard in his own. “It would be good if we used part of this nine hundred and seventy-three million francs to build prisons in those six countries,” he said. “This country spends more than a hundred million francs a year on imprisoning them in our prisons.” I share his irritation. I agree that we must do much more than we have for so many years,” he said. He confessed that his officials had warned him to keep me in line and read my speech, but I won’t. text: A petition calling for Nathan Gill to be removed as UKIP Wales leader has been sent to the party's ruling body. It follows allegations that party leaders wish to impose candidates from outside Wales for the assembly election. Six general election candidates signed the petition, which asserts there is no coherent plan to contest the campaign and no effective leadership in Wales. UKIP has questioned the petition's credibility, with its Wales chairman stating disgruntled members signed it. Numerous Welsh activists have objected to former Conservative MPs Mark Reckless and Neil Hamilton being considered for selection, accusing the party of parachuting them in. Earlier in February, Mr Gill announced that local members would determine the rankings of candidates for regional list seats, rather than the party's national executive committee. However, some Welsh members remain dissatisfied with how the issue has been managed, with UKIP Vale of Glamorgan councillor Kevin Mahoney resigning from the party. It is understood by all that UKIP in Wales operates on the basis of mutual respect and understanding, the petition states. In light of the extraordinary circumstances prevailing and indeed, as a last resort, to prevent further harm and disharmony within 'the party' it is necessary to censure and remove those responsible forthwith. The petition accused Mr Gill of demonstrating a lack of leadership in all aspects pertaining to this matter. It stated through his inactivity or unwillingness to resolve the prevailing circumstances, [he] has exacerbated the situation to the point where members no longer have faith in his ability to lead UKIP in Wales in any effective way. UKIP general election candidates supporting the petition were Joe Smyth (Islwyn), Darran Thomas (Brecon and Radnorshire), Ken Beswick (Torfaen), Blair Smillie (Alyn and Deeside), Nigel Williams (Delyn), and Paul Davies Cooke (Vale of Clwyd). Mr Williams, one of the petition organisers, said it was better late than never to express their concerns with the assembly election so imminent. He called for a leadership election, stating UKIP Wales could choose any one from ten great people but Wales chairman David Rowlands said it adds nothing to the debate. Gethin James, a UKIP councillor and assembly election candidate for Ceredigion, told BBC Radio Cymru: It's not a good situation, but I'm 100% behind Nathan Gill. People don't know how much work he's done. The problem is with the national executive, not with Nathan Gill. On Tuesday, Mr Gill told BBC Wales he had no intention of resigning, stating claims that he had failed to support rank-and-file members in Wales were nonsense. A UKIP Wales spokesman said: Despite efforts of one or two individuals phoning around the party membership in Wales, their petty 26-person petition included someone from England, six people who were not even members and a growing number who denied ever signing it.

text: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and what is now known as the World Bank, were set up to manage the post-World War II global economy. These are external links and will open in a new window. They were conceived in 1944 at a conference in Bretton Woods, in the US state of New Hampshire. By promoting economic cooperation and assisting countries with balance of payments issues, the founders aimed to prevent a recurrence of the 1930s Great Depression. The IMF seeks to maintain economic stability and address - or ideally avert - financial crises. Over time, its focus has shifted to the developing world. The World Bank's predecessor - the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development - was established to promote post-war recovery. Now, it stands as the world's leading development organisation, advocating for growth and poverty alleviation. Owned by the governments of its 187 member states, the Bank provides loans and grants and offers advice to low and middle-income countries. The IMF is financed by a charge - known as a quota - paid by member nations. The quota is based on a nation's wealth and determines voting power within the organisation; those contributing more have greater voting rights. The IMF serves as a lender of last resort, disbursing its foreign exchange reserves for short periods to any member in difficulty. Since their inception, the IMF has been led by a European and the World Bank by a US national. The IMF and the Bank have become focal points for various causes - from environmentalists to anarchists - and meetings have sometimes been accompanied by violent street protests. Protesters and critics cite the exploitation of the poor and the environment, arguing that freer trade threatens the livelihoods of millions. The IMF has acknowledged that compelling developing countries to open their markets to foreign investors can heighten the risk of financial crises. Its former managing director Horst Koehler stated in 2002 that the benefits of globalisation had not been equally distributed. However, he added that the objective should not be less globalisation but more and better globalisation. Conceived: Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, USA. Date: 1944. Headquarters: Washington DC. IMF-World Bank membership: 187 countries. World Bank staff: 10,000. IMF staff: 2,500. IMF managing director: Christine Lagarde. Christine Lagarde is the first woman to lead the IMF in the organisation's 65-year history. She trained as a lawyer and worked for over two decades at a Chicago-based international law firm, specialising in major labour and anti-trust cases. She served as French trade minister from 2005 to 2007, when she was appointed finance minister, becoming the first woman to hold such a post in any of the G8 major industrial countries. Ms Lagarde assumed leadership of the IMF in July 2011 during a period of significant challenges, with the eurozone in deep crisis and fears that countries such as Greece might default on their loans. Never hesitant to express her views, she has partly attributed the 2008 global financial crisis to the male-dominated, testosterone-driven culture at global banks. She is highly regarded internationally and was named best finance minister in Europe by the Financial Times in 2009. She has committed to enhancing diversity at the IMF and advancing reforms to grant emerging economies more influence within the organisation. She succeeded Dominique Strauss-Kahn, who resigned over charges of sexual assault, from which he was later cleared. World Bank president: Jim Yong Kim. Jim Yong Kim was appointed as the new president of the World Bank in April 2012. The Korean-American health expert was president of Dartmouth College in the US state of New Hampshire. He faced a strong challenge for the position, traditionally held by an American, from Nigerian Finance Minister Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala. Dr Kim succeeded Robert Zoellick and is serving a five-year term. Jim Yong Kim is a doctor acclaimed for his pioneering work in treating HIV/Aids and mitigating the impact of tuberculosis in the developing world. The IMF and World Bank strive to assist countries or regions in economic turmoil - often acting as a lender of last resort for nation-states. Past IMF interventions have included providing funds for countries affected by the 1997 Asian financial crisis and loans to help South American countries like Argentina and Brazil avoid debt default crises. In October 2008, the IMF activated an emergency funding scheme for countries facing economic distress due to the global financial crisis. As of August 2010, it had committed around $200bn in lending to several economies impacted by the crisis. The largest borrowers then were Hungary, Romania, and Ukraine. The recent eurozone crisis also prompted extensive IMF intervention, including substantial bailouts for countries such as Greece, Portugal, and Ireland in collaboration with the European Union. It is currently contributing to the second international bailout of Greece and discussing further loans to Hungary. The IMF can also provide emergency loans following natural disasters; these have included the 2004 Asian tsunami. Developing countries have expressed dissatisfaction with what they perceive as their lack of influence in the IMF and World Bank. This includes the so-called Bric countries - Brazil, Russia, India, and China - whose economic power has grown significantly. They have called for changes to the quota system, where votes in the IMF are weighted according to member nations' financial contributions. Under this system, the US holds 17% of the vote in the IMF, while India, with more than three times the US population, has less than one third. And because constitutional changes in the IMF require 85% of the vote, the US has a veto. The long-standing arrangement under which the IMF is typically led by a European, while the World Bank is led by an American, has also been questioned. Ms Lagarde swiftly appointed Zhu Min - a former deputy governor of the People's Bank of China - to the newly created post of deputy managing director upon assuming her role.

text: The landlocked mountainous region of Nagorno-Karabakh is the subject of an unresolved dispute between Azerbaijan, in which it lies, and its ethnic Armenian majority, backed by neighbouring Armenia. In 1988, near the end of Soviet rule, Azerbaijani troops and Armenian secessionists initiated a bloody conflict, resulting in the de facto independent state being controlled by ethnic Armenians when a truce was signed in 1994. Negotiations have yet to yield a lasting peace agreement, and the dispute remains one of post-Soviet Europe's frozen conflicts. The conflict's origins extend back over a century into competition between Christian Armenian and Muslim Turkic and Persian influences. Populated for centuries by Christian Armenians and Turkic Azeris, Karabakh became part of the Russian Empire in the 19th century. Profile compiled by BBC Monitoring. The two groups coexisted in relative peace, although acts of brutality on both sides in the early 20th century persist in popular memory. Following World War I and the Bolshevik revolution in Russia, the new Soviet rulers, as part of their divide-and-rule policy in the region, established the Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Region, with an ethnic Armenian majority, within the Soviet Socialist Republic of Azerbaijan in the early 1920s. As Soviet control weakened towards the end of the 1980s, simmering Armenian-Azeri tensions erupted into violence when the region's parliament voted to join Armenia. During the fighting, in which an estimated 20,000 to 30,000 people lost their lives, the ethnic Armenians gained control of the region. They also advanced to occupy Azerbaijani territory outside Karabakh, creating a buffer zone linking Karabakh and Armenia. With the dissolution of the Soviet Union in late 1991, Karabakh declared itself an independent republic, further escalating the conflict into a full-scale war. That de facto status has not been recognised internationally. While Armenia itself has never officially recognised the region's independence, it has become its primary financial and military supporter. A Russian-brokered ceasefire was signed in 1994, leaving Karabakh and large areas of Azeri territory around the enclave in Armenian hands. During the fighting, in which more than one million people fled their homes, the ethnic Azeri population—about 25% of the total before the war—fled Karabakh and Armenia, while ethnic Armenians fled the rest of Azerbaijan. Neither population group has been able to return home since the war's end. Karabakh is the Russian rendering of an Azeri word meaning 'black garden', while Nagorno is a Russian word meaning mountainous. The ethnic Armenians prefer to call the region Artsakh, an ancient Armenian name for the area. Both sides have suffered soldier casualties in sporadic ceasefire breaches. The closure of borders with Turkey and Azerbaijan has caused landlocked Armenia severe economic difficulties. Since the truce, a simmering stalemate has prevailed. Azeris resent the loss of land they consider rightfully theirs, while the Armenians show no inclination to return it. Russia, France, and the US co-chair the OSCE's Minsk Group, which has been attempting to broker an end to the dispute. In a December 2006 referendum, declared illegitimate by Azerbaijan, the region approved a new constitution. Nonetheless, there have been signs of life in the peace process, with occasional meetings between the Armenian and Azeri presidents. Significant progress was reported at talks between the leaders in May and November 2009, but progress stalled, and since then there have been several serious ceasefire violations. The most serious occurred in April 2016, when dozens of soldiers on both sides died in a fresh outbreak of hostilities.

After World War I and the Bolshevik Revolution in Russia, the new Soviet government, as part of its policy of division and occupation in the Caucasus, established in the early twenties in the Socialist Republic of Azerbaijan, an autonomous region of Nagorno-Karabakh, with an ethnically Armenian majority. After fighting, in which between twenty and thirty thousand people died, the region was occupied by Armenians. At the end of the '80s, when the waning of the Soviet system began to manifest itself in the Caucasus, the Armenians occupied the region. Karabakh declared independence at the collapse of the Soviet Union, in the autumn of 1991, and thus raised the conflict to a war. It also occupied lands of Azerbaijan around Karabakh, which have since become a buffer between Karabakh and Armenia. This independence was only de facto, and has not been recognized internationally. In the year 1994 a cease-fire was negotiated by the Russians, and Karabakh and large areas of Azerbaijani territory around the enclave passed to the control of the Armenians. In the course of the fighting, during which more than a million people were forcibly displaced, approximately one quarter of the Azeri population (one million or one million three hundred thousand) fled from Armenia to Karabakh, while from Azerbaijan the ethnic Armenians fled from Armenia to Karabakh.1 Although Armenia has not yet recognized the independence of Karabakh, it is its principal financial and military support. Since the truce, the simmering stalemate has continued. Karabakh is the Russian transcription of the Azeri word for 'black garden', Nagorno is the Russian word for'mountainous'; and the Armenians of Artsakh prefer to call it by its ancient Armenian name. Since the war, neither group has been able to return home. At the end of December 2006, the region voted for a new constitution, which was deemed illegal by Azerbaijan. Both sides have suffered casualties in the sporadic violation of the cease-fire. The Armenian border with Turkey and Azerbaijan is closed, causing serious economic difficulties for the landlocked country. Despite all this, the peace process continues to move forward; occasional meetings take place between the presidents of Armenia and Azerbaijan. Azerbaijan resents the loss of the land it considers its own, and the Armenians do not wish to return it. Russia, France and the United States are the co-chairs of the Minsk Group, which is trying to resolve the conflict. The negotiations between the two leaders in May and November, 2009, had a positive outcome, but then a stalemate occurred in the negotiations, and since then several breaches of the ceasefire have occurred, the worst being in April this year, when dozens of soldiers on both sides were killed in renewed fighting.

text: Tortoises, Roald Dahl and the man behind Love Actually are just three of the ingredients in Esio Trot, a romantic comedy for BBC One starring Dustin Hoffman and Dame Judi Dench. Collectively, 77-year-old Dustin Hoffman, 79-year-old Dame Judi Dench, and Richard Curtis—considered youthful at 58—have a combined age of over 214 years. However, as Dame Judi remarks, age is merely a figure, particularly in a new TV comedy drama that demonstrates one can still discover love later in life. Based on Roald Dahl's 1990 children's novel, Esio Trot narrates the story of a solitary London bachelor whose attention is captured by the flirtatious widow residing directly below him. Her fondness for tortoises appears to be an insurmountable obstacle to their romantic prospects—until Mr Hoppy (Hoffman) devises an unusual method to capture Mrs Silver's (Dench) attention. The fact that Esio Trot is 'tortoise' spelled backwards hints at the nature of Mr Hoppy's plan, for those yet to read Dahl's 1990 original for their own enjoyment or their children's. Suffice it to say that reading backwards plays a crucial role in a narrative that also features James Corden as the neighbour who acts as the story's guide and narrator. Curtis, known for successes such as Four Weddings and a Funeral, Notting Hill, and the Blackadder TV series, confesses to being a huge fan of an author he compares to Charles Dickens. Adapting Esio Trot, however, was particularly enticing as it enabled him to explore something about love between older people. I was writing all these films about people for whom, if it doesn't work out, they can try again, he told reporters in November. But if you're older and lonely, the stakes are higher. I wanted to do something about people finding love who both presumed they wouldn't. I thought that would make it even more dramatic. Curtis's enthusiasm for the project was shared by Dame Judi, who stated she wanted to play Mrs Silver unconditionally even if the character is somewhat stupid. After they said Dustin's name I would have come in to walk across the street, says the actress, who will appear next year in the sequel to the box office hit The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel. That film, like Esio Trot, focused on mature characters who are relatively under-represented by an industry that often favours storylines aimed at a younger audience. It is not a situation with which Dench is content. Age is a number that's imposed on you, she asserts firmly. It's that thing that everyone says—'you're as old as you feel.' It drives me absolutely spare when people say 'Are you going to retire?' or 'Don't you think it's time you put your feet up?' I don't want to be told I'm too old to do something, continues Dench, who won an Oscar for Shakespeare in Love in 1999 and portrayed M in seven James Bond films. I want to try it first. It's not to do with age; it's to do with the engine. As long as you keep it going, you won't fall over. Falling over was a genuine concern for Hoffman in a scene in Esio Trot where he and Dame Judi dance to music by jazz legend Louis Armstrong. I'm not a dancer, nowhere near it, admits the veteran US star of The Graduate, Tootsie, and many other classic films. I thought after the first two lessons it wasn't going to work and I wasn't going to be ready. But it wasn't a problem because [Mr Hoppy] wasn't supposed to know how to dance, he continued. We were just naturally doing it. Hoffman is full of admiration for his latest screen partner, describing Dench as an extraordinary talent with great energy who allows you right into her bone marrow. Yet he is less enthusiastic about his other co-stars—the large group of tortoises who assist Mr Hoppy in his romantic endeavour. You've never smelled anything until you've smelled 60 tortoises, he sighs. That tortoise poo was the real thing—there was no CGI for us. I always get warm [on set] so I always want air conditioning, Hoffman continues. We brought in these big machines, but by the third day we weren't using them anymore. It was all because of the tortoises. If they get too cold, they won't act. So did Hoffman and Dench get to spend any time together when they weren't filming Esio Trot in London earlier this year? Judi wanted to socialise, but I was always too tired, says the former with a shrug. I don't socialise when I'm working, he adds. I don't socialise when I'm not working. Other than that, I love people! Esio Trot will be broadcast on BBC One on 1 January at 1830 GMT.

text: Pupils at a County Antrim school have developed a new tool to target cyberbullying. The new reporting system, named 'Step Up', is operational at Ballyclare High School and can be utilised at home, in school, or on a smartphone. The school asserts it is the first system of its kind in Northern Ireland. It allows pupils to raise concerns directly with the appropriate teacher via the school website. Emma Blacoe, aged 14, who contributed to its development, stated that teachers could receive extensive information about alleged incidents. Pupils can upload files and pictures of screenshots and chats if they feel someone's in danger, she mentioned. They can also simply report if they're being pressured or bullied or if anyone else is. When pupils click a button on the school website, they are directed to an online form where they specify their year group and who they wish to handle their concerns. The information they provide is visible only to themselves and teaching staff, and they can opt to disclose their name or remain anonymous. David Andrew, who also contributed to 'Step Up', remarked that it was user-friendly and accessible to pupils. If pupils genuinely feel there's something that needs resolution, they can address it, he stated. Bullying is never acceptable, and the sooner someone steps up, the sooner it can be resolved. The school's head of cyber safety, Mhairi Hill, said teachers would investigate every allegation they received information about. Staff will address it at the earliest opportunity and follow the existing procedure for dealing with incidents, she said. With online bullying, pupils can present us with screenshots, which serve as concrete evidence to advance the investigation. We would establish the facts before proceeding but would follow up every report. If a child has deemed it necessary to raise the concern, then it's worth pursuing in our view. We have a duty of care for our pupils, and if a pupil is upset or distressed in class, they're unlikely to learn to their full potential, so it's important that we address these issues.

text: Colombia's President Juan Manuel Santos has met 30 rebels of the ELN, the country's second largest armed group, who laid down their arms. Mr Santos described the development as a great step towards peace. The ELN, or National Liberation Army, is not involved in the peace talks with Colombia's largest rebel group, the Farc, but its leaders have shown interest in joining the negotiations. The government has maintained that the ELN must first release its hostages. Officials report that the left-wing group consists of approximately 1,500 members. The 30-member group surrendered their arms in the south-eastern region of Cauca. Speaking in Cali, Mr Santos personally welcomed the rebels, including three pregnant women, who surrendered their arms and equipment. This is what the [peace] process is about. So every member of the ELN and the Farc follows their path fighting for their ideals, but without violence and without arms, he stated. This is the largest single ELN contingent to surrender, Mr Santos noted. On Monday, Farc's chief peace negotiator remarked that the armed conflict, which has lasted nearly five decades, was nearing its conclusion. Ivan Marquez, participating in talks with the Colombian government in Cuba, urged left-wing parties and unions to join the effort to achieve peace. The government aims to sign a peace accord by November. However, Mr Marquez cautioned against hastily reaching a settlement. It is possible [to reach an agreement by November]. But to achieve peace you need time. A bad peace deal is worse than war, he said in an interview with Colombian network RCN. The first direct talks between Colombia's largest rebel group and the government commenced in November last year. Thus far, however, the ELN has been excluded from the talks. Chief government negotiator Humberto de la Calle stated that the objective of the Cuban peace talks was to persuade the rebels to abandon their armed struggle and engage in the political process. Agreement has already been reached on land reform, but negotiations are ongoing on five other agenda items. The Farc negotiator recently suggested that a Constitutional Assembly should be convened to endorse the agreements reached in Cuba. The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) are estimated to have around 8,000 fighters, down from approximately 16,000 in 2001. text: Nottingham Forest have made an approach to Burton Albion to speak with former player Nigel Clough in relation to their managerial vacancy. Clough, aged 50, played over 300 matches for the Reds across two periods, the first under his father Brian. He is currently in his second tenure as manager of Burton, having returned in December 2015 and led the Brewers to promotion to the Championship last season. Forest dismissed former manager Philippe Montanier on 14 January. Burton are three places below Forest, who are 19th and five points clear of the relegation zone, in the Championship. Forest declined to comment when approached by BBC Radio Nottingham, as did Burton when BBC Radio Derby sought a response. Clough addressed the speculation linking him with a move to Forest following Montanier's exit from the City Ground in his latest press conference. It's an easy and logical link from many perspectives, Clough stated to BBC Radio Derby on Wednesday. All these allegiances you have, yes they're strong, but in football, people often join rivals. It's challenging when you've spent 18 years—I'm just over 50 years old—so a third of my life associated with a certain club [Nottingham Forest]. Despite his connections to Forest, Clough has never managed the club since concluding his playing career. His popularity among fans only waned during his managerial stints at traditional rivals Derby County and Sheffield United. However, he was warmly welcomed when he returned with Burton for the EFL season opener in August, which Forest won 4-3. Clough may have been the son of manager Brian during much of his time at Forest, but his contributions ensured no awkwardness in the dressing room or derision from supporters. Only Grenville Morris has scored more than his 131 goals, and he was part of a late 1980s generation that made Wembley an almost annual spring destination. He scored twice in the 1989 League Cup final victory against Luton, the club's first trophy in nearly a decade, while his vision and skill made him the ideal partner to strikers such as Lee Chapman, Nigel Jemson, and Teddy Sheringham, earning him England honours. When his father departed the club at the end of a dismal 1992-93 season that concluded with relegation from the top division, Nigel left to join Liverpool after nine years of service, only to return on loan in an unsuccessful short-term effort to keep Forest in the top flight in 1996-97.

text: ScottishPower customers will soon be able to buy gas and electricity in bundles of days rather than signing up to standard or fixed-price deals. The system is modelled on how individuals refuel their vehicles with petrol or purchase data bundles for mobile phones. The company states it is an effort to simplify energy bills. ScottishPower chief executive Keith Anderson remarked: We're advising people to buy it by the day, not by kilowatts or a complex tariff you don't comprehend. Customers will utilise an app featuring a gauge to measure consumption. The company will customise each customer's day based on a personalised forecast of their typical energy usage. This will also fluctuate according to the season. Customers will have the option to purchase gas and electricity packages ranging from one day to a month, and up to 180 days in advance. The firm has been trialling the scheme and claims it could revolutionise how consumers purchase energy. Mr Anderson stated they started from scratch and examined how people purchase petrol for their vehicles. You visit the garage and put £50 in your car. You inherently know that will last two to three weeks. We thought, why not apply the same concept to energy? A fuel gauge within the app will inform customers of their energy usage and remaining balance. Under the scheme, named PowerUp, customers will not incur a standing charge. ScottishPower stated its tariffs for the scheme would feature some of the firm's most competitive prices. It will initially be launched to existing customers, and the company will then consider expanding it to the broader market. A two-year investigation into the energy industry by competition authorities revealed that many consumers were disengaged from the energy market and failed to switch to the cheapest deals. The new approach to purchasing energy has been endorsed by the industry regulator. In a statement, Ofgem expressed: We desire more competition to enhance choice and reduce prices for consumers. We encourage suppliers to offer new innovative tariffs to assist people in engaging with the market and finding the best deal that suits them. Innovative tariffs can be tailored to an individual consumer's needs and provide people with more control over their energy bill and payment methods. Claire Osborne, energy expert for Uswitch.com, commented: Energy bills are notoriously difficult to understand, and this approach, akin to how we buy petrol, should aid consumers in using less, wasting less, and paying less for their gas and electricity. The absence of a standing charge will appeal to many customers—particularly those with second homes unoccupied for part of the year—as there's nothing to pay on days when no energy is used.

text: The Dalai Lama has called on his fellow Nobel Peace Laureate, Aung San Suu Kyi, to do more to help persecuted Rohingya Muslims in her country, Myanmar. The Tibetan spiritual leader informed The Australian that he hoped Ms Suu Kyi could address the issue. The Dalai Lama expressed particular concern over the plight of thousands of Rohingyas stranded at sea. Ms Suu Kyi has faced international criticism for her refusal to speak out on the Rohingya issue. The Rohingya are not recognised as citizens of Myanmar (Burma) by the authorities and are effectively stateless. In his interview with The Australian, the Dalai Lama urged all of Myanmar's Buddhists to remember the face of the Buddha when dealing with the Rohingya minority. He stated that he had urged Ms Suu Kyi to act on the issue twice since 2012, when interfaith violence erupted in Myanmar's Rakhine state. It's very sad. In the Burmese case, I hope Aung San Suu Kyi, as a Nobel laureate, can do something, he told the newspaper. I met her twice, first in London and then in the Czech Republic. I mentioned this problem, and she told me she encountered difficulties, that things were not simple but very complicated. But despite that, I feel she can do something. Ms Suu Kyi, 69, has defended her reticence over alleged Rohingya persecution by stating she is a politician and not a human rights defender. She contends that the issue of thousands of Rohingya migrants who have fled Myanmar—and are now believed to be stranded at sea—was for the government to resolve. The BBC's Jonah Fisher in Myanmar reports that the Dalai Lama is the latest international figure to urge Ms Suu Kyi to speak out. South African Archbishop Desmond Tutu has also expressed concern over their plight. Our correspondent notes that Myanmar is scheduled to hold a general election in November, and many view her silence as political pragmatism—she knows that many Burmese are openly hostile to the Rohingya minority. However, it is unclear whether she actually has much sympathy for the Rohingyas, our correspondent adds.

text: Thousands of Yemenis have taken to the streets of the capital, Sanaa, to protest after an air strike killed more than 140 people at a wake on Saturday. Protesters assembled outside the United Nations headquarters, demanding an international inquiry into the strike attributed to the Saudi-led coalition. Saudi Arabia has not admitted any involvement but has promised to investigate. It joined Yemen's civil war last year, supporting the internationally recognised government. Influential former Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh, allied with the Houthi rebels controlling Sanaa, has urged attacks on soldiers at the Saudi border in retaliation. Over 500 individuals were injured in Saturday's bombing, which targeted the wake of the father of Houthi-appointed Interior Minister Gawal al-Rawishan. Numerous Houthi officials were present, and Mr Rawishan was severely injured in the attack. A rescuer described the aftermath as a lake of blood. The attack has been denounced by the UN, European Union, and the US. UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon stated that any deliberate attack against civilians is utterly unacceptable and called for accountability for those responsible. The Saudi-led coalition has vowed to immediately investigate this case along with the Joint Incidents Assessment Team in Yemen and experts from the United States who participated in previous investigations. The US announced an immediate review of its already-reduced support for the coalition. White House National Security Council spokesman Ned Price stated that US cooperation with Saudi Arabia was not a blank cheque. Houthi leader Abdul-Malek al-Houthi claimed in a televised address that the strike occurred with a green light from Washington and using US weapons. The rebels' spokesman termed it an act of genocide. Yemen faces a dire humanitarian crisis, with four out of every five of its 28-million population requiring assistance, according to the UN's humanitarian office. Nearly three million people have been displaced since the conflict began in 2014. The Houthis captured the capital then, forcing President Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi's government to flee. The Saudi-led coalition has conducted thousands of air strikes against the rebels, of the Zaidi Shia sect, whom it fears are Iranian proxies. A recent UN report estimated that 3,799 civilians have been killed since the Saudi-led air campaign began in March last year, with coalition strikes responsible for 60% of civilian deaths over a yearlong period.

text: The Pope's plea to tackle climate change is likely to get a cool reception from some key energy politicians in the US. Republican Marsha Blackburn, the second-highest ranking member on the House energy committee, states the jury is still undecided on global warming. Pope Francis is scheduled to address Congress on the subject on Thursday. He informed a White House audience on Wednesday that the issue could no longer be left to a future generation. Earlier this year, as part of a forthcoming Radio 4 documentary series Climate Change - Are we Feeling Lucky?, she claimed the earth had cooled by 1F over the last 13 years. She also stated no evidence would convince her of man-made warming. She further rejected the theory of evolution. Scientists describe her views as complete nonsense. The jury is still out saying man is the cause for global warming, after the earth started to cool 13 years ago, she asserts. When challenged that the earth's surface temperature had not risen substantially in 13 years - but had definitely not cooled, she responded: I think we've cooled almost 1 degree (F). The earth's scientific authorities - including the US space agency Nasa - assert the earth is still warming, with ice melting, sea level rising and oceans warming. Ms Blackburn - who represents Tennessee, a major coal user - declined to disclose the sources of her scepticism about mainstream science. We have met with different researchers, she states. We have had numerous committee meetings in which we've had individuals come to present and from all of that and what we have been able to read you come to an opinion. There are some that feel like human activity is the cause for carbon emissions and because of that we need to revert to where we were in the 1870s for carbon emissions. I just choose to disagree with that. Asked what scientific evidence would convince her that climate change was a threat, she replied: I don't think you will see me being persuaded. Asked whether she accepted the theory of evolution she said: No, I do not. Ms Blackburn's views are significant because Republicans in Congress are attempting to reverse President Obama's efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Professor Brian Hoskins, a leading climate scientist at the Royal Society, described her remarks as absolutely staggering. It is nonsense to say the world has cooled, Hoskins stated. If no evidence will persuade Ms Blackburn of climate change, that shows how well-founded her views are. Correction 25 September 2015: An earlier version of this report implied that Marsha Blackburn's comments were made in relation to the Pope's address. They were actually given in an earlier interview and the headline and text have been amended to make this clear. Follow Roger on Twitter @rharrabin.

text: A police force criticised for not doing more to stop a porn-obsessed murderer is being investigated over its handling of another man who went on to kill. West Mercia Police acknowledged shortcomings in their previous interactions with Jamie Reynolds, who was subsequently imprisoned for hanging 17-year-old Georgia Williams. The force contacted the police watchdog because Jason Conroy allegedly strangled a teacher in March 2013. He was later imprisoned for strangling 18-year-old Melissa Mathieson in Bristol. A spokesperson for the Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) stated: We received a referral from West Mercia Police in January 2015. It pertained to the police handling of allegations against Jason Conroy related to an incident in Shropshire in March 2013. The IPCC investigation was paused due to Mr Conroy's criminal prosecution but has now resumed following his convictions. Reynolds, described in court as having morbid sexual fantasies, attempted to strangle a girl in 2008, before proceeding to hang Georgia five years later. The force and social services faced criticism in a serious case review last week after it was revealed they were aware of the earlier attack. A subsequent investigation led to misconduct meetings for four officers and a member of police staff. Reynolds is now serving a rare whole-life prison term after a judge stated he had the potential to become a serial killer. Conroy allegedly strangled a teacher at a school in Shropshire in March 2013, but it was not reported to police at the time. A West Mercia Police spokesperson said: Police were informed of the incident several months later when an officer attended the address for an unrelated matter. It is understood the officer advised the victim that no action could be taken as a time limit had passed. Conroy, 18, strangled Melissa Mathieson last year at the Bristol centre where they both resided and was sentenced to a minimum of 19 years in prison. His trial at Bristol Crown Court revealed he had expressed as a child a desire to have sex with a deceased woman and was described as having an abnormal sexual drive.

text: BBC Ouch wants your funny, confusing or embarrassing stories about those awkward situations which occurred because you're disabled or have mental health difficulties. These are external links and will open in a new window. Re-experience those unique moments at Tales of the Misunderstood - a live storytelling event this summer. Perhaps the humorous story you shared about losing your leg in a shark attack backfired when your employer, believing it to be true, recounted it at a conference. The occasion when a waiter provided you with a children's menu at dinner because you are a person with restricted growth. Or how acquaintances awkwardly avoid words like mad or crazy because they know you consult a therapist. We are aware your story is likely more captivating than our examples here, and we eagerly anticipate hearing them. Whatever the narrative, we are interested. All we request is that the story is true, you are disabled or have a mental health issue, and your story includes this. If selected, you will collaborate with a leading comedy script producer and perform it before an audience at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival this August. Interested in participating? Write your story and send it to us by 9 July, along with some details about yourself. If you prefer to submit a summary for now, that is acceptable, but most successful applicants last time submitted lengthy stories in their initial email. Email ouch@bbc.co.uk or direct message us on Facebook. If you possess a great story but require some access to tell it, we will assist you in refining and communicating it. The final story should last approximately seven minutes. It could be humorous like stand-up or provide an engaging insight into something the audience may not have considered. In addition to performing it to a supportive crowd, we will also film it for the BBC. This is the second time we have organised a storytelling event; the first was in March 2017. View two of the acts from the initial show in London, where many participants had never performed on stage before. Remember, the deadline for your stories is 9 July. If we find yours appealing, we will contact you to inform you of the next step. Accommodation is available if you are travelling a long distance, and travel funding is available if you are based in the UK. We will strive to accommodate all access needs. We can also answer any questions via the aforementioned email address. Please share this on social media, especially with those you know who can tell a compelling story. Bookmark this page and follow Facebook for updates about becoming an Ouch storyteller and how to obtain free tickets. What Ouch's storytelling team said about participating in our first live event: Performing for the all-embracing BBC Ouch! audience has encouraged me to be courageous and creative in response to my difficulties, opening up a whole world of opportunities. The experience has taught me that sharing stories about our disabilities is something we owe not just to ourselves, but to each other. (John Servante) Disabled people are uniquely placed to tell stories about people, kindnesses and weirdness ... but often these stories remain within disability circles and do not reach a wider audience. (Damon Rose, Ouch editor)

text: Two people have been killed and two others injured in a stabbing in a house in Canterbury. A man believed to have been acquainted with the victims was apprehended at the house on Dickens Avenue shortly after 19:30 BST on Tuesday. Kent Police reported that two individuals had sustained fatal injuries and two others were transported to hospital. Neighbour Rab Hendry informed the BBC he assisted in treating a man, in his 20s, who had been stabbed in the abdomen. I saw two lads, whom I believe were brothers, and the elder one stated his brother had been stabbed in the stomach. I got him to the ground and observed the wound was fully open. I applied tea towels and pressure until paramedics arrived. Mr Hendry mentioned the boy was panicking and white as a sheet, so he continued speaking to him to attempt to calm him. Another resident, identifying himself only as Jamie, said he observed a woman lying in the doorway of the house and what appeared to be the body of a man further inside. He stated police performed CPR in an attempt to revive them, but he understood they had died. The man detained by police was arrested at the Dickens Avenue location. Kent Police indicated it was believed he and the victims were known to each other. Residents expressed their shock at the murders occurring in such a quiet area. Charlotte Bunn, 83, residing opposite the house where the incident occurred, remarked that people often lived there for one or two years then move on. I only knew the residents there to exchange greetings when out in the garden or walking in the street. They seemed all right. I can't find any fault. It's a quiet area. In all the time I have lived here, I have only had trouble once, stated Ms Bunn. Another neighbour, who wished to remain anonymous, speculated the property might have housed people placed there by the authorities. The vicinity around the house was cordoned off, and serious crime officers were summoned to the scene. Forensic investigation experts visited the property on Dickens Avenue, with a forensic tent erected outside the front door. Kent Police stated they were in the process of notifying the victims' next of kin, but formal identification had not yet occurred. Detectives are currently endeavouring to establish the circumstances of the incident, according to a spokesman.

text: Welsh exiles Taulupe Faletau, George North, Jamie Roberts and Rhys Priestland will have to rely on being picked as wildcards for future Wales selection. The Welsh Rugby Union's (WRU) senior player selection policy (SPSP) stipulates that only three players who play outside Wales may be chosen. Dominic Day, Nicky Thomas, and Rhodri Williams are the others impacted. Bath lock Luke Charteris is exempt from the rule and available for selection. This marks the first occasion the WRU has disclosed its seven-man list, from which three wildcard selections are available for each Wales campaign, commencing from the 2016-17 season. The Six Nations, summer tour, and autumn internationals constitute different campaigns, and the wildcard selections may vary for each. Known as 'Gatland's Law' in reference to Wales head coach Warren Gatland, the policy is designed to ensure more players participate in domestic rugby in Wales. In August 2014, the WRU and Wales' four professional regions signed a £60m, six-year agreement that resolved a long-standing dispute over the sport's future. That agreement included regulations that allow players based outside Wales to be overlooked in favour of home-based talent. The policy stipulated no player based overseas should represent Wales, although exceptions can be made. The SPSP does not affect players who signed contracts with clubs outside Wales before the policy was implemented, such as Toulon's Leigh Halfpenny and Exeter's Tomas Francis. Robert Howley will act as deputy for Gatland, who will lead the 2017 British and Irish Lions tour to New Zealand. Wales will host Australia, Argentina, Japan, and South Africa at Cardiff's Principality Stadium in November. The squad for those Test matches will be announced on Tuesday, 18 October. Players have been aware that there would come a point, if they left or signed new contracts outside Wales, that the policy would impact on selection, stated WRU chief executive Martyn Phillips. We are aware that supporters may be concerned that we will not be selecting from a full list of players, but the alternative where players increasingly play outside Wales isn't sustainable for the long-term success of our game whether that be professional or community rugby. Clearly, the player ultimately has the choice, but we will do all we can to ensure that playing in Wales provides the player with the best professional rugby experience possible.

text: Mark Percival scored 14 points for St Helens as they won a fiery derby against Wigan Warriors and secured a fifth straight Super League victory. Following Percival's early penalty, Lewis Tierney scored for Wigan, but tries from Percival and Morgan Knowles put Saints ahead 16-4 at half-time. Luke Walsh's drop-goal and James Roby's late try secured victory for the visitors in challenging, wet conditions. Saints advance to fourth place for the start of the Super 8s, while Wigan remain second. With leaders Hull FC defeating Salford, the Warriors missed the opportunity to stay level on points with the Black and Whites. Wigan were on a nine-match winning streak before their loss to Leeds last Friday, but they will now enter their Challenge Cup semi-final against Hull FC next week following consecutive defeats. It was an impressive defensive display throughout by Keiron Cunningham's St Helens team, highlighted when Joe Greenwood thwarted Sam Tomkins' effort on the line in the second half. New Zealand prop Frank-Paul Nuuausala was sent to the sin-bin on his home debut for Wigan for his strike on Louie McCarthy-Scarsbrook, who also received a yellow card. Wigan forward John Bateman returned after his eight-week ban and £10,000 fine for an alleged altercation with another player. Wigan head coach Shaun Wane stated: I'm gutted, devastated. We didn't turn up and got what we deserved. The smartest team won. They were good on the floor and were allowed to be good. Our defence was very good for large parts of the game but our attack was off. Too many individual players had a poor game. We've got seven hard days of work ahead of us now. We need to make sure we turn up against Hull with the same commitment to defence but we've got to be better on attack. St Helens head coach Keiron Cunningham commented: I'm just pleased for my players, they stood up to everything Wigan threw at us - they could probably still be playing now and not score. That's what self-belief brings to a side. We went through a tough spell but we're a real close-knit group and now we're heading in the right direction. Wigan are a great attacking side and were fully stacked tonight. They had lots of threats but I thought we stuck to the plan. We're not going to fall in love with ourselves, we give ourselves a good shot for the top four. Attendance: 20,049.

text: The owner of Atlanta's new Major League Soccer team says David Beckham should ground share with an American football side for his Miami-based MLS franchise. Beckham and his co-investors announced in February their intention to establish a new team in the MLS. The former England captain has had two proposals for a 25,000-seat stadium in central Miami rejected this summer. When asked if Beckham should share a venue, Arthur Blank, who also owns the NFL's Atlanta Falcons, said: Yes. It's a challenge Beckham must overcome. It's crucial he finds a balance between the commercial side and the special, emotional atmosphere desired for a football stadium. Blank, speaking before the Falcons' game against the Detroit Lions at Wembley on Sunday (13:30 BST), is constructing a new stadium in Atlanta with a capacity of 65,000 for Falcons games, and 29,000 for his as-yet-unnamed MLS team. Media playback is not supported on this device. This smaller capacity will be achieved through a retractable lower tier and mechanised curtains to close off the top tier, and Blank believes this should ensure the more intimate, football-specific atmosphere the MLS seeks for its expansion clubs. Blank's relatively smooth progress towards a state-of-the-art home for his two franchises (he has even secured £125m in public funding for the project) contrasts with the difficulties of Miami Beckham United, the group of investors led by the former Manchester United, Real Madrid, and LA Galaxy star. There are currently 19 teams in the MLS but none in the southeast quarter of the US. This will change when Orlando City begins next year. However, part of the MLS's growth strategy has been to promote local rivalries, which is why it is hoped a second Florida franchise in Miami will join the league in 2017, the same year Blank's Atlanta team, in neighbouring Georgia, is scheduled to join. The Miami team, however, cannot be given a start date until it secures a suitable home, and Blank believes it should reconsider its opposition to sharing an existing venue with an American football team. The NFL's Miami Dolphins play at the renowned Sun Life Stadium in northern Miami, sharing it with the University of Miami's American football team. The stadium was designed with football in mind, so its dimensions and pitch are adequate, but it lacks a roof and is far too large for a new MLS team's fan base. Another option is Florida International University Stadium, home to the public university's American football team. With a capacity of 20,000, it is a better size, but its pitch and facilities would require updating, and its location is not ideal as it is situated in the middle of a college campus.

text: A former chaplain and an ex-principal of a Roman Catholic care home have been found guilty of abusing boys. Anthony McCallen, aged 65, served as chaplain at the now-defunct St William's Children's Home in East Yorkshire, where James Carragher, aged 75, was the head. The duo denied a total of 87 sexual offences against children at the home between the 1970s and the 1990s. Leeds Crown Court was informed that Carragher, a convicted sex offender from Merseyside, took boys for naked swimming sessions late at night. The jury was told they both targeted boys aged between 10 and 16 years old. In total, 18 men provided evidence describing how they were indecently touched. One victim left the courtroom after informing the jury that the pair had visited him while he slept and sexually assaulted him. Another witness recounted how boys were taken swimming after lights-out at the home and instructed not to wear any swimming trunks. Following the verdict, Judge Jeffrey Marson QC commended the jury members for their conduct. He remarked: I've never ever in many years of doing this had a jury who had to consider so many charges, it is way beyond the norm, and they are some of the most difficult charges to deal with. Carragher, who was imprisoned for seven years in 1993 and 14 years in 2004 for sex offences, pleaded not guilty to 50 counts of indecent assault and 12 other serious sex offences. McCallen, also from Merseyside, who was convicted of abusing two boys in the 1990s, denied 18 indecent assaults and seven other serious sexual offences. After a 10-week trial and 11 days of deliberations, the jury found Carragher guilty of 21 indecent assaults and three serious sex offences, but he was acquitted of a further 30 charges. McCallen was found guilty on a total of 11 charges, including a serious sexual offence. He was cleared of eight other charges. However, the jury could not reach verdicts on 13 charges and were discharged by the judge. The pair are scheduled to be sentenced on 4 January. St William's in Market Weighton, which closed in 1992, was owned by the Diocese of Middlesbrough and operated by members of the De La Salle Brotherhood. In a statement, the diocese expressed hope that those affected by the abuse can move on with their lives. We condemn any behaviour which harms young people. The behaviour of Anthony McCallen whilst he was a priest was a betrayal of the trust that was placed in him from the Diocese of Middlesbrough.

text: Shares in the UK's biggest estate agent, Countrywide, have plummeted following the publication of its gloomy report on the property market. Thursday's 12% decline follows a previous 5% drop after the announcement that letting agents' fees are to be abolished. In its third-quarter trading update, Countrywide stated it anticipated a decrease in transactions due to stamp duty changes and the Brexit vote. Group revenue was £188.5 million compared with £197.1 million for the same period last year. The group, which includes 55 high street brands such as Bairstow Eves, John D Wood, and Gascoigne Pees, predicted a 6% decline in transactions this year, with further reductions expected in 2017. The company stated that the reduced market transactions observed in the second half of this year would result in 2016 profits being at the lower end of expectations. Countrywide reported that figures for the three months to the end of September showed overall house exchanges were down by 1% compared with the same period last year, while in London they were 29% lower. It also noted that mortgage approvals were 12% lower than the same time last year. The lettings sector was impacted by the rush to avoid stamp duty changes at the end of the first quarter, leading to an unusually high supply of rental properties, according to its statement. In the three months to the end of September, residential lettings increased by 14%, with a 1% rise in London. The announcement of the ban on letting agents' fees in Wednesday's Autumn Statement was described as a hammer blow to estate agents. Countrywide's chief executive Alison Platt expressed eagerness to collaborate with the government on the consultation. We have made good progress this year despite challenging market conditions since the EU referendum, said chief executive Alison Platt. Particularly pleasing is our growth in market share in both sales and lettings. However, ETX Capital markets analyst Neil Wilson remarked: Countrywide shares are tumbling again this morning after it provided a very downbeat assessment of the property market. The company claims it's making good progress, but today's trading statement confirms that estate agents are facing a troubled future. Yesterday's Autumn Statement bombshell banning letting agents from charging upfront fees to tenants couldn't have come at a worse time for the sector. The trading statement presumably doesn't account for this change, so we could see a greater adverse effect as a result, he added.

However, doubts have been raised about the largest portion of this extra funding, with uncertainty over whether the government will proceed with abolishing free meals for all infants. Without a majority in the House of Commons, it would be more challenging to pass legislation to abolish the free meals for infants, introduced three years ago. The proposal to remove the meals faced criticism from chef and healthy-school-food advocate, Jamie Oliver. The funding warning letter will be sent by head teachers to parents in over 4,000 schools, indicating that many schools will need to reduce staff and subject offerings. Parents will be informed about analysis from the Institute for Fiscal Studies, which stated that the Conservatives' plans for school spending would result in a real-terms cut of 2.8% in per-pupil funding between 2016 and 2022. text: The flagship Conservative election pledge to open a further 500 free schools in England is being put into practice, with applications invited for new schools. The government intends to create 270,000 additional places in free schools over the next five years. Education Secretary Nicky Morgan described them as modern engines of social justice. Labour's Tristram Hunt criticised it as an irresponsible use of public funds. The opening of the application process on Friday signifies the start of the next wave of free schools. Among the proposals to be submitted are New Croydon Academy, focusing on science and technology, and Gipsy Hill Secondary Academy, where a group of primary schools in south London aims to establish a secondary school. Free schools, with over 250 already open and more than 150 approved, are new state schools with the same independence as academies, operating outside local authority control and with greater flexibility over curriculum and staffing. During the election campaign, Prime Minister David Cameron stated these start-up schools were raising standards and restoring discipline. They were introduced under the coalition government to bring more choice and innovation, allowing local parents and community groups to create their own schools if they perceived a lack of good quality local schools. However, the trend has shifted towards free schools being opened by existing professional school groups. An analysis by the Policy Exchange think tank revealed that in the most recent waves of free schools, over two-thirds were opened by academies or academy chains, while fewer than a fifth were opened by parents and community groups. They have faced opposition from Labour and teachers' unions, who have accused the free-school project of failing to deliver extra school places where most needed. However, the Department for Education states that nearly three-quarters of the 125,000 free school places created were in areas with a shortage, with half in the most deprived communities in the country. Free schools are at the heart of the government's commitment to deliver real social justice by ensuring all pupils have access to a world-class education, said Mrs Morgan. This is central to our commitment to govern as one nation - creating a country where everyone, regardless of their background, can achieve their high aspirations. Free schools provided a fresh chance for families to break the cycle of disadvantage by providing a quality of schooling never before seen in many communities, stated the education secretary. Sarah Pearson, interim director of the New Schools Network, which supports the opening of free schools, says they have been working with about 30 groups wanting to set up schools. text: Wrexham's appointment of Dean Keates as manager is not the first time the Welsh club have turned to a familiar face to lead them. Keates, who made over 150 league appearances and captained the club to an FA Trophy victory in 2013, has been appointed to his first managerial role as Gary Mills' successor. Arfon Griffiths, Brian Flynn, and more recently Andy Morrell were all former players who received their first management opportunity from the north Wales club. All three left their mark on a club now in its eighth season outside the Football League. Wrexham have not mounted a serious play-off challenge since the tenure of Morrell, who had Keates as club captain. Morrell, now manager of National League North side Tamworth, was among the first to send Keates congratulations on his appointment. He's perfect for it, Morrell told BBC Radio Wales Sport. He's ambitious, enthusiastic, and has Wrexham at heart. He fought tooth and nail as a player for them and put his body on the line, and he'll do exactly the same in the manager's role. It's a great opportunity for him because these don't come along often. Morrell, like Keates, initially took over on an interim basis in September 2011 when Dean Saunders departed for Doncaster Rovers and was later made permanent. However, Morrell took over a side that was second in the Conference, while Keates' Wrexham are currently 14th and eight points off the play-off places. I was in a better position because we had won seven out of the 10 games, Morrell recalls. All I had to do was continue what we were doing, and the lads were great. Dean has to somehow change the players' mind-set. They've got to change that mentality into a winning one, and he can do it. He'll lead from the front and tell them exactly what he wants. The appointment has also drawn comparisons with another diminutive midfielder turned Wrexham manager, Flynn. Although 5ft 5ins, Keates joked at his press conference: I'm a bit taller than Flynnie though. Flynn, the former Wales international, transitioned from player to manager at Wrexham as Dixie McNeil's successor in November 1989. He transformed a side that finished bottom of the Football League into FA Cup giant killers, with notable victories over Arsenal and West Ham United during his 12-year tenure. It's a very similar situation to when Brian Flynn came in, and look at the success he had at the football club, said Peter Jones, chair of Wrexham Supporters' Trust. We felt the opportunity for Dean was the right time. He knows the club, he knows everyone here. Flynn was renowned for giving young players their chance at Wrexham, and Morrell says home-grown talent is key to the club's development and sustainability. I hope they can get a plan in place not just to try and make the play-offs this season or next season, Morrell told BBC Wales. Media playback is not supported on this device. It's got to be a longer-term plan. What are they going to do with the academy? Are they going to use that properly and bring players from there into the first team? You've got assets there that you can sell, whereas at the moment they seem to be ignoring that. If they can get those players through, it gets the fans on board. If there's a plan in place, there's no reason why in a few years' time you can't be pushing again. There are so many big teams struggling to get back to where they should be, and Wrexham are a Football League club in mine and many people's eyes. Keatsy will be positive, and he'll push them on and make them play well.

text: The growing buy-to-let property market in the UK could post a threat to wider financial stability, a Bank of England committee has said. Buy-to-let mortgage lending had the potential to amplify a housing boom and bust, the Bank's Financial Stability Committee (FPC) concluded. Lending in this sector has increased by 40% since 2008, the FPC stated. It refrained from suggesting any intervention by government or regulators at this stage. The FPC is alert to the rapid growth of the market and potential developments in underwriting standards, the committee remarked. As the market continues to grow, particularly if driven by loosening of underwriting standards, the sector could pose risks to broader financial stability, both through credit risk to banks and the amplification of movements in the housing market. The 40% rise in the outstanding stock of buy-to-let mortgage lending since 2008 compares with an increase of just 2% in owner-occupier mortgage lending. The share of buy-to-let in the stock of outstanding mortgage lending has increased to 16% from 12% in 2008. The Bank indicated that buy-to-let landlords were much more likely to sell if there was a significant drop in house prices, causing property values to decline further. A similar amplified effect could occur should prices rise sharply. Any increase in buy-to-let activity in an upswing could add further pressure to house prices. This could prompt owner-occupier buyers to take on even larger loans, thereby increasing overall risks to financial stability, the FPC noted. Over the Bank of England's three centuries of history, it has had to grapple repeatedly with the problem of boom and bust. The doorman standing outside the Bank of England, as I entered today, was a reminder of this enduring struggle. He was clad in the usual pink tails: the colour is Houblon pink, named after the first governor, Sir John Houblon, who took office in 1694. Could the rise of buy-to-let be putting us in danger again? The Bank's Financial Policy Committee says it has the potential to amplify the housing and credit cycles. It is careful not to designate either the dash for buy-to-let or recent house price increases as a boom. But it is clear that bank officials see investors' enthusiasm for bricks and mortar as a problem which needs to be monitored. Buy-to-let investors push prices up faster. Because they are more prone to sell if the market hits the buffers, they make prices plunge more steeply. Cuts to the amount of tax relief that can be claimed on mortgage interest payments by buy-to-let landlords were announced by Chancellor George Osborne in his Budget in July. The amount that landlords will be able to claim will be set at the basic rate of tax, which is currently 20%. The change will be introduced over four years from April 2017. Mr Osborne suggested this would help to create a level playing field between homeowners and investors. The FPC said that no intervention was needed in the Help to Buy scheme - which sees the government guarantee part of a low-deposit home loan - as it posed no risks to financial stability in its current form.

text: Rakesh Shukla is a software engineer who's found his life's calling in looking after dogs that no-one wants, writes the BBC's Geeta Pandey in Bangalore. These are external links and will open in a new window. The car arrived outside a dusty farmhouse near the capital of Karnataka, a southern Indian state, and suddenly dogs were everywhere, yelping and barking, jumping with joy. Within moments, they surrounded Rakesh Shukla, nuzzling and licking him, and Mr Shukla was equally delighted to see them. He spoke to them, patted some, scratched one behind the ears, and lifted another onto his shoulder. He then gave me a tour of his three-and-a-half-acre farm. At the last count, Mr Shukla had 735 dogs. The farm hosts Labradors, Golden Retrievers, Great Danes, Beagles, Dachshunds, Rottweilers, Saint Bernards, and even a pug. There are also hundreds of mongrels. Most of the dogs are strays, while others have been abandoned by their owners. The latest arrivals were a group of 22 pedigreed dogs whose owner, a city businessman, was recently shot dead by criminals. Geeta Pandey recently spent 10 days working on a series of stories in Bangalore. This is her fourth report. You can find the other reports here: Why is Bangalore stuck in traffic jams? Women from Mars? The restaurant that has a city eating out of its hands. I'm the last stop for these dogs. They are no longer cute and cuddly. Many are sick and no longer wanted, said Mr Shukla, aged 45. Affectionately known as the Dog Father, he refers to the dogs as his babies and himself as their papa. Mr Shukla, who founded a software company with his wife 10 years ago, spends three to four days each week on the farm, caring for his canines. I had worked in Delhi, in the United States, and then set up my own company in Bangalore, he said. Life was all about buying big cars and expensive watches and living a fancy life. I had travelled and seen the world many times over, but then I was not happy. Then Kavya entered his life: a beautiful 45-day-old Golden Retriever with whom he fell hopelessly in love. It was in June 2009, and Mr Shukla clearly recalls the day he brought her home. When we got home, she went and hid in a corner. I got down to her level on the floor and I was calling out to her. She was looking at me, she was scared, but I could see she wanted to trust me, he said. And that's when the moment happened - it was a physical feeling, my hair was tingling, I could feel a warm glow. And I've never needed to ask myself that question - 'why am I here?' - again after that. Mr Shukla's second dog, Lucky, came to him three months later when he rescued her from the streets. It had been raining for 12-13 days, she was wet and miserable, so I brought her home too, he said. Over the following days and weeks, whenever he encountered a stray or abandoned dog, he brought it home. Initially, he kept them there, but when his wife protested, he moved some to the office, where the top floor was converted into a home for dogs. In 2012, as the pack grew, Mr Shukla purchased land in Doddballapur town and established the farm - a haven for dogs that are old, ailing, or simply unwanted. The farm is designed for its canine residents, with ample open spaces for them to run around and ponds to swim in, and there's double fencing to ensure their safety. Each time we entered an enclosure, a cacophony of barks greeted us. The farm employs about 10 people, including trained veterinary assistants, to care for the dogs, cook for them, and feed them. The dogs are fed 200kg of chicken and another 200kg of rice daily, and many of the sick ones require regular medicines and attention. The daily cost of running the centre is 45,000 to 50,000 rupees (£532 to £592; $663 to $737), according to Mr Shukla, who stated he provided 93% of the funds. In the past year, however, he has encountered issues with some animal activists, who have demanded access to the farm. He has also faced complaints that he is causing public unrest by keeping so many dogs. There have also been demands that he shut down the farm. He has refused to concede. I've made a pact with my dogs, he said. We will part only when one of us kicks the bucket.
