text: It's that time of year again where we put the clocks forward and all get one hour less in bed! The clocks will advance on Sunday, 26 March at 1am, so you will likely be asleep in bed when it occurs. When the clocks change in this manner, we transition from Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) to British Summer Time (BST), also known as Daylight Saving Time (DST) or GMT+1. Last year was particularly notable as it marked 100 years since we first altered our clocks in this way. The change on Sunday morning will result in lighter evenings during the summer months. After reading about the reasons for this practice, try our quiz at the end to test your memory. An American politician and inventor named Benjamin Franklin first proposed the idea while in Paris in 1784. He suggested that rising earlier, when it was lighter, would conserve candles. However, it was introduced in the UK after Coldplay singer Chris Martin's great-great-grandfather, a builder named William Willett, also found it appealing. In 1907, he published a leaflet titled The Waste of Daylight, urging people to rise earlier. Willett was an avid golfer and became frustrated when his games were cut short due to the sunset, leaving insufficient light to continue playing. The concept of adjusting the clocks forwards and backwards was debated by the government in 1908, but many opposed it, so it was not legislated. Willett dedicated his life to persuading people of its merits, but it was only implemented in the UK in 1916, a year after his death. It was initially introduced by the Germans during World War One, shortly before the UK adopted it. During World War Two, the UK utilised what was termed British Double Summer Time (BDST), with clocks advanced by an additional hour in summer, though this was short-lived. Currently, the UK's clocks always revert by one hour on the last Sunday in October and advance by one hour on the last Sunday in March. Adjusting clocks in this manner is now practised in some countries worldwide, though many do not. Opinions vary on whether we should continue this practice. Some believe BST is beneficial as it conserves energy by optimising natural daylight and helps reduce traffic accidents. Others oppose it, arguing it does not genuinely save energy and can make mornings darker for children going to school, posing a danger. They also contend it is detrimental to health. text: Political sketch writer Quentin Letts has apologised for an article he wrote mocking the disability of broadcaster Andrew Marr. In a Daily Mail review of the new Robert Peston show on ITV, Letts referred to Marr as Captain-Hop-Along, growling away on BBC One, waving his arm like an inebriated conductor. Marr suffered a stroke in January 2013. Letts issued his apology via Twitter after media commentator Roy Greenslade's article appeared in the Guardian. Greenslade stated in his article, titled It isn't Funny or Smart for Quentin Letts to Poke Fun at Andrew Marr: I don't want to appear overly sensitive. I recognise that no-one should be immune to criticism and that Letts was exercising his right to press freedom. But really Quentin, that was an ungracious comment. He subsequently urged Letts to apologise. Letts conceded his remarks about the admirable Marr were horrid. His apology tweet was met with responses labelling him utterly disgraceful and appalling. The Daily Mail article was published in both the print edition and its online version. Marr's wife, journalist Jackie Ashley, tweeted about Letts' article, criticising the message it conveyed to disabled individuals. The Stroke Association stated: A stroke is not a joke. Stroke survivors deserve our respect and support, and Andrew Marr deserves an apology, before urging people to lodge complaints with the Independent Press Standards Organisation. In a statement to the BBC, the Independent Press Standards Organisation said: we have received a total of 11 complaints about the article. All of the complaints are under Clause 12 (Discrimination), with one or two also citing Clause 1 (Accuracy) or Clause 4 (Intrusion into grief or shock). It is IPSO policy not to comment on the identity of individual complainants, so I am unable to confirm the names of anyone who has contacted us on this article. text: JPeg pictures could soon have built-in restrictions making them harder to copy, if recommendations by the body overseeing the format are implemented. The Joint Photographic Experts Group (JPeg) committee has advocated for controls over how image data in .jpg files is accessed. It is believed this would protect copyright and safeguard the privacy of individuals in images. However, rights groups have argued that the features might impede creativity. In an online summary of the proposals, the JPeg committee stated that photographs were often redistributed without relevant rights information attached, allowing them to be easily copied or republished without permission. In some instances, the privacy of the photographer could be compromised if metadata embedded in the images, which might include the geo-location of where the photo was taken, was accessible. Currently, these concerns are not well addressed and [are] an inhibiting factor in the further proliferation of digital content distribution, the JPeg committee briefing stated. The JPeg committee has no concrete plans to alter the JPeg format yet, but hopes to seek technological solutions once the specifics of the new proposals have been determined, according to the committee's convener, Touradj Ebrahimi. Speaking to the BBC, Dr Ebrahimi said any changes made would still allow JPeg files to be freely shareable if their authors desired. One thing that's important to note is that this is not something we're imposing, he said. We are just saying, 'Let people have a choice.' Those who are perfectly happy with today's situation and want to have security-free image sharing [will still be able to]. Currently, when someone wishes to protect an image from being viewed by certain people, it is possible to publish it on websites with their own privacy-protecting software, such as Facebook. However, if the photograph is taken from that site by someone with access to it and sent elsewhere, it could then be distributed to anyone. Dr Ebrahimi suggested it might be preferable to have access controls built into the file. It would be best if you have one image that is protected in such a way that if you have the rights, you see it clear; if you don't have the rights, you don't see it, he said. The idea has raised concerns among rights groups such as the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF). In a blog, the EFF warned against imposing tight restrictions on JPeg files and suggested the move could stifle creativity—hindering an artist from using a photograph in a new work, for example. It might also be challenging to secure the restrictions from those intent on bypassing them, said Jim Killock, executive director of the Open Rights Group. He compared the situation to digital rights management (DRM) software, which is found on products such as DVDs and prevents copying of the content. DRM tends to be easily broken, he told the BBC. People who want to break the rules would still do that. Mr Killock also expressed concerns that companies might charge excessive fees for allowing certain levels of access to restricted images. You're going to want to edit pictures, crop them, alter them, all of these sorts of things that DRM potentially restricts, so I guess the other major beneficiary would end up being software publishers, he said. The JPeg format is the most widely used image format on the internet, and according to the JPeg committee, several billion JPeg images are produced every day.

text: How can busy working mums and dads keep tabs on their toddlers and stay connected to them during the working day? An increasing number of technology entrepreneurs assert they have a solution. However, does employing more technology provide time-constrained parents with valuable new methods to engage with their children, or does it merely increase their anxiety? Molawa Adesuyi, co-founder and chief executive of Mytoddlr, an app that provides updates on a child's activities at nursery or creche, is convinced of the technology's utility. Most working parents drop off their children at day nurseries as early as 8 or 9am and cannot collect them until 5 or 6pm, he states. During this period, they have no means of staying in touch or informed about their children's welfare throughout the day. This is a significant problem. With the Mytoddlr app and website, nurseries input data regarding the child's routine and behaviour throughout the day—from potty breaks to naps—and parents receive these updates in real time on their phones or computers. The nursery is content, parents are content, it's a win-win for everyone, says Mr Adesuyi. But does this not impose an additional administrative burden on nursery staff? Mr Adesuyi argues it does not, as it can actually decrease paperwork and offer a simpler, quicker way of communicating with parents, he says. There are excellent apps available now for parents... solutions to real problems parents face. It's just gratifying to see technology transform parenting, he concludes. Launched in 2015, Mytoddlr is utilised by 2,000 parents in Lagos, Nigeria, and is currently being trialled by some nurseries in London. Harsh Songra, the 19-year-old founder and chief executive of the smartphone app My Child, was inspired to create his child development monitoring app after experiencing dyspraxia during his upbringing. This developmental disorder affecting coordination and movement can be challenging to diagnose if parents are unaware of the signs. I have experienced the struggles of a family with a child who has a disorder, he says. It took my parents over nine years to identify the specific issue, and I still encounter some health challenges, says Mr Songra. The My Child app assists parents in monitoring the development of a child up to 24 months old, posing questions, aggregating relevant content, and identifying local experts. Launched in early 2015, the app has been downloaded over 11,000 times in more than 140 countries and is particularly popular in the US, India, Singapore, and the UK. Mr Songra believes technology is a beneficial parenting tool but admits it may occasionally interfere with professionals' work. Sometimes it does affect their relationships with doctors, as parents become anxious about their child due to what they find on Google, he says. The issue is that we tend to trust the content of one link over 100 others and then act based on that information. But we believe this will surely change over time, as there will be increased awareness of these issues in the future. Parenting apps—from webcam baby monitors to location-tracking services, interactive games to health checkers—are undoubtedly on the rise, as busy parents incorporate the latest technology into their lives. One woman in Australia even used Siri, Apple's voice-activated iPhone assistant, to call an ambulance when her toddler daughter stopped breathing. However, for New Jersey-based entrepreneur Amit Murumkar, the motivation for developing an app was purely practical. My daughter was three... and would bring a piece of art home daily from her Montessori school, but there is only so much you can display on a refrigerator door, he says. I was also a good artist as a child, and when I became a parent, I thought, 'If only I could show the art I created to my own children.' Thus, he developed a smartphone app called Canvsly, which allows parents to capture these artworks on the app, organise them into albums, and invite grandparents or other family members to view and comment on them. The artwork can also be printed through the app and used to create gifts. Provided you trust the app's cloud storage provider, you could then dispose of the originals. Parents can go guilt-free and clutter-free, Mr Murumkar says, adding that the app has been downloaded in more than 100 countries. Anesu Charamba, a tech analyst at research consultancy Frost & Sullivan, believes such apps are assisting parents in raising and interacting with their children in new and exciting ways. As smartphones and more affordable, reliable internet access extend beyond developed economies to the rest of the world, early adopters will be joined by the majority, he believes. text: In our series of letters from African journalists, filmmaker and columnist Farai Sevenzo considers the role of cameras in conflict. An intriguing moment occurred at the recent Cannes Film Festival when Mauritania-born film director Abderrahmane Sissako responded to questions following the screening of his film Timbuktu - The Silence of Fear. Timbuktu film lauded at Cannes The film is a fictional account of the uncertain months when jihadists seized control of this ancient Malian town, enforcing various rules such as banning music and football, and introducing lashings and stoning. Sissako, one of Africa's most consistent storytellers, was moved to tears during his press conference, stating that he wept for all Malians who endured the experiences depicted in his film. The real courage, he remarked, was found among those who faced this daily. Timbuktu was eventually liberated, but the true freedom was for those who internally sang the banned songs and music. Dramatists among us focus on recent African events to provide moments of reflection. However, in our 24-hour news culture, the camera is omnipresent, initially in the hands of news reporters—and in the hands of the jihadists as well. At the turn of the century, the late Osama bin Laden frequently supplied footage to news channels, which became embroiled in a perverse competition over who would receive the next diatribe from the man residing in the mountains. Who are Nigeria's Boko Haram Islamists? Fifteen years later, we have YouTube, and fighters from Syria to Somalia have embraced the camera as a soldier does a weapon. Combatants on our continent have begun providing footage with increasing frequency. In the past month, the rising toll of the dead and missing in north-east Nigeria has brought two issues into sharp focus—the leadership of President Goodluck Jonathan and the face of Abubakar Shekau, the Islamist militant responsible for the kidnapping of over 200 schoolgirls in Chibok. The Boko Haram leader has appeared before the camera with theatrical enthusiasm, declaring: I abducted your girls; I will sell them in the market. Since 14 April 2014, we have been compelled to listen to his every word in new videos, hoping that the anguish of Chibok's parents will soon be alleviated. From Shekau's tirades, some might conclude this was an actor in a Nollywood film portraying the archetypal villain, ready to declare something outrageous—such as having already sold his own mother, aunts, and sisters, with these schoolgirls destined for the same fate. Negotiations of a sort may be underway, and the Nigerian military, perhaps stung by persistent rumours of their conspicuous absence from remote Nigerian villages under attack, now claim they know the girls' location and are assessing the situation. It is one of the ironies of our age that in a world saturated with cameras and recording equipment, where the earth's firmament is populated by satellites, we cannot locate a plane or several hundred missing children who are not at sea but on land within heart-breaking distance of their longing parents. When the dust settles on such events, artists, novelists, and filmmakers can offer what TV bulletins cannot—the chance to reflect and extract meaning from the combatants' propaganda. Who are these people and what do they seek? How do the villagers relate to them? Is it fear or faith that is awakened? Where do the imams stand? Can the tension be defused in a more traditional African manner with the elders rather than soldiers? Yet, the artists and their cameras have the luxury of time, which those on the frontline of this new struggle do not. While answers to these significant issues remain elusive, the quest to find them cannot cease. Whether or not Nigeria's militants release another video, the seismic clash of ideas in Nigeria's north, as represented by Boko Haram's existence, persists and presents a very real and present danger that is spreading fear. Such fear exists in other African cities—Nairobi, Mogadishu, and recently Djibouti. The silence of fear is no more desirable than the fear of the silence that met Chibok's parents when their daughters first vanished weeks ago—before celebrities held aloft hashtag signs. Still, in this era of instant footage and digital imagery, the most poignant images remain those of mothers and fathers holding up ageing portraits of teenage daughters they may never see again. Sissako, one of the most eloquent storytellers in Africa, was moved to tears during his conference. Timbuktu, acclaimed in Cannes, was a film whose success was welcomed with enthusiasm. Our dramatists have drawn their materials from the recent events in Africa. He said that he wept for all the Malian boys who lived the adventures of his film. He has noted that true courage is that of those who have faced it every day. Who are the dreadful Boko Haram guerrillas of Nigeria? Timbuktu was liberated, but the real liberation was that of the men who sang the forbidden songs and music inside themselves. Fifteen years later we have combatants on our own continent, and the frequency of combatant-made films is growing. text: Zayn Malik has revealed that, in leaving One Direction, he has let the fans down. He announced he was quitting the band on Wednesday. In an interview with The Sun, he stated: I can't do this anymore. The star admitted his decision was crazy and wild and a bit mad. But I've never felt more in control in my life. I feel like I'm doing what's right, right by myself and right by the boys. Zayn gave his interview just hours after announcing he was leaving the world's biggest band. He denied any rifts between the band members, saying those claims couldn't be more wrong. However, he confessed he had wanted out of the band for some time. He said: You know, I did try to do something that I wasn't happy doing for a while, for the sake of maybe other people. Basically, I'm only upset [because] I feel like I may have let them down. It's not that I've turned my back on them [the fans] or anything, it's just that I just can't do that anymore because it's not real to me. He also dismissed rumours it was the beginning of the end for the band, who were put together on The X Factor in 2010. He refused to comment on speculation he could return in the future. Zayn quit the globally successful pop group a week after leaving their world tour due to stress. This followed the singer being pictured with his arm around a blonde girl in Thailand, prompting speculation he had cheated on his fiancée, Little Mix singer Perrie Edwards. Immediately after the announcement, he flew back to the UK and wrote on Twitter: I'm 22 years old... I love a girl named Perrie Edwards. And there's a lot of jealous [people] in this world. I'm sorry for what it looks like. Announcing he was leaving One Direction for good on Wednesday, Zayn said: After five years, I feel like it is now the right time for me to leave the band. Asked about his relationship by The Sun, Zayn said his two-year engagement had not been broken off. He described Perrie as a good girl who was supportive of his decision. Meanwhile, Zayn has reportedly visited a west London recording studio to work on solo material with Naughty Boy, who helped launch the careers of Emeli Sande and Sam Smith. text: England women began their World Twenty20 campaign with a routine 36-run victory over Bangladesh in Bangalore. England, champions in 2009 and runners-up in the last two tournaments, reached a total of 153-7 thanks to 60 from captain Charlotte Edwards. Bangladesh, who have only secured five victories in their 29 T20 matches, never posed a threat to the target. Katherine Brunt conceded 17 runs from her four overs, while Anya Shrubsole took 2-27 as Bangladesh finished on 117-6. England faces tougher challenges ahead, beginning with hosts India in Dharamsala on Tuesday. Here, led by Edwards, the highest run-scorer in T20 internationals—men or women—they efficiently handled the mediocre opposition. The captain combined accumulation with powerful shots against poor deliveries, steering England through a potentially tricky phase when they lost Sarah Taylor and Heather Knight for just one additional run. At 71-3, she was joined by Nat Sciver, who contributed 27 in a partnership of 47, while Danni Wyatt and Brunt added late power as England scored 35 from the final three overs. The chase was always likely to be beyond Bangladesh, a team that had never previously surpassed 115 in a T20 international. Opener Sharmin Akhter was bowled by the impressive Brunt in the first over of the reply, and from that point, England maintained control. Nigar Sultana and Salma Khatun did set a Bangladesh record with a 64-run partnership for the fifth wicket, but the match was already decided. England coach Mark Robinson told Sky Sports: I thought we regressed today. We played it safe, and we do not want to be safe. We lost our way in the middle with the bat and made poor decisions with the ball. Perhaps that's beneficial, as it leaves room for improvement. We weren't bad—six out of 10. We're progressing in the right direction, but today we didn't quite reach our potential. That's not how we said we would play. In the middle of the innings, you cannot settle for six an over. We're better than that. England captain Charlotte Edwards remarked: It's always nice to start with runs, but the win was the most important thing. It was a good total, and there's some work we can do on our bowling and fielding, but we're fairly pleased. Bangladesh played really well towards the end, and we've got a big game next against India. The new coaches have challenged us to express ourselves, and there's still a lot to come from us as a team. Former England batter Ebony Rainford-Brent on BBC Test Match Special commented: I'd like to have seen more from the middle order, where there was a bit of a collapse. That will be punished by Australia or India. We've discussed the reliance on Edwards and Taylor, and I'd like to see a big score from Heather Knight as this tournament progresses, because she represents the next generation.

text: Wales women's footballer Jess Fishlock says more must be done to provide an environment in which gay players feel comfortable to come out. Fishlock, aged 29, has previously discussed the challenges she has encountered as a prominent gay athlete. No current Premier League players are openly gay, yet a recent BBC survey revealed that 82% of fans would have no issue with a gay player. The environment and the timing are crucial, Fishlock stated. That's what we need to achieve - an environment that says 'it's okay and it's not a problem'. That's what we're striving for and need to work on. She informed BBC Radio Wales Sport: You don't want a footballer to come out for the wrong reasons and then experience negative repercussions. What you do want is for them to feel comfortable, to be themselves, and to be happy with that. Former England women's captain Casey Stoney publicly disclosed her sexuality for the first time in February 2014, becoming the most prominent active gay footballer in England. Stoney remarked that homosexuality was more accepted in the women's game than in the men's. Justin Fashanu was the first player in England to come out as gay in 1990 but tragically took his own life at age 37 in 1998. No male professional player has come out while playing in England since. The Seattle Reign player, currently on loan at Melbourne City, mentioned she had faced abuse during her career for being gay but was also proud she had inspired others to accept their own sexuality. I've received letters from people saying how my openness and comfort with who I am at the highest level in a major sport has made them realise it's okay and they don't need to consider suicide or have dark thoughts anymore, she added. When you hear that and receive that, I suppose nothing else truly matters because that is such a significant impact to have. Former Germany and Aston Villa player Thomas Hitzlsperger became the first player with Premier League experience to publicly announce his homosexuality in January 2014 after he had stopped playing in England. Football Association chairman Greg Clarke informed a Commons Select Committee in October that Premier League players would still endure significant abuse if they chose to reveal they were gay. This weekend, football and rugby union will support a campaign to raise awareness of issues faced by lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) fans and players. The Rainbow Laces campaign, launched by LGBT equality charity Stonewall in 2013, aims to combat homophobic, biphobic, and transphobic attitudes in sport. Rainbow flags will be displayed at Premier League fixtures, while referees will wear rainbow-coloured laces, and Fishlock expresses her support for the campaign's objectives.

text: Eastern Ukraine has become a testing ground for Russia's new military capabilities. When Russia last engaged in warfare, in Georgia in 2008, it appeared to be an easy victory. However, Russia's generals were deeply troubled by their forces' poor performance in certain key areas of modern warfare. Russia has spent the subsequent seven years rearming, re-equipping, and retraining to address those deficiencies and attempt to close the capability gap with modern Western armies. The results are now evident in eastern Ukraine, where pro-Russian separatists have gained ground against Ukrainian government troops. Ukraine's army has not undergone the same intensive modernisation process and is suffering the consequences, facing the newer weapons and systems supplied by Russia. Two key examples are the use of UAVs (drones) for surveillance and targeting, and the employment of electronic warfare. Both technologies were identified as weaknesses in the Russian forces in 2008, and both have been intensively developed since. They are now in widespread use in eastern Ukraine, placing Ukrainian government forces at a significant disadvantage. Ukrainian forces lack secure communications systems. Consequently, their communications are vulnerable to jamming and often reveal their location to Russian direction-finding equipment. This can lead to swift targeting by Russian artillery, including Grad and other, more powerful, rocket systems. As part of the non-lethal aid provided by the US, Ukraine has received special radar to attempt to pinpoint the source of incoming mortar fire. However, their use is limited by the difficulty in communicating the results to other forces. For the time being, Ukraine has not received the more sophisticated systems that would pinpoint the source of fire from longer-range artillery systems. Ukrainian forces are also outmatched by the tanks arriving from Russia. These are not only more modern than Ukrainian models, but Ukraine is also lacking effective anti-armour weapons in working order. All of these systems, along with medical support and field hospital equipment, are on the list of Ukrainian requests for support, to enhance the survivability of their forces when confronting new Russian military equipment. Losses of Ukrainian aircraft over the conflict zone demonstrate how well-equipped the Russian-backed separatists are for air defence. This includes not just the Buk missile system - blamed for downing Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 - but also others like Strela for use at lower altitudes and shorter ranges, and a wide range of lighter, shoulder-launched missiles. Independent experts, as well as NATO, Western leaders, and the Kiev government, assert there is clear evidence of direct Russian military involvement, despite Russian denials. As part of its military transformation process, Russia has been preparing for conflict with an intensive programme of exercises and manoeuvres, involving tens of thousands of servicemen across the country. These exercises have been increasing in size and complexity and often feature a storyline that is directly hostile to the West. Now, additionally, Russia has the advantage of a live testing ground in eastern Ukraine, where it can trial its new weapons, systems, and tactics. The results - especially if all of these are tested against any potential new US defensive systems supplied to Ukraine - will assist Russia in assessing how its forces would fare in a direct confrontation with NATO. Keir Giles is an analyst with the Conflict Studies Research Centre in Oxford and an Associate Fellow with the Russia and Eurasia Programme at Chatham House in London.

The team at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine hopes to revolutionise eye care for millions in remote areas worldwide. Trials involving 233 individuals in Kenya, published in JAMA Ophthalmology, demonstrated that the phone yielded results comparable to eye charts. The London team, alongside Scottish colleagues, adapted a smartphone to create a series of eye tests requiring minimal training and easy portability. The Portable Eye Examination Kit (Peek) utilises the phone's camera to scan the eye lens for cataracts. Its Acuity App displays a shrinking letter on screen for a basic vision test. The camera's flash illuminates the eye's back to check for disease. Initial clinical data from Kenya show the vision test matches results from traditional eye charts. Examinations were conducted both at homes and eye clinics. Further results on retina scanning are forthcoming and described as 'compelling'. The phone is relatively inexpensive, costing about £300 compared to bulky equipment exceeding £100,000. However, even if universal testing were possible, the significant issue remains of funding treatment for millions.

text: Organisers of this summer's music festivals have been asked by the government to warn about legal highs. Minister for Crime Prevention James Brokenshire has written to festival organisers, urging them to caution attendees about the potential dangers of such substances. He also announced that drug laws would be amended to allow temporary bans on emerging substances while scientific advice is obtained. Letters have also been dispatched to councils and police forces in festival regions. Mr Brokenshire stated: During the festival season, we recognise that individuals may be tempted to experiment with potentially hazardous new drugs, especially when marketed as 'legal' or 'herbal'. That is why we are requesting festival organisers and police to collaborate with us to communicate that these substances may be unsafe and could contain illegal drugs. We intend to amend our drug laws to enable a swift response to emerging substances by imposing a temporary ban while we acquire comprehensive scientific advice. text: The leader of Colombia's largest armed rebel group, the Farc, has said he ordered the organisation in September to stop buying guns and ammunition. Rodrigo Londono Echeverri, known as Timochenko, stated the decision demonstrated the Farc's dedication to reducing the conflict with the Colombian army. The left-wing group and the Colombian government have been engaged in peace negotiations for nearly three years. Both parties indicate they anticipate signing an agreement in March. Approximately 220,000 people are estimated to have been killed since the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia commenced its armed struggle in 1964. Peace negotiations were initiated in the Cuban capital, Havana, in November 2012. The objective is for the rebels to abandon their armed struggle and enter the legal political process. Timochenko's announcement was made in a tweet to Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos. There has been consensus on four broad points on the agenda: the political participation of the rebels, land rights, drug trafficking, and most recently, transitional justice. Transitional justice—how rebels who have committed crimes will be penalised—had been regarded as one of the most challenging issues on the agenda. When the two sides announced a deal on the matter on 23 September, President Santos travelled to Cuba. The president shook hands with Timochenko for the first time. He also set a deadline of six months, until 23 March 2016, for the signing of a final peace agreement. The rebels have expressed a desire to sign a peace deal even before that date. However, both sides are still addressing a number of issues and the implementation of the agreement. A final deal will require approval by the Colombian people in a referendum. Last month, Mr Santos announced he was prepared to join the Farc in a bilateral ceasefire from 1 January 2016 if there is significant progress in the negotiations. The rebels have already declared a truce. Mr Santos has also suspended radio and television campaigns to encourage the rebels to leave the Farc, describing it as a goodwill gesture. Demobilisation campaigns would typically be intensified in the weeks leading to Christmas.

text: You may not have heard of Judith Hill, but you've almost certainly heard her voice. The Californian singer has provided backing vocals for Stevie Wonder, Elton John, Josh Groban, Carole King, Robbie Williams, and Rod Stewart throughout her illustrious career. Most notably, she was set to be a featured singer on Michael Jackson's ill-fated This Is It tour in 2009 and can be seen performing a spine-tingling duet with the star in the posthumous film of the rehearsals. She later appeared on the US version of The Voice, where her unexpected elimination prompted judge Adam Levine to declare: I hate this country. Hill's attempts to launch a solo career were then documented in the Oscar-winning film 20 Feet From Stardom, which highlighted the (mainly African-American) backing singers who have supported rock's biggest stars. However, the catalyst for her solo career turned out to be Prince, who read about her in a newspaper and invited her to record an album at his Paisley Park Studios in Minneapolis. Hill discusses with the BBC their collaboration, her experiences as a backing singer, and the day Michael Jackson died. What is the first song you remember hearing? Walk With Me by Vanessa Bell Armstrong. Who was the first person who told you you could sing? My mother was the first person to tell me I could sing. She recounts the story of how I was singing in the back car seat as a little girl, and she noticed my talent. We wrote our first song together when I was four. How did you secure a job on Michael Jackson's This Is It tour? I did a small gig in Los Angeles and became friends with some musicians there. One of them knew Michael's musical director and invited me to audition. I did a small audition at the vocal director's house and a couple of weeks later I was hired. I remember them telling me, Michael is on your Myspace page. Change the picture! At the time, I was also hired to work at a clothing shop, so I quit that job and joined the This Is It tour. He was a master of stagecraft—what tips did he give you? Michael was fascinating to watch. Working with him taught me the importance of seizing every moment on stage. He painted pictures with every lyric and movement in his body. What do you remember of the day he died? I was sitting at a restaurant when my phone started blowing up. There were rumours of his death but I didn't believe it. It wasn't until later that day when this nightmare became a reality as I arrived at the Staples Center for rehearsal. It was a very tragic day. They had already begun to collapse the stage and pack up the gear. Just the night before we were rehearsing… It was surreal. What was it like to sing at the memorial service? It was an overwhelming experience. I mean, that was the same stage we rehearsed with him [on] two weeks prior. But it was a beautiful service. You were eliminated from the US version of The Voice—what did that experience teach you? When I was on The Voice, I made discoveries about my vocal style. No matter what the song was, I always managed to turn it into a soul song whether I wanted to or not. I learned that at the heart of it, I'm a soul singer. My roots run deep, starting from the early days of jamming with my parents on Sly and the Family Stone and Curtis Mayfield songs. What difference did 20 Feet From Stardom make to your career? 20 Feet From Stardom was a special project that resonated with so many people. We were honoured with an Oscar and Grammy and many wonderful opportunities have come my way because of it. People were inspired by the stories in the film and they continue to follow my story to see what happens next. How much of a struggle was it to make the leap to solo artist? It's a very rough road—that 20 feet from being a backing singer to an artist is a long 20 feet! But what keeps me going is a passion for music. No matter what, it makes me happy to do it. What's the biggest difference between working as a backing vocalist and fronting your own material? Working as a backing singer is being a part of a group effort to give the artist what they need. It's a fun community to be a part of. Being a solo artist is a totally different experience. There is more responsibility and pressure, yet it is very rewarding. I love sitting in the driver's seat, directing everybody to achieve the sound I'm looking for. There's nothing more fulfilling than making the sounds you hear in your head become a reality. Who's the most demanding artist you've sung for? The most demanding was Natalie Cole. It was a short show, but she was very particular about how she wanted the vocals. I have much respect for her. She kept the singers on their toes! How did you end up working with Prince? I did an interview and was asked who is my dream collaborator. I said Prince! He saw the interview and personally reached out to me. I remember receiving the unknown call on my mobile phone and freaking out while I was talking to him. I officially met him at his album listening party in Los Angeles. Shortly after, he invited me to Paisley Park and that was the beginning of the collaboration. He's got a wicked sense of humour... Has he ever caught you out with a prank? He once called me and I didn't recognise his voice because he pretended to be someone else. He can do great impersonations. What did he contribute to your album? He's a fantastic producer and arranger. He played many instruments, sang, arranged, and even wrote. He was very involved in the process, yet it was a great collaboration between his ideas and my ideas. Most of the songs were already written and he helped me come up with great grooves and effective edits. Why did you call it Back In Time? I wanted people to feel like they have travelled back into a golden era of funk/soul music. For me, personally, this record celebrates my childhood and upbringing in a musical family. Many of the lyrics are autobiographical—describing where I came from, my old stomping grounds, and the amazing musical community that inspired me along the way. The whole record feels like a dusty jam session in the basement of my parents' house. What song means the most to you? Angel In The Dark. I think about the many times I felt like I was trapped in a dark tunnel, yet God has always managed to rescue me at the right time. He is that Angel in the dark. Judith Hill's debut album Back In Time is out now on NPG Records.

text: Egyptians go to the polls on 26 and 27 May to elect a new president. Results are anticipated on 5 June, with minimal doubt that former defence minister Abdul Fattah al-Sisi will secure a comfortable victory. The sole opposing candidate is veteran left-winger and previous presidential contender Hamdeen Sabahi. Why is the election being held early? The military ousted Islamist President Mohammed Morsi following mass protests last July, subsequently outlining a roadmap to democracy that scheduled presidential elections two years earlier than planned. A parliamentary poll was initially intended to precede, but the interim government reversed the order in January. Parliament will be elected later this year, once the president is securely in office. The new constitution of January 2014 restricts the president to two consecutive four-year terms. Mohammed Morsi is currently on trial, accused of inciting the murder of anti-government protesters, killing prison officers during a 2011 jailbreak, espionage, and conspiracy to commit terrorist acts. What are the candidates' programmes and support base? Mr Sisi has proposed an ambitious plan to develop agriculture, housing, education, impoverished areas, and employment. He is unclear on how the substantial funds required would be raised, aside from calling for hard work from all and reduced profit margins for state and private enterprises. He campaigns under the slogan Long live Egypt! and asserts that his victory would signify the end of the Muslim Brotherhood as a political force. Mr Sisi enjoys support from several prominent businessmen, as well as a broad spectrum of political parties from the Islamist right to the moderate left. Hamdeen Sabahi, a prominent left-winger since the 1970s, presents an alternative to young voters who prefer a civilian candidate over a military one. Under the slogan We will pursue our dream, he pledges to combat corruption and incompetence while promoting civil rights. Like Mr Sisi, however, he states he will not re-legalise Mr Morsi's Muslim Brotherhood, which was banned as a terrorist organisation. The parties and movements supporting Mr Sabahi are predominantly left-wing. Abdul Fattah al-Sisi: New face of Egypt's old guard Who is Abdul Fattah al-Sisi? Who is Hamdeen Sabahi? Egyptian election: Voters' views Is the vote likely to be free and fair? Two factors hinder this. Firstly, the election occurs amid security and political unrest. The Muslim Brotherhood continues to protest against President Morsi's removal, and the authorities have responded with a violent crackdown on the Brotherhood and its supporters. Hundreds have perished in clashes with security forces since last summer, and hundreds more face imprisonment or even death sentences, prompting further protests. Secondly, Mr Sisi receives overwhelming support from the mainstream media, which are already depicting him as the next occupant of the presidential palace. Furthermore, the Muslim Brotherhood's media within Egypt have been banned, restricting this major opposition voice to online television and news portals hosted abroad. These do not possess the reach of the mainstream media. Who is monitoring the polls? Major Western monitoring groups are not observing the vote. The US Carter Centre states it will not participate, though the European Union says it will monitor the poll across the country. The Arab League will dispatch 100 monitors, and the African Union will also send a mission despite having suspended Egypt from membership last year. Who is calling for a boycott? Several but not all Islamist parties have declared they will boycott the vote, though some have endorsed Mr Sisi. The Muslim Brotherhood considers Mr Morsi the legitimate president and refuses to recognise the new election. The pro-Morsi National Alliance to Support Legitimacy describes the vote as a farce, and the Salafist Front has labelled it illegitimate. The political arm of the Gamaa Islamiya (Islamic Group), the Building and Development Party, states most of its members also favour a boycott. The secular 6 April Youth Movement - prominent in the uprising against Hosni Mubarak - has also called for a boycott, claiming the elections are merely a means of enthroning Mr Sisi. What problems will the new president face? Domestically, the new president will need to address severe political, economic, security, and social issues. The public expects the president to tackle unemployment, inequality, and corruption, but restoring security may be his most significant challenge. Internationally, the new leader will aim to maintain friendly relations with the US and the West while attempting to improve ties with countries that supported Mr Morsi - Turkey and Qatar and, to some extent, Iran. text: The centuries-old tradition of church bell-ringing is under threat because of a shortage of new recruits. A BBC local radio survey indicates it is becoming increasingly challenging to persuade newcomers to engage in the practice. Three-quarters of delegates at the annual conference of the Central Council of Church Bell Ringers reported it had become more difficult over the past decade to attract new members. Approximately eight out of ten delegates stated it was challenging to recruit individuals under the age of 21. Tower captain at St James Garlickhythe in London, Dickon Love, remarked that bell-ringing is often associated with Morris dancing as an activity for older men with beards, but this perception is misleading. Bell-ringing is stimulating for the mind, he stated. It's the ultimate form of heavy metal; it produces a big loud noise, keeps you fit, and has a competitive aspect. Additionally, it is a very social activity—after each practice, without exception, you can find us at the local pub. They have managed to attract some new recruits and possess a new set of eight bells, installed four years ago, and a newly-recruited team of ringers, including a professor of astrophysics and the art director of a renowned magazine. Pete McCoy, the tower captain at St Mary's Church in Walkley, Sheffield—who met his wife Judith through bell-ringing—commented that teenagers today face more distractions than in his youth. He said: There weren't as many activities for teenagers or young people as there are today. And is it cool to ring bells? I think it is. But does everyone else? Although there are nearly 40,000 ringers in the UK, just over half of the 180 delegates surveyed at the conference in May in Portsmouth believed that declining church attendances have made recruitment more difficult. 54% Agree 43% Disagree Kate Flavell, of the Central Council of Church Bell Ringers, states that the 66 affiliated societies need to enhance the promotion of their hobby. They have collaborated with the Heritage Open Days initiative to ring bells for the public at 500 sites, including St Peter Mancroft in Norwich, where the first full peal was performed in May 1715.

text: UK Chancellor George Osborne is to embark on a week-long visit to China to boost commercial and political ties with the country. Mr Osborne, accompanied by business leaders and ministers, aims to foster a new era in UK-China relations, according to the Treasury. His visit, commencing on Sunday, will take him to Beijing, Shanghai, and Chengdu. China is the world's second-largest economy, but there is increasing evidence of its slowdown. Speaking prior to the seven-day trip, the chancellor stated the delegation's purpose is exploring new opportunities to open up new markets. This precedes a state visit to the UK by Chinese President Xi Jinping in October, the first by a Chinese leader in 10 years. Mr Osborne met China's Vice Premier Liu Yandong in Downing Street on Friday to prepare for the trip. The senior Chinese minister also held discussions with Prime Minister David Cameron and Foreign Secretary Philip Hammond on enhancing UK-China ties. Mr Osborne stated: I want us to forge closer economic and cultural links with China. Our partnership for growth, reform, and innovation is facilitating record levels of investment and trade in both directions, but there is much more we can achieve. This trip is focused on exploring new opportunities to open up new markets for the benefit of both economies. The centrepiece of Mr Osborne's visit will be the UK-China Economic and Financial Dialogue in Beijing. Accompanying him will be Treasury minister Lord O'Neill, Business Secretary Sajid Javid, and Energy Secretary Amber Rudd. Mr Osborne will also promote his Northern Powerhouse plans in England, accompanied by a delegation of senior business and local government figures, including Liverpool Mayor Joe Anderson and Manchester City Council leader Sir Richard Leese. The trip signifies a further warming in UK-Chinese relations following a dispute over Prime Minister David Cameron's decision to meet the Dalai Lama in 2012. Both Mr Cameron and Mr Osborne visited China last year, when the PM encouraged the country to invest in UK infrastructure, including nuclear power stations and high-speed rail. Earlier this year, the UK became a member of the Chinese-backed Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank. China recently revised its 2014 growth figures from 7.4% to 7.3%—its weakest performance in nearly 25 years. For this year, the government targets annual economic growth of about 7%. Increasing evidence of the world's economic powerhouse slowing has caused significant investment market declines.

text: David Cameron has visited a Lebanese refugee camp amid the crisis triggered by war in neighbouring Syria. Mr Cameron, on his inaugural visit to Lebanon as Prime Minister, met a family in a camp in the Bekaa Valley who are scheduled to be flown to the UK. He stated: I wanted to come here to see for myself and to hear for myself stories of refugees. The UK will accept up to 20,000 Syrian refugees over the next five years, Mr Cameron informed MPs earlier this month. He has appointed Richard Harrington as Minister for Syrian Refugees to ensure the arrivals receive a warm welcome in the UK. The Prime Minister's visit coincides with European Union interior ministers meeting in Brussels to discuss plans to distribute 160,000 asylum seekers across 23 EU states through mandatory quotas. Home Secretary Theresa May is expected to attend and oppose plans for an EU-wide quota system for refugees. Under EU law, the UK, Ireland, and Denmark are exempt from the quota plan. James Landale, BBC Deputy Political Editor It is David Cameron's first visit to Lebanon, and he is here with a clear aim: to address criticism that Britain is not doing enough to tackle Europe's refugee crisis. Thus, he toured a refugee camp in the Bekaa Valley just one mile from the Syrian border to meet some families benefiting from British aid. He also visited a school in the heart of Beirut supported by British funds where Syrian and Lebanese students study together. The PM's argument is that this is the assistance Syrian refugees need rather than any encouragement to risk the perilous journey to Europe. So, to a nation now familiar with television images of Syrian refugees fleeing across Europe, Mr Cameron wants to remind people of where the vast majority are, namely in Lebanon, Turkey, Jordan, and Syria itself. Mr Cameron asserts British aid is deterring hundreds of thousands of refugees from heading to Europe. Aid agencies on the ground suggest poverty and an inability to pay traffickers are more significant factors. While welcoming British aid, they also suggest it is insufficient. Today is about the PM attempting to reframe a debate that has raged for many weeks, a debate that has not always favoured him. Migrant crisis: Why is it erupting now? EU migration: Crisis in graphics Mr Cameron said: I want to focus on how we help Syrian refugees here in Lebanon, in Jordan, how we make sure we discourage people from making this dangerous journey to Europe but instead we take people from these camps and we make them welcome in the United Kingdom, in our country. Following a meeting with Lebanon's Prime Minister Tammam Salam, Mr Cameron said the UK was determined to do all we can to bolster Lebanon's security. He mentioned training had already been provided to more than 5,000 Lebanese soldiers, and the UK had helped to construct a series of watchtowers on the border with Syria. The UK will also train, equip and mentor the Lebanese armed forces, he said. Lebanon is to receive £29m of the additional £100m in UK aid for Syria and surrounding countries announced by the Prime Minister earlier this month. This will fund food packages for thousands of refugees, as well as clean water, blankets, stoves, mattresses, counselling support, and play areas for children. There are 1.1 million Syrian refugees registered in Lebanon, which is more than a quarter of Lebanon's population. The camp visited by the Prime Minister is operated by the UN's refugee agency and is one of 1,500 in the Bekaa Valley, which is less than a mile from the Syrian border. Mr Cameron also observed the enrolment of pupils on the first day of the academic year at the Sed el Bouchrieh school in Beirut. At the school, Syrian children are joining classes alongside Lebanese children as part of a drive, part-funded by UK aid, to integrate refugees into the wider society. The former Labour Foreign Secretary David Miliband criticised the UK government for only agreeing to resettle 20,000 refugees over the next five years. Mr Miliband, who leads the aid agency International Rescue Committee (IRC), said it was inadequate to take just 4,000 refugees from Syria per year and noted it was the equivalent of the number arriving on the beaches of the Greek island Lesbos every day. Each country needs to shoulder the burden and agree to both relocate refugees who have reached the continent and resettle the most vulnerable from the Middle East, he said.

text: Russia will not compete at next month’s Paralympics in Rio after losing an appeal against a ban imposed for state-sponsored doping. Media playback is not supported on this device. The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the International Paralympic Committee's (IPC) ban on all Russian athletes. The IPC made this decision following the McLaren report, which detailed a Russian state-sponsored doping programme. Russian Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev labelled the decision as cynical. Medvedev claimed certain leaders of the Paralympic movement aimed to squeeze out strong competitors, describing the decision as a blow to all people with disabilities, not just Russians. The CAS panel, which intends to release the full rationale for its decision later, stated that the IPC's decision to ban the entire Russian team was proportionate in the circumstances. It noted that the Russian Paralympic Committee did not present any evidence to counter the facts provided by the IPC. The Paralympics are set to commence on 7 September. The IPC's decision contrasts with that of the International Olympic Committee (IOC), which opted not to impose a blanket ban on Russia from the Olympic Games. The IOC faced widespread criticism for disregarding the World Anti-Doping Agency's (WADA) recommendation to ban Russia. Instead, each individual sporting federation was granted the authority to decide if Russian athletes could compete, with a three-person IOC panel having the final say. Ultimately, over 270 Russian athletes were cleared to compete at the Olympics, with Russia securing 56 medals in total and finishing fourth in the medal table. Russia had planned to send 267 athletes across 18 sports to the Paralympics. The CAS statement added that it had not considered the natural justice rights or personality rights of individual Russian athletes in its decision. Russia's Paralympic team's lawyer, Alexei Karpenko, confirmed the decision was final, stating they would attempt to file an appeal with the Swiss Federal Supreme Court, though it would take one to two years for the court to review the case. So I'm afraid Russian Paralympians will not be going to the Games in any case, Karpenko added. IPC president Sir Philip Craven, who has described Russia's anti-doping system as broken, corrupted and entirely compromised, and claimed it prioritised medals over morals, expressed he was greatly encouraged by the CAS decision. He stated it was not a day for celebration, adding: We have enormous sympathy for the Russian athletes who will now miss out. It is a sad day for the Paralympic movement, said Craven. But we hope also a new beginning. We hope this decision acts as a catalyst for change in Russia and we can welcome the Russian Paralympic Committee back as a member safe in the knowledge that it is fulfilling its obligations to ensure fair competition for all. Russian sports minister Vitaly Mutko described the ban as political and not within legal framework, while lawyer Karpenko termed it a black day for the sports judiciary. He said: I can only express huge disappointment at the ruling. The rights of Russian Paralympians have been blatantly violated. Regardless of whether the Russian Paralympics Committee is guilty of the charges, punishing innocent athletes and not allowing them to defend themselves - which was an opportunity afforded to the Russian Olympics athletes - this is a flagrant violation of human rights. Meanwhile, Dmitry Svishchev, head of Russia's parliamentary sports committee, called the CAS decision an inhumane act. Speaking to the state-owned Tass news agency, he added: [CAS has shown] an unprecedented impudence and lack of principle. How is it possible to bar the people who with their courage have earned the right to a proper life from the Games? Whatever this court is called, it is an inhumane court. One can punish officials, coaches, but by no means should athletes be punished: when looking at what they do in spite of hardships and strain, one wants to pull off their hat. Such people should only be respected. Richard McLaren, a Canadian law professor, published a WADA independent report that found Russia's sports ministry manipulated urine samples provided by its athletes between 2011 and 2015. The report identified 27 samples relating to eight Para-sports, five of which are summer sports, including some governed by the IPC. The IPC also found evidence that samples were swapped during the Sochi 2014 Paralympic Games, adding that it planned to reanalyse every Russian sample given at the event. Oksana Savchenko, an eight-time Russian Paralympic champion, said: Yesterday evening the mood seemed to be positive. Everyone thought that everything had gone well, everyone thought that our guys would finally go. Many received the equipment yesterday already and now there is this decision, which actually is shocking. And partly, yes, perhaps that is the reason why we have not been allowed - [because] we are a leading team, which shows great results, gets most medals and constantly brings fame to our country. Roman Petushkov, a six-time Russian Paralympic champion, stated: We all are shocked, of course - we all are depressed. Guys still don't know - they are practising right now. This is inhumane treatment. This is humiliation. Such treatment of people with disabilities is... there are no words. Simply, we have been [trodden] to pieces. Karen Pickering, a four-time British Olympic athlete and four-time world champion, commented: Hats off to the IPC for making a very strong stand - CAS did the right thing by upholding it. I think it's a shame that the IOC didn't do the same because there is a real appetite right now amongst athletes that we don't want any former drug cheats in the Olympic Games. I believe that if an athlete cheats you sanction them, if a team cheats you sanction them and if a country cheats you sanction them. That means that Russia should not have been competing in Rio, and I think there are a number of athletes who can say 'I should have been on the medal podium'. The Paralympics are proceeding as planned, but face significant budget cuts as Rio's organising committee has not raised sufficient funds to support the event due to Brazil's struggling economy and poor ticket sales. Cuts will impact venues, workforce, and transport. Delayed travel grants will now be paid to athletes, but 10 countries may struggle to get teams to Rio.

text: Generally speaking, England will be very happy to have won the Test series against Sri Lanka without really breaking sweat. Although they did not complete the task as swiftly as in the first Test, their nine-wicket victory in the second Test at Chester-le-Street was still thoroughly convincing, with Sri Lanka never really competing. England coach Trevor Bayliss rated their performance an eight out of 10. I would rate them a seven—they are not yet fully operational, and as captain Alastair Cook conceded, there were instances when they eased off. However, that might be considered overly critical. It is always challenging to accurately evaluate a team when their opponents are as weak as Sri Lanka have been throughout most of this series. Nonetheless, one thing is evident: James Anderson is bowling exceptionally well. Even against top-tier batsmen, he would still be making the ball behave in the same manner. He is performing at his peak, and his rise to the top of the Test bowling rankings is well-earned. Fast bowling is an unpredictable game, heavily reliant on rhythm—a difficult concept to define or measure. Anderson lacked rhythm in South Africa, but now he is running up confidently, 'kissing' the pitch and claiming numerous wickets. One might argue that superior batsmen would handle him better, but in these conditions, with the ball moving both ways, Anderson poses a threat to any batsman globally. The significance of the overs he bowled for Lancashire earlier in the season cannot be underestimated, where he took 12 wickets at an average of 20.75 in three matches. Regardless of who you are and how much Test cricket you have played, you cannot regain your rhythm in the nets. In stark contrast is Steven Finn. Finn was arguably the standout bowler in the series in South Africa, where Anderson struggled, but now his rhythm appears to have eluded him once more. He is not doing anything wrong—I know from my own playing days that sometimes you can put in just as much effort and believe you are releasing the ball just as quickly, but it simply does not come out with the same sharpness. My concern is that he has no opportunity to regain his rhythm before the final Test at Lord's on 9 June—there is only one T20 Blast match for Middlesex in which he might participate. Finn must play at Lord's. There has been some discussion that England might consider giving Jake Ball, who has been part of the squad for the first two Tests, a chance, but he can wait. Finn is familiar with Lord's, and this could be his chance to regain form. Even in victory, it is essential to seek improvements, and there are a few areas that may be causing concern for the England management at present. Jonny Bairstow has excelled with the bat this summer, but his wicketkeeping remains a work in progress. He does make errors: dropping catches and missing stumpings. It is an extremely challenging role, and slow-motion replays can be harsh on keepers because you wonder, 'how did he miss that?' But it occurs in an instant. However, I do not believe his position behind the stumps is in jeopardy. Unfortunately, those mistakes can sometimes be costly, and if he makes too many, his role as a keeper will be scrutinised. Another issue is Nick Compton's form at number three. Although he will be greatly relieved to have scored 22 not out in the second innings as England chased 79 to win in Durham, his issue is that he has not amassed significant runs all summer—for England or Middlesex. Lord's is a venue he knows well, and he will be eager to perform well. It will be a flatter pitch than we have seen so far this summer, and the conditions should be more favourable for batting. If England can win the toss and bat first, he will have an excellent opportunity to secure that position—that is how he will view it. I do not believe his England place necessarily depends on his performance in the third Test—there is a considerable gap between that match and the first Test against Pakistan on 14 July, and he could go away and score a substantial number of runs for Middlesex. However, if he does not achieve a good score, people will scrutinise him even more. One individual whose position is certainly not under scrutiny is Cook. What an extraordinary achievement for him to become the first Englishman to reach 10,000 Test runs. He has accomplished it in the most challenging manner—opening the batting, much of it with the responsibility of captaincy, and with uncertainty over his partner at the other end. These are three factors that most people would find incredibly difficult to overcome. You must have immense admiration for him. He is not a stylist, and he does not attract crowds eager to watch him, but that is Test cricket. You need players like Cook to blunt attacks and lay the foundation of an innings for the team. He has fulfilled that role exceptionally well, and he will continue to do so. For a time, he was as stubborn in his captaincy as he was in his batting, and as a leader, you do not really want that. However, he has certainly become more open over the past year, and his confidence has grown significantly. Yet he can still go out to bat, set everything aside, and concentrate on what he needs to do with a bat in hand—and that is a great testament to him. That focus has, in some ways, been Cook's defining quality as a Test batsman, and it was evident from the very start. I recall him arriving in Nagpur after that lengthy journey from the West Indies, just two days before making his debut, and he scored 60 and a century. You thought, 'this chap is quite special', because he can concentrate entirely on batting. Long may he continue. Jonathan Agnew was speaking to BBC Sport's James Gheerbrant.

text: After months of secrecy, the sequel to the late Stieg Larsson's best-selling Millennium series has been published. These are external links and will open in a new window. The Girl in the Spider's Web, authored by David Lagercrantz, continues the tale of punk super-hacker Lisbeth Salander, which commenced in The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo. However, as Lagercrantz elucidates, crafting the new instalment brought the challenge of remaining faithful to Larsson's characters and criticism from Larsson's long-term partner. There has been so much secrecy surrounding this book, so I am eager to see what people think, says Swedish writer David Lagercrantz, speaking to the BBC just days before The Girl in the Spider's Web was released globally. With over 80 million copies of Stieg Larsson's Millennium Trilogy already sold, Lagercrantz can be excused for experiencing some pre-publication nerves. I have felt pressure from the beginning, he confesses. I am absolutely terrified. Yet, I believe the pressure actually improved my writing. It would be a disgrace if I did not live up to [Stieg Larsson's] books or at least attempt my best. Larsson, who passed away from a heart attack at the age of 50 in 2004, did not witness his novels—The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo, The Girl Who Played with Fire, and The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet's Nest—become a publishing phenomenon. The books were all adapted for the screen—three Swedish films and an American remake of Dragon Tattoo featuring Rooney Mara and Daniel Craig. Despite being with him for 32 years, Larsson's partner Eva Gabrielsson was not entitled to anything from his estate under Swedish law, as they were not married and there was no valid will. She has been embroiled in a legal dispute for several years with his father and brother, who inherited Larsson's estate. In December 2013, the estate and Swedish publisher Norstedts commissioned Lagercrantz to take on the characters of hacker and social misfit Lisbeth Salander and journalist Mikael Blomkvist. In the lead-up to publication, Gabrielsson has described Lagercrantz as a totally idiotic choice and told The Sunday Times that the sequel was a money-making stunt that would have appalled Larsson. How has he coped with the criticism? It was difficult, he responds without hesitation. All I wanted to do was follow my passion and tell a good story. This has been the thrill of my life. text: David Cameron's hurried visit to Paris on Monday night is yet another significant sign that his EU reforms - dismissed as weak by critics in the UK - are seen by some in the EU as going too far. France is concerned about the Prime Minister's efforts to shield non-euro countries from eurozone regulations. This may seem entirely reasonable. Most EU nations use the euro. Why should they be permitted to collaborate to the detriment of non-euro countries like Britain? However, France believes David Cameron and George Osborne, the UK Chancellor, are being underhanded. It suspects they are using the argument to secure an unfair advantage for the City of London and a covert veto on eurozone and broader EU financial legislation. The French economy is sluggish, to put it politely, and the French President is about to enter the political race for re-election. He cannot be perceived as allowing Britain to excel financially while his eurozone options are limited. Two weeks ago, on the eve of the publication in Brussels of David Cameron's draft reform plans, we were informed by a high-level source close to the negotiations that the French delayed them for hours, concerned about the wording regarding safeguards for non-eurozone countries. All leaders must agree to the reforms this Thursday for them to be approved at the EU summit. The French could again dispute, clash over, and even thwart the Prime Minister's hopes of a deal if they choose. A real possibility, however, is that after hours of closed-door negotiations, the summit will conclude with the kind of EU compromise so criticised by the bloc's detractors. Yet, in typical EU fashion, all parties wish to depart claiming they have achieved something. The French will likely boast that the British failed to secure a veto over eurozone legislation (even though David Cameron never requested one). The countries of Central and Eastern Europe received Britain's promise to help strengthen NATO in Eastern Europe as a pre-summit incentive. They also aim to limit reductions in EU migrant in-work and child benefits to the UK only. The European Commission and Council played key roles as facilitator and mediator respectively and, as such, received some respectful press coverage in Europe—something they are not accustomed to in these days of eurozone and migration crises. And David Cameron should secure his deal in time for him to call the referendum as soon as possible—believed to be 23 June. He is fully aware that, regardless of the deal's content, his critics will denounce it. Thus, he seems to prefer to tick just enough boxes, particularly the one addressing migration—the primary concern of many of his voters. He knows that persuading the British public to support any deal ahead of the referendum is a far tougher challenge than gaining the support of 27 fractious and distracted EU leaders. The Prime Minister wishes to leave his EU colleagues to return to arguably the toughest issue they face: refugees, boats, and migrant quotas. On Monday, European Council President Donald Tusk urged EU leaders to assist David Cameron in securing his reforms. It is high time we started listening to each other's arguments, the risk of break-up is real. What is broken cannot be mended, he said. If those are Mr Tusk's words on Brexit (the idea of Britain leaving the EU), what might he say about the refugee and migration crisis, combined with the steady disintegration of European unity? text: I have been working now for more than two decades and I've not seen a measles epidemic of this severity, says Doctor Raza Hasan, as he shows me around the measles isolation ward of the Lahore Children's Hospital. The ward is so crowded with infants and young children that they are sharing beds. At one point, up to 70 new patients were arriving at the hospital daily. They are covered in rashes and suffering from high fevers, with some fighting for their lives. In one corner, a boy lies motionless on his back, his eyes rolled back as flies crawl across his face. At least 40 children have died in this hospital since the epidemic spread from southern Pakistan to Lahore and other parts of Punjab province at the year's start. The burden of managing the epidemic weighs heavily on Dr Hasan, who recounts incidents of families attacking medical staff at the hospital after learning their children had died. While measles itself is rarely fatal, it can lead to life-threatening complications such as meningitis and pneumonia, especially in developing countries where malnutrition leaves many children with low immunity. Some of them are arriving very late at the hospital, says Dr Hasan. After developing complications at home, their parents don't take them to doctors, they don't get any treatment and so when they come here... there is not much we can do. Some are in the final stage of life or already dead with meningitis or pneumonia, he continues. However, while this may be true, it is not the complete story. It does not explain why so many children in Pakistan are contracting measles initially. The epidemic has spread rapidly with thousands of cases nationwide and 239 deaths between January and April 2013, according to Pakistan's national measles co-ordinator. One reason is the low vaccination coverage of the population, says Dr Tanvir Ahmed, the director-general of health services for Punjab province. In the districts there are even pockets where there is no vaccination coverage. The average [coverage] for Punjab is 58%. Through an entrance off a narrow street in Lahore, we ascend the stairs to the home of Nasara and Mohammed Ashfaq. The walls are bare and despite daytime temperatures exceeding 40C, there are no fans. Mohammed is cradling his daughter Yasmeen, who will turn two this summer. She is covered in the measles rash and has had an alarmingly high fever. Just a few days ago, her brother Ehsan died at the Lahore Children's hospital from complications arising from measles. He was nine months old. Now the family is afraid to take Yasmeen to hospital and hope she will recover at home. Yasmeen, like her brother, had not been properly vaccinated against measles. I didn't get him vaccinated because I was on my own at home with so many children, says Nasara. And we had to go out to get the vaccinations, so it was difficult because they were small. While doctors here say families need to take more responsibility for ensuring their children are vaccinated, they acknowledge the official vaccination programmes have often been poorly managed, leading to people missing out. We have removed nine district managers on the basis of poor performance of the programmes, says Dr Tanvir Ahmed, head of health services in Punjab. And we have improved our monitoring and supervision. There has also been an emergency measles vaccination campaign in recent weeks covering 2.6 million children in Lahore. In June, another 11 million children are scheduled to be inoculated in other parts of Punjab. Health experts hope this will bring the epidemic in the province under control by mid-July. They say they have the large stocks of vaccine necessary to achieve this in the province. However, they say this is not the case in the southern province of Sindh, where the outbreak began. It is believed mass vaccination programmes will not commence in Sindh until the autumn. So in this area, which has already had by far the highest number of cases in the country, the epidemic could worsen in the coming months.

text: Labour remains committed to renewing the Trident nuclear weapons system, new shadow defence secretary Nia Griffith has said. She informed Forces TV she had serious doubts about it in the past, but Labour policy was to support it, and that was unlikely to change. Ms Griffith replaced Clive Lewis when Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn reshuffled his shadow cabinet earlier this month. Mr Lewis's conference speech on Trident was altered at the last moment. He was reportedly prevented by the leader's office from committing categorically to Labour renewing the UK's nuclear weapons system. Labour's official policy is to support renewing the Trident system, but leader Jeremy Corbyn—a longstanding CND campaigner—wants to change the party's position and initiated a defence review to examine the issue. In her interview, Ms Griffith stated Labour delegates at the party conference in September had backed the weapons system and that is a commitment that we will stick to. She said Labour can't be shilly-shallying about on Trident, but added the UK must advocate for multilateral disarmament. What we do need to do now, and there is a very strong mood for this, both within the Labour Party and in the broader public, is really push forward on the multilateral nuclear disarmament, on the multilateral approach of bringing people together across the globe to try to make our world a safer place, she stated. Renewing Trident would involve the manufacture of four replacement submarines at a current estimated cost of £31bn. The controversial nuclear arms issue caused a split within Labour when MPs voted in favour of renewal in July, with 140 Labour MPs supporting renewal, 47 voting against, and the remainder abstaining. CND, which advocates for a global ban on nuclear weapons, expressed disappointment at Ms Griffith's comments, saying the issue appeared to be being sidelined. Labour hasn't debated Trident for 20 years but it insists on clinging to its old policy in spite of the fact that the majority of Labour members oppose Trident and the party leader has been elected twice with a strong anti-Trident position, said its general secretary Kate Hudson. We urge Labour Party members to ensure that the defence review be published, together with a full democratic debate within the party and at its next conference. Meanwhile, Mr Corbyn has announced the appointment of seven more shadow ministers, bringing his team to 68 frontbenchers. Those assuming shadow ministerial positions are Paula Sherriff (women and equalities), Richard Burden (transport), Wayne David (defence), Khalid Mahmood (foreign office), Rupa Huq (home affairs), Lyn Brown (home affairs), and Gill Furniss (business). And the former chief whip, Dame Rosie Winterton, has been appointed the party's envoy with responsibility for relations with Labour's international sister parties on the Party of European Socialists. Her dismissal as chief whip, as part of a reshuffle following Mr Corbyn's re-election, had angered many Labour MPs.
