text: China's Communist Party and its more than two-million-man army aren't supposed to like video games. Home-video consoles, which gained popularity during the 1990s, were officially banned in 2000 due to concerns they were corrupting Chinese youth. It resembled a King Canute-style communism—an effort to resist the rising tide of capitalism and the influx of Western cultural products. Ultimately, this effort failed, and the loud warnings about electronic heroin were overwhelmed by consumer demand. Consoles remained accessible on the grey market, and the gaming industry simply transitioned online. Today, it is an industry valued at over 50bn Chinese RMB ($7.9bn; £5.2bn) annually, with the Communist Party and its military now fully engaged. Since its public release a few months ago, Glorious Mission, a video game initially developed for and by the Chinese military, has been downloaded over a million times. It may appear to be just another violent shoot 'em up, but it is, in fact, China's latest propaganda instrument. It was created as a training tool for Chinese soldiers, and state-run television has broadcast images of them enthusiastically gaming, controlling virtual People's Liberation Army troops in various battlefield scenarios. Interestingly, the virtual enemy they confront sometimes bears at least a passing resemblance to the US and its allies, raising questions about the real-life scenarios for which they are training. Regardless of its impact on soldiers, the decision to make the game available to the general public was made to instil patriotic values, the core values of the military, according to army sources. Gu Kai, vice-president of the software developers behind the game, Giant Network Technology, believes the game will help attract new army recruits. I would hope that somebody will play the game and fulfil their dream, he states. Most young boys, from the bottom of their hearts, want to be a soldier. They like to fight, they like to win, and if this video game can make that dream come true, I won't be surprised. The propaganda appears, at times, less than subtle. One stage of the game recreates the fiery atmosphere of camp life, according to one news report. In one Shanghai internet café, nearly every one of the approximately 100 terminals is occupied with someone engaged in intense online combat with a variety of foes; goblin, alien, or human. One young man claims he spends more than 10 hours a week there, and he agrees that online games might be a powerful tool for influencing thoughts and ideas. It's possible, he says. Most of the players here are young. A military video game could make you feel familiar with and then develop an affinity for the army. Glorious Mission, therefore, represents a rapid shift for the Chinese military as well as an indication that China is not only censoring the internet, banning search terms, and deleting posts, which it does routinely, but also now attempting to harness its power. The country already has an army of Communist Party bloggers posting comments in support of the government. The seemingly rehabilitated gaming industry is simply the latest weapon. This year, reports on state media suggest that the authorities might be about to officially abandon their moral concerns about the gaming industry entirely, with the consoles ban apparently under review. Gu Kai from Giant Network Technology tells me that he believes China is now well and truly over it. I've met some of the officials, he says. They stopped worrying about video games years ago. Most of them are promoting gaming as a new, hopeful, and fast-growing industry. At least here in Shanghai, all the officials are very open and supportive. China is not the first to design a video game for military training purposes—Glorious Mission bears some resemblance to a game created 10 years ago as a tool for the US military and also as a lure for army recruitment. However, influencing the thoughts of the wider public and attempting to mould and foster nationalist sentiment and loyalty is a more ambitious endeavour, and in China's virtual world, it is a struggle that is likely to intensify.

text: Christian Eriksen scored twice as Tottenham proved far too strong for spirited Hull City at White Hart Lane. The Denmark international scored in both halves as Spurs strengthened their hold on fifth place in the Premier League with their eighth victory of the season. Danny Rose set up Eriksen's first goal within 15 minutes after effective work down the left, and Kyle Walker did the same from the right to extinguish any hope of a Hull comeback after the interval. Eriksen was extremely unfortunate not to secure the match ball after his excellent free-kick was tipped onto the post by Hull goalkeeper David Marshall, allowing Victor Wanyama to convert the rebound from a few yards out. Hull have no grounds for complaint about the defeat, but the one-sided final score was somewhat harsh on the Tigers after they matched their hosts for extended periods. However, conceding 35 goals in 16 games is a damning statistic for the side second-bottom of the league, as is the fact they have now lost six consecutive away games, equalling their top-flight record. Spurs dominated possession and opportunities, having 27 shots in total, but clear-cut chances were scarce. Wing-backs Rose and Walker were a constant threat, and it was through them that Spurs found the most success. With 14 minutes elapsed, Rose sprinted down the wing to latch onto Jan Vertonghen's long ball, advanced and cut inside his marker before setting up Eriksen to power the ball high into the net. With Spurs deploying Eric Dier alongside Vertonghen and Toby Alderweireld in a three-man defence, Spurs' wing-backs had greater freedom to advance, and their second goal was similar to the first. This time it was Dier with a ball over the top for Walker to collect and move into the area, and when he crossed low across the face of goal, it was an easy task for Eriksen to slot home his second at the back post, marking his fifth goal in his last four Premier League matches. Rose then won the free-kick from which Spurs scored their third, completing a fine display by the England full-back. Despite the disparity between the sides in terms of league position and resources, Hull delivered a performance that was, for a time, on par with their hosts. They managed 10 shots on goal away from home against a top-five side, something they have struggled to do at home against lesser opposition this season, and with a bit more composure, they might have pegged Spurs back at 1-1. Jake Livermore was the standout player for Hull against his former club and nearly brought them level. His first chance came during a sustained spell of Hull pressure after falling behind, but Hugo Lloris got down well to save his poked effort. The Tigers' second good chance came as the Spurs fans were beginning to grumble at their team's inability to impose themselves on the visitors at the start of the second half. Spurs had several penalty appeals turned down by referee Andre Marriner, and it was following one of those, after Eriksen was bundled over by Andrew Robertson, that Hull nearly equalised. The breakaway ended with Livermore being played in on the right of the area, but his initial shot was blocked and his follow-up cleared away by the left boot of Lloris. Three minutes later, Eriksen slotted in his second goal of the night, and the game was up for the Tigers. Spurs manager Mauricio Pochettino said, I think it was a game we dominated. I think the most important is the three points, to be close to the top four. In some parts, the team played well, which is hard against a team playing for survival. On Christian Eriksen, he commented, He was very close to a hat-trick. It was a very good performance for him; he played very, very well. On Eric Dier, he remarked, I know there are a lot of rumours, but he's 100% our player. He's very important for us. He signed a contract after the Euros and showed his commitment to the club. There's no doubt his future is at White Hart Lane. Media playback is not supported on this device. Hull manager Mike Phelan stated, We came here with a fabulous attitude. text: The Football League season is poised for another dramatic climax as six teams aim to be promoted by winning their respective play-off finals at Wembley. Saturday's Championship final between Hull City and Sheffield Wednesday is valued at approximately £170 million for the victors. Barnsley and Millwall will compete in the League One final on Sunday, with AFC Wimbledon and Plymouth Argyle concluding the 2015-16 season in League Two on Monday. Saturday 28 May, 17:00 BST Hull manager Steve Bruce is experienced in securing promotion, having led Birmingham City to the Premier League in 2002 and 2007 and guiding the Tigers there in 2013. However, Saturday will mark his first visit to Wembley for a play-off final, and the journey has been challenging for Bruce and his team. Their season was marred by inconsistency, and they nearly lost a 3-0 first-leg advantage in their play-off semi-final against Derby County. You can sense there's a significant match approaching, Bruce told BBC Radio Humberside. The players are tackling each other and eager to play. Sometimes you need to restrain them a bit because we need to let them go on Saturday. Hull last appeared at Wembley in 2014 for their FA Cup final loss to Arsenal, and the experience Bruce has gained over his 18-year managerial career could be vital as they aim to return to the top division at the first attempt. Media playback is not supported on this device On the other hand, the closest Sheffield Wednesday head coach Carlos Carvalhal has come to Wembley is watching English league football on television as a child in Portugal. Carvalhal had a modest managerial career in his home country and Turkey before joining Wednesday in June 2015. His team has steadily climbed the table throughout the season, and their play-off performances were decisive, defeating Brighton over two legs to secure their place at Wembley. The South Yorkshire team has not visited the national stadium since appearing in both domestic cup finals in 1993 and has only finished in the top half of the Championship table twice since their relegation from the top division in 2000. Hull City are a strong team with a very spirited coach - they are a premier team and it will be very tough, Carvalhal told BBC Radio Sheffield. My players know exactly what they need to do and we will prepare for this game like any of the others. We expect a very good response from the players to the plan we will implement. Sunday 29 May, 15:00 BST In November 2015, Barnsley were at the bottom of the League One table, having won just five of their 20 league matches. Six months later, they have won the Johnstone's Paint Trophy, secured the last third-tier play-off spot, and decisively defeated Walsall 6-1 on aggregate in their semi-final tie. Caretaker manager Paul Heckingbottom built on the foundation laid by Lee Johnson, leading Barnsley through a series of 12 victories in 15 league games between December and March. Everything is bigger about the play-offs, Heckingbottom, who was part of the Barnsley squad promoted via the play-offs in 2006, told BBC Radio Sheffield. It's not just the prize at the end, but the bigger opposition, better-quality football, and away games at larger stadiums that come in the Championship. It's a cup final after 46 rounds and a two-legged semi-final, and that brings its own unique tension, adrenaline, and excitement for everyone. That's what makes a win that much sweeter. Millwall are seeking an immediate return to the Championship after their five-year stay in the second tier ended last season. Club legend Neil Harris has led their promotion push, having overseen a player clear-out following relegation. We have come a long way as a group. We have a terrific bunch of lads, and they have great spirit, the 38-year-old told BBC Radio London. Whatever happens on Sunday, the pride is back in the club, and we have foundations to build on. Harris, Millwall's record goalscorer, was part of the Lions side that won the League One play-off final in 2010, defeating Swindon 1-0 at Wembley. Barnsley played there this year, but they didn't play against Millwall or in front of our fans there, he said. The noise at The Den in the second leg against Bradford was something special. That is what we will have at Wembley, with 35,000 passionate fans going to support their team. Every time we have had that, the players have performed. You must have the link between the terraces and the pitch at this club. Monday 30 May, 15:00 BST Phoenix club AFC Wimbledon could reach the third tier for the first time in their brief history on Monday. Formed in 2002 after an independent panel allowed the old Wimbledon FC to relocate to Milton Keynes, the Dons achieved five promotions to enter the Football League in 2011. Neal Ardley, in charge at Kingsmeadow since October 2012, guided the club to seventh in the table following seven victories in their last 10 matches of the campaign. Someone asked me if it is the biggest game in the club's history, former Wimbledon midfielder Ardley told BBC Radio London. Terry Brown getting them into the Football League would have been, and maybe us staying in the Football League on the last day in 2013. But it is the biggest occasion in the club's history. Wimbledon and Wembley have a lovely ring to it, and we know why. To take these fans to Wembley, it is a most unique club and a wonderful feeling for me and the players to do that for this group of fans - who, 14 years ago, were dealt the biggest blow you could possibly imagine and rolled their sleeves up and said 'no, it's not happening'. Plymouth Argyle have not visited Wembley since 1996. During that time, the Devon club has gone from leading the Championship in August 2004 to nearly going out of existence seven years later. Relegation from the Championship in 2010 led to financial instability at Home Park, and administrators arrived soon after, with Argyle dropping to League Two in 2011. The club's players threatened to strike that September, having not been paid in full since the previous December, and only avoided relegation out of the Football League in the penultimate week of that season. We nearly died, so to be here in this position is absolutely fantastic, Argyle president Chris Webb, who helped rescue the club, told BBC Sport. We had a torrid time with the players and staff not being paid for 10 months, but out of that, we united the fans, the staff, and the city, and the club was almost reborn. I believe if we can make that step at Wembley, then we're well set up to challenge in League One as well. text: Sharks have patrolled the oceans for at least 400 million years and evolved into a huge range of remarkable species. These are external links and will open in a new window. There are deep sea lantern sharks that emit a glow in the dark, wobbegong sharks that develop shaggy beards, and majestic, plankton-filtering whale sharks, which are the largest fish in the ocean. Nonetheless, when many individuals think of these creatures, one thought prevails: shark attacks. As a beachgoer, diver, or surfer, your likelihood of encountering a shark, let alone being killed by one, is remarkably low; lightning strikes, bee stings, and car accidents all pose significantly greater threats than sharks. In truth, humans kill millions more sharks than sharks kill humans. A quarter of all shark species, along with their relatives the rays, are at risk of extinction, according to a recent report from the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN). The primary threat to sharks is overfishing, with the largest species facing the greatest danger. However, a controversial shark cull was recently ordered in Western Australia following a series of attacks. Scientists are now exploring alternative methods to address the shark attack issue. Professor Shaun Collin is leading a team of neurobiologists at the University of Western Australia (UWA) who are learning to think like sharks. We're trying to tread this very fine line of protecting both humans and sharks at the same time, Professor Collin told the BBC World Service programme Discovery. By studying shark brains and senses, the team is developing and testing various non-lethal repellents. The goal is to manipulate the sharks' finely-tuned senses to discourage them from approaching and attacking people. One such innovation is a shark-proof wetsuit designed to resemble poisonous, black and white banded sea snakes, which many sharks tend to avoid. The stripy wetsuit was initially conceived years ago by marine biologist Walter Starck. Now, a detailed understanding of shark vision is assisting the UWA team in updating this concept. Nathan Hart, assistant professor at UWA, explained to me that sharks do not see as well as humans. We've ensured that the size of the bands can be detected by a shark from a certain distance, he says. Tests of the new wetsuit design are currently underway. This involves wrapping the fabric around a barrel filled with dead fish and observing how sharks respond to it in the wild. It is still early days, but so far, Nathan informed me, the results have been promising. Based on what we know about the sensory systems of sharks, they should reduce your risk to some extent, he says. Just like a seatbelt in a car, it doesn't reduce your risk to zero; it's a matter of reducing your risk by a certain amount and by as much as possible, he adds. In addition to trying to protect individual swimmers, another strategy is to make certain areas off-limits to sharks. We can try and define areas on the beaches where people are confident they can go and swim, says Dr Hart. Bubble curtains could be deployed to deter sharks from popular beaches. The idea is to lay perforated hosepipes across the seabed and pump air through them to create a plume of bubbles that sharks may choose not to swim through. Sharks can see and hear the bubbles and also feel them with their lateral line, a system of sense organs many fish possess. It's a system of what's known as 'distant touch'; it detects vibrations and very low-frequency sound in the water, Nathan explained. Early tests showed that tiger sharks eventually muster the courage to cross a barrier of bubbles, suggesting they have the capacity to learn. Eugenie Clark, a veteran marine biologist at the Mote Marine Laboratory in Florida, pioneered studies of shark learning in the 1950s. Nicknamed The Shark Lady, Dr Clark trained captive sharks to press targets with their snouts and ring bells for a food reward. She demonstrated for the first time that sharks can learn and remember things. Eugenie recounted to me the time she took a trained baby nurse shark as a gift for the Crown Prince of Japan, who shared her fascination with fish. The airline gave me an extra seat for the shark. Most people didn't know, he was such a tiny thing he was less than two feet long. But he never made a mistake, says Eugenie. Recently, I witnessed firsthand the capacity sharks have to learn, particularly that they can learn not to attack people. I went diving off the Pacific island of Fiji and saw my first bull sharks, notorious as one of the most aggressive shark species. Locals from Beqa Adventure Divers have trained a population of around 100 bull sharks to approach a diver, one-by-one, and gently take a piece of fish offered to them by hand. The sharks have learned how to behave if they want food. They know us very well, Fijian divemaster Papa told me before I entered the water. That's the good thing, they know what's going on. Preparing for the dive, I was unsure how I would react to seeing these giant predators. But as soon as I descended beneath the waves, my nerves dissipated, and I saw just how graceful and calm bull sharks can be. There was no safety cage or any sort of repellent, and I never felt in any kind of danger. In addition to helping to change the sharks' negative reputation as insatiable killers, the Fijian divers are demonstrating that a live shark in the water is worth far more than a dead one. In Fiji and elsewhere around the world, sharks are under immense pressure from the demand in Asia for shark fin soup. Back in Western Australia, the shark cull continues amid beachside protests. The problem has been an unusually high number of shark attacks, with seven fatalities over the last three years compared with 20 in the last century. The response of the Western Australia government has been to lay baited hooks offshore from popular beaches. Any great white, tiger, and bull sharks that are caught and are larger than 3m long are shot and discarded at sea. One opponent of the cull is shark attack survivor Rodney Fox. Fifty years ago, he suffered a horrific attack from a great white in South Australia but has since become a dedicated shark advocate. We just have to learn how to live with the sharks and not just kill them from fear, he told me. He believes killing sharks deliberately is an unscientific and irrational strategy to try to reduce the attack rate. However, Western Australia's government asserts the cull is in place to protect swimmers and surfers. text: Poland's Prime Minister Beata Szydlo has vowed to press on with judicial reforms, saying the government would not yield to pressure from the street and from abroad. These are external links and will open in a new window. On Monday, President Andrzej Duda vetoed a controversial law to replace Supreme Court judges with government nominees. This occurred after thousands protested across Poland. Mr Duda stated he made his decision after consulting legal experts and judges. The European Commission had threatened sanctions this week if the changes were not reversed. European Council President Donald Tusk, a former Polish prime minister, warned of a black scenario that could ultimately lead to the marginalisation of Poland in Europe. In a televised address, Ms Szydlo insisted that the Law and Justice (PiS) government would not relent. We all want to live in a fair Poland, which is why the reform of the courts is needed... Today's veto by the president has slowed down work on the reform. We cannot yield to pressure from the streets and abroad... We have a stable majority. We won't give in to pressure. We will realise our plan. As president, I don't feel this law would strengthen a sense of justice, Andrzej Duda said in a statement on national television. These laws must be amended. He stated he was vetoing two of the new laws but approving a third, which grants the justice minister the right to appoint the heads of Poland's lower courts. Many were surprised, as the president is a former member of the right-wing ruling party pushing the legislation. The PiS government has strongly rejected claims that the reforms are a move towards authoritarian rule and expressed disappointment at President Duda's decision. The president had already intervened last week in an attempt to find a compromise. He said he had discussed the reforms at the weekend, including with Zofia Romaszewska, a veteran dissident from the communist era. She was jailed during the years of martial law in the early 1980s but is now one of the president's advisers. The activist had told Mr Duda she did not want to return to the days when the general prosecutor could do virtually anything. Ms Romaszewska told Polish media it was completely out of the question for the attorney-general to take charge of the Supreme Court. Opposition MPs also praised the role of protesters in influencing the decision. Demonstrations have taken place in dozens of Polish cities, from Poznan and Lublin to Krakow, Gdansk and Warsaw, and there have been calls for the protests to continue. Mr Duda warned that no change should lead to a separation of the state from society. Poland's judicial system is widely viewed as slow, and reforms are seen as necessary. I'm absolutely a supporter of this reform, but a wise reform, said President Duda. The three reforms give the justice minister and MPs broad powers and have prompted alarm from the US, as well as the EU. The president's initial compromise plan last week watered down the government's bid to push through its nominees for the National Judiciary Council by requiring the support of another political party. In his statement, the president said he regretted that a draft law on reforming the Supreme Court had not been handed to him before a vote in the lower house of parliament, the Sejm. The president also took issue with the strengthened role of the justice minister, who also acts as attorney general in Poland. In theory, the Polish parliament could now challenge the president's veto. Law and Justice has a simple majority in the Sejm but needs a three-fifths majority if it decides to reject Mr Duda's decision. It could theoretically achieve that with the support of a smaller party, Kukiz'15, but that is not seen as certain. A more likely step would be to spend the next weeks redrafting the two bills that the president has turned down and seek his approval. The protest movement has celebrated its success so far but is now pushing for the president to veto the third reform as well. Much now depends on the man seen as the real power behind the government, PiS co-founder Jaroslaw Kaczynski.

text: Returning to Cold Feet after more than a decade since it was last seen on TV felt like putting on an old jumper, Fay Ripley has said. The actress expressed her delight at reviving the role of Jenny, likening it to bumping into an old friend. Co-star John Thomson stated that the timing was ideal to revisit the show, citing a great need for nostalgia. Eight new episodes of the comedy-drama, which concluded in 2003 after five series, will be aired this autumn. Following the lives of three 30-something couples, over 10 million viewers tuned into the final episode, which included the funeral of central character Rachel, portrayed by Helen Baxendale. The new series will explore how life has treated friends Jenny and Pete, Karen and David, and widower Adam over the years, as they navigate middle age and parenting teenage children. Ripley initially thought it might be challenging to return to character but found: Within a minute, it was the same. It was like stepping back in time. We have a shorthand when working together, all of us, which is incredibly useful. She joked that this meant they didn't have to do any of the polite stuff when reunited on set. You can just go in and say, 'I've got a banging headache, my menopause is giving me gip', she quipped. Thomson remarked the timing couldn't be better to revive something so feel-good as Cold Feet. The world isn't in a great place at the moment, and there's a great need for nostalgia, to look back at the days when things seemed okay, he said. Hermione Norris concurred it was comforting to see the old characters together again but admitted she was initially hesitant to reprise the role of Karen. It's that thing in life - you think 'Don't go back, just move forward', she said. It was so of its time and it was so loved, I thought maybe it should be left as I didn't want to do anything that would have undone that. She said the show's creator, Mike Bullen, convinced her it was not a remake, but rather a case of revisiting these characters in this chapter of their life - and revealed Karen uses the dating app Tinder in the new series, illustrating how technology and dating have evolved. Norris said she did not re-watch any old episodes before filming began, stating: It was amazing how much I'd forgotten - I couldn't remember how many children David and I had. She also mentioned she felt strange not having Baxendale there, adding: I missed Helen hugely - because Rachel was Karen's best friend. I really felt her absence. It's like it would be in real life, if you've lost a really good friend. Ripley joked there would be no shower moment for Rachel - referring to the scene in US soap opera Dallas when character Bobby Ewing returned, with his death the previous year explained away as a dream. She added Baxendale was happy with the show continuing without her, saying: She's cool with it. Norris also said she loved working with people her own age on the show: I really appreciate being with my own generation. As an actor, and as Karen. I find as a woman, I love being older. The weight of experience - you just don't have that as a 30-year-old. Robert Bathurst commented on his decision to return as David: It's all very much down to the script. I wouldn't have done it for the sake of it. He said the secret of the show's success was that it has never been about anything - it's about ordinariness, adding: It's about people and how they rub along together. Bathurst also hopes the new series will stand alone and attract a new generation of fans. Among the new cast members is BBC Radio 1 presenter Cel Spellman, who plays Adam and Rachel's teenage son Matthew - last seen as a baby in the final episodes of the previous series. He admitted it was daunting to join the hit show - and that he binge-watched the box set to prepare for the role. I started to realise why the show was so successful, he said, adding that his mother was a huge fan who pecked his head for details of the new storylines. But Mrs Spellman and Cold Feet fans will have to wait a bit longer to find out what's in store for the characters, with show bosses keen to avoid any spoilers before it begins. text: An electrical fire in a tunnel under a pavement in central London is still burning as firefighters have reported difficulty tackling the blaze. London Fire Brigade (LFB) stated that firefighters would be working most of the night on Thursday. It reported that the fire, which has been burning for over 24 hours, had been contained within the tunnel. Approximately 5,000 individuals were evacuated in Holborn on Wednesday after smoke was observed emanating from an inspection cover. Over 100 businesses have been impacted. LFB mentioned that the cordon in Kingsway had been reduced, but the road remained closed. Assistant Commissioner Dany Cotton remarked: This is a technically difficult and unusual incident to tackle as it is underground. She noted that fighting fires in tunnels was very hazardous, and precautions had to be taken to prevent the risk of a gas explosion. Firefighters have, however, been applying water through access points throughout the night, to control the spread of the fire, she added. She urged people to avoid the immediate area if possible. A total of 35 firefighters and six fire engines are present at the fire on Kingsway. Local road closures remain in effect. The cause of the fire is still unknown, but it is believed the blaze originated among underground cables. Speaking to BBC London 94.9, Met Police Insp Neil Johnson stated: I imagine this road will be closed a long time after this is finished because of damage the heat does to the road. It will have to remain closed until a structural engineer examines it properly and either he or she says what work has to be done and that work is completed - this is not an overnight job. On Wednesday, onlookers reported difficulty in breathing and chaos in and around Holborn. UK Power Networks reported that the number of customers currently affected by the power cuts stood at about 1,000 and it had restored power to about 2,000. It is hoped power will be restored to everyone affected by the end of Thursday. Apologising to customers, Matt Rudling from the firm said: The gas is still burning under there and until we can gain access to that particular area we won't understand what's caused it and what we can do. He added that emergency generators were being used to supply power to the area and engineers were also attempting to connect some of the damaged cables to unaffected ones. Several West End theatres were forced to cancel performances on Wednesday evening, including Beautiful - The Carole King Musical, Charlie And The Chocolate Factory, Disney's The Lion King, Gypsy, Mamma Mia! The Play That Goes Wrong and The Woman In Black. Thursday's matinee performances at the Novello and Aldwych theatres were also cancelled. Councillor Richard Beddoe, from Westminster City Council, said: We are relieved to hear that there were no serious casualties but the losses to big businesses in the West End, due to poor infrastructure, is just not acceptable. We want to see action. The National Grid stated it was working with emergency services to isolate the gas supply. In a statement, the company, which operates gas transmission infrastructure in the UK, said the fire had affected one of its pipes. This is a challenging operation due to the fire's location, access to our gas pipe and other utilities in close proximity. We cannot just turn a valve and switch off the gas because of safety reasons and [the] impact on the gas network, the statement said. Transport for London stated Holborn station is open, however, nine bus services are being diverted, the 1, 59, 68, 91, 168, 171, 188, 243 and 521. text: US illustrator Norman Bridwell, creator of the Clifford the Big Red Dog books, has died at the age of 86 following a fall at his home in Massachusetts. His beloved character first appeared in 1963 and went on to feature in over 40 stories, selling 120 million copies globally. Clifford's image has been used on merchandise and in US buildings, including the White House. Bridwell had completed two additional books scheduled for release next year. Dick Robinson, president of the author's long-time publisher Scholastic, stated: We are deeply saddened by the loss of our loyal and talented friend whose drawings and stories have inspired all of us and generations of children and their parents. His wife of 56 years, Norma, remarked: A lot of people were Clifford fans and that makes them Norman fans too. She was responsible for naming the character Clifford after her imaginary childhood friend. Over the decades, the bright red dog appeared in numerous stories, including Clifford Goes To Hollywood and Clifford and The Grouchy Neighbours, which became popular bedtime reading for children across the US and beyond. The dog often got into trouble before redeeming himself with a daring rescue or performing a good deed. Bridwell's wife noted there were parallels between the author and his creation. He's never been able to recognise that. Clifford tries to do the right thing, Norman tries to do the right thing, and he makes a mess of it. But he's the most lovable grown-up man. He's just a nice guy. Before achieving fame with Clifford, Bridwell worked as a commercial artist during the 1950s. He made numerous attempts to break into children's publishing until a New York book editor suggested he create a story around an illustration he had submitted of a child and her oversized dog. Further rejections followed until publishers Scholastic recognised his creation's potential—a move which led to lasting success for the company. I said to my wife, 'Now don't count on there being any more. This one is just a fluke. I don't know if there will ever be another one,' Bridwell said. In more recent years, the character was animated in a series of cartoons for US television, while a feature film—Clifford's Big Red Movie—was produced in 2004. Bridwell is survived by his wife, a son, and three grandchildren. A small private funeral service will be held along with a more public celebration of the author's life and work, his family announced.

text: Residents of a mid Wales village have voted on proposals to install a new train station in the area. The Welsh Government requested Carno Station Action Group and the community council to consult residents on two potential locations. One of the sites is the original station, closed in 1963 due to the Beeching cuts to Britain's railways. The old station subsequently became part of the Laura Ashley site in Carno. The village is situated on the Cambrian line between Aberystwyth and Shrewsbury. A campaign to reopen Carno station commenced in 2002. In 2011, Mid Wales Transportation, a group collaborating with the Welsh Government, stated there was a strong case for future investment in the station after conducting an appraisal. The site could be developed into a tourist information centre and a Laura Ashley museum if plans receive approval. Action Group chairman Jeremy Barnes said the week-long consultation concluded on 22 March, and the results would be processed before submission to the Welsh Government. He added: We have discussed with the Welsh Government the possibility of the new station including a tourist information centre, cafe, an office for the community council's clerk, and a small museum dedicated to Laura Ashley should the existing site be selected. Carno is a growing village with a population of about 750, and this proposed development will create employment and allow residents affordable access to work further afield. It is located on the longest stretch of railway without an intermediate station in the whole of Wales, the 22 miles between Caersws and Machynlleth. There is a strong consensus that the capital asset of the railway line passing through the village is being wasted as long as the trains pass through without stopping. The consultation followed a meeting between the action group and Transport Minister Edwina Hart last October. Fashion designer Laura Ashley had strong ties with Carno for nearly a quarter of a century before her death in 1985. Carno was the original Welsh base of the Laura Ashley company when she relocated with her husband Bernard from Kent in 1961. She is interred in a churchyard in the village. Laura Ashley's former headquarters in Carno, where many of her products were manufactured, closed in 2004.

text: A US Senate report has condemned the CIA's use of enhanced interrogation on al-Qaeda suspects after the 9/11 attacks. The 480-page summary outlines the treatment experienced by some of the organisation's prominent figures. Details of the interrogation of three of the most renowned individuals have now been disclosed. Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, Abu Zubaydah, and Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri were captured after the 9/11 attacks and remain in US custody at Guantanamo Bay. Once labelled by US intelligence as one of history's most infamous terrorists, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed is the self-confessed architect of the 9/11 attacks. He asserts that he personally beheaded the captured US journalist, Daniel Pearl. Born in Kuwait to Pakistani parents, he graduated from a US university before travelling to Afghanistan to combat the Soviets. There, he is believed to have first encountered Osama Bin Laden. He has been implicated in, or confessed to, several plots, including a plan to blow up US airlines over the Pacific in 1995. After his capture in Pakistan in 2003, he was taken to detention centres reportedly in Europe. According to the Senate report, he was subjected to waterboarding at least 183 times. A CIA officer described the procedure as a series of near drownings. However, the report stated that some of the information provided by Mohammed was fabricated. He remains detained at Guantanamo Bay after an attempt to try him in a New York court failed amid widespread opposition. Abu Zubaydah is believed to have been al-Qaeda's chief recruiter in the 1990s and later became a key organiser, linking Osama Bin Laden to other al-Qaeda cells. Although he is not thought to be directly connected to the 9/11 attacks, he is believed to have operated several camps in Afghanistan where some of the attackers trained. Born in Saudi Arabia, he used over 30 aliases and gained a reputation as a master of disguise. He was captured in Pakistan in 2002 and taken to a detention camp reportedly in Thailand. At the time, US intelligence officers claimed he was planning a terror attack in Israel. He was subjected to so-called enhanced interrogation techniques for extended periods and waterboarded more than 80 times. On one occasion, the treatment rendered him completely unresponsive with bubbles rising through his open full mouth. Accounts in the Senate report describe how Zubaydah spent 266 hours in a tiny, confined space barely larger than a coffin, and 29 hours in an even smaller box just 21 inches (53cm) wide and 2.5ft (76cm) deep and tall. In obtaining permission to use harsh treatment on Zubaydah, US Justice Department lawyers relied on inaccurate CIA representations about him, the report found. He is currently held at Guantanamo Bay prison camp. Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri gained notoriety as the suspected orchestrator of the terrorist attack on the USS Cole, a destroyer targeted by suicide bombers while docked in the port of Aden, Yemen. According to US intelligence, the Saudi-born Islamist was the leader of al-Qaeda's operations in the Gulf region. Besides the USS Cole attack, which killed 17 sailors, US intelligence chiefs believed the 49-year-old was involved in plots against various Western targets in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, the Straits of Gibraltar, Morocco, and Qatar. He allegedly fought with the Taliban in Afghanistan and was involved in earlier Chechen and Tajik insurgencies. After being arrested in Dubai in 2002, he was held for four years in several secret CIA facilities worldwide, including in Poland and Thailand. During this period, he endured waterboarding and mock executions, according to the report. In 2006, he was transferred to the Guantanamo Bay detention facility, where he has remained ever since.

text: France rounded off their Euro 2016 preparations with a classy and comprehensive victory over Scotland. Didier Deschamps' team dominated to affirm their status as pre-tournament favourites. Olivier Giroud responded to his critics with the first two goals, and his Arsenal colleague Laurent Koscielny headed a third before half-time. Substitutions mercifully disrupted the second-half flow, allowing the Scots to retain their dignity. The truth is that this performance and result do not help answer that question, but the tournament hosts certainly seem to possess the quality to do so. Their midfield options are enticing—the trio of N'Golo Kante, Paul Pogba, and Blaise Matuidi appear masterful, exuding power and athleticism. Giroud has faced boos from French fans and criticism from local media ahead of the Euros, but a clever back-heel and an alert close-range rebound earned him a standing ovation from the Metz crowd. Kingsley Coman, Dimitri Payet, Antoine Griezmann, and Anthony Martial were also given playing time as Deschamps assessed his options before Friday's competitive debut against Romania in Paris. Concerns have been raised about the strength of their defence, but Scotland provided no challenge to that. Gordon Strachan lamented his team's inability to pass and control the ball in Sunday's 1-0 defeat by Italy, and there was little to be pleased about on this occasion either. They had more possession than against the Italians but rarely used it effectively and once again failed to register a shot on target. Goalkeeper David Marshall, as he did six days ago, kept the damage to a minimum with a series of excellent saves and will be hard to displace when the World Cup qualifiers commence in September. Another small consolation for the Scotland coach will be a confident display from young Swansea full-back Stephen Kingsley when he came on in the second half, with Rangers winger Barrie McKay also making his senior international debut from the bench. Pogba controlled the match in commanding fashion and twice came close to adding a fourth goal, first hitting the post with a powerful free-kick before curling another onto the roof of the net. text: The body set up to probe deaths during the Troubles in Northern Ireland investigated cases where the state was involved with less rigour than others, a police watchdog has found. These are external links and will open in a new window. HM Inspectorate of Constabulary stated that it seemed the Historical Enquiries Team's (HET) policy was founded on a misrepresentation of the law. It noted their approach was inconsistent and had significant shortcomings. HET was established in 2005 to re-examine 3,260 murders. The report also assessed that the HET's approach to cases involving the state was inconsistent with the European Convention on Human Rights. When questioned if HET had acted outside the law, Her Majesty's inspector of constabulary, Stephen Otter, stated: We believe it was acting unlawfully concerning state cases because it treats them differently in policy terms and in the way that then manifests in practice. So state cases were less effective as a result, and effectiveness is a key test of whether it's Article 2 compliant. HMIC stated the Historical Enquiries Team risked undermining the confidence of the families of those who died during the Troubles in its effectiveness and impartiality. Northern Ireland's chief constable Matt Baggott agreed to a policing board request to commission the review by the HMIC following criticism of HET in a University of Ulster report. The report, by Dr Patricia Lundy, alleged the HET gave former soldiers preferential treatment and did not adequately investigate deaths caused by the military. The HET rejected the allegations in her report. Responding to the HMIC report, Dr Lundy stated: I believe the HET as an organisation itself is irretrievable at this point. I think it has implications for many different cases, not just the army cases, because we've heard the structural problems, there's no oversight, there's no complaints procedure, and really it seemed to me that it was a bit of a law unto itself. Mr Otter stated Dr Lundy had presented a report that at the time was made out to be untrue. I do think she deserves an apology from the chief constable on behalf of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI), he said. What is indefensible is that she did make these findings in 2009, so for four years nothing was being done to address those findings, and I do find that very difficult to believe. Chief Constable Matt Baggott stated that all military cases investigated by HET will now be re-examined, and he accepted that HET put in place a policy that was wrong. A differential approach to military cases is wrong, and I assure you this has ended, he said. He also accepted the recommendations of the HMIC report in full and would work to implement them. The HET is reviewing more than 150 killings by soldiers between 1970 and September 1973. The HMIC inspection focused on whether the HET's approach to reviewing military cases conformed to current policing standards and policy. It examined material relating to 31 cases that the HET had reviewed. HET treats cases involving military differently as a matter of policy. HET not conforming to current policing standards in a significant number of important areas. A lack of explicit systems and processes. Different teams adopting different working practices. No clearly defined complaints process. No independent review of the HET's processes (until now). HMIC examined if the HET adopted a consistent approach to both military and paramilitary cases. It also considered if the HET's review process met requirements to ensure it was compliant with human rights legislation. The report found the HET treats cases involving military differently as a matter of policy, and this appeared to be based on a misinterpretation of the law. It also found that the HET did not always seek verification where a potential interviewee in a state involvement case claimed to be unfit for interview due to illness. HMIC stated this was entirely wrong and had led to military cases being reviewed with less rigour in some areas than cases not involving military. The inspection found that none of the 39 cases referred back to the PSNI for investigation since 2010 had involved state involvement. It is striking that not one state involvement case relating to the British Army has to date been referred to the PSNI for further investigation or prosecution, the report said. Mr Otter stated: HMIC is concerned that the inconsistencies we found in our review may seriously undermine the capability of the HET's processes to determine whether the force used in killings during the Troubles was justified in state involvement cases, therefore potentially preventing the identification and punishment of those responsible. Our recommendations set out fundamental improvements that the PSNI and the HET need to make in order to ensure the team is effective in delivering its objectives in a way that is consistent with the requirements of Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights; and commands the confidence of the public of Northern Ireland, and in particular, of the families of the victims of the Troubles. Mr Otter stated the HET was created and continued to operate within an extraordinary complex social and political context which presented those who established it with challenges unparalleled in UK terms. This context makes it even more important for the HET to operate to the highest standards of effectiveness and impartiality, so that the people of Northern Ireland, and the families of the victims whose cases are being reviewed, can have confidence in it, he added. HMIC interviewed more than 180 people from a range of organisations, including HET, criminal justice agencies, and non-governmental bodies. It also spoke to the families of 13 of the victims, some in Belfast and others in Londonderry. HMIC stated although many people it had spoken to would have preferred the HET to be independent from the PSNI, they also expressed an almost universal desire for it to be retained so long as improvements were made to the way it operates. The HET is a special investigative unit attached to the PSNI to re-examine the deaths of thousands of people in Northern Ireland between 1968 and 1998. It is an independent unit which is directly accountable to Northern Ireland's chief constable.

text: Progressive music, the oft-maligned genre that had its heyday in the 1970s, is to be endorsed by the Official Charts Company (OCC). Next week marks the release of the inaugural monthly Official Progressive Albums Chart Top 30. It will include classic prog bands such as Pink Floyd, but the top position is claimed by 21st Century rock act Tame Impala. We felt it was an oversight not to have done this a long time ago, stated OCC chief Martin Talbot. Progressive music is as vibrant as it has ever been. It's more a mindset than a genre. The chart's announcement coincides with the annual Progressive Music Awards at Shakespeare's Globe Theatre in London on Thursday night. Among those being honoured is Genesis founder member Tony Banks, who will receive the 2015 Prog God Award. Rick Wakeman, who received the same honour in 2012, told the BBC that a chart dedicated to the progressive genre was long overdue. It's only 45 years too late, but better late than never, said the former Yes keyboardist. Prog rock is the healthiest it's ever been... the standard of musicianship of young bands is overall much higher than it was in the 1970s. The first official progressive album chart, to be published in Prog Magazine next week, features Tame Impala's album Currents at number one, ahead of Muse's Drones. Official Progressive Albums Chart - Top 10 © Official Charts Company 2015 It shows that wonderful wide spectrum that prog rock has, said Wakeman. It's no longer something to be sneered at and looked down on. With so many bands taking elements from it, it's widely accepted as a genuine contributor to the modern music scene. Prog rock, which emerged from 1960s psychedelia, was initially associated with bands such as Pink Floyd, Rush, Genesis, Yes, and King Crimson. It experienced a resurgence in the 1980s with bands like Marillion, while Muse, The Mars Volta, and Porcupine Tree are among the best-known progressive acts of the 21st Century. Jerry Ewing, editor of Prog Magazine, said: Prog artists have always pushed the boundaries of musical convention, and by doing so, many have become some of the best-selling and most influential artists of all time, but prog didn't stop in the 1970s, there are many people out there who are into prog artists and just don't seem to know it. You look at some of the best-selling and acclaimed artists of the modern era, like Muse, Radiohead, Mogwai, Tame Impala, what they do is incredible, they are challenging themselves, their audience and inspiring a new generation, and the Official Progressive Albums Chart is the platform in which this will be recognised. The last new chart created by the Official Chart Company was the vinyl chart, in spring 2015. The new progressive chart joins other musical genres such as dance, urban, jazz and blues, and country. The monthly Top 30 will feature the biggest selling titles ranked on physical and digital sales and audio streaming data. There are some artists who embrace the term 'progressive', and there might be many others who don't because it is a tainted word, said the OCC's Martin Talbot. The punk wars were fought to do away with prog music. Part of what we are saying is that it was prog and disco that won the punk wars - maybe more than punk did. text: On Friday 11 May 2012, Derby woke up to the news there had been a fire at a house in the Allenton area. These are external links and will open in a new window. The six children, Duwayne, 13, Jade, 10, John, nine, Jack, eight, Jesse, six, and Jayden, five, were all upstairs. Philpott claimed he used a ladder in what Derbyshire Police described as apparent valiant attempts to rescue them. However, Det Supt Kate Meynell began hearing a different narrative from the Philpotts' neighbours, who had also attempted to rescue the children that night. She stated: Within a few days they commented on how they felt they were making more effort to rescue the children and that Michael Philpott was not as instrumental as he should have been. The fire originated in the hallway, below the letterbox, where petrol had been poured. Police discovered a petrol can near Victory Road and a glove which was taken as evidence. The blaze was clearly arson. The police commenced their investigation by eliminating those closest to the family. A man Philpott was accused of assaulting was also ruled out. text: Doctors who carry out cosmetic procedures should give patients time to think before agreeing to go ahead, new guidance says. It will now seek feedback from doctors and the public regarding the guidance. Plastic surgeons stated they were already implementing a two-week cooling-off period. In 2013, a report by NHS England's medical director underscored the risks linked to the cosmetic sector. This followed safety concerns after nearly 50,000 women in the UK received PIP breast implants. The French implants were made from unauthorised silicone filler and were found to have twice the rupture rate of other implants. In January, the Royal College of Surgeons released a consultation on proposals to raise standards in cosmetic surgery. The GMC establishes the standards expected of all UK doctors performing cosmetic procedures. It also aims to help patients understand what to anticipate from their doctor. Some of the principal points in the new guidance state that doctors should: Prof Terence Stephenson, chairman of the General Medical Council, stated that some patients in this field were vulnerable and required protection. We are clear that doctors must not pressure patients to make rushed decisions they may end up regretting and they must give them enough information so they can make an informed choice. Rajiv Grover, consultant plastic surgeon and former President of the British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons (Baaps), endorsed the GMC's guidance, noting that some patients were psychologically unsuitable for cosmetic surgery. Cosmetic surgery has for too long been seen as a commodity but unfortunately once an operation is done - it can't be taken back to the shop. He said Baaps had advocated for a two-week cooling-off period for many years and also promoted a second consultation with a surgeon before a decision was made. The association is exploring the development of a screening tool to help identify patients who should not undergo surgery. The final GMC guidance is anticipated to be published in early 2016.

text: Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp endured a frustrating first game at Anfield as the Reds were held to a draw by 10-man Rubin Kazan in the Europa League. The visitors took the lead through Marko Devic's impressive half-volley but soon had captain Oleg Kuzmin dismissed for a second yellow card. Liverpool responded with Emre Can stabbing in after a free-kick. Substitute Christian Benteke hit the post late on as Liverpool were held to a third consecutive Group B draw. Despite late pressure, it was ultimately a challenging evening for Klopp and Liverpool as they struggled to break down their Russian opponents for much of the match. The result leaves Liverpool second in their group on three points, four behind leaders FC Sion. Klopp's arrival has been met with excitement by Liverpool fans since he was confirmed as Brendan Rodgers' successor. The 48-year-old's first appearance in a Liverpool dugout was at Tottenham last weekend, but Thursday marked his first competitive appearance at Anfield. In his programme notes, Klopp praised the special atmosphere created by the fans, who certainly extended a warm welcome to the German. Stall traders sold scarves outside the ground boasting the Klopp revolution, while fans eagerly awaited autographs and photos with their new manager. It was not only the fans keen to witness Klopp's first game in charge, with the club's owners flying in for the match. Klopp's appearance from the tunnel just before kick-off was met with rapturous applause, but any excitement about a new era gave way to frustration as Liverpool's familiar failings this season were once again evident. Under Klopp, Dortmund reached the Champions League final in 2012-13 and rose from 110th to 13th in the UEFA rankings. Liverpool fans hope he can have a similar impact at the Reds, who are currently ranked 54th in Europe, between FC Genk and APOEL. Europa League success may not be the supporters' priority, but they will welcome improved performances in the competition after disappointing draws against Bordeaux and FC Sion this season. Liverpool's early efforts against Rubin Kazan were encouraging as they played quick, one-touch football and attacked at pace. However, when Rubin took the lead, albeit against the run of play, Liverpool - along with the home fans' enthusiasm - faded. Kuzmin's sending-off - he received a second yellow card for stopping Can - and Can's subsequent equaliser lifted Anfield again. Liverpool, though, failed to capitalise on that. Despite a late flurry as Rubin Kazan's players retreated further into their own half to protect the point, the hosts lacked the creativity to score a winner. Klopp felt Liverpool had their moments but accepted the sending off made it more difficult for his side. It was a very interesting game, a big challenge because of the quality of Rubin, he said. Sometimes it is a big advantage against 10 men, most of the time they stop playing football and defend in a compact block. It was not a masterclass but it was not the worst day in my life. Klopp appreciated the reception from the Liverpool fans, adding: It was one of the best moments for me. I felt everything positive and then I concentrated on the game. text: Careers services for young people in England need to be urgently improved, says a report from an advisory body set up by the government. The National Careers Council, which has been examining the current state of careers provision, emphasises a lack of consistency and availability. It warns that too many young people do not receive the necessary advice about work. Deirdre Hughes, who chaired the council, stated that a culture change in careers provision was urgently needed. The report from the National Careers Council indicates there are massive variations in the advice available, depending on where young people reside. It notes that in one region there are 134 careers advisory services, while in another there is only one. There are also concerns that the National Careers Service has been structured to primarily address the needs of adults, leaving a gap in advice services for school-age individuals. The service provides over a million face-to-face advice sessions for adults, but there is no provision for such individual advice for young people. Instead, young people are offered phone advice lines and online information. The council expresses disappointment with the slow progress in enhancing careers services for young people. It calls for the establishment of an employer-led advisory body to oversee the creation of a better careers advice system. Furthermore, it urges the government to provide all schools with free or subsidised access to independent and impartial career development. It suggests there should be a fund to invest in successful models of careers advice so they can be more widely implemented in other schools and regions. There have been a series of critical reports about the quality of careers provision and doubts regarding the decision to transfer responsibility for careers advice to individual schools. It is worrying that the new arrangements are failing to provide good guidance, said Ofsted chief Sir Michael Wilshaw last year, when the education watchdog warned that too few schools had the skills to provide good quality advice. The Education Select Committee also reported last year that careers services were showing a worrying deterioration. Neil Carberry, of the CBI, remarked: The shift of responsibility for careers advice to schools has been a failure. Schools, government and businesses all have a role to play in fixing the problem; it cannot be shouldered by schools alone. Brian Lightman, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said schools had been working hard to provide careers advice, but many are finding it extremely difficult. A stark postcode lottery is putting many young people at a real disadvantage, said the head teachers' leader. Far too many young people are having to make vital and incredibly important decisions about their futures without access to good and reliable information, said Nick Chambers, director of the Education and Employers Taskforce charity. Deirdre Hughes, who chaired the group that produced the report, stated: Some progress has been made in the last 12 months, but this has been far too slow. Meanwhile, our education and labour markets remain complex and confusing for young people, parents and teachers, and there are significant costs associated with this. We urge government and others to take action across England to halt the rapid decline in careers services for young people. Labour's shadow education secretary, Tristram Hunt, commented on the careers service: There is surely no other policy agenda where the government has so miserably failed our young people. He said he would reverse the decision to make work experience placements optional and would want every school to have a governor responsible for developing links with local businesses to help provide careers advice and experience of the world of work.

text: Former Arkansas Governor Mike Huckabee has launched a second attempt at getting the Republican nomination for the presidency. At a rally in his hometown of Hope, Arkansas, Mr Huckabee employed the phrase hope to higher ground as a theme. The bass guitar-playing, foreign policy hawk has pursued a media career since losing the nomination in 2008. He enters a crowded Republican field that includes three senators, a businesswoman, and a neurosurgeon. Folks, it is a long way from a little brick rent house on Second Street in Hope, Arkansas to the White House, he stated. Here in this small town called Hope, I was raised to believe that where a person started didn't mean that's where he had to stop. I always believed that a kid could go from Hope to higher ground. Following his announcement, the crowd erupted in chants of We want Mike! The former Southern Baptist minister acknowledged his pro-gun-ownership stance, recounting to the audience how he received a BB gun at the age of five. He stated that the US Department of Education should be abolished, a stance popular with conservatives who oppose recent national education reforms. On immigration, he asserted that US borders should be secured but provided few details. He also reaffirmed his unwavering opposition to same-sex marriage. Mike Huckabee has returned. Eight years ago, he launched a surprisingly successful presidential bid, finishing second to Arizona Senator John McCain and winning the Iowa caucuses and seven other states. Four years ago, there were widespread rumours that Mr Huckabee would run again. Supporters and analysts watched and waited... and waited. The former Arkansas governor, who held a lucrative position as a television and radio host, chose to sit out the campaign, despite some polls showing him leading the Republican field. He said his heart says no. Now, however, Mr Huckabee's heart is saying yes. He has resigned from his media commitments and is entering the 2016 race. He will face a much more crowded field than he would have in 2012, both in the total number of candidates and in opponents who will compete with him for the evangelical voters who supported his 2008 campaign. Mr Huckabee has many advantages—name recognition, a developed fundraising network, and experience from his previous presidential campaign. But given the strength of his Republican opponents—new, engaging, and also well-funded—will that be sufficient? Early in his speech, Mr Huckabee noted that he was the first male in his family to graduate from high school. My dad wasn't an educated man, but he was a smart man. And he and my mother didn't have a whole lot, but they had honesty to the bone, he said. As his campaign progresses, Mr Huckabee may face challenges within his own party. Many conservatives may not appreciate the fact that overall, taxes and spending increased during his tenure as Arkansas governor. In 2008, Mr Huckabee won eight primaries in socially conservative states, but this time he has pledged to focus more on the economy and national security. To secure the Republican nomination, he will have to overcome Senators Marco Rubio, Ted Cruz, and Rand Paul, as well as former Hewlett-Packard boss Carly Fiorina and retired neurosurgeon Ben Carson. Jeb Bush has not officially announced but is the frontrunner in the party.

text: The way alcohol is sold in airports is to be examined after a number of recent incidents involving drunk passengers, the new aviation minister has said. These are external links and will open in a new window. Lord Ahmad stated he did not wish to kill merriment, but he would consider the times alcohol was available for sale and passenger screening. Statistics indicate 442 individuals were detained on suspicion of being drunk at an airport or on a plane in the past two years. The government stated there were no plans to specifically tackle the issue. In a recent incident, a female passenger struck an EasyJet pilot in the face after being instructed to disembark an aircraft before take-off from Manchester. In February, six men on a stag party were detained by German police after an in-flight altercation forced a Ryanair flight from Luton to Bratislava, Slovakia, to divert to Berlin. Lord Ahmad remarked: If you're a young family travelling on a plane, you want to travel from point A to B without disruption. I don't think we want to eliminate merriment entirely, but it's crucial that passengers boarding planes act responsibly and consider other passengers, which should certainly be a factor we consider. He added: Regarding specific regulations on the timing of outlets [selling alcohol] and their operations, I clearly want to examine that. He also emphasised the importance of screening travellers before they boarded planes. Glasgow and Manchester airports have tested a scheme with shops selling alcohol in sealed bags to reduce issues on flights. Police data obtained by the Press Association through Freedom of Information requests revealed at least 442 individuals were detained on suspicion of being drunk on a plane or at an airport in the UK between March 2014 and March 2016. Trade bodies representing UK airlines and airports stated such incidents were a very rare occurrence, but warned they could result in serious consequences. They highlighted that disruption on board an aircraft was an illegal offence which could incur a severe penalty, including a travel ban, fine, or imprisonment. According to the Civil Aviation Authority's latest passenger survey, approximately 238 million passengers passed through UK airports in 2014. Earlier this week, budget carrier Jet2.com released a code of practice on disruptive passengers following collaboration between airlines, airports, the police, and retailers. The zero tolerance policy includes airport shops advising passengers not to consume alcohol they have purchased before or during their flight, and training staff in bars and restaurants to limit or halt the sale of alcohol to prevent or manage disruptive behaviour. A Department for Transport spokeswoman stated: Airport security is always under review; however, there are no plans to specifically address the issue of alcohol at airports.

text: The fact that a record-equalling 10 Wales players have been selected to start the British and Irish Lions' crucial final Test against Australia is a source of great national pride. Head coach Warren Gatland has opted to retain the players he knows best from his tenure with Wales. They secured the Grand Slam in 2012, defeated England in the final match to clinch this year's Six Nations, and reached the 2011 World Cup semi-final. Gatland is aware of their capabilities, but his decision places some pressure on him. If they win, he is hailed as a hero. If they lose, he will face criticism for selecting so many Welsh players. His choice also increases the pressure on the Welsh players to deliver. All selections involve some risk, but it is somewhat surprising that five changes were made for the second Test and another six for the Sydney Test. It is uncommon to have so many changes, as successful teams usually remain settled. Gatland's front-row selection appears robust, although I believe England lock Geoff Parling is rather fortunate to retain his position in the second row. In the back row, I would have included another Welshman—flanker Justin Tipuric—in the starting line-up. The Welsh players will also be driven by the nation's recent poor record—they have lost eight consecutive matches—against Australia. Wales have been quite unlucky against the Wallabies recently, and they could have easily won two of their last three encounters. Bearing those defeats in mind, they will be eager for revenge. I am surprised that Ireland centre Brian O'Driscoll has been omitted, as he would have been the ideal captain. However, Wales lock Alun Wyn Jones is performing excellently and will undoubtedly lead by example. Provided Wales centre Jamie Roberts is fully fit upon his return at the weekend, he possesses the ability to breach the gain line. A failure to do so was a significant issue last Saturday, when the Lions made no breaks at all. To defeat the Australians, we need someone who can put us on the front foot. While our regional sides have performed poorly in recent years, fortunately, the national team has been very consistent. Reflecting on the 1971 and 1974 Lions teams, of which I was a member, we also had a strong Welsh influence. The positivity from the national side can indeed be transferred to the Lions—that certainly occurred in 1971 when we were series victors in New Zealand, and in 1974 when we remained unbeaten in South Africa. Let us hope the same outcome occurs for the Lions on Saturday. The last two games have been decided by two-point and one-point margins, and it could come down to the final minute again. It will be very close, and I believe Australia will start as slight favourites. JPR Williams was speaking to BBC Sport's Matt Monaghan.

text: Hospital beds in England may fill up with the elderly and vulnerable because of cuts to local authority social care funding, a top NHS figure has warned. The assertion was made by Nigel Edwards, head of the NHS Confederation, in a letter to the Daily Telegraph. Mr Edwards stated that individuals requiring medical treatment might be denied a hospital bed due to the cuts. The Department of Health responded by stating that an additional £2 billion was being allocated to safeguard social care. Health spending was protected in Chancellor George Osborne's Spending Review. However, councils in England are facing a 27% reduction in central government funding over the next four years. Mr Edwards, whose organisation represents health service bodies in England, remarked that the £2 billion interim solution to social care funding announced in the Spending Review would be a welcome relief to many. Yet he indicated that the funding constraints could still have a knock-on effect on the health service. In his letter to the Telegraph, Mr Edwards wrote: Less support from council services will quickly lead to increased pressure on emergency services and hospitals. Hospital beds will be blocked for those who badly need care because the support services the elderly require after discharge will not be available. • £81 billion cut from public spending over four years • 19% average departmental cuts - less than the 25% expected • £7 billion extra welfare cuts, including changes to incapacity, housing benefit and tax credits • £1.8 billion increase in public sector pension employee contributions by 2014 • Rise in state pension age brought forward • 7% cut for local councils from April next year • Permanent bank levy • Rail fares to rise 3% above inflation from 2012 He added: When it comes to the care of the most vulnerable in our society, it really is essential that the NHS and local authorities are in it together. The Department of Health stated it recognised that social care can impact on NHS demands. A spokeswoman commented: That's why we are strengthening programmes like re-ablement and the 30-day re-admission tariff, which will integrate hospital care with care in the community. We have allocated an additional £2 billion by 2014-15 - this extra boost, alongside an ambitious programme of efficiency, will ensure that there is enough funding available both to protect people's access to services and deliver new approaches to improve quality and outcomes. We expect local health and social care professionals will work together to ensure that the funding is spent on joint health and social care priorities and improve outcomes for everyone. Councillor David Rogers, from the Local Government Association, stated the extra £2 billion would not extend very far. Of course that is very welcome, but as part of what councils said to the government before the Spending Review, there's likely to be a gap over that same time of about £6 billion. So, there are still going to be difficulties. But I think that the important thing is to ensure that both councils and the NHS locally work increasingly closely together to provide the best service to our residents. On Thursday, critics expressed concerns over whether the £2 billion earmarked for social care, half of which is to come from a direct grant to local government, would reach its intended target. Jennifer Dixon, chief executive of the Nuffield Trust think tank, said: The reality is that local authority budgets will be stretched and funds for social care are not ring-fenced, so the extra £1 billion per year is by no means certain.

text: Antrim lost 2-06 to 0-09 to Limerick in their All-Ireland Qualifier Round 1B game at Corrigan Park on Saturday. Limerick had not secured a competitive victory all year, but early goals from Ian Ryan and Sean McSweeney, a penalty, set them on their path to triumph. The hosts led 2-2 to 0-6 at halftime and secured the win with points from McSweeney, Ryan, and Stephen Cahill. Goalkeeper Donal O'Sullivan made three crucial saves for Limerick. Antrim's championship campaign ended disappointingly as the Saffrons failed to build on their promotion to Division Three of the Football League. Antrim utilised the wind advantage in the first half, with a free from Ryan Murphy after 40 seconds and a Kevin Niblock score from the right putting the home side ahead 0-2 to 0-0. The visitors received a significant boost when Seanie Buckley found Ryan at the edge of the square, and the St Senan's player scored with a low shot past Chris Kerr after five minutes. Antrim conceded a second goal three minutes later from McSweeney's penalty. Midfielder Darragh Treacy was fouled after getting behind the Antrim defence. McSweeney maintained his composure to drill the ball into the bottom right corner, giving Limerick a 2-01 to 0-02 lead. Those goals boosted Limerick's confidence, but Antrim responded well. Matthew Fitzpatrick was the first Antrim player to score with a good shot from the right in the 13th minute—perhaps he could have aimed for a goal—and four minutes later, Patrick McBride kicked his side's fourth point, reducing the gap to three points. Tommy Childs was a late substitute for injured Limerick captain Iain Corbett, impressing in midfield and setting up a fine score from the right for Ryan after 18 minutes. Ryan had a great chance for his second goal nine minutes from time when he got ahead of substitute Martin Johnson, only for Kerr to deny him with a superb save with his feet. Antrim finished the half strongly, with McBride and Sean Burke scoring to make it a two-point lead at halftime. With a two-point lead and a strengthening wind at their back, Limerick started brightly in the second half, and after solid defensive play, corner-back Cahill extended their lead to three in the 44th minute. After scoring just six points in 50 minutes, Antrim needed a goal to mount a comeback, and that chance fell to Martin Johnson as he cut in from the right, but Donal O'Sullivan made an excellent save to keep his goal intact. The introduction of Tomas McCann gave Antrim a much-needed injection of pace up front, and he followed a free from Ryan Murray with one of his own to cut Limerick's lead to two points with nine minutes remaining. Ryan extended that to a goal with a free, but Antrim came close to finding the net twice in the closing stages, only for O'Sullivan to produce great saves to deny Ryan Murray and Martin Johnson, securing their place in the next round.
