text: Saturday's FA Cup final between Arsenal and Aston Villa at Wembley will be watched by half a billion viewers in more than 120 countries. Nearly 90,000 fans are expected at Wembley for the 134th final of the world's oldest cup competition as two teams of elite, millionaire athletes compete for glory. But what was the scene like at the original final in 1872? An estimated 2,000 spectators watched 22 amateurs play on a cricket pitch without nets, as Wanderers defeated Royal Engineers 1-0 with a goal from Morton Betts. BBC Sport, with assistance from Matthew Taylor, professor of history at De Montfort University, examines the first final 143 years ago. Before the 1872 FA Cup, there were no regular competitive matches in England. Football Association secretary Charles Alcock devised plans for the first FA Cup, which saw 15 teams enter the first round in November 1871. Barnes, Civil Service, Hitchin, Crystal Palace (not the current Palace but their predecessors dissolved in 1876), Maidenhead, Marlow, Queen's Park, Donington School, Upton Park, Clapham Rovers, Royal Engineers, Reigate Priory, Wanderers, Harrow Chequers, and Hampstead Heathens, who received a bye, stepped forward. Initial issues and the logistical challenges of scheduling matches across Britain in the steam era meant that Scottish side Queen's Park reached the semi-finals without playing a match. The semi-finals, both goalless draws, were held at Kennington Oval. The Royal Engineers secured their place in the final with a 3-0 replay win over Crystal Palace, while Wanderers advanced when Queen's Park withdrew, unable to afford another costly trip to London for the replay. The historian's view: The consensus is that the FA Cup was modelled on knockout competitions between 'Houses' at major public schools like Harrow. However, Alcock may have also drawn inspiration from existing provincial competitions, such as Sheffield's Youdan Cup, launched in 1867. Football was certainly as established and popular in Sheffield as it was in London at this time, and the elite ex-public schoolboys in the capital knew and played against teams from Sheffield, Nottingham, and elsewhere. Alcock, the mastermind behind the idea, played in defence for Wanderers. Formed in 1859 as Forest Football Club, the team mainly comprised former Harrow public schoolboys and adopted the name 'Wanderers' because they played at various grounds. By 1869, the club was based at Kennington Oval, where Alcock was also the secretary of Surrey cricket club. The Royal Engineers were founded in 1863 by Major Francis Marindin, an extraordinary figure. Having served in the Crimean War, he played in the 1872 final, became president of the FA in 1874, and refereed eight more FA Cup finals. The 1872 final took place at Kennington Oval, also the venue for the first international football match between England and Scotland in 1870. The Oval hosted 20 of the next 21 FA Cup finals, with the 1873 final held at Lillie Bridge, near Chelsea's modern home at Stamford Bridge. The historian's view: Many football clubs played on cricket grounds in the late 19th century. Football clubs often emerged from existing cricket clubs as a way for players to stay fit in winter. Purpose-built football grounds did not appear in significant numbers until the 1880s and 1890s. While fans at this year's final will navigate crowds at Wembley, the 1872 event was more sedate. Football had yet to gain widespread popularity, and around 2,000 attended the Oval. Much has changed beyond recognition in football, but the cost of attending remains an issue. The historian's view: Attendances for football matches were not large in the early 1870s, partly due to ticket prices, which at one shilling (five pence today) were higher than most matches at the time. The Oval crowd was described as 'very fashionable', likely comprising the well-to-do and upper middle-class, as well as those connected with the 'old boys' public school network running the Football Association. The Royal Engineers could claim to be the Barcelona of their day, with their revolutionary tactic of 'passing' the ball to a team-mate contrasting with the usual approach of chasing the ball into space. The final's only goal came after 15 minutes when Betts, playing under the pseudonym A H Chequer from his membership of the Harrow Chequers club, collected the ball after a long dribble from Walpole Vidal and scored. Goalkeeper was not yet a specialised position, with keepers often playing outfield. The historian's view: It was not unusual for teams to line up with six or seven forwards in the early 1870s. Most teams relied primarily on individual dribbling, with team-mates supporting the dribbler to move the ball towards the opponents' goal. Some authorities claim the Royal Engineers were the first to develop a passing game, doing so around the time of the first FA Cup final. It is fair to say footballers of Oscar Wilde's era were a different breed from today's stars. The Wanderers' group of ex-public schoolboys and aristocratic elite produced notable sportsmen. Besides the pioneering Alcock, the team included several first-class cricketers, a goalkeeper capped by England as a defender, and a forward capped by England in goal. Forward Edward Bowen was noted for walking 90 miles between Cambridge and Oxford in 26 hours between football and playing cricket for Hampshire; full-back Edgar Lubbock became deputy governor of the Bank of England, and wing-wizard Walpole Vidal, known as the prince of dribblers, later became a vicar. As expected, the Royal Engineers had all seen military service worldwide, with experiences from India to Crimea, Bermuda, Gibraltar, and the Zulu War. Forward Henry Waugh Renny-Tailyour played football and rugby union for Scotland and cricket for Kent, later becoming a managing director of Guinness, while half-back Alfred Goodwyn became the first international footballer killed in a riding accident in India two years after the final. The historian's view: Most players in the first final learned the game in elite public schools and at university. The Wanderers was open only to those who attended leading public schools and Oxbridge. Three of the Cup final line-up attended Eton, and four went to Harrow. The early rules were very different. In a nod to cricket, players had to appeal for a goal and changed ends after each goal, not at half-time. This once allowed Walpole Vidal to score three times without the opposition touching the ball. The historian's view: Modern fans would be surprised by some features of football in 1872. Instead of a crossbar, a tape was stretched between two posts eight feet above the ground. Throw-ins were not determined by the team whose player kicked the ball off the pitch but by the first player to reach the ball. These rules were not consistent nationwide. Variations existed in different areas, and it was not until 1882 that a uniform set of rules was established by the FA. The 2015 final will be refereed by Jon Moss, who can expect some criticism from the stands. It was different for civil servant Alfred Stair, the referee for the first three FA Cup finals. Stair was the head of the Inland Revenue, presumably seen as a trustworthy gentleman of his time, and also played football for Upton Park. The historian's view: In football's earliest days, referees were literally peripheral figures. They stood outside the playing area and were only called upon to adjudicate if the umpires (appointed by each club and standing in either half of the pitch) could not agree. For winners Wanderers, it was the start of a golden, albeit brief, era of success. They retained the trophy in 1873 by defeating Oxford University 2-0 and won three more trophies before the decade's end. Their five FA Cups have only been surpassed by Blackburn Rovers, Newcastle, Aston Villa, Chelsea, Liverpool, Tottenham, Manchester United, and Arsenal. By 1881, Wanderers could not field a team as players left for newer clubs emerging nationwide, and the team folded in 1887. A reformed side was established in 2009, and the club currently plays in the Surrey South Eastern Combination. They are seeking a new manager to return to the FA Cup by 2022. The Engineers reached four finals and won the Cup in 1875. They continue to play and are currently managed by Capt Simon Mayers, who has a 25-man squad selected from around 8,000 men worldwide. The historian's view: Football's popularity grew over the next decade as it became embedded in British working-class culture. Its popularity was aided by entrepreneurs who saw opportunities in enclosing playing fields and charging entry fees. As teams began to represent their localities, ambitious club committees 'poached' the best players and paid them to play. Within less than a decade of the first FA Cup final, professional football emerged in England, though it was not legalised by the FA until 1885.

text: A gay man has won a landmark ruling which will give his husband the same pension rights as a wife would receive. These are external links and will open in a new window. The Supreme Court unanimously decided that if John Walker, aged 66, passes away, his husband is entitled to a spouse's pension, provided they remain married. The former cavalry officer stated it would drag the government into the 21st century, while human rights group Liberty claimed thousands could benefit. A government spokesman stated it would review the implications of the decision. BBC legal affairs correspondent Clive Coleman remarked that the decision will have a dramatic effect on the entitlement of thousands of civil partners and spouses in same-sex marriages. They will now enjoy the same pension rights and entitlements as those in heterosexual marriages, our correspondent added. The ruling means Mr Walker's husband, who is in his 50s, will now be entitled to a spousal pension of about £45,000 a year, rather than approximately £1,000 a year. Mr Walker said it was to our government's great shame that it has taken so many years, huge amounts of taxpayers' money and the UK's highest court to drag them into the 21st Century. He added: Finally this absurd injustice has been consigned to the history books and my husband and I can now get on with enjoying the rest of our lives together. Mr Walker pursued legal action as he wanted to ensure that, should he die first, his husband would receive an adequate pension. The majority of occupational pension schemes provide 50% of the value of a pension to a spouse for the rest of their lives after their husband or wife dies, without considering the marriage date. However, the Equality Act 2010 has an exemption for employers, allowing them to exclude civil partners from spousal benefits paid in before December 2005. The Supreme Court has now ruled the exemption under the 2010 act is incompatible with EU law and must be disapplied. Emma Norton, a lawyer from Liberty, which represented Mr Walker, urged the government to assure that Brexit would not threaten the ruling. This ruling was made under EU law and is a direct consequence of the rights protection the EU gives us, she said. We now risk losing that protection. The government must promise that there will be no rollback on LGBT rights after Brexit. A government spokesperson said the rights of same-sex couples had been transformed for the better since 2010. During the hearing, it stated the cost of applying the ruling retrospectively would be £100m for private sector schemes and a further £20m for the public sector.

text: At one of the shops serving the troops in Camp Bastion there are plenty of reminders that this war is nearly over, at least for those who have travelled from Britain and America. There are fewer products available for purchase. Some of the remaining items are offered at special prices. The souvenirs on display remain at full price, yet they also suggest that the end is near. There are drinking glasses inscribed with Been there; Done that, while a mug states Happiness is Helmand in the rear view mirror. Bastion was once a bustling military metropolis, comparable in scale to Reading. However, it is now gradually becoming more of a ghost town. Compounds that once housed tents or military vehicles now stand empty. There are fewer personnel in uniform walking around, and the constant sound of helicopter blades has become more sporadic. While Bastion is slowly reducing in size, most other British bases in Helmand have already vanished. At the peak of the conflict, approximately 10,000 British military personnel occupied 137 bases across the province in southern Afghanistan. Currently, around 4,000 UK personnel occupy just two: the main operating base at Bastion and an observation post named Sterga 2, which offers a strategic view over the Helmand valley. In the forthcoming months, Sterga will be transferred to Nato command, with the British-led Task Force Helmand integrated into Regional Command South West under the leadership of a US Marine Corps brigadier general. Lashkar Gah, a main operating base and former British headquarters, has been handed over to the Afghans. The buildings that recently housed a British provincial reconstruction team are to be converted into a health centre. There will be no UK presence to witness this transformation when it occurs. Make no mistake: this is a complete withdrawal by the British from one of Afghanistan's most violent regions. Camp Price once accommodated 2,000 troops. In recent weeks, it has been demolished. Chainsaws and diggers are the new tools for British soldiers. The saws dismantle the Hesco walls that once protected them, while the diggers level the ground. From dust to dust. Even the concrete barriers, which served as makeshift memorials with graffiti honouring fallen comrades, have been removed. Capt David Goodman observes as the last shipping containers are loaded onto lorries. A total of 600 containers have departed Price since October. He states: I am now dreaming of ISO containers. We have been sending out 20 or 30 a day and it is a nightmare, waking up thinking 'did this container go?' Hardly anything has been left behind. This raises questions about the lasting legacy of British forces after eight years in Helmand and 448 British military deaths. It is certainly not peace. As the last containers are loaded onto lorries at Camp Price, gunfire can still be heard in the distance. Lt Col Mike Caldicott of the Royal Logistic Corps led the final military convoy out of Price, likely one of the last logistic patrols in Helmand. He is convinced they have made a difference. I only wish that people at home could see the changes I have seen through my eyes, he says. I think they would feel a lot better about the investment we have made. This view contrasts with some soldiers we spoke to who appear more eager to focus on returning home than on what they leave behind. One simply states: Job done, get home. Another comments: I will miss the sun, that is probably about it. Most soldiers we speak to believe they have made a difference. However, few in uniform echo David Cameron's claim last year that it is already mission accomplished. The most senior British general in Afghanistan, Lt Gen John Lorimer, says extraordinary things have been achieved across the country. But when asked if it is mission accomplished, he carefully avoids the phrase. Instead, he states: There is still a lot to be done. One senior British officer tells me that if Iraq was the A-level exam, Afghanistan is the PhD. Back home, the assessment is likely more stark. The current hesitance over military intervention reflects the public's wariness of conflict. Margaret Evison lost her only son, Mark, in Helmand in 2009. She says she has had time to adjust to her loss but adds: There is nothing in my mind that would justify my son's death. On the broader question of what has been achieved, she says she is unsure if the British withdrawal comes at a time when Afghanistan is more stable. As for David Cameron's assertion that it is mission accomplished, her response is Well he has to say that! Brig James Woodham will be the last commander of Task Force Helmand. He too states there is still much work to do. He believes there has been progress but admits that ultimately history will be the judge of what has been achieved. What seems peculiar is that after investing so much here for the past eight years, there will soon be no British military presence to help write the final chapter.

text: Basketball's biggest star LeBron James has announced his return to the Cleveland Cavaliers - the team where he began his NBA career 11 years ago. The 29-year-old announced his decision in an interview with Sports Illustrated on Friday. James has been a free agent since 1 July after opting out of the final two years of his contract with Miami Heat. I always believed I'd return to Cleveland and finish my career there, stated James. James, who has been named the NBA's most valuable player four times, terminated his contract in Miami last month. He would have earned $42.7m (£25.1m) over the remaining two years of his contract. His decision initiated a scramble for the player, but he disclosed that returning to his home state of Ohio was always on his mind. After last season, free agency wasn't even a thought, said James, who is from Akron, 40 miles from Cleveland. But I have two boys, and my wife, Savannah, is expecting a girl. I began considering what it would be like to raise my family in my hometown. I considered other teams, but I wasn't going to leave Miami for anywhere except Cleveland. The more time passed, the more it felt right. This is what makes me happy. After joining the Cavaliers as the first draft pick in 2003, James rose to superstardom over the next seven years before being lured to Miami in 2010, where he formed a formidable partnership with Chris Bosh and Dwyane Wade. His announcement of leaving for Miami was made during a staged ESPN television show called The Decision. It resulted in a backlash from Cleveland fans who burned James jerseys in anger. James, who would have earned $20m (£11.7m) next season, won NBA titles with the Heat in 2012 and 2013. He also led Miami to the NBA Finals in 2011, when they lost to Dallas, and in 2014, when they were heavily defeated by San Antonio. Speaking of his time in Miami, James said: The hardest thing to leave is what I built with those guys. I've talked to some of them and will talk to others. Nothing will ever change what we accomplished. We are brothers for life. News of James' departure was announced over the loudspeaker at Cleveland airport, and Cavaliers ticket phone lines crashed, reported ESPN. In 2010, Cavaliers owner Dan Gilbert wrote an open letter criticising James and describing his departure as a shocking act of disloyalty and a shameful display of selfishness and betrayal. But on Friday, he tweeted: My eight-year-old: 'Daddy, does this mean I can finally wear my LeBron jersey, again?' Yes it does, son. Yes it does! In Miami, a mural featuring James was defaced, according to South Florida news station WPLG Local 10. Heat owner Micky Arison tweeted: I am shocked and disappointed in today's news. However, I will never forget what LeBron brought us for four years. Thanks for the memories. The situation could yet worsen significantly for the Heat. Wade and Bosh both joined James in opting for free agency this summer and may now follow their former teammate's lead by confirming moves away from Miami. In addition to the Sports Illustrated interview, James posted a photo of himself in a Cavaliers uniform on Instagram with the phrase I'm coming home. He told Cleveland fans not to expect immediate success, however. When I left Cleveland, I was on a mission, James said. I was seeking championships, and we won two. But Miami already knew that feeling. Our city hasn't had that feeling in a long, long, long time. I'm not promising a championship. I know how hard that is to deliver, James stated. We're not ready right now. No way. Of course, I want to win next year, but I'm realistic. It will be a long process, much longer than it was in 2010. My patience will get tested. I know that.

text: The jobs market has seen a substantial decline in people starting full-time jobs since the start of the year, according to a regular survey of recruiters. The hiring index is compiled by the Markit data firm, in collaboration with recruitment consultants REC. It indicated a significant decline in both permanent placements and the availability of candidates for them. There was, however, an increase in demand for permanent and temporary staff during January. The sector consistently showing the highest demand for recruits is nursing, medicine, and care, followed by engineering and construction. A forecast by the Construction Industry Training Board (CITB), also released on Wednesday, estimates there will be a need for 12,000 recruits over the next five years, as workers exit the sector or the country. It anticipates the total number of construction workers to decrease, as major infrastructure projects, including the Queensferry Crossing, wind down from very high levels. Growth in the home-building and repair market is expected to be between only 1% and 2%. Ian Hughes, a director at CITB, stated: While we have factored Brexit into this forecast, many unknowns remain regarding life after leaving the EU. We will be working with our industry to understand what it means for our migrant workforce and what we must do to attract and grow more of our own. The REC/Markit recruitment survey indicated starting salaries are rising, but not as rapidly as a parallel survey showed for the rest of Britain. Overall, the situation appeared weaker than the figures across the rest of Britain, where other recent survey evidence has shown the jobs market to be markedly stronger. Recruitment consultants reported an increase in the employment of temporary staff, at the fastest pace for more than a year. Hourly rates of pay for temporary staff increased, but the pace of wage inflation slowed. Kevin Green, chief executive of REC, remarked: The jobs market in Scotland continued to deteriorate in January, with recruiters reporting a decline in permanent placements for the fourth consecutive month. Scotland's economy is not as strong as the rest of the UK. The energy sector has weakened, and ongoing political uncertainty is affecting business confidence. Vacancies in Scotland remain in growth, so demand for staff is robust, despite employers showing hesitancy regarding investment decisions. This suggests the market could pick up again if confidence is restored. The survey encompasses around 100 recruitment and employment consultants in Scotland.

text: The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge have visited a bereavement centre to mark its one-year anniversary. Prince William, who inaugurated Child Bereavement UK's Stratford centre in east London in 2015, has served as the charity's royal patron since 2009. The charity assists parents who have lost children and supports bereaved children. William and Kate were introduced to staff and volunteers before meeting families who have utilised the service. The Duke made a rare public admission regarding his emotions following the death of his mother, Princess Diana, telling a grieving boy he was very angry when she passed away. The Duke was a teenager and his brother, Prince Harry, was 12 when their mother died in a car crash in Paris on 31 August 1997. He spoke candidly during his visit to the centre, where he and Kate sat with families and created memory jars in honour of deceased loved ones. As Lorna Ireland, 36, and her son Shinobi Irons, 12, filled their jars with layers of coloured salt—symbolising memories of the boy's grandmother who died three years ago and godmother who died in 2015—the future king discussed his feelings. Miss Ireland said: He told my son that when his mum died he was 15 at the time and he was very angry and found it very difficult to talk about it. So it was very important that Shinobi talked to somebody about how he was feeling even now years on. Ann Chalmers, Child Bereavement's chief executive, expressed she was honoured by the Duke and Duchess's visit to the centre. The charity was established in 1994, and Princess Diana attended its launch. One of the charity's supporters, actor Jason Watkins, spoke to BBC Breakfast on Wednesday about the loss of his two-year-old daughter in 2011. Maude became ill with a cough and a cold and was treated with steroids by a GP. She died from sepsis. Mr Watkins said: We put her to bed, did all the things we were told to do by the medical professionals. My older daughter had been trying to play with her in the bedroom... and I went in to see if she was alright and she had clearly died. He told the programme it was an awful, traumatic, hysterical and terribly painful event for the entire family. You never get out of bed, you spend days in bed, you can't get out. It's like people who have had an operation you feel completely obliterated and have no energy. You feel like you're trying to get out of a dark pit that you can't get out of. Your heart aches...you feel your heart is broken. But that acute phase of trauma, it does pass and you do come through that, he said. His eldest daughter, Bessie, is nine years old, and wrote in her diary: When Maude died I was three, I didn't know what death was. I was in shock for a long time that I would never see her again. Maudey will never come back but she will always be in our hearts.

text: Pakistan's Supreme Court is considering corruption allegations against Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, amid mounting pressure over his family's wealth. These are external links and will open in a new window. The development follows investigators' claims that his family failed to explain the origins of its financial assets. The investigation commenced after the Panama Papers leaks connected his children to offshore companies used to purchase London flats. This sparked suspicion that the companies were utilised to launder illicit wealth, allegations Mr Sharif vehemently denies. He asserts the London properties were acquired lawfully and that he does not personally own them. However, the matter is becoming a significant challenge for him. Opposition groups accuse his family of leveraging political influence to accumulate wealth unlawfully and are urging him to resign. Thus far, Mr Sharif has refused, describing the investigators' report as a compilation of allegations and assumptions. His decision to remain in power was supported by the federal cabinet last week. Hundreds of security personnel have been stationed around the Supreme Court, parts of which have also been enclosed with barbed wire. The Joint Investigation Team (JIT), established in April, claims it has found significant gaps/disparity among the known and declared sources of income and the wealth amassed by Mr Sharif and his family. It accuses Mr Sharif of concealing assets, overstating his father's wealth to justify his family's wealth, and failing to reflect an exorbitant hike in his family's wealth during his first decade in power (1985-93) in his wealth statement. It accuses his heir-apparent, daughter Maryam Sharif, of being the beneficial owner of offshore firms through which the London flats were acquired, and of forging documents to show she was a trustee for her brother, the actual owner. This allegation is based on a copy of a trust deed she signed in February 2006. The JIT states the document was printed in Calibri font, which was not commercially available until January 2007. The existence of the flats and the offshore companies linked to them was revealed in the leak of 11 million documents held by the Panama-based law firm Mossack Fonseca. The family claimed the money for the flats, as well as the family's businesses in the UK and the Gulf region, originated from the sale of their UAE-based Gulf Steel Mills. The mill was established by PM Sharif's father, the late Mian Mohammad Sharif, in the early 1970s, and he later invested the proceeds from its sale in a Qatar-based business. The Sharif family have presented a letter from former Qatari Prime Minister Prince Hammad bin Jassim al-Thani explaining the money trail. He was unavailable for an interview by the JIT. However, the JIT claims it found no evidence of a money trail leading from Pakistan through Dubai and Qatar to the London flats. The JIT report has divided the nation - something very evident in media coverage. Audiences tuned to any of the pro-government TV channels would conclude that the JIT report was a pack of lies, but debates on pro-opposition channels leave no doubt in their viewers' minds that they believe Mr Sharif and his family are involved in corruption. The report addresses complex issues of international finance, involving a maze of financial regulations from various states and regulatory bodies. Therefore, while much of what it states may be based in reality, experts have noted instances where the JIT appears to have either concealed its lack of access or understanding or included opinions lacking a sound basis. Questions have also been raised over the Supreme Court's decision that the two military intelligence services, the MI and the ISI, would contribute one representative each to the six-member JIT, which ideally should consist of financial experts only. Additionally, the Supreme Court's decision to allow the ISI to exclusively arrange secretarial services to the JIT has not been well-received by those who believe this service has been actively involved in political management of Pakistan's ruling superstructure since the 1980s. Many suspect the ISI is interfering ahead of elections due in 2018 to retain its influence over the political establishment. There are three options: A disqualification would mean that Mr Sharif would be barred from politics for life, as required under the honest and sagacious provision of the constitution. His daughter and political heir would face the same prospect. It is unclear how the situation will be managed by the Supreme Court, which is itself under immense pressure. Creating the JIT to investigate the prime minister's wealth was an unprecedented move. The JIT is not a product of the constitution or the executive, but a creation of the Supreme Court. As such, few consider it likely that the court would reject the JIT's report entirely. If disqualified, the prime minister is likely to announce a successor - possibly his brother Shahbaz, who is chief minister of Punjab - and allow the government to complete its term. In any other scenario, analysts expect him to remain and, if necessary, to go down fighting.

text: A recovering alcoholic has been jailed for four months for stealing £11,000 from a faulty Ulster Bank cash machine. A judge informed Peter Anthony Young, 58, of Hunter's Way, Ardglass, that he had deliberately taken advantage of a significant glitch in the bank's system nearly four years ago. This glitch allowed customers to withdraw funds from ATM machines without affecting their balance. Upon investigation, the bank discovered that Young had withdrawn the money. A prosecution lawyer informed Downpatrick Crown Court that on 22 June 2012, Ulster Bank had experienced a computer malfunction in its system. Following a check, Ulster Bank discovered that Young, who was one of its customers, had £11,000 withdrawn from his account on that day, stated Ms Ivers. The judge was informed there had been 22 separate withdrawals of £500 on the day in question. The prosecution lawyer stated the bank made repeated attempts to contact Young without success before eventually reporting the incident to police as fraudulent. The PSNI commenced an investigation, and Young voluntarily attended a police station, admitting to making the withdrawals and stating he had spent the money on drink. The prosecution lawyer said the accused, a customer of Ulster Bank, had made no effort to pay back the funds, with the outstanding balance now at £10,908.40. A defence lawyer described it as an unusual case and mentioned that when Young was interviewed by police in September 2014, he made frank admissions to his crimes. Reading between the lines from the court papers, it appears Mr Young was in the company of other people drinking with them that day, and when he was taking money out, it became apparent to him and the others that there was a fault with this machine, he told the court. This was always going to come home to him. He is not in the least blaming others. The defence lawyer stated that Young's life had taken a downward spiral following his mother's death in 1991 and that by the age of 34, he was an alcoholic, homeless, and living on the streets of Belfast. The lawyer added that the father-of-five was now a recovering alcoholic, attending Alcoholics Anonymous meetings, part of a church group, and also participating in a rehabilitation programme. The defence lawyer suggested Young could be subject to a community order which would leave something hanging over his head that would remind him not to stray from the straight and narrow again. I would urge the court to give him a chance to continue to improve himself, the lawyer added. The judge stated Young had gone to the machine on one occasion to withdraw £500 on the day in question. He chose to return to this machine a further 21 times to withdraw the money when he knew he did not have the funds in his account, he said. He knew full well what he was doing and he deliberately took advantage of the defective ATM. The judge noted Young, who is living on social security benefits, had not repaid any money he had stolen from Ulster Bank. I don't believe I could deal with this case by way of a suspended sentence. The least sentence I can impose is one of four months in custody.

text: Schools in Beijing are closed and outdoor construction halted as the Chinese capital's first ever pollution red alert came into effect. These are external links and will open in a new window. The alert, the highest possible warning level, was issued late on Monday and will remain in effect until midday on Thursday. Restrictions have been imposed on car usage, and some factories have been instructed to cease operations. This occurs as China, the world's largest polluter, participates in discussions on carbon emissions in Paris. It is the first instance of China declaring a red alert under the four-tier alert system, which was implemented just over two years ago, although pollution levels were not the worst the city has experienced. At 07:00 local time on Tuesday (23:00 GMT on Monday), when the alert took effect, the US Embassy's air pollution monitor in Beijing reported that the concentration of tiny particles known as PM 2.5 was at 291 micrograms per cubic metre. By 11:00, it had decreased slightly to 250, still a level described as very unhealthy. Levels of the toxic particles in the suburbs were reported to be several times higher. The World Health Organization recommends 25 micrograms per cubic metre as the maximum safe level. As I cycled into the office this morning, wearing a smog mask firmly in place, the traffic was noticeably lighter. Beijing's first red alert means half of all cars must stay off the roads; odd-numbered licence plates today, even-numbered ones tomorrow. However, although the air is indeed an unpleasant, filthy grey, the pollution index is actually considerably lower than it was this time last week, when the quantity of hazardous particulate matter (PM 2.5) surged to around 40 times the World Health Organization's maximum guideline. Coal-powered industries and heating systems, along with vehicle emissions and dust from construction sites, all contribute to the smog, which has been exacerbated by humidity and a lack of wind. Analysis: Matt McGrath, BBC environment correspondent, Paris. China's air quality is a crucial factor in its push for a new global deal on climate change. Its negotiators here highlight their continued investment in renewable energy sources, in an effort to reduce coal consumption, particularly in urban areas. Around 58% of the increase in the country's primary energy consumption in 2013-14 came from non-fossil fuel sources. These efforts to go green may not be having an immediate effect on the air in Beijing, but they have impacted global carbon dioxide output. This year's figures, just published, show carbon levels have stalled or declined slightly even as the world economy has expanded. A strong agreement here in Paris will not immediately solve China's air problems, but if it ultimately reduces the cost of renewables further, it could contribute to solving the issue long term. You have to do whatever you can to protect yourself, Beijing resident Li Huiwen told the AP news agency. Even when wearing the mask, I feel uncomfortable and lack energy. While the smog's effects have been worsened by weather conditions and the city's geography—bordered to the south and east by industrial areas that generate pollution and to the north and west by mountains that trap it—it has prompted increasing concern that China has prioritised economic growth at too high an environmental cost. It is a sharp warning to us that we may have too much development at the expense of the environment, and it is time for us to seriously address air pollution, said Beijing worker Fan Jinglong. The scale of the health impact is vast. There have been 1.4 million premature deaths in China due to air pollution, according to a study led by Jos Lelieveld of Germany's Max Planck Institute and published this year in Nature magazine. Activists reported that the level reached 1,400 micrograms per cubic metre in the north-east city of Shenyang last month, claiming it was the worst seen in China. In comparison, London's PM 2.5 average on 6 December was 8 micrograms per cubic metre, the Environmental Research Group at King's College reported. It stated that more than 70 was reached during spring 2014 and 2015, with the highest recorded on bonfire night, 5 November 2006, at 112. Last week, activists from Greenpeace urged the Chinese government to declare a red alert. Another Chinese city, Nanjing, issued a red alert in December 2013. On 30 November, Beijing issued an orange alert, the second-highest of the four-tier system adopted in 2013. Pollution in the capital had actually improved in the first 10 months of the year compared with the same period last year, although pollution levels remained frequently high. Correspondents say Chinese officials had been reluctant to commit to strict targets on reducing carbon emissions, but have now realised the country must reduce its dependence on fossil fuels. President Xi Jinping promised to take action over China's emissions at the global climate change talks in Paris. China still relies on coal for more than 60% of its power, despite significant investment in renewable energy sources.

text: An elderly woman was beheaded by a man who went on a rampage in north London, the Old Bailey has heard. Palmira Silva, aged 82, was in her garden when she was attacked by Nicholas Salvador, who stabbed and beheaded her, prosecutors stated. The court was informed he was armed with a wooden pole and machete and was arrested following a violent struggle during which he was tasered six times. The 25-year-old from Enfield denies murder by reason of insanity. Prosecutor Jonathan Rees QC informed the jury the killing occurred three days after Mr Salvador had lost his job, and there was no dispute over his responsibility for her death. He stated that at the time of the killing, on the afternoon of 4 September last year, the defendant resided three doors away from Mrs Silva on Nightingale Road. On the day of the attack, the defendant armed himself and beheaded two of his hosts' cats, believing they were demons, the court was told. He then proceeded through several back gardens, broke into a house, and attacked a car containing two members of the family he was living with. Mr Salvador then jumped over a wall into Mrs Silva's garden, where she was repeatedly stabbed before being beheaded, the court heard. It was stated Mr Salvador believed he was killing a supernatural entity disguised as Hitler resurrected, or a demon in the form of an elderly woman, Mr Rees said. The prosecutor informed the jury the defendant fled and was arrested in the front room of another house following a violent and chaotic struggle with police, during which he was tasered multiple times and kicked and punched, but with little effect. He exhibited signs of mental illness, repeating phrases such as red is the colour and I am the king. An eyewitness described how, prior to the attack, he appeared like a headless chicken and seemed to be searching for more cats to kill, the court heard. In the weeks leading up to the attack, Mr Salvador had exhibited signs of odd behaviour and developed an interest in shapeshifters—supernatural entities that can transform into another being or form. After being charged, the 25-year-old was remanded in custody at Belmarsh prison before being transferred to high-security Broadmoor Hospital due to his mental illness. Mr Rees stated that psychiatrists would testify he was suffering from paranoid schizophrenia. Mrs Silva came to Britain from Italy in 1953 and ran a cafe with her husband. She had two children, six grandchildren, and one great-grandchild. Mr Salvador also denies a charge of assault by actual bodily harm by reason of insanity and assaulting a police officer after Pc Bernard Hamilton sustained a leg injury requiring hospital treatment. The case continues.

text: Ahead of the general election on 7 May, BBC Radio Merseyside is holding three special debates in front of a live audience. Three crucial constituencies—Wavertree, Southport, and Wirral West—have been selected, offering you the opportunity to question the candidates aspiring to represent you at Westminster for the next five years. Roger Phillips will host the first of the hour-long debates in Wavertree, one of Liverpool's so-called safe Labour seats, starting at 12:00 BST. Located to the east of the city centre, the constituency is mainly residential. It features a large technology park closely linked to the university and has a significant student population that boosts the local economy. Voters hope to avoid a repeat of the 2010 incident when the polling station on Dunbabin Road ran out of ballot papers as the polls were about to close. Liverpool City Council states, The problems last time at a small number of polling stations were caused by a number of people turning up at the close of polls and not all of the polling stations had a full allocation of ballot papers. We are ensuring that all stations have a full allocation and additional training has been provided for staff. Also, anyone in the queue by 22:00 BST will be given the chance to vote. So, who will be competing for those votes? Luciana Berger, the shadow health minister, retained the seat for Labour five years ago with a majority of over 7,000. She succeeded Jane Kennedy, the constituency's MP since its creation in 1997, who was elected Merseyside's Police Commissioner in 2012. At one point, it seemed former Labour Councillor Jake Morrison would challenge Ms Berger. He was only 18 when elected in 2011, but his relationship with the party soured last year when he announced his retirement at the age of 22. If re-elected, Ms Berger says she would take practical action to support people who are looking for a job, for example by holding another jobs fair to bring together employers and local people. I'll promote apprenticeships and opportunities for young people and back our fantastic small businesses. She added: I will continue to campaign for changes to law around dangerous dogs to make our neighbourhoods safer, and I will build on my strong record of standing up for the people of Liverpool Wavertree to ensure their concerns are heard where it matters and that real change is delivered for our community. The Liberal Democrats targeted this seat in 2010 without success. Their hopes this time rest with 20-year-old student Leo Evans. He pledges to protect green spaces like Calderstones Park, increase the NHS budget by £8bn annually with a focus on mental health, work to ensure Liverpool benefits from any devolved power—especially ensuring connection to HS2 and HS3—and continue the biggest expansion of apprenticeships since the 1950s. James Pearson is the Conservative candidate. The former Trafford councillor unsuccessfully stood for the Church ward in last year's Liverpool City Council elections, and this is his first parliamentary race. Mr Pearson has three main priorities for Wavertree: He aims to support business and investment, safeguard the NHS, and stand up for the armed services and their families. He feels passionately about the last of these aims, being an officer in the Army reserves and having served in Afghanistan and Cyprus. His party won only 7.5% of the vote in 2010, and it would be a significant surprise if they were to win this time. Adam Heatherington represents UKIP, hoping to attract votes from disaffected traditional Tories and Labour supporters alike. A former candidate for Liverpool Mayor, the supply teacher argues more needs to be done to boost the Wavertree economy, which he claims is performing below the national average. He wants more investment in Wavertree Technology Park, where there's a lot of vacant offices and retail spaces… business rates are just too high. We have a brain drain in this city—too many students are leaving to work in Manchester, Leeds, and London. We need more of a focus on vocational qualifications and bring them up to equal par with academic qualifications and we need more investment in our young people, he said. The Green Party also hopes to make an impact in Wavertree. Peter Cranie, the party's former election co-ordinator, missed out on a European Parliament seat last year. He is realistic about his chances next month, admitting the party is focusing much of their efforts on nearby Liverpool Riverside, where Martin Dobson is standing. But he believes he is giving everyone in Wavertree the opportunity to express their support for the more radical policies against austerity. We think it is obscene that the five richest families in Britain own the same wealth as the 13 million least well-off, he said. That's why the Greens will commit to ending austerity and real redistribution of wealth for a fairer and better society. The Trade Unionist and Socialist Coalition are also contesting this seat. Council worker Dave Walsh is their candidate. He aims to get those who have been disenfranchised and disengaged in politics re-engaged as well as defending local services including libraries and Sure Start Centres. The party is fielding more candidates than ever before—130 across the country—vowing to push for an increase in the minimum hourly wage to £10 and renationalise the railways. Finally, Leo Evans is standing as an independent after gaining a taste for politics by participating in Until They Kick Us Out—a theatre production from Liverpool's Young Everyman Playhouse, which addresses themes of young people and democracy. The 18-year-old student from Edge Hill wishes to support school leavers, push for a higher minimum wage, introduce rent caps for students and low-income families, and improve social housing. He insists his campaign is more than just a protest vote. With seven candidates standing, Wavertree is one of the most highly contested constituencies on Merseyside. To hear the candidates respond to questions from our listeners, please tune in to BBC Radio Merseyside from 12:00 until 14:00.

text: Italian Prime Minister Mario Monti claimed Europe had one week to save the euro ahead of yet another crunch EU summit on Thursday and Friday. The President of France has called for a growth pact, Tony Blair has advocated a grand bargain, the markets demand a big bazooka, while in Germany there are discussions about federalism. However, the economic and financial solutions to the eurozone crisis are surprisingly straightforward. How so? Simple. Consider how the same issues have been addressed by members of another large and more effective single currency area—the United States of America. Europe's real challenge is that almost all solutions are politically unpalatable. The eurozone's fundamental issue is that the southern European economies have become fundamentally uncompetitive—their wages increased too rapidly during the boom years, leading them to import more than they exported and borrow the difference. The excessive debts, persistent uncompetitiveness, and ongoing need to borrow in southern economies—along with Germany's reluctance to provide funds—have driven the financial panic that has made it more difficult for southern European governments and banks to borrow from markets. Furthermore, the freezing of European financial markets—not to mention the collective determination of Europe's governments to cut spending, and the European Central Bank's focus on price stability—is threatening to push the entire continent into a prolonged and deep recession, which would only exacerbate the debt issues. So, if the eurozone were to look to the US model for inspiration in its time of need, what sorts of changes—economic, financial, and ultimately political—might need to be considered? Europe's most immediate task is to restore confidence in its banks. All the bad loans made by eurozone banks (loans to mortgage borrowers, property speculators, and even governments that may not be fully repaid) may need to be cleaned up (by injecting money into the banks), with the potential losses borne by the eurozone as a whole—because many national governments probably cannot afford it. In the case of Spain's banks, the current bailout deal leaves Spain's government bearing all the losses. Deposits at all eurozone banks may need to be guaranteed in euros by the eurozone as a whole, to prevent panicky investors from moving their money from banks in southern European countries at risk of exiting the euro, to Germany (and increasingly to Switzerland and Denmark). All of Europe's banks may need to be placed under a common regime of regulation and supervision, with troubled banks given equal access to rescue loans and being wound up by a central authority when they fail. Europe's biggest long-term conundrum is how to prevent governments like Spain or Italy from going bankrupt—and restore confidence in their commitment to remain within the euro—while ensuring that all governments are more responsible with their finances in future. The biggest sticking point is eurobonds. A significant portion of eurozone government debt may need to be amalgamated—with governments standing behind each other's finances—to reinforce the commitment of governments to staying in the euro. In the long run, a US-style federal budget may be needed to cover the cost of recessions, so that individual governments do not risk going bankrupt when their national economies encounter difficulties. For example, the cost of a minimum level of social security—especially unemployment benefits—could be permanently shared across the eurozone, funded by a common income tax. The new French President, Francois Hollande, was elected on a platform demanding a growth pact in Europe—a set of reforms designed to boost European economies and mitigate the pain caused by government spending cuts across the continent. The European Central Bank may need to have its mandate changed so that it has an explicit dual target to support employment as well as price stability, similar to its American counterpart, the US Federal Reserve, as proposed by Mr Hollande. The eurozone may need to fund large-scale investment in infrastructure, particularly in southern Europe, much like West Germany invested in rebuilding East Germany after reunification in 1990. Proposals on the table include increasing the European Investment Bank's ability to lend and creating common project bonds to finance major construction. All Europeans (and especially southerners) are having to implement structural reforms that will increase their long-term growth and strengthen government finances (although at the risk of hurting growth in the short term). These include removing restrictions on market competition, raising the retirement age, laying off (over many years) a significant number of state employees, and making it much easier to hire and fire employees. Mr Hollande has resisted many of these reforms in France. Rebalancing means solving the significant underlying competitiveness problem faced by southern Europeans that led to their economies accumulating so much debt initially. The ECB and German government may need to stimulate high wage inflation in Germany for several years to eliminate the country's current massive competitive trade advantage over southern Europe—something that is already beginning to occur. In the same way that Washington assists struggling US states, the southern European governments may need to be given money (given, not lent) by the rest of the eurozone via direct fiscal transfers, so they can afford to support their economies until they regain competitiveness. These transfers could end up taking the form of bailout loans that are never repaid. Structural reforms—particularly labour market reforms—also play a key role in rebalancing, by ensuring that wages in southern Europe do not rise too quickly, as they did in the past decade. To make a full banking, fiscal, and monetary union work, the eurozone governments would need to hand power to a central authority (the European Commission) that can fund and supervise all of the above, while national governments accept that in future they have to keep their own spending strictly within their limited means. As most of the above reforms involve Germany sharing its wealth with the rest of Europe (and all European nations handing power to Brussels), Berlin is insisting on the principle of no taxation without representation—in other words, a move towards full federalism, with spending and regulation controlled by a directly elected presidency of the European Commission.

text: And so it begins. The campaign for the assembly's fifth election has finally commenced, although politics in Cardiff Bay has had a pre-election atmosphere for some time now. Much of the campaign style and events will seem familiar, but this time there will be fundamental differences. Firstly, all parties will strive to make their voices heard against the noisy backdrop of the EU referendum campaign. Additionally, there is the UKIP factor—the party has a realistic chance of winning several seats for the first time, thereby altering the political dynamic at the assembly. All parties face challenges to overcome. Labour faces the triple challenge of criticism over their NHS management, appearing fresh after 17 years in power, and the unknown impact of their UK leader Jeremy Corbyn in marginal seats where they compete against the Conservatives. Regarding disappointing elections, the Liberal Democrats must attempt to recover from their crushing result last year. The Tories must ensure divisions over the EU referendum do not derail efforts to maintain the party's momentum in Wales, following some notable victories in the general election. Plaid Cymru must generate some electoral momentum after several disappointing election results. UKIP has a significant opportunity to return a handful of AMs, which would provide them with a power base they have lacked in any UK political institution so far, but they have been plagued by serious internal divisions. A new Welsh Government will eventually have more powers than any previous administration, but expect the campaign to be dominated by the NHS, which has been devolved since 1999. Policymakers will have to address the challenge of supporting a health service under significant financial pressure while maintaining support in areas such as education and the economy. There are numerous policies where there is broad consensus among the parties, such as the need for apprenticeships and business rate relief for small firms, but there are several highly divisive issues, including plans for an M4 relief road and council reorganisation, where voters face genuine choices. The outcome on voter turnout, which was 42% last time, remains uncertain. The risk is that assembly politics will be overshadowed by the EU referendum, but media interest in the NHS, particularly over the past five years, will have also raised the profile of devolution in the public's mind.

text: Mfon Udoh scored a hat-trick as Nigeria's Enyimba beat visitors Etoile du Sahel of Tunisia 3-0 in the first leg of their last 16 African Champions League tie on Sunday. Earlier on Sunday, DR Congo's AS Vita Club defeated visiting Mamelodi Sundowns of South Africa 1-0. The overall winners of the tie will advance to the group stages. Meanwhile, the losers will have a second opportunity in the Confederation Cup. Udoh scored his first goal after nine minutes, added a second for Enyimba after the break, and completed his hat-trick with a powerful shot just before the match concluded. This achievement makes Udoh the top scorer in the tournament with seven goals so far. Etoile played the last 19 minutes of the match with 10 men after Ghazi Abderazek received a second yellow card for dissent and was sent off. The tie is a repeat of the 2004 final, which Enyimba eventually won on penalties after both legs had finished 2-1 to the home team. Uganda goalkeeper Dennis Onyango kept Sundowns in the game in Kinshasa with some fine saves as Vita Club's Ghanaian star Bernard Morrison proved challenging. The only goal of the game was scored in injury time at the end of the match as Morrison was once again given too much time, and while his shot was well saved by Onyango, his parry fell to Kule Mbombo, who scored. Vita's compatriots TP Mazembe face a tough task if they are to defend their title after a 2-0 loss on Saturday at Morocco's Wydad Casablanca. Abdellatif Noussir scored his first goal of the campaign just before half-time for Wydad, and Reda Hajhouj converted a penalty midway through the second half in Marrakech. Coached by twice Real Madrid manager John Toshack, Wydad are attempting to win the competition a second time, having previously succeeded in 1992. Mazembe are pursuing a sixth title, which would make them the second most successful club after eight-time champions Al Ahly of Egypt. Also on Saturday, record eight-time title-holders Al Ahly earned a 1-1 draw in Tanzania with Young Africans. Guided by former Tottenham manager Martin Jol, the Cairo Red Devils took an early lead when Amr Gamal headed in after 11 minutes to give Ahly an away goal. The home side responded eight minutes later, forcing an equaliser from an Ahmed Hegazi own-goal. Ahly's great rivals Zamalek, guided by another ex-English Premier League boss, Alex McLeish, defeated debutants Mouloudia Bejaia of Algeria 2-0 in Cairo. Mahmoud 'Kahraba' Abdel Moneim put Zamalek ahead just before the hour, and they doubled the lead eight minutes from time via Ahmed Hamoudi. Asec Mimosas of Ivory Coast capitalised on home advantage to beat Al Ahly Tripoli of Libya 2-0. Dao Youssouf put the Ivorians ahead after 59 minutes, with Aka Serge adding a second 10 minutes from time. Al Merreikh of Sudan and Entente Setif of Algeria drew 2-2 as they met for the second successive season. On Saturday, Merreikh went behind to a Eude Dagoulou strike after 15 minutes. Raji Abdalati put the hosts level after 20 minutes, only for Abdelmoumene Djabou to give Setif the lead again just three minutes later. But Abdalati ensured the first leg would end in a draw with his second of the game to make it 2-2. Stade Malien had hopes of becoming the first qualifiers from Mali all but dashed after a shock 3-1 home loss to Zesco United of Zambia. The game began promisingly for the hosts as Moussakoye Diallo scored, but Mwape Mwelwa levelled before half-time and Idris Ilunga bagged a late brace.

text: The HS2 link between Birmingham and Crewe marks a sad day for Stoke-on-Trent, Tristram Hunt has said. City MP Mr Hunt stated that the line from London to Manchester could have been completed more swiftly and economically with a route through the Potteries. The HS2 line from Birmingham to Crewe is scheduled to open in 2027. Transport Secretary Patrick McLoughlin has proposed constructing a junction in South Staffordshire to serve Stoke-on-Trent. According to the new plans, a 43-mile HS2 section between Birmingham and Crewe will be operational six years earlier than originally planned. Further updates on this story and others concerning Stoke and Staffordshire. The HS2 project seeks to enhance transport links with northern England. The government anticipates the London to Birmingham route will be finished by 2026. Crewe has been selected over Stoke-on-Trent as the next significant staging post on the route to Manchester. Stoke-on-Trent had previously submitted a bid for an HS2 railway station in its city centre. Responding to Crewe's selection over the city, Labour MP Mr Hunt remarked: With Crewe rather than Stoke benefitting from this substantial investment, plans for a northern gateway partnership between Stoke-on-Trent and east Cheshire become more crucial. Mark Winnington, Staffordshire County Council member for the economy, environment and transport, stated the current route will traverse miles of countryside and be a significant blow to communities. Mr Winnington commented: HS2 will cut through 45 miles of Staffordshire countryside, and from the outset, we have been concerned about the impact a project of this magnitude will have not only on the environment but also on residents living near the proposed route. For six years, Crewe will be the sole location in the North West with an HS2 connection—in theory, this means Cheshire can fulfil its self-designated title as gateway to the Northern Powerhouse. In reality, it is unsurprising, given the government-owned company responsible for HS2 has consistently recommended Crewe should have a stop. However, it is evidently a setback for Stoke-on-Trent, which launched a rival bid to host a hub and even threatened legal action if unsuccessful. Now the government and Cheshire officials assert their commitment to ensuring North Staffordshire benefits from high-speed rail. Michael Jones, leader of Cheshire East Council, stated the HS2 Birmingham to Crewe link would be a game-changer for Crewe and its surrounding areas. It's a real once-in-a-generation opportunity, the like of which Cheshire East has not seen before, he said. Conservative MP for Lichfield, Michael Fabricant, described the announced route as environmentally damaging to beautiful parts of Staffordshire. Labour MP for Stoke-on-Trent South, Robert Flello, stated: Crewe might appear on a map as if it is next door to Stoke-on-Trent, but the reality is it's a good hour by car from my constituents. Conservative MP for Stafford, Jeremy Lefroy, urged Mr McLoughlin to reconsider the proposed route.

text: An own goal from goalkeeper Ryan Clarke in the 95th minute denied Neal Ardley's AFC Wimbledon their first win of the season as Rochdale earned a share of the spoils at the Crown Oil Arena. Andy Barcham's first-half header appeared sufficient for the Dons to climb out of the bottom four, but Clarke punched Jamie Allen's corner into his own net, leaving the visitors at the bottom of League One. The Dons took the lead 12 minutes into the match, with the goal originating from a Rochdale attack. Donal McDermott's corner was inadvertently returned to him by Matt Lund, and when McDermott attempted to beat Chris Whelpdale, he was dispossessed deep in Wimbledon territory. Whelpdale sprinted the length of the field down the right before delivering a cross into the centre for Barcham to head past Conrad Logan. Dale pressed hard for an equaliser after the break, with Jamie Allen hitting the crossbar and Clarke denying Calvin Andrew twice. The home side's task became more challenging when Callum Camps was sent off for a second bookable offence, but Clarke's good work was undone when he diverted Allen's corner into his own net deep into added time. text: A schoolgirl has become the first child in Wales to be given an official hearing dog. Poppy is among over 45,000 children in the UK for whom being deaf is a part of daily life. The 14-year-old, who is profoundly deaf, states the yellow Labrador has boosted her confidence and aids her in sleeping at night. She is one of 27 children in the UK to have received a hearing dog from the charity Hearing Dogs for Deaf People. It was not until Poppy was nine years old that civil engineer Richard and housewife Rebecca noticed subtle changes in their daughter's behaviour which concerned them. She was turning the volume up on the TV, said Rebecca. When she was in the car she wouldn't hear me when I was talking to her, even though her brothers and sister could hear in the back. Concerned, they had Poppy, from Cwmbran, Torfaen, referred to an audiologist who was shocked to discover the schoolgirl was profoundly deaf and could barely hear anything, but had been concealing this by lip-reading. Despite her severe deafness, there was no impact on her schoolwork so the early signs had not been noticed. Rebecca said: What we realised when she was diagnosed was that she had become quite proficient in lip reading, which was how she had managed to wing her way through school. No-one had noticed as there was no change in her schoolwork. She was diagnosed with the rare disease Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome type 1. Although she was given hearing aids to wear in each ear, she became withdrawn and lacked confidence both socialising and doing small tasks like going to the shops. She had trouble getting to sleep at night as she could not wear hearing aids, which meant she could not hear anything at all and was constantly on edge about someone entering her room. Poppy struggled for three years feeling increasingly isolated until her mother discovered hearing dogs, who assist deaf people similarly to guide dogs. There are 850 deaf people, mostly adults, partnered with dogs in the UK. Due to her profound deafness, Poppy was the first child to be partnered with a hearing dog in Wales. The dog was named Tanni after Baroness Tanni Grey Thompson and was one of just 12 given out that year. Source: Hearing Dogs for Deaf People. A year on, Poppy says Tanni has transformed her life. Having her has built my confidence, said Poppy. She gives me more independence. Before when my mum went out I would be left at home, now I can go with her and go into shops. Before I was very reluctant to go into a shop and pay by myself. I was worried as they wouldn't know I was deaf, but now they can see from Tanni that they need to speak clearly as she wears a special harness when we're out. Another good thing is that people ask questions about Tanni and I feel happy talking about her. It has made me more confident answering questions in general. I have got a best friend. Tanni accompanies Poppy everywhere, except school. She has been trained to alert Poppy if there is a fire alarm or if her mother wants her. Poppy said: She wakes me up in the morning, if my mum wants to let me know we are going out or it is tea time she will write a note and put it in a purse which Tanni then brings in her mouth to me. So she will come up to get me and then nudges me. As I get older and more independent we could train her to do the doorbell, phone and text messages. And Poppy has finally enjoyed the good night's sleep she had hoped for. She said: I used to sleep with the door open as I didn't know who was coming into the room, I had the bed so I could see straight down the landing with the door open. Now Tanni wakes me up if someone comes in, so I can sleep with the door shut. Andrew James, National Client Services Manager for Hearing Dogs for Deaf People, said: We have now placed 27 hearing dogs with deaf children across the UK, and we are so pleased that Poppy and Tanni are the first child partnership in Wales. The Hearing Dogs for Deaf Children project has been a huge success since it was launched in 2012 and we have seen increasing interest each year, so the charity plans to expand our work with children over the coming years. Hearing dogs have an important influence on a deaf child's life, and we couldn't be happier with the positive difference that Tanni has made to Poppy and her family. There are currently 29 deaf people with hearing dogs in Wales.

text: Six years ago Yingluck Shinawatra, a novice who had only been in politics for two months, led the Pheu Thai party, founded and funded by her older brother Thaksin, to a resounding election victory. These are external links and will open in a new window. It was a remarkable outcome for a party that had experienced two prior administrations being toppled by a coup and a contentious court ruling, and whose supporters had been involved in a Bangkok occupation the previous year, which concluded in violence. A crucial element of Ms Yingluck's successful manifesto was a generous pledge to rice farmers, which is central to the legal case against her. Under the new programme, the government was to purchase the entire rice crop and pay 15,000 baht (£350; $450) per tonne, significantly above the 11,000 baht guaranteed by the previous administration. It was extremely popular with farmers. However, economists and agricultural experts immediately questioned its feasibility. The price of 15,000 baht was considerably higher than the global rice price, and Thailand exported more of its crop than any other nation—it was the world's leading rice exporter at the time. It was anticipated that its main competitors, India and Vietnam, would simply boost their exports at Thailand's expense, offering a price much lower than the Thai government could afford, unless it was prepared to incur substantial losses. There were numerous warnings that the scheme was susceptible to corruption. Six years later, Ms Yingluck faces a potential 10-year prison sentence on charges of malfeasance, or dereliction of duty, over the rice scheme. She has not been charged with corruption but with failing to prevent it, in her role as prime minister and as chair of the National Rice Policy Committee. If found guilty, she could be permanently barred from politics—she has already been banned for five years following her impeachment in 2015. Unsurprisingly, Ms Yingluck and her party have protested. After all, her government was overthrown in 2014 by the same military officers who now govern Thailand. They justified their coup by claiming a need to restore order but had conspicuously failed to support her as she faced prolonged protests in Bangkok, which had paralysed her administration. The military is not perceived as impartial and wields authoritarian powers, even extending to judicial matters. The rice scheme was excessively costly and wasteful. The exact cost of rice that rotted in storage, was stolen, or improperly sold is still contested. However, the government estimates it cost the state at least $8bn—some estimates reach as high as $20bn, although these include the overall cost of the subsidy, not just losses through corruption and mismanagement. The scheme did improve farmers' living standards but was almost certainly unsustainable. There is ample anecdotal evidence of corruption, although few cases have yet reached court. The most notable case, involving a former commerce minister and 27 other defendants accused of an allegedly fraudulent government-to-government deal to sell rice to China, will conclude on the same day Ms Yingluck hears her verdict. Ms Yingluck argued in court that she was not responsible for the day-to-day management of the scheme and that as a key policy platform when she was elected, she could not order its cancellation. She highlighted what she believes are multiple procedural flaws in the case. Regardless of the merits of the case against her, few observers doubt that the military government seeks to weaken Thaksin Shinawatra's political movement before allowing some form of democracy to be restored. Ms Yingluck is very popular and an effective vote-winner. With Mr Thaksin entering his 10th year of exile, his party is struggling to find a replacement leader. However, her fate presents Thailand's current rulers with some dilemmas. If she is acquitted, Mr Thaksin, who is protective of his younger sister, might be emboldened to push for a greater share of power in a post-election Thailand than the military is willing to accept. An acquittal would outrage hard-line conservatives and those who led the protests against the Yingluck government. If she is imprisoned, hard-line opponents of the Shinawatra clan would be satisfied, and she would be completely removed from politics. Convicting her would also help the generals justify their coup as part of a fight against corruption. However, it risks turning the telegenic Ms Yingluck into a symbol of resistance for the so-called red-shirt mass movement that supports her. Red-shirt leaders acknowledge that organising large-scale protests against a conviction would be difficult under a military government. They have ruled out any repeat of the central Bangkok occupation that ended so badly seven years ago. However, they say they would view a conviction as the first shot in a re-ignited conflict with the military, as an end to any pretence of reconciliation. They do not rule out localised demonstrations of anger by Ms Yingluck's supporters. This concerns the government, as it seeks calm in the lead-up to the elaborate cremation of the late King Bhumibol Adulyadej in October. It will also need to be mindful of the wishes of King Vajiralongkorn, who is expected to hold a coronation ceremony shortly after the cremation. A possible compromise might be a suspended prison sentence for Ms Yingluck. This is possible if she receives less than five years. Even if she is given a custodial sentence, government legal experts say she can appeal. However, that would depend on her. She might choose not to. Behind all of this lies the jostling for a new balance of power once the generals permit an election to take place. In that election, polls suggest Pheu Thai will be the largest party, as it has been in every election since 2001, although the new electoral system will almost certainly ensure it does not win a majority of seats in the lower house of parliament. However, the political parties will have to contend with a 250-seat senate entirely appointed by the military and with a military-drafted reform blueprint for the next 20 years, which all governments are legally required to honour. In this environment, no-one is certain who is in line to be the next prime minister. In the past in Thailand, elected governments were able to concentrate a lot of power and patronage in their hands. That will no longer be the case. Some in Pheu Thai believe it might actually be better for the party to have a period in opposition—that the first elected government will be so constrained by the courts and the generals it is not a prize worth having. The military itself is factionalised, and it is not clear that the current ruling clique will remain dominant. Another important unknown is what King Vajiralongkorn desires. The intimidating shadow of the lese majeste law makes any discussion of his role impossible in Thailand, but he has already made it clear that he wishes to be consulted on important decisions and that he is willing to exercise his influence in ways that his father did not. He may prove to be one of the most important factors in reshaping Thailand's future.

text: The number of people who think you must speak English to be considered truly British has increased over the past 10 years, a survey suggests. These are external links and will open in a new window. The annual British Social Attitudes survey of 3,000 individuals found that 95% agreed it was important to speak English to be British, an increase from 86% in 2003. It also revealed that 61% believed EU immigrants should wait three years before being eligible to claim benefits. Nearly a quarter stated the primary reason immigrants came to the UK was for benefits. NatCen Social Research has conducted the report for 31 years, assessing changing social attitudes in Britain. The report's authors state a key finding of their latest work is that the threshold to being considered British has got higher over time. The proportion of individuals who agreed it was important for a person to have lived in Britain for most of their life to be considered British is now 77%, up from 69% in 2003. Approximately 74% agreed it was important to have been born in Britain to be considered British, down from 76% in 2003. Additionally, 85% agreed respecting institutions/laws was very or fairly important to be considered British, an increase from 82% in 2003. Regarding immigration, 77% of people wanted immigration reduced a lot or a little, a figure that has sharply increased since 1995 but is largely unchanged since 2008. The report's authors stated the British view that current immigration was too high was well established and stable. Half believed the main reason immigrants came to Britain was for work, but 24% said the main reason was to claim benefits. The proportion of people who believe immigrants increase crime rates in Britain rose from 37% in 2003 to 43% in 2013. London divide. The authors stated the survey also reflected the divide on attitudes to immigration between London and the rest of Britain, as seen in the performance of the anti-EU party, UKIP, in recent elections. The survey suggested 54% of Londoners thought immigration was beneficial for the economy, but this figure fell to 28% outside the capital. Referring to the 61% who believed EU immigrants should wait at least three years before being able to claim benefits, the report's authors said this contrasted with rules that came into force this year requiring EU migrants to show they are earning at least £149 a week for three months before accessing a range of benefits. This, the report stated, demonstrated a considerable gap between public opinion and reality. Other findings include: Penny Young, chief executive of NatCen Social Research, stated: In an increasingly diverse, multi-cultural country, we might expect people to be more relaxed about what it means to be British, yet the trend is going in the opposite direction. It is now harder to be considered British than in the past and one message comes through loud and clear; if you want to be British, you must speak English. She added that the public want tougher rules on benefits and many are unaware of the policies that are in place to control immigration. Rules on immigrants claiming benefits vary depending on which benefit they wish to claim. The government has been imposing new restrictions in recent months, including one which came into force in January requiring migrant jobseekers to be in the UK for three months before they can claim Jobseeker's Allowance. The survey interviews were conducted from June to November 2013, before the so-called Trojan Horse attempt by Islamists to take control of schools in Birmingham became public knowledge. Education Secretary Michael Gove responded to the Trojan Horse issue by stating schools should promote British values.
