text: The Church of England's ruling body has decided that women bishops should be allowed, but there are further steps to take before they can be ordained. The General Synod has offered minimal concessions to traditionalist Anglicans who opposed the move. They had sought to be under the care of a male alternative bishop on terms acceptable to them. However, the synod decided that women bishops should determine the identity and functions of any such bishop. The BBC's religious affairs correspondent Robert Pigott stated that women bishops would only need to consult a code of practice guiding them in their interactions with traditionalists. He reported that the decision made during a synod meeting at York University had resulted in considerable division. Members of the synod decided there was no need for further delay to the progress of a draft law permitting women to become bishops. The law must now receive approval from a majority of the Church's 44 diocesan synods before returning to the General Synod. It must then secure a two-thirds majority at the General Synod before obtaining parliamentary approval and the Royal Assent. Our correspondent described it as an extraordinary weekend of intense emotion, noting that while supporters were celebrating a breakthrough, some traditionalists had left the synod chamber in tears. Proposals to establish a class of male-only bishops to oversee traditionalist parishes were rejected on Saturday. The Archbishop of Canterbury, Rowan Williams, and Archbishop of York, John Sentamu, had supported the compromise plan, which would have allowed parishes unwilling to serve under a woman bishop to seek the oversight of a male alternative. It would also have granted that alternative bishop considerable legally-backed independence and autonomy as part of a joint jurisdiction over those parishes. Although the proposal received a majority of votes in the synod as a whole, it failed because clergy—who vote separately from lay people and bishops—defeated it by just five votes. Our correspondent said Dr Williams had risked his reputation with the compromise plan and would now face a challenging situation as he attempted to address discontent among traditionalists who would likely remain in the church. The proposals will now be sent to dioceses and return to the synod in a year's time for a final vote. Campaigner Christina Rees, a member of the General Synod and chairwoman of Women in the Church, told the Press Association the synod's decision on Monday was a wonderful outcome. She stated: This is wonderful news. It is entirely consistent with what synod indicated it wanted two years ago. In one sense I am not surprised but I am delighted, it is very, very good news. However, traditionalists have warned that the decision could lead many of them to leave the Church of England. The Reverend Prebendary David Houlding, a leading member of the Catholic Group on the General Synod, expressed concern and felt as if traditionalists were running out of options. He told PA: There are several people who will be making hard decisions about their future. I am staying in the Church of England for the time being until I am driven out. I am not going willingly, I will only go if forced. The more this goes on in this manner, the more it seems as if the door is shutting. The scope for remaining in the Church of England is getting more and more narrow and the options are rapidly closing.

text: Chris Evans and Nick Grimshaw both lost listeners over the last three months, according to the latest industry figures from Rajar. Evans's breakfast show on BBC Radio 2 experienced a decline of 414,000 listeners compared with the previous quarter, reaching 9.06 million. However, the programme remained the most popular radio show in the UK. Grimshaw attracted 5.25 million weekly listeners between July and September, a decrease of 184,000 from the last quarter. The declines are likely due to fewer people tuning in to breakfast shows during the summer months. Meanwhile, digital station BBC Radio 6 Music attracted a new record audience of 2.34 million listeners. It marks the fifth consecutive quarter that the digital station has achieved record ratings. Helen Boaden, Director of BBC Radio, expressed her delight that more people are discovering the station's compelling mix of outstanding alternative music and witty presenters. While Grimshaw's figures decreased, Radio 1 as a whole increased from 9.46 million last quarter to 9.87 million weekly listeners between July and September. The figure rose further to 10.9 million when listeners aged 10 to 14 were included in the data. The station is currently aiming to attract a younger audience. Ben Cooper, controller of Radio 1, stated the figures should be considered alongside the increase to 1.5 million views a day on their YouTube channel and their 8.5 million users on social media. BBC Radio 4 reported a weekly reach of 11.2 million, its second highest audience to date. The network's flagship Today programme lost 250,000 listeners, falling to 7.1 million, but its sister programme The World At One reached an all-time high of 3.75 million. In commercial radio, LBC, Heart, and Capital all increased their number of weekly listeners compared with the previous quarter, while Absolute Radio added more than half a million. The breakfast shows on Classic FM and talkSPORT increased their reach nationally, but several commercial breakfast programmes lost listeners. Kiss's Rickie, Melvin and Charlie fell from 2.13 million national listeners in the last quarter to 1.83 million between July and September. The Chris Moyles breakfast show on Radio X lost 36,000 listeners in London but increased the overall number of listeners across the UK, reaching 703,000. However, Capital's breakfast show, hosted by Dave Berry, George Shelley, and Lilah Parsons, dropped slightly but remained the most popular commercial breakfast show in the UK. Overall, Rajar, the official body responsible for measuring radio audiences in the UK, reported that 89% of British people, or 48.2 million adults, listened to the radio at least once a week over the quarter, an increase of 320,000 on last year. text: It sounds like the screenplay from a heist movie. Burglars have broken into a vault filled with diamonds, watches, and priceless family heirlooms, selecting items from the hundreds of safe deposit boxes inside while no one outside was aware. The row of unassuming shops and traders comprising London's jewellery quarter in Hatton Garden has long been the subject of secretive and intriguing stories about underground passageways leading to gold stores and highly secure workshops where precious items are meticulously crafted by hand. However, with such a closed network of family businesses rarely opened to outsiders, it is difficult to ascertain how many of the stories are true. Hatton Garden's reputation for diamond dealing initially emerged at the end of the 19th Century when De Beers began selling their South African stones through London. The Hatton Garden area encompasses a small number of streets in Holborn surrounding the street of the same name. In an area covering roughly a tenth of a square mile, there are 300 shops and companies, including dealers, suppliers, and craftsmen. Joanna Hardy, an independent jewellery expert who worked in Hatton Garden for over 20 years, is reluctant to confirm any of the myths or rumours because she says it contradicts what the industry represents. It's not so much a secret, it's that this is a trade that is built on trust. People think that it's all about top secret stuff, but it's because of the high value of the goods that make it a very closed community. The people who work there have been doing it for generations, and when something like this happens, it shocks everybody. The manner in which the thieves have targeted the Hatton Garden Safe Deposit company only seems to add to the mystery. You don't see people holding up banks now; these crimes are done online behind a computer, but this seems all the more shocking because it's so old-school, Ms Hardy says. And with so much gold and so many precious gems contained in the row of East London buildings, most people would assume security is high, with alarms, double door entry systems, and CCTV on every exit. However, Peter Kirkham, a former detective chief inspector of the Metropolitan Police's specialist Flying Squad, says it's best not to assume. There is a huge amount of difference in the way premises are protected. From my experience, this trade can actually be very complacent and think it just won't happen to them. It's not unheard of for thieves to trigger the system, wait for the response, and then act when it's thought [by others] it was just a false alarm. If it is the case that there weren't strong security systems and procedures in place, thieves could have had the run of the place all weekend. There is just something that feels very odd about it all. In whatever way the raid was carried out, Mr Kirkham says the chances of high-value pieces being recovered are not high. Jewellery is notorious for disappearing completely. It's broken up, recut, and sold on the black market because no one wants anything that is identifiable. Like any trade when it comes to crime, no one is bothered by the sentimentality.

text: Welsh Secretary Stephen Crabb has said the Nato summit in Newport has raised the profile of Wales abroad and would attract investment. It has been a significant showcase for all that is positive, strong, and commendable about Wales, he stated. Mr Crabb mentioned that the relationship with the Welsh government and First Minister Carwyn Jones functioned remarkably well. He noted they were determined that daily politics would not hinder the demonstration of Wales working in unison. Over 60 world leaders, 4,000 delegates, and 1,500 journalists have spent two days at the Celtic Manor Resort for one of the largest international gatherings ever held in the UK. Mr Crabb remarked: We intended it to be an opportunity to present the very best of Wales in terms of hospitality, quality of infrastructure, and facilities. I believe this week has demonstrated precisely that. We have been clear that this NATO summit needs to have a lasting economic impact for Wales. I believe the global profile of Wales this week will assist in that. And with the investment summit we are organising following the NATO summit, we are determined it will attract more inward investment. Bringing world leaders, prime ministers, and ambassadors here this week has all been part of that plan. The UK Investment Summit, on 20 and 21 November, will also take place at the Celtic Manor. US President Barack Obama expressed his approval for the warm Welsh welcome on Thursday, commending the country for its extraordinary beauty, wonderful people, and great hospitality. Despite hopes for long-term benefits to Wales, traders in the centre of Cardiff have complained that security barriers and road closures severely affected their businesses by deterring customers in the lead-up to the summit and during the event. First Minister Carwyn Jones paid tribute to residents and businesses for their support for the summit and tolerance of some inevitable disruption. What a fantastic week this has been for Wales, he stated. President Obama himself gave us the highest endorsement, praising the extraordinary beauty, wonderful people, and great hospitality of our country and saying he would encourage people from the United States to visit here. The next step is to ensure we maintain this momentum. Cardiff council promised that security barriers in the city centre would be removed by Sunday afternoon. text: The gang behind a Halloween ride-out in Leeds which was likened to scenes from the film Mad Max has been jailed. These are external links and will open in a new window. More than 100 bikers gathered on Kirkstall Road before entering the city, disrupting traffic and riding through pedestrianised areas. David Armitage did not participate in the event but organised it via social media, Leeds Crown Court was informed. Also imprisoned were 12 other defendants, who had all admitted to causing a public nuisance at an earlier hearing. The judge stated their actions on 31 October could not be tolerated. Read more about this and other stories from across Yorkshire. Armitage, 26, of Brookfield Road, Headingley, had been recorded on 31 October instructing riders to shut down the city centre. Sentencing him to two years in prison, Judge Geoffrey Marson QC said: This is a case which calls for a deterrent sentence. Behaviour of this sort, having serious effects on this city, cannot be tolerated. West Yorkshire Police received approximately 160 calls from the public, some comparing it to scenes from the Mel Gibson film, Mad Max. Chief Superintendent Paul Money said: The behaviour of these individuals and others that night put people's safety at risk, caused unnecessary fear to the public and created an image of lawlessness in the heart of the city that we simply could not allow to go unchallenged. text: Pedro Caixinha insists his Rangers players proved their commitment in the comeback win at Partick Thistle. Barrie McKay's goal and a stoppage-time header from Joe Garner secured three Premiership points for the Ibrox men following Kris Doolan's opener for Thistle. Caixinha conceded the performance was disorientated but believed his players demonstrated they are fighting for him. If we were not united as a group, I do not think the players would celebrate like that at the end, Caixinha stated. I really appreciate the way the players understood and were committed. There were numerous moments I truly felt the passion from the players. The outcome ensured a top-four finish and European football for Rangers next season, although for much of the match they were second best to Alan Archibald's side. Caixinha implemented a series of system and personnel changes, with substitute McKay making a significant impact, but for extended periods the Ibrox men struggled to find any rhythm. The manager, however, defended his changes as his side responded to consecutive Old Firm defeats. Today was crucial for us to demonstrate a reaction, he added. We showed it in the second half and I need to be pleased with that. We needed to alter the course of the game and we succeeded. My passion and dedication to this sport is such that I would rather die trying than be alive to see what happens. And that is what the players did. Jags boss Archibald was left to account for another late collapse against Rangers. In November at Firhill, the Jags had taken the lead only for a late Joe Dodoo double to secure victory for the Ibrox men. It's a sore one, he remarked. We invested a lot into that first-half performance. We created several good opportunities - the only negative was not adding to our 1-0 lead. We were not outdone by tactics or anything like that. It's one long ball that defeats us. You feel guilty about criticising, but we must learn from it. We must move on. We aspire to be a top-six side, we want to stay away from the bottom end of the league. You must see games out, manage them, and learn from it. Once we conceded the goal, we did not react appropriately. We did not execute the basics. With 30 seconds to go, you must defend your box as if your life depends on it.

text: Donald Trump has said his sons will run his businesses during his presidency but there will be no new deals. These are external links and will open in a new window. He tweeted that he would hold a news conference in the near future after postponing an announcement on managing his business interests. The US president-elect had been scheduled to hold a rare press conference on the matter on Thursday. Mr Trump also stated that he would announce his choice for secretary of state on Tuesday. On his Twitter account, Mr Trump mentioned that, although not legally required, he would divest from his businesses before 20 January, when he is inaugurated as president. Two of my children, Don and Eric, plus executives, will manage them, he tweeted. No new deals will be done during my term(s) in office. No mention has been made of the role of Mr Trump's prominent daughter, Ivanka, fuelling speculation that she might have a role in his administration. If Mr Trump retains ownership or some financial interest in his business, then the threat of a constitutional crisis looms over his presidency. His insistence that no law forces the president to be free of business interests ignores decades, even centuries, of convention. It is also an explicit disavowal of the constitution itself. The US federal government's founding document specifically prohibits US office holders from receiving presents or emoluments (defined as the returns arising from office or employment - i.e., payment) from foreign governments. It is difficult to see how even the most straightforward business transactions between the Trump organisation and an overseas company would not threaten to put President Trump in breach of that clause. Commentators and political rivals have raised this issue repeatedly, first during Trump's campaign, but particularly since his stunning victory. That he still will not address it directly suggests either that he is still seeking a way to reconcile his business interests with his presidential obligations - and will unveil it later. Or that he intends to risk Congress one day deciding that his conflicts of interest are so significant that he must be impeached. Mr Trump's transition team spokesman, Sean Spicer, said Thursday's press conference had been postponed to ensure proper protocols are put in place. With so many iconic properties and successful entities, moving the announcement to January ensures the legal team has ample time to ensure the proper protocols are put in place so his sole focus will remain on the country and achieving his ambitious agenda with the help of the world-class cabinet he has built, Mr Spicer wrote in an email statement to Associated Press. Critics have said Mr Trump runs many businesses which all present possible conflicts of interest. It makes no sense to say 'no new deals,' said Richard W Painter, a White House ethics adviser under President George W Bush. Is he going to continue to borrow money from foreign banks like Bank of China? That is a deal, Mr Painter told the New York Times. Or collect rent from foreign government-owned companies? That is a deal. Will he still be hiring people, or having people stay in his hotels? Mr Trump's extensive domestic and international business interests include hotels and golf courses, including two in Scotland, as well as a variety of real estate holdings: ownerships or investments in hotels, offices, and residential buildings. Last month, Mr Trump issued a series of tweets pledging to leave my great business in total, saying it was visually important to in no way have a conflict of interest. Media reports suggested that the delay in outlining how he plans to separate his business interests from his presidency was also due to his focus on several high-profile cabinet appointments he has been making. Mr Trump said he was appointing Goldman Sachs President Gary Cohn as his top economic adviser. text: Governor Scott Walker's campaign for president is premised on more than just his conservative achievements in Wisconsin, of which there are many. The candidate frequently, almost incessantly, boasts about what he has had to overcome—and whom he has defeated—to implement them. Conservative audiences across the United States seem to admire him for it. For the past five years, Democratic opponents in a state with a long tradition of progressive policies have contested the governor over every inch of political ground. Now many are questioning if they are partly responsible for his emergence as a presidential contender. Is Candidate Walker a creation of their own making? I regard Walker as one of the most destructive forces in American politics today, says Dave Obey, a retired Democratic congressman from Wisconsin. However, Mr Walker's rise, he continues, would not have been possible without the misguided recall efforts that took place in the state. The recall drive was a 2012 initiative to hold a special election to remove Mr Walker from office during his first term as governor. It followed months of protests by over 100,000 demonstrators in Madison, the state capital, in a failed attempt to block a law significantly reducing the collective bargaining power of the state's public employees' unions, including teachers. I don't blame the unions for thinking they ought to vote for the recall because he was literally putting them out of business economically as well as politically, Mr Obey adds. But sometimes it is helpful if you don't think with your spleen. The unsuccessful recall efforts, Mr Obey says, made Mr Walker a hero among grass-roots conservatives, allowed him to establish a national fundraising network, and provided him with a unique talking point in the crowded Republican field. Including his 2014 re-election, he has won three elections in five years—in a state that has not voted for a Republican president in more than 30 years. Another Wisconsin Democratic insider, speaking on condition of anonymity, was more blunt about the recall effort. It was something you just couldn't politically be against, because the activists were so angry, he says. I just wanted this to go the [expletive] away. I was praying they wouldn't get the signatures, but I couldn't stand up in public and say that. He says the protests, although well-intentioned, were destined to fail due to Republican control of the state legislature. And the recall election was a disaster because the Wisconsin public was not convinced of the effort's legitimacy. At its core was a sort of purity and innocence and stuff that would almost make you believe in American democracy—but it was just so tragically flawed, he says. It was not going to work; it was just a children's crusade. During his presidential announcement event on Monday, Mr Walker's political war record was repeatedly mentioned. There was talk of agitators being bussed in from out of state during the Madison protests and death threats made against Mr Walker and his family. Do you remember what it was like to see your governor persecuted for simply putting you back in charge? Wisconsin Lieutenant Governor Rebecca Kleefisch asked the audience of around 300. Like a David to Goliath, Governor Scott Walker had your back. And America, he will again. After Mr Walker spent nearly 40 minutes boasting of his conservative achievements, members of the audience echoed a similar sentiment. Democrats threw everything at him that they could, and he still won, says Jeff Bishop, of Richfield, Wisconsin, who attended the event with his wife. That says a lot. Chris Taylor, then a Wisconsin lobbyist for Planned Parenthood, was among the protesters at the state capitol in 2011, and she bristles at the characterisation of the gathering as an unruly mob. The protests were nonviolent, she says. These were teachers, and kids, and grandmas. They were as Wisconsin as you can get. Progressives should not regret the demonstrations and recall drive, she says, as they reflected the will of the people independent of Democratic leaders. Mr Walker, she adds, is just a tricky guy who has been able to convince the Wisconsin public he is something he is not. He's very moderate in his speech, he's not bombastic, he's very earnest, he's very Mid-Western, Ms Taylor, now a Wisconsin state representative, says. He's very appealing in that way, but he governs like an extremist. According to Joel Rivlin, a Wisconsin-based Democratic political consultant, the protests and recall efforts gave Mr Walker a significant boost, even if it was fairly clear from the governor's first days in office that he was positioning himself for an eventual presidential bid. Even before the recall, he was receiving a ton of money from outside of Wisconsin, he says. People just assumed he was gearing up for something and had bigger ambitions. But now, riding a wave of liberal spite, Mr Walker has emerged as a force to be reckoned with in national Republican politics. He is the front-runner in neighbouring Iowa, the first of the 2016 nomination battlegrounds, and is near the top in national approval polls. While the Republican primary field is filled with high-calibre governors with records of accomplishment—Florida's Jeb Bush, Rick Perry of Texas, and New Jersey's Chris Christie, to name but a few—Mr Walker's stands apart. No other Republican candidate has built a throne of his enemies' skulls, as the Federalist's Rich Cromwell puts it, quite like the Wisconsin governor. There is a line by Ralph Waldo Emerson that is often trotted out for coups and revolutions, but could prove equally applicable to the leader of a certain northern dairy state. Never strike a king unless you are sure you shall kill him. Scott Walker, despite all efforts to unseat him, still wears the crown—and now he is eyeing a much larger dominion.

text: Los Angeles, known as the homeless capital of the US, has passed a $1.87bn (£1.29bn) plan to help get an estimated 40,000 people off the streets. City authorities aim to expand homeless shelters and construct quality housing over the next decade. It is the most serious humanitarian crisis confronting our county today, stated city official Sachi Hamai. Los Angeles declared a state of public emergency last year as the homeless population surged by 12.4% in two years. Residents and officials attribute the growing problem to a combination of unemployment, drugs, and rising rents and house prices. An estimated 40,000 homeless individuals are expected to be living throughout Los Angeles County, with two-thirds residing on the streets, in tents, or in vehicles. Measures to be implemented as part of a 10-year plan include investing in short and long-term housing, permitting overnight parking for those living in vehicles, and establishing a city-wide network of mobile showers and toilets. Officials plan to release $150 million over the next two years, designated for housing the homeless. Some lawmakers are questioning the source of the funds, but the city's mayor has suggested it could come from new revenue and reallocating existing funds. It may include things related to revenue growth or shifting priorities of money. We don't have 100 million extra dollars lying around to allocate solely to homelessness. It will require difficult decisions, stated Mayor Eric Garcetti. The plans still require adoption by the city, which will not vote on its budget until April. Los Angeles already spends approximately $1 billion annually on medical, psychiatric, and social welfare costs for its homeless residents. The City of Angels has another nickname: the homeless capital of America. The accuracy of the title may be disputed—there are many ways to count, none definitive—but no one else wants it, and it has persisted. The heart of this capital lies in the shadows, beneath the gleaming skyscrapers, on Skid Row in downtown Los Angeles. In this land of glitz and glamour, the forgotten people have established camp. Block after block, the homeless and their scant belongings—tarpaulins, tents, and trolleys—are scattered on the concrete in the baking sun. Most of the faces are African-American. Read more here.

text: Quentin Tarantino's first western, 2013's Django Unchained, was his highest grossing film in the USA - and now the 52-year-old director's latest movie, The Hateful Eight, is also set in the wild west, fulfilling his desire to breathe life into obsolete or dormant genres and make them my own, or even remake them. Set in Wyoming following the American Civil War, The Hateful Eight brings together a cast of Tarantino regulars, including Samuel L Jackson, Kurt Russell, and Reservoir Dogs stars Tim Roth and Michael Madsen. It also features Single White Female actress Jennifer Jason Leigh as the sole woman among the eight, while Tarantino jests that Channing Tatum interns for a debut role in one of his films. Similar to Django Unchained, which faced criticism for the director's perceived insensitivity towards slavery, The Hateful Eight is reported to have caused discomfort at early Hollywood screenings due to its race-related language and the violence directed at Leigh. However, Harvey Weinstein, the film's executive producer, has dismissed accusations of misogyny against Tarantino as fishing for stupidity, and both Tarantino and Leigh have been nominated for Golden Globes for screenplay and actress, which Tarantino says he is thrilled about. Leigh portrays Daisy Domergue, a captured gangster en route to execution. Russell, who spent the four-and-a-half-month shoot handcuffed to Leigh for the storyline, explains that they had worked out the violence we were expected to carry out on each other carefully. When this sort of thing is involved, you need to trust that actor, because if you don't, you can't do your scenes properly. I wanted to make it look effortless, and it was important that she was safe in my hands, that she could play the part as she needed to. Tarantino himself defends his script: The violence is meant to send shockwaves through the audience, to create sympathy with Daisy, but also I have trapped all my characters in a cabin during a blizzard. It's a pressure cooker in terms of storyline, and you know the way I go; that any piece of outrageous violence can happen. So you're telling me I can cross all the lines with seven characters, but the eighth I have to protect? It goes against the entire plot. On the race issues in the film, however, with Jackson portraying a former Union soldier with a letter from Abraham Lincoln in his pocket, Tarantino admits that over the last 18 months, many of the themes we were dealing with in the film, we were watching on our TV screens—referring particularly to the riots that followed the shooting of 18-year-old Michael Brown in 2014 by a white police officer in Missouri. The director's first draft of The Hateful Eight was leaked online in January 2014, after which Tarantino initially cancelled the film. Now he says he's grateful that the first draft got out after all, because it's on record that I wasn't writing a script in response to these events happening. He does believe his scripts have a deeper meaning, saying: I like masking what I want to say under a story. I think in history, no other genre deals with modern America better than the western. The westerns of the 1970s after Vietnam and Watergate were very cynical, for example. Django Unchained did really well, and I hope it did reinvent the genre a little, so now we've got two big westerns coming to cinemas—The Revenant with Leo DiCaprio and this one. I've always said if you want to be known as a western director, you have to make three of them, so I guess I might have to do one more. But cowboy shows like the 1960s TV series Bonanza were also an inspiration for the creation of The Hateful Eight; and the film has a retrospective feel throughout, with a three-hour running time, a musical overture from composer Ennio Morricone, and a 12-minute interval for audiences. The movie itself was shot on 70mm film, employing the very lenses used to shoot the Ben Hur chariot race in 1959. (However, many cinemas will be showing a shorter non-70mm version of the film as few venues have the specialised equipment necessary.) Last year, Tarantino announced he might retire after making 10 films—The Hateful Eight is his eighth, if Kill Bill is included as one film. Russell, who starred for Tarantino in 2007's B-movie homage Deathproof, believes it would be a tragedy if he did, saying the director is in a league of his own. You just know within a few frames of this film opening who is directing it. Every couple of generations someone comes along like him, and I wish everyone in the industry got a chance to work with him. Trust me, it's a crazy circus everyone should be a part of. The Hateful Eight is released in the UK on 8 January.

text: A motorised wheelchair user has been convicted of ramming a policeman during a loyalist protest in north Belfast. Samuel Baxter trapped the officer's leg against a police vehicle after being prevented from passing through security lines on Twaddell Avenue, Belfast Magistrates Court was informed. The 53-year-old was also convicted of disorderly behaviour during one of the nightly demonstrations in the area. Baxter, of Canmore Close, will be sentenced next month. Police witnesses testified that one constable sustained a bruised shin in the incident after Baxter repeatedly directed his wheelchair, weighing up to 28 stone, at them. Baxter stated he was in the area for family reasons and was not involved in the protests over a disputed Orange Order parade. He claimed he was attempting to pass through the police cordon to take his friend, who had a blood clot, to hospital. He alleged the officer he was accused of assaulting told him: Sit down, you're not getting through, OK. He contended that the constable's flak jacket had caught on his wheelchair's gear stick, causing it to move forward about an inch. A police inspector testified that Baxter was swearing and abusive. He stated the incident was part of attempts to incite a crowd who were filming on their mobile phones. This set-up happens on a nightly basis and has done for the past 400-odd nights, he stated. Things like that are staged to try and rile the crowd up. I was made aware he had come out with a whole crowd round him and their cameras already on. The inspector said police had been trying to calm the situation. We do this protest on a nightly basis. If there was a medical emergency it would have been quite obvious and we would certainly facilitate that, he added. When I spoke to this man and gave him numerous chances to tell me what the problem was, he was just extremely verbally abusive and playing to the crowd. The judge convicted Baxter of both counts of assault on police and disorderly behaviour and ordered a pre-sentence report to be prepared.

text: Pupils in schools in London and other parts of England are wearing green to show support for those affected by the fire at Grenfell Tower. These are external links and will open in a new window. The campaign requests pupils and staff to donate £1 to charity in exchange for wearing green for the day. The concept emerged when students at Fulham Cross Girls' School in London wanted to express solidarity with the fire victims. Fulham Cross headteacher Peter Haylock stated that more than 100 schools in west London wore green for Grenfell on Friday. He added: The idea originated from the students themselves, who have relatives and friends severely affected by the fire. Some of our students also pass the tower on their way to school. We devised the idea of wearing green for Grenfell and consulted the local authority, which spans the three boroughs, Hammersmith, Kensington and Chelsea, and Westminster, and over 100 schools have adopted it. From there, it has spread across the entirety of London and the whole of the UK, he said. Approximately 100 balloons were released at Fulham Cross Girls in memory of those who perished in the fire. Pupils from three other schools, dressed in green, were invited to participate in the balloon-releasing ceremony. Mr Haylock added: For me as a headteacher, I know that some of my colleagues have faced the worst imaginable task - informing an assembly that some of their friends will not be returning. Meanwhile, Belmont School in Chiswick, west London, tweeted that it raised £705.40 for the Grenfell Disaster Fund. Thank you for your generosity Belmont, a tweet stated. The senior leadership team at Outwood Grange School in Sheffield prepared green jelly to commemorate the day and support the affected families. Meanwhile, pupils at Oswald Road Primary in south Manchester are also supporting the day by wearing green clothes and collecting donations for those who have lost loved ones and their homes. The idea is to conduct fundraising to assist and show support for those who've lost everything in the fire, the school tweeted. Schools participating are donating funds to various charities supporting work in the affected community.

text: The group representing many of Scotland's councils has urged them to reject the Scottish government's funding settlement offer. Council leaders at the Convention of Scottish Local Authorities voted 21 to 7 to reject the unacceptable deal. The motion stated the Scottish government's approach was wholly misguided and threatens grievous injury to communities and citizens. Finance Secretary John Swinney described the offer as a deal worth taking. Councils have until 9 February to respond to the settlement offer. All councils in the Cosla grouping not run by the SNP united against the deal, with some considering a legal challenge. Scotland's four other councils not part of Cosla also convened and are examining the legality of the deal's terms. The funding package prioritises maintaining the council tax freeze, in place since 2007, with any councils breaking it facing a loss of Scottish government funding. However, some councils are contemplating tax increases due to budget pressures. Discussions have occurred between Mr Swinney and council leaders, with the deadline for acceptance repeatedly extended. Following a Cosla meeting in Edinburgh, President David O'Neill announced the rejection of the funding package as totally unacceptable and an attack on our democratic mandate. He stated: The Scottish government is basically forcing individual councils into having to accept the deal. Sadly, I fully accept that individual councils, due to the horrendous sanctions they would face, will find that they have no other option but to give in to central direction on this occasion. In imposing the deal on individual councils, the most vulnerable in our communities will be left to pick up the pieces. Today's vote at Cosla is largely symbolic but illustrates the extent of some councils' anger over the budget offer. 21 of 28 councils supported a motion condemning the funding offer, with only SNP councils opposing. The move complicates local government's ability to present a united front. Some councils are genuinely angry, even considering the politically charged atmosphere as the Holyrood election nears. Initially, they feared they would need to make larger cuts and savings than expected. Their concern intensified when it emerged the deal made it even harder to contemplate raising council tax to compensate. One council, Moray, had proposed an 18% rise in its council tax rates, but the calculations leading to this figure are now obsolete. Meanwhile, SNP councils, while acknowledging the funding offer's challenges, believe it is, on balance, the best they can expect. The government made a manifesto commitment to freeze council tax for the entire parliamentary term, believing it has been a popular policy aiding family budgets. It also argues it has shielded councils from the worst of what it terms Westminster spending cuts. The move by the four councils not in Cosla, including Glasgow and Aberdeen, to explore the offer's legality rests on a specific point. However, their consideration of this option demonstrates their deep concern and highlights the Scottish government's numerous advantages. Realistically, councils have little choice but to accept the government's funding offer. This raises longer-term questions about the entire system of council funding. A recent report, commissioned jointly by the government and Cosla, detailed several possible alternatives to the council tax. There is also a debate over whether councils should be less dependent on the government and have more local revenue-raising options. The parties are likely to outline their proposals ahead of May's Holyrood election. The motion accepted by Cosla stated the deal would slash council budgets by £350m and would be undeliverable without an unacceptable level of cuts to services and staffing. Trade union GMB Scotland has claimed 8,785 local authority jobs are under threat due to budget cuts and is planning a rally outside the Scottish Parliament next week. Jenny Laing, leader of Aberdeen City Council, which is not part of Cosla, said the relationship between the Scottish government and councils was broken. Speaking after the Scottish Local Government Partnership (SLGP) met in Glasgow, she said: This is the most significant grant cut ever applied to local government. And when we've carried out our civic duty to question the settlement on behalf of our residents, we've been held to ransom by the Scottish government's attempt to control decisions which should be made by democratically-elected representatives. She stated the group was seeking legal advice on the matter. Scottish Labour and the Lib Dems said it was now time for Mr Swinney to re-think the deal on the table. Responding to the Cosla and SLGP votes, John Swinney said: This is a deal worth taking. Our funding proposals deliver a strong but challenging financial settlement for local government, despite cuts to the central budget by the UK government. It is a deal that will see an additional £250m invested in social care, it will help councils deliver the Living Wage giving 40,000 people a pay rise, it will freeze council tax for a ninth consecutive year, and it protects the pupil-teacher ratio, helping improve attainment. Overall, as a percentage of total revenue expenditure, the reduction in local authority budgets is around just 2 per cent. So while I recognise this will not be easy for councils to accommodate, some of the language used to describe the deal has been unnecessary. I hope and expect cooler heads will come to realise this is a deal councils can and should accept.

Plane 2 crashed on the Syrian side of the Turkish-Syrian border. text: For the cynics among us, Valentine's Day is an annual nightmare: everything turns pink and heart-shaped, restaurants slap a premium price on a sub-par special menu, and Hallmark shareholders are laughing all the way to the bank. However, beyond the cuddly toys and red roses, the tradition elicits mixed reactions globally. From the stringent to the utterly bizarre, here are just some of the ways Valentine's Day is embraced—or rejected like an unwanted lover. Authorities in certain regions of Indonesia have prohibited students from celebrating Valentine's Day, claiming it promotes casual sex. In Makassar, police raided shops and dismantled condom displays. The mayor informed the BBC that condoms were removed from view following customer complaints, but would still be sold discreetly. Valentine's Day has its origins in a Roman fertility festival but later evolved into a Christian feast day—a fact that concerns conservatives in some Muslim-majority nations. In Indonesia's second-largest city, Surabaya, students were instructed to reject the festival as it contravenes cultural norms. Neighbouring Indonesia, Malaysia has also experienced a Valentine's backlash. A group called the National Muslim Youth Association has advised women and girls to avoid using emoticons or overdoing the perfume in a pre-Valentine's Day message. The group's guidance included advice on countering the celebration of romance by creating anti-Valentine posters and avoiding Valentine-themed attire. Robben Island will forever be linked with the notorious prison that held Nelson Mandela—but since 2000, it has hosted a mass celebration of love on 14 February. The tradition was initiated by South Africa's Department of Home Affairs and the Robben Island Museum and now attracts couples worldwide. This year, 20 couples are planning to say I do in the island's small white chapel. The service is offered for a nominal fee and includes a tour of the island. Organisers state that 2017's couples were chosen by the department based on their diversity and interesting romantic stories. Thailand's civil servants are distributing free pre-natal pills on the streets of Bangkok on Valentine's Day, aiming to boost the country's declining birth rate. Approximately 1 million baht ($28,600; £22,900) has been spent on the pills for prospective mothers aged 20 to 34. The very magical vitamins (as termed by the government) contain folic acid and iron. In 1970, Thai couples had an average of six children, but the figure now stands at 1.6. The High Court in Pakistan's capital, Islamabad, has prohibited public celebrations of Valentine's Day, stating it is not part of Muslim culture. The festival has gained traction in recent years, but local critics argue it is a decadent Western invention. The court order bans the media from covering Valentine's events and prohibits festivities in public places and government offices. Saudi Arabia's religious police are vigilant at this time of year for love-themed merchandise, including flowers, cards, and suspicious red items. Florists have been known to deliver bouquets in the middle of the night to evade detection, as determined lovers defy the nationwide ban. A black market in roses and wrapping paper enables some to express their feelings. However, for others, it is the ideal time of year for a romantic getaway—to nearby Bahrain or the UAE, where celebrations are more tolerated. As Japan prepared for the 14th, a group of Marxist protesters unfurled a giant Smash Valentine's Day banner in Tokyo. The Kakuhido, or Revolutionary Alliance of Men that Women find Unattractive, seeks an end to public displays of love that hurt their feelings. Members have been known to chant slogans such as public smooching is terrorism. Our aim is to crush this love capitalism, said Takayuki Akimoto, the group's PR chief. People like us who do not seek value in love are being oppressed by society, he added. It's a conspiracy by people who think unattractive guys are inferior, or losers—like cuddling in public, it makes us feel bad. It's unforgivable! The protests occurred as Japan's family planning association revealed that sexless marriages in the country are at a record high. Nearly 50% of married Japanese couples had not engaged in sexual activity for more than a month and did not expect that to change soon, it stated.

text: Comments made by Northern Ireland Health Minister Jim Wells linking child abuse with gay relationships have been rejected by a child protection body set up by his own department. The Safeguarding Board for Northern Ireland (SBNI) is a coordinating organisation that advocates for the welfare of children and young people. Independent chair Glenys Johnston stated: There is no evidence that children raised by same-sex couples are at greater risk of abuse than those raised by heterosexual couples. She further commented: In many European regions, children who have been abused, possibly by a man or woman, are sometimes best cared for by same-sex couples of a different gender. I do not wish for children and young people with same-sex carers or parents to fear increased likelihood of abuse, nor do I want those caring for the children to face adverse comments or criticism, and I do not want the children themselves to be bullied because their carers are of the same gender. SBNI was founded by Northern Ireland's Department of Health in 2012. Mrs Johnston declined to comment specifically on remarks made by Mr Wells, whose wife is seriously ill. I know he has experienced an extremely difficult personal period for several months, she remarked. He actually appointed me to my position, and I have no indication whatsoever that he is not committed to safeguarding children in Northern Ireland. Mr Wells, the DUP South Down candidate in the 7 May election, stated during an election hustings discussion on gay marriage: You do not bring a child up in a homosexual relationship. That a child is far more likely to be abused and neglected... In a subsequent statement, he said: I accept that one line of what I said caused offence and deep concern. Mr Wells added: I regret having wrongly made that remark about abuse and I am sorry those words were spoken. The comment did not reflect my view nor that of my party. His comments during the election debate have also been contested by a leading academic. Prof Susan Golombok of the University of Cambridge's Centre for Family Research told BBC Radio Ulster's Talkback programme: The minister has got his facts wrong because the evidence points to completely the opposite conclusion. More than 35 years of research on the well-being of children with lesbian mothers, and more recently with gay fathers, have shown that these children do just as well as children with traditional families. A ban on gay and unmarried couples applying to adopt children in Northern Ireland was lifted in December 2013. Mr Wells' predecessor as Stormont health minister, his DUP colleague Edwin Poots, had attempted to challenge an appeal court decision to extend adoption rights to gay couples. text: Security forces in Gabon have arrested more than 1,000 people during a second day of violence following disputed presidential elections. Three individuals were killed in clashes in the capital, Libreville. Protests erupted following the announcement that President Ali Bongo had been narrowly re-elected in Wednesday's election. Opposition leader Jean Ping, currently in hiding, informed the BBC that his party headquarters had been bombed. The UN, US, and former colonial power France have urged restraint and greater transparency regarding the results. A 98% or 99% turnout is not typical in an honest election. Voting is mandatory in Gabon, but it is not enforced; even in Australia, where it is enforced, and voting can be done by post or online with fines for non-compliance, turnout only reaches 90-95%. The primary reason a full turnout is practically impossible is that electoral registers, even if recently compiled, can rarely be 100% current. Even if no one falls ill or needs to travel, people still die. When a register is updated, new voters are eager to add themselves to the list. However, there is little enthusiasm for removing the names of deceased individuals, leading to an increase in non-existent voters over time. How to identify signs of potential election rigging. I know who has won and who has lost, Mr Bongo told local media. Who has won? 1.8 million Gabonese with whom we will progress together. Who has lost? A small group aiming to take power to exploit Gabon instead of serving it. Interior Minister Pacome Moubelet Boubeya stated on Thursday that 800 people had been arrested in Libreville and 400 in other parts of the country. Security forces cracked down after protesters attacked the national assembly building late on Wednesday, tearing down its main gate and setting parts of it ablaze. On Thursday, the building's facade was blackened by fire, and its windows were shattered. Burned-out cars were scattered on nearby streets. Democracy does not sit well with an attack on parliament, Mr Bongo said. Police used tear gas to prevent crowds from gathering there again and arrested individuals as they emerged from the building's remains. The BBC's Charles Stephane Mavoungou in Libreville reports that people there have been unable to access the internet. Meanwhile, Jean Ping told the BBC that a presidential guard helicopter had bombed his headquarters, resulting in two fatalities. They attacked around 01:00 (00:00 GMT), he said. They were bombarding with helicopters and then attacked on the ground. Security forces surrounded the building on Thursday night and detained members of the opposition National Union party inside, according to a party spokeswoman. It was not immediately clear where Mr Ping had gone into hiding, but a European diplomat quoted by AFP news agency stated he was safe. Witnesses reported that security forces had sealed off central Libreville. The official election result, announced on Wednesday afternoon, granted Mr Bongo a second seven-year term with 49.8% of the vote to Mr Ping's 48.2%—a margin of 5,594 votes. However, Mr Ping claimed the election was fraudulent. He cited the result in Mr Bongo's home province of Haut-Ogooue, where turnout was 99.93% and 95% of votes were for the president. Turnout in other provinces ranged from 45% to 71%, according to Gabon's interior ministry. EU election monitor spokesperson Sarah Crozier told BBC Newsday, it's not a very common result, that's for sure. Mr Bongo assumed office in 2009 after an election marred by violence, succeeding his father Omar Bongo, who had come to power in 1967. Mr Ping had been a close ally of Omar Bongo, serving him in ministerial roles and having two children with his daughter, Pascaline, a former Gabonese foreign minister.

text: Jane Haining was a quiet farmer's daughter from the south of Scotland who ended her life as a slave labourer in the most notorious extermination camp the world has ever known. These are external links and will open in a new window. She is the only Scot to be officially honoured for sacrificing her life for Jews during the Holocaust. However, her life began far from the barbed wire fences of Auschwitz, amidst the rolling hills of rural Dumfriesshire. Jane Haining was born in Dunscore in 1897. Her mother passed away when she was just five years old, and she assumed much of the care for her younger sisters. After leaving Dumfries Academy, where she excelled as a student, particularly in languages, Jane took a secretarial position at the large JP Coats weaving factory in Paisley. While there, she attended church at Queen's Park West in the Crosshill area of Glasgow. It now features stained glass windows in memory of a woman driven by a strong Christian faith. In 1932, she responded to an advertisement for a position as matron at the Scottish Mission to the Jews in Budapest. Dr David Kaufman, director of the Centre for the Study of Modern Conflict at the University of Edinburgh, states that the Hungarian city had a burgeoning middle-class Jewish population. He notes it was often referred to as 'Jewdapest' because 60% of the doctors and half of the lawyers in the city were Jewish. The life and worship at the Church of Scotland mission school were overtly Christian, yet Jewish parents were eager to have their children educated there. Rev Aaron Stevens, minister at the present-day St Columba's Church of Scotland in Budapest, remarks: I think it had to do with the quality of the education the girls received and also with the way the girls were accepted. Jewish girls who came here were not seen as second-class pupils. They were just as welcome. Rev Stevens describes Jane's role as a mother figure for those no longer living at home. Former pupil Katalin Packard told BBC Scotland documentary Jane Haining: The Scot who died in Auschwitz that she remembered Jane as kind and welcoming and warm. For her pupils, Jane Haining embodied the values of fairness, tolerance, and equality that drove the entire Scottish mission. We never felt we were not equal with each other or with the Christian pupils, says another former pupil, Dr Zsuzanna Pajzs. We did not even notice who was Christian and who was Jewish. Less than a year after Jane arrived in Budapest, Hitler was elected Chancellor of Germany. He became the most powerful force in the turning against Jews that occurred across Europe in the 1930s. Dr David Kaufman states: The Hungarian political elite tended to gravitate towards Nazi Germany in the 1930s. The Hungarian Jewish population see themselves as different from the rest of the Jewish populations of Eastern Central Europe. They see themselves as successfully assimilated within Hungarian culture. But in social terms, they are not really accepted because there is still a latent, casual anti-Semitism which pervades Hungarian society. In 1939, the Nazis invaded Poland, and Britain declared war on Germany. Hungary's Nationalist government began to concede anti-Semitic laws in an attempt to appease its more demanding fascist sympathisers before eventually allying itself with Germany. The authorities began detaining Jews who had lived in Budapest for decades without citizenship. As more territories fell to the Nazis, Hungary's alliance with Germany kept invasion at bay. The government continued to protect the lives of its Hungarian Jews, but they did lose jobs, social position, civil rights, and respect. Former pupil Eve Haller, now a prominent social activist in America, has never forgotten how the Scottish Mission school restored that respect. However, the Church of Scotland became increasingly alarmed for the safety of its missionaries and sent repeated letters urging Jane Haining to return home. She refused and wrote: If these children needed me in days of sunshine, how much more do they need me in these days of darkness? She could not grasp the evil in which she was functioning, says Annette Lantos, a former pupil. It was not part of her ability to understand what she was confronted with. She lived in a different world. A world that was civilised and reasonable and rational, where people did not kill each other for no reason. Then the outlook suddenly darkened further when Hitler turned his attention to Hungary and its Jews. On a Sunday afternoon in March 1944, Nazi troops marched into Budapest. Jane Haining is said to have wept as she sewed on the yellow stars that branded her children as Jews. Her open sympathy placed Jane in grave danger. It only took one incident to ignite the situation. Within weeks of the invasion, Jane scolded the cook's son-in-law for consuming food intended for the girls. He informed on her. The next morning, a Gestapo police car arrived at the school. She was arrested on suspicion of espionage on behalf of England. She was initially taken to the local prison but was soon transferred to Poland, to Auschwitz, as the industrial slaughter of Jews was reaching its peak. Approximately 12,000 Hungarian Jews were being sent to Auschwitz every day. Most went directly to the gas chambers. In total, more than a million human beings were killed at Auschwitz. Jane Haining was a political prisoner, so she was sent to the labour camps where inmates were screamed at, beaten, and chased with dogs. She survived just two months. She was only 47. According to her death certificate, she died of cachexia following intestinal catarrh. Whether Jane died of starvation, illness, or disease, and whether she died in hospital or was actually gassed like many women who became too ill to work, cannot be known for certain. It took a long time before Jane Haining's death was recognised. In 1997, following an initiative from Queen's Park Church and a 10-year investigation by an Israeli board, Jane was named as Righteous Among the Nations in Jerusalem's sacred Yad Vashem. In 2010, she was awarded a Hero of the Holocaust medal by the British government. Her death was anonymous and without ceremony, but her quiet sacrifice for those Jewish children has now been recognised worldwide. text: Reports of child rape to police in England and Wales have risen by 37% over the last five years, figures show. There were 5,674 recorded cases of child rape in 2009/10 and 7,775 cases in 2013/14, according to Her Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary (HMIC). However, less than a third of child rape cases result in suspects being charged or summoned, the figures indicate. Recorded adult rapes increased by 38% from 9,383 in 2009/10 to 12,952 in 2013/14, the report states. Approximately a fifth of adult cases result in suspects being charged or summoned. The Metropolitan Police recorded the highest number of adult rapes per 100,000 people in 2013/14 with 3,056, while Dyfed-Powys recorded the lowest with 62. The North Wales force recorded the highest number of child rape cases per 100,000 people with 144 in 2013/14, while Hertfordshire recorded the lowest with 73. Essex, Kent, and Suffolk forces ranked lowest in the table of charges or summons for child rape cases, with 21% of cases resulting in action. Northumbria topped the same table with 47% of cases leading to charges or a summons. Shadow Home Secretary Yvette Cooper stated: These figures are extremely disturbing and a shocking indictment of the widening justice gap created by this government. Over the last four years, there has been a dire trend in recorded incidents of rape going up, but prosecutions and convictions going down. Rape and the sexual abuse of a child are some of the most abhorrent and heinous crimes. And victims deserve justice. Crime Prevention Minister Lynne Featherstone noted that rape sentencing lengths had increased and the total number of rape prosecutions in England and Wales rose from 3,819 in 2009/10 to 3,891 in 2013/14. The coalition government is clear that every report of rape must be taken seriously, every victim must be treated with dignity and every investigation must be conducted thoroughly and professionally, she said. The increase in the number of rapes being reported to police is encouraging as it shows more victims are finding the courage to come forward. Paul Ford, Secretary of the Police Federation National Detectives' Forum, remarked: Policing is under significant pressure through budget cuts and this is having an impact on the level of service that policing can provide to victims. Devon and Cornwall have one of the highest rates of recorded adult and child rape. Yet only 15% of adult rape cases and 27% of child rape cases result in a charge or summons, according to the figures. The force's Police and Crime Commissioner Tony Hogg stated that police performance on rape was under regular review. Fee Scott of Devon Rape Crisis commented: We will get a lot better outcomes if we believed people and we don't judge them on what they were wearing, doing, saying or drinking. All of that stops women coming forward because they are fearful of the reaction they will get from the authorities. This report gives a very depressing picture of what the outcome might be.

text: Nine landless farmers in Paraguay have been charged with murder after six police officers died during clashes in eastern Canindeyu province. At least nine farmers also perished in the clashes. Police had earlier reported the number of officers killed as seven. President Fernando Lugo has deployed the army to the area to restore order. Territorial disputes are not uncommon in Paraguay, but Friday's incident was the most violent in decades. Police stated that one officer injured in the confrontation remains in a serious condition. Relatives of the landless farmers claimed they had discovered two more bodies at the clash site, raising the civilian death toll to 11, though this has not yet been officially confirmed. Murder charges have been filed. Police reported that nine suspects, including a 15-year-old boy, are in custody. They stated that some are receiving treatment for injuries sustained during the eviction attempt. They have been charged with murder, attempted murder, and criminal association. The confrontation began in the early hours of Friday when police moved onto private land occupied by over 100 landless farmers. According to police official Walter Gomez, the officers were ambushed in a wooded area. He stated they had not anticipated violence and had sought to negotiate a peaceful eviction. Mr Gomez said his officers were attacked with high-calibre weapons. Among those killed was the chief of the Police Special Operations Force, Erven Lovera. Battle for land Farmers' leader Jose Rodriguez told Paraguayan radio that those killed were humble farmers, members of the landless movement, who'd decided to stay and resist. The farmers claimed the land was illegally taken during the 1954-1989 military rule of Gen Alfredo Stroessner and distributed among his allies. According to the Paraguayan Truth Commission, 6.75 million hectares of land were sold or transferred under irregular circumstances during military rule. The Commission states that nearly 20% of Paraguayan land can be classified as ill-gotten gains. Interior Minister Carlos Filizzola and Chief of Police Paulino Rojas were replaced over the incident. The new Interior Minister, Ruben Candia, stated that the evictions would continue and that they would be conducted with the full backing of the law.

text: The SNP won every seat in Tayside on the way to a Scotland-wide landslide in the general election. These are external links and will open in a new window. text: England need to work on how they play spin bowling after their tour of India ended in a crushing Twenty20 defeat, says head coach Trevor Bayliss. England lost eight wickets for eight runs in 19 balls, resulting in a 75-run defeat in Bangalore, with spinner Yuzvendra Chahal taking 6-25 in his four overs. This defeat confirmed a 2-1 T20 series loss for England, who also lost the Test and one-day series during the tour. We're certainly not world-class players of spin, admitted Bayliss. We're playing against players that are very good at spin, and they've got very good spinners themselves. When you don't grow up on it, as players here do, it is difficult. It's a learning process. England lost 86 wickets to spin across all formats on their tour of India, having also struggled against it in their previous tour in Bangladesh. Chasing 203 to win on Wednesday, they remained competitive at the halfway stage of their reply, but after Chahal dismissed both skipper Eoin Morgan and vice-captain Joe Root, the tourists collapsed. It is a little bit disappointing the way we finished our series, said Bayliss. It doesn't reflect the type of cricket we have played over here. But it's what can happen in a T20 match when you're chasing a big total. Morgan said: Everybody is gutted. Today was a big game for us. There was a series on the line and we wanted to produce a good performance but in fact we have produced one of our worst in a long time. If we can take anything from it, it is that it is the first time it has happened in two and a half years. England won only three of their 13 matches during the tour - one ODI, one T20 and a tour match against India A. However, they produced their best cricket in the limited-overs series, scoring more than 300 in each of the ODIs and producing some improved bowling displays in the T20s. The results haven't gone the way we'd have liked, said Bayliss. We've played some pretty good cricket here at times. We've still got a lot of work to do - the boys have been very honest about where they stand. We've got to put together a batting and a bowling performance in one game - we seem to bat well in some games, and bowl well in others. Morgan added: There hasn't been a lot between the sides, particularly in the one-day series. There was 15-20 runs between the winning and losing of the series. The improvements we have shown since then have been considerable in our bowling department. When you are going well you have to take advantage of it. But we are really strong at the moment. Home advantage is huge, around the world. We have pushed India right to the cusp in both [limited-overs] series. In the wake of the 4-0 Test series defeat in India, Alastair Cook said he had questions about his role as England captain, admitting Root was ready to be his successor. Australian Bayliss said he had not spoken to Cook since he departed the tour but said he would contact him in due course. I'm heading home to Australia for a little while in the next day or so, added Bayliss. I'll put the feet up for a little bit and I'm sure I'll speak to him at some stage. I'll give it a couple of days - I'm sure we'll exchange a text message or something. As I said to him when he left, and there was a lot of speculation, it is totally up to him. He will know if it's time to step down. I'm happy either way, whether he stays or goes. There is plenty of time.

While his detractors question whether Sanusi’s real motive is to undermine President Goodluck Jonathan’s re-election prospects, many others are likely to see the president’s action as an attempt to silence the whistleblower rather than to investigate fraud.

text: Rail passengers have been speaking of their frustration after overrunning engineering works saw services thrown into chaos. No trains have been running between Paddington in west London and Reading for most of the day, impacting routes to the West Country and Wales. At King's Cross in London, which serves northern and eastern England and Scotland, all services were cancelled. There were long queues at Finsbury Park station as passengers waited for trains to Peterborough and further north. The 12:15 train from Peterborough to Edinburgh departed Peterborough at 13:05 and was overcrowded. An elderly German couple expressed disbelief. There was no chance of reaching the buffet car, and when they finally could, it had been closed since Newcastle. Seats were only available from Doncaster and York, although people were still standing in the doorways. Alternative, less crowded trains from Peterborough were available, but these came and went without information from staff who appeared leaderless. There seemed to be no management involvement today, possibly still on holiday. It was freezing waiting an hour on the Peterborough station platform. There are insufficient waiting rooms. Soon to be home, but no Christmas spirit on Network Rail. The train was almost an hour late at Edinburgh. People stood in the aisles and vestibules between carriages. Although it was very busy, people were generally relieved to be on a train. The atmosphere was friendly, with passengers chatting, helping each other with bags, and giving up seats to those in greater need. I boarded the train at Finsbury Park, but passengers who joined at Peterborough said they had been told the train was empty, so there would be plenty of seats. This was clearly not the case. Most of us had been waiting on platforms for over an hour without adequate information. Additionally, there were not enough staff to provide information. I arrived at Finsbury Park at 09:50 and was informed there would be no train until 11:00, with no East Coast staff available to tell us where trains were going. The website was not up to date, so more people kept arriving. Eventually, I left without knowing the destination at about 11:20. I was planning to visit my friend in Bradford and her family for the first time before travelling to Liverpool to see friends I had not seen for over a year. Finsbury Park was very busy, and passengers had to carry luggage and small children up a steep spiral staircase to reach the train platforms from the Tube platform. At the top of the spiral staircase, a tunnel was filled wall-to-wall with passengers—elderly passengers, young children, crying babies, prams, luggage—and it was impossible to reach any platforms. There was no one to advise on what to do or where to go. We were all stuck in this tunnel, and it was becoming busier as more passengers arrived, causing me to feel slightly anxious as a crowd management issue seemed imminent. Several rail staff pushed through the tunnel of passengers, but they were quite rude and unhelpful when questioned. Some staff members acted unprofessionally and did not seem to know how to handle the situation. I stood in the bitter cold trying to determine if any destination options would get me close to Leeds or Bradford. I overheard that I could get a train to Peterborough and change there, and there was a Peterborough train on the screen, but it never materialised. By this point, I was very tired and cold. I decided I had enough and would return to Reading. I had to leave the platform and descend into the tunnel full of people. Upon exiting Finsbury Park, there was a large crowd of several hundred people standing outside. I had to navigate through and around to the Tube entrance and make my way back across the city to Waterloo to return to Reading. I cannot believe I have had to completely abandon my plans, which I had been looking forward to. I am utterly exhausted and too worried to risk travelling again tomorrow.

text: An outspoken member of South Africa's African National Congress (ANC) party has been charged with ill-discipline for speaking out against President Jacob Zuma. These are external links and will open in a new window. MP Makhosi Khoza has consistently urged Mr Zuma to resign. Last week, she described him as a disgrace. She has received death threats warning her to cease advocating for a secret ballot when MPs vote on Mr Zuma next month. Parliament and the police have decided to provide her with security. Last week, the ANC stated she had overstepped and must face disciplinary action for criticising the president. The ANC in her home province of KwaZulu-Natal labelled her remarks a blatant betrayal of the core values of the party. Ms Khoza, aged 47, has also criticised corruption within the ANC. Mr Zuma has faced numerous corruption allegations, all of which he denies. The National Assembly is expected to vote on a motion of no-confidence in him on 8 August. Milton Nkosi, BBC News, Johannesburg. The decision to charge Makhosi Khoza with ill-discipline exemplifies how the ANC is undermining itself. Following its poor performance in last year's local government elections, the party vowed to self-correct. However, the South African electorate is witnessing the ANC inflicting self-harm that may not heal before the next general election in 2019. Ms Khoza is a PhD MP and one of the most popular among the over 200 in the National Assembly. She is being penalised for speaking truth to power. This is precisely what Nelson Mandela warned South Africans about regarding his party's impunity when he stated: If the ANC does to you what the apartheid government did to you, then you must do to the ANC what we did to the apartheid government. The ANC resembles an unstoppable train hurtling downhill at breakneck speed. If there was ever a time for the 105-year-old party to apply the brakes, it is now. However, the public is likely to penalise these leaders in two years' time. Last week, Ms Khoza received a death threat stating she had 21 days left to live. She called Mr Zuma a disgrace at a ceremony marking Nelson Mandela's birthday on 18 July. She was addressing civil society groups, unions, and business leaders advocating for Mr Zuma's removal in next month's no-confidence vote. There is no suggestion that he is linked to the death threats. Jacob Zuma has survived several previous votes of no-confidence. The constitutional court ruled in June that parliament could conduct a secret ballot, but the speaker has yet to announce a decision on the matter. Mr Zuma is set to step down as ANC president in December, and whoever succeeds him would lead the party into the 2019 elections.

text: A rugby fan was nearly six times over the drink-drive limit after downing a bottle of vodka in the NekNominate craze, a Cardiff inquest has heard. Stephen Brookes, aged 29, from Rumney, passed away after a friend filmed him consuming three-quarters of a 75cl bottle during an online drinking challenge. He was nominated by a friend to consume the drink for Facebook. The coroner recorded a verdict of death by acute alcohol poisoning and cocaine use. The inquest was informed that Mr Brookes had been drinking earlier in the day on Sunday, 9 February, after watching Wales play Ireland in the Six Nations. However, he was dared by friends to consume the vodka. The inquest heard that labourer Mr Brookes stated he would be OK just before undertaking the stunt. Yet, within minutes, he collapsed and became unconscious. He was taken home by friends but was later found deceased. His cousin Jodie Cummings informed South Wales Police: Stephen had been watching a rugby match with friends at a house. He had taken a 75cl bottle of vodka. A few weeks ago, he had been NekNominated. This involves someone nominating a friend to consume something like a bottle or a pint. After midnight, while I was in the bathroom, Stephen consumed the bottle of vodka. It was filmed, and I saw it on a friend's phone. I saw him drink back the bottle of vodka. He just held the bottle in the air. Afterwards, he was in good spirits and said, 'you know me'. He was dancing around. But 10 minutes later, his balance had gone. He was slurring his words - it all happened so quickly. Friends informed police how people were encouraging him to consume the vodka at around 01:30, the day after he had watched Wales play Ireland in the Six Nations rugby. Another friend, Shaun Chivers, stated the vodka disappeared within seconds as he was filmed at the party near his home. I saw Stephen had three-quarters of the bottle left and I knew he was going to drink it, he said and advised his friend to stop messing around. He added: The next thing, he drank the bottle, and it was gone in seconds. Soon after, he was swaying all over the place. Mr Brookes died within an hour of the NekNominate stunt and was later found to have 458 millilitres of alcohol in his blood - the drink-drive limit is 80. He also had a high level of cocaine in his blood and had taken between 10 and 20 lines of cocaine. Pathologist Thomas Hockey stated he was clearly well over the fatal range for alcohol.
