text: After months of sotto voce claims that some businesses were simply too scared to put their head above the independence parapet, tonight comes the most significant move by anti-independence members of the UK business community ahead of the September vote. A letter endorsed by 133 globally interested businesses asserts that the uncertainty of a Yes vote is detrimental to business. The signatories span various sectors, including banking, mining, engineering, food, whisky, technology, and a selection of SMEs. Some have previously expressed anti-independence views, while many are new. The letter is signed by individuals such as Douglas Flint, chairman of HSBC; Andrew Mackenzie, CEO of mining giant BHP Billiton; and Sir John Grant, executive vice president of policy at BG Group (and formerly the UK government's representative in Brussels). Audrey Baxter, executive chairman of Baxters Food Group; Simon Thomson, CEO of Cairn Energy; and Ian Curle, CEO of Edrington, which owns whisky brands The Macallan and The Famous Grouse, also support the letter. It will be published in Wednesday's Scotsman newspaper. The letter was organised by Keith Cochrane, CEO of engineering firm Weir Group, who has already warned of substantial risks if Scotland votes for independence. Its supporters claim that no political organisations were involved in compiling the list. One source mentioned it arose from frustration over a perceived lack of cohesiveness in the business and independence debate. The signatories represent approximately 50,000 jobs in Scotland, I have been informed, from large companies like Babcock shipbuilding to small engineering firms in Glasgow's east end. Advocates of an independent Scotland can, of course, highlight their own array of supporters from business and economics. Former chairman of The Royal Bank of Scotland, Sir George Mathewson, has stated that Scotland's vital financial services sector would thrive if Scotland votes yes. There is nothing to suggest that being part of a smaller country hinders a financial services industry. Switzerland, for example, has - in Geneva and Zurich - not one, but two of the world's Top 10 financial centres. Singapore, with 5 million people, is ranked 4th, he has said. Investment is an increasingly global business, where success depends much more on people than on borders. Economist and former head of Scottish Enterprise, Sir Donald MacKay, has argued that an independent Scotland would be in better fiscal condition than the UK currently is. An independent Scotland should use that financial advantage to invest in re-engineering our economy towards industrial, manufacturing and trade-able services development, he has argued. Jim McColl, one of Scotland's wealthiest individuals and head of the engineering investment business Clyde Blowers Capital, has disclosed that he is so enthusiastic about independence he would consider relocating back to Scotland in the event of a Yes vote. For now, Mr McColl resides in Monaco. Willie Walsh, CEO of IAG, owner of British Airways, also suggests that independence could potentially benefit Scotland. I wouldn't be surprised if more names are disclosed this week. Both sides of the debate have emphasised that it is up to the voters to decide. With this letter, voters will certainly have a clearer understanding of the issues concerning those businesses worried about a possible Yes vote. These concerns centre around five key topics: the currency, an independent Scotland's relationship with the European Union, potential tax and regulation changes post-independence, pensions, and how exports may be affected (an issue linked to the EU debate). The letter states that much is at stake: Our economic ties inside the United Kingdom are very close and support more than a million Scottish jobs. As job creators, we have examined the arguments made by both sides of the debate. Our conclusion is that the business case for independence has not been made. I am informed that this is not the beginning of a new campaign by businesses against independence but is a one-off. However, it does precede a CBI dinner in Glasgow on Thursday evening, where Sir Mike Rake, president of the CBI and chairman of BT Group, is likely to present similar arguments against independence. Business for Scotland responded tonight, issuing this statement: Business for Scotland has 2,500 members who run businesses in Scotland, employ people across the country in a range of industries, and all believe that Scottish independence is in the best interests of Scotland and Scottish business. It's a position reached after examining the facts and figures and realising that, from a simple balance sheet point of view as well as other considerations, our best interests lie in becoming an independent country. It will be for the Scottish voters to decide the weight they assign to either side in this debate.

text: A tipper truck which killed four people when its brakes failed had clocked up almost 450,000 miles (724,000km), the driver's trial has heard. Mitzi Steady, aged four, Robert Parker, 59, Philip Allen, 52, and Stephen Vaughan, 34, perished in the crash in Bath in February 2015. Bristol Crown Court was informed the truck was an accident waiting to happen. Driver Phillip Potter, 20, denies causing the deaths by dangerous and careless driving. His employer Matthew Gordon also denies 14 offences, while the truck company's mechanic Peter Wood denies four charges. Mr Potter and Mr Gordon were operating two trucks carrying 30-tonne loads from a Wiltshire quarry on 9 February, the court was told. Mr Gordon, who was driving ahead of Mr Potter, halted his truck on Lansdown Lane in Weston village, but Mr Potter's brakes failed, forcing him to swerve to avoid a collision, the court heard. The truck struck several pedestrians, including Mitzi and her grandmother Margaret Rogers, and a car containing Mr Allen and Mr Vaughan, both from Swansea, and Mr Parker, from Cwmbran, south Wales. Prosecutor Adam Vaitilingam QC stated: (Mr Potter's) lorry continued to career down Lansdown Lane out of control. It caused absolute devastation. By the time it finally came to a stop, four people had suffered fatal injuries - a four-year-old girl who had been crossing the road with her grandmother and three men who had been travelling together in the same car. Mr Vaitilingam described Mr Potter as an inexperienced driver who had only been in the company for a matter of days. He stated Mr Gordon's firm, Grittenham Haulage Limited, was established in December 2013 and was a shambles from start to finish with no transport manager in place at the time of the crash. The firm did not conduct the recommended brake efficiency tests on the vehicle, which was an accident waiting to happen, he said. Mechanic Peter Wood was employed to perform inspections on the trucks. The final safety check on the vehicle occurred in January 2015, weeks before the crash, when he deemed it safe to drive, the court heard. Mr Vaitilingam said: If Mr Wood did carry out a safety inspection that day it was wholly inadequate. On the date of the crash the lorry had serious and long-standing defects with its braking system, meaning that it was and had been for some time in a dangerous condition. This sort of catastrophic brake failure doesn't just happen through bad luck. Mr Potter, of Dauntsey, Wiltshire, is also charged with causing serious injuries to Karla Brennan and Margaret Rogers - Mitzi's grandmother - by dangerous driving. He denies a total of 10 charges against him. Mr Gordon, 30, also of Dauntsey, denies 14 charges against him. Mr Wood, 55, from Brinkworth, Wiltshire, denies the four charges against him. The trial continues.

text: Great Britain will have a team of 264 athletes competing at the Rio Paralympics in 19 sports. The British team have consistently finished within the top five in the medal table. MacGirrre is the current world champion in the BC4 category, while Smith won gold in the team competition in Beijing with Murray, a two-time Paralympic champion. text: California regulators have accepted an offer from farmers to reduce their water usage by 25% in an effort to combat the record four-year drought. A group of several hundred farmers conceded after state officials threatened to revoke their water rights. California has already mandated a 25% reduction in cities and towns. However, critics argue that state Governor Jerry Brown has not sufficiently reduced usage by the farming industry's influential water rights holders. The agreement between California's Water Resources Control Board and the farmers—who have previously resisted pressure to commit to reductions—indicates the worsening impact of California's drought. The US Drought Monitor reported on Thursday that 94% of California was experiencing severe drought or worse, with farmers using 80% of all water extracted from the land in the state. The agreement is the first of its kind in over 30 years and involves farmers in the delta of the Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers. Others in this category—known as senior rights holders—include irrigation districts, utilities with hydropower stations, and cities, including San Francisco. Thousands of the state's junior water rights holders—those whose claims to water usage date back only to 1914—have already had their water use restricted this year. These are primarily farmers receiving no federal irrigation deliveries. Under California's system, junior water rights holders must cease taking water from rivers and streams to ensure sufficient flow for those with older claims. About 350 farmers convened on Thursday to discuss an attempt to avoid deeper mandatory cuts to their water allowance. That doesn't necessarily mean they'll all participate in the voluntary 25% reduction, said Michael George, the state's water master for the delta. However, he expressed confidence that many would. The farming industry has faced criticism in recent weeks from residents who have been compelled to turn off their sprinklers and time their showers under threat of heavy fines. The agreement grants the farmers until 1 June to present plans for implementing the proposed cuts.

text: Jacob Boehme remembers when he knew something was seriously wrong. In 1998, Boehme had been suffering from a persistent cold for months. An Aboriginal elder sat me in the middle of her legs and started to sing over me, he recalls. During a healing ceremony, she wiped sweat from his armpits and applied it to his head and neck. Eventually, she murmured: Ahh, you need to go to a Western doctor. Everything is red. I cannot help you. Boehme was diagnosed with HIV. At a time when antiretroviral treatments were in their early stages, it was the first such news his doctor had delivered. He was choked up and almost crying, Boehme says. I had to console him. Now 43, Boehme is not only still alive, but he has channelled his experiences as a gay, indigenous, HIV-positive man into a solo show. Blood on the Dance Floor, recently performed at the Sydney Festival, examines what our understanding of blood signifies, from heritage to health. Combining storytelling and dance, the work features a skit on being a camp gay elder in drag, discussion of HIV stigma in the gay community (particularly when seeking a partner), and moments when Boehme is framed, moving, against streams of blood, with bubbling red cells projected on the wall. Most importantly, he says, is reshaping the conversation on what it means to be HIV-positive. Anything shown in the media or entertainment, it's always been some kind of memorialisation of the Aids crisis back in the '80s. Everybody dies, he elaborates. That's not relevant to me and to many of the other men and women that I know living with HIV. There isn't an image of a healthy functioning person with employment and prospects—you don't see that portrayed anywhere. Another crucial step, he says, is expanding our understanding of who is affected by the virus. According to the University of New South Wales, notification rates (the reporting of newly-diagnosed cases) of indigenous men with HIV doubled in the past five years from 6.2 per 100,000 to 12.4 per 100,000. In contrast, non-indigenous notification rates fell by 12%, stated the report by the university's Kirby Institute. Despite this, education campaigns largely remain targeted at white men, says Boehme. Tell me the last time you saw an HIV education campaign with someone from the Aboriginal, Asian or African identity on those posters? You just see gay white men in their underwear, he points out. It makes quite a lot of people feel completely dismissed and it's not just the gay male community—it's heterosexual males living with HIV, kids living with HIV too. It's never been a gay white man's disease. Born in Melbourne to a non-indigenous mother and a father from the Narungga and Kaurna peoples of South Australia, Boehme knew he was gay from the age of four. The dancer—who is the incoming creative director of the Melbourne Indigenous Arts Festival—has always had the support of his family. Others are often not as fortunate. In some Aboriginal communities, stigma towards homosexuality persists, insists Boehme. When you go into communities that are very much still holding up the values of the old mission days, that's when you get a problem, through those Christian and very Victorian ideas of sex, gender and sexuality, he says. Blood on the Dance Floor was conceived after rehearsals in a warehouse. Boehme was obsessed about my blood, about the cleanliness of my blood. After cutting his heel on an exposed nail, I sat back down and realised I left a trail of blood on the dance floor. And [my friend] went 'ah, there's your title'. Blood, it's a life force that connects us, it can be used to define us and can be used to discriminate, to separate, or to actually unite, Boehme says. When writing the show, the artist kept a small crystal decanter of his own blood on his desk. Suddenly I was connected to my dad, then my grandmother, then a whole line of our ancestors that I never met and through that, those voices started to then speak through me. In that blood, in those codes, there are thousands of generations sitting in that little decanter. Boehme says blood connects him to his past and, above all, to his illness. But it also releases him. Regardless of what features or skin colour we have, really our blood is the thing that ties us together, he says. A particularly raw moment in Blood on the Dance Floor touches on the suicide of Boehme's friend in 1996 after discovering he was HIV-positive. It was a time when there was still this spectre hanging around like it was a death sentence. There was a lot more shame around HIV and he just couldn't cope. Boehme still remembers when he found out. His friend's boyfriend, drunk, announced at a dinner party that his partner was positive. I looked at him. And he said, 'I don't want that look. I don't want anyone's pity. Don't you dare give me that look.' Just two years later—as antiretroviral drugs were being rolled out to the larger population—Boehme received his own diagnosis. In Australia in the 1990s around 1,000 people died each year of Aids. Today, deaths are so low they are not recorded. That's exactly why I insisted we honour him, Boehme says of his friend. He didn't get a chance. If you are feeling emotionally distressed and would like details of organisations in the UK which offer advice and support, go online to bbc.co.uk/actionline. In Australia, you can find similar information at Lifeline and Beyond Blue.

text: On 15 November 37 police and crime commissioners will be elected in England, along with four in Wales. The Police and Crime Commissioners (PCCs), as they will be known, will be responsible for scrutinising their police force and holding it accountable. They will also have the authority to hire and dismiss the chief constable and set the budget for the force. The commissioners will receive remuneration and are intended to empower local residents to have a say in how crime is addressed in their area. Nominations for candidates in South Yorkshire have now officially closed. BBC News has reviewed each of the police forces ahead of the elections. The county comprises a mix of urban areas alongside regions with a history of large-scale mining, steelworks, and engineering. By James Vincent, BBC Yorkshire Political Reporter. As police forces reduce in size and begin sharing services, the significant challenge for South Yorkshire's police commissioner will be ensuring the public feels secure. We are frequently informed that crime is decreasing here, but so is the number of police officers available. A council tax increase to fund an additional hundred officers is mitigating the impact of losing 400 in recent years, but there are genuine concerns that South Yorkshire is being asset-stripped. Divers, mounted officers, and firearms teams might soon be shared across Yorkshire, and the challenge will be to maintain a high-quality service while attempting to save money; a common theme across the public sector. The force decided to retain its own police helicopter and join the new National Police Air Service, which is expected to begin serving South Yorkshire in April 2013. The helicopter's popularity is unquestioned, but the long-term feasibility of funding two services may be an early decision for the individual elected to lead the police. Officers at South Yorkshire Police cover an area of 600 square miles (1,554 sq km), with several population centres, including the city of Sheffield, and other areas of open countryside. Priorities identified by the force include improving public confidence and satisfaction, along with enhancing community safety. Senior officers have identified tackling serious and organised crime, terrorism, and extremism as priorities across the county. Currently, the force is led by Chief Constable David Crompton, who has a deputy and two assistant chief constables, a director of finance, and an assistant chief officer responsible for human resources. South Yorkshire Police states it works closely with the county's police authority and the rank and file officers' union, the Police Federation. The force is also part of the Regional Chief Constables' Group (RCCG) and the Joint Police Authorities Committee (JPAC). Together, they outline the principles to guide policing delivered locally by individual forces to communities within Yorkshire and the Humber. South Yorkshire Police Authority has set a budget of £251 million for 2012/2013. The figure is based on an increase in the police authority council tax precept of 3.95%. For the average Band D property, this was a rise of £5.22 from the previous year. The budget would enable the authority to defer a reduction of 110 police officers in 2012/13 and fund an additional 22 police and community support officers (PCSOs) for the next three years, it claimed. The authority had also committed to offsetting some other planned reductions in police resources in 2013 and 2014. By increasing the council tax precept, the county's police authority said it hoped to secure around £2 million a year, which would balance the need for further cuts in policing from 2013 onwards. South Yorkshire Police reported that a snapshot of the year 2010/11 showed total crime had decreased by 9% - burglaries had been reduced by 5%; criminal damage was down by 17%; vehicle crime had dropped by 17%, and incidents of robbery were down by 14%.

A small bundle is wrapped in white plastic sheeting, and stern-faced men are loading yellow disinfectant cans into a pick-up truck. This is the final resting place of the latest Ebola victim: a four-month-old baby boy named Faya. He contracted the virus from his mother, who passed away a few weeks earlier. His is the 20th anonymous grave in this bleak and isolated clearing. I was there with him just before he died, says Adele Millimouno, a Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) nurse recruited from a nearby village. I had been feeding him milk. I stepped away for a short break, but then I was called back and he was dead. I was utterly devastated. This is merely another day on the front line of the latest Ebola outbreak. Gueckedou was where the first case of the disease was reported in March. Médecins Sans Frontières and the International Federation of the Red Cross, which together have nearly 400 international staff combating the outbreak, state the situation across West Africa remains out of control. A treatment centre in Gueckedou, operated by MSF, had - until 22 July - treated 152 Ebola patients, of whom 111 have died. It is the survivors that Adele says provide her with the strength to continue this distressing work. I muster the courage to come and work here to help save my community. I feel very proud of our work. We have been able to save around 40 people. The next morning we drive in a convoy with health officials to a village 12km away called Kollobengou. The last time health workers attempted to enter this village, they were attacked and told not to return. Many people died in front of me. It was a very difficult time for me, especially when the young children died. Sometimes I went outside and cried. Residents slowly emerge from their huts and gather in the centre of the village. The local ministry of health official in charge of co-ordinating the fight against the virus stands up and urges people not to be afraid and to permit health workers to ask them questions and assess people who could be ill. text: More black, Asian and ethnic minority lives will be saved under an opt-out organ donation system, a charity says. Roy Thomas, the chairman of the Kidney Wales Foundation (KWF), stated that these groups are three times more likely to require a transplant compared to the rest of the population. However, he noted that fewer than 2% have registered with the NHS Organ Donation Register. This follows a donor expert's accusation that the Welsh government misled the assembly regarding its organ donation bill. John Fabre, professor of clinical sciences at King's College London, claimed the policy was misinterpreted based on information from Spain's system. Professor Fabre, the author of several papers on international organ donation systems, asserted that Spain's high donation rate resulted from the available facilities and coordination within the Spanish health service, rather than legislation. The Human Transplantation Bill, which could become law by 2015, would require adults living in Wales to opt-out of the organ donation system if they did not wish to donate after death. Currently, individuals must actively opt-in to become donors. KWF cited Belgium as an example, where only 2% of the population opted out of a presumed consent system, claiming it was a great success with donor rates increasing by 55% in the first five years. In evidence to the assembly's health and social care committee, Mr Thomas stated that a change in the law was a key component to altering organ donation. He added: It is, however, key that the proposed legislation is implemented with the goodwill of the people of Wales. A transplant law provides only a legal environment which can influence the extent to which potential donors can be used. The law in proper practice will be essential. Mr Thomas informed the committee: We have been campaigning for the change in the law over many years and we have a determination to see the successful implementation of the law because of the clear effect it will have in changing the cultural approach in Wales and the UK on organ donation. A Welsh government spokesman stated that the Spanish government's website points to the adoption of appropriate legislation as one element of the success of their model for organ donation.

text: One million people who work in crowded places in the UK are to be trained over the next 12 months in how to deal with a possible terrorist attack. The plan, to be announced by the National Police Chiefs' Council, will involve staff passing on police terror training and advice to colleagues. The initiative will expand an existing scheme, which currently involves police training approximately 100,000 workers annually. Police stated they require everyone to play a part in keeping the public alert. Det Ch Supt Scott Wilson, the national counter-terrorism coordinator, will announce an extension to Project Griffin to enable existing trainers at companies to pass on police training and advice to colleagues. Public limited companies located in busy city centres, as well as those in the entertainment, sports, and retail sectors, will be targeted. We need everyone to play a part in keeping the public alert, not alarmed, Det Ch Supt Wilson added. Project Griffin was initially established by the City of London and Metropolitan police forces in 2004 to advise and train managers and security officers of large organisations on handling security and counter-terrorism issues; it has since been extended to other forces across the UK. Police can help explain what the threats and risks to different sectors are, but companies are better placed to explain to staff exactly what action they can take to enhance their security and how to respond if the worst happens, Det Ch Supt Wilson stated. He added: Individual organisations possess vital protective security information such as building layouts, security equipment, and safety procedures. They have the local knowledge that could be crucial to keeping staff and the public safe. BBC security correspondent Frank Gardner said the issue of preparing for a potential terror attack had been troubling the police and intelligence agencies ever since the marauding terrorist attacks in Mumbai in 2008. In the wake of the recent attacks in Brussels and Paris, efforts to prepare workers in busy areas will now be massively stepped up to brief one million staff in the next 12 months, our correspondent said. Terror attacks in Mumbai in 2008 resulted in 174 fatalities, while attacks by gunmen and suicide bombers left 130 people dead in Paris in November last year. Last month, bomb attacks at Brussels airport and a metro station resulted in 32 fatalities. The move comes amid an increase in the number of trained police firearms officers to cope with the possibility that criminals inspired by the so-called Islamic State could open fire in a public place using automatic weapons smuggled in from mainland Europe, added our correspondent.

text: A mother who took her toddler son to Syria has been jailed for six years for joining the so-called Islamic State. Tareena Shakil, aged 26, is the first woman from the UK to return from the self-declared caliphate and be convicted of the offence. Sentencing her, Mr Justice Inman stated she had shown no remorse and was aware her son's future would ultimately be as an IS fighter. He informed Shakil: You allowed him to be photographed next to an AK47. Shakil, from Birmingham but formerly of Burton-upon-Trent in Staffordshire, admitted travelling to Syria but denied joining IS and encouraging acts of terrorism through messages posted on Twitter. Passing sentence at Birmingham Crown Court, the judge remarked: Most alarmingly you took your toddler son to Syria knowing how he would be used. You embraced your role in providing fighters of the future. Shakil posed the boy, who was 14 months old at the time, for pictures wearing an IS-branded balaclava, which the judge described as one of the most abhorrent aspects of the case. Mr Justice Inman told Shakil she had embraced Isis, sending messages on the day she arrived in Syria stating she was not returning to the UK, telling her family it was part of her faith to kill the murtadeen (apostates) and that she wished to die a martyr. He said it was evident she had been radicalised following online conversations with prominent members of the terrorist group. Shakil, who was convicted on Friday, maintained she took her son to Syria, in October 2014, to escape an unhappy family life. Shakil flew from East Midlands Airport to Turkey, telling friends she was going on a family beach holiday, before crossing the border into Syria. However, once in the war-torn country, she claimed she became unhappy there too and decided to return of her own free will because she realised she had made a mistake. She said she caught a bus and bribed a taxi driver to take her part of the way before crossing the border back into Turkey in January 2015. Sentencing her to four years for IS membership, and two years, to run consecutively, for encouraging acts of terror, Mr Justice Inman stated she would be entitled to release on licence after serving half her sentence. As she was jailed, members of Shakil's family shouted that the hearing was a farce. Speaking after the sentencing hearing, children's charity the NSPCC said: This is a deeply disturbing case which could have resulted in tragedy for the toddler involved.

text: Worcester chief executive Jim O'Toole says giving head coach Carl Hogg sole charge of the first team was necessary because players weren't getting the dual-management structure. Following the departure of former director of rugby Dean Ryan on 30 June, Hogg and high-performance director Nick Johnston initially shared responsibilities. However, the Warriors have decided to alter their approach after a series of poor performances. Granting Carl sole leadership is now appropriate for us, O'Toole informed BBC Sport. It all traces back to Dean Ryan's departure in the summer. When he left, aside from his considerable experience and rugby intellect, we effectively lost his level of management at short notice just before the season began. Carl, as head coach under Dean, was in charge of the first team. Nick was responsible for the athletes and their preparation. We decided at the time to experiment with a duo-management system, which I've heard (England boss) Eddie Jones discuss as being the method used in the southern hemisphere. He strongly supports that type of structure. After six months, we reviewed it. My view, shared with my fellow directors, was that the players were not understanding it. Nick continues in his role, but streamlining the management by granting Carl sole leadership is the correct course of action. Ultimately, the players must be clear about their objectives. The injury-plagued Warriors have secured only two wins in 14 matches this season, achieving just one victory and two draws in the Premiership. Following Sunday's 26-12 home defeat by Wasps, they are positioned 11th in the table, six points above the bottom club Bristol, where they will travel on Boxing Day. Having twice previously faced relegation since first reaching the Premiership in 2004, their current struggles, although worsened by a significant injury list, have led to criticism from frustrated supporters. O'Toole has addressed this by organising a meeting with 40 of the club's more regular critics and regards managing dissatisfied customers as a significant aspect of his role. Modern communication channels are accessible to everyone, he stated. I have daily communication with supporters on Twitter, on club forums, via e-mail, telephone, and text messaging. I've even received messages on Facebook Messenger from individuals who are not my friends, who insist on conveying their message and like to suggest improvements. I did not come to manage a rugby club to socialise with the players. For me, it's about the excitement and passion of engaging with a large number of committed supporters and the environment that creates. People like to express their opinions, and I'm here to receive them. If people approach me and communicate politely, I consider their views. It's the old adage that 'the customer is king'. They are not always right, and some individuals get a bit carried away, but people are not unpleasant without reason. You know it's only because they care.

text: Afghanistan's two presidential election candidates have agreed to an audit in an attempt to resolve a dispute over the result of last month's vote, US Secretary of State John Kerry has said. Both contenders, Abdullah Abdullah and Ashraf Ghani, have consented to accept the outcome. The review of all 8 million ballots would commence within 24 hours, Mr Kerry stated. Preliminary results indicate Mr Ghani has emerged victorious, yet both candidates accuse each other of electoral fraud. Results declared by Afghanistan's election officials show Mr Ghani with 56.44% of votes in the 14 June run-off, while Mr Abdullah received 43.45%. The results were significantly different from those in the first round of voting, held in April, when Mr Ghani was a distant second. Afghanistan's current President Hamid Karzai, who assumed office following the US-led overthrow of the Taliban, is stepping down after more than a decade. He has endorsed the audit and agreed to postpone his successor's inauguration to allow time for the review, anticipated to take several weeks. At a news conference with the two candidates, Mr Kerry stated that every single ballot would be audited. This is the strongest possible signal by both candidates of a desire to restore legitimacy to the process and to Afghan democracy, he remarked. Ballots in Kabul would be examined first, and the International Security and Assistance Force (Isaf) would transport the remainder from the provinces, he added. The agreement was reached after two days of intense discussions and exceeds what many Afghans had anticipated, the BBC's Karen Allen in Kabul reports. It reflects the extent of international political, military, and financial commitment to ensuring Afghanistan does not regress into violence, our correspondent notes. At the press conference, Mr Ghani described the move as the most comprehensive audit in the history of elections... such a process would remove any ambiguity about the result. Meanwhile, Mr Abdullah stated the two sides had reached a technical and political agreement. I hope this is for the benefit of Afghan people, he added. Counting of votes is set to begin early on Sunday morning, with the ballot boxes being transported under tight security to counting locations. The votes will be under constant guard until new results are announced. The framework for a unity government may be being outlined, but the specifics about the potential division of power remain unclear. Mr Kerry arrived on Friday for a hastily organised visit, amid concerns over reports that Mr Abdullah was planning a parallel government. Speaking on Saturday as the audit was announced, Mr Kerry cautioned of a difficult road ahead due to important obligations required and difficult decisions to be made. He added: We hope that the promise of the next weeks will deliver the authenticity and credibility that the people of Afghanistan deserve. Analysts state Mr Ghani and Mr Abdullah both have strong support and any division in the government or armed forces could jeopardise the country's stability.

text: The number of hours that ambulances spent waiting at A&Es in the North West of England has more than doubled in the past two years, the BBC has found. Freedom of Information (FoI) data indicates an increase from 17,413 hours in 2013-14 to 46,160 in 2015-16 beyond the standard 15-minute handover period. All of the region's trusts except one have experienced increases, with wait times rising six-fold at the Royal Liverpool Hospital. North West Ambulance Service stated that demand for emergency care is increasing. The Royal Liverpool and Broadgreen University Hospitals' Trust reported it had recently employed several hospital-trained paramedics in its emergency department to assist in the safe handover of patients to return ambulances to the road. Nationally, only one of the UK's 13 ambulance services is currently achieving its target to reach seriously ill and injured patients, the investigation revealed. Delays have also been attributed to a crisis in social care provision leading to bed-blocking caused by delays in the discharge of elderly patients. During the period covered by the FoI, the number of hours spent by ambulance crews waiting to hand over patients at North West A&E units increased by 167%, with many hospitals experiencing even larger increases: Aintree Hospital in Merseyside, where last week 20 ambulance staff were photographed waiting to hand over patients due to a surge in 999 calls, recorded a 234% rise. One paramedic at Aintree reported spending more than half of their shift standing in corridors. The only hospital where handover times actually decreased was Wythenshawe in Manchester, where the number of hours has fallen by 9%. We have all heard stories of long waits at A&E—detrimental for patients and ambulance crews alike. Put simply, if they are stuck in a hospital, they are not on the road attending to other emergencies. To clarify these totals, ambulance services allow 15 minutes to hand patients over. These figures represent the number of additional hours they have had to spend waiting to do that. For the last financial year, that totalled 46,160 hours for the North West—a significant increase from two years earlier when it was just under 17,500. So why are the figures rising so dramatically? The number of people attending A&E is steadily increasing as the population ages. However, several hospital trusts are also highlighting the gaps in social care provision, particularly for the elderly. One trust informed me they currently had the equivalent of three wards occupied by people who should not be in hospital at all, simply because there was nowhere satisfactory for them to go. And if those beds are occupied, that means there are fewer for the patients arriving at A&E. Overall, handover delays at hospitals across England, Wales, and Northern Ireland have shown a 52% increase in the last two years. Lisa Grant, chief nurse at the Royal Liverpool and Broadgreen University Hospitals, stated: Hospitals across the area are working together with partners in community and social care to help to safely discharge patients who no longer require hospital care, providing beds for those in the emergency department who need to be admitted to a ward. A statement from the North West Ambulance Service said: We are seeing more and more people in need of our services, especially for Red incidents for patients with serious and life-threatening conditions. This contributes to additional activity at hospital emergency departments. During busy periods this can unfortunately result in ambulance crews having to wait longer to hand over patients into the care of hospital staff before they can be clear to respond to other emergencies.

text: A chronology of key events: 9th century - The County of Barcelona is established alongside several other counties due to Charlemagne's efforts to create a buffer zone between his Frankish Empire and Muslim-ruled Spain. 1023-76 - Under Ramon Berenguer I, the County of Barcelona attains a dominant position in the region. 12th century - The term Catalonia is mentioned for the first time. 1131-1162 - During the reign of Ramon Berenguer IV, his marriage to Queen Petronilla of Aragon leads to the county's dynastic union with the Kingdom of Aragon. Although part of the Crown of Aragon, Catalonia retains its own traditional rights and parliament, the Corts Catalanes. 14th-15th centuries - Aragon acquires the kingdoms of Sardinia, Sicily, and Naples, becoming a significant Mediterranean maritime empire. 1469 - Ferdinand I of Aragon and Queen Isabella of Castile marry, creating a dynastic union of their kingdoms and laying the foundations of the Kingdom of Spain. 1492 - Christopher Columbus's discovery of the Americas initiates the creation of Spain's overseas empire, shifting commercial activity from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic and diminishing Catalonia's economic and political significance. 1640-52 - The Reapers' War sees Catalonia revolt against the taxation policies of Philip IV of Spain, briefly declared a republic under French protection before Spanish troops reoccupy it. 1705-14 - During the War of the Spanish Succession, Catalonia supports Archduke Charles of Austria, a rival claimant to the Spanish throne, against King Philip V. This results in the suppression of its parliament and traditional liberties upon Philip's victory. 1716 - The Nueva Planta decree dismantles the separate Catalan legal system, subjects Catalonia to direct rule from Madrid, and abolishes the administrative use of the Catalan language. 1812-13 - Napoleon briefly annexes Catalonia to France before French troops withdraw from Barcelona under an armistice signed with the Duke of Wellington. 1808-33 - Catalonia becomes a battleground during the First Carlist War between liberal supporters of Queen Isabella II and the absolutist supporters of her uncle and rival, the Infante Carlos. 19th century - Catalonia leads Spain's industrialisation and experiences a cultural renaissance, initiating a movement to revive Catalan culture and language, leading to the rise of Catalan nationalism. 1901 - The Catalan nationalist Regionalist League is formed. The legacy of General Franco's dictatorial rule continues to affect relations between Catalonia and Madrid. Buried unpleasant truths? 1913 - The four provinces of Catalonia are granted limited joint self-government in the Commonwealth of Catalonia under Enric Prat de la Riba's leadership. 1925 - The Commonwealth is suppressed during the dictatorship of Spanish Prime Minister Miguel Primo de Rivera. 1931 - Spain becomes a republic; an autonomous Catalan regional government, the Generalitat, is established under the Revolutionary Left of Catalonia. 1936 - An insurrection by Spanish nationalist troops led by General Francisco Franco sparks the Spanish Civil War. Catalonia remains loyal to the Republic, with both the Generalitat's regular forces and popular militias fighting on its side. 1938 - English author George Orwell publishes Homage to Catalonia, a memoir of his time fighting with left-wing Republican forces in the region. 1938-9 - Franco's forces overrun Catalonia, paving the way for the collapse of Republican resistance elsewhere in Spain. 1939-75 - During Franco's dictatorship, political opposition and Catalan autonomy, language, and culture are suppressed. Thousands of Catalan activists are executed or go into exile. 1960s - Catalonia benefits from the onset of mass tourism in coastal Spain and increasing industrialisation. Barcelona attracts large numbers of migrants from other Spanish regions. 1975 - Franco's death initiates a process of democratisation under the new king, Juan Carlos. 1977 - A provisional regional government, again named the Generalitat, is restored under Josep Tarradellas's leadership. 1978 - A new democratic Spanish Constitution recognises the existence of distinct national communities within Spain, beginning the process of regionalisation. 1979 - Catalonia is granted a statute of autonomy and recognised as a nationality. Catalan becomes the joint official language of Catalonia alongside Spanish. 1980 - The centre-right moderate nationalist Convergence and Union wins the first elections to the new regional parliament. Its leader, Jordi Pujol, becomes the first president of the new regional government. 1992 July-August - The Summer Olympic Games are held in Barcelona. 2003 - Jordi Pujol retires as president of the regional government after 23 years in the post. 2003 November - Despite winning the largest number of seats in regional elections, Convergence and Union is ousted for the first time in 23 years by a coalition of Socialists, the Revolutionary Left, and Greens. Socialist Pasqual Maragall becomes regional president. 2006 June - Pasqual Maragall steps down and is replaced by fellow Socialist Jose Montilla. 2006 August - A reformed version of Catalonia's autonomy statute comes into force, granting the regional government greater powers and financial autonomy. Its preamble also uses the word nation to describe Catalonia. 2009 December - Between December 2009 and April 2011, Catalan nationalists hold a series of informal, non-binding votes on independence in regional towns and cities, including the capital Barcelona. 2010 July - The Constitutional Court in Madrid strikes down part of the 2006 autonomy statute, ruling that there is no legal basis for recognising Catalonia as a nation within Spain and that Catalan should not take precedence over Castilian in the region. The decision is criticised by the regional government. Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy rejects a call by regional leader Artur Mas for greater fiscal independence. 2012 November - Snap elections held to support a referendum on independence see the governing Convergence and Union losing ground to the left-wing Republican Left (ERC) party. text: As Westminster does from time to time, there is a frothing row this morning over where a memo - which purports to reveal the government's private Brexit woes and is splashed on the front of The Times - actually comes from. To describe Downing Street as cross is an understatement. They are enraged by the emerging story, not only because the claims are embarrassing and criticise the prime minister's style, but also because they assert the document was not authored by anyone with a genuine understanding of the situation, but by a consultant, believed to be from the firm Deloitte, whose analysis was part of a pitch for work. The Times contests this, stating that senior civil servants were indeed also involved. Regardless of who is correct, the document is significant because it highlights what we have reported and others have written about numerous times. Five months after the referendum, the cabinet is struggling to agree on a common position regarding what Brexit means Brexit truly signifies. There is a range of opinions around the table, and a substantial amount of work has been commissioned across government to help reach a consensus. The department working on the plan, DEXEU, (or Dexit as it might be easier to call it if it catches on) has commissioned 51 different studies of various parts of the economy to 'assist'. However, as a senior source suggested this week, they just don't know what they are going to do - the whole thing is a frightful mess. Information is accumulating, decisions are not. And with a very small majority in the Commons, ministers are concerned about losing the arguments and are trying to avoid major confrontations. The prime minister's holding position of Brexit means Brexit is now under real pressure. Downing Street was always aware that it could not endure. But while there is an expectation that the PM might provide more details in a speech at the CBI next week, there is little public indication that the government is actually any closer to any conclusions. Until that changes, they will remain vulnerable to the charges outlined in the memo, regardless of its author, and the accusations of chaos from the opposition.

text: More than 150 people in Wales have been reported to police for meeting children following sexual grooming over the last five years, new figures show. Dyfed-Powys Police recorded the highest number of complaints with 60, whereas North Wales had the lowest with 26. Nearly 60% of the crimes reported from 2011 to 2015 involved online grooming. NSPCC Cymru advocates for mandatory online safety lessons to be included in the curriculum. Data obtained by the charity under the Freedom of Information Act revealed 155 complaints were lodged against adults accused of meeting a child under 16 following sexual grooming. South Wales Police received 35 reports, while Gwent Police received 34. Dyfed-Powys Police reported the highest number of crimes involving online grooming with 37, followed by Gwent Police with 22, North Wales Police with 17, and South Wales Police with 16. NSPCC Cymru has urged for compulsory online safety lessons in schools from September to educate pupils about the dangers of social media and online grooming. NSPCC chief executive Peter Wanless stated: Education is the key to teaching children how to use the internet safely so they do not find themselves at risk of serious harm. Online safety is a 21st-century child-protection challenge and it is something that we need to tackle head on. The Welsh Government stated it had an extensive e-safety education programme, which included online resources and classroom materials to help pupils think critically, behave safely, and participate responsibly online. We have also created an online one-stop shop, Hwb, providing help for children and young people to stay safe on the web, a spokesman said. South Wales Police, Dyfed-Powys, and Gwent Police stated they worked with schools to educate pupils on issues including grooming, sexual exploitation, the taking and sharing of inappropriate images, and staying safe online. Gwent Police Supt Leanne Brustad said the force delivered 1,874 lessons to nearly 50,000 pupils in 2014/15, while South Wales Assistant Chief Constable Con Jon Drake said it collaborated with agencies to ensure those working with young people understood the signs of such abuse. Dyfed-Powys Police stated it had allocated more resources to addressing the issue and had a team of digital detectives, forensic computer, and mobile phone investigators. North Wales Police has been asked to comment.

text: A US appeals court has overturned the money laundering conviction of a once-powerful former Republican congressman, citing insufficient evidence. Tom DeLay was convicted in 2010 of illegally channeling corporate money to Texas Republican political candidates. By a 2-1 decision, the Third Circuit Court of Appeals overturned the jury verdict, ruling that prosecutors failed to prove the funds were tainted. Mr DeLay, first elected to Congress in 1984, ascended to majority leader in 2003. Known as the hammer, Mr DeLay was famed for his ability to keep the Republican caucus firmly aligned with the party line in close votes. The Texas congressman and former pest control magnate resigned in June 2006 following his indictment on charges of money laundering and conspiracy to commit money laundering. Federal prosecutors stated that during the 2002 mid-term election campaign, Mr DeLay's aides took $190,000 (£121,935) donated by corporate lobbyists to a campaign committee he controlled and transferred it to an arm of the Republican National Committee. That group then distributed the funds to seven state legislative candidates. Six of those candidates won, granting the Republican Party control of the Texas House of Representatives, which later enacted a redistricting plan that sent more Republicans to Washington in 2004, strengthening Mr DeLay's grip on power. Mr DeLay argued the swap was legal and that no corporate money was given to state-level candidates. He condemned the prosecution as a political vendetta. A Texas jury convicted him in November 2010. The following January he was sentenced to three years in prison but was permitted to remain free pending appeal. On Thursday, the appeals court ruled that the prosecution had failed in its burden to prove that the funds that were delivered to the seven candidates were ever tainted. Mr DeLay's attorney, Brian Wice, informed the Associated Press that Mr DeLay felt vindicated. He's ecstatic. He's gratified. He's just a little bit numb, he said. I'm hoping with today's victory, he will be able to resume his life as he once knew it.

text: A Taser gun was used three times in less than 30 seconds as police tried to apprehend a man who had killed a woman, an inquest has heard. These are external links and will open in a new window. Matthew Williams was discovered attacking Cerys Yemm, 22, at the Sirhowy Arms Hotel, Argoed, on 6 November 2014. Williams, aged 34, was Tasered by police who arrested him, and he subsequently died. Gwent Coroner's Court in Newport also heard that there were bites on Miss Yemm's body and cuts that could have been caused by a broken ceramic cereal bowl. Michael Rees, a South Wales Police armourer, examined Tasers used by all officers involved in the attempt to arrest Williams. He informed the inquest that only one had been used, it was partially covered in blood and had been activated four times during the incident. It was deployed at 01:37:11 and then at 01:44:14, 01:44:28 and 01:44:41. Forensic scientist Gillian O'Boyle examined the scene and stated it contained 15 pieces of broken crockery that fitted together to form an almost complete cereal bowl. Most of these had blood on them, with DNA analysis indicating it belonged to Miss Yemm and Williams. She concluded: The pattern of the blood was as if the bowl had been used to hit an individual and had broken as part of this, but stated she could not determine who had been holding it. There were also cuts in Miss Yemm's clothing that could have been caused by a sharp-edged item, such as a ceramic piece, Ms O'Boyle added. Forensic dentist Romina Carabott concluded that three bite marks on Miss Yemm's abdomen and another on her wrist were probably all caused by Williams. Williams, released from prison two weeks prior to the incident, was found to have 12.2 grams of class B mephedrone, 9.9 grams of mephedrone mixed with monosodium glutamate, and 1.02 grams of amphetamine sulphate mixed with caffeine. Forensic pathologist Dr Richard Jones, who conducted Miss Yemm's post-mortem examination, informed the inquest he found 24 areas of injury across her body with at least 89 separate injuries. Half of the injuries were to her head, and Dr Jones stated the cause of death was given as sharp force trauma to the face and neck. He added that bite marks had no bearing on her death, nor did traces of amphetamines and cannabis in her body. The inquest continues.

It was established that two weeks before the event, two weeks after his release from prison, Mr. William was found in possession of twelve grams of mephedrone, nine grams of mephedrone mixed with monosodium glutamate, and one gram of amphetamine sulfate mixed with caffeine. text: All photographs by Olivia Acland These are external links and will open in a new window. During its 11-year civil war, Sierra Leone gained notoriety for blood diamonds. Rebel and government factions engaged in brutal conflict over diamond-rich regions in the north of the country, financing themselves by selling the gems to international buyers. Fourteen years after the conflict concluded, diamond mining operations persist in the northern district of Kono. A South African firm, Koidu Holdings, operates a large mine employing advanced machinery to blast through kimberlite and locate diamond-dense areas deep underground. Nearby, artisanal miners work along riverbanks, equipped with sieves, spades, and buckets. One such miner, Philo, has been working in Kono for the past 23 years but was displaced during the conflict and lived as a refugee in Guinea. When the war subsided in December 2000, he returned home and resumed diamond mining a year later. Many artisanal miners confess they have not found a diamond in months and remain desperately poor. Yet in a nation with 70% youth unemployment, mining offers some form of livelihood. Most men mine in teams of three. Philo collaborates with two friends. One dives to scoop a bucket of mud and grit from the riverbed, while another holds him down to prevent drifting with the tide. The third collects the bucket and empties it into a mound. Once sufficient material is gathered, the sifting begins. The three men rotate roles regularly to avoid getting too cold. Philo complains of chills upon exiting the water and consumes a packet of cheap rum to warm up, stating: This work is tough and physically straining—if I had the qualifications or opportunity to do another job then I would at once. The swampy area around the river has been excavated by artisanal miners, who are scattered throughout, urgently scooping mud and sifting through it. Finally, after three hours of sifting, Philo is delighted to have found a tiny diamond. Some miners can invest in what is known as a rocker. They employ a power hose to spray water through a layer of mud piled onto fine mesh. Once the mud is cleared, they are more likely to spot a glinting diamond. However, Philo lacks this luxury. We are not able to afford this kind of machinery, we have to manage with just a bucket, spade, and shaker [sieve], he says. In the local market, each shaker sells for 25,000 Leones (about £3.50). Shortly after Philo discovers a diamond, he packs up early and heads into town with his team. He is content, saying: This was a very good day, we hadn't seen a diamond for nearly a month. On his way home, he encounters his elder brother outside a shop. They greet each other in front of the rocky kimberlite mountain created by Koidu Holdings' blasts. Philo expresses envy of their machinery and wealth, especially as diamonds in shallow ground are depleting. Back home, Philo relaxes in his room with his uncle. During the conflict, his mother was shot and killed by rebels just outside the room in which he now sits. His entire house was burned down and had to be rebuilt. The following day, Philo heads into Koidu town to sell his diamond in an office just off the high street. The current rate is $3,200 (£2,520) for a carat that is 40% pure, and much less for gems of lower purity. Philo receives only $35 (about £28) for his find, but he is pleased as it exceeds his expectations.

text: A US judge in Seattle has issued a temporary nationwide block on President Donald Trump's ban on travellers from seven mainly Muslim nations. Federal Judge James Robart ruled against government lawyers' assertions that US states lacked the standing to challenge Mr Trump's executive order. Mr Trump's action last week sparked mass protests and caused confusion at US airports. The State Department reports that 60,000 visas have been revoked since then. Mr Trump's executive order imposed a 120-day suspension of the US Refugee Admissions Programme. There is also an indefinite ban on Syrian refugees. Individuals arriving from Iraq, Syria, Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, and Yemen face a 90-day visa suspension. Trump border policy: Who is affected? The lawsuit against President Trump's ban was initially filed by Washington state, with Minnesota joining subsequently. Washington State Attorney General Bob Ferguson has described the ban as illegal and unconstitutional, arguing it discriminates against people based on their religion. The ruling poses a significant challenge to the Trump administration and theoretically allows nationals from the seven countries to apply for US visas, reports the BBC's David Willis in Washington DC. The administration can appeal the decision. President Trump has maintained that his directive is intended to protect America. He stated that visas would be issued again once the most secure policies were established and denied it was a Muslim ban. Several state attorneys general have declared the order unconstitutional. Several federal judges have temporarily halted the deportation of visa holders, but the Seattle ruling is the first to apply nationwide. Courts in at least four other states—Virginia, New York, Massachusetts, and Michigan—are hearing cases challenging Mr Trump's executive order. Earlier on Friday, a judge in Boston declined to extend a temporary ban that prohibited the detention or removal of foreigners legally authorised to enter America. The ban, which only applied to Massachusetts, is set to expire on 5 February.

text: This morning on the Today programme, Ed Miliband prayed in aid Sir Nick Macpherson when repeating his view that the big economic mistake of the last Labour government was a failure to regulate the banks properly, rather than to spend too much. Sir Nick serves as the Treasury's permanent secretary, ranking as the second most powerful civil servant in the nation, and is the individual upon whom George Osborne, as chancellor, most relies for fiscal advice and the implementation of his policies. In a review of a book on austerity by Bill Keegan, the leading Keynesian economic commentator, Sir Nick stated: The 2008 crisis was a banking crisis pure and simple. Excessive risk had accumulated in the system; the regulators failed to recognise the scale of that risk or to address it. It was 'a failure of the Group of Seven economic policymaking establishment', myself included. Inevitably, countries with larger banking sectors, notably the UK, were more severely affected. In other words, Sir Nick is admitting that he and the rest of the economic decision-making elite in wealthy developed countries were oblivious to the excessive risks taken by banks in pursuit of profits and bonuses. He acknowledges that the UK Exchequer depended excessively on revenues generated by the inflated financial services sector: corporation taxes paid by banks on their inflated profits proved unsustainable; equally fleeting were capital gains tax and stamp duty generated by bubbles in the housing market and financial securities, both inflated by banks' reckless provision of finance. This explains why when the Tories claim that Labour overspent and Ed Miliband insists the UK's economic turmoil was entirely due to a global banking crisis, they are contradicting each other far less than it might seem. As I mentioned on Friday, Gordon Brown and his economic advisers—including Nick Macpherson from the impartial civil service, alongside Ed Balls and Ed Miliband from his party—felt comfortable increasing spending by four percentage points of GDP from 2000 to 2007, partly due to their optimism that the growth of the City and associated tax revenues would not be a temporary boost to the Exchequer. Brown was mistaken, as were Macpherson, Balls, and Miliband. That error has been officially acknowledged, so to speak: with hindsight, both the IMF and the OECD have calculated that the UK's cyclically adjusted deficit—the portion of the gap between spending and revenues that normal growth will not eliminate—was larger in the UK than in other major wealthy countries. Thus, according to the IMF, in 2007 the cyclically adjusted deficit was 5.3% in the UK, compared with 3.5% in the US and 3.7% in France. One significant reason for the UK's larger so-called structural deficit was that financial services constitute a significantly larger share of the UK economy than of the US economy and those of any other major competitors. None of this absolves the Labour government of Brown, Miliband, and Balls. They must be held accountable for making significant long-term public spending commitments based on money generated by an inflated banking sector that could not be relied upon. However, it is worth noting that just days before Northern Rock collapsed, and City euphoria dissipated, George Osborne as shadow chancellor was pledging to match the Labour government's promises to continue increasing public expenditure. In other words, Osborne was effectively part of Sir Nick Macpherson's blinkered economic establishment. Even so, it does not lessen the culpability of Brown, Miliband, and Balls that Osborne also failed to recognise that the government was living beyond its means. They were in power, he was not. This is why many voters seem to be saying that if Miliband and Balls wish to argue that Cameron and Osborne have failed to restore living standards for millions, they need to better accept responsibility for the initial blow to those living standards.

text: Pressure is increasing on world powers and Iran to sew up a deal on Iran's nuclear programme after many months of negotiations. If an agreement is reached, crippling sanctions impacting daily life in Iran will be lifted. BBC Persian spoke to ordinary Iranians about their expectations for the talks. The nuclear negotiations influence every Iranian's life due to inflation caused by sanctions. Many families can no longer maintain their previous standard of living. If an agreement is not reached while President Rouhani is in office, both sides will encounter significant difficulties in the future. Iran's economy has been severely affected since the last round of sanctions on the oil and banking sectors. I own three factories. Eight years ago, they operated at full capacity; now all three are closed. Approximately 400 workers, technicians, and engineers have lost their jobs. There are many like me who once owned small manufacturing companies in industrial cities. Nowadays, our cemeteries are expanding faster and performing better than our industrial cities. I followed every moment of the last round of negotiations. If you recall, the stress was evident on John Kerry's face. It indicates Mr Obama needs to find a resolution to this issue. Regardless of the strength of lobbies on the other side, I believe the US president is determined to secure a deal and can accomplish that. I am not optimistic. As our leader states, we do not trust the US, the UK, or the West in general. Now we observe that some in Iran have placed their trust in them and believe they can advance matters through negotiation, and the [Supreme] leader has consented to that. It is occurring, but personally, I believe the process will fail. It is merely a question of when. I do not think a deal is feasible. There are numerous entrenched groups in Iran, such as the Basij [volunteer paramilitary force], and most importantly, those connected to the office of the Supreme Leader. These groups will not permit it, and people will continue to feel the pressure. I am a farmer but cannot sell the rice I produce. It is unfair to our people. I am a teacher. I am following negotiations with excitement. However, sometimes it seems to drag on indefinitely. Regardless, I do not believe we will witness any significant changes immediately. Change will require time to achieve. It will not occur the day after an agreement.

text: Almost half (45%) of young people are checking their mobile phones after they have gone to bed, a poll suggests. These are external links and will open in a new window. A survey of 2,750 individuals aged 11 to 18 found that one in 10 admitted to checking their mobile phones for notifications at least 10 times a night. The poll was conducted by Digital Awareness UK and the Headmasters' and Headmistresses' Conference. The organisations warn that night-time mobile usage results in pupils arriving at school tired and unable to concentrate. They recommend a digital detox by putting mobile devices away for 90 minutes before lights-out or keeping them out of the bedroom. text: So Eddie Jones has gone from South Africa's Stormers to England's strugglers, from Cape of Good Hope to capable of good, it is to be hoped. The agreement has been swiftly finalised, yet it remains significant. The England rugby union team has never before been managed by a foreign coach. This change is largely due to Jones' extensive coaching expertise and his availability compared to other ideal candidates. It is also attributed to the tendency of English sports authorities to appoint the polar opposite of the previous unsuccessful candidate, rather than the rubber-soled footwear popular on Australian beaches. This strategy, perfected by the Football Association, has been adopted by others since. The pattern can be traced back through the years: the low-cost and low-profile Roy Hodgson replaced the expensive and autocratic Fabio Capello, an experienced foreign coach succeeding the inexperienced and outmatched Englishman Steve McClaren, who was the loud antithesis of the detached Sven Goran Eriksson, initially hired for his calm tactical genius compared to the passionate yet naïve Kevin Keegan. Keegan, a populist figure, succeeded the eccentric and isolated Glenn Hoddle. The born-again Christian Hoddle followed Terry Venables, who resigned to clear his name regarding off-field business dealings. Venables' international experience and attractive style contrasted with Graham Taylor's long-ball British basics. This pattern extends to other sports. England cricket replaced the taciturn foreigner Duncan Fletcher with the lively homegrown Peter Moores. When Moores lacked international expertise and influence, he was succeeded by the stern Zimbabwean Andy Flower, a former world number one-ranked batsman. When Flower was considered too dour, the cheerful Moores returned, only to be replaced again when the same shortcomings emerged, this time by the experienced Australian Trevor Bayliss. Media playback is not supported on this device. The RFU has followed a similar approach since Sir Clive Woodward's departure from the Twickenham position. Was Andy Robinson too dour? Introduce Brian Ashton's attacking ethos. Ashton lacked authority? Call for Martin Johnson's dark charisma. Johnson was exposed in his first coaching role? Enter Stuart Lancaster, a grassroots coach with minimal public profile. This brings us to Jones. Lancaster had one season of Premiership experience before taking the England job, a season ending with a financially struggling Leeds team being relegated to the Championship. He had never attended a rugby match at the Millennium Stadium or the Stade de France. Jones, however, has coached extensively—at two Super Rugby teams in Australia, as an assistant to Jake White for South Africa, in England with Saracens, and with Japan leading up to the last World Cup. He led the Wallabies to a World Cup final and helped the Springboks win the next in 2007. Whether he is the right choice for England is uncertain. No other union has the financial or playing resources of the RFU. This is one reason why, unlike Wales, Scotland, and Ireland, it has traditionally chosen a leader from within its vast pool. Even now, the rationale is debatable. RFU chief executive Ian Ritchie insisted Lancaster's successor must have international experience. This makes sense if Lancaster's shortcomings were the sole benchmark, but not on other criteria. Lancaster failed for various reasons. Not all these issues are present in every English coach, merely due to shared nationality. Had Wales followed Ritchie's approach, they would not have appointed Warren Gatland, who led them to two Grand Slams during England's barren years and a World Cup semi-final despite limited resources. It would have meant Ireland passing on Joe Schmidt, who secured the Six Nations title last spring, and would have denied Scotland the wisdom of Vern Cotter, who was one controversial refereeing decision away from leading his adopted nation to their own World Cup semi-final. Michael Cheika, praised for revitalising the Wallabies over the past year, had never coached at the international level before. Woodward, who elevated the team to its peak, was an international novice when he took charge. Jones has achieved significant success, most recently inspiring Japan to the greatest World Cup upset, their 34-32 victory over South Africa two months ago. He deserves credit for both their unprecedented success and the manner in which it was achieved. Will the same approach work in England's vastly different environment, where he will have neither the same control over his players nor the same eager players to shape in his image? His Brumbies team of the late 1990s was among the best in Super Rugby history. That alone will not provide him with a breakdown specialist like the great George Smith if, as it seems, he considers current captain Chris Robshaw lacking the necessary specialist skills. Jones has also faced failures. Japan may have won more matches at the World Cup than England, but Jones was dismissed by Australia in 2005 after eight defeats in nine matches and resigned from the Queensland Reds in 2007 after finishing last in the Super 14 table. Selecting the coach is the easy part. Transforming the system to produce more world-class players capable of playing with the same skill set as world champions New Zealand is arguably more important but also much more challenging. Like those players, a coach requires the right environment to thrive—a fortunate combination of human and financial resources, the right specialists below him, and the right leader above. Otherwise, we risk another reversal, and one pair of those is sufficient for anyone.

text: Mexico's Congress has approved sweeping changes to the country's energy industry which will see private oil contracts awarded in the country for the first time since 1938. New legislation passed on Wednesday will open the market to foreign oil companies. Consequently, the state-owned energy group Pemex will lose the monopoly it has held since nationalisation. President Enrique Pena Nieto has made energy reform the cornerstone of his administration. He anticipates the changes will boost production back to 2004 levels by 2025. Deteriorating infrastructure, bureaucracy, and corruption have reduced Mexican production from 3.6 million barrels a day in 2004 to just 2.5 million. The end of Pemex's monopoly required constitutional changes, signed into law last year. The reforms are expected to attract billions of dollars of investment into the country, the world's ninth-largest oil producer. They also permit private electricity production. President Pena Nieto tweeted: A more competitive and prosperous Mexico. They have laid the foundation for a new era of development and prosperity for Mexican families. Pemex, officially known as Petroleos Mexicanos, will have to compete with international giants such as Chevron, Exxon Mobil, and BP. Bidders are expected to begin signing new contracts with the Mexican state from 2015 to explore, produce, and refine oil. Until now, they were only permitted to hold service contracts with Pemex. The break-up of the oil industry is the culmination of years of attempts to liberalise the Mexican economy that began in the early 1980s. In July, new legislation forced the break-up of billionaire Carlos Slim's America Movil empire, Latin America's largest telecoms company. The most controversial aspect of the energy reforms is a provision to transfer about one-third of the state oil company's pension debts to the federal government's balance sheet. Opponents of the bill argued taxpayers would have to bear the cost of years of mismanagement of the pension fund. To emphasise their point, they carried a life-size picture of the late President Lazaro Cardenas, who nationalised the industry in 1938, onto the floor of the Senate.

text: The fastest animal on land rarely uses its top speed to capture prey, according to a new analysis. A study on cheetahs has revealed that the animal utilises remarkable acceleration and rapid speed changes when hunting. The animals achieve this acceleration by exerting nearly five times more power than famed sprinter Usain Bolt during his record-breaking 100m run. The results have been published in the journal Nature. The findings astonished the lead researcher, Prof Alan Wilson of the Royal Veterinary College in Hatfield, UK. They are remarkable athletes—not just in terms of their speed, but also with their ability to accelerate and manoeuvre in capturing the prey, he informed BBC News. The top speed often quoted for a cheetah is 65mph (105km/h)—a result measured in 1965 and published in the Journal of Zoology three decades later by a scientist in Kenya. He timed the run of a semi-domesticated cheetah running in a straight line on a firm dirt track. However, a well-fed zoo cheetah is not accustomed to running very fast—it does not need to. Consequently, few measurements of zoo cheetahs have found speeds greater than that of a greyhound, about 40mph (64km/h). Thus, for years, researchers speculated whether cheetahs might run much faster than 65mph in the wild to capture prey. Prof Wilson and his team at the college's Structure and Motion Laboratory sought to find out by tracking five animals in the wild for a year using collars equipped with movement detectors and GPS systems. They discovered that the cheetahs did indeed run very fast at times—close to 60mph—but only occasionally. In most hunts, they reached about 30 to 35 mph, but they were accelerating and changing direction much more rapidly than any other land animal. They found that cheetahs could increase their speed by nearly 7mph (10km/h) in a single stride. They've arranged to have a low gear so they can accelerate very rapidly up to their top speed, stated Prof Wilson. Short bursts of speed can be quantified in power per kilogramme of the animal's weight. Jamaican sprinter Usain Bolt exerted 25 W/kg during his record-breaking run in 2009. A horse used in a polo match exerts slightly more power per kg, around 30 W/kg, and a greyhound's is double that at 60 W/kg. However, a cheetah can reach 120 W/kg. The researchers also found that cheetahs have a very strong grip, so much so that they rip up the ground as they run. They discovered it was the use of the animals' claws that enabled them to turn very sharply and to accelerate and decelerate very quickly. The measurements have only been made possible due to the collars developed by Prof Wilson specifically for the experiment. It is very hard for GPS to work on an animal that is ducking and diving, so the collar is an innovation in its own right, he remarked. We've been working on GPS for 12 years, and the collars are the result of those labours. They are not your typical GPS tracking system that you get in the car or phone. The GPS is far more accurate; we are getting positions and speeds five times a second. We combine those with readings from other instruments, and we finish up with something that is very much more accurate both in terms of speed and position and very much more robust, Prof Wilson explained. The team are currently using the collars to track lions and African wild dogs to obtain comparative measurements. Follow Pallab on Twitter.
