text: There may be one positive that comes out of the negative number issued on Wednesday morning by the Scottish government. These are external links and will open in a new window. With a decline of 0.2%, the October-to-December output from the Scottish economy certainly attracts attention, as another quarter of contraction would be termed a recession. Recessions are not the end of the world as we know it. Indeed, an absence of recessions would break with the world as we know it. The economic cycle is precisely that—a cycle that tends to deliver slowdowns. Australia is the only major country in modern times to have avoided recession for decades. However, they are more difficult to explain when neighbouring regions are not experiencing the same downturn. Thus, the disparity with the UK figures is challenging to dismiss or overlook. Nothing can be done to prevent a recession for Scotland now, as the relevant quarter—January to March—has just concluded. We can only confirm a recession long after it has begun, and usually after it has ended. Confirmation of recession, or not, is scheduled for 3 July. The figures provide a bit more insight into the economic situation, but often raise more questions than they answer clearly. They show services were flat in the final quarter of the year, which constitutes three-quarters of the economy. Over the year, these figures indicate stagnant public sector services. It is difficult to measure the output of health and education, but by this measure, they hardly changed. The strongest performers were financial services and, even more so, firms classified as technical, scientific, and administrative support services. Construction has declined from a high level in its measure of output over the past three years—a factor that has kept Scotland out of recession in previous quarters. Within the production sector, there are some particularly steep declines. Manufacturing is down 8% in two years, textiles by more. Metals and machinery have decreased by 24% in two years. It plays a significant role in the supply chain for the oil and gas sector. The category including computer equipment has fallen 6% since 2013, and 44% since the start of the century. That was roughly when we stopped discussing Silicon Glen. Even food and drink—touted as the big hope for production and exports—saw output fall slightly from 2015 to 2016. Overall, if you compare the end of 2016 with the final three months of 2015, the economy is producing the same amount. It has stalled, while the UK economy is estimated to have grown by 1.9%. If you add up the four quarters of 2015 and compare them with the four quarters of 2016, you reach the anaemic growth rate of 0.4%, while the UK economy is up 1.8%. How does that compare with other economies? While Scottish output stalled, the US was up 2% between December 2015 and December 2016, the Eurozone up 1.7%. Developing economies grow faster. India was up 7% and China by nearly as much. Closer comparators to Scotland include Ireland, rebounding from the depths with 7.2%, and Iceland doing likewise, with a substantial 11.3% growth. Norway saw 1.8% growth, not aided by the oil and gas downturn either. Sweden and Denmark saw 2.3% growth. Down in the doldrums with Scotland was Russia on 0.3% growth. Those overly reliant on oil revenues, as well as those afflicted by war, dominate the list of contracting economies: Brazil continued a severe contraction with 2.5% less output last year, and Venezuela has deteriorated significantly, down 18%. The numbers for the final quarter of 2016 make it difficult to argue that the downturn is solely about the oil and gas slump, as the stalled, stagnant, and contracting parts of the economy are much more widespread. A boost from the weakening of the pound following the June referendum is not evident. Export sectors have not performed as might have been expected. And the service sector—representing three-quarters of the economy—has been flat. So what has changed that might explain this? The Scottish government attributes it to Brexit uncertainty. Its newly-commissioned measure of consumer sentiment declined after the referendum—less for individual household expectations than for expectations for the economy as a whole. I asked finance secretary Derek Mackay—he was on a life science business visit just after the results were released—why Scotland is feeling the Brexit effect any differently from the rest of the UK. Perhaps Scots are better informed about what Brexit entails, he suggested. Perhaps it is because they are more pro-Europe, and therefore feel the loss of that trading relationship more acutely. Perhaps so, but something more than that must be occurring. What else could that be? The distinctive parts of the story in Scotland include the low business start-up and growth rates, the lack of corporate headquarters in the country, and relatively poor research and development spending by businesses. Some blame over-reliance on the public sector. With a squeeze on spending, there could be a proportionately larger effect for a country with a bigger public spend. There are issues of being at the periphery of Europe, though that does not seem to be holding back Ireland or Iceland. A more subdued (and sensible?) property market releases less equity to homeowners on which they can borrow to spend and invest more. Plus, yes, there is politics. If Brexit is identified as the key source of uncertainty which has affected consumer confidence and thus economic growth, I asked the finance secretary if the prospect of another independence referendum is a help or a hindrance to the economy. The answer: independence can be beneficial for the economy. Even the debate about independence can, he says, be a positive. Meanwhile, the release of the latest Gross Domestic Product figures brings to mind the debate about how much statistics can be trusted, when they are based on survey evidence, on what economists can infer and impute, on educated guesses, and seasonal adjustment to smooth out volatility. There is a lively debate (some well-informed, some not) on whether the Government Expenditure and Revenue Scotland (GERS) figures can be trusted. In 2013 and 2014, they were trusted as the basis for the economic case made in the Scottish government's independence white paper. With less oil and gas revenue changing fiscal circumstances, they are much less helpful to the cause now. So what does the finance minister think, given that it is his part of the Scottish government that compiles them? GERS is a range of estimates, he tells me. A number of the statistics are based on estimates. I do not believe GERS is the starting position of an independent Scotland. It's a reflection of where we are now. So I'll take those statistics at face value. But that's separate to the argument we can have about what you could do with the economic levers of an independent nation, where we could make different choices. I accept the estimates as they are, but I think we could do so much better. So if they are a reflection of where we are, are they an accurate reflection? In terms of the statistics available between the UK government statistics, the ONS (Office for National Statistics) and what the Scottish government produces, yes, they are accurate, says Mr Mackay. But they are an accurate assessment of estimates of where we are right now—not the starting position of an independent Scotland. The next set of GERS figures, covering the financial year which ends within a few hours of me writing this, is due for publication around August.

text: First-time buyers are being warned they could pay tens of thousands of pounds more interest if they sign up for 40-year mortgages. Sales of longer-term mortgages have reached unprecedented levels, with the majority of young buyers opting to borrow for more than the traditional 25 years. The monthly repayments are reduced, enabling them to afford larger loans to purchase their dream homes. However, one of the UK's largest mortgage brokers warns that the interest bill can soar, as buyers must continue making payments for an extended period. Fifteen years ago, nearly every first-time buyer had a 25-year mortgage, but high prices have compelled people to seek new strategies to navigate the market. Currently, 60% borrow for longer. The typical term is 30 years, but many are selecting terms of 35 or 40 years to make larger strides onto the housing ladder. The short-term gain was more beneficial than the long-term pain, says Chris Pearson, who has recently purchased a house with his partner Katie Baynes in Cheadle, Manchester. We had spent a long time saving for a deposit and needed a house that was sufficiently large. They have secured a 40-year mortgage from Nationwide and managed to borrow £300,000. I think I'll be 72 when we've just paid it off, Chris admits. The appeal is evident. You pay £948 a month for a typical 25-year mortgage, but only £716 if you extend the term to 40 years. You save well over £200 a month. What occurs is that the interest paid each month remains constant, but the repayments of capital, which are part of the monthly bill, are distributed over a longer period. That is the positive aspect. The issue is that you must pay interest for an additional 15 years. In this scenario, you would pay an extra £60,000. Interest over 25 years amounts to around £84,000, but the total over 40 years is £144,000, a substantial bill for borrowers. It's a real danger, warns David Hollingworth from London & Country Mortgages, who calculated the figures. They need to understand that they are going to pay thousands more in interest over the life of the mortgage. Katie and Chris say they are depending on house prices continuing to rise to support their finances. We're stuck in a rut really, Katie says. We're taking a massive risk. Mortgage regulation has been tightened, with stricter controls on what people can afford with their regular incomes. However, there are no rules limiting the length of mortgage terms or preventing families who are already struggling from committing themselves for four decades. Essentially, these borrowers are postponing the day of reckoning and depleting their future wealth. David Hollingworth suggests they keep their mortgages under review and shorten the repayment period as soon as they can afford to make higher payments. Such a strategy, he says, will save them a fortune. But what if interest rates rise, making mortgages more expensive, or if the family income remains unchanged? Homeowners like Katie and Chris in Cheadle could find that the 40-year deal is all they can ever afford, and their mortgage becomes a burden in later life.

text: Technology developed by a professor at Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh could help millions of people exposed to high levels of arsenic in their water supplies. If the same water is used for irrigation, arsenic can accumulate in their crops as well. We owe the golden age of British crime fiction for arsenic's reputation as a deadly poison. It is not typically immediately fatal in drinking water. Instead, it is associated with various debilitating diseases: cancers, disfiguring skin conditions, and even type 2 diabetes. Professor Sen Gupta is a water technologist whose current focus is on Bangladesh. There, the arsenic in the water supply occurs naturally. It is carried as silt in the rivers flowing down from the Himalayas, as it has for millions of years. Until just a few decades ago, it remained harmless and inert in the banks of rivers and streams. However, it is now dissolving, colourless and tasteless, into the shallow aquifers from which people draw their water. It may originate from a natural source, but human activity has caused the problem. In a classic example of the law of unintended consequences, the introduction of new, improved types of rice has disrupted nature's balance. The new, high-yielding varieties of rice require much more water and fertiliser, Professor Sen Gupta states. Fertiliser-rich water from the rice fields reaches the sub-surface, but due to lack of oxygen, the arsenic-bearing minerals become by default a kind of participant in the reaction and break up, producing a very toxic type of arsenic. Professor Sen Gupta's solution involves, in effect, deceiving nature. Water is pumped out of a well, gradually oxygenated in the air, and then sent back down the well again. The oxygenated water encounters bacteria that usually live in an oxygen-free environment. That is why the rise in oxygen level must be gradual. Doing it suddenly would cause the bacteria to die. The oxygen encourages them to transform the arsenic from a liquid to an inert solid, which is absorbed onto the surface of grains of sand in the aquifer. All this occurs out of sight down the well. At no point does the arsenic reach the surface. The technique, known as subterranean arsenic removal or SAR, uses no chemicals and produces no waste. Professor Sen Gupta and his colleagues have been working on SAR for nearly a decade. What is new is that it now operates on solar energy and is an autonomous system. Once the delicately balanced process is established, the equipment can be operated remotely. The first plant is now operational in the Comilla district of Bangladesh. The World Health Organisation's safe guideline for arsenic in water is 10 micrograms per litre. The level in the well was 239 micrograms per litre. And, almost inevitably in this connected world, Professor Sen Gupta says there is an app to manage it all: We can operate the plant from anywhere in the world as long as you have a wifi connection. Professor Sen Gupta aims to transfer his knowledge from Heriot-Watt to the world. He states: We as a global university would like to be responsible for global problems and global issues - and be part of the solution. He is hoping to establish a charity to advance the work further. It will have a simple selling point: with £5,000, you can improve a thousand lives.

text: Bradford City's three-match winning run came to an end as they were held to a draw by Oldham Athletic at Valley Parade despite dominating the game. Oldham took the lead in the fifth minute when Marc Klok delivered a free-kick from the right to the far post, where unmarked defender Peter Clarke scored with a downward header. Bradford dominated the remainder of the opening period as the visitors' defence endured a series of narrow escapes. Goalkeeper Connor Ripley made a brilliant one-handed save to deny winger Mark Marshall, Timothee Dieng and Josh Cullen both had shots deflected for corners, and Billy Clarke missed a good opportunity when he turned James Meredith's cross wide. Oldham somehow maintained their lead until half-time, but Bradford deservedly equalised after 57 minutes when Ousmane Fane dragged Cullen to the ground and Clarke scored from the penalty spot. Bradford continued to dominate, but could not convert possession into goals as Oldham's defence remained resolute. Report supplied by the Press Association. text: The ever-expanding emissions crisis at VW is having a direct effect on sales. The initial evidence indicating that customers are turning away from VW is expected to be disclosed in the new car registration figures to be released by the Society of Motor Manufacturers & Traders (SMMT) on Thursday morning. I understand that VW sales in the UK have decreased by more than 8% compared to the same period last year. Two other VW brands, Seat and Skoda, are also experiencing sales declines. However, I understand that Audi sales are stable. These figures represent only one month's data and follow years of rising and record numbers. Other manufacturers have reportedly also experienced significant declines, even if they are not involved in the emissions scandal. Industry sources indicate that VW is attributing the sales decline to the events of the past six weeks. With its share price now a third lower than at the crisis's onset, it is evident that VW is incurring a substantial commercial cost due to the expanding emissions scandal. The BBC has been informed that Patrick McLoughlin, the transport secretary, has spoken to Herbert Diess, a senior VW official in Germany, today and demanded compensation for any reduced resale value of cars involved in the crisis. Whitehall sources inform me that VW has conceded that payments may need to be made. Louise Ellman, chair of the Transport Select Committee, has also informed the BBC that the committee is likely to broaden its inquiry into VW and the testing of all motor vehicles. She has written to the German carmaker requesting further details on how defeat devices were utilised. The committee will review the responses we receive, but I anticipate the committee will wish to conduct further work on this very important issue, she told the BBC. It's about the scandal of Volkswagen, but it's also about the broader policy of testing, where there are significant questions about the testing of all vehicles. The credit rating agency, Moody's, has also downgraded the German carmaker, which could result in VW having to pay more to borrow funds. Today's downgrade reflects mounting risks to Volkswagen's reputation and future earnings following its announcement on 3 November regarding irregularities in CO2 and fuel consumption levels for certain Volkswagen group vehicles, stated Yasmina Serghini-Douvin, a Moody's senior credit officer and lead analyst on Volkswagen. She mentioned that Moody's was also considering fresh allegations [which VW denies] from the US on 2 November that defeat devices were also installed in certain Audi, Porsche and Volkswagen models in the US. With sales declining and the company's share price reduced by a third, VW's relentless quest for the truth is proving to be a costly and damaging endeavour.

text: Chinese central bank governor Zhou Xiaochuan has accused speculative forces of targeting the country's currency, the yuan. He stated there was no justification for the yuan to continue depreciating in value and that China would not allow international speculators to dominate market sentiment. Mr Zhou's remarks come as Chinese markets prepare to reopen on Monday after a week-long New Year holiday. Efforts to defend the yuan have eroded China's foreign currency reserves. At $3.23 trillion (2.84 trillion euros; £2.2 trillion), China still possesses the world's largest reserve of foreign currency holdings. However, this has declined by $420 billion over six months and stands at the lowest level since May 2012. In January alone, the reserves plunged by $99.5 billion as the People's Bank of China sold dollars in an effort to support the value of the yuan. Mr Zhou's comments were made in an interview published in the Caixin financial magazine. International speculative forces have recently focused on shorting China, the People's Bank of China governor told the magazine, without providing further details. He dismissed concerns that China's currency reserves were declining too rapidly, stating: It is normal for foreign reserves to rise and fall as long as the fundamentals face no problems. The Chinese economy posted growth of 6.9% in 2015, its slowest rate since 1990. Fears of an economic slowdown have prompted some investors to move their money out of China in search of better returns elsewhere. However, Mr Zhou stated China would not tighten its capital controls as a result. Capital outflow and capital flight are two different concepts, he added. The Chinese authorities fear a rapid devaluation of their currency, as it could destabilise the economy. Many Chinese businesses hold debt in dollars, and managing those debts with a severely weakened yuan could cause problems and lead some companies to fail. Thus, China has been attempting to engineer an ordered devaluation of the yuan, but that is proving difficult to achieve. Investors have been trying to withdraw funds from investments priced in yuan, and speculators have been betting on further declines in the currency. To stabilise the situation, China has been selling dollars and purchasing yuan. Additionally, it has been employing other tactics, including curbing currency speculation and instructing offshore banks to retain their reserves of yuan.

text: Championship side Oldham Roughyeds stunned last season's Challenge Cup finalists Hull KR to reach the last 16. The Roughyeds, positioned fourth from the bottom of the second tier, led 24-6 at half-time with tries from Will Hope, Richard Lepori, Steve Roper, and Adam Clay. Shaun Lunt, Dane Tilse, Maurice Blair, and Joe Wardill scored after the break to give the Super League side hope. However, missed conversions proved costly as Gary Middlehurst and Lepori's second try secured victory for Oldham. Hull KR coach James Webster described his team's performance as an utter embarrassment. Media playback is not supported on this device. Rovers, who lost 50-0 to Leeds in last year's final at Wembley, have only won twice in Super League this season and lost 40-0 to Catalans Dragons in their last match. They were still expected to defeat part-timers Oldham, who are in their first season in the Championship after winning promotion from League 1. Yet Oldham outscored them six tries to five, while Lewis Palfrey's six goals to Ben Cockayne's one gave the second-tier side an ultimately comfortable margin of victory against the hosts, who finished with 12 men after Cockayne was sent to the sin-bin moments before Lepori's try with the game's last move. Meanwhile, last season's Championship winners and Challenge Cup giant killers Leigh, who knocked out Super League sides Wakefield and Salford, are out after losing 10-8 at League 1 side Toulouse. Batley Bulldogs are also through to the sixth round after a 28-10 victory over fellow Championship side Featherstone Rovers. Oldham Roughyeds coach Scott Naylor: This is probably the biggest win since the club reformed [in 1997]. We spoke about getting to 20 minutes, then 30 minutes and see what happens. We didn't expect the half-time score to be 24-6 and we knew they would come out in the second half and have a go after getting a bit of a roasting. For the club, this is something we'll cherish. It's a massive day for Oldham and it could be a massive night for the players. I'll go home and have a few beers with my family. Hull KR coach James Webster: It was the biggest embarrassment of my career since before I left school. What we dished up was utter embarrassment. I've protected these boys since I've been here, but I have to apologise to everyone associated with this club. That is not of a level that's needed to pick up the wage they pick up. Supporters give up cars, holidays to follow this club because I deal with these people every day. I understand what people think and it's all true. Well done to Oldham because I thought they played very well. Hull KR: Cockayne, Wardill, Sio, Thornley, Dixon, Blair, Marsh, Tilse, Lunt, Green, Greenwood, Clarkson, Walker. Replacements: Mulhern, Donaldson, Boudebza, Lawler. Oldham: Lepori, Clay, Gee, Grimshaw, Chisholm, Palfrey, Roper, Joy, Owen, Spencer, Middlehurst, Langtree, Hope. text: Japanese carmaker Toyota has regained its slot as the world's biggest vehicle maker, capping a year of a dramatic turnaround in its fortunes. Toyota reported it sold 9.75 million vehicles in 2012, marking an increase of over 22% from the previous year. General Motors, which was the largest vehicle manufacturer in 2011, sold 9.29 million vehicles in 2012. Toyota's 2011 sales were impacted by natural disasters in Japan and Thailand, which disrupted production at its factories. However, Toyota and other affected Japanese carmakers have experienced a steady recovery since then and have been regaining market share in key regions such as the US. The last two years have been very difficult for Toyota, Vivek Vaidya, an automotive analyst with Frost & Sullivan, told the BBC. Regaining the top position would definitely be encouraging for the company and is good news for its investors and shareholders, he added. Toyota's competitors also reported record vehicle sales numbers for 2012. Nissan Motor announced it sold 4.94 million vehicles globally, an increase of nearly 6% from the previous year, while Honda Motor reported a 19% rise from a year earlier, selling 3.82 million vehicles. In addition to natural disasters, Japanese carmakers have also been affected by a strong yen. A strong currency not only makes Japanese goods more expensive for foreign buyers but also impacts firms' profits when they repatriate their foreign earnings. This particularly affects companies like Toyota, which depend heavily on overseas sales. However, Japanese carmakers have benefited in recent weeks as the yen has depreciated against the US dollar. The Japanese currency has fallen nearly 15% against the US dollar since last November. It was trading close to 90.8 yen against the US dollar in Asian trade on Monday. Analysts indicated the decline is likely to positively impact Toyota's growth. The drop in the yen is a welcome relief for Toyota, said Frost & Sullivan's Mr Vaidya. We are likely to see profit margins increase, providing more cash in hand and the ability to invest in developing new technologies, which should support its growth momentum moving forward. The Japanese carmaker raised its annual profit forecast in November. It projected a net profit of 780bn yen ($8.6bn; £5.4bn) for the financial year ending 31 March 2013, up from its earlier forecast of 760bn yen. However, the carmaker does face some potential challenges, particularly from the ongoing territorial dispute between Japan and China. China is the world's largest car market and is considered crucial for the future growth of firms like Toyota. However, the dispute over a group of islands in the East China Sea, which escalated late last year, has strained relations between the two countries and led to a decline in Japan's exports to China. The dispute remains unresolved, and there are concerns it may escalate again in the coming months, further damaging trade relations between the two nations. The concern is that any such development may increase anti-Japan sentiment and negatively impact sales of Japanese brands in China. Analysts suggested that any such decline is likely to adversely affect Toyota's growth.

text: History, they say, is written by the victors. Standing beneath the shade of a towering windmill at what was once among the most productive sugar plantations in the West Indies, it is easy to envision the legion of imperious Englishmen at its helm. However, while extensive documentation meticulously records the details of the industry that helped build the British Empire, very little is known about the lives of the African slaves upon whom it depended. Researchers investigating an 18th-century slave village amid a major excavation project at Betty's Hope plantation in Antigua aim to change that. One of just a few ever unearthed in the Caribbean, the discovery of the site and recent artefacts is set to illuminate a grim past. Dr Georgia Fox, leading the project, describes the initial discovery of the village in 2013, which had eluded archaeologists for decades, as a eureka moment. Aligning high-tech electronic surveying equipment with maps dating back to 1710 enabled one of her team of students from California State University, Chico, to pinpoint its location. It felt like a miracle, she told the BBC. We'd seen all these dots on the maps and we now realised they signified the slave village. It was an amazing discovery. Subsequent excavation works have uncovered a wealth of fascinating relics which, for the first time, offer a glimpse into the daily lives and culture of the plantation's 400 slaves. First we found what appeared to be a very specific type of rough pottery, called Afro-Antiguan ware, made by slaves. Pots were created by coiling pieces of local clay and would have been used for cooking stews, Dr Fox explains. Recently we were able to delve deeply into the heart of the village and we found some remarkable items like cowrie shells from East Africa which were used as currency, for games or good luck charms. This in itself raises interesting questions as slaves in Antigua tended to be from West rather than East Africa. Then we found Dutch delftware which was probably bartered for, traded or given to the slaves as hand-offs, followed by two corners of a beautifully made limestone wall which was tantalising as most slave homes were standard wattle and daub, Dr Fox continues. Excavation by Dr Fox's team began in 2007 at the plantation's Great House, followed by the Still House where rum, then sugar's most important by-product, was made. The once 700-acre site dates back to around 1650 and comprised a largely self-sustainable living complex accommodating everyone from field workers, servants and overseers to tradesmen, a blacksmith and a doctor. At its peak, each of the plantation's twin windmills could have produced 12 tonnes of sugar crystals a day. Less than 5% of the sprawling site has been investigated so far. Items uncovered at the Great House include children's toys, musket balls, buttons, cutlery, a door knocker, clay tobacco pipes and a cod liver oil bottle. The organic materials used to build slave houses, such as palm fronds, sticks and mud, made the adjacent village's identification difficult. Local historian and Unesco representative Reg Murphy, who oversees all of Antigua's archaeology projects, said the work was vital to piece together a complete history of the island where most of the population are slave descendants. Everything we learn is about the glory of sugar and the industrial colonial legacy, he says. You never hear about the day-to-day lives of the workers, the other side of the coin. This is a way of learning about their daily routine, what they ate, how they lived, seeing it from their perspective. There were over 400 slaves at Betty's Hope at one time - their stories have never been told. For Dr Fox, the significance goes further still. There were sugar plantations throughout the world but the Caribbean was the gateway to the New World and had a tremendous impact on the development of America. This was the beginning of capitalism and it all started in the Caribbean. It's important to remember how the New World was created - this is everybody's history. Although slavery was abolished in 1834, Antigua's sugar production remained an economic mainstay until the 1960s when it was replaced by tourism. Dr Fox adds: Sugar changed the world. Every time you bite into a chocolate bar or add sugar to your tea or coffee, you are taking part in a long history and reaching into the past.

text: Ulster secured a home quarter-final and condemned Leicester to an away tie as they ended the Tigers' unbeaten home run of 25 matches in the Heineken Cup. It was 9-9 at the interval, courtesy of a hat-trick of penalties from fly-half Toby Flood for Leicester and scrum-half Ruan Pienaar for the visitors. A Flood penalty and Niall Morris's converted try put the Tigers 19-9 ahead. However, a Pienaar penalty and his converted try levelled the score before his fifth penalty secured a dramatic win for Ulster. When Leicester led by 10 points with half an hour remaining, it appeared they would not only end the only unbeaten record in this season's tournament but also secure a home quarter-final. Yet, the Ulster players tackled fiercely and contested every breakdown, pushing the hosts back and allowing South African scrum-half Pienaar to guide the Irish province to a victory at Welford Road, ensuring they qualify as top seeds. The 1999 champions and 2012 beaten finalists are currently redeveloping their Ravenhill ground to accommodate 18,000 supporters. They promise it will be ready for the quarter-finals on the weekend of 4-6 April, and given their fans' enthusiasm, it is unlikely to be anything other than a sell-out when they host Saracens, who will be the eighth and final qualifiers after Leicester's losing bonus point meant the Tigers finished as the best runners-up in the group stages. Leicester initially dominated in a brutal encounter with their scrum performing well and full-back Mathew Tait, who later limped off injured, appearing lively. Second row Graham Kitchener nearly added a try to his fine line-out work as he was brought down just short after a 40m burst, but despite not crossing the line, Flood's boot guided the Tigers into a 9-3 lead. However, Ulster combine Irish defiance with a blend of strength and rugby intellect from South Africa, and with Pienaar, the mastermind of their operation, orchestrating play and landing his penalties, they drew level at the break. Again, it was the hosts who started better after the restart, and when Ulster open-side flanker Chris Henry broke early from a scrum, Flood restored the Tigers' lead, which they soon extended to 10 points. Tom Youngs surged forward from a high Flood kick, and when the Tigers recycled, the fly-half threaded through a precise grubber kick, and winger Morris won the race to touch down. Flood converted to make it 19-9, and surely Leicester were on their way, but Ulster were in no mood to accept defeat and responded five minutes later when hooker Youngs went off his feet at a ruck, and Pienaar found the target with the penalty. Then came the decisive moment of the game as Pienaar charged down Flood's kick and won the race to touch down, before converting his own score from wide out to make it 19-19. Media playback is not supported on this device. The game was open, and Leicester went close after Flood's superb penalty to the corner earned them an attacking line-out, only for the fly-half to drop a pass five metres from the line as the Tigers pressed forward. Ulster once again fought their way back into Leicester territory, and Pienaar confirmed his class with a long-range penalty to put the visitors in front. Leicester had a late scrum in the Ulster half, but the visitors won the ball against the head, and with it went the Tigers' hopes as the Irish province made it six wins out of six and set up what promises to be a lively housewarming party at Ravenhill. Ulster captain Johann Muller: It seems like it's happening every week, when Ruan scores all the points - he was outstanding. We came here to get a home quarter-final. Sarries totally outplayed us last season - they are a great side and don't mind going away to get a result. It's two months away, and at this stage, we will just enjoy the moment. We have not achieved anything yet, and there's a huge amount of work left if we are to achieve something. Leicester boss Richard Cockerill: We're disappointed with the result, but it was a good game. Ten points up, we needed to control the game better, but we did not manage the backfield as well as we would have liked, and they exposed us. At the moment, it's probably Toulon [away in the last eight], tomorrow it may be Clermont, who have an average home record - what is it, 73 games unbeaten? We are in the quarter-finals, and we have suffered a lot of adversity [through injuries], so that's not a bad effort from us. text: Auditors have warned MSPs about severe problems faced by three health boards. An Audit Scotland report has revealed that a new IT system at NHS24 has incurred 50% more costs and taken two years longer to install than initially planned. The watchdog also cautioned that NHS Tayside failed to break even for the third consecutive year, relying on a £14 million loan from the Scottish Government. Concerns were also highlighted regarding finances at NHS Highland, which auditors stated needs to reduce reliance on one-off savings. In a report to MSPs, Audit Scotland indicated that delays in implementing the new computer systems at NHS24 resulted in substantial additional costs and risks, with the completion timetable shifting from June 2013 to October 2015. The estimated cost of the system is now £117.4 million, 55% higher than the original estimate of £75.8 million. Auditors discovered overspending on staffing, holiday pay, and primary care prescribing left NHS Tayside dependent on loans for the third consecutive year. The health board required £14.2 million from the Scottish government merely to break even in 2014/15. In addition to repaying the loan, auditors warned the board would need to achieve savings of £27 million in 2015/16. NHS Highland received a critical report on its 2013/14 accounts, and auditors noted improvements had been made. However, they stated more needed to be done to develop longer-term financial planning and decrease reliance on one-off savings. Responding to the report, NHS24 chief executive Ian Crichton said the report outlines a series of weaknesses dating back to 2011. He stated: Delays in this major IT programme have led to a significant increase in costs. During the last 16 months, an expert team has been working hard to bring the project back on track. The new system will be in place by the end of October. NHS Tayside chief executive Lesley McLay said the board was facing challenges due to increasing demands on services. She stated: NHS Tayside's board has been building a programme of improvement and transformation since the beginning of this financial year. This medium-term programme, led by clinical staff who are partnered with managers, prioritises the delivery of service improvement and benefits for patients and also supports the delivery of sustainable financial balance for NHS Tayside. NHS Highland chairman Garry Coutts welcomed the report, saying it reflected the robust measures taken to improve following the 2013/14 audit. He stated: It is heartening to read in this latest report that the auditor has concluded that we have strengthened our financial management arrangements, transparency, and scrutiny of our financial performance. This latest report makes the point that it is important for the board to build on these improvements given the challenges ahead. That is something we are determined to do.

text: The Beast's beastliness falls well short of savage these days, and generates only faux outrage in the stilted setting of green benches. Veteran Labour MP Dennis Skinner, long nicknamed the Beast of Bolsover, has been expelled from the chamber for referring to the prime minister as Dodgy Dave. While Mr Skinner's anger is undoubtedly genuine, he has become the establishment's sanctioned jester, the undignified element of the constitution. His taunts are insignificant compared to the grievances of some right-wing Labour MPs regarding their treatment by activists. They scarcely provoke the same reaction as tweets lauding Hitler. Meanwhile, across the Atlantic, a presidential hopeful is labelling his critics, particularly women, as ugly, dogs, dummies, and clowns, albeit not simultaneously. Far more refined, and likely more distressing to the recipient, are Petronella Wyatt's comments on Chancellor George Osborne, a man she claims to like: His complexion is Eastern, with the fish-belly pallor of Vlad the Impaler. His eyes have a Mongolian slant and his voice the twang of a Gypsy's zither. Despite Jeremy Corbyn's call for a new politics, has it truly become cruder and ruder than ever before? Perhaps not. Churchill referred to Ramsey MacDonald as the boneless wonder and Stanley Baldwin as that great turnip. According to a book I am currently reading, James II was insulted to his face by one disgruntled subject, who called him an ugly lean-jawed, hatchet-faced, Popish dog. His successor William of Orange fared little better—one gentleman of Holborn was fined for remarking the new king was a rogue and a son of a whore. However, politicians and public figures must do better than mere abuse. While I have only the vaguest notion of what the 18th Century Prime Minister Lord North looked like, Horace Walpole's description amuses me. Two large prominent eyes that rolled about to no purpose (for he was utterly short-sighted) a wide mouth, thick lips and inflated visage, gave him the air of a blind trumpeter, Walpole said. A deep untunable voice which, instead of modulating, he enforced with unnecessary pomp, a total neglect of his person, and ignorance of every civil attention, disgusted all who judge by appearance. Of course, the insults that endure are those that blend venom with wit, and, better still, insight. The poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge's observations on Pitt the Younger may lack poetic quality but strike to the heart of that distant, peculiar and brilliant man. Coleridge said: He has patronised no science, he has raised no man of genius from obscurity; he counts no prime work of God among his friends. He has no attachment to female society, no fondness of children, no perception of beauty in natural scenery; but he is fond of convivial indulgences, of that stimulation which, keeping up the glow of self-importance and the sense of internal power, gives feelings without the mediation of ideas. Perhaps, brevity is preferable. Told by Lord Sandwich he would die either on the gallows or of the pox, radical MP John Wilkes replied: That depends, my Lord, whether I embrace your mistress or your principles. Not only clever but concise enough to fit on Twitter. But there lies a clue to what may have changed. I am inherently opposed to lamenting changes brought by technology, or claims the world today is descending into chaos, but social media has influenced the public mood. First, the constraints on Twitter make it ideal for recommending and linking to longer articles and blogs. However, they do not promote reasoned debate, instead summoning the mood of the mob. A fleeting thought is preserved in text, the irritable grumble over a news item transformed into a barrage of arrows aimed at a target. Serious harassment has become so prevalent, it has spawned a new lexicon of offence, from flaming to trolling. Much less seriously, I cannot be the only journalist who feels somewhat disgruntled when tweets criticising my work for bias or stupidity never delve into identifying the specific cause of offence. Abuse has become the focus, rather than merely the dramatic outburst of an argument. If you respond, it worsens. Twitter exchanges, due to their brevity, become more heated. Email correspondence (or the even more traditional kind) tends to cool the atmosphere and even lead to greater understanding. Social media also encourages the gathering of like-minded individuals, who reinforce each other's values, refusing to consider the opposing side. The less they listen, the less they understand, the greater the reason to attribute base motives to their opposition. There is no point wondering if their values might be valid or their views worth considering—they are simply sons of whores or hatchet-faced dogs. The mobs move through the virtual city, and all that can be clearly heard through the chaos are curses and imprecations. Social media can be an ally of the instinctively clenched fist. Reaction is immediate—swifter than thought—with no time to ponder, reflect and debate, and with no need to associate a human face with a despised meme. Such reactions remain largely in the virtual realm—but they are the enemy of the sort of politics that seeks resolutions and solutions to often complex problems.

text: The cost of a basket of shopping at the same shop in Jersey and the UK can cost up to 10% more. BBC Radio Jersey's business reporter, Chris Rayner, has been investigating the cost of a basket of shopping at three supermarkets in Jersey and in Hampshire. He compiled a basic shopping list using items recommended by Jersey's Consumer Council. It included a litre of milk, a kilo of white potatoes, cat litter, soap, toothpaste, and ketchup. The research found items such as coffee at the same shop in the UK cost £1.32 more in Jersey. Mr Rayner stated: While the quality of life here may be better, many feel we pay more for the privilege, whether it's through higher rents, more expensive food and travel costs. The BBC visited three supermarkets in Jersey, the Co-op in Charing Cross, Waitrose at Rue des Pres, and Marks & Spencer in King Street; and three in Petersfield in Hampshire: Tesco, Waitrose, and Marks & Spencer. He discovered that conducting business in Jersey was not inexpensive either. The Channel Islands Co-op is one of the supermarkets that imports tonnes of food and other items from the UK every week, costing the business £60,000 a month. Colin Mcleod, the Co-op's chief executive, stated: We've got high land costs, we've got high build costs, we've got high labour costs. But we're doing the best we can in that environment for our members. A spokesman for Waitrose in Jersey said: We continually monitor our prices to ensure we remain as competitive as possible, and because of this shoppers may find that many of our products now cost less than when we first opened our shops in the island. We need to reflect the additional costs of getting products to the Channel Islands in our prices but we pass on the savings of UK VAT to our shoppers in Jersey and have hundreds of relevant and meaningful promotions across our branches each week. Tony O'Neill, the chief executive of Sandpiper CI, said over half their products in Marks & Spencer are sold on promotion. The Citizens Advice Bureau and the Community Savings Bank informed the BBC they were seeing more clients. Brian Curtis, executive chairman of the Community Savings Bank, said it was not just those who find themselves unemployed. He stated: I know some people on middle incomes who have not had any increase [in wages] for three years. They have still got a job, so that's fine in itself, but adjusting to a different scenario is not easy for some of these people.

text: The world's highest paid YouTube star, PewDiePie, has defended himself over allegations of anti-Semitism in a new YouTube video. The Swede described the allegations, which led Disney to sever ties with him, as insane and unfair. He claimed any offensive remarks he made were taken out of context and that he had been blatantly misrepresented. Some of his recent videos were found to include Nazi references or anti-Semitic imagery. PewDiePie, whose real name is Felix Kjellberg, stated in his YouTube video: I am sorry for the words I used as I know they offended people. He expressed a strong belief that one can joke about anything, but also acknowledged there is a right and wrong way to joke about things. He admitted that as a rookie comedian he might take jokes too far. He asserted that he did not support right-wing groups advocating hatred and claimed recent articles by newspapers, including the Wall Street Journal, highlighting his alleged anti-Semitism were personal attacks and attempts to discredit him. The Swede reportedly earned $15m through YouTube in 2016. He was associated with Disney via Maker Studios, a company with a network of YouTube stars. The YouTuber has garnered several billions of views per month and generated significant income from advertising. Disney stated on Tuesday that while Mr Kjellberg had a reputation for being provocative and irreverent, some of his videos were inappropriate. In one controversial video, Mr Kjellberg paid two Indians through a crowd-sourcing website to hold a sign reading Death to all Jews. In response to criticism, he said he aimed to demonstrate how people would say anything for $5. In other videos, he showed swastikas drawn by a fan, played the Nazi Party anthem, and performed a brief Hitler salute, all of which he claims were jokes taken out of context. Mr Kjellberg argued he had been accused of normalising hatred in the jokes, whereas he believed it was his media critics who were doing so through their unfair attacks. YouTube earlier announced it had cancelled the release of Mr Kjellberg's new series Scare PewDiePie 2 and removed him from its Google Preferred scheme, which highlights advertiser-friendly content creators. In 2016, PewDiePie was temporarily suspended from Twitter after making jokes about so-called Islamic State.

Dr. Jim Swire, whose daughter died in the bombing, claimed that the prosecution must be based on much better evidence than that used against Megrahi, who, he believes, is not the culprit. “It’s too long ago, people have died, stories have been forgotten, I would like to see some small degree of rapprochement, but I’m not expecting the kind of justice we all hope for.” Abdel-Hamid al-Senussi is, unlike his dark companion, no ordinary man. It is known that he is in prison in Tripoli, but there is no certainty about Masud’s whereabouts. He is undergoing a ten-year term of imprisonment, but reports are contradictory as to whether he is in Tripoli or in the prison of Misrata. It is extremely improbable that any Libyan government would consent to an extradition by American or Scottish authorities, to enable them to interrogate the two men. He is Gaddafi's black box on every crime, atrocity, and clandestine affair that he is accused of having committed during his reign. It was always suspected in Libya that the West was after him for that reason and would never let him go. Both of the newly-identified suspects are imprisoned in Libya, which is in the midst of a storm of rival factions. The question of having them interrogated in Libya was complicated by the absence of Western diplomatic offices and the lack of an international government in Tripoli. Senussi, who is waiting to be executed in a Libyan prison, was the brother-in-law and head of intelligence of the former dictator Colonel Gaddafi. The Crown Office said that a request for the interrogation of the suspects was sent through the British embassy in Tripoli. The two suspects are not in the custody of the government-in-exile in Tobruk, but with the Islamist-backed regime in Tripoli. Masud is allegedly serving a sentence for bombmaking. Some relatives of the victims welcomed the name of these two new suspects. These two names had been mentioned as possible suspects in a recent American documentary. The film was made by Ken Dornstein, whose brother, David, died in the Lockerbie disaster. He declared to the BBC: “I started with a list of names drawn up by the first investigation, a list drawn up from tens of thousands of pages of documents. I realized that many were dead or disappeared. In the end I came to the conclusion that there were perhaps three of them.” In the question of the existence of Al-Masud, Dr Dornstein said that even his existence alone would explain many of the open questions about the bombing, because, according to the best available information, he was with Megrahi at the Malta airport on the day when the bomb was allegedly put in the suitcases and from there on to the Pan Am 103. The question of Megrahi's involvement in the bombing has been raised in several books and documentaries.

text: Before February 2015, I'd never heard of the word sepsis. When the doctors informed us my father had the condition, I was unfamiliar with it and had to search online for information. I discovered it is blood poisoning, a response to infection when the body attacks its own organs and tissues. Just a few weeks later, I learned even more—that it would lead to my father's death. Besides my day job forecasting the weather for Wales Today, I have been collaborating with BBC Wales' Week In Week Out programme to examine sepsis more thoroughly—its devastating impact on lives and whether hospitals are equipped to detect and address it promptly. What I have uncovered has been shocking. Sepsis claims 44,000 lives annually in the UK—more than breast, bowel, and prostate cancer combined—enough to fill a large football stadium. Alarmingly, sepsis is a silent killer that can strike with alarming speed. Regardless of age or fitness, anyone could be affected. My father, Cliff, was 82 and had several health issues, including vascular dementia. He required care home assistance towards the end of his life and had been battling various infections in the months preceding his death. It was Christmas 2014 during lunch at my sister Kathryn's house—weeks before he developed sepsis—that I noticed his frailty. I felt immense sadness, thinking it could be my last Christmas with him. My father was a devoted family man. He drove a petrol tanker for Esso, and I recall him stopping at the bottom of our street in Barry, where I would climb into the cab and accompany him on deliveries across south Wales, singing along to his favourite Johnny Cash and Kenny Rogers songs. He loved boxing and football and would take my brother and me to Ninian Park to watch Cardiff City play. As I grew older, he supported my ambition to become a meteorologist—an interest sparked by the 1976 heatwave when my fascination with weather began. My father bought me my first thermometer, took me to visit the Cardiff weather centre, and years later, drove me to my job interview at the Met Office in Bracknell. He was immensely proud of my achievements, and towards the end of his life, when he was in a care home, my mother would show him episodes of my TV show Weatherman Walking, and each time, she said he would tear up at the mention of my name. I miss my father and, of course, wish he were still here, but I find solace in knowing he lived to a good age despite poor health in later years and led a fulfilling life with a loving family. The experiences of individuals I encountered while making the documentary are heart-wrenching. Michelle Christopher's beautiful 17-year-old daughter Chloe passed away just weeks before my father. Just before Christmas, she exhibited cold and flu symptoms, nothing alarming, Michelle told me. On the night Chloe died, 30 December 2014, she was at home with a friend while her mother was caring for her grandmother nearby. When Michelle returned home later that evening, she found Chloe collapsed on the upstairs landing. Mam, I'm frightened, I don't feel well, Chloe told her. Michelle called 999. She was answering the operator's questions when Chloe went into cardiac arrest. Chloe's colour drained… I had to lay her down and attempt CPR on her, and then she just left us, she says. Attempting CPR on your own daughter is surreal. The inquest into her death revealed Chloe had been suffering from an E. coli urine infection, leading to multi-organ failure and cardiac arrest. Sepsis was the cause of her death. Michelle is haunted by what ifs but told me there were no signs of what was to come. One moment her daughter was eagerly planning a New Year's fancy dress party, the next she was lifeless in her arms. Her death was shockingly swift. Michelle is determined to raise awareness of this critical factor—it is vital to catch sepsis very early, within an hour of suspicion. If antibiotics and intravenous fluids are administered swiftly, survival chances are good. There are days when Michelle wants to shut out the world, but she has channelled her grief into campaigning with the UK Sepsis Trust charity to save lives. We need to spread the word to everyone, she says. If only we'd known, maybe Chloe would still be here. For the programme, I returned to the University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff, where my father died. The staff did their utmost for my father, but sadly he was too ill to overcome sepsis. I spoke with medics about sepsis and their efforts to save lives. Research by Cardiff University indicates that sepsis treatment varies between hospitals. I asked Wales' Health Secretary Vaughan Gething if a more coordinated, consistent approach is needed to tackle sepsis more effectively. He assured me he is seeking advice on this matter. Jayne Carpenter, 49, a nurse from Merthyr Tydfil, developed sepsis and received timely treatment that saved her. Nonetheless, her life would never be the same. In May this year, Jayne felt unwell; she thought it was a cough, at worst a chest infection. When her condition worsened, she visited the out-of-hours service at Prince Charles Hospital in Merthyr. I went to GP out-of-hours and then I woke up two-and-a-half months later, having nearly lost my life, she says, but I did lose my legs, my left arm, and the fingers on my right hand. Unbeknownst to Jayne, she had contracted pneumonia and was developing sepsis. Surgeons had no choice but to amputate her limbs to halt the infection's spread. Honestly, I had no clear recollection of a moment when I realised I had no limbs, she says. A nurse said I kept asking 'where's my hand?' When I was informed of how ill I'd been, it seemed less important than the fact I could have died. Jayne's inspiring, positive outlook has facilitated her significant progress. She has undergone intensive physiotherapy at Cardiff's Rookwood Hospital and is determinedly rebuilding her life with the support of her husband Rob and her beloved Weimaraner dog Harriet. Her lifelong passion for shoes continues as she adapts to prosthetics, and she has relearned how to apply her makeup, no longer needing Rob's assistance. She is determined to return to work and resume her previous activities. I see myself in the future back to walking my dog on the beach, she says. I want to return to work because I want my life back. It was nearly taken from me so suddenly. I want myself back. The experiences of Jayne, Chloe, and their families—the destruction and pain it causes to so many—highlight the critical importance of awareness about sepsis and its potential impact. It claimed my father and has taken countless other fathers, mothers, brothers, daughters, and even infants. I loved my father dearly, and nothing will bring him back. It is the same for Chloe Christopher's mother. But if by sharing our experiences, Michelle and I can help prevent even one unnecessary death, it would be a fitting tribute to two people who meant the world to us both; who are missed even more acutely at this time of year, Christmas, around the anniversaries of their deaths. Derek Brockway: Understanding Why My Dad Died is broadcast on BBC One Wales at 20:30 GMT on Monday, 28 November.

text: The Easter Rising was one of the most important, fundamental events in the history of Ireland. The six-day rebellion in Dublin witnessed republican insurrectionists attempting to overthrow British rule. Over 450 individuals were killed, thousands injured, and square miles of Dublin's city centre were reduced to rubble under a barrage of artillery fire. For Ireland's press, it was the story of the century—yet it was a story hardly anyone could publish. The chaos and confusion in the capital, a lack of reliable eyewitness reports, and restrictions imposed by a British government on a war footing meant Ireland's major newspapers were prevented from printing detailed coverage of the fighting. Ultimately, it was a small, weekly newspaper in County Fermanagh that outpaced the larger dailies to the story. The Impartial Reporter, based in Enniskillen, is believed to be the first newspaper in Ireland to publish a first-hand, eyewitness account of the Rising. In 1916, the newspaper was owned by William Copeland Trimble, whose son—William Egbert—happened to be in Dublin when the Rising began on Monday, 24 April. Thanks to William Egbert's presence in the city, the Impartial Reporter was able to provide the first on-the-ground reports of the fighting in Dublin, published on Thursday, 27 April. The outburst of rebellion in Dublin has astounded the country! its report read. Like a flash of lightning the carefully-matured plans of the Sinn Feiners were carried out on a religious festival and holiday. It continues to report armed Sinn Fein volunteers seizing government buildings and points of vantage, and virtually holding control of the chief portions of the city. Dr Éamon Phoenix, head of history at Stranmillis College, Belfast, stated that William Egbert's position on the ground gave the Impartial Reporter an invaluable scoop. He was able to very quickly track down people from Fermanagh who were caught up in the fighting, such as British troops, he said. He was able to get reports of British soldiers who were killed, or about troops being sent out from barracks. He was the only trained reporter on the ground who was able to send out reliable reports, so the Impartial Reporter had a first. Sarah Saunderson, current editor of the Impartial Reporter, said William Egbert—or Bertie—had strong connections with Dublin that helped him get the Rising story. He studied law at Trinity College, Dublin, until his legal career was brought to an end when he was home for holiday in 1901 and found himself fighting a fire on the paper's premises. Bertie Trimble never returned to Trinity as he was needed at home to help with the family business. However, Trinity's loss was the Impartial's gain. With Bertie's Dublin connections, he was in the right place at the right time to deliver an impressive scoop for the Impartial Reporter. While the small County Fermanagh weekly newspaper was able to publish the first verified reports of violence, other newspapers were struggling to print anything. In Dublin, said Dr Phoenix, the Irish Times was unable to distribute and the Irish Independent offices were damaged in the fighting. Meanwhile, newspapers in Belfast knew about a serious state of affairs in Dublin but could not publish details due to a lack of first-hand reports and the Defence of the Realm Act. This wartime law prevented newspapers from spreading reports likely to cause disaffection or alarm among Her Majesty's forces or among the civilian population. Dublin isolated reported the Belfast Telegraph headline for Tuesday, 25 April, the day after the Rising began, but added that we are precluded from publishing details. The News Letter was similarly limited, reporting that the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland had been forced to cancel a planned trip to Belfast to stay in Dublin. Shortly before six o'clock certain very alarming rumours began to be whispered about in the city of serious trouble in Dublin, it reported. It added, Up till the time of going to press no reports of the happenings in Dublin have come to hand. Under these circumstances we refrain from publishing the facts which we have in our possession. The first people in Belfast would have heard about the Rising would have been when the viceroy did not turn up on Easter Monday, said Dr Phoenix. A group waited all afternoon at the train station and, when he didn't come, they rang Dublin. What they heard back was that the viceroy would not be able to come as he was 'attending to an emergency'. On Thursday, it could finally report what it knew—albeit without the benefit of a first-hand account, like the Impartial Reporter, and with the caveat: We hope these reports are correct but it is right to remember the difficulty in maintaining communications. On the same day, the Belfast Telegraph was able to attribute its story, headlined 'Stamping Out Rebellion', to the many Belfast people who had winged their way back to the north after being in Dublin. It also included a scathing takedown of the Rising and those that supported it: It is a sad reflection on the Irish race that a very substantial body of ostensibly sane men could be misled by a parcel of frothy ranters whose history is the very negation of commonsense conduct. Public opinion would change in the days after the Rising, particularly with the execution of 16 of the Rising's leaders. By then, newspapers were able to freely print stories on Ireland's ongoing political strife. But, for one history-making week in April, it was one small paper that got the jump on its rivals.

He was on the point of joining the staff of the Impartial Reporter when a fire broke out in the offices of the paper. Sarah Saunderson, present editor of the paper, told how William Egbert - Bertie - had many connections in Dublin, which had helped him to get the news of the Rising. He could easily find out about people from Fermanagh, about British soldiers, etc. Bertie Trimble never returned to Trinity College, as he was so much needed at home in the business. But the loss of Trinity was the gain of the Impartial Reporter. He was the only experienced reporter on the spot who could send accurate reports, and so the Impartial Reporter had a first-rate correspondent. The newspapers in Belfast knew of the serious situation in Dublin, but were not able to report details because of the lack of first-hand reports and the Defence of the Realm Act. The little Fermanagh paper was able to publish the first verified reports of the violence, but other papers had great difficulty in printing anything at all. Bertie’s connections in Dublin proved invaluable in getting the paper the first word on the situation. On the morning of Tuesday, 25 April, the headline of the Belfast Telegrahic read: "Dublin isolated"; and added that it was forbidden to give details. In Dublin, Doctor Phoenix said, the Irish Times could not be delivered, and the offices of the Irish Independent were damaged in the fighting. This law prevented the newspapers from publishing anything which might embarrass or alarm the troops or the civilian population. Until the moment of going to press, no news of what happened in Dublin came to hand. The News Letter was similarly restricted in its report of the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland’s forced postponement of his proposed visit to Belfast, and his remaining in Dublin. “The absence of the Viceroy on Easter Monday was the first news of the Rising in Belfast,” said Dr. Phoenix. “A number of people had been waiting all afternoon at the station, and when he did not appear they telephoned Dublin. In these circumstances, it said, we refrain from publishing facts which are in our possession.” On the same day, the Belfast Tele-graph was able to attribute its article, which was headed “The Stamping of Rebellion,” to the many of its readers who had returned from Dublin. It was also able to attack the Rising and those who had supported it, saying: “It is a sad reflection on the Irish race that a large number of supposedly reasonable men have been misled by a band of frothy ranters whose history is the antithesis of good sense. They were told that the Viceroy could not come, as he was engaged in an important affair. But for one week in April, one small newspaper stayed ahead of the rest. Opinion changed during the days following the uprising, and particularly after the execution of sixteen of the leaders of the uprising. On Thursday it could report without the benefit of first-hand information, like the Impartial Reporter, and with the following disclaimer: “We hope that these reports are correct, but we must bear in mind the difficulty of communication.” In this case the newspapers were able to freely publish articles about the political turmoil that was going on in Ireland.

text: Some doctors in England are being offered thousands of pounds to cut the number of patients being sent to hospital, an investigation has found. GP practices are receiving payments to assist local NHS groups in limiting patient referrals and reducing costs, the doctors' magazine Pulse has discovered. Appointments affected include scans and specialist consultations, including those for cancer patients. The British Medical Association described such incentives as misguided. Pulse's investigation revealed that at least nine clinical commissioning groups (CCGs) were offering GP practices payments for meeting targets. In one instance, Birmingham South Central CCG was offering practices over £11,000 to decrease new outpatient attendances, follow-ups, A&E attendances, and emergency admissions by 1%, compared to 2014/15. The schemes, excluding cancer referrals, were intended to incentivise best quality practice and drive improvements in the quality of primary medical care. A spokesperson for Birmingham South Central CCG stated, Our priority is to ensure that patients have access to services that they need, when they need them. Another CCG informed Pulse it had considered the full impact of the incentive scheme and was confident that there is no conflict of interest. Pulse reported that one scheme had already been reviewed by the General Medical Council, the body regulating medical standards in the UK, after local GP leaders raised concerns. The magazine noted that initial hospital referrals for cancer patients should occur within two weeks of a GP first suspecting the condition. Dr Chand Nagpaul, chairman of the GPs committee of the doctors' trade union the British Medical Association, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that such schemes were a financial contaminant to patient-doctor trust. He stated: It's short-sighted and misguided of CCGs to introduce such mechanisms, because they do lead to the potential for patients questioning the motives of GP referrals. We believe it is far more appropriate for CCGs to introduce clinical pathways that ensure patients are referred appropriately rather than these crude, salesman-like bonuses which pay GPs simply to make reduction to referrals in numerical terms. Dr Peter Melton, local GP and clinical chief officer for North East Lincolnshire CCG, which offers the equivalent of more than £6,000 to practices that reduce outpatient referrals to the same level as the 25% with the lowest referral rates (including two-week urgent cancer referrals) in 2014/15, said the CCG was already among the best in England for referring suspected cancer patients to a consultant within two weeks and the scheme was not about avoiding sending people to hospital. It is not focussing on referral reduction per se but on better clinical and quality standards for the patient, he explained. The expectation is practices will be encouraged to investigate more locally and monitor the patient in the first instance rather than automatically refer in to a secondary care service. Analysis by the BBC's Helen Briggs The NHS is under pressure to make savings, with a target of achieving £22bn of efficiency savings by 2020. NHS leaders aim to reduce patient referrals deemed inappropriate, particularly when patients could be cared for locally. Clinical Commissioning Groups (CCGs) are groups of GPs collaborating to plan and design local health services. There are over 200 CCGs across England and, according to Pulse, at least nine are offering payments for maintaining targets for outpatient referrals and follow-ups. It is unclear how widespread the practice is elsewhere. Some have questioned the wisdom of the move, suggesting patients could miss out on vital care. However, CCGs have defended their stance, asserting it is about good practice, not about keeping people who need treatment out of hospital. In November, the NHS advisory board stated GPs in England should nearly double the number of patients referred to hospital for cancer tests. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence indicated delays in spotting symptoms could be costing thousands of lives each year. NHS England stated: We explicitly want to increase not deter appropriate referrals for cancer checks. Dr Rosie Loftus of the charity Macmillan Cancer Support described the findings outlined in Pulse as very worrying. This is yet another sign of an NHS which is seriously overstretched and not giving GPs the resources and support they need, she said. NHS Lambeth Clinical Commissioning Group, which offers payments for practices moving towards the average referral rate, stated, like all CCGs, it aimed to reduce the number of patients being sent to hospitals unnecessarily. The part of the payment relating to the rate of referrals is a small part of the funding and is not designed to stop GPs referring patients who have a clinical need for hospital treatment such as cancer patients, said a spokesperson.

text: A villain-turned-leading man of Bollywood, a bohemian at the feet of a hippy guru, a successful politician: Vinod Khanna was a man who lived many lives, writes Sudha G Tilak. These are external links and will open in a new window. Vinod Khanna, who has passed away at the age of 70, was part of the second wave of Punjabi heroes who dominated Bollywood, known as Partition Punjabis. His family originated from Peshawar in Pakistan and relocated to India in 1947 during the partition. The screen heroes of that era were swashbuckling figures known for their handsome appearances, cultivated on-screen mannerisms, and unique styles. He embodied all these qualities while also bringing the flair of 1970s cinema to his performances. Khanna graduated from college in Mumbai but had been captivated by films since school and soon focused on acting full-time. He made his film debut in 1968 with Man ka Meet. Film writer Jai Arjun Singh notes that Khanna's Bollywood path was unusual for his times. He was the first modern Bollywood hero to begin his career by playing antagonistic roles. Khanna's villainy was remarkable as it combined his dashing looks with an edgy dangerous menace that made him impressive on screen. He excelled more in villain roles than as the conventional Bollywood hero, says Singh. If Dharmendra was the original beefcake of Bollywood in the 1970s, the 1980s were dominated by Amitabh Bachchan's angry young man persona. However, Mr Singh mentions there was a period when Bollywood observers predicted that Khanna was a threat to superstar Bachchan's popularity. The two appeared in several films together. In Amar Akbar Anthony, one of Bollywood's biggest hits, a scene features Khanna beating Bachchan severely and carrying him over his shoulders, leaving many fans of the superstar astonished. It was inconceivable for me to imagine my hero getting beaten. Even by his elder brother in the film, writes Diptakirti Chaudhuri in a book on Bollywood. Khanna was a hunk with dreamy eyes, and the combination of his muscularity and good looks helped him rise to the top. He performed in action films, thrillers, and romances and, for a time, dominated the Bollywood marquee. His notable films include Mera Gaon Mera Desh, Gaddar, Imtihaan, Muqaddar ka Sikander, Inkaar, Amar Akbar Anthony, Qurbani, Kudrat, Dayavan among others. However, in the 1980s, Khanna, by then a family man and leading hero, abandoned acting to retreat to an ashram run by Rajneesh, an unconventional spiritual guru popular with Westerners, in the western Indian city of Pune. The tabloids dubbed him Sexy Sanyasi, referring to an ascetic follower of Hinduism. I am, I guess, a human being who does what feels right to him at the time, does what he really wants to do, he once told a journalist who asked him whether he was a star or a sanyasi. Sure, it is easy to latch onto one thing, to be and do that all your life - but within you is a voice saying there must be something more to life. I look for that something more. After returning from the ashram, his marriage ended, and he faded from public consciousness. However, he remarried and gradually returned to acting at his own pace. Much later, in 1997, he entered politics, subsequently being elected to parliament four times. He was once appointed a junior foreign minister. Khanna is survived by his wife, daughters, and sons. He will be eternally remembered as an actor who crafted his own distinctive narrative.

text: Fighting has eased in parts of Syria where a Russian-led initiative to halt the country's six-year war took effect from midnight, activists say. These are external links and will open in a new window. The agreement revealed by Russia on Thursday to establish four de-escalation zones is supported by Turkey and Iran. However, the main Syrian opposition group expresses little confidence in the agreement. Elsewhere in Syria, activists report that government aircraft have targeted central Hama province, with additional reports of shelling and gunfire in other areas. The opposition High Negotiations Committee (HNC) stated on Friday that the safe zones plan lacked safeguards and compliance mechanisms. It also rejected Iran as a guarantor of the agreement. The UN special envoy for Syria, Staffan de Mistura, informed the BBC that the agreement was significant because it was being implemented by three countries capable of making it effective. The UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR) reported that Syrian fighter jets bombed rebel positions in Hama on Saturday. A rebel commander confirmed that fighting erupted after midnight, according to Reuters. The Syrian military has not yet commented on the matter. The memorandum on the creation of de-escalation areas was announced by the Russian military following discussions in Kazakhstan's capital, Astana. Russia's foreign ministry released the full text of the agreement on Saturday. The aim is to halt attacks by all parties and to provide the conditions for the safe and voluntary return of refugees along with the rapid delivery of relief supplies and medical aid. The four zones will remain for six months, but their boundaries must be finalised by Russia, Iran, and Turkey by 4 June. Under the plan, the four zones will be established in: Russian Deputy Defence Minister Alexander Fomin stated on Friday that there had been no bombing raids by Russian aviation in the four zones since 1 May. However, he emphasised that Russia's air force would continue targeting militants from the Islamic State (IS) group elsewhere in Syria. The US has voiced concern over Iran, stating that the country had only contributed to the violence, not stopped it. The Syrian government of President Bashar al-Assad is not a signatory, but its state news agency has indicated it supports the plan. The Astana talks aimed to reinforce a frequently violated ceasefire initially agreed upon in December. A partial cessation of hostilities was declared at the end of last year, but violence has persisted on several fronts. Syria's conflict has claimed more than 300,000 lives since it began in 2011.
