text: The people who have been closely involved with the Kevin Pietersen story recognised it was always destined to finish in a dramatic parting of the ways. It has consistently concluded in this manner, regardless of his location. Media playback is not supported on this device. However, if England have been unsuccessful in their efforts to manage him, so has everyone else. At least the decision not to select him again was unanimous and made by those at the England and Wales Cricket Board who are aware of the true circumstances. It was made by individuals within the dressing room, not by journalists or supporters. Players have made various off-the-record comments about Pietersen and his behaviour, yet when a camera or dictaphone is presented to them, they will describe him as a great lad. On the field, he may have been England's leading run scorer in the 5-0 Ashes whitewash in Australia, but he only truly fought once, scoring 71 and 49 in Melbourne. Had he averaged 40 and been caught behind each time, he might have survived. However, the manner of his dismissals in the first three Tests in Brisbane, Adelaide, and Perth likely influenced the ECB's decision. Pietersen has always batted according to his mood on a given day, but if he could not focus and play for the team when they were struggling, could he ever do so? His international career could have easily ended 18 months ago when he sent text messages to the South Africa dressing room, undermining then-captain Andrew Strauss. That was disgraceful—and Pietersen was aware of it. The ECB did everything possible to reintegrate him, but when you have been so thoroughly dismantled, as England have been this winter, a line must be drawn. Nov 2004: Makes England one-day debut, scoring 27 not out against Zimbabwe. Jan/Feb 2005: Scores three centuries in one-day series in South Africa. July 2005: Makes Test debut in opening Ashes Test, scoring 57 & 64 not out. Sept 2005: Scores 158 on the final day of the Ashes series as England win the urn for the first time in 18 years. text: Matteo Renzi came to power in February 2014 with a promise of widespread reform, at the head of Italy's powerful centre-left Democratic Party (PD). Before Matteo Renzi, at the age of 39, stepped into Rome's Chigi Palace, his political journey was largely defined by his tenure as mayor of Florence. Remarkably, he had never held a seat in parliament. Yet, in a dramatic political maneuver, just two months after seizing leadership of his party in December 2013, Renzi orchestrated the ousting of Prime Minister Enrico Letta, a rival within his own party, and swiftly assumed office.Renzi's ascent to national politics symbolized a much-needed generational shift in a country long dominated by aging leaders. Known as Il Rottamatore or The Scrapper, Renzi had already gained a reputation for advocating the dismantling of Italy's entrenched political establishment, often criticized for being corrupt and failing the nation over the decades.Although Renzi led his party to a resounding victory in the European elections shortly after becoming prime minister, by May 2015, his party's share of the vote in local elections had plummeted to below 24%. Notably, he has yet to contest a general election.Renzi's political acumen was honed in Florence, where he garnered praise for promoting the city and implementing an ambitious pedestrianization plan. However, he was not without detractors. A former Florentine councillor criticized him for prioritizing Facebook updates over fiscal management, while opposition councillor Ornella De Zordo accused him of being better at making promises than fulfilling them. He's used the slogan 'Said, Done!' many times, she remarked. I would say 'Said, But Not Done!' because Matteo Renzi is very good at a communicational level - at making announcements. But when you look at his record, things are very different. He sells himself very well.Renzi believed in transforming politics and once called for the removal of the old guard. People are weary and disillusioned, he asserted. They don't believe anymore. I believe, and that's why I do politics - because I still believe.Some drew parallels between Renzi and former British leader Tony Blair, who revitalized the Labour Party in the mid-1990s. Like Blair, Renzi aimed to reposition his Democratic Party (PD) towards the center, appealing to voters traditionally aligned with the right. Describing himself as hugely ambitious, he vowed to bring all the courage, commitment, energy, and enthusiasm of which I am capable.Renzi exudes boundless energy, appearing relaxed on television and in parliament, delivering speeches with speed and fluency. His legacy, however, will likely hinge on the success of his reform agenda, which has been overshadowed by Italy's Mediterranean migrant crisis. Since January, an estimated 45,000 migrants have arrived in Italy, and over 1,830 have perished attempting the perilous Mediterranean crossing. Renzi has criticized other European nations for ignoring the crisis, a stance that has bolstered his right-wing, anti-immigrant adversaries, the Northern League.Renzi's reform efforts have found an ally in Federica Mogherini, who became EU foreign affairs chief after the 2014 European elections. Nonetheless, his decision to meet publicly with Silvio Berlusconi, the former centre-right prime minister, angered the left wing of his party. Berlusconi, although expelled from parliament, remained a key figure in the Forza Italia movement. Renzi defended his actions, saying, It's a contradiction in terms to say 'You should have spoken to FI but not to Berlusconi'. Should I have spoken to [Berlusconi's fiancee's dog] Dudu?In a matter of weeks, Renzi orchestrated a party coup. After dining with President Giorgio Napolitano, Renzi reportedly remarked that the government's energy was waning and a decision was needed on whether to recharge or change it. Following a meeting with Letta, Renzi expressed gratitude but emphasized that Italy stood at a crossroads, necessitating a new phase with fresh leadership. Shortly thereafter, Letta announced his resignation.Leading the picturesque Renaissance city of Florence and managing its traffic was vastly different from governing Italy and reforming its political landscape. Renzi succeeded in overhauling the electoral system, introducing proportional representation that ensured a substantial majority for the winning party, though this victory alienated some party members. He faces further challenges as he strives to elevate standards in Italy's educational system and reform the labor market to boost employment, all while contending with opposition from trade unions and dissent within his own ranks.

text: Being in a wheelchair doesn't mean that I can't do it or anyone else can't do it - we're just as capable as any other models. Gemma Flanagan made her debut on the catwalk at a London fashion event this Wednesday, rolling herself down the runway with grace. It was amazing to do it without falling off, she shared, relieved that her fear of rolling off the end or side did not materialize. Before an illness confined her to a wheelchair, Gemma had a vibrant career as an air hostess and part-time model. Reflecting on her experience, she said, I surprisingly felt just as confident as I have done in the past. Given it was my first time in a chair, I wasn't sure how I'd handle it. When you're walking, you can strut and really show off the clothes. I was worried I couldn't do that as well. But the designer was thrilled with how I showcased their items, and that's what modelling is all about.The fashion show, organized by Models of Diversity—a group advocating for inclusivity in fashion and beauty—took place at the Ideal Home Show in London's Olympia. Celebrating her 32nd birthday this week, Gemma hopes for a future where disabled models are a standard in the industry. The more people open to using models with disabilities, the more it will be seen as normal. Many of us have been in one-off campaigns, often unpaid. It would be great to use models with disabilities as just models, not as novelties—we're better than that, she emphasized.Looking ahead, Gemma has exciting plans: I've got a hair show in May and some shoots with local photographers. I want to do more in my chair. I'm in it almost all the time now. Part of doing this show was to embrace myself and see the chair not as an enemy but as part of me. It's about looking past the metal and wheels and seeing 'a gorgeous model' rather than 'a girl in a chair.'Gemma's journey took a turn in 2011 when she was diagnosed with Guillain-Barré Syndrome, a severe condition affecting the nervous system. She spent seven months in rehab relearning to speak, write, and walk. However, walking has become increasingly challenging, and she now relies more on her wheelchair. When I got ill, they hoped for a full recovery, she explained. But I've started getting worse again, and the consultant thinks this might be my best. I've had ups and downs, but mostly I feel OK now. I want to show others they don't need to be defined by their disabilities.Stay updated by following @BBCNewsbeat on Twitter, BBCNewsbeat on Instagram, and Radio1Newsbeat on YouTube.

text: A monthly record of 218,394 migrants and refugees reached Europe by sea in October, the UN says, almost as many as the total number of arrivals in 2014. According to the UNHCR, Greece has seen 210,265 arrivals, while Italy has received 8,129. Many of these individuals are refugees fleeing the conflict in Syria. Tragically, in the past week alone, at least 70 people have drowned attempting to reach the Greek islands. On Monday, the Aegean Sea yielded the bodies of four men after their boat sank, and another seven individuals remain missing near the island of Farmakonisi.Just a day earlier, on Sunday, a capsized boat near Samos resulted in the recovery of 10 bodies, including six children, with another child's body discovered on a nearby beach. This year, the perilous journey across the Mediterranean has claimed 3,440 lives, either drowned or missing, according to the UN agency. The International Organization for Migration reports that over 400 people have died on the route to Greece alone.The UN states that 744,175 people have arrived on European shores this year, primarily landing on Greek islands like Lesbos and Samos. Despite the dangerous conditions, rough seas and deteriorating weather have not deterred migrants, who often pay exorbitant fees to smugglers for passage in overcrowded, unseaworthy boats.Most migrants continue their journey northwards through the Balkans, aiming to seek asylum in Germany. Germany anticipates at least 800,000 asylum seekers this year, with some estimates suggesting the number could reach 1.5 million—at least four times the number from the previous year.Chancellor Angela Merkel is working to reach a consensus with her coalition partners on managing the influx to Germany. Horst Seehofer, from the Christian Social Union (CSU), advocates for establishing transit zones near the borders to process new arrivals. While Merkel's CDU party supports this proposal, Social Democrat leader Sigmar Gabriel opposes it, fearing the zones might resemble concentration camps.

Many of these are refugees fleeing the Syrian war. This year, according to the United Nations agency, 3,440 have died or gone missing in the Mediterranean, according to the International Organization for Migration; and, on Greek waters alone, the International Organization for Migration reports that more than 400 people have perished. On Monday, the sea drew the bodies of four men after a boat sank, and seven other people were missing off the island of Farmakonisi, a day after a boat capsized on Samos, resulting in the recovery of 10 bodies, six of them children, and one more body was recovered on the beach. The day before, on Sunday, a boat capsized near Samos, resulting in the recovery of 10 bodies, including six children, and another child was found on the beach. The majority of the refugees continue their journey northward through the Balkans and hope to reach Germany as asylum seekers. Chancellor Merkel is trying to agree with her coalition partners how to handle the inflow; Horst Seehofer of the Christian Social Union wants to set up transit camps on the borders to process new arrivals. Although the danger is great, the rough seas and bad weather have not stopped the refugees, who often pay a smuggler an enormous sum of money to get into the crowded, unseaworthy ships. The CDU supports this, but Social Democratic leader Gabriel opposes it, fearing the zones would become concentration camps.

text: Fireworks scratched colours into the slate grey sky after being unleashed from the top of Tower Bridge as the historic royal flotilla finished gliding along the Thames. The Diamond Jubilee pageant in London concluded under a persistent drizzle, but not all planned festivities withstood the wet weather. The confetti cannons remained silent, and a helicopter flypast was scrapped due to poor visibility. Despite the rain, singers bravely performed the national anthem during the event's closing moments, soaked but undeterred.This marked the end of a day filled with merriment, food, and celebration, including multiple renditions of the national anthem and even a protest against the monarchy. The festivities proceeded resolutely, rain notwithstanding. Earlier, some revelers faced disruptions as overcrowding on the train network left passengers stranded on platforms. Meanwhile, nearly 9,500 roads were closed across England and Wales for local parties as others chose to celebrate at home.In London, the spirit of celebration was palpable, especially at the Big Jubilee Lunch on Piccadilly, where tables lined the usually bustling street. Among the crowd were three friends, Jodie Merrylees from Cheltenham, Charlotte Symonds from Brighouse, and Jodie Cosgrove from Leeds, adorned in tiaras and patriotic colors. I really like the Royal Family and the tradition it represents, said Ms. Symonds. We wanted to dress up for the Jubilee and get involved with the atmosphere.The event took on an even more regal air with the arrival of the Duke and Duchess of Cornwall, who mingled with attendees, even braving potentially damp seats to chat with those enjoying their meals.Street parties thrived, especially in Bristol, which saw more road closure applications than any city outside London. Revelers gathered in Millennium Square, adorned in red, white, and blue, featuring a make your own corgi attraction. Inspired by the Thames pageant, Andrew Southerden transformed his pub in Kibworth, Leicestershire, into HMS Coach & Horses, complete with portholes and liferafts.In Gainsborough, Lincolnshire, party-goers enjoyed food at 1950s prices, with hot dogs for 7p and tea for just 2p. In Belfast, Samuel and Margaret Sloan celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary alongside the Jubilee at a tea party hosted by the city's Lord Mayor. It is a great honor, Mr. Sloan remarked. She is a very gracious Queen and she does care for the people.Wales hosted over 300 official street parties, including a Big Lunch in Cardiff's St Mary's Street, while hundreds gathered for a similar event in Swansea. Despite rain canceling a beach party in Rhosneigr, Anglesey, a village hall picnic went ahead, drawing hundreds.Edinburgh saw ten street parties, accounting for a third of Scotland's applications. However, not all participants supported the monarchy. Abigail Burnyeat, at a street party in Stockbridge, told the BBC she enjoyed the community spirit but didn't see it as support for the monarchy. It's a celebration of community, she noted.As the pageant commenced, its 1,000 vessels were greeted by 1.2 million spectators, organizers reported. Crowds lined the Thames, with some climbing window ledges for better views, grateful the rain had paused. On Lambeth Bridge, a controlled number of onlookers chose sides to watch the pageant's arrival or departure. Cheers erupted as smaller boats led the procession, culminating in a crescendo when the royal barge appeared, prompting a sea of mobile phones and cameras to capture the moment.Among them was Marilyn Griffiths from Ledbury, Herefordshire, proudly sporting a union jack hat and earrings. I just love the Royal Family and admire them all for what they do, she said. I wanted to come here to show my support.By the pageant's end, the rain intensified, soaking everyone, yet the crowd's good humor endured. The last steam boats sounded their horns, drawing cheers from flag-wavers along Tower Bridge. I saw the Queen, a small child exclaimed to his mother, marking a memorable achievement for all.For more Diamond Jubilee news and features, visit bbc.co.uk/diamondjubilee.

text: Michael Bostwick's second-half strike secured a comfortable win for Peterborough over MK Dons. In an impressive display, Peterborough United surged past MK Dons with a 2-0 victory, climbing above their opponents in the League One standings. The match kicked off with Andrew Hughes scoring within the first minute. Marcus Maddison's precise free-kick found Hughes unmarked at the near post, allowing the former Newport defender to skillfully volley the ball into the net from six yards.Despite a slow start, Karl Robinson's team carved out their first significant opportunity nearly 30 minutes into the game. Nicky Maynard broke through on goal and delivered a pass to Daniel Powell, whose shot was expertly saved by the experienced Posh goalkeeper, Mark Tyler.Peterborough doubled their lead in the 71st minute, capitalizing on a brief resurgence by the hosts. Once again, Maddison played a pivotal role, delivering another free-kick that found Michael Bostwick. Bostwick leapt and headed the ball past Dons' goalkeeper David Martin, securing the second goal.The match concluded with MK Dons unable to find the back of the net. Dean Bowditch's effort from outside the box went wide, while Ben Reeves saw his shot narrowly miss the top right corner. The Dons struggled to convert their chances, with multiple attempts saved or blocked by the Posh defense.Several fouls and yellow cards punctuated the game. George Baldock and Darren Potter of MK Dons, along with Paul Taylor of Peterborough, were booked for bad fouls. Substitutions saw Jermaine Anderson, Shaquile Coulthirst, and Callum Chettle enter the fray for Peterborough, while Kabongo Tshimanga replaced Nicky Maynard for MK Dons.The match ended with Peterborough United firmly in control, as they celebrated a well-deserved win. The Press Association provided this report. Final score: MK Dons 0, Peterborough United 2.

text: Labour MP Simon Danczuk has been suspended by the party after newspaper allegations about his private life. The Sun has reported allegations against Rochdale MP Simon Danczuk, claiming he exchanged explicit messages with a 17-year-old girl. Responding on Twitter, Danczuk acknowledged the incident, describing it as an extremely low point in his life and admitting his behavior was inappropriate. He expressed regret, stating, I was stupid [and] there's no fool like an old fool.In light of these allegations, a Labour Party spokesperson announced, The general secretary of the Labour Party has today suspended Simon Danczuk's membership of the party, pending an investigation into allegations published in the media today. A full investigation will now take place under the authority of the National Executive Committee, which will be responsible for determining any further action.Danczuk, who has represented Rochdale since 2010 and separated from his wife earlier this year, has been a vocal critic of Labour leaders Jeremy Corbyn and Ed Miliband. He has also led a prominent campaign to uncover historical child abuse. On Twitter, he expressed concern that this incident might overshadow his efforts in Rochdale, emphasizing, That's where my focus lies.Known as an outspoken backbencher, Danczuk has often challenged Jeremy Corbyn and called Ed Miliband one of the worst Labour Party leaders in history. He gained recognition for his work on historical child sex abuse, co-authoring a book on former Rochdale MP Cyril Smith's alleged abuses and advocating for action regarding a missing 1980s dossier about alleged paedophiles at Westminster. In July, he announced he was stepping back from this work to address his depression, acknowledging its impact on his marriage.Following his suspension, Danczuk will sit as an independent MP, having had the Labour whip withdrawn. Although the girl involved was over the age of consent, BBC political correspondent Chris Mason noted the allegations are particularly embarrassing for Danczuk, given his focus on child protection.Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and shadow chancellor John McDonnell emphasized the independence of the National Executive Committee's investigation. Ken Livingstone, a Corbyn ally and NEC member, cautioned against premature conclusions, stating, We won't be rushing to any judgement. He added that while the actions might not be illegal, a lot of people are going to disapprove of that sort of age gap and that sort of texting, especially from an MP who prioritized exposing child abuse in his political career.

text: Manchester City earned their first Premier League home win in almost three months as they battled past Watford at Etihad Stadium. In a match that saw Manchester City eager to break a streak of two consecutive defeats, they emerged victorious against Watford with a 2-0 win. The Blues, currently fourth in the league, initially took the lead when Pablo Zabaleta, left unmarked, coolly side-footed Kevin de Bruyne's precise cross into the net. Raheem Sterling came close to doubling the lead but only managed to hit the crossbar after the interval. Watford's best opportunity fell to Odion Ighalo, who failed to capitalize by poking the ball over the bar. As the Hornets slipped to 11th place, City sealed the win with a late goal from David Silva on his 200th league appearance, following a swift counter-attack. However, the victory was marred by a serious knee injury to Germany midfielder Ilkay Gundogan, which manager Pep Guardiola confirmed would sideline him for several months.Reflecting on City's journey since September, they had enjoyed a dream start under Guardiola, winning their first 10 matches, including six Premier League games, establishing a four-point lead at the top. By mid-December, however, their form had dipped, winning only four of the last 15 games before facing Watford. This downturn has led to scrutiny over Guardiola’s tactics, which previously brought him success at Barcelona and Bayern Munich.City had not won a home league game since their 4-0 triumph over Bournemouth on September 17. Despite lacking the flair of their early-season performances, the Blues will be satisfied with a determined display that keeps them fourth. It has been a long time without a win playing at home, it has been strange, Zabaleta remarked. City now trail leaders Chelsea by seven points and sit just behind Liverpool and Arsenal, with the latter visiting the Etihad on Sunday.City's recent struggles have largely been due to defensive frailties, having kept just one clean sheet in their previous 17 matches. After a humiliating 4-2 loss to Leicester City, Guardiola opted for a defensive reshuffle, switching from three to four at the back and benching John Stones. This change brought a more organized and resolute defensive display. It was not the prettiest game tonight but we had determination to win the game, Zabaleta added. Despite a couple of scares, including Ighalo's miss and a crucial save by Claudio Bravo from Etienne Capoue, City held firm. Guardiola defended Bravo, saying, It is not easy to come to a new club and a new country... When moments arrive he has to be brave. Today he was excellent.Under Walter Mazzarri, Watford have shown mixed performances, capable of beating teams like Manchester United but also suffering heavy defeats such as a 6-1 loss to Liverpool. Against City, they displayed resilience but struggled to create clear chances. Despite scoring three against Everton recently, Watford's goal-scoring has been inconsistent all season. Troy Deeney, without a goal since October 1, was benched, leading to a new strike partnership of Ighalo and Jerome Sinclair. Sinclair, in his first start since a £4m summer move, was largely ineffective, while Ighalo squandered his best opportunity late on. The defeat, combined with results for West Brom and Southampton, saw Watford drop to 11th.Mazzarri lamented their missed chance, saying, We were unlucky because of the chance for Ighalo. If he had scored, we would have drawn the game and in my opinion that would have been the fair result. On leaving Deeney out, he explained, We wanted to get Deeney ready for Sunderland. We have three games in a week and he is on four yellow cards.Former England defender Phil Neville commented, It was not about the performance tonight, it was about getting the result. They did not play at their fluent best but scored a couple of really good goals. It's pathetic that Pep Guardiola has been getting criticism so soon into a season.City now prepare to face Arsenal at home on Sunday, while Watford travel to Sunderland on Saturday. The match concluded with a 2-0 victory for Manchester City.

However, their fortunes have dipped of late, and before playing Watford on Saturday they had won only four of their last 15 games, prompting questions about Pep Guardiola’s tactics, which had worked so well at Barcelona and Bayern. They are now seven points behind leaders Chelsea, and only two behind Liverpool and Arsenal, who will both be visiting the Etihad next Sunday. “We’ve had a bad run at home,” Zabaleta said. “We haven’t won for a long time and it’s been strange.” The problems had been mainly caused by defensive weaknesses: in their last seventeen matches they had not kept a single clean sheet. After a humiliating 4-2 defeat by Leicester City, Pep Guardiola made changes, reverting to a back four and dropping John Stones. Despite a few scares, with Ighalo’s miss and Claudio Bravo’s crucial save, City held firm. “We didn’t play the prettiest game but we had the determination to win,” Zabaleta said. But their goals have been inconsequential. Under Walter Mazzarri, Watford have a mixed record, having beaten the likes of Man Utd but also suffered crushing defeats, such as losing 6-1 at Liverpool. Guardiola defended Bravo, saying: “It's not easy, to come to a new club and a new country... But when the time comes, you have to be brave. Today he was excellent.” At City they defended well, but failed to create any clear chances. This defeat, together with the results of West Brom and Southampton, meant that Watford slipped down to eleventh place. Troy Deeney, who had not scored since 1 October, was not in the game, and the two strikers Ighalo and Jerome Sinclair were introduced. Phil Neville, former England defender, remarked, “Tonight it wasn’t about performance, it was about result.” The luckless goal that Ighalo failed to score was lamented by Mazzarri, who said, “We were unlucky because of Ighalo’s chance. If he’d scored, we would have drawn level and I think it would have been fair.” The game ended 2-0 in favour of Manchester City. They played a less fluent game but scored a couple of really good goals. He said of Deeney’s absence: “We’ve kept him for Sunderland. We have three games in a week and he’s on four yellow cards.” Now City have to face Arsenal at home on Sunday, while Watford go to Sunderland on Saturday. It's sad that Pep Guardiola is being criticized so soon in the season.

text: A Carmarthen school at the centre of a police investigation into claims of historical abuse has been criticised by care inspectors in a new report. The Care and Social Services Inspectorate Wales (CSSIW) has reported that the residential unit at Rhydygors School in Carmarthen is not meeting the required minimum standards. This follows criticism from school inspectors Estyn in September of last year. The school's governors have stated they are working to build on the progress made in response to the Estyn report's concerns.In a separate development, Dyfed Powys Police announced earlier this month the arrest of six former staff members as part of Operation Almond. This investigation is examining allegations of abuse at the school spanning from 1976 to 1986. Rhydygors School, located in Johnstown, specializes in education for students with social, emotional, and behavioral difficulties.The CSSIW report highlighted, Overall, we found that young people and their representatives cannot be confident that due care and attention has been paid to the national minimum standards for residential special schools in the period since our last inspection, as the service has not fully met these standards. As a result, Carmarthenshire council will now conduct monthly visits to monitor the quality of care provided to pupils.The report urged the acting head teacher, Margaret Davies, and the governing body to become more familiar with national minimum standards. It noted that 80% of care staff should possess a relevant qualification, a target the residential unit has not achieved. Additionally, the service failed to conduct an annual review of the school's welfare provision for boarding students.Estyn inspectors rated the school's performance as adequate but expressed that prospects for improvement were unsatisfactory. They stated, The school's arrangements for safeguarding pupils generally meet requirements but a few areas give a cause for concern.Matthew Harries, the chair of governors, remarked, Rhydygors was inspected by Estyn in September 2014 and, as the new chair of governors, I will be looking to build on the progress that has been made to address the recommendations of the report. Indeed, we are pleased that progress has been made in many of these areas as noted in the more recent CSSIW report.A spokesperson for CSSIW commented, We do not have any significant concerns about Rhydygors School.Operation Almond is also investigating abuse allegations at Cartref-y-Gelli children's home in Carmarthen from 1986 to 1990.

text: The spacecraft which made a spectacular landing on a comet last year has discovered a rich array of carbon compounds. A prominent scientist has intriguingly referred to the chemicals found on comet Churyumov-Gerasimenko 67P as a frozen primordial soup, a discovery that bolsters the theory that comets might have delivered the essential ingredients for life to early Earth. This revelation emerged after the Philae lander successfully touched down on the comet in November, a mission orchestrated by the European Space Agency's Rosetta mothership that marked the climax of a decade-long journey.The groundbreaking results from Philae's seven instruments have been documented in a special collection of papers published in the journal Science. Notably, the COSAC instrument team identified 16 organic compounds, including four previously unknown to exist on comets. Professor Ian Wright of the Open University, who leads the Ptolemy instrument team, described the findings as really interesting, likening the cometary material to a primordial soup that, under the right conditions, could potentially spark life. What we may be looking at here is our abiological ancestral material, he explained. This is life before life happened.Among Ptolemy's significant findings is polyoxymethylene, a polymer of formaldehyde composed of simple molecules. Professor Wright remarked, The simplest unit of this polymer repeats a ratio of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen similar to that in carbohydrates and sugars, which is crucial to Earth's biological cycle.In another study, Fred Goesmann and his colleagues elaborated on the 16 compounds identified by COSAC, highlighting their potential role in life's development. They noted that hydroxyethanal acts as an efficient initiator in the prebiotic formation of sugars, while methanenitrile is key in the prebiotic synthesis of amino acids and nucleobases, offering a pathway to sugars. The researchers concluded that the comet's complex chemical composition and nitrogen-containing organics suggest that early solar system chemistry could foster prebiotic material in significant concentrations.Though no sophisticated compounds like amino acids have been identified, further analysis may reveal more. Professor Charles Cockell, director of the UK Astrobiology Centre, who was not involved in the mission, told the BBC the results were very significant. He emphasized the excitement of discovering simple organic compounds on a comet, suggesting they might have been delivered to early Earth, contributing to our understanding of life's origins. It confirms there is organic chemistry throughout the universe, he said, with complex carbon-containing compounds possibly forming on comets in our solar system.Professor Mark McCaughrean, the European Space Agency's senior science advisor, offered an analogy to BBC News: Imagine building a house with raw materials from a forest versus pre-made building blocks from a hardware shop. Our findings suggest the comet provides the latter, giving a head start. He posed a crucial question: Is this material made on the comet or in space before being incorporated? We don't know yet.The data published today was collected during Philae's tumultuous landing. Ptolemy was programmed to activate ten minutes post-landing. Professor Wright explained to the BBC that the initial data collection was intended as a quick check to ensure the instrument's survival. However, as Philae bounced off its intended landing site, Ptolemy's data collection occurred while airborne, capturing significant readings from the dust around it.Despite Philae's recent sporadic contact, the lander's status remains uncertain. One theory suggests a gas jet from beneath might have dislodged it, while another posits it could have been struck by debris as the comet nears its closest approach to the Sun on August 13. The mission team remains hopeful for renewed contact, although even if Philae remains silent, the data from its initial 60 hours on the comet is still under analysis and holds promise for future revelations.

text: Nigeria's main opposition party has condemned a weekend raid of its Lagos offices by state security agents. Lawal Shuaibu, the deputy chairman of the All Progressive Congress (APC), has called for an independent commission to investigate the reasons behind the armed raid on their office. We call for an independent commission of inquiry to ascertain the reasons why armed officers raided our office, he told the BBC. The APC reported that during the raid, computers were destroyed and documents seized.The State Security Service (SSS) has stated it is investigating allegations of voter card cloning ahead of the February elections. According to the SSS, The petition alleged that those behind the activities were cloning Inec [Independent Electoral Commission] permanent voters cards, with the intention of hacking into [the] Inec database, corrupting it and replacing them with their own data. The SSS explained that, based on this information, surveillance was conducted on the building, leading to the raid when suspicious activities were confirmed.During the operation, SSS agents confiscated a server, three hard drives, and 31 bags of documents on Saturday. In contrast, the APC described the raid as another one in the string of attacks and illegal actions of the administration. They claimed more than a dozen computers were destroyed, a server was vandalised, and 28 people were arrested.Nigerians have been witnessing the way and manner the government have been using force in oppressing us, Shuaibu expressed to the BBC Hausa service. This is to be condemned and we have been restraining ourselves from taking actions based on the provocations by the government and the security personnel.APC spokesman Lai Mohammed likened the raid to the infamous Watergate scandal in the U.S., which resulted in President Richard Nixon's resignation in 1974. Just like the Watergate scandal in the USA, the state-sponsored security operatives apparently acting at the behest of the ruling PDP [People's Democratic Party] government turned the office upside down, and pulled out and vandalised everything in sight, he told AFP news agency.The APC asserted that the office functioned as a data centre for processing party membership registrations and maintained that it was a legitimate operation. Formed in 2013 from a merger of four opposition parties, the APC has emphasized the need to challenge President Goodluck Jonathan, whose PDP has dominated Nigerian elections since the military rule ended in 1999.The International Crisis Group has recently warned that the upcoming February election could be volatile and vicious. They cautioned, If this violent trend continues, and particularly if the vote is close, marred or followed by widespread violence, it would deepen Nigeria's already grave security and governance crises. The think tank urged the government, its agencies, and all national figures to work swiftly to ensure the elections are not conducted in an explosive environment, as this could further destabilize the country.

text: Writer and humourist Shovon Chowdhury gives his perspective on a recent advert featuring lesbians in India, arguing that we shouldn't be surprised, given India's ancient liberal tradition, which accepted all forms of sexuality and sexual expression. They did an ad about lesbians! a friend exclaimed to me. At first, I misheard, thinking he had said librarians, which left me puzzled but pleased, as I often worry about the state of reading habits in our country. However, when he showed me the ad, the reality was quite different.It was a commercial for a women's clothing brand, featuring two women in love. The ad was impressively directed and acted, making it difficult to mock. Was this a significant leap forward? Initially, it seemed so, until I recalled the legacy of Parveen Babi.Parveen Babi, a beloved actress of our youth, brought pride to India by gracing the cover of Time magazine. The portrayal of lesbian relationships isn't as novel as it's made out to be. In the 1983 film Razia Sultan, Parveen Babi and Hema Malini shared an intimate scene on a luxurious boat. Hema Malini, half-asleep, is serenaded by Parveen Babi, who gazes at her lovingly. They share a concealed kiss, hidden behind feathers, a common technique of that era to obscure onscreen kisses.This TV commercial offers a more contemporary setting, with fewer feathers and more relatability. One might think, That girl could be my cousin or my best friend's sister. Yet, cinema paved the way long before. Post-independence filmmakers, fueled by newfound freedom, weren't shy about embedding positive social messages in their work, contributing to nation-building.However, with the advent of television in the 1990s, cinema's influence waned. TV allowed audiences to stay home, leading to a surge in advertising, driven by economic factors. TV serial producers, known for their frugality, often stretch plots thin. Meanwhile, advertisers and copywriters, who are better compensated, sometimes succeed in delivering powerful social messages.Indian advertising has evolved through three distinct phases. Initially, in the 1970s and 1980s, ads educated the masses on basic hygiene and social etiquette. I vividly remember encountering a woman in a bikini for the first time in a Liril soap ad, an image that left an indelible mark on me.As society progressed, so did advertising. Women began to be portrayed as independent, capable of purchasing clothes, owning credit cards, and driving convertibles. Today, in the third phase, advertisers address issues like stuttering, cancer survival, and even partition, alongside topics like lesbian relationships.But why the uproar over lesbians? Is it a conspiracy against women? Is it forbidden in the Kama Sutra? Historically, Indian society hasn't been as hostile towards homosexuality as some might think. The ancient Laws of Manu prescribed a simple purification ritual for homosexuality, while the Artha Shastra imposed a small fine. The Kama Sutra even provided detailed instructions for homosexual acts.The Sushruta Samhita, a medical treatise from around 600 BC, recognized sexual orientation as innate, distinguishing between transgender and homosexual individuals. Despite challenges, transgenders have found a place in Indian society, hosting TV shows and participating in elections.The temples of Khajuraho, built around 1000 AD, depict various sexual activities, including some seemingly implausible combinations. So, when did prudishness take hold? The blame often falls on Queen Victoria, but we share responsibility too. After the 1857 revolt, the British introduced the Indian Penal Code (IPC) in 1861 to suppress dissent, reflecting Victoria's disapproval of sex by criminalizing most sexual activities outside the missionary position.Despite nearly 75 years of independence, the IPC remains in force, suggesting a lingering mistrust. Thus, the film celebrated by millions on YouTube is more than just a film—it's an act of civil disobedience. It portrays an act punishable by up to 10 years in prison under Section 377. The fate of the directors remains uncertain, but if the authorities act as prescribed by the outdated law, we might soon find out.Shovon Chowdhury, a Delhi-based amateur humorist and advertising professional, is the author of Murder with Bengali Characteristics, his second novel.

text: There has been a 65% increase in children recorded as home educated in the UK over six years. Parents are choosing to home educate their children for various reasons, including lifestyle choices, dissatisfaction with local schools, special needs, bullying, and religious beliefs. Data obtained through Freedom of Information requests from 190 local authorities reveals that 36,609 children are being home educated. The government maintains that it will respect the rights of parents to home educate their children.While there is no legal requirement for children to attend school, parents must ensure their children receive a suitable education at home. The figures indicate a rise of at least 10,399 pupils, bringing the total to nearly 37,000 within a school population of approximately 9.5 million pupils. This number might be underestimated, as children who have never been enrolled in school may not be included in the statistics.Among 190 councils providing data for 2014-15, 178 have records for the past three years, showing a 26% increase in home education. Data from 133 local authorities spanning from 2009-10 to 2014-15 reveals an almost two-thirds rise in numbers. Graham Stuart, chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group on Home Education, suggests that councils may have improved their data recording, and the actual figures are likely underestimated. Local authorities have created groups to share best practices, and there's an encouraging trend to view home education as an opportunity for support rather than a problem to regulate, said the Conservative MP and former education select committee chairman.Parents are not required to provide reasons for withdrawing their children from school, but in 41 council areas, information sheds light on their motivations. Leading the list is a difference in philosophy or lifestyle at 13.4%, with Gloucestershire reporting this as the reason for 235 out of 641 home-educated children. Dissatisfaction with local schools or conflicts account for 9.3%, with 240 out of 724 parents in Hertfordshire citing this reason.Cultural or religious reasons are mentioned in 6.2% of cases, bullying in 4.8%, and special needs or medical issues in 4.3%. Additionally, 3.4% of parents cite the inability to secure a place in a preferred school due to rising pupil numbers. Dr. Helen Lees from Newman University Birmingham, an expert on alternative education, suggests some parents oppose structured assessments and testing in schools. She notes that parents are inspired by successful home education stories online, saying, If they can do it, why can't we? They find support from online groups, where they hear that home education is working well, and the children are happy.The motivations of parents are not comprehensively recorded, as they are not obligated to explain their decision. Similarly, detailed data about the families is limited. In a small number of local authorities with religious information, about 31% of home educators are affiliated with a faith group, though this may not be their reason for choosing home education. Among these, half identify as Christian and a third as Muslim.The growth in home education varies across regions, suggesting multiple factors are at play. In counties with grammar schools, such as Kent and Essex, numbers remain high, with 1,429 and 1,191 home-educated children, respectively. In Rhondda Cynon Taf, the number has increased from five in 2009-10 to 65.Concerns have been raised by Ofsted regarding the potential misuse of home education rights to place children in unregistered, possibly illegal schools. Education Secretary Nicky Morgan has tasked Chief Inspector of Schools Sir Michael Wilshaw with gathering evidence for potential prosecutions. The government is considering stricter regulations on part-time education settings offering more than six to eight hours of weekly tuition. However, it emphasizes that it does not intend to infringe on parents' legal rights to decide their children's educational path. The government continues to respect the rights of parents to home educate their children, whether at home or in a combination of other settings, provided a suitable full-time education is being arranged.

text: Scotland's first minister has warned David Cameron against fighting a miserable, negative, fear-based EU referendum campaign. In a recent speech in London, Nicola Sturgeon criticized former Prime Minister David Cameron for his negative approach during the Scottish independence referendum, which she believed cost him votes. Sturgeon emphasized her desire for a decisive vote in favor of remaining in the European Union. David Coburn, UKIP's Scottish MEP, countered by arguing that the Scottish National Party (SNP) sought Scottish independence while still being under Brussels' influence. He suggested that leaving the EU would return more powers to Scotland.Addressing an audience at the Resolution Foundation, Sturgeon highlighted her intention to use the referendum campaign to advocate not only for the economic advantages of EU membership but also for the social and employment rights it provides. She reiterated that if Scotland voted to remain in the EU on June 23, but the UK overall chose to leave, it might prompt calls for a second independence referendum. Polls have consistently shown that EU membership is more favored in Scotland than in other parts of the UK.Sturgeon's comments coincided with the UK government's release of an analysis warning that an EU exit could result in a decade of uncertainty, affecting the economy and jobs. She stressed that the Scottish government believed EU membership was in Scotland's best interests. Sturgeon vowed to present a positive, constructive case for staying in the EU and to campaign wholeheartedly for a decisive victory across the UK.Reflecting on the Scottish referendum, Sturgeon noted the recurrence of similar arguments in the early stages of the EU referendum, albeit in different contexts. She urged all involved to heed the lessons from the Scottish experience in the coming weeks and months.BBC Scotland political editor Brian Taylor observed Sturgeon's intriguing stance on EU membership. She reaffirmed her support for Scottish independence but clarified she did not want it to result from the UK leaving the EU. This position might seem like a rejection of a potential path to independence, but Taylor suggested the reality was more nuanced.Sturgeon pointed out that the Scottish referendum demonstrated the potential for a thriving democratic debate by engaging people with the issues. However, she warned that a miserable, negative, fear-based campaign had caused supporters of remaining in the UK to lose a significant lead.Despite acknowledging the EU's imperfections, including its bureaucratic nature and mishandling of the Greek debt crisis, Sturgeon praised its achievements in areas like environmental protection and workers' rights, which she said had made millions wealthier, healthier, happier, and freer. These benefits should be celebrated, not renounced, she insisted.Sturgeon saw no contradiction in supporting both Scottish independence and EU membership. She reiterated, I do want Scotland to be independent, but I don't want Scotland to become independent because the UK chooses to leave the European Union.David Coburn, UKIP's leader in Scotland, criticized the SNP's stance, questioning the notion of independence while being governed by Brussels. He argued that Brexit would return many powers to Holyrood and allow Scotland to regain control over policies such as fishing limits and industrial tariffs, thus preserving industries like steel and keeping facilities like Longannet Power Station operational.

text: David Cameron has said world leaders are miles apart in the search for a solution to the Syria crisis. In a revealing interview with CBS, the Prime Minister described the challenge of ending his country's civil war as the toughest problem he has encountered. This conversation took place before his participation in a United Nations anti-terror summit in New York.The Prime Minister expressed his willingness to collaborate with any party but firmly rejected any phoney solution that would involve cooperation with Syrian President Bashar al-Assad. The stance of the UK and the United States is clear: President Assad must step down. However, this perspective is not shared by Russia and Iran.During a meeting with Iranian President Hassan Rouhani on Monday, Mr. Cameron acknowledged the significant influence of Iran and Russia on Syria's future. He emphasized the importance of persuading both nations that establishing a new Syria with a different leader aligns with their interests and is crucial for eliminating the so-called Islamic State (IS), also known as ISIL. The challenge has been Russia and Iran's reluctance to envision a Syria without Assad, he noted.He further remarked, Is this the most complex and stubborn issue that President Obama and I have faced? Absolutely. We are four years into this conflict. Countless lives have been lost, and many have fled the country. But that doesn't mean we give up. Nor should it lead to a misguided solution of aligning with Assad to combat ISIL, as that would be counterproductive. We must adhere to the correct approach, regardless of the time it takes, and work to convince others.The Prime Minister also criticized Western governments for their insufficient efforts to train moderate opposition forces in Syria. He highlighted the impact of a UK drone strike last month that killed three British IS fighters in Syria, stating it effectively thwarted terrorist plots against both the US and the UK.Later, at the anti-terror summit led by US President Barack Obama, he outlined the extent of the UK's involvement and stressed the importance of winning the propaganda war and the battle of hearts and minds.

text: General Motors chief executive Mary Barra has apologised for an ignition switch fault in some cars linked to at least a dozen deaths in road crashes. During a US congressional hearing on Tuesday, General Motors (GM) chief executive Mary Barra expressed her concern over the company's previous reluctance to address the high cost of replacing defective parts. This issue has led to the recall of 2.6 million vehicles. GM has faced criticism for its delayed response, as problems with ignition switches in certain models like the Chevrolet Cobalt and Saturn Ion were reported over a decade ago. However, recalls only commenced in February this year, shortly after Ms. Barra assumed leadership.Testifying before a US House of Representatives panel, Ms. Barra stated, I cannot tell you why it took years for a safety defect to be announced... but I can tell you that we will find out. She emphasized that upon learning of the problem, GM acted swiftly and transparently. We told the world we had a problem that needed to be fixed, she said. Whatever mistakes were made in the past, we will not shirk from our responsibilities now and in the future. Today's GM will do the right thing.Ms. Barra offered a heartfelt apology to those affected by the recall, particularly the families and friends of victims who lost their lives or were injured. I am deeply sorry, she added. She also expressed her disturbance over the possibility that cost concerns delayed the replacement of the faulty switches.Republican Fred Upton, chairman of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, remarked to Ms. Barra, With a two-tonne piece of high-velocity machinery, there is zero margin for error; product safety is a life or death issue. But sadly, vehicle safety has fallen short.Initially, GM's recall targeted 1.6 million cars manufactured before 2007, but last week, the company expanded the recall to include over 800,000 vehicles produced between 2008 and 2011. The defect involves an ignition switch flaw that can cause the key to unintentionally shift from the run position to accessory or off, even while the vehicle is moving at full speed.In response, GM has launched an internal investigation and established a new senior role dedicated to overseeing vehicle safety and recalls. In a move towards potential victim compensation, Ms. Barra announced that GM would enlist consultant Kenneth Feinberg to assist in planning reparations for those most affected by the tragedy. Feinberg has previously managed compensation efforts for the September 11 attacks, the BP oil spill, and the Boston Marathon bombing.Additionally, on Monday, GM announced a separate recall of over 1.3 million vehicles due to an electronic power steering issue that could increase the risk of a crash.

text: A law has come into force in France which makes it an offence for a Muslim woman to conceal her face behind a veil when in public. France has become the first European nation to openly prohibit a form of dress that some Muslims consider a religious obligation. The BBC News website has received numerous reactions from its readers in France regarding this controversial development. Below is a compilation of their perspectives.Sabrina from Lille shares her concerns: In my opinion, this law infringes on individual freedoms. Although I am a Muslim, I do not wear a headscarf as it doesn't align with my beliefs. However, this ban will undoubtedly stigmatize Islam. It affects a small number of Muslim women in France, making it seem extreme and unjust. These women might end up confined to their homes, leading to severe social repercussions. This law suggests that Islam is viewed as a threat to French values and society.Jean Paul Baptiste, residing in Paris, expresses relief: As a Muslim living in Paris, I'm pleased with this new law. There has been a growing issue with the radicalization of young Muslims, and some extremists have used dress as a statement against French society. This extreme interpretation of Islam contradicts what Muslims in France stand for—living in harmony with other religions and beliefs.Rachel Sword from Aix en Provence supports the law wholeheartedly: Finally, a law that upholds the dignity and human rights of women. This is not a racist law but a courageous and progressive measure to end the persecution of women in the Muslim community. Although I am not a fan of Sarkozy, I support this law entirely because the global plight of women forced to wear this garment deeply saddens me.Fiona Ricard from Gailhan agrees with the legislation: Women wearing burqas in public evoke both fear and pity. It's not surprising that these women often feel ignored, as concealing one's identity breeds wariness and suspicion in others.Andy, a human rights lawyer in Strasbourg, has mixed feelings: While freedom of religion should allow people to express their faith, the state can impose restrictions if justified. An outright ban seems excessive; perhaps it should be limited to employment or certain societal areas. The state must respect diverse values, but immigrants must also respect the secular values of France.Naveen Webber from Gex warns of potential division: Banning face-covering veils may polarize and entrench opinions. Few Muslim women choose to wear veils, but prohibiting them might provoke a defensive response. text: The museum at Cuba's most famous beach, the Bay of Pigs, is under renovation. Inside the museum, workers are diligently setting up new multimedia exhibits, while outside, a construction crew is busy laying a concrete patio and painting the entrance. The grand reopening is scheduled for April, commemorating the 55th anniversary of the ill-fated Bay of Pigs invasion, where hundreds of CIA-trained Cuban exiles landed at Playa Giron in a failed bid to overthrow Fidel Castro and his socialist revolution.This botched invasion marked a low point in US-Cuba relations, a nadir only eclipsed by the Cuban Missile Crisis the following year. It remains a symbol of Washington's covert interventions in Latin America. Many of the original Cuban fighters, both militias and regular army troops, are still alive today, though only a few remain in Playa Giron, and several are in poor health.One resident, 83-year-old Dolores Vic Hernandez, vividly recalls fleeing the invading forces. Though not a fighter herself, she remembers escaping with her sister-in-law and their children into the hills surrounding the coastal town. We only had the clothes we were wearing, and the babies were in nappies. We collected our friend who had six children, whose husband was in Havana, and took her with us to the mountains, she recounts.Despite her failing mobility and eyesight, Dolores’s determination as a young mother trying to protect her family is palpable. I'm a person who's never been afraid of anything, she asserts, recalling how she entered an abandoned house to gather a little coffee and sugar, some biscuits for the children for their journey.Ultimately, Fidel Castro led the revolutionary forces to a renowned victory at Giron, a triumph that would humiliate Washington for decades. As US-Cuba relations began to thaw, Fidel, the elder statesman of the Cuban Revolution, offered only brief remarks on the new relationship: I don't trust in the United States' policy nor have I exchanged a word with them, he wrote in Granma, a state-run newspaper, over a year ago. His skepticism isn't surprising, given the numerous assassination attempts he survived during his rule.Fidel further commented that his brother, President Raul Castro, was taking the pertinent steps in accordance with his prerogatives and the faculties bestowed on him by the National Assembly and the Cuban Communist Party. To some, this sounded less than enthusiastic. However, Cuban academic Esteban Morales argues otherwise: That didn't mean to say he doesn't support the process, Morales contends, having extensively studied Cuba's relationship with the United States. Fidel is wise enough to know that this is the only possible path. What is the alternative? Stand against the US canons firing across the bow like we did in the past? No. That's why Fidel intellectually understands that this is a moment to advance.Morales believes Castro was alerting the Cuban people to Washington's true intentions: Fidel knows international relations is a wide battlefield. We don't expect the United States to become our best friends or allies overnight, not by a long way. But perhaps in time, they might become trusted neighbors.Yet, skepticism isn't limited to Fidel alone. There are Cubans who are nervous about the opening, notes Jon Lee Anderson of the New Yorker, author of a definitive biography of Che Guevara. They seem to be people who were already of a certain age when the revolution came along and this has been their life, the true believers in Fidel Castro's long project of socialism. Their concerns span social, cultural, economic, and political arenas. They fear the potential for Miami Cubans to buy everything and shut them out, and the erosion of their values by capitalism. However, Anderson suggests that erosion began long ago, with changes following the Soviet Union's collapse.While it may seem improbable to Fidel's generation that US-Cuba relations could progress so quickly, most young Cubans are eager for even swifter change. President Obama's upcoming visit, where he plans to walk the streets of Old Havana, meet dissidents, and deliver a major speech, underscores this shift. Earlier this month, tens of thousands of young Cubans gathered on the Malecon in Havana for a concert by Major Lazer, an American dance music group, promoting 'Musicabana,' an upcoming electronic music festival in Cuba.This is the first international music band to come to Cuba at the top of their game, says Fabien Pisani, the concert organizer and director of 'Musicabana.' This is the music that every kid who is 12 through to 17 is listening to right now. You can see the excitement here, to be able to touch that and dance and sing together. The concert took place near the US embassy, in the 'Anti-Imperialist Plaza,' a site once synonymous with government-organized demonstrations against US policy. This time, an estimated 150,000-200,000 people gathered not to protest, but to dance in the late afternoon sun.Back in Playa Giron, Dolores Vic remains a true believer in Fidel Castro's socialist vision, even decades after the Bay of Pigs fiasco. Fidel is like a god to me, she says, recalling how she once cooked him a traditional Cuban meal when he visited the region. While she shares some unease about renewed US relations, she acknowledges, I have a few doubts as there are always a few bad people over there who'd want to harm us. But there are a lot of good ones too.Nonetheless, Dolores is excited about President Obama's visit. I never dreamt I'd see this, she says, her eyes shining with disbelief. I never thought that in my lifetime a US president would come to Cuba.

text: A teachers' union is warning that schools are increasingly likely to use unqualified teaching staff. Parents today face uncertainty about whether their children are being taught by qualified teachers, according to Chris Keates, leader of the NASUWT union. This is jeopardising the educational progress of children, she stated, criticizing the employment of unqualified staff as a crude cost-cutting measure. Tristram Hunt of the Labour Party described the situation as nothing less than a scandal.The NASUWT, during its annual conference in Cardiff, is addressing claims of increasing use of teachers without qualified status in schools. A survey conducted by the union revealed that out of 4,600 respondents, 61% reported working alongside unqualified staff, and 66% said the situation was worsening due to funding issues. Teachers expressed concerns, noting that these unqualified staff lack any training in classroom management and discipline, and warning that parents might be misled about the teaching quality in schools.This issue has become a point of contention in the general election. Labour opposes the practice of allowing academies and free schools to hire teachers who lack qualified status or are still in training. Shadow Education Secretary Tristram Hunt criticized the current government, saying, The rising number of unqualified teachers in our schools shows yet again that the Tory plan is threatening standards and failing children and working families. He pointed out that over 400,000 children are being taught by unqualified teachers who lack essential training in classroom discipline and safeguarding.The Liberal Democrats also advocate for mandatory qualified status for teachers. However, both the Liberal Democrats and Conservatives argue that the number of unqualified teachers was higher when Labour was in power. A Conservative spokesperson highlighted that the percentage of unqualified teachers has decreased since 2010, noting, Only 3.7% of teachers are 'unqualified'.The Conservatives defend their policy by emphasizing the autonomy given to head teachers in hiring decisions, suggesting that many unqualified teachers, such as nuns, linguists, and engineers, bring valuable expertise from other sectors. There are some brilliant teachers who have not got qualified teacher status, the spokesperson said.Meanwhile, a Liberal Democrat representative stated, We would change the law to guarantee a qualified teacher in every classroom, emphasizing the need to uphold teaching as a high-status profession to attract top talent. They acknowledged the decrease in unqualified teachers since Labour's tenure but insisted that every child deserves instruction from a qualified teacher.According to the Department for Education's 2013 figures, the number of unqualified teachers rose from 14,800 to 17,100 compared to the previous year, yet this is still lower than the 17,800 recorded in 2010. However, for academies, the proportion of unqualified teachers has increased annually since 2010, rising from 2,200 to 7,900.

text: Shaun Johnson scored a winning drop-goal as New Zealand beat England in a tense and physical Four Nations match at a sell-out Huddersfield. Media playback is not supported on this device.Shaun Johnson, the man of the match who famously scored a decisive try against England in the 2013 World Cup semi-final, once again proved his mettle. With just 14 minutes remaining, Johnson's try put the Kiwis ahead 17-16, a lead they fiercely defended to secure two crucial points, propelling them closer to the final on November 20.Initially, England surged forward, with Gareth Widdop kicking two penalties and the team consistently threatening the Kiwi line, dominating the first 20 minutes. However, New Zealand turned the tide. Jordan Kahu's penalty and a try by Jordan Rapana in the right corner saw David Kidwell's squad take a narrow 6-4 lead into halftime. The Kiwis extended their advantage when Johnson intercepted a pass from Widdop, racing 80 yards to score, with Kahu adding the conversion. England fought back as Huddersfield Giants winger Jermaine McGillvary scored in the corner, narrowing the gap to two points. Although Rapana added another try after a brilliant offload from Manu Ma'u, England responded with Ryan Hall's converted touchdown, set up by Widdop's exquisite flick pass, leveling the score at 16-16. Johnson's decisive strike from in front of the posts sealed the victory for New Zealand.Media playback is not supported on this device.Before the game, New Zealand captain Jesse Bromwich noted that the Four Nations' round-robin format gave the Test a semi-final atmosphere. With both teams yet to face favorites Australia and underdogs Scotland, winning at Huddersfield was critical. England's next match is against Scotland in Coventry next Saturday, but they will likely need to defeat the Kangaroos in London on November 13 to reach the final at Anfield. Wayne Bennett's squad faces a daunting challenge as they aim to end a long drought since Great Britain's World Cup win in 1972.The match marked Sam Burgess's return to the England team and his debut as captain, as well as Australian Wayne Bennett's first meaningful fixture coaching England after a warm-up win over France in Avignon. England began with strong intent, led by Canberra hooker Josh Hodgson, taking an early 4-0 lead. Yet, by halftime, the Kiwis had taken control, and England found themselves defending against repeated attacks.Despite England's resilience following Johnson's intercept try, they were constantly on the back foot during a scrappy second half as the Kiwis demonstrated why they are ranked as the world's top side, expertly closing out the game. Hopes for a new era for England, a team with a history of falling short in crucial matches, were dashed, leaving many players dejected at the final whistle.Last year, England defeated New Zealand 2-1 in a Test series, and the Kiwis had only won two of their last 10 away games against Great Britain or England. Coach Kidwell faced challenges in 2016, with his team managing just two line breaks and one try in their previous two matches, both losses to Australia. However, with a formidable forward pack and the dynamic hooker Issac Luke, along with the unpredictable Johnson, the Kiwis secured a much-needed win ahead of their upcoming clash with the Kangaroos in Coventry.The Kiwis defended staunchly early on, building pressure and seizing the initiative from England, earning a valuable two points in the process.Subscribe to the BBC Sport newsletter to receive the latest news, features, and videos directly to your inbox.

text: Chelsea underlined their title credentials with a superb come-from-behind victory over Manchester City at the start of an engrossing weekend of Premier League action. Arsenal delivered a commanding performance at West Ham, while Bournemouth shocked Liverpool in a thrilling seven-goal encounter. Tottenham, Sunderland, Crystal Palace, Stoke, and West Brom also secured victories. Meanwhile, Manchester United and Everton ended in a stalemate at Goodison Park.Do you agree with my Team of the Week? Or would you choose differently? Create your own Team of the Week from the shortlist curated by BBC Sport journalists and share it with your friends.In the early moments of the game, Sergio Aguero's attempt was expertly tipped over the bar, appearing effortless. His subsequent save against Kevin de Bruyne was crucial, but it was his denial of Aguero's second strike that truly stood out. By then, Aguero must have felt Courtois was insurmountable. It took an exceptional finish to beat the Belgian goalkeeper initially, but Courtois quickly demonstrated his resolve not to be beaten again. Manchester City's frustration grew as chance after chance was thwarted by Courtois, who seemed impervious to their efforts.What I admire about Courtois is his lack of theatrics; he consistently shows up for big games, focusing solely on making the save. He doesn't act like a star, preoccupied with his appearance; instead, he looks somewhat awkward with his preppy hairstyle. Yet, his goalkeeping prowess is undeniable.The tackle by Aguero on Brazil's Luiz was charged with animosity from past encounters. Neither player was willing to yield, and once again, Luiz emerged victorious against the Argentine. The fierce rivalry between their nations only intensified the Premier League title chase. Luiz, in top form, constantly pressured Aguero, ultimately provoking a reaction that led to Aguero's dismissal and a suspension for upcoming matches. Luiz's performance was monumental, leaving Manchester City to reassess their title ambitions without Aguero.At Stoke, Muniesa caught my attention with a standout performance against an overwhelmed Burnley. His ball control as a defender reflected his Barcelona upbringing. His goal was reminiscent of Gerard Pique, starting a move in his own half, advancing into the opponent's penalty area, demanding the ball, and finishing with Messi-like finesse. It was pure class, echoing Barcelona's style.West Brom's rise to the top six on Saturday night seemed almost dreamlike. Tony Pulis has transformed them into a cohesive unit, with defenders like McAuley shining. McAuley consistently contributes goals, mainly from set-pieces, and rarely misses games, showing total dedication. His crucial block against Troy Deeney prevented Watford's captain from scoring his 100th goal. Pulis is doing an excellent job, but he must rein in James McClean, whose unnecessary scrapes could hinder West Brom's success.Tottenham's early cross for Harry Kane's header set the tone against Swansea. Despite the warning, Swansea couldn't cope with Spurs' mood, especially Walker's. Spurs can be devastating when they want to, but I would have preferred a draw with Chelsea and a straightforward win over Swansea. Tottenham often crush lesser teams but falter against bigger clubs, creating false optimism about their title chances. Walker doesn't shy away from big moments, but this 5-0 win might mask underlying issues. Last week's defeat at Chelsea was a clear sign that Spurs still have work to do before being serious title contenders.McArthur delivered an outstanding performance for Crystal Palace, securing vital points. The Scot was commanding, and manager Alan Pardew needed this win desperately. Despite recent struggles, Palace is exceeding expectations. Their victory over Southampton was impressive, and with players like McArthur in key roles, they should be fine. Last week's decision to have Christian Benteke mark players in the box was baffling; defenders should defend, attackers should attack.Bournemouth's Fraser emerged 10 minutes into the second half against Liverpool, reigniting the game. Liverpool's defensive vulnerabilities were exposed, and Fraser's energy brought Bournemouth back. He won a penalty, scored the equalizer, and energized the crowd. Liverpool's defensive issues are evident, and manager Jurgen Klopp must address them swiftly.The clash between Arsenal and West Ham resembled a scene from Game of Thrones, with West Ham under siege. Arsenal breached their defenses early, with Monreal's crosses causing chaos. Monreal defended with intensity, nullifying Manuel Lanzini's threat. I've had doubts about Monreal's consistency, but against West Ham, he seemed determined to prove himself.Phillips, once at QPR, showed potential but lacked consistency. Under Tony Pulis at West Brom, he's thriving. His transformation is evident, and it's puzzling why Scotland's Gordon Strachan overlooks him for international duty.Sanchez's hat-trick was a masterclass, showcasing his selflessness and skill. Watching Match of the Day, Gary Lineker challenged Alan Shearer's view that Aguero was the only world-class striker in the Premier League. Sanchez belongs in that elite group, and it's hard to see why he wouldn't be considered world-class.Costa's improvement is remarkable. During the Aguero-Luiz incident, Costa stayed uninvolved, a testament to Antonio Conte's influence. Costa doesn't need to engage in altercations; his skill speaks for itself. His play against Otamendi, setting up Willian's goal, was sensational. It's ironic that Aguero now exhibits behavior once criticized in Costa. Pep Guardiola must be cautious; there's a fine line between aggression and thuggery.

text: Welsh cyclist Elinor Barker believes there is less pressure on GB's women's Olympic pursuit team in Rio because they are not clear favourites to win. In a stunning display at the London 2012 Olympics, Team GB clinched the gold medal, but by the 2016 World Championships, they had slipped to third place. As the British team, consisting of Barker, Laura Trott, Ciara Horne, and Joanna Rowsell Shand, gears up for the next challenge, they face formidable competition from the USA and Canada.Barker, 21, expressed that the pressure might be less intense this time around. There's maybe less pressure now because it's not necessarily ours to lose, she stated. It's still ours to win, but there's not a dominant force in women's team pursuit now which there had been for many, many years.The current landscape of women's team pursuit is more unpredictable, according to Barker. I think it makes it much more exciting but it also means no one is watching any one team, she explained. We're all watching each other, we're all interested in what everyone is going to do and there's probably about five teams who could quite easily win it if it goes well for them on the day which makes it pretty exciting.Reflecting on her journey, Barker recalled watching the 2012 Games on television as a 17-year-old when Trott, Rowsell Shand, and Danielle King triumphed over the USA in the final. Fast forward four years, and Barker finds herself competing in Rio, a prospect she finds hard to fathom. Probably a combination of luck and very hard work has got me here, she admitted. I wouldn't be here if I hadn't worked very hard and been very specific in my training but I've also been very lucky in the opportunities I've been given.Hailing from Cardiff, Barker was part of the squad that secured a bronze medal at this year's World Championships. Their hopes of reaching the final were dashed by a subpar performance in an early round, drawing criticism after years of dominance. However, Barker sees this setback as a learning experience. It just goes to show people make mistakes all the time but it doesn't mean that we're not a good team, she remarked.The team managed to rebound and claim bronze with the same lineup, which Barker believes demonstrates their resilience. We came back from it [to take bronze] with exactly the same line-up so it shows it was that ride rather than us - it was a bad race and it doesn't define us as a team.For those inspired by Team GB's journey, a special guide is available to help you get into cycling.

text: Jeremy Corbyn says he will ask his MPs to vote for the Article 50 Brexit process to begin, if the government is forced to seek Parliament's approval. Amidst the political turmoil surrounding Brexit, Jeremy Corbyn has emphasized his party's stance on the referendum result, stating it is very clear that Labour accepts the outcome. In the wake of a heated debate within party ranks, Mr. Jones announced a cabinet that included Conservatives, igniting controversy. The national party had previously declared that its councilors should not collaborate with the Tories. Among the critics was Assembly Member Simon Thomas, who stated that the Plaid Cymru group on Conwy Council never wanted Mr. Jones to accept the position initially. Thomas further remarked that disciplinary consequences for Mr. Jones would follow.The dispute lingers on, with Mr. Jones, a former Aberconwy Assembly Member from 1999-2003 and 2007-2011, expressing his bewilderment on BBC Radio Cymru's Post Cyntaf program. He questioned the central party's strategy, which refused to endorse his cabinet that included Conservative councilors. What is the rule regarding working with Labour that is as much a threat as the Conservatives? he asked. I can't comprehend Plaid Cymru's strategy—there's nothing in the constitution referencing any party... yet suddenly, there's this business... we're not working with the Conservatives, but collaboration exists with them in several places across Wales, including the National Assembly.He added that his intention in forming a coalition was to govern openly. The Conwy cabinet comprises two Plaid Cymru members, including Mr. Jones, five Conservatives, and one independent councilor. Labour councilors declined the invitation to join. Initially, two other Plaid Cymru members were part of Mr. Jones's plans, but they are not in the final cabinet.Mr. Jones described his decision to resign as difficult, stating, Of course, there was no choice because I must respect the decision made by the national working group. He explained, There was a discussion, and the majority opposed supporting what we're trying to achieve in Conwy's cabinet, and what's become clear from that decision is that Plaid could not support any Plaid Cymru member as part of this cabinet in Conwy.
