text: Police are too sensitive about asking victims of crime if they are disabled, an inspection has found. A comprehensive review by joint inspectorates has revealed that disability hate crime in England and Wales is both overlooked and under-reported. This investigation scrutinized the police, probation services, and the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), urging the establishment of a new common definition to ensure these crimes are addressed swiftly and effectively. Despite efforts, senior police officers acknowledge the need for continued improvement.In the 2011-12 period, police recorded over 1,700 disability hate crimes across England and Wales. This review was initiated in the aftermath of the tragic case of Fiona Pilkington, who, in 2007, took her own life and that of her disabled daughter, Francecca Hardwick, following persistent harassment from local youths and inadequate police response. The report cautions that without urgent reforms, similar tragedies could recur.Inspectors conducted interviews with personnel from six police forces, along with CPS and probation trust offices in Cleveland, Cumbria, Derbyshire, Hertfordshire, Greater Manchester, and the West Midlands. They also attended seven court hearings and engaged with disabled victims, witness care units, victim support services, and independent disability advocates.Disabled individuals expressed to inspectors that police officers and control-room staff were overly cautious about causing offense, leading to a hesitance in inquiring about a victim's disability. Steve Ashley, HM Inspectorate Constabulary's programme director, highlighted this reluctance, noting a failure to ask critical questions that could differentiate between crime and anti-social behavior, and assess the impact of disability on the victim.Ashley further pointed out confusion surrounding the definition of disability hate crime, contrasting it with more readily identifiable religiously or racially motivated attacks. He emphasized the discomfort officers feel when directly asking individuals if they are disabled. When questioned about the possibility of a repeat of the Pilkington case, Ashley affirmed, Yes, it could.The disability charity Mencap reported that its research indicates nine out of ten people with a learning disability have experienced hate crime. Emma Harrison, an assistant director at Mencap, stated the review highlights ongoing failures in the criminal justice system at every stage. She welcomed the review's call for collaborative efforts between police, probation, and CPS to address these issues.The review recommends a single, clear and uncomplicated definition of disability hate crime to mitigate confusion. It urges the three agencies to enhance training for their frontline staff and encourages police to actively solicit reports from victims to tackle under-reporting. Additionally, the review suggests the Law Commission consider establishing a stand-alone offense for disability hate crime.CPS Chief Inspector Michael Fuller, speaking for the three agencies, acknowledged that disability hate crime has been largely neglected and stressed the need for systemic change to better serve disabled individuals. Javed Khan, CEO of Victim Support, insisted on improved police services for disabled victims.The Association of Chief Police Officers stated that the police have made significant efforts to improve their handling of disability hate crime by engaging with disabled communities to understand their challenges and working to eliminate barriers to reporting. A Home Office spokeswoman added that the department has enhanced the methods for collecting and recording hate crime data, including those targeting disabled people, and remains committed to working with disability groups to bolster victim confidence in coming forward.

text: A dog owner whose pet was the latest victim to die from from Alabama Rot says more needs to be done to inform owners of the risks. Steve Kirwan from Lyndhurst, Hampshire, is convinced that his Labrador-collie mix, Bodhi, fell ill after a walk in the Whitefield Moor area of the New Forest. Bodhi, who was three years old, succumbed to kidney failure in February, two weeks after showing symptoms. The mysterious disease, responsible for the deaths of 24 dogs in the UK since 2012, remains an enigma to experts.According to the Forestry Commission, between November 2012 and March of last year, there were 12 confirmed cases of the disease, with five occurring in the New Forest, alongside two unconfirmed cases. Since December of last year, another 12 cases have emerged, half of which were also in the New Forest. Tests are ongoing for an additional 22 suspected cases. The disease, known as cutaneous and renal glomerular vasculopathy (CRGV), was first identified in the United States during the 1980s.Early symptoms often include lesions or wounds on the legs, paws, and face, though these are not always present. Within two to seven days, affected dogs may exhibit signs of kidney failure, such as vomiting, a loss of appetite, and fatigue. Notably, the disease does not seem to be contagious among dogs.Anderson Moores Veterinary Specialists have noted cases outside Hampshire in Northamptonshire, Yorkshire, Monmouthshire, Dorset, Shropshire, Surrey, Cornwall, Worcestershire, and County Durham. In response, the Forestry Commission has initiated a poster campaign across 29 car parks in the New Forest to alert dog owners to the threat. However, Mr. Kirwan expressed dissatisfaction, stating, I don't think it's enough. There are far more than 29 car parks in the New Forest. I believe the warnings should cover the entire forest, given the concentration of cases here as part of the national picture.Bodhi never developed lesions but showed signs of dragging his back legs. Vets suspected Alabama Rot, but despite treatment efforts, Bodhi did not recover and had to be euthanized. The investigation into the disease's cause is being spearheaded by Anderson Moores Veterinary Specialists in Hursley, near Winchester. They are collaborating with the Forestry Commission, the Environment Agency, the Suffolk-based Animal Health Trust, and local veterinarians.David Walker from Anderson Moores commented, There's a significant amount of research ongoing, exploring multiple different avenues, but at this stage, we are no closer to knowing what the trigger is. Research will continue, but we may find ourselves researching this disease for five, ten years without discovering the underlying cause. However, that doesn't mean we will stop looking.

text: A £5 note engraved with a tiny portrait of Jane Austen and said to be worth up to £50,000 has been found in a Christmas card. On Thursday, a second of four unique £5 notes, intricately engraved by micro-artist Graham Short, surfaced in Scotland. Earlier this month, the first was discovered in a café in South Wales. Meanwhile, two more notes, released in England and Northern Ireland, continue to circulate.The special notes, identifiable by their serial numbers AM32 885552 and AM32 885554, are part of a project initiated by the Tony Huggins-Haig Gallery in Kelso, located in the Scottish Borders. The gallery has advised anyone who finds one to get in touch.Tony Huggins-Haig shared with BBC WM that the latest recipient, who stumbled upon the note by chance, prefers to stay anonymous. He explained, It was tucked inside a Christmas card from a loved one, unbeknownst to the giver. He added, That's two found, but two are still out there. Keep an eye on your change.The notes are distinguished by Mr. Short's engraving of a 5mm portrait of Jane Austen on the transparent section of the new plastic Bank of England £5 notes, commemorating the 200th anniversary of her death next year. Each note features a unique quote, enhancing their individuality.Both individuals who have found the notes have decided to hold onto them rather than sell. Short expressed mixed feelings about this decision: I don't know whether I'm disappointed that they haven't wanted to sell them because I wanted them to have some money for Christmas, but the fact that they are so happy to keep them, that's nice as well.Short also confessed to checking his own change, jokingly admitting his fear of finding one himself. When someone gives me a £5 note in my change now, I always check. Wouldn't it be awful if it came back to me? People would say it was a fix, he remarked.

text: The family of a 20-year-old woman from Glasgow who has travelled to Syria and married an Islamic State (IS) fighter have said that she has betrayed them. Khalida and Muzaffar Mahmood were devastated upon discovering their daughter Aqsa had fallen into radicalization. This revelation came after Twitter comments attributed to Aqsa urged individuals in Britain to replicate the brutal terrorist acts seen in Woolwich and the United States.The Mahmoods expressed their enduring love for their daughter, desperately wishing for her return. In a heartfelt statement, they declared, We still love you, Aqsa, but now we must prioritize your family, your brother, and sisters, as you have betrayed us, our community, and the people of Scotland with your actions. You have torn the heart out of our family and changed our lives forever. Please come home.They warned other families, saying, If our daughter, who had every opportunity and freedom, could become a bedroom radical, then it could happen to any family.Aqsa, who was privately educated, reportedly used a Twitter account under the alias Umm Layth to advocate for terrorist activities. The account has since been removed. She traveled through Turkey to Aleppo, Syria, in November and was reported missing to the police. Before her disappearance, she was a well-integrated part of society, attending Craigholme School and then university, according to her parents. They emphasized she was raised with love and affection in a happy home.At a news conference in Glasgow, Mrs. Mahmood, wiping away tears, listened as their solicitor, Aamer Anwar, read a statement on behalf of her and her husband. They stated, She may believe that the jihadists of ISIS are her new family, but they are not; they are simply using her.Remaining silent during the conference, the parents described Aqsa as always a very sweet, peaceful, intelligent child, inquisitive about everything. They had envisioned a future where she might become a doctor, save lives, and eventually marry and have children. Sadly, that no longer looks likely, they lamented. As parents, we would have liked for her to listen to us, but we gave her everything possible in terms of love, freedom, and education, and she chose a path we could never approve of.They added, All parents want to be proud of their children, but sadly we now feel nothing but sorrow and shame for Aqsa. We are not in denial and do not make any excuses for her and absolutely condemn her involvement in ISIS and recent comments. But she is our daughter, and we still love her, fear for her life, and urge her to return home while she still can.After Aqsa's arrival in Syria, she maintained contact with her parents through social media until Tuesday, when news of her involvement with ISIS emerged. Mr. Anwar stated, Due to yesterday's events, all contact with their daughter appears to have ceased. They hope this plea reaches her, prompting her to reconsider and return home. They want her back while she still can come. They are telling her that she is wrong, deluded if she thinks she is helping people in Syria.The solicitor explained that Aqsa, a British national, had become concerned and upset by media and online reports of the violence in Syria, expressing to her parents a desire to help. Mr Anwar then said that since the events of the previous day, all contact with their daughter had been broken off. They hope that their daughter will return to them before it is too late. They added, “As parents we would like to see her listen to us, but we have given her everything that is possible to love, freedom, and education, and she has chosen a path that we can never approve of.” The lawyer said that Aqsa, a British national, had been deeply disturbed by the reports of the violence in Syria in the press and on the Internet, and had told her parents that she wanted to help. Her parents, who are police officers in Scotland, told him: ‘Isis kills in the name of religion and pretends to defend the weak. Our daughter, by joining them, is being brainwashed and lulled into helping those who commit genocide.’ In the days and months ahead we will be looking for clues on social media, to find out whether our daughter is alive. They tell her she is wrong, a fool, if she thinks she is helping people in Syria. They are also worried about the increasing climate of fear in the country, where young people are prevented from discussing their opinions with parents and friends, and that is dangerous for society. Today, while we try not to cry, we feel we have lost our child. Like many young people in our society, Aqsa was understandably distressed and angry over the innocent victims in the Middle East, but that won't help.”

text: Home Secretary Theresa May's internet monitoring plans need significant work, a committee has ruled. The proposed Investigatory Powers Bill is set to compel internet service providers to retain records of all web activity for a year. It will also authorize the mass collection of personal data and the hacking of smartphones by British intelligence agencies. Government ministers argue that these measures will modernize legal frameworks to combat terrorism and organized crime, aligning with the evolving technology used by criminals.However, civil liberties advocates argue that these provisions amount to mass surveillance of UK citizens. They contend that the committee's report indicates the home secretary needs to reconsider the approach. Shami Chakrabarti, director of Liberty, remarked, This report shows just how much homework the government has to do on this landmark legislation.Labour's shadow home secretary, Andy Burnham, has communicated to Mrs. May that while Labour supports the bill's aim to empower police and security services, the government must reassess its strategy to ensure a balance between security and privacy. Mrs. May responded by stating that the government would carefully consider the findings of three committees that have reviewed the bill before finalizing their proposals. She emphasized, This is vital legislation, and we are absolutely determined to get it right. Our draft Bill followed three independent reports on investigatory powers, whose authors were unanimous a new law was necessary. We are clear we need to introduce legislation which responds to the threats we face in the digital age, protects both the privacy and security of the public, and provides world-leading oversight and safeguards.While consensus exists on the necessity of a new surveillance law, the specifics remain contentious, as highlighted by several parliamentary reports. The current law is widely viewed as complex and opaque, and the proposed bill has yet to fully address these issues. The pressing concern is whether the Home Office will adequately address the criticisms and if there is sufficient time to do so, given that the final bill is expected to be introduced soon for debate and passage by the year's end.The Joint Committee on the Draft Investigatory Powers Bill, in a comprehensive 194-page report, acknowledged the potential value of Internet Connection Records for law enforcement, stating it could outweigh the intrusiveness involved in collecting and using them. Nonetheless, it echoed tech firms' concerns about the feasibility of safeguarding user privacy as promised by Mrs. May, particularly in collecting only website names instead of individual web pages. The committee was informed that this might not be technically feasible, but noted the Home Office is collaborating with the industry to find a solution.Ministers must also clarify their stance on encryption to ensure tech firms are not compelled to provide a back door for intelligence agencies, as urged by the parliamentary committee. Additionally, the Home Office must justify the collection of emails and other internet traffic passing through the UK, as revealed by US whistleblower Edward Snowden, and other bulk data gathering practices.Committee chairman Lord Murphy of Torfaen highlighted that the Home Office has a significant amount of further work to do before Parliament can be confident that the provisions have been fully thought through. Former Deputy Prime Minister Nick Clegg criticized the bill as a dragnet approach and disproportionate. He had previously blocked Mrs. May's earlier attempt at passing similar legislation, dubbed the snooper's charter by critics.Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Clegg accused the Home Office of wanting to collect everything on everyone to identify terrorists or criminals. He questioned whether it was proportionate in a liberal democracy to retain information on everything from the music you download on Spotify, to the app that you open, to the supermarket website that you visit, in order to go after the bad guys? Clegg advocated for a narrower approach to data retention, suggesting other countries focus on individuals who flicker on the radar screen of security services in the first place.A significant portion of the bill addresses the operations of Britain's intelligence agencies, aiming to clarify their legal mandate following Edward Snowden's disclosures. It proposes equipment interference warrants, enabling agents to hack into suspects' devices and extract data, both domestically and internationally. Additional warrants would allow the download of bulk personal data databases, potentially including medical records, and the interception of internet traffic traversing the UK for future analysis by GCHQ. Many of these techniques were unknown to the public until recently and were governed by a patchwork of outdated legislation, some predating the internet. The draft bill also proposes further measures.

text: Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has said the inconclusive election result means no party can govern alone. The AKP, led by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, is currently engaged in discussions to form a government after losing its parliamentary majority for the first time in 13 years in the latest general election. The party secured 41% of the vote, a significant decrease from its 2011 performance, necessitating the formation of a coalition or the prospect of governing as a minority.Erdogan has urged all political parties to maintain stability in Turkey, stating, I believe the results, which do not give the opportunity to any party to form a single-party government, will be assessed healthily and realistically by every party.The AKP faces the challenge of forming a coalition, as no other party has expressed willingness to collaborate. Meanwhile, opposition parties might explore forming a coalition to counter the AKP. However, Numan Kurtulmus, one of Turkey's four deputy prime ministers, asserted that a government without AKP representation is unlikely.Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoglu is convening with AKP cabinet members and officials in Ankara to evaluate the election outcomes. Once the final results are officially confirmed, Davutoglu will have a 45-day window to establish a government. Kurtulmus mentioned that another election remains a possibility.This election marks a potential shift in Turkey's political landscape. Despite the setback, the AKP still garnered over 40% of the vote, a figure that many parties worldwide would envy. The party maintains a strong base among religious and conservative Turks, who feel empowered by both the party and Erdogan. Nevertheless, the AKP's long-standing dominance, characterized by a singular political narrative over the past 13 years, has been significantly challenged.The election results have dealt a blow to Erdogan's ambitions to expand presidential powers, as he had hoped to secure a two-thirds majority to transition Turkey into a presidential republic. Meanwhile, the pro-Kurdish HDP surpassed the 10% threshold, earning parliamentary seats for the first time. HDP leader Selahattin Demirtas remarked, The discussion of executive presidency and dictatorship have come to an end in Turkey with these elections.On the economic front, the Turkish lira plummeted to near-record lows against the dollar, and the Istanbul stock exchange saw shares drop by over 8% after opening. In response, the central bank swiftly reduced the interest rate on foreign currency deposits to stabilize the lira.For those in Turkey wishing to share their reactions to the election results, they can contact haveyoursay@bbc.co.uk. If you are open to speaking with a BBC journalist, please include your phone number. Pictures can be shared via email at yourpics@bbc.co.uk, uploaded online, or tweeted @BBC_HaveYourSay. text: Overall crime in England and Wales fell by 15% in 2013, official figures show. The Crime Survey for England and Wales (CSEW) has revealed a significant drop in crime, reporting 7.5 million crimes against households and adults for the year, marking the lowest level since the survey's inception in 1981. Meanwhile, police figures indicated a 2% decrease in crime for 2013, though there were notable increases in certain areas, such as a 25% rise in fraud and a 17% increase in reported sex offenses, the latter influenced by the Jimmy Savile scandal.Government ministers hailed these statistics as good news, asserting that they demonstrate the effectiveness of ongoing reforms. The CSEW, published by the Office for National Statistics (ONS), estimates crime levels by surveying individuals about their experiences as crime victims. The data suggested a 15% reduction in crimes against households and adults for the year ending December 2013 compared to the previous year.According to BBC News Home Affairs correspondent Danny Shaw, the decline in crime was anticipated, as crime rates have been steadily decreasing since the mid-1990s. However, the magnitude of the reduction—a 15% drop—was unexpected, representing the largest percentage decrease since the survey began 33 years ago. A notable 22% decline in violence further supports recent findings from Cardiff University's study on crime-related injuries.While police statistics present a different narrative, they should be approached with caution due to concerns about data manipulation and the reliance on victims reporting crimes. The ONS attributed the overall crime reduction to fewer offenses, including a 25% drop in household theft and a 22% decrease in violence. Vandalism reports also fell by 15% during the year.Additionally, the survey indicated that 762,000 crimes were experienced by children aged 10-15 in 2013, marking a 13% decrease from 2012. Danny Shaw noted that the overall decline was not surprising, but the scale of the reduction was unexpected.Police data for England and Wales showed a decline in most major crime categories, with 3.7 million offenses recorded for the year ending December 2013, a 2% decrease from the previous year. However, some categories saw increases, such as a 6% rise in shoplifting and a 1% increase in violence against individuals, potentially due to better recording practices and increased public reporting. The rise in fraud followed efforts to centralize crime recording, and high-profile cases like those involving the late DJ Savile contributed to the surge in recorded sexual offenses.Crime Prevention Minister Norman Baker commented, Under this coalition government, overall crime is down by more than 10% according to both the independent crime survey and police-recorded crime. Today's statistics are more good news, and the evidence is clear: police reform is working and crime is falling.Adam Pemberton, assistant chief executive at Victim Support, expressed approval of the crime decline but emphasized, It is important to remember that for many of the victims of 7.5 million crimes committed last year, the impact will have been severe and long-lasting.Chief Constable Jeff Farrar, head of crime statistics for the Association of Chief Police Officers, noted that the figures reflect the impact of significant operations on sexual abuse and fraud. The statistics do not include data from Scotland and Northern Ireland. In June of the previous year, the Scottish government reported a 13% decline in recorded crime for the year ending March 2013. In Northern Ireland, crime fell by 2.9% in 2012/13 compared to the previous year.

text: About one-third of workers in Clackmannanshire and Dumfries and Galloway will benefit from the national living wage, according to research. The Resolution Foundation has conducted an analysis revealing that the impact of the new national living wage will differ significantly across Scotland. Starting in April, workers aged 25 and over will see a new wage floor of £7.20 per hour. According to the UK government, this change will result in pay increases for millions.The study indicates that approximately 500,000 employees in Scotland will be affected by this wage adjustment. In regions like Clackmannanshire and Dumfries and Galloway, one-third of the workforce is expected to benefit, whereas only 16% of employees in Aberdeen will see a change. Similarly, Edinburgh (17%), Dundee (18%), and Glasgow (19%) show lower percentages of affected workers.The Foundation praises the introduction of the new wage but warns that its implementation poses greater challenges in areas with lower pay. It urges collaboration among the Scottish government, the Fair Work Convention, local leaders, and businesses to prevent job losses and ensure workers do not remain at the minimum wage threshold. Employers are encouraged to enhance productivity in sectors like retail, hospitality, cleaning, and care to make the national living wage sustainable.Furthermore, the Foundation criticizes the UK government's new pay structure, arguing it is not genuinely a living wage. They advocate for the broader adoption of the voluntary living wage of £8.25 nationwide.Conor D'Arcy, a policy analyst at the Resolution Foundation, remarked, The welcome new national living wage will significantly impact low pay, especially as it approaches £9 an hour by 2020. Our analysis suggests the pay rise should be manageable for most businesses, though implementing it will be challenging for some, particularly in lower-wage areas. Politicians must collaborate with employers to ensure the success of the national living wage, especially in low-paying sectors.A UK government spokesperson responded, The government is committed to ensuring Britain receives a pay rise while equipping businesses with the skills needed for success. We are witnessing record employment rates and real wage growth not seen since before the recession. The report highlights that workers in certain cities will experience even greater benefits, supporting our efforts to rebalance the economy through initiatives like the northern powerhouse and the devolution of powers to local governments and cities.

text: Algerian militant Mokhtar Belmokhtar is reported to have masterminded the two suicide bombings in Niger on Thursday. A spokesman from the Signed-in-Blood Battalion informed the Mauritanian news agency Alakhbar that he had supervised the recent attacks in collaboration with the group Mujao. These assaults targeted a military base in Agadez and a French-operated uranium mine in Arlit, resulting in the deaths of 21 individuals.On Friday, French special forces, alongside Nigerien troops, eliminated two militants who had taken refuge inside the Agadez base. Niger's Defence Minister, Kardijo Mahamadou, explained that the militants had barricaded themselves in a dormitory with two soldiers, who were subsequently rescued during the operation. Our military forces and French special forces assaulted the building, and the hostages—a total of two people—were freed, he told the Associated Press. The two kidnappers hiding in the military dorm were killed. The operation is now finished.Mahamadou further disclosed to RFI radio that eight Islamist militants were killed in the Agadez operation and two others in Arlit, noting, All of them were wearing belts packed with explosives. France's Defence Minister, Jean-Yves Le Drian, confirmed on BFM television that French troops intervened at the request of Nigerien President Mahamadou Issoufou, and the situation had stabilized. A French defence ministry official corroborated to AP that the two soldiers held hostage were freed during the assault, contradicting earlier reports from local and military sources to the BBC that they had been killed.The bombing on Thursday at the Agadez barracks claimed 19 lives, including 18 soldiers. Four attackers perished, while a fifth was subdued by security forces. The attack on the Somair mine in Arlit resulted in one death and 14 injuries, according to its operator, Areva.Alakhbar quoted El-Hassen Ould Khalil, a spokesman for al-Muwaqqioun bi-Dima (Signed-in-Blood Battalion), stating, It was Belmokhtar who himself supervised the operational plans of attacks. He added that the attacks targeted elite French forces providing security at the Areva-majority-owned uranium mine. An online statement, purportedly signed by Mokhtar Belmokhtar, declared, This is the first of our responses to the statement of the president of Niger—from his masters in Paris—that he eliminated jihad and the mujahideen militarily.The Movement for Unity and Jihad in West Africa (Mujao) also claimed responsibility for the attacks. However, Khalil's statement to Alakhbar indicated a joint effort with Mujao. Mujao spokesman Abu Walid Sahraoui told AFP on Thursday that their militants targeted the enemies of Islam in Niger, attacking France and Niger due to their cooperation in the war against Sharia. This was likely a reference to French and Nigerien efforts to expel Mujao and other Islamist groups from northern Mali earlier this year.Belmokhtar's group issued a warning against Western intervention in the region, stating, Columns of commandos and those seeking martyrdom are ready and waiting for their targets. They threatened further operations, asserting, We will have more operations, by the strength and power of Allah, and not only that, but we will move the battle to the inside of his country if he (the president of Niger) doesn't withdraw his mercenary army, as stated to Mauritania's ANI news agency.In response, French President Francois Hollande vowed on Thursday to safeguard French interests and collaborate with Niger in its fight against terrorism. Mokhtar Belmokhtar, believed to have orchestrated the deadly January attack on an Algerian gas plant that killed 37 hostages and 29 insurgents, had previously split from al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (AQIM) to form a new jihadist group known by various names, including the Signed-in-Blood Battalion.Chadian forces claimed he died in a raid in northern Mali on March 2, though no confirmation followed, and his death has been reported multiple times before. Mujao, a splinter group of AQIM operating mainly in northern Mali, aims to extend jihad throughout West Africa rather than limit it to the Sahel and Maghreb regions, AQIM's primary focus.

text: A judge in Argentina has been told to reopen a criminal investigation into former Top Gear host Jeremy Clarkson's infamous drive through the country. The filming of a special episode of Top Gear was abruptly halted last year due to protests over a controversial number plate on a Porsche driven by Jeremy Clarkson. The plate, which seemed to reference the 1982 Falklands War, was eventually replaced. Earlier this year, a local judge had determined that the Top Gear team did not act in bad faith when they changed the plates. However, a court has now decided to reopen the investigation, asserting that the crew swapped the plates with the knowledge that it was illegal.In 2014, the show sparked outrage among locals by featuring the registration number H982 FKL, which was perceived as a nod to the Falklands conflict. The situation escalated, forcing the Top Gear team to leave South America amidst intense protests. The show's vehicles were abandoned by the roadside as the crew faced a barrage of stones and had to be escorted to the airport.Andy Wilman, the executive producer of Top Gear, defended the show, insisting that the number plate had not been intentionally selected and that it was most definitely not a publicity stunt. Despite this, a group of Falklands War veterans appealed the case's closure, leading the court of appeals in Tierra del Fuego province to reopen it. The prosecution accuses Clarkson of falsifying, altering or suppressing the number of a legally registered object.Osvaldo Hillard, a spokesperson for the Centre for Malvinas Veterans, stated, We think that the Top Gear team changed the plates with full knowledge of the fact that it was illegal. The case will now proceed at Tierra del Fuego's High Court, a process that could take years to resolve. In Argentina, altering or suppressing a number plate can result in a prison sentence ranging from six months to three years.At the time, Wilman remarked, Top Gear production purchased three cars for a forthcoming programme; to suggest that this car was either chosen for its number plate, or that an alternative number plate was substituted for the original is completely untrue.Earlier this year, Clarkson was dismissed from the show after an altercation with a Top Gear producer. His colleagues, James May and Richard Hammond, along with Wilman, also departed to create a new car show for Amazon TV.

text: Manchester United have criticised the fans who sang chants about the Hillsborough disaster during Thursday's Europa League defeat at Liverpool. During Liverpool's 2-0 victory at Anfield in the first leg of their last-16 tie, offensive chants echoed through the stadium. These chants referenced the tragic Hillsborough disaster of 1989, where 96 Liverpool fans lost their lives during an FA Cup semi-final against Nottingham Forest. Manchester United swiftly condemned the chants, stating they have no place in the game.A Manchester United spokesperson emphasized, It has always been the position of Manchester United that chants of this nature, which refer to historical tragedies, do not reflect the values the club holds. The club is actively engaging with fans' groups to prevent such behavior in the future.Former Liverpool midfielder Ray Houghton expressed his dismay on BBC Radio 5 live, labeling the chants as dreadful. He stressed the importance of eradicating such behavior from the sport, noting, There were people in the crowd who lost loved ones at Hillsborough, and that's really hard to take. It's something we don't want to hear. Houghton also recalled similar incidents involving Liverpool fans referencing the Munich air disaster, which claimed the lives of eight United players and three club officials in February 1958. When you lower yourself to that level, it's quite remarkable, he remarked. It should have been a night of celebration; the fans should have been supporting their own team.BBC Sport's Juliette Ferrington, present at Anfield, described the atmosphere, noting that chants such as the Sun was right, a reference to the controversial coverage of the Hillsborough tragedy by The Sun newspaper, could be heard intermittently. The newspaper remains heavily boycotted in Merseyside. Ferrington added, It wasn't continuous but was clearly audible, maybe four or five times. It kind of got drowned out. The noise at the game was deafening. After the match, these chants were overshadowed by Liverpool fans singing You'll Never Walk Alone and celebrating their five European Cup victories.Former United striker Dion Dublin shared his disgust on BBC Radio Manchester, calling the songs disgusting. He commented, It leaves a bad taste in your mouth. It's not in good taste, and the people that were actually singing it should feel embarrassed.

text: Northern Ireland sprinter Leon Reid says he has no idea when he is going to be able to represent Ireland in international competition. Earlier this year, English-born athlete Reid, who has earned European junior and U23 medals for Britain, sought to change his international allegiance. However, his plans hit a roadblock due to the IAAF's decision to pause all nationality changes pending a comprehensive review. I don't really know what's going on now with it, Reid expressed to BBC Sport NI. He added, Athletics Ireland have been working on my behalf, but since the IAAF announcement by Sebastian Coe in February, there seems to be no progress.In February, IAAF President Sebastian Coe announced the formation of a working group to draft new regulations, responding to the backlash over the significant number of African athletes changing national allegiance in recent years. Countries like Bahrain and Qatar have attracted talented Kenyan and Ethiopian athletes, while several European nations have also benefited from the existing IAAF rules to bolster their teams with African athletes.At the Northern Ireland Championships in Belfast on Saturday, 22-year-old Reid showcased his talent by achieving a sprint double. He clocked 10.59 seconds in the 100m final, surpassing Paralympic star Jason Smyth. However, in the 200m semi-final, Reid narrowly missed the Commonwealth Games standard by 0.04 seconds, finishing in 20.81 seconds. The 200m final saw him struggle with less favorable wind conditions, resulting in a time of 21.12 seconds. I'm not having much luck at the moment. My blocks slipped back in the 100m final, which affected my start a lot, Reid explained. Yet, he remains optimistic, stating, I know I'm going to get the Commonwealth standards (100m 10.26, 200m 20.77). It's just a matter of time.Reid has improved his 100m personal best to 10.33 seconds this year and has recorded several wind-assisted times under 10.30 seconds. His 200m personal best stands at 20.62 seconds, set in 2015, with a best of 20.79 seconds this year.Meanwhile, Jason Smyth was satisfied with his 100m performance at the Mary Peters Track as he prepares for the IPC World Championships in London next month. The five-time Paralympic gold medallist recently spent three weeks at his former training base in Florida. However, he faced setbacks as one scheduled race was canceled due to a thunderstorm, and a date change prevented him from competing in another. So to an extent, I'm still trying to gather where I am at in terms of my form, Smyth noted. Despite these challenges, he remains positive, saying, I've been able to put in the work, which is very positive. So in that respect, a good foundation has been set down, and it should be just a matter of executing the races.After a successful period with coach Stephen Maguire and later Clarence Callendar in London, Smyth is now training with various coaches in Belfast, including Tom Reynolds from Athletics Northern Ireland. I am kind of going back to what worked in the past for me, Smyth shared.Smyth aims for a sprint double in London, having missed the opportunity to defend his T13 200m title at the last championships in Doha due to the birth of his daughter, Evie. However, he did secure the 100m title during those championships.

text: Prosecutors in Austria say former Kazakh ambassador Rakhat Aliyev, found dead in a Vienna prison on Tuesday, appears to have killed himself. Links provided will open externally. A post-mortem examination of Mr. Rakhat Aliyev, found hanging in an Austrian prison while awaiting trial for the murder of two Kazakh bankers, has prompted his lawyers to demand an investigation. Mr. Aliyev, formerly married to the daughter of Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev, had previously been sentenced in absentia in Kazakhstan for attempting to overthrow the government. Austria had consistently denied requests to extradite Aliyev, who was dismissed as Kazakhstan's ambassador to Vienna in 2007.On the day of his death, Aliyev was scheduled to testify against two ex-cellmates accused of blackmailing him with threats of orchestrating his murder to appear as a suicide. Austrian authorities have stated that no evidence suggests third-party involvement in his death. Vienna's deputy chief prosecutor, Gerhard Jarosch, confirmed that an experienced forensic expert examined Aliyev's body. The inspection of his body, the prison cell, and CCTV footage revealed no signs of violence or external interference.Deputy Chief Prosecutor Jarosch noted that results from a toxicological test, standard in judicial post-mortems, were expected shortly. These results would determine if Aliyev's blood contained substances other than his prescribed heart medication at the time of his death. After the alleged threats against him surfaced, Aliyev was relocated to a single cell but was not placed under suicide watch.One of Aliyev's attorneys, Klaus Ainedter, has called for a thorough investigation, expressing skepticism to the Austrian press agency APA. I have significant doubts, Ainedter stated. I visited him just [on Monday]. There was no indication of a suicide risk.Aliyev faced charges in 2007, with Austria twice rejecting extradition requests, citing concerns over the fairness of a potential trial in Kazakhstan. He had been in custody since June after voluntarily surrendering once Austria agreed to hold a trial. Aliyev denied the murder charges, labeling them as politically motivated. A businessman with extensive connections within the Kazakh elite, he had criticized President Nazarbayev following his dismissal as ambassador. Aliyev was previously married to Dariga Nazarbayeva, President Nazarbayev's eldest daughter.Since Kazakhstan's independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, President Nazarbayev has maintained a firm grip on power, prioritizing economic reform while resisting political democratization. Aliyev's case attracted significant attention in Austria, involving prominent lawyers and allegations that the Kazakh secret service attempted to sway the judicial process.

text: Apple has just turned 40 years old - a timely reason to track down a man who helped start the firm and then walked away. Venture an hour beyond the glittering lights of Las Vegas into the vast Nevada desert, and you'll stumble upon Pahrump, a place seemingly at the edge of civilization. Here resides Ronald G Wayne, co-founder of what has become the world's most valuable and influential company. Wayne, now 81, reflects on a pivotal moment in his past when he was 41, working at Atari, where he met a young Steve Jobs. Jobs often sought Wayne's counsel, asking questions ranging from starting a slot machine business—advised against—to embarking on a soul-searching journey to India, to which Wayne cautiously agreed.The question that altered the course of history came when Jobs asked for help in persuading Steve Wozniak, his brilliant partner, to focus on their shared vision. Wayne invited them to his Mountain View, California home for a discussion. Known for his charm and ingenuity, Wozniak, or Woz, was transforming business computers into personal devices, a project that captivated the Homebrew Computer Club. This group of tech enthusiasts was as passionate about reinventing electronics as children with a new box of Lego. Wozniak's creation, a circuit board, laid the groundwork for the Apple 1, later auctioned for $365,000 in 2015.Jobs wanted Wozniak's genius exclusively for Apple, but Wozniak was hesitant. Wayne, perceived by Jobs as more diplomatic, managed to convince Wozniak during a 45-minute conversation. He bought into it, Wayne recalls. Thus, the Apple Computer Company was born, with Wayne drafting the foundational documents on an IBM typewriter, much to Wozniak's amusement at Wayne's ability to produce legal language from memory.Ownership was divided straightforwardly: Jobs and Wozniak each took 45%, while Wayne received 10% and a role as the mediator in disputes. Yet, just twelve days later, Wayne opted out. Despite Apple's subsequent $600 billion market cap, he stood by his decision, citing very excellent reasons. Jobs had secured Apple's first major order of 50 machines from the Byte Shop, necessitating a $15,000 loan. However, Wayne, wary of the Byte Shop's payment reputation, feared personal liability for the debt. Jobs and Wozniak didn't have two nickels to rub together, Wayne noted, contrasting his own financial stability.Though stepping back from official duties, Wayne left his mark by designing Apple's first logo—an ink drawing of Newton under an apple tree. Jobs, however, instructed him to remove his signature. Months after parting ways, Wayne received an offer to relinquish any claims to Apple for $1,500, which he accepted, viewing it as found money.Pahrump, 500 miles and a world apart from Cupertino, Apple's headquarters, is where Wayne resides, surrounded by mementos of a life spent engineering and collecting. An old silver slot machine and a functioning 1930s radio in mahogany grace his home. He once crafted a detailed model of the Nautilus from 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea, relying on film stills rather than blueprints, later donating it to a museum.Despite the staggering value his 10% Apple share would hold today—nearly $60 billion—Wayne harbors no regrets. I would've been stuck heading a documentation department, shuffling papers for 20 years, he muses. I chose to pursue what appealed to me over money. His advice to youth is to find joy in one's work, ensuring it never feels like labor.Wayne's study houses fan mail, including a letter from Jason, who humorously questions whether the notoriously headstrong Jobs could handle Wayne's critiques. Reflecting on Jobs, Wayne acknowledges his pivotal role in Apple's success, despite not always being a nice guy. Wayne saw himself as the adult supervision to Jobs' ambition, even encouraging him to focus on financial success to pursue broader goals, though Jobs ultimately became consumed by Apple's operations.One regret lingers for Wayne: selling his original signed Apple contract for $500, a document that later fetched $1.6 million at auction in 2011. His home, devoid of Apple products, reflects his preference for building and customizing his own technology. Even an iPad 2, gifted in 2011, was given away, consistent with his life's pattern.Follow Dave Lee on Twitter @DaveLeeBBC and on Facebook.

We were convinced it was going to go down to the wire, remarked Archibald, 22, reflecting on the intense competition.America came out harder than us. In all the previous rides, we hadn't been leading until the last kilo, she added, acknowledging the formidable challenge posed by their American rivals, who clocked in at four minutes 12.454 seconds but couldn't keep up with the British team's momentum.Hailing from Milngavie, near Glasgow, Archibald shared her exhilaration in the immediate aftermath: I had a sneaky look at the end to see if we were there, and once you get that champing-on-the-bit sensation, we felt like superheroes, I suppose. It's pretty special. I've not won a team pursuit since the Europeans this year.The victory was an emotional moment for Archibald, who expressed, It's all the clichés at the moment; it's overwhelming, it's a dream come true, because nobody really expects that they'll make that gold medal. Every athlete goes through their injuries and trials and tribulations and whatnot. It will kick in in about 10 minutes, no doubt, and the legs will start hurting.Archibald's triumph is particularly noteworthy, considering her recovery from a severe motorbike accident last December, which resulted in a ruptured posterior cruciate knee ligament and a fractured elbow, forcing her to miss the World Championships in March.Her gold medal contribution has propelled Team GB to new heights at the Rio Games, marking Scotland's most successful Olympics on foreign soil with 10 medals, surpassing the previous record of eight at Sydney 2000. It's pretty mad, with Callum [Skinner, also a gold medal winner] getting in the track cycling scene, that progression over the last few years. I train as GB most of the year until the Commonwealth Games, so it's exciting when you see people that you've seen for years go through different programmes and different levels and now we're all at the top.

text: Hourly pay rates for Tesco store staff will rise by 10.5% over the next two years, the supermarket has said. Tesco is set to increase its hourly wage for workers from the current £7.62 to £8.42 by November 2018. Despite this rise, Tesco's pay will still lag behind competitors Aldi and Lidl, and the company plans to cut overtime pay for Sundays and Bank Holidays. By 2018, the pay hike will place Tesco employees above the anticipated National Living Wage of £7.90, which serves as the minimum wage for adults aged 25 and over. Presently, the National Living Wage stands at £7.50, with younger workers entitled to a lower rate.Government Budgets indicate that statutory minimum pay rates will continue their upward trend until at least 2020. Companies are adapting to these changes while also trying to stay competitive to attract and retain staff. In the UK, wage growth has been sluggish, yet inflation and wage increases at other supermarkets have prompted action. Aldi recently raised its hourly rate to £8.53, and Lidl offers £8.45 to store staff.Tesco plans to implement its wage increase in three phases: £8.02 in November 2017, £8.18 in July 2018, and finally £8.42 in November 2018. This reward package marks our largest store pay investment in a decade, providing colleagues with a sustainable pay deal that acknowledges their contributions while helping us attract new talent, stated Tesco UK chief executive Matt Davies. The retailer has also enhanced maternity pay terms. However, starting July 2018, extra pay for Sundays and Bank Holidays will be reduced from time-and-a-half to time-and-a-quarter.This adjustment aligns with government legislative requirements concerning the minimum wage, explained retail analyst Steve Dresser. As anticipated, many businesses facing this wage rise have had to cut premiums and perks to meet the core wage increases.

text: With the #OscarsSoWhite controversy and calls for the Brit Awards to be more truly representative, there has never been more discussion about diversity in the arts. In recent stage productions, such as Hamlet and King Lear, predominantly black, Asian, and ethnic minority (BAME) casts have taken center stage. Yet, some industry insiders argue that you can walk onto a building site and see more diversity than in the average theatre.Paapa Essiedu, currently starring as Hamlet with the Royal Shakespeare Company, believes theatre is caught between two worlds. He acknowledges the optimism about the future but feels the impact is not yet tangible. What is required is for people to be more bold and more adventurous in what they back, he asserts.In Manchester, the Royal Exchange's King Lear featured veteran actor Don Warrington in the lead role, a decision that should not be startling, according to Warrington. However, many reviews highlighted his race, which Warrington views as an indictment of where we are. While he acknowledges improvements since he began acting nearly 50 years ago, the fact that his casting sparks discussion indicates a lingering problem. He notes, There's a higher visibility, but the question is about the quality of that visibility and the quality of the parts. I don't think that is where it should be.Hamida Ali, Equity's equalities and diversity organizer, shares Warrington's concerns. She points out the surprise that still greets seeing a black actor in a lead role, not just in Shakespeare but across the board. It says something in itself that that remains something of note, she remarks. Ali notes a consensus on the existence of a problem, but debates continue about its causes, responsibility, and solutions.The Lear production was staged with Talawa, a theatre company founded in the 1980s to address the lack of opportunities for minority ethnic actors. Artistic director Michael Buffong insists that even after three decades, there is a rapid need for change. He emphasizes the necessity of diverse perspectives to avoid a narrow viewpoint.Essiedu concurs, stating that theatre needs to diversify the stories and storytellers. By doing that, there will be more opportunity for a more diverse group of actors, he says. We're in 2016 in an international, multicultural, integrated society, and we've got a responsibility as artists to reflect that in the work that we create.Matthew Xia, associate artistic director at the Royal Exchange, believes theatre has regressed in many ways. It's not just about the art; it's also about the organizational structure, he explains. Leadership roles lack proportional representation of the cities they serve. It's beyond me, because you can walk onto a building site and see more diversity than you can see in what is meant to be the liberal end of the work spectrum.Buffong emphasizes the need to change the gatekeepers, because that's where the power is. Casting a couple of black actors is not equivalent to telling a story from a particular perspective. Dawn Walton, founder of Sheffield's Eclipse, agrees, noting that theatre often focuses on stage diversity rather than systemic change. She argues that theatre boards remain stuck in old patterns while the country has evolved.Xia points out that actors of color are still expected to play peripheral roles unless race is a central theme, which he finds absurd. The human experience is so much broader than that, he states. He has heard directors express troubling views about casting, indicating a lack of understanding. Ultimately, people are always going to represent their world on stage, so if their world has been monocultural, it's highly likely that's how the work will be rendered.Neil Darlison, Arts Council England's director of theatre, acknowledges diversity as an ongoing issue. He warns that theatres not addressing it risk their business. However, he notes positive signs, especially in metropolitan areas where diversity in organizations is improving.Warrington calls for direct action to drive change, advocating for deliberate policies to make diversity an everyday practice. Buffong supports immediate measures like targets, quotas, and funding to achieve results now. The idea of more initiatives and training is so over, he says, emphasizing the need for opportunities.Ali highlights legal complexities that can hinder progress. While laws support equality, exemptions in casting for realism can impede it. She stresses that artistic decisions have industrial impacts, disproportionately affecting work opportunities.Essiedu suggests a straightforward solution: visibility. We mimic what we see, so we need to put that in front of people to get that machine started, he explains. He recalls not considering a Shakespearean lead until seeing Chiwetel Ejiofor in Othello. People from whatever background are only going to be inspired to write or perform if they see it.Hamlet will be screened in cinemas from June 8 and performed at the Royal Shakespeare Theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon from August 13.

text: Edinburgh Capitals captain Jacob Johnston was delighted as his team ended their losing run of games - but was then left to rue another defeat. The Edinburgh Capitals finally put an end to their seven-game losing streak with a 3-2 victory against the Dundee Stars at home on Saturday. However, their joy was short-lived as they suffered a 6-0 defeat in the rematch on Sunday at Tayside. This weekend's mixed results left coach Johnston with conflicting emotions, especially after the promising start at Murrayfield.Reflecting on the weekend, Johnston remarked, Saturday's win felt really good. We've faced some challenges recently, so breaking that losing streak was a relief. We aimed for a successful four-point weekend, given Dundee's proximity to us in the standings, but we fell short on Sunday. We must approach every game with the expectation of winning if we want to climb the ranks.Despite the weekend's ups and downs, the Capitals remain three points behind Dundee, though they have two games in hand over Marc LeFebvre's team. The Capitals' losing streak, during which they conceded a staggering 47 goals, finally ended with the 3-2 triumph at Murrayfield. Ian Schultz and Matt Tipoff scored in the first period, while Mason Wilgosh added a third goal early in the second. Although Dundee's Matt White and Kevin Bruijsten responded, they couldn't equalize, extending their poor form to 13 losses in 14 games.Sunday's rematch in Tayside saw the Stars break their own seven-game losing streak with a commanding 6-0 victory. Mikael Lidhammar, Brett Switzer, and two goals from Matt White gave Dundee a comfortable lead in the second period. Justin Faryna added two more in the third, sealing a satisfying night for the Stars.Meanwhile, the Fife Flyers had a successful weekend, starting with a 4-2 win against the Manchester Storm on Saturday. After a goalless first 35 minutes, Ryan Dingle broke the deadlock, only for Taylor Dickin to equalize. Dingle restored the lead, followed by Sebastien Thinel's goal. Matt Bissonnette pulled one back for Manchester, but Flyers debutant Bryan Cameron secured the victory with a fourth goal.In the return game on Sunday in Kirkcaldy, the Flyers completed their perfect weekend with a 3-1 win. Paul Phillips put Manchester ahead late in the first period, but the Flyers responded with goals from Brendan Brooks and Dingle, with Justin Fox scoring a late empty-netter.The Braehead Clan faced a challenging weekend, starting with a visit to the in-form Nottingham Panthers. Despite missing five players, the Clan secured a point in a 4-3 overtime loss. Lee Baldwin scored first, but the Panthers turned the game around with goals from Brian McGrattan and Matt Carter. Mike Hammond equalized for the Clan, and after goals from Jeff Brown and Alex Leavitt, the game went into overtime, where Robert Farmer scored the winner.Back in Glasgow, the Clan hosted league leaders Cardiff Devils and, despite a valiant effort, suffered a penalty shot defeat after a 2-2 draw. text: Sinn Féin has dismissed a proposal to stand independent anti-Brexit candidates as part of a general election pact in Northern Ireland. In the lead-up to the 8 June election, the SDLP proposed a collaborative strategy among parties that favored remaining in the EU, suggesting they field non-affiliated candidates. Colum Eastwood, the party's leader, believed this approach could unite pro-Remain factions. However, Sinn Féin's John O'Dowd dismissed the idea as not a credible offer.Despite some anti-Brexit parties discussing a progressive alliance, as described by Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill, to challenge pro-Brexit seats in the Westminster election, the proposal faced hurdles. The Democratic Unionist Party and the Ulster Unionists, both supporters of Brexit in the Commons, also explored the possibility of a unified unionist candidate in certain constituencies.Eastwood's suggestion aimed to introduce independent anti-Brexit candidates in East Londonderry, Fermanagh and South Tyrone, and North Belfast. However, O'Dowd made it clear that Sinn Féin would not support this plan, emphasizing that any alliance should focus on political party representation. He argued, We don't believe that's an acceptable way forward. It is political parties that will drive forward change in this society. He further suggested that the proposal seemed designed to hinder Sinn Féin and boost the SDLP, which he deemed contrary to the essence of a progressive alliance. Nonetheless, he expressed willingness to discuss potential agreements with other parties.Acknowledging the slim chances of his proposal's success, Eastwood admitted, If Sinn Féin have ruled that out, I think it's very, very difficult. He stressed the importance of a broad, non-nationalist coalition, stating, We wanted this to be broad; we wanted this to be non-nationalist; we wanted to go right across the political spectrum.Meanwhile, the Green Party, led by Steven Agnew, declared it would not align with parties that didn't share its vision for a progressive society. Agnew noted that the SDLP's choice of Alasdair McDonnell as their South Belfast candidate effectively ended any possibility of a local agreement.

text: Police Scotland has said that it does not collate or hold specific figures on child sexual exploitation. BBC Scotland, through a series of Freedom of Information requests, sought to uncover the number of recorded cases, concerns, and complaints regarding child exploitation and child sexual exploitation over the past four years. However, Police Scotland revealed that such data is not consolidated within a single system, a disclosure that Scotland's Children's Commissioner described as disturbing.Coinciding with this revelation, a new police unit was launched to tackle the intricate issues of child abuse and neglect across Scotland. This unit aims to bolster local teams in conducting thorough investigations into cases of child sexual exploitation, online offenses, and other forms of abuse.In response to the BBC's inquiries, Police Scotland clarified: Child exploitation encompasses a wide range of criminal activities and does not align with a specific offense. It involves various offenses, and the level of data requested is not held on a single system.This situation emerges in the aftermath of the Jay report published last summer, which exposed the harrowing sexual exploitation of over 1,400 children in Rotherham, South Yorkshire. Last year, Glasgow City Council reported that 97 children in the city were either victims of or at risk of sexual exploitation. While the Association of Chief Police Officers noted that most forces in England and Wales now mark such offenses in their records, senior officers in Scotland highlight the challenges in implementing a similar system. Children's Commissioner Tam Baillie expressed concern: I am disturbed that we do not yet collect police figures on children who are the subject of sexual exploitation. This was a recommendation of the Scottish Parliament and is part of the Scottish government action plan on child sexual exploitation. Understanding the scope of the problem is crucial for an appropriate and proportionate response.Assistant Chief Constable Malcolm Graham of Police Scotland remarked on the challenges of addressing child sexual exploitation, noting that victims are unlikely to report abuse. He stated, Our priority is to focus on identifying as many victims as we can and targeting perpetrators to prevent these devastating crimes. Scotland is at the forefront of approaches to child sexual exploitation. While sexual exploitation is a form of abuse, it is not recorded as a specific crime type. Victims may suffer repeated rapes, physical assaults, or grooming offenses, and we categorize all these in crime recording.He emphasized, Our main focus is on identifying victims and addressing child protection issues to keep children safe.Martin Crewe, director of Barnardo's Scotland, highlighted the importance of the Rotherham case as a wake-up call, leading to the Scottish government's national action plan. We welcome the police's efforts but acknowledge that more needs to be done. Our concern is that we do not fully understand the extent of the problem, he said.In January 2013, Aileen Campbell, Minister for Children and Young People, responded to an inquiry into Child Sexual Exploitation in Scotland, announcing measures to improve the identification of such exploitation by Scotland's new single police force. However, sexual exploitation remains unrecorded and not centrally collated.The Scottish government stated that while figures on the broader issue of child abuse are available, the safety of children is a top priority. A spokeswoman noted, The launch of the National Child Abuse Investigation Unit will help bring to justice those who harm our young people. The unit addresses all forms of child abuse, including sexual exploitation. We have robust legislation for various offenses, including online abuse, and are working to strengthen the law further.She added, Assessing the problem is challenging due to the concealed nature of abuse. Prevention and swift action to safeguard children are central to our strategy against these crimes. Victims may have been subjected to repeated sexual assaults, assaults or grooming, all of which is recorded on the system of recording offences,” the minister said. It was in January, 2013, that the Minister for Children and Young People, Aileen Campbell, in answer to an inquiry into the sexual exploitation of children, announced measures to improve the identification of such exploitation by the new police force in Scotland. The Scottish government said that, although no figures are available, it is committed to the safety of children. A spokeswoman said: "The National Child Abuse Investigation Unit will help to bring to justice those who are guilty of harming our children." The director of Barnardo's in Scotland, Martin Crewe, has described the Rotherham case as a "wake-up call" that has led to the Scottish government's national action plan. She added, “It is difficult to estimate the extent of the problem, because of the hidden nature of such abuses. But the prevention and quick reaction to protect children is at the heart of our strategy against such crimes. This includes sexual exploitation.” We have good legislation for all sorts of crimes, including cybercrime, and we are working to strengthen the law still further. It includes a sound national child protection plan, the fight against new forms of child abuse, such as sexual exploitation, a national awareness campaign and advice for employees of night-time establishments such as taxi drivers and hotel workers, who may encounter vulnerable children.

text: The range and quality of research at Scotland's universities has been praised in a new UK-wide survey. Scottish universities have largely upheld or enhanced their positions in the latest league table, with the University of Edinburgh securing an impressive 4th place and the University of Glasgow landing at 13th. Over 85% of research conducted by Scottish universities was deemed to have an outstanding or very significant impact on society and the economy, surpassing the UK average, according to an analysis by Research Fortnight based on the 2014 Research Excellence Framework (REF 2014). This comprehensive evaluation scrutinized the quality of research across various subjects at UK universities, involving panels of experts who assessed work from more than 52,000 academics across 154 institutions.Both Edinburgh and Glasgow universities ascended by one position compared to the previous 2008 rankings. Other Scottish institutions, including St Andrews, Strathclyde, Aberdeen, Dundee, Heriot-Watt, and Stirling, also made it into the top 50. Notably, Strathclyde's physics department was celebrated as the best in the UK, outshining prestigious institutions like Oxford, Cambridge, and Imperial College. While Aberdeen and Dundee experienced a slight decline in overall rankings, the other universities showed progress.The data broadly indicates that Scottish universities have either maintained or improved their research standings since the abolition of tuition fees for Scottish students. International rankings further suggest that the overall status of Scottish universities remains stable. All 18 higher education institutions in Scotland conduct research recognized as world-leading, and the country exceeds the UK average in research impact assessments.For the first time, REF 2014 also evaluated the influence of research on the economy, society, public policy, culture, and quality of life. Laurence Howells, chief executive of the Scottish Funding Council, remarked, Today we have had confirmation that our universities' research is world-leading and impacts on almost every aspect of daily life, from the way we treat patients in hospital, to the way we communicate with smartphones. By making the most of our investments in research, Scotland's universities are rightly on the podium with the best in the world. It is particularly satisfying that Scotland's pioneering approach to collaboration through research pooling has helped to bring this success in the REF.The University of Edinburgh's three colleges each had at least one research area ranked top in the UK. Specifically, Edinburgh's research in Sociology, Earth Systems and Environmental Sciences, and Computer Science and Informatics was rated the best in the UK, based on the breadth and quality of research. Prof Sir Timothy O'Shea, the principal, stated, Research at the University of Edinburgh is constantly expanding the depth of human knowledge and making an impact on the wider world—whether it be improving the effectiveness of youth justice policy and practice, or shaping the technologies used to manage the world's data. Our outstanding researchers enable us to forge links with charities, businesses, policymakers, and other universities, so that together we can tackle long-standing challenges at home and overseas.The University of Glasgow highlighted its achievements in pioneering medical research with new drugs and treatments, innovative software for electric motor design, novel methods for controlling animal diseases like TB in cattle and rabies, and positive impacts on knife crime policy. Additionally, they contributed to transforming Stirling Castle into a leading heritage site in the UK. Principal and vice-chancellor Prof Anton Muscatelli noted, It is particularly pleasing that, in line with the aspirations of the university set out in the university's 2020 Global Vision, 31% of our output was judged to be of 'world-leading' quality. This success lies at the very heart of our contribution to the UK's economy and, in particular, Scotland's economy.Education Secretary Angela Constance welcomed the report, emphasizing Scotland's global recognition for pioneering research, with four universities ranking among the world's top 200—more per capita than any country except Switzerland. She added, The 2014 Research Excellence Framework has now shown that all of our institutions are producing world-class research in a variety of areas. Research is also key to our economic growth and prosperity. Figures published earlier this year showed that our £124m investment in eight innovation centers has the potential to generate up to £1.5bn and around 5,000 jobs for the economy, through sectors such as energy, aquaculture, and construction.However, the University and College Union (UCU) warned that world-leading research is often conducted by individuals on zero-hours contracts. They urged institutions not to use any perceived low scores as a pretext for staff reductions. Mary Senior, a UCU Scotland official, stated, Our universities must be free to continue pushing the boundaries in their cutting-edge work. We must also recognize that a lot of research not included or rated highly in the REF is still incredibly important. Too often our world-leading research is being conducted by people with little or no job security. Universities must avoid any knee-jerk reactions to the results or use perceived low scores to try and make unnecessary cuts. We are not alone in criticizing what we see as a flawed process when it comes to the REF and have outlined the need for a fundamental overhaul of the research system. We want to see better funding that expands our research base, covering more institutions and more diverse areas of research.

text: The mother of an RAF airman who went missing more than three weeks ago has said she absolutely believes her son is still alive. Corrie Mckeague, a 23-year-old gunner stationed at RAF Honington in Suffolk, disappeared following a night out in Bury St Edmunds in the early hours of September 24. His mother, Nicola Urquhart, expressed her disbelief over his sudden disappearance during an interview on the BBC's Victoria Derbyshire programme, stating, Nobody can just disappear.Ms. Urquhart mentioned that it wouldn't be out of character for her son to accept a ride from a stranger. Originally from Dunfermline in Fife, Mr. Mckeague was last seen on CCTV at 03:20 BST, strolling alone and eating takeaway food in Bury St Edmunds. His mobile phone was traced in Bury St Edmunds on the morning of September 24, before moving to the Barton Mills area.According to Ms. Urquhart, phone data indicates that the journey between the two locations took 28 minutes, which aligns with the driving time. However, it remains unclear if Mr. Mckeague had the phone with him during this time. She remarked that getting into a stranger's car was genuinely something Corrie would do, noting his tendency to offer lifts to strangers if he saw them walking while he was driving.Despite ongoing efforts, police have yet to locate either Mr. Mckeague or his phone. Ms. Urquhart mentioned several reasons why the phone's signal might be lost, such as a dead battery or damage. She highlighted the extensive amount of CCTV footage police are reviewing, stating, They've got so much CCTV they've still not been able to watch it all.The search has expanded, with authorities examining private CCTV footage, yet no new images of Mr. Mckeague have surfaced. Ms. Urquhart believes that somebody does know something about her son's disappearance, although the public has been eager to assist. But nothing, not one person [has been able to] give us anything - and that just doesn't make sense, she lamented.Anyone with potentially relevant information is urged to contact the Suffolk Police incident room at 01473 782019. The Victoria Derbyshire programme airs weekdays from 09:00 to 11:00 on BBC Two and the BBC News Channel.

text: UN human rights chief Zeid Raad Al Hussein has described the Syrian city of Aleppo as a slaughterhouse. In a recent address, a speaker highlighted the siege and relentless bombardment of Aleppo's rebel-held east as crimes of historic proportions occurring in Syria. Over the past month, nearly 500 lives have been lost and 2,000 individuals injured since government forces, bolstered by Russian airstrikes, initiated an offensive on the eastern part of the city.The Syrian government has attributed civilian suffering to the actions of terrorists. Meanwhile, the United Nations announced that a lack of security guarantees had compelled them to postpone planned medical evacuations from Aleppo. This delay coincided with the second 11-hour humanitarian pause unilaterally declared by the government and its ally, Russia, on Friday. Russia also announced a suspension of airstrikes between 08:00 and 19:00 local time (05:00-16:00 GMT) on Saturday, ostensibly to allow civilians and rebels to exit the city through designated safe corridors. However, reports indicate that very few have utilized this opportunity, with rebel groups arguing that it equates to forced displacement and surrender.Aleppo, once Syria's largest city and a bustling commercial and industrial center, has been ravaged by conflict since 2012, leaving it divided. President Bashar al-Assad's forces control the west, while rebels hold the east. In early September, government troops and Iranian-backed militias cut off the rebels' final access route to the east, placing its 275,000 residents under siege. Two weeks later, following the breakdown of a US-Russia brokered nationwide truce, the government launched a ground offensive to seize full control of the city, accompanied by an aerial assault of unprecedented ferocity.During an emergency session of the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva on Friday, Mr. Zeid cautioned that crimes of historic proportions were being perpetrated in eastern Aleppo and elsewhere in Syria. He described Aleppo, once a beacon of ancient civility and beauty, as now resembling a slaughterhouse, where the lifeless bodies of small children are trapped under streets of rubble and pregnant women deliberately bombed.Mr. Zeid further stated that his team had documented violations of international humanitarian law by all parties in Aleppo. He noted that while armed opposition groups continue to launch mortars and other projectiles into civilian areas of western Aleppo, it is the indiscriminate airstrikes by government forces and their allies across the eastern part of the city that account for the vast majority of civilian casualties. These violations constitute war crimes, he emphasized. And if knowingly committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack directed against civilians, they constitute crimes against humanity.The commissioner criticized the international community, particularly the UN Security Council, for failing to protect civilians and stop the violence, stating that this failure should haunt every one of us. In response, Syria's permanent representative to the UN, Hussam al-Din Ala, delivered an impassioned statement, asserting that the Syrian government was engaged in a battle against terrorism.Subsequently, the charity Save the Children issued a warning, citing reports from aid workers and medical professionals in eastern Aleppo about the widespread use of cluster bombs, which are prohibited under international law. They referenced the Violations Documentation Centre, an activist-run organization, which recorded 137 cluster-bomb attacks in Aleppo from 10 September to 10 October—a staggering 791% increase compared to the average of the previous eight months.
