text: Sipping from a cup of tea in the Hampden dressing room, surrounded by jubilant players and coaches, Roy MacGregor might have dwelled upon how far Ross County have come. In a moment of triumph that seemed to encapsulate the spirit of Ross County, the club's chairman watched with pride as long-time staff members, some carrying on a legacy from their parents, celebrated on the pitch at the national stadium. The team had just secured a 2-1 victory over Hibernian to claim the Scottish League Cup. This victory was a tapestry of individual stories, yet all threads seemed to converge on MacGregor.Jim McIntyre, the victorious manager, affectionately referred to his chairman as Mr. Ross County and expressed his joy at delivering the club's first major trophy to him. As the players paraded the cup, MacGregor and McIntyre shared a heartfelt embrace. A particularly poignant moment came when MacGregor lifted his grandson, drawing loud cheers and applause from the County supporters.Though MacGregor appeared modest in the limelight, he has long maintained that County should function as a community club, grounded in family values. His leadership, both in personality and financial backing, has been instrumental in County's rise. Reflecting on 1985, when County languished at the bottom of the Highland League, underscores the magnitude of this achievement.This isn't the end of the journey, MacGregor remarked, acknowledging the shared path with McIntyre. The manager, valuing discipline, insisted that celebrations would be brief due to training on Monday and an important match against St Johnstone on Wednesday. County’s sights are set on a top-six finish, so the revelry would have to wait.A man of deep faith, MacGregor built a global engineering business but always prioritized his local community. He humorously noted that Dingwall, with its 6,000 residents, seemed deserted as over 9,000 Ross County fans flocked to Hampden.The match itself was challenging, with Hibs dominating possession for much of the first half. However, County's victory was punctuated by inspiring moments. Jackson Irvine was a relentless force in midfield, his energy and strategic play creating the opening goal for Michael Gardyne. Irvine's boots bore his grandfather's name, a nod to the man who introduced him to football in Australia. He flew his family from Melbourne to witness the final.The winning goal was emblematic of determination. Brian Graham, impactful as a substitute, helped County gain ground with his forward play. In the 90th minute, he won the ball, allowing Gardyne to dash down the left. Despite an earlier injury scare, Gardyne pressed on, delivering a cross that was cleared only to land at Alex Schalk's feet. Schalk, overcoming cramp, tapped the ball in and sprinted to celebrate with County fans.The goal was a harsh blow for Liam Fontaine, who had equalized in the first half. Desperate to make amends, he pushed forward, but his late overhead kick was saved by Gary Woods. Fontaine, along with several Hibs players, was visibly emotional at the end. Despite their contributions—Henderson's energy, McGinn's creativity, and McGregor's steadfast defense—they fell short. Alan Stubbs acknowledged his team's superiority in the first half, but lamented their lack of composure in the final third, as Cummings and Stokes struggled to connect effectively.McIntyre's bold decision to field a back three for the first time this season could have backfired, and County initially struggled with the unfamiliar formation. Yet, they emerged victorious. MacGregor's investment, both financial and personal, coupled with McIntyre's strategic acumen, culminated in this historic win for County. It also marked a significant moment for Highland football, with Ross County and Inverness Caledonian Thistle now holding Scotland's major cup trophies. This thought surely brings an extra smile to MacGregor's face.

text: UK astronaut Tim Peake has begun his life in space with tea and a bacon sandwich. On Tuesday, Tim Peake reached the International Space Station after launching from Kazakhstan's Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Soyuz rocket. Enthusiastically sharing his experiences on Twitter, he expressed that he was loving every minute of his initial days in space.Later today, Peake will engage with journalists through a live link from the European Astronaut Centre in Cologne, Germany. Peake is part of a six-member crew currently residing and working aboard the ISS. Among them is US station commander Scott Kelly, who is undertaking a year-long mission on the station. In a lighthearted tweet, Peake, a 43-year-old from Chichester in Sussex, praised Kelly: What makes a good leader? @StationCDRKelly having a hot bacon sarnie waiting as my 1st meal on #ISS. Boy that tasted good! #Principia. He continued, 1st 48hrs on ISS - busy but incredible. Amazing how fast the body adapts to new environment. Found my tea ... life is good!The former Army aviator and helicopter test pilot received warm wishes from notable figures such as the Queen and Sir Elton John following his successful launch and docking. In a nod to Sir Elton John, Peake tweeted a line from the iconic song Rocket Man in response to a good luck message. He also acknowledged the Queen's support after Buckingham Palace's Twitter account shared a letter of encouragement from the monarch.Today, Peake will briefly pause his busy schedule to address the press via a live stream on the European Space Agency's website. As outlined by the European Space Agency, his packed agenda includes tasks such as unpacking cargo, exercising on a stationary bike for an hour, and participating in an experiment examining the effects of microgravity on bone marrow.For those eager to learn more about Tim Peake's journey in space, a special report page offers the latest news, analysis, and videos. Additional content includes a video titled Bye bye Daddy, a photo gallery of the space station flight, and an explainer on how to become an astronaut.

text: The wife of Turkey's president has described the harem of the Ottoman era as an educational establishment that prepared women for life, reports say. During an official event in Ankara focusing on Ottoman sultans, Emine Erdogan made remarks that have stirred debate, as reported by Turkish TV stations. Her statements followed closely on the heels of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s assertion that a woman is above all a mother, which he made in a speech commemorating International Women's Day.In the Ottoman Empire, the sultans resided in Istanbul's Topkapi Palace, where they maintained a harem, now a museum since 1924. This harem was home to the sultan's wives, female relatives, and numerous concubines, with male staff being eunuchs. Emine Erdogan described the harem as an educational institution for the Ottoman dynasty's women, suggesting that the legacy of these women could serve as an inspiration, according to Turkish media.While concubines in the harem received some education and were well-fed, they were not free to leave the palace at will, and not all were used for sexual purposes. This characterization of the harem as a school provoked swift backlash on social media. Critics, like @GaziCaglar, dismissed the notion, stating, Receiving education in harem doesn't make it a school. This is nonsense, estimating there were about 400 concubines. Another user, @anlam75, questioned, If the Ottoman harem was a scholarly institution then why were the men who worked there castrated? Meanwhile, @kizmonot noted, Those who mention harem do not send their daughters to anything less than American universities, highlighting that the Erdogans' daughters attended Indiana University.However, some, including pro-government journalist Ceren Kenar, defended Mrs. Erdogan's comments, acknowledging that women did receive education in the harem. This controversy echoes past remarks by President Erdogan, who in 2014 sparked outrage by declaring that women and men are not equal. His recent comments on women's roles have also led to street protests in Istanbul.

text: All living flowers ultimately derive from a single ancestor that lived about 140 million years ago, a study suggests. A groundbreaking study has pieced together the visage of the ancestral flower by merging evolutionary models with an unprecedented dataset of living flower characteristics. This research, published in Nature Communications, provides a glimpse into the flower that existed over 140 million years ago. The reconstructed ancestral bloom featured multiple concentric cycles of petal-like organs in trios, arranged in whorls, and was bisexual in nature.Hervé Sauquet from Université Paris-Sud, France, a co-author of the study, remarked, There is no living flower that looks exactly like the ancestral one - and why should there be? This is a flower that existed at least 140 million years ago and has had considerable time to evolve into the incredible diversity of flowers that exist today.Flowers, the reproductive structures of approximately 90% of all terrestrial plants, captivate us with their beauty, yet their origins and initial evolution remain shrouded in mystery. The scarcity of fossilized flowers from the era when the ancestral flower is believed to have existed complicates this enigma.Dr. Jason Hilton from the University of Birmingham, UK, who was not involved in the study, commented, The structure and organisation of the ancestral flower has remained enigmatic. For instance, we don't know if the oldest flowers were unisexual or bisexual, or if they were pollinated by wind or insects.To visualize the first flower, scientists meticulously recorded traits such as petals and sepals from 792 extant species. They then mapped these traits onto the evolutionary tree of flowering plants, constructing an image of flowers at critical historical junctures, including the last common ancestor of all current flowers.The ancestral flower was reconstructed with petal-like structures in a whorl pattern, akin to a common lily but with more whorls, contrasting with a spiral arrangement seen in flowers like the lotus. Hervé Sauquet noted, For some of the features we studied, the result was surprising, especially the fact that organs (such as sepals and petals and the stamens) were probably arranged in whorls instead of spirals, as commonly assumed for the ancestral flower.The evolution of sex in flowers has been a topic of intense debate. This study suggests that the earliest flowers were likely bisexual, containing both male and female organs. Dr. Jason Hilton emphasized the significance of these findings, stating, This study is important as it tells us how complicated the ancestral flower is likely to be - now the search is on to find it or something closely resembling it in the fossil record. That's if the model is correct - only time (and further study) will tell.

text: The Solar Impulse plane has broken the record for the longest non-stop solo flight without refuelling. Seventy-six hours into the latest leg of its global circumnavigation attempt, a significant milestone was reached. Pilot Andre Borschberg is steadily advancing in his groundbreaking endeavor to complete the first solar-powered flight across the Pacific Ocean. After departing from Nagoya, Japan, early Monday local time, Borschberg has successfully passed Midway Island and is now en route to his destination in Kalaeloa, Hawaii.At the 76-hour mark, Borschberg shattered the record for the longest non-stop solo flight without refueling, surpassing the previous record set by American Steve Fossett in 2006. Fossett's jet-powered Virgin GlobalFlyer had circled the globe in that time, covering over 41,000 kilometers. In contrast, Borschberg's Solar Impulse, which operates entirely without fuel, covered approximately 5,500 kilometers in the same duration.On Wednesday, the Swiss pilot flew in a holding pattern to time his approach to an impending cold front, expected on Thursday. To successfully navigate the final stretch into Kalaeloa on Friday, Borschberg requires optimal sun conditions to elevate his aircraft above the weather system. The exact timing of this historic landing remains uncertain, as the Solar Impulse has stringent constraints for safe landing, including a maximum crosswind of four knots and an overall wind speed cap of ten knots. If ground-level winds are excessive, Borschberg will continue circling until conditions improve. By the journey's end, he is likely to have spent over 120 hours in the air.Remarkably, Borschberg has managed on minimal sleep and even found time to indulge in some humor on Wednesday, donning a wig and fake beard in his cockpit. Upon arrival in Hawaii, he will be greeted by fellow adventurer and business partner, Bertrand Piccard. The duo has shared piloting duties in the single-seater plane's global quest, which commenced in Abu Dhabi, UAE, in March. Piccard, known for completing the first non-stop global circumnavigation in a balloon, will pilot the next leg from Kalaeloa to Phoenix, Arizona. Although shorter than the current segment, this leg is expected to take four days and nights.From Phoenix, Solar Impulse will journey to New York, followed by an Atlantic crossing that will ultimately return the plane to Abu Dhabi. Throughout their global expedition, Borschberg and Piccard have used various stopovers to advocate for clean technologies. The Solar Impulse is not intended as a future aviation model but as a demonstration of solar power's current capabilities. The aircraft is equipped with 17,000 photovoltaic cells that either power its electric motors directly or charge its lithium-ion batteries for nighttime flight.The journey's legs have included: - LEG 1: 9 March. Abu Dhabi (UAE) to Muscat (Oman) - 772 km in 13 hours and 1 minute - LEG 2: 10 March. Muscat (Oman) to Ahmedabad (India) - 1,593 km in 15 hours and 20 minutes - LEG 3: 18 March. Ahmedabad (India) to Varanasi (India) - 1,170 km in 13 hours and 15 minutes - LEG 4: 18 March. Varanasi (India) to Mandalay (Myanmar) - 1,536 km in 13 hours and 29 minutes - LEG 5: 29 March. text: Online touts who bulk buy tickets and sell them for inflated prices will face unlimited fines under government plans. An amendment to the Digital Economy Bill will soon make it illegal to use bots to circumvent limits on ticket purchases. These bots have been notorious for snapping up tickets, which then appear on resale websites at exorbitant prices, far exceeding their original value. A spokesperson from the Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) condemned this profiteering as simply not fair.Prominent artists like Adele and Ed Sheeran have spoken out against such practices, urging fans to avoid buying tickets from secondary platforms. Last month, Viagogo, a resale site, faced accusations of moral repugnance for listing tickets to an Ed Sheeran Teenage Cancer Trust concert for as much as £5,000. Similarly, tickets for Adele's show at the O2 in London, originally priced at £85, were reportedly sold for an astonishing £24,840.In response to these issues, ministers are adopting the full recommendations from a review by Professor Michael Waterson. His report advocates for stricter anti-bot measures, a mechanism to report bot attacks, more rigorous enforcement of existing consumer rights laws, and potential further actions against unscrupulous ticket traders if the industry fails to self-regulate.The government is pressing major players in the secondary ticket market to better identify ticket touts and distinguish them from genuine fans reselling tickets they can no longer use. Heavy metal enthusiasts Brian and Jane O'Donoghue, who aim to attend a concert monthly, describe the ticket-buying experience as incredibly frustrating due to touts. Recently, they paid £250 each for Black Sabbath tickets at Birmingham's O2 Arena, more than double the face value, via a secondary site. It was the only way, said Brian, 51, from Hereford. He explained that they even considered traveling to Copenhagen to see Metallica, as the total cost, including flights and a hotel, was comparable. Despite his efforts to purchase tickets directly, they often sell out within minutes. For their next concert, Iron Maiden, they managed to secure face-value tickets and have been instructed to bring their payment card and photo ID. That's the way ahead, Brian remarked, though he anticipates many might show up with just their ticket and face disappointment.Should progress stall, ministers are prepared to take further steps to ensure compliance with consumer law. The government has faced mounting pressure from celebrities to address ticket touting. Josh Francheschi, lead singer of You Me At Six, testified before a committee last year, advocating for a ban on bots, stating fans are the main losers. In New York, the use of such technology was criminalized last year after a report revealed a bot purchased 1,000 tickets in a single minute for a U2 concert at Madison Square Garden.Jo Dipple, CEO of UK Music, praised the move. Massive profit is made by people who are taking value out of the music industry and putting tickets out of the reach of music fans, she stated. Banning bots is a step towards ensuring the ticketing market for live events works more fairly for gig-goers.Minister of State for Digital and Culture, Matt Hancock, expressed his disapproval: It's unacceptable that touts are misusing technology to bypass security measures and buy up vast numbers of tickets before real fans get the chance, only to sell them on at rip-off prices. It's a growing problem that affects too many people.In December, the Competition and Markets Authority launched an investigation into any suspected breaches in this market. Mr. Hancock added, This profiteering is simply not fair, so we are acting to put fans first and improve the chances of seeing our favorite musicians and sports stars at a reasonable price. Ticket sellers need to do more, by improving transparency and ensuring that they are acting in the best interests of consumers and help the market work for everyone.

text: A petition calling for jousting to be made an Olympic sport has been launched by English Heritage. Dominic Sewell, a jousting expert with the charity English Heritage, shared with BBC Radio 5 live that jousting is a worldwide phenomenon that should be recognised. Despite only around 20 competitive jousters in the UK, the charity highlighted that tournaments occur globally. However, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) reported being unaware of any formal request for the sport's recognition.For a sport to be considered for the Olympic Games, it must be governed by an international federation, widely practised, and meet several criteria before the IOC's executive board considers it. English Heritage has initiated contact with both the IOC and the Federation Equestre Internationale (FEI), which oversees all Olympic equestrian disciplines, as the first step towards jousting's potential Olympic inclusion.English Heritage stated that jousting must first gain recognition from the FEI before the IOC can consider it as an Olympic sport. Mr. Sewell, who competes in jousting, remarked, Just like the Olympic British equestrian team, we ride beautiful horses to an exceptional level. He emphasized that jousting demands a huge amount of skill and a daily training regime, requiring competitors to be strong, not just physically but mentally, so you can sit fearlessly in your saddle, face your rival, and offer yourself as a target.A former furniture assembler, Sewell explained, This has gone from being a hobby to being a sport and a career. Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, he recounted how his interest sparked from attending historical re-enactments, yet clarified, I'm a sportsman, I'm not an actor. He added, As soon as I got on a horse everything changed and I thought: this is what I want to do, I want to be good at this.English Heritage acknowledged the long road ahead for jousting's Olympic recognition but noted encouraging signs. The sport's popularity is rising, with tournaments now held in Belgium, Brazil, and New Zealand. In the United States, where jousting has been Maryland’s official state sport since 1962, there is a similar push for Olympic recognition.Sewell describes modern jousting as quite a safe sport to take part in. He explained, The rules are essentially that you are in a single combat situation, in a designated area, in a pitch—or 'tilt-yard'—and in that yard is a tilt rail. Competitors charge down the rail towards each other, earning points based on the style and strength of their hit. Clad in armor weighing about 20kg, athletes wield a 12ft lance in one hand and reins in the other, galloping towards opponents at speeds up to 30mph. These days injuries are few and far between... but the odd un-horsing might result in a few bruises, Sewell noted.The IOC is currently reviewing its programme as part of Olympic Agenda 2020, aiming to make it more flexible by shifting from a sport-based to an event-based programme. A spokesman revealed, One recommendation was to make the Olympic programme more flexible by moving from a sport-based to an event-based programme. Earlier this month, the IOC supported a bid to include karate, skateboarding, sports climbing, surfing, and baseball/softball in Tokyo 2020, potentially adding 18 events and 474 athletes.Jousting, with roots in Ancient Greece as a war preparation activity, emerged in England in the 10th Century for knights to refine their equine and lance skills. The first recorded tournament in England was organized by Frenchman Godfrey de Preuilly in 1066. The sport's popularity led King Henry II to ban it in the 12th Century due to its danger, although King Richard I later lifted the ban. Jousting remained popular, particularly during the Tudor era, but declined after the death of French King Henry I in a joust in 1559. The sport saw a resurgence in the 19th Century, romanticized by writers like Lord Byron, Percy Shelley, and Sir Walter Scott, who celebrated chivalry through tales of knights and fair maidens.

text: Two 15-year-olds have been given life sentences with 20-year minimum terms for the murder of a mother and daughter in Lincolnshire in April. In a chilling case that has shocked the nation, dinner lady Elizabeth Edwards, 49, and her 13-year-old daughter Katie were brutally murdered in their sleep at their home in Spalding. The crime, committed by two teenagers who were both 14 at the time, has been described by Mr. Justice Haddon-Cave at Nottingham Crown Court as a terrible crime which has few parallels in modern criminal history.The young perpetrators, now recognized as Britain's youngest double murderers, carried out the heinous act on April 13 at Dawson Avenue, Spalding. Following the murders, the pair engaged in a bizarre sequence of events, sharing a bath, having sex, and watching four Twilight vampire films. The judge condemned their actions, describing them as grotesque and highlighting the defining and particularly chilling nature of the case.Addressing the teenagers, the judge remarked, There is a clear intention to kill both victims—both defendants admitted wanting to murder them. He emphasized the remarkable premeditation and planning, which was described as substantial, meticulous, and repeated. The brutal nature of the killings was likened to executions, with Elizabeth Edwards suffering immensely in her final moments.The court heard that the couple, likened to Bonnie and Clyde, repeatedly stabbed their victims. The boy stabbed Mrs. Edwards eight times, including twice in the throat, to prevent her from alerting her daughter. Katie was then stabbed twice in the neck with severe force before being smothered. The judge stated both teenagers shared equal responsibility and revelled in what you achieved. He added that if they were adults, they might have faced life imprisonment.Outside the court, Karen Thompson, deputy chief crown prosecutor for the East Midlands, described the case as one of the most distressing she had encountered. She extended sympathies to the victims' family and friends, who are grappling with the aftermath of this horrific crime.Det Ch Insp Martin Holvey of Lincolnshire Police called it a rare and unprecedented case, noting the cold and ruthless planning involved. The lack of remorse shown by the juveniles further highlighted the chilling nature of the crime.In court, Peter Joyce QC, prosecuting, revealed the boy's account following his arrest. The boy claimed the girl had instigated the plan, expressing a dislike for the smell of blood. He detailed the attack on Elizabeth Edwards, recounting how she struggled and scratched him before going limp. He then removed his trainers to avoid creaking floorboards, proceeded to Katie's room, and attacked her with a knife before smothering her with a pillow.Simon Myerson QC, defending the boy, argued that the children were trapped in a self-created fantasy. Andrew Stubbs QC, representing the girl, described their relationship as toxic, suggesting they were daring each other to commit the crime.Initially, the pair pleaded guilty to manslaughter in September. However, the boy later admitted to murder, while his girlfriend maintained her innocence. She was ultimately found guilty of two counts of murder.

text: Steven Wilson is often dubbed the hardest working musician in the world of progressive rock. In a triumphant showing at the Progressive Music Awards in London this month, multi-talented musician Steven Wilson secured three prestigious accolades, including the coveted Album of the Year for Hand. Cannot. Erase. The Guardian lauded the album as a smart, soulful and immersive work of art in its five-star review.Since the 1980s, Wilson has been the creative powerhouse behind numerous musical ventures, most notably the renowned rock band Porcupine Tree. As he gears up for two sold-out performances at the Royal Albert Hall, Wilson is also launching Transience, a vinyl-only double LP that highlights the more accessible aspects of his solo work.In a conversation with the BBC, Wilson shared his passion for vinyl, his jam-packed schedule, and the unexpected collaboration with comic actor Matt Berry as his support act. Reflecting on his connection to vinyl, Wilson remarked, I grew up at the very tail end of the vinyl era. Back then, we eagerly awaited CDs because vinyl could be frustrating. You'd buy a record, take it home, and it might have a scratch, forcing you to return it. While CDs are fantastic, especially for genres like classical music, they lack the tangible, cherished quality of vinyl. Vinyl is akin to owning a beautiful painting; it's something you can hold, explore, and lose yourself in.When asked about a treasured vinyl piece, Wilson admitted, I parted with all my vinyl in the '90s. What I have now is repurchased. Initially, I aimed to recreate my collection from when I was 15, but it's grown beyond that. The first record I convinced my parents to buy was Electric Light Orchestra's 'Out of the Blue.' If I still had that original copy, it would hold sentimental value, but it's probably in a charity shop now.Discussing the decision to release Transience on vinyl, Wilson explained, It was initially an idea for Record Store Day, but we missed the opportunity. My record company suggested compiling some of my shorter, more accessible tracks. I became fixated on creating 'an introduction to Steven Wilson,' and insisted it be a vinyl-only release. Buyers will also receive a high-resolution download.Wilson dismissed concerns that Transience might not fully represent his work, stating, While I often focus on long-form pieces, melody has always been paramount for me. Many progressive rock tracks emphasize technical complexity over melody. Pink Floyd, the most successful progressive rock band, endured because they prioritized melody and atmosphere.Regarding his upcoming Royal Albert Hall shows, Wilson teased, I don't want to reveal too much. Each night will feature a completely different repertoire. The first night will be an enhanced version of the 'Hand. Cannot. Erase.' show with special guests. The second night will delve into my history, catering to long-time fans.On the collaboration with Matt Berry, Wilson shared, Everyone on the tour bus and I are huge fans of 'Toast of London.' We quote it endlessly. I decided to explore Matt's music and picked up 'Music for Insomniacs.' After discussing our shared admiration for Mike Oldfield, I invited him to perform at the Royal Albert Hall. I'll be starstruck by my opening act.Wilson has also been busy remixing albums for iconic bands like XTC, Tears for Fears, and Yes. He noted, I don't consciously draw from these projects, but deconstructing classic albums inevitably influences me. My last solo album, 'The Raven That Refused to Sing,' was my most traditional progressive work, coinciding with a year of remixing King Crimson, Jethro Tull, and Yes. 'Hand. Cannot. Erase.' opened up more, influenced by working on Tears for Fears and XTC.Known as one of progressive rock's busiest musicians, Wilson reflected, You can drop 'progressive.' I'm probably one of the most work-obsessed people in the music industry, and it's a curse. My father had a strong work ethic, and if I'm idle for a day, guilt creeps in. Remixing has been a blessing, allowing me to stay productive without constantly creating my own music.Wilson acknowledged the challenges of the music industry, saying, It's tough to make a living. I wouldn't recommend it as a profession now. I work daily, and while I'm not rich, I make a good living. I love what I do, and it's a privilege, but laziness wouldn't allow me to survive.Transience will be released in the UK on September 25. Steven Wilson's performances at the Royal Albert Hall are scheduled for September 28 and 29, as part of his 2015-16 European tour.

text: Food bank use in Scotland has increased to record levels, with more than 60,000 referrals over a six-month period, according to a charity. The Trussell Trust has revealed that, on average, individuals require 1.7 referrals, indicating that approximately 35,000 people have received assistance. Between April and September, the charity's food banks distributed 60,458 three-day emergency food supplies, marking a 17% increase from the previous year. The primary reason for financial hardship remains delays in receiving benefits, with 28% of recipients citing this issue, consistent with last year's figures. Meanwhile, referrals due to benefit changes have slightly decreased from 18% to 16%, whereas those attributed to low income have risen from 18% to 21%.Ewan Gurr, the trust's Scotland network manager, expressed concern about the growing impact of low income. Welfare benefit difficulties still drive most people to Scottish food banks, but now one in five referrals is due to low income, he noted. Gurr highlighted the plight of individuals in low-paid jobs who struggle to make ends meet when a crisis occurs. He also pointed to the instability in the oil, gas, and steel industries, which has led to significant redundancies and a rise in unemployment in Scotland, contrasting with the rest of the UK.The trust also worries about a repeat of last December's surge in low-income referrals, as increased fuel costs strain household budgets. Responding to these figures, SNP MSP Kevin Stewart described them as alarming. He criticized UK government benefit changes and delays, labeling them the most common reasons for emergency food aid. Stewart condemned further cuts to the incomes of the poorest families, highlighting the Scottish government's £300 million investment over three years to counteract Tory social security cuts. He noted, George Osborne is set to proceed with £12 billion more in social security cuts.In defense, a UK government spokesperson argued that their reforms have led to record employment, a near-record number of job vacancies, and a growing economy. They emphasized the complexity of food bank usage reasons and rejected the notion that welfare changes are the primary cause. Work remains the best route out of poverty, the spokesperson said, crediting the government's economic plan for enabling many to experience job security and family support for the first time.In terms of food donations, Scotland ranks second only to the northwest of England. The statistics also suggest that, relative to population, Scotland sees a disproportionately high number of food bank referrals compared to other UK regions, according to the trust. Neil Findlay, Scottish Labour's equality spokesman, called the reliance on food banks in a wealthy country like Scotland unacceptable. He warned that as winter approaches, the demand for support will only grow. Findlay urged both Scottish and UK governments to address the persistent wealth gap after years of SNP and Tory leadership.The Trussell Trust, a charity driven by Christian values, operates 50 food banks in Scotland as part of its network of 425 across the UK. Individuals accessing these food banks are referred by professionals such as social workers, health visitors, or school liaison officers.

text: Skier Dave Ryding matched Britain's best ever alpine World Cup result when he finished second in the Kitzbuhel slalom in Austria. After leading the first run, he was surpassed by local favorite Marcel Hirscher, yet still celebrated his first career podium finish. This marked the best result for a British male skier in over 35 years, since Konrad Bartelski's second place in an Italian downhill race in 1981. At 30, he had already achieved sixth and seventh positions earlier in the season.The first run was just insane, he shared with BBC Sport. I knew I had skied it clean, but couldn't believe it when I crossed the finish line. Between runs, I tried to keep calm and not stress. I kept telling myself I wasn't the last to go, but it was tough. It was a mental battle, but I won it.Acknowledging Hirscher's performance, he added, Hirscher skied so well, so coming second almost felt like a victory. It's crazy. I'm just really proud of what I've achieved.Despite losing UK Sport funding for alpine skiing in 2010, the Lancastrian continues to race with the help of other sponsorships. Ryding, who honed his skills on a dry slope at Pendle Ski Club, has been with the British ski team since 2006 and competed in the 2010 and 2014 Winter Olympics, finishing 17th.Ryding had a 0.29-second lead over Italy's Stefano Gross before the second run, with Hirscher trailing by 1.02 seconds. However, the Austrian, a three-time overall slalom titleholder and 2013 race winner, delivered an outstanding second run, climbing from seventh to first, leaving Ryding 0.76 seconds behind.The event drew over 60,000 spectators, with Ryding describing the atmosphere as deafening. Kitzbuhel is like the FA Cup final in England. The downhill race is the number one, but the slalom is also massive. The fans are incredible, he remarked.Since the alpine ski World Cup's inception in 1967, Ryding and Bartelski are the only British men to have reached the podium. On the women's circuit, Gina Hathorn (1967) and Divina Galica (1968) have also achieved top-three finishes. Bartelski's success in Val Gardena, Italy, prompted a French commentator to exclaim, This is not possible, he is English!In the pre-World Cup era, Britain's Gordon Cleaver won the combined race on Kitzbuhel's Hahnenkamm course in 1931. Although the alpine team no longer receives UK Sport funding, the Great British freestyle ski and snowboard team does. Following Jenny Jones' historic slopestyle bronze in Sochi, they secured £4.9m for the cycle leading to the 2018 Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang, South Korea.The team has achieved numerous World Cup victories, with Katie Ormerod becoming the first snowboarder to win a World Cup big air, and cousin Jamie Nicholls claiming slopestyle victories. Lesley McKenna and Rowan Cheshire have triumphed in halfpipe, while Zoe Gillings-Brier excelled in snowboardcross. Skier James Woods boasts three World Cup slopestyle wins.In cross-country skiing, Briton Andrew Musgrave achieved his best World Cup result, finishing sixth in a 15km race in Sweden on Saturday.

text: An archive of sketchbooks, drawings and letters belonging to artist Lucian Freud has been acquired by the nation through the acceptance in lieu scheme. The National Portrait Gallery, known for its record-breaking Lucian Freud Portraits exhibition in 2012, has been entrusted with a remarkable collection of the artist's work. Among this collection are items that have never been published or displayed before, with plans to exhibit them next summer.Spanning Lucian Freud's career from the mid-1940s until his death in 2011, the sketchbooks offer a unique window into his artistic journey. Culture Minister Ed Vaizey commented, This rare collection of Lucian Freud drawings and letters provides a fascinating glimpse into the work of one of our most pioneering artists. Bringing these never seen before treasures into public collections means that everyone can enjoy and see the early beginnings that shaped his most celebrated work.The archive is rich with studies for many of Freud's significant works and includes 162 childhood drawings that capture family life. These drawings, made during his time in Germany before fleeing to England in 1933 due to Hitler's rise to power, were preserved and dated by his mother.According to the National Portrait Gallery, the archive will give added context to two existing works in its collection: a self-portrait in oils and a charcoal drawing of Lord Goodman from 1985. Several sketches in the collection reveal the initial stages of portraits, such as Lord Goodman's, beginning with the nose and eyes and expanding outward.The collection also features early book cover designs by Freud, including one for his daughter Esther Freud's 1992 novel Hideous Kinky and Nigel Dennis's 1955 Cards of Identity.Dr. Nicholas Cullinan, director of the National Portrait Gallery in London, described the archive as a very important, extensive and generous gift to the nation and a vital source of reference. The 47 sketchbooks, drawings, and letters have settled an inheritance tax bill of £2,940,000 from the Lucian Freud Estate through the inheritance in lieu scheme.Sir Peter Bazalgette, chair of Arts Council England, remarked that the collection provides a real insight into the life of one of Britain's most compelling and influential artists.

text: Three years ago thousands of Tunisians protested on the streets, demanding, among other things, more economic opportunity. The ousting of President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, prompted by widespread protests, ignited the Arab Spring across North Africa and the Middle East. Yet, despite his removal in 2011, Tunisia's economic reforms have been sluggish, hampered by persistent political instability that lingered until late last year.Optimism is on the rise with the formation of a moderate interim government of independent figures in December and the adoption of a new constitution in January. These developments have rekindled hopes for pro-business reforms aimed at fostering entrepreneurship and the growth of small businesses. The World Bank has bolstered this sense of confidence by granting Tunisia $1.2 billion in loans last month to support economic and political reform. This includes $750 million to aid government reforms for economic equality and job creation, and $100 million to enhance lending to small and medium-sized enterprises.For many Tunisian entrepreneurs, swift reform is crucial. Ramzi el Fekih, the 46-year-old CEO of Viamobile, a mobile banking and payments app, believes a more effective judicial system is essential for business growth in Tunisia. After spending 25 years abroad, including two decades in California's mobile technology sector, he returned to launch his business in 2009. The biggest difference between working here and in California is the lack of trust, he notes. There's so much control that it becomes constraining. We need a judicial system that enforces the law.El Fekih also advocates for reduced regulation and bureaucracy, citing the two-year delay in getting Viamobile approved by Tunisia's central bank. Despite these challenges, he remains optimistic about Tunisia's potential. I really believe there is huge potential in Tunisia and among Tunisian entrepreneurs, he asserts. With the new constitution in place, he hopes that reforms will accelerate, likening the need for a conducive business environment to an easy and accessible operating system for entrepreneurs.For 29-year-old entrepreneur Zied Jallouli, securing financial backing is the primary hurdle for start-ups in Tunisia. Raising funds here for a big idea is really, really tough, he admits. Jallouli and his partner developed Disrupt CK, a smartphone app that helps users purchase items seen on TV shows or films. Although he struggled to find support from local banks or investors, he eventually gained backing from Swedish expatriate Thomas Adner, a former Tetra Pak executive, who was so impressed with the app that he joined as chief marketing officer.There are great business opportunities in Tunisia, Adner observes, citing the affordability of hiring skilled web developers and programmers. However, he acknowledges the challenges posed by extensive bureaucracy. In Sweden, it takes about 30 minutes to register a new business, and within two days, all paperwork is done. Here, it takes months, if not longer, he says, urging the government to simplify the process.Laurent Gonnet, the World Bank's financial sector specialist in Tunisia, concurs that significant improvements are needed. He highlights the extreme caution of commercial banks, especially towards technology firms, and notes the absence of a private credit rating system, which complicates entrepreneurs' efforts to secure bank loans.Fortunately, Tunisia's politicians appear committed to pro-business reforms, driven by the World Bank's influence and a challenging economic landscape, with unemployment at 16%. The hope is that this momentum will persist beyond the general elections scheduled for the end of the year.We are reviewing the investment code to reduce red tape, says Dhamir Mannai, an assembly member from the CPR party of current President Moncef Marzouki. Meanwhile, Moncef Cheikhrouhou, from the opposition Democratic Alliance and deputy chairman of the parliament's finance, planning, and development committee, emphasizes the urgency of fostering entrepreneurship to generate wealth. We are treating this as an urgent matter and are seeking input from entrepreneurs as well, he states.

text: A former Labour chief whip has urged Jeremy Corbyn to reflect on Tony Blair's approach when party leader by ruling out the de-selection of MPs. Baroness Hilary Armstrong, in a conversation with the BBC, described Jeremy Corbyn as the greatest rebel ever during his tenure as a backbencher, noting that Tony Blair, the then prime minister, hesitated to take disciplinary action against him. Blair viewed Labour as a broad church, Armstrong explained.Amidst speculation that Corbyn's adversaries might face expulsion, Armstrong emphasized the need for him to demonstrate tolerance. During an interview on BBC Radio 4's The Westminster Hour, she expressed satisfaction that Labour party chairman Ian Lavery had dismissed de-selection as a viable approach. However, she remarked, I know MPs who are essentially subjected to harassment, facing criticism and challenges at every meeting, being told they don't represent the attendees. This tactic is designed to wear them down, to make them question their place in the Labour party.Armstrong pointed out that sectarianism seemed to be prevailing in certain areas. She urged Corbyn to seize the opportunity over the summer and at the party conference to clearly communicate that he intends to lead a broad church rather than a narrow sectarian faction. She added, The real test for Jeremy is whether he is up to it.Corbyn, who had voted against his own government over 500 times, had stirred discontent among some party members in his Islington North constituency, Armstrong recalled. I had a couple of people from Jeremy's constituency approach me, expressing concern about his consistent opposition to the Labour government and contemplating de-selection, she said. Armstrong advised them that the leadership would not support such a move.Reflecting on those times, she noted, The prime minister was very clear about not pursuing de-selection when Jeremy was a backbench MP. And he was right; it wasn't something we should have done. But I hope Jeremy now considers this and is resolute in ensuring it doesn't occur under his leadership.

text: Brighton kept the pressure on their Championship automatic promotion rivals with victory at Birmingham, whose hopes of a play-off place all but ended. Birmingham initially took the lead when Kyle Lafferty, the on-loan striker from Northern Ireland, scored a debut goal. However, Brighton quickly responded with a goal from Connor Goldson, who expertly headed the ball into the net. Soon after the break, Lewis Dunk, a defender in excellent form, rose above the rest to score with a header from a corner, putting Brighton ahead.As the match progressed, Brighton faced little resistance and maintained their advantage, remaining just one point behind the top two teams. Birmingham, on the other hand, stayed in ninth place and fell 11 points behind the top six, following victories by Sheffield Wednesday and Derby. Gary Rowett's team has only managed two wins in their last ten games, while Brighton extended their unbeaten streak to eight matches.Both of Brighton's goals were the result of precise set-piece deliveries by Jiri Skalak. Goldson and Dunk successfully out-jumped their defenders to capitalize on his exceptional crosses. Birmingham struggled to create meaningful opportunities in the second half, allowing Brighton to secure their lead with relative ease. Substitute James Wilson nearly added a third goal for Brighton in the final moments.Reflecting on the game, Birmingham manager Gary Rowett expressed his disappointment, stating, I've warned the players if they think they can take their foot off the gas then they'll be coming in on Sundays and their days off. I think I'd look a bit stupid if I said we could still get into the play-offs now, the gap's 11 points. He praised Lafferty, saying, I was really pleased with Kyle Lafferty, when I took him off a fan was screaming he was our only chance of a goal, but he hasn't played a lot of football and needs to be fitter.Brighton's assistant manager, Colin Calderwood, commented on their approach, saying, If you really want to go for it you have to chase the three points and get them. Winning tonight helps us but it won't take us up. He added, We weren't aware of Middlesbrough being 2-0 up at half-time, but whether Middlesbrough win or lose, if we win every game we'll have a chance. Well, we won't have a chance, we'll be up. text: Formula 1 is the most technologically advanced sport on the planet, and the latest radical rule changes have imposed a whole new set of challenges on the teams. **Special Report: The Business of Technology****Hey You, Get On to My Cloud****Domain Shift Sends Cyber World Dotty****How to Cash In with Off-the-Peg Apps****Taj Mahal Comes to Your Living Room****Sochi 2014: Hi-Tech Winter Games**The BBC recently visited the Lotus F1 Team at their headquarters in Enstone, Oxfordshire, to explore how they are gearing up for the 2014 race season, set to commence in Melbourne, Australia, on March 16. Despite operating with less than half the budget of leading F1 teams and facing additional challenges, Lotus is leaning heavily on technology to stay competitive.The team is navigating the departure of team principal Eric Boullier to McLaren and dealing with a new leader who must address a £140 million financial shortfall from the previous year. This financial strain contributed to the loss of star driver Kimi Raikkonen to Ferrari. In Formula 1, every fraction of a second can significantly impact a team's annual revenue, explains Chief Executive Matthew Carter, who was appointed by owners Genii Capital to stabilize the organization. We are operating on half the budget of some of the big boys, so we have to think of different ways of making that work and being competitive, he notes.This necessity pushes the team to enhance their use of technology in all facets of the business. Recent rule changes have been substantial, requiring a smaller turbo-charged engine, a more potent electric battery and energy recovery system, as well as modifications to the front wing and chassis to reduce downforce. These changes have led to the creation of thousands of new drawings, parts, and tests. They're the biggest rule changes I've seen in 20 years of working in the sport, says Nick Chester, Chief Technical Director for Lotus F1 Team. We had to start developing this car two and a half years ago.To boost efficiency, Lotus abandoned its fragmented software approach and secured a £4 million, four-year agreement to implement Microsoft's Dynamics enterprise resource planning (ERP) software across the organization, Chester explains. This partnership, while not exclusive to Lotus, allows the team to customize the software to their needs and access Microsoft's research and development team in Redmond, Washington.The ERP system facilitates the complex journey from computer-aided designs, informed by computational fluid dynamics, to wind-tunnel-tested carbon-fiber speed machines. It helped us cope with an increase from 12,000 to 14,000 drawings that the new car required, Chester says. It also enables us to run parallel design programs and allocate resources accordingly. Over the season, a car might undergo 200 to 250 aerodynamic and mechanical upgrades, necessitating an additional 6,000 drawings, all of which must be planned, resourced, and delivered on time.The team has cut development costs by adopting laser 3D printing, which allows for quicker and more affordable prototype part creation. Enhanced technology also minimizes time wasted on basic administration by automating routine processes, according to IT Director Michael Taylor. If you can free up an aerodynamicist's time by just one minute a day, over the course of the year that's a significant amount of time. And if you can extend the design lifecycle, in theory, you create a better design, he explains.When a part fails, identifying the exact cause and pinpointing the stage of failure—from material purchase to the moment of breakage—is crucial. We need a single source of truth, Taylor asserts. Data plays a pivotal role in the sport, with the car's onboard computer and numerous sensors generating up to 50 gigabytes of data per race, all requiring immediate analysis. As the car races at speeds up to 200mph in Abu Dhabi, the team in Enstone monitors this real-time data remotely via VMware's virtual desktop technology.All this sensitive data is securely stored in two concrete bunkers at the Oxfordshire site, as external cloud storage services are not yet trusted, though Taylor foresees potential use in the future. Top-secret files are shared securely with partners, such as engine supplier Renault, using EMC's Syncplicity software. It's like a commercial version of Dropbox, Taylor says. IT enables everything inside this business. And the be-all and end-all of our IT strategy is to give us a competitive edge.In-season testing on tracks, in wind tunnels, and simulators has been limited by the FIA, the sport's governing body, to reduce costs and help smaller teams survive. While these restrictions are absolutely essential, according to Carter, they place a greater reliance on IT to fill the void. The lack of testing in F1 means we have to do an awful lot of work back here, making sure there's a real good correlation between the information we get from the simulator and wind-tunnel testing and what happens on the track, so that we can continue punching above our weight, he states. If you stop investing in technology and stand still, others overtake you very rapidly in this sport.

This month the BBC visited the Lotus F1 Team at its headquarters in Enstone, Oxfordshire, to find out how they were getting ready for the 2014 race season, which will begin in Melbourne, Australia, on March 16th. Although operating with less than half the budget of the leading Formula One teams, Lotus has to overcome additional difficulties, and despite having lost its star driver, Kimi Rakkonen, to Ferrari, it is still investing heavily in technology. And in F1, where a fraction of a second can have a considerable influence on the annual revenue of a team, this need has forced the team to redouble its efforts to improve technology in all aspects of its business. Recent rule changes have been substantial, requiring a smaller, turbo-driven engine, a more powerful electric battery and energy recovery system, and modifications to the front wing and chassis to reduce downforce. “We operate on half the budget of some of the big boys, and we have to think of different ways of making that work,” says chief executive Matthew Carter, who was appointed to stabilize the team by its new owners, Genii Capital. These changes involved the creation of thousands of new drawings, parts and tests. “They’re the most radical changes I’ve seen in my twenty years in the sport,” says Nick Chester, Lotus F1 Team’s Chief Technical Director. “We started developing the new car two and a half years ago.” This Enterprise Requirements Planning system makes it possible to make the complex transition from CAD-influenced fluid-dynamically influenced designs to wind-tunnel-tested, carbon-fibre-fused speed machines. “This helps us cope with the increase from twelve to fourteen thousand drawings, and allows us to run parallel design programmes and allocate the resources accordingly,” says Chester. It also allows us to run parallel design programmes and allocate the resources according to the outcome of the wind-tunnel testing. This partnership is not exclusive, but Lotus is able to influence the development of the software to meet their needs and access the research and development teams in Redmond, Washington. The development costs have been reduced by the use of a new technique of prototyping parts, the 3D printing of materials by a rapid and inexpensive process. During a season, the car may undergo 200 to 250 aerodynamic and mechanical modifications which necessitate some 6,000 new drawings, all of which must be planned, resourced and delivered on time. The new techniques have reduced the amount of time spent on routine procedures, according to IT Director Michael Taylor, and the time that an aerodynamicist would spend daily has been reduced by one minute per day, and that over a year has made a difference. Data plays a crucial role in the sport: the on-board computer and the various sensors on the car, which can produce up to 50 gigabytes of data per race, must be analyzed immediately. When a component fails, it is essential to determine the exact cause and to know the exact point of failure from the purchase of the material to the moment of breakage. “A single source of truth is essential,” says Taylor. Until now all sensitive data has been stored in two concrete bunkers on the Oxfordshire site. Taylor says he is now starting to trust cloud services, but not yet. In the meantime, secret files are shared securely with partners such as engine supplier Renault using EMC's Syncplicity software, which is like a commercial version of Dropbox. As the car speeds up to 200 mph in the race in the United Arab Emirates, the team in Enstone monitors real-time data remotely using virtual desktop technology. In the racing season, the governing FIA, in the interest of reducing costs and helping smaller teams to survive, has limited track, wind tunnel and simulator tests. “These limitations are necessary, but the more we rely on IT, the more important IT becomes,” says Carter. “IT enables everything in this business, and the purpose of our IT strategy is to increase our competitiveness.” If you stop developing technology and you stand still, others quickly overtake you in this sport. The lack of testing in F1 means that a great deal of work has to be done in the background, ensuring that the simulator and wind tunnel results are as close as possible to what happens on the track, so that we can continue to punch above our weight, he said.

text: A financial scam was committed once every 15 seconds in the first half of the year, prompting a new campaign to highlight the risks. Over a million instances of card, cheque, phone, or online fraud were documented from January to June, according to Financial Fraud Action (FFA). This represents a staggering 53% increase compared to the same period last year. Funded by banks and payment card companies, the FFA is actively disseminating advice to curb fraud.Although banks frequently refund losses, this is not guaranteed for every case. Many victims feel too ashamed to admit they have been deceived. To combat this, the Take Five campaign, supported by police, the banking sector, and consumer organizations, encourages individuals to pause and think before responding to any financial inquiries or sharing personal data.Katy Worobec, director of FFA, stated, We are asking people to take five - to take that moment - to pause and think before they respond to any financial requests and share any personal or financial details.Home Office Security Minister Ben Wallace highlighted the severe impact financial fraud can have on victims, noting that fraudsters use increasingly sophisticated and persuasive tactics. They prey on people who are trying to get on with their lives but in a moment where they are busy or distracted become vulnerable, he said. The government, alongside law enforcement and the banking industry, is actively working through the Joint Fraud Taskforce to dismantle the organized networks behind these crimes.Banks assert they prevent £7 out of every £10 in potential fraud losses, yet fraudsters still manage to siphon off millions. Last year's financial fraud losses soared to £755 million, marking a 26% rise from the previous year. This figure likely underestimates the true scale, as many cases go unreported.Modern-day fraudsters frequently employ email deception, as well as phone and text-based scams, a trend now reflected in official crime statistics that include fraud data. According to the British Crime Survey, fraud and cybercrime constitute nearly half of all offenses.Despite consumers' awareness of the risks of sharing personal information, police experts acknowledge that people can still fall victim. An FFA survey revealed that victims often believed the caller was genuine. Nearly 40% were caught off guard because they felt pressured, while a similar percentage were vulnerable when distracted.A separate survey by a comparison website found that over 40% of people had to cancel credit or debit cards due to fraud in the past year. Jody Baker, head of money at comparethemarket.com, remarked, Most of the transactions we make now are digital and our research suggests that over a quarter of people carry as little as £10 in cash. With so many of us shopping and banking on the internet, combined with a rise in contactless payments, it is more important than ever to be vigilant when managing your money.For further guidance, see The Met Police's Little Book of Big Scams.

text: Families of football fans who died in the Hillsborough disaster are pursuing High Court misconduct action against the South Yorkshire and West Midlands police forces, lawyers have said. After a relentless 27-year campaign by the families of the victims, a jury has determined that the 96 fans who perished at the FA Cup semi-final were unlawfully killed, with the match commander, Ch Supt David Duckenfield, found responsible for manslaughter by gross negligence due to a breach of duty. The inquests also highlighted significant police failings that exacerbated the already perilous situation on April 15, 1989.In response to these findings, families have filed claims of misfeasance in public office, as reported by Saunders Law Solicitors. This legal action, initiated in 2015, was paused pending the inquests' outcomes. Misfeasance in public office is a civil claim against a public official accused of abusing their power. The claims focus on the events of the disaster and its subsequent handling.Both South Yorkshire Police, responsible for the planning and operations on the day, and West Midlands Police, tasked with the original investigation into officer conduct, have been approached for comments. A statement from Saunders Legal team alleges a systematic cover-up by these forces, accusing them of shifting blame onto innocent parties through falsifying evidence, pressuring witnesses, and suppressing the truth. The statement further describes the misconduct as abuse on an industrial scale, pointing to institutional misfeasance rather than isolated incidents.The current chief constable of South Yorkshire Police, David Crompton, was suspended on Wednesday due to the force's handling of the inquest. In 2012, Crompton acknowledged grave errors during the disaster and issued a profound apology. Following the jury's conclusions on Tuesday, he admitted the match's policing was catastrophically wrong and accepted the findings without reservation.Despite the inquests' damning conclusions, a message on a website for retired South Yorkshire police officers encouraged them to take pride in their service, sparking outrage among the families. These families are now calling for criminal prosecutions in light of the hearings' outcomes.The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) has stated it will formally consider whether any criminal charges should be brought against any individual or corporate body based on all available evidence. Two ongoing investigations into the disaster and its aftermath are expected to conclude by the year's end. Operation Resolve is examining the events leading to the fatal crush, while the Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) is probing allegations of a cover-up.

text: The botched Renewable Heat Incentive (RHI) scheme was set up to encourage uptake of eco-friendly heat systems over the use of fossil fuels. The Renewable Heat Incentive (RHI) scheme scandal, which could burden taxpayers with an additional £490 million due to overly generous fuel subsidies, has led to the collapse of the Northern Ireland Executive's power-sharing arrangement. BBC News NI delves into the key figures embroiled in this controversy.Arlene Foster, Northern Ireland's former first minister, was at the helm of the Department of Enterprise, Trade and Investment (Deti) during the RHI scheme's design phase. She later expressed that her deepest political regret was the failure to implement crucial cost-control measures. Despite vehemently denying allegations from Jonathan Bell, her successor as enterprise minister, that she instructed him to keep the scheme open, Foster faced calls to step aside for a judge-led public inquiry. In January, she reiterated her decision not to resign, attributing some demands for her departure to misogynistic motives. Ultimately, Martin McGuinness's resignation as Deputy First Minister forced an election, abruptly ending her tenure.Jonathan Bell, who served as Deti minister when the RHI scheme inflicted significant financial damage, revealed in a BBC interview with Stephen Nolan that he attempted to close the scheme before the surge of applications in late 2015, only to be obstructed by DUP advisers. He accused them of altering documents without his consent and has been suspended by his party after calling for a public inquiry.Behind the scenes, Timothy Johnston, a long-time influential figure within the DUP, has been implicated by Bell as one of the advisers preventing the scheme's closure. Johnston, who has served as an adviser to several DUP leaders, including Arlene Foster, refuted these claims. He is one of the highest-paid special advisers, earning £91,809.Dr. Andrew Crawford, another adviser to Foster during the RHI scheme's inception, has also been accused by Bell of keeping the scheme open. Despite denying these allegations, Crawford was named by senior civil servant Andrew McCormick as having influenced the scheme's continuation, though McCormick lacked evidence. Crawford's brother, a poultry farmer, benefits from the RHI scheme.Richard Bullick, a prominent DUP policy adviser, was accused by Bell of attending a hostile meeting with Foster, which Bullick denied. He has been involved in significant political negotiations and, like other advisers, earns the maximum salary permitted.Stephen Brimstone, another adviser linked to the RHI scheme, resigned in November. Bell claims Brimstone witnessed a heated exchange over the scheme's closure, a claim Brimstone disputes. He is also a claimant of the RHI scheme, as is his brother.Timothy Cairns, Bell's adviser at Deti, advised on the RHI scheme but stated that the final decisions rested with the minister. He previously worked with Peter Robinson but is no longer a DUP adviser.Dr. Andrew McCormick, permanent secretary at the Department for the Economy, has been tasked with addressing the RHI scheme's fallout. He highlighted significant concerns to Bell in 2015 and mentioned a whistleblower's unheeded warnings two years prior to the scheme's closure.David Sterling, a former Deti permanent secretary, has accepted responsibility for failures during the RHI scheme's setup but admitted to lacking answers for why a planned review in 2014 never occurred. He now holds a top civil service position in the Department of Finance and Personnel.Chris Stewart, Bell's deputy permanent secretary at Deti, was named by Bell as seeking to expose DUP advisers' attempts to remove Foster's references from RHI documents. Stewart disputed this, acknowledging some document alterations but stating Bell assured him the issue was resolved.John Robinson, previously the DUP's director of communications and now a special adviser, was named by Bell as having interests in the poultry industry. Robinson clarified that his family farm's chicken houses were not part of the RHI scheme, although his in-laws had benefited. The DUP dismissed Bell's remarks as mud-slinging.

text: Taking Northern Ireland out of the EU would be an act of profound legal and constitutional, as well as political, significance the High Court has heard. During the third day of judicial review hearings concerning legal challenges to the UK's EU withdrawal, a barrister voiced significant concerns. Representing a cross-party group of assembly members opposed to Brexit, he argued that the Brexit process demands parliamentary scrutiny rather than unilateral action via royal prerogative. He criticized Secretary of State James Brokenshire for failing to offer guidance on broader issues, emphasizing, It is his role to speak for Northern Ireland's interests. He further insisted, The Northern Ireland Office must take a position on whether Brexit is good or bad for Northern Ireland and make that position known to the British government.Simultaneously, a separate legal challenge is being pursued by victims' campaigner Raymond McCord, whose son Raymond Jnr was tragically murdered in 1997. McCord's legal team contends that the Good Friday Agreement renders Northern Ireland's exit from the EU unlawful. A barrister for McCord proposed that Northern Ireland might have the power to veto Brexit for the entire UK. After the hearings concluded in Belfast, McCord expressed confidence, stating, I believe that enough has been done for us to stop Brexit and for Northern Ireland not to exit out of Europe.In response, barristers representing the secretary of state and the Northern Ireland Executive countered these claims, arguing that the Good Friday Agreement does not legally impede EU withdrawal. A barrister for the secretary of state noted there was no obstacle preventing the Northern Ireland Executive from initiating a debate and conveying its views to the Westminster government.On Wednesday afternoon, Attorney General John Larkin, QC for the NI Executive, addressed the court, asserting that the Good Friday Agreement poses no hindrance to EU withdrawal. He questioned whether the Belfast Agreement could function if any participants were not EU members, confidently answering, The answer is inevitably yes. We already have that. He referenced the Isle of Man, Jersey, and Guernsey, none of which are part of the UK or the EU.Mr. Justice Maguire, after hearing three days of submissions at Belfast High Court, announced he would give immediate consideration to the case. The court is expected to reconvene following the outcome of similar legal challenges to Brexit, which are scheduled to be heard in London next week.

text: There is a new class of planet out there that astronomers are calling the mega-Earth. A remarkable discovery has prompted scientists to redefine planetary classifications. A newly identified planet, Kepler-10c, boasts a mass 17 times that of Earth, yet shares a hard surface similar to our own world. This giant planet orbits a star located approximately 560 light-years away. Its unusual characteristics were unveiled at an American Astronomical Society meeting in Boston, leaving experts puzzled.Traditionally, theorists believed that a planet of such magnitude would accumulate vast amounts of hydrogen, resembling gas giants like Neptune or Jupiter. However, Kepler-10c defies these expectations. The proper way to call it is something bigger than a 'super-Earth,' so how about 'mega-Earth,' suggested Prof. Dimitar Sasselov from the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics. He also dubbed it the Godzilla of Earths!The planet was discovered using NASA's Kepler telescope, which identifies new worlds by detecting slight dips in starlight as planets transit their parent stars. This method provided Kepler-10c's diameter—29,000 kilometers, over twice Earth's width—but not its mass. To determine the mass, astronomers employed the Harps-North instrument on the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo in the Canary Islands. This tool measures gravitational interactions between a planet and its star.The findings revealed that Kepler-10c's mass, combined with its diameter, indicates it is not a gaseous planet but composed of very dense material. It's 17 - in fact, it's more than 17 - Earth masses, and that brings the density to 7.5 grams per cubic centimeter, which is a lot more than what we know of rock here on Earth (5.5g/cm3), explained Prof. Sasselov. He noted that the planet's density results primarily from compression rather than composition differences, suggesting a mix of rocks and some volatiles, likely including 5-15% water.This discovery enhances our understanding of the diverse types of planets and offers insights into when rocky worlds might evolve into gaseous planets. Intriguingly, the host star of Kepler-10c is around 11 billion years old, a period early in the Universe's evolution when heavy elements necessary for rocky planets were scarce. Thus, Kepler-10c suggests that rocky planets may have formed earlier than previously believed, highlighting the potential for very ancient star systems to host life.Prof. Sasselov remarked, It is [on] solid planets that is the place, as far as we know—and we know very little about the origins of life—where we think the chemistry is capable of building those molecules that lead to the emergence of life from geochemistry.Follow Jonathan on Twitter for more updates.

text: Terror attacks can be difficult for adults to understand - so how should we talk to children about terrorism? Last year, an NSPCC report highlighted a growing trend of children feeling anxious about global issues. Many who reached out to Childline expressed worries about the EU referendum, the US presidential election, and conflicts in the Middle East. This raises the question: can we discuss troubling news with children without exacerbating their fears?Psychologist Emma Kenny and Nicky Cox, editor of the children's newspaper First News, tackled this topic on BBC Radio Scotland. Despite efforts by parents to shield their children from distressing news, kids often hear about these issues from friends or through social media. Nicky Cox argues that parents who believe they are successfully protecting their children might actually be doing them a disservice.If you think as a parent you've done a really good job in shielding your child, you're doing them a disservice because they're going to go into school, they're going to be talking about it in the playground, in the lunch hall, and they're going to be getting information second, third and fourth hand, Cox explained. She emphasized that parents cannot control how their children access information. Instead, they should ensure that their children receive accurate information and feel empowered to discern the truth in conversations with peers.At First News, Nicky Cox and her team strive to deliver factual reporting to young readers. She stressed the importance of teaching children to distinguish between reliable news sources and fake news. We tell the truth, Cox stated. There's absolutely no reason not to tell them the truth because they are going to hear all sorts of misinformation if they're on the internet or just talking at school. There is so much fake news out there, and it is important that they are educated to recognize where to go to get proper information. I think kids are more savvy than most adults give them credit for.Emma Kenny noted that while very young children might be comforted by parental reassurance, older children might not share their concerns about distressing news or graphic images they encounter online. She emphasized the need for parents to initiate open dialogues. Ask them if they've heard the news and allow them to have that conversation, she suggested. That's how they can start to ask you the questions that really most people want to ask each other.Kenny shared a personal anecdote on BBC Radio Scotland about her eldest son's reluctance to return to London after the Westminster attack. She reassured him by saying, We're going to London in April because the reality is you're more likely to die by falling out of bed than in a terrorist attack. She highlighted that the UK is predominantly full of good people, despite the actions of a few bad or sick people.She further noted, When you look at what happened yesterday, it was full of people running towards that attack to help, not people running away to save themselves. Kenny advised parents to use their own experiences as a framework for discussion and to provide statistical context to alleviate fears. Ask your child, in all the years you've been here, how many times has that occurred for you, how many times have you been involved in it? she recommended.

text: London Underground office staff have voted for industrial action in a row over ticket office closures. In a significant move, nearly 68% of the Transport Salaried Staffs' Association (TSSA) members have voted in favor of strikes, with the turnout for the vote at 44%. The union has highlighted that its members have faced unprecedented levels of abuse following the closure of ticket offices. A survey conducted by the TSSA revealed that most staff feel less secure since transitioning from ticket offices to station concourses.Tom Edwards, the BBC London Transport Correspondent, noted that the closure of ticket offices marks one of the most substantial changes to the tube in generations. The shift to automatic payment methods like the Oyster card and contactless systems aimed to relocate staff from behind glass screens to the ticket gate lines. However, unions have consistently opposed this change, arguing that it has resulted in increased lone working and staff shortages.Representing station staff, the TSSA is expected to decide, likely tomorrow, on the specific industrial action they will undertake in response to the dispute. While strikes are a possibility, an overtime ban is also under consideration. Other forms of industrial action received overwhelming support, with a nine-to-one backing.The union has reported that staff are often targeted by frustrated passengers when ticket machines malfunction. TSSA General Secretary Manuel Cortes stated, This vote is about our members being prepared to strike to make it clear that the Tube is not fit for safe purpose. He emphasized, Our customer service assistants are trying to warn the public that the Tube is not safe. We simply don't have enough staff.In response, Steve Griffiths, London Underground's chief operating officer, urged the TSSA leadership to engage constructively with them on the issues raised instead of threatening strikes that would disrupt customers. The closure of ticket offices was part of the Fit for the Future programme, initiated by former London mayor Boris Johnson. His successor, Sadiq Khan, has since ordered a review of the project.In related developments, Tube drivers are planning 24-hour strikes on December 6 and 7, aligning with a walkout by Southern Rail guards.

text: The new Harry Potter play in London has removed the use of live owls from the production. Following an unexpected incident during the premiere of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child on Tuesday, the decision has been made to remove live owls from the production. During the show, an owl failed to return to its handler after a brief flight, causing it to escape into the auditorium. The play, which is being previewed in two parts, began its run this week. At the Palace Theatre on Thursday, a sign informed attendees that no real birds would be used in the performance. In a statement, the producers explained, The production of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child is currently in its preview stage, allowing the creative team time to rehearse changes or further explore specific scenes before the play's official opening. Earlier this week, it was decided that live owls would no longer feature in the production. The statement emphasized the care given to the owls, noting they were looked after by certified trainers and an on-site specialist veterinary surgeon, Steve Smith, MRCVS, ensuring their welfare and enrichment needs were prioritized.Animal rights organization Peta praised the decision. Peta commends the production team for coming to its senses and recognizing that treating owls like props goes against every message of respect and kindness that JK Rowling's wonderful books taught us, said director Mimi Bekhechi. She added that Harry Potter can now join innovative productions like War Horse, The Lion King, and Running Wild, which demonstrate that animals need not be exploited for theatre and that prop design is limited only by creativity.Adding to the excitement of Thursday's show, JK Rowling was spotted in a box stage right just before the second half began, prompting screams and eager attempts from the audience to catch a glimpse of her.The play, which officially opens on July 30, is based on an original story by Rowling, writer Jack Thorne, and director John Tiffany. Set 19 years after the events of the seventh book, The Deathly Hallows, it features a grown-up Harry Potter, portrayed by Jamie Parker, working at the Ministry of Magic. Meanwhile, his youngest son Albus, played by Sam Clemmett, struggles with the heavy burden of the Potter legacy. The show will continue its West End run until May 2017.
