text: Liam Neeson and Graham Norton have called for the introduction of same-sex marriage in Northern Ireland ahead of a planned protest in Belfast. Snow Patrol's frontman Gary Lightbody and The Fall's star Bronagh Waugh have joined the chorus of voices advocating for same-sex marriage in Northern Ireland, the last region in the UK and Ireland where such unions remain prohibited. This contentious issue has become a significant hurdle in the ongoing discussions to reinstate power-sharing at Stormont.The topic has garnered increased media scrutiny following the Democratic Unionist Party's (DUP) alliance with UK Prime Minister Theresa May, after her failure to secure a majority in the general election. The DUP, known for opposing same-sex marriage, denies allegations of homophobia, asserting instead that they are safeguarding the traditional concept of marriage.A host of celebrities, including actor and writer Stephen Fry and Neil Hannon of The Divine Comedy, have expressed their support through Amnesty International, a key member of the Love Equality coalition orchestrating a march in Belfast on Saturday, July 1.Liam Neeson, an actor hailing from Ballymena, remarked, We've had enough of a history in our society in Northern Ireland of discrimination, mistrust and hatred. Yet, we're also an open-hearted, welcoming and terrific people. Let us show that to the world by treating gay, lesbian and transgender peoples as our brothers and sisters and allowing them to marry, if they so wish.TV presenter Graham Norton reflected on the historic referendum in the Irish Republic that legalized same-sex marriage, calling it a proud gay day. He shared, My own mother was from Northern Ireland, so of course I have a huge affection for the place and its people. I know it is hugely frustrating for gay people there that it is the last part of these islands still without marriage equality. Especially when there is such overwhelming support for it among the public.County Down's own Gary Lightbody recalled marching with 20,000 fellow citizens for marriage equality two years ago. It was a beautiful day of hope, joy, and solidarity, and I was so proud to be from 'Norn Iron'. Two years on and somehow—defying reason given it's the will of the people—we still do not have marriage equality in Northern Ireland, he lamented.Bronagh Waugh, an actress from Coleraine and the host for the parade rally at Belfast City Hall, emphasized the urgency of the moment: With the spotlight on Northern Ireland at the minute, now is our chance to really step up our campaigning a gear and give Northern Ireland what it so clearly wants and deserves, finally—equal marriage.

text: Chinese internet giant Tencent insists its profits won't take a hit from a decision to limit the time children can play one of its most popular games. Access to the popular game Honour of Kings is now restricted for children in China, with those under 12 limited to one hour of play per day, and those aged 12 to 18 restricted to two hours. This decision follows criticism from the government-owned People's Daily, which described the game as poison and advocated for stricter regulations.Honour of Kings, also known as Kings of Glory, is a fantasy role-playing game classified as a multiplayer online battle arena. It bears resemblance to Tencent's other hit, League of Legends, the world's leading PC game. However, Honour of Kings distinguishes itself by featuring characters from Chinese history and being tailored for mobile play, a crucial factor in its popularity in China, where many lack access to gaming consoles or PCs.While the app is free to download, players can spend money to enhance their characters or costumes, facilitating progression to higher levels. Estimates suggest that the average player spends between $1.50 and $6 monthly. Though seemingly modest, these expenditures accumulate significantly with over 50 million active users each month.Concerns about gaming addiction among children have been longstanding, but Honour of Kings has faced particular criticism from the People's Daily, which labeled it a drug harmful to teenagers and called for more stringent online game regulations.Tencent, the company behind Honour of Kings, relies heavily on its revenue model, which encourages gamers to spend more time on their offerings. Their strategy, as outlined in their last annual report, aims to convert casual gamers into more dedicated midcore or hardcore players. In the first quarter of this year alone, Tencent earned $7.2 billion, with gaming contributing $3.9 billion of that total. While League of Legends is its top title globally, Honour of Kings leads in China as the highest-grossing mobile game.According to Chinese gaming industry database CNG, Honour of Kings generated approximately $810.5 million in the first quarter, accounting for about 11% of Tencent's revenue. text: I'm not a tech person. Chad Mureta, a quintessential tech millionaire, has a story that defies expectations. Known for his success in app development, Mureta's creations, such as the Emoji app and Fingerprint Scanner Pro, have been downloaded over fifty million times. His company, App Empire, generates between $3 million and $5 million annually. Yet, his journey to success was anything but typical, marked by a near-fatal accident that changed his life's trajectory.In 2009, Mureta's life was in disarray. After stints in various jobs, including selling on eBay and managing a nightclub, he found himself as a dissatisfied real estate agent. Driving home from a basketball game, his life took a dramatic turn when he swerved to avoid a deer on the motorway, resulting in a horrific crash. His car flipped multiple times, leaving his left arm severely damaged. Doctors almost amputated it.The aftermath was grueling: six months in the hospital followed by six months of rehabilitation, and a staggering $100,000 medical bill that his insurance wouldn't cover. I was at such a low place, Mureta recalls. Very depressed, couldn't sleep, tonnes of medication – and actually very suicidal. I was in so much pain I didn't think I could go on any more.Amidst this turmoil, a serendipitous discovery sparked a new beginning. His smartphone, remarkably intact after the crash, inspired him from his hospital bed. Observing doctors casually using their phones, he envisioned enhancing phone security. Though initially a fleeting thought due to heavy medication, a friend's visit with a magazine article about apps reignited his interest. I just had this 'A-ha' moment, he says. I was sitting there, on all these IV drips, morphine, and I looked around and I finally saw the picture. I entertained a different destiny.Despite lacking coding skills and resources, Mureta had one invaluable asset: time. He immersed himself in studying apps, seeking to understand their appeal. This insight became his competitive edge. A doctor mentioned a cousin in India who was dabbling in app development. Mureta took a leap, borrowing $1,800 from his stepfather, and surmounted language and technical barriers to create his first app.Two months later, Fingerprint Security Pro hit the app store. Though it was a gimmick, simulating fingerprint scanning with a hidden unlock button, users loved it. It earned $12,000 in its first month, setting Mureta on his path to success.Since then, Mureta, now 34, has built and sold three app companies, developing over fifty apps. App Empire now focuses on teaching others how to create and launch their own apps, offering personalized tutoring and publishing instructional books.Mureta attributes his success to focusing on his strengths and delegating the rest. He maintains a lean operation, relying on freelancers and a small core team, while working just one or two hours a day to ensure smooth operations. I work probably one or two hours a day on App Empire, he says. I just make sure things are running smoothly.While he doesn't consider himself a tech expert, Mureta is passionate about technology. He may not code, but he excels at guiding others to create and launch apps successfully.Despite the trauma of his accident, Mureta is open about his experience, recognizing that his recovery story inspires others. Although his arm will never fully function, he retained it thanks to groundbreaking surgery. I have titanium all the way up from my elbow, he notes. It was groundbreaking and unbelievable surgery. Because I still have feeling in my arm, I can use it for the most part, and most people wouldn't even know – aside from the crazy, bear-like scar I have on there!

text: If this secret left-wing plan to take over the Labour Party comes to pass, our electoral existence is in peril. Tom Watson did not hold back in his conversation with me on Monday morning. His concerns seemed to straddle both the future of his political party and the union, Unite, which now seems misnamed given the current discord. The fates of both are undeniably intertwined.Once, Watson shared a close friendship with Len McCluskey, Unite's general secretary; they even shared a flat. However, their relationship soured when Watson, Labour's deputy leader, failed to persuade McCluskey to get Jeremy Corbyn to set a date to step down as party leader. This came after a significant no-confidence vote from eight out of ten Labour MPs against Corbyn last summer. The fallout has led to both political and personal tensions.With McCluskey facing re-election next month, Watson and his allies see an opportunity to weaken both McCluskey and Corbyn. McCluskey's main challenger is Gerard Coyne, a West Midlands organiser, who stands politically to the right of McCluskey. Watson supports Coyne, partly because under McCluskey's leadership, Unite has heavily funded Corbyn's leadership campaigns. A change in leadership could potentially halt financial support to any future left-wing leaders.Coyne initially campaigned on the premise that McCluskey focused too much on Westminster politics, neglecting the union members' interests. However, critics of Corbyn at Westminster felt Coyne's message was too subtle to attract significant media attention. They suggested reframing the contest as a proxy battle for Labour's future.This weekend, Watson received potent ammunition for his campaign. Jon Lansman, who founded Momentum to sustain the spirit of Corbyn's initial leadership campaign, was recorded expressing more interest in altering Labour than in changing the government. He mentioned that an early election would disrupt our plans and emphasized the need to change the nature of the Labour Party.Even more advantageous for Watson was the implication of a closer relationship between McCluskey and Momentum. Lansman speculated that if McCluskey won re-election, Unite will affiliate to Momentum and will fully participate in Momentum. Watson argued that McCluskey preferred to support a left-wing faction within Labour rather than the party itself, a revelation he hoped would mobilize moderate Unite members to vote for a change in leadership.Gail Cartmail, acting leader of Unite, refuted any plans to affiliate with Momentum and claimed Watson did not verify his information before going public. Yet, with or without union funding, Watson fears a hard-left plot that could dismantle Labour.Momentum seeks to amend Labour's leadership rules. Currently, a leadership candidate needs the backing of 15% of MPs and MEPs before the wider membership can vote. Corbyn only made it onto the 2015 ballot because some MPs lent him support to broaden the debate. Those MPs, regretting their decision, are unlikely to repeat it. Lansman stressed the importance of reducing this threshold, should Corbyn resign. At the Labour conference in September, delegates will likely vote on lowering the threshold from 15% to 5%, easing the path for a left-wing candidate.Internal groups like Labour First and Progress, representing Brownites, Blairites, and so-called modernisers, are collaborating in local constituencies to select delegates aligned with their views. They share Watson's belief that replacing Corbyn with someone of similar politics would squander the chance to appeal to a broader electorate. To prevent changes, they aim to outnumber pro-Corbyn delegates at the autumn conference.Watson's dire warnings are partly to alert demoralized moderate members. Conversely, Lansman's transparency about Momentum's goals may rally newer, left-leaning Labour members to attend delegate-nominating meetings.Watson also suspects Momentum aims to unseat MPs and councillors deemed hostile or right-wing. Momentum asserts its right to express views, leaving local members to choose their representatives. Lansman's remarks were made at a public meeting, not in secrecy.It's possible McCluskey could secure his leadership and Momentum may not achieve its desired changes. This stalemate between Corbyn's supporters and detractors could harm the party electorally. Leadership sources caution that Watson's actions have jeopardized local election prospects, exacerbating existing challenges.If election results disappoint, the anti-Corbyn faction may cite this as proof of leadership failure. Corbyn's supporters, however, are preemptively shifting blame to Watson. Following a shadow cabinet away day on Monday, Corbyn and Watson released a statement claiming robust and constructive discussions. Yet, it seems there might have been more robustness than constructiveness.

text: The daily commute to work is something to be put up with rather than enjoyed, yet how we get there and how long it takes has an impact on how we feel. In Britain, the typical worker dedicates an average of 54 minutes daily to commuting, a significant and growing portion of the workweek that comes with more than just financial costs. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) reveals that with each additional minute spent traveling to work, feelings of happiness, life satisfaction, and the perception that one's activities are meaningful tend to diminish. Essentially, personal wellbeing suffers as commutes lengthen.The ONS study highlights that commutes lasting between one and one-and-a-half hours have the most detrimental impact on personal wellbeing. Among various commuting options, taking the bus for more than 30 minutes is most likely to sour one's mood. Consider the experience of a commuter from Porthcawl, Wales: I live in Porthcawl and travel a minimum of five days a week to Watford. My alarm goes off at 03:30 each day and my journey takes two-and-a-half to three hours. My day can last as long as 12 hours. I then travel home when there is a lot more traffic than there is in the mornings, with an average of three to three-and-a-half hours being the norm for this single journey.According to the 2011 census, 7.2% of workers in England and Wales commute by bus or coach, while 5% use trains and 3.8% rely on the underground or tram. The majority, 59%, drive or carpool. Ideally, commuting should not impact mental health since it is a choice. People often move away from urban centers to enjoy better housing, more green space, and an improved quality of life, leading to longer commutes.Professor Jenny Roberts from the University of Sheffield has explored the effects of commuting on wellbeing by studying 7,000 men and 7,000 women over 13 years. Her findings contrast with the ONS report, which is based on a one-time survey of over 60,000 employed individuals between 2012 and 2013. Roberts found that women are more negatively affected by commuting than men, despite commuting less and working fewer hours. This was determined after considering factors like income, job satisfaction, and housing quality. So why are women more sensitive to commuting time? The only reason we could come up with was trip-chaining, explains Prof. Roberts. Women tend to make more interim stops on their journey, via the nursery or the school or the shops, so they have less flexibility and do more multiple activities. This adds stress to commuting.Commuting impacts wellbeing due to the well-established connection between stress and mental health. Stress arises from a lack of control during commuting, such as delayed trains, traffic jams, and unpredictable weather. Additionally, research shows that boredom and social isolation among commuters can lead to unhappiness. However, some find benefits in commuting, using the time to work, read, or relax.Interestingly, 'extreme commuting'—journeys of three hours or more—is becoming more common, and the ONS suggests these lengthy commutes might be more enjoyable than shorter ones. This could be because extreme commuters often have higher incomes and use their travel time more productively.Cyclists and walkers benefit from the physical activity that boosts wellbeing, but cycling can also be stressful, especially if it’s done out of necessity or through heavy traffic.Ultimately, the psychological health of commuters is crucial since everyone commutes, yet we rarely examine how it affects us, notes Prof. Rogers. Do people really make that calculation when moving out to a suburban house of how much time, how much income it's going to cost, and how it's going to affect their mental health?

text: In a football match, it is not usual to start 3-0 down. As the government gears up for the Autumn Statement at the end of the month, it finds itself in a precarious economic situation. The previous Chancellor, George Osborne, had established three fiscal rules to demonstrate to a doubtful public that the government was committed to reducing the national deficit—the gap between public service spending and tax revenue—and curbing debt accumulation. However, these rules have been either broken or discarded: the cap on welfare spending, the pledge to decrease debt relative to national income, and the promise to balance the budget by 2020 have all been abandoned.The target to eliminate the deficit was particularly impacted by the referendum's outcome, which triggered a series of economic downgrades for the UK. If these downgrades materialize, government revenue will decrease, making it even more challenging to eliminate the deficit without resorting to further tax hikes or cuts to public services.This is the challenging landscape that the current Chancellor, Philip Hammond, faces as he prepares for his inaugural Autumn Statement in two weeks. A report released today by the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) highlights the hurdles ahead. It indicates that, given the anticipated economic slowdown, the outlook for public finances is £25 billion worse than the projections made in last March's Budget. Without policy changes—a significant assumption considering Mr. Hammond is both a new chancellor and has mentioned a fiscal reset—the IFS predicts tax revenues will fall by £31 billion. This shortfall could be partially mitigated by the £6 billion the government might save by halting EU budget contributions, although this too is a substantial assumption.Many government insiders suggest that to facilitate a smooth transition to a free trade agreement with the EU, particularly if no consensus on freedom of movement is reached, the UK might need to continue some budget payments. Nonetheless, Brexit's impact on public finances is not entirely negative. The Bank of England's decision to lower interest rates to 0.25% reduces the cost of servicing government debt. Additionally, the depreciation of the pound, which increases import prices, helps shrink Britain's trade deficit by boosting export performance. The rise in dollar earnings and profits for UK-based global companies also benefits government tax receipts. However, these positive aspects are overshadowed by the broader negative implications of the predicted economic slowdown.Some analysts argue that the bleak forecasts may be overly pessimistic, similar to how recession predictions earlier this year failed to materialize. If this optimism is justified, public finance estimates will need another revision. Such is the volatile nature of economic forecasting.With the Autumn Statement approaching, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), the official economic watchdog, is providing weekly updates to the Treasury on future public finance projections. The OBR is expected to lower its growth forecasts for the UK, echoing the Bank of England's stance, which implies reduced government revenue predictions. The government might react by implementing further spending cuts (undesirable), raising taxes (undesirable), or relaxing the deficit reduction target (probable). Should economic growth indeed falter, Mr. Hammond will have limited options to recover the lost fiscal objectives.

text: Motorists trying to access a new system for hiring a car have been experiencing problems with the DVLA website. On Monday, June 8, a new system abolishing the paper counterpart for driving licenses came into effect, sparking mixed reactions. While this change does not impact drivers in Northern Ireland, some car hire companies faced challenges, including long queues, as they adapted to the new process.The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) reported that over 20,000 drivers accessed the new online system without any issues. However, some motorists expressed frustration, claiming parts of the website were inaccessible. Richard Stock from U-drive in Bristol noted, The DVLA system has fallen over a dozen times this morning, highlighting the difficulties faced by car hire firms, which resulted in a queue of 20 people.Under the new system, drivers renting a car must now present a temporary code, valid for only three days, as proof of their driving endorsements and convictions. This change means that all such records are now maintained online. The DVLA has been preparing for this transition for months, according to their statement.Despite the DVLA's assurances, the car hire industry criticized the rapid implementation of the system. Gerry Keaney, CEO of the British Vehicle Rental and Leasing Association (BVRLA), remarked, The project's being rushed through. It's not brilliant. Concerns were echoed by the RAC, which previously warned that many drivers were unaware of the new requirement. A survey by money.co.uk found that 73% of drivers did not know they needed a code to hire a car.To assist motorists, the DVLA created a step-by-step guide and emphasized the simplicity of the process. Oliver Morley, the DVLA's chief executive, stated, It's very easy to view and share your driving record. Just go to gov.uk and search for 'view driving licence'. He added that drivers could save their records as a PDF on a mobile device. For those without internet access, a phone service is available, though only during specific hours.Despite the changes, the AA advised drivers to still carry their paper counterparts, even though they are no longer valid. The government defended the new system, citing potential savings of millions of pounds and a reduction in bureaucracy. Last year, the DVLA replaced 445,000 paper counterparts, charging motorists £20 for each lost replacement.The BVRLA suggested an online IT system allowing hire companies to directly check convictions would be more efficient. Meanwhile, drivers are urged to confirm with their car hire company what documents are necessary before traveling, as smaller or international companies might be unaware of the new rules.Although eight million old-style paper licenses remain valid, courts will no longer add endorsements to them. The changes apply only within Britain, with Northern Ireland maintaining a separate licensing system.

text: The number of people playing golf is falling and Rory McIlroy believes speeding the game up at grassroots level could reverse that trend. Sport England's data reveals a dramatic decline in golf participation among 16 to 25-year-olds, with numbers nearly halving between 2009-10 and 2012-13. This has sparked a conversation about how to revitalize the sport's appeal. Cost is a significant barrier. Golf is an expensive hobby for young people, says a user known as bigted, suggesting that some of the substantial earnings at the top level could be used to support struggling clubs and young players. Peter shares a similar concern, noting that his son, once a junior member of a prestigious London club, couldn't afford full membership after university. He believes clubs should facilitate a smoother transition from junior to full membership.AndyL highlights the prohibitive joining fees, explaining that it would cost him £3,000 to join a decent course nearby. He worries that clubs may suffer in the long run for excluding younger generations. Dave Harrison echoes this sentiment, pointing to the high costs of green fees, lessons, and equipment. Chrisf offers a different perspective, noting that many clubs provide payment plans and that there's a wealth of used equipment available. He suggests that players could benefit from using a half set in a lightweight bag, rather than cumbersome equipment that damages courses in winter.Gary R emphasizes that the primary issue deterring young players is cost, not slow play. Christian Porter proposes several solutions: widening the gap between groups on the time sheet, offering varied hole competitions, and introducing zone golf with different difficulty levels. He stresses the need for golf to be more affordable, less stressful, and more enjoyable.Sam Hatton believes that showcasing the fun side of golf and relaxing dress codes would make the sport more inviting. Ray Bundell shares that a family-friendly nine-hole game rekindled his interest in golf after years of playing tennis. Christian suggests adding urgency with a timer for each shot, while Electric Kid proposes designated times for junior fourballs to foster camaraderie. Nozzie recommends shorter courses that emphasize club selection and ball accuracy. Lyle Hill suggests that the first player to putt should complete their turn to save time.Alan envisions courses with three six-hole loops, allowing players with time constraints to play six or twelve holes. He also suggests that an 18-hole round could be completed over a week. In a more whimsical vein, Kennedy Maswaure jokes about making golf a contact sport, and Jay imagines golfers using jet packs instead of walking or using carts. These varied suggestions reflect a shared desire to make golf more accessible and appealing to younger generations.

Christian recommends a time limit for each shot, and the electric boy says that the junior foursomes should be given a set time, so as to encourage camaraderie. Nozzie suggests a course of shorter length, to encourage good play and a better choice of clubs. He suggests a half-score in a light bag, instead of heavy equipment that damages the course in winter. On the more whimsical side, Kennedy Maswaure joked about making golf a contact sport, and Jay pictured golfers flying around the course in jetpacks instead of walking or driving. Ray Bundell says a family-friendly nine-hole game has brought him back to golf after years of playing tennis. Alan imagined a golf course with three six-hole loops, allowing people with limited time to play six or twelve holes. He also proposed playing an 18-hole game over the course of a week. A desire to make golf more open and more attractive to the younger generations unites these different suggestions. Lyle Hill suggested that the first player to putt should end his turn to save time.

text: The makers of the Raspberry Pi computer have created a version of its graphical front end that can run on ordinary desktop computers. The Raspberry Pi Foundation has revamped its Pixel desktop to operate on both PCs and Apple Mac machines, ensuring users enjoy a consistent experience across different platforms. This development aligns with the Foundation's ambition to deliver the best desktop computing experience, as highlighted in their recent announcement.Eben Upton, co-creator of Raspberry Pi, emphasized the benefits for students who utilize the compact Pi device in educational settings or personal projects. The new software allows them to seamlessly continue their work on PCs or Macs. Upton explained that both the Pi edition of Pixel and the version adapted for larger machines feature exactly the same productivity software and programming tools, in exactly the same desktop environment. This uniformity eliminates the need for adjustments when transitioning between systems, as there is no learning curve involved.Moreover, Upton noted that creating this version of Pixel helps the Raspberry Pi Foundation maintain integrity by allowing its developers to identify areas of the user interface that require improvement. Given that Pixel's core software is based on an older computer architecture, Upton suggested it should run smoothly even on vintage machines. However, he cautioned that the software remains experimental and may contain bugs or minor issues that could affect performance on some devices.Initially released in September, Pixel overhauled the main graphical interface used on the Raspberry Pi, drawing from Debian, an open-source Linux software. The desktop version, however, does not include Minecraft and Mathematica, as the Pi organization has not secured licenses for these applications on non-Pi machines.As of April last year, the Raspberry Pi achieved the status of the most popular British computer ever, with over 10 million units sold since its 2012 debut. It continues to serve as a valuable educational tool for programming enthusiasts and learners worldwide.

text: Doctor Who's Peter Capaldi has passed on his sonic screwdriver to Jodie Whittaker who becomes the 13th doctor and first woman to take on the role of television's famous Time Lord. The lineage of actors portraying the iconic Doctor in the beloved sci-fi series stretches back to its inception in 1963. William Hartnell was the pioneering actor to step into the Doctor's shoes, gracing the BBC show from 1963 until 1966. Before his tenure as the Doctor, Hartnell, who passed away in 1975, was known for roles in The Army Game and the inaugural Carry On film, Carry On Sergeant, in 1958. Health issues eventually compelled Hartnell to vacate the role, marking the first-ever regeneration of the Doctor into Patrick Troughton.Troughton, remembered for his quirky, unkempt style, navigated time and space for three years until 1969. His successor, the dashing Jon Pertwee, became the third Doctor and the first to be seen in color television. Pertwee's era, from 1970 to 1974, was notable for the Doctor's exile to Earth, where he collaborated with Unit, the United Nations Intelligence Taskforce. It was also during Pertwee's time that the series introduced ensemble stories featuring multiple Doctors. The Three Doctors, aired between December 1972 and January 1973, united Pertwee with Troughton and Hartnell, in what would be Hartnell's final acting role.Tom Baker assumed the mantle in 1974, becoming the longest-serving Doctor with a seven-year stint. His deep voice, curly hair, and iconic scarf won him a massive fan base, further delighted by his cameo in the 50th-anniversary special in 2013. When Baker left the role in 1981, Peter Davison, with his youthful charm, became the Fifth Doctor. Davison's three-year term coincided with the show's 20th anniversary, celebrated with a special featuring Jon Pertwee, Patrick Troughton, and a stand-in for Hartnell by Richard Hurndall. Tom Baker opted out of The Five Doctors, with his absence covered by footage from an unbroadcast adventure. A 1983 photo shoot creatively included a mannequin in place of Baker, alongside Hurndall, Davison, Pertwee, and Troughton.Davison's exit in 1984 paved the way for Colin Baker (unrelated to Tom) to take the helm. His time as the Doctor was brief, shortened by an 18-month production hiatus. Despite limited episodes, Colin Baker's Doctor reunited with Troughton in The Two Doctors in 1985, marking Troughton's final reprise. Years later, Troughton's sons, David and Michael, would also appear in the series.Sylvester McCoy succeeded Colin Baker in 1987, leading the show until its cancellation in 1989. BBC One controller Michael Grade was a critic of the show, which struggled against the backdrop of more polished cinematic offerings. However, some argue this era has been unfairly criticized. A revival attempt in 1996 saw McCoy regenerate into Paul McGann during a TV film set in America. The film was intended to launch a new series but ultimately did not, rendering McGann's tenure the briefest.Doctor Who's resurgence came in 2005 as a well-funded, ambitious series with Christopher Eccleston as the Doctor. Despite the show's success, Eccleston departed after one series, his exit confirmed shortly after his debut episode aired. David Tennant then stepped into the role, delighting audiences with his first full appearance in The Christmas Invasion on Christmas Day 2005. Tennant's engaging portrayal lasted until January 2010.The youthful Matt Smith, at just 27, became the 11th Doctor, serving for four years and coinciding with the show's 50th anniversary. This milestone was celebrated with The Day of the Doctor, a special featuring Smith alongside Tennant and introducing Sir John Hurt as the War Doctor.Peter Capaldi, a lifelong fan of the series, became the Doctor in 2013, bringing a mature intensity to the role. His tenure included a notable appearance alongside the original Doctor, portrayed by David Bradley, who will return in the upcoming Christmas special. Bradley had previously played William Hartnell in the 2013 dramatization An Adventure in Space and Time.Jodie Whittaker has been announced as the 13th Doctor, making history as the first woman to assume the role. Her debut is set for the Christmas episode when Capaldi's Doctor regenerates.Stay connected with us on Facebook, follow our updates on Twitter @BBCNewsEnts, or join us on Instagram at bbcnewsents. text: Celtic reached an important milestone by beating Aberdeen in the League Cup final, says manager Brendan Rodgers. Media playback is not supported on this device.Celtic celebrated a landmark victory with a 3-0 triumph, courtesy of goals from Tom Rogic, James Forrest, and Moussa Dembele, securing their 100th major trophy and marking Brendan Rodgers' first as manager. The Northern Irishman praised his team's performance, emphasizing the need to build on this success.It's a winning club, that's what the history of this club has been based on, Rodgers, the former Liverpool manager, stated. Reaching the century of trophies is significant, and now we must focus on the next century. That's crucial for us and the club.Celtic, maintaining an unbeaten domestic record this season, dominated the match. Rogic and Forrest found the net in the first half, while Aberdeen showed some fight after the break. However, their efforts were thwarted when Anthony O'Connor's foul led to a penalty, which Dembele converted.Rodgers expressed his delight, saying, It's a great night for the Celtic supporters to celebrate, and we push for the next one. Reflecting on his tenure, he added, It's been six months and a week since I arrived, and we've been clear about our goals and the way to achieve them. We're making good progress.The manager highlighted the ongoing efforts to enhance standards on and off the field, shaping the team to play in a distinctive style. We'll analyze what we can do better and how we can improve, he noted. Ultimately, the goal was to win the cup, and thankfully, we've achieved that.Rodgers shifted the spotlight from his personal milestone to his players' contributions, particularly praising Scott Brown's midfield command. I've a huge job to do here in terms of building on it and sustaining it, he remarked. It's a great achievement, and for the players, it's a testament to their hard work. It boosts confidence and sets us up for the rest of the season.He added, Having Scott as the captain is a huge honor. He really dominated the game and pulls the team together on the field.Meanwhile, Aberdeen's manager, Derek McInnes, urged his players to channel their disappointment as motivation to reach another cup final this season. He acknowledged that some players fell short of their potential but insisted that Celtic are beatable in a one-off match.There's a lot of pain and not feeling good about ourselves, McInnes admitted. We were beaten by a better team. The key is, when facing them in a cup final, everyone must be at their maximum.He encouraged his team to regroup, saying, It's important we try to pick ourselves up. We're capable of reaching another final this season. This isn't an end-of-season defeat. There's so much more to come this season. We expect more of ourselves, and people perhaps expect more of us.McInnes concluded, It's important that we stick together and recognize there's plenty to play for. I don't mind putting ourselves up there to be shot down. We were huge underdogs, but I still expected us to win and thought we would win the game.

text: A team of UK scientists hopes to shed light on the mysteries of bleeding canker, a disease that is threatening the nation's horse chestnut trees. Researchers have successfully sequenced the genome of a bacterium strain responsible for a severe infection affecting horse chestnuts. According to a 2007 survey, the disease, known as bleeding canker, had spread rapidly, with nearly half of the two million horse chestnuts in the UK showing symptoms.The study's findings have been detailed in the journal PLoS One. One of the most noticeable symptoms of this disease is a lesion on the bark, which secretes a resin onto the trunk or branches. This infection kills the bark beneath the canker, and if it encircles the trunk completely, it can cut off the tree's food supply, ultimately leading to the death of the horse chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum).To understand more about this disease, researchers sequenced the genome of the bacterium Pseudomonas syringae pathovar aesuli (Pae) from three UK samples. These were then compared with a historical sample from an Indian horse chestnut collected in India during the 1960s. The three British samples were all identical, stated Dr. David Studholme, a co-author of the study, currently at the University of Exeter but affiliated with The Sainsbury Laboratory in Norwich during the research. This suggests a single introduction source, he explained to BBC News.However, Dr. Studholme emphasized that further research is necessary to determine whether the bacterium originated from India, where the pathovar was initially recorded. He noted that the Indian specimen had only been known to cause leaf spots, with no evidence of it causing cankers.Sarah Green, a co-author and plant pathologist at Forest Research, the research division of the UK Forestry Commission, described Pae as very mobile, very aggressive and stressed the importance of studying it. We found some intriguing genes that might contribute to its aggressiveness, she said. She also noted that Pae affects the woody parts of trees, unlike other bacterial diseases that target soft tissues like leaves.Since its first recorded appearance in 2002, Pae has spread throughout the UK, with over 70% of horse chestnuts in some areas showing signs of infection. Roddie Burgess, head of plant health at the Forestry Commission, expressed hope that the research would aid in developing a strategy to combat the disease. It's shocking to discover that nearly half of your tree population might already be infected, he told BBC News.Burgess mentioned that local authorities had felled a few thousand trees due to concerns about the potential risks posed by infected trees to the public. A significant number were cut down before we realized that some trees might go into remission and recover. Our current advice is to avoid hastily resorting to chainsaws, he advised.Further research is being conducted to explore whether the disease could kill trees by means other than cutting off their nutrient supply. These are the crucial aspects we need to understand before considering how best to manage infected trees, Burgess added.

text: Head teachers warning that they face financial meltdown are furious that the government has been pledging funds to create grammar schools in England. On Wednesday, it was disclosed that ministers extended an invitation to grammar school leaders to apply for a £150 million fund over three years, aimed at creating new selective school places. Meanwhile, school leaders have been vocal in their demand for the return of £384 million, initially designated to convert schools into academies.The Department for Education claims that school funding has reached unprecedented levels. However, school leaders express their frustration, arguing that while they have been raising alarms about inadequate funding, the government has managed to allocate hundreds of millions for initiatives such as expanding grammar schools and transitioning schools to academy status.In West Sussex, head teachers have been campaigning against what they describe as severe budget deficits. They have reached out to local MPs, expressing their incredulity at the funds seemingly available for grammar schools and are urging political leaders to justify their financial decisions.In a private meeting with the education secretary and schools minister, the Grammar School Heads' Association discussed plans to expand selective places and establish new grammar schools by 2020. Meeting notes, released by the grammar heads, detail how to apply for £50 million annually for new selective places.West Sussex school heads have called for emergency funding of £20 million, warning that without it, schools might face reduced hours, larger class sizes, or the removal of certain subjects. text: Double Olympic champion Alistair Brownlee says he may not return to triathlon for the 2020 Tokyo Olympics. Media playback is not supported on this deviceThe World Triathlon Series kicks off in Abu Dhabi this Friday, but Alistair Brownlee, the 28-year-old Olympic champion from Yorkshire, will be absent from the starting line. Instead, he is focusing on transitioning to the longer half-Ironman distance. Brownlee, who clinched triathlon gold at the Rio 2016 Olympics, successfully defended his title from London 2012.Reflecting on his Olympic future, Brownlee remarked, There's a chance I could never be at an Olympic Games again, but to say I'll never do it is impossible. The Olympic Games are just fantastic and I'd definitely love to be there, but the course in Tokyo is going to play a big part in terms of whether I feel I can go there and win. It's going to be a case of sitting down at the end of 2018 and weighing it up—am I enjoying the long distance stuff? Am I still able to be competitive enough to win a medal in Tokyo?Brownlee is set to defend his World Series title in Leeds on June 11, marking his only confirmed race of the season. Meanwhile, his brother Jonny, who won silver in Rio, will start his season with the second race on the Gold Coast on April 8.Throughout the year, Alistair will juggle standard Olympic-length events—comprising a 1.5km swim, 40km bike ride, and 10km run—with half Ironman distance competitions, known as Ironman 70.3, referring to the total miles covered. He has identified the Ironman 70.3 World Championship in September as an obvious goal as he gears up for the full Ironman distance, which he has long aspired to tackle. Ironman has got to be one of those things you always want to do—it's like the London or Boston marathon of triathlon, he commented.The two-time gold medallist acknowledged that his Rio 2016 victory was slightly overshadowed by the absence of his long-time rival, Javier Gomez. The London 2012 silver medallist was forced to withdraw from the Games after fracturing his elbow in a cycling accident. It definitely took a bit away from my gold in Rio that Gomez wasn't there, Brownlee admitted. You want to be there in your best shape and race the best athletes in their best shape—we were fortunate to have that in London, and it would have been fantastic to have had that in Rio as well, but what happened happened. But on that day, on that course, I'm fairly confident I'd have had him anyway.With Gomez, now 33, having recovered from his injury, Brownlee anticipates that the Spaniard will be a strong contender for the World Series title, alongside fellow Spaniard and current champion Mario Mola, 27. Brownlee also sees his brother Jonny, 26, as a podium contender, suggesting that with a bit of luck and a fair wind behind him, Jonny could seize the title.Alistair Brownlee admits that returning to World Series racing might have left him bored, having faced the same kind of racing against basically the same people for the last 10 years. However, he is invigorated by his new ambitions, which might include competing in 10,000m running races and marathons. I now have an opportunity to try these other things without hurting my chances if I do decide I want to compete in four years in Tokyo, he explained.After Rio, Brownlee contemplated various pursuits. I definitely want to run a marathon and that might be in the not too distant future. The other obvious thing is cycling and trying to make a wholehearted jump into being a professional cyclist, but although that's possible, I'm very aware that in that arena and in running, I can be good and get to a level where I could be professional, but never to a level where I can win stuff. I still feel like I want to be the best at what I'm doing, so that's why I'm choosing things I feel like I can win, he concluded.

text: Donald Trump made a string of promises during his long campaign to be the 45th president of the United States. As President Trump and his administration near the 100-day milestone, it's evident that several of his initial positions have evolved. During his campaign, Trump made headlines with bold promises, such as banning all Muslims from entering the U.S. and constructing a wall along the Mexican border. However, the reality of governing has led to shifts in many of these stances.Initially, Trump dismissed climate change as a fabrication by China and criticized the Paris Agreement for hindering American economic growth. Yet, after months of deliberation at the White House, he ultimately decided to withdraw from the Paris accord, a commitment involving nearly 200 countries, thus fulfilling a campaign promise.On healthcare, Trump fervently promised to dismantle Obamacare, deemed a job killer by Republicans. Although he initially wanted to retain its strongest assets, the plan proposed by House Republicans, which he supported, faced widespread criticism from medical professionals and was predicted to leave millions uninsured. Despite passing in the House, the Senate plans to rewrite it entirely.Trump's pledge to build a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border was one of his most contentious campaign promises. While he insisted Mexico would foot the bill, Mexico refused, and Trump conceded that the U.S. would initially pay, seeking reimbursement later. Congress is exploring funding options, but many Republicans balk at the potential $21.5 billion cost, significantly higher than Trump's $12 billion estimate. Landowners and environmental groups have also raised objections.Regarding trade, Trump labeled NAFTA a disaster and criticized the TPP. True to his word, he withdrew from the TPP shortly after taking office and has since initiated renegotiations of NAFTA with Canada.Trump's stance on immigration also softened over time. Initially advocating for a complete ban on Muslims entering the U.S., he later pivoted to extreme vetting. As president, he introduced two travel bans, both challenged in court. The revised ban was blocked by judges in Hawaii and Maryland, citing constitutional violations and campaign statements as evidence. Trump has criticized this judicial overreach and may appeal to the Supreme Court.On undocumented immigrants, Trump initially called for the removal of all 11.3 million individuals but later narrowed his focus to deporting two to three million with criminal records. The Migration Policy Institute estimates around 890,000 undocumented immigrants have criminal records, but deportations have declined since peaking in 2012.Trump's view on NATO has also evolved. Once questioning its relevance, he acknowledged its significance in combating terrorism during a meeting with NATO Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg, stating, It's no longer obsolete.In foreign policy, Trump threatened to label China a currency manipulator but later acknowledged China's efforts to prevent the yuan from devaluing. He also dropped the largest non-nuclear bomb in Afghanistan, targeting ISIS, fulfilling his aggressive rhetoric against the group.Domestically, Trump promised to appoint conservative judges, successfully nominating Neil Gorsuch to the Supreme Court. He also shifted on torture, deferring to Defense Secretary James Mattis and CIA Director Mike Pompeo, who opposed such methods.The call to lock her up regarding Hillary Clinton faded post-election. Trump expressed gratitude towards Clinton and decided against pursuing further investigation to help her heal.On infrastructure, Trump reiterated his commitment to revitalizing roads, railways, and airports, though concrete actions remain pending. Lastly, while he pledged to move the U.S. embassy in Israel to Jerusalem, he signed a waiver to keep it in Tel Aviv for now, suggesting the relocation is a matter of timing to aid peace negotiations.As the Trump presidency progresses, these shifts illustrate the complex transition from campaign rhetoric to the realities of governance.

text: A Venezuelan teenager taking part in an anti-government protest has been killed in Caracas, the chief prosecutor's office has confirmed. In the Altamira neighborhood, a tragic incident unfolded as 17-year-old Fabián Urbina was fatally shot during a confrontation between security forces and demonstrators. Interior Minister Néstor Reverol acknowledged the possibility of improper and disproportionate use of force by security personnel and confirmed that several officers are under investigation for their actions. Reverol also criticized the Venezuelan opposition for inciting violence and promoting an uprising. Meanwhile, rights ombudsman Tarek William Saab announced via Twitter that two National Guard members have been detained for the undue use of a firearm.For the past 80 days, Venezuela has been gripped by almost daily anti-government protests, as the nation’s economic and political turmoil deepens. These demonstrations often escalate into violence, with protesters hurling petrol bombs and stones, while police respond with tear gas. Since April 1, protest-related violence has claimed over 70 lives, according to the chief prosecutor's office. A list from the information ministry suggests a higher toll, indicating most victims were involved in anti-government demonstrations. However, casualties also include security personnel, bystanders, and a group of men electrocuted during a bakery looting.On Monday, the opposition organized a march to oppose the government's proposal to form a citizens' assembly for drafting a new constitution. Critics argue that President Nicolás Maduro aims to consolidate power and circumvent the opposition-controlled National Assembly through this constituent assembly. President Maduro, however, claims the new constitution is intended to protect the social programs established by his socialist administration and that of his predecessor, Hugo Chávez.While anti-government protesters clashed with security forces in Altamira, government supporters participated in an anti-imperialist march in support of the constituent assembly in the city center. This demonstration aimed to convey a message to the Organization of American States (OAS) meeting in Mexico, urging non-interference in Venezuelan affairs.Foreign ministers of OAS member states once again deliberated on Venezuela's crisis but failed to reach a consensus on a resolution condemning the Venezuelan government. A draft resolution urging President Maduro to abandon the constitutional assembly plans garnered support from 20 countries, faced opposition from five, and saw eight abstentions. The resolution required 23 votes for adoption but fell short.

text: On 2 May 2011, Barack Obama announced that al-Qaeda leader Osama Bin Laden had been killed by US forces in Pakistan. In a compound near Islamabad, a man was shot dead, thrusting Pakistan once more into the global spotlight for unsettling reasons. Despite being accustomed to political and economic turmoil, Pakistan has long been perceived as South Asia's struggling economy, grappling with dwindling foreign reserves, a frail currency, and scant foreign investment. It seemed an unlikely destination for foreign investors.However, Mattias Martinsson defied expectations. In October 2011, just six months after the incident, he launched Pakistan's first-ever foreign equity fund. Initially, support was scarce, prompting Martinsson to invest $1 million (£780,000) of his own and his partners' money. Today, that fund has grown to $100 million. It was a tough sell at the time, the soft-spoken Swede admits from Stockholm, chuckling at the memory.This understatement belies the challenges he faced. Following the killing of Bin Laden, investors, enraged by plummeting share prices, even resorted to stoning the stock exchange. Then the US military bombed a Pakistani base, leading to Pakistan's blockade of NATO supply routes. The market plummeted by 10%, Martinsson recalls. Yet, he persevered, and by 2012, a government tax amnesty aimed at encouraging the Pakistani diaspora to repatriate funds began to turn the tide. The market surged, and we raised $50 million in just three months, he reflects.For the first time in decades, more money flowed into Pakistan than out. Nearly a decade later, Martinsson's gamble appears vindicated. On June 1, 2017, Pakistan rejoined the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, signaling a positive shift. Investors are already taking notice. This index, comprising 23 high-growth economies like India, China, and Brazil, now includes Pakistan, whose main index, the KSE 100, has consistently outperformed it. A $100 investment in the KSE in January last year would now be worth $164, compared to $137 if invested in the MSCI.Rejoining the Emerging Markets Index offers investors reassurance about the growth and transparency of Pakistan's companies. Previously part of the index, Pakistan was downgraded to a frontier market after the 2008 financial crisis prompted the exchange to shut down for four months, trapping foreign investments. We were kicked out because of measures taken to prevent foreign funds from fleeing, explains Nadeem Naqvi, managing director of the Karachi Stock Exchange. We lobbied hard and implemented reforms to regain our place, he adds, assuring investors of the KSE's liquidity.The Pakistan Stock Exchanges Act of 2012 bolstered corporate governance and introduced reforms to prevent a repeat of 2008. Pakistan's GDP has also surged, fueled by a burgeoning middle class and China's $46 billion investment in the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) as part of its One Belt One Road initiative. It's just beginning, Naqvi notes. The real impact will be seen in the next 12 to 24 months, boosting the growth rate. Chinese investors now own 40% of the Pakistan Stock Exchange, further bolstering confidence.Despite these promising developments, security issues along CPEC routes have raised concerns about the project's long-term viability. Investors must weigh these challenges before entering the market. It's great for Pakistan's ego, says Mark Mobius, executive chairman at Templeton Emerging Markets Group, acknowledging the country's pride in leaving the frontier market index. However, he cautions about potential government changes and tensions with India.Despite significant setbacks, including the assassinations of Osama Bin Laden and former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, the KSE has thrived, outperforming other regional indices to become one of Asia's best performers. text: Five disabled social housing tenants have lost their Court of Appeal bid to have benefit cuts for those deemed to have spare bedrooms ruled unlawful. Judges have ruled that the court cannot intervene in the government's contentious housing benefit reforms, often referred to as the bedroom tax by its critics. Legal representatives for the claimants argued that the regulations in England, Wales, and Scotland do not adequately consider the accommodation needs of disabled individuals. Despite the setback, they expressed their intention to continue their legal battle.The court also dismissed the claims of two single parents who argued that the government's cap on total benefits infringes on human rights laws and common law, particularly affecting vulnerable families. Lord Dyson, Master of the Rolls, acknowledged that these legal challenges targeted two of the government's most debated benefit measures. However, he stated that the court could only intervene if the measures were manifestly without reasonable foundation, a standard he concluded was not met, resulting in the dismissal of both challenges.Ugo Hayter, representing some of those contesting the changes, expressed confusion over the Court of Appeal's decision and indicated a potential appeal to the Supreme Court. The court recognized that our clients and thousands of disabled people across the UK have unmet accommodation needs under the new housing benefit rules, Hayter said. Yet, it decided that disabled tenants should not have their housing needs met equivalently to their able-bodied counterparts.Jayson Carmichael, one of the appellants from Southport, Merseyside, voiced his frustration, saying, I hope we can appeal it in the Supreme Court. It must be the worst High Court decision that's ever been made. I'm very angry about it. We are determined to fight for justice because we don't have a spare bedroom due to my wife's severe disabilities. To claim that disabled people are justifiably discriminated against is unacceptable in Britain in 2014.Carmichael detailed the challenges he faces as a full-time carer for his wife, who requires around-the-clock care due to her condition. He expressed concerns about their financial situation, noting that while they have received some discretionary housing payments, they have been told no more will be available this year, risking their ability to keep up with rent.Anne McMurdie, representing three of the appellants, emphasized, Disabled tenants are not asking for extra funds. They are asking for housing benefits to be paid at a level that meets their needs, the same right as others. Discretionary payments are not the answer.Richard Kramer, deputy chief executive of the national deaf-blind charity Sense, expressed disappointment with the ruling, stating, Although this decision concerns five individuals, the policy's impact has been devastating for many disabled people.Kevin Williamson, head of policy at the National Housing Federation, remarked that the court action highlighted the desperation of those affected, stating, Disabled people across the country are being forced to cut back on food and heating to pay the bedroom tax.Richard Hawkes, chief executive of disability charity Scope, described the ruling as a setback for campaigners and a significant blow to the 400,000 disabled people impacted by this policy.The Department for Work and Pensions, a defendant in both cases, welcomed the judgments. A spokesperson commented, Reform of housing benefit in the social sector is essential for the benefit's long-term sustainability. We have ensured extra discretionary housing support is available for vulnerable people. Regarding the benefit cap, the spokesperson added, We are pleased that the courts have again ruled that the benefit cap complies with the European Convention on Human Rights. The cap sets a fair limit on what people can receive from the welfare system, ensuring claimants do not receive more than £500 a week, the average household earnings.Since April of the previous year, individuals with one spare bedroom have seen their housing benefit reduced by 14%, while those with two or more spare bedrooms have faced a 25% reduction. Initially, the challenge involved 10 families, but five cases involving disabled children have been dropped due to exemptions from the benefit cut.The group includes Richard Rourke, a 46-year-old wheelchair user from Bakestone Moor, Derbyshire, who requires an additional bedroom for his mobility equipment. Also involved is Charlotte Carmichael, who, due to her spina bifida, cannot share a bedroom with her husband, who serves as her full-time carer.

text: Argentina's economy minister Axel Kicillof has returned to the negotiating table in a last-ditch attempt to prevent the country defaulting on its bonds. Late on Tuesday night in New York, Mr. Kicillof's negotiations with the hold-out investors concluded without reaching an agreement. These investors are insisting on a full payment of $1.3 billion (£766 million) for the bonds they possess. A U.S. judge has mandated that if no deal is struck, these hold-outs must be paid by Wednesday night.Meanwhile, in Buenos Aires, thousands of miles away, skepticism abounds regarding the possibility of any agreement. The government's stance has been unequivocal. The hold-outs consist of U.S. hedge funds that purchased debt at a discount during Argentina's financial crisis and never consented to restructuring. President Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner has labeled them vultures, accusing them of exploiting Argentina's debt woes for profit.The situation is further complicated by the fact that if the hold-outs succeed, other bondholders who accepted reductions of up to 70% in their claims might also demand full repayment. On the streets, when asked about Argentina's debt issues, most people admit the complexity is beyond their understanding. However, they are familiar with the term fondos buitres, or vulture funds in Spanish.Despite the government's defiant rhetoric, resignation seems to have settled among the populace. Argentina has defaulted before, and many anticipate it may happen again. I spoke with Carina Etchegaray, a mother of two teenagers, aged 14 and 16. She recounted how, during Argentina's last default at the end of 2001, she lost significant savings intended for purchasing a house. The government had implemented the corralito, a policy that froze bank accounts and restricted withdrawals. When we finally had the money, because of devaluation, we could only buy a car for the same quantity of money we had for a house, she shared. Yet, she remains pragmatic. We live with this shadow of crisis. You have to continue with your life because you have children and have to work. You have to adapt - in this country, it's the way of life.Entrepreneur Federico Dumas is also adapting, though not in the way Argentina might hope. He runs a software company but hesitates to invest as he would prefer. I'm afraid of everything and my customers are not willing to invest, so that will affect my business, he explained, though he remains hopeful for a reasonable resolution to Argentina's problems. But if the country goes into default, I'm very afraid of what's going to happen to my business and my employees.Whether a default occurs or not, Guillermo Nielsen, who led the debt restructuring negotiations in 2005, expressed disbelief at the current situation. I never imagined this - not in my wildest dreams, he remarked. People, although they were unsatisfied and they were very tough negotiations, they knew that Argentina was not able to pay, so that's a very big difference. Today, Argentina has the money - back then, we didn't have the money. In my own perception, I think the incoming negotiations are going to be much tougher than the ones we had to go through.Nielsen is particularly concerned about the potential activation of an acceleration clause if the country defaults. This clause could require Argentina to repay bonds much sooner than originally agreed, posing a significant threat. Yet, all of this remains speculative. With only a few hours left, no concrete decisions have been made, and discussions continue. The details of what has been discussed remain unclear. As is often said, in Argentina, negotiations tend to extend until the very last moment. Until then, the vultures will continue to circle.

text: Military landing craft have been suggested as a possible solution to a breakdown of Lochaber's Corran Ferry. In a recent report to Highland councillors, the idea of seeking assistance from the Royal Navy was floated to address a ferry disruption that occurred last month. However, council officers pointed out that multiple landing crafts would be required due to the high volume of vehicles transported, and the ferry's slipways are incompatible with military vessels.Last month, the Corran Ferry, managed by Highland Council and operating on Loch Linnhe in Lochaber, was grounded for several days due to a breakdown. The vessel had drifted and collided with rocks near a slipway. The usual backup, the Maid of Glencoul, was unavailable as it was undergoing refurbishment. After necessary repairs and an inspection, the Corran Ferry resumed its services.The incident report presented to the Lochaber Committee on Tuesday revealed that the local authority incurred costs of £39,000, attributed to lost income and expenses for repairs and inspections, which included the use of a remotely operated vehicle. The report also commended the ferry staff's meticulous and diligent efforts in maintaining a low frequency of breakdowns.During the disruption, Highland Council faced criticism for suspending the service, with complaints about insufficient information regarding the service's status and contingency measures. In response, the council asserted it had taken everything possible to restore operations, disseminating updates via its website and Twitter. Additionally, Traffic Scotland was requested to alert travelers to the ferry issues using electronic signs on the A82 trunk road, although roadworks and heavy rain warnings took precedence.The Corran Ferry is a crucial link for communities in Ardgour, Morvern, and Ardnamurchan, crossing a narrow section of Loch Linnhe. It also serves residents and businesses on Mull, who initially reach the mainland via the Fishnish-Lochaline ferry. Together, the Corran Ferry and Fishnish-Lochaline services provide tourists with an alternative route to the Oban to Mull ferry.

text: Housing is too expensive for would-be buyers to take advantage of the government's Help to Buy Isa (HTB Isa), savers have told the BBC. A BBC investigation has uncovered that in numerous regions, the average price of a starter home surpasses the maximum purchase cap allowed by the scheme. Here, we delve into your experiences.Claire Etheridge, a 28-year-old solicitor from Greenwich, south-east London, works in the capital but finds homeownership there unaffordable. She advocates for raising the £250,000 cap in areas surrounding London. I am looking to buy in St Albans and commute, she explained. However, this area is outside London, meaning I can't utilize what I've saved in the Isa, as the properties I'm interested in exceed the £250,000 cap for areas outside London. It's a beneficial scheme for outside London, but I believe places like Kent or Hertfordshire should have allowances, as prices remain high, and the £250,000 cap is insufficient.Liane Reilly from Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, and her partner face a similar struggle. The 30-year-old shared, We rent a one-bedroom flat for £900 monthly, which consumes nearly one of our salaries. Saving enough to buy seems impossible as our incomes go towards rent and bills.The Help to Buy Isa is part of a broader initiative, including government equity loans covering up to 20% of a new build home's cost, with no fees for the first five years. Matthew Taylor, a 27-year-old management consultant, and his wife Anne, a research client manager, utilized this loan scheme to purchase a home in Dartford, Kent. Help to Buy genuinely works, Matthew stated. People should consider the practical reasons for this scheme's existence. I'd love a central London home with a garden, but that's not feasible. text: William Hague is standing down as an MP after an illustrious 25 year career in the House of Commons. In a reflective interview with the BBC's Norman Smith, former Foreign Secretary and Conservative Party leader William Hague expressed minimal regrets about his political career, apart from his loss in the 2001 general election. I'm not one for having a lot of regrets but I do regret that we didn't get things back together again faster in the Conservative Party, he admitted. As the general election approaches on May 7, Hague is among a notable wave of MPs stepping away from the House of Commons. According to BBC Analysis and Research, 86 MPs have announced their decision to retire. Although this number might seem significant, it pales in comparison to the 2010 election, when 149 MPs exited following the expenses scandal, marking the largest turnover in Commons history.Among those retiring are 17 former cabinet ministers, including 12 from Labour and five from the Conservatives. With the departure of Hague, Sir George Young, and Stephen Dorrell, the number of John Major-era cabinet members still serving dwindles to three: Ken Clarke, Peter Lilley, and John Redwood, each of whom also served under Margaret Thatcher.The Conservative Party will see three female MPs elected in 2010 retire, accounting for 6% of their female representation. In total, seven MPs from the 2010 Conservative intake will step down after just one term. Notable Conservative retirees include former Health Secretary Andrew Lansley, Sir George Young, and Sir Peter Tapsell, the Father of the House, who was first elected in 1959 and has served for 54 years, with a brief hiatus in the mid-1960s.Sir Malcolm Rifkind, now an independent after losing the Tory whip, is also retiring. On the Labour side, only three members of Tony Blair's first cabinet—Nick Brown, Margaret Beckett, and Harriet Harman—will remain, provided they retain their seats. High-profile Labour retirees include former Prime Minister Gordon Brown and ex-cabinet ministers Alistair Darling, David Blunkett, and Dame Tessa Jowell. Jack Straw, who now sits as an independent after his suspension, will also leave.Labour will see 11 female MPs, or 16% of their female representation, retire, all of whom are long-serving. Meanwhile, the Liberal Democrats will lose 10 MPs, including two women. Noteworthy among them are former leader Sir Menzies Campbell and former minister Jeremy Browne.Below is the comprehensive list of MPs standing down in 2015:- Stephen O'Brien, Eddisbury - Francis Maude, Horsham - text: The Irish government arranged for a doctor to visit Ibrahim Halawa in jail in Egypt following concerns about the health of the 21-year-old Dubliner. He has been imprisoned without trial for over three years and has staged multiple hunger strikes in protest. According to his lawyer, by last month, he had become so frail that prison staff needed a wheelchair to transport him to family visits. On medical advice, the Irish government urged Egypt to release him for further medical examinations.Prior to a visit, Irish Prime Minister Enda Kenny expressed his concern over reports of Mr. Halawa's deteriorating health, stating he wanted an assessment from an Irish medical point of view. On Monday, Irish Minister for Foreign Affairs, Charlie Flanagan, confirmed that a prison assessment was conducted last week at the request of the Irish government.Mr. Flanagan reiterated the government's longstanding desire for Mr. Halawa's return to Ireland, noting that direct appeals have been made to the Egyptian government on several occasions. Following the doctor's report, Mr. Kenny wrote to the Egyptian president, seeking Mr. Halawa's release for further testing.The foreign minister also mentioned discussing the case with Abou El Gheit, the Secretary General of the League of Arab States, on Monday. I also raised the case again with the EU's High Representative, Vice President Federica Mogherini, who has taken a personal interest in the matter, Mr. Flanagan added. He emphasized that the case is receiving unprecedented attention and resources both in Dublin and Cairo.Despite these efforts, the Halawa family insists that the Irish government must intensify its actions and has previously urged Mr. Kenny to initiate international legal proceedings against the Egyptian government. Mr. Halawa, the son of the Republic of Ireland's most senior Muslim cleric, was just 17 when he was arrested alongside his three sisters during a 2013 siege at Cairo's Al-Fath mosque. While his sisters were released after three months, Mr. Halawa remained imprisoned, with his court case being adjourned 20 times.For years, Mr. Halawa faced the threat of a death penalty if convicted in a mass trial. However, in January, the Egyptian president assured a delegation of Irish politicians that he would pardon Mr. Halawa once his trial concluded. The Egyptian parliament has previously resisted calls from the Irish parliament to release the Dubliner, arguing that such requests interfere with the Egyptian judiciary's affairs.

text: A County Down couple, who foster five boys including two sets of siblings with a range of complex needs, have been named Northern Ireland's Foster Carers of the Year. Glen and Regina Mahon, seasoned foster carers for 15 years, have been lauded for their unwavering dedication, generosity, and kindness. The couple was taken aback when their names were announced as award winners. Regina expressed their joy to the BBC, saying, We were ecstatic.We were gobsmacked, she added. I couldn't believe it when they said our names. After hearing the stories of other carers, we thought so many others deserved this recognition.Despite raising five boys ranging from seven to 17 years old, their Ballykinler home remains a serene haven. The kitchen, bustling with football kits and boots, serves as the home's hub. Regina credits their calm to a well-structured routine. The boys all have chores. One brings out the bin in the morning, another sets the table. That's what makes us work, she explained.The Mahons opened their doors to children who arrived in vulnerable states, craving love and support. Among them are kids with various health challenges, including ADHD, epilepsy, and a boy with a hypoplastic heart. Despite their diverse backgrounds, a strong bond has formed among the children and with the Mahons.I visited the Mahons after a celebratory weekend with the children. In their lively kitchen, Regina shared their gratitude. Every one of them is a character, no doubt, she said. These children, traumatized for various reasons, seek reassurance, compassion, and someone to listen. Each has complex needs, which is tough, but we wouldn't be without them.What set the Mahons apart from other finalists was a touching story. Glen took leave from work to accompany one child to Birmingham for critical heart surgery, a commitment lasting 16 weeks. Why did I do it? How could I not, Glen said. If it was one of your own, you'd be there. I was at his bedside 24/7, before the operation and during intensive care. It was harder on him as he took longer to mend.Why choose to foster? You do it because these children need love and care. They need a family, Glen explained. They arrive cowering at the door, then gradually feel part of the family. When they call you mum and dad, it brings a lump to your throat. It feels good.Currently, over 2,150 children are living with more than 2,000 foster families across Northern Ireland. Despite these numbers, the Fostering Network estimates a need for at least 170 new foster families annually. There is a pressing demand for carers for teenagers, disabled children, and sibling groups.Kathleen Toner, director of the Fostering Network, highlighted the importance of fostering. Foster carers can provide children with a home for as long as they need it, she said. Survey results show children need stability. If you have room in your heart and home, 2016 could be the year you make a lasting positive difference to a child.Foster care needs have surged by 14% over the past four years due to increased awareness of child protection and family challenges in Northern Ireland, according to Toner. The Fostering Network aims to debunk myths about fostering, such as the belief that single people cannot foster or that there is an upper age limit. You don't need to be a parent to foster.For the Mahons, winning the award has been humbling. They are thrilled that their son and his wife, inspired by their example, have registered as foster carers, continuing the family tradition.

text: The board of Rangers discussed putting the club into administration months before it was bought by businessman Craig Whyte. These are external links and will open in a new window.Former financial director Donald McIntyre testified that the club's significant financial liabilities made it essential to address them. Craig Whyte, accused of fraudulently acquiring Rangers, faces two charges: one of fraud and another under the Companies Act. During his second day on the witness stand, McIntyre detailed the financial challenges Rangers faced before Whyte's acquisition in May 2011. The club was confronted with a potential £50 million bill from HMRC, known as the Big Tax Case. Defense QC Donald Findlay likened the debt to a nuclear missile targeting Rangers, describing it as like an exocet, unstoppable.McIntyre revealed that Rangers' board hoped to contest the amount owed, with legal counsel at the time suggesting they had a strong case. However, Findlay argued that the tax bill represented a potentially terminal event for the club. He inquired when McIntyre first realized the board was considering administration for Rangers. McIntyre couldn't specify a date but acknowledged the topic would have cropped up in 2010.The court learned about a March 2011 meeting of Rangers directors discussing the HMRC debt and its implications. Findlay pressed McIntyre: Rangers could not contemplate paying up that size of debt? McIntyre concurred. The jury later heard that Rangers eventually went into administration, though it was unrelated to the Big Tax Case.The trial also revealed that former owner Sir David Murray, who acquired the club in 1988, reportedly called Whyte's bid the only show in town. Findlay asked McIntyre if it became clear that Murray would do anything to secure the deal with Whyte. McIntyre disagreed, saying, I would not put it like that. I don't think a deal would have been done under any circumstance. Findlay countered, A deal was done under any circumstance...Rangers was bought for a pound. text: Huddersfield Giants climbed off the bottom of the Super League table to leave Hull Kingston Rovers as the only winless side in the top flight.
