The Rovers managed to cut the deficit with a converted try by Thomas Minns. However, Aaron Murphy's try reestablished the 12-point advantage for the Giants, who then pulled away with additional tries from Jermaine McGillvary, Larne Patrick, and Ukuma Ta'ai.Danny Brough, instrumental with his tactical kicking, successfully converted all six tries and added a penalty, contributing a personal tally of 14 points. His efforts included a conversion following McGillvary's landmark 100th Super League try. This victory marked Huddersfield's first win after losing their initial four Super League matches, allowing them to surpass Rovers in the standings. Rovers, having secured only one point from their first six games, were still reeling from a draw with Castleford last month.James Webster, the interim head coach and former Rovers captain, faced a challenging debut as his team was outclassed throughout the match. Despite the return from injury of ex-Huddersfield players Shaun Lunt and Graeme Horne, and the reinstatement of James Green and John Boudebza from suspension, the Rovers struggled. He mentioned Sir Edward Heath, whom he said he had always hated and whose house he said was fully equipped with a system of surveillance, and whom he had never been able to enter, since a whole troop of watchmen and armed guards guarded it. He mentioned some names, some of whom he knew, others he had heard of, and others he did not know at all. text: Remains found on the raised Sewol ferry that were thought to come from one of the disaster's missing victims are from animals, South Korean officials say. The National Forensic Service has confirmed that bone fragments discovered during the salvage of the Sewol ferry are of animal origin, according to the maritime ministry. The Sewol ferry tragically sank off Jindo Island on April 16, 2014, resulting in the deaths of 304 people, most of whom were schoolchildren. Despite extensive efforts, the bodies of nine individuals remain unaccounted for, prompting relentless campaigns by their families for recovery.After nearly three years submerged, the ship was raised last week and placed on a platform for transport to port. On Tuesday morning, South Korean officials reported that bones had been found protruding from a window in a passenger room during the draining process. Lee Cheol-jo of the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries initially indicated that tests were necessary to ascertain whether the bones belonged to one or more individuals. However, a later statement from the ministry clarified that the bones were not human.The Sewol disaster deeply affected the nation, as most passengers were teenagers from a single high school. Many followed incorrect crew instructions to stay in their cabins as the ferry went down. The nine missing victims include four students, two teachers, and a family of three.The ship is anticipated to arrive at Mokpo port later this week, where it will be greeted by the victims’ families before undergoing cleaning and a thorough search for remains. On Tuesday, the relatives of the nine missing individuals held a memorial service aboard a boat near the raised ferry. The ship has come up, but not the nine people inside it, Lee Geum-hee, whose daughter is among the missing, expressed to local media. She implored, Please don't forget there are people inside the dirty, rusty, and smelly wreckage... Please do the best and let us bring them back home.The disaster has been attributed to illegal modifications, excessive cargo, the inexperience of the crew member piloting the vessel, and insufficient government oversight. The ferry's captain was eventually convicted of murder.

text: A leading Liverpool fans' group has warned members they need to discuss the issue of safe standing or risk the conversation happening around them. Media playback is not supported on this device.The Spirit of Shankly (SOS) is set to cast votes on the matter this Saturday. Jay McKenna, the chair of SOS, commented that the Hillsborough disaster's aftermath might have caused fans to lag in discussions about reintroducing standing areas in stadiums.Liverpool FC has stated that they will listen to the opinions of their supporters if the legislation mandating all-seater stadiums is ever revised. The club acknowledged that their fans face a uniquely complex and difficult position when considering safe standing. This is due to the fact that the requirement for all-seater stadiums in England's top league was a direct response to the Hillsborough tragedy, where 96 fans lost their lives in a crush during an FA Cup semi-final in 1989.Since September, SOS has been engaging with its members on this issue, and on Tuesday, they will meet with survivors and families of the disaster's victims. An open meeting is scheduled in the city this weekend, followed by an online vote. This vote aims to establish an official stance on safe standing for SOS members, while a separate poll will gather the opinions of non-members to form a broader consensus among supporters.McKenna emphasized, We think it's important that everybody has a say. It can be a factual and emotional debate. We are fully aware of that. In the past, nobody has wanted to talk about it, perhaps for fear of upsetting people. If we don't have this conversation, it will happen around us. We just want to know, are you in favor of it or not?For safe standing to be implemented, changes in government legislation would be required. Last month, the Premier League reached out to its 20 clubs to gauge their interest in piloting safe standing.The discussion around this issue has intensified since Celtic introduced approximately 3,000 rail seats at Celtic Park at the start of last season. Representatives from the Scottish club and the Sports Ground Safety Authority, which managed the transition to all-seater stadiums, will attend Saturday's SOS meeting.Margaret Aspinall, chair of the Hillsborough Family Support Group, which aids families of over 70 victims from Hillsborough, reaffirmed the group's opposition to safe standing. We have had a vote not so long ago with the families and they voted against any form of standing whatsoever, she stated. We don't call it safe standing; we call it unsafe standing.Meanwhile, the Hillsborough Justice Campaign has maintained a neutral stance on safe standing. However, its chair, Kenny Derbyshire, stressed that it is now imperative for people to express their views.In April 2016, inquests determined that the 96 individuals who perished at Hillsborough were unlawfully killed. By June, it was announced that six senior figures would face charges related to the disaster.

text: Listening to new music is rewarding for the brain, a study suggests. A groundbreaking study by a team of Canadian scientists has revealed intriguing insights into how our brains respond to hearing a song for the first time. Utilizing MRI scans, researchers discovered that the brain's reward center, specifically the nucleus accumbens, becomes highly active when people listen to new music.Published in the journal Science, the study highlights that the more a listener enjoys a song, the stronger the neural connections in the nucleus accumbens. Dr. Valorie Salimpoor of the Rotman Research Institute in Toronto explained to the BBC's Science in Action program, We understand that the nucleus accumbens is linked to reward. But music is unique. Unlike tangible rewards like food, sex, or money, which trigger excitement because of their physical nature, music excites us with its abstract anticipation.The research was conducted at the Montreal Neurological Institute at McGill University, where 19 volunteers listened to 60 new music excerpts tailored to their tastes. Each 30-second track was accompanied by the option to purchase it in a simulated online music store, all while participants were inside an MRI machine.Through the analysis of brain scans, scientists observed that the nucleus accumbens lit up during music listening. The level of activity was so telling that researchers could predict whether a participant would buy a song based on their brain's response. Dr. Salimpoor noted, By examining brain activity, we can gauge how much someone appreciates or enjoys music before they even express it. This is part of a new direction in neuroscience—understanding thoughts, motivations, and behaviors through brain activity.Additionally, the study found that the nucleus accumbens interacts with the auditory cortical stores, a brain area that holds sound information from past musical experiences. This brain region is unique to each person, reflecting the diverse music we've all heard, Dr. Salimpoor added.The team aims to delve deeper into how these brain interactions drive our musical preferences and whether they can explain individual inclinations towards different music styles.For more insights on this research, tune into the BBC World Service's Science in Action program. Broadcast schedules are available here, and you can also listen or download the podcast anytime.

text: Engineers have produced an alloy that springs back into shape even after it is bent more than 10 million times. Memory shape alloys hold vast potential, yet their current versions often succumb to wear and tear. A groundbreaking material composed of nickel, titanium, and copper has now emerged, setting new resilience records. This innovation, as reported in Science Magazine, could revolutionize artificial heart valves, aircraft parts, and next-generation solid-state refrigerators.Already utilized in various fields, memory alloys are found in surgical procedures. For instance, a stent can be compacted to fit a small space, then expand to support a blood vessel. Despite their uses, these alloys have struggled to break into high cycle fatigue applications.Typically, shape memory alloys—like those in minimally invasive surgery—regain their shape once or a handful of times, not repeatedly, explained Prof. Manfred Wuttig, a senior author of the study from the University of Maryland. This development is extraordinary. It's a significant leap forward, he shared with the BBC.Prof. Wuttig collaborated with colleagues at the University of Kiel, Germany, to develop this new alloy. The secret to its exceptional properties lies in its crystallization. The nickel, titanium, and copper atoms are structured to toggle between two configurations repeatedly.This phase transition enables the alloy to revert to its original shape after being bent, triggered by heat or released tension. Crucially, tiny particles of an impurity—a compound of titanium and copper, Ti2Cu—facilitate this process. This precipitate is fully compatible with both crystal structures, ensuring complete transformation from A to B and back, Prof. Wuttig noted.The team crafted the alloy into small 1cm-square pieces, less than 1mm thick, and subjected them to rigorous testing using heat and stress. Achieving 10 million cycles required patience and automation, Prof. Wuttig admitted. With stress, it's manageable. You can automate stress-strain machines, but it takes weeks to accumulate the cycles. Temperature is more challenging.A specialized furnace system was employed to rapidly heat and cool the samples 10 million times. The experiment spanned several weeks, Prof. Wuttig added. The alloy's structural changes were scrutinized using advanced microscopes and X-rays. Experiments at a synchrotron provided precise crystal structure data, he elaborated.In a commentary for the journal, Prof. Richard James from the University of Minnesota described the 10 million cycle achievement as breathtaking. text: Former soap-actress Tracy Brabin has been selected as Labour's candidate for the Batley and Spen by-election prompted by the killing of Jo Cox. In a significant development for the Batley and Spen constituency, the well-known actress from Coronation Street, EastEnders, and Emmerdale, has been selected as the Labour Party's candidate, surpassing fellow nominee Jane Thomas. This decision comes in the wake of the tragic loss of MP Jo Cox, who was brutally shot and stabbed on June 16 in Birstall, West Yorkshire. The by-election is scheduled for October 20.Tracy Brabin, a native of Batley, had previously collaborated with Mrs. Cox on a campaign dedicated to preserving the town's library. Her acting career includes memorable roles as Tricia Armstrong in Coronation Street during the 1990s, Roxy Drake in EastEnders, and Carole in Emmerdale. Additionally, she has contributed as a writer to popular shows such as Family Affairs, Tracy Beaker, and Hollyoaks.At a hustings event on Friday, Ms. Brabin expressed her deep sense of honor and responsibility in being chosen to follow in Mrs. Cox's footsteps. Jo was my inspiration. I intend to do her proud, she asserted. She emphasized, Obviously no-one wanted this, but I'm the only person on the ballot paper that can stand up for everyone in Batley and Spen. I'm hoping people will put party politics to one side and we can work together.In a related event, Brendan Cox, Jo Cox's husband, along with their two children, met with US President Barack Obama at the White House in Washington, DC. Brendan shared on Twitter that their conversation with the president revolved around Jo and the fight against extremism. He commended President Obama for being excellent with the kids, noting that the kids gave him their best drawings.Following Ms. Brabin's selection, Yorks&Humber Labour tweeted their congratulations: Many congratulations to @Tracy4MP who has been selected as Labour's candidate for Batley and Spen. She'll be a strong voice for everyone.Jane Thomas, Ms. Brabin's rival, had previously contested as a Labour candidate in the 2010 general election but was defeated by the Conservatives in Keighley, West Yorkshire. In a gesture of respect, the Conservatives, Liberal Democrats, and UKIP have announced they will not present candidates in the upcoming by-election. However, the English Democrats have declared that their deputy chairman, Therese Hirst, will contest, and Jack Buckby will represent Liberty GB.In the 2015 general election, Jo Cox secured a majority of 6,057 votes in Batley and Spen, with the Conservatives finishing second and UKIP third.

text: Parents who restrict their children to a vegan diet could face a jail term if a controversial bill is passed by the Italian parliament. Elvira Savino, a member of the centre-right Forza Italia party, has introduced a draft bill targeting parents who impose a vegan diet on their children, claiming it lacks essential nutrients necessary for children's healthy and balanced growth. This proposal comes in the wake of several high-profile incidents in Italy where malnourished children, fed vegan diets, were taken into care. Over the past 18 months, four such cases have resulted in hospitalisation.Despite these concerns, the American Dietetic Association asserts that vegan diets can be suitable for children, provided careful attention is given to ensuring they receive all necessary nutrients, particularly vitamin B12. Some doctors speculate that the guardians of hospitalised children may not have been adequately informed about how to supplement a vegan diet to make it safe for young ones.A vegan diet excludes all animal-derived products, and its rising popularity prompts questions about its impact on physical endurance and part-time adoption. Savino's bill, which is set to be reviewed by parliamentary committees before a potential debate in the chamber later this year, according to Reuters, aims to address this issue.In contrast, three competing bills seek to increase the availability of vegan and vegetarian options in Italian canteens. In the introduction to her bill, Savino acknowledges the growing belief in Italy about the health benefits of vegetarian and vegan diets. She states, There is no objection if the person making this choice is an informed adult. The problem arises when children are involved... The vegetarian or vegan diet is, in fact, deficient in zinc, iron, vitamin D, vitamin B12, and omega-3.The draft legislation is designed to stigmatise the reckless and dangerous eating behaviour imposed by parents pursuing a vegan diet to the detriment of minors. If passed, the bill would impose penalties of up to a year in jail, escalating to four years if a child suffers illness or permanent injury, and six years in the event of death.While some nutrition experts question the bill's validity, others warn that its vague language could lead to penalising a broader spectrum of parents beyond just vegans or vegetarians, such as those with obese children. Critics suggest that enhancing public health education might be a more effective strategy for improving children's nutrition than punitive measures.

text: Is Facebook a media company? This abstract question, often associated with Palo Alto tech enthusiasts, Lower East Side podcasters, and local media critics, actually touches on the core of modern democracy. Understanding Facebook's recent announcement about combating fake news requires addressing this question first. Facebook has introduced measures to tackle fake news, such as simplifying the process for flagging false stories and reducing the financial incentives for their creators. While these steps are appreciated, they fall short of the demands of some critics. The media landscape has evolved, with platforms like Facebook increasingly assuming roles traditionally held by publishers.In a recent episode of the Wall Street Journal's Media Mix podcast, Tony Haile noted, Publishers do five things: they create, post, curate, distribute and monetize content. Facebook now does four of those five... [But] they don't create. This point, however, is debatable. While Facebook doesn't commission original journalism, the introduction of Facebook Live brings it closer to content creation. Lavish Reynolds' live broadcast of the aftermath of Philando Castile's shooting exemplifies this shift. Facebook didn't commission her report, but through Facebook Live and Instant Articles, it facilitates original journalism, much like Amazon's Web Services support for entrepreneurs.Supported by advertising, generating vast story amounts, and serving as a primary news source for millions globally, Facebook undeniably resembles a media company. Yet, Facebook resists this label in a crucial way: it refuses to exercise human judgment in distinguishing truth from falsehood.I recently discussed this with Adam Mosseri, Facebook's Vice President of Product for News Feed. He detailed Facebook's new initiatives to combat fake news, which some argue contributed to Donald Trump's presidential victory. Although Mark Zuckerberg initially dismissed this claim as crazy, he has since shown commitment to addressing the issue. Facebook's strategy involves four key actions to curb fake news. According to Zuckerberg and Mosseri, fake news constitutes a small fraction of Facebook's shared content, and complete eradication is unfeasible.However, Facebook remains firm on one controversial point: it will not employ editors to determine truth. Mosseri explained that the effort is algorithmic, relying on algorithms and user judgments to identify potential fake news, without direct editorial intervention.Years ago, Zuckerberg likened Facebook to a utility company, but utilities operate in regulated environments. The narrative shifted to Facebook being a technology company. In Rome, this past August, Zuckerberg reiterated, we are a tech company, not a media company.Despite this stance, Facebook's influence on the media industry is undeniable, attracting advertising and vast audiences. Critics from outlets like the New York Times and The Sun lament the perceived duopoly of Facebook and Google over media. Although Facebook denies being a media company, its significant impact on the industry and role in spreading misinformation continue to draw condemnation from publishers. They argue that Facebook, despite its global stature, is neglecting a vital public duty: serving as arbiters of truth.In essence, Facebook functions as a media company, even if it refuses to acknowledge it.

text: The plays of William Shakespeare have endured for centuries, and so have many of the names he created for his characters. As we commemorate the anniversary of Shakespeare's death, we delved into the lives of individuals named after his timeless characters. We spoke with a Hero, a Lysander, a Macbeth, and even a William Shakespeare to uncover how their names have shaped their experiences.William Shakespeare from London reflects on his name's legacy. My parents never explained why they chose William, but I suspect it was after my father, he shared. His father was the first William in the family, yet William himself did not continue the tradition, naming his children Peter and Susan. Growing up during the war, his name rarely drew comments. Curious about a possible family connection to the bard, William explored his ancestry but remains uncertain. I once visited Stratford-upon-Avon and jokingly offered to sign books in a shop, but the owner didn't catch on, he chuckled.In Sweden, Shuna Macbeth Blankenhaus embraces her Shakespearean middle name. Surrounded by diverse cultures, my name remains constant, and my lecturers enjoy it, she said. Studying literature, she feels destined for this path. Collecting Shakespeare's works in English and German, she appreciates his influence on post-colonial and world literature. I love the reactions my name evokes and never have to introduce myself twice, she noted. While some associate her name with bad luck, her family affectionately calls her and her sisters the three little witches.Ariel Ophelia Meadows from New Zealand shares a deep connection with her Shakespearean namesakes. Her father loved the character Ariel, while Ophelia was her great-grandmother's name. It's an icebreaker, and I can spot a Shakespeare fan when they reference 'The Tempest' instead of 'The Little Mermaid,' she said. Her name fostered an early interest in Shakespeare, with fond memories of attending A Midsummer Night's Dream in Savannah. Both Ariel and Ophelia taught me about strength and kindness, she reflected.In Belgium, Lysander Fockaert's name often surprises people. Inspired by A Midsummer Night's Dream, his parents chose it without hesitation. Some mistake me for a girl due to the similarity with Lisanne, but it's rare, he explained. Though not widely recognized in Belgium, once people learn its origin, they are impressed. My name sparks conversations and has fueled my interest in literature and culture, he added.Hero Selwood from Cornwall initially disliked her name due to childhood teasing. They'd ask why I wasn't called Heroine, she recalled. However, as Hero became more common, she grew to appreciate its uniqueness. It's a conversation starter, but I struggle to remember others' names, she admitted. Her job involves frequent customer interactions, often leading to surprise when they realize she's a woman.Puck Creemer from Holland faced bullying over her name, which was unusual at the time. I thought I was named after a dog, she said. Learning about her Shakespearean namesake, she found comfort despite Puck's mischievous reputation. Older people always said it was a great name, she noted. Over time, Puck has come to cherish her connection to Shakespeare.Portia Miller from Berkshire experiences frequent mispronunciations of her name. People think I'm named after the car, she explained. Her parents were inspired by Portia de Rossi and later discovered the Shakespearean character. I admire Portia's conviction and believe it's a unique name, she shared.In Northern Ireland, Lynsey Richards chose the name Arden for her daughter, inspired by Shakespeare's Forest of Arden. Living in Stratford-upon-Avon, we wanted a meaningful name, she said. The name suits her daughter perfectly and serves as a cherished reminder of their connection to Stratford.Compiled by Andree Massiah.

text: Children's mental health services are in a state of emergency and must be prioritised, a leading doctor has said. The government has pledged a substantial £1.4 billion investment aimed at overhauling mental health services for the youth. However, Dr. Richard Vautrey, a Leeds-based GP and deputy chair of the British Medical Association (BMA), has urged the government to translate its promises into tangible actions. This is an emergency, he stated. We've discussed it extensively but have not taken adequate steps to address the issue. The longer we delay, the more severe the problem becomes.Recent statistics reveal that one in 50 children under 18 are engaged with specialist mental health services across England. NHS Digital's data collection on under-19s using mental health services began in January, and by June, the number had reached 235,189. These figures also highlight significant regional disparities in treatment wait times, with the BBC reporting that in 40% of the areas providing data, the average wait exceeded a month.The challenge in addressing mental health care for the youth is compounded by limited data availability. Since NHS Digital only started gathering specific information on children and young people in January, only 65% of mental health care providers have submitted high-quality data. This incomplete picture complicates strategic decision-making for mental health care provision.The Oxford Health NHS Foundation Trust reported the longest average waiting time nationwide, with patients typically waiting 18 weeks to start treatment. However, Oxford Health contested these figures, claiming their median waiting time in June was 34 days. NHS Digital clarified that mental healthcare providers are responsible for ensuring the accuracy of the data they submit.In Bradford, patients faced nearly two-month waits to commence treatment. Our local target is to see all patients within 11 weeks, and we are meeting 100% of urgent cases within a week. text: A court in Egypt has sentenced one of the country's most prominent pro-democracy activists, Alaa Abdul Fattah, to 15 years in jail for illegal protest and attacking a police officer. The family of Mr. Abdul Fattah revealed that his verdict was delivered in absentia, as he was denied entry into the courtroom. A pivotal figure in the 2011 uprising against Hosni Mubarak, Mr. Abdul Fattah was sentenced just three days after ex-army chief Abdul Fattah al-Sisi assumed the presidency. Since the military ousted former President Mohammed Morsi in July 2013, authorities have aggressively targeted both Islamists and secular activists, leading to hundreds of deaths and thousands of arrests.Mr. Abdul Fattah was detained in November following his participation in a protest opposing a new law that prohibited unauthorized demonstrations. His mother, Laila Soueif, told the BBC on Wednesday that her son was barred from entering the courtroom for the verdict. Alaa and his lawyers were outside the court. They were refused entry, she explained. She criticized the judge's decision to issue the verdict without Mr. Abdul Fattah present, stating, There was no justification for the judge to issue this verdict in absentia... we expected a court hearing with the prosecution and witnesses speaking. She further expressed her belief that Egypt's judicial system is disconnected from law and justice and confirmed that the family plans to appeal the verdict.Previously, Mr. Abdul Fattah had been detained under Mubarak's regime and interrogated over protests against the Muslim Brotherhood in 2013. According to the BBC's Orla Guerin in Cairo, this severe sentence raises further concerns about democracy and free speech in Egypt. In a recent interview with the BBC, Mr. Abdul Fattah remarked that the authorities aimed to imprison him for an extended period, claiming the current regime is even more oppressive than Mubarak's.President Sisi, who secured 96.9% of the vote in May's elections, faced a turnout of less than 50%. This low participation was influenced by calls from Mr. Morsi's Muslim Brotherhood and various liberal and secular activists to boycott the election. Sisi's victory came nearly a year after he deposed Mr. Morsi, Egypt's first democratically elected president, following widespread protests against his governance. Mubarak, Morsi's predecessor, had resigned in 2011 after nearly 30 years in power, following mass anti-government demonstrations.

text: Scunthorpe gave their League One play-off prospects a boost with victory over second-placed Bolton. The visitors' only notable attempt came six minutes before halftime, when Conor Wilkinson's effort soared high and wide into the crowd.The Iron nearly extended their lead early in the second half. Neal Bishop's low strike deflected slightly before hitting the post, narrowly missing the chance to double the advantage. Scunthorpe's goalkeeper, Joe Anyon, played a pivotal role in maintaining the team's first clean sheet in nearly two months. He made a crucial save by tipping over a powerful shot from James Henry and later demonstrated his skill again by diving to stop Max Clayton's header.As the match drew to a close, Scunthorpe made strategic substitutions, with Craig Davies replacing Stephen Dawson, and Sam Mantom coming on for Paddy Madden. Bolton applied pressure, earning several corners, but Scunthorpe's defense held firm. David Mirfin, instrumental at both ends of the pitch, conceded a corner, while Scott Wiseman and Stephen Dawson also contributed defensively.Bolton's attempts to equalize were thwarted by Scunthorpe's resilience. Dorian Dervite's header was saved, and Max Clayton's shot was blocked. Ivan Toney of Scunthorpe had a couple of chances, but his shots from outside the box failed to find the target.The match saw several fouls and yellow cards, with Murray Wallace and Neal Bishop of Scunthorpe both booked for bad fouls. The match concluded with Scunthorpe United victorious, holding onto their slim lead to defeat Bolton Wanderers 1-0. This report was provided by the Press Association.

text: Police officers carrying Tasers will now patrol outside the Scottish Parliament. Links to external content will open in a new window. In the wake of the Westminster attack, Members of the Scottish Parliament (MSPs) have been briefed about heightened security measures. Police Scotland clarified that these measures are precautionary and not prompted by any specific intelligence threat concerning Holyrood. Despite this, the proposal to equip all police officers in Scotland with Tasers has been turned down. The suggestion, originating from the Scottish Police Federation (SPF) during a debate on increasing the number of armed officers, was rejected by Deputy Chief Constable Johnny Gwynne. Speaking to BBC Scotland, Gwynne emphasized the need for a nuanced approach to counter-terrorism and organized crime, heavily reliant on community cooperation. For the avoidance of doubt, we as a command team in Police Scotland pride ourselves in being an unarmed service with the ability to draw on armed capability when we need it, Gwynne stated. We are committed to remaining what looks like an unarmed service, because that's what we believe makes policing work here. It is, in essence, a policing model that works right across the UK and that's what we're committed to. Where we need armed capability, we can draw on it at speed and in numbers.He further praised the rapid response of Assistant Chief Constable Bernard Higgins and his team during the Westminster incident, describing the Scottish force as match-fit for such events. Higgins added that Tasers should not be considered in isolation but as part of the broader capability to address all threat levels. It's not just about Tasers, it's about Police Scotland's ability to mitigate every threat level. When we look at the threat level, we assess it throughout the country. My firm belief is that the number of officers we have trained in the use of Taser and firearms is proportionate to that level of threat.An emergency motion at the SPF's annual conference questioned whether budget cuts undermine counter-terrorism efforts and if officers are sufficiently equipped, including with firearms, for protection during terrorist incidents. Calum Steele, the SPF's general secretary, argued that officers should have all necessary equipment, asserting their right to protection. He noted the Westminster attack unfolded in under 90 seconds, a timeframe comparable to deploying tactical officers in Scotland. This has got to be about more than tactical police responses, Steele insisted. It's got to be about more than machine guns. It's got to be about more than police officers with ballistic helmets, wearing their balaclavas and carrying out a very dangerous role. The terrorist attack in Nice, with the truck, was brought to an end by ordinary armed police officers. The terrorist attacks at Charlie Hebdo and the Bataclan theatre were brought to an end by tactical firearms officers. There is room for both. You need both.Khalid Masood's attack last Wednesday resulted in three fatalities when he drove a car into pedestrians before fatally stabbing PC Keith Palmer. Masood, 52, was then shot dead. Following this, Scotland saw an increase in armed response vehicles on its streets for 36 hours. Police Scotland, after reviewing intelligence, deemed this response proportionate to the threat level around Holyrood.In a letter to Holyrood staff before Police Scotland's announcement, Holyrood chief executive Paul Grice stated, Police Scotland will announce this morning that police officers carrying Tasers will patrol the public area outside of the Scottish Parliament building with effect from today. Police Scotland has assured us that the move is an operational contingency measure and is not based on any intelligence threat in relation to the parliament or Scotland. text: Twelve people were hurt, including seven teenagers, when fires broke out at two neighbouring refugee hostels in the south German region of Bavaria. A man has been taken into custody after fires broke out in Wasserstein, with police suspecting arson as the cause. Fortunately, no one in the hostels suffered serious injuries. This incident occurs in a year when Germany has seen the arrival of over a million refugees and migrants, with Bavaria being the initial destination for most of them.President Joachim Gauck dedicated his Christmas message to addressing this significant influx. He commended the German people for their goodwill and professionalism, as well as their ability to improvise in response to the crisis. We have shown what we are capable of, he stated, while also urging that the full force of the law be applied against those who resort to violence against newcomers. Arson and attacks on defenseless people deserve our contempt and deserve punishment, he emphasized.According to Die Zeit newspaper, refugee hostels in Germany have experienced over 200 attacks this year, yet only a few perpetrators have been convicted. In light of this, Chancellor Angela Merkel recently pledged that Germany would noticeably reduce the number of refugees, a move aimed at addressing criticism from her center-right CDU party.A significant portion of the arrivals, up to 40%, hail from Balkan countries like Albania and Kosovo, deemed safe, while the rest are primarily refugees from Syria, Iraq, and Afghanistan. European nations are grappling with the challenge of accommodating the large influx of people entering the EU. This week, international migration officials reported that over a million irregular migrants and refugees have reached Europe by land and sea, with the majority passing through Greece.Czech Prime Minister Bohuslav Sobotka criticized Mrs. Merkel, accusing her of sending a message that encouraged illegal migration to Europe from the Middle East and Africa. Meanwhile, UN refugee officials reported that 3,716 people have died or gone missing this year while attempting to reach Europe.Amidst these grim statistics, there is a glimmer of hope for an Afghan family who feared their 10-year-old son had drowned off the Turkish coast. The Rabani family, now in Lower Saxony, Germany, was separated from their son during a boat boarding in Turkey. His boat capsized, resulting in numerous drownings. However, a German Red Cross official managed to locate the boy at a refugee hostel in Switzerland, and the family anticipates reuniting in a few weeks.In another development, Reem Sahwil, a 14-year-old Palestinian refugee who made news in July after crying in front of Mrs. Merkel, has reportedly been informed by German immigration officials that her family can remain in the country until 2017. During a live TV event, Reem expressed her desire to attend university, only to break down in tears when Mrs. Merkel explained the harsh realities of migration policies. The chancellor attempted to console her by stroking her head.

text: A dog which went missing on a mountain, sparking a social media campaign by more than 6,000 people to find him, has been rescued. Jasper, a Border Collie, disappeared during a walk on Scafell Pike in the Lake District with his owner, Adam Nolan. The search for Jasper, which involved a mountain rescue team, a helicopter, police, and dog enthusiasts, concluded successfully on Thursday. By 19:00 GMT, a JustGiving page created by Mr. Nolan to support the rescue efforts had amassed over £25,000.Jasper was last spotted around 14:00 on Sunday at Cam Spout Crag, beneath Scafell Pike. According to Mr. Nolan, from Cleator Moor, the outing was routine, as Jasper was accustomed to navigating the fells. Desperate to find his beloved pet, Mr. Nolan turned to social media, launching the #FindJasper campaign, which quickly gained traction.After a potential sighting in Seascale on Wednesday, Mr. Nolan expressed his determination to continue the search until Jasper was home and in front of the fire. The local community rallied behind the effort, and Wasdale Mountain Rescue successfully located Jasper early Thursday morning.Mr. Nolan shared his joy on Facebook, writing, I'm over the moon to announce the safe return of my best friend Jasper. This morning, Geoff Horky [from the rescue team] ascended Scafell Pike in response to yesterday's sighting report near the summit. Geoff found Jasper at 2:00 am in excellent condition. The Wasdale Mountain Rescue Team was then alerted and initiated the rescue. Upon receiving the news, I joined the team at Lingmell Col, where I was reunited with Jasper. I owe a huge thank you to Geoff and the Wasdale Mountain Rescue Team for their heroic efforts this morning.A spokesman for Wasdale Mountain Rescue expressed the team's satisfaction, stating, The team is pleased to announce that we have been involved in the successful rescue of Jasper. The team responded and brought Jasper back to the valley to reunite with Adam.

text: India's space agency has successfully launched its heaviest rocket. A monumental day unfolded for India as a 640-tonne rocket soared into the sky from Sriharikota, located off the Bay of Bengal. This significant launch marks a pivotal moment for the Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro), as it reduces its dependency on European vehicles for launching heavy satellites. The event has been met with vibrant enthusiasm, with media outlets drawing vivid comparisons: the rocket's weight is likened to that of 200 elephants or five jumbo jets. Such analogies underscore the launch's importance as India seeks to carve out a larger slice of the global commercial satellite launch market.Historically, India has relied on international partners to send heavy satellites into orbit, a costly venture that strains Isro's budget. The newly launched GSLV Mark III, however, can transport payloads exceeding three tonnes into the high-altitude orbits used by satellites that facilitate television, telephone, and broadband communications.Despite its capabilities, the GSLV Mark III is not the world's heaviest rocket. That title belongs to NASA's Saturn V, which was operational between 1967 and 1973 and boasted a lift-off mass approximately four times greater than India's latest rocket. According to NDTV, the rocket's weight is equivalent to five jumbo jets, a notable factor given the substantial mass of communication satellites.Experts highlight that this development grants India greater flexibility in deploying various types of satellites. Ajay Lele from the Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses remarked to AFP, We were able to send satellites weighing up to two tonnes previously. This is a double quantum jump for India.Isro aspires for the rocket, dubbed the monster by some media, to eventually carry an astronaut to space by 2024. Achieving this would place India among the elite ranks of the US, China, and Russia, who have already accomplished manned space missions. Experts suggest that this successful launch will further energize India's indigenous space program.This achievement follows a series of Isro's recent successes, including a mission to Mars and the launch of over 100 satellites in a single mission earlier in the year. Adding to the excitement, the BBC discovered the rocket stands taller than the Statue of Liberty. Measuring 43 meters (141 feet) in height, it surpasses the statue, which is 33.83 meters tall, excluding its pedestal. The BBC's Kirtish Bhat captured the event's essence through cartoons, adding a creative touch to the coverage.

text: The EU's latest Earth observer has returned its first pictures. Launched just two weeks ago, Sentinel-3a is set to revolutionize ocean monitoring by focusing on measuring sea surface color, temperature, and height. This data will be crucial for weather forecasters and marine biologists aiming to assess the health of global waters. The first images captured by the satellite’s Ocean and Land Colour Instrument (OLCI) feature the Strait of Gibraltar, the Californian coast, and the ice-covered Svalbard archipelago.As its name implies, the OLCI sensor isn't limited to oceanic observations; it also collects data on land surfaces, such as monitoring global vegetation health. We received the first images on 29 February, but we've had to spend a bit of time working on them to get the calibration right, explained Volker Liebig, director of Earth observation at the European Space Agency (ESA). We're not ready with everything onboard the satellite yet, that's clear; but we thought it important to get the pictures out there, he told BBC News.Before Sentinel-3a begins routine operations, it will undergo several months of testing. This satellite is part of the European Union's Copernicus programme, a multi-billion-euro initiative expected to support a wide range of applications, from air quality monitoring to crop performance, water resource management, and transport infrastructure planning. ESA is responsible for the technical design of the satellites, while industry handles their construction. Contracts for Sentinel-3's follow-on models—b, c, and d—are already in place, ensuring operational continuity in orbit until at least 2030.In addition to the OLCI, Sentinel-3a is equipped with a radiometer for measuring ocean and land surface temperatures, and an altimeter for gauging ocean height. These instruments will be invaluable for tracking phenomena like El Niño, which causes warm waters to accumulate in the eastern Pacific every few years, leading to global weather disruptions. Europe's national meteorological agencies are eager to integrate Sentinel-3 data into their forecasting models.Yes, Sentinel-3 is an ocean workhorse, but it's also a global workhorse, said ESA senior scientist Dr. Craig Donlon. The vegetation products we'll get from OLCI in 21 bands will be really excellent, so there will be a huge amount we'll get out of it just looking at land surfaces. And then there's all the work it will do measuring ice surfaces, and rivers and lakes using its altimeter, he told BBC News.Sentinel-3a joins two other satellites already in orbit: Sentinel-1a, launched in 2014 with radar capabilities to measure Earth's surface shape, and Sentinel-2a, launched last year with a color camera to monitor land use changes over time. More Sentinels are on the horizon, with the European Commission and ESA considering expanding the initial suite of sensors. There is interest in developing a space-borne carbon-monitoring capability to ensure countries adhere to carbon dioxide and greenhouse gas reduction policies.This would be a multi-satellite mission, said Prof. Liebig. The idea would be to have a first prototype satellite by 2025, let's say; and then a full system around 2030. But if we want to achieve this we have to start in this (EU) financial perspective.The European-funded Sentinel series is a key component of the Copernicus programme. For further updates, follow Jonathan Amos on Twitter: @BBCAmos.

text: It didn't much look like a protest. On a sunny Sunday afternoon, a group of casually dressed, smiling middle-class Germans gathered in a picturesque park on the outskirts of Hamburg. Some had children, others brought their dogs, and all were engaged in lively conversation. Despite the relaxed atmosphere, this was a protest group, rallying to collect signatures for a petition aimed at halting the construction of a new refugee center on the green space.The protesters were quick to clarify that they were not opposing immigrants per se. Their primary concern, they said, was preserving the natural beauty of the area. However, as conversations unfolded, deeper anxieties emerged. Birgit mentioned the difficulty Germans already face in finding housing. Hamburg, suffering from a chronic housing shortage, is now straining under the influx of tens of thousands of immigrants, pushing the city to its limits. Authorities have resorted to converting shipping containers into refugee accommodations and repurposing vacant commercial properties and open spaces for new migrant centers.I don't think Angela Merkel has any idea what she started, Birgit remarked. Meanwhile, Hanno expressed his worries, shaking his head as he said, I just don't think Germany can integrate this number of people. It's a real worry. A real worry.This gathering was not a demonstration by the far-right anti-immigrant minority in Germany, known for grabbing headlines. Instead, it was made up of Angela Merkel's core supporters: the comfortable middle classes, now beset by doubt and insecurity. While most Germans acknowledge their duty to assist those fleeing war or human rights abuses, the sheer number of arrivals is unsettling for many. By the year's end, Germany is expected to receive over a million refugees, with some experts predicting the figure could rise to 1.5 million.Chancellor Merkel, echoing Barack Obama's Yes We Can, continues to assure the nation with Wir schaffen es! (We can do it!). Yet, more Germans are asking: How? Recent polls indicate that only one in three supports her migrant policy, and her popularity is declining. Once known for her cautious, step-by-step approach, Merkel's decisive actions during a summer of refugee crises have taken many by surprise. A month ago, she unilaterally declared all Syrian refugees welcome, refusing to set an upper limit on Germany's intake. It seemed an impassioned move, a departure from the stable, strong, and stoic demeanor for which she is traditionally admired.Florian Juerg, a branding consultant, speculates that Merkel is revealing her other self. Until now she has acted like the sensible scientist that she is, he explained, referencing her background as a physicist. But suddenly she's transformed back into the moral-driven pastor's daughter of her youth. In Hamburg, a hub for marketing and brand imaging, I asked Juerg if the migrant crisis would tarnish Brand Merkel. Not in the long-term, he replied. Building a brand takes time, and Merkel's decade as Chancellor has been beneficial for Germans. Hers is a solid brand.Nevertheless, if her refugee policy fails, it could mar her political legacy. Known affectionately as Mutti, or Mummy, Merkel has consistently been trusted by Germans to make the right decisions. Her handling of the migrant crisis is the most significant gamble of her career. While Brand Merkel has bolstered Brand Germany, it now risks unintended consequences. The influx of asylum seekers will undoubtedly affect Germany's economy, society, and politics, with divisions already surfacing within Merkel's conservative bloc.We have to get the balance right, stated Lorenz Caffier, CDU Interior Minister of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The German constitution mandates care for refugees, but the benefits we offer are too generous. Frankly, I'm amazed at any migrant who doesn't choose Germany. Our benefit system is like a travel agency. We must prioritize our own citizens' welfare.German media has highlighted the disparity between benefits for refugees and those for German citizens on welfare, fueling a sense of injustice. There are also widespread concerns about the strain on the national health and education systems. Germany can't take everyone in, Mr. Caffier asserted. Angela Merkel didn't open the door to refugees; they were already at the door. What was she to do—send tanks to the Austrian border? Closing borders is impossible, and any politician suggesting otherwise is lying.He stressed the necessity of shared responsibility across Europe. We Germans can't do this alone. Brussels must decide whether it will focus on trivial regulations or address significant European issues. Yet, other European leaders are not rushing to accept asylum seekers in large numbers. Chancellor Merkel's leadership in the migrant crisis is as contentious abroad as it is domestically. The once queen of consensus politics is no more.

text: Former bouncer Levi Bellfield, 43, has been convicted of murdering three young women and trying to kill another in south-west London and Surrey. Here are the profiles of the women who became victims in a harrowing campaign of violence.Amanda Dowler, affectionately known as Milly, was a vibrant 13-year-old described as pretty, popular, and intelligent. In every sense, she was an ordinary girl blossoming into a fine young woman, prosecutor Brian Altman revealed at the Old Bailey. Milly lived in Walton with her parents, Bob and Sally, and her older sister Gemma, with whom she shared a close bond. Gemma recounted in court, We would go to bed at the same time and chat about our day. Milly and I had no secrets; she'd tell me about the boys she fancied at school. Milly was a fan of Gareth Gates and had recently seen him at a Pop Idol concert. She was eagerly anticipating a school event to see a boy she liked. However, the court also learned of a darker side, as poems and a goodbye letter found after her death suggested she was unhappy. Milly was in Year 9 at Heathside School in Weybridge, where her mother taught math. By chance, she took a route home that led her across Bellfield's path; normally, she would have disembarked at another station but had stopped at a cafe with friends. She was one of the funniest people I had ever met, always trying to make people laugh and smile, said her friend Danielle Sykes.Marsha McDonnell, 19, had just completed her A-levels and was enjoying a gap year before university when tragedy struck. Described in court as an attractive blonde, she was brutally attacked by Bellfield just yards from her Hampton home, which she shared with her parents, Phil and Ute, two sisters, and a younger brother. On the night of her attack, Ms. McDonnell, who worked in a Kingston gift shop, had been to the cinema with friends. Her sister Nathalie remembered her as someone who always thought of other people and was a free spirit. Her uncle, Shane McDonnell, expressed the family's grief, saying, Five years have passed since the night our beloved Marsha was so cruelly taken, a girl with only love in her heart, brutally slain by a man filled with hate. He described their loss as devastating, adding, Marsha, we miss you. Our world is incomplete, like a rainbow missing a color. We thank you for the joy you brought us in your short life. Your goodness, sense of fun, and passion for life remain with us. Ms. McDonnell's love for music is commemorated with a music room at a local children's hospice in her honor. Her uncle further stated, For her family, life will never be the same. The pain and hurt we carry is a sentence with no remission.Amelie Delagrange, 22, had a deep passion for the English language and moved to Britain to advance her studies. Originally from Amiens, France, she had easily passed her baccalaureate exams and spent six weeks in Manchester for a language course. She enjoyed her time there and wanted to return to the UK. At the time of her death, Ms. Delagrange had been living in Twickenham for just three months, working at a patisserie in Richmond, and had a close-knit group of English and French friends. Her parents, Jean Francois and Dominique Delagrange, traveled from France to attend the Old Bailey hearings. Her mother described her as a good student, sensible, and never a problem. Her boyfriend, Olivier Lenfant, echoed these sentiments, saying she believed she lived in a safe area. In a statement, her parents expressed their ongoing anguish: It is nearly four years since our lives were so seriously disrupted, descending into a horror—a living nightmare. They added their disappointment in not hearing any remorse from Bellfield, saying, We would have liked to hear some confession of sorts. A memorial tree and bench on Twickenham Green honor her memory, placed by the community and her family.Kate Sheedy was an 18-year-old head girl at her Isleworth convent school when she was attacked in 2004. After spending the evening bidding farewell to friends on her last day at Gumley House School, she was struck by a car while walking home. The attack forced her to miss her A-levels, but she was awarded her predicted grades and later pursued history and drama at York University. The trial revealed that she remains mentally and physically scarred. In a statement, Ms. Sheedy shared, On the day I was attacked, I was celebrating moving on to a new and exciting time in my life. All that hope and excitement was taken from me, and I thought my life had changed forever. The incident delayed her university start by a year. I will never be able to forget what happened to me; the scars and memories are something I will never be rid of, but hopefully, I can move on, she said. Beyond the physical and mental trauma, Ms. Sheedy also endured stress from the police investigation.

text: A new chair-based gymnastics exercise programme has significant benefits for people with dementia, says a report. Media playback is not supported on this device.The Love to Move initiative, orchestrated by the British Gymnastics Foundation (BGF), has engaged over 150 participants. Research from Age UK highlights its demonstrable benefits across physical, emotional, and cognitive dimensions for the elderly. With aspirations to broaden its reach, organizers are focused on training more individuals to deliver this transformative program.Patrick Bonner, the BGF manager, expressed enthusiasm about the program's impact, stating, This age and dementia-friendly programme is astonishing people with its life-changing benefits. So many people involved are seeing their lives improving as a result and it is unthinkable that people are regaining functions which were thought to be lost because of participating in the Love to Move classes. Initially, Bonner anticipated the program might merely decelerate dementia’s progression, but has observed participants reclaiming previously lost functions.In South Korea and Japan, the program's success has led to complete state funding, with its implementation in every care home. Exercise, in any form, can significantly benefit those with mental and physical ailments, and dementia is no exception.The BGF, inspired by a chair-based exercise program flourishing in Japan and South Korea, was determined to introduce it to the UK. The original Japanese program, whose results were published in 2016, demonstrated that exercises focused on cognitive stimulation, memory arousal, and music could profoundly affect dementia patients. By integrating these core principles into a pilot scheme, adapted for British culture, the BGF crafted the Love to Move program.Can you tap your head while rubbing your stomach simultaneously? This simple exercise demands substantial concentration, enhancing the brain's ability to process information independently on each side. The Love to Move program capitalizes on bilaterally asymmetrical movement, which involves performing different actions with each side of the body. This increases neural connections, thereby boosting cognitive abilities.For dementia patients, Love to Move has been shown to improve their ability to handle everyday tasks like eating, crafting, and socializing. If you know someone with dementia—a family member, friend, or coworker—you understand the desire for any improvement in their condition.The BGF is eager to share its exercises with the public, hoping to provide a gentle, practical approach to health improvement for those affected by dementia. A downloadable booklet, featuring exercises and tips from head coach Kim Hall, offers insights into the program’s structure and history, along with key coordination exercises.Over two years in Cambridgeshire, Love to Move sessions have centered on enhancing coordination, posture, movement, and core strength. Feedback from care home staff revealed that residents eagerly participated, sometimes even convincing visitors to join in.Key findings from the pilot scheme reveal that exercises like hand rotations, finger tapping, and drawing shapes in the air enhance coordination, while balance and core-focused activities help participants sit unaided. Those with severe cognitive decline showed improved emotional states, visibly enjoying the classes and anticipating future sessions. The program also fostered social interaction, allowing residents to build connections and support each other.The BGF aims to replicate the success seen in Japan, offering Love to Move across the UK. Achieving this requires extensive staff training, a nationwide awareness campaign, and a cadre of trained coaches to lead the sessions.

text: Southern rail commuters are facing more travel misery after drivers walked out for the third day this week following the failure of conciliation talks. The ongoing dispute over driver-only operated trains has once more brought the rail network to a standstill. Labour's transport spokesperson, Andy McDonald, is urging the government to step in before another conductors' strike takes place next week. He emphasized the need for a pause and a thorough examination of the situation, stating, People need to step back and let's have a thorough examination of this.Speaking on Radio 4's Today programme, McDonald expressed his frustration with Southern and the Department for Transport, accusing them of intransigence and stupidity in their handling of the situation. He highlighted the importance of the issue, citing concerns over safety and security, and criticized the trivialization of these concerns. McDonald called for the intervention of Chris Grayling, urging him to agree to a moratorium to get passengers back on trains, stating, It's what a Secretary of State should be doing right now.On Thursday evening, enraged passengers held a protest at London Victoria station, subsequently delivering a letter to the Department for Transport (DfT) demanding government intervention. The protest, organized by the Association of British Commuters, has gained support in its efforts to pressure ministers into resolving the industrial disputes and other issues plaguing Southern.A spokesperson for the association remarked, We have suffered a year-long nightmare because of the collapse of Southern rail. We have desperately called for government action and have been repeatedly ignored—even while many of us have lost our jobs or had to move house. The DfT informed the BBC that the dispute is between Southern and the unions, stating that it is not something the government is involved in. A spokeswoman declined to comment further but mentioned that splitting the franchise was not planned as it would not solve the problems and might cause more disruption. The focus, she said, should be on resolving the strikes.The Aslef and RMT unions are in conflict with Southern's parent company, Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR). Due to the strike, Southern announced there would be no service on any route on Friday and warned of a revised service on Saturday. However, Thameslink is running a normal schedule, and the Gatwick Express is operating every 30 minutes from 05:00 to 22:00 GMT between London Victoria and Gatwick Airport.Under Southern's proposed changes, drivers would manage the opening and closing of train doors, while guards would assume the role of on-board supervisors. The RMT has expressed concerns over potential job cuts and safety issues. Aslef has labeled the changes inherently unsafe, though GTR maintains that both the Office of Rail and Road and the Rail Safety & Standards Board have deemed the practice safe.Talks between GTR and Aslef at the conciliation service Acas on Thursday failed to yield an agreement, with both parties remaining open to further discussions. In a letter to union members on Friday, Aslef leader Mick Whelan stated that no formal offer had been made regarding the core issue of the dispute. text: In our series of letters from African journalists, Nigerian writer and novelist Adaobi Tricia Nwaubani looks at the clamour for assistance that accompanies a politician's rise to office. As Nigeria's political party primaries conclude, citizens now have a clearer view of who might next enjoy the spoils of power following the February 2015 elections. Yet, it's not just the victorious candidates who will benefit from the nation's wealth. In Nigeria, the news of an electoral win spreads rapidly, crossing rivers, mountains, fields, and forests to reach relatives worldwide. Many unemployed individuals anticipate the end of their joblessness, while those without formal education foresee new opportunities to ascend the corporate ladder. Meanwhile, Nigerians abroad begin plotting their return home.Soon, relatives and friends converge on the successful candidate. They flood his phone with calls, send messages, and appear at his doorstep. Offers of campaign assistance abound, and prayer sessions for his triumph are organized, often late at night in his living room.A Lagos-based friend recently shared his travel plans to Benin City, where his acquaintance had secured a seat in the House of Assembly. Another associate was poised for a prominent position. He's a good friend of my elder brother in Florida, he noted. I've told my brother: 'You'd better come down, connect with him, and introduce us.'Another acquaintance, whose husband closely associates with a victorious candidate in one of Nigeria's prestigious states, reported her phone ringing nonstop with congratulatory calls. Even I called to extend my congratulations.In Nigeria, it is customary for anyone who rises to power and gains control of the national wealth to include their clan in the feast. Forgetting his people after taking office is the gravest error a politician can make. He must remember his extended family and friends, ideally through contracts, appointments, or jobs. Failing to do so leads to ridicule and ostracism, leaving him isolated at the end of his term. Long after his death, his legacy will be one of neglecting his kin.Stories abound of the influx of people from the Niger Delta to Abuja after Goodluck Jonathan's election as president in 2011. A favorite tale comes from a British-Nigerian friend teaching at an elite Abuja school. She was astounded when a student displayed extensive knowledge about crustaceans, detailing their capture, cleaning, and cooking. Curious, she inquired about his expertise. The boy revealed he grew up in the creeks, where his family traded crustaceans.This is why a candidate's potential rise to power brings such joy. Globally, economic transformation typically requires years of effort. In Nigeria, an election and a new political appointment can swiftly elevate one's circumstances, taking a child from creek-side crustacean trading to an exclusive Abuja school.The insatiable demands of relatives and friends fuel Nigeria's corruption woes. Picture the thousands with outstretched hands behind each political officeholder. Convincing them of reform when it's finally their turn to share the wealth is a daunting task.If you wish to comment on Adaobi Tricia Nwaubani's column, please do so below.

The water's surface was coated with a thin film of oil, which villagers had to skim off before collecting water. They reported that no fish had been seen in the stream for over five years and that oil pipe explosions had claimed lives and caused health problems due to inhaling fumes from burning oil well heads. By 2011, the situation had worsened, forcing villagers to walk up to four hours to find drinkable water.Over the past two decades, successive Nigerian governments have failed the people of Ogoniland, and I remain skeptical that this report will bring about change. Meanwhile, calls for secession in Ogoniland are likely to grow louder. Some areas that appeared unaffected were actually severely contaminated underground, according to Unep. In one community, families were found to be drinking from wells contaminated with benzene, a known carcinogen, at levels 900 times the recommended limit. Scientists discovered oil slicks eight centimeters thick on the water, attributed to a spill over six years ago.The report, which examined around 200 locations over 14 months, criticized Shell for not adhering to its own procedures in maintaining oilfield infrastructure, creating public health and safety issues. However, it also noted that locals were sabotaging pipelines to steal oil. The restoration of the region could cost $1 billion (£613 million) and take 25 to 30 years to complete. The environmental restoration of Ogoniland could be the most comprehensive and long-term oil clean-up ever undertaken if we are to restore contaminated drinking water, land, creeks, and vital ecosystems like mangroves to full health, Unep stated.Regarded as the most detailed study on any area in the oil-rich Niger Delta, the report was partially funded by Shell at the Nigerian government's request. All oil spills are detrimental—harmful to local communities, the environment, Nigeria, and SPDC, he stated. We clean up all spills from our facilities, regardless of the cause, and restore the land to its original state, he added. The SPDC managing director also urged authorities to intensify efforts to curb illegal refining and pipeline sabotage.Ogoni communities have long lamented the damage to their environment, often feeling ignored. The issue was famously highlighted by writer Ken Saro-Wiwa, who was executed in 1995 by Nigeria's military government, drawing international condemnation. text: Learning a foreign language should be made compulsory in primary schools here, a new report has said. In Northern Ireland, the primary school curriculum does not mandate learning a second language, unlike in England and Scotland, where students are expected to study a foreign language. Researchers from Stranmillis University College recently reviewed the state of primary language education in Northern Ireland, surveying over 100 schools. Their findings revealed that Spanish and French were the most commonly taught languages, with some schools also offering German or Mandarin. However, not all primary schools provide language instruction, leading to what the researchers described as a lack of equity in provision for children nationwide.The study also highlighted inconsistencies in the frequency and starting age for language instruction. Many primary school principals voiced concerns about inadequate support and resources for teachers and students. Despite these challenges, most principals and teachers involved in the study recognized the importance and value of learning an additional language. Nevertheless, they noted that foreign language instruction is not prioritized, as it is neither assessed nor measured.The authors of the report emphasized that developing language skills is vital for economic prosperity, social cohesion, and the acceptance of diverse cultural identities. They expressed hope that their findings would encourage policymakers, businesses, and educational providers to advocate for revising and enhancing the current curriculum to better support language learning. The report also noted that language education can drive economic growth and improve the future employability of young people.In the European Union, more than 80% of primary pupils learn an additional language, highlighting a stark contrast with Northern Ireland's approach. The research was commissioned by the Northern Ireland Languages Council, an organization established by the Department of Education that includes representatives from over 20 entities spanning business, education, and the community sector.

text: Lewis Hamilton collided with Mercedes team-mate Nico Rosberg on the last lap before passing him to win a thrilling Austrian Grand Prix. In a dramatic turn of events at the Austrian Grand Prix, Lewis Hamilton emerged victorious after a contentious collision with his Mercedes teammate Nico Rosberg. The incident, which occurred as Rosberg attempted to defend his position late in the race, resulted in a damaged front wing for the German driver, relegating him to a fourth-place finish. The race stewards penalized Rosberg with a 10-second penalty and two license points for causing the collision, narrowing Hamilton's gap to Rosberg in the championship standings to just 11 points.The controversy at Mercedes is likely to intensify following this pivotal move. As Hamilton attempted to overtake around the outside at Turn Two, Rosberg delayed his turn-in, leading to contact between the two cars. This maneuver forced Hamilton off the track, but Rosberg's damaged front wing sparked along the circuit, allowing Hamilton to pass and also enabling Red Bull's Max Verstappen and Ferrari's Kimi Raikkonen to overtake Rosberg.On the podium, Hamilton addressed the crowd, which had booed him, stating, He made a mistake into Turn One and I had an opportunity to go around the outside in Turn Two. I left a lot of room on the inside and I guess he locked up and crashed into me. Rosberg, who also received a reprimand for continuing to drive with a damaged car, offered a different perspective. Absolutely gutted, he said. We were battling and I was struggling a little with my brakes. I went a bit deep but that is fine because I am on the inside so I can dictate. So I was surprised Lewis turned in and caused a collision. It's unbelievable.Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff initially described the collision as brainless, refraining from assigning specific blame. The team revealed that Rosberg suffered a brake-by-wire failure affecting the rear axle on the penultimate lap, which contributed to the incident.Hamilton's victory was a relief, considering the earlier pit stop errors and strategy questions that had jeopardized his race. Despite starting from pole and leading for 21 laps, Hamilton found himself behind Rosberg due to a slow pit stop caused by a left rear wheel issue. This allowed Rosberg to close the gap after initially starting sixth due to a gearbox penalty.Hamilton's engineer's decision to fit the more durable soft tires during his first pit stop, while Hamilton remained on ultra-softs, enabled Rosberg to gain ground. Although initially appearing to be on a two-stop strategy, Mercedes eventually opted for both drivers to make a final pit stop within a lap of each other, with Hamilton taking used soft tires and Rosberg new super-softs. Hamilton questioned this choice but was assured by his engineer, Bonnington, that they were the best option, a decision that ultimately proved correct.The race's dynamics shifted dramatically following a safety car deployment triggered by Sebastian Vettel's right rear tire exploding on the pit straight on lap 27. Vettel, leading at the time, was left frustrated by another missed opportunity in a challenging season for Ferrari. Out of nowhere the tire decided to blow up, said Vettel, recalling a similar incident at last year's Belgian Grand Prix.Behind Hamilton, Red Bull's Daniel Ricciardo and McLaren's Jenson Button delivered strong performances. Button, who had started third on the grid, managed to convert his position into a commendable points finish despite a fierce midfield battle, holding onto second place for the initial laps.The Austrian Grand Prix results have undoubtedly set the stage for further intrigue in the championship race, with Hamilton's win tightening the title contest.

text: Thirteen schoolgirls have been on a hunger strike for six days to protest against daily sexual harassment in the northern Indian state of Haryana. In a harrowing revelation, teenage girls aged 16 to 18 from a village in Rewari district have spoken to the BBC about the sexual harassment they endure while traveling to school in a neighboring village. Frustrated by the lack of protection from local officials, these students have taken a stand, demanding change.In response to their plight, police have vowed to enhance security measures for the girls. Additionally, the government has committed to upgrading the current school in their village to a higher-secondary level, eliminating the need for the girls to commute.Despite these promises, the students, who have been on a hunger strike, consuming only water, insist they will not relent until they receive written confirmation of these changes. Their protest has garnered support from fellow students and parents who, although not on hunger strike, have joined the cause.Almost every day, we face eve teasing, Sheetal, one of the 13 students, told BBC Hindi's Nitin Srivastava. Should we stop studying? Should we stop dreaming? Are only rich people and their children allowed to dream? The government should protect us or open a higher-secondary school in our village.Another student, Sujata, shared her distressing experiences, stating that men often try to touch us inappropriately and write our phone numbers on walls, make nasty comments. Actually much worse happens, but not everything can be described.This protest has been a significant chapter in the lives of these girls, who are determined to secure better educational opportunities and safety. Their parents have also joined the demonstration, setting aside their farm work and daily jobs to support their daughters.Haryana, known for its skewed gender ratio, frequently witnesses crimes against women. However, this marks a rare occasion where young girls have decided to protest openly, receiving robust support from their community, including men advocating for gender equality.One mother expressed her anguish, saying it was painful to see these girls suffer. She added, These young girls face the kind of harassment that I can't even describe. When we complain to the police, they put pressure on us to take such cases back.Rohtash Kumar, the father of one protesting girl, acknowledged that harassment has been a long-standing issue. It's the first time that girls have taken the matter into their own hands. The men in our village support their struggle, he stated. Mr. Kumar emphasized the need for concrete assurances from authorities, wary of unfulfilled promises. Such promises have not been fulfilled in the past. We want to be sure that our struggle doesn't go waste because of a false promise, he concluded.

text: In our series of letters from African journalists, veteran Ghanaian journalist Elizabeth Ohene reflects on why in Ghana a person's age is not etched in stone. In Ghana, numbers, especially those related to age, often take a backseat in importance. Unlike in many parts of the world where a date of birth is a fixed marker from cradle to grave, in Ghana, it is not uncommon to see newspaper announcements of changed birth dates. This is particularly prevalent as individuals approach retirement age. With the official retirement age set at 60 for most public officers, some people resort to swearing affidavits to shave years off their age, allowing them to extend their careers and continue drawing a salary.Remarkably, some have adjusted their birth dates to suggest they were in Primary Class One before they were even born. The most striking instance I encountered involved an official who reduced their age by seven years. This widespread phenomenon recently made headlines when it was reported that approximately 800 teachers had petitioned the Ghana Education Service to alter their ages. While many sought to appear younger, a few aimed to make themselves older than their records indicated.The news sparked widespread outrage, with many Ghanaians expressing disbelief. How can people want their dates of birth to be changed? was a common sentiment among the younger generation. In defense, a teaching union leader argued that these requests stemmed from errors made by payroll departments at the time of employment.The root of this issue lies in the fact that few births are officially recorded. Historically, illiterate parents often neglected to document their children's births, leading to dates being forgotten over time. Although a birth certificate is required for school enrollment, many manage to bypass this requirement.This disregard for birth date accuracy affects various aspects of life in Ghana. For instance, I've seen children no older than 14 holding voter registration cards, despite the legal voting age being 18. Such discrepancies can haunt individuals unless they continually adjust their records through affidavits.Police recruitment ads cap eligibility at 25 years, yet someone might present as 26 due to earlier falsifications. Similarly, young athletes sometimes alter their ages to qualify for age-restricted competitions. However, advancements in technology now make it harder for older participants to infiltrate under-17 events.Efforts to enforce birth and death registration have largely failed. A civil service regulation prohibits public officials from changing their birth dates during government employment, yet enforcement remains challenging. Many Ghanaians view their age as confidential, leading to evasive responses when asked.The new government has promised a national identification system within its first year, aiming to provide all Ghanaians with cards containing immutable biometric data. This would prevent the alteration of birth dates through affidavits. As we anticipate this change, I ponder any potential benefits of the current system where age remains flexible and private.Reflecting on a British newspaper article about tennis, I recall the vivid description of players' ages: Serena Williams, 35, joined her 36-year-old sister, Venus, in the women's final, defeating the 34-year-old Mirjana Lucic-Baroni. Federer, 35, performed magic against Stan Wawrinka, 31. Such detailed age reporting might deter Ghanaians from embracing fixed birth dates.For more insights, follow us on Twitter @BBCAfrica, on Facebook at BBC Africa, on Instagram at bbcafrica, or email africalive@bbc.co.uk.
