text: A chronology of key events: A journey through Mexico's rich history reveals a tapestry of ancient civilizations, colonial conquests, and modern political shifts. From the Classical Maya city-states flourishing around AD 250-900 in southern Mexico, Guatemala, and Belize to the enigmatic Teotihuacan culture between AD 0-500, Mexico's past is a mosaic of cultural achievements and mysteries. The rise and fall of the Toltec culture in Tula (800-1000) and the resurgence of the Maya civilization in the northern Yucatan Peninsula (10th-16th centuries) laid the groundwork for the Aztec Empire, which dominated central Mexico from 1428 until the Spanish conquest began in 1519 under Hernan Cortes.The Spanish conquest, marked by the capture of Tenochtitlan in 1521, initiated a new era, with Mexico becoming part of the Viceroyalty of New Spain until 1820. The struggle for independence (1810-1821) culminated in the short-lived Mexican Empire, which included territories stretching to modern-day Costa Rica. By 1824, Mexico transitioned into a federal republic, although internal strife persisted, fueled by tensions between conservative elites and the indigenous populace.The 19th century witnessed significant territorial losses, including Texas's secession in 1836 and the Mexican-American War (1846-1848), which resulted in the cession of northern provinces like California and New Mexico to the United States. The La Reforma period (1855-1872) introduced liberal reforms, challenging the Catholic Church's power. Meanwhile, the turbulent era of foreign intervention saw Archduke Maximilian of Austria's brief reign (1864-1867) end in execution.Porfirio Diaz's dictatorship (1876-1911) ushered in modernization and economic growth but at the cost of political repression, eventually sparking the Mexican Revolution (1910-1920). The revolution led to the establishment of a constitutional republic, though political instability persisted, with figures like Zapata leading peasant revolts.The 20th century saw Mexico grappling with social and economic challenges. The PRI's long rule began in 1929, while President Lazaro Cardenas implemented oil nationalization and land reforms in the 1930s. The Tlatelolco massacre in 1968 and the discovery of massive oil reserves in 1976 marked significant events in the nation's history.Mexico's political landscape shifted in the 1990s with the rise of opposition parties and the Zapatista uprising in Chiapas. The PRI's dominance waned, culminating in Vicente Fox's presidential victory in 2000. Meanwhile, drug-related violence escalated, with drug cartels wreaking havoc across the country.The 21st century has been marked by the ongoing battle against drug cartels, economic reforms, and social issues. High-profile arrests, like that of Zetas leader Miguel Angel Trevino Morales in 2013, and energy sector reforms in 2014, demonstrate the government's efforts to address these challenges. However, incidents such as the 2014 disappearance of 43 students in Guerrero highlight persistent issues of violence and corruption.In recent years, Mexico has faced international scrutiny and domestic unrest over drug violence and human rights abuses. The extradition of drug lord Joaquin El Chapo Guzman to the United States in 2017 symbolized a significant step in the fight against organized crime. As Mexico continues to navigate its complex socio-political landscape, its history remains a testament to resilience and transformation.

Burnley-born goalkeeper Ryan Fulton has committed to a two-year contract and is eager to catch the eye of head coach Gordon Strachan. Having played for Scotland Under-21s, Fulton is optimistic about his future prospects. He'll watch a lot more matches up here, the 21-year-old shared. So there's a good chance, if something happens with the first-team lads, I might get a chance.Reflecting on his development, Fulton credits current Celtic manager Brendan Rodgers for his growth during Rodgers' tenure at Liverpool. When Brendan Rodgers was there, I was training with the first team day in, day out, said Fulton, whose father hails from Paisley. I got to see a lot of him. He's a really good guy. He would give me a lot of pointers and tips where to go. I have full respect for him.Fulton recognized three years ago that breaking into Liverpool's first team was beyond reach at this point in his career, making his departure from the English Premier League club an easy decision. It's tough to get in the team there, he explained. I'm at that age now where I need to start playing first-team football and be challenged at the same time. I was going out on loan to try to get that experience. I think the best thing for me is to move on and get playing. This is a good challenge for me. I think it's what I need. It's a good stepping stone, it's a good club to be at and it's a good league to be in, so I think it was a no-brainer for me.Fulton gained valuable experience playing 13 times in a six-month stint with Portsmouth in League Two, followed by 29 appearances last season for Chesterfield, despite their relegation from League One. He has no regrets about joining a team struggling against the drop, believing it has prepared him well to help Accies, a team often battling in the bottom six, avoid a similar fate. That was good for me because I gained a lot of experience from that, he added. It was a challenge for me. You have to slug it out at some stage, so it is great to have it under my belt.

text: Comedian Bob Mortimer has revealed that he got married less than an hour before he went into hospital for a triple bypass operation. Last October, heart complications forced Bob Mortimer and his comedy partner Vic Reeves to cancel the initial leg of their 25th anniversary UK tour. Mortimer recounted, I thought I had a chest infection and went to the doctor—five days later I was under the knife. He revealed the shocking news that his arteries were 95% blocked.During a press conference in central London to announce the 2016 continuation of their tour, Mortimer shared a personal story about marrying his partner of 22 years, Lisa Matthews, on the morning of his surgery. I found out I needed heart surgery on the Thursday, so I made a will on the Friday, he explained. Initially, they were unable to marry due to a 21-day notice requirement. However, after his consultant emphasized the severity of his condition, a London registrar granted special permission for the ceremony. I got married at half nine on the Monday and went to hospital at 10 to have the operation, Mortimer recounted.Following the press conference, Mortimer tweeted a photo with Lisa, calling her the love of his life. He also mentioned to the BBC that his doctors assured him he wouldn’t need to alter his physical comedy routines for the 15-date tour. I've just done all my tests and they said if I was a builder or scaffolder I would be fine to do it. We don't do any heavy labour in the show so I should be fine. Whether I'll be funny—no comment, he joked. Reeves, whose real name is Jim Moir, humorously added, You had that part of you removed.Mortimer also shared a health update, saying, I've got my cholesterol down from 8.5 to 2.7—that's through eating seeds. I'm basically a chaffinch now.The tour, titled 25 Years of Reeves and Mortimer: The Poignant Moments, marks the duo's first live tour since 1995. It will feature elements from their TV shows, including Vic Reeves Big Night Out, Shooting Stars, and House of Fools. Fans can look forward to beloved characters such as Judge Nutmeg, the Stotts, and Man with the Stick. Mortimer emphasized their goal for the tour, stating, The main thing we want to do with the tour is to leave people thinking that particular night was unique for them.

text: Stoke City boss Mark Hughes says Liverpool were incredibly fortunate to reach the League Cup final. The Potters' journey ended in heartbreak after they were eliminated on penalties, following a 1-1 aggregate draw in their two-leg semi-final. This came after their historic victory at Anfield, their first since March 1959. Stoke's goal, scored by forward Marko Arnautovic in first-half injury time, was somewhat fortuitous.It was offside, but we deserved it. We got the goal that won us the game, but not the tie, Stoke manager Mark Hughes told BBC Stoke. He added, We always believed we had a chance, even if others doubted us, but we just couldn't find that second goal, even though we seemed the more likely to score. The reaction of their fans and players shows they were incredibly fortunate to advance to the final. Once it goes to penalties, it's a toss-up, and unfortunately for us, it didn't go our way. These things happen in sport, but it doesn't make it any easier.Despite lying ninth in the Premier League, just a point behind Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool in seventh, Stoke faced an uphill battle after a lackluster performance in the first leg at the Britannia Stadium three weeks prior. Without their skipper Ryan Shawcross, replaced by Marc Muniesa, the Potters managed to keep Liverpool from registering a single shot on target.Employing a strategy reminiscent of Tony Pulis, Stoke's use of towering forwards Jon Walters and Peter Crouch provided a greater attacking threat than the home team. I can't fault any of them, Hughes remarked. They all delivered fantastic performances. Peter Crouch, alongside Marc Muniesa, stood out despite not having played for a long time. We hope to receive the credit we deserve. We came here under difficult circumstances after losing the home leg, but we were very positive, made a few changes, and on the night, we were clearly the better team. I'm really proud of the players' efforts, but unfortunately, we're not the ones heading to Wembley.Hughes now faces injury concerns ahead of Saturday's FA Cup fourth-round tie at Crystal Palace, with doubts over Arnautovic and Charlie Adam. Arnautovic sustained a back injury after two heavy falls following tackles from Liverpool's Jon Flanagan. Meanwhile, Adam, who came on as a second-half substitute, lasted just half an hour before exiting in the first half of extra time with a calf issue.Adam was one of three players on the pitch from the last time Liverpool clinched a trophy, the 2012 League Cup final, which also ended in a penalty shootout. Back then, he missed his penalty against Cardiff City. Stoke right-back Glen Johnson was also part of that Liverpool team, scoring one of their three penalties. The only remaining player from Kenny Dalglish's 2012 Reds team still on the field was Jordan Henderson, now the captain. Lucas Leiva, one of the penalty shootout heroes for Liverpool on Tuesday night, had missed that Wembley final due to injury.

text: The debate over flying the Confederate flag has reignited in the US, but the American South isn't the only place in the world you'll see the emblem - it's also proudly displayed in the rural Brazilian town of Santa Barbara D'Oeste. Each year, descendants of approximately 10,000 Confederates who fled to Brazil after the US Civil War gather for what resembles a family reunion. They engage in activities typical of the American South, like square dancing, eating fried chicken and biscuits, and enjoying George Strait's music, reports Asher Levine, a Reuters correspondent based in Sao Paulo. And there's an abundance of Confederate flags everywhere.Although these descendants are now six or seven generations removed from their Southern ancestors, many Brazilian locals continue to embrace Southern culture and prominently display the Confederate flag. According to Levine, for these individuals, the flag serves more as an ethnic emblem rather than a political statement. They consider themselves ethnically American to some extent, he explains. It's akin to people waving an Italian flag at an Italian festival or an Irish flag on Saint Patrick's Day. They perceive it that way, devoid of political connotations.Over the years, the Southern white settlers have intermingled with Brazilians, leading to a diverse population with varying skin tones proudly displaying the Confederate flag. This visual might surprise many Americans. Many descendants of these Confederates have African ancestry, so you might see people with dark skin waving the Confederate flag at the gathering, Levine notes.Levine recounts speaking with an American at the festival who was taken aback by the sight of a young girl singing Amazing Grace—a hymn commonly sung in African American churches in the US—while standing on a Confederate flag. The flag is omnipresent, with children waving miniature versions and women donning dresses adorned with the emblem. To them, the symbolism is completely lost, but for us, it's quite a stark contrast, Levine remarks.In Brazil, a nation known for its mixed-race populace, the recent Charleston shootings are perceived more as a matter of gun safety than a racial issue. When they hear about incidents like the one in South Carolina, they question whether the US is genuinely safer, Levine adds.This story was initially broadcast on PRI's The World. But even though the descendants of some 10,000 Confederate refugees who emigrated to Brazil after the American Civil War are now six or seven generations removed from their southern ancestors, they continue to embrace the southern culture and the Confederate flag. These people, Levine says, are ethnically American, who wave the American flag as they might wave an Italian flag at a festival, or an Irish flag on St. Patrick’s Day. They view the flag in this way, without political connotations. They see it as a symbol of ethnicity rather than a political statement. It has been said that many of the descendants of the Confederates have an African blood, and it is not uncommon to see blacks at these gatherings. There has been a mingling among the white Southerners and the black population of Brazil, which is why one can see at the Confederate festivals a mixture of people of all skin colors. Levine tells of an American who was astonished to hear a little girl singing on the Confederate flag the hymn, ‘Amazing Grace,’ which is very popular in the black churches of the United States. The flag is everywhere, children carry little flags, women wear dresses with the flag motif. “When they hear of the events in South Carolina, they ask if the United States is really safer,” says Levine. Brazil, with its mixed population, regards the recent shootings in South Carolina as a gun issue rather than a racial issue. You can hear it here. Required field. text: Portsmouth made history in staging the The America's Cup World Series, the city council leader has said, despite criticism from some spectators. Donna Jones, the city council leader, announced that a detailed analysis of the event would be conducted.The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge were among those left disappointed by the cancellation of the races. Team Origin, the event organizers, assured that Fanzone Arena and Grandstand ticket holders would receive refunds. Many attendees voiced their grievances on the organizers' Facebook page, highlighting issues with ticket prices, viewing quality, toilet facilities, and catering services. Paul Dornan remarked that the £45 Fanzone entry fee was a lot for what you got.Local businesses, including the Blue Reef Aquarium, reported a decline in trade, attributing it to the event. Lindsay Holloway, the aquarium's manager, criticized the organizers for miscommunication and frankly poor management. A spokesperson for Team Origin Events defended the Fanzone's location, stating it was positioned directly in front of the racing and allowed access to the free waterfront festival arena and a dedicated kids' area. We have set out from the start to engage with the existing seafront attractions to ensure that everyone benefited from this event, he explained.Mark Askey, a local boat tour operator, reported a 70% drop in revenue compared to the same week last year, saying, It was a big deterrent for us and numerous other small businesses. Record-breaking yachtsman Sir Robin Knox-Johnston supported the decision to cancel the races, noting, The real tragedy is Portsmouth built up so hard, but it has lost out on this big event.On Friday, those holding tickets to a canceled South Coast proms concert were offered refunds plus free entry to Saturday's pop concert, a move that angered individuals who had paid up to £48 for Saturday's tickets. Organizers labeled the free tickets as a gesture of goodwill.Reflecting on the weekend, Ms. Jones remarked, We need to remember this is the first time since 1861 this cup has been back on British soil, so regardless of what happens in the future, we've created history this weekend.

text: The Labour Party has made legal checks to ensure its leadership contest is complying with the law and try to avoid challenges to the result. Newly introduced regulations now permit individuals to register as supporters and participate in voting for a fee of £3. This development has stirred unease, with allegations surfacing that members from rival parties are attempting to sway the election's outcome. Despite these concerns, Harriet Harman's acting leadership team firmly dismissed any notions of halting or postponing the election process. The party is focused on ensuring full compliance with the 2014 rules, a spokeswoman for Harman stated. We've sought legal counsel to confirm adherence and are exercising thorough due diligence. However, there are no intentions to halt or suspend the contest. We remain vigilant.In a related incident, a Labour spokeswoman revealed that a Conservative activist, who joined the Labour Party at a discounted rate of £1 for former armed forces members, was disqualified and barred from voting. Alan Pearmain, a parish councillor and deputy chairman of the South Ribble Conservative Association, admitted on the BBC's Victoria Derbyshire programme that his actions were a form of mischief-making.In the midst of the leadership race, Scotland's Daily Record has thrown its support behind Jeremy Corbyn, a left-wing candidate. This endorsement follows the Daily Mirror's backing of Andy Burnham just a week prior. Corbyn expressed his gratitude, saying, I'm obviously pleased to have the backing of a paper that has such a long tradition of support for the Labour Party. This endorsement likely considers Labour's future in Scotland, which is crucial as we strive to reconnect with Scottish communities to succeed across the UK.Meanwhile, former Home Secretary David Blunkett, who supports Andy Burnham, voiced concerns about a potential Corbyn victory. Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, he remarked, Jeremy Corbyn has been effective in opposing the Tories, but he's also been effective in opposing my party. If you want to remain in opposition, vote for someone skilled at opposition.Blunkett emphasized the need for someone who can address the world of tomorrow rather than reverting to Old Labour or even New Labour from the 90s, as we face an entirely different world.In another development, Sarah Brown, wife of former Prime Minister Gordon Brown, endorsed Yvette Cooper for leadership, with Andy Burnham as her second choice. Opinion polls indicate a tight race between Cooper and Burnham as they vie to challenge Corbyn, with Liz Kendall in fourth place.The contest sees Burnham, Cooper, and Kendall competing against Corbyn. Meanwhile, former Labour leader Ed Miliband has faced criticism regarding the voting system used to elect his successor. The switch from an electoral college system to one member, one vote, allowing public participation as registered supporters for £3, was overwhelmingly approved at a special Labour conference last year. However, backbench Labour MPs Simon Danczuk and Graham Stringer argue that the new system is vulnerable to manipulation.The election results are set to be revealed at a special conference on September 12.

text: Nearly 15 years ago, successful Nigerian businessman Anselm Okoukoni was one of the desperate African migrants prepared to do anything to get to Europe. As the eldest son of a widowed farmer, Anselm Okoukoni was customarily expected to shoulder the responsibility for his six siblings immediately upon graduating from university. Determined not to join the ranks of unemployed graduates in his country, he pursued a degree in statistics, yet faced a series of visa rejections from embassies of Italy, Germany, Spain, Austria, France, Belgium, the UK, and the US.His fortunes shifted when a contact offered to facilitate a visa to Greece for about 400,000 naira, then equivalent to approximately $3,500 (£2,350). My uncle in America had already told me to let him know whenever I got a visa, Okoukoni recalled. True to his word, his uncle sent $5,000 to cover the visa, airfare, and travel expenses—a gift to support his nephew's future.In December 2002, at 24, Okoukoni left Nigeria for Greece, a country where he knew no one. He quickly made his way to Italy, where he had friends. I felt I was doing something professional. I was paying taxes. I was sending money home to Nigeria, he said. When his visa expired weeks later, he followed his friends' lead and applied for asylum, though he admitted, I don't remember what story I told.The next two years were challenging. Struggling with the Italian language and unable to secure a decent job, he resorted to street hawking, an illegal activity in Italy. Arrests and confiscations of his goods became part of his routine. It wasn't the kind of life I wanted to live, he lamented, noting that his earnings barely covered his siblings' school fees.A stroke of luck introduced him to a man with a European passport who resembled him, enabling him to travel to the UK in the summer of 2004. Arriving in London, Okoukoni was both shocked and thrilled. I saw Africans driving buses and cabs, and working in McDonald's and in hospitals, he observed, contrasting this with Italy, where he mostly saw black people in low-wage jobs.His Nigerian friends in London helped him find accommodation and a job as a parking attendant, using someone else's identity. Within one year, I had job satisfaction, he reflected. I felt I was doing something professional. I was paying taxes. I was sending money home to Nigeria. Earning £8.50 an hour, he soon decided to further his education after seeing a community college open day advertisement. He chose plumbing, recalling, I'd never entered a house in Nigeria where the plumbing was done properly.Though the course cost £1,400 for non-citizens and required proof of residency, Okoukoni managed to enroll by claiming he forgot his passport. After a year, he left his job to become an apprentice plumber, earning £9.70 an hour. Over the years, he gained qualifications in plumbing, heating, gas, and building services engineering, investing roughly £10,000 in his education.By 2012, Okoukoni planned to return to Nigeria, confident his skills would be invaluable. In 2013, he shipped a van filled with tools to Nigeria and left his £12-an-hour job in London for a property development firm in Lagos. His efficiency impressed his boss, but Okoukoni was eager to start his own business. Although his initial plans for aggressive marketing didn't materialize, referrals from satisfied clients quickly brought in contracts.In Nigeria, the scarcity of skilled workmen made his services in plumbing, fire protection, air conditioning, and ventilation highly sought after. Right now, I shuttle between Port Harcourt and Lagos doing jobs, he said. Many Nigerian developers, aiming for quality, import artisans from Togo and Benin, known for their superior skills. Okoukoni attributes the poor quality of Nigerian artisans' work to their focus on earning money quickly, neglecting proper training.His company, Ansko Building Services Ltd, employs 12 plumbers and two apprentices. Though initially claiming experience, his plumbers required retraining, for which they were paid, as were the apprentices, above the minimum wage. Since the beginning of this year, I've not touched any tool. They now do all the work while I supervise, he said.Okoukoni aspires to open a training center for building services professionals, emphasizing tool usage. Nobody has ever taken the time to teach them, he remarked. Despite regrets over the illegal steps taken during his journey through Europe, he is pleased with his life's outcome. He now provides employment for young Nigerians, supports his wife, cares for his mother, and funds his brother's education in the US.His advice to migrants in Europe or those planning to go: When they get to Europe, they should obey the law and do the right thing. They should look for unique skills that they can develop and use to improve society over there and also back home. If you go to Europe to simply look for money, you are wasting your time.

text: Planning permission for a controversial peace centre at Northern Ireland's former Maze prison has been granted. Years of political discord have surrounded the future of a site near Lisburn, once home to paramilitary prisoners during the Troubles from 1971 to 2000. The notorious prison witnessed the deaths of ten men during the 1981 republican hunger strikes. Concerns from Unionists have persisted that the site might transform into a republican shrine.Although protests have erupted against the new center, planners have reportedly received only a single formal objection to the construction proposal. Renowned architect Daniel Libeskind, known for his work on New York's Ground Zero, designed the new building. This standalone structure is flanked by two other preserved buildings, including remnants of the former prison such as a watchtower, a prison hospital, a compound, and an H Block. Additionally, the site contains two World War II hangars from the old Long Kesh RAF airfield.Northern Ireland Environment Minister Alex Attwood, announcing the decision, stated, There is learning to be taken from the conflict here. The centre can contribute to sharing this learning and perhaps to help inform the resolution of conflict in other places. He praised Libeskind's design, emphasizing that good planning needs good design, and highlighted Libeskind as both a world leader in architecture and a friend of Northern Ireland.The peace-building and conflict resolution center will largely be funded by an £18 million grant from the European Union. The redevelopment of the former prison's 350-acre site is part of a £300 million project, with a significant portion allocated to the Royal Ulster Agricultural Society (RUAS).Since the prison's closure in 2000, the site's future has been a topic of continuous debate. Initially slated for a national sports stadium, the proposal was eventually dismissed after prolonged disagreements. In April, DUP MLA Edwin Poots announced on BBC NI's The View that his party had made a corporate decision to support the site's redevelopment. He expressed optimism about the project's progress, assuring that it would not become a republican shrine.Simultaneously, Seanna Walsh, a senior republican ex-prisoner, emphasized that any new peace and reconciliation center must represent the stories of all involved parties, including loyalists and the British Army.

text: The US and Russia say world powers will meet in New York on Friday to pass a UN resolution endorsing the Syria peace process. In a bid to resolve the ongoing Syrian conflict, US Secretary of State John Kerry recently engaged in discussions in Moscow with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov and President Vladimir Putin. Lavrov emphasized the commitment of both nations to address contentious issues, such as the composition of the opposition delegation. Meanwhile, Kerry noted that some progress had been made, particularly regarding agreements on terrorist groups.Since September, Russia has been conducting an air campaign to support President Bashar al-Assad's government, claiming to target terrorists, primarily jihadist militants from the Islamic State (IS) group. However, activists argue that these strikes have predominantly impacted Western-backed rebel factions.Lavrov announced that an upcoming meeting in New York on Friday aims to pass a UN resolution reaffirming the peace process principles established in Vienna last month. Kerry's visit to Moscow was an effort to bridge differences over strategies to end the Syrian conflict. He conveyed to President Putin that the US and Russia possess the ability to make a significant difference.A major point of contention between the US and Russia remains the role of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad in any transition. The US insists on Assad stepping down, while Russia maintains that his fate should be determined by the Syrian people.Confusion persists regarding Russia's alleged supply of weapons and ammunition to the Free Syrian Army (FSA). President Putin initially confirmed the support, only for his spokesman Dmitry Peskov to later deny it. The Russian general staff chief echoed Putin's initial statement, but a Kremlin aide subsequently refuted any supply claims. Attempts to clarify this during a Kremlin conference call proved unsuccessful, with Peskov stating, I have nothing to add to what's already been said.Ahead of the meeting, President Putin remarked, Together, we are looking for ways out of the most urgent crises. Since September 2014, a US-led coalition has targeted IS positions in Syria without coordinating with the Damascus authorities.Kerry highlighted past collaborations despite differences, noting, Even when there have been differences between us, we have been able to work effectively on specific issues. He added, The world benefits when powerful nations can find common ground.Kerry's discussions with Russian officials included insights from a recent meeting in Riyadh, which united various Syrian political and armed opposition groups. Russia contested the meeting's outcome, which excluded Assad and his aides from any transitional period, and demanded consensus on a terrorist blacklist before proceeding further.The humanitarian situation in Syria remains dire: $3.2 billion in aid is needed, 13.5 million Syrians require assistance, 6.5 million are internally displaced, 4 out of 5 families live in poverty, 72% lack access to drinking water, and 2 million children are out of school.BBC's Barbara Plett-Usher, accompanying Kerry, noted that Russia's involvement is crucial as it holds the key to bringing Assad to the negotiating table. On IS, Kerry acknowledged that both Russia and the US view it as a threat to every country. Lavrov expanded on this, stating IS activity extends beyond Syria to Iraq, Afghanistan, and Yemen.The meeting also touched on Ukraine, where conflict persists between the Western-backed government in Kiev and Russian-backed separatists. Kerry expressed a desire for resolution, saying, Nothing would please us more than to solve the problem of Ukraine and move forward on the economic front.The US, backing the Syrian opposition, advocates for a settlement based on the 2012 Geneva Communique, which calls for a transitional governing body and Assad's departure. Russia, supporting Assad since its September air campaign, also endorses the Geneva Communique but insists Assad's future should be decided by Syrians.While Syria's opposition factions now largely agree on the necessity of a managed transition, they demand Assad's exit at its outset. Assad, however, insists that peace talks cannot commence until terrorism is eradicated, and he refuses to consider stepping down before elections.

text: Married couple Dilshad and Barinder Hothi are joint founders of the international training company, the Knowledge Academy, which they aim to turn into the Amazon of the education world. When a husband and wife team runs a business, it's natural to wonder who's really calling the shots. With the Hothis, however, the lines blur. Their conversations are a lively dance of enthusiasm, with each often finishing the other's sentences.Barinder Hothi is particularly animated about their company's unique edge in the crowded professional training market. The future is about blending, she explains. Our online courses are traditional, computer-based, but we also offer walk-in clinics. If someone wants to discuss an issue, they can find a local instructor, pop in, ask questions, and get that human interaction.Dilshad Hothi shares a grand vision for their venture. From the outset, he recognized the internet's transformative power on consumer habits, from books to groceries, and thought, Why not training? He declares, I knew there was a phenomenal opportunity. In the next decade, we'll be a global household name, much like Google or Facebook—perhaps even bigger.This may sound ambitious, but the Knowledge Academy has experienced remarkable growth in its first six years. It stands as one of the largest training companies worldwide, offering over 5,000 courses across numerous locations. By year's end, they plan to provide training in 3,000 cities across 210 countries, from the US to Australia, Bhutan to Chile. Their offerings span diverse fields, including project management, IT, social media, aviation, and animation, and they've trained employees from companies like Rolls Royce, HSBC, PwC, and Disney.Despite their global reach, the Hothis’ story is rooted in a rich cultural blend of Indian and English influences. Barinder's parents, immigrants from Punjab, ran a restaurant in Harrow, London. Neither of them spoke any English, she recalls, which meant she and her siblings helped with the business from a young age. Yet, education was paramount. I can still hear my mum saying, 'Study, because this is what will help you in life,' Barinder notes.While Barinder's upbringing was steeped in Indian values, Dilshad's was a mirror image. Born and raised in India, his father served in the Indian Air Force. He attended Lawrence School, Sanawar, akin to a British public school. It's the Eton equivalent of India, he says. As house captain, he thrived in a competitive, sports-driven environment, excelling in cricket and field hockey.At 21, Dilshad moved to the UK, where he met Barinder through his aunt. He worked for a UK-based training company while she was at Microsoft. They launched their business in 2009, amid the global economic crisis—a decision Barinder calls the best ever. The downturn created a demand for formal qualifications as people sought new jobs. There were so few positions that you needed more badges on your CV, Dilshad explains. Now, platforms like LinkedIn make qualifications even more crucial by keeping them visible.One potential pitfall looms: the business consuming their lives entirely. Their workdays, from 8 am to 6 pm, leave little time together, but at home or on weekend walks, work dominates the conversation. Their nine-year-old daughter, familiar with the office, can operate the franking machine and knows most staff members by name. We often have to tell each other to turn the iPads off, Barinder admits.They've established a rhythm of intense work followed by luxury breaks in places like Dubai. Neither seems to mind the dedication required, though their approaches differ. I'm more conservative, Barinder says. Typically British. Without her restraint, Dilshad jokes, I'd try to do 10 things at once.So, who's in charge? Barinder's in charge of the people. I'm probably in charge of the strategy, Dilshad concedes. Do they argue? Barinder has been very supportive, he says. If she's supportive, is he really in charge? She laughs but stands her ground, maintaining the mystery of their partnership dynamics.

text: Prestonpans' Josh Taylor feels the calming influence of stable-mate Carl Frampton is helping him focus before his debut in Las Vegas on Saturday. The undefeated Commonwealth super-lightweight champion is set to face Mexico's Alfonso Olvera on the undercard of Carl Frampton's WBA featherweight world title defense against Leo Santa Cruz. Reflecting on Frampton, Taylor remarked, He doesn't put any pressure on himself, he just keeps calm. I'm not getting too excited about it.At 26, Taylor clinched Commonwealth Games gold as an amateur in 2014 and swiftly captured the Commonwealth title in his seventh professional fight, defeating Derby's Dave Ryan in five rounds at Meadowbank last October. Since turning professional in July 2015, Taylor has secured victories in Texas and New York. However, the upcoming fight against Olvera marks his debut in the famed fight capital of the world.Expressing his excitement, Taylor, a product of Terry McCormack's Lochend club in Edinburgh, shared, I'm dazzled, star-struck, being here. You dream of fighting in Vegas and the MGM Grand, where legends like Floyd Mayweather and Manny Pacquiao have fought, when you first turn professional. I just never imagined it would be at such an early stage in my career on such a massive undercard. I'm pinching myself but at the same time, I'm relaxed and looking forward to the fight.Taylor finds inspiration in sharing the same stable as Carl Frampton. Seeing his face up on the MGM gives me massive motivation to be in his position one day, fighting for a world title. If I dedicate myself like he has done, there's no reason why I can't, he said. Taylor admires Frampton's ability to switch off between training sessions, emphasizing its importance for recovery and sharpness.Amidst the madness of Las Vegas, Taylor is captivated by the city's casinos and hotels and humorously mentions his plan to tackle a 10,000-calorie burger after the fight. Before indulging, though, he must overcome Arizona-based Olvera. Describing his opponent, Taylor noted, He's had 11 fights, he's drawn one, lost two, and they were against unbeaten opponents. He can fight and he comes to win, so I'm taking it very seriously. I take every fight seriously, like it could be my last fight. A lot of fighters underestimate opponents and they get beat or get hurt.Taylor is being considered as a potential challenger for fellow Scotsman Ricky Burns, the WBA world super-lightweight champion. I feel I am ready to go in with anybody, but it's just about being smart, Taylor stated. I need to earn the right to fight Ricky Burns. He's world champion and I've only had seven fights. I've got to climb the ladder. If I was in against him I'd be confident, but it's not my style to call fighters out. I have massive respect for Ricky Burns. He has put Scottish boxing back on the map.Interview by Mike Costello.

text: Pop stars have always been clothes horses for fashion designers - but more and more of them are turning to designing themselves. This year has seen Skepta launch his debut fashion line and Zayn Malik unveil his Versace Versus collection. They join the ranks of musicians-turned-designers like Victoria Beckham, Kanye West, and Rihanna. But how straightforward is it for a pop star to transition into a successful designer in a field traditionally dominated by those who have honed their craft over years?Victoria Beckham, once known as Posh Spice, has firmly established herself as a leading British fashion designer. Her journey began in 2008 with the launch of her first fashion line, which initially faced skepticism. However, her debut collection of just ten dresses was met with critical acclaim. Nicole Phelps of Vogue noted, The woman formerly known as Posh Spice has launched a dress collection, and, believe it or not, it's one of the hottest things going in New York this week.Since then, Beckham's reputation in fashion has only grown. Glamour's fashion director, Natalie Hartley, remarked, With Victoria Beckham, everyone wanted to hate her and put her down, but she learned from the beginning how to do everything from scratch. Despite not being able to pattern-cut, Beckham's dedication and personable nature won over the fashion community. She has received multiple accolades, including two British Fashion Awards for Best Brand in 2011 and 2014. Her collaborations extend to the US high street brand Target, offering affordable options for a broader audience. Beckham once stated, I want a woman to look and feel like the best version of herself.Kanye West, another music star who ventured into fashion, began with a Nike collaboration in 2009, introducing the Air Yeezys. He furthered his fashion education with an internship at Fendi the same year. His first women's fashion label, DW Kanye West, debuted at Paris Fashion Week in 2011 but faced criticism. Lisa Armstrong of The Daily Telegraph described it as a stupendously vacuous enterprise, while Suzy Menkes of The New York Times was unimpressed. However, Kanye's subsequent collections, including his Yeezy line, have been more favorably received. Natalie Hartley appreciates his dedication, saying, I love sportswear and think he has done a great job making simple, modern sportswear.Gwen Stefani entered the fashion scene with her label L.A.M.B in 2004, named after her debut solo album. Her collections, often showcased during New York Fashion Week, blend classic Hollywood glamour with modern street influences. Despite taking a break to focus on family, Stefani has returned to the runway, continually expanding her fashion empire with lines like Harajuku Lovers and Design With Purpose. Natalie Hartley acknowledges Stefani's unique style, saying that her fans embrace dressing like her.Rihanna has become a fashion icon, not just for wearing designer clothes but for creating them. Her collaborations include Armani Jeans and River Island, and she became Puma's creative director in 2014. Her Puma trainer line, including creeper-style trainers and furry sliders, has been a massive success. Rihanna's fashion ventures extend to collaborations with Manolo Blahnik and Dior, as well as her own perfume and jewelry lines. Natalie Hartley admires Rihanna's authenticity, noting, Rihanna does stuff that's true to her. She wouldn't put anything together she would never wear herself.Tinie Tempah, the south London rapper, ventured into fashion with his label Disturbing London. Known for his street-meets-high-fashion style, he launched the What We Wear line, emphasizing sustainability. Tinie expressed his motivation to Reuters, saying, I got a little bit bored of people just saying I was really stylish just for wearing other people's clothes. He aims to shift the focus from clothes to the person wearing them and is open to designing a women's collection in the future. As he told GQ, Regardless of what you're wearing, confidence is key.Follow us on Facebook, Twitter @BBCNewsEnts, or Instagram at bbcnewsents. text: The UK is to spend £25m on building a prison in Jamaica so that foreign criminals in the UK can be sent home to serve sentences in the Caribbean. During his visit to Jamaica, Prime Minister David Cameron revealed a significant agreement aimed at resolving the stalemate over a prisoner transfer deal between the UK and Jamaica. This initiative addresses the issue of over 600 Jamaican nationals currently incarcerated in UK prisons who cannot be deported due to inadequate prison conditions in Jamaica.The deal, funded by foreign aid, is projected to save UK taxpayers £10 million annually once prisoner transfers commence in 2020. Under the Jamaica prison scheme, more than 300 current offenders, each serving sentences of at least four years with 18 months or more remaining, are expected to be returned to Jamaica. Currently, these transfers are hindered by concerns that the conditions in Jamaican jails could lead to successful human rights challenges.Jamaica ranks third among foreign countries with nationals serving sentences in the UK, with nearly 70% of Jamaican inmates convicted of violent and drug-related crimes. The UK has pledged to cover about 40% of the cost of constructing the new prison, which will accommodate 1,500 inmates.Prime Minister Cameron, fresh from discussions at the United Nations in New York on combating the Islamic State group, stated, It is absolutely right that foreign criminals who break our laws are properly punished, but this shouldn't be at the expense of the hard-working British taxpayer. He emphasized the importance of the agreement, noting that it would ensure Jamaican criminals serve their sentences back home, thus saving British taxpayers millions while still delivering justice. Additionally, he highlighted the benefit to Jamaica through the enhancement of their criminal justice system with the new prison.As the first British prime minister to visit Jamaica in 14 years, Cameron is also poised to announce £300 million in aid for infrastructure projects across the Caribbean, including roads, bridges, and ports. This regional infrastructure fund, to be implemented in partnership with the Caribbean Development Bank, aims to bolster economic growth in the region.Upon his arrival at Kingston Airport, Cameron was welcomed with an honor guard and national anthems. He then toured the RFA Lyme Bay, a British ship engaged in anti-drug smuggling and emergency relief efforts in the Caribbean. The day's itinerary includes discussions with Jamaican Prime Minister Portia Simpson-Miller and attendance at a reception.BBC political correspondent Carole Walker reports that Cameron has expressed a desire to strengthen the historically neglected relationship between the UK and Jamaica.

text: Australian politician Bob Katter has defended a video that depicts him killing his electoral rivals. Mr. Bob Katter, an independent politician from north Queensland, has stirred controversy with a provocative advertisement. In the ad, Katter is depicted blowing smoke from a toy gun, with two faceless men from major political parties sprawled lifeless on the ground. Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull criticized the ad, urging Katter to retract it, calling it in the worst of taste.Despite this, the 71-year-old Katter, leader of Katter's Australia Party and representative of the Kennedy electorate, stands by the ad, describing it as brilliant and screamingly funny. The ad, produced in collaboration with the satirical website Betoota Advocate, opens with members of the Labor Party and the Liberal-National coalition erecting a sign that reads Australia for sale. Katter is shown discarding the sign and, when it reappears, altering it with a bold black marker to say Australia not for sale, before transitioning to the gun scene.I think most people will enjoy the humour. I found it very funny, I must admit, Katter remarked to the ABC. What's not funny is the selling off of this country. We hate it and we're tenaciously opposed to it.Queensland Senator Barry O'Sullivan condemned the ad as abhorrent, while Finance Minister Mathias Cormann deemed it unfortunate. During an appearance on the Sunrise breakfast show, host David Koch questioned Katter on the timing of the video's release, given its proximity to the tragic shooting at the Pulse nightclub in Orlando, Florida, where 49 people were killed. Katter claimed ignorance of the shooting and pointed out that similar ads had not sparked controversy.If this represents Australia's peak political scandal, it underscores the dullness of the current election campaign. Katter's ad embodies Australia's irreverent sense of humour—politically incorrect, shocking, and perhaps not as amusing as intended. But is it truly abhorrent or in the worst of taste? Should its release have been postponed in light of the Orlando shootings?Australia is far removed from Florida, and many in regional areas might appreciate Katter's audacious humour. Humour can be rough or tasteless, sometimes missing the mark. If Katter's constituents disapprove, they can express their dissatisfaction at the polls on July 2.Clancy Overell, editor of Betoota Advocate and one of the actors portraying the shot men, acknowledged the potential for the video to wind people up, but doubted Katter shared this awareness. Overell defended the video's timing, telling the BBC that shootings occur daily in the US. Australians can't be prevented from making jokes about cowboys and western-style gunplay, he stated.Katter is no stranger to unconventional campaign tactics. A video from the 2012 Queensland state election showed him line dancing with a group of young people and even performing a headspin, though it's likely a body double was used for the latter stunt.

text: Oldham Athletic are hoping to complete the signing of convicted rapist Ched Evans on Thursday. The Welsh striker, 26, is on the verge of finalizing a deal, despite facing significant backlash, including a petition with 60,000 signatures. Legal hurdles remain, potentially delaying the agreement. A board member revealed to the BBC that they are inclined to sign Evans, noting the Professional Footballers' Association's significant role in the decision. Club owner Simon Corney stated on Wednesday that there is an 80% likelihood of signing the striker, with the club currently 14th in League One.Ched Evans, formerly of Manchester City and Sheffield United, was imprisoned in April 2012 for raping a woman and was released in October after serving half of his five-year sentence. Guardian sports writer David Conn criticized Evans' lack of empathy, stating, There's been no decency shown to her after the event. You can still say 'I maintain my innocence of the crime, while apologizing for what I did which I don't dispute,' and show some decency and empathy for this woman. Conn added that the treatment of the victim by Evans' supporters was a tipping point, making him feel Evans isn't ready for a second chance.Former England international Danny Mills remarked on the unique nature of the dressing room, describing it as a sanctum of protection. He noted, If Ched Evans goes into that dressing room and starts to play good football and starts to score the odd goal then, rightly or wrongly, whatever you think should happen, those players will forget about everything off the pitch if he's doing the business on the pitch.BBC commentator Guy Mowbray questioned the impact on the squad, wondering how players might feel if the club is desperate to get that sort of player in. Former Sunderland striker Kevin Phillips highlighted Oldham's need for a center forward and pondered the supporters' reactions if Evans scores, predicting that, despite initial resistance, fans might eventually celebrate his goals.Mills further argued that Evans has served his sentence and should be allowed to work, while Conn countered, You have the right to work in theory, but you don't have a right to walk back into your chosen profession. No employer, no football club has a duty to employ him.Oliver Holt, chief sports writer for the Daily Mirror, expressed his belief in rehabilitation, stating, I believe in a society where once criminals have served their sentence they deserve the chance to rehabilitate. He cautioned against making arbitrary judgments about which criminals can return to work.Mowbray expressed surprise at Oldham's decision, citing potential financial and security implications, and doubted the move would end positively for the club or Evans, given the immense pressure involved.Mills, Phillips, Mowbray, Conn, and Holt shared their views on BBC Radio 5 live.

text: Eye doctors are warning about bird-scaring explosives, called bangers, being modified and used as fireworks. In Sussex last year, five people suffered severe eye injuries when agricultural bangers were thrown into a crowd during a Bonfire Night celebration. These bangers, designed to scare wildlife away from crops, are becoming a concerning trend when misused in public gatherings, according to medical professionals.Doctors expressed their alarm in a letter to the British Medical Journal (BMJ), warning about the potential spread of this dangerous practice. The bangers, also known as rookies and deer scarers, feature a slow-burning rope fuse that ignites several explosives. When the rope is cut down, the fuse and explosives can be lit and thrown. Edward Pringle, a retinal fellow at Sussex Eye Hospital and one of the letter's authors, explained, These banger fireworks are easy to throw into a crowd. People look at them, and debris shoots into the eye. It's like a hand grenade going off—a flash in front of the eye, and then the feeling of a blunt injury.Pringle highlighted that such injuries are typically seen in war zones, not in small market towns. He noted that both those throwing the bangers and attendees at public events are often unaware of the potential dangers. On the evening of November 5, 2011, Sussex Eye Hospital treated eight patients from the Lewes bonfire event, which attracted over 60,000 people. Two individuals were blinded, and three others now face the risk of lifelong glaucoma.St John Ambulance offers guidance on dealing with eye injuries: - Stand beside the injured person and gently separate their eyelids, asking them to look in different directions while examining the eye. - If a foreign object is visible, try washing it out with clear water from the inner corner. - If unsuccessful, attempt to lift the object with the damp corner of a clean tissue. - If the object cannot be removed, seek medical assistance.The Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents (RoSPA) expressed concern: It is worrying that some people feel it is appropriate to throw very dangerous agricultural products around crowds of people. Deer scarers, and indeed real fireworks, are not toys. They are explosives, and the injuries they can cause can be devastating, as this story sadly shows.RoSPA emphasized that attending a public fireworks display remains the safest option. However, there is a need for greater awareness that throwing fireworks and other explosives is both dangerous and illegal. The BMJ letter advocates for stricter firework regulations, noting that countries with such legislation have seen a reduction in blinding injuries. While the UK has laws limiting firework distribution, deer scarers are exempt because they are not classified as fireworks.The authors of the BMJ letter also call for enhanced safety measures at public events, suggesting that organizers engage audiences in safer firework practices and promote eye protection. According to the British Ophthalmic Surveillance Unit, an average of eight eye injuries occur across the UK on Guy Fawkes Day each year. Of those injured, half require surgery, half become blind, and one in six may need eye removal. Alarmingly, about a third of those injured are under 18.

text: It was a final chance for MPs to rehearse their campaign slogans. Gerald Jones, shadow Wales Office Minister, accused the government of risking Welsh jobs and livelihoods with their extreme Tory vision of Brexit.Cairns, however, dismissed these concerns, saying, We want the freest, most open trading agreement, and it seems to me that the real investors, who are creating real jobs, are taking us towards our ambition.Labour's Christina Rees pressed for updates on projects from the last Conservative manifesto, questioning the progress on the electrification of the Great Western Railway to Swansea, the north Wales growth plan, and the HS2 hub in Crewe. text: History is useful when trying to make sense of present tensions between Russia and the West. At the Defence Academy near Shrivenham, Oxfordshire, a warehouse houses an extraordinary collection of military volumes, meticulously arranged on library shelves. This collection, now known as the Russian Military Studies Archive, includes numerous books in Russian and other languages from the former Soviet bloc, compiled over the past fifty years to understand the adversary better. It serves as a vital record of the USSR's rise and fall, the Cold War, and ongoing tensions between Russia and the West.With the collapse of the USSR and Warsaw Pact and the rise of digital records, maintaining archives like this has become increasingly challenging. In today's cost-conscious climate, some argue that physical libraries are luxuries we can ill afford. Fortunately, this military archive has been preserved, not discarded. Recently, the notion of Russia as a security concern has resurfaced, making the archive's historical insights more relevant as we attempt to decipher Moscow's actions and future moves.Among the archive's memorabilia are reminders of a pivotal moment in my career: the August 1991 coup attempt in Moscow, where defense, KGB, and Communist leaders sought to reverse Mikhail Gorbachev's perestroika reforms. They believed these reforms endangered their nation. I'll never forget those tense days when history seemed poised on a knife-edge. I ventured from our BBC office in Moscow to find tanks lining the inner ring road, with bewildered young soldiers peering from turrets, uncertain of their location. The tanks were intimidating, but the young soldiers were not. Our cleaning lady, Masha, clad in her usual headscarf and apron, scolded them, What do you think you are doing here? Your mothers would be ashamed of you. Take yourselves back to the barracks where you belong.The coup failed when Russia's new President, Boris Yeltsin, declared the actions illegal, urging the armed forces to disregard orders and calling on Moscow's citizens to stand against the coup leaders. The response was both astounding and humbling. Soviet citizens, who not long ago feared speaking publicly, now courageously took to the streets. Young women with pushchairs, civil servants with briefcases, musicians with guitars and violins all flocked to the Russian parliament, demonstrating through sheer numbers that they would not be silenced or allow a return to the past.The archive contains leaflets from that era, some still muddy from being trampled, quickly printed and distributed by Yeltsin's supporters to counter the coup leaders' state media broadcasts. I recall them plastered throughout the metro, their words urgent and compelling. Over Russia storm clouds are gathering, clouds of dictatorship and terror… Soldiers! I believe at this tragic hour that you will make the right choice, read one appeal. Another, from Yeltsin to Moscow's citizens, expressed my heartfelt thanks to you all for your courage.Lately, I've pondered 1991, wondering if Russians might once again flood the streets if economic conditions worsen and desperation sets in. Would they risk protest, or focus solely on survival? Do they now feel differently about their nation and leader, more supportive and less willing to risk upheaval? These are questions that Russian opposition leaders, and Vladimir Putin's inner circle, must consider. The political climate of 1991 was vastly different. Russians were encouraged to protest, with Yeltsin's urging and Gorbachev's endorsement of free speech over six years. This empowerment was a factor again in 2011, when Muscovites protested election fraud during Dmitry Medvedev's presidency.Today, the atmosphere has shifted. Public space for dissent has diminished, and grassroots movements are often perceived as threats. New laws and the murders of top opposition figures discourage critics from speaking out or compel them to emigrate. Since Russia's 2014 annexation of Crimea, a wave of patriotism has bolstered the government's message: Russia faces external threats from NATO and jihadists and needs a strong leader to maintain unity and security. Putin's supporters argue that Russia cannot afford another revolution and the bloodshed it would bring, recalling the devastation of the Bolshevik revolution nearly a century ago.Reflecting on my experiences in Russia over the past 30 or 40 years, I am reminded that it is often when the giant seems dormant that it surprises us by awakening. I recall those Moscow citizens, young and old, who gathered in 1991 to prevent a Communist resurgence. No one, likely not even the demonstrators themselves, anticipated such a street uprising. So, who can predict Russia's future path? History offers many parallels, each teaching different lessons. Perhaps the most likely outcome is an unforeseen twist that catches us all off guard.

text: More than 60% of Australia's major organised crime figures now deal in crystal meth, a new report has found. The Australian Crime Commission (ACC) has released a report highlighting ice, a form of methylamphetamine, as the most dangerous illegal drug threatening Australian communities. The report reveals that the purity of this substance has risen significantly over recent years, heightening its peril.Methylamphetamine is available in various forms, but the crystal ice variant is predominantly found across Australia. The ACC notes that the price of crystal meth in Australia ranks among the highest globally, incentivizing organized crime syndicates to intensify their involvement in its trade. These criminal groups are reportedly mixing other illicit drugs with crystal meth to boost addiction rates, according to the report.The ACC has observed a considerable increase in the number and weight of detections at the Australian border, while domestic production shows no signs of decline. Alarmingly, Mexican drug cartels have expanded their operations to include supplying this drug internationally, collaborating with distribution networks in countries like Australia. The report also identifies India and China as primary sources for the precursor chemicals used by Australian producers to manufacture the drug.Chris Dawson, the ACC's chief executive, emphasized the severe impact of crystal meth's availability and addictive nature, which has spurred demand in urban, rural, and disadvantaged areas. Ice is a devastating, insidious drug, he stated. It affects everyone from users, their families, and their communities, to the authorities who deal with the users.Significant drug busts underscore the growing crisis. In November of last year, New South Wales police confiscated over 800 kilograms of methylamphetamine and two tonnes of MDMA, with a street value estimated at A$1.5bn (£800m; $1.2m). More recently, authorities uncovered 230 kilograms of liquid methylamphetamine hidden in a shipment of 20,000 bottles of flavored water intended for a Sydney warehouse.In response to this escalating issue, the ACC report calls for a collective national response to combat the drug's spread. Everyone plays a role in the fight against illicit drugs, Mr. Dawson stressed, including governments, law enforcement, health and education sectors, industry, non-government organizations, and the wider community.

text: Former Chancellor George Osborne is to become editor of the London Evening Standard newspaper, in a surprise move that has angered opposition MPs. In a surprising career twist, Tory MP George Osborne expressed his excitement at succeeding Sarah Sands as editor of the Evening Standard. Sands is departing to take the helm of the BBC's Today programme. Osborne, set to edit the paper four days a week, plans to maintain his role as MP for Tatton, Cheshire, despite mounting pressure to leave politics altogether. Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn criticized the dual role, calling it a joke and demanding an immediate by-election in Tatton, a constituency Osborne has represented since 2001 and which will be dissolved at the next election.Corbyn argued that Osborne's appointment undermines media independence, adding, It takes multitasking to a new level and insults the electors he is supposed to serve. Meanwhile, Evgeny Lebedev, the Standard's owner, praised Osborne as London through and through, expressing confidence in his ability to build on Sands' legacy. I am proud to have an editor of such substance, Lebedev tweeted, emphasizing Osborne's alignment with the paper's socially liberal and economically pragmatic stance.The newspaper announced Osborne would work an average of four days a week as editor, allowing him to fulfill his parliamentary duties. Osborne, addressing the Standard's newsroom, called it a great honor to lead one of the UK's most influential newspapers. He assured that his editorial stance would be independent and fearless in advocating for Londoners. Growing up as a Londoner, I've always known the Evening Standard as an institution, Osborne stated, promising to give voice to all Londoners.Osborne, 45, emphasized that his role as editor would not compromise his position as a Conservative MP. We will judge the actions of the government, London's politicians, and political parties by one criterion: is it good for our readers and London? he declared. Osborne admitted to the Standard's staff, I've got to learn from you because I may have run the country, but I haven't actually run a newspaper.BBC media editor Amol Rajan noted that the Standard, an afternoon paper, is sent to print by 11:00 GMT, allowing Osborne to arrive at the office by 05:00 GMT and work until midday before attending to other duties. Rajan highlighted Osborne's lack of traditional journalistic experience, noting that most editors have years of experience in crafting headlines and reporting—skills Osborne must quickly acquire.Tatton Conservative Association's president, Patti Goddard, expressed full support for Osborne's new venture, describing it as exciting and affirming his reputation as a hard-working MP. London Mayor Sadiq Khan congratulated Osborne, noting he would cover the world's greatest city. However, Labour's John Mann criticized Osborne as invisible in Parliament, arguing that his new job devalues democracy. Fellow Labour MP Paul Flynn condemned the revolving door between government and private sectors.Green Party co-leader Caroline Lucas called for assurances that the Conservatives would not exert undue influence over the newspaper and suggested Osborne be removed from the Privy Council to prevent access to confidential briefings. Robert Barrington of Transparency International described the situation as an astonishing conflict of interest that damages democracy.Former Tatton MP Martin Bell expressed disbelief, likening the news to fake and suggesting Osborne would need to be superman to juggle his roles. Former Labour leader Ed Miliband humorously tweeted about his own potential editing role, while Lib Dem leader Tim Farron joked about Osborne's next job.Since leaving frontline politics, Osborne has taken roles as a visiting fellow at a US university and an adviser to BlackRock, earning £650,000 for four days of work a month. Osborne, who once aspired to journalism, defended his new role by citing historical examples of MP editors. He pointed to Boris Johnson, who edited The Spectator while an MP, as a precedent. Johnson, now foreign secretary, called Osborne's appointment brilliant and good for London.The National Union of Journalists criticized the move as a blatantly cynical political maneuver, especially amid staff pay cuts and reduced hours, but welcomed Osborne's potential application for union membership.

text: Video sites such as YouTube will be forced to pay more to musicians and record companies under plans to reform European copyright laws. A draft directive is set to mandate that publishers and producers disclose the profits generated by performers' or authors' works. The music industry has long criticized YouTube for inadequate compensation for music content. For the first time, news publishers will be recognized as rights holders, and platforms like Google News will be required to pay fees for using news snippets.Carlo Perrone, head of the European Newspaper Publishers' Association, hailed the creation of a copyright for news publishers in Europe as a significant and historic step. European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker emphasized the need for fair compensation for creators, stating, I want journalists, publishers, and authors to be paid fairly for their work, whether it is made in studios or living rooms, whether it is disseminated offline or online, whether it is published via a copying machine or hyperlinked on the web.While the Commission has not specified how it will compel sites like YouTube to increase payments to artists, the plans also aim to simplify access to online content across EU countries and reform copyright rules in research and education. Andrus Ansip, Vice-President for the Digital Single Market, remarked, Our proposal will ensure that more content will be available, transforming Europe's copyright rules in light of a new digital reality.These proposals, however, face potential challenges from lobbyists and must be approved by the European Parliament and EU states, a process that could take years. A Google spokesperson responded, We believe there's a better way. Innovation and partnership - not subsidies and onerous restrictions - are the key to a successful, diverse and sustainable news sector in the EU.Earlier this year, over 1,000 artists, including Lady Gaga and Coldplay, urged the Commission to address the value gap, criticizing platforms like YouTube for unfairly siphoning value away from the music community and its artists and songwriters. YouTube, which profits from advertising and shares these profits with rights owners, operates differently from streaming services like Spotify and Apple Music, which pay record companies for each song play.The BPI, representing the UK recorded music industry, welcomed the recognition of the need for a level playing field for digital music. Geoff Taylor, BPI's chief executive, criticized platforms like YouTube for building huge businesses using music and other content while paying only a fraction of the royalties paid to artists and labels by services such as Spotify and Apple Music.PRS for Music, representing nearly 120,000 UK songwriters, composers, and music publishers, supported the move to require licenses for searchable sites like YouTube. The European Commission's proposed new copyright directive provides the framework for this essential legal clarity, stated Robert Ashcroft, PRS's chief executive.The IFPI, representing the global recording industry, viewed the proposals as a positive initial step towards fairer content licensing in Europe. Frances Moore, IFPI's chief executive, asserted, Importantly, it confirms that user-uploaded content services such as YouTube, which are the largest source of on-demand music, should not be able to operate outside normal licensing rules. However, there is a lot more to do to make this a workable proposal.UK Music criticized YouTube for insufficiently compensating artists, stating the platform has yet to provide fair returns to rights owners and creators. The band Two Door Cinema Club expressed dissatisfaction, saying, I don't think things at the minute are fair. YouTube don't pay a fair royalty.Google claims it has paid the music industry over $3 billion (£2.3 billion) since 2007. However, the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC) argued that the Commission's proposals fall short in preventing geo-blocking of online content and criticized plans to require websites to automatically detect and remove videos containing copyrighted material. BEUC warned, This would punish millions of consumers who share a self-made remix of a song, family videos, or holiday pictures which contain parts of a music tune or video clip.Additionally, the Commission proposed an overhaul of EU telecoms rules to ensure faster internet access across Europe. It aims for schools, universities, hospitals, transport hubs, and companies reliant on digital technologies to have connectivity exceeding 1 gigabit per second. All homes, rural and urban, should have broadband speeds of at least 100 megabits per second. The Commission also calls for 5G wireless coverage in all urban areas and major roads and railways, with each EU country having 5G in at least one major city by 2020.

text: Back in the heady days of May 2010, when the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats united in government, they set out a detailed set of policy proposals called the Coalition Agreement. In a bid to cleanse politics of big money, a statement once declared, We will... pursue a detailed agreement on limiting donations and reforming party funding. This pledge emerged after the divisive cash-for-honours scandal, offering a glimmer of hope for reform. Shortly thereafter, the independent Committee on Standards in Public Life deemed the issue significant enough to warrant an investigation. Sir Christopher Kelly, the committee's chairman, acknowledged the significant difficulties that lay ahead. Yet, he remained optimistic, asserting, there is sufficient will to reform the system to give us some hope that it ought to be possible to find a solution. Such optimism, in Whitehall's cautious language, was nothing short of bold, with Sir Christopher's outlook overflowing with hope.After months of anticipation, Sir Christopher unveiled his proposals. He suggested capping individual donations to political parties at £10,000. Furthermore, he recommended that union members should individually decide whether to contribute to the Labour Party, reversing the current system where they must opt out to withhold their funds from Ed Miliband's coffers.In exchange for these changes, which would significantly cut the income of the three main parties, Sir Christopher proposed that the public should help fund political parties. Parties with representation in Parliament or the devolved assemblies would receive approximately £3 for each vote they garnered. With around 30 million voters participating in the last general election, this plan could potentially funnel £90 million to political parties over a five-year term. Additionally, the public could make substantial donations to parties without incurring tax.However, consensus on these proposals is elusive. Oliver Heald, the Conservative member of the committee, expressed opposition to the £10,000 cap, advocating instead for a £50,000 limit. He also suggested that union members should have the option to allocate part of their fees to parties beyond Labour. Meanwhile, Labour's Margaret Beckett opposed the union reforms. Deputy Prime Minister Nick Clegg, despite his party's need for state funding, dismissed any immediate increase in taxpayer support for parties. It would not be right to ask our hard-pressed taxpayers to pay more to political parties at a time when they are having to deal with so many cuts and savings elsewhere, he told MPs just last week. Many in government share his sentiment.Sir Christopher Kelly insists that the public is wary of party funding and skeptical of large donors. He points out that all three major parties have committed to reform in their manifestos. The Conservatives, Labour, and the Liberal Democrats agree that progress hinges on consensus. Yet, consensus remains elusive. The coalition agreement pledged to pursue reform, but it stopped short of guaranteeing success.

text: Ahead of Kenya's elections in August, we asked you what issues you want us to report on. External links will open in a new window. We will keep updating this page with more questions.Kenya lacks a law governing election campaign funding, a situation that persists after the electoral commission's attempt to introduce one last year was thwarted by MPs. The commission had suggested spending caps for various electoral seats, but in the absence of such a law, candidates remain free to spend without limits.According to the privately owned Daily Nation, most of the money is spent on logistics and advertisements, but many candidates and parties also bribe voters. The publication notes that during the 2013 election, the opposition coalition Cord spent over $50 million (£40 million), while the ruling Jubilee Party expended more than $100 million on its presidential campaign. Politicians typically raise funds from businessmen and through fundraisers, although opposition parties accuse the ruling party of exploiting state resources for its campaigns.Ken Opalo from Georgetown University in the US anticipates some trouble but not on the scale of the violence a decade ago that resulted in over 1,000 deaths and displaced approximately 600,000 people. I am not too worried about the national elections. The real action will likely be at the county level, he remarked. There will most certainly be violence. But again, that will be more a reflection of what is at stake, rather than some descent into complete chaos and state failure.Nic Cheeseman, professor of democracy at the UK's University of Birmingham and a commentator on Kenyan politics, shares this perspective. He believes disorderly party primaries are a reason to be concerned, but they may not lead to greater conflict come election day.Kenya has experienced a steady economic growth rate, averaging 5% annually over the past five years. However, inflation has surged to 12% due to rising prices of essentials like milk, bread, and maize flour, leaving many Kenyan families struggling. The hashtag #CostOfLivingKe has emerged as Kenyans share the costs of basic items and their lifestyle adjustments.Kwame Owino, CEO of the Institute of Economic Affairs, told the BBC, Every election year, the economy also experiences a shrinkage, and that's no different this year as investors wait out on the election period. He added, Some companies are currently cutting down employment, but not in big numbers, and the informal sector remains the biggest employer.Kenya attracted $1 billion in new investments in 2014 following reforms such as reducing business costs, cutting bureaucracy, investing in infrastructure, and lowering visa costs, which boosted tourism. However, corruption, political tension, and state-controlled bank interest rates have strained the economy. The UN's development agency (UNDP) reports that Kenya has the highest unemployment rate in the region, with four out of ten Kenyans unemployed.Mr. Owino suggests that voters may be swayed by candidates they believe will best serve their economic interests. Transparency International's 2016 report ranked Kenya 145 out of 176 countries, attributing the low ranking to the ineffectiveness of anti-corruption agencies and the failure to punish those implicated in graft. Anti-corruption advocate John Githongo has labeled President Uhuru Kenyatta's administration the most corrupt in Kenya's history. Mr. Kenyatta, however, claims his anti-corruption efforts are hindered by sluggish court proceedings and an ineffective anti-corruption agency.Mr. Githongo highlights several scandals involving inflated project costs and payments to phantom companies. In 2015, Mr. Kenyatta suspended and eventually dismissed five ministers and other high-ranking officials over corruption allegations, with another minister resigning under public pressure. Opposition members have also been implicated in scandals, but some accuse the government of scapegoating.Constitutional bodies established to combat corruption face criticism for being partisan and lacking independence. Kenyan political analyst Barrack Muluka blames ordinary Kenyans for the corruption issue, citing ethnic biases: A government can steal as much as it wants, and Kenyans will be happy as long as it's 'our thieves'. He references the April party primaries where candidates with questionable integrity and corruption accusations won their races. Mr. Githongo calls it normalisation of the absurdity, noting that theft has become commonplace: Those we used to call thieves are now hustlers, he says.
