text: New rules for moving livestock will be disastrous for small agricultural shows, the Farmers Union of Wales said. Farmers have voiced their concerns over the Welsh Government's new livestock movement regulations, labeling them as overly stringent and costly. Starting June 10, farmers must register a quarantine unit (QU) on their farms to move livestock without adhering to the six-day standstill rule. This system, according to the Welsh Government, was created in collaboration with the farming industry. Previously, introducing new stock to a farm triggered a six-day lockdown, prohibiting any animal movement. However, exemptions existed for certain seasonal events, such as agricultural shows. Farmers could utilize an approved isolation unit, like a field or shed separate from other livestock, to bypass these restrictions. Yet, post-June 10, these isolation units will no longer be permissible, compelling farmers to apply and pay for the new quarantine units.The new system encompasses 61 rules, including requirements for double gates, double fences, and specialized clothing. The cost for a single QU stands at £172.80, while two units cost £244.80. Gwilym Jones, a farmer from Blaenau Ffestiniog, expressed his frustration, stating, It makes no sense to show, it's not worth it. The rules are going backwards instead of forwards. Similarly, Geraint Jones from Ystrad Meurig declared, I will break the law, and if they want to put me in jail, they can - I've got nothing to lose. If they want to kill the countryside, they're doing the right thing.Sian Davies, who exhibits her texel sheep nationwide, criticized the changes for being costly, bothersome, and increasing paperwork. She remarked that the Welsh Government seemed out of touch, sharing her experience of contacting the Aberystwyth office, only to find they were unaware of the new regulations. Geraint Jones reported similar experiences with the offices in Cardiff and Carmarthen.Despite these complaints, the Welsh Government has not acknowledged any registration delays. Brian Walters, vice-president of the Farmers Union of Wales, described the impact on smaller agricultural shows as disastrous. He stated, We don't feel there is enough evidence to indicate that diseases are passed between livestock at agricultural shows to justify such draconian measures.While England has postponed these rule changes until autumn, avoiding the show season, the Welsh Government maintains that the new QU system aims to simplify the standstill regime, offering added flexibility while upholding disease movement restrictions. This system, developed alongside the farming industry, is intended for all types of animal movement, not just shows. The alternative to the six-day standstill was a result of the industry's request through the Working Smarter review and involved extensive collaboration with the Livestock Identification Advisory Group over the years.The Welsh Government clarified that these recommendations were published in January 2012, and they have communicated with industry members twice in 2017, in April and May, supported by an extensive communications campaign.

text: Supermarkets and other big businesses could face higher business rates under a Welsh Conservative government, with a tax cut for smaller companies. The Welsh Conservatives have unveiled a proposal to change the calculation of business rates, emphasizing their commitment to prioritize small businesses within the Welsh government's agenda. Andrew RT Davies, the leader of the Welsh Tories, highlighted the crucial role small firms play in Wales, stressing the need for support to enable their development and growth.Retailers, however, have cautioned against reforms that might create disparities or add to the existing complexity. If victorious in the upcoming assembly election in May, the Conservatives plan to establish a dedicated team within the Welsh government focused on small businesses, which would be accountable to the assembly.Among other initiatives, some previously announced, the Tories intend to remove the age limit on a job creation scheme and simplify the process for businesses to secure loans from the Welsh government. Wales is a nation of shopkeepers, stated Mr. Davies. These small firms are the lifeblood of the Welsh economy, and they require support to thrive and expand.Currently, business rates, which are paid to local councils, are determined by property values. The Welsh government already offers rate relief, providing discounts to small businesses. For instance, businesses with property valued up to £6,000 are exempt from paying rates. The Conservatives propose extending this rate relief to encompass more businesses and introducing differential rates for large and small businesses, ensuring that larger entities contribute more.While England and Scotland have distinct rates, Wales has yet to implement such a system. The Welsh Retail Consortium, representing shop owners, has called for a comprehensive reform of business rates across all business sizes. A spokeswoman for the consortium remarked, The proposed small firms' relief is a welcome step towards cost reduction. However, many high street retailers stand to gain little, and we would be concerned if the new rate for medium and larger commercial premises led to increased taxes, as seen in Scotland.

text: A Chinese authority has banned the importation of brown crabs from Anglesey after claiming they contain a metallic contaminant. On Wednesday, the Centre for Food Safety (CFS) in Hong Kong declared a ban on certain sea creatures and issued a warning to the public against their consumption. This move followed the discovery of excessive cadmium levels in samples collected from the region.The UK's Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) emphasized that all crabs sold in the UK must adhere to EU regulations regarding permissible cadmium levels. Defra also mentioned its collaboration with Hong Kong authorities to devise a workable solution to resume trade as soon as possible.The CFS reported that two crab samples, intended for export to China, contained cadmium levels of 15 and 22 parts per million (ppm), significantly surpassing the acceptable limit of 2ppm. Consequently, Hong Kong officials have detained over 220kg of meat from one exporter, although 160kg had already been distributed.Officials cautioned that while occasional consumption of cadmium-laden crabs may not pose immediate health risks, prolonged exposure could adversely affect kidney function. The CFS has informed the relevant authorities in the United Kingdom and the local trade and will continue to closely monitor the situation, taking necessary actions such as enhanced surveillance of aquatic products imported from the United Kingdom, the statement read.Anglesey council noted its awareness of the situation, though it had not been directly contacted by Chinese authorities. Brown crab is known to accumulate cadmium in the hepatopancreas due to its detoxifying role, a spokesperson explained. The council added that export certificates for brown crab to China had not been issued for several months, following Defra's advice about China's restrictions due to high cadmium levels.The Food Standards Agency (FSA) in Wales pointed out that cadmium concentrations in brown crab meat, found in the hepatopancreas, differ significantly from those in white crab meat, which comes from the legs and claws. The NHS advises regular fish consumers to limit their intake of brown crab meat.An FSA spokesperson stated, The FSA is continuing to work with the crab industry to explore methods of reducing cadmium levels in brown crab meat through alternative processing techniques.

text: Respected by his peers and loved by millions, guitarist BB King was a blues legend who influenced a generation of musicians. Riley B King, born in Mississippi in 1925, became known as BB King, a nickname derived from Beale Street Blues Boy after his move to Memphis in 1947. King honed his craft on the Chitlin' Circuit, a series of venues across the racially segregated southern United States, named after chitterlings, or stewed pig intestines. In 1968, King embarked on his first European tour, gaining international acclaim. A memorable moment was captured in 1994, showing him on the Great Wall of China. During a 1996 European tour, he paused to perform for NATO troops at the Tuzla airbase in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Over his illustrious career, King amassed numerous accolades, including over a dozen Grammy Awards. In 2001, he won the Grammy for Best Traditional Blues Album for Riding with the King, a collaboration with Eric Clapton, whom he had admired since the 1960s. Reflecting on their friendship in 2007, King remarked, I've never met a better man, a more gracious man than my friend Eric Clapton.Another notable collaboration was in 1988 with U2 on their Rattle and Hum album, and he reunited with Bono at a tribute concert in 2008. King's distinguished career also included visits to the White House. In 1990, he received the National Medal of Arts from George and Barbara Bush. Sixteen years later, he was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by another Bush family member.In 2001, between these honors, King jammed with President Bill Clinton in Beverly Hills, accompanied by saxophonist Reverend Dave Boruff. That same year, King returned to the White House with his guitar, Lucille, named after a woman whose actions nearly led to the destruction of his first guitar in a fire.In 2004, King was honored with the Polar Music Prize in Stockholm by King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden, recognizing his immense contributions to the blues and modern popular music. Reflecting on his career in 2010, King humbly stated, I think that I know my job pretty well. But I'm never any better than my last job. I think that I'm here and, just as easy, cannot be here. So I never think that I've got it made.

text: British reggae band UB40 have praised Jeremy Corbyn as an incorruptible politician who will put working people first as they backed his campaign to remain as Labour leader. The renowned music group UB40, with a record of 70 million albums sold, has voiced its support for Jeremy Corbyn, highlighting his appeal to young voters and presenting him as a believable alternative to the status quo. Corbyn, who is currently in a leadership battle against Owen Smith, will find out the results on September 24. He has garnered endorsements from various celebrities, including actor Daniel Radcliffe. However, JK Rowling, the acclaimed author of the Harry Potter series, has criticized him as an ineffective leader.UB40, originally named after the British unemployment benefit form, was a dominant musical force in the 1980s and 1990s, achieving 50 hit singles with songs like Red Red Wine, Can't Help Falling in Love, and I Got You Babe. Despite a legal dispute resulting from the departure of three original members, the band, now led by guitarist and vocalist Robin Campbell, has thrown their support behind Corbyn. Campbell praised Corbyn for rekindling interest in politics among those who felt excluded and inspiring new young voters who see him as an incorruptible representative.Drummer Jimmy Brown added that Corbyn stands out as the only prominent politician advocating for working people marginalized by successive governments, including New Labour. Despite facing opposition from most of his MPs and losing a no-confidence vote after the EU referendum, Corbyn welcomed UB40's endorsement, noting their inspiring story of cultural diversity and creativity overcoming prejudice.Corbyn's arts manifesto, released last month, promises additional funding for arts activities in all primary schools in England and the establishment of a national arts scholarship scheme. Speaking to the Guardian, Corbyn expressed his willingness to meet with JK Rowling to discuss their disagreements after she accused him of leading Labour astray. Rowling's comments, suggesting Corbyn's leadership could harm Labour and that the poorest need a viable alternative to the Conservatives rather than mouthy, impotent socialism, sparked a strong backlash from Corbyn supporters on social media.

text: Almost four million children in the UK do not own a book, according to a report by the National Literacy Trust. A growing number of children are without books, according to a recent report by a charity, which highlights a concerning trend. Currently, one in three children lack books, a significant increase from one in ten in 2005. The study, which involved 18,000 children, indicates that those with personal books are more likely to excel in reading and perform better academically. The survey, conducted in September, involved school-aged children from 111 schools across the UK. It found that 33.2% of children, equating to 3.8 million across the country, do not own books. The data revealed that children from wealthier backgrounds are more likely to have their own books compared to those who receive free school meals. Additionally, it noted that poorer children and boys are less likely to own books.Jonathan Douglas, the trust's director, expressed alarm over the sharp increase in children without personal books. He stated, We know there is a direct correlation between book ownership and children's reading abilities. With one in six in the UK struggling with literacy, it is very worrying that many children could be missing out on opportunities to develop these essential skills.The study further demonstrated that children who own books are more inclined to read daily, and there is a clear connection between book ownership and reading proficiency. Among those with books, over half surpass the expected reading level for their age, while less than one in ten fall below it. In contrast, nearly 20% of children without books fail to meet the expected reading level, and only a third exceed it.The survey was launched to coincide with an appeal for public donations to provide books and reading support to disadvantaged children. As part of this initiative, several children's book illustrators have designed cards for the trust's Christmas Gift of Reading campaign.Additionally, the survey uncovered a link between reading skills and receiving books as gifts. Approximately 20% of children reported they had never visited a bookshop or library. However, the survey also found that reading any material, such as magazines, outside of class at least once a month, is associated with improved reading achievement.

text: Conservative backbenchers are demanding radical changes to school funding in England within months. Ministers are under mounting pressure from numerous MPs within their own ranks to commit to rapid reform, or face a campaign demanding action. Without intervention, there are warnings of teacher redundancies and increasing class sizes. Daniel Kawczynski, a backbench MP, emphasized the urgency, noting that huge numbers of Conservatives in the Commons are calling for change. Speaking on BBC Radio 4's World at One, he remarked, I think you would be fascinated by how strong the feelings are on this issue and the sort of campaign that is going to be pursued in the course of this year.Graham Stuart, the former chairman of the education select committee and a Conservative, echoed this sentiment. He anticipated that many Tories would push for an announcement at the earliest possible opportunity, ideally during July's Budget. Stuart warned, Schools are facing the prospect of deficits unless they take significant action to reduce headcount. We could potentially see redundancies as a way to cope with the funding pressures.Backbenchers argue that the current method of allocating government funds to local authorities for schools must be revised by next April. There are stark disparities nationwide, with some areas receiving up to £7,000 per pupil, while others get just over £4,000. Although ministers have pledged to reform the system since 2010 and reiterated this promise in the 2013 Conservative manifesto, the funding formula remains unchanged. An additional £390 million was allocated to the most underfunded authorities at the end of the last Parliament, but a comprehensive rewrite of the funding formula has yet to occur.The proposed changes would likely result in well-funded inner-city authorities losing money, whereas some rural areas might benefit. A Department for Education spokeswoman commented, The last government made considerable progress in reforming the school funding system. In 2014, an additional £390 million was allocated to boost 69 of the least fairly funded areas in the country in 2015-16—the biggest step toward fairer schools funding in 10 years. But we recognize there is still work to be done, which is why we are committed to looking at what more needs to be done to ensure that all local areas are funded justly.

text: Brightly coloured murals adorn the walls of the 'Little Hands' nursery. Concrete walls and a plastic tent roof define the classroom where young children, aged four and five, sing and dance. Beyond the chicken wire fence, dusty roads stretch out, yet this could be any kindergarten in the world. However, this is Zaatari camp in Jordan, home to thousands of Syrians who have fled their war-torn country.Neil Mathers, head of Save the Children in Scotland, observes, Many of the children we see here were born in the camp. They've known no other existence. The charity operates three nurseries in Zaatari, reaching 52% of the camp's children. Mathers highlights a pressing need: There are 40,000 children requiring this kind of support in Zaatari alone. Our kindergartens reach around 2,000, so much more is needed.Situated a few miles south of the Syrian border, Zaatari camp spans 8 square kilometers of barren desert. It has transformed from nothing into Jordan's fourth-largest city, with over 80,000 residents, making it the world's second-largest refugee camp. Refugees live in a mix of tents, tin shacks, and makeshift huts, enduring scorching summer temperatures exceeding 50°C and freezing winter nights.Dominic Graham, Jordan country director for Edinburgh-based charity Mercy Corps, describes camp life as tough. Mercy Corps, along with numerous other NGOs, has been active in Zaatari since its inception four years ago, as the Syrian civil war intensified. While essentials like water, sanitation, and shelter are in place, and rudimentary commerce has developed, life remains bleak and stagnant.Initially, many refugees believed their stay would be brief, expecting the fall of President Assad's regime. Hassan, who arrived last year, shares this sentiment. He and his family, devoid of savings, yearn to return to Syria but remain cautious. I will go back as soon as it is safe, he says, though he doubts it will be soon. Graham acknowledges, The prospects of returning to Syria are getting thinner and thinner.Zaatari represents only a fraction of the refugee crisis. Inside Syria, nearly eight million people are internally displaced. Those who reach camps like Zaatari often do so because of proximity or the ability to pay smugglers. The most vulnerable remain trapped within Syria, making aid delivery crucial. Steve Gordon, Mercy Corps' security manager, stresses the importance of assisting those inside Syria to prevent them from becoming a burden on neighboring countries.The challenges are daunting, with shifting front lines and Russia's intervention altering dynamics. Mercy Corps reports significant population movements, and Gordon emphasizes the need to pre-position supplies in potentially isolated areas.In Zaatari, children play in water sprayed from a tanker to settle the dust. The distant Syrian hills are just visible through the haze, a reminder of an uncertain future. Refugees face a difficult choice: stay or attempt to return. A silver bus waits at the camp's security checkpoint, bound for the Syrian border. Despite the dangers that once drove them away, some choose to return, while others set their sights on Europe, hoping for a new life.The Syrian refugee crisis has prompted billions in aid. The UK alone has contributed over £1 billion, with £330 million allocated to Jordan. Jeff Tudor, head of the UK's international development program in Jordan, acknowledges the complexity of the crisis. We're hanging on in there, he says, but ultimately we need a political solution in Syria. Even if that happens tomorrow, it's at least a decade before refugees can return. The situation won't allow it.

text: Asian stocks opened higher after turmoil on financial markets saw European and US indexes tumble following another oil price fall. Despite Thursday's gains, financial markets have yet to recover from the downturn experienced in recent days. Investor anxiety persists, fueled by plummeting oil prices and China's decelerating economic growth. On Wednesday, stocks plunged to their lowest since May 2009, with UK, French, and Japanese shares falling over 20% below their 2015 peaks.The turbulence did not spare Wall Street, where the Dow Jones closed 1.6% lower after a tumultuous trading session that saw stocks dip as much as 3%. Overnight, markets in Europe and the US had a terrible day, as worries from a 'drunk' Asia spilled over, noted Bernard Aw, a market strategist at IG, in a statement.In China, the Shanghai market dipped slightly by 0.3%, reinforcing global apprehensions about the world's second-largest economy. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's Hang Seng index managed a modest recovery, climbing 1.3% after a nearly 4% drop the previous day. According to the BBC's Juliana Liu in Hong Kong, traders express skepticism about the rally's durability. The gains are modest and susceptible to any negative news. This could be a 'dead cat bounce,' a term from the 1980s describing a brief recovery in a declining market, she explained.Earlier, Australia diverged from the market rout, with the ASX/200 rising 1.1%, despite its economy's heavy reliance on Chinese demand for commodities. Japan and South Korea also saw positive movements, with the Nikkei up 1.4% and the Kospi gaining 0.5%.Markets are deeply uncertain about China's economic slowdown, remarked Stephen Koukoulas, chief strategist at TD Securities, to the BBC. Official figures have been released, but many doubt their accuracy, instead looking to commodity prices as indicators of China's economic health.Oil prices have slid below $28 a barrel, while coal, iron ore, and other metals continue their prolonged slump. Analysts have drastically reduced their 2016 oil price forecasts. Morgan Stanley suggests oil in the $20s is possible if China further devalues its currency, while economists at the Royal Bank of Scotland predict oil could drop to $16. Standard Chartered forecasts prices might plummet to just $10 a barrel.Investors are particularly jittery about China's loss of momentum, Koukoulas added. The critical question is whether this is merely an adjustment from previous excesses or the onset of a more severe downturn that could significantly weaken growth.Some observers believe markets were poised for a fall, with asset prices inflated by ultra-low interest rates and central banks' quantitative easing, which involved purchasing financial assets with newly minted money. This inflation affected shares, bonds, and commodities. The commodity boom has definitively ended, partly due to China's slowdown and, in oil's case, an oversupply.These issues are indeed troubling, prompting a warning from the IMF: If these key challenges are not successfully managed, global growth could be derailed. Ultimately, this is the core concern for markets.

text: Scotland's largest council has said the greater Glasgow area will suffer unless there is specific government action to mitigate the effects of Brexit. One key recommendation is for both governments to assume responsibility for projects previously funded by the EU.Frank McAveety, leader of Glasgow City Council, stressed the urgency of governmental action to prevent a looming crisis. I believe that Brexit will confront Glasgow with major economic challenges, McAveety stated. If that happens, then the problems associated with Brexit can become an opportunity for economic growth and not a threat of crisis.Titled Brexit and the Glasgow Economy: Impacts, Actions and Asks, the report was collaboratively produced by the council, Glasgow Chamber of Commerce, and the Glasgow Economic Leadership board. This partnership includes the council, chamber of commerce, Scottish Enterprise, and Skills Development Scotland. text: The UK's home secretary has expressed concerns about plans to make it easier for Chinese tourists to get visas. text: The SNP's national executive has ruled not to endorse two sitting MPs as candidates in the general election. Michelle Thomson and Natalie McGarry, once elected as SNP MPs but now serving as independents, have been informed by the party's governing body that they will not be considered for candidacy. Expressing her disappointment, she confirmed, after careful consideration, her decision not to seek re-election for Edinburgh West.On Saturday, the SNP announced that all 54 of its current MPs would be backed as candidates for the upcoming election. Angus Robertson, the party's leader at Westminster, stated, SNP MPs have been the hardest working group at Westminster and, with Labour in complete disarray, the only real opposition to the Tory government. text: Lufthansa pilots have begun their eighth strike this year, forcing the cancellation of 1,511 flights over Monday and Tuesday. text: AMs have agreed that the National Assembly for Wales should change its name. Elin Jones, the presiding officer of the assembly, announced that Assembly Members (AMs) have several options to consider regarding a potential name change for the Welsh Assembly. Although Welsh Parliament has been suggested before, some AMs believe the name Senedd should also be on the table.Gareth Bennett, a UKIP AM, controversially remarked that organizations with Welsh-only names are primarily recognized in the Welsh-speaking colony of Pontcanna in Cardiff. This drew criticism from First Minister Carwyn Jones, who stated that such comments might be offensive to some.During a recent assembly debate on Tuesday, no consensus was reached on a new name. However, the presiding officer and assembly commission will now explore the implications of a name change. AMs unanimously approved a motion, without a formal vote, supporting the idea that the assembly should adopt a name reflecting its status as a national parliament.The Wales Bill, currently moving through the UK Parliament, will soon empower the assembly to rename itself with the consent of two-thirds of its members. This change is intended to mirror the assembly's expanding powers. Although the Welsh Government had intended to propose a vote to unofficially rename the assembly as the Welsh Parliament before any legal amendments, the vote was withdrawn.Elin Jones stated that the next step involves consulting on the potential new name. There are several possibilities and many associated terms which would stem from that choice, she explained, emphasizing that the name should instill confidence and pride among the Welsh people. She plans to inform the assembly of further developments at the start of the autumn term.Bethan Jenkins, a Plaid Cymru AM for South Wales West, advocated for adopting Senedd, a term already used for the assembly building, as the official name. Let us be self-confident enough to discard our mental baggage and take this opportunity to be unique by adopting an official Welsh name for our Senedd, she urged during the debate. While some AMs prefer to keep the name National Assembly, Jenkins noted that Senedd is widely used at the grassroots level.Andrew RT Davies, leader of the Welsh Conservatives, who first proposed the name change to Welsh Parliament in 2012, expressed openness to using both Senedd and Parliament. He remarked, Over time I think the word Senedd could be readily taken on board.UKIP group leader Neil Hamilton questioned whether the public might view the debate as pretentious navel gazing. However, he acknowledged that as the Wales Bill progresses and tax-raising powers are devolved, there is a strong case for calling the institution a Parliament. Personally, he found the idea of the name Senedd appealing, humorously pondering whether it would make them Senators.Conversely, Gareth Bennett advocated against the term Senedd, arguing it would alienate the assembly from most Welsh people. He suggested that in areas like Canton, the term is not commonly understood. Bennett's comments, particularly those referring to organizations with Welsh-only names such as the Urdd and Chwarae Teg, sparked laughter and derision from Jenkins. He claimed, The problem is most people outside the Welsh-speaking colony of Pontcanna, most people in Cardiff don't know what these things are.First Minister Carwyn Jones criticized Bennett's remarks, stating that labeling English speakers in areas like Ceredigion or Gwynedd as a colony would cause outrage. He argued that such language implies that Welsh speakers don't belong in the capital, which he deemed a wholly wrong remark and potentially offensive, though he was unsure if Bennett intended it that way.

text: The stories of those visiting and working at the Royal Welsh Show are being told on social media by a PhD student for his thesis. Greg Thomas, hailing from Builth Wells in Powys and currently studying at Aberystwyth University in Ceredigion, initially embarked on his research journey at the show by conducting surveys. However, he quickly realized that these surveys only provided numerical data. I didn't want my thesis to be really dull, explained Mr. Thomas, who plans to submit his work in October. I didn't want it to be read by five bearded academics and that's it—I wanted it to be useful and for everyone to get something out of it.This realization led him to focus on the people behind the statistics. It's 100,000 words—but there's so much going on here and the show means so much to so many people, is that even enough? he pondered. Thus, Mr. Thomas decided to enrich his doctoral work—which examines the interactions between farmers and non-farmers, Welsh identity, and politics—with photographs and quotes from a diverse group of individuals, including farmers, visitors, stewards, and organizers. Essentially, he aimed to capture the essence of the Royal Welsh Show's human element.Inspired by the popular Humans of New York social media phenomenon, Mr. Thomas conducted interviews during the show and approached individuals he encountered who might have intriguing stories to share. Although he noted that his most popular posts typically spotlight real people rather than celebrities or politicians, rugby referee Nigel Owens proved to be an exception. Owens contributed bilingual posts, reflecting, I've been coming to the Royal Welsh for years really, coming from a farming community and working on a farm, that was the interest originally. But then over the last few years, I've been president of Wales Young Farmers clubs, and most of the time I've been coming here to compete with the Young Farmers when I was a member and then coming to help out in the YFC office during the competitions. The last four or five years, I've been coming here to referee the final of the sevens tournament.The familiar voice that resonates across the showground belongs to chief announcer and commentator Nicola Davies, whom Mr. Thomas also interviewed for his Facebook page. I've been coming here as a child with my family, exhibited Welsh cobs here for many, many years, she shared. But I was asked to commentate here on an equine display back between 10 and 15 years ago, and I got the bug. I was part of the team, some say it was a promotion, some not. But I'm now chief commentator, so I'm in charge of the commentators at the main ring, horse ring, the sheep, the cattle, and the pig section. So I don't know anything much about pigs and cattle, but I try to find people that do.Wales UKIP leader Neil Hamilton and his wife, author and media personality Christine Hamilton, added a touch of humor to the project by joking that they attended the show solely for Mr. Thomas's thesis. We're Neil and Christine Hamilton, and we are basically here to give you a couple of extra paragraphs for your thesis, Mr. Hamilton quipped. But apart from that, it is of course the biggest agricultural show in northern Europe, and I believe this brings in £20m a year to the mid Wales economy. It is a vitally important event in the year.Mr. Thomas found that people were generally receptive to his interview requests, enjoying more success than with his previous survey approach. Among those who agreed to share their stories was police officer Matthew Howells. I'm a police officer with Dyfed-Powys Police, I'm working here at the show for three days this week. I'm from a farming background myself, so the interest is there anyway for me to come to the show. I would be coming anyway, so I do a bit of work, and I'm helping my partner show a horse tomorrow as well, he said.Steward Barbara Green, who is presenting a barren mare in the main ring this week, also shared her experience. It will be the first time I've shown in the main ring for many years, she said. I was showing here for the first time when I was 16 years old, and quite a few years have passed since then. I'm quite excited about it, but I'm also very nervous.Curiously, one person has yet to feature as a Human of the Royal Welsh Show—Greg Thomas himself. Reflecting on his own journey, he shared, I'm Greg Thomas, a PhD student in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University. This week at the show I have been conducting the Humans of the Royal Welsh Show project, it is great to get so many stories from the people who work tirelessly to make the show the best in Europe. Being from Builth Wells, and having a farming background, it is a privilege to be able to study an event that means so much to so many.

text: The final leaders' debate gave the opposition parties what they wanted in throwing the focus of the campaign well and truly onto the NHS. The first thirty minutes of the debate were a whirlwind of emotion, policy discussions, and spirited exchanges—truly compelling to watch. Carwyn Jones set the stage with his opening remarks, zeroing in on health services and highlighting the absence of a junior doctors' strike in Wales. This ongoing dispute in England has provided Labour with a strategic advantage, especially with the strike coinciding perfectly with the lead-up to polling day next week.In stark contrast to last week's leaders' debate, where opposition parties united against Carwyn Jones, this time saw a fragmented dynamic with various leaders clashing at different intervals. Nathan Gill and Kirsty Williams debated fiercely over EU steel dumping, while Andrew RT Davies criticized Kirsty Williams and Leanne Wood for their alliances with the Labour administration.A notable theme throughout was Carwyn Jones's persistent attacks on Leanne Wood regarding Plaid Cymru's proposals to restructure the NHS and their plan to forgive student debt only for those who return to Wales. This was unexpected, given Labour's repeated emphasis that the election battle is primarily between them and the Conservatives. Eventually, a visibly frustrated Leanne Wood accused Jones of distorting her policies. Following the debate, Plaid Cymru interpreted the criticism as a backhanded compliment, suggesting it revealed Labour's unease about a potential Plaid threat. Labour, on the other hand, believes there are Plaid supporters who might be swayed in key battlegrounds like the Vale of Glamorgan and the Vale of Clwyd, where they face off against the Tories.Meanwhile, Nathan Gill adopted a different approach. Throughout the assembly campaign, he has been eager to distance discussions from the EU, aiming to demonstrate the party's serious commitment to devolution. However, during the debate, he frequently referenced the EU, seemingly to rally the party's core supporters. The pressing question is whether UKIP voters, energized by the EU referendum, will be motivated enough to vote next week. With no historical data to guide predictions, the potential impact of UKIP's turnout, especially in marginal seats, remains uncertain but could be significant.An insider from one party likened a strong UKIP showing in a tight contest to a bomb going off, due to its potential to disrupt the vote distribution among other parties and consequently alter the final outcomes in many constituencies.

text: Sri Lanka's Kumar Sangakkara became the first player to score four successive one-day international centuries as his side beat Scotland at the World Cup. In a thrilling display at Hobart, 37-year-old Kumar Sangakkara smashed 124 runs, contributing to Sri Lanka's formidable total of 363-9. This marked his fourth century in the tournament, adding to his previous hundreds against Bangladesh, England, and Australia. Meanwhile, Sangakkara also reached a milestone of over 500 ODI dismissals as Scotland crumbled to 215 all out.Despite valiant half-centuries from Scotland's captain Preston Mommsen and Freddie Coleman, Sri Lanka concluded Pool A with four victories. They are poised to face South Africa in the quarter-finals in Sydney on Wednesday. Scotland, having suffered their fifth defeat, remain winless and are set to play co-hosts Australia in their final match on Saturday in Hobart.The day at Bellerive Oval was one for the record books. Left-hander Sangakkara notched his fifth World Cup century, trailing just one behind Sachin Tendulkar's record of six. With 14,189 ODI runs to his name, only Tendulkar, who retired in 2013 with 18,426 runs, surpasses him in the 50-over format. Sangakkara, the first player to score four centuries in a single World Cup, has hinted at retiring from ODI cricket after the tournament.In recent months, the wicketkeeper-batsman has been in prolific form, becoming the fastest to reach 12,000 Test runs in January, and scoring his 11th double century, just one shy of Don Bradman's record. Reflecting on his performance, Sangakkara said, I've been batting and keeping for a long time, it's getting harder and the joints are creaking and aching, but I consider myself lucky to be part of a great team. No matter how hard you try, it's hard to pinpoint why I'm playing so well. Maybe I'm making better decisions at the crease, I don't know. Whatever it is, it's working for me at the moment.Sangakkara's 124 against Scotland followed scores of 105 not out against Bangladesh, 117 not out against England, and 104 against Australia. Sri Lanka's innings was bolstered by a 195-run partnership for the second wicket between Sangakkara and Tillakaratne Dilshan, who also scored 104. Both reached their centuries in consecutive balls before being dismissed in quick succession by Scotland's Josh Davey. Davey, with figures of 3-63, topped the World Cup wicket-takers list with 14, edging ahead of New Zealand's Trent Boult and Tim Southee.Sri Lanka's captain Angelo Mathews added fireworks with a rapid 20-ball half-century, including four consecutive sixes off Matt Machan's bowling, setting them on course for a potential 400-plus score. However, a late collapse and sharp Scottish fielding curtailed their innings.Scotland's chase began disastrously as Kyle Coetzer fell to a simple return catch off Lasith Malinga's second ball. text: Too many patients are locked into mental health rehabilitation wards far from home, a review of England's psychiatric services suggests. The Care Quality Commission (CQC) has revealed that 3,500 beds are currently occupied in locked facilities across the UK, yet it maintains that a significant number of individuals could benefit from care in residential settings closer to their homes. The report highlights that safety on mental health wards remains a pressing issue.NHS England has acknowledged progress in mental health care, attributing it to increased funding. Claire Murdoch, NHS England's head of mental health, expressed cautious optimism but emphasized the need for further improvements aligned with the NHS's five-year plan priorities.The CQC's comprehensive review of specialist mental health services across England included both NHS and independent sector provisions. It found that nearly all services were rated as good or outstanding for their caring and compassionate staff, with numerous examples of exceptional care. However, several concerns were identified.Particularly troubling are the locked rehabilitation wards, two-thirds of which are managed by independent providers. CQC leaders criticized these facilities for not offering a suitable model of care for the 21st Century. Patients often endure extended stays, averaging 341 days, which raises the risk of institutionalization and undermines the aim of community reintegration.Dr. Paul Lelliott, the CQC's mental health lead, remarked, We weren't expecting to find this many [locked rehabilitation beds]. He expressed suspicion that a significant proportion of these patients could be better served in residential settings closer to home, with more independence and community support rather than hospital confinement.The report also noted that about one-third of services require safety improvements, with one in 20 deemed inadequate, posing real and sometimes immediate risks to patient safety. Inspectors cited old and unsuitable buildings, such as those with blind spots in corridors, as contributing factors. Additionally, a 12% decrease in mental health nursing staff from January 2010 to 2017 exacerbates safety concerns.Brian Dow of the charity Rethink Mental Illness acknowledged the sector's strong commitment but stressed that substantial progress is still needed. He questioned whether adequate funding and the right personnel are in place to deliver effective care and whether patients are actively involved in their treatment.Claire Murdoch described the report to the BBC as a really fair evaluation of the nation's mental health services. She noted that most providers are progressing towards or achieving good status, with some moving towards outstanding. However, she agreed that the report rightly identifies areas needing further improvement.

text: Safety inspections will be carried out at schools across Scotland following the collapse of a wall at an Edinburgh primary, BBC Scotland has learned. In the capital, four buildings were temporarily closed after defects were discovered in schools constructed by Miller Construction a decade ago. This prompted new surveys focusing on schools built by the same company in Glasgow, Fife, and Inverclyde. The contractor described these inspections as a precautionary measure.The issue came to light when Storm Gertrude hit in January, causing hundreds of bricks to be blown from the wall of Oxgangs Primary School. A subsequent safety inspection revealed problems with the construction of the external wall, which was built in 2005 under the Public Private Partnership 1 (PPP1) project. Oxgangs was part of a broader initiative that involved the construction or refurbishment of 17 schools, following an agreement between the council and a private finance consortium.The wall collapse led to further inspections, uncovering similar issues at three other Edinburgh schools: St Peter's RC Primary, Firrhill High, and Braidburn Special Schools. All these schools, built around the same time by Miller Construction, were deemed unsafe and temporarily closed. Galliford Try, which acquired Miller Construction in 2014, stated the schools are expected to reopen after the Easter holidays.A spokesperson for Galliford Try explained: The four schools temporarily closed in Edinburgh were part of the second phase of the PPP1 programme, completed by Miller Construction in 2005. We have already started remedial work at Oxgangs Primary School and are assessing the need for work on the other three schools. Any necessary remedial work will be carried out swiftly to minimize disruption to the children's education. Although we are not aware of any defects, we have contacted the clients of the PPP school projects Miller Construction undertook in Glasgow, Fife, and Inverclyde as a precautionary measure. Further investigations will be conducted as needed.The Public Private Partnership deal for Edinburgh schools, signed in 2001, was valued at £360 million. In exchange for 30 years of fixed payments from the council, a private consortium designed, built, and managed the schools. Miller Construction was part of this consortium, as well as others that were constructing schools in other parts of Scotland. A PPP1 deal signed in Glasgow a year earlier was valued at three times Edinburgh's and involved 29 secondary schools and one primary school across the country.Glasgow City Council announced that its PPP contract would now include surveys on the handful of schools built by Miller Construction. Galliford Try also contacted clients of schools built by the company in Inverclyde, and inspections are currently being conducted by the council in Fife. Shelagh McLean, head of education and children's services (equity and system improvement), stated: Fife Council has contacted both of our PPP Contractors, who are monitoring the situation in Edinburgh. They will be carrying out inspections in Fife during the school Easter holidays. Both contractors also perform annual inspections of the building fabric and freestanding walls as part of their ongoing maintenance.Oxgangs Primary School and St Peter's are scheduled to reopen on April 11.

text: The head of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), Martin Wheatley, is to stand down from his post after just two years in charge. Martin Wheatley, head of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), will step down in September, as announced by the FCA. Chancellor George Osborne expressed gratitude for Wheatley's service, praising his brilliant job of launching the FCA in tough circumstances. However, Osborne noted, The government believes that different leadership is required to build on those foundations.Tracey McDermott, Wheatley's deputy, will assume the role on an interim basis while the search for a permanent successor begins. Reflecting on his tenure, Wheatley stated he was incredibly proud of the achievements made with his team over the past four years in establishing the FCA. He expressed confidence that the organization would continue to thrive and bolster the financial services industry.The decision for Wheatley to step down was influenced by the Treasury. Sources indicate that recent discussions made it clear to Wheatley that the Chancellor would not renew his contract, set to expire in March 2016. Facing this reality, Wheatley opted to leave early. His relationship with the Treasury has been tense, particularly after his assertive declaration to shoot first when addressing misconduct in the financial sector. This stance drew criticism from senior banking executives.Andrew Tyrie, chairman of the Treasury Committee, acknowledged Wheatley's contributions, recognizing the challenges he faced in transforming the culture of both the regulated community and the regulator. Tyrie emphasized the importance of finding a high-caliber successor to protect consumer interests and enhance competition in the financial services sector.Wheatley's journey with the FCA began in September 2011 when he joined the Financial Services Authority (FSA), the FCA's predecessor. He succeeded Hector Sants as chief executive of the newly empowered City regulator, launched in April 2013. Known for his tough regulatory approach, Wheatley had previously built his reputation in markets like Hong Kong and at the Securities and Exchange Commission in the US, which contributed to his appointment as FCA chief.In recent weeks, Wheatley has sought to reassure industry leaders that the FCA is not pursuing a punitive agenda under new accountability rules in the banking sector. Nevertheless, the FCA has imposed some of the largest regulatory fines in the City's history. The regulator has faced its own controversies, notably last year's incident with the insurance industry. A leaked story to the Daily Telegraph suggested an impending investigation into 30 million pension policies, some dating back to the 1970s. This leak led to significant financial repercussions for major insurance companies, a parliamentary inquiry, and the loss of annual bonuses for four senior executives, including Wheatley.

text: Crime involving mopeds has gone up by more than 600% in London in the past two years, BBC London can reveal. In 2016, the Metropolitan Police recorded over 7,500 moped-related offences, including attacks, robberies, and thefts, averaging about 22 incidents daily. This surge, primarily driven by teenagers stealing mopeds to facilitate crimes, is a huge concern, according to the Met. However, they maintain that the issue is not out of control.While moped-enabled crime has touched other major UK cities, London remains the most affected. The city's allure for criminals stems from its abundance of tourists with mobile phones and a high concentration of luxury shops.Scotland Yard's internal statistics reveal a dramatic rise in such crimes: 7,668 incidents in 2016 alone, compared to 1,053 in 2014 and 4,647 in 2015. Superintendent Mark Payne, who leads Operation Venice—a dedicated initiative to combat this issue since its inception two years ago—remarked, I think it's a huge concern because it is a change in criminal behavior. The fact of the matter is it's much more difficult to deal with people on mopeds than it was people who were committing those sorts of crimes before on foot or on bicycles.The Met has identified 200 individuals suspected of moped-related crimes, yet prosecutions are often hampered by insufficient evidence. Furthermore, suspects frequently evade pursuit if not wearing helmets, due to safety concerns.This cautious approach follows incidents like the death of teenager Henry Hicks, which led to disciplinary actions against four officers from Islington, North London, after an inquest jury found he died during an unauthorized pursuit in 2012. Additionally, the police watchdog is investigating the death of 18-year-old Lewis Johnson, whose scooter crashed during another chase.To address repeat offenders who elude prosecution for suspected crimes, the Met employs an Achilles Heel strategy, reminiscent of the tactic used to apprehend gangster Al Capone. This involves targeting them for lesser offences, such as driving without insurance or a license.Despite criticisms, the police assert that criminals do not feel emboldened by the unlikelihood of helmetless pursuits. They believe they are maintaining an appropriate balance in assessing the risks of high-speed chases.In a bid to curb thefts, police also advise moped owners to enhance security by using additional locks.

text: Banking giant JP Morgan Chase plans to raise the hourly wages of 18,000 US staff over the next three years. Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has taken a stand on income inequality, urging the private sector to step up its efforts. In an opinion piece for The New York Times, Dimon declared, A pay increase is the right thing to do. Wages for many Americans have gone nowhere for too long. This announcement will see a boost in salaries for bank tellers and customer service representatives, with hourly wages rising from $10.15 (£7.71) to between $12 and $16, depending on the location. Dimon emphasized that this move enables more people to begin to share in the rewards of economic growth. He also noted that higher wages would benefit the bank by attracting and retaining talent.On Tuesday, JP Morgan's shares experienced a 1.2% increase. This decision aligns with a broader trend among major US companies. Just a day prior, Starbucks revealed plans to raise wages for 150,000 hourly workers, and in April, McDonald's announced a pay hike for employees at its non-franchised outlets.Despite a recovering job market, wage stagnation has persisted since the recession. Federal Reserve Chair Janet Yellen has pointed out that this is a sign the labor market has yet to reach its full potential, and the central bank is monitoring wage growth closely. The disparity between the highest and lowest earners has also been a focal issue in the US election.In his article, Dimon urged businesses to do more for their employees. He suggested that even companies unable to increase wages could still support their workforce through training and mentoring programs. Additionally, he called on the government to expand the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), a tax refund for low-income workers with children, to a broader group of workers.We face many challenges. But they can be overcome by government, business and the non-profit sectors working together to build on models of success that advance economic opportunity and create more widely shared prosperity, Dimon concluded.

text: Police have said the number of people caught drink-driving during the annual Christmas crackdown increased significantly on the previous year. Between November 27 of last year and January 2, a total of 396 arrests were made, marking a significant 42% increase from the 282 arrests during the same period in 2014-15. Among those apprehended was a police officer, and one individual was halted with their children present in the vehicle. Notably, one driver was found to be four times over the legal drink-drive limit, and another was caught on two separate drink-driving occasions. The statistics encompass drivers who were deemed unfit, refused, or were unable to provide a sample.Assistant Chief Constable Alan Todd of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) expressed grave concern over the rise in drink-driving incidents. He described the offenders as disregarding the safety of themselves and others by engaging in this shameful and incredibly dangerous practice. Todd warned that those caught would likely face a minimum one-year driving ban, with many also risking job loss or imprisonment. Every year across Northern Ireland, drinking and driving kills, maims, and wrecks families, he emphasized. He recounted an incident involving a driver, detected at three o'clock in the afternoon, with their children in the car after consuming alcohol. Todd urged the public to consider the dire consequences of a serious collision on themselves and their families. How would you feel if your actions resulted in you or one of your family being paralyzed? How would you feel if some innocent person was killed? he questioned. The arrested police officer is expected to face court and disciplinary measures within the PSNI, which could result in suspension or dismissal.The majority of those apprehended for drink-driving were men, totaling 325, while 71 women were caught. The youngest individual detected was 16, and the oldest was 83. Environment Minister Mark H Durkan highlighted the severe impact of drink-driving, stating, Drink-driving has caused over 2,000 deaths and serious injuries since 2000. That is the shocking reality of mixing alcohol with driving. He affirmed that society today views drink-driving as unacceptable. Durkan also noted that the recently passed Road Traffic Amendment Bill in the Northern Ireland Assembly will impose lower drink-drive limits.

text: The amount of nursery and pre-school provision for children in special schools is to be reduced. Starting in September, all 39 special schools across Northern Ireland will see a significant change in their pre-school schedule. Children with moderate to severe learning difficulties will now attend school for just 2.5 hours daily, a reduction from the previous minimum of 4.5 hours. This decision was disclosed by the Education Authority (EA) in a letter addressed to a parent, confirming that all pre-school children will receive 2.5 hours in pre-school per day from September 2016.The EA explained that this adjustment aims to increase the opportunity for children to access special school places and ensure greater regional consistency. However, the decision has sparked concern among special school principals and governors. The Strategic Leadership Forum for Special Schools (SLFSS), representing these stakeholders, expressed strong opposition, stating the reduction will hold back and restrict the development of children with complex needs.In a submission to the Northern Ireland Assembly, the SLFSS articulated their disagreement, highlighting the potential negative impacts of the move. Francine Wilson, whose three-year-old son Aodhan is set to begin pre-school at a special school in September, shared her concerns. Aodhan has Down's Syndrome, and we were hoping he would receive five hours of nursery placement, she said. Receiving two and a half hours will, I believe, result in delayed development in Aodhan, both educationally and socially.Despite these concerns, a spokesperson for the EA defended the reduction, stating it aligns with the Department of Education's 'Learning to Learn' policy. There has been a progressive move towards part-time places in all sectors, the spokesperson noted. They emphasized that research indicates no significant difference in development at the start of primary school between children who attended part-time versus full-time pre-school. The EA spokesperson further explained that the change is intended to offer more children the opportunity to attend special schools, ideally closer to their homes. The provision of increased access and greater regional consistency is a priority, they added.

text: Speaking at Prime Minister's Questions, Theresa May refused to say whether the Conservatives will keep the same protections for the state pension if they win the general election. The claim that pensioners would be £872 worse off without the triple-lock has sparked debate. The triple-lock ensures the basic state pension rises by the highest of average earnings, inflation, or 2.5%. In the long run, pensioners would indeed face financial setbacks without this mechanism, though the extent depends on its replacement. Ian Blackford's assertion, based on a House of Commons Library study, suggested a £872 loss over five years if pensions only matched inflation predictions. However, the actual figure from the research indicates a £817 loss over the same period.When questioned by Angus Robertson, SNP's leader in Westminster, the government reaffirmed its commitment to increasing pensioners' incomes but stopped short of detailing the specifics. The current government policy maintains the triple-lock until 2020, ensuring pensions rise by the highest of the three metrics. Political parties including Labour, the Liberal Democrats, and the SNP support this policy. However, the Work and Pensions Committee has labeled the triple-lock as unsustainable and unfair to younger generations, suggesting pensions should only rise with earnings, safeguarded against inflation surpassing earnings, but without a minimum annual increase.John Cridland, in a recent report on state pensions, also recommended eventually replacing the triple-lock with an earnings link. The long-term implications of the triple-lock are significant, with the Office for National Statistics forecasting a sharp increase in the ratio of pensioners to working-age individuals over the next half-century.On BBC Newsnight, Mr. Blackford referenced the House of Commons Library's findings, which compared the impact on pensions under various scenarios using Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts. It showed minimal difference if pensions rose with earnings, as these are expected to exceed 2.5% throughout the period. Aligning only with inflation would result in a £642 loss over five years for a basic state pensioner and £817 for someone on the new state pension. Mr. Blackford's £872 figure appears to be a misquote of these findings.These projections, inherently uncertain, contrast with historical analyses by the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS), which found the triple-lock added about £6 billion annually compared to earnings protection alone, and £4 billion compared to inflation-only adjustments. The IFS charted the variance in national income allocation to pensions with or without the triple-lock, based on OBR forecasts.The IFS suggests the government should determine a fixed proportion of earnings for the state pension, avoiding arbitrary increases via the triple-lock. The significance of the triple-lock is underscored by its impact on pensioner versus worker incomes. Pensioners have seen more generous protection than in-work benefits, with the Resolution Foundation noting that, post-housing costs, pensioner households often fare better financially than working ones. This disparity arises as pensioners are more likely to own homes with minimal or no mortgages.Baroness Altmann, a former pensions minister, criticized the triple-lock's fairness, highlighting its pressure on the government to raise the pension age, delaying younger families' access to their pensions. As discussions on the triple-lock's future continue, various alternatives are being considered.

text: They call Lynton Crosby the Wizard of Oz - the political magician who has been hired by the Conservatives to mastermind their next election campaign. Lynton Crosby, often likened to a shadowy wizard in the political realm, is a figure of both admiration and controversy. While some critics argue he is not as formidable as his reputation suggests—highlighting the Conservative Party's loss at the last general election he managed—others point to his triumphs, particularly in Australia and more recently in London, where he orchestrated Boris Johnson's successful re-election as mayor.Born 55 years ago in rural South Australia, Crosby's early life was marked by a move from a farm, where his father, more artist than farmer, opened an arts and crafts shop in Kadina. Crosby enjoyed a happy and somewhat indulgent childhood, according to his sister Robyn Hewett, who recalls his love for debating, performing plays, and his academic prowess. His parents, though not overtly political, were instinctive supporters of the Liberals, Australia's conservative party, which perhaps set the stage for Crosby's later career in politics.After studying economics at Adelaide University, where his parents relocated to support him, Crosby ventured into Liberal politics following a stint in the private sector. Although his attempt as a candidate was unsuccessful—he humorously admits he wouldn't have voted for himself—he found his niche behind the scenes. Rising to become campaign director for Liberal Prime Minister John Howard, Crosby helped secure four consecutive election victories, albeit amid accusations of employing divisive tactics, such as dog-whistle campaigns and exploiting wedge issues.Cheryl Kernot, a former Australian Senator, vividly recalls Crosby's strategic focus on controversial topics like immigration and refugees, which she argues played on fears and prejudices. Despite such criticisms, John Howard defends Crosby as a professional campaigner dedicated to victory, dismissing allegations of unscrupulous methods as the complaints of those opposed to the Liberal Party's success.Crosby's contentious reputation followed him to the UK, where he assisted Michael Howard's Conservatives in the 2005 election. Daniel Finkelstein, who introduced Crosby to Howard, praises his political acumen and ability to sharpen campaign focus, although some of Crosby's hard-hitting slogans contributed to the Tories' nasty party image. Despite the election loss, Crosby left a lasting impression, leading to his recruitment by Boris Johnson for the 2008 London mayoral race.In London, Crosby's strategy and discipline helped Johnson secure a Tory victory in a traditionally Labour-leaning city. Johnson recalls Crosby's candid feedback, which, despite its bluntness, proved effective. However, Ken Livingstone, Johnson's Labour opponent, criticizes the negative personal attacks he attributes to Crosby's campaign tactics.With Boris Johnson's endorsement, Crosby was recommended to David Cameron as the ideal strategist for the next general election, though not without reservations from Tory modernisers wary of his focus on core issues like immigration and crime. Finkelstein, however, believes Crosby will align with Cameron's direction, ensuring a disciplined approach.As Labour and the Liberal Democrats prepare to counter Crosby's strategies, Ken Livingstone warns Ed Miliband to study Crosby's methods closely. Crosby's ability to secure a Tory victory in London amid broader Conservative losses underscores his formidable skills, making him a key figure in future political battles.For more insights into Lynton Crosby's career and influence, tune in to Radio 4's Profile or download the Profile podcast.

text: China's economy is slowing down. The economic landscape of China is a significant concern as President Xi Jinping visits the United States. Once boasting an average annual growth rate of 10% over three decades, China's growth has decelerated markedly, hitting 7.4% last year. Many economists doubt the accuracy of China's official figures, suspecting the real growth rate is much lower. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasts a further decline to 6.8% for the coming year, noting that this slowdown was inevitable.The IMF describes China's ongoing transformation as a shift to a new normal, characterized by slower but more sustainable and secure growth. This new phase is necessary because the factors that once fueled China's rapid expansion are diminishing. The aging population limits the economic contribution of a growing labor force. Moreover, China's technological advancements have reduced the gap with the rest of the world, curbing the potential for rapid catch-up growth.Investment, another growth driver, is already at a high level in China. In fact, the IMF indicated back in 2012 that China's investment was excessive, diverting resources from other sectors like household spending and leading to economically inefficient projects.The pressing question for financial markets is whether China's transition will be smooth or result in a hard landing, an abrupt slowdown or recession. This outcome is critical globally, as China is the world's largest economy by some measures, contributing 17% to global economic activity. While the U.S. economy is similarly large, it is not growing as quickly, and this dynamic is expected to persist for years, even decades, as China stabilizes at a more sustainable growth rate. Consequently, China's influence on global growth and its demand for international goods is substantial.Economists are divided on the issue, but Willem Buiter, Citigroup's chief economist and former Bank of England and London School of Economics figure, offers a bleak perspective. He warns of a high and rising likelihood of a Chinese, emerging market, and global recession scenario.Buiter's definition of a recession hinges on an economy's growth potential, considering global growth below 2% for a year as a recession, with China's threshold at 2.5%. He is skeptical of China's official data, believing the economy is closer to recession than reported figures suggest. Buiter estimates a 40% chance of a moderate global recession, with a 15% chance of a severe downturn and financial crisis. He attributes the risk mainly to slow growth in key emerging economies, particularly China, stating, We consider China to be at high and rapidly rising risk of a cyclical hard landing.Buiter points to classic recession indicators: excess capacity in industries, high borrowing and debt levels, and irrational exuberance in asset markets, such as real estate and stocks. Should a recession occur, its effects would ripple globally, impacting other emerging economies like Brazil and Russia, already in recession.China is a crucial export market for many countries, ranking first for South Korea, Saudi Arabia, and Iran. It's the second-largest market for Japan and Germany (outside the EU) and the fourth for the U.S. Even countries with minimal direct trade with China could feel the impact of a hard landing if they supply nations that do trade with China or if they export commodities sensitive to Chinese demand fluctuations.Prices for key industrial commodities like crude oil and copper have plummeted, with crude oil prices halving since June last year due to supply factors and weaker-than-expected Chinese demand. Copper, essential for construction and electrical installations, has also seen its price halved since 2011, largely due to China's slowdown.However, not everyone shares this pessimism. The London consultancy Capital Economics recently suggested that China's growth has stabilized after an early-year slowdown, with stronger growth expected in the months ahead.Ahead of his U.S. visit, President Xi assured the Wall Street Journal, The Chinese economy is still operating within the proper range. President Barack Obama, hosting Xi, undoubtedly hopes this remains true, as do many others worldwide.

text: An error with the Global Positioning System (GPS) network has been blamed for causing problems with digital radio broadcasts last week. A software error emerged after the US Air Force removed a satellite from service, leading to disruptions in digital radio signals, the BBC reported. This issue arose following the decommissioning of a GPS satellite, which affected listeners' ability to receive BBC digital radio.The BBC has confirmed that not only one, but several satellites were impacted. A user, Darcy72, shared on Digital Spy's online forums: I live on the Worksop side of Sheffield and for the past two days, the reception of the BBC National Ensemble [BBC radio stations] has been virtually non-existent indoors.The BBC explained, The outages were caused by a rogue GPS satellite (SVN23), which was taken out of service on the evening of 26 January. This decommissioned satellite led to software glitches affecting multiple satellites.For DAB transmitters to function correctly, they must broadcast at identical frequencies, which requires synchronization with GPS satellite signals. These signals are expected to be accurate to within a few nanoseconds. However, when the GPS satellite SVN23 was decommissioned on 26 January, it unexpectedly disrupted the network.The US Air Force stated, While the core navigation systems were working normally, the coordinated universal time timing signal was off by 13 microseconds, which exceeded the design specifications. This issue was resolved at 06:10 MST, but global users may have experienced GPS timing problems for several hours.The time discrepancy, noted by the Metsahovi Radio Observatory in Finland, could have thrown off GPS positioning by nearly 4km. It's still unclear if other global systems, such as navigational tools, were affected. The BBC is seeking more information from the US Air Force.Prof Danielle George from the University of Manchester questioned the foresight of the decommissioning process: They knew they were decommissioning it, so shouldn't they have been aware this would happen? She noted that the satellite, decommissioned after 25 years, had already outlived its expected 7.5-year lifespan.Prof George suggested that if only one satellite had been problematic, DAB transmitters might not have faced issues. They shouldn't have seen an issue with that because as far as I understand the way they work is they need two frequencies to lock and there are a number of GPS [signals] to look at, she explained to the BBC.Martyn Thomas, a fellow at the Royal Academy of Engineering, warned of the dangers of over-reliance on GPS technology. The world is dependent on GPS for a vast range of critical applications from navigation to financial trading, and precision docking of oil tankers to high-tech farming, he stated. Prof Thomas emphasized the necessity of having backup systems in the future.

text: Councils have warned they may be charging more for services despite some already increasing such revenue by more than 100% in three years. In the fiscal year 2014/2015, councils across the UK generated over £11 billion through fees, charges, and sales, according to government data. This marked a 3% increase in revenue from these sources since 2012/2013. The Local Government Association highlighted the challenging balancing act councils face when determining these fees.These charges encompass a range of services, such as car parking, adult social care, planning, and country parks. While some councils have seen their income from these sources soar by tens of millions, others have experienced declines. Notably, six councils in England—Breckland, Devon, Hinckley and Bosworth, South Northamptonshire, and Sedgmoor—witnessed their income from fees, sales, and charges more than double over three years. Meanwhile, Derbyshire, Westminster, Bristol, and Shropshire emerged as the biggest gainers in real terms, each collecting tens of millions more annually.A spokeswoman for Derbyshire, which saw a £33 million increase in revenue from fees, charges, and sales between 2013/2014 and 2015, explained: Like all councils, we aim to boost our income where possible, as we need to find £157 million in savings from 2013 to 2018. We've increased charges in various areas, such as co-funding for adult social care, home-to-school transport for faith school pupils, and parking at some countryside sites.Sharon Taylor, acting leader of the Local Government Association, commented on the delicate nature of setting council charges: There's a law of diminishing returns. Raising prices can lead to reduced service usage. It must be a reasonable increase; it's a balancing act. Councils, regardless of political affiliation, recognize that family budgets are tight and are cautious about raising costs. Ultimately, fees and charges must be weighed against council tax increases.In Cambridge, where revenue from fees and charges climbed from £20.5 million to £23.1 million over three years, any department wishing to raise fees above inflation must justify the necessity. Lewis Herbert, leader of the Labour-led council, stated: We strive to balance service costs without burdening residents. We're not sounding alarms, and our situation isn't as dire as some councils, but it's precarious as we await details of the government's local government plans. We're more business-oriented, exploring options like building a café at the crematorium, selling flowers, or renting more space in the Guildhall to boost income through sales rather than higher charges.The Department for Communities and Local Government did not respond to requests for comment.

text: Brazil's President Michel Temer has nominated his justice minister to the Supreme Court as it prepares to rule on one the biggest corruption scandals in the country's history. Alexandre de Moraes, a close ally of President Michel Temer, has been nominated to fill the vacancy left by Judge Teori Zavascki, who tragically died in a plane crash last month. Despite calls for a less politically charged appointment, given the numerous corruption charges facing senior politicians, Temer defended his choice, citing Moraes's solid academic credentials.At 49, Moraes is a lawyer affiliated with the PSDB party, part of Temer's governing coalition. He joined the cabinet in May when Temer took over from President Dilma Rousseff amid her impeachment proceedings. Earlier this year, Moraes faced a significant challenge when over 100 prisoners were killed in a series of riots. In response, he proposed establishing police intelligence units and enhancing collaboration with neighboring countries to curb the influence of gangs controlling Brazilian prisons.Moraes's nomination requires Senate approval, for which he has requested a 30-day leave to prepare. Analysts predict a smooth confirmation process, given the government's substantial Senate majority. Meanwhile, the Supreme Court is set to review extensive evidence from the Petrobras corruption investigation later this month. This investigation, known as Operation Car Wash, was previously overseen by Judge Zavascki, who had compiled a list of politicians allegedly bribed by Odebrecht to secure Petrobras contracts. Odebrecht has confessed to paying $1 billion in bribes across 12 countries.Judge Zavascki, respected for his integrity, lent significant credibility to the Car Wash probe. text: New Edinburgh centre Sasa Tofilau is primed for his Pro12 debut after a rapid switch from the 'jungle rugby' of the Scottish club game's third tier. He suggested, 'why don't you come over here and experience Edinburgh?' I had heard great things about Edinburgh, so I decided to check it off my bucket list, and that's how it all happened.Previously, Tofilau was part of the Chiefs development squad in Waikato and also played for Australia's Under-20s. text: Arkansas will become the first US state in 17 years to hold two executions on the same day, if two inmates are put to death as planned on Monday evening. Lawyers representing Jack Jones and Marcel Williams are urgently seeking stays of execution, citing their clients' poor health as a primary concern. Arkansas initially scheduled the execution of eight inmates over an 11-day period, aiming to use the lethal drugs before their expiration. Last Thursday, Ledell Lee was executed, marking the state's first execution since 2005. Kenneth Williams is slated for execution this Thursday, although his legal team argues he is intellectually disabled.Currently, court orders have halted four of the eight planned executions. However, the state's chief prosecutor is determined to navigate through legal challenges to carry out the sentences. The last instance of a U.S. state executing two inmates on the same day occurred in Texas in 2000.Both Jones and Williams, who have admitted guilt, are set for execution on Monday. Jones was convicted in 1996 for the rape and murder of Mary Phillips and the attempted murder of her 11-year-old daughter. Additionally, he was found guilty of rape and murder in Florida. Williams received a death sentence in 1997 for kidnapping, raping, and murdering Stacy Errickson, and he also abducted and raped two other women.Jones is scheduled for execution at 7:00 PM local time (midnight GMT) at the Cummins Unit prison, with Williams following at 8:15 PM. On Sunday, they sought a stay of execution from the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals, which has not yet issued a ruling. Jones's attorneys warn he may experience a torturous death due to potential resistance to midazolam. He is currently on high doses of medications for diabetes, high blood pressure, and neuropathy. Williams's lawyers highlight the difficulty of locating a vein for the lethal injection due to his 400-pound (180kg) weight.A federal judge in Little Rock, Arkansas, dismissed the health-related challenge from Jones and Williams last Friday. James Phillips, whose wife was murdered by Jones, expressed to the BBC his lack of sympathy, stating, It don't matter if they suffer a little bit as far as I'm concerned, because my wife suffered big time. Among numerous legal challenges, a lawsuit from the manufacturer of one of the execution drugs argued that the state failed to disclose its intent to use the drugs for executions. However, the Arkansas Supreme Court recently dismissed this lawsuit.

text: Saudi King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz has died, royal officials have announced, weeks after he was admitted to hospital.
