Many residents gathered at mosques for Friday prayers, grappling with the loss of a monarch they held in high regard. The kingdom will only begin to adjust to this new reality once the late king is laid to rest.An official statement named another of Abdullah's half-brothers, Muqrin, in his late 60s, as the new crown prince. Abdullah, Salman, and Muqrin are all sons of King Abdulaziz, the founder of modern Saudi Arabia, commonly known as Ibn Saud, who passed away in 1953. King Salman urged the royal family's Allegiance Council to recognize Muqrin as his successor. He quickly appointed Interior Minister Prince Mohammed bin Nayef as deputy crown prince, positioning him second in line, and named his son, Mohammed bin Salman, as defense minister. State TV reported that other key ministers, including those of foreign, oil, and finance, retained their positions.King Salman's official Twitter account reflected his new role, with a message asking for divine assistance in serving the Saudi people. In accordance with Wahhabism, the ultra-conservative form of Sunni Islam practiced in Saudi Arabia, King Abdullah will be buried in an unmarked grave after Friday prayers. The kingdom's religious doctrine dictates submission to God's will, and thus, no official mourning period occurs; government offices remain open, and flags stay at full mast.As King Salman takes the reins, Saudi Arabia faces significant challenges. text: St Johnstone extended their unbeaten streak against Hearts to six games as they held the hosts to a draw at Tynecastle. In a thrilling encounter at Tynecastle, Prince Buaben's header initially put Heart of Midlothian in the lead, but a skillful strike from Danny Swanson leveled the score for St. Johnstone before the break. The match saw late drama as substitute Chris Kane nudged home a David Wotherspoon cross with just five minutes remaining, giving the visitors a temporary advantage. However, Callum Paterson salvaged a point for the hosts, heading in Don Cowie's corner in the dying moments.The draw propels Hearts above Rangers into third place on goal difference, with Rangers set to play Ross County on Sunday. Meanwhile, St. Johnstone remains in fifth, tied on points with the two teams directly above them.Both teams entered the match struggling with form: Hearts had conceded five goals across two winless matches, while St. Johnstone had secured just one victory in their last four outings. Recent history favored the Saints, who had not lost in their previous five encounters with Robbie Neilson's side. Hearts, however, started brightly, dominating possession and creating more opportunities. Buaben's goal midway through the first half, albeit controversial, was awarded after Don Cowie's shot rebounded off the crossbar. There was debate over whether the ball had crossed the line, but the goal stood, igniting the home crowd.Buaben soon tested Saints' goalkeeper Zander Clark again, but Swanson's brilliance turned the tide. Steven MacLean set up Swanson, who effortlessly maneuvered past John Souttar to score his 10th goal of the season, and his third against Hearts in this campaign. The second half began with significant chances for both sides. Wotherspoon forced a save from Hearts' Jack Hamilton and then struck the post with a stunning free-kick, which Joe Shaughnessy tapped in, only for it to be ruled offside. Moments later, Bjorn Johnsen's close-range effort was heroically blocked by Steven Anderson, preserving the Saints' hopes.As the match progressed, both teams seemed to lack the creativity to break the deadlock again. However, with five minutes left, Wotherspoon found Kane, who slotted past Hamilton, sparking offside protests from Hearts that went unheard. Yet, Hearts' resilience shone through as Paterson headed in from a corner, securing a deserved draw.Hearts manager Robbie Neilson reflected, It was a really tough game. We knew St Johnstone would make it difficult, and it turned out that way. We managed to get ourselves in front, then gave away a poor goal. But we fought back and showed our quality to equalize. We are disappointed not to take the three points, but the manner in which we fought back was really pleasing.St. Johnstone's Tommy Wright commented, It maybe lacked quality at times, but I think it was end to end and entertaining, and I think we picked up a very good point. I've seen the first Hearts goal back and the referee's assistant had a clear view of it. Brian Easton doesn't think it's over, but the angle I've got doesn't clear it up. For the disallowed goal, the assistant seems to think Joe Shaughnessy was offside, but he looks level to me. We maybe got the wrong end of the stick.The match concluded with a 2-2 draw, a result that reflected the competitive nature of the game. As the final whistle blew, both teams had reasons to feel both satisfaction and frustration, with Hearts looking ahead to their next challenge and Saints content with a hard-earned point.

text: A woman has told the Surjit Singh Chhokar murder trial she did not tell police who attacked her partner because she was distraught. Elizabeth Bryce initially provided police with the name of only one of the three men she alleges were involved in the attack: Andrew Coulter. However, she has now identified the other two as Ronnie Coulter and David Montgomery. Ronnie Coulter, 48, stands accused of the murder of Mr. Chhokar from Gowkthrapple, North Lanarkshire, but he denies the charges, instead pointing the finger at the other men.Ms. Bryce, aged 56, gave her testimony on the second day of the trial. During cross-examination, Ronnie Coulter's defense lawyer, Donald Findlay QC, pressed her on why she hadn't disclosed the identities of all three men to the police initially. She responded, I was distraught. At the time I wasn't thinking. I was distraught at my man lying dead at my feet. She further explained that although she was aware of all three men, she specifically named Andrew Coulter out of anger towards him.Earlier in court, Ms. Bryce recounted confronting Andrew Coulter on the day of 32-year-old Mr. Chhokar's death. Her partner had mentioned a missing giro cheque, and she learned through inquiries that Andrew Coulter had allegedly cashed it at the post office.Mr. Findlay accused Ms. Bryce of tailoring her evidence, suggesting she altered her partner's final words. Initially, in a police statement the day after Mr. Chhokar's death, she quoted his last words as I've been stabbed. However, in court, she claimed he actually said, they stabbed me. Ms. Bryce refuted the accusation of tailoring her evidence.When questioned further by Mr. Findlay, she admitted to having probably told a few lies but not in the case of what happened to Chhokar. She also acknowledged a prior conviction for £13,000 in benefit fraud, dismissing it as not relevant to this case.Mr. Findlay also challenged her assertion that she saw both Coulters and David Montgomery walking past her window twice on the day in question. Testifying on Wednesday, she described grabbing a garden spade and rushing outside her home on Garrion Street, Wishaw, to confront the trio, who she claimed were dragging her partner across the street. She recounted the moment when the blood just flew out of Mr. Chhokar, leading to his death.Ronnie Coulter faces charges of murdering Mr. Chhokar by repeatedly attacking him with a knife or similar weapon. He is also accused of forging Mr. Chhokar's signature on a £100 giro cheque, breaking into Mr. Chhokar's residence at Caplaw Tower, Gowkthrapple, on the day of the murder, and stealing a cooker. Additionally, he is charged with attempting to defeat the ends of justice by destroying or disposing of a knife and clothing. The trial, presided over by Lord Matthews, continues.

text: Ministers have said the growth of high-stakes roulette machines on the High Street is concerning and they do not rule out action to restrict them. Culture Minister Helen Grant has warned MPs that the future of fixed-odds betting terminals remains unresolved, urging bookmakers to swiftly enhance player protection measures. These machines allow bets of up to £100 every 20 seconds, a situation criticized by Labour as emblematic of David Cameron's Britain. They propose granting councils new powers to restrict these machines.Despite Labour's appeal, their motion to empower local authorities to control the proliferation of these terminals was defeated in a Commons vote, with 314 MPs opposing and 232 supporting. Across the UK, there are over 33,000 such machines, a surge attributed to the relaxation of gambling laws by the previous Labour government. Labour now accuses the gambling industry of exploiting these changes, particularly targeting economically disadvantaged areas.Labour argues that fixed-odds betting terminals contribute to crime and anti-social behavior, advocating for local authorities to manage clusters of betting shops. They propose a review of the number of machines allowed per premises and suggest measures to reduce their addictiveness, such as mandatory pop-ups and breaks in play.Shadow culture minister Clive Efford emphasized that the last government intended for these machines to be regularly reviewed. He noted the significant growth of the online gambling industry, now valued at over £2 billion, since the machines were first licensed. These machines are an example of Cameron's Britain, Efford stated, highlighting a perceived disparity between rules for constituents and those for businesses running betting shops. Labour MP Brian Donohue compared the machines to cocaine, describing them as absolutely and totally addictive.Ministers maintain that local authorities already have the power to reject new gambling premises and review existing licenses. However, Ms. Grant admitted the expansion of these machines is concerning, expecting the industry to voluntarily implement player protection measures, such as play suspensions and alerts when stakes reach certain levels, by March. She stated the government is awaiting the results of a study on the machines' usage and their impact on players before deciding on further actions. There is no green light for these machines. Their future is unresolved pending the research we have started, she assured MPs.Ms. Grant accused Labour of rank hypocrisy, total cynicism, and outright opportunism, pointing out that Labour had initially liberalized gambling laws. Labour brought these machines into being and now blame the government for any harm caused, she added.The gambling industry, meanwhile, refutes claims of targeting deprived areas and has implemented a code of conduct for player protection. The Association of British Bookmakers stated, Betting is a pursuit enjoyed by millions of working-class people throughout Britain, and we aim to reach a broad audience by being present on High Streets. They acknowledged concerns about gaming machines and expressed openness to dialogue with politicians regarding local authorities' powers. The association also contested claims of widespread problem gambling, emphasizing their ongoing efforts to mitigate harm for the minority of gamblers who face issues.Previously, MPs rejected Labour's proposals to reduce the maximum stake from £100 to £2 and cut the top prize from £500.

text: A Llandudno hotel's service has been named best in the world by travel website TripAdvisor. The Lawton Court Hotel, where a night's stay begins at £78, has triumphed over a slew of luxury hotels worldwide. Meanwhile, the nearby Elm Tree Hotel has been crowned the world's best bargain hotel. Llandudno has outshone other UK locations, aside from London, receiving more accolades with eight hotels garnering 20 travellers' choice awards.TripAdvisor revealed that these honors were determined by millions of reviews and opinions gathered on their platform. Hannah and Scott Lawton-Jones, owners of the Lawton Court Hotel, expressed their gratitude, stating, We're here to help - and that's what we love to do. The couple further shared, We are so grateful and lucky to have welcomed so many lovely guests over the last three years, not forgetting the fantastic hardworking team we have that share the same principles as us.In a remarkable family achievement, Mr. Lawton-Jones' parents, Carol-Lynn and Ian Robbins, own the nearby Lauriston Court Hotel. This hotel was named the best in the world for service in 2013 and has secured the fifth spot this year.The Elm Tree Hotel not only clinched the top spot in the world's bargain hotels category but also ranked sixth among the world's best small hotels and third for service in the UK. text: A top NFL official has acknowledged a link between head trauma in American football and the brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). For the first time, a league executive has openly acknowledged a connection between football and neurodegenerative diseases like CTE. Jeff Miller, the NFL's vice president of health and safety, faced questions from U.S. politicians about the matter. When asked directly if there was a link, Miller responded, The answer to that question is certainly yes.This marks a significant shift from previous statements within the NFL. Earlier this year, leading up to Super Bowl 50, neurosurgeon Mitch Berger, head of the NFL's subcommittee on long-term brain injury, claimed that no connection had been established between American football and CTE. However, Illinois Representative Jan Schakowsky criticized Berger's remarks, accusing the league of peddling a false sense of security by downplaying the risks of head injuries. Schakowsky emphasized that football is inherently high-risk due to routine hits, not just concussions, and called for transparency and more research into the health risks.The NFL has previously conceded that head trauma, especially concussions, can threaten players' long-term health. Yet, definitive public admissions from NFL commissioner Roger Goodell and other senior officials have been notably absent.In his testimony, Miller referenced the research of Boston University neuropathologist Ann McKee. Addressing the committee, McKee stated unequivocally, I think there's a link between playing football and CTE. Her research has identified CTE in 90 out of 94 examined NFL players' brains, as well as in 45 out of 55 college players and six out of 26 high school players.The disease, which manifests symptoms like memory loss, depression, and progressive dementia, can only be diagnosed posthumously. It has been discovered in the brains of numerous former American football players. Around 5,000 former players have filed lawsuits against the NFL, alleging the league concealed the dangers of repeated head trauma.

text: Stoke held Southampton to a goalless draw despite having Marko Arnautovic sent off in Mark Hughes' 400th match as a Premier League manager. In a match marked by missed opportunities and a controversial sending off, Southampton and Stoke City played out a goalless draw at the Bet365 Stadium. The game, which saw plenty of possession from the visitors, was marred by a lack of clear chances. The pivotal moment came early, as Stoke's Marko Arnautovic received a red card for a reckless studs-up challenge on Sofiane Boufal in the 23rd minute, leaving his team with ten men for the majority of the contest.Despite the numerical advantage, Southampton struggled to capitalize. Substitute Jay Rodriguez squandered the best chance of the game, failing to connect with Boufal's precise low cross in the second half. James Ward-Prowse also missed a golden opportunity to clinch the win after a mistake by Glen Johnson, only for his shot to be deflected wide.The draw nudged Southampton up to ninth in the standings, while Mark Hughes' Stoke remained in 12th. Claude Puel's men controlled possession after the red card but lacked the cutting edge in the final third. They displayed neat passing and buildup play, yet the decisive final ball was consistently absent. A rare direct attempt came from Ryan Bertrand, whose powerful shot from the edge of the box tested Stoke's goalkeeper, Lee Grant. However, Rodriguez's miss proved to be the turning point.Stoke's defense held firm, aided by Southampton's inefficiency up front. Steven Davis dispossessed Joe Allen, setting up Boufal for a simple finish that Rodriguez failed to deliver, seemingly uncertain about which foot to use. The home crowd voiced their displeasure at Arnautovic's dismissal, though the challenge was undeniably high and late.Hughes lamented the impact of the red card on his team's performance, noting that Stoke failed to pose a threat after Allen's early near-post effort was thwarted by Fraser Forster. Xherdan Shaqiri's frustration was evident as he punched a seat in the dugout following his substitution for Mame Biram Diouf, having contributed little to the game.The result was a reflection of Southampton's poor finishing rather than Stoke's defensive prowess. Johnson's misstep in his own box should have been punished by a sharper Ward-Prowse finish, while Allen's hesitation led to the game's only clear-cut chance. For Hughes, the milestone of his 400th match in the English top flight became a forgettable affair. His win rate stands at 36%, on par with Alan Pardew but trailing behind Harry Redknapp (37%) and David Moyes (41%).Reflecting on the match, Hughes commented on Arnautovic's red card: It's unfortunate because he obviously caught him high on the thigh, but the ball was bouncing around and it wasn't a violent movement to take the player out. The ref wasn't great on the night, he missed a number of decisions and clearly missed an elbow from Shane Long on Bruno Martins Indi - that needs looking at again. Overall the ref put us in a situation and we had to show real work ethic and understanding of what was required. Given the circumstances, the point we gained was magnificent.Southampton's manager, Claude Puel, expressed his disappointment: We're disappointed. Eleven against ten you have to do better. In the first half, we were too nervous, in the second half we were better and created a few possibilities, but it was not enough. There were good crosses and good combinations, but our play was too slow and not effective in the final third. It was two points lost and it's a shame. On Arnautovic's red card, he added, I think it's an important foul, it was very dangerous, he does not play the ball.Stoke will face Leicester at home on Saturday, with a 15:00 GMT kickoff, while Southampton will travel to Bournemouth on Sunday for a 13:30 start. The match concluded with a 0-0 stalemate, leaving both teams to rue missed opportunities and reflect on what might have been.

text: Two black former Scottish top-flight footballers claim the colour of their skin is holding them back from making the transition to management. Russell Latapy and Kevin Harper, both former Hibernian players, argue that the lack of diversity in Scottish football management highlights a significant issue. Despite numerous applications for coaching roles, both have faced repeated rejections. Scotland's football authorities, alongside the managers' union, insist they are committed to enhancing diversity. Yet, John Barnes, who briefly managed Celtic in the late 1990s, remains the sole black manager in Scottish football history.Latapy, originally from Trinidad and a former manager of his national team, has held coaching roles at Inverness Caledonian Thistle and Falkirk. However, he finds the managerial path in Scotland particularly challenging. Young black managers are not given the same chances as their white counterparts, the 47-year-old stated. He emphasized, We play side by side as players, and all we seek is equal opportunity. Since John Barnes, no other black manager has emerged. I don't want a job because of my skin color; I want it based on what I can contribute to a football club.Harper, who is pursuing his A Licence in coaching, shares similar sentiments. I've applied for at least 10 jobs in Scotland but received only two responses, the 40-year-old disclosed. Being new to this, it's concerning to have so few responses and no interviews. There's clearly an issue.Recent statistics from the Scottish government indicate that about 4% of the population is non-white, and of the 10,000 registered Scottish FA coaches, just under 6% are from non-white backgrounds. However, Harper, a former Scotland Under-21 forward, believes the problem is more pronounced at higher levels. There might be 6% in the coaching system, but there are 0% at the clubs, he pointed out. There's definitely an issue.Alex Smith, head of the Scottish Coaches' and Managers' Association, expressed surprise at these claims. We don't see this as a problem, he remarked. When clubs appoint coaches or managers, color, creed, or sexual orientation is never a factor. The only criterion is ability.The Scottish Professional Football League echoed this sentiment, stating, We are confident that our member clubs assess each management and coaching application on its own merit, appointing only the best candidates, regardless of skin color. Our clubs fully support the Show Racism The Red Card campaign and engage extensively in promoting diversity within their communities.

text: Oxfordshire could be voting for its first elected mayor by 2018, according to a council leader. Bob Price, leader of Oxford City Council, has voiced strong support for the introduction of a county mayor in Oxfordshire, suggesting it could reclaim powers back from Whitehall. Price argues that such a move would not only increase central government funding but also enhance the county's control over housing and transport across its six council authorities.The idea of an elected mayor is currently under consideration by authority leaders. This comes after a revelation in November that the Oxfordshire Local Enterprise Partnership (OxLEP), responsible for stimulating the county's economy, had only tentatively secured £15 million of the £382 million requested for countywide infrastructure projects.Price, who is affiliated with OxLEP, commented, We think that in the latest round of local growth fund allocations there was a strong bias in the allocations made by government to places which had elected mayors and combined authorities. There's no evidence to really prove that, but that seems to be the evidence in terms of allocations.He believes that a political consensus could be reached between the mayor and the Labour and Conservative-led Oxfordshire authorities, as all parties are eager to improve roads like the A34 and tackle the county's housing crisis.BBC Oxford's political reporter, Bethan Phillips, analyzes the situation, noting that the absence of an elected mayor might be why Oxfordshire has missed out on substantial government funding for major projects. The councils and OxLEP had sought £382 million for projects such as railway station upgrades and new road junctions, but the county is expected to receive only a fraction of this amount.Price claims there is a bias towards funding areas with elected mayors or plans for one. However, there is no unanimous agreement among the councils on the mayoral proposal, which requires collective approval to proceed. The potential for significant funding makes the change appealing to the councils.The six councils—Oxfordshire County Council, Oxford City Council, and the district councils of Cherwell, West Oxfordshire, South Oxfordshire, and Vale of White Horse—are contemplating lobbying the government for an elected mayor, possibly as part of a devolution bid.A spokesperson for Oxfordshire County Council, responsible for transport infrastructure, social care, and other services, stated, We cannot pass up the chance to secure infrastructure investment from the government, so we will work closely with the district and city councils on a devolution bid—which is likely to include an elected mayor and combined authority. But we still need to be convinced that adding another layer of council administration is right for Oxfordshire.Nigel Tipple, OxLEP's chief executive, added, Ultimately, proposals will be submitted to central government for consideration and final decision. OxLEP will continue to work closely with all local authorities, universities, business, and other partner organisations to create the conditions that will best enable the county's already thriving economy to flourish and grow in future.

text: Sinn Féin and the SDLP have criticised the government's plan for Brexit, but a White Paper published on Thursday has been welcomed by unionists. Prime Minister Theresa May recently articulated the government's 12 principles for Brexit in a pivotal speech delivered in London. text: A study confirming a link between atmospheric pollution and heart-attack risk strengthens the EU case for tougher clean-air targets, experts say. A comprehensive study published in the BMJ, analyzing long-term data from 100,000 individuals across five European countries, has uncovered evidence suggesting harm from air pollution even at levels currently deemed acceptable. Although experts emphasize that the risk to individuals remains relatively minor, some contend the findings are not definitive, as they do not consider prior exposure to higher pollution levels. Additionally, factors such as smoking and high blood pressure are considered more significant contributors to heart attack risk than pollution from traffic and industry.Nevertheless, the research, conducted in collaboration with various European universities and institutes, indicates that prolonged exposure to air pollution, such as residing near a bustling city road, does have detrimental effects. The study highlights that each 5 µg/m3 increase in annual exposure to fine-particulate (PM 2.5) air pollution, known for its ability to penetrate deeply into the body, correlates with a 13% relative rise in heart attack incidence, even when accounting for other risk factors like smoking. Similarly, elevated levels of larger-particulate air pollution (PM 10) were also associated with increased heart attack risk, and these links persisted even when exposure concentrations were below current European standards.Authors of this extensive study—the largest of its kind examining pollution exposure's impact on Europeans—argue that their findings bolster the argument for reducing EU limits on particulate matter air pollution. Currently, EU regulations set the annual mean limit for PM 2.5 at twice the level recommended by the World Health Organization. Jon Ayres, a professor of environmental and respiratory medicine at the University of Birmingham, stated, There is no doubt that further reduction of PM levels would result in improvements in cardiac health in Europe. One can only hope that our European politicians will be persuaded of the importance of these findings and reassess their position on air pollution in Europe.In contrast, Prof. David Coggon from the University of Southampton's Department of Occupational and Environmental Medicine expressed caution. He noted, This study adds to the evidence that particulate air pollution is a cause of heart disease, but it does not establish that there are important health risks from levels of exposure below current exposure limits. This is because the differences in risk that were observed may have been a long-term effect of exposures in the past when levels of pollution were higher.In the UK, estimates indicate that nearly 30,000 people die prematurely each year due to air pollution exposure, which has been linked to asthma, other lung diseases, cancer, and heart problems. A recent report by Defra suggests there is no safe limit for PM 2.5 exposure, highlighting that this form of man-made pollution reduces the average life expectancy of UK residents by seven to eight months. A Defra spokeswoman commented, Air quality has improved significantly in recent decades and the UK currently meets the EU limits for this type of pollution. We want to keep improving air quality and reduce the impact it can have on human health and the environment.

text: Restoration work has started on a World War I cemetery in Surrey built for Muslim soldiers killed in combat. The Horsell Common Preservation Society is racing against time to complete a significant restoration project by August 4 next year, marking the centenary of World War I's outbreak. The Grade II listed memorial in Woking has suffered from years of neglect and vandalism. The first phase of the restoration, partially funded by English Heritage, is targeted for completion by November. In addition to restoring the structure, the society plans to establish a memorial garden at the site.Woking council leader John Kingsbury emphasized the site's significance, stating it holds deep meaning for the local community and the descendants of those who sacrificed their lives in the war. Paul Stamper, a senior designation adviser at English Heritage, highlighted the site's architectural and historical value, noting its unique role as a memorial for Muslims who died fighting for Britain in both world wars. Its architectural interest and unique status as a site of memory for Muslims who died fighting for Britain in two world wars is recognized in its national designation as a Grade II listed structure, he said.David Robbins, chairman of the Horsell Common Preservation Society, expressed his hope that the town would take pride in this unique war memorial once the work is completed.During World War I, over a million troops from pre-independence India served Great Britain. The wounded were treated in hospitals across the South East. While Hindu and Sikh soldiers were taken to crematoriums, Muslim soldiers initially lacked a proper burial ground until the Woking site was established in 1917. The preservation society reports that 17 burials took place there that year, each marked with a west-facing round arched headstone, adhering to Islamic tradition. A Sandhurst military academy cadet was laid to rest there in 1920, before the War Graves Commission assumed responsibility for the site's maintenance in 1921. World War II saw an additional eight Muslim soldiers buried there, including three from the Free French forces.However, in 1968, following a series of vandalism incidents, all the remains were transferred to Brookwood Cemetery, and the site was de-consecrated. Despite these changes, the structure continues to be recognized as a Registered War Memorial.

text: Coach Vern Cotter insisted Scotland can still secure a top-half finish in this year's Six Nations despite a record points defeat by England. Scotland's aspirations for their first victory at Twickenham since 1983 were dashed as they suffered a crushing 61-21 defeat, matching the margin of their 43-3 loss in 2001. The Scots faced a series of setbacks with Stuart Hogg, Mark Bennett, Tommy Seymour, and Ryan Wilson all leaving the field due to injuries, three of which were head-related.We have had two away games and eight concussions, Vern Cotter revealed to BBC Scotland. It's not the sole reason, but early substitutions were necessary. We ended up with Ali [Price] on the wing and Duncy [Weir] at full-back, so there were quite a few adjustments.Cotter acknowledged England's strong performance while lamenting Scotland's missed opportunities. We take it on the chin. England played well, but we didn't, despite scoring three tries. We hoped for four tries to earn a losing bonus point.His immediate concern was assessing the injured players to prepare for their upcoming home match against Italy. Cotter also admitted that Fraser Brown's yellow card, just two minutes into the game, hindered their start. We aimed to start strong against a good team but ended up aiding them in many ways, he explained.He emphasized the need to address certain issues to improve future performances. We scored three tries when we had possession, but we struggled with fast possession in the first half. Once we gained tempo, we crossed the advantage line. However, our set-piece defense, especially from line-outs, was lacking. There's much to work on. We'll analyze and train hard.Despite the setback, Cotter remains optimistic about finishing at the top end of the table. Our feet are firmly on the ground now, and we'll strive for a strong performance next week.Scotland, currently fifth and tied on points with Wales, but trailing Ireland and France by one point, will face Italy in next Saturday's early match. Meanwhile, France hosts Wales, and England travels to Ireland later in the day.At Twickenham, Gordon Reid's try, along with two from Huw Jones, all converted by Finn Russell, provided some consolation. John Barclay, captaining in Greig Laidlaw's absence, reflected, It certainly wasn't a good day. It wasn't for lack of effort, just too many errors. England executed well under pressure, perhaps not enough pressure from us.

text: The first new design of an electricity pylon in almost 90 years has been erected at a site in Nottinghamshire. After nearly a century of service, the iconic steel lattice pylon has received a modern makeover. The newly designed T-pylon stands at approximately 120 feet (36 meters), a noticeable reduction from the traditional 165 feet (50 meters) of its steel predecessors. This innovation by the National Grid aims to support the growing demand for energy derived from lower-carbon sources.The T-pylon's innovative design allows it to operate at 400,000 volts despite its shorter stature, thanks to a unique cable arrangement. Instead of the conventional three-arm attachment, the cables are now carried in a diamond configuration on a single arm, optimizing space. Each arm is engineered to support 60 tonnes. With only eight main structural components and bolts, the T-pylon is not only quicker to erect—requiring just a day compared to a week—but also easier to install.The National Grid emphasizes the necessity of these new pylons to facilitate the transition from coal to alternative energy sources like wind, solar, and nuclear power. These renewable sources are often located in different regions compared to the traditional coal-fired plants concentrated in central England.A test line for the T-pylon has been constructed, though it will not be connected to the main grid. Instead, it serves as a training ground for staff and contractors to practice stringing the conductors—a process that requires a distinct technique unique to this design.The T-pylon emerged victorious in an international competition held by the National Grid in 2011, designed by the Danish firm Bystrup. Its proponents argue that the pylons are less visually intrusive, not only due to their reduced height but also because their design allows them to blend seamlessly with the landscape's natural contours.Project manager Alan Large notes that maintenance will be more straightforward, as operators can work from elevated platforms rather than climbing the towers. Additionally, the smooth, robust surface of the pylons makes them more resistant to vandalism.These new pylons will not replace the 88,000 lattice towers currently scattered across the UK countryside. Instead, they will be employed primarily for new power lines in England and Wales. The National Grid has already applied to use them for connecting the upcoming Hinkley Point C nuclear power station to the national grid.The story of the UK's electricity transmission network dates back to 1928, with the construction of the first pylon near Edinburgh. While some view these structures as eyesores, others find a skeletal beauty in them. For a dedicated few, these towering giants are a source of enduring fascination.Follow Claire on Twitter for more updates. Read more about the allure of pylons: Pylon passion.

text: The final of this year's Britain's Got Talent drew the lowest audience in the show's 10-year history, according to overnight figures. An impressive average of eight million viewers tuned in live to witness the finale of Britain's Got Talent, with an additional 500,000 catching the action on ITV+1. The audience reached a staggering peak of 9.7 million as Richard Jones, an Army bandsman and magician, was declared the winner. This marked a significant dip from previous years, with the lowest viewership since 2014, when 10.7 million watched Collabro's victory.Jones, a 25-year-old lance corporal in The Household Cavalry, captivated both judges and the public with his military-themed magic act. I can't believe it, thank you so much to everyone that voted - it's been an incredible experience, it means the world to me, he expressed. As the first magician to clinch the title, he takes home a £250,000 prize and a coveted spot at the Royal Variety Performance.Live viewership accounted for a 39.7% share of all TV viewing, though comprehensive figures, including on-demand and catch-up services, will be available in a week. An ITV spokeswoman noted that when ITV+1 figures were considered, the audience peaked at 10.5 million.The finale aired concurrently with the Uefa Champions League Final between Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, which was available on BT Sport and YouTube for free. Last year's finale attracted an average of 11.7 million viewers, with a 46.6% audience share. The show's peak viewership was in 2009, drawing over 17 million viewers when Diversity triumphed over Susan Boyle. Although typically among the most-watched programs annually, this year's finale might not make the top 10.Jones, donning his Household Cavalry uniform, performed a poignant card trick narrating the story of Fergus Anckorn, Britain's oldest living magician, who used magic to endure his time as a prisoner of war in Singapore. The act concluded with the 97-year-old joining him on stage, earning a standing ovation. Alesha Dixon praised the performance as poignant, noble and brilliantly British.Head judge Simon Cowell, speaking on Britain's Got More Talent, suggested that Jones won not just for his magical prowess. text: The BBC has argued the case for popular shows like Strictly Come Dancing and Sherlock in its response to the government's green paper on its future. When the green paper was introduced in July, Culture Secretary John Whittingdale stated that hard questions would be posed about the BBC's size and ambitions. He emphasized the need for a decision on whether the corporation should aim to do all things or focus on being more precise.Earlier this week, Mr. Whittingdale informed the Conservative Party Conference that over 80,000 people had participated in the public consultation. The BBC's response, spanning more than 100 pages, concurs that the government consultation is right to insist that the BBC should be distinctive. However, it argues that distinctiveness should not mean retreating from popular content. The BBC makes good popular programmes - if we withdrew, audiences would have less choice, the response states.The BBC counters the idea of stepping back from crowd-pleasing shows, asserting, Competition on a Saturday night has been part of the TV landscape for generations and drives up quality - with the viewer being the winner. Cox nearly doubled his tally soon after, hitting the crossbar, before Atkinson scored following an excellent setup by Marc-Antoine Fortune.In the second half, Smith continued his strong performance by denying Tom Elliott. text: The SNP leader has hit back at claims that too much cash comes over Hadrian's wall during the ITV leaders' debate. In a heated debate, UKIP leader Nigel Farage expressed frustration over the financial contributions England makes to Scotland, claiming English taxpayers are cheesed off with the public funds allocated north of the border. In response, Nicola Sturgeon, leader of the Scottish National Party, countered by highlighting that Scots have paid more taxes per capita annually for the last 34 years.The debate brought together leaders from seven political parties across the UK, marking the only joint television appearance of Prime Minister David Cameron and Labour leader Ed Miliband before the general election on May 7. Cameron defended the Conservative economic strategy, asserting, Let's not go back to square one, Britain can do so much better than that. Meanwhile, Miliband outlined his plans as potential prime minister, including raising the minimum wage, eliminating exploitative zero-hours contracts, and revitalizing the NHS.Joining the debate were Liberal Democrat leader Nick Clegg, Plaid Cymru's Leanne Wood, and the Green Party's Natalie Bennett. A YouGov poll of 1,100 viewers declared Sturgeon the winner with 28% support, followed by Farage at 20%, Cameron at 18%, Miliband at 15%, Clegg at 10%, Bennett at 5%, and Wood at 4%. However, a ComRes poll for ITV showed a tie between Cameron, Miliband, Farage, and Sturgeon, with Cameron seen as the most capable leader. An ICM poll for the Guardian placed Miliband slightly ahead with 25%, Cameron at 24%, Farage at 19%, and Sturgeon at 17%. A Survation poll for the Daily Mirror had Cameron and Miliband neck and neck at 25%, Farage at 24%, and Sturgeon at 15%.In the debate, Sturgeon emphasized the SNP's commitment to advocating for Scotland while extending friendship to England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, promising to help to bring about change for you too. Farage, however, argued that Scots had secured a favorable deal under the Barnett formula, which determines the distribution of public funds. He remarked, This all has to be rebalanced because frankly English taxpayers are a bit cheesed off with so much of their money going over Hadrian's wall, giving people no prescription charges and no university tuition. Sturgeon retorted that Scots have consistently paid more tax per head for decades.Sturgeon also criticized Cameron's deficit-reduction strategies, insisting that the NHS is the nation's most precious public service. Cameron framed the election as a choice between continuing a successful economic plan or reverting to the debt, taxes, borrowing and spending that got us in this mess in the first place. He added, The real choice is with Ed Miliband, who still thinks the last government didn't tax too much and borrow too much. Miliband accused Cameron of focusing on the past rather than the future, declaring, Some people will tell you that this is as good as it gets for Britain. I say Britain can do so much better than it has done over the last five years.The debate symbolized a shifting political landscape, with seven leaders on stage, including three women. Sturgeon, dressed in bold red, took aim at the old boys' network in SW1, while Bennett and Wood joined her in challenging the austerity measures of Westminster's main parties.Miliband criticized Cameron for isolating Britain in Europe, stating, I don't think our place lies outside the EU. I think that would be a disaster for jobs, a disaster for families and business. He also accused Clegg of betraying young people over tuition fees. Clegg, in turn, attacked Miliband's pious stance and demanded an apology for crashing the economy. He also challenged Cameron on not asking the wealthy to contribute more to deficit reduction, opting instead for ideologically-driven cuts.The SNP claimed a surge in membership, gaining 1,200 new members during the debate. Deputy leader Stewart Hosie noted that an average of post-debate polls indicated Sturgeon as the winner, showcasing her strong and persuasive performance. Scottish Labour leader Jim Murphy remarked that the debate clarified the choice for Scots in the upcoming election, emphasizing, In the debate there were seven passionate speakers but only two potential prime ministers. There are lots of ways to protest against David Cameron but only one way to replace him.UKIP's Scottish MEP David Coburn defended Farage's debate comments on Radio Scotland's Good Morning Scotland, stating, I think most reasonable Scots believe in the fair allocation of money. I think the SNP may make a big fuss about this but I think fair minded Scots like myself and everyone else believe we should give the English a reasonable deal too.

text: Restrictions put on terror suspects by the home secretary may be withering on the vine, a group of MPs and peers has warned. In a call for urgent action, the next government in 2015 has been advised to scrutinize the role and effectiveness of Terrorism Prevention and Investigation Measures (TPims). The Joint Committee on Human Rights' report raised alarms about the potential for individuals to disappear while under TPims. According to the Home Office, these measures represent the most robust options permissible by the courts.TPims impose several restrictions, including mandatory overnight residence at a designated location, GPS tagging, reporting obligations, and limitations on travel, movement, association, communication, finances, work, and study. By the end of this month, six individuals under TPims will be released, leaving only one person still under surveillance. Due to the system's secrecy, it's uncertain whether other suspects exist.Previously, control orders—a more stringent system—faced criticism for their oppressive, house-arrest-like conditions. TPims inherited these critics and faced additional scrutiny from security experts who argued the new system was overly lenient. However, a more effective strategy seems to be emerging: charging suspects earlier with preparing acts of terrorism. This approach targets individuals who might have previously been considered for a TPim due to intelligence concerns but lacked concrete evidence for prosecution.Implemented in December 2011, TPims replaced control orders to prevent terrorist-related activities. As of November last year, eight TPim notices were active, all concerning British citizens. However, seven of these are set to expire by month's end. The committee urged a broader review of counter-terrorism powers, advocating for greater transparency and engagement with the independent reviewer of terrorism legislation's recommendations.The report expressed skepticism about TPims' practical utility, suggesting they may be losing relevance as a counter-terrorism tool. It proposed renaming them as Terrorism Prevention Orders, reflecting their limited investigative function. Agreeing with the independent reviewer, the committee highlighted an inherent risk of subjects absconding under TPims. It also called for the public release of more information from an internal review initiated after two subjects went missing.One such case involved Mohammed Ahmed Mohamed, linked to the Somali militant group al-Shabab, who vanished in November after disguising himself in a burka at a west London mosque. This followed Ibrahim Magag's disappearance in December 2012, when he fled in a black cab after removing his electronic tag.Hywel Francis, the committee chairman, stated, There is no evidence that they serve any investigative function and even as preventive measures they seem to be going out of favour with the agencies. With most TPims nearing expiration, Mr. Francis emphasized the lack of information about the individuals subjected to these measures, questioning the necessity of such powers. He stressed the need for the next government to reevaluate these measures within the broader context of counter-terrorism powers.David Anderson, the independent reviewer of terror legislation, described TPims as a necessary evil on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, noting, One thing it shows is that police and prosecutors are doing their job. He cited numerous convictions, guilty pleas, and heavy sentences in recent years. However, he acknowledged that TPims don't present a long-term solution.Home Secretary Theresa May argued that TPims could aid in gathering evidence for prosecutions. Yet, the committee reported finding no evidence that these measures had resulted in more charges. With TPim restrictions lifted or soon to be lifted from seven suspects, including those allegedly involved in plotting terrorist attacks, the measures, imposed two years ago, cannot be renewed.A Home Office spokesperson defended the introduction of TPims, stating, TPims were introduced because control orders were not working and their powers were being struck down by the courts. They now provide some of the strongest possible protections that the courts will allow.

text: The idea that party leaders are decisively important in the winning or losing of general elections is implicit in much political journalism and it is a belief that some political leaders themselves - Tony Blair, in particular - have been eager to propagate. In the world of politics, it is a rare occurrence for the personality of a leader to decisively sway an election outcome, even in a tightly contested race. Often, the less popular leader's party can triumph over its rival. A prime example is the 1979 UK election, where despite Labour leader James Callaghan enjoying a 20-point lead over Margaret Thatcher, it was the Conservative Party that emerged victorious, not Thatcher herself.A comprehensive analysis of UK elections post-World War Two identified Harold Wilson as the only leader whose popularity might have tipped the scales for his party, in the closely fought contests of October 1964 and February 1974. In both instances, Wilson's appeal far exceeded that of his Conservative opponents, Sir Alec Douglas-Home in 1964 and Edward Heath in 1974. Yet, the Conservatives managed a win in 1970, despite Wilson's continued popularity over Heath.As the May 2015 election loomed, predictions pointed to another nail-biter, raising questions about the media's intense focus on party leaders like David Cameron and Ed Miliband. However, this scrutiny might not be warranted. It would be prudent for major parties to spotlight other prominent figures during the lengthy four-month campaign, rather than overexposing their leaders. Nick Clegg, leader of the Liberal Democrats, might benefit from sharing the spotlight, perhaps with Vince Cable, as he is unlikely to replicate his standout 2010 campaign performance. Despite the Cleggmania of that year, the Lib Dems saw only a marginal increase in votes and ended with fewer MPs.Nigel Farage remains the face of UKIP, although the party's recent successes are less about his charisma and more due to its stance on immigration—a topic largely sidestepped by the major parties. UKIP's challenge to EU membership resonates less with the general public, except as it relates to immigration. While UKIP might not secure many seats, they could significantly impact the election by drawing more votes from Conservatives than Labour. This dynamic could advantage Labour, provided they reconnect with their core supporters.The Green Party, though holding just one seat, could influence outcomes in several constituencies. Media focus on party leaders often overshadows the Greens, despite their growing support, particularly among young voters. Few can name their leader, Natalie Bennett, as the party's collective leadership style limits media exposure. Nonetheless, they have surpassed the Liberal Democrats in popularity, standing at 7% compared to the Lib Dems' 6%, and could siphon votes from both the Lib Dems and Labour.Among the smaller parties, the Scottish National Party (SNP) stands out as potentially pivotal in the UK election. Unlike UKIP, the SNP has proven governance capabilities, having led Scotland as a minority government from 2007 to 2011, before winning a majority in 2011. Historically, Scots have voted differently for Westminster than for the Scottish Parliament, with Labour securing 41 out of 59 Scottish seats in 2010. However, a December 2014 poll showed the SNP 17 points ahead of Labour, threatening Labour's hold on these crucial seats.The SNP's rise is often linked to Alex Salmond's leadership, but his successor, Nicola Sturgeon, has continued to bolster the party's support. The SNP has vowed not to support a Conservative government, but might back a Labour administration, albeit at a cost. Such a scenario could provoke an English backlash, fueling the separatist agenda and potentially destabilizing the British state as it currently exists.

text: Swedish journalists Johan Persson and Martin Schibbye have been speaking to the BBC about their time in prison in Ethiopia. After enduring over 400 days of an 11-year sentence, Martin Schibbye and Johan Persson have been released. Convicted of illegally entering Ethiopia and supporting the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF), their imprisonment drew international attention to Ethiopia's treatment of journalists. Captured alongside ONLF rebels in June 2011, Schibbye and Persson insisted they were merely fulfilling their journalistic duties. Amnesty International supported this view, stating they were prosecuted for legitimate work.However, Ethiopian government spokesman Bereket Simon justified their imprisonment, claiming they were caught red-handed collaborating with terrorist organizations. The journalists were reportedly pardoned by former Prime Minister Meles Zenawi before his death in August, facilitating their release.Johan Persson described the dire conditions of their imprisonment to the BBC World Service programme Newsday. It was 200% overcrowded. It was very hot. There was a lack of water. It was dusty. There were rats, fleas, and many people were sick with HIV or tuberculosis, he recounted. Yet, he emphasized the significance of their fellow inmates: What's interesting is who they put in there: journalists and the political opposition.Although they concede to entering Ethiopia illegally, Schibbye and Persson argue their trial was unjust. The trial was a joke, Persson said, noting that Zenawi had declared their guilt on national television weeks before the trial began. They also contend that the charge of providing moral support for terrorism has been misapplied to suppress other journalists in Ethiopia. For the last few years Ethiopia has been using its anti-terror legislation to crack down on the media and to crack down on journalism, Schibbye explained to Newsday.The freelance journalists had been in the Ogaden region, an ethnic Somali area in eastern Ethiopia, for four days prior to their arrest. Schibbye recounted their capture: The Ethiopian army spotted us. Then they followed in our footsteps for three to four days. Then they ambushed us. We were attacked by about 150 Ethiopian army soldiers who opened fire on us. We got hit quite quickly. I got hit in the shoulder and Johan got hit in the arm. Somebody shouted, 'media, media, international press,' and we were arrested.Post-arrest, they claimed they were coerced at gunpoint into participating in a staged film depicting their alleged collaboration with the ONLF. Two civilians, who we'd never seen before, were dressed up as rebels. The soldiers gave them guns and stood them in front of us, and they testified against us and said that we came with them from Somalia, Schibbye said. The journalists alleged that senior Ethiopian civilian officials orchestrated the filming. This was not being done by some crazy militia: the director was the vice president in the region, and in the evening the regional president called us and said, 'We are not satisfied by your performances in the film,' Schibbye added. The film later served as evidence in court.The Ogaden region has been embroiled in an insurgency led by local ethnic Somalis. We were walking through villages where there had been people living till recently, but now they had fled, forced out by the conflict. There was heavy fighting and that was one of the reasons why we were detected and followed and ambushed by the Ethiopian army, Persson explained.Despite their lengthy incarceration, neither journalist regrets their time in Ethiopia. For Schibbye, the role of a foreign correspondent inherently involves risk and defying restrictions on journalistic access. Persson concurred: As long as governments make laws to protect themselves against journalists, our job is to break those laws. I would do the same again today.

text: Belfast bantamweight Michael Conlan earned a morale boosting win for the Ireland boxing team at the Olympics as he clinched a quarter-finals place. World champion Michael Conlan, at just 24, delivered a commanding performance to secure a unanimous victory over Armenia's Aram Avagyan. Conlan, alongside fellow London 2012 medallist Katie Taylor, remains one of the last hopes for the eight-member Irish boxing team still competing in the Games.Despite high expectations, fighters like Paddy Barnes were eliminated last week. However, Conlan, a close friend of Barnes, triumphed with a decisive score of 30-27, 30-27, 29-28 against the world-ranked 28th Avagyan. From the outset, Conlan set an aggressive pace, landing a powerful right hand that shook Avagyan, whose most notable achievement was a European Championship bronze three years prior.Although Avagyan improved in the latter half of the first round, Conlan had already secured a 10-9 advantage on all judges' scorecards. Conlan, who previously won a flyweight bronze in 2012, faced a moment of vulnerability when caught with a strong left while trapped on the ropes early in the second round. Nevertheless, he responded with several effective shots, again winning the round 10-9 across the board.Entering the final round with a solid lead, Conlan forced Avagyan to take risks. Although one judge favored the Armenian in the last round, Conlan's earlier dominance ensured his advancement. Meanwhile, defending women's lightweight champion Taylor is set to begin her journey with a quarter-final match against Finland's Mira Potkonen on Monday afternoon, where a win would assure her at least a bronze medal.Ireland's boxing campaign in Rio faced a rocky start with Laois middleweight Michael O'Reilly's positive drug test. The disappointment continued with a surprising defeat for 2012 bronze medallist Barnes, adding to a challenging week for the Irish team. Another strong contender, light-heavyweight Joe Ward, was among the early eliminations.Ballymena welterweight Steven Donnelly's medal aspirations were dashed in a quarter-final loss to Morocco's world champion Mohammed Rabii on Saturday. Additionally, Brendan Irvine from Belfast became the fifth Irish boxer to exit the competition.

text: A year into power, if there is one thing that becomes clearer about the Xi Jinping leadership of the Communist Party of China, it is that it understands the value of political symbolism. In November, shortly after assuming the role of party secretary, Mr. Xi Jinping made a significant visit to Shenzhen, a city symbolic of China's Reform and Opening-up Process since 1978 and a pioneer among Special Economic Zones. This visit echoed the historical meeting at Beijing's Jingxi Hotel in December 1978, where pivotal ideological shifts enabled the acceptance of foreign capital and the establishment of a market economy in China.Fast forward over three decades, and the same venue hosted around 400 elite members of the Communist Party for another crucial gathering. This setting alone fueled expectations of landmark decisions. However, the communique issued on November 12, following the Third Plenum of the 18th Party Congress, dispelled any notion that this leadership would replicate the dramatic economic reversal of 1978.The circumstances today are vastly different. Unlike the post-Mao era, when China was desperate for radical economic rejuvenation, the nation now stands as a formidable global economy. The challenge, as Premier Li Keqiang articulated, is to unlock new sources of growth internally. A fundamental shift in direction is not on the agenda. Instead, the focus is on refining the market and liberalizing new growth sectors, a key takeaway from this plenum.The foundational principles of the Reform and Opening-up era remain unchallenged. The party's dominance is unequivocally affirmed in the plenum report, emphasizing its central societal role and the importance of internal unity and collective leadership, values upheld since the Hu Jintao and Wen Jiabao administration. The goal, guided by Deng Xiaoping's theory and Socialism with Chinese characteristics, remains the attainment of the primary state of socialism, a process expected to span many years, according to the communique.The plenum also highlighted the establishment of a national security coordination body, reflecting a continuation of the pro-stability measures favored by Hu and Wen. This move aims to streamline decision-making in security, especially since the current Politburo Standing Committee lacks a dedicated security lead, unlike its predecessor.The leadership's commitment to stability is underscored by recent violent incidents, such as the Tiananmen car explosion and the Taiyuan bomb attack in early November, reinforcing the necessity to maintain a firm stance on security.Politburo member Yu Zhengsheng hinted at impending reforms, particularly regarding rural-urban migration. The government is keen to accelerate urbanization, offering rural residents the means to relocate, secure employment, access social welfare, and educate their children in urban areas. However, the success of these reforms hinges on effective implementation and convincing provincial governments to support the influx of new residents.Although the plenum did not explicitly address whether provinces will gain broader tax-raising powers, this seems a logical step to accommodate the new urban population.Economic reform discussions prominently featured the development of a finance market, with Li Keqiang's influence evident. He is closely linked to the recent establishment of a Free Trade Zone in Shanghai, a potential catalyst for liberalizing China's capital account and expediting yuan trading. Finance is poised to be a pivotal sector, instrumental in creating a high-value-added economy.The plenum's framework reinforces the leadership's existing themes: gradual ideological and political continuity, prioritizing material well-being, and striving for robust growth. A significant emphasis is placed on achieving high urbanization levels by 2020, a bold strategy to tackle growth challenges, sustainability issues, and inequality.This ambitious urbanization plan is a high-stakes gamble, as China aims to urbanize at an unprecedented rate. Questions linger about achieving social cohesion and the eventual social and political structures needed to realize the harmonious society previously envisioned by past leaders.Kerry Brown, a professor of Chinese politics at the University of Sydney, leads the Europe China Research and Advice Network (ECRAN) funded by the European Union and is an Associate Fellow of the Asia Programme at Chatham House.

text: Spain and Germany sought to reassure investors that Spain would not need a full international bailout, after its borrowing costs hit a record high. German Finance Minister Wolfgang Schaeuble and his Spanish counterpart Luis de Guindos have expressed concern over the financial markets' response to Spain's economic situation. In a joint statement, they argued that the record 7.6% yield on Spain's 10-year bonds, observed on Tuesday, did not accurately reflect the country's economic fundamentals. Meanwhile, Mr. Guindos is set to meet with French Finance Minister Laurent Fabius on Wednesday to discuss the situation further.Spain's financial troubles continue to unsettle investors, with rising borrowing costs and the Catalonia region declaring its need for government support. On Tuesday, Spain announced that Italy and France support a plan for the swift execution of measures agreed upon in the previous month's eurozone summit. These measures include providing aid to Spanish banks without increasing national debt. Spain has indicated a worrying delay in implementing the agreements made at the 29 June eurozone leaders' summit. A key provision is the activation of the European Stability Mechanism (ESM) to directly fund struggling banks like those in Spain, bypassing national governments. However, constitutional challenges in Germany have delayed Berlin's ratification of the fund until at least 12 September.The Spanish foreign ministry emphasized the urgency, stating, Speed is an essential condition for the success of any European action. However, France's European Affairs Minister Bernard Cazeneuve refuted claims of an agreement with Italy and Spain for immediate implementation, stating, It makes no sense to say that. We are following the decisions taken at the European summit and are working on them. Similarly, Italy denied any involvement in a joint initiative with Spain.The market's tension is reflected in the record high yield on Spanish 10-year bonds, highlighting the financial strain. Moody's, a credit rating agency, has warned that Spain may require a full bailout, increasing pressure on Europe's strongest economies, such as Germany. Higher borrowing costs can escalate a financial issue to an unsustainable level, although the impact on Spain's interest obligations is gradual. This situation is akin to slowly steering an oil tanker towards perilous rocks. As Spain continues to seek new market funds, the interest rates on these borrowings contribute to the overall financial burden, potentially necessitating a new bailout to stabilize costs.In light of these developments, Moody's has revised Germany's AAA credit rating outlook to negative, indicating a potential downgrade within two years. On Monday, Spain's market regulator attempted to curb investment volatility by imposing a ban on short-selling, a practice where traders sell stocks they don't yet own, hoping to repurchase them at lower prices.Other developments include Spain securing a 100 billion euro loan package for its banks, differing from the bailout models of Greece, Ireland, and Portugal. However, several of Spain's 17 autonomous regions are heavily indebted and are turning to an 18 billion euro public fund for support. Catalonia, the second-largest region, has already requested assistance following Valencia's appeal. text: In January 1842, Charles Dickens arrived on American shores for the first time. In Boston, Massachusetts, the celebrated novelist Charles Dickens was welcomed with the fervor typically reserved for rock stars. Yet, his visit was driven by a serious mission: to combat the rampant distribution of pirated copies of his work in the United States. At the time, the U.S. offered no copyright protection to foreign authors, allowing unauthorized copies to flourish unchecked.In a poignant letter to a friend, Dickens likened his plight to being robbed and then humiliated in public. He wrote, Is it tolerable that besides being robbed and rifled, an author should be forced to appear in any form - in any vulgar dress - in any atrocious company? His metaphor, though dramatic, underscored a complex issue: the need for legal safeguards for intellectual creations, which otherwise could be freely copied and adapted.The debate over intellectual property is featured in 50 Things That Made the Modern Economy, a program on the BBC World Service that delves into the innovations shaping our economic landscape. Patents and copyrights grant creators a temporary monopoly, allowing them to profit from their works. For instance, Dickens's British publishers charged premium prices for Bleak House, pricing out many avid readers. However, such profits incentivize creativity and innovation. Without intellectual property rights, Dickens might not have invested the time to write Bleak House.Intellectual property represents an economic balancing act. If protections are overly generous, the dissemination and adaptation of ideas slow down. Conversely, insufficient protections may stifle innovation altogether. This balance is often influenced by politics. In the 1800s, Britain robustly defended its authors and inventors, bolstering its cultural and innovative dominance. Meanwhile, the U.S., in its developmental phase, prioritized cheap access to European ideas, filling its newspapers with copied content and criticisms of Dickens.As American creators gained prominence, the U.S. gradually embraced intellectual property rights. Newspapers that once opposed copyright now depend on it. This evolution mirrors trends in developing countries today, where the shift from imitation to innovation prompts stronger protections. Notably, China established its copyright system only in 1991.The concept of intellectual property dates back to 15th-century Venice, where patents were designed to spur innovation. An inventor received a patent if their creation was deemed useful, with the patent being transferable and inheritable. However, it could be revoked if unused or if the invention was too similar to existing ideas. These principles soon led to modern challenges.During the British Industrial Revolution, James Watt developed an improved steam engine design. Securing a patent took precedence over production, aided by his partner Matthew Boulton's lobbying efforts. They used the patent to demand licensing fees and suppress competitors like Jonathan Hornblower, who was ultimately financially ruined. While Watt's invention was groundbreaking, economists Michele Boldrin and David Levine argue that the true industrial breakthrough came after the patent expired in 1800, unleashing pent-up innovation.Despite this, intellectual property protections have expanded over time. Copyright terms in the U.S. have extended from an initial 14 years to 70 years posthumously. Patents now cover vague concepts, such as Amazon's one-click purchase method. The U.S. intellectual property framework has also achieved global influence, thanks to its inclusion in trade agreements. Consequently, intellectual property now encompasses diverse areas, including plants, buildings, and software.The expansion of intellectual property rights is easily explained by their immense value to owners, who invest in legal and lobbying efforts to maintain them. Meanwhile, the costs are dispersed among consumers, who often remain unaware. Figures like Matthew Boulton and Charles Dickens have strong incentives to advocate for stringent laws, while consumers of steam engines and literary works lack the organization to oppose them.Boldrin and Levine propose a radical solution: abolish intellectual property entirely, suggesting that inventors have alternative incentives such as market advantage, brand strength, and product knowledge. Tesla's 2014 decision to open its patent archive aimed to benefit the electric car industry as a whole, reflecting this perspective.While most economists find the idea of eliminating intellectual property extreme, they acknowledge its necessity in fields like pharmaceuticals, where invention costs are high and copying costs minimal. Nonetheless, current protections are deemed sufficient to encourage new ideas.Ironically, Dickens later found a silver lining in the lack of U.S. copyright protection. On a return visit to America 25 years later, he capitalized on his fame from pirated editions by embarking on a lucrative lecture tour, amassing a fortune in today's terms. Perhaps, in some cases, intellectual property yields greater value when shared freely.Tim Harford, author of the Financial Times's Undercover Economist column, explores these themes in 50 Things That Made the Modern Economy, available on the BBC World Service. More details about the program and its sources can be accessed online, with options to listen or subscribe to the podcast.

In a pathetic letter to a friend Dickens wrote: “It is like being robbed and then publicly humiliated.” The question of intellectual property is part of the series “50 things that made the modern economy,” which deals with innovations that have made our economy what it is. Intellectual property is a balancing of economic interests. He wrote: “Is it tolerable that, pillaged and robbed, the author is forced to appear in any form, in any vulgar attire, in any abominable company?” His metaphor, though it was a flight of fancy, underlined a complex question: the necessity of legal protection of intellectual works which would be freely copied and modified without any legal protection. These profits, on the other hand, encourage the author to create and to experiment. Without such profits, Dickens might not have taken the trouble to write Bleak House. For instance, Dickens’s English publishers charged a premium for the first edition of Bleak House, and many avid readers could not afford to pay it. This balance is often influenced by politics. In the eighteenth century, England, which was a nation of innovators and inventors, protected its authors and inventors, and so increased its supremacy in culture and innovation, while the United States, in its early growth, favored cheap access to European ideas and filled its newspapers with pirated Dickens stories and reviews. If protection is too great, the diffusion and adaptation of ideas are slowed down; on the other hand, inadequate protection can stifle innovation completely. The invention of intellectual property dates back to fifteenth-century Venice, where a patent system was instituted to encourage innovation. The inventor received a patent if his invention was considered useful, and it was transferable and hereditary. text: How often do we really look into someone's eyes? We often exchange fleeting glances with strangers and gaze lovingly at friends and family, but how often do we truly hold someone's gaze for more than a few seconds? According to Nuala McKeever, a self-proclaimed happiness teacher, not often enough. Nuala advocates that prolonged eye contact can reconnect us in a profound and spiritual way. At 40, she possesses a deep understanding of the human spirit.Nuala's journey began after she left a high-pressure role in the financial services sector. This path of self-discovery led her to become a 'laughter-yoga' instructor. Originally from Londonderry, she now resides in Belfast and, alongside her friend Michelle Major, runs the Sunshine Project. Their mission to spread peace and love took them to Victoria Square, Belfast, on Thursday, where they invited the public to engage in 60 seconds of eye contact with a volunteer.Curious about this intimate experience, I joined the event at Belfast's Corn Market during lunchtime. Volunteers were stationed inside hula hoops, seated on cushions or chairs, with an empty space inviting participants to sit or stand before them. The challenge was simple: maintain silent eye contact for a full minute.I was paired with Nuala, who instructed me to focus on her left eye to avoid the distraction of shifting my gaze. As our 60 seconds commenced, I initially felt uneasy. Nuala, however, appeared serene, her head slightly tilted in calm composure. As the seconds passed, my urge to look away subsided, and I began to relax, experiencing the calming effects of the exercise. The bustling city faded into the background, and for a fleeting moment, it felt as if we were the only two people there.When our session concluded, Nuala embraced me warmly, an act that felt surprisingly natural after our shared gaze. I often see myself when I stare into someone's eyes, she confessed, adding, Eye contact is how we connect as human beings. It always reminds me that I am part of something much bigger than myself. In Belfast, looking beyond our differences is more important than ever.Participant Marcela Vojacova, 44, shared her reasons for joining the project. I wanted to see what could be achieved by staring into another person's eyes and what I might see, she explained. When I participate, I feel a sense of fulfillment, love, and happiness—I hope others feel the same.Mark Graham, who attended the event hoping to alleviate stress before a job interview, was pleasantly surprised by the experience. Sharing 60 seconds with Marcela really helped me to relax, he remarked. For that moment, it was as if no one else was around. People might laugh at the idea, but it could be genuinely beneficial for some.

text: Free movement of workers in the EU has made life tougher for low paid workers in the UK, Andy Burnham has said. In his inaugural major address as shadow home secretary, Andy Burnham set his sights on reclaiming Labour supporters who had drifted to UKIP. He challenged the longstanding Labour narrative, asserting it was not true that free movement had universally benefited everyone. UKIP responded, calling it a welcome recognition of the blindingly obvious, but urged Mr. Burnham to advocate for leaving the EU if he was serious about change.Meanwhile, Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, who had significantly outpaced Burnham in the Labour leadership race, underscored the positive impact of EU migrants on the UK. Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Corbyn emphasized, People that have migrated to this country over many years have made an enormous contribution to our society, helped our economic growth, helped our health service and helped our social services and our education services, so don't look upon immigration as necessarily a problem, it's often a very great opportunity.Corbyn acknowledged that during the leadership campaign, Burnham had highlighted the need for the government to focus more on issues like the shortage of doctors' surgeries, school places, and housing in certain areas. However, Burnham, in his speech, criticized Labour for not confronting the realities of EU migration's impact, which he claimed made the party seem out of touch.Addressing delegates in Brighton, Burnham declared, To win back the voters we lost to UKIP, I want to reframe the debate about immigration and the way Labour approaches it. For too long, we have argued that free movement across Europe benefits everyone and affects all areas equally. That's just not true.He continued, In some areas, a free market in labor benefits private companies more than people and communities. Labour hasn't faced up to that, and that's why we look out of touch. Burnham argued that David Cameron's renegotiation of Britain's EU relationship, ahead of a planned in/out referendum, was a chance to safeguard workers.The truth is that free movement under the current rules is widening inequality. It has bolstered the economic power of the big cities, which is good. But it has also made life harder for people in our poorest communities, where wages have been undercut and job security lost, he stated. The coming referendum presents a chance to change that. Let's seize it as an opportunity to put Labour back on the front foot and back in touch.He called for a new vision of a social Europe, advocating for a Europe that prioritizes people over profits and multinationals, and establishes a safety net for all workers. The Tories and UKIP want to take those protections away, he warned. Let's have the strength to take on their scapegoating rhetoric which won't pay anybody's bills, feed anybody's kids or protect anybody's job. We welcome people here to work, as we always have. But let's make it work for everyone with new EU rules to stop undercutting, protecting the going rate for skilled workers.In response, UKIP employment spokeswoman, MEP Jane Collins, criticized Burnham's remarks as the desperate attempts of a man who has ignored the plight of the working classes due to mass immigration for years.
