text: Justin Timberlake has said he'll be performing at this year's Eurovision Song contest in Stockholm, Sweden. In an unprecedented move, 35-year-old global superstar Justin Timberlake will grace the Eurovision stage during the interval of the grand final this Saturday. Eurovision officials have clarified that his appearance will be purely non-competitive. This marks the first occasion in the contest's history that an artist of such international renown will perform independently.Sven Stojanovic, one of the show's producers, expressed his enthusiasm in a statement: This is a fantastic opportunity. We are very happy and excited that Justin Timberlake will perform his new song together with his band in our show. It makes it extra special that the Swedish songwriters Max Martin and Shellback have co-written and co-produced the song together with Justin Timberlake.The nine-time Grammy award-winner is set to perform Can't Stop the Feeling, his latest track written for the DreamWorks animation Trolls. Meanwhile, BBC Radio 1's Scott Mills and The Great British Bake Off's Mel Giedroyc will team up to host BBC Four's live coverage of the two semi-finals on May 10 and 12. Graham Norton will once again provide commentary for BBC One's live broadcast of the final from the Globe Arena.Currently on a promotional tour for his single, Timberlake recently presented the best drama series award at this year's Bafta TV awards alongside actress Anna Kendrick. The accolade was claimed by BBC Two's Wolf Hall.The announcement of Timberlake's performance follows the news of Romania's expulsion from Eurovision due to unpaid fees. Additionally, Eurovision organizers have recently relaxed their flag regulations, allowing the UK entry to display a Welsh flag. Previously, the red dragon was banned as a political statement, as only flags of contest members and UN states were permitted to maintain the event's non-political stance.Representing the UK, Joe Woolford from Ruthin, Denbighshire, and Jake Shakeshaft from Stoke-on-Trent will perform You're Not Alone. The Eurovision Song Contest will air on BBC One at 2000 BST.

text: Pupils have been so violent or disruptive that on eight occasions last year teachers held ballots to refuse to teach them in their classes. Members of the NASUWT teachers' union recently cast votes in cases where students who had assaulted teachers were allowed to remain in school. Following these ballots, some students faced expulsion or were relocated. Nick Gibb, the Schools Minister, assured that teachers have been provided with the backing they need to tackle poor behaviour.Chris Keates, the leader of NASUWT, has pointed out that these incidents highlight a growing trend of worsening student behaviour. The number of refusal to teach ballots has increased for the third year in a row across the UK, rising from three in 2012, to four in 2013, and reaching eight in 2014. At the union's annual conference in Cardiff, it was revealed that many more potential ballots were averted by making alternative arrangements for disruptive students.One notable incident involved a 16-year-old in the west of England who assaulted peers, teachers, the headteacher, and even the police. After a teachers' ballot, this student was educated off-site. In north Wales, a secondary school student with a history of disruptive behaviour threatened to slit the throat of another pupil and was subsequently expelled following a ballot. In the English Midlands, a student accused of assaulting and threatening staff and peers was kept in school but barred from classes taught by NASUWT members. Another case involved a ballot after a dispute over teachers' intervention with a pupil known for aggression, leading to the pupil's removal from the school after allegations against the teachers.Keates remarked on the widespread and increasing problem of pupil indiscipline in schools. A survey conducted by the union gathered around 3,500 online responses from its members about their experiences with student behaviour. Nearly three-quarters of respondents reported a widespread behaviour problem in schools today, a higher percentage than a similar survey the previous year. Although not a representative sample, 82% of respondents faced verbal abuse from a student, and 38% from a parent in the past year. Additionally, 23% were physically threatened, and 16% reported being assaulted.Respondents identified an excessive focus on data-driven targets as a major factor in deteriorating behaviour, with nearly two-thirds of teachers citing this issue. text: Is banning a person from contesting for public office if he or she does not have a toilet at home a good idea? In a bold move, the western Indian state of Gujarat has taken a significant step towards improving sanitation by passing a bill that requires candidates to have toilets in their homes to qualify for elections to local municipalities and village councils. This legislation, enacted earlier this week, also mandates that current elected officials must declare within six months that they have home toilets or face disqualification.Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who governed Gujarat for over a decade before ascending to power in Delhi in May, has prioritized eradicating open defecation. Although this initiative is commendable, critics argue that it does not adequately address the issue of manual scavenging. Nonetheless, legislators from Modi's ruling BJP in Gujarat have eagerly supported his sanitation campaign.Open defecation remains a severe health hazard affecting millions of Indians, with nearly half of the population still resorting to this practice. Despite being one of India's wealthiest states, Gujarat has struggled with sanitation issues. The new Chief Minister, Anandi Patel, has set an ambitious goal for the state to become open defecation free within two years. A recent report highlighted that over 70,000 people in Ahmedabad, Gujarat's main city, defecate in the open. However, economic prosperity does not automatically translate into improved sanitation.The question arises: is linking the democratic right to contest elections with the requirement of having a private toilet a sound policy? Critics, including economist Hemant Shah, argue that the bill is fundamentally undemocratic and discriminatory and should be contested in court.In Gujarat, 40% of the population resides in 159 municipalities and eight municipal corporation areas, making it one of India's most urbanized states. With over 18,500 villages and 13,500 village councils, elections are vital for the state's democratic and developmental health. The right to run for office is an essential freedom for all citizens.Many residents in Gujarat's crowded cities live in chawls—densely packed buildings where multiple families share a single toilet. Should these residents be denied the right to contest elections because they lack a private toilet? What about those living in cramped shantytowns where space is limited and toilets are nonexistent?Professor Shah raises a pertinent point: The government should first provide space and funds to build toilets for the poor. Urban planning has consistently ignored them, and now, without the space or money to construct their own toilets, they can't aspire to public office? This question challenges the fairness of the new legislation.

text: Scientists have discovered another eight pieces of genetic code linked to osteoarthritis, bringing the total number to 11. External links will open in a new window.Experts assert that inherited factors are responsible for at least half of an individual's likelihood of developing osteoarthritis, a prevalent joint condition. Understanding these genetic influences could pave the way for new treatments.Published in *The Lancet*, the study analyzed the DNA of 7,400 UK osteoarthritis patients and compared it with that of 11,000 healthy volunteers. This comparison enabled scientists to identify the most promising genetic regions for further investigation.The researchers extended their study to another group, comprising 7,500 individuals with osteoarthritis and approximately 43,000 without the condition, from various countries including Iceland, Estonia, the Netherlands, and the UK. This follow-up confirmed three previously identified gene variants and uncovered eight additional ones associated with osteoarthritis.Further research is necessary to pinpoint specific DNA changes in these genetic regions to understand precisely how they lead to osteoarthritis. Among these, the region with the most significant impact was linked to the GNL3 gene, which is vital for cell maintenance. Three other regions were connected to the regulation of cartilage, bone development, and body weight.John Loughlin, a lead scientist and professor of musculoskeletal research at Newcastle University, explained, We know that osteoarthritis runs in families due to the genes passed down, rather than shared environments. In this study, we confidently identified the major genetic risk factors for developing osteoarthritis—an unprecedented achievement for this complex disease. It's an important first step.Prof. Alan Silman, medical director of Arthritis Research UK, the charity that funded the study, remarked, Understanding the cause of this complex disease is crucial for finding a cure. This breakthrough significantly advances our comprehension of osteoarthritis, and we hope it will help us unlock the genetic basis of the disease.

text: The number of young men using steroids in London is rising on a regular basis a drugs charity has warned. The South Westminster Drug and Alcohol Service has reported a troubling rise in young male clients seeking help for anabolic steroid use. Home Office statistics indicated that in 2014, 60,000 individuals in the UK used steroids. However, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) warned that this figure might be just the tip of the iceberg, urging gyms to provide sharps bins for safe needle disposal.Roy Jones, a representative from the South Westminster service, highlighted the growing trend, stating, Our numbers are increasing on a regular basis. I've been working with steroid users for 16 years, and initially, the users were bodybuilders in their 30s. Now, the average age is 23.Professor Gillian Leng, deputy chief executive of NICE, expressed concern over the increasing normalization of steroid use among young professionals. She remarked, It's fair to say it is becoming a much more normal thing to do among some groups of young men who are concerned about the way they look...injecting steroids has become a solution.Although official figures from 2014 suggest 60,000 steroid users, experts believe the actual number is significantly higher, as the data only accounts for those apprehended by police. Professor Leng commented, I think it is inevitable that the number is a lot higher. From the epidemiology (the data) we have about the kind of people who use steroids - it's a group that's not all going to appear in custody, so that figure is bound to be the tip of the iceberg - it might be three times that number.A 25-year-old City of London worker, who wished to remain anonymous, shared with BBC London his two-year experience with steroids, which he purchased from a dealer at his local gym. I started taking them because I felt I couldn't get any bigger training naturally, he explained. It was the next step for me. There's immense pressure to look good - it's part of the culture we live in, we all want that big figure.In response to the issue, Easygym has installed sharps bins across all its locations, while Fitness First, Virgin Active, and David Lloyd have implemented them in select clubs. These gyms maintain a zero-tolerance policy towards steroids, emphasizing that the bins serve as a health and safety measure for diabetic members and razor disposal.The Department of Health stated it had given local areas the power and the funding to tackle public health issues like this. Despite increased awareness, tragedies persist. Matthew Dear, a 17-year-old from Southend, died following an adverse reaction to steroids. We are now at that point where it is boiling over and somebody needs to take ownership.Rolandas Malinauskas, a natural bodybuilder from east London and former British Champion, advocates for steroid-free bodybuilding. He cautioned, In the long term, you do not win with steroids - they create a mirage. You can build muscle naturally, but it takes time and dedication. It's all about precision, training, and diet.

text: England seem set to end the series in South Africa with a defeat after a horrible start to their second innings. After England quickly crumbled to 18-3, the prospect of averting a heavy defeat seemed bleak, with the overnight score at 52-3 and a daunting target of 382 appearing purely academic. South Africa's pace attack not only exposed England's familiar frailties but also underscored the challenging nature of the Centurion pitch, especially with the new ball in play. The pressure was palpable: poor light conditions, the impossibility of an England victory, and the need to bat for a draw—all typical hurdles faced by the team.While some might argue that England should have performed better, the reality of facing a new ball is undeniably tough. The unpredictability of the pitch was evident in Captain Alastair Cook's experience, as he faced deliveries that either skidded along the ground or rose sharply towards his armpit, leaving him with mere moments to react and increasing the uncertainty.Top-order batsmen are expected to handle such conditions, but executing this is far more challenging than it seems. Alex Hales, for instance, fell to a delivery that kept low, marking another failure in his series. Over four games, he has managed only 136 runs. My opinion remains unchanged: any opening bowler would consider Hales an easier target than he ought to be as an opening batsman. Despite this, England may persist with him, having already dismissed Adam Lyth after seven matches. With eight opening batsmen tried since Andrew Strauss's retirement in 2012, their options are dwindling.Nick Compton could be an alternative, but his performance has been underwhelming both as an opener and at number three. His loose shot made him the third England wicket to fall within the first 10 overs. England faces a crucial decision regarding their opening position, which they must resolve before their three-Test series against Sri Lanka in early summer. In those conditions, Hales might score runs, potentially kickstarting his Test career, but his technical issues remain a concern. His single score of 60 aside, his dismissals have been disappointing.The pressure is mounting on Hales, Compton, and James Taylor, as their places are under scrutiny. Meanwhile, players like Gary Ballance and Ian Bell, who have been sidelined, will be eager to perform well in the domestic season to reclaim their spots. Early-season county cricket will be their battleground, with competition for places becoming increasingly fierce. As the selection for the first Test against Sri Lanka at Headingley on 19 May approaches, none of these players are likely to rest easy.Returning to Bell seems unlikely, as the team appears to have moved on after the 2-0 defeat against Pakistan in the UAE last year. Ballance, who has scored four centuries and six fifties in his 15 Tests, is someone they are keen to reintegrate, but he must earn his place back.Despite losing the series, South Africa can take solace in the excellent form of some players, offering hope for the future. Hashim Amla delivered another masterful innings, showing resilience despite being hit on the thumb, though it was unfortunate he missed a second hundred in the match. Temba Bavuma, who impressed with a stellar century in Cape Town, continues to shine with his excellent attitude, footwork, and technical prowess. Alongside him, young fast bowler Kagiso Rabada has been a revelation, claiming two more wickets to dismantle England's top order in a brief session before the close.Rabada, who seeks one more wicket to become the youngest South African to claim 10 in a Test, has already made a significant impact with his first innings haul of 7-112. Despite having bowled 29 overs, he showed no signs of fatigue and, with Morne Morkel, promises to be a formidable force. South Africa is undoubtedly the favorite to clinch victory on the final day.Surprisingly, South Africa batted longer than expected. Many thought they would declare with a 270 lead and put England to bat before an impending storm, testing them under dim conditions. As a new captain, AB de Villiers faced the challenge of timing declarations, with many believing an hour earlier would have been ideal. Nevertheless, they have ample time left, and with the second new ball available after 60 overs on Tuesday, they are well-positioned to seal the win.Jonathan Agnew shared these insights with BBC Sport's Jamie Lillywhite.

text: Young people who went through pre-school education are much more likely to do well in international Pisa tests when they are teenagers, says the OECD. External links will open in a new window.The international think tank OECD has highlighted the need for early years education to include provisions for the poorest families to maximize its benefits. According to the OECD, the UK provides a relatively low number of hours in pre-school education. Although plans in England aim to increase free childcare to 30 hours, this extension applies only to working families.The OECD's latest study underscores the substantial economic and personal gains from investing in early childhood education, endorsing England’s initiative to broaden pre-school access. Currently, the UK offers 15 hours of free childcare, one of the lowest among OECD nations, but this will increase to 30 hours in the autumn for families with at least one working parent.Andreas Schleicher, the OECD's Director of Education, acknowledges the rationale behind prioritizing childcare for working families, which enables parents to maintain employment. However, he cautions that this focus might diminish the educational advantages of early years support, which are particularly significant for children from disadvantaged backgrounds. The study reveals that the UK has a high proportion of children in workless households, especially in single-parent families, who might be excluded if the emphasis remains on working families.Mr. Schleicher emphasized the critical role of pre-school education in providing children with a robust foundation, noting that its benefits extend beyond academics to include improved health outcomes, such as lower obesity rates. Nevertheless, the report warns of inconsistent funding in this sector and highlights that pre-school staff are often paid less than their counterparts in the school system. Since 2010, UK pre-school staff wages have declined in real terms, according to the OECD survey.Parents searching for quality pre-school options face challenges due to the fragmented and complex nature of available information, unlike the more accessible data on schools. Mr. Schleicher described the landscape of early years provision as very fragmented and hard to navigate.Neil Leitch, Chief Executive of the Pre-school Learning Alliance, expressed frustration: We have long argued that, given current limited resources, the government should focus its spending on where it is needed most. As such, we remain at a loss as to why there has been no attempt to rethink the current eligibility criteria for the 30-hour offer.A spokeswoman from the Department for Education responded, We are investing more than ever before into childcare—£6bn per year by 2020—and doubling our existing offer of free childcare for all three and four-year-olds to 30 hours for working parents. We are also supporting the most disadvantaged families with 15 free hours per week for two-year-olds, our pupil premium worth over £300 a year per child, and our new Disability Access Fund, providing £615 per eligible child.

text: A Spanish MP has provoked criticism by taking her baby into parliament and breastfeeding him during its first session since an inconclusive general election last month. Carolina Bescansa captured everyone's attention as she stood as a candidate for the parliamentary speaker. Among those seen cradling her young son was Pablo Iglesias, the leader of the anti-austerity Podemos party. Meanwhile, political leaders remain embroiled in discussions about forming a government after the December 20 election. Although the conservative People's Party (PP) secured the most seats, they did not achieve a majority.A member of Podemos, which finished third in the election, Bescansa had pledged to breastfeed in parliament during her campaign, according to various reports. On Wednesday, she defended parents' rights to raise their children as they see fit, responding to criticism from some politicians who deemed her actions unnecessary, as reported by Spanish news agency Efe. Bescansa expressed her gratitude for the privilege of not being separated from her baby, Diego, since his birth.However, acting Interior Minister Jorge Fernandez Diaz, from the PP, labeled her actions as lamentable, according to El Mundo. Socialist MP Carme Chacon echoed this sentiment, calling it frankly unnecessary. Bescansa reportedly requested photographers not to show her baby's face, yet some critics accused her of seeking attention, noting the availability of a nursery in the parliament building since 2006 to assist MPs with childcare.In her quest to become parliamentary speaker, Bescansa was unsuccessful. The position went to Socialist MP Patxi Lopez, marking a historic moment as he became the first speaker from a party that did not win the most seats in an election. Bescansa has previously brought her son to parliament for ceremonial occasions, including her swearing-in as an MP.In 2012, Iolanda Pineda of the Socialists' Party of Catalonia (PSC) also took her baby into Spain's upper house of parliament. Similarly, Italian politician Licia Ronziulli was photographed with her baby in the European parliament in September 2010 when the child was just six weeks old. Since then, images of the MEP with her daughter have chronicled the child's growth. Last year, a group of UK MPs called for the reversal of a ban on new mothers breastfeeding in the House of Commons chamber.The first parliamentary session in Spain on Wednesday saw MPs convene, yet the government formation remains at an impasse. Mariano Rajoy's Popular Party is advocating for a coalition with the Socialists (PSOE) and the center-right Ciudadanos (Citizens) party, which ranked fourth in the election. Conversely, the Socialists aim to forge an agreement with Citizens and Podemos. However, Podemos maintains a demand for a Catalonia independence referendum, which the other two parties oppose.Should the main parties fail to reach a consensus, King Felipe VI will designate a party leader to form a government, and MPs will vote on this nomination. If no agreement is reached, new elections may be necessary.

text: Newcastle Falcons survive a second-half fightback from Bristol at Kingston Park to earn their third win of the season. In a gripping encounter, Newcastle Falcons managed to hold off a spirited Bristol fightback to secure a narrow victory. The Falcons soared to a 19-point advantage in the first half, thanks to tries from Juan Pablo Socino, Will Welch, and Joel Hodgson. However, Bristol, still searching for their first win since rejoining the Premiership, responded with tries from John Fisher and Mitch Eadie, narrowing the gap to just five points.Despite a valiant effort, Bristol could not complete their comeback and suffered their sixth consecutive defeat, leaving them anchored at the bottom of the table. The match concluded with both teams reduced to 14 players, as Newcastle's Alex Rogers and Bristol's Gaston Cortez were sent to the sin bin.In the dying minutes, Bristol applied intense pressure but fell short of overturning the deficit. They did, however, earn their second losing bonus point of the season, doubling their points tally.Both Joel Hodgson and Mike Delany missed crucial second-half penalties for Newcastle, which could have extended their lead. Nevertheless, the Falcons' commanding first-half performance, highlighted by Hodgson's crucial try just before the break, ultimately secured the win.Reflecting on the game, Newcastle's director of rugby, Dean Richards, expressed mixed emotions: If you'd asked me 15 minutes before kick-off if I'd take a 19-14 win, I'd have said yes. But now, there's a sense of frustration among us. We're in the top half of the Premiership with three wins and a couple of losing bonus points, but injuries to key players have been challenging. We excelled in the first half and could have scored more, which would have helped in the second half. Our kicking faltered, and that was probably the root cause of the problem. I never thought we'd lose, but we could have thrown it away.Meanwhile, Bristol's director of rugby, Andy Robinson, acknowledged the team's early struggles: We started reasonably well but lost our discipline, gifting Newcastle their first try and momentum. In the second half, we improved, made our tackles, and gained momentum, scoring two excellent tries. Unfortunately, we couldn't maintain it. The second half showed we have the talent to succeed in the Premiership. We did some good things today and in our season opener, but we aimed for at least one win in the first six games, and it's frustrating not to have achieved that.The teams lined up as follows: Newcastle fielded Hammersley; Tait, Waldouck, Socino, Sinoti; Delany, Young; Vickers, Lawson, D Wilson, Green, Olmstead, M Wilson, Welch (capt), Hogg, with replacements Sowrey, Rogers, Welsh, Witty, Temm, Takulua, Hodgson, Agulla. text: On a warm Saturday afternoon in March a group of campaigners heads to the Golden Lane estate in central London. With local council elections looming, volunteers from the campaign group We Can Win are not rallying for councillors but instead aim to raise awareness about the unique electoral system of the City of London Corporation. This system, which they oppose, covers the financial hub known as the Square Mile and differs from the Greater London Authority that governs the entire UK capital.The City of London, home to fewer than 8,000 residents, sees a daily influx of approximately 450,000 workers. Remarkably, the City Corporation allows a portion of these workers to vote, increasing the electorate to nearly 19,000. I thought democracy was about one person, one vote, says Dan Firth, the campaign director. But here, businesses have almost twice the votes of ordinary people, which feels unjust.We Can Win's campaign is focused on challenging the influence of big business votes and boosting resident turnout. The City is divided into 25 wards, with most residents in Portsoken, Queenhithe, Aldersgate, and Cripplegate, which includes Golden Lane. Each ward elects Common Councillors every four years, with the next election on March 23, while aldermen are elected every six years as terms expire.Georgia O'Brien, a campaigner, notes that while some residents are aware of the voting system, many are shocked to learn that workers have nearly double the votes compared to residents. Golden Lane resident Beverley Bytheway, active in her residents' association, was unaware that workers could vote and expressed skepticism about the Corporation's interest in residents.Despite this, the City of London Corporation openly provides information on voting registration for both residents and workers. The City is a democratic institution, a spokesman stated, emphasizing that all councillors are elected. Residents have one vote each, while business votes are based on employee numbers. Smaller businesses get one vote, while larger organizations can appoint voters proportionally to their workforce size.The Corporation advises businesses to ensure their nominated voters reflect the organization's diversity. Deloitte, with over 10,000 employees, values its 260 votes across two wards. A spokesperson highlighted the importance of local issues like road safety, noting the valuable role of councillors as links between businesses and the community.The City of London's governance dates back to medieval times, making it Britain's oldest local authority. While non-residential votes were abolished elsewhere in 1969, the City's system, revised in 2002, continues to allow business votes. This includes not just financial institutions but also diverse entities like shops, charities, and churches.Mukesh Gaglani, a long-time voter and small business owner, feels his vote is equal to anyone else's, dismissing concerns about big business dominance. The City gets most of its revenue from commercial properties, he argues against proposals to restrict voting to residents.Sophie Fernandes, an independent Common Councillor since 2009, handles a range of issues from infrastructure to landlord complaints. Her ward, primarily business-oriented, has few residents. Workers, not businesses, have votes, she clarifies, supporting the system that balances business and residential needs.Fernandes refutes claims that the Corporation wants to remove residents, citing their contribution to the City's diversity. To stand as a councillor, one must be a registered voter and a Freeman of the City of London, with no cost barrier for voters to obtain freedom. Fernandes, like most councillors, serves as an independent, advocating for a non-partisan approach to governance.The Labour Party, challenging this independence narrative, first fielded candidates in 2009 and is contesting wards in 2017. Paul O'Brien, running for Coleman Street, acknowledges the necessity of worker representation in wards with few residents, aligning with Fernandes on this point.Both critics and supporters agree on the City's unique nature, with influence extending beyond the Square Mile, managing estates and open spaces like Hampstead Heath and Epping Forest, and funding London boroughs through the City Bridge Trust. The Common Councillor elections are set for Thursday, March 23, with a complete list of candidates available online.

text: All it takes to officially run for the Republican presidential nomination is a one-page form sent to the Federal Election Commission, the US government entity in charge of overseeing campaign laws. This year, a staggering 213 hopefuls have taken the initial step towards the presidency by announcing their candidacy. Yet, the real challenge lies ahead. Declaring one's intention and filing the necessary federal paperwork doesn't automatically secure a spot on any state-level primary or caucus ballot, which are crucial for amassing delegates needed for the Republican National Convention in July.The path to these ballots is a grueling state-by-state battle, each with its own set of rules and regulations. Success demands significant time, money, and organization. For instance, getting on the ballot in New Hampshire, a pivotal early-voting state, costs $1,000 (£600). But that's a mere drop in the bucket compared to South Carolina, the third state in the nominating process. To compete there, Republican candidates had to pay a hefty $40,000 (£26,500) fee by Wednesday—half of which is allocated to the state government for administrative expenses, while the rest goes to the state Republican Party.This is extortion, claims Richard Winger, editor of Ballot Access News, adding that such fees might not even be legal. He cites a 1972 US Supreme Court decision that deemed a fee of up to $8,900 for a local office run unconstitutional, arguing that excessive fees could preclude qualified candidates lacking wealth or affluent supporters. If every state did this, it could soon cost a million dollars, Winger warns.South Carolina and New Hampshire are just the beginning. Eight other states impose filing fees, mostly around $1,000. Arkansas charges $25,000 for its primary, due by November 9, while entering caucuses in Kansas or Kentucky costs $15,000 each. These fees must come from candidates' campaign funds, which are subject to contribution limits and strict reporting, not from external donors or Super PACs.The prohibitive cost in South Carolina reportedly influenced former Texas Governor Rick Perry to end his presidential bid in mid-September. Wisconsin Governor Scott Walker paid the fee but exited the race the following month, with his campaign over $750,000 in debt. Despite these challenges, none of the 15 remaining Republican candidates have contested the fee legally. All, including New Jersey Governor Chris Christie and former New York Governor George Pataki, met the deadline, preferring to pay up rather than stir controversy.Democrats face fees too, but generally lower. In South Carolina, candidates like Hillary Clinton pay $2,500 to the state party, which covers the remaining $20,000 administrative cost. Beyond financial hurdles, candidates must often gather up to 5,000 signatures from registered voters, a task requiring a robust organization or funds for professional help.In 2012, Virginia required 10,000 signatures for ballot access, with only Mitt Romney and Ron Paul succeeding. For March 1, 2016, Virginia reduced this to 5,000, with at least 200 from each of the 11 congressional districts. Similar district-specific requirements exist in many states, where missing even one district's quota can disqualify a candidate.Some states offer alternatives. In Texas, candidates can either pay a $5,000 fee or submit 300 signatures from at least 15 congressional districts. Florida presents a unique case: candidates can pay $25,000, collect 3,375 signatures, or attend the Sunshine Summit in Orlando, a potential party fundraiser with tickets ranging from $200 to $1,000.Iowa stands out with no filing fees, petitions, or ballots. Voters can support any candidate in caucuses, but mobilizing supporters on a cold February evening can be as challenging as South Carolina's financial demands.The journey for Republican presidential candidates, both in and out of the race, is fraught with obstacles, from steep financial requirements to logistical challenges, underscoring the complexities of the American electoral process.

text: Venezuela has donated $500,000 to US President Donald Trump's inauguration, newly released records show. Citgo Petroleum, the U.S. subsidiary of Venezuela's state-owned oil company, has been named in a filing with the Federal Election Commission. This revelation comes amid Venezuela's severe economic turmoil, marked by food shortages, rampant crime, and soaring inflation.On Wednesday, protests erupted in Venezuela, with tens of thousands demanding new elections. Tragically, the unrest resulted in the deaths of three individuals. In stark contrast, documents reveal that major corporations, including Pepsi and Walmart, contributed $250,000 and $150,000 respectively to political causes, while NFL team owners and their companies collectively donated over $5 million. Casino magnate Sheldon Adelson also contributed $5 million.Venezuela, an oil-rich nation, is grappling with a profound economic crisis, teetering on the edge of hyperinflation. Amid this chaos, protests on Wednesday called for President Nicolas Maduro's resignation, leading to at least two fatalities. In this turbulent environment, Venezuelan media have largely overlooked the news of their government's $500,000 contribution to Donald Trump's inauguration, facilitated through Citgo.Despite the lack of media attention, some Venezuelan analysts are voicing outrage. We have been experiencing four consecutive years of recession, we have the highest inflation in the world, and are facing scarcity in many basic goods. It is scandalous that Venezuela, facing such a crisis, would make those donations to the inauguration of a US president, who at least in theory, is ideologically confronted with the revolution, said Jose Manuel Puente, a public policy professor at IESA university in Caracas, speaking to the BBC.The payment was reportedly funneled through Citgo, continuing a pattern of the company's involvement in politically charged activities in the U.S. In the past, under President Maduro's predecessor Hugo Chavez, Citgo provided subsidized fuel to low-income Americans, an act critics labeled as propaganda aimed at antagonizing the U.S. government.However, the current Maduro administration appears less confrontational towards Washington. President Maduro recently remarked that Trump has been subjected to a brutal hate campaign, adding that he won't be worse than Obama. According to Puente, The (Bolivarian) revolution is pragmatic. Eighteen years after the beginning of the revolution, the US is still their main trading partner. It is business as usual.

text: Neil Gaiman's The Ocean at the End of the Lane has been voted 2013's Book of the Year, winning the public vote by a considerable margin. Neil Gaiman's enchanting fantasy novel triumphed over fellow National Book Award recipients, such as Kate Atkinson and David Walliams. The narrative, which follows a man's poignant return to his childhood home for a funeral, captured the public's admiration, winning the popular vote from a shortlist of ten National Book Award winners this year.The renowned graphic novelist expressed his delight, stating, I've never written a book before that was so close to my own heart - a story about memory and magic and the fear and danger of being a child. Gaiman admitted his uncertainty about the book's reception, adding, I wasn't sure that anyone else would like it. I'm amazed and thrilled that so many other people have read it, loved it, and made their friends read it too.Gaiman further expressed his gratitude for the recognition, saying, Winning a National Book Award was thrilling; discovering that the public have made The Ocean at the End of the Lane their Book of the Year is somewhere out beyond wonderful. Thank you to everyone who voted.His novel had already clinched the Audiobook of the Year honor. It emerged victorious in the public vote, surpassing competitors like Gillian Flynn's hit Gone Girl, David Jason's autobiography My Life, and Malala Yousafzai's inspiring I Am Malala, to claim the prestigious Book of the Year title. The online voting, unique for being solely decided by readers, concluded on December 19.In previous years, the award has been claimed by EL James' provocative Fifty Shades of Grey, Caitlin Moran's insightful How To Be A Woman, and David Nicholls' romantic One Day.Dame Mary Perkins, founder of Specsavers, the award's sponsors, extended her congratulations to Gaiman for this fantastic award. She acknowledged the stiff competition, noting, The competition was tough but to be chosen by members of the public as well as your industry peers truly is a tribute to hard work, dedication and creativity.Gaiman, who gained fame with his graphic novels, including The Sandman series and Coraline, has also written two recent Doctor Who episodes featuring Matt Smith. He is currently working on a prequel to The Sandman, and a television adaptation of his book American Gods is underway.

text: Derby County climbed into the Championship play-off zone for the first time under new boss Paul Clement as they proved too good for Wolves. In a thrilling encounter at Derby County, Chris Martin's first-half brilliance set the stage for a 4-2 victory over Wolverhampton Wanderers. Martin opened the scoring with a stunning 20-yard curler and later added a powerful header, sandwiching Benik Afobe's well-executed equalizer for Wolves. Martin's attempt to secure a hat-trick was thwarted when Emiliano Martinez saved his penalty, but Bradley Johnson's somewhat fortuitous strike ensured a 3-1 lead at halftime.Johnny Russell extended Derby's advantage with a fourth goal, before Adam Le Fondre pulled one back for Wolves with a looping volley, assisted by Sheyi Ojo's knockdown. Despite Scott Carson's fingertips grazing the shot, it found the net. This was a small consolation for Wolves, who were denied a penalty earlier when Jason Shackell blocked a shot with his elbow. Controversy also surrounded Derby's second goal, as Martin appeared to use Kortney Hause's shoulders for leverage. Johnson's goal, meanwhile, came after a scramble following Martin's missed penalty, initially awarded for Danny Batth's foul on Tom Ince.Wolves had earlier showcased a well-rehearsed set-piece, with Afobe lashing in James Henry's corner to level the score after Martin's opener. However, Derby's sustained pressure paid off, and Russell's toe-poke from 12 yards put the Rams firmly in control. The final scoreline, slightly flattering to Wolves, reflected Derby's dominance as they collected 16 points from a possible 18, climbing to sixth in the standings. Wolves, who had enjoyed back-to-back 3-0 wins before the international break, slipped to 11th, now trailing the play-off spots by five points.Reflecting on the match, Derby head coach Paul Clement praised his team's performance, telling BBC Sport, Our best performance of the season. We've had some good first halves and some good second halves, but this time we were solid throughout and were deserved victors. Chris Martin put in the best performance I've seen from a Championship centre forward this season. A great finish for the first, a brave header for the second, and he led the line well. It was a shame he didn't finish off the penalty for what would have been a first-half hat-trick. But he was a well-deserved man of the match. Against a good side, it was also a great response from the team to come back and score the way we did following the penalty miss. We could have gone in at half-time on a low. But to make it 3-1 was a big moment.On the other side, Wolves head coach Kenny Jackett lamented his team's defensive lapses, saying, Derby were strong and take some stopping, but our defending was poor. We didn't work hard enough to put in enough blocks and cut down things at source. There were too many key moments when we didn't defend well enough. They had too many shots and far too many of them we gifted them. Their penalty was the right decision. I also thought we should have had one for the handball, but it would be hard to get those sort of decisions here. Our keeper's held his hand up for the second goal. He should have left it to Kortney Hause to deal with, but he's a good keeper and he'll learn from that.The match concluded with Derby County triumphing 4-2 over Wolverhampton Wanderers. The second half ended with the same scoreline, as Derby's defensive and attacking prowess outshone Wolves' efforts.

text: A fund to raise money for the families of the five Birmingham wall collapse victims has passed £20,000. Tragedy struck at Hawkeswood Metal in Nechells on Thursday when a 15-foot wall of concrete and scrap metal collapsed, claiming the lives of five workers. The victims, all Spanish citizens originally from Gambia, were identified locally as Bangaly Dukureh, Ousman Jabbie, Alimamo Jammeh, Mohammed Jangana, and Saibo Sillah. Each was reportedly married with children. A sixth worker, also of Gambian heritage and Spanish citizenship, survived but sustained a broken leg.In the wake of this disaster, the Birmingham Mail initiated a fund, receiving what its editor described as an overwhelming response. Donations have been pouring in nationwide to support the bereaved families. Mr. Reeves, commenting on the initiative, stated, No money can ever fill the void left by a loved one, especially in a tragedy of this sort. But at least if the families are freed from the concerns of paying for funerals, travel for family members, and all the other immediate financial worries that get in the way of grieving, then it is worthwhile to raise some money to help. The response is overwhelming, and as well as the financial support, we hope this sends a message to the families that Birmingham cares about them and feels their pain.By Friday, all the bodies had been retrieved from the debris. Police have closed the site, and post-mortem examinations are scheduled for Monday. Meanwhile, detectives believe they have a reasonable idea of the incident's cause. The victims' relatives have expressed a desire for a swift recovery of the bodies for burial, in line with Muslim customs.Hawkeswood Metal Recycling Ltd, a company with over 40 years of history and a workforce of about 50, processes more than 500,000 tonnes of scrap metal annually at its Nechells location. The company has faced safety issues in the past, including a £50,000 fine in 2012 after an employee's arm was trapped in machinery, a violation of health and safety regulations. Earlier this year, the plant was also the site of a significant fire, where 700 tonnes of scrap metal were engulfed in flames.

text: Women who wore pantsuits in support of Hillary Clinton on US election day are now being urged to donate them to poor and homeless women. text: Hosts France advanced to the Euro 2016 final with their first victory over Germany in a major tournament since 1958 on a night of high emotion in Marseille. Antoine Griezmann, the standout scorer of the tournament, proved pivotal in both halves, propelling France to a Euro 2016 final against Portugal at the Stade de France on Sunday. Just before the break, Griezmann coolly converted a penalty after Italian referee Nicola Rizzoli penalized Germany's Bastian Schweinsteiger for a handball during an aerial duel with Patrice Evra. Despite Germany's relentless pressure, Griezmann cemented France's victory with 18 minutes left, seizing on a loose ball after Manuel Neuer's partial clearance of a Paul Pogba cross. Joshua Kimmich came close for Germany, hitting the post and forcing a brilliant save from French keeper Hugo Lloris, but the reigning World Cup champions couldn't find a way back.France, who had a sluggish start to Euro 2016, found renewed vigor at Marseille's Stade Velodrome. Didier Deschamps' squad seemed buoyed by a national wave of emotion, especially poignant given the stadium's history. It was here, during a friendly between France and Germany, that the first explosions of the Paris attacks were heard in November, claiming 130 lives. Fourteen players from that night took the field in Marseille.The atmosphere was electric, amplified by the day's scorching heat. A defining moment came when the entire stadium erupted into a passionate rendition of La Marseillaise, rallying the team as Germany pressed for an equalizer. France now faces one final challenge against Portugal, with the nation eagerly anticipating victory.Griezmann, the diminutive forward from Atletico Madrid, has shouldered the hopes of a nation, emerging as a key figure and match-winner. With six goals in the tournament, he has matched Thierry Henry's European Championship tally, achieved over three tournaments. Though not yet at the level of Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo, or Luis Suarez, Griezmann's performances are edging him closer to that elite group.In the last 16, he overturned a deficit against the Republic of Ireland, and against Germany, he was again the decisive factor. He tested Neuer early with a low shot after a slick exchange with Blaise Matuidi, and even under German dominance, he remained a constant threat. His penalty was executed with confidence, and he was composed as he capitalized on Neuer's error with Pogba's cross.Griezmann's all-around play, first touch, and goal-scoring ability make him an indispensable asset for France. With Olivier Giroud struggling, Griezmann has often carried the attack alone, providing hope and inspiration for the final in Paris.Germany, unable to emulate France and Spain's feat of holding both the European Championship and World Cup, have been a formidable force in past tournaments, often eliminating host nations. However, on this occasion, France broke the curse, emerging victorious.Joachim Low's side displayed impressive skill but lacked the finishing touch, thwarted by France's resolute defense and Lloris's outstanding goalkeeping. Germany's tendency to concede penalties proved costly, with Schweinsteiger's raised arm inviting punishment, echoing Jerome Boateng's error against Italy.Despite this, Germany remains a European powerhouse, but France exploited every weakness before their ecstatic home crowd.Thierry Henry, speaking on BBC One, praised France's opportunism, likening them to classic Italian or German sides. Two opportunities, two goals, he noted, expressing pride in the team's unity and the fans' support. He hailed Griezmann as a hero, capable of winning tournaments, and looked forward to the final against Portugal, where Ronaldo and Griezmann would face off once more.Germany's manager Joachim Low reflected on the match, asserting, We were the better team, but luck wasn't on our side. He praised his players' courage and discipline, lamenting missed chances and the unfortunate goal conceded.France's manager Didier Deschamps expressed delight for his players, acknowledging the challenge posed by Germany. He credited Lloris's crucial saves and emphasized that both France and Portugal have equal chances in the final, despite France's home advantage.Antoine Griezmann, reflecting on the victory, said, We knew it would be tough, but we held firm. Now, we prepare for the final, where anything can happen.The match concluded with France defeating Germany 2-0, setting the stage for an eagerly anticipated showdown with Portugal.

text: Another City shareholder has called on Sky's independent directors to explain why they have backed a takeover by Rupert Murdoch's 21st Century Fox. Last Friday, the US media conglomerate announced its intention to acquire the remaining 61% of Sky that it doesn't already own, offering £10.75 per share. This price has been tentatively agreed upon by the independent directors from both companies. However, Richard Marwood from Royal London Asset Management is calling for greater transparency. Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Marwood stated, Those independent directors have taken advice, and we think that they should share that with shareholders, to actually allow the rest of us to see [if] £10.75 is the right price, so we are all acting from the same information.As a member of the FTSE 100, Sky's shares are held by numerous investment firms in the City. On Wednesday, shares were trading at 982p, amidst increasing demands for the government to refer any bid to Ofcom, the media regulator. Royal London holds a relatively small stake in Sky, with just 2.4 million shares, representing 0.14% of the total. Nonetheless, their comments echo a broader discontent among some shareholders, urging Sky's directors to justify their decisions and push for a better offer.Concerns about the independence of Sky's board have been raised by Standard Life and Jupiter Asset Management, particularly given that James Murdoch, Rupert Murdoch's son, serves as both chairman of Sky and CEO of Fox. Additionally, the Sky board includes Chase Carey, a former Fox Television CEO and Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation co-chief operating officer, as well as John Nallen, the chief financial officer of 21st Century Fox.Marwood expressed doubts about Sky's corporate governance, saying, We had concerns when he [James Murdoch] was appointed to be the chairman of Sky, just for this situation. We felt if there were ever to be a bid, there would be a conflict, and our fears have been realised with what's happened.He further commented, To some extent, Sky have tried to allay the fears of investors by having these independent directors opining on the bid. But I think more transparency to give us some confidence that there is some independence there would be very good.

text: Hungary has passed a law that critics say could undermine the independence of its central bank. In a decisive move, Hungary's ruling Fidesz party, wielding a two-thirds majority, has pushed through a controversial constitutional amendment during the last parliamentary session of the year. This change has sparked significant international concern, contributing to Standard & Poor's decision to downgrade Hungary's debt to junk status last week.The proposed constitutional changes have already led to a breakdown in negotiations with EU and IMF officials, who have suspended aid discussions with Hungary. The nation had been seeking a substantial standby credit line, ranging from 15 to 20 billion euros ($19.5 billion, £12.6 billion), to safeguard against potential difficulties in issuing new debt. However, both the International Monetary Fund and the European Commission have expressed skepticism about providing aid under the current circumstances.Investor confidence has been shaken, as evidenced by Hungary's decision to cancel part of a planned bond auction on Thursday when faced with demands for higher interest rates on its debt. The bill has been sharply criticized by Andras Simor, Hungary's central bank governor, who described it as a central bank takeover. The European Central Bank has also voiced concerns, stating that the law could potentially compromise the independence of the central bank by influencing its decision-making process.Amid this international pressure, the Hungarian government aims to maintain low interest rates to stimulate economic growth. However, the central bank has raised rates for the second consecutive month, increasing them from 6.5% to 7% last week. Inflation in Hungary is currently at 4.25%, significantly surpassing the official target of 3%.BBC's Eastern Europe correspondent, Nick Thorpe, reported, While some amendments have been made since the original draft was presented before the Christmas holiday, the law's core issues remain unresolved. He noted that the reform could introduce deputy governors and allow the government greater sway over critical monetary policy areas, such as interest rates.Back in 2008, Hungary secured a 20 billion-euro standby loan from the IMF to avert a debt default. However, newly-elected Prime Minister Viktor Orban chose not to renew this facility last year. Standard & Poor's has highlighted increased risks to Hungary's debt repayment capabilities, citing a deteriorating domestic and global economic outlook. In our view, the predictability of Hungary's policy framework continues to weaken, harming Hungary's medium-term growth prospects, stated S&P.Adding to the financial strain, Moody's downgraded Hungary's credit rating to junk status last month, attributing the decision to the economy's high debt levels and bleak growth prospects.

text: The OFT has made a move to try to help people access discounts when booking online, after closing an investigation into competition practice between three companies. An inquiry into online travel agents Booking.com, Expedia, and the hotel group InterContinental Hotels (IHG) has taken a new turn. Initially, the investigation raised concerns that these companies might be violating competition laws by restricting price competition. However, regulators have now permitted such arrangements, provided certain conditions are met.The Office of Fair Trading (OFT) has decided to allow online agents to offer discounts on hotel room prices, aiming to foster a more competitive market. Previously, these platforms were unable to provide such discounts. According to the OFT, consumers must join a membership program with a hotel, one of the agents, or another online agent to qualify for discounts. Additionally, they must have previously booked at least one room at full price with the online agent or hotel.Booking.com and Expedia stand among the UK’s largest online travel agents. The OFT initiated its investigation in 2010 to explore claims of agreements and practices that might result in fixed or minimum resale prices. Whether this decision will indeed spur competition and lower prices remains a topic of debate.Gaucho Rasmussen, the OFT’s enforcement director, emphasized the thoroughness of their review, stating, We did some consumer research and a significant amount of people would shop around and use smaller websites and new starters. He noted that the OFT had conducted two consultations and believed the decision represented the best possible outcome. Rasmussen added that as the market evolves, smaller websites might innovate to stay competitive.In contrast, Dorian Harris, founder of the discount booking site Skoosh, expressed skepticism about the decision's impact. I am baffled by the outcome, he remarked. Harris argued that smaller companies like Skoosh lack the resources to adapt their marketing strategies and hotel contracts to meet the OFT's conditions, making it challenging to offer discounts. He criticized the conditions for potentially discouraging consumers from trying smaller, lesser-known websites over established giants like Booking.com or Expedia. The OFT have not understood the market. It is a huge failure in assessment, Harris asserted.Harris also pointed out that consumers are unlikely to pay full price for a room on a new platform like Skoosh just to qualify for future discounts. Instead, they would prefer immediate discounts from larger sites such as Expedia, where they might have already booked premium-rate rooms. He argued that these conditions could further entrench the dominance of Booking.com and Expedia, accusing the OFT of catering to the interests of these major companies.Acknowledging the potential for increased market dominance, Rasmussen assured that the OFT would be vigilant in monitoring market developments.

He expressed concerns that the association and trade deal might jeopardize enterprises that heavily rely on Russian trade.Despite his eventual intention to sign the EU deal, Yanukovych has acknowledged substantial pressure from Moscow, which is urging Kiev to join a Russian-led customs union. text: Swiss pilot Andre Borschberg has begun his bid to cross the Pacific, from China to Hawaii, in the zero-fuel Solar Impulse aeroplane. In the early hours of the morning, at precisely 02:39 local time (18:39 GMT), an extraordinary aircraft took off from Nanjing. This experimental plane, boasting a wingspan larger than a jumbo jet yet weighing only as much as a large car, is piloted by Mr. Borschberg, who is embarking on a daring five to six-day non-stop flight to the central Pacific. Throughout this ambitious journey, he plans to remain mostly awake, catching only brief naps.From a control room in Monaco, a team will meticulously track his progress. Meteorologists and flight strategists will provide him with continuous updates on the optimal route to take. This journey marks the seventh leg of the single-seat, propeller-driven aircraft's mission to circumnavigate the globe powered solely by solar energy.Since its departure from Abu Dhabi in March, the project has made consistent headway. However, it faced a significant delay of over a month on China's eastern coast, waiting for favorable weather conditions over the ocean. The Solar Impulse relies not only on favorable winds to aid its forward motion but also on clear skies. Its 17,000 photovoltaic cells, mounted on the wings, need to function at maximum efficiency to charge the plane's lithium-ion batteries by dusk, ensuring it can fly through the night until dawn.Mr. Borschberg, a seasoned pilot and trained engineer, is intimately familiar with the aircraft's systems. Despite his expertise, he acknowledges the formidable nature of the mission. It's more in the end about myself; it's going to be an inner-voyage, he shared with the BBC before takeoff. It's going to be a discovery about how I feel and how I sustain myself during these five or six days in the air.Bertrand Piccard, who has piloted the Solar Impulse on other legs of the journey, explained to the BBC, There's one pilot at a time, so the pilot needs to do everything on his own. And it's a very large aeroplane, big wingspans, sensitive to turbulence, flying quite slow. So sometimes it's difficult to handle when the air moves. But we have an auto-pilot, we have toilets on board, we have food for days, water reserves and everything, and we are well trained.The destination is Kalaeloa Airport on Hawaii's O'ahu island, over 8,000 kilometers (5,000 miles) away. If adverse weather or a significant technical issue arises early in the flight, Mr. Borschberg has the option to return to China or Japan. However, a point will come when turning back is no longer feasible, and preparations have been made for the possibility of ditching in the Pacific should a serious problem occur. In such a scenario, Mr. Borschberg would not remain with the plane due to the risk of electrocution in the water. Instead, he would evacuate with a dinghy and await rescue by ship.Should he successfully reach Kalaeloa Airport, Mr. Borschberg will set multiple aviation records, including the longest-duration solo flight. The Solar Impulse project aims to highlight the potential of clean technologies rather than propose a specific future for aviation.The journey so far has included: - LEG 1: 9 March, Abu Dhabi (UAE) to Muscat (Oman) - 441 km in 13 hours and 1 minute - LEG 2: 10 March, Muscat (Oman) to Ahmedabad (India) - 1,468 km in 15 hours and 20 minutes - LEG 3: 18 March, Ahmedabad (India) to Varanasi (India) - 1,215 km in 13 hours and 15 minutes - LEG 4: 19 March, Varanasi (India) to Mandalay (Myanmar) - 1,398 km in 13 hours and 29 minutes - LEG 5: 29 March, Mandalay (Myanmar) to Chongqing (China) - 1,459 km in 20 hours and 29 minutes - LEG 6: 21 April, Chongqing (China) to Nanjing (China) - 1,241 km in 17 hours and 22 minutes

text: There is no obvious link between tough laws and levels of illegal drug use, a government report has found. Norman Baker, the Liberal Democrat Home Office minister, has called for an end to the mindless rhetoric surrounding the UK's drugs policy, following a report that compares the nation's approach to that of other countries. He accused the Conservatives of withholding the report's findings for several months. Prime Minister David Cameron, however, dismissed the idea of decriminalising drugs, stating that the research did not provide specific conclusions.The debate on drugs policy was reignited in the House of Commons, with Green MP Caroline Lucas urging a review of what she described as failing drugs laws. Under current legislation, individuals can face up to seven years in prison for possessing Class A drugs, and life imprisonment for producing or supplying them.The Home Office report examined the UK's drug misuse strategies alongside those of 13 other nations. Among these, nine countries, including Canada, Denmark, and Switzerland, have introduced drug consumption rooms. Eight countries, such as Switzerland, the Netherlands, and the UK, are experimenting with treating addicts using pure heroin instead of methadone. Additionally, four countries, including the US, have established drug courts where offenders can choose treatment over incarceration. Portugal stands out with its dissuasion commissions, treating drug possession as a health issue since 2001.The report concluded that drug use is influenced by factors more complex and nuanced than legislation and enforcement alone. Notably, it highlighted significant health improvements among drug users in Portugal post-decriminalisation. However, the Home Office cautioned against attributing these outcomes solely to decriminalisation.Baker argued for treating drug use as a health issue rather than relying on incarceration. Alex, a recovering heroin and crack addict from London, shared his personal story, emphasizing that current laws do not deter addicts. He criticized the Home Office's stance on drug policy as out of touch, highlighting the devastating impact of addiction on his life and family.Lib Dem leader Nick Clegg accused the Conservatives of holding a totally misplaced, outdated, backward-looking view on drugs policy. Baker echoed this sentiment, criticizing the mindless rhetoric of the past 40 years that dismisses alternative solutions. He claimed the Conservatives suppressed the report due to its inconvenient truths, but Tory MP Michael Ellis countered, accusing the Lib Dems of exploiting the report for political gain and branding their policies as dangerous and irresponsible.Cameron defended the government's approach, stating, Under this government drug use is falling, attributing this to an evidence-based strategy focused on education, prevention, and treatment. He acknowledged the report as interesting but argued it did not justify any specific policy change.BBC home affairs correspondent Danny Shaw noted the stark divisions within the coalition. While the Home Office maintains its drug strategy is effective, Baker calls for radical change, supported by the report's findings that tough drug laws do not necessarily reduce usage. The study emphasized the complexity of drug policy, cautioning against directly applying foreign strategies to the UK.Nick Barton of Action on Addiction stressed the need to treat addiction as a health condition rather than a criminal issue, noting that incarceration rarely solves the problem. Danny Kushlick, founder of Transform, hailed the report as a significant step, stating it marks the first time in over 40 years that the Home Office acknowledged tough drug laws don't necessarily curb drug use.Reflecting on Portugal's experience, BBC Europe correspondent Matthew Price highlighted the country's dramatic reduction in heroin addiction since treating it as a health issue. Despite initial opposition, the policy has led to improved public health outcomes, including reduced rates of AIDS and hepatitis infections.In a separate report, the Home Office proposed a comprehensive ban on all psychoactive substances to combat legal highs, following Ireland's example, which exempts substances like alcohol and tobacco.

In the House of Commons, the Green MP Caroline Lucas renewed the debate on the laws against drugs, which she said were ineffective. Under current legislation, a person can be sentenced to seven years in prison for possession of a class A drug, and up to life imprisonment for selling or producing it. The Home Office report compared Britain's drug policy with that of 13 other countries. Nine of them, including Canada, Denmark and Switzerland, operate a programme of drug consumption rooms; eight, including Switzerland, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom, are experimenting with the use of pure heroin to treat addicts instead of methadone. Portugal also stood out in its dissuasion commissions, which, since 2001, have viewed possession of narcotics as a health issue. The report concluded that drug use is influenced by factors that are more complex and ambiguous than the law and its implementation. Specifically, the report showed that the health of drug users has improved in Portugal since decriminalization. The Home Office cautioned against attributing these results solely to decriminalization. Alex, a former crack and heroin addict from London, told his own story and pointed out that current laws do not deter addicts, accusing the Home Office of a backward and outdated approach, recalling the disastrous consequences of drug addiction for him and his family. The Liberal Democrat leader, Clegg, accused the Conservatives of being completely misguided, outdated, and backward in their attitude towards drugs. Prime Minister David Cameron defended the government's policy on drugs, saying that drug use was declining under his government, and that he attributed it to a well-researched programme of prevention, education and treatment. BBC home affairs correspondent, also noted the sharp divisions within the government. Dan Baker also referred to forty years of mindless rhetoric, which had rejected all other solutions. In spite of the Home Office’s insistence that its drug policy is working, Baker demands radical reforms, and he uses the report’s conclusion that strict drug laws do not necessarily reduce drug abuse. The Home Secretary admitted that the report was interesting but argued that it did not justify any particular policy change. In a separate report, the Home Office proposed a ban on all psychoactive substances in order to combat the emergence of so-called legal highs, following Ireland's example. Alcohol and tobacco are excluded. Mr. Barton, from the Action on Addiction group, expressed the need to treat addiction as a health issue rather than a criminal matter, saying that imprisonment rarely solves the problem. Despite the initial opposition to this policy, it has proved very beneficial for public health. Infections with hepatitis and AIDs have dropped.

text: Vital health services in England including stop smoking, obesity and sexual health clinics are at risk, experts are warning. Earlier this year, the Chancellor revealed plans to slash £200 million from the £2.8 billion public health budget starting in January. This budget, managed by local councils, falls outside the government's pledge to protect the health service. However, key figures in the medical community, including doctors, nurses, and senior health officials, argue that these funds are crucial for alleviating pressure on the broader NHS. A coalition of 11 organizations, such as the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges, Royal College of Nursing, NHS Confederation, and Faculty of Public Health, have collectively addressed a letter to George Osborne, urging him to reconsider the proposed cuts.The letter warns that depleting these funds would only exacerbate health disparities and increase illness within the population. It highlights that NHS England's chief executive, Simon Stevens, had justified the need for an additional £8 billion annually—promising £22 billion in efficiency savings by 2020—by emphasizing the importance of health improvements.We urge you to consider very seriously the position we have outlined, to reverse these cuts in your forthcoming spending review and give a clear commitment that no further cuts will be made to public health budgets in future years, the letter states.The Chancellor is expected to present his spending plans for this Parliament in November. Prof. John Ashton from the Faculty of Public Health commented, The legacy of a decision to cut the public health grant will be major further burdens on the health service within the foreseeable future. Avoidable ill health, heart disease, sexual health problems, unplanned pregnancies—these are the kind of things which are being affected by this irrational cut to funding.Rob Webster, CEO of the NHS Confederation, echoed these concerns, stating, There is an unprecedented consensus that we can only address the problems facing the NHS if we invest in the future of our nation's health by helping people to stay well. Open any report from any director of public health in any part of the country and you can see health inequalities and poor health putting pressure on NHS services and blighting people's lives. We need the upcoming spending review to protect public health budgets.A government spokesperson emphasized that the NHS remains a priority for investment, which will be evident in the additional funds to be announced in the spending review. However, the spokesperson also noted, Difficult decisions need to be made across government to reduce the deficit and ensure the sustainability of our public services.

text: The RMT union is staging a day of protests in support of safer Scottish railways. The rail union is urging the Scottish government to immediately outline a plan for removing Abellio from its management of the ScotRail franchise. The union argues that only a publicly-owned service can ensure safer railways in Scotland. Meanwhile, ScotRail has emphasized its significant investment, amounting to hundreds of millions of pounds, in new trains and advanced technology. Protests are currently taking place at railway stations nationwide. text: In just a few years, Wonga has become one of the country's biggest, and certainly fastest growing, money lenders. Since its inception in the fall of 2007, Wonga has issued four million small, short-term loans, totaling over a billion pounds. Despite its success, the company has faced significant criticism, with detractors labeling it a digital loan shark that preys on the financially vulnerable. In January, the firm was embroiled in controversy for advertisements urging employed students to take loans for expenses like overseas trips. By March, football club fans were demanding the removal of Wonga's ads from their teams' websites. This week, Wonga drew further attention by launching a loan service targeting cash-strapped businesses. Errol Damelin, Wonga's founder, remains unfazed by the backlash. At a recent press briefing, he appeared optimistic about his business's future and the legitimacy of short-term lending. Damelin likened Wonga to iTunes in the financial sector, stating, Wonga is a platform for the future of financial services; the digital revolution has not yet begun in financial services.Damelin compared his company to tech giants like Google, Amazon, PayPal, and Netflix, emphasizing that technology and customer data are pivotal to success. Wonga is on a multi-year and multi-decade journey to build the future of financial services, using data and technology to make objective and unprejudiced decisions, he asserted.Wonga's loan process is straightforward: customers apply online, receive a rapid decision, and funds are transferred to their bank accounts within 15 minutes. The company employs over 100 staff dedicated to technology development and site maintenance. A key feature is its extensive in-house credit scoring system, which evaluates potential borrowers.Damelin explained that Wonga's AI software analyzes up to 8,000 data points on applicants to determine loan eligibility. We have built the world's first completely straight-through processing system for credit, he noted, highlighting the automation for both individuals and business owners seeking cash advances. This eliminates the need for traditional bank loan applications for short-term cash flow issues.Wonga's technology filters out high-risk applicants, currently rejecting about 66% for poor creditworthiness. Applicants must have a regular income, a bank account, a debit card, a mobile phone, and a good credit record. Consequently, only about 7% of Wonga borrowers have defaulted, a lower rate than the 10% default rate on credit card lending.The credit scoring process extends beyond simple inquiries, utilizing technology to gauge customer interactions with the website. For example, borrowers use online sliders to set loan amounts and durations. Wonga found that those who immediately select the maximum loan amount, currently £400 for 30 days for first-time applicants, are more prone to default.Damelin argued, Our decisions are always objective; we are not subject to the same imperfections as traditional lenders, where biases can affect credit access. Regarding costs, Wonga is transparent about its staggering 4,214% APR, displayed prominently on its homepage. Borrowers are informed of exact repayment amounts and schedules. Damelin contended that for Wonga's target market, speed, convenience, and transparency are more critical than price. We have dared to ask hard questions, like how to make loans instant and available 24/7, and how to be totally transparent, he said.Wonga counters criticism by highlighting customer satisfaction, boasting a net-promoter score over 90%, indicating most users would recommend its services. In contrast, many banks have negative scores, with even top-rated banks like First Direct scoring below 50%.Despite this, the payday lending industry faces scrutiny. The Office of Fair Trading (OFT) announced in February a renewed examination of payday lenders' practices, concerned about unethical selling, such as targeting loans at those unable to repay and allowing debt rollovers.Wonga distances itself from the less reputable end of payday lending. Damelin aims to expand by offering loans to small businesses facing short-term cash shortages. Financial services is a challenging place to innovate, so we are responding where we can deliver a better service, he said. Businesses have been crying out for a solution available 24/7 to solve relatively small, short-term cashflow problems.
