text: A senior Labour MP has called for its leadership contest to be paused over fears it has been infiltrated by supporters of other parties. Barry Sheerman has claimed that individuals from a range of political affiliations, including the Socialist Workers Party, the Green Party, the Conservatives, and UKIP, have registered to participate in the Labour leadership election. However, Labour has dismissed allegations that hard left and Conservative supporters are rallying behind Jeremy Corbyn, a prominent left-wing candidate. A Labour spokeswoman has firmly rejected calls to suspend the leadership contest, assuring that a very robust system is in place to thwart fraudulent and malicious registrations. She emphasized that additional checks are being conducted to ensure compliance with the rules. An exclusion list is currently being compiled to bar those who have previously opposed Labour or assisted others in doing so. According to the BBC, up to 1,000 applications have already been rejected.In response to Sheerman's claims, one of Corbyn's supporters labeled the suggestion as ridiculous. Backbench MP Diane Abbott argued that such comments stem from individuals who think their side will lose, adding, This election is being fought under rules that were agreed by the whole party last year.These rules, introduced by former leader Ed Miliband, allow individuals to register as supporters for £3 and participate in the vote, provided they affirm their support for Labour's aims and values. Corbyn's campaign has gained significant momentum, prompting warnings from fellow candidates Andy Burnham, Yvette Cooper, and Liz Kendall about the party potentially veering too far left.Sheerman's remarks echo concerns from backbench MPs Graham Stringer and John Mann, who have also called for the leadership contest to be paused. Sheerman, the Huddersfield MP and former select committee chairman, who has served since 1979, told the BBC that a substantial number of people are joining Labour with malign intentions to influence the leadership election. He described the process as being in real trouble, leaving Labour MPs dumbfounded by its execution.Labour's acting leader, Harriet Harman, has reached out to the party's MPs via email, providing a list of new members in their constituencies and asking them to identify any suspicious names. Sheerman admitted that while he might recognize some usual suspects, many others would likely go undetected. He denied that his concerns were influenced by his support for Liz Kendall, asserting that he has previously opposed entryism and believes the current system is flawed.Labour maintains that the verification process is ongoing, with ballot papers yet to be distributed. Recently, the party rejected an application from Conservative MP Tim Loughton, who attempted to register as a supporter to expose perceived flaws in the system. Liz Kendall, speaking on BBC Radio 4's The World at One, expressed her approval of the increased interest in Labour, stating she had not encountered any issues of concern. The important thing is that the checks are put in place, she noted.The Trade Unionist and Socialist Coalition, which fielded candidates in 135 constituencies in May's general election and includes the Socialist Workers Party, dismissed infiltration reports as Blairite manoeuvres against Corbyn's campaign. The coalition clarified that one of its members, former councillor Chris Flood, was incorrectly identified in a Times report as having signed up.Meanwhile, Labour's former communications director, Alastair Campbell, warned that the party could be finished if Corbyn wins. In a blog post, he cautioned of a car crash scenario and urged supporters to back anyone but Corbyn, highlighting the difficulty of replacing him if he were to win and Labour faced challenges in the polls.

text: The UN special envoy for Syria, Staffan de Mistura, says he is appalled and shocked that rebels in Aleppo are targeting civilians in the city. In the past 48 hours, relentless and indiscriminate rocket attacks in western Aleppo have resulted in numerous civilian casualties, according to Mr. de Mistura. He suggested these assaults might constitute war crimes. On Friday, rebel forces launched an offensive to break the government’s siege on eastern Aleppo, where approximately 275,000 residents have been trapped for months.Since September, Aleppo has endured intense bombardment by Russian and Syrian government aircraft, leading to over 2,700 casualties, both dead and injured. Although Russia paused its air strikes on October 18 to facilitate the evacuation of the sick and wounded, few have taken the opportunity to leave.On Sunday, Syrian state media accused rebels of deploying chemical weapons in government-controlled areas of Aleppo. However, a spokesman from a rebel faction refuted this, asserting that the rebels do not possess such weapons, as reported by the Associated Press. The Sana news agency reported that 35 individuals in Dahiyet al-Assad and Hamdaniya experienced symptoms like shortness of breath and numbness.Activists report that since the rebel attacks commenced, over 40 civilians have died in western Aleppo, including 16 children, according to the UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights. Additionally, it noted the deaths of 55 soldiers and 64 rebels, though these figures remain unconfirmed.Rebels from outside Aleppo are leading this new offensive, focusing on Hamdaniya, a district currently under the control of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad’s forces. The rebel coalition includes Jabhat Fateh al-Sham, formerly known as the Nusra Front, alongside Ahrar al-Sham and other Islamist groups.This marks the rebels' second attempt to break the siege. In August, they briefly opened a corridor between the eastern and western parts of Aleppo after the government had fully encircled them in July. Once Syria's economic powerhouse, Aleppo has been a battleground divided between opposing forces since 2012.

text: Undercover journalist Mazher Mahmood plotted to change a witness statement in a case against pop singer Tulisa Contostavlos, the Old Bailey has heard. The infamous reporter known as the Fake Sheikh, along with his driver Alan Smith, stand accused of conspiring to pervert the course of justice, charges they both deny. The case against singer Tulisa Contostavlos, who had faced allegations of supplying cocaine, fell apart in 2014. Prosecutors argue that Mr. Mahmood had a vested interest in her prosecution.The court was told that Miss Contostavlos became a target of the so-called king of the sting, who masqueraded as a prominent film producer offering her a role in a Hollywood film. She allegedly arranged for Mr. Mahmood to purchase half an ounce of cocaine for £800 through one of her contacts. This led to her arrest and charge for involvement in the supply of a class A drug after Mr. Mahmood presented evidence to the police.Mr. Mahmood, 53, from Purley, south London, and Mr. Smith, 67, from Dereham, Norfolk, are accused of conspiring to alter a favorable police statement Mr. Smith had made regarding Miss Contostavlos's defense. During the trial's opening, Sarah Forshaw QC addressed the jury, stating, The hearing in June 2014 effectively put Mr. Mahmood and his journalistic methods on trial.She highlighted Mr. Mahmood's self-proclaimed title as the king of sting and noted his boasting in a book about numerous convictions he claimed responsibility for. Forshaw argued that if it were proven he acted improperly as an agent provocateur, persuading Miss Contostavlos to act against her nature, his credibility and the likelihood of conviction could be severely compromised.Miss Forshaw revealed that Miss Contostavlos had expressed disapproval of hard drugs to Mr. Smith, a statement that was later altered. Mr. Smith initially told police he recalled Miss Contostavlos speaking negatively about cocaine, mentioning a family member's dependence on it. However, a day later, he sought to retract that part of his statement, the court heard.It is alleged that within those 24 hours, Mr. Smith sent his interview copy to Mr. Mahmood, and they exchanged several texts and calls. During a pre-trial hearing at Southwark Crown Court in June 2014, Mr. Mahmood testified under oath, denying any discussion with Mr. Smith about Miss Contostavlos's comments. Every school is categorized by color, ranging from green to yellow, orange, and red. This marks the third year that this system of grading schools has been in use. Last year, 333 primary and secondary schools achieved the top category, green, showing a 41% increase from the previous year. The number of schools in the red category, those needing the most improvement, decreased from 81 to 58. The Welsh Government believes that this categorization system helps identify schools that need the most assistance, allowing them to offer support and guidance. The report highlighted that seven out of ten primary schools are good or better, but this figure drops to four out of ten for secondary schools. Teacher unions have generally given cautious approval to the system, as long as it is part of a broader evaluation framework. Rob Williams from the headteachers' union NAHT Cymru stated, We still believe that for the categorization system to work best, it needs to be part of a broader system coordinated to improve schools. As Estyn highlighted in their recent report, performance variation still exists across Wales, and the additional focus on schools in the orange and red categories does not hide the funding disparities between schools. We know that the Welsh Government is listening to school leaders and their concerns about a system that uses such data in isolation without recognizing individual pupil progress while at school. The National School Categorization System was jointly agreed upon by education authorities and the Welsh Government, with the understanding that the system's purpose is neither to label schools nor to create simplistic league tables.

text: Nurses and midwives who complete their training in hospitals outside Europe will now face shorter tests to check they are fit to work in the UK. The Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) has unveiled plans to overhaul the assessment process for overseas-trained nurses and midwives, introducing a computer-based exam and simulated clinical scenario tests. These new assessments are set to replace the existing requirement of a minimum three-month supervised practice period.However, nurse leaders are calling for more detailed information to ensure these new checks are thorough and adequate. Currently, nurses and midwives trained outside the UK constitute about 10% of the registered workforce. Each year, approximately 1,000 nurses from outside the European Economic Area, primarily from Australia, India, and the Philippines, come to work in the UK.The NMC cites the change as a response to the current system's inefficiency, where supervised placements can extend from three months to a year, failing to meet the urgent demand for healthcare professionals. The regulator describes the current process as not agile enough for employers who need to recruit quickly. Additionally, there have been reports of applicants struggling to secure spots in these programs due to limited availability.Scheduled to commence in the autumn, the new testing system includes two parts. Similar assessments have already been implemented by other healthcare regulators, as noted by the NMC. The council emphasizes that this approach will ensure that hundreds of nurses and midwives trained overseas are evaluated in a proportionate and robust way to safeguard the public.Jackie Smith, the NMC's chief executive, clarified, The new system will not replace the need for employers to ensure that the staff they recruit display the behaviors, skills, and knowledge necessary for the specific role to which they are recruited, and provide further support and development as required.Janet Davies, executive director of nursing at the Royal College of Nursing, commented, Healthcare in the UK relies on the hard work and dedication of many nurses who trained overseas. These proposals may well form part of a more robust and consistent mechanism for ensuring that nurses who work in the UK are equipped to practice here. However, we need more information about how nurses will be evaluated under this system before we can determine its adequacy.Davies further stressed the importance of recruiting nurses for the right reasons and providing them with adequate support once they arrive, noting, Too often, nurses are recruited from overseas to fill short-term gaps and given inadequate support to care for patients well.Official statistics indicate that around 67,000 nurses and midwives trained outside Europe currently hold NMC registration. This is in addition to the workforce of over 600,000 nursing and midwifery staff who have trained within Europe and registered with the UK regulator.

text: Plans to help nearly 100,000 small businesses due to be hit by changes to rates next month are being considered by Communities Secretary Sajid Javid. A looming cliff edge threatens approximately 25,000 firms due to the new business rates revaluation, as reported by the ratings agency CVS. In response, CVS presented a series of proposals to Secretary of State Sajid Javid during a meeting on Wednesday, aiming to alleviate the burden on small businesses.The Treasury is under pressure to devise additional support for these firms following significant backlash from the business community. Although ministers have assured that the revaluation—the first since 2010—will result in unchanged or reduced rates for three-quarters of businesses, there is mounting pressure on Mr. Javid and Chancellor Philip Hammond to assist those in regions where rental values have soared.Critics argue that the current system disproportionately benefits large retailers and online companies at the expense of high street shops. During the discussions with Mr. Javid, CVS proposed a relief package potentially worth up to £150 million. The government is anticipated to introduce measures in the upcoming Budget to soften the revaluation's impact.Mark Rigby, CEO of CVS, remarked, The Secretary of State was clearly in listening mode and it was evident to me that he was acutely aware of the potential impact that the revaluation will bring to some communities and the anger felt by small businesses, particularly the retail and leisure sectors. He was clear in his determination to find a meaningful, targeted solution to ease the financial burden for those most in need ahead of the April tax changes.Prime Minister Theresa May, during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, hinted that Mr. Hammond would tackle the issue in the Budget. She stated that both Mr. Hammond and Mr. Javid had been tasked with ensuring that the support provided is suitable and available for the most affected cases, adding that she expects the Chancellor to elaborate on this in the Budget next week.Currently, the government has implemented a transitional relief system valued at £3.6 billion to gradually introduce the increases over five years. Additional measures might include a package akin to the previous retail relief scheme, which provided £1,500 to firms before it concluded in April last year. The threshold for tapered relief could also be raised as part of these efforts.

text: The publisher of GQ magazine has been found guilty of contempt of court over its coverage of the News of the World (NoW) phone-hacking trial. The High Court has determined that GQ magazine created a substantial risk of seriously impeding or prejudicing the trial of Rebekah Brooks, Andy Coulson, and others. This ruling came after a GQ article, published by Conde Nast Publications Ltd, was said to have potentially influenced jurors by suggesting that the owners of News of the World (NoW) were aware of or directed phone hacking activities.Rebekah Brooks was ultimately acquitted of all charges. In contrast, Andy Coulson was found guilty of conspiracy to hack phones and received an 18-month prison sentence. Lord Thomas, the Lord Chief Justice, announced that a future hearing would determine the penalty for Conde Nast.The contentious article, penned by Michael Wolff, was featured in the April 2014 edition of the men's magazine, during the fourth month of the trial at the Old Bailey. The Attorney General, represented by Andrew Caldecott QC, initiated legal action against Conde Nast. Caldecott argued that the article implied Rupert Murdoch, owner of News International, was likely involved in voicemail interception and should have faced prosecution. He stated that this suggestion was absent from the prosecution's case in court.Furthermore, Caldecott pointed out that the piece insinuated defense lawyers had a hidden agenda to protect Murdoch's interests and obscure his involvement. In defense, Adrienne Page QC, representing Conde Nast, described the article as a highly subjective, personal and impressionistic sketch based on the experience of visiting the trial courtroom.However, Lord Thomas, alongside Mrs Justice Nicola Davies, concluded that the article was seriously prejudicial. Following the decision, Attorney General Jeremy Wright QC emphasized the rarity of pursuing legal action against publishers. He remarked, The GQ article contravened the fundamental principle of our criminal justice system: everyone is entitled to a fair trial, and it is not for the press to decide who deserves this protection.

Lord Thomas, the Lord Chief Justice, announced that a further hearing would be held to determine the penalty to be imposed on Conde Nast. In her defense, Adrienne Page, defending Condé Nast, argued that the article was a highly subjective, personal, and impressionistic sketch of her visit to the court. She said there was no suggestion in the case that the defense was secretly protecting Murdoch’s interests or hiding his involvement. But Lord Thomas, with Mrs. Justice Nicola Davies, decided that the article was seriously prejudicial. The article in GQ violates the fundamental principle of the judicial system, he says: that everyone is entitled to a fair trial. And it is not up to the press to decide who deserves that protection.

text: A major children's musical drama is being made in Northern Ireland by the Disney Channel. The Disney Channel is set to premiere a new 10-part series titled The Lodge this September. Nearly 100 cast and crew members are involved in the production, which is being filmed across various locations in County Down, Northern Ireland. David Levine, head of the Disney Channel in the UK and Ireland, remarked that this marks the first time such a large-scale production has been brought to Northern Ireland by the channel. Northern Ireland is typically associated with swords and dragons, but we're introducing songs and dancing, Levine commented. Our investment is significant, with production, post-production, set construction, and filming happening in multiple locations.Filming is primarily taking place at Montalto Lodge near Ballynahinch, with additional scenes being shot in Castlewellan and Tollymore Forest, close to Newcastle. The show features a cast of 22 and a crew of 67, with 46 crew members hailing from Northern Ireland, including local producer Raymond Lau.The Lodge follows the story of Skye, a 15-year-old girl who, along with her father, moves from the city to manage their family's country lodge. Skye discovers her father's plans to sell the business and has the summer to change his mind. Sophie Simnett, known for her role in the BBC series Dickensian, stars as Skye. She shared, There are numerous sub-plots, filled with activity. Besides singing and dancing, I had to learn rock climbing for a scene where I go on a date, and kayaking for a group scene.Thomas Doherty, who has appeared in the TV series Dracula and the film Hercules, plays Sean. He's fun-loving, sporty, and has a romantic interest in Skye, Doherty explained. I initially trained in musical theatre, so landing this role was fantastic. We've had extensive training with choreography and singing coaches, making it an enjoyable experience.Filming for The Lodge is expected to wrap up before summer, with its debut on the Disney Channel in both the UK and the Republic of Ireland. Following its initial release, the series is anticipated to air on the channel across other parts of Europe.

text: On a small yet busy lane in central Bangalore is a three-storey white house with a bright orange gate. In the bustling city of Bangalore, often hailed as India's start-up capital, a seemingly ordinary property is nurturing the next generation of business innovators. This southern Indian metropolis, known for its thriving computer industry, attracts entrepreneurs from across the globe seeking inspiration, investment, and workspace. However, these ambitious individuals also need a place to stay—a challenge when the typical hotel room or dormitory doesn't suit their entrepreneurial spirit.Enter the Construkt Start-up Hostel, a white house with an orange gate that opened its doors in May. It proudly claims the title of India's first start-up hostel, offering a 20-bed haven where budding entrepreneurs can live among peers, exchanging ideas around the clock. More than half the hostel's bunk beds are occupied during my visit, and alongside essential amenities like a kitchen and laundry, it provides the indispensable wi-fi and coffee maker.One wall on the ground floor serves as a chalkboard calendar, listing upcoming start-up and technology events in the city. These include a boot camp for pitching to investors and a data analysis conference. The founders of Construkt explain that this is part of their effort to integrate residents into Bangalore's vibrant start-up ecosystem.The hostel's residents are a mix of men and women, some still refining their business concepts, others conducting market research. Krishna Elakara, a 42-year-old of Indian origin recently living in Australia, is developing a fitness training product. In a cozy mini-library on the first floor, he shares his reasons for coming to Bangalore: All the elements you need to put together a start-up, they're here, he explains. I'm staying at this hostel to build my network. Other accommodations might have tourists, but here, you meet like-minded individuals.In the semi-circular living room downstairs, an open hack session is underway. Residents gather to critique each other's business ideas. Krishna is first to present, facing questions like What's unique about your idea? and Who would you partner with? Shashikiran Rao, 36, a hostel founder, smiles as he describes the process: We take the idea and tear it apart, let everyone jump in and poke holes into it. We're very good at it. The idea is to help entrepreneurs develop their plans.Next up is Aashna Kaur, a 24-year-old with a business administration degree and a year of consulting experience with start-ups. She's exploring two business ideas: technology for solo female travelers or products to encourage more Indian women in the workforce. Having stayed at Construkt for over a week, Aashna values the networking opportunities over the cost, which is about $14 a night or $220 a month. I could find a cheap hotel at the same rate, but it's the connections here that matter, she says.Besides aspiring entrepreneurs, Construkt also attracts those still deciding their career paths. Prerna Gautam, a university student from Mumbai, is interning at Microsoft Accelerator in Bangalore, a program that aids entrepreneurs in bridging the gap between ideas and execution. Though uncertain about her future career, her time in Bangalore is drawing her toward the start-up scene.As Construkt plans to open a second hostel, Sudhir Singh, an analyst from PricewaterhouseCoopers, acknowledges the concept's niche appeal. There's definitely a space for something like this, but I don't know if it'll catch on like wildfire, he comments. Aspiring entrepreneurs may flock here for networking, but established ones might not unless innovative programs are offered.Back at Construkt, the atmosphere is lively. Music plays, food and drinks are shared, and conversations about business, technology, and politics fill the air. Once seen as a risky venture, starting a company in India is now almost expected of graduates. Though challenges like securing funding and hiring persist, they do little to deter India's enterprising youth.

text: Jurassic World has become the first film to take more than $500m (£322m) at the global box office on its opening weekend. In the United States, Jurassic World raked in an impressive $204.6 million (£132 million) over its opening weekend, making it the second-largest debut in history, just behind 2012's Marvel's The Avengers, which earned $207.4 million (£133.8 million). What contributed to this film's remarkable success? Chris Pratt, who has transitioned from supporting roles and comedic stints in the cult US sitcom Parks and Recreation, has emerged as one of Hollywood's most bankable stars. In 2014, he headlined two of the top five grossing films at the US box office: The Lego Movie and Guardians of the Galaxy. Pratt's unique blend of charm, vulnerability, and humor allows him to bring a human touch to even the most effects-heavy blockbusters. He demonstrated this talent in Guardians of the Galaxy, where his co-stars included a talking raccoon and a giant animated tree. Defying expectations, the film grossed $774 million (£499 million) worldwide, securing its place as the third highest-grossing film of 2014. Not to mention, Pratt's good looks haven't hurt his appeal either.China, with its film market ranking as the second largest globally after the US, imposes a strict limit on foreign films, allowing only 34 per year. However, securing a spot in China can significantly boost box office earnings. Unlike most Hollywood blockbusters, Jurassic World had a simultaneous release in China and the US, contributing to its massive success. The film debuted in 66 international markets, bringing in $307.2 million (£198 million), with China alone accounting for $100.8 million (£65 million)—nearly 20% of its total earnings.When the original Jurassic Park premiered, Imax screens were a rarity, typically reserved for short films, documentaries, and theme park attractions. Today, with approximately 800 Imax screens worldwide, the opportunity to witness dinosaurs larger than life has proven irresistible. The added thrill of seeing a T-Rex in 3D has enticed audiences to pay premium prices, significantly boosting box office revenues. According to box office analysts Rentrak, nearly half of Jurassic World's US earnings came from 3D screenings.Steven Spielberg's 1993 blockbuster Jurassic Park holds a cherished place in the hearts of many cinema enthusiasts. It set a new benchmark for CGI and became a defining film of the 1990s, igniting the imaginations of a generation. Actress Bryce Dallas Howard reminisced to the BBC, I was 12 when Jurassic Park came out and it just blew me away. I remember watching it and thinking, 'I'm seeing real dinosaurs right now.' It felt so real. Her co-star Chris Pratt shared a similar sentiment, recalling, I was 13 years old and I felt the same. I had complete Jurassic-mania and saw it twice in one weekend.Following two sequels that failed to replicate the original's success both critically and commercially, fans eagerly anticipated that the new film would recapture the magic, thrills, and horror of Spielberg's classic. Many parents brought their children along, hoping to share the wonder they experienced decades ago.

text: Scottish rugby suffered two body blows this week and, rather like boxer Ricky Burns who drew with his opponent after getting one heck of a hiding from opponent Raymundo Beltran, it's a little battered, a little broken and in need of time off the canvas. The rugby world has been rocked by two unexpected developments: the first positive steroids test in Scottish rugby history and the ongoing debate over the fairness of team qualifications for the Heineken Cup. However, let's focus on the former and leave the Heineken Cup controversy for another time.Sam Chalmers, son of rugby legend Craig Chalmers, has publicly apologized for his actions, admitting he sourced the banned substance online. His explanation echoes the familiar lone wolf narrative. Yet, questions linger: Was Chalmers truly acting alone, or did he discuss these substances with fellow players?Coaches involved in youth rugby report a troubling trend: the combination of weight training and supplements is becoming commonplace. The pressure to bulk up and gain weight is undeniable. While the rugby field has remained unchanged for 150 years, players have evolved, with the game now focusing more on physical power than agility.However, the notion that players feel compelled to resort to steroids is unacceptable. Using steroids is unequivocally cheating. Purchasing them is a conscious decision to break the rules, banking on evading drug testers. Some players may have considered steroids but ultimately rejected them, understanding that rugby may no longer be a sport for all body types.Coaches observe that young athletes often consume supplements before, during, and after gym sessions. This reliance might lead them to believe that natural nutrition is insufficient, nudging them toward illegal aids like steroids. But can players achieve the desired physique through diet alone?According to the International Rugby Board (IRB), 1,542 drug tests were conducted in 2012, covering all IRB tournaments and events. This resulted in 21 anti-doping violations, about 1.36% of the total. Some offenders, like Chalmers, were caught using stanozolol, the steroid linked to disgraced sprinter Ben Johnson.The 2011 World Anti-Doping Agency figures show 5,553 rugby drug tests globally, with 61 violations, over 1%. It suggests a higher incidence of doping in lower leagues or among those trying to break into the system, though this remains speculative.Reflecting on my time in South Africa during the 1995 Rugby World Cup, I recall the surge in schoolboys seeking steroid prescriptions, often with parental support. Could such a scenario unfold here?Chalmers belongs to the vulnerable demographic of young players aspiring to professional rugby. His path will be challenging, but adversity is part of the game. Many before him, caught in scandals like Bloodgate or drug violations, have faced similar trials. This is a test for Chalmers. He must serve his time and then return to the sport.One can't help but wonder if Chalmers was truly alone in this. Are there younger players who haven't been caught yet? What pressures drive players to consider steroids?You can join the conversation with John Beattie on Twitter @bbcjohnbeattie.

text: England footballer Adam Johnson asked a girl for a naked picture and offered to meet her for money, a court has heard. text: Donald Trump's plan to erect a huge sea wall at his Irish golf course has been withdrawn in the light of stiff opposition. The initial proposal for a protective barrier at the Trump International Hotel and Golf Links in Doonbeg, County Clare, highlighted the threat of rising sea levels due to climate change. However, environmental activists strongly opposed the two-mile development, arguing it endangered the rare whorl snail, Vertigo angustior. A revised plan featuring a smaller wall is anticipated soon.Acquired in 2014, the Doonbeg resort faced severe erosion of its sand dunes after storms that year. In response, the Trump organization submitted plans to Clare County Council for a two-mile (2.8km) limestone wall, intended to mitigate the sea's impact. The proposed structure, standing 4 meters high and 20 meters wide, would have required approximately 200,000 tonnes of rock and cost €10 million.The original application emphasized the wall's role in protecting against erosion exacerbated by global warming, which increases sea levels, storm frequency, and wave energy. Additionally, it claimed the coastal protection would benefit the local community. While many residents and businesses supported the project, environmental groups raised concerns about its impact on the protected snail species.Six months ago, the local authority requested more information from the Trump group regarding the wall's effect on the Carrowmore dunes conservation area, but received no response. We got notification from the applicant yesterday that they were withdrawing their application, a council spokesman told BBC News. The Trump group cited the lengthy planning process as a reason for withdrawing.In a statement, the organization noted that the resort contributes approximately €6 million annually to the local economy. While expansion plans are under consideration, they stressed the necessity of coastal protection. The realization of these plans, however, is fundamentally dependent on the provision of adequate protection from coastal erosion, the statement read. Since 2002, an estimated 15 to 20 meters of dune face has eroded, and attempts at soft coastline management have failed.The group now plans a scaled-down version of the wall, extending 900 meters in two sections. This design will involve metal sheet piles inserted into the golf course ground, surrounded by limestone boulders. Some campaigners suggest that the international attention on Donald Trump's proposed wall on the US-Mexico border negatively impacted the Doonbeg plans. You could tell that they were upset, because there were already analogies being made with the Mexican wall, said Tony Lowes from Friends of the Irish Environment, who met with the Trump team. You could tell that they didn't like that because they could sense that this could turn into something more than a little planning battle in Ireland.A petition organized by the surfing group Save the Waves garnered signatures from around 100,000 people worldwide opposing the original plans. Campaigners argue that criticism of President-elect Trump's perceived environmental indifference did not significantly fuel opposition. In this case, I think the absurdity of the proposal, the outrage at what was about to be inflicted was so great, that no one could look at the proposal without being shocked, said Lowes. I have very rarely seen an environmental case that looked so absolutely horrific.The new proposal is expected to be submitted before Christmas, with a decision likely by March next year. Analysts will scrutinize the documents for any further mentions of climate change and the impact of rising seas. Follow Matt on Twitter and Facebook for updates.

text: A new loan scheme is to be offered to Scottish farmers to prevent a repeat of the problems caused by delays to Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) payments. Rural Affairs Secretary Fergus Ewing has acknowledged that the IT system responsible for delays in farm payments is still not fully operational. Ewing admitted that next year's payments are not risk-free but announced that farmers and crofters can apply for loans covering 80% of their total entitlement. This new scheme has been welcomed by the farming union NFU Scotland, which believes it will offer farmers much-needed clarity and certainty.However, opposition parties argue that the loan scheme is an implicit admission that the issues with the CAP payment system remain unresolved. The CAP Futures programme was designed to streamline Scotland's rural payment process, but the introduction of a new IT system by the Scottish government led to significant delays in disbursing funds to farmers.In May, Audit Scotland, the public spending watchdog, reported that these delays severely impacted farmers, many of whom were already facing financial hardships due to low milk prices and severe flooding. Speaking at Holyrood, Mr. Ewing reported that 17,744 out of 18,479 eligible businesses have received their 2015 payments, with most remaining cases expected to be settled by the October 15 deadline. He also expressed confidence that the 2016 payments would be substantially completed by next June's deadline.Ewing emphasized that the new loan scheme is designed to provide farmers and crofters with certainty over the winter, aiming to inject up to £300 million into the rural economy, safeguarding jobs and local agricultural businesses. He stated, Having learned lessons from the 2015 CAP payment round, I am committed to providing as much certainty as possible, not just for farmers and crofters, but for our rural communities' wider economy. Farmers won't have to wait until 2017 for their CAP entitlement. Letters will be sent out by the end of the month, inviting applications. Those who apply by the October 12 deadline will receive a loan of 80% of their entitlement in November.NFU Scotland president Allan Bowie responded positively, noting the impact on the rural economy. Knowing that up to 80% of your support package will be delivered in early November gives clarity and certainty to farm businesses, he said. The flawed 2015 payment run continues to cast a shadow, and the cabinet secretary has once again apologized for ongoing issues. We will keep pressuring the Scottish government until all 2015 payments are settled.Peter Chapman, Scottish Conservative rural affairs spokesman, criticized the loan scheme as an admission of unresolved IT issues. He can't deliver 100% payments in December as expected, so he offers an 80% loan for November, Chapman said. These loans signify failure. This won't restore trust among farmers, who have lost patience with the SNP on this matter. Mr. Ewing should agree to a parliamentary inquiry.Mike Rumbles of the Scottish Liberal Democrats dismissed Ewing's claim of injecting £300 million into the rural economy as complete nonsense, arguing that farmers should already be receiving full payments if the system worked properly. Today's statement is a dreadful admission of the Scottish government's failure, Rumbles said. The 80% loan plan will be available to all applicants, but the average farm business will still be over £6,000 short, with no end in sight.

text: European banking stocks have fallen sharply despite the victory of the pro-bailout New Democracy party in Greece's elections on Sunday. The election results in Greece have sparked a glimmer of hope that the nation will adhere to austerity measures and retain its position in the eurozone. However, analysts caution that significant uncertainties linger.Across Europe, banking shares took a hit, with Germany's Commerzbank and France's BNP Paribas both declining by 4.4%. Spanish bond yields remained erratic, climbing past the critical 7% threshold.The broader European stock markets presented a mixed picture. France's Cac 40 ended the day down 0.7%, while Germany's Dax edged up by 0.3%, both having initially risen by 1%. London's FTSE 100 managed a 0.3% gain after early losses, whereas New York's Dow Jones dipped by 0.2%.In the banking sector, Deutsche Bank saw a 1.1% drop, and Credit Agricole fell 3.4%. In the UK, Royal Bank of Scotland and Lloyds Banking Group were the biggest losers on the FTSE 100, plummeting 5.0% and 3.6%, respectively.Spain, considered at high risk of requiring a full international bailout, experienced its 10-year bond yield soaring to a new peak. After initially dipping to 6.767%, it surged to 7.144%. Italy's 10-year bond yield also rose, reaching 6.08% from an earlier 5.85%. The main stock indexes in Spain and Italy declined as well.Spain's Ibex closed with a 3.0% loss, and Italy's FTSE MIB dropped 2.9%. In currency markets, the euro fell slightly against the dollar, settling at $1.2579 from $1.2637 late Friday.Earlier, Asian markets showed robust gains. Japan's Nikkei 225 and South Korea's Kospi both climbed 1.8%, while Australia's ASX 200 increased by 1.9%.Antonis Samaras, leader of Greece's New Democracy party, declared on Sunday, The Greek people voted today to stay on the European course and remain in the eurozone. There will be no more adventures. Greece's place in Europe will not be put in doubt.Adrian Slack, head of equities at Bastion Capital, remarked that the initial reaction to the Greek election results was too euphoric, adding, Fundamentally, the problems [in Greece and the eurozone] haven't changed. Peter Schiff from Euro Pacific Capital questioned, How long is it going to take for people to worry about Spain again?Spain's borrowing costs have soared to euro-era records, reflecting lenders' skepticism about Madrid's debt repayment capabilities. Last week, Moody's downgraded Spain's credit rating to just above junk.Yet, some analysts remain hopeful. Masayuki Doshida, a senior market analyst at Rakuten Securities, noted that Greece's New Democracy victory temporarily eased eurozone fears, expressing, There'll be a definite sense of relief spreading around today. David Lennox of Fat Prophets told the BBC that the worst of the Greek crisis might be over, suggesting, We think that early punters are already taking the view that a floor has been put under the crisis for now.Global investors closely monitored Greece's elections, as did eurozone leaders. Such a scenario risked spreading economic turmoil across the eurozone and globally.However, the BBC's business editor, Robert Peston, highlighted that Greece's new government faces a formidable challenge. He noted that bankers indicated Greece needs eurozone governments and the European Central Bank to write off a big slug of what they are owed.

text: Researchers attempting to learn why people snack are to study the health and habits of more than 100 Scots. As part of a Scottish government initiative to combat obesity, Aberdeen's Rowett Institute of Nutrition and Health is embarking on a study that seeks to recruit 120 volunteers for a week-long monitoring project. The research team will track participants' heart rates, activity levels, and snacking habits using heart sensors, GPS devices, and electronic diaries.The study aims to uncover connections between brain executive functions and snacking behavior. Dr. David McMinn, who leads the study, explained the modern challenge: We live in an environment where snack foods are readily available, and where desk jobs and labour-saving devices mean that we are less active than in previous generations. Because our environment makes it easy to consume high-calorie snack foods and spend long periods of time inactive, eating well and being active requires considerable self-regulation. It requires us to make an effort, such as deciding not to snack in order to maintain a healthy weight.Dr. McMinn further elaborated on the focus of the research: We are particularly interested in the way food choices and physical activity behaviours are linked to psychological processes in the brain called the 'executive functions'. We use executive functions to achieve goals, for example, planning actions in advance, solving problems, ignoring distractions and resisting temptations. The executive functions can be depleted if used intensively, or due to particularly stressful situations. We are interested to know if reductions in executive functions are associated with behaviours such as snacking on unhealthy foods or sedentary behaviour.The researchers are seeking volunteers over the age of 18 who are not taking beta-blockers and can visit the university's health sciences building at the Foresterhill campus for psychological testing before the monitoring begins. Dr. McMinn highlighted the study's objective: Information from the different monitoring devices will be used to identify where periods of snacking, activity, sedentary behaviour, and stress occur. The aim is to try to understand why people snack, because we all know that sticking to a healthy diet is easier said than done.

text: The head of MI5, Sir Jonathan Evans, is to step down from the post next month, Home Secretary Theresa May has said. text: Every year charitable trusts are set up in memory of people who have met violent or tragic deaths. Some charitable organizations, like the Stephen Lawrence Charitable Trust—founded following the racially motivated murder of Stephen Lawrence—grow into major entities, celebrating milestones like their 20th anniversary. Others, however, briefly thrive before folding. What drives families affected by tragedy to establish charities or trusts, and how does this endeavor aid them in their grief?The Williams family from Wellington, Shropshire, faced an unimaginable loss when their teenage daughter, Georgia, disappeared in May. Her body was discovered near the Nant-y-Garth pass, Wrexham, days after she went missing. Jamie Reynolds, a 22-year-old from Avondale Road, Wellington, has been charged with her murder.In the wake of Georgia's death, friends and community members quickly raised funds for a memorial bench. The overwhelming response led to the creation of the Georgia Williams Trust, aimed at ensuring her memory endures. It's been heartwarming to see people getting involved and reading their supportive comments, Georgia’s father, Steve Williams, expressed. We've found comfort in how people remember her.The trust's mission is to provide young people in Telford and Wrekin with opportunities for enrichment activities like canoeing, rock climbing, and volunteering. Richard Langton, chair of the trust, acknowledges its role in supporting the family and is committed to maintaining a close relationship with them.The Charity Commission notes that when new charities are established, particularly in response to tragedies, they often encounter an initial surge of generosity. Over time, however, donations tend to decrease, challenging the sustainability of smaller charities. The Commission advises founders to consider long-term viability to avoid disappointing beneficiaries.A West Mercia Police inspector hopes the charity offers the family a positive focus during this difficult period and ensures Georgia’s legacy continues. We’re working closely with the family, including trustee Scarlet Williams, Georgia's sister, to fulfill their vision for the charity, the inspector stated. Mr. Langton emphasized the importance of building a charity that can endure beyond these painful months, urging the trust's 5,200 Facebook followers and 500 Twitter followers to engage and participate.Ann Oakes-Odger, who lost her son Westley in a stabbing incident in Colchester in 2005, understands the desperate emotion parents feel after losing a child. She found solace in creating knifecrimes.org and Victims' Advocate, organizations aimed at helping others facing similar tragedies. Setting up these organizations helped after losing Westley, she shared. I knew a void would follow the trial if there wasn’t something to focus on in his memory.Karen Prior from Shropshire also turned to charity following the loss of her two-year-old son Lewis, who died awaiting a heart transplant. A collection at his funeral inspired Karen and her husband, Colin, to establish a foundation in his memory. The funds supported the Rainbow Ward at the Royal Shrewsbury Hospital and Hope House hospice. Though they recently wound down the charity, Mrs. Prior does not regret the decision. It helped us through 10 years and made us stronger, she reflected. We didn't seek publicity; our goal was to keep Lewis's condition and name alive.

text: Fidel Castro, who has died aged 90, was a huge figure in our lives, Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn has said. Jeremy Corbyn lauded Fidel Castro's revolutionary heroism, his influential role on the global stage, and Cuba's advancements in health and education. The announcement of Castro's death came from his younger brother, Raul Castro, who succeeded him as Cuba's president. Boris Johnson, the UK's Foreign Secretary, recognized Castro as a historic, if controversial figure and extended condolences to Cuba's government and people. Johnson remarked that Castro's passing signified the end of an era for Cuba and the start of a new one for Cuba's people. He emphasized the UK's commitment to collaborating with Cuba on various foreign policy matters, including human rights.Ken Livingstone, former Labour mayor of London, hailed Castro as an absolute giant of the 20th century. Meanwhile, ex-Labour MP George Galloway shared a photo with Castro, calling him the greatest man I ever met and the man of the century. However, other Labour figures offered more critical perspectives.Corbyn, a staunch advocate of the Cuba Solidarity Campaign, which opposes the blockade and foreign intervention in Cuba, described Castro as a huge figure of modern history, national independence, and 20th-century socialism. He praised Castro's achievements in developing a world-class health and education system and noted Cuba's international solidarity efforts. Corbyn acknowledged Castro's role in aiding Angola's fight against apartheid in South Africa, labeling him an internationalist and champion of social justice. He admitted there were problems and excesses under Castro's regime but stressed the importance of considering the broader picture, noting Castro had seen off a lot of US presidents.Former Labour Home Secretary Jacqui Smith countered, stating Castro saw off many US presidents because they were democratically elected. text: There is one sentence in the press release announcing Nicholas Serota's departure from Tate that stands out. Nicholas Serota, reflecting on his departure from Tate, remarked, I leave an institution that has the potential to reach broad audiences across the UK and abroad, through its own programmes, partnerships and online. The word potential is particularly striking. What does he imply by potential?Under Serota's leadership, Tate has transformed from a respected but modest gallery in Pimlico into an international art powerhouse. It now includes the world's most visited modern art museum, Tate Modern, along with two popular regional galleries and a network of partnerships. Tate's British art collection is exhibited in major museums from Beijing to Boston. By most standards, Serota has already realized Tate’s potential.However, Serota’s perspective suggests otherwise, revealing his character and the reasons behind his successful tenure. He is not one for complacency. His use of potential underscores three traits: humility, relentless ambition, and a challenging spirit. He aims to ensure that his successor understands the work is far from finished.Who might take on the challenge of fulfilling Tate's potential? Leading the speculation is Maria Balshaw, who has excelled at the Whitworth in Manchester and leads the city's cultural program. Iwona Blazwick, director of the Whitechapel Gallery and a key figure in shaping Tate Modern's curatorial vision in the late '90s, is also a strong contender. Her path from Whitechapel to Tate mirrors Serota's own journey.Among internal candidates, Frances Morris stands out, though she has only recently become director of Tate Modern. Jessica Morgan, recently appointed at the DIA Art Foundation, could also be a possibility, but she is still new in her role.The search may extend beyond immediate circles. Klaus Biesenbach from MoMA PS1, super-curator Carolyn Christov-Bakargiev, and Michael Govan of the LA County Museum might be considered. Additionally, Tim Marlow from the Royal Academy and Matthew Slotover, co-founder of Frieze, are notable figures who could bring fresh perspectives to Tate.

text: Gatwick Airport has been given approval to run six narrower flight paths to allow planes to fly in less airspace. The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) has announced that aircraft departing from Gatwick Airport will now follow more concentrated flight paths, a change facilitated by advancements in aviation navigation technology. This move aims to lessen the environmental impact of flights by reducing the number of people affected by aircraft noise.Sally Pavey from the Gatwick Area Conservation Campaign likened the change to creating a superhighway of planes. Currently, Gatwick's single runway handles an average of 350 flights daily. The CAA's decision comes after reviewing the effects of an airspace change implemented in 2013.With the help of advanced satellite navigation technology, aircraft can now bypass ground-based beacons, allowing them to fly closer together and utilize less airspace. This shift aligns with new European legislation mandating the UK to optimize such technology, and Gatwick's concentrated flight paths are a direct response to this requirement.Phil Roberts, head of airspace, air traffic management, and aerodromes at the CAA, stated, We absolutely understand that aircraft noise disturbs many people and we have taken the required amount of time to fully assess the considerable amount of feedback we have received from across the local communities. As we have done throughout this review, we will continue to consider the environmental impact of all our airspace decisions.Despite these efforts, some critics argue that Gatwick is causing significant disruption in parts of the southeast. Tom Tugendhat, Conservative MP for Tonbridge and Malling, expressed his concerns, stating he intends to examine the changes more closely. He urged Gatwick to become a better neighbor, highlighting that communities from Hildenborough and Tonbridge, through Leigh and Penshurst, Chiddingstone, Edenbridge, and even his own home south of Edenbridge, are severely affected by the noise, which he described as absolutely unbearable.Gatwick Airport responded by indicating that over time, the narrowing of flight paths would enable the airport to alternate some of them, offering occasional relief to those experiencing concentrated over-flight.

text: After two days of talks, Labour and Plaid Cymru have got a deal. Carwyn Jones was reappointed as First Minister on Wednesday following Plaid Cymru's decision to withdraw Leanne Wood as a candidate. The agreement between Labour and Plaid Cymru touches on several areas of mutual interest while sidestepping contentious issues, potentially setting the stage for future disagreements.Both parties have agreed to focus on initiatives that garner widespread support within the assembly. These initiatives include the creation of a National Infrastructure Commission and a Welsh development bank, along with three committees dedicated to financial, legislative, and constitutional collaboration. These proposals reflect shared elements in the manifestos of both parties.Labour and Plaid have pledged to prioritize apprenticeship programs, with Labour aiming to create 100,000 all-age apprenticeships and Plaid proposing 50,000 additional positions. Both parties also agree on the need to increase the number of healthcare workers in Wales. Plaid's proposal includes adding 1,000 doctors and 5,000 nurses, while Labour is committed to attracting more GPs.In terms of new medical treatments, Plaid suggested a £50 million New Medicines and Treatments Fund for Wales, whereas Labour proposed an £80 million fund. Childcare is another common ground, with Labour promising 30 hours of free childcare weekly for working parents of three and four-year-olds, and Plaid aiming for full-time early education by 2021.Economically, both parties support the establishment of a financial institution to aid Welsh businesses, with Plaid advocating for a national bank and Labour for a Welsh development bank. Both have also pledged to address business rates, with Labour offering cuts for small firms and Plaid supporting similar measures.The issue of a potential smacking ban remains contentious. Plaid intends to legislate the removal of the reasonable chastisement defense, while Labour seeks cross-party support for similar legislation.Plaid Cymru claims success in securing agreement on five of its nine main manifesto pledges, highlighting the National Infrastructure Commission as a major achievement not featured in Labour's manifesto. On overlapping issues like apprenticeships and childcare, Plaid insists it ensures Labour's prioritization.Labour managed to re-elect a first minister without compromising its governmental commitments. However, some critical issues remain unresolved, such as the M4 Relief Road. Labour favors a new six-lane motorway south of Newport, while Plaid prefers upgrading existing roads following Professor Stuart Cole's blue route proposal.Local government reform is another area of divergence. Labour proposes reducing Wales' 22 councils to eight or nine, whereas Plaid suggests maintaining the current structure with added regional authorities. Labour's 2016 manifesto did not specify details on the M4 route or council mergers, despite previous commitments.Other issues, such as the single transferable vote, remain unaddressed in the agreement. Leanne Wood acknowledged in the chamber on Wednesday that there wasn't enough time to negotiate complex issues like the M4, steel industry measures, fair voting, or student finance. She assured that Plaid would revisit these topics through budget discussions and other available channels.

Labour wants a new six-lane motorway south of Newport, Plaid wants improvements to existing roads along Professor Stuart Cole’s blue route. Where there are issues in common, such as apprenticeships and child care, Plaid wants to make sure that Labour puts them first on its list. Despite previous promises, the 2016 manifesto did not contain any details about the route of the M4 or the proposed amalgamation of councils. Labour proposes to reduce Wales's 22 councils to eight or nine, but Plaid Cymru wants to retain the existing structure and add new regional authorities. text: Some businesses hit by malware in a cyber-attack that began on 27 June are still struggling to return operations to normal, the BBC has learned. Nuance Communications, known for its transcription software tailored for medical professionals, has been gradually restoring its services. Despite these efforts, an IT worker informed the BBC that two hospitals in the United States continue to face challenges. This worker, who opted to remain anonymous, expressed frustration: We have been waiting for [Nuance Communications'] iChart [product] since they were first hit with the ransomware and are still waiting for it to come back. We will likely have to move to another product or even another vendor to get the same type of benefit.While Nuance Communications chose not to comment directly, they referred the BBC to an update from July 5. Security researcher Kevin Beaumont described the ongoing situation as alarming but commended some companies for their transparency in handling the crisis.Meanwhile, logistics giant FedEx revealed that its TNT Express division is still grappling with widespread service and invoicing delays. Shipping behemoth Maersk also suffered due to the Petya attack, leading to temporary shutdowns at some port terminals operated by its APM Terminals subsidiary. A Maersk spokesman assured the BBC that all major systems and customer interfaces have been restored. However, he acknowledged: There are some delays on some processes due to manual workarounds or backlogs that needed to be cleared. In some cases, our turn time to customers might be longer than usual, but we are nevertheless providing them with the services they expect from us.The financial implications of the attack are significant. Companies like Mondelez International, which owns Cadbury, and consumer health manufacturer Reckitt Benckiser, anticipate a slight dip in their quarterly sales figures. French construction titan Saint-Gobain, which reported €39.1bn (£34.7bn) in sales in 2016, predicts a potential 1% decline in sales for the first half of the current financial year.Kevin Beaumont remarked on the dual nature of the situation: On one hand, it is alarming to see large multinational corporations still feeling the impact and attempting to recover systems. On the other hand, it is good to see some of the businesses communicating so openly about the problems they are experiencing. Both Beaumont and Mikko Hypponen from F-Secure have lauded Maersk's transparency.The Petya cyber-attack, which began in Ukraine at the end of June, has left a trail of disruption. Approximately £8,000 in Bitcoin ransom payments have been traced from a digital wallet, but the perpetrators remain unidentified.

text: Malaga have been banned from European competition for at least one season because of unpaid bills. Malaga's suspension from European competitions won't impact their current campaign as they strive to reach the Champions League quarter-finals. However, should they qualify for Europe again in the next four seasons, the ban will take effect. This decision marks the first by Uefa's club financial control body, prompted by significant overdue payables.Uefa, aiming to curb clubs from excessive spending through Financial Fair Play, has issued the ban. Currently, Malaga sits in fourth place in La Liga. In a statement, Uefa declared, Uefa's club financial control body has taken its first decision due to the presence of significant overdue payables. Malaga is excluded from participating in the next Uefa club competition for which it would otherwise qualify in the next four seasons.In response, Malaga expressed strong disapproval, claiming they have been unfairly targeted. Malaga wishes to express its total disagreement at the decision issued today by Uefa and considers the intended actions against the club to be completely unjustified, the club stated. These clubs include Hadjuk Split and Osijek from Croatia, Rapid Bucharest and Dinamo Bucharest from Romania, and Partizan Belgrade from Serbia.

text: German Chancellor Angela Merkel has warned the UK that countries at the bargaining table negotiate better deals than those outside the room. Chancellor Angela Merkel expressed her hope that the United Kingdom would choose to remain in the European Union during the upcoming referendum on June 23, though she emphasized that the decision ultimately rests with the British people. She described the UK as an integral component of the EU, beneficial to all member states.Campaigners advocating for the UK to leave the EU argued that while staying might align with Germany's interests, it does not necessarily serve the UK's interests. BBC political editor Laura Kuenssberg noted the significance of Merkel's comments, highlighting that just weeks prior, German sources indicated Merkel was unlikely to comment on the referendum.During a press conference in Berlin with NATO General Secretary Jens Stoltenberg, Merkel stated, Obviously, it is up to the citizens of the UK themselves how they wish to vote on the upcoming referendum. I've said repeatedly before that I personally would hope and wish for the UK to stay part and parcel of the EU.Although Merkel has been cautious about intervening in the referendum debate, she has been clear about her desire for Britain to remain in the EU, recognizing it as a crucial economic and political partner for Germany. Her caution stems from concerns about how her remarks might be perceived by British voters, making her recent statements particularly noteworthy. Merkel was careful to underline that the decision is fundamentally a British one. In her typically reserved manner, Merkel issued a warning: the EU would not negotiate with an outsider as it would with a member state. Her comments appeared to align with those of other European leaders who have signaled reluctance to expedite renegotiation of the UK's rights and access in the event of a Brexit. This reflects a growing unease in Berlin over the possibility of the UK leaving the EU.Merkel emphasized the collaborative relationship with the UK, especially in developing new EU regulations. We work well together with the UK particularly when we talk about new rules for the EU, she said. Merkel stressed the importance of being at the bargaining table, highlighting that countries outside the EU will never get a really good result in negotiations.She underscored the significance of the single market, which facilitates the free movement of goods, people, and capital, arguing that the UK's political influence is best exerted within the EU framework. It would be not only in our interest but it could also be in the interest of Britain when it can bring its whole political weight to the negotiating table as part and parcel of the EU, Merkel stated.Labour MP and Leave campaigner Kate Hoey advised Merkel to refrain from influencing what she described as a critical vote for British democracy. I really don't think that Angela Merkel telling the British people how they should vote in a democratic referendum in three weeks' time will affect anyone's vote, Hoey remarked. She argued that the UK could thrive outside the EU and the single market, noting, We are the fifth largest economy, we can look outwards.Merkel joins a chorus of EU leaders speaking out as the UK's referendum campaign nears its end. Dutch Prime Minister Mark Rutte recently warned of a reciprocal response if the UK adopts a points-based immigration system, while Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy cautioned that an exit vote would have very negative consequences for British citizens.

text: There was a standing ovation in Venice at the world premiere of the new film about Ian Paisley and Martin McGuinness but tougher audiences lie ahead. Regardless of its reception at the international film festival, Northern Ireland audiences will form their own opinions on 'The Journey' and whether the political drama of Stormont can successfully transition into entertainment. Colin Bateman, the scriptwriter from Bangor, County Down, was not concerned with pleasing a global audience when crafting the screenplay. His primary focus was on resonating with viewers in Northern Ireland.Bateman humorously admitted he wanted to avoid the embarrassment of hiding in the back of his local cinema to escape the wrath of disgruntled viewers. Fortunately, such a scenario seems unlikely as European critics have largely given positive feedback. Bateman is ready to celebrate with a vintage bottle of Buckfast, though the Daily Telegraph's critique might give him pause. The review labeled the film as a graceless Wikipedian plod through the Irish peace process. Ouch, indeed.As the first journalist from Northern Ireland to watch the film, I found some scenes particularly uncomfortable. My instincts nearly had me leaping from my seat in a luxurious Venice cinema, shouting, That never happened! Paisley and McGuinness were never in a car together, let alone in a graveyard or a remote forest near Loch Lomond trying to save a dying deer. This is fiction!Of course, it is fiction. The filmmakers clarify from the outset that this is a dramatized narrative. While Paisley and McGuinness genuinely developed a bond, the film imagines a more rapid and adventurous evolution of their political relationship. Once you accept this creative liberty, the urge to protest diminishes, though it takes some adjustment.Opinions in Northern Ireland are bound to be divided. Nick Hamm, the Belfast-born director and former Campbell College student, describes it as a feel-good film. But with 90 percent of the dialogue centered on the Troubles—from Bloody Sunday to the hunger strikes to the Enniskillen bombing—it doesn't immediately strike as uplifting. In one poignant scene, Ian Paisley, portrayed by Timothy Spall, lists the names of those killed in the Enniskillen IRA bombing to Martin McGuinness, played by Colm Meaney. The film intertwines fiction with a heavy dose of reality.Despite the somber themes, Hamm highlights the film's conclusion, where former adversaries Paisley and McGuinness discover more common ground than differences, eventually becoming friends. They maintained contact after Paisley's retirement and even prayed together, a testament to their remarkable journey.In an era where global tensions seem to escalate, the filmmakers believe this story of reconciliation and friendship is one the world needs to hear.

text: Levels of unconscious racist and sexist bias have been reduced by manipulating the way the brain learns during sleep. In a groundbreaking study, researchers at Northwestern University in Chicago have explored the potential of using sounds during sleep to reinforce memories of exercises performed earlier in the day. This intriguing trial, involving 40 participants and detailed in the journal Science, revealed that the effects of this technique could last for at least a week. Experts have noted the promising applications of these findings across various fields, while also highlighting ethical concerns. The Northwestern team points out that biases related to race and gender are prevalent, often occurring unintentionally. They reference studies where participants in computer games disproportionately targeted black characters over white ones or favored male applicants over equally qualified female candidates.To measure participants' biases, researchers administered a series of publicly available tests at the beginning of the study. Subsequently, participants underwent counter-bias training, which involved pairing images of faces with words that contradicted common stereotypes. For instance, female faces were linked with terms like maths, and black faces were associated with positive words such as sunshine. During this training, distinctive sounds were played, which were then replayed at a low volume during a 90-minute afternoon nap.The outcome was a notable reduction in sexual and racial bias scores, with the effects persisting for at least a week. But can this approach genuinely diminish sexism or racism? Professor Ken Paller, director of the cognitive neuroscience program at Northwestern University, remarked to the BBC News website, We didn't have people interact with or make decisions about other people, so that sort of experiment is needed to know the full effects of the methods we used. But we suggest that modifying unconscious social bias is likely to influence the extent to which decisions are influenced by racist or sexist attitudes.Paller believes this technique could also be useful in addressing issues like addiction or unhealthy eating habits. In a commentary, Gordon Feld and Jan Born from the University of Tubingen lauded the study, stating, This is the first to demonstrate that this method can be used to break long-lived, highly pervasive response habits deeply rooted in memory. However, they warned that sleep is a vulnerable state where people lack wilful consciousness. They added, Aldous Huxley's portrayal of a dystopian 'brave new world' where young children are conditioned to certain values during sleep reminds us that this research also needs to be guided by ethical considerations.Professor Paller acknowledged the parallels to subliminal advertising, noting the necessity for ethical discourse. He emphasized, More importantly, perhaps, is the question of whether people in positions of authority in society, such as judges and police officers, and perhaps people who make hiring decisions, should have their unconscious bias evaluated and perhaps trained to some standard.

text: Romania's Prime Minister Victor Ponta has rejected claims that he plagiarised large sections of his doctoral thesis, which was published in 2003. In a revealing report by the science magazine Nature, it is alleged that more than half of Prime Minister Victor Ponta's doctoral thesis consists of copied text. Despite these serious accusations, Ponta vehemently denies any wrongdoing and remains steadfast against calls for his resignation. He claims that the allegations are politically charged, with President Traian Basescu orchestrating the smear campaign against him.According to the British-based magazine, an anonymous whistleblower provided documents indicating that substantial portions of Ponta's thesis on the workings of the International Criminal Court are identical to the writings of other legal scholars. The evidence suggests that over half of the 432-page dissertation, submitted to the University of Bucharest, is plagiarized. This thesis, published as a book in 2004, later served as a foundation for a 2010 publication on liability in international humanitarian law, co-authored by former PhD student Daniela Coman.Nature quoted Marius Andruh, a chemist at the University of Bucharest and the president of the Romanian council for diploma recognition, stating, The evidence of plagiarism is overwhelming.Ponta, however, defends his work by noting that the bibliography includes all consulted papers. Demonstrating his willingness to cooperate with the investigation, the prime minister expressed his readiness to submit his thesis to the education ministry commission for scrutiny. text: A firm has been handed a record fine for nuisance calls after making more than six million automated calls in a solar panel marketing campaign. Home Energy & Lifestyle Management Ltd, a company based in Glasgow, has been slapped with a £200,000 fine by the Information Commissioner for its involvement in a large-scale automated call marketing campaign. The campaign, which aggressively promoted free solar panels, left many complainants feeling overwhelmed, with some reporting their answering machines were inundated with messages.The company, however, shifted the blame to a third-party firm it had contracted to make the calls, and announced plans to appeal the decision. According to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO), the company's actions violated regulations requiring explicit consent from individuals before making automated calls. One distressed complainant recounted to the ICO how they were unable to ignore the incessant calls while awaiting critical news about a terminally ill family member.Christopher Graham, the Information Commissioner, emphasized, The bottom line is companies trying to sell a product have got to stick to the rules. Nuisance phone calls are a modern pest. He assured the public that the ICO, alongside other agencies, is committed to shutting down these phone pests.The ICO pointed out that companies must obtain permission, specifically naming the concerned company, to make automated calls. Shockingly, Helms admitted ignorance of these rules. This company's ignorance of the law is beyond belief, remarked Steve Eckersley, head of enforcement at the ICO. It did not even bother to find out what the rules were and its badly thought out marketing campaign made people's lives a misery.Moreover, the company failed to provide an adequate means for individuals to opt out of receiving such calls. While the Telephone Preference Service allows people to avoid unsolicited calls, it only applies when a human is on the line. In contrast, Helms employed software to disseminate automated messages repeatedly.The ICO further revealed that Helms, part of the government's Green Deal initiative, misled consumers since the solar panels touted as free were not genuinely without cost. In response, Helms argued that the campaign had ceased before the ICO's investigation began and attributed the problems to another company. Helms had significant difficulty in fully co-operating with the ICO, owing to the failure of the third party company to give any information to verify and explain the extent of the calls made, stated the company through its legal representative.The company criticized the ICO for seemingly disregarding its explanations and expressed its intention to appeal the ruling while also pursuing legal action against the third-party firm.
