text: This week three senior figures were appointed to oversee investigations into claims that a small group of hard-line Muslims had tried to take over schools in Birmingham. The inquiry into the so-called Operation Trojan Horse plot has revealed a far larger scope than initially anticipated, with over 200 complaints involving 25 schools in Birmingham, all situated in areas with Muslim populations exceeding 90%. This raises the question: what exactly is Operation Trojan Horse, and will we ever uncover the truth behind it?Central to the controversy is a document first received by the city council in early November. Accompanied by a letter from a concerned citizen, it urged Sir Albert Bore, the council leader, to act swiftly. The sender claimed the document was discovered in their superior's office at a Birmingham school. In February, similar letters reached four additional schools.The document, though incomplete, outlines a five-point plan dubbed Operation Trojan Horse, allegedly crafted in Birmingham with directives for someone in Bradford. It purports to detail a strategy for taking over schools, which has led many to question its authenticity due to its seemingly too-convenient format. Conspiracies rarely present themselves so openly.However, some allegations within the document, particularly concerning Adderley School, had not been publicly disclosed before. These claims are now part of an unfair dismissal case set for an industrial tribunal later this year. The West Midlands Police economic crime unit is scrutinizing related documents, and four women have been arrested in connection with this case, limiting current reporting on the matter.The document suggests targeting schools with predominantly Muslim populations in impoverished areas, rallying a group of hard liner parents to challenge staff, curricula, and teaching methods. It advocates infiltrating the governing body to instigate disruption until leadership aligns with the group's religious views. The plan claims invisibility, allowing operations under the radar, and boasts of past successes in replacing head teachers at four schools: Saltley School, Adderley School, Regents Park Community School, and Park View Academy. Tahir Alam, a Park View governor, is named as a conspirator, an accusation he has consistently denied. Highfield is mentioned as a potential target.Skeptics argue the document is a hoax, citing language issues and questionable accuracy. They point out that much of its content had already been reported locally before gaining national attention, questioning why a genuine conspiracy would leave such an explicit paper trail. Supporters, however, note that some allegations were previously unknown and that the document has been under scrutiny by Birmingham City Council and detectives for months. If it were fake, they ask, why hasn't it been definitively dismissed?Authorities have been cautious, labeling the document probably a fake or likely to be spurious, but without certainty. Until the author is identified, its authenticity remains unproven. Even if fabricated, it might have been a whistleblower's attempt to flag real concerns about school governance.Regardless of its origins, the document has sparked numerous allegations of bullying, intimidation, and claims that state-funded schools are being stealthily converted into faith schools. Accusations include gender-segregated classes, female staff being marginalized, Arabic replacing European languages, strict dress codes, and praise for a radical cleric linked to al Qaeda during an assembly.Many accusers have remained anonymous, fearing backlash as racist Islamophobes. Nonetheless, these claims are being taken seriously, prompting multiple inquiries. Ofsted is investigating on behalf of the Department for Education, focusing on leadership, curriculum, and teaching quality.Birmingham City Council has appointed Ian Kershaw to lead its main inquiry into the allegations, involving Ofsted, the DfE, West Midlands Police, and the National Association of Head Teachers. A second review, led by Stephen Rimmer, former Home Office director general, will include the education sector, local leaders, and community representatives. Rimmer previously headed the government's anti-radicalization strategy, Prevent.The appointment of Peter Clarke, former head of the Met's counter-terrorism unit, as an education commissioner by Michael Gove has been contentious, particularly in the predominantly Muslim areas implicated in the allegations. This community feels targeted and isolated, especially given past terror plots in the vicinity. The language used by the DfE, including terms like extremist and Islamist, has shifted the narrative from school governance to something more ominous.Behind the scenes, another inquiry is quietly examining financial misconduct at some schools, led by the Education Funding Agency. Ofsted's reports are expected soon, following inspections at 15 of the 25 schools under investigation. These snap inspections, conducted under Section 8 of the 2005 Education Act, involve thorough questioning of staff, parents, governors, and students. Park View Academy was the first to be inspected on March 6 and 7, with a follow-up visit a week later. Although the report is overdue, Ofsted is likely to release all findings together after Easter.The Kershaw and Rimmer reviews aim to publish by July's end, with interim reports anticipated in early May. Clarke's inquiry will run concurrently. As part of the Rimmer review, the Youth Parliament has been tasked with defining what constitutes a good inclusive education in Birmingham and envisioning a safe, resilient future citizen. This work is expected to be published over the summer.The Education Funding Agency's findings lack a definitive publication date, leaving the community and authorities waiting for further clarity.

The plan boasts of having succeeded in four schools already: Saltley School, Adderley School, Regents Park Community School and Park View Academy. The plan names Tahir Alam, governor of Park View Academy, as a conspirator, a charge which he has always denied. Highfield is mentioned as a potential target. Those who argue that the document is a hoax point to the fanciful language and the disputed accuracy of much of what it says, and point out that a lot of what is said has already been reported, both locally and nationally, and they wonder why a real conspiracy would leave so much detail. But those who support it point to the fact that some of the information in it is unknown, and that it has been under investigation by the council and police for months. However, this document was the object of numerous allegations of bullying and intimidation, and of the clandestine conversion of state schools into religious schools. And if it was a forgery, they say, why not deny it definitively? The authorities have taken a cautious view, declaring that the document is probably a forgery or is likely to be a forgery, but without determining the authorship; until the author is identified, the authenticity of the document remains uncertain. But the accusations are being taken seriously, and investigations have been launched. Ofsted is carrying out an investigation on behalf of the Ministry of Education, focusing on the leadership, the curriculum and the teaching quality. There are many accusations, mostly anonymous, of sexism, the exclusion of female staff, the substitution of Arabic for European languages, strict dress code and the lauding of a radical cleric linked to Al-Qaeda. The Birmingham City Council has appointed the historian, Professor Ian Kershaw, to lead an investigation of the allegations, which includes Ofsted, the Ministry of Education, the West Midlands police and the National Association of Heads of Schools. The appointment of Peter Clarke, former head of the police counter-terrorism unit, as an education commissioner by Michael Gove has caused much debate, especially in predominantly Muslim areas that are subject to the allegations. A second review, led by Stephen Rimmer, former head of the Home Office, will also include the education sector, local leaders and community representatives. This community feels particularly isolated and targeted, in the context of past terrorist attacks in the area. The reports of the Ofsted investigations of 15 of the 25 schools under investigation are expected soon. In the background, the Education Funding Agency is conducting a second inquiry into the financial misdemeanours in some schools. Rimmer was responsible for the government's counter-radicalization strategy. These unannounced inspections, under Section 8 of the 2005 Education Act, entail extensive questioning of staff, parents, governors and pupils. Kershaw and Rimmer aim to publish by the end of July, with interim reports in early May. The language used by the Department for Education, with terms such as extremist and Islamist, has shifted the narrative from school management to something more sinister. The inspections at Park View Academy were the first, on March 6 and 7, followed by a visit a week later. The report is overdue, but Ofsted will probably release all the findings together after Easter. Inspectorate is expected to conduct a further investigation in parallel. As part of the Rimmer review, the Youth Parliament has been asked to define what a good inclusive education in Birmingham looks like and to imagine what a resilient, safe citizen will look like in the future. This work is expected to be published this summer. The date of publication of the Education Funding Agency's report is uncertain, leaving both the public and the authorities in limbo.

text: Female workers continue to face a rapid rise in pay inequality when they get into their 30s and 40s, according to the Resolution Foundation. Women born between 1981 and 2000 are likely to face a 9% pay disparity compared to men by the time they reach 30, according to a recent report. This gap contrasts with a 5% difference observed in their 20s. The report highlights that having children imposes a sharp and long-lasting financial penalty on women, potentially costing them hundreds of thousands of pounds over their lifetimes.Laura Gardiner, a senior policy analyst at the Resolution Foundation, remarked, Young women today face relatively little disadvantage in terms of their pay packets compared to what their parents' and grandparents' generation faced. However, she noted that many millennial women, who have not yet encountered significant pay gaps, are likely to experience them in their 30s, coinciding with starting families. Gardiner emphasized that this pay penalty remains substantial and enduring, affecting even younger generations despite initial career progress.The research indicates that the gender pay gap for women in their 30s has remained largely unchanged over generations. A similar study by the Institute for Fiscal Studies last year found that while men in their 30s typically see wage increases, women's earnings tend to stagnate.Jo Swinson, former coalition government member and current director of Equal Power Consulting, attributed part of this issue to persistent sexism. There is some occupational segregation, with more men going into science and engineering-type roles, but we also know there is discrimination at work, she told the BBC. Others argue that the gap is not solely due to gender discrimination but also because more women of child-bearing age work part-time, which generally offers lower pay rates than full-time positions.The Resolution Foundation urges policymakers and businesses to intensify efforts to close the pay gap. However, Jill Kirby, former director of the Centre for Policy Studies, cautioned against imposing changes on women who may not desire them. Women who are highly-qualified will choose to take less demanding jobs—more nine to five, and less nine to nine-type jobs—when they have a family because they actually feel there are better things in life than spending all their time at the office, she explained to the BBC.Starting in April 2018, companies with over 250 employees will be mandated to disclose detailed information about their pay gaps. A government spokesperson stated, The gender pay gap is at a record low, but we have to push further to eliminate it completely. Shining a light on organisations' pay gaps means employers can take action to tackle the causes and drive change.

text: Almost a third of dogs checked at random across the UK were found to be carrying a tick, researchers say. In a groundbreaking survey, researchers have revealed that the risk of dogs picking up ticks is as prevalent in urban areas as in rural ones. This finding emerged from the largest study of its kind conducted in the UK, focusing on ticks in dogs. Ticks are notorious for carrying various diseases, including Lyme disease, and a newly discovered parasite in the UK that poses a potentially fatal threat to dogs.Lyme disease, transmitted by ticks infected with Borrelia burgdorferi bacteria, can lead to severe health issues such as meningitis and heart failure, with fatal outcomes in extreme cases. The study, conducted by Bristol University last year, examined nearly 15,000 dogs across the UK. Astonishingly, 31% of these randomly selected dogs were found to be carrying ticks.The research highlighted that ticks are widespread across the UK, with Scotland, East Anglia, and the South West identified as high-risk areas. Surprisingly, urban environments are just as susceptible as rural ones. Initiated in April 2015, the project enlisted vets to examine dogs weekly and complete detailed questionnaires on each dog's clinical history, including the tick species, life-cycle stage, sex, origin, and any pathogens present.Professor Richard Wall, who led the Big Tick Project at the University of Bristol, stated, Our work shows that ticks are extremely widely dispersed. We have observed an increase in tick numbers nationwide. Our primary concern is the diseases ticks carry. While the UK currently has low pathogen prevalence, continental Europe experiences much higher rates of disease. With rising tick numbers, we must remain vigilant and aware of potential problems.He advised pet owners to be cautious in woodlands and areas with long grass, emphasizing that urban areas are not exempt from risk. Conservationist Chris Packham, responding to the findings, described the project as a tremendously significant effort that unveiled shocking insights into tick distribution and their disease potential for pets and humans. He noted the surprising presence of ticks throughout the UK, not just in isolated regions.Ticks, which do not jump or fly, attach to clothing when brushed against. They are commonly found in woods, urban parks, heathland, fields, and even gardens. Lyme disease manifests through a tick bite, similar to how mosquitoes transmit malaria. Public Health England estimates 2,000 to 3,000 new confirmed cases of Lyme disease annually in England and Wales, though not all are laboratory-confirmed. About 15% of cases involve individuals returning from abroad.Initial symptoms may include a red circular bullseye rash around the bite, but this is not always present. Victims may experience flu-like symptoms, muscle and joint pain. Lyme disease is treatable with antibiotics, but if neglected, it can severely impact health, affecting the nervous system and potentially causing meningitis or heart failure.Despite the relatively low prevalence of Lyme disease in the UK, with only about 3% of ticks carrying the bacteria, the study's results underscore the need for awareness and preventive measures against tick bites. The Big Tick Project has introduced an online tool for tracking tick prevalence.Sarah Bignell, a once-active vet, shared her harrowing experience with Lyme disease after a walking holiday in Aberfeldy, Scotland, in 2011. Unaware of the area's Lyme disease risk, she developed severe symptoms six weeks later, including bone, joint, and nerve pain. Misdiagnosed initially, Sarah's persistence led to a Lyme disease test, confirming her condition despite the absence of a bullseye rash.Her ordeal escalated to encephalitis, rendering her unable to tolerate sound or light and requiring constant care. I spent eight-and-a-half months locked in a room, she recounted, unable to care for her pets. Over the next four-and-a-half years, she faced life-threatening challenges, describing her survival as very lucky.Sarah's recovery, aided by intensive treatment, has improved, though she still battles fatigue and tough decisions about daily tasks. She emphasizes awareness and prevention over research investment, noting the complexity of the bacteria and the necessity of avoiding bites. I'm not saying avoid the outdoors, she insists. I returned to the woods with my dog Matty as soon as I could, wearing protective clothing.Determined to regain her fitness, Sarah hopes to resume part-time veterinary work next year. Follow Claire on Twitter for more updates.

text: The violence and murder of a protester in Charlottesville, Virginia, over the weekend has been attributed to far-right elements that descended on the city to demonstrate against the proposed removal of a statue of Confederate war hero Robert E Lee. President Donald Trump faced a storm of criticism on Saturday after attributing the violence in Charlottesville to many sides, initially failing to directly condemn the white supremacists who organized the rally. By Monday, under mounting pressure, Trump specifically denounced the KKK, white supremacists, and neo-Nazis. However, many conservatives argue that the blame should also fall on Antifa, a loosely organized group of far-left activists. Critics claim the media often overlooks the violence perpetrated by Antifa, simply because they oppose white supremacists and their detestable beliefs.So, what is Antifa? Short for anti-fascist or Anti-Fascist Action, Antifa's social causes are distinctly left-leaning. Most members are staunchly against all forms of racism and sexism, and they vehemently oppose what they perceive as the nationalist, anti-immigration, and anti-Muslim policies implemented by President Trump. Yet, as their name suggests, Antifa is more focused on combating far-right ideologies than promoting leftist policies.Unlike the mainstream left, Antifa does not aim to gain power through conventional means like elections or legislative processes. Instead, they are anti-government and anti-capitalist, often aligning more with anarchists than traditional leftists. Their protest methods are militant, sometimes involving property destruction and physical violence. Antifa was present at the 2017 Berkeley protests against far-right speaker Milo Yiannopoulos, the violent demonstrations during Trump's inauguration, and the events in Charlottesville.Globally, Antifa is a patchwork of groups, with the most active branches in the US, UK (known as Anti-Fascist Action), and Germany (Antifaschistische Aktion). The German movement originated in 1932 to counter the Nazi party's rise, disbanded in 1933 after Hitler's parliamentary takeover, and was revived in the 1980s in response to neo-Nazism post-Berlin Wall. Trump's election has been a catalyst for Antifa, which has connections with the Black Lives Matter movement and various anarchist groups. James Anderson, part of the team behind the anti-fascist and anarchist news site It's Going Down, notes a surge in interest since Trump's rise to power. The site, which had about 300 daily visits in 2015, now sees 10,000 to 20,000 hits daily. Following the Charlottesville events, their Twitter gained 2,000 new followers.Despite this increased interest, quantifying active Antifa members remains elusive. Like the far-right, Antifa chapters are loosely connected and highly secretive, organizing primarily through message boards like Reddit and social media platforms such as Twitter and Facebook. Antifa has become a hot topic on right-leaning websites and among conservative commentators. Erick Erickson, a Fox News commentator, stated in The Resurgent, a conservative blog, Antifa and the white supremacists are two sides of a common coin. The people dead in Charlottesville died because of one neo-Nazi, but there were dozens left bleeding in the streets because of Antifa. Meanwhile, a change.org petition urging Trump to label Antifa a domestic terror organization has attracted nearly 100,000 signatures.While Antifa has received limited attention in mainstream media, this may soon change. According to Anderson, the Charlottesville events mark a sea change in how Antifa is viewed. This is a huge turning point and vindication for our movement, he stated. We are collaborating with Black Lives Matter and local clergy; this isn't a movement that wants to stand alone as a militant group. This is about popular power. Sometimes that looks controversial, but this is a broad movement, and we are looking to engage a wide variety of people.

text: Kenya's Julius Yego, who refined his javelin technique watching YouTube videos, says his World Championship gold medal was really unbelievable. Media playback is not supported on this device.Standing at 5 feet 9 inches, 26-year-old Julius Yego may not be the tallest in his sport, but he made a towering statement by throwing 92.72 meters—a new Commonwealth record—to clinch victory by nearly four meters. Reflecting on his achievement, Yego admitted, I had a serious injury and thought I won't compete in Beijing. He proudly added, Very few athletes have done what I have done.The 85-kilogram Commonwealth champion had initially aspired to join the ranks of Kenya's celebrated runners. However, he honed his javelin technique by studying videos of Olympic and world champions Jan Zelezny from the Czech Republic and Norway's Andreas Thorkildsen. Yego confidently stated, There will not be another YouTube athlete coming through. I want to go back and watch my throw; it was almost perfect.Earlier, news broke that his teammates Joyce Zakary and Koki Manunga had tested positive for doping at the championships. Currently, thirteen Kenyan athletes face suspensions for doping violations. Addressing this issue, Yego remarked, I can't dwell on that, it's a shame. I always believe you can win clean. In sport, you win clean.According to his IAAF profile, Yego is the fourth of seven siblings, hailing from Nandi South County in Kenya. Initially recruited by the police near Nairobi, Nicholas Kilisio, the head coach of the national force, claimed he spotted Yego's talent early on. We saw the talent in him and decided to take him. He had a small frame, but we have bulked him up, Kilisio explained.After securing national junior titles, Yego represented Kenya at the 2010 African Championships, winning bronze. His career gained momentum when he met Finnish javelin coach Petteri Piironen, who also coaches world silver medallist Ihab El Sayed of Egypt. Yego traveled to Finland on an IAAF scholarship for two weeks during the winter of 2011-12, enduring temperatures as low as -30°C. text: More than one body has been discovered during a search for one of the Disappeared in the Republic of Ireland. The Independent Commission for the Location of Victims' Remains (ICLVR) recently uncovered remains initially thought to belong to Joe Lynskey, who was abducted in west Belfast in 1972 and subsequently murdered and buried in secret by the IRA. However, following the initial discovery on Thursday, the ICLVR announced that additional remains had been located at a bog in County Meath.The term the Disappeared refers to individuals who were killed and covertly buried by republicans during the Troubles. Jon Hill, a senior investigator, indicated that the identification process was still in its early stages, emphasizing the complexity of the recovery effort. He noted that the bodies of Seamus Wright and Kevin McKee, two other victims, were believed to be buried within a couple of hundred yards of the current search area. Hill stated, There are most certainly two bodies—we're at quite an early stage, but there may be more. We were looking for Joe Lynskey, expecting it to be a single grave, and quite clearly that isn't the case.Joe Lynskey, a former Cistercian monk from the Beechmount area of west Belfast, later joined the IRA and was abducted near his home in August 1972. Seamus Wright and Kevin McKee, both IRA members, were also abducted and murdered by the organization in 1972. Hill confirmed that their families had been informed of the developments.The discoveries were made on Thursday by contractors working under the guidance of a forensic archaeologist, with the recovery process set to continue on Friday. Following this, the state pathologist will perform post-mortem examinations to formally identify the remains.Excavations at the Coghalstown bog began in March, with forensic investigators narrowing the search to approximately 15 acres of bogland. Last month, Maria Lynskey, Joe Lynskey's niece, visited the site and appealed for assistance in locating his body, expressing that her family had endured years of pain since his abduction. In a brief statement on Thursday, she thanked the ICLVR and those who had contributed to the search for Joe, adding, Our thoughts are with the other families whose loved ones remain disappeared.Sinn Féin president Gerry Adams acknowledged the distress faced by families due to the uncertainty over the recovered bodies' identities, stating, I thank everyone who has helped in the search of the remains of those who were killed and secretly buried by the IRA. Republicans have co-operated fully with the commission and we now need to continue to do our utmost to bring closure for the remaining families.Established in 1999 through a treaty between the British and Irish governments, the ICLVR's mission is to gather confidential information that could aid in locating the bodies of missing victims, although such information cannot be used in criminal proceedings. Over the past 16 years, the ICLVR has searched for 16 individuals officially listed as the Disappeared, successfully recovering and identifying the remains of 10 victims to date.

text: A 15-year-old Austrian synchronised swimmer suffered severe injuries when she and two other teenagers were in a collision with a bus in the athletes' village at the European Games in Baku. Vanessa Sahinovic has suffered multiple fractures and a head injury, though her condition is not life-threatening. Meanwhile, 15-year-old Luna Pajer sustained injuries to her arms and has also returned to Vienna for specialized medical care. Despite these unfortunate events, the Austrian Olympic Committee (AOC) confirmed that the team will continue to compete. Dr. Karl Stoss, President of the AOC, expressed his sorrow, stating, It's a very, very sad day. It's a tough day for the team. Sporting motives and goals are not important at this moment. The incident is currently under police investigation, according to event organizers.Dr. Robert Kandelhard, the team doctor, accompanied Sahinovic and Pajer back to Vienna aboard a private jet provided by Azerbaijan President Ilham Aliyev. They have already landed and can get the best care there, Stoss mentioned, adding, I'm not a medical expert but the treatment has been really good so far. It's a real shock for us and tough to motivate the team to focus on sport.The AOC reported that the collision occurred at 08:30 local time on Thursday as the athletes were walking on the pavement in the Olympic village. Another athlete, 15-year-old Verena Breit, was also injured, suffering a thigh injury. She spent an hour in a Baku hospital but has since returned to the athletes' village.A Baku 2015 spokesperson commented, This is a terrible accident, and at this time our thoughts and concerns are for the athletes involved, their families, and the remainder of the Austrian delegation. The incident is now a matter of a police investigation and until that process is complete we will be making no further statement.The inaugural European Games, featuring 20 sports—16 of which will be part of next year's Olympics—are set to begin on June 12. In another development, the British newspaper, The Guardian, claims it has been banned from entering Azerbaijan to cover the event. The newspaper suggests this decision appears to be linked to its report on the country's event preparations, which criticized the government's clampdown on freedom of speech and any political opposition.

text: British artist Benedict Drew is aiming to challenge a culture of unhealthy body image through pieces of art work being unveiled across digital screens in the London Underground today. Art on the Underground, an initiative launched by London Underground in 2000, has commissioned a new series of works aimed at promoting contemporary art throughout the city. Among these is a video piece by artist Benedict Drew, titled de-re-touch, which draws inspiration from the unique atmosphere of London's underground system and cleverly manipulates advertising language. Lasting just eight seconds, de-re-touch serves as a brief but impactful disruption to the usual stream of images and advertisements that commuters encounter daily. The video features a close-up of an ear, a pulsating fist, and flashing text, alluding to the crowded conditions of tube travel and the advertising world. Accompanying this visual piece is an electronic, experimental audio track available for download, intended to be experienced during one's commute.Drew, whose artistic journey began in the '90s, has a background in video, sculpture, and experimental music. Reflecting on his early influences, he shared, I was very privileged with my mother running a gallery in Canterbury, so I was brought up around amazing art. It was like a family trade. I went to Middlesex Arts School in the '90s, which was an amazing time. Some really good people had come out of that art school, like Hayley Newman—she was totally inspiring. I then went back to doing an MA at the Slade School of Fine Art about five years ago; it was amazing.When asked about his attraction to the current project, Drew expressed enthusiasm: It's really wonderful to be invited to work with Art on the Underground. It's an organization that's very public, and I've been aware of their works for quite some time. Being asked to make something about this sight of the underground and within that kind of space was really challenging. It was quite nice to engage with something I'm so familiar with. The underground is such an intense place.Drew finds London's underground environment particularly unique due to its shared nature. It's a very shared space, and you're very close to people you don't know, which is kind of unusual in a city where we are all trying to mark our own territory. It's quite archaic at times as well, and the underground can be super confusing. I think it's quite remarkable how well people behave towards each other on the tube, given the crampedness of it all—people give up their seats for the elderly, people will stand on the right side of the escalator.His frustration with advertisements stems from their portrayal of distorted images, particularly of female bodies. We're confronted with distorted images of bodies, especially female bodies. I see [advertisements] this as a kind of oppression. We're confronted with photos that aren't even real; they are digital drawings. Making the video work that sits amongst real advertisements was important to me, and when given this project, I felt it was impossible not to address this issue. The misrepresentation of bodies through a male gaze is a destructive thing, and it's harmful and warps our perception—enough is enough.The title de-re-touch is a deliberate call to cease the practice of retouching photos. The video contrasts sharply with the polished advertisements it sits alongside, presenting a messy, scrawling, and fast-moving protest against the dominant world of image-making in advertising today. Drew questions, Why will this unrealistic, imagined idea of a perfect body sell me an item of clothing or a gym membership? It's so messed up, and it seems so obvious to say it.Drew is uncertain whether he will continue to explore themes of body image and self-perception in future works. I don't know. I often think of my work as songs, like this piece is gestural.Regarding the impact he hopes his work will have, Drew wishes for viewers to reject these distorted images. I want people to stop accepting these distorted images of bodies. I'd like everyone to just say it's unacceptable because it is—it's oppression. When you see television programmes from the '60s and '70s and you just see obvious racism or homophobia, now you think, 'Gosh, that's so unacceptable,' like that wouldn't happen now, which is good, we've moved on. I think there will be a time where we just look back and think, 'Oh my gosh, what were people thinking?'Discussing his creative process, Drew describes it as emergent and influenced by various cultural elements. It's complicated. It's emergent and comes out of a set of things I indulge in—the things I see, music I listen to, or books I've read. It's kind of like constructing a cultural universe, and then out of that emerges a voice and forms the way you think. My work is excreted out of that.When facing artist's block, Drew finds deadlines helpful. Deadlines help! he laughs. It's tough, but I'm quite productive, and I work a lot. What I like about art, as an arena, is that anything can be allowed into it—if you wish to make shoes, you could do it, and that is artwork. I make drawings, prints, sculptures, videos, and music; so when I'm blocked with one medium, I can jump onto another, which I find quite useful.Determining when a piece is finished is often a matter of timing for Drew. Generally the day before the exhibition opens, he laughs. There's a sense that you can tinker with things forever, but it's quite good to keep hold of immediacy. Like if you overwork something, you can lose the energy within it. I think that's the case across all forms of work.Looking ahead, Drew is participating in the British Art Show, which recently opened in Leeds and will travel to other locations, including Edinburgh. He is also teaching at the Slade School of Fine Art and hopes to create more music, possibly even a record.Benedict Drew's latest works can be found throughout various underground stations across London, offering commuters a thought-provoking artistic experience amidst their daily routines.

Misrepresentation of the body through the male gaze is a destructive thing, it harms us and distorts our perceptions – enough. “It is so distorted, and so obvious, that it is hardly necessary to mention it. I often think of my art as songs, and this is a gesture. As to what he hopes to achieve with his art, he hopes that the viewer will reject these distorted images. I would like everyone to say that it’s unacceptable, because it is. It’s oppression. When you watch a film from the sixties or seventies and you see people being openly racist or homophobic, you think: “How can it be possible that we still have that sort of thing now?” 'It's complicated. I think we'll look back and say 'what on earth were they thinking about?'. Asked about his creative process, Drew describes it as an emergent process, influenced by various cultural elements. “It comes out of a combination of things, from what I see, from the music I hear, from the books I read. I build up a universe of knowledge, and out of it a voice emerges, it creates the way I think, and my work comes out of that. It is difficult, but I am a man of considerable productivity, and I do a great deal. When he feels he’s blocked, he finds a deadline helps. He laughed. What I like about art, as a field, is that you can put anything into it; if you want to make shoes, you can, and that’s art; I draw, print, sculpt, film, make music, and then, when I get stuck in one medium, I can jump to another, which I find useful. Deadlines are a help.’ Benedikt Drew's latest works are displayed in all the underground stations, where they invite reflection from the busy commuters; he also teaches at the Slade School of Fine Art, and plans to make more music, perhaps even a record. Benedikt Drew also participates in the British Art Show, which recently opened in Leeds and is now travelling to other places, including Edinburgh. "It's tempting to tinker with things for ages, but it's best to keep the immediacy, because if you work at something too much, it loses its energy, and I think that's true in all art."

text: There are few areas of life in which comic and actor Lenny Henry has not made an impact - working in theatre, television, film and charity. The star expressed his delight at receiving a knighthood, stating he was very chuffed when the news broke in the press last weekend. Over an impressive five-decade career, he has weathered occasional criticism without losing the affection of the British public.Lenworth George Henry, born to Jamaican parents on August 29, 1958, in Dudley, West Midlands, catapulted to fame in 1975 at just 17 after his appearance on the TV talent show New Faces. His victory led to roles in the comedy series The Fosters and the lively children's show Tiswas, where he began to develop his unique, energetic comedy style.However, a controversial career decision soon followed. He joined the Black and White Minstrel Show, where white performers, in blackface, sang songs from the American South—a concept now widely criticized. Henry spent five years touring with the show, later describing it as a grotesque parody of black people. Reflecting on this period, he told The Telegraph last year, I sort of wish it had never happened, but I don't regret that I did it. Although it was a weird, reprehensible position to be in, I was working in huge venues and learning how to work a crowd.His career took a positive turn with the BBC sketch series Three of a Kind, alongside Tracey Ullman and David Copperfield. First aired in 1981, the show used cutting-edge video effects and graphics to deliver fast-paced comedy, though some elements now seem dated.Around this time, the alternative comedy scene was gaining momentum. Through TV producer Paul Jackson, Henry met the innovative comedians of the Comic Strip team, including Dawn French. Initially, French was critical of Henry's style, which had evolved in northern working men's clubs. Despite this, the two grew close and married in 1984 at St Paul's Church in London's Covent Garden.Henry's political awareness also matured. In 1984, he declined to judge a Miss Blackpool beauty contest, calling it degrading to women. His TV career continued to flourish with BBC One's The Lenny Henry Show and The Delbert Wilkins Show. As a charity fundraiser, he co-founded Comic Relief in 1985, which has since raised over £1bn.In 1993, Henry starred in the successful BBC One series Chef!, while also working to promote new black comedy talent, contributing to the creation of BBC Two's The Real McCoy. He began taking on more serious roles, including playing an embattled head teacher in Hope and Glory on BBC One in 1999, and co-creating the 1996 BBC drama serial Neverwhere with Neil Gaiman.Henry's stage career began in 2009 with the title role in Northern Broadsides' production of Othello at the West Yorkshire Playhouse in Leeds. The performance transferred to London, earning him the best newcomer title at the London Evening Standard theatre awards.In 2010, after his 25-year marriage ended in divorce, Henry faced personal tragedy when his older brother Hylton lost his wife and two children to cancer and TB. These cataclysmic events, as Sir Lenny described them, helped him reassess his life and deepen his love for his family. He immersed himself in work, making his debut at the Royal National Theatre in London in 2011 as Antipholus of Ephesus in Shakespeare's The Comedy of Errors. His stature as a serious actor was solidified in 2014 when he received the best actor award at the Critics' Circle Theatre Awards for his role in Fences.In recent years, Sir Lenny has been a vocal critic of the lack of ethnic diversity in British television. I'm used to being the only black person wherever I go, he remarked. There was never a black or Asian director when I went to the BBC. Eventually, I thought, 'where are they all?' I spent a lot of time on my own. Things have changed a bit, but rarely at the BBC do I meet anyone of colour in a position of power. In a 2014 Bafta speech, he called the lack of minorities appalling, and has continued to address the issue publicly.Upon learning of his knighthood, Sir Lenny said his mum would have absolutely been chuffed, admitting he was overwhelmed himself. It was lovely, it was a lovely feeling, it was like being filled with lemonade for 10 or 15 minutes, he shared with BBC Radio 2.

While Cordia is striving to ensure schools operate normally, some disruptions cannot be ruled out. text: Iran has confirmed some of its computer systems were infected with the Duqu trojan, but said it has found a way to control the malware. Iran has been identified as one of at least eight countries targeted by a sophisticated spyware, believed to be designed for data theft to facilitate further cyber attacks. While the origin of the malware remains unknown, researchers have uncovered a curious reference to a US television show within Duqu's code.Iran's cyber defence unit is actively combatting the infection, according to reports from the Iranian news agency, IRNA. Brigadier General Gholamreza Jalali, head of Iran's civil defence organisation, stated, The software to control the virus has been developed and made available to organisations and corporations. All the organisations and centres that could be susceptible to being contaminated are being controlled. He added that a final report on the targeted organisations is still in progress.Previously, Iran had accused Western nations of attempting to disrupt its nuclear facilities with the Stuxnet worm. In April 2011, officials reported a second malware attack, dubbed Stars. Now, the Duqu attack is described as the third virus to strike Iran.Kaspersky Lab, a computer security firm, speculates that Stars might have been a keylogging program linked to the same campaign that deployed Duqu. Keyloggers can gather system information, capture passwords, take screenshots, and search for files. The firm further detailed Duqu's operation, revealing that an unidentified company received an email from someone using the alias Mr. B Jason, proposing a business venture. This reference is believed to allude to the Jason Bourne series of books and films.The email included a Microsoft Word attachment, seemingly legitimate as it bore the targeted company's name, which helped it evade spam filters. Kaspersky noted that for each victim, a unique set of attack files was generated using a different control server, with this method employed at least 12 times. Upon opening the file, the malware activated via a Truetype font exploit but remained dormant until ten minutes of inactivity.Kaspersky identified the font as Dexter Regular, humorously linked to Showtime Inc., the network behind the TV series Dexter, about a serial-killing CSI doctor. The exploit then loaded a driver, believed to have been compiled as early as August 2007. If this information is correct, then the authors of Duqu must have been working on this project for over four years, the report noted.Once installed, the driver initiated the Duqu trojan, enabling attackers to introduce new modules, infect other networked systems, and gather intelligence. Efforts to trace the perpetrators have been hindered by their deactivation of several control servers thought to be involved in the attacks.

text: Parents should have lessons provided by the government on how to raise their children, Britain's leading public health expert has said. text: Germany's second-biggest lender, Commerzbank, is planning to cut 9,600 jobs over the next four years and end dividend payments for the first time. Commerzbank announced plans to sustainably increase its profitability by the end of 2020, while simultaneously aiming to create 2,300 new positions in its expanding business sectors. The bank's board is set to discuss this strategy on Friday. As of last year, Commerzbank employed approximately 51,300 people.This announcement emerges amidst denials from the German government regarding a potential rescue plan for Deutsche Bank. Germany's largest bank, Deutsche Bank, is currently grappling with a $14 billion fine in the United States for mis-selling mortgage-backed bonds before the 2008 financial crisis.Commerzbank's new strategy focuses on strengthening its core operations, which include services for private and small business customers and corporate clients, alongside digitizing several processes. As part of a €1.1 billion restructuring, Commerzbank plans to merge its Mittelstandsbank, which serves medium-sized German firms, with its corporates and markets division. Consequently, the bank may write off about €700 million in the third quarter of this year. Additionally, it plans to scale back investment banking activities to reduce earnings volatility and regulatory risk, thereby freeing up capital for core client businesses.As Germany's second-largest bank, Commerzbank is embarking on a significant restructuring effort, which includes nearly 10,000 job cuts and the suspension of dividends for shareholders. This restructuring aims to save billions of euros annually, enabling the bank to invest in new business sectors and create jobs in growth areas.The German government owns a 15% stake in Commerzbank, acquired during the 2008 financial crisis to support the bank. Critics argue that Germany's banks have been sluggish in addressing the credit crunch's aftermath, facing challenges such as new competition, increased regulatory costs, and ultra-low interest rates impacting profits.Despite anticipated write-offs and increased loan loss provisions due to weaknesses in the shipping markets, Commerzbank expects to achieve a modest net profit for 2016. The bank plans to initiate discussions with employee representatives regarding the job cuts, which, after accounting for the 2,300 new positions, will result in a net loss of 7,300 full-time jobs.On Thursday, Commerzbank's shares dropped by 3% in Frankfurt. In contrast, Deutsche Bank shares, which had recently hit a 30-year low, rose by 1% on the German stock exchange, following a 2% increase on Wednesday. Despite these gains, a significant portion of Deutsche Bank's shares continued to be shorted. Investors have been selling off Deutsche stock, anticipating the need for the bank to issue more shares, which would decrease the value of existing holdings. This strategy allows them to repurchase shares at a lower price and potentially profit from the difference.

text: More than 150 beavers living in Tayside waterways have adapted well to life in Scotland, studies have found. The future of beavers in Scotland is under serious consideration by the Scottish government, with a trial currently in progress at Knapdale, Argyll. A decision is being pondered on whether to permanently reintroduce these creatures into the wild. The Tayside beavers, which either escaped or were released illegally, have reportedly adapted well to their surroundings, according to recent studies.Back in 2012, when the issue of the beavers was raised, the government opted to monitor the situation for three years rather than removing the animals or accepting their presence outright. The current findings from the Tayside Beaver Study Group, in conjunction with the Knapdale reintroduction trial, will play a pivotal role in shaping the government's decision on the beavers' future in Scotland.Concerns had been raised about potential ecosystem damage and disease spread, but the study group, led by Scottish Natural Heritage, indicates that the beavers have integrated effectively, despite some challenges in land management. These Eurasian beavers, once native to Britain, have been discovered in various rivers and lochs, spanning from Kinloch Rannoch, Kenmore, and Crieff in the west to Forfar, Perth, and Bridge of Earn in the east. They likely hail from Bavarian or German ancestry.The beavers are thriving, reproducing successfully, and expanding throughout Tayside, free from diseases that could affect humans, domestic animals, or other wildlife. However, their most significant impact is on agricultural land, particularly where they construct dams on the River Isla or the Tay, potentially causing nearby arable land to flood. While methods to protect trees from being gnawed and felled have been effective in preventing flooding, managing the impact of beavers burrowing into flood banks and damming drainage ditches remains challenging.The study group highlighted that these issues need addressing if the beavers are to remain, as 70% of reported negative impacts from beaver activity have financial implications. David Bale, chair of the study group and SNH's area manager for Tayside and Grampian, described the findings as very useful. He stated, The findings show there is no evident risk of diseases being transmitted from the Tayside beavers to other animals, or indeed to humans. The genetic tests tell us that they would be suitable for permanent reintroduction to Scotland, because they are Eurasian rather than North American beavers. They are also varied enough genetically to make a reasonable first step towards a full reintroduction if that was the decision of the Scottish Government.Bale further noted that while beavers may cause minimal concerns in many situations, if they are to be permanently reintroduced, it is crucial to find efficient, effective, and affordable ways to manage and reduce their potential impact on intensively farmed land and other interests.The study group's reports, along with other beaver research, will be presented to the government in May. A Scottish Land and Estates spokesman expressed their active involvement in the Tayside Beaver Study Group and their desire for comprehensive information to be available to the government before making a decision. We are not opposed to beaver ever being reintroduced to Scotland; we simply want to ensure that any reintroduction, whatever the species, is only progressed after a robust assessment and justification process which ensures a competent decision in which impacts on land management have been fully acknowledged and accommodated, the spokesman said.They also mentioned that Scottish Land and Estates had recently hosted the environment minister on a visit to Tayside farmers to discuss the beaver impacts on land management. They appreciate the report's acknowledgment of the Tayside population's impact, emphasizing the need for effective management solutions if beavers are to be reintroduced permanently.

text: Babies born by Caesarean are at higher risk of becoming obese, especially compared with siblings born by vaginal delivery, a large study suggests. In an article published in JAMA Pediatrics, researchers suggest that the mode of delivery might influence a child's future weight, with vaginal births potentially offering exposure to beneficial gut bacteria crucial for dietary regulation. The study tracked over 22,000 infants into adulthood, revealing that those delivered via Caesarean were 15% more likely to become obese, even after accounting for variables like maternal age and weight. Experts, however, emphasize that a multitude of factors likely contribute to obesity risk, including maternal diet, gestational diabetes, and breastfeeding. Babies born by Caesarean are less frequently breastfed, which is associated with a heightened risk of obesity. Additionally, children's diets play a significant role in their long-term weight outcomes.In the UK, Caesarean sections account for about 26% of births, a figure that has been rising, according to the Royal College of Midwives. The procedure involves making an incision in the abdomen and uterus to deliver the baby. Researchers from Harvard Medical School and other institutions noted that in families with children born through different delivery methods, those born via Caesarean had a 64% higher likelihood of obesity compared to their siblings delivered vaginally. Despite these findings, the researchers could not definitively attribute obesity to Caesarean sections or fully explain the underlying mechanisms. They hypothesize that variations in gastrointestinal microbiota, or gut bacteria, might play a role.Microbiota refers to the diverse microbes inhabiting our bodies, which differ among individuals and are linked to various diseases, though they can also promote health. A method known as vaginal seeding, which involves transferring maternal vaginal fluid to Caesarean-born infants to introduce healthy bacteria, has been suggested, but doctors warn of potential infection risks.Dr. Simon Cork, a research associate at Imperial College London, stresses the complexity of obesity risk factors, noting that delivery method is just one element. Overall, the literature suggests a possible link between Caesarean sections and obesity, but this connection is neither fully proven nor understood, he said. He added that most Caesareans are medically necessary, which should alleviate concerns about future weight issues.Prof. Neena Modi, President of the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, calls for further research to determine if Caesarean births contribute to obesity. Caesarean sections can be life-saving for mothers and babies. However, many women choose this option without a medical need, she noted. She emphasized the importance of informing women about the potential increased obesity risk to help them make informed decisions about childbirth.Prof. Modi also highlighted the significance of factors parents can control, such as maintaining a healthy weight before and during pregnancy, to positively impact their child's health.

text: Ian Bell has stepped down as captain of Warwickshire in all formats of the game to focus on batting. In September 2016, at 35 years old, Ian Bell led the Bears to a One-Day Cup triumph. However, less than a year later, the team finds itself languishing at the bottom of the Division One Championship table. Bell, who last represented England in November 2015, was recently excluded from the Bears' T20 lineup.This is the right time for me to stand down, Bell announced. He expressed his commitment to supporting the team in any way possible, emphasizing his belief in the promising future of the squad. It's been an absolute honor to lead my home county over the last 18 months, and my decision to step down is one I've contemplated for weeks, he added.Bell will be succeeded by former England batsman Jonathan Trott as the captain of Warwickshire's Championship team. Ashley Giles, the county's sports director, praised Bell's brave choice to concentrate on his batting. Having him focused solely on scoring runs for Warwickshire and Birmingham Bears is a huge asset to the club, Giles remarked.Despite winning limited-overs silverware in Bell's inaugural season as captain, Warwickshire is now grappling with relegation threats in Division One, losing five of their nine matches, four of which were by an innings. Bell, Warwickshire's most capped international player, has played 118 Tests, 161 one-day internationals, and eight T20 matches. This season, he has scored 345 runs in 14 innings, averaging 24.64, without reaching a Championship century since April 2016. In the T20 Blast, he accumulated 251 runs in 12 matches at a strike rate of 117.29 but was demoted from the opening position after a series of low scores.In the Bears' penultimate game, Bell didn't bat at all and was left out of the final group match on Friday, which the Bears won against Lancashire at Old Trafford, securing a quarter-final spot. New Zealand international Grant Elliott captained the side and is expected to do so again in the upcoming last-eight tie against Surrey at The Oval.Bell, who was part of the Birmingham Bears' T20 Blast title-winning team in 2014, also celebrated victory with the Perth Scorchers in the Big Bash League in Australia last winter.

text: Heinz has been taken to court in Australia after a watchdog said it falsely marketed a children's food as healthy. The lawsuit revolves around Shredz, a snack made from fruit juice concentrates and pastes. Heinz, denying any wrongdoing, maintains that these bars have a similar nutrition profile to sultanas. However, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) argues they should be classified as confectionery. The ACCC claims the snack, targeted at toddlers, contains over 60% sugar.Although no longer available on the market, Shredz was offered in three flavors: peach apple and veg, berries apple and veg, and strawberry and apple with chia seeds. The packaging prominently displayed a variety of fruits and claimed to be 99% fruit and veg.During a Federal Court session in Adelaide, ACCC's lawyer, Tom Duggan, highlighted that the berries, apple and veg Shredz contained up to 68.7 grams of sugar per 100 grams. Nutritionist Rosemary Stanton, a contributor to Australia's dietary guidelines, likened the bars to sweets rather than fruits or vegetables. Confectionery with added vitamins is still confectionery, she stated, noting that while the product included dietary fiber and various vitamins, many unhealthy foods do as well. Sure, there are some positive nutrients in there, just as there are positive nutrients in a Big Mac, she added, suggesting that Shredz should be considered an occasional treat.Heinz strongly refutes the allegations of misleading marketing. In a statement, the company dismissed the ACCC's assertions regarding the bars' packaging. The Shredz products were snack foods available in small individually-packaged serves appropriate for children aged one to three, Heinz stated. The Shredz products had a similar nutrition profile to dried apple or sultanas. Heinz stands behind the Shredz products and their packaging.The legal proceedings were initiated in June 2016 following a complaint about toddlers' foodstuffs by the advocacy group, the Obesity Policy Coalition. The ACCC seeks financial penalties, corrective notices, and costs from Heinz.

text: High street stores had a disappointing October, according to figures from the Scottish Retail Consortium (SRC). In the UK, total sales experienced a modest rise of 0.9% compared to the previous year, yet Scotland's figures told a different story, showing a decline of 2.4%. According to the SRC/KPMG Scottish Retail Sales Monitor, like-for-like sales, which exclude variables like new store openings, fell by 2.8%.The unseasonably mild autumn weather appeared to have dampened clothing sales, while consumers seemed to be delaying purchases of electrical goods, possibly in anticipation of upcoming sales. David McCorquodale, KPMG's head of retail, described the statistics as a sobering reminder of the frailty of the economic recovery. He remarked, The declines in Scottish retail sales in October, compared to a relatively weak month last year, are disappointing for retailers, especially given the mainly dry weather and temperatures only slightly above average.McCorquodale noted that the weather wasn't cold enough to boost sales of coats or boots. He also suggested that with consumers perhaps waiting for heavy promotions, retailers were left pushing themed products for Halloween. He emphasized that the forthcoming weeks would be crucial for retailers, as strategies surrounding Black Friday and the Christmas season start to emerge.In the food sector, sales dropped by 3.2% compared to October 2014. Retailers were unable to capitalize fully on the Rugby World Cup, as Scotland's early exit from the tournament dampened potential sales. The SRC indicated that Halloween, which fell on a Saturday, led some Scots to choose guising over shopping.Despite Scotland experiencing its driest and sunniest October since 2003, sales of autumn and winter clothing were sluggish, although Halloween costumes reportedly sold well. Many shoppers postponed purchasing electrical items, waiting for Black Friday deals at the month's end, resulting in a 1.8% decrease in total non-food sales from the previous year.David Lonsdale, SRC director, commented, This rather pallid set of results paints a disappointing October overall for Scotland's retailers, with total retail sales edging down again once falling shop prices are taken into account. He speculated that consumers might be holding out for better deals as Christmas approaches, possibly eyeing online discounts at the month's end, despite shop prices already being at record lows.Lonsdale highlighted the upcoming Autumn Statement and Scottish Budget, expressing hope that they would introduce measures to increase consumer spending and encourage investment and growth among retailers.

text: The singers of global hit Despacito have lashed out against the Venezuelan president, accusing him of using their song for political gains. During his weekly television broadcast on Sunday, President Nicolas Maduro unveiled a controversial remix of the hit song Despacito to promote his contentious new citizen's assembly. This assembly, set to be elected on Sunday, aims to rewrite Venezuela's constitution. The remix has sparked outrage among the song's original creators, Puerto Rican artists Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee.Maduro was seen clapping along to the altered version as his supporters danced. The revised lyrics include a line that says, Our call to the 'Constituent Assembly' only seeks to unite the country ... Despacito! This reimagining of the song did not sit well with Fonsi, who took to social media to express his anger. At no point was I asked, nor did I authorise, the use or the change in lyrics of Despacito for political means, and much less so in the middle of the deplorable situation experienced by Venezuela, a country I love so much, he stated. He further emphasized that his music is meant for enjoyment, not as a tool for political propaganda.Daddy Yankee also voiced his disapproval, posting an Instagram image of Maduro with a large red cross over his face. That you illegally appropriate a song [Despacito] does not compare with the crimes you commit and have committed in Venezuela, he wrote, condemning Maduro's regime as a global joke.Originally, Despacito is a song about seduction, translating to slowly in English. However, the Venezuelan version has stripped away the sensual elements, replacing them with a call for peaceful political expression: Slowly, take your vote rather than weapons, and express your ideas. Always in peace and calm. Maduro introduced this new version to his supporters, claiming a creative group had reworked it and he was eager for feedback. What do you think, eh? he asked the crowd with a grin.In recent months, Venezuela has been rocked by violent protests, with millions participating in a general strike last week. The unrest has claimed around 100 lives and exacerbated an already collapsing economy suffering from severe shortages of food and medicine. Maduro's proposed constituent assembly would have the authority to rewrite the constitution and bypass the opposition-controlled legislature, leading critics to accuse him of attempting to solidify a dictatorship. Maduro, however, insists this is the only path to restoring peace in the fractured nation.The original version of Despacito by Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee, featuring Canadian pop sensation Justin Bieber, has achieved global success, becoming the most-streamed song of all time. Meanwhile, Diosdado Cabello, another prominent figure in Venezuela's Socialist Party, has also used Despacito for political gain. As the song says, step by step, slowly and suavely, they [the critics] want to create a coup, he remarked, according to local media. Opposition parodies have also gained traction on social media, with versions like Madurito and Bien Flaquito (Very Skinny) highlighting the country's dire food shortages.

text: A BBC sitcom has been criticised as Islamophobic during a Commons debate about whether the BBC's programmes and staff reflect UK diversity. Labour MP Rupa Huq has voiced criticism of the BBC sitcom Citizen Khan, describing its portrayal of a Muslim family as quite backward. The show, which has faced accusations of perpetuating stereotypes since its debut in 2012, was created by Adil Ray, who revealed to the Radio Times that he has received death threats over the series.Despite the controversy, the BBC has defended the award-winning show, highlighting the positive feedback it has received. The fact that Citizen Khan returns for its fifth series this year is a sign of its popularity with all audiences, a BBC spokesperson stated. The show has garnered accolades from the Royal Television Society and Asian Media Awards, including Best TV Character.Ms. Huq, representing Ealing Central and Acton, expressed her concerns during a backbench debate initiated by former culture minister David Lammy. She remarked, If I didn't know what year it is, you would think it's an everyday tale of a Birmingham family of Muslims, but they're really quite backward. She added that while the show stops short of extreme depictions, it flirts with potentially offensive stereotypes.David Lammy criticized the BBC for lacking diversity, accusing it of recycling the same old faces from the same old schools. He claimed that black and Asian staff within the BBC felt unable to voice their concerns for fear of being labeled troublemakers. Lammy also pointed out the absence of the Chinese community in BBC programming and urged the new charter to address the representation of ethnic minorities. He noted that despite 29 initiatives aimed at improving diversity between 1999 and 2014, the proportion of ethnic minority staff had decreased from 13.1% in 2015 to 12.2% currently.While praising the diversity in children's programming, BBC Three, and documentaries, Lammy questioned the diversity within management. He challenged the representation within Broadcasting House, contrasting the visible diversity among junior staff with the lack of it in editorial roles.Conservative MP Helen Grant proposed that the BBC voluntarily disclose data on the recruitment, retention, promotion, and pay of ethnic minority staff. Julie Elliott, Labour MP for Sunderland Central, emphasized the need for the BBC to reflect every UK region, noting that Salford, home to MediaCity UK, should not be seen as the northern boundary.Earlier, Labour MP Chuka Umunna criticized TV portrayals of Muslim communities, suggesting that rising Islamophobia is partly fueled by broadcasters using so-called community leaders who lack genuine representation. In response, the BBC stated it is making good progress towards greater diversity and is committed to developing new and innovative ideas to improve further. Almost half of our workforce is made up of women, and the proportion of our workforce who are black, Asian, and other ethnic minorities is at an all-time high, the spokesperson added, promising to soon unveil a new diversity strategy.

text: Roger Ailes revolutionised cable news in the US, creating the hyper-partisan, opinion-based environment that currently dominates the American media landscape. The passing of the man who founded Fox News, a conservative media juggernaut, has sparked sharply divided reactions across partisan lines. Some view him as a monster who corrupted American society, making it dumber and angrier, while others hail him as a great American patriot and a media genius. This dichotomy reflects a nation with two starkly different worldviews.Recent discussions have highlighted the fragmentation of U.S. culture, where Americans retreat into echo chambers that reinforce their political and social beliefs. Over the past two decades, Roger Ailes constructed Fox News into one of the largest such echo chambers.In 1996, Rupert Murdoch recruited Ailes to launch a new network at a time when CNN reigned supreme in cable news. CNN's format mirrored the authoritative, supposedly unbiased evening news programs that had become staples of American life since the advent of television, featuring figures like Walter Cronkite and Tom Brokaw. These networks delivered news with a semblance of neutrality, interspersed with talk shows like Crossfire and Capital Gang, where politicians and pundits sparred, and Larry King, who provided a platform for public figures.Ailes, a long-time Republican strategist who had served Richard Nixon, Ronald Reagan, and George H.W. Bush, transformed cable news by infusing it with a partisan slant. He turned television news into an ideological instrument, whether viewed as a megaphone or a cudgel. Fox News' nightly programming eschewed impartiality, offering conservative content that audiences eagerly consumed in record numbers. Ailes recognized that many Americans sought confirmation, not just information, from their TV news.However, Ailes' legacy cannot be divorced from his dramatic downfall. Accusations of serial sexual harassment surfaced, with over 25 women alleging predatory behavior. Fox Corporation paid millions in legal settlements due to these claims. The powerful media empire Ailes built faced a series of crises, leading to the departure of top talents like Megyn Kelly, who detailed Ailes' misconduct in her book, and Bill O'Reilly, who faced his own sexual harassment scandal.Fox News, once unrivaled, has struggled during the Donald Trump era. Its rosy portrayal of the Republican president often clashes with the constant turmoil surrounding the White House. Should the Trump presidency falter, Fox News risks becoming the band that plays on as the ship sinks.This week, while Washington reeled from James Comey's memos and Trump's Oval Office conversations with Russian officials, Fox hosts Tucker Carlson and Sean Hannity focused on Hillary Clinton's email server and a debunked conspiracy theory about a murdered Democratic staffer.Even Fox News' once-dominant ratings have shown vulnerability, with left-leaning MSNBC frequently surpassing it during evening hours recently. With Ailes' departure, the future of Fox News remains uncertain. Murdoch has toured the network's New York headquarters, announcing plans for extensive structural renovations, hinting at potential programming changes that could reshape Ailes' creation.Regardless of what lies ahead, Ailes' legacy—both its triumphs and controversies—remains firmly entrenched.

text: The European Space Agency (Esa) has turned off one of its most successful ever missions. In 2015, LISA Pathfinder was launched into orbit to validate technologies for a future mission aimed at detecting gravitational waves—those ripples in space-time caused by colliding black holes. Exceeding all expectations, the satellite's success paved the way for the LISA mission's selection in June. This ambitious billion-euro project plans to deploy a trio of satellites between 2030 and 2034, incorporating many of Pathfinder's systems, notably its crucial laser interferometer, now proven capable of detecting gravitational waves in space.LISA Pathfinder has shown that LISA is feasible at full sensitivity, more than we could hope for, stated principal investigator Stefano Vitale. He described the mission as a stepping stone for GW astronomy and an incredibly rewarding experience for the team. Thank you, and stay tuned on LISA! he remarked to BBC News.Prof Vitale had the honor of sending the final kill commands to Pathfinder, which had been operating 1.5 million km from Earth in the sunward direction. These commands, sent from the European Space Agency's mission control in Darmstadt, Germany, forced the satellite to reboot with corrupted software, effectively shutting down its systems, including the transmitter. The only way you could recover the spacecraft would be to go up there and attach an umbilical and restart from another computer, explained Ian Harrison, Pathfinder's spacecraft operations manager.This shutdown process, known as passivating the satellite, ensures it poses no threat to future missions by preventing collisions or radio interference. In April, the Darmstadt team had already fired Pathfinder's thrusters to move it away from its station, a favored spot for Sun-studying missions. Now, it drifts harmlessly around the Sun. There's a very, very small chance it could return to the Earth-Moon system; it's so remote but you can't actually say it's zero, Harrison noted. The mission analysis actually looked at the planetary positions 500 years into the future.Gravitational waves are currently a hot topic in science. Ground-based labs in the US have begun detecting these waves from massive objects merging, which are 20-30 times the mass of our Sun. By placing an observatory in space, scientists hope to identify sources millions of times larger and track their activity to the farthest reaches of the observable Universe. This could significantly enhance our understanding of gravity and potentially reveal flaws in Einstein's equations.LISA will detect gravitational waves by bouncing laser light between three spacecraft arranged in a triangle, each side measuring 2.5 million km. The laser beams will precisely measure the positions of small, free-floating blocks inside the satellites. When gravitational waves pass through, the distances between these blocks should shift by minuscule amounts, mere fractions of an atom's width.LISA Pathfinder's technology demonstration involved a laser and gold-block monitoring system compact enough to fit in a single satellite. Although it couldn't detect gravitational waves itself, the system's sensitivity proved the metrology principles sound. LISA Pathfinder did more than we ever asked for, said Paul McNamara, ESA's Pathfinder project scientist. It met its requirements on day one, the day we switched on its science. But we then met and surpassed the requirements of LISA. So, it's been a phenomenal mission. It's sad to turn Pathfinder off but at some point we have to look to the future, he told BBC News.For more updates, follow Jonathan Amos on Twitter: @BBCAmos or contact him at Jonathan.Amos-INTERNET@bbc.co.uk.

text: Police investigating the murder of a man in a car shooting in Glasgow have issued a fresh appeal for witnesses. Despite efforts to save him, he succumbed to his injuries in the hospital. His 29-year-old passenger emerged unscathed from the incident.The shots were fired from a dark-colored Audi Q5, which swiftly fled the scene toward the M8 motorway and Kingston Bridge. Shortly before midnight, police responded to reports of a vehicle ablaze on Bracken Street in Glasgow's Parkhouse area. Forensic experts are currently examining the burnt car to determine any potential connection to the Shields Road murder.Detectives are urging witnesses who may have seen a car speeding in the vicinity to step forward. Det Supt Jim Kerr of Police Scotland's major investigations unit emphasized, Our priority remains tracing whoever is responsible, and a team of highly experienced detectives are working on this murder inquiry.Kerr acknowledged that Johnston was likely the intended target of a calculated attack, expressing concern over the blatant disregard for public safety. I completely understand that people will be concerned regarding this, he stated, assuring that police are diligently reviewing CCTV footage from the area to identify the shooter.The crime scene on Shields Road has been thoroughly examined, with forensic and search operations concluded, and the area has since reopened. Supt Kerr appealed to the public for assistance, noting, Even the smallest piece of information could be vital to our investigation. We have support mechanisms in place for those who feel vulnerable about contacting us. I urge people to do the right thing and report any information they have.An incident room has been established at Baird Street Police Office in Glasgow to manage incoming information. On Wednesday, Supt Kerr disclosed that Johnston, who hailed from the Maryhill area, was known to police, though he withheld further details. Johnston was reportedly returning home after dining out when he was ambushed.The 29-year-old passenger in Johnston's car is being regarded as a significant witness, according to the detective. Additionally, the shooting was witnessed by members of the public, adding urgency to the ongoing investigation.

text: UK scientists have successfully germinated seeds from the critically endangered Japanese Birch, a species that has just 21 known trees remaining. In a bid to rescue the endangered Betula chichibuensis, seeds were collected last year during a daring expedition to a secluded mountain area near Tokyo. Experts warn that the dwindling wild population of this tree species is too small to survive without intervention. To aid in its conservation, young trees will be distributed to various arboretums.The International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) paints a grim picture for the tree's survival in the wild. According to its Red List of Threatened Species, the tree's limited population and restricted habitat make it vulnerable to natural disasters and disease. The tree's self-incompatibility, which requires two nearby individuals for successful cross-pollination, further complicates seed production in small groups. Additionally, deforestation and habitat degradation in the region pose significant threats to the species' survival.In 2014, researchers from the University of Oxford Botanic Gardens and the University of Tokyo embarked on a mission to gather seed samples from these endangered birch trees. Among them was Dan Luscombe, a dendrologist from the Forestry Commission's Bedgebury National Pinetum and Forest. Luscombe described their fortunate timing: I guess we got a little lucky in terms of being there at the right time. It is found in a very, very remote location and it is not an easy place to get to. It has got very, very low viability so we were very lucky that we were able to collect a lot of seeds... as birch seeds shatter and shed everywhere, so once it has done that you will never find it.The team managed to gather approximately 1,000 seeds, resulting in about 100 seedlings at Bedgebury Pinetum. Luscombe emphasized the importance of growing trees from wild sources to preserve genetic diversity. At the end of the day, we have got these really rare trees and their habitats are highly threatened. If you want to put them back or want to put them somewhere else then you need to know how to grow them, he stated.The project aims to plant Japanese birch saplings in arboretums nationwide, collaborating with Japanese colleagues to ensure the species' survival in the wild. We will share the love so then other arboretums can try growing this species in different climates and soils etc, Luscombe added. Planting these trees across the UK also mitigates the risk of losing the species to storms or disease. Plans are underway to establish a seed orchard, ensuring a continuous supply of seeds for the future.
