text: Almost 1,500 secondary pupils across Aberdeen have been given anti-weapons lessons in the wake of the killing of schoolboy Bailey Gwynne. In a tragic incident at Cults Academy, 16-year-old Bailey was fatally stabbed during an altercation with another student. His assailant is currently serving a nine-year sentence for culpable homicide. An independent review into the incident, which occurred last October, revealed that Bailey's death could have been prevented if teachers had been aware that his attacker was carrying a knife. In response, educational sessions are set to be introduced next year for P7 students in Aberdeen, although some critics express skepticism about whether students would report their peers. Addressing an S1 class at Hazlehead Academy in Aberdeen, PC Seb Cook of Police Scotland emphasized, You'll have heard about the tragic incident that happened a year ago in Aberdeen. We never, ever want anything like that to happen again. You guys will never need to take anything sharp or dangerous into school.Jim Purdie, head teacher at Hazlehead, highlighted the broader implications of carrying weapons: It's not just about carrying weapons or blades, it's about the legal aspect of that, and then the consequences for the pupils, for their families, for their friends. There's an expression we often use, which is if we don't know things are happening, we can't do anything about them. We are constantly reminding our children to take responsibility. If there's something that is upsetting them, they know who to tell.When asked how they would react if they knew someone had a weapon, one pupil told BBC Scotland, I would probably just go up to a teacher, maybe even up to the person and just say 'why are you doing that, think of the consequences'. Another student added, People say don't grass up a mate, but if it's serious I think you should.Police Scotland was questioned about weapon-related incidents in schools. Superintendent Andy McKay, of Police Scotland Safer Communities, stated, Police Scotland relies on local authorities to report all incidents of weapon possession so that accurate figures can be collated. Following the report into Bailey Gwynne's death, Aberdeen City has been working closely with Police Scotland to ensure each and every incident of weapon possession is reported. However, it will be up to other local authorities to consider this recommendation moving forward. As a result, the figures collated to date may not offer a true reflection of the national picture in relation to possession of weapons in schools due to inconsistent reporting and recording methods. Figures represent a snapshot in time, and may not accurately portray a divisional or national perspective.Last month, a strategy to prevent knives and weapons from entering Aberdeen schools was approved. This plan includes providing staff with clear guidelines on recording incidents, conducting pupil searches, and confiscating weapons, including knives. Additionally, the council has approved professional learning opportunities for teachers to enable them to deliver lessons on anti-weapon and knife crime.The review, led by child welfare expert Andrew Lowe, resulted in 21 recommendations aimed at enhancing the safety and well-being of students in schools.

text: Sydney is marking the first anniversary of the cafe siege which left three people, including the gunman, dead. On December 15 last year, Man Haron Monis, an Iranian self-proclaimed Muslim cleric, took 18 hostages inside the Lindt cafe. As the anniversary of this tragic event approaches, a twilight vigil is set to take place outside the cafe on Tuesday, drawing thousands, including the families of victims Katrina Dawson and Tori Johnson.The Dawson family expressed their gratitude for the global support they have received over the past year. In a heartfelt statement on Tuesday, they said, While nothing can fill the void left by Katrina's death, the warmth from countless voices has been a tremendous help during our darkest days. Today is one such day. However, we choose to remember Katrina not for the circumstances of this anniversary but for the extraordinary joy, hope, and inspiration she brought to many lives.New South Wales Premier Mike Baird also shared his sentiments on Tuesday, expressing that Sydney continues to mourn alongside the families of Tori and Katrina. He remarked that a year ago, terror came right to our doorstep, yet emphasized that the city remains unbroken by those who seek to sow division and fear.In a gesture of remembrance, Premier Baird announced plans for a permanent memorial to be installed in Martin Place. This tribute will feature clear cubes filled with flowers, embedded into the pavement, and illuminated with special lighting, inspired by the vast floral tributes left in the aftermath of the siege.Meanwhile, Jarrod Morton-Hoffman, a siege survivor and Lindt cafe employee, penned an emotional essay reflecting on the harrowing experience. Writing for the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, he shared his ongoing struggle to comprehend the senselessness of the event. He noted, Terrorism is an inherently violent performance aimed at capturing public attention and broadcasting the terrorist's goals. For Monis, that goal was to threaten us for our involvement in Syria and Iraq. His aim was to instill fear. Whether he succeeded or not depends solely on our decision to remain afraid or choose bravery.

text: When Wes Metcalfe bought a cucumber from a Tesco shop in Dinnington, South Yorkshire, he did not expect it to come with a dead worm. When Mr. Metcalfe discovered an unexpected guest in his cucumber packaging, he turned to Facebook to share his experience with Tesco, humorously vowing to avoid cucumber sandwiches for a while. The exchange between Tesco and Mr. Metcalfe quickly gained viral traction.The saga began on Saturday when Mr. Metcalfe posted: Dear Tesco, yesterday I bought one of your fine cucumbers for my favorite dish - a cucumber sandwich. Upon opening it, I found a worm inside the wrapping. I thought - finally, Tesco has outdone Aldi’s free-spider-with-bananas offer. I called the kids down to meet our new pet, whom we named William. However, William seemed unresponsive. We assumed he was just sleepy, but 24 hours later, he still hadn't moved. On closer inspection, he appeared quite flat, and I suspect the tight shrink wrap may have squashed him. Though Aldi's banana spiders were deadly, at least they were alive. Now, I have three upset children, a worm funeral to plan, and I've lost my taste for cucumber sandwiches, a wake favorite. So, Tesco, how will you wiggle out of this one?Tesco’s witty reply began: I’ll soon be at a muddy festival, much like William would have enjoyed. I can’t attend the funeral, but I’ve written a poem you might read: 'An ode to William. Though life takes funny turns, we learn from William the worm. Gather, light a candle, and celebrate William. He wriggled many miles and gave us smiles. William will return, like Arnie, but now we check before making a sarnie!' #PoemsforWilliam. Best wishes, Rob - customer care.Mr. Metcalfe, touched by Tesco's tribute, shared a photo of William’s grave, posting: Funeral update: it was an emotional day, but everything went smoothly. Tesco Rob, your poem was read, and there wasn’t a dry eye. Here's another poem to sum up today. #RIPWilliam #justiceforwilliam #poemsforwilliam. As we gather for William the worm, we reflect on lessons learned. His life was cut short, crushed in a cucumber I bought. Tesco, don’t let this happen again. William’s death brought us together, sharing jokes and cheer. Once unknown, William is now a viral superstar!The conversation continued with Tesco offering their version of Oasis's Wonderwall, followed by Mr. Metcalfe's rendition of Blur's Parklife, renamed Worm life. Since Saturday, this Facebook exchange has been shared over 30,000 times, with more than 10,000 comments.Mr. Metcalfe, a trainee electrician from Sheffield, told BBC News: I love making people laugh, but you never know what will go viral. Tesco's fun responses were key. Without them, it wouldn’t have blown up online. Most reactions were positive, though one person didn’t get the joke and scolded me for fussing over a worm.Tesco offered Mr. Metcalfe a £10 gift voucher to cover William's funeral costs. Tesco has more than made up for it, he said. If people can laugh, that’s great. There’s enough seriousness in the world. He also confirmed his return to cucumber sandwiches.

text: Mark Wigglesworth has resigned as musical director of the English National Opera. In an email, Mark Wigglesworth announced his departure from the English National Opera (ENO), stating it was evolving now into something I do not recognise. The company, which has been navigating a tumultuous period, confirmed that he would leave at the end of the current season. Despite his exit, Wigglesworth will fulfill his contractual obligations as a conductor and expressed enthusiasm about continuing to collaborate with ENO's talented musicians.Wigglesworth, who took on the role of musical director in 2014, had described his appointment as a huge privilege. At that time, he emphasized the company's commitment to taking risks and pursuing adventurous projects, even in the face of funding challenges. However, in his email to colleagues, the 51-year-old conductor expressed his inability to support the ENO's future plans, which the board and chief executive were aware of. As hard as I have tried to argue to maintain what I believe to be the fundamental pillars of our identity, I have failed to persuade others of this necessity, he lamented. He stressed the importance of efficiencies that enhance value for money without compromising the opportunity to present high-quality opera to a wide audience.A familiar face at the Proms since 1991, Wigglesworth has conducted works by notable composers such as Olivier Messiaen and Richard Wagner. His resignation follows a series of challenges for the English National Opera. In February of the previous year, the Arts Council of England reduced the ENO's core funding by £5 million, removing it from the national portfolio of organizations for 2015-18. In response, the ENO lowered ticket prices two months later in a bid to stabilize its financial situation.Earlier this year, the company proposed changing chorus members' contracts from 12 months to nine months, prompting the chorus to vote for a strike, arguing that the change effectively reduced their pay. As part of their protest, the chorus threatened not to participate in a segment of the performance of Akhnaten at the London Coliseum. The ENO had warned that failing to implement these changes could lead to bankruptcy. Eventually, the pay dispute was resolved, and the strike was called off.

text: When Avi Yaron was 26 years old he had a motorbike accident - a day he describes as the luckiest of his life. In a twist of fate, a routine scan for potential head injuries unveiled a hidden threat deep within an Israeli student's brain—a tumor that might have otherwise gone unnoticed. In 1993, doctors informed the electronic engineering student, Mr. Yaron, that this mass was perilously close to brain regions vital for movement and cognition. Confronted with a daunting decision, he had to choose between undergoing risky, invasive surgery with a chance of paralysis or seeking alternative solutions.Determined to find a less perilous option, Mr. Yaron embarked on a year-long search that led him to a New York surgeon who successfully removed part of the tumor. Tests revealed it was benign, yet doctors advised him to wait for technological advancements before proceeding with further surgery. However, the looming threat of the tumor exerting pressure on critical brain areas was unacceptable to Mr. Yaron. I was young and thinking of starting a family. I could not be passive about this sword hanging over my head, he reflected.His relentless pursuit of safer surgical methods spanned five years, culminating in a successful conventional operation to remove the remaining tumor. This journey sparked a curiosity in Mr. Yaron, driving him to explore less invasive brain surgery techniques. Over the years, he developed a groundbreaking method to perform brain surgery in 3D.While minimally invasive procedures have become standard for easily accessible body parts, such as keyhole surgeries on the abdomen, brain surgery presented unique challenges. Traditional 2D imaging systems required surgeons to mentally translate flat images into three-dimensional perspectives. Recent advancements introduced 3D technology for certain operations, but achieving this in neurosurgery proved particularly challenging due to the need for ultra-small scopes.Most 3D scopes rely on dual optical channels to create a three-dimensional image, akin to human vision. However, crafting a device small enough for neurosurgery that also delivers high-quality images has been elusive. Mr. Yaron's team, however, approached the problem from a different angle. Instead of mimicking human eyes, they designed a scope inspired by the compound eye of a bee. This innovative scope uses a single sensor with hundreds of thousands of micron-sized elements, capturing the surgical field from multiple angles. Specialized software then translates these into images for both eyes, resulting in a scope compact enough for brain surgery.Visionsense, Mr. Yaron's company, has successfully developed this pioneering scope, now in use in the US and Europe. Shahzada Ahmed from Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Birmingham, who performed one of the UK's first 3D endoscopic neurosurgical procedures, likens the experience to watching a movie like Avatar in 3D: When I use the scope, there is a better appreciation of depth, and the pictures feel more real to me. This enhanced depth perception allows surgeons to better navigate complex anatomy.Ongoing studies are evaluating whether this 3D approach surpasses traditional 2D high-definition systems. Hani Marcus, a neurosurgeon at the Hamlyn Centre, Imperial College London, conducted a study using a model brain and novice surgeons. The research suggests that 3D imaging leads to quicker operations and improved depth perception. However, Mr. Marcus cautions against assuming 3D is inherently superior, emphasizing the need for further research. Some surgeons accustomed to 2D may find the transition challenging, and just as some people experience discomfort with 3D films, similar issues may arise for surgeons.For Mr. Yaron, the development of this 3D scope represents a silver lining to a personal ordeal. If I hadn't had this accident, I wouldn't have been able to offer this solution. And I really know how it feels to need options, he stated, reflecting on his journey from patient to innovator.

text: Sony's film The Interview has been pulled after hackers threatened a 9/11 style attack on any cinemas which screened the comedy. Hackers, identifying themselves as the Guardians of Peace, have issued a stern warning, predicting a bitter fate for anyone who watches the awful film.Speculation is rife that North Korea is behind the cyberattack, which exposed scripts for upcoming movies, celebrities' salaries, and personal emails of employees. Although North Korea denies any involvement, it has labeled the movie an act of terrorism, threatening merciless retaliation if it is released. Recently, they described the hacking incident as a righteous deed, suggesting it might have been executed by their supporters and sympathisers.However, North Korea might have more pressing concerns than a film criticized as muddled muck by one reviewer. The nation faces significant issues affecting its citizens. WARNING: This article includes distressing details.Over a quarter of North Korean children suffer from stunted growth due to malnutrition. According to the UN, around two-thirds of the population, nearly 16 million people, are unsure of their next meal. This food scarcity has resulted in North Korean men being, on average, 3 to 8 cm (1.2 to 3.1 inches) shorter than their South Korean counterparts. A United Nations report highlights that North Korea has prioritized its military arsenal and nuclear program over feeding its people. The situation is exacerbated by the state's strict control over family movements, hindering their ability to find food.Earlier this year, Michael Kirby, who led a UN Commission of Inquiry into North Korean human rights abuses, told BBC World Service that families resort to using the ashes of their relatives as fertilizer due to a lack of resources. Inside these camps, prisoners endure back-breaking labor, torture for disobedience, and are left to die when injured or deliberately starved. Former inmate Jeong Kwang-il, who escaped North Korea in 2003, testified to a UN panel that he lost a third of his body weight in just three months at a detention center. Then they hang you so you would not be able to stand or sit, he recounted. text: The number of people seeking to buy guns in Colorado has soared since last week's mass shooting in the US state's town of Aurora, say law officials. In the wake of the tragic cinema shooting, which claimed 12 lives and left 58 injured, there has been a significant surge in gun background check applications. Over the three days following the incident, applications rose by 43% compared to the previous week.The suspected shooter, James Holmes, 24, made his first court appearance on Monday. He is accused of unleashing chaos during a midnight screening of The Dark Knight Rises by hurling gas canisters into the crowd before randomly opening fire. Prosecutors revealed that Holmes had legally acquired his weapons and amassed thousands of rounds of ammunition, while his apartment was rigged with explosives.The Colorado Bureau of Investigations reported that on Friday, July 13, just days before the shooting, 880 people applied for state-approved background checks. This number jumped to 1,216 on the day of the shooting, July 20, and reached 1,243 on Saturday. In total, 2,887 individuals were cleared to purchase a firearm over the weekend, marking a 43.5% increase from the previous weekend. Although these figures do not directly indicate gun purchases, local gun shop owners confirmed a spike in sales.Dick Rutan, owner of Gunners Den in Arvada, described the sales as off the hook. He explained to the Denver Post, What they're saying is, 'they want to have a chance.' They want to have the ability to protect themselves and their families if they are in a situation like what happened in the movie theatre.Jake Meyers, an employee at Rocky Mountain Guns & Ammo

text: After leaders of the billion-euro Human Brain Project hit back at critics, six top neuroscientists have expressed dismay at their public response. Last week, an open letter signed by over 600 researchers expressed concerns that the Human Brain Project (HBP) was veering off course, calling for an independent review. In response, HBP members expressed disappointment, describing the protest as divisive rather than unifying in their quest to understand the brain. Prof. Henry Markram, the project's chair, dismissed the protest as a personal crusade.In a letter to Nature, six neuroscientists, who did not sign the original protest, urged for a more open-minded attitude and voiced their disappointment with the HBP leadership's stance. Prof. Richard Morris from the University of Edinburgh, along with five colleagues, criticized the project leaders for dismissing the concerns of over 600 signatories as misguided.Identifying themselves as European neuroscientists invested in the success of research projects, the six authors emphasized the importance of addressing the scientific community's concerns. Prof. Richard Frackowiak, a co-executive director of the HBP, countered claims of dismissiveness, asserting that the project leaders take the matter very seriously.The HBP, alongside graphene research, was announced as a flagship technology project by the European Commission (EC) in January 2013. Last week, hundreds of neuroscientists raised alarms over the project's narrow focus and closed management style, demanding an independent review and threatening to boycott HBP-related funding if ignored.In a subsequent email to the BBC, Prof. Markram from EPFL in Switzerland questioned the motivations behind the protest, attributing it largely to Dr. Zachary Mainen, Director of the Champalimaud Neuroscience Programme in Portugal, who had been repositioned outside the project's core.However, Dr. Alexandre Pouget from the University of Geneva, who helped organize the open letter, argued that the support of 600 people could not be dismissed as a one-man crusade. Dr. Pouget, who withdrew from the HBP in 2012 due to concerns over its increasing focus on simulations, emphasized the need for a balanced approach.Prof. Frackowiak acknowledged that communication could have been more proactive but insisted that the project was not autocratic. He described the HBP as an open initiative building infrastructures for the entire community and noted that changes in governance were underway, including the appointment of a new chair separate from Prof. Markram, who will assume the role of CEO.Support for the HBP also came from US Congressman Chaka Fattah, a proponent of the BRAIN Initiative, who described the HBP as a potentially disruptive force in a field too focused on incremental advances.The EC responded to the open letter by acknowledging the feedback and highlighting a rigorous annual review scheduled for January 2015. When asked about the transparency and independence of this review, an EC spokesperson assured that it would consider the open letter's requests while adhering to data protection rules.Dr. Pouget and Dr. Mainen met with the head of the EC's FET Flagships Unit, which funds the HBP and the Graphene Flagship, and found the meeting positive. Dr. Pouget expressed hope that the EC would take the situation seriously, noting the unusual nature of last week's events.Prof. Frackowiak, however, did not perceive the situation as a crisis, viewing it instead as an opportunity to bring the issue into the public eye. Our next scientific review is in January, and we look forward to it, he stated.

text: Six young voters from Wales who took part in an election debate geared around young people have described it as brilliant to a lot of hot air. In an electrifying debate hosted by BBC's Newsbeat at Leeds City Museum on Tuesday evening, over 100 young adults aged 18-24 engaged with five prominent politicians. Trust emerged as the central theme, while discussions on tuition fees, gender equality, and the voting age also took center stage.The political panel featured Sam Gyimah from the Conservatives, Labour's Sadiq Khan, Sal Brinton of the Liberal Democrats, Mhairi Black from the SNP, and Rhun ap Iorwerth of Plaid Cymru, all facing a barrage of questions from the young audience.BBC Wales followed the experiences of six Welsh participants, capturing their reactions to the lively exchange.Guto Gwilym, 21, from Lampeter, expressed his enthusiasm: It was brilliant to have that one hour purely focused on young people and the issues we face. It felt like a night where politicians truly listened to us, and I hope they took notes. We urgently need to address diversity among MPs.Aled Illtud, 20, from Aberystwyth, appreciated the debate's energy: It was nice to see a different kind of debate—it was much more energetic. Although there seemed to be more questions than answers, it reflected the audience's passion. We bombarded politicians with questions, which was great, but I would have liked more answers.Peter Gillibrand, 18, from Carmarthen, critiqued the focus: The debate concentrated too much on tuition fees. I wanted to hear more about support for disabled people like my brother, who's severely autistic and affected by service cuts. I vote Plaid Cymru, but I think the SNP and Lib Dems shone in this debate. The SNP representative was inspirational, and the Lib Dems' admission of their mistake on tuition fees felt genuine.Robyn Holley, 21, from Cwmbran, was less impressed: It was everything I expected—people shouting, opinions flying, and politicians being politicians. Their responses felt like hot air. I've considered not voting, but I might just to try and effect change.Gwion Dafydd, 20, from Pembrokeshire, found some politicians relatable: I appreciated that Labour, Plaid Cymru, and the Lib Dems supported lowering the voting age to 16. It shows they care about young voices. I've gained more respect for some parties.Rhys Taylor, 21, from Bangor, emphasized accountability: I stood up during the tuition fees discussion. It's crucial for politicians to admit mistakes and apologize when promises aren't kept. We need more politicians to own up to their errors to build trust.The debate highlighted the pressing concerns of young voters and the need for politicians to engage meaningfully with their issues.

text: When BBC Alba was launched in 2008, as a collaboration between the BBC and the Gaelic TV body MG Alba, it was a huge achievement for supporters of the Gaelic language. Proponents of a dedicated Gaelic channel have long contended that it would serve Gaelic speakers more effectively than isolated Gaelic programs scattered across major channels. They believe such a channel could be pivotal in preserving the language's future. Uniquely within the UK, this BBC service is a collaborative effort. Some programs are funded by the BBC, while others fall under the purview of MG Alba, which receives government funding.There was, however, disappointment when it was revealed that the channel would only be available via satellite TV, which reaches just 43% of Scottish homes. Nonetheless, programs can also be accessed online through the BBC iPlayer. Advocates insisted that the channel should also be accessible on Freeview, similar to other public service channels. In response, BBC management devised a plan to make this possible. The compromise was that BBC radio stations would have to be removed from Freeview whenever BBC Alba was broadcasting.Earlier this year, the BBC Trust delayed a decision as it was planning a broader review of how all BBC services should be broadcast. After extensive research, the Trust has now endorsed the scheme, although no specific date has been set for BBC Alba's Freeview debut. Some optimistically anticipate its Freeview launch by the time of the digital switchover in central Scotland next May and June.In practice, BBC Alba will soon be accessible in nearly every Scottish home, posing a challenge for the station to prove its value to a broad audience, including non-Gaelic speakers. Some newspaper commentators argue that it is difficult for Alba to demonstrate this value due to the absence of standard viewing figures. Alternative research methods have been employed, partly because the typical ratings sample excludes viewers from Scotland's islands.Although BBC radio stations will be removed from Freeview, they may return in the future with technological advancements. Meanwhile, main radio stations will continue broadcasting on FM and medium wave, and digital stations like 1 Extra and BBC7 will remain available via satellite, cable, digital radios, and online.The decision to prioritize BBC Alba over radio stations was challenging. However, the alternative could have involved the BBC purchasing commercial capacity on another part of the Freeview system, which might not have reached viewers using relay transmitters. The BBC Trust has also decreed that Gaelic programs should stay on BBC Two Scotland, though it will no longer be designated as the primary channel for Gaelic content. The scheduling of Gaelic on BBC Two Scotland is evolving, with programs previously aired in a two-hour block on Thursday evenings now appearing in various time slots, while the overall Gaelic content during peak hours is expected to remain constant.

text: Pirelli will be told to produce a tyre drivers can push to the limit in 2017 as Formula 1 bosses seek to make the sport more exciting. The current state of Formula 1 tires is preventing drivers from racing at full throttle due to their rapid degradation, requiring careful management. However, this is set to change in 2017, with cars anticipated to be up to five seconds faster per lap. Pirelli, the tire supplier, has expressed its readiness to develop more competitive tires for the upcoming season but insists on more track testing to achieve this goal. The company has been allocated 12 days in 2016 for this purpose.The BBC has learned that the FIA, the governing body of F1, will direct Pirelli to create a tire that allows drivers to maintain high performance for longer periods. In a recent meeting with teams and drivers, where dissatisfaction with the current tires was a hot topic, Pirelli chairman Marco Tronchetti Provera assured that the company could produce any tire the F1 community desired, provided they received a clear mandate.Pirelli has already received preliminary data on the expected performance of the 2017 cars, allowing them to commence tire design. The FIA plans to specify the desired tire performance and will supply all necessary data to Pirelli by the end of March.Since entering F1 in 2011, Pirelli was tasked with ensuring races featured multiple pit stops, achieved through tires that degrade thermally. These tires lose performance once a certain temperature is exceeded and do not recover, leading drivers to often race conservatively to manage tire wear and optimize race times. This limitation sometimes even affects qualifying laps, as drivers must avoid overheating the tires.The issue reached a critical point last season after two high-speed tire failures at the Belgian Grand Prix. Alexander Wurz, chairman of the Grand Prix Drivers' Association, stated that drivers desire tires suitable for maximum-attack racing.In response, Pirelli has altered the tire characteristics for 2016 to make grip loss less predictable, hoping this would allow drivers to push harder. However, world champion Lewis Hamilton, after testing the new tires in Barcelona, expressed dissatisfaction. It's definitely not better, that's for sure, he remarked. It just feels like a harder tire and it's not giving me any more grip. I think I prefer last year's.Efforts to enhance car speed in 2017 faced a temporary setback when Pirelli indicated that its tires would require unusually high pressures to withstand the planned increases in cornering forces. This prompted teams and the FIA to consider a less ambitious set of changes, but analysis revealed these would not achieve the desired performance levels.The new rules, agreed upon this week, represent a compromise based on a proposal from McLaren. The focus is on increasing aerodynamic downforce from the underfloor and enhancing mechanical grip. Cars will be wider, both in terms of the distance between the wheels and the bodywork, and will feature larger tires. As a result, cars are expected to be four to five seconds faster per lap in 2017.

text: First Minister Carwyn Jones has launched Welsh Labour's general election campaign - making no reference to UK party leader Jeremy Corbyn in a speech to activists in Cardiff. Mr. Jones unveiled the party's five key pledges, focusing on the NHS, housing, schools, and policing. The first minister emphasized that the general election should not center around Brexit but rather highlight seven years of Tory failure.He justified not mentioning Mr. Corbyn by explaining that it was a Welsh-specific launch. Addressing activists on Monday, Mr. Jones declared that Labour's achievements are limitless when the party stands united. In Welsh Labour, we are together—councillors, MPs, and AMs—we are united, he affirmed.The Welsh Labour leader proudly announced that the party had thwarted Tory efforts in Conservative-targeted areas like Flintshire, Newport, and Swansea during last Thursday's local elections. We did face some setbacks, but we'll learn from them, he acknowledged.Mr. Jones urged voters to return a battalion of Welsh Labour MPs, asserting that Welsh Labour has no apology for its local campaigning and proudly highlighted its governance achievements in Wales. The party's election pledges include three commitments in the devolved areas of health, education, and housing.This election must focus on seven years of Tory failure, Mr. Jones stated, criticizing ongoing austerity. This is not the Brexit election, he insisted, noting that the referendum had already decided that issue last year. I was a Remainer, as was Theresa May, he added, questioning the prime minister's lack of an EU exit plan. All she is doing is posturing, he claimed. We produced a plan; where's theirs?In April, Mr. Corbyn visited Cardiff for a campaign rally shortly after the election announcement. Accompanied by the first minister, he encouraged a crowd of about 700 at Whitchurch Common to embark on a journey of hope and excitement, commending Labour's governance in Wales.Mr. Jones explained to BBC Wales that Mr. Corbyn was not mentioned at Monday's event because it was a Welsh Labour campaign launch that he was leading. It's clear who would be prime minister if we secured a majority, the first minister stated, denying any belief that Mr. Corbyn was a liability in the election.We live in an era of devolution. That's why it's crucial for parties to present their Welsh pledges, he pointed out. This strategy by Carwyn Jones' Welsh Labour aims to distinguish itself from Jeremy Corbyn's UK Labour party.This approach is understandable, as the focus on Welsh Labour is believed to have helped the party retain several councils last week and fend off the Tories in marginal assembly seats last year. However, the challenge remains: in a general election, it would be Jeremy Corbyn, not Carwyn Jones, entering Downing Street.Labour's minimal emphasis on the UK leader contrasts sharply with the Conservatives, who frequently highlight Theresa May's leadership in their rhetoric.

text: Official figures released today by the Forestry Commission show that the government is falling far short of its own tree-planting targets. The Woodland Trust has expressed deep concern over the drastic decline in new woodland planting, describing the situation as appalling and warning of potential severe environmental repercussions. The organization has criticized the government for falling short of its target in England by a staggering 86%.Defra, the environment department, insists it is committed to increasing woodland cover. However, data released today by the Forestry Commission, the governmental body tasked with expanding Britain's woodlands, reveals that only 700 hectares (seven km²) of woodland were planted in England last year, far below the intended 5,000 hectares (50 km²).Austin Brady of the Woodland Trust remarked, These figures are all the more shocking against the backdrop of the growing evidence of the importance of trees and woods in tackling air pollution, improving water quality, and offering scope to deliver natural flood management. Something is drastically wrong with the way woodland planting is being supported across the various government departments that share responsibility for trees and woods.The government has pledged to plant 11 million trees between 2015 and 2020. Environment Minister Elizabeth Truss highlighted their role in flood prevention, stating in the House of Commons in December 2015 her desire to address the environment on a catchment level, ensuring tree-planting programs reduce flood risk and enhance the environment.Despite these commitments, Mr. Brady noted, There have been lots of really interesting and well-informed conversations - all the signals are positive, but the system of delivering the grants and getting things moving on the ground is not matching up with the fine words. It is not fit for purpose.With only 10% of England covered in trees, the UK remains one of Europe's least wooded nations, compared to the EU average of 37%. Although government funding is available, changes to grant schemes for tree planting last year have caused delays in processing contracts and payments. Under the Countryside Stewardship Scheme, stringent rules dictate the amount of land and planting density required to qualify for grants.Confusion persists over whether planting trees affects farmers' eligibility for EU farm subsidy payments, leading many farmers and landowners to shy away from new planting initiatives.A Defra spokesperson stated, Woodland cover in England is at its highest level since the 14th Century, and we are committed to growing it even further. The Countryside Stewardship scheme is an important opportunity to help expand our nation's woodlands, which is why the Forestry Commission is supporting landowners to make applications through a series of workshops and online support.The Woodland Trust argues for more flexible schemes to enable landowners with limited space to qualify for funding and calls for greater clarity. Currently, government departments involved in tree management include Defra, the Forestry Commission, Natural England, and the Environment Agency.Beyond environmental benefits, the government's Natural Capital Committee report suggests that woodland planting of up to 250,000 additional hectares near urban areas could yield net societal benefits exceeding £500 million annually.Follow Claire on Twitter for more updates.

text: An NHS trust has apologised unreservedly after a misdiagnosis resulted in a three-year-old boy having his legs and seven fingers amputated. In July 2015, Lou Harvey-Smith took her son Reuben to Ipswich Hospital after he sustained a burn. Two days later, she returned with him, concerned about his fever, and was informed that he had tonsillitis. However, Reuben was eventually diagnosed with toxic shock syndrome, leading to amputations. The hospital trust has admitted full liability, and settlement discussions are currently underway.Initially treated for his burn, Reuben soon developed a fever and sore throat. When Ms. Harvey-Smith brought him back to the hospital, he was prescribed antibiotics for tonsillitis. The next day, his condition worsened critically. Seeking further advice, his mother contacted the burns unit at Chelsea and Westminster Hospital. There, doctors suspected toxic shock syndrome, a severe infection caused by bacteria entering the wound and releasing toxins into the bloodstream.Reuben was urgently taken back to Ipswich Hospital, then transferred to St Mary's Hospital in Paddington, London, where amputations were performed. Reflecting on the ordeal, Ms. Harvey-Smith, 41, from Chelmondiston near Ipswich, recalled her son's words: [Reuben] looked at his amputated legs and said 'poorly feet gone, get new ones.' He just accepts it and gets on with things.Despite his resilience, Ms. Harvey-Smith pursued legal action against Ipswich Hospital NHS Trust. The trust conceded that toxic shock was a significant possibility given Reuben's symptoms at the time, and that timely diagnosis and treatment could have prevented the amputations. Her solicitor, Tim Deeling, expressed concern, stating: It is extremely concerning they were aware of the link between burns and toxic shock, yet didn't consider this for Reuben's case.The trust has made an interim payment of £50,000. A spokesperson commented, In an ongoing legal case, the trust has admitted full liability for shortcomings in the A&E care provided to Reuben in July 2015 and have offered an unreserved apology. He further mentioned that staff have received additional training to better recognize the signs of septic shock syndrome. The trust is committed to ensuring that Reuben is appropriately compensated so that he has the care, prostheses, and equipment that he needs throughout his life, he added.

text: The maker of the EpiPen will start selling a generic version in the wake of criticism about steep price increases. Mylan has announced plans to introduce a more affordable generic version of its EpiPen, with a list price set at $300 (£230) expected to hit the market in several weeks. This price is approximately half of the current $600 cost for the branded EpiPen, a critical emergency treatment for severe food and insect allergies. Over the past decade, the price of EpiPens in the United States has soared by 500%.The upcoming generic version will be identical to the branded EpiPen, which is sold in packs of two doses. Allergy sufferers often need multiple pens for different locations such as home, school, work, or the car, and these pens have a shelf life of just 12 months.Heather Bresch, Mylan's chief executive, stated that the company has invested hundreds of millions of dollars in enhancing the product since acquiring it from Merck in 2007. Our decision to launch a generic alternative to EpiPen is an extraordinary commercial response, Bresch explained. We determined that bypassing the brand system in this case and offering an additional alternative was the best option.This move is particularly unusual as the branded EpiPen remains under patent protection, and other competing treatments have not received regulatory approval. The EpiPen generates $1 billion in annual sales for Mylan.Ronny Gal, an analyst at Bernstein, commented, We suspect Mylan will continue to receive some heat for its price increases and there will be heightened pressure on the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] to bring competition to the market.Bresch attributed the price increases to the complexities of the U.S. healthcare system, noting that Mylan receives only $274 of the $600 list price, with the remainder divided among insurers, pharmacies, and other parties. The cost to individuals for an EpiPen prescription can vary significantly depending on their insurance coverage.The price hikes have sparked backlash from politicians and parents, with Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton denouncing them as outrageous and unjustified. The controversy led to a 12% drop in Mylan's shares last week, although the stock remained steady at $43.04 in afternoon trading in New York.Actress Sarah Jessica Parker, who had previously endorsed EpiPens, announced last week that she was severing ties with Mylan. She had previously highlighted the importance of the treatment for her family due to her son's peanut allergy.In recent months, other pharmaceutical companies such as Valeant, Turing, and Pfizer have also faced criticism for substantial price hikes.

text: Former England captain David Beckham is being cast away for the 75th birthday celebrations of BBC Radio 4's Desert Island Discs next weekend. Since its debut on January 29, 1942, Desert Island Discs has welcomed over 3,000 guests. To celebrate the show's 75th anniversary, former football star David Beckham, 41, will share his favorite music selections. Presenter Kirsty Young described Beckham's participation as the perfect gift for the milestone episode.Beckham expressed his excitement, stating, I'm delighted to join Desert Island Discs for its 75th anniversary celebrations. Music has been a huge part of my—and my family's—life, and it is a real pleasure to highlight that on such an iconic programme. Music indeed plays a significant role in Beckham's life, as he is married to former Spice Girl turned fashion designer Victoria Beckham. Their youngest son, Cruz, 11, even released a Christmas-themed single last month. However, it remains a mystery whether Beckham will choose any of his wife's hits or her solo work for the show.Kirsty Young praised Beckham, noting, His sporting legacy is of course extraordinary. And along with his charisma, cultural impact, and humanitarian work, he is a modern man of many parts. He'll be a fascinating guest to welcome on to my little interview island.The anniversary will be commemorated with a special three-hour broadcast on BBC Radio 4 Extra on January 28, hosted by Young. This program will feature highlights from past guests, including Cilla Black discussing her early days singing with The Beatles and Richard Dimbleby recounting his experience of taking a cutlery set from Hitler's bunker after the dictator's death. Additionally, extracts from recently rediscovered episodes will be added to the show's online archive.In a nostalgic nod, Beckham's episode will reintroduce the sound of the sea to the opening and closing of the programme, a feature absent since the 1960s. Gwyneth Williams, controller of BBC Radio 4 and Radio 4 Extra, remarked, A sure way to uncover an elusive British national identity is to listen to this programme week after week. The broad range of guests is a measure of contemporary talent and achievement, and the music opens up different eras and prompts emotional memory in all of us.Stay connected with us on Facebook, follow our Twitter handle @BBCNewsEnts, or find us on Instagram at bbcnewsents. text: Derbyshire were denied a chance of a first Championship win for two years as bad light and rain saw their match with Nottinghamshire end in a draw. Rain postponed the start of play until 13:45 BST, with Nottinghamshire resuming at 313-6. They managed to add only 36 runs, being bowled out for a total of 349, as Tom Taylor claimed three swift wickets, finishing with figures of 4-67.Chasing a target of 216 for victory, Wayne Madsen led Derbyshire's response with a solid 61, forming a crucial 67-run partnership with Shiv Thakor, who contributed 25. Derbyshire found themselves at 190-5, needing just 26 runs from 7.5 overs when rain interrupted play for the final time, dashing their hopes of securing a first Championship win over Notts since 2002.After an early setback at 36-2, Madsen and Thakor accelerated the scoring rate, exceeding five runs per over, swinging the momentum in Derbyshire's favor. As the victory loomed, bad light halted play, leaving Derbyshire with nine overs to achieve the 36 runs required. The match resumed briefly, lasting only seven balls, during which Alex Hughes, who had scored 24, was trapped lbw by Luke Fletcher, who took 2-46. However, heavy rain soon forced the players off the field, leaving Derbyshire tantalizingly close to a remarkable win.Nottinghamshire now lead the standings by 13 points over second-placed Kent, who did not play this week. Derbyshire sit eighth with 36 points from five matches.Peter Moores, Nottinghamshire's head coach, remarked, I think we have to give credit to them. Derbyshire were in a great position to win the game. It was unfortunate for them that the weather came at the wrong time, but credit to how they played. Now with all the weather apps around, we get that many reports, but at the start of the day we knew we'd have a chance of some cricket. We prepared as if we were going to play but we wanted to get a lead of 250-270. They bowled well at us and it was a good run chase from them. They put us under pressure.Derbyshire captain Billy Godleman expressed his disappointment, saying, Obviously we are disappointed that we weren't able to play the game through and seal the victory. We've spoken internally about putting together quality first-class cricket across four days, not just a session or a day, so I'm really pleased the group were able to play good solid cricket across all four days. I think everyone has played their part. It has been a real team effort and everyone has contributed. We are just disappointed that the weather and light intervened and stopped us from a certain victory.

text: Terry Flanagan has accused fellow Mancunian and lightweight world champion Anthony Crolla of ducking him. On July 9, at the Manchester Arena, 27-year-old Terry Flanagan will defend his WBO title against South African veteran Mzonke Fana. Just a couple of months later, on September 24, the same venue will host Anthony Crolla, 29, as he puts his WBA title on the line against Jorge Linares from Venezuela.Flanagan recently addressed the potential matchup with Crolla, saying, We offered Crolla the fight and he didn't want it. If he wants the fight, he should go to his coach and promoter and say he wants it. Flanagan suggested that it might be Crolla’s team that is hesitant, although ultimately, the decision rests with Crolla. It's an easy fight to make. Frank [Warren, Flanagan's promoter] isn't making it hard for them. If anything, he's bending over backwards to make it happen, Flanagan emphasized. Warren has even agreed to let the fight air on Sky Sports, despite Crolla’s promoter Eddie Hearn having an exclusive deal with the network. Yet, the fight remains elusive. Flanagan expressed doubt about the matchup happening soon, saying, If we both keep winning, it might happen down the line, but I'm not confident it will. He knows my style will give him problems and I don't think his team believe he can beat me.Flanagan, undefeated in 30 professional bouts, is set for his third title defense against the 42-year-old Fana, a former super-featherweight world champion who turned professional in 1994. Addressing critics questioning his choice of opponent, Flanagan remarked, People say: 'Why are you fighting this old man [Fana]?' He added, We want the big fights that the fans want to see. All we can do is keep pushing for them and hopefully one of them will come off.Promoter Frank Warren revealed that Crolla was offered £500,000 to face Flanagan, but instead opted to fight his mandatory challenger, Ismael Barroso. In his first title defense last month, Crolla stopped Barroso, who was previously unbeaten, bringing his professional record to 31 wins out of 38 fights.Both Barroso and Linares, Crolla's upcoming opponent, have previously defeated Britain's Kevin Mitchell, showcasing their formidable skills in the ring.

text: The Swiss government has defended its law requiring asylum seekers to hand over assets in excess of $1,000 (£700; €900) following international criticism of similar proposals in Denmark. In Switzerland last year, assets were seized in just over 100 cases from nearly 30,000 asylum applications, a practice that has sparked criticism from the Swiss Refugee Council, labeling it as unworthy. However, the government defends this policy, asserting that it aligns with the will of Swiss voters.Meanwhile, Denmark faces backlash from the UN refugee agency and human rights groups over proposed measures to confiscate migrants' cash and valuables exceeding 10,000 kroner (£1,000; €1,340, $1,450) to cover their expenses. Danish MPs debated these plans on Wednesday, with a vote expected later this month.In Switzerland, asylum seekers must declare their assets upon arrival, with anything exceeding $1,000 subject to seizure. In 2015, authorities collected a total of 210,000 Swiss francs ($210,000; €200,000) from 112 individuals under this regulation, according to public broadcaster SRF.Lea Wertheimer, a government spokeswoman, explained on Swiss television, Swiss law states that asylum-seeking refugees who have money have to contribute to the costs that they cause while being here. And that's why we take their valuables away once they arrive in Switzerland.Stefan Frey of the Swiss Refugee Council criticized the policy as daylight robbery, insisting, This is unworthy. This has to change.A Syrian man recounted to Swiss television how he had to sell his house to pay traffickers to help his family escape their war-torn country. Upon arriving in Switzerland, the remaining funds were confiscated. In Zurich, we were controlled by the police. They took away all our money, he said, noting he had about £2,000 at the time. It seems that it is their right to take it away. They gave us a receipt. The officers promised that the money would be returned, but until now this has not happened.On Wednesday, the UNHCR criticized Denmark's proposals, expressing disbelief that the country would seize the few belongings asylum seekers managed to save. However, Integration Minister Inger Stojberg argued that the measures place migrants on equal footing with unemployed Danes, who must sell assets above a certain threshold to receive benefits. Items of sentimental value, such as wedding rings, are exempt from the plans.Unlike Denmark, Switzerland is not an EU member but is part of the Schengen Agreement, which allows passport-free travel between participating countries. Yet, some nations have reinstated border controls due to concerns over the influx of more than a million migrants into Europe last year.

text: In the Mansion House speech that was abandoned last week due to the murder of Jo Cox MP, George Osborne was due to warn on the impact on financial services if Britain leaves the European Union. Major banks like JP Morgan and HSBC have raised alarms about potential job losses in the capital, a concern now echoed by one of France’s leading economists. Mathilde Lemoine, a former advisor to French Prime Minister Dominique de Villepin and a current member of France's economic watchdog, supports this claim. Speaking to the BBC, Lemoine warned that Brexit could drive euro-denominated asset transactions, a crucial component of the City's financial operations, to relocate to the eurozone.The European Central Bank has long held that euro-denominated transactions, valued at hundreds of billions of euros, should be conducted on the continent. The UK Treasury, however, successfully challenged this notion in the European Court of Justice, emphasizing the importance of these transactions to London's financial health. Lemoine, now the chief economist at Edmond de Rothschild private bank, argued that this legal victory would be nullified if Britain exits the EU. If the United Kingdom leaves the European Union, this clearing house dealing with euro transactions will relocate to the eurozone, prompting many foreign, European, and non-European banks to follow suit, she stated.She highlighted London's status as a premier financial hub, attributing it to the talent pool, which could shift to the eurozone, enhancing its financial sector. Lemoine described it as an abnormality that euro transaction clearing houses are based in London, outside ECB supervision, posing a systemic risk. She noted that the market could be worth between €600bn and €1tn, potentially affecting thousands of jobs, though the exact number remains uncertain.Proponents of Brexit argue that, despite potential service losses, London could thrive without EU regulations, especially concerning pay. A major bank's CEO expressed confidence that London would remain Europe's only globally significant financial center due to its vast, liquid markets and professional services, dwarfing smaller centers like Paris and Frankfurt.Gerard Lyons, former economic advisor to Boris Johnson and chief economist at Standard Chartered, asserted that the EU would still rely on London. London will remain Europe's major financial center, regardless of the Referendum's outcome, he said, emphasizing London's potential to compete globally with cities like Hong Kong, Singapore, and New York.Concerns also loom over a possible economic downturn post-Brexit. However, Lemoine suggested the impact might not be as severe as some economists predict. Many models foresee disaster if Brexit occurs, she acknowledged, but argued, That's not my evaluation. She believes the UK government would implement measures to mitigate GDP decline, and exporters could swiftly adapt to new trade policies.Drawing parallels with the UK's 1992 exit from the European monetary system, Lemoine recalled how UK exports to the EU plummeted, yet those to non-EU countries surged, resulting in an unexpected 5% overall export growth.

text: India's Supreme Court has struck down a controversial law which allowed police to arrest people for comments on social networks and other internet sites. In a landmark decision, the Supreme Court declared Section 66A of the Information Technology Act unconstitutional. This controversial law had led to the arrest of several individuals for their social media posts on platforms like Facebook and Twitter, sparking widespread public outrage. The government had argued in favor of the law, claiming it was designed to prevent the spread of offensive content online. However, a two-judge bench of the Supreme Court, responding to petitions from civil rights groups and a law student, found that Section 66A infringed upon the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression. Justice RF Nariman, quoted by news agency AFP, stated, Section 66A is unconstitutional and we have no hesitation in striking it down. He further remarked, The public's right to know is directly affected by section 66A.The now-nullified Section 66A had broad powers, allowing for up to three years of imprisonment for sending electronic messages deemed annoying or inconvenient. The law first came under scrutiny after the 2012 arrest of two young women in Mumbai. Shaheen Dhada was detained for criticizing the city's shutdown following the death of politician Bal Thackeray, while Renu Srinivasan was arrested for merely liking the comment. Both were eventually released on bail, but their arrests ignited demands across India for the law to be abolished.Since then, numerous arrests under Section 66A have been criticized as abuses of power. The Supreme Court's decision on Tuesday was met with widespread approval, quickly becoming a trending topic on Twitter under #Sec66A. The ruling was welcomed by Delhi's governing Aam Aadmi Party. Journalist Swati Vashishtha emphasized the significance of the right to dissent for citizens, while popular author Chetan Bhagat expressed he was super happy with the outcome. Pankaj Pachauri, former communications advisor to Prime Minister Manmohan Singh, succinctly commented, good riddance to the law.

text: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and what is now known as the World Bank, were set up to manage the post-World War II global economy. In 1944, a pivotal conference in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, laid the groundwork for the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and what would become the World Bank. These institutions were envisioned to foster global economic cooperation and prevent a recurrence of the 1930s Great Depression by aiding countries with balance of payments issues. Initially focused on post-war reconstruction, the World Bank, originally known as the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, has since evolved into the leading global development organization, dedicated to promoting growth and reducing poverty. It operates by providing loans, grants, and advice to low and middle-income countries, with its 187 member states as stakeholders.The IMF's mission is to maintain economic stability and mitigate financial crises, particularly in the developing world. Funded by member nations through a quota system based on each country's wealth, the IMF also determines voting power within the organization: greater contributions equate to more significant voting rights. Acting as a lender of last resort, the IMF provides short-term foreign exchange reserves to members in distress. Historically, the IMF has been led by a European, while a US national has headed the World Bank.The IMF and World Bank have often been focal points for protests, drawing criticism from various groups, including environmentalists and anarchists. Detractors argue that their policies exploit the poor, damage the environment, and threaten livelihoods through freer trade. The IMF has acknowledged that opening developing markets to foreign investors can heighten the risk of financial crises. In 2002, former managing director Horst Koehler admitted that globalization's benefits had not been evenly distributed, advocating for more and better globalization instead of less.Christine Lagarde made history in 2011 as the first woman to lead the IMF in its 65-year history. With a background in law and experience as France's finance minister, she took charge during the eurozone crisis, where fears of Greek loan defaults loomed large. Known for her candidness, Lagarde has criticized the male-dominated culture of global banks for contributing to the 2008 financial crisis. She aims to enhance diversity at the IMF and reform voting to give emerging economies more influence. Her predecessor, Dominique Strauss-Kahn, resigned amid sexual assault charges, from which he was later cleared.Meanwhile, Jim Yong Kim became the World Bank president in April 2012, succeeding Robert Zoellick. A Korean-American and former Dartmouth College president, Kim is celebrated for his work in combating HIV/AIDS and tuberculosis. Despite facing a strong challenge from Nigerian Finance Minister Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, Kim secured the position traditionally held by an American.The IMF and World Bank often step in during economic turmoil, providing critical financial support. The IMF has played roles in the 1997 Asian financial crisis, assisted South American nations like Argentina and Brazil, and activated emergency funding during the 2008 global financial crisis. By August 2010, it had committed around $200 billion to economies in distress, with Hungary, Romania, and Ukraine as major borrowers. The eurozone crisis prompted significant IMF interventions, including substantial bailouts for Greece, Portugal, and Ireland. The IMF also provides emergency loans for natural disasters, such as the 2004 Asian tsunami.Developing countries, including the BRIC nations (Brazil, Russia, India, and China), have criticized their limited influence in the IMF and World Bank. They argue for reforms to the quota system, which ties voting power to financial contributions. The current system grants the US 17% of the vote, enabling it to veto changes requiring an 85% majority, while India, despite its large population, has less than one-third of the US's voting power.The traditional leadership structure of the IMF and World Bank, favoring Europeans and Americans respectively, has been increasingly challenged. Upon assuming her role, Lagarde appointed Zhu Min, a former deputy governor of the People's Bank of China, as deputy managing director, signaling a shift towards greater inclusivity.

text: The landlocked mountainous region of Nagorno-Karabakh is the subject of an unresolved dispute between Azerbaijan, in which it lies, and its ethnic Armenian majority, backed by neighbouring Armenia. In 1988, as the Soviet Union neared its collapse, a brutal conflict erupted between Azerbaijani forces and Armenian secessionists. This war, which concluded with a truce in 1994, left the de facto independent state of Nagorno-Karabakh under the control of ethnic Armenians. Despite numerous negotiations, a lasting peace agreement remains elusive, and the conflict is one of post-Soviet Europe's enduring frozen conflicts.The roots of this strife stretch back over a century, tied to historical tensions between Christian Armenian and Muslim Turkic and Persian influences. Karabakh, inhabited for centuries by both Christian Armenians and Turkic Azeris, was absorbed into the Russian empire in the 19th century. Although the two communities coexisted relatively peacefully, early 20th-century violence lingers in collective memory.Following World War I and the Bolshevik revolution, Soviet authorities established the Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Region within the Soviet Socialist Republic of Azerbaijan in the early 1920s. This move, part of a broader divide-and-rule strategy, placed an ethnic Armenian majority under Azerbaijani jurisdiction. As Soviet power waned in the late 1980s, tensions flared into open conflict when the region's parliament voted to unite with Armenia.The ensuing violence, claiming an estimated 20,000 to 30,000 lives, saw ethnic Armenians seize control of Karabakh and push into surrounding Azerbaijani territories, creating a buffer zone linking it to Armenia. In late 1991, amid the Soviet Union's dissolution, Karabakh declared independence, escalating the situation to full-scale war. This self-declared status, however, remains unrecognized internationally. Armenia, while not officially acknowledging Karabakh's independence, has been its primary military and financial supporter.A Russian-brokered ceasefire in 1994 left Karabakh and adjacent Azerbaijani areas in Armenian hands. The conflict displaced over a million people, with ethnic Azeris—once 25% of Karabakh's population—fleeing to Azerbaijan, and ethnic Armenians leaving Azerbaijani territories. Neither group has been able to return.The region's name, Karabakh, is derived from an Azeri term meaning black garden, while Nagorno is Russian for mountainous. Ethnic Armenians prefer the ancient name Artsakh. Sporadic ceasefire violations have resulted in casualties on both sides, and Armenia, landlocked due to closed borders with Turkey and Azerbaijan, faces significant economic challenges.Since the truce, a tense stalemate persists. Azeris lament the loss of land they claim as theirs, while Armenians show no inclination to relinquish it. The OSCE's Minsk Group, co-chaired by Russia, France, and the US, continues efforts to mediate the conflict. A 2006 referendum in the region, deemed illegitimate by Azerbaijan, saw the approval of a new constitution. Nonetheless, there have been sporadic diplomatic engagements, with Armenian and Azeri leaders meeting occasionally.While talks in May and November 2009 suggested progress, negotiations stalled, and ceasefire breaches have continued. The most severe incident occurred in April 2016, when renewed hostilities resulted in the deaths of dozens of soldiers from both sides.

In the midst of the break-up of the Soviet Union in 1989, the Parliament of Karabakh voted to join Armenia, and in the ensuing conflict, which lasted until the end of 1991, Karabakh declared its independence, which is unrecognized. The Karabakh Parliament in 1989 voted to join Armenia, and a war broke out in Karabakh which escalated into a full-fledged war. The war, which lasted from 1992 to 1994, ended with a Russian ceasefire and left the region in Armenian hands. Around one million people were displaced, many of them Armenians, many Azeris who had fled to Azerbaijan, and Armenians who had fled the regions of Azerbaijan. Neither side has been able to return. The name Karabakh derives from the Azeri Kara-Bagh, which means ‘black garden’, while the Russian name Nagornaya means ‘mountainous’. In the years following the ceasefire, the tension has continued. Armenia, landlocked by Turkey and Azerbaijan, faces serious economic difficulties. The Azerbaijanis lament the loss of what they consider theirs, while the Armenians are in no mood to give it up. The so-called "Minsk group" (Russia, France and the United States) led by mediation in the conflict continues to negotiate. In the year 2006, a constitutional referendum in the region, which was considered illegitimate by Azerbaijan, adopted a new constitution. Diplomatic contacts have been continuing, with occasional meetings between Armenian and Azerbaijani leaders, but, despite some progress, negotiations have stagnated, and cease-fire violations continue. The worst case was that of April of the year 2016, when renewed fighting resulted in the deaths of dozens of soldiers on both sides.

text: Tortoises, Roald Dahl and the man behind Love Actually are just three of the ingredients in Esio Trot, a romantic comedy for BBC One starring Dustin Hoffman and Dame Judi Dench. Dustin Hoffman, Dame Judi Dench, and Richard Curtis collectively boast more than 214 years of life experience. Yet, as Dame Judi aptly puts it, age is just a number. This sentiment is at the heart of a new TV comedy-drama that showcases the ability to find love later in life.Adapted from Roald Dahl's 1990 children's book, Esio Trot tells the tale of a solitary London bachelor whose affection is captured by the charming widow living in the flat below. Her love for tortoises seems an insurmountable barrier to romance, until Mr. Hoppy, portrayed by Hoffman, devises a clever scheme to win over Mrs. Silver, played by Dench.For those unfamiliar with Dahl's original story, the title Esio Trot is simply tortoise spelled backwards, hinting at the unique plan Mr. Hoppy concocts. Reading backwards, or sdrawkcab, becomes a key element in the narrative, which also features James Corden as the neighbor who guides and narrates the story.Richard Curtis, known for hits like Four Weddings and a Funeral, Notting Hill, and the Blackadder series, confesses to being a huge fan of Dahl, whom he compares to Charles Dickens. Curtis found the project particularly enticing because it allowed him to explore love between older people. He explained, In my previous films, if things don't work out, characters can try again. But when you're older and lonely, the stakes are higher. I wanted to show people finding love when they thought it was impossible. That adds drama.Dame Judi shared Curtis's enthusiasm, eagerly accepting the role of Mrs. Silver, even if she finds the character a bit stupid. She quipped, After they mentioned Dustin's name, I would have joined just to walk across the street. Dench, who will appear in the sequel to The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel, is passionate about portraying older characters, often overlooked by an industry skewed towards younger audiences.Dench is vocal about her disdain for age-related stereotypes. Age is just a number imposed on you, she asserts. It irritates me when people ask if I'm retiring or suggest I should relax. I don't want to hear I'm too old for something. I want to try it first. It's not about age; it's about the spirit. Keep moving, and you won't fall.For Hoffman, staying upright was a concern during a dance scene with Dame Judi to Louis Armstrong's music in Esio Trot. I'm not a dancer, admits the star of The Graduate and Tootsie. After two lessons, I thought it wouldn't work, but it was fine because Mr. Hoppy wasn't supposed to be a dancer. We just went with it.Hoffman praises Dench as an extraordinary talent with great energy, allowing him to connect deeply with her on screen. However, he was less enamored with his other co-stars—the tortoises crucial to Mr. Hoppy's plan. You've never smelled anything like 60 tortoises, he laments. That tortoise poo was real—no CGI. We stopped using air conditioning because the tortoises wouldn't act if they got too cold.While filming in London, Hoffman and Dench had little time to socialize. Judi wanted to, but I was always too tired, Hoffman admits. I don't socialize when I'm working or when I'm not. Other than that, I love people!Catch Esio Trot on BBC One on January 1 at 18:30 GMT.

text: Pupils at a County Antrim school have developed a new tool to target cyberbullying. Ballyclare High School has introduced an innovative reporting system known as 'Step Up', which students can access from home, school, or even via their smartphones. The school claims this is a pioneering initiative in Northern Ireland. This system allows students to directly communicate their concerns to the appropriate teacher through the school's website.Emma Blacoe, a 14-year-old student who contributed to the system's development, explained, Pupils can upload files and pictures of screenshots and chats if they feel someone's in danger. They can also simply just say if they're being pressured or bullied or if anyone else is. By clicking a button on the school website, students are directed to an online form where they can specify their year group and choose which teacher should handle their issue. The provided information remains confidential, visible only to the student and teaching staff, with the option to remain anonymous.David Andrew, another contributor to 'Step Up', highlighted its user-friendly nature. If pupils really feel there's something which needs to be sorted out, they can do it, he said. Bullying is never acceptable, and the sooner someone steps up, the sooner it can be sorted out.Mhairi Hill, the head of cyber safety at the school, assured that all allegations would be thoroughly investigated by teachers. Staff will pick it up at the earliest opportunity and follow the procedure already in place for dealing with incidents, she stated. With online bullying, pupils can come to us with screenshots, and that's concrete evidence we can use to take the investigation forward. We would establish the facts before proceeding but would follow up every report. If a child has felt it's necessary to raise the concern, then it's worth following up in our eyes. We have a duty of care for our pupils, and if a pupil's upset or distressed in class, they're not going to learn to their full potential, so it's important that we address these issues.

text: Colombia's President Juan Manuel Santos has met 30 rebels of the ELN, the country's second largest armed group, who laid down their arms. In a significant stride towards peace in Colombia, President Santos hailed the recent developments as a great step towards peace. The National Liberation Army (ELN), despite not being part of the ongoing peace talks with the country's largest rebel faction, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc), has shown interest in joining these negotiations. However, the Colombian government maintains that the ELN must first release its hostages.The ELN, a left-wing group with approximately 1,500 members, saw a contingent of 30 rebels surrender in Cauca's southeastern region. Among them were three pregnant women, who handed over their weapons and equipment in the presence of Mr. Santos. Speaking in Cali, he welcomed the rebels and emphasized, This is what the [peace] process is about. So every member of the ELN and the Farc follows their path fighting for their ideals, but without violence and without arms. This marks the largest single group of ELN members to lay down arms, according to Mr. Santos.On Monday, Farc's chief peace negotiator, Ivan Marquez, expressed optimism about ending the nearly five-decade-long armed conflict. Engaged in talks with the Colombian government in Cuba, Marquez urged left-wing parties and unions to join the peace efforts. The government aims to finalize a peace accord by November, but Marquez cautioned against a hasty settlement. It is possible [to reach an agreement by November]. But to achieve peace you need time. A bad peace deal is worse than war, he stated in an interview with RCN, a Colombian network.The first direct talks between the Colombian government and its largest rebel group began in November of the previous year, yet the ELN remains excluded from these discussions. Last month, in an apparent effort to involve the ELN, the Farc announced that the two groups were exploring unification. Nonetheless, the government stands firm that the rebels must first disarm and release all hostages. Although the ELN recently freed a Colombian soldier, they are believed to still hold other captives.Humberto de la Calle, the chief government negotiator, reiterated that the goal of the Cuban peace talks is to persuade the rebels to abandon their armed struggle and join the political process. While consensus has been reached on land reform, negotiations continue on five additional agenda items. A Farc negotiator recently proposed convening a Constitutional Assembly to ratify the agreements made in Cuba.The Farc, whose numbers have dwindled from about 16,000 fighters in 2001 to an estimated 8,000 today, are part of the fourth attempt at negotiating peace since the conflict began in the 1960s.

text: Nottingham Forest have made an approach to Burton Albion to speak with former player Nigel Clough in relation to their managerial vacancy. Nigel Clough, aged 50, is a familiar face at Nottingham Forest, having played over 300 games for the club during two separate stints, the first under the management of his father, Brian Clough. Currently, he is in his second tenure as the manager of Burton Albion, a role he resumed in December 2015, successfully leading the Brewers to the Championship last season. On January 14, Nottingham Forest dismissed their former manager, Philippe Montanier. Currently, Burton trails Forest by three positions in the Championship standings, with Forest sitting at 19th place, five points clear of the relegation zone. When contacted by BBC Radio Nottingham, Forest declined to comment on the managerial situation, and Burton similarly withheld remarks when approached by BBC Radio Derby.In a recent press conference, Clough addressed the rumors linking him to the Forest managerial vacancy following Montanier's exit. It's an easy link and a logical one from lots of points of view, he remarked to BBC Radio Derby on Wednesday. Despite strong allegiances, in football, people often join rival clubs. Having spent 18 years with Nottingham Forest, it’s a significant part of my life.Although Clough has never managed Forest, his connection to the club remains strong. His popularity with fans only waned during his managerial periods at Derby County and Sheffield United, both traditional rivals. Nevertheless, he received a warm welcome when Burton faced Forest in the EFL season opener in August, a thrilling match that ended 4-3 in Forest's favor.During his playing days at Forest, Clough, despite being the manager's son, carved out his own legacy, ensuring his presence was respected both in the dressing room and among supporters. Only Grenville Morris has surpassed Clough’s tally of 131 goals for the club. He was part of a late 1980s squad that frequently graced Wembley, notably scoring twice in the 1989 League Cup final victory over Luton, securing Forest's first trophy in nearly ten years. His vision and skill complemented strikers like Lee Chapman, Nigel Jemson, and Teddy Sheringham, earning him international recognition with England.After his father’s departure following the dismal 1992-93 season that saw Forest relegated from the top division, Clough moved on to Liverpool after nine years with Forest. He briefly returned on loan in 1996-97, attempting, albeit unsuccessfully, to help Forest retain their top-flight status.
