text: Manchester City's Claudio Bravo is one of the world's top keepers when it comes to build-up play, manager Pep Guardiola said after beating Hull 3-1. On Saturday, a weak shot from Tigers defender Andrea Ranocchia found its way past the goalkeeper, marking the visitors' only attempt on target. This adds to an unsettling trend for Claudio Bravo, who has now let in seven goals from the last seven shots he has faced in the Premier League.Despite this, Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola remains confident in Bravo's abilities, particularly praising his footwork. His footwork is on par with Bayern Munich's Manuel Neuer and Barcelona's Marc-Andre ter Stegen, Guardiola stated. The Chilean goalkeeper returned to the starting lineup against Hull, replacing Willy Caballero, for his first league appearance since January 21.Bravo played a role in City's second goal, contributing to a sequence of skillful passes that culminated in Raheem Sterling's cross to Sergio Aguero, who netted his 28th goal of the season. Guardiola emphasized Bravo's contribution, saying, With his feet, he helps us significantly in building up play and maintaining possession in midfield.In his previous Premier League outings, Bravo conceded twice against Tottenham and four times at Everton. His last save of a shot on target in the league came against Burnley on January 2. City's victory over Hull marked their first Premier League win since defeating Sunderland 2-0 on March 5, snapping a four-match winless streak. They currently sit fourth in the standings, trailing Liverpool by two points but with a game in hand. They are seven points ahead of Arsenal and Manchester United, both of whom have played two games fewer. The much-anticipated Manchester derby against United is set for January 27.Guardiola, who took over from Manuel Pellegrini at the Etihad Stadium last summer, believes the battle for a top-four finish and Champions League qualification will go down to the wire, concluding on May 21. He remarked, The gap isn't large. We must stay vigilant. We still face teams like Leicester, West Brom, and Southampton, which have challenged us this season. I'm confident we'll be competing with Arsenal, United, and Liverpool for the third and fourth spots until the very end.

text: ScottishPower customers will soon be able to buy gas and electricity in bundles of days rather than signing up to standard or fixed-price deals. ScottishPower is revolutionizing the way consumers purchase energy by introducing a system inspired by the familiar processes of filling up a car with petrol or buying mobile data bundles. This initiative aims to simplify energy bills, according to the company's chief executive, Keith Anderson. We're saying to people buy it by the day, not by kilowatts or a fancy tariff you don't understand, Anderson explained.Customers will engage with an app featuring a consumption gauge, allowing them to monitor their energy usage. Each customer's day will be customized based on a personalized forecast of their typical energy use, which will also adjust with seasonal changes. Consumers will have the flexibility to purchase gas and electricity packages ranging from a single day to a month, and even up to 180 days in advance.The company has been testing this scheme, named PowerUp, which they believe could revolutionize consumer energy purchasing. Anderson shared their inspiration: You go to the garage and put £50 in your car. Inherently you know that will last you two to three weeks. We thought why don't we do the same thing with energy. The app will feature a fuel gauge that informs customers of their current energy usage and remaining balance.Under the PowerUp scheme, customers will not incur a standing charge. ScottishPower promises that the tariffs under this plan will include some of their most competitive prices. Initially, the scheme will be available to existing customers, with potential expansion to the broader market under consideration.A two-year investigation by competition authorities revealed that many consumers are disengaged from the energy market and fail to switch to the most cost-effective deals. The industry regulator has welcomed this novel approach. Ofgem stated: We want more competition to increase choice and drive down prices for consumers. We encourage suppliers to offer new innovative tariffs to help people engage in the market and find the best deal which suits them. Innovative tariffs can be tailored to an individual consumer's needs and give people more control over their energy bill and how they pay for it.Claire Osborne, an energy expert at Uswitch.com, endorsed the initiative, noting, Energy bills are notoriously difficult to understand and so this approach, similar to how we buy petrol, should help consumers use less, waste less and pay less for their gas and electricity. text: The Dalai Lama has called on his fellow Nobel Peace Laureate, Aung San Suu Kyi, to do more to help persecuted Rohingya Muslims in her country, Myanmar. In a recent interview with The Australian, the Dalai Lama expressed his hope that Aung San Suu Kyi would address the ongoing Rohingya crisis. The Tibetan spiritual leader voiced particular concern about the thousands of Rohingyas left adrift at sea. Suu Kyi has been criticized internationally for her silence on this issue.The Rohingya people, not recognized as citizens by Myanmar (formerly Burma), remain stateless. The Dalai Lama urged Myanmar's Buddhists to remember the face of the Buddha when addressing the plight of the Rohingya minority. He revealed that since 2012, following interfaith violence in Myanmar's Rakhine state, he had twice encouraged Suu Kyi to take action.It's very sad. In the Burmese case, I hope Aung San Suu Kyi, as a Nobel laureate, can do something, he told the newspaper. I met her two times, first in London and then the Czech Republic. I mentioned this problem, and she told me she found some difficulties, that things were not simple but very complicated. But in spite of that, I feel she can do something.Suu Kyi, 69, has defended her reluctance to speak out on the alleged persecution of the Rohingya by asserting that her role is that of a politician, not a human rights advocate. She contends that the issue of thousands of Rohingya fleeing Myanmar and being stranded at sea is a matter for the government to resolve.According to the BBC's Jonah Fisher in Myanmar, the Dalai Lama joins a growing chorus of international voices, including South African Archbishop Desmond Tutu, urging Suu Kyi to address the situation. With Myanmar's general election approaching in November, many interpret her silence as political pragmatism, given the widespread hostility toward the Rohingya among the Burmese population. However, it remains uncertain whether she harbors any genuine sympathy for the Rohingyas, our correspondent notes.

text: Thousands of Yemenis have taken to the streets of the capital, Sanaa, to protest after an air strike killed more than 140 people at a wake on Saturday. Outside the UN headquarters, demonstrators rallied, demanding an international probe into a deadly strike attributed to the Saudi-led coalition. Although Saudi Arabia has not admitted involvement, it has committed to an investigation. The kingdom entered Yemen’s civil war last year, backing the internationally recognized government.Former Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh, now aligned with the Houthi rebels controlling Sanaa, has urged attacks on Saudi border soldiers as retribution. Saturday's bombing, which left over 500 injured, targeted the wake of Gawal al-Rawishan, the Houthi-appointed Interior Minister's father. Many Houthi officials were present, and Mr. Rawishan was gravely injured. A rescuer described the scene as a lake of blood.The attack has drawn condemnation from the UN, European Union, and the US. UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon declared, any deliberate attack against civilians is utterly unacceptable, demanding accountability for those responsible. The Saudi-led coalition has promised to immediately investigate this case with the Joint Incidents Assessment Team in Yemen and US experts who participated in previous investigations. They acknowledged reports about the regrettable and painful bombing in Sanaa, emphasizing that their troops are instructed to avoid targeting populated areas and civilians.In response, the US announced an immediate review of its already-reduced support for the coalition. White House National Security Council spokesman Ned Price stated that US cooperation with Saudi Arabia is not a blank cheque. Houthi leader Abdul-Malek al-Houthi, in a televised address, claimed the strike occurred with Washington's green light using US weapons. The rebels' spokesman described it as an act of genocide.Yemen faces a dire humanitarian crisis, with the UN reporting that four out of every five of its 28 million people need assistance. Since the war's onset in 2014, nearly three million have been displaced. The Houthis seized the capital, forcing President Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi's government to flee. The Saudi-led coalition, fearing the Zaidi Shia rebels as Iranian proxies, has conducted thousands of airstrikes against them.A recent UN report estimated that 3,799 civilians have been killed since the Saudi-led air campaign began in March last year, attributing 60% of civilian deaths over a year to coalition strikes.

text: The Pope's plea to tackle climate change is likely to get a cool reception from some key energy politicians in the US. Republican Marsha Blackburn, who holds the position of the second-highest ranking member on the House energy committee, has expressed skepticism about global warming, asserting that the debate on its causes remains unresolved. Notably, Pope Francis is set to address Congress on Thursday, emphasizing the urgency of climate action. During a White House speech on Wednesday, the Pope declared that the climate crisis can no longer be left to a future generation.In a forthcoming Radio 4 documentary series titled Climate Change - Are we Feeling Lucky?, Blackburn claimed earlier this year that the earth had cooled by 1°F over the past 13 years. She firmly stated that no evidence could convince her of the existence of man-made global warming. Additionally, Blackburn rejected the theory of evolution, a stance that scientists have criticized as complete nonsense.The jury is still out saying man is the cause for global warming, after the earth started to cool 13 years ago, Blackburn remarked. When confronted with the fact that the earth's surface temperature had not significantly risen in the past 13 years, she insisted, I think we've cooled almost 1 degree (F).Contrary to Blackburn's assertions, major scientific bodies, including NASA, report that the earth continues to warm, with observable phenomena such as melting ice, rising sea levels, and warming oceans. Representing Tennessee, a state heavily reliant on coal, Blackburn declined to specify the sources of her skepticism towards established scientific consensus.We have met with different researchers, Blackburn explained. We have had numerous committee meetings with presentations from various individuals, and from all of that and what we have been able to read, you come to an opinion. There are some who believe human activity is responsible for carbon emissions, and because of that, we need to revert to 1870s levels of carbon emissions. I just choose to disagree with that.When asked what scientific evidence might change her stance on climate change as a threat, she responded, I don't think you will see me being persuaded. On the topic of evolution, Blackburn simply stated, No, I do not.Blackburn's views hold significance as Republicans in Congress aim to dismantle President Obama's initiatives to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Professor Brian Hoskins, a prominent climate scientist at the Royal Society, described her remarks as absolutely staggering. It is nonsense to say the world has cooled, Hoskins commented. If no evidence will persuade Ms. Blackburn of climate change, that shows how well-founded her views are.Correction 25 September 2015: An earlier version of this report inaccurately implied a connection between Marsha Blackburn's comments and the Pope's address. Her statements were actually made in an earlier interview, and the headline and text have been amended for clarity. Follow Roger on Twitter @rharrabin.

text: BBC Ouch wants your funny, confusing or embarrassing stories about those awkward situations which occurred because you're disabled or have mental health difficulties. Experience the magic of storytelling at Tales of the Misunderstood, a live event this summer. Imagine the moment when your humorous shark attack tale, meant as a joke, was taken seriously by your boss and retold at a conference. Or the time you were handed a children's menu at dinner due to your restricted growth. Perhaps your friends tiptoe around words like mad or crazy because they know you see a therapist. text: Two people have been killed and two others injured in a stabbing in a house in Canterbury. A man, believed to be acquainted with the victims, was apprehended at a residence on Dickens Avenue shortly after 19:30 BST on Tuesday. According to Kent Police, two individuals succumbed to fatal injuries, while two others were hospitalized.Neighbor Rab Hendry recounted to the BBC his efforts to assist a man in his 20s, who had sustained a stab wound to the stomach. I saw two lads, who I think were brothers, and the older one mentioned his brother had been stabbed in the stomach, Hendry explained. I got him to the ground and saw the wound was completely open. I used tea towels to apply pressure until paramedics arrived. Hendry added that the young man was extremely panicked and appeared white as a sheet, so he continued talking to him to help keep him calm.Another local resident, identifying himself only as Jamie, described seeing a woman lying in the doorway and what appeared to be a man's body further inside the house. He noted that police attempted CPR to revive them but believed they had already passed away.The suspect was detained at the scene on Dickens Avenue, with Kent Police indicating that he likely knew the victims. The community expressed their disbelief, as the tragic incident unfolded in what they described as a quiet area.Eighty-three-year-old Charlotte Bunn, living opposite the crime scene, remarked that residents typically stayed for one or two years then move on. She added, I only knew the people there to say hello to in passing. They seemed fine. I can't find any fault. It's a quiet area. In all my years here, I've only had trouble once.Another neighbor, choosing to remain anonymous, speculated that the property might have been used for housing by the authorities. The vicinity around the house was sealed off, with serious crime officers and forensic experts dispatched to the scene. A forensic tent was erected at the front entrance of the property on Dickens Avenue.Kent Police stated they were in the process of notifying the victims' next of kin, although formal identification had yet to be completed. Detectives are actively working to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident, according to a police spokesman.

text: Welsh exiles Taulupe Faletau, George North, Jamie Roberts and Rhys Priestland will have to rely on being picked as wildcards for future Wales selection. The Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) has implemented a senior player selection policy (SPSP) that limits the number of players who can be chosen from outside Wales to just three. Among those impacted are Dominic Day, Nicky Thomas, and Rhodri Williams. However, Bath lock Luke Charteris is not bound by this rule and remains eligible for selection. For the first time, the WRU has disclosed its seven-man list, which provides three wildcard options for each of Wales' campaigns, beginning with the 2016-17 season. These campaigns include the Six Nations, summer tours, and autumn internationals, with the flexibility to alter wildcard selections for each event. This policy, colloquially dubbed 'Gatland's Law' after Wales head coach Warren Gatland, aims to encourage more players to compete in domestic leagues within Wales.Back in August 2014, the WRU and Wales' four professional regions resolved a longstanding conflict over the sport's future by signing a £60 million, six-year agreement. This deal incorporated regulations favoring home-based players over those playing abroad. While the policy generally excludes overseas-based players from representing Wales, exceptions can be made. Notably, the SPSP does not apply to players like Toulon's Leigh Halfpenny and Exeter's Tomas Francis, who had already signed contracts outside Wales before the policy's introduction.With Warren Gatland set to lead the 2017 British and Irish Lions tour to New Zealand, Robert Howley will step in as his deputy. In November, Wales is set to face Australia, Argentina, Japan, and South Africa at Cardiff's Principality Stadium, with the squad for these Test matches slated for announcement on Tuesday, 18 October.Martyn Phillips, WRU chief executive, stated, Players have been aware that there would come a point, if they left or signed new contracts outside Wales, that the policy would impact on selection. He acknowledged potential concerns among supporters about not selecting from a full roster but emphasized that relying heavily on players outside Wales is unsustainable for the long-term success of both professional and community rugby. Ultimately, the player has the choice, Phillips added, but we will do all we can to ensure that playing in Wales offers the best professional rugby experience possible.

text: Mark Percival scored 14 points for St Helens as they won a fiery derby against Wigan Warriors and secured a fifth straight Super League victory. In a gripping clash under challenging wet conditions, St Helens emerged victorious against Wigan with a decisive 26-4 win. The match kicked off with an early penalty from Percival, followed by a try from Lewis Tierney for Wigan. However, St Helens quickly gained the upper hand with scores from Percival and Morgan Knowles, leading 16-4 at the break.Luke Walsh extended the lead with a drop-goal, and James Roby's late try sealed the triumph for the visitors. This win propels St Helens to fourth place as the Super 8s commence, while Wigan remains in second. Meanwhile, Hull FC's victory over Salford meant Wigan missed the chance to equal their points.Wigan, having previously enjoyed a nine-match winning streak, now faces consecutive defeats, including last week's loss to Leeds. They head into their Challenge Cup semi-final against Hull FC next week, needing to regroup.St Helens, under Keiron Cunningham, showcased a formidable defensive performance, notably when Joe Greenwood thwarted Sam Tomkins at the line in the second half. The game also saw New Zealand prop Frank-Paul Nuuausala sin-binned on his home debut for Wigan after clashing with Louie McCarthy-Scarsbrook, who also received a yellow card.Returning to the field after an eight-week suspension and a £10,000 fine, Wigan forward John Bateman was back in action. Wigan's head coach Shaun Wane expressed his disappointment, stating, I'm gutted, devastated. We didn't turn up and got what we deserved. The smartest team won. They were good on the floor and were allowed to be good. Our defence was very good for large parts of the game, but our attack was off. Too many individual players had a poor game. We've got seven hard days of work ahead of us now. We need to make sure we turn up against Hull with the same commitment to defence but we've got to be better on attack.In contrast, Keiron Cunningham of St Helens praised his team, saying, I'm just pleased for my players, they stood up to everything Wigan threw at us - they could probably still be playing now and not score. That's what self-belief brings to a side. We went through a tough spell but we're a real close-knit group and now we're heading in the right direction. Wigan are a great attacking side and were fully stacked tonight. They had lots of threats but I thought we stuck to the plan. We're not going to fall in love with ourselves, we give ourselves a good shot for the top four.The teams lined up with Wigan Warriors featuring S Tomkins, Tierney, Gildart, Sarginson, Manfredi, Williams, Smith, Sutton, Powell, Flower, Bateman, Isa, and O'Loughlin, with replacements Crosby, Nuuausala, Mossop, and Shorrocks. St Helens fielded Lomax, Owens, Fleming, Percival, Swift, Turner, Walsh, Walmsley, Roby, Richards, Greenwood, McCarthy-Scarsbrook, and Wilkin, with Amor, Vea, Thompson, and Knowles as substitutes. Referee Phil Bentham officiated the match, which drew an attendance of 20,049.

I admire his moxie—he's self-assured, and that's essential. Despite setbacks at the Masters and last year's Open, I was confident he wouldn't falter again, and he hasn't.I first heard about him when he shot a 61 at my home course in Portrush. Seeing him fulfill his potential is fantastic; he's been like an inevitable success waiting to happen.While McIlroy's Masters collapse is etched in history, his triumph at Congressional could become legendary. His talent has been evident for some time, and seeing him put it together is remarkable.As I've said before, he probably has the most talent I've ever seen from a golfer. Watching him play is a joy; his fluid motion and long drives are impressive.Rory has always had the potential to reach this level. text: Hospital visits for alcohol poisoning have doubled in six years, with the highest rate among females aged 15 to 19, a report has found. Emergency hospital admissions in England due to alcohol-related conditions, like liver disease, have surged by over 50% in the past nine years, reaching 250,000 annually. According to the Nuffield Trust, these rates are most prevalent in deprived regions, particularly in the north, and among men aged 45 to 64. The government has responded by banning the cheapest alcoholic drinks.The Nuffield Trust cautioned that their statistics might underestimate the true impact of alcohol consumption, as they exclude incidents like alcohol-fueled falls and fights, focusing only on illnesses such as alcohol poisoning and liver disease. Furthermore, the data does not account for individuals who arrive at A&E intoxicated and are sent home without treatment or admission.A staggering half of all A&E visits attributed to alcohol poisoning—defined as consuming a toxic amount of alcohol in a short span—occurred on weekends, peaking between midnight and 2 a.m. The report highlights that three-quarters of these cases arrived by ambulance, placing additional strain on already overburdened resources.Alarmingly, young women aged 15 to 19 were hospitalized for alcohol poisoning 1.4 times more often than their male counterparts. The likelihood of A&E visits due to alcohol poisoning and related emergency admissions was three to four times higher among the poorest fifth of the population. The north of England and urban areas also reported higher hospital admission rates.The report delves into the demographics of those admitted for alcohol-related issues, with middle-aged men (45-64) comprising the largest group. Claire Currie, co-author of the report, expressed concern about the pressures on the NHS, especially during the holiday season, urging the government to consider policies like minimum unit pricing and restrictions on alcohol marketing.In 2013, around 18% of men and 13% of women in England consumed alcohol at levels considered harmful. During 2013/14, about 5% of emergency admissions were alcohol-related. Contrastingly, Scotland has seen a decline in such admissions, while Wales has stabilized. The Office for National Statistics indicates a decrease in binge-drinking among young adults in Britain, with over 20% of UK adults abstaining from alcohol entirely.Jackie Ballard from Alcohol Concern highlighted the issue of middle-aged and older individuals exceeding recommended drinking limits, often at home. She emphasized the complex health care needs arising from excessive alcohol consumption, which is linked to over 60 medical conditions. Ballard warned that without serious societal and governmental acknowledgment of these health risks, the NHS will continue to face mounting challenges.A government spokesperson reiterated the importance of responsible drinking, noting the strain on ambulance services and A&E staff. The government has already taken steps to address cheap alcohol by banning the lowest-priced drinks, resulting in a decline in regular alcohol consumption among young people.

text: The owner of Atlanta's new Major League Soccer team says David Beckham should ground share with an American football side for his Miami-based MLS franchise. In February, David Beckham and his group of investors announced their intention to establish a new Major League Soccer (MLS) team. However, the former England captain faced setbacks this summer when two proposals for a 25,000-seat stadium in central Miami were rejected.Arthur Blank, owner of both the NFL's Atlanta Falcons and an upcoming MLS team, was asked about Beckham's situation and suggested that sharing a venue might be a viable solution. Yes, Blank stated, It's a challenge Beckham has to overcome. It's crucial to strike a balance between the commercial aspects and the unique, emotional atmosphere desired in a soccer stadium.Speaking before the Falcons' game against the Detroit Lions at Wembley, Blank shared insights into his own stadium project in Atlanta. The new venue will accommodate 65,000 fans for Falcons games and 29,000 for his MLS team, thanks to a retractable lower tier and mechanized curtains to section off the top tier. Blank believes this design will create the intimate, soccer-specific environment that MLS expansion teams aim for.While Blank's stadium project progresses smoothly, even securing £125m in public funding, Miami Beckham United—the investment group led by the former Manchester United, Real Madrid, and LA Galaxy star—faces significant challenges. Currently, MLS has 19 teams, with none located in the southeastern United States. This will change with the introduction of Orlando City next year. MLS's strategy to foster local rivalries includes adding a second Florida franchise in Miami by 2017, coinciding with the launch of Blank's Atlanta team in Georgia.However, Miami's team cannot move forward without a suitable venue. Blank suggests reconsidering the opposition to sharing an existing stadium with an American football team. The NFL's Miami Dolphins and the University of Miami's football team both play at Sun Life Stadium in northern Miami. Although its dimensions suit football, the stadium lacks a roof and is too large for an MLS fan base.Another possibility is the Florida International University Stadium, which hosts the public university's football team. With a 20,000-seat capacity, it is more appropriately sized, but would require pitch and facility upgrades. Its location, in the middle of a college campus, is also less than ideal.

text: A former chaplain and an ex-principal of a Roman Catholic care home have been found guilty of abusing boys. Anthony McCallen, 65, once served as the chaplain at the now-closed St William's Children's Home in East Yorkshire, where James Carragher, 75, held the position of head. Both men faced a total of 87 charges related to sexual offenses against children at the home spanning from the 1970s to the 1990s, charges they both denied.During the proceedings at Leeds Crown Court, it was revealed that Carragher, a known sex offender from Merseyside, would take boys for late-night naked swims. The jury heard disturbing accounts of their predatory behavior towards boys aged between 10 and 16. In total, 18 men testified, detailing instances of indecent touching.One victim, visibly upset, left the courtroom after recounting how he was sexually assaulted by the pair while he slept. Another witness described how boys were taken for swimming sessions after lights-out and instructed not to wear any trunks.Following the verdict, Judge Jeffrey Marson QC commended the jury for their diligence, remarking, I've never, in many years of doing this, had a jury who had to consider so many charges. It is way beyond the norm, and they are some of the most difficult charges to deal with.Carragher, who had previously been sentenced to seven years in 1993 and 14 years in 2004 for similar offenses, pleaded not guilty to 50 counts of indecent assault and 12 other serious sexual offenses. McCallen, also from Merseyside and previously convicted of abusing two boys in the 1990s, denied 18 counts of indecent assault and seven other serious sexual offenses.After a grueling 10-week trial and 11 days of jury deliberation, Carragher was found guilty of 21 counts of indecent assault and three serious sexual offenses but was acquitted of 30 additional charges. McCallen was convicted on 11 charges, including a serious sexual offense, but was cleared of eight others. The jury could not reach a verdict on 13 charges, leading to their discharge by the judge.Sentencing for McCallen and Carragher is scheduled for January 4. St William's, located in Market Weighton and closed in 1992, was owned by the Diocese of Middlesbrough and operated by the De La Salle Brotherhood. In response to the trial, the diocese expressed hope that those affected by the abuse can move on with their lives and condemned any behavior that harms young people. They stated, The behavior of Anthony McCallen whilst he was a priest was a betrayal of the trust that was placed in him from the Diocese of Middlesbrough.

text: Shares in the UK's biggest estate agent, Countrywide, have plummeted following the publication of its gloomy report on the property market. On Thursday, Countrywide's shares plummeted by 12%, following a previous 5% decline after the announcement that letting agents' fees would be abolished. In its third-quarter trading update, Countrywide revealed expectations of a drop in transactions due to changes in stamp duty and the Brexit vote's aftermath.The group's revenue stood at £188.5 million, down from £197.1 million during the same period last year. Countrywide, which operates 55 high street brands including Bairstow Eves, John D Wood, and Gascoigne Pees, predicted a 6% decline in transactions for the year, with further reductions anticipated in 2017.The company indicated that the decreased market activity observed in the latter half of the year would result in 2016 profits hitting the lower end of expectations. For the three months ending in September, Countrywide reported a 1% decrease in overall house exchanges compared to the previous year, with London experiencing a sharp 29% drop. Additionally, mortgage approvals fell by 12%.The lettings sector was impacted by a surge to complete transactions before the stamp duty changes at the end of the first quarter, leading to an unusually high supply of rental properties, according to the company's statement. Despite this, residential lettings increased by 14% overall, with a 1% rise in London for the three months to September.The announcement of the ban on letting agents' fees in Wednesday's Autumn Statement was labeled a hammer blow for estate agents. Countrywide's CEO, Alison Platt, expressed the company's eagerness to collaborate with the government on the consultation. She noted, We have made good progress this year despite tough market conditions since the EU referendum. Particularly pleasing is our growth in market share in both sales and lettings.However, ETX Capital markets analyst Neil Wilson commented, Countrywide shares are tumbling again this morning after it offered a very downbeat assessment of the property market. The company says it's making good progress, but today's trading statement confirms that estate agents are facing a troubled future. Yesterday's Autumn Statement bombshell banning letting agents from charging upfront fees to tenants couldn't have come at a worse time for the sector. The trading statement presumably doesn't take stock of this change, so we could see a greater adverse effect as a result, he added.

text: A Monmouthshire school has warned parents their children could be sent home if they do not wear a new official uniform. Monmouth Comprehensive School is set to introduce a new uniform policy starting in September, mandating parents to purchase attire from a designated supplier. This decision has sparked discontent among parents, who are frustrated by the requirement to buy £20 trousers and £16 skirts from Trutex, instead of opting for more affordable alternatives.This move by the school runs counter to the Welsh Government's guidelines on school uniforms. Monmouthshire Council, however, has defended the decision, stating that the school engaged in extensive consultations with the entire school community, aligning with government recommendations.In a letter to parents, Deputy Head Andy Williams emphasized that sending students home for uniform violations, as per Welsh Government guidance, would be a measure of last resort. The issue has ignited a flurry of responses on a community Facebook page, with parents expressing their concerns.One parent, Paula Beddis Simpson, voiced her frustration: I am a single parent juggling two or three jobs to make ends meet. It's totally unfair. As long as they are proper grey school trousers and pupils look smart, what is the problem? Another parent, Alex Watkins, remarked, It's not as if people are refusing to adhere to the uniform; they just want the freedom to choose where to buy trousers, skirts, and shirts. It's hardly unreasonable.For year seven and sixth form students, a branded blazer and tie will replace the current polo shirt and jumper, which the school described as tired, inconsistent, and not fit for purpose. Other students can opt for the new uniform if they wish or if their existing attire needs replacement.Parents argue that the new uniform will exceed £100 if purchased from the specified supplier, though the school estimates the cost at £97 for boys and £93 for girls. The Welsh Government advises that governing bodies should specify basic items and colors but not styles, allowing purchases from various retail chains at reasonable prices.Acknowledging concerns over the cost of items from their suppliers, the school, which plans to relocate to a new £33 million building in 2018, defended its decision. Mr. Williams explained, We trialed barcodes for parents to buy cheaper (but often less ethically sourced) items from high street retailers. However, we quickly found that codes and styles changed, leading to a wide variety of uniforms, including tight, skinny jean-type trousers and inappropriate skirts. The school simply cannot keep up with brand and style changes, which would lead to inconsistency in a school with over 1,500 students.Council officer Will McLean noted, The design of school uniforms and the rules which apply to them are determined by school governing bodies. To assist families, pupils eligible for free school meals will receive free uniform items in their first year.

One parent, Alex Watkins, remarked: “It’s not that parents are refusing to buy the uniform, it’s just that they want the freedom to buy trousers, skirts, and shirts where they want to.” “The uniform regulations are set by the school’s governing body, and schools have been unable to keep up with the constant changes in styles and brands which would lead to chaos in a school of 1,500 pupils,” he said. “We tried the bar code system to allow parents to buy cheaper, though often less ethically sourced, uniforms from high street shops, but we soon found that bar codes and styles changed, resulting in a very mixed bag of uniforms with tight, ill-fitting trousers and inappropriate skirts,” he explained. As an assistance to the family, pupils who receive free meals will be given a uniform in their first year of school.”

text: Head teachers in England are keeping up the pressure on school funding, sending a letter warning about cash-starved schools to almost two million families. As the government gears up to outline its agenda in the Queen's Speech, school leaders from 17 councils are urgently calling for action to address a funding gap. School funding shortages emerged as a key issue during the election, resonating with voters and becoming a contentious topic. The Conservative manifesto pledged an additional £1 billion annually, sourced from savings. However, doubts loom over the largest portion of this funding, as uncertainty surrounds the government's plan to eliminate free meals for all infants.With the government lacking a majority in the House of Commons, pushing through legislation to scrap free infant meals, introduced three years ago, presents a significant challenge. This proposal has faced criticism from chef and healthy-school-food advocate Jamie Oliver.In response, head teachers are preparing to send a warning letter to parents of over 4,000 schools, indicating that many institutions may need to cut staff and reduce subject offerings. Prior to the election, there were already warnings that some schools might have to shorten school hours or even implement a four-day week for certain students.School governors have expressed their support for these funding concerns, exemplified by the first-ever strike by governors in West Sussex. The letter will reach parents in councils including Brighton, East Sussex, Northamptonshire, Surrey, Cambridgeshire, Essex, Oxfordshire, Thurrock, Cornwall, Hertfordshire, Peterborough, Wokingham, Devon, Norfolk, Suffolk, West Sussex, and Dorset.Parents will be informed about an analysis from the Institute for Fiscal Studies, which indicates that the Conservative plans for school spending could result in a real-terms cut of 2.8% in per-pupil funding between 2016 and 2022. The head teachers involved are part of a regional campaign addressing school funding shortages, and teachers' unions are also demanding increased investment in education.Kevin Courtney, general secretary of the National Union of Teachers, stated: The general election has forced the government to accept that there is a major problem with school funding that must be addressed. This matter cannot wait—unless the government acts now, class sizes will be higher and fewer subjects will be taught in September.Beyond the debate over the overall school budget, the government must decide whether to proceed with a new funding formula for individual schools. The government has committed to creating a fairer system for distributing school budgets. Ministers have defended their record on school funding, with a Department for Education spokeswoman stating, The core schools budget has been protected in real terms since 2010 and is set to rise from £41bn in 2017-18 to over £42bn in 2019-20 with increasing pupil numbers. But we recognize that schools are facing cost pressures and will continue to provide support to help them use their funding in cost-effective ways.

text: The flagship Conservative election pledge to open a further 500 free schools in England is being put into practice, with applications invited for new schools. The government has announced an ambitious plan to create 270,000 additional places in free schools over the next five years. Education Secretary Nicky Morgan praised these institutions as modern engines of social justice, highlighting their role in transforming education. However, Labour's Tristram Hunt criticized the initiative, calling it an irresponsible use of public funds.The application process for the next wave of free schools began on Friday, signaling the start of this educational expansion. Among the proposals are the New Croydon Academy, which will emphasize science and technology, and the Gipsy Hill Secondary Academy, a project by a group of primary schools in south London aiming to establish a secondary school.Free schools, which number over 250 with more than 150 approved, are new state schools that enjoy the same independence as academies. They operate outside local authority control, offering greater flexibility in curriculum and staffing. Prime Minister David Cameron, during the election campaign, lauded these schools for raising standards and restoring discipline. Introduced under the coalition government, free schools were designed to increase choice and innovation, allowing parents and community groups to establish schools if they saw a lack of quality local education.Despite the original vision, most free schools are now opened by existing professional school groups. A Policy Exchange think tank analysis revealed that in recent waves, over two-thirds of free schools were established by academies or academy chains, while fewer than a fifth were initiated by parents and community groups. Critics, including Labour and teachers' unions, argue that free schools have not delivered additional places where they are most needed. However, the Department for Education counters that nearly three-quarters of the 125,000 free school places created were in areas with shortages, with half located in the country's most deprived communities.Mrs. Morgan emphasized that free schools are at the heart of the government's commitment to deliver real social justice by ensuring all pupils have access to a world-class education. She stressed that this initiative is part of a broader commitment to creating a nation where everyone, regardless of background, can achieve their aspirations. According to the education secretary, free schools offer families a fresh chance to break the cycle of disadvantage by providing unprecedented quality education in many communities.Sarah Pearson, interim director of the New Schools Network, which aids in opening free schools, mentioned that they are collaborating with about 30 groups eager to set up schools. These groups have been diligently working to complete their applications in recent months. The New Schools Network highlighted several expected applications, including the Gipsy Hill bid led by Sir Craig Tunstall. Tunstall, executive head teacher of the federation, expressed a desire to address the issue of bright primary pupils falling behind in secondary school. In our area, there is a shortage of outstanding secondary places, and too often the first year is spent treading water academically as teachers and pupils get to know each other from scratch, he said.In contrast, Tristram Hunt, shadow education secretary, criticized the government's approach. When there is a shortage of school places, rising class sizes, widespread teacher shortages, and significant real-terms budget cuts, parents will find it odd that David Cameron continues to invest hundreds of millions of pounds into building new schools in areas with a surplus of places, he argued.Christine Blower, leader of the National Union of Teachers, echoed these concerns, stating that free schools and academies do not raise standards more effectively than maintained schools. She argued that the initiative is far more about privatisation and ideology than social justice and equality. Chris Keates, leader of the NASUWT teachers' union, added that local authorities should manage place provision and determine the type of school provision that best meets local community needs.

text: Pro12 leaders Ulster will be without injured pair Charles Piutau and Franco van der Merwe for the derby against Connacht in Galway on Friday night. In the aftermath of their victory over the Ospreys, Piutau is dealing with delayed onset concussion, while van der Merwe is grappling with an ankle ligament injury from the same match. Meanwhile, Tommy Bowe makes a triumphant return, providing a significant boost for the team. The Ireland wing, sidelined for six months due to a knee injury, is set to make his first start.Connacht has reshuffled their lineup with six changes following their win against Edinburgh last Saturday. Cian Kelleher steps in on the left wing, replacing the injured Matt Healy. With Peter Robb and Kieran Marmion out due to injuries, Craig Ronaldson is set to make his season debut at inside centre after recovering from a long-term injury, while Caolin Blade will start at scrum-half.In the forward pack, Dave Heffernan will make his first start of the season, taking over from the injured Tom McCartney. With Denis Buckley unavailable, Finlay Bealham, an Ireland international, returns to fill the loosehead position. Andrew Browne, back from injury, will make his season debut, partnering with Ultan Dillane in the second row.Ulster's director of rugby, Les Kiss, has opted to rest scrum-half Ruan Pienaar, with Callum Black stepping into the front row. A new second-row partnership is formed with Robbie Diack and Peter Browne, while Clive Ross takes over from Sean Reidy at openside flanker.Defending champions Connacht, who have managed just one victory over Ulster in their last 20 encounters, currently sit ninth in the standings.Connacht's lineup features T O'Halloran; N Adeolokun, B Aki, C Ronaldson, C Kelleher; J Carty, C Blade; F Bealham, D Heffernan, C Carey, U Dillane, A Browne, E McKeon, J Heenan, and captain J Muldoon. Their replacements include S Delahunt, R Loughney, JP Cooney, L Stevenson, J Connolly, S Kerins, S O'Leary, and S Ili.Ulster fields J Payne as captain, joined by T Bowe, L Ludik, D Cave, C Gilroy; P Jackson, P Marshall; C Black, R Best, R Ah You, R Diack, P Browne, I Henderson, C Ross, and R Wilson. The bench features R Herring, A Warwick, R Kane, K Treadwell, S Reidy, D Shanahan, B Herron, and R Lyttle.

text: Wrexham's appointment of Dean Keates as manager is not the first time the Welsh club have turned to a familiar face to lead them. Dean Keates, who graced the field over 150 times for Wrexham and led the team to victory in the FA Trophy in 2013, is stepping into his first managerial role, succeeding Gary Mills. The club, known for giving former players their managerial start, has seen Arfon Griffiths, Brian Flynn, and Andy Morrell take the helm in the past. Each left a distinct mark on the team, which is now enduring its eighth season outside the Football League.Under Morrell's leadership, with Keates as captain, Wrexham last made a significant play-off push. Morrell, currently managing National League North side Tamworth, was quick to congratulate Keates on his new role. He's perfect for it, Morrell shared with BBC Radio Wales Sport. He's ambitious, enthusiastic, and deeply connected to Wrexham. He gave everything as a player and will do the same as a manager. It's a rare opportunity for him.Morrell himself began as interim manager in September 2011, following Dean Saunders' departure to Doncaster Rovers, before securing the position permanently. However, Morrell inherited a team in second place in the Conference, while Keates now faces a Wrexham side sitting 14th, eight points shy of the play-offs. I was in a better spot, Morrell recalls. We had won seven out of 10 games. Dean needs to shift the players' mentality to a winning one, and he can do it. He'll lead by example and be clear about his expectations.Keates' appointment draws parallels to another former player-turned-manager, Brian Flynn. Despite standing at 5ft 5ins, Keates humorously noted at his press conference, I'm a bit taller than Flynnie though. Flynn, a former Wales international, transitioned from player to manager at Wrexham in November 1989, succeeding Dixie McNeil. He famously turned the team from bottom of the Football League to FA Cup giant killers, with memorable victories over Arsenal and West Ham United during his 12-year reign.Peter Jones, chair of the Wrexham Supporters' Trust, remarked, It's a very similar situation to when Brian Flynn came in, and look at the success he had. Jones emphasized the timeliness of Keates' appointment, highlighting his familiarity with the club. Flynn was known for nurturing young talent, and Morrell believes that homegrown players are crucial for Wrexham's growth. I hope they establish a long-term plan, not just aiming for play-offs this season or next, Morrell told BBC Wales. They need to utilize the academy effectively, bringing young players into the first team. These are assets that can engage fans and bolster the club's future.Morrell envisions a bright future if Wrexham can capitalize on their resources. With a plan, there's no reason why they can't push forward in a few years. Many big teams struggle to reclaim their status, but Wrexham is a Football League club in my eyes and many others'. Keatsy will be positive, driving them to perform well.

text: The growing buy-to-let property market in the UK could post a threat to wider financial stability, a Bank of England committee has said. The Bank of England's Financial Stability Committee (FPC) has raised concerns about the potential impact of buy-to-let mortgage lending on the housing market. According to the FPC, this type of lending could amplify both housing booms and busts. Since 2008, lending in the buy-to-let sector has surged by 40%, a sharp contrast to the mere 2% increase in owner-occupier mortgage lending during the same period. Despite these figures, the FPC has not recommended any immediate government or regulatory intervention.The FPC is alert to the rapid growth of the market and potential developments in underwriting standards, the committee stated. It warned that if the market's expansion is driven by more lenient underwriting, it might threaten broader financial stability through increased credit risk to banks and intensified housing market fluctuations.The proportion of buy-to-let lending within the total stock of outstanding mortgage lending has climbed from 12% in 2008 to 16%. The Bank highlighted that buy-to-let landlords are more likely to sell properties if house prices drop significantly, which could exacerbate the decline in property values. text: Rakesh Shukla is a software engineer who's found his life's calling in looking after dogs that no-one wants, writes the BBC's Geeta Pandey in Bangalore. In the heart of Karnataka, near its bustling capital, a dusty farmhouse becomes a haven of joy and chaos as a car pulls up. Suddenly, a symphony of barks and wagging tails erupts, welcoming Rakesh Shukla with unrestrained enthusiasm. The dogs, jumping and yelping, swarm around him, each vying for his affection. Mr. Shukla, equally delighted, greets them with pats, scratches, and even hoists one onto his shoulder.As he leads me through his sprawling three-and-a-half-acre farm, the scale of his commitment becomes evident. At last count, Mr. Shukla was caring for 735 dogs. Among them are Labradors, Golden Retrievers, Great Danes, Beagles, Dachshunds, Rottweilers, Saint Bernards, a pug, and hundreds of mongrels. Many are strays; others were abandoned. The most recent arrivals—a group of 22 pedigreed dogs—were left homeless after their owner, a businessman, was tragically murdered.This is Geeta Pandey's fourth report from Bangalore, following her 10-day stint covering various stories, including the city's notorious traffic jams and its culinary delights.I'm the last stop for these dogs, Mr. Shukla, 45, explains. They are no longer cute and cuddly. Many are sick and no longer wanted. Lovingly nicknamed the Dog Father, he calls the dogs his babies, and himself their papa.A decade ago, Mr. Shukla, along with his wife, founded a software company. He now dedicates three to four days a week to the farm, nurturing his canine family. Reflecting on his past, he shares, I had worked in Delhi, in the United States, and then set up my own company in Bangalore. Life was all about buying big cars and expensive watches. I had traveled the world, but happiness eluded me.Everything changed in June 2009 when Kavya, a 45-day-old Golden Retriever, entered his life. When we got home, she hid in a corner. I got down to her level, calling out to her. She looked scared but wanted to trust me, he recalls. It was a transformative moment—I felt a warm glow and never questioned my purpose again.Three months later, Mr. Shukla rescued Lucky from the streets, drenched and miserable after weeks of rain. I brought her home too, he says. Soon, every stray or abandoned dog he encountered found a place in his heart and home. Initially, the dogs lived with him, but as their numbers grew, his wife suggested relocating them. The top floor of his office became their new abode.By 2012, with the pack expanding, Mr. Shukla purchased land in Doddballapur and established the farm—a sanctuary for the old, ailing, and unwanted. Designed with open spaces and ponds, the farm is a paradise for its residents, safeguarded by double fencing.The cacophony of barks accompanies us as we tour the enclosures. A team of about 10, including trained veterinary assistants, cares for the dogs, preparing meals and administering necessary medicines. Each day, the dogs consume 200kg of chicken and 200kg of rice. The center's daily operation costs range from 45,000 to 50,000 rupees ($663 to $737), with Mr. Shukla funding 93% of it.Despite his dedication, Mr. Shukla has faced challenges from animal activists demanding access to the farm, alongside complaints of public disturbance due to the large number of dogs. Calls for the farm's closure have been made, but Mr. Shukla stands firm.I've made a pact with my dogs, he declares. We will part only when one of us kicks the bucket.

text: The father of fugitive former US intelligence contractor Edward Snowden is in Russia to visit his son. Lon Snowden expressed profound relief over his son's safety, telling journalists in Moscow, extreme gratitude that my son is safe and secure and he's free. According to local media, he later reunited with Edward Snowden. Edward Snowden, who leaked a vast trove of U.S. intelligence documents, was granted asylum in Russia in August after being stranded for weeks in a transit area at Moscow airport due to the revocation of his travel documents by the U.S. government. The 30-year-old's revelations, widely disseminated by The Guardian and The Washington Post, exposed extensive surveillance operations by U.S. and British intelligence agencies on internet and phone communications.In the United States, Snowden faces serious charges, including theft of government property, unauthorized communication of national defense information, and willful communication of classified intelligence. Each charge carries a potential 10-year prison sentence.On Wednesday, Edward Snowden met with four former U.S. security officials in Russia, who are now advocates against what they see as the misuse of state secrecy. They presented Snowden with the Sam Adams Associates for Integrity in Intelligence award, an honor bestowed annually by a group of retired CIA officers. The officials informed Russian media that Snowden had no regrets about his actions, believing he had acted correctly. He's remarkably centred, former FBI agent Coleen Rowley remarked to state-funded RT television.Upon arriving at Moscow's Sheremetyevo airport on Thursday, Lon Snowden was greeted by his son's Russian lawyer, Anatoly Kucherena. I'm here to learn more about my son's situation, he stated to reporters. My hope is to learn more about his circumstances and his health and to discuss legal options. In televised comments, he added, If the opportunity presents itself, I certainly hope that I have the opportunity to see my son. I'm not sure that my son will be returning to the US. That's his decision, he's an adult.Although Lon Snowden later met with his son, Russian state-run TV channels Rossiya 24 and Channel One reported that the details of the meeting were kept confidential for security reasons. Lon Snowden has previously lauded his son for speaking the truth and making significant sacrifices, while expressing concern that Edward would not receive a fair trial if he returned to the U.S.Edward Snowden accessed the classified documents while employed by the defense contractor Booz Allen Hamilton in Hawaii, where he resided with his girlfriend. As the disclosures emerged, Snowden fled to Hong Kong, where he consented to The Guardian revealing his identity in June. To avoid U.S. extradition efforts, Snowden traveled to Russia, remaining in Sheremetyevo airport's transit zone until granted asylum.Russia's decision to grant asylum to Snowden further strained its relations with the U.S., leading Washington to cancel a bilateral summit in September.

text: It's that time of year again where we put the clocks forward and all get one hour less in bed! As you sleep soundly in your bed, the clocks will spring forward at 1 a.m. on Sunday, March 26. This annual shift marks our transition from Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) to British Summer Time (BST), also known as Daylight Saving Time (DST) or GMT+1.Last year was noteworthy as it celebrated a century since we first adopted this practice. The upcoming change ensures longer, lighter evenings throughout the summer months.Curious about the origins of this tradition? Test your knowledge with our quiz at the end. The concept was first proposed by American politician and inventor Benjamin Franklin in 1784 while he was in Paris. He suggested that rising earlier with the daylight could conserve candle usage.The idea reached the UK thanks to William Willett, a builder and the great-great-grandfather of Coldplay's Chris Martin. In 1907, Willett published a pamphlet titled The Waste of Daylight to encourage earlier risers. An avid golfer, Willett was frustrated when his games were cut short by the setting sun.The UK government debated the idea in 1908, but widespread opposition delayed its implementation. Despite Willett's persistent advocacy, it wasn't until 1916—after his death—that the UK adopted the practice. Interestingly, it was first introduced by the Germans during World War I, just before the UK followed suit.During World War II, the UK experimented with British Double Summer Time (BDST), advancing the clocks by an additional hour in summer, though this was short-lived. Today, the UK's clocks reliably fall back an hour on the last Sunday of October and spring forward an hour on the last Sunday of March.While many countries worldwide adopt this clock-changing tradition, others choose not to. Opinions remain divided. Proponents argue that BST conserves energy by maximizing natural daylight and reducing traffic accidents. Critics, however, contend that it fails to save energy and poses risks, such as darker mornings for schoolchildren, which can be hazardous. They also argue it may negatively impact health.Now, put your knowledge to the test with our quiz and see how much you've remembered!

text: Archaeologists and officials have expressed outrage about the bulldozing of the ancient Assyrian city of Nimrud by Islamic State militants in Iraq. Iraqi officials reported that on Thursday, the Islamic State (IS) initiated the destruction of the ancient site of Nimrud, founded in the 13th Century BC. This act has drawn severe condemnation from the head of the UN's cultural agency, who labeled the systematic destruction in Iraq as a war crime.IS, which holds significant territories in Iraq and Syria, justifies its actions by declaring that shrines and statues are false idols that must be obliterated. They are erasing our history, lamented Iraqi archaeologist Lamia al-Gailani.Nimrud, located about 30km (18 miles) southeast of Mosul along the Tigris River, remains partially intact, with many artefacts having been relocated to museums in Baghdad and abroad. However, numerous items still reside at the site. BBC Middle East correspondent Jim Muir noted that the attempt to destroy Nimrud is reminiscent of the Taliban's demolition of the Bamiyan Buddha sculptures in Afghanistan in 2001.In addition to destroying artefacts, IS engages in the trade of these items, which serves as a crucial revenue stream for the group. On Thursday, the tourism and antiquities ministry reported that IS assaulted the historic city of Nimrud and bulldozed it with heavy vehicles. The ministry urged the UN Security Council to convene a meeting to address the protection of Iraq's cultural heritage, accusing the militants of defying the will of the world and the feelings of humanity.While it remains uncertain whether Nimrud has been entirely destroyed, a local tribal source informed Reuters that IS members looted valuables from the archaeological city before leveling the site. There used to be statues and walls as well as a castle that Islamic State has destroyed completely, the source added.Irina Bokova, head of UNESCO, strongly condemned the attack, stating, This is yet another attack against the Iraqi people, reminding us that nothing is safe from the cultural cleansing underway in the country. She emphasized that the deliberate destruction of cultural heritage is a war crime, without any political or religious justification.Dr. Gailani expressed her dismay to the BBC, saying, Nimrud for us in Iraq and for me as an archaeologist is one of the most important [sites]. There are still quite a lot of things that are standing - the reliefs and the statues, the famous winged bulls. They are erasing our history. I wish it was a nightmare and I could wake up.John Curtis, president of the British Institute for the Study of Iraq, described the destruction as a horrific crime against the cultural heritage of the whole world, calling Nimrud the best preserved Assyrian site in Iraq.This destruction follows a video released last week by IS, showing militants using sledgehammers to destroy historic artefacts in a Mosul museum. The video depicted a militant drilling through a stone winged bull, with the artefacts labeled as false idols and their destruction justified on religious grounds. The UN also condemned this attack as a war crime.IS has controlled Mosul, Iraq's second-largest city, and surrounding areas since June 2014, a region that encompasses nearly 1,800 of the country's 12,000 registered archaeological sites.In response, Iraqi forces and Shia militia, supported by Iran, have joined forces to reclaim the northern city of Tikrit from IS militants. Additionally, a US-led coalition is conducting air strikes against the militants. On Friday, Iraqi forces, backed by US-led strikes, reportedly cleared IS fighters from the town of al-Baghdadi in the western Anbar province. This town, seized by IS last month, lies about 8km (5 miles) from an air base where hundreds of US troops are training Iraqi soldiers.

text: Political sketch writer Quentin Letts has apologised for an article he wrote mocking the disability of broadcaster Andrew Marr. In a review for the Daily Mail, Quentin Letts made controversial remarks about Andrew Marr, referring to him as Captain-Hop-Along, growling away on BBC One, throwing his arm about like a tipsy conductor. These comments, made in the context of Letts' critique of Robert Peston's new ITV show, drew significant backlash. Marr, a respected broadcaster, suffered a stroke in January 2013, which adds a layer of insensitivity to Letts' words.The controversy gained further attention when media commentator Roy Greenslade addressed the issue in the Guardian. In his article titled It isn't Funny or Smart for Quentin Letts to Poke Fun at Andrew Marr, Greenslade expressed his disapproval, stating, I don't want to come off all namby-pamby. I understand that no-one should be beyond criticism and that Letts was exercising his right to press freedom. But really Quentin, that was a graceless remark. He urged Letts to issue an apology.Responding to the criticism, Letts conceded that his comments about the admirable Marr were indeed horrid. He issued an apology via Twitter, which prompted further reactions, with users describing his remarks as utterly disgraceful and appalling.The Daily Mail published the article both in print and online, sparking a wider conversation. Marr's wife, journalist Jackie Ashley, took to Twitter to express her discontent, highlighting the negative message Letts' comments sent to disabled individuals.The Stroke Association also weighed in, stating, A stroke is not a joke. Stroke survivors deserve our respect and support, and Andrew Marr deserves an apology. The organization encouraged the public to file complaints with the Independent Press Standards Organisation (IPSO).In a statement to the BBC, IPSO confirmed receiving 11 complaints regarding the article. These complaints primarily cited Clause 12 (Discrimination), with some also referencing Clause 1 (Accuracy) and Clause 4 (Intrusion into grief or shock). IPSO, adhering to its policy, declined to disclose the identities of the complainants.Amidst this controversy, Robert Peston's new Sunday politics talk show on ITV received mixed reviews following its premiere. Letts described Peston's show as breathless and batty - and bound to be a hit, despite the lukewarm reception.

text: JPeg pictures could soon have built-in restrictions making them harder to copy, if recommendations by the body overseeing the format are implemented. The Joint Photographic Experts Group (JPeg) committee has proposed implementing controls on how image data in .jpg files is accessed, aiming to protect copyright and privacy. However, rights groups have raised concerns that these measures could stifle creativity.In a summary presented online, the JPeg committee highlighted that photographs are often redistributed without the necessary rights information, leading to unauthorized copying or publishing. Additionally, the privacy of photographers could be at risk if metadata, such as the geo-location of where a photo was taken, is accessible.The committee noted, Currently, these concerns are not well addressed and [are] an inhibiting factor in the further proliferation of digital content distribution. Although there are no immediate plans to alter the JPeg format, the committee, led by convener Touradj Ebrahimi, hopes to find technological solutions once the specifics of the proposals are finalized.Dr. Ebrahimi assured the BBC that any changes would still allow JPeg files to be freely shareable at the author's discretion. One thing that's important to note is that this is not something we're imposing, he emphasized. We are just saying, 'Let people have a choice.' Those who are perfectly happy with today's situation and want to have security-free image sharing [will still be able to].Currently, images can be protected on websites with privacy software, like Facebook. However, if someone with access removes the image and shares it elsewhere, it could be widely distributed. Dr. Ebrahimi suggested that embedding access controls within the file itself could be more effective. It would be best if you have one image that is protected in such a way that if you have the rights, you see it clear; if you don't have the rights, you don't see it, he explained.The proposal has sparked concern among rights groups such as the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF). In a blog post, the EFF cautioned that imposing strict restrictions on JPeg files could hinder creativity, potentially limiting an artist's ability to incorporate a photograph into new work.Jim Killock, executive director of the Open Rights Group, warned that securing these restrictions could be challenging, likening the situation to digital rights management (DRM) software used on DVDs. DRM tends to be easily broken, he told the BBC. People who want to break the rules would still do that.Killock also expressed worries that companies might impose high fees for access to restricted images. You're going to want to edit pictures, crop them, alter them, all of these sorts of things that DRM potentially restricts, so I guess the other major beneficiary would end up being software publishers, he remarked.As the most widely used image format online, the JPeg format sees billions of images produced daily, according to the JPeg committee.

text: How can busy working mums and dads keep tabs on their toddlers and stay connected to them during the working day? An increasing number of tech entrepreneurs are convinced they've found a solution for busy parents. But does more technology provide time-strapped parents with valuable ways to connect with their children, or does it simply heighten their anxieties? Molawa Adesuyi, co-founder and CEO of Mytoddlr, an app designed to update parents on their child's activities at nursery or daycare, is certain of the benefits such technology offers. Most working parents drop off their children at day nurseries as early as 8 or 9 am and can't pick them up until 5 or 6 pm, he explains. During this time, they have no way of keeping in touch or staying informed about their children's well-being throughout the day. This is a significant issue.Mytoddlr's app and website allow nurseries to log data about a child's daily routine and behavior—from potty breaks to naps—providing parents with real-time updates on their phones or computers. The nursery is happy, parents are happy; it's a win-win for everyone, Mr. Adesuyi asserts. Concerns about increased administrative work for nursery staff are dismissed by Mr. Adesuyi, who argues that the app can actually streamline paperwork and facilitate quicker communication with parents. There are fantastic apps available now that address real problems parents face. It's exciting to see technology transforming parenting, he concludes. Launched in 2015, Mytoddlr is already used by 2,000 parents in Lagos, Nigeria, and is being trialed in select nurseries in London. Meanwhile, Harsh Songra, the 19-year-old founder and CEO of the My Child app, was inspired by his own experiences with dyspraxia to create a tool for monitoring child development. This condition, which affects coordination and movement, can be challenging to diagnose without proper knowledge.I understand the struggles of a family dealing with a child's disorder, Mr. Songra shares. It took my parents over nine years to pinpoint my specific issue, and I still face some health challenges. The My Child app supports parents in tracking their child's development up to 24 months by posing questions, curating relevant content, and identifying local experts. Since its launch in early 2015, the app has been downloaded over 11,000 times across more than 140 countries, with notable popularity in the US, India, Singapore, and the UK.While Mr. Songra acknowledges technology's role as a valuable parenting tool, he admits it can sometimes disrupt professional relationships. Sometimes it affects interactions with doctors because parents become paranoid about their child based on what they find online, he notes. The issue is that we often trust the content of one link over 100 others and make decisions based on that information. But I believe this will change over time as awareness grows.Parenting apps, ranging from webcam baby monitors to location-tracking services, interactive games, and health checkers, are on the rise as parents increasingly integrate cutting-edge technology into their lives. In Australia, a mother even used Siri, Apple's voice-activated assistant, to call an ambulance when her toddler stopped breathing.For Amit Murumkar, an entrepreneur from New Jersey, the inspiration to create an app was born out of practicality. My daughter was three and would bring home a piece of art every day from her Montessori school, but there's only so much you can display on a refrigerator door, he recalls. I was also a good artist as a kid, and as a parent, I thought, 'If only I could show my art to my children.'This led him to develop Canvsly, a smartphone app that enables parents to capture their children's artwork, organize it into albums, and share it with family members who can view and comment on it. The app also allows for printing the artwork to create gifts, potentially eliminating the need to keep the originals if you trust the app's cloud storage. Parents can go guilt-free and clutter-free, Mr. Murumkar says, noting that the app has been downloaded in over 100 countries.Anesu Charamba, a tech analyst at Frost & Sullivan, believes these apps are enabling parents to engage with their children in new and exciting ways. As smartphones and affordable, reliable internet access continue to expand beyond developed nations, he predicts that early adopters will soon be joined by the majority.Follow Technology of Business editor @matthew_wall on Twitter for more insights. text: In our series of letters from African journalists, filmmaker and columnist Farai Sevenzo considers the role of cameras in conflict. At the Cannes Film Festival, a poignant moment unfolded as Mauritanian director Abderrahmane Sissako fielded questions following the screening of his film, Timbuktu - The Silence of Fear. This film, celebrated at Cannes, offers a fictional narrative of the tumultuous period when jihadists seized the ancient Malian town of Timbuktu, enforcing draconian rules that banned music and football, and introduced harsh punishments like lashings and stoning.During the press conference, Sissako, a steadfast African storyteller, was moved to tears. He expressed his sorrow for the Malians who endured the real-life events his film depicted. The real courage, he remarked, was found among those who lived this on a daily basis. Timbuktu was eventually freed, but true liberation was for those people who, in their minds, sang the songs and music that had been banned.While dramatists spotlight recent African events for reflection, our 24-hour news cycle ensures cameras are everywhere—wielded by reporters and jihadists alike. In the early 2000s, Osama bin Laden frequently delivered footage to news outlets, sparking a bizarre competition over who would broadcast his latest tirade. Fast forward to today, and platforms like YouTube have become a stage for fighters from Syria to Somalia, who now wield cameras with the same familiarity as weapons.Recent events in north-east Nigeria have highlighted two figures: President Goodluck Jonathan and Abubakar Shekau, the Islamist militant responsible for the abduction of over 200 schoolgirls in Chibok. Shekau's theatrical video appearances, where he declared, I abducted your girls; I will sell them in the market, have kept the world on edge since April 14, 2014, as the global community hopes for relief for the grieving parents of Chibok.Shekau's performances might seem like scenes from a Nollywood film, with him as a villain proclaiming outrageous statements, such as hypothetically claiming to have sold his own family members. Meanwhile, negotiations are reportedly in progress, and the Nigerian military, possibly motivated by criticism of their absence in affected villages, claims to know the girls' location and is assessing the situation.In an era saturated with cameras and technology, it is ironic that we struggle to locate a missing plane or hundreds of children who remain on land, painfully close to their longing parents. Once the dust settles, artists, novelists, and filmmakers offer a perspective beyond the immediate news, allowing us to reflect and discern truth from the combatants' propaganda.Who are these militants, and what drives them? How do villagers perceive them? Is it fear or faith that stirs them? Where do the imams stand? Can traditional African methods, involving elders rather than soldiers, defuse tensions? Artists have the luxury of time to explore these questions, a luxury not afforded to those on the frontlines of this struggle.Despite the elusive nature of answers, the quest to find them must continue. Whether or not militants release another video, the ideological clash in northern Nigeria, epitomized by Boko Haram, presents a growing threat that instills fear across African cities like Nairobi, Mogadishu, and Djibouti.The silence of fear is no less daunting than the fear that enveloped the parents of Chibok's missing daughters before global attention turned to their plight. Yet, amidst the flood of digital imagery, the most heart-wrenching pictures remain those of parents holding faded portraits of daughters they may never reunite with.If you wish to comment on Farai Sevenzo's column, please share your thoughts below.

text: Zayn Malik has revealed that, in leaving One Direction, he has let the fans down. On Wednesday, Zayn Malik shocked fans by announcing his departure from the band. In a candid interview with The Sun, he revealed, I can't do this anymore. Acknowledging that his decision might seem crazy and wild and a bit mad, he added, But I've never felt more in control in my life. I feel like I'm doing what's right, right by myself and right by the boys.Zayn's revelation came just hours after he declared his exit from the globally renowned band. He firmly denied any rumors of discord among the members, insisting such claims couldn't be more wrong. However, he admitted he had been contemplating leaving for some time. You know, I did try to do something that I wasn't happy doing for a while, for the sake of maybe other people, he explained. Basically, I'm only upset [because] I feel like I may have let them down.He emphasized that his decision wasn't a rejection of the fans, saying, It's not that I've turned my back on them or anything, it's just that I just can't do that anymore because it's not real to me. Zayn also dismissed speculation that his departure signaled the band's end, which had formed on The X Factor in 2010. He remained silent on whether he might rejoin the group in the future.His departure from the chart-topping pop group came a week after he left their world tour, citing stress as the reason. This followed a media frenzy after he was photographed in Thailand with his arm around a blonde woman, sparking rumors of infidelity towards his fiancée, Little Mix singer Perrie Edwards. Shortly after his announcement, Zayn returned to the UK and took to Twitter, stating, I'm 22 years old... I love a girl named Perrie Edwards. And there's a lot of jealous [people] in this world. I'm sorry for what it looks like.When questioned by The Sun about his personal life, Zayn confirmed that his two-year engagement to Perrie was still intact, describing her as a good girl who was supportive of his choice. Meanwhile, Zayn has reportedly been spotted at a recording studio in west London, working on solo projects with Naughty Boy, the producer known for helping launch the careers of Emeli Sande and Sam Smith. For more updates, follow @BBCNewsbeat on Twitter, BBCNewsbeat on Instagram, and Radio1Newsbeat on YouTube.

text: England women began their World Twenty20 campaign with a routine 36-run victory over Bangladesh in Bangalore. England, the 2009 champions and recent runners-up, reached a total of 153-7 thanks to a commanding 60 from their captain, Charlotte Edwards. Bangladesh, with only five wins in 29 T20 matches, never posed a threat to this target.
