text: The jobs market has seen a substantial decline in people starting full-time jobs since the start of the year, according to a regular survey of recruiters. The latest hiring index, compiled by the data firm Markit in collaboration with recruitment consultants REC, reveals a significant drop in both permanent job placements and the availability of candidates for these roles. Despite this, the beginning of January saw a rise in demand for both permanent and temporary staff. Among various sectors, nursing, medicine, and care continue to lead with the highest recruitment demand, closely followed by engineering and construction. On Wednesday, the Construction Industry Training Board (CITB) released a forecast predicting a need for 12,000 new recruits over the next five years as workers exit the sector or the country. They anticipate a decline in the total number of construction workers, as large infrastructure projects like the Queensferry Crossing wind down from their peak activities. Meanwhile, growth in the home-building and repair market is expected to hover between just 1% and 2%.Ian Hughes, a CITB director, commented, While we have factored Brexit into this forecast, there remain many unknowns to life after leaving the EU. We will be working with our industry to understand what it means for our migrant workforce and what we must do to attract and grow more of our own.The REC/Markit recruitment survey indicates an increase in starting salaries, although not as rapidly as a similar survey suggests for the rest of Britain. Overall, the employment situation appears weaker in comparison to the rest of the UK, where other surveys have shown a notably stronger job market. Recruitment consultants have observed a surge in temporary staff employment, marking the fastest pace in over a year. Although hourly pay rates for temporary employees have increased, the rate of wage inflation has slowed.Kevin Green, the chief executive of REC, remarked, The jobs market in Scotland continued to deteriorate in January, with recruiters reporting a decline in permanent placements for the fourth consecutive month. Scotland's economy is not as strong as the rest of the UK. The energy sector has weakened, and ongoing political uncertainty is affecting business confidence. Vacancies in Scotland remain in growth, so demand for staff is robust, despite employers showing hesitancy when it comes to investment decisions. This suggests the market could pick up again if confidence is restored.The survey encompasses insights from approximately 100 recruitment and employment consultants based in Scotland.

text: Southampton manager Ronald Koeman says the club are now looking to sell record signing Dani Osvaldo. In August 2013, Italian striker Osvaldo joined Southampton for £15 million, but by January, he found himself loaned out following a training-ground altercation. The former Roma forward failed to report for pre-season training and was subsequently granted a leave of absence. Southampton manager Ronald Koeman explained to BBC Radio Solent, It was a difficult situation for him to come back to.Osvaldo's stint in English football was fraught with challenges. He managed to score three goals in 13 appearances for the Saints, but his time was marred by controversy. In January, he was suspended for three matches and fined £40,000 due to violent conduct during an incident at Newcastle. That same month, a clash with Saints defender Jose Fonte led to his loan move to Juventus, ultimately costing him a spot in Italy's World Cup squad.His absence from pre-season training prompted the Southampton board to consider selling him. text: Ex-captain Michael Vaughan has backed Kevin Pietersen's claims that England's bowlers were an intimidating clique, adding they could be disrespectful. Reflecting on his early days at Yorkshire, Vaughan recalled his own fear of making mistakes due to a similar environment. In her school in Merseyside, on the day a month had passed since her death, all the pupils wore orange, her favourite colour. The organisation Victim Support has already received over 350 calls in connection with the bombing in Manchester, many of them from children, and is still receiving an average of fourteen calls a day. Psychologist Emma Kenny explained, “First, when you are in the eye of the storm, everybody supports you. At first, most people feel estranged and horrified, but they don’t know what they themselves are feeling because they’re thinking about how others are feeling. But when things have settled down, that’s when they can realize what has happened and where they stand.” Usually it takes four to six weeks to see whether there are any lingering problems. Children will then start to talk of nightmares, and adults will fear going into shopping malls. Eve Senior, a teenage girl from Bradford, described her nine-day stay in hospital, and her return when the doctors found more of the metal in her foot. Ellie Cheetham, who was not physically injured in the attack, shared her experience with BBC Three. She said her mother, Natalie, had called the last month the strangest of her life and expressed her concern about how they were going to cope, but also pointed out the strong support they had around them. “My friends don’t understand how long it will take me to recover, and I don’t even understand it myself,” she said. “That’s when you really notice whether or not you’ve been affected.” The 14-year-old’s film, which she shot when she and her friends heard the explosion in the arena, went the rounds of the social media. The world has moved on, and so has the news, but the victims must not be forgotten.

text: Pakistan's Supreme Court is considering corruption allegations against Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, amid mounting pressure over his family's wealth. The investigation into Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif and his family has intensified after they failed to clarify the origins of their financial assets. This scrutiny began following the Panama Papers leak, which linked Sharif's children to offshore companies used to purchase luxury apartments in London. These revelations have sparked allegations of money laundering, which Sharif vehemently denies, insisting the properties were acquired legally and he holds no personal ownership.The controversy has become a significant political hurdle for Sharif, with opposition groups accusing his family of exploiting political power for financial gain and demanding his resignation. Despite these pressures, Sharif remains defiant, dismissing the investigators' findings as mere allegations and assumptions, a stance supported by the federal cabinet last week.In anticipation of potential unrest, hundreds of security personnel have been stationed around the Supreme Court, with parts of it secured by barbed wire. The Joint Investigation Team (JIT), established in April, reported significant gaps/disparity between the declared income sources and the wealth amassed by Sharif and his family. It accuses Sharif of asset concealment, inflating his father's wealth to justify his family's riches, and failing to account for a substantial increase in wealth during his initial tenure from 1985 to 1993.Maryam Sharif, Sharif's daughter and political successor, is alleged by the JIT to be the beneficial owner of the offshore companies used to acquire the London flats and of forging documents to pose as a trustee for her brother, the actual owner. This claim hinges on a trust deed she signed in February 2006, which used the Calibri font, not commercially available until January 2007.The Panama Papers leak, which exposed 11 million documents from the Panama-based law firm Mossack Fonseca, revealed the existence of these flats and the offshore companies linked to them. The Sharif family maintains that the funds for the flats and their businesses in the UK and Gulf originated from the sale of Gulf Steel Mills in the UAE, established by Sharif's father, Mian Mohammad Sharif, in the early 1970s, with subsequent investments in a Qatar-based enterprise. A letter from former Qatari Prime Minister Prince Hammad bin Jassim al-Thani detailing the money trail was presented by the family, though he was unavailable for JIT questioning. However, the JIT found no evidence of a financial trail from Pakistan through Dubai and Qatar to the London flats.The JIT report has polarized the nation, as seen in media coverage. Pro-government TV channels dismiss the report as false, while pro-opposition channels assert it confirms corruption by Sharif and his family. The report's intricate financial details, spanning multiple international regulations, have led experts to identify areas where the JIT may have either lacked access or misinterpreted information, raising questions about its conclusions.The Supreme Court's decision to include representatives from the military intelligence services, MI and ISI, in the six-member JIT, which ideally should consist solely of financial experts, has also been controversial. The ISI's exclusive role in providing secretarial services to the JIT has fueled suspicions of political interference ahead of the 2018 elections.There are three potential outcomes: disqualification could permanently remove Sharif and his daughter from politics under the honest and sagacious constitutional provision. The Supreme Court, under immense pressure, must decide the course of action. The JIT, a unique creation of the Supreme Court rather than the constitution or executive, is unlikely to see its report entirely dismissed. If disqualified, Sharif might name a successor, possibly his brother Shahbaz, the Punjab Chief Minister, to ensure the government completes its term. Otherwise, analysts anticipate Sharif will remain in power and, if necessary, fight to the end.

text: A recovering alcoholic has been jailed for four months for stealing £11,000 from a faulty Ulster Bank cash machine. In a case that unfolded nearly four years ago, Peter Anthony Young, 58, from Hunter's Way, Ardglass, faced stern words from a judge who accused him of deliberately taking advantage of a significant glitch in a bank's system. This glitch allowed customers to withdraw cash from ATMs without it impacting their account balance.The incident came to light after the Ulster Bank conducted a review and discovered that Young had withdrawn £11,000 from his account on June 22, 2012, the day the bank experienced a major computer malfunction, as noted by prosecution lawyer Ms. Ivers at Downpatrick Crown Court. On that day, Young made 22 separate withdrawals of £500 each.Despite numerous attempts by the bank to contact Young, he remained unresponsive, leading them to report the matter to the police as a case of fraud. The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) launched an investigation, during which Young voluntarily attended a police station. He admitted to making the withdrawals, candidly stating that he had spent the money on drink.The prosecution highlighted that Young, a customer of Ulster Bank, had not made any effort to repay the funds, leaving an outstanding balance of £10,908.40. Describing the situation as an unusual case, a defense lawyer explained that Young had made frank admissions during a police interview in September 2014. The lawyer suggested that Young discovered the ATM fault while drinking with others, realizing he could withdraw money without funds in his account.This was always going to catch up with him, the defense lawyer remarked, emphasizing that Young was not attributing blame to others. The lawyer also detailed Young's troubled past, noting that his life spiraled downward after his mother's death in 1991, leading to alcoholism and homelessness in Belfast by age 34. However, Young is now reportedly on a path to recovery, attending Alcoholics Anonymous, participating in a church group, and engaging in a rehabilitation program.The defense proposed that a community order could serve as a deterrent for Young, keeping him on the straight and narrow. I would urge the court to give him a chance to continue to improve himself, the lawyer implored.The judge, however, was firm in his assessment, pointing out that Young had initially withdrawn £500 but then returned to the ATM 21 more times, fully aware he lacked the funds. He knew full well what he was doing and he deliberately took advantage of the defective ATM, the judge asserted. Living on social security benefits, Young had yet to repay any of the money taken from Ulster Bank.I don't believe I could deal with this case by way of a suspended sentence, the judge concluded. The least sentence I can impose is one of four months in custody.

text: A primary school in Leeds has introduced a temporary ban on children playing tig during break times after clothes were torn and pupils were left upset. In an effort to give children a chance to settle down a bit, a school has put a halt to the game commonly known as tag or you're it, according to the headmaster. This recent ban is part of a broader trend in England where schools are prohibiting activities that many fondly recall from their own school days. BBC News revisits other school activities that have faced similar fates:One of the more predictable bans involves the game British Bulldog, where students charge at each other, attempting to outmaneuver 'bulldogs' and dash to safety on the other side of the playground. Although the data is somewhat dated, a 2011 survey by the Association of Teachers and Lecturers found that over 25% of 653 school staff reported the game was banned at their schools. A secondary school teacher explained the ban was due to the number of broken bones it generates!In Wiltshire, Cumbria, and Clackmannanshire, schools have prohibited the game of conkers over concerns that horse chestnuts could cause anaphylactic reactions. The Anaphylaxis Campaign advocates for a common sense approach, suggesting that conkers be put away safely after play and that everyone wash their hands thoroughly. Some schools have allowed conker fights if children wear protective goggles. A headteacher in Carlisle described this as a sensible measure to protect children's eyes from flying chestnut fragments.In January, a primary school in Blackpool banned birthday cakes because teachers lacked the time to verify ingredients for students with allergies. At Norbreck Primary Academy, parents were informed that cakes brought to school would be sent home uneaten. The headteacher expressed reluctance in saying, I hate to be a killjoy... there are many reasons for this, some of them serious.In Birmingham, students were dismissed from school for wearing incorrect footwear. Baverstock Academy in Druids Heath issued letters to families mandating plain black shoes. A parent described the decision as ridiculous, leading to chaotic scenes with around 300 children sent home. The school later eased the rule slightly, according to parents.Meanwhile, in Darlington, it was the parents who created a stir at a primary school. The headteacher of Skerne Park Academy requested that parents wash in the morning and refrain from dropping off their children in pyjamas. The tipping point came when parents attended parents' evenings and even the Christmas show in their PJs, according to the head.In West Yorkshire, a headteacher removed books featuring stories about pigs from key stage one classrooms at Park Road Junior Infant and Nursery School in Batley, to avoid offending Muslim students. Head Barbara Harris stated that while the books would remain in the school library, We try to be sensitive to the fact that for Muslims talk of pigs is offensive.In South Gloucestershire, students were prohibited from wearing tinsel on a non-uniform day. Teachers at Chipping Sodbury School cited potential litter and safety hazards, such as the risk of students using tinsel to strangle each other. A letter sent home cited health and safety reasons for the ban. The local council clarified that the day, supporting the charity Crisis, was far from being against the spirit of Christmas.

text: Schools in Beijing are closed and outdoor construction halted as the Chinese capital's first ever pollution red alert came into effect. Late Monday, Beijing issued its first-ever red alert for air pollution, the highest warning level in its four-tier system, which will remain in effect until midday Thursday. This unprecedented move has led to restrictions on car usage and the temporary shutdown of certain factories. The alert coincides with China's participation in global talks on carbon emissions in Paris, highlighting its status as the world's largest polluter.When the alert was activated at 07:00 local time on Tuesday (23:00 GMT Monday), the U.S. Embassy in Beijing recorded PM 2.5 levels at 291 micrograms per cubic meter. By 11:00, this figure had only slightly decreased to 250, a level deemed very unhealthy. In the suburbs, the concentration of these harmful particles was reported to be even higher. The World Health Organization recommends a maximum safe level of 25 micrograms per cubic meter.Cycling to work through the smog this morning, with a mask securely fastened, I noticed a significant reduction in traffic. The red alert mandates that half of all vehicles remain off the roads, alternating between odd and even numbered license plates. However, despite the oppressive grey haze, current pollution levels are significantly lower than last week, when PM 2.5 levels soared to roughly 40 times the WHO's safe limit. Today, it's about 10 times over.The question arises: why declare a red alert now? The absence of such alerts previously drew increasing public criticism. People questioned what it would take for the government to act as children navigated through toxic air to get to school. It seems mounting public pressure may have finally prompted this decision.The smog, worsened by humidity and stagnant air, results from coal-powered industries, heating systems, vehicle emissions, and dust from construction sites. The alert will end at 12:00 on Thursday when a cold front is expected to disperse the pollution. Schools lacking adequate air filtration systems have been advised to close, and car usage is restricted based on license plate numbers. Authorities have promised to bolster public transport to accommodate increased demand.China's air quality is a pivotal issue in its quest for a global climate agreement. Negotiators in Paris highlight the country's investments in renewable energy to reduce coal dependency, particularly in urban areas. Between 2013 and 2014, 58% of China's primary energy consumption increase came from non-fossil fuels. While these efforts haven't immediately improved Beijing's air, they have impacted global carbon dioxide output. Recent data shows a stabilization or slight decline in carbon levels despite economic growth. A robust agreement in Paris could further reduce renewable energy costs, aiding long-term air quality improvement.Beijing resident Li Huiwen told AP, You have to do whatever you can to protect yourself. Even with a mask, I feel uncomfortable and lack energy. The smog's severity is exacerbated by Beijing's geography, surrounded by industrial zones to the south and east and mountains to the north and west, which trap pollutants. This situation has sparked concerns that China has prioritized economic growth at the environment's expense. Beijing worker Fan Jinglong remarked, It is a sharp warning that we may have too much development at the cost of the environment. It's time to seriously address air pollution.The health implications are staggering. A study led by Jos Lelieveld of Germany's Max Planck Institute, published in Nature magazine, attributes 1.4 million premature deaths in China to air pollution. Last month, Shenyang's PM 2.5 levels reportedly hit 1,400 micrograms per cubic meter, the worst recorded in China. In contrast, London's PM 2.5 average on December 6 was 8 micrograms per cubic meter, according to King's College's Environmental Research Group. The city has seen levels surpass 70 in spring 2014 and 2015, with a peak of 112 on November 5, 2006.Greenpeace activists recently urged the Chinese government to issue a red alert, a step previously taken by Nanjing in December 2013. On November 30, Beijing had issued an orange alert, the second-highest level. Despite some improvement in air quality in the first 10 months of this year compared to last, pollution remains a persistent problem. Chinese officials, once hesitant to set firm carbon reduction targets, now recognize the need to reduce fossil fuel reliance. President Xi Jinping has committed to addressing emissions at the Paris climate talks. Despite substantial investments in renewables, China still relies on coal for over 60% of its energy.

text: An elderly woman was beheaded by a man who went on a rampage in north London, the Old Bailey has heard. In a chilling incident, 82-year-old Palmira Silva was brutally attacked and beheaded in her garden by Nicholas Salvador, as revealed by prosecutors. The court was informed that Salvador, wielding a wooden pole and machete, was subdued only after a violent confrontation involving six taser deployments.Salvador, a 25-year-old resident of Enfield, has pleaded not guilty to murder, citing insanity as his defense. Prosecutor Jonathan Rees QC informed the jury that the horrific event occurred merely three days after Salvador had been dismissed from his job, and there was no contention regarding his responsibility for Silva's death. At the time, Salvador lived just three houses away from Silva on Nightingale Road.On September 4th of the previous year, the day of the attack, Salvador allegedly armed himself and decapitated two cats belonging to his hosts, believing they were demons. He then traversed several back gardens, forcibly entered a house, and targeted a car occupied by two family members with whom he was staying.Salvador subsequently vaulted into Silva's garden, where he repeatedly stabbed and beheaded her, according to court accounts. Mr. Rees explained that Salvador was under the delusion he was confronting a supernatural being, either Adolf Hitler resurrected or a demon disguised as an elderly woman.After the gruesome act, Salvador fled but was apprehended in another house's living room. There, he engaged in a violent and chaotic struggle with police, enduring multiple taser shocks, punches, and kicks, which seemed to have little impact. His erratic behavior included muttering phrases like red is the color and I am the king, suggesting signs of mental instability.An eyewitness recounted Salvador's frantic demeanor before the assault, likening him to a headless chicken as he appeared to search for more cats to kill. In the weeks leading up to the incident, Salvador exhibited odd behavior and developed a fascination with shapeshifters—mythical beings capable of changing form.After his arrest, Salvador was initially held at Belmarsh prison but was transferred to the high-security Broadmoor Hospital due to his mental health condition. Prosecutors indicated that psychiatrists would testify that Salvador was suffering from paranoid schizophrenia.Palmira Silva, who immigrated to Britain from Italy in 1953, operated a café with her husband and was a mother to two children, with six grandchildren and one great-grandchild.Salvador also faces charges of assault causing actual bodily harm and assaulting a police officer, after Pc Bernard Hamilton sustained a leg injury requiring hospital care. The trial is ongoing.

text: Ahead of the general election on 7 May, BBC Radio Merseyside is holding three special debates in front of a live audience. Three pivotal constituencies—Wavertree, Southport, and Wirral West—have been selected for public scrutiny as candidates vie for the honor of representing constituents at Westminster over the next five years. The first of these hour-long debates will be hosted by Roger Phillips in Wavertree, a traditionally secure Labour seat in Liverpool, commencing at 12:00 BST.Located east of Liverpool's city center, Wavertree is a primarily residential area that boasts a significant technology park closely linked to the university. The presence of a large student population significantly contributes to the local economy. Voters in Wavertree are hopeful to avoid a repeat of the 2010 debacle when the polling station on Dunbabin Road ran out of ballot papers just before closing.Liverpool City Council has acknowledged previous issues, stating that they were caused by a surge of people arriving at the polls' closing time, combined with some stations lacking a full allocation of ballot papers. This year, they are ensuring all stations are fully stocked and have provided additional staff training. Furthermore, anyone in line by 22:00 BST will be allowed to vote.So, who are the contenders for this seat? Luciana Berger, the shadow health minister, retained the seat for Labour five years ago with a comfortable majority exceeding 7,000. She succeeded Jane Kennedy, the constituency's MP since its inception in 1997, who became Merseyside's Police Commissioner in 2012. Initially, it seemed former Labour Councillor Jake Morrison might challenge Ms. Berger. Elected at 18 in 2011, Morrison's relationship with Labour soured, leading him to retire at 22.Ms. Berger, seeking re-election, promises to take practical action to support people who are looking for a job, for example by holding another jobs fair to bring together employers and local people. I'll promote apprenticeships and opportunities for young people and back our fantastic small businesses. She also pledges to campaign for changes to law around dangerous dogs to make our neighborhoods safer, and to continue advocating for Liverpool Wavertree's residents.The Liberal Democrats, unsuccessful in their 2010 bid, are pinning their hopes on 20-year-old student Leo Evans. His campaign focuses on protecting green spaces like Calderstones Park, increasing the NHS budget by £8 billion annually with a focus on mental health, ensuring Liverpool benefits from devolved powers, particularly HS2 and HS3 connections, and expanding apprenticeships.James Pearson represents the Conservatives, marking his first parliamentary contest after an unsuccessful bid for Liverpool City Council's Church ward. His priorities for Wavertree include supporting business and investment, safeguarding the NHS, and advocating for the armed services and their families—a personal commitment, as he serves as an officer in the Army reserves with deployments in Afghanistan and Cyprus. Despite the Conservatives securing only 7.5% of the vote in 2010, Pearson remains hopeful.UKIP's Adam Heatherington, a former Liverpool Mayor candidate, seeks support from disillusioned Tory and Labour voters. As a supply teacher, he argues for enhanced investment in Wavertree Technology Park, citing high business rates and vacant spaces. Heatherington highlights a brain drain as students leave for jobs in other cities and calls for equal emphasis on vocational and academic qualifications.The Green Party's Peter Cranie, who narrowly missed a European Parliament seat last year, acknowledges his limited chances but aims to offer Wavertree voters a voice against austerity. He criticizes wealth inequality, stating, We think it is obscene that the five richest families in Britain own the same wealth as the 13 million least well-off, and advocates for wealth redistribution.Dave Walsh, representing the Trade Unionist and Socialist Coalition, seeks to re-engage disenfranchised voters and defend local services like libraries and Sure Start Centres. The party, fielding 130 candidates nationally, calls for a £10 minimum wage and railway renationalization.Lastly, Leo Evans, running as an independent, draws inspiration from his involvement in Until They Kick Us Out, a play about youth and democracy. The 18-year-old Edge Hill student supports school leavers, a higher minimum wage, rent caps for students and low-income families, and improved social housing, asserting that his campaign is more than just a protest vote.With seven candidates competing, Wavertree is among Merseyside's most hotly contested constituencies. Tune in to BBC Radio Merseyside from 12:00 to 14:00 to hear the candidates answer questions from listeners.

text: Italian Prime Minister Mario Monti claimed Europe had one week to save the euro ahead of yet another crunch EU summit on Thursday and Friday. France's President has proposed a growth pact, while Tony Blair advocates for a grand bargain. The markets clamor for a big bazooka, and whispers of federalism echo through Germany. Yet, the economic and financial solutions to the eurozone crisis are surprisingly straightforward. How so? Simply look to how the United States, another large single currency area, has tackled similar issues. However, Europe's challenge lies in the political unacceptability of most solutions.The core issue plaguing the eurozone is the fundamental uncompetitiveness of southern European economies. During the boom years, wages in these regions soared too quickly, leading to higher imports than exports and resulting in substantial borrowing. This debt, coupled with ongoing uncompetitiveness and a reliance on further borrowing, has fueled financial panic. Germany's hesitation to finance these debts exacerbates the situation, making it increasingly difficult for southern European governments and banks to secure market loans.Additionally, the stagnation of European financial markets, alongside austerity measures by governments and the European Central Bank's (ECB) focus on price stability, threatens a deep recession across the continent, further worsening debt woes.If the eurozone seeks to emulate the US model in its crisis, what economic, financial, and political transformations might be necessary? The immediate priority is restoring confidence in banks. Eurozone banks burdened with bad loans—whether to mortgage borrowers, property speculators, or governments—may require recapitalization, with losses absorbed collectively by the eurozone. This is crucial as many national governments lack the resources for such measures. Spain's current bailout illustrates this, as its government bears all losses.To prevent investors from shifting deposits from at-risk southern European banks to safer havens like Germany, Switzerland, or Denmark, a eurozone-wide guarantee of bank deposits in euros may be essential. Moreover, a unified regulatory and supervisory regime for all European banks is necessary, ensuring equal access to rescue loans and central authority intervention for failing banks.The long-term challenge is preventing defaults by governments like Spain or Italy, while reinforcing their commitment to the euro and promoting fiscal responsibility. Eurobonds could be key, allowing shared responsibility for a significant portion of eurozone debt and reinforcing the commitment to the euro.A US-style federal budget might be needed to manage recession costs, preventing national economies from collapsing. For instance, a shared eurozone income tax could fund a minimum level of social security, particularly unemployment benefits.Newly elected French President Francois Hollande champions a growth pact aimed at revitalizing European economies and alleviating the strain of spending cuts. He also suggests revising the ECB's mandate to include employment support alongside price stability, akin to the US Federal Reserve's dual mandate.The eurozone may need to finance substantial infrastructure investments, particularly in southern Europe, similar to West Germany's post-reunification efforts in East Germany. Proposals include enhancing the European Investment Bank's lending capacity and introducing project bonds for major construction projects.Europeans, especially in the south, must implement structural reforms to boost long-term growth and stabilize government finances, though these may hinder short-term growth. Such reforms include deregulating markets, raising retirement ages, downsizing state employment, and easing hiring and firing processes. Hollande has resisted many of these reforms in France.Rebalancing requires addressing the competitiveness issues that initially led southern Europe into debt. The ECB and Germany may need to encourage several years of high wage inflation in Germany to neutralize its trade advantage over southern Europe—a trend already emerging.Similar to US federal support for struggling states, southern European governments might require direct fiscal transfers from the eurozone to sustain their economies until competitiveness is restored. These could manifest as bailout loans that remain unpaid.Structural reforms, particularly in labor markets, are vital for rebalancing by ensuring controlled wage growth in southern Europe, unlike the previous decade's rapid increases.For a comprehensive banking, fiscal, and monetary union, eurozone governments must delegate authority to a central body, such as the European Commission, to oversee and finance these initiatives. National governments would need to adhere to strict budgetary constraints.Most reforms necessitate Germany sharing its wealth with Europe, and all nations ceding power to Brussels. Berlin demands no taxation without representation, advocating for full federalism with spending and regulation managed by a directly elected European Commission presidency.

text: And so it begins. The race for the assembly's fifth election has officially begun, though the atmosphere in Cardiff Bay has been charged with a pre-election vibe for some time. text: Mfon Udoh scored a hat-trick as Nigeria's Enyimba beat visitors Etoile du Sahel of Tunisia 3-0 in the first leg of their last 16 African Champions League tie on Sunday. On Sunday, AS Vita Club from DR Congo clinched a narrow 1-0 victory against South Africa's Mamelodi Sundowns. The winner of this matchup will advance to the group stages, while the loser will have another shot in the Confederation Cup. In an impressive display, Udoh scored his first goal just nine minutes into the game, added a second for Enyimba after halftime, and completed his hat-trick with a powerful strike near the end. Udoh now leads the tournament scoring chart with seven goals. Etoile faced a setback, playing the last 19 minutes with only ten men after Ghazi Abderazek was dismissed for dissent following a second yellow card. This tie echoes the 2004 final, which Enyimba won on penalties after both legs ended 2-1 in favor of the home teams.Ugandan goalkeeper Dennis Onyango kept Sundowns in contention in Kinshasa with remarkable saves, as Vita Club's Ghanaian player Bernard Morrison posed a constant threat. The game's only goal came in injury time when Morrison's shot, initially saved by Onyango, was converted by Kule Mbombo.Meanwhile, TP Mazembe's title defense faces a challenge after a 2-0 defeat to Morocco's Wydad Casablanca on Saturday. Abdellatif Noussir netted his first campaign goal just before halftime, and Reda Hajhouj scored a penalty in the second half. Under the guidance of former Real Madrid manager John Toshack, Wydad aims to secure their second title, having last won in 1992. Mazembe, seeking a sixth title, aspires to become the second most successful club after Egypt's Al Ahly, who have claimed eight championships.On Saturday, Al Ahly, the record eight-time champions, secured a 1-1 draw against Tanzania's Young Africans. Managed by former Tottenham coach Martin Jol, the Cairo Red Devils took an early lead with Amr Gamal's header in the 11th minute. However, eight minutes later, an own-goal by Ahmed Hegazi leveled the score.Zamalek, Al Ahly's fierce rivals, triumphed over debutants Mouloudia Bejaia of Algeria with a 2-0 win in Cairo. Mahmoud 'Kahraba' Abdel Moneim put Zamalek ahead just before the hour mark, and Ahmed Hamoudi sealed the victory eight minutes from time. Ivory Coast's Asec Mimosas capitalized on home advantage, defeating Al Ahly Tripoli of Libya 2-0. Dao Youssouf opened the scoring after 59 minutes, with Aka Serge adding a second ten minutes from the end.In a repeat encounter from last season, Sudan's Al Merreikh and Algeria's Entente Setif drew 2-2. Eude Dagoulou gave Setif an early lead after 15 minutes, but Raji Abdalati equalized five minutes later. Abdelmoumene Djabou restored Setif's lead shortly after, but Abdalati's second goal ensured a draw by the final whistle.Stade Malien's hopes of becoming Mali's first qualifiers were severely dented by a surprising 3-1 home defeat to Zambia's Zesco United. Despite Moussakoye Diallo's early goal for the hosts, Mwape Mwelwa equalized before halftime, and Idris Ilunga's late brace sealed the win for Zesco.

text: The HS2 link between Birmingham and Crewe marks a sad day for Stoke-on-Trent, Tristram Hunt has said. City MP Mr. Hunt argued that a route through the Potteries could have expedited and reduced the cost of the HS2 line from London to Manchester. The HS2 segment from Birmingham to Crewe is scheduled to commence operations in 2027, six years ahead of previous projections. Transport Secretary Patrick McLoughlin has proposed constructing a junction in South Staffordshire to enhance access to Stoke-on-Trent.The overarching aim of the HS2 project is to bolster transport links to northern England, with the government aspiring to complete the London to Birmingham section by 2026. Despite Stoke-on-Trent's bid for an HS2 station in its city center, Crewe has been selected as the next pivotal stop on the route to Manchester. Reacting to this decision, Labour MP Mr. Hunt emphasized the importance of a northern gateway partnership between Stoke-on-Trent and east Cheshire, stating, With Crewe rather than Stoke benefitting from this massive investment, plans for a northern gateway partnership become more important.Mark Winnington, a member of Staffordshire County Council responsible for the economy, environment, and transport, expressed concerns about the environmental and community impact, noting, HS2 will cut through 45 miles of Staffordshire countryside and from the outset we have been concerned about the impact a project of this scale will have not only on the environment but also on residents living close to the proposed route.For the next six years, Crewe will be the sole HS2 connection in the North West, positioning Cheshire as the gateway to the Northern Powerhouse. This decision, while anticipated due to recommendations by the government-owned company behind HS2, is a setback for Stoke-on-Trent, which had launched a rival bid and even considered legal action. Nevertheless, government and Cheshire officials have pledged to ensure North Staffordshire reaps the benefits of the high-speed rail.Michael Jones, leader of Cheshire East Council, described the Birmingham to Crewe link as a transformative opportunity for Crewe and its neighboring areas, calling it a real once-in-a-generation opportunity, the like of which Cheshire East has not seen before.Conservative MP for Lichfield, Michael Fabricant, criticized the route as environmentally damaging to beautiful parts of Staffordshire. Meanwhile, Labour MP for Stoke-on-Trent South, Robert Flello, pointed out the practical distance issues, stating, Crewe might look on a map [as if it is] next door to Stoke-on-Trent but the reality is it's a good hour by car from my constituents.Conservative MP for Stafford, Jeremy Lefroy, urged Mr. McLoughlin to reconsider the proposed route, highlighting the need for a thorough reassessment.

text: An own goal from goalkeeper Ryan Clarke in the 95th minute denied Neal Ardley's AFC Wimbledon their first win of the season as Rochdale earned a share of the spoils at the Crown Oil Arena. In a dramatic clash at Spotland, Andy Barcham's early header seemed destined to lift AFC Wimbledon out of League One’s relegation zone. However, a late own goal by goalkeeper Clarke ensured Rochdale salvaged a 1-1 draw, leaving the Dons anchored at the bottom.The visitors took the lead just 12 minutes into the match. A Rochdale attack unraveled when Donal McDermott’s corner was inadvertently returned to him by Matt Lund. Attempting to outmaneuver Chris Whelpdale, McDermott lost possession deep in Wimbledon’s half. Whelpdale seized the opportunity, sprinting down the right flank and delivering a precise cross to Barcham, who nodded it past Rochdale's goalkeeper, Conrad Logan.After the interval, Rochdale intensified their efforts to equalize. Jamie Allen came agonizingly close, his powerful shot rattling the crossbar, while Clarke twice denied Calvin Andrew. The home side faced further challenges when Callum Camps received a red card for a second bookable offense, reducing them to ten men. Yet, in a cruel twist of fate, Clarke’s earlier heroics were overshadowed when he misjudged Allen’s corner, punching it into his own net during stoppage time.The Press Association provided the match report, which concluded with the scoreline reading Rochdale 1, AFC Wimbledon 1.In the closing stages, Allen's long-range shot from a tight angle found the top right corner, leveling the score. Rochdale earned a corner after George Francomb's deflection, while Calvin Andrew's attempt was saved from the center of the box. Both Nathaniel Mendez-Laing and Jake Reeves received yellow cards amidst the intense exchanges.Numerous fouls punctuated the game, with AFC Wimbledon’s Dannie Bulman and Rochdale’s Jamie Allen among the offenders. As tensions flared, Callum Camps was shown his second yellow card, reducing Rochdale to ten players. Despite this disadvantage, they managed to clinch a point thanks to Clarke's late error.Rochdale made strategic substitutions, bringing on Sanmi Odelusi and Calvin Andrew, while AFC Wimbledon introduced Tyrone Barnett and Dean Parrett. Injuries and tactical adjustments saw George Francomb replace Lyle Taylor for the visitors.In the end, despite several missed opportunities and a flurry of corners, neither side could secure a decisive victory. The match concluded with Rochdale and AFC Wimbledon sharing the spoils in a hard-fought draw.

text: A schoolgirl has become the first child in Wales to be given an official hearing dog. In the UK, over 45,000 children live with the reality of being deaf, and among them is 14-year-old Poppy. Despite her profound deafness, Poppy's yellow Labrador, Tanni, has significantly boosted her confidence and improved her sleep. Poppy is one of 27 children in the UK who have been matched with a hearing dog by the charity Hearing Dogs for Deaf People.Poppy’s parents, Richard, a civil engineer, and Rebecca, a housewife, first noticed subtle changes in their daughter’s behavior when she was nine. She was turning the volume up on the TV, Rebecca recalled. In the car, she couldn't hear me, even though her siblings in the back could. Alarmed, they consulted an audiologist who was astounded to find that Poppy was profoundly deaf. She had been relying on lip-reading to get by, which explained why her school performance hadn’t suffered.Diagnosed with the rare Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome type 1, Poppy was fitted with hearing aids. However, they failed to alleviate her struggles with social confidence and nighttime anxiety, as she couldn't wear them while sleeping. For three years, she felt increasingly isolated until Rebecca discovered hearing dogs, which assist the deaf similarly to guide dogs for the blind. In the UK, 850 deaf individuals, mostly adults, have these canine companions.Poppy became the first child in Wales to receive a hearing dog due to her profound deafness. Her dog, Tanni, named after Baroness Tanni Grey Thompson, was one of just 12 distributed that year.A year later, Poppy describes Tanni as life-changing. Having her has built my confidence, she said. She gives me more independence. Before, I was reluctant to shop alone, worried people wouldn't know I was deaf. Now, Tanni's special harness alerts them to speak clearly. Tanni's presence has also made Poppy more comfortable engaging in conversations, as people often inquire about the dog.Tanni accompanies Poppy everywhere except school and has been trained to alert her to fire alarms or when her mother needs her. In the morning, if my mum wants to let me know we are going out or it is tea time, she writes a note and puts it in a purse that Tanni brings to me, Poppy explained. As I get older, we might train her to respond to the doorbell, phone, and text messages.Finally, Poppy enjoys restful nights. I used to sleep with the door open, afraid of who might come in. Now, with Tanni, I can sleep with the door shut, she said.Andrew James, National Client Services Manager for Hearing Dogs for Deaf People, expressed his satisfaction with the program. We have placed 27 hearing dogs with deaf children across the UK, and we are thrilled that Poppy and Tanni are the first child partnership in Wales. The project has been a huge success since 2012, and we plan to expand our work with children in the coming years. Hearing dogs have a profound impact on a deaf child's life, and we couldn't be happier with the positive difference Tanni has made for Poppy and her family.Currently, there are 29 deaf individuals partnered with hearing dogs in Wales.

text: Six years ago Yingluck Shinawatra, a novice who had only been in politics for two months, led the Pheu Thai party, founded and funded by her older brother Thaksin, to a resounding election victory. In a dramatic turn of events, the political landscape of Thailand has been shaken by a party whose past is marked by coups and contentious court rulings. Just a year prior, its supporters were embroiled in a violent occupation of Bangkok. At the center of this upheaval is Ms. Yingluck's electoral promise to rice farmers, which now forms the crux of the legal proceedings against her.Yingluck's manifesto included a bold pledge to purchase the entire rice crop at 15,000 baht (£350; $450) per tonne, significantly higher than the previous government's guarantee of 11,000 baht. This scheme was immensely popular among farmers. However, economists and agricultural experts immediately raised concerns about its sustainability. The proposed price far exceeded global rice rates, and as the world's leading rice exporter, Thailand faced stiff competition from India and Vietnam, who could offer lower prices unless Thailand was prepared to absorb substantial losses. Additionally, warnings about the potential for corruption within the scheme were rampant.Fast forward six years, and Ms. Yingluck is confronted with a possible 10-year prison sentence, accused of malfeasance for failing to prevent corruption in the rice scheme during her tenure as prime minister and chair of the National Rice Policy Committee. While she hasn't been charged with corruption herself, if convicted, she faces a permanent political ban, adding to her existing five-year ban following her impeachment in 2015.Unsurprisingly, Ms. Yingluck and her party have expressed their grievances. Her government was toppled in 2014 by the same military officers now governing Thailand, who justified their coup by claiming a need to restore order. Yet, they conspicuously failed to support her amidst the protests in Bangkok that crippled her administration. The military, wielding considerable authority, is viewed as lacking neutrality, even in judicial matters.The rice scheme proved to be exorbitantly costly and inefficient. The exact financial toll, including rice that spoiled, was pilfered, or improperly sold, is still debated. Government estimates place the cost at a minimum of $8 billion, though some estimates soar to $20 billion, factoring in the subsidy’s total cost rather than just losses from corruption and mismanagement. While the scheme did improve farmers' living standards, its sustainability was highly questionable.Despite anecdotal evidence of corruption, few cases have reached the courts. A prominent case involves a former commerce minister and 27 others, accused of a fraudulent government-to-government rice deal with China. This case will conclude on the same day as Ms. Yingluck’s verdict.Ms. Yingluck defended herself in court, arguing that she wasn't responsible for the scheme's daily operations. She contended that, as a key electoral promise, she couldn't simply cancel it. She also highlighted what she perceives as multiple procedural flaws in the case against her.Regardless of the case's merits, many believe the military government aims to weaken Thaksin Shinawatra's political influence before any democratic restoration. Ms. Yingluck remains a popular figure and an effective vote-winner. With Mr. Thaksin in his 10th year of exile, his party struggles to find a new leader.The outcome of Ms. Yingluck’s trial presents a conundrum for Thailand's current rulers. An acquittal might embolden Mr. Thaksin to seek more power than the military is willing to concede, potentially angering hard-line conservatives and those who protested against Yingluck’s government. On the other hand, a prison sentence would satisfy her staunch opponents and justify the military's coup as part of an anti-corruption effort. However, it could also transform the charismatic Ms. Yingluck into a symbol of resistance for her red-shirt supporters.Red-shirt leaders admit that organizing large-scale protests would be challenging under military rule. They have ruled out repeating the disastrous occupation of Bangkok from seven years ago but warn that a conviction could ignite localized demonstrations, marking the end of any pretense of reconciliation.The government is concerned about maintaining peace ahead of the late King Bhumibol Adulyadej’s elaborate cremation in October and King Vajiralongkorn’s expected coronation. A potential compromise could be a suspended sentence for Ms. Yingluck, dependent on her receiving less than five years. Even with a custodial sentence, she has the option to appeal, though that decision rests with her.The backdrop to this drama is the ongoing struggle for power as the generals prepare for an eventual election. Polls suggest Pheu Thai will likely be the largest party, continuing its winning streak since 2001, but the new electoral system will likely prevent it from securing a majority. Additionally, political parties must navigate a military-appointed 250-seat senate and adhere to a military-drafted 20-year reform blueprint.In this uncertain political climate, the identity of Thailand's next prime minister remains unclear. Historically, elected governments wielded considerable power, but that era seems to be over. Some in Pheu Thai argue that a stint in opposition might be advantageous, given the constraints imposed by courts and the military.The military itself is not monolithic, and it's uncertain if the current ruling clique will maintain its dominance. Another significant unknown is King Vajiralongkorn’s stance. The strict lese majeste law stifles discussion of his role, but he has already signaled his desire for consultation on crucial decisions, suggesting he may play a pivotal role in shaping Thailand’s future.

text: The number of people who think you must speak English to be considered truly British has increased over the past 10 years, a survey suggests. The annual British Social Attitudes survey, conducted by NatCen Social Research, has revealed significant shifts in public opinion. This year, 95% of the 3,000 respondents agreed that speaking English is crucial to being considered British, a notable increase from 86% in 2003. The survey, which has been tracking the evolution of social attitudes in Britain for 31 years, also highlighted that 61% of participants believe EU immigrants should wait three years before claiming benefits.The authors of the report emphasize that the criteria for being regarded as British have become more stringent over time. Currently, 77% of people think it is essential for someone to have lived in Britain for most of their life to be considered British, compared to 69% in 2003. Meanwhile, 74% believe being born in Britain is important, slightly down from 76% a decade ago. Respecting British institutions and laws remains a priority, with 85% considering it very or fairly important, up from 82% in 2003.On the topic of immigration, 77% expressed a desire for reductions, a sentiment that has remained stable since 2008 but is significantly higher than in 1995. The report notes that the perception of current immigration levels as too high is well established and stable. While half of the respondents believe immigrants come to Britain primarily for work, 24% think the main reason is to claim benefits. Furthermore, the belief that immigrants contribute to increased crime rates has risen from 37% in 2003 to 43% in 2013.The survey also highlights a geographical divide in attitudes towards immigration, particularly between London and the rest of the UK. In London, 54% view immigration as beneficial to the economy, whereas this opinion drops to 28% outside the capital. The report also points out a disconnect between public perception and reality regarding benefit claims by EU immigrants. While 61% think EU immigrants should wait three years to claim benefits, recent rules require them to earn at least £149 a week for three months before accessing various benefits.Penny Young, chief executive of NatCen Social Research, remarked, In an increasingly diverse, multicultural country, we might expect people to be more relaxed about what it means to be British, yet the trend is going in the opposite direction. It is now harder to be considered British than in the past, and one message comes through loud and clear: if you want to be British, you must speak English. She also noted that the public desires stricter benefit rules and remains largely unaware of existing immigration control policies.The government has introduced several restrictions in recent months, including a rule implemented in January requiring migrant jobseekers to be in the UK for three months before claiming Jobseeker's Allowance. The survey interviews were conducted from June to November 2013, prior to the exposure of the so-called Trojan Horse plot by Islamists to take over schools in Birmingham. In response to this issue, Education Secretary Michael Gove stated that schools should promote British values.

text: The Church of England's ruling body has decided that women bishops should be allowed, but there are further steps to take before they can be ordained. In a significant yet contentious decision, the General Synod offered limited concessions to traditionalist Anglicans opposing the ordination of women as bishops. These traditionalists had hoped for the option of being under the care of a male alternative bishop, under terms they found acceptable. However, the synod ruled that women bishops would have the authority to determine the identity and roles of any such bishops.BBC's religious affairs correspondent, Robert Pigott, reported that women bishops are required only to consult a guiding code of practice when dealing with traditionalists. This decision, made during a synod meeting at York University, has intensified divisions within the Church.The synod members agreed there was no need to delay further the draft law allowing women to become bishops. Before it returns to the General Synod, this law must gain approval from the majority of the Church's 44 diocesan synods. Following this, it requires a two-thirds majority in the General Synod, parliamentary approval, and the Royal Assent to come into effect.Pigott described the weekend as extraordinary, marked by intense emotions. While supporters celebrated a breakthrough, some traditionalists exited the synod chamber in tears. On Saturday, proposals to establish a class of male-only bishops to oversee traditionalist parishes were rejected.Archbishop of Canterbury Rowan Williams and Archbishop of York John Sentamu had strongly supported a compromise plan. This plan would have allowed parishes opposed to female bishops to seek oversight from a male alternative, who would have significant legal independence and autonomy under a joint jurisdiction arrangement. Despite gaining a majority in the synod, the proposal was defeated by just five votes from the clergy, who vote separately from laypeople and bishops.Pigott noted that Dr. Williams, having staked his reputation on the compromise, now faces challenges in addressing the dissatisfaction among traditionalists who are likely to remain in the church. The proposals are set to be reviewed by dioceses and will return to the synod for a final vote in a year.Christina Rees, a campaigner and chairwoman of Women in the Church, expressed her elation to the Press Association, calling the synod's decision a wonderful outcome and consistent with the synod's intentions from two years prior. This is wonderful news, she remarked. In one sense I am not surprised but I am delighted, it is very, very good news.Meanwhile, traditionalists have cautioned that this decision might lead many to leave the Church of England. Reverend Prebendary David Houlding, a prominent member of the Catholic Group on the General Synod, voiced his concerns, feeling that traditionalists were running out of options. He told PA, There are several people who will be making hard decisions about their future. I am staying in the Church of England for the time being until I am driven out. I am not going willingly, I will only go if forced. The more this goes on in this manner, the more it seems as if the door is shutting. The scope for remaining in the Church of England is getting more and more narrow and the options are rapidly closing.

text: Chris Evans and Nick Grimshaw both lost listeners over the last three months, according to the latest industry figures from Rajar. BBC Radio 2's breakfast show, hosted by Chris Evans, experienced a decline of 414,000 listeners, bringing its audience down to 9.06 million compared to the previous quarter. Despite this drop, it continues to hold the title of the UK's most popular radio show. Meanwhile, Nick Grimshaw's show on Radio 1 saw a decrease of 184,000 listeners, reaching 5.25 million weekly from July to September. This decline is attributed to a seasonal dip in breakfast show listenership during the summer months.Conversely, BBC Radio 6 Music celebrated a milestone with a record audience of 2.34 million, marking its fifth consecutive quarter of growth. Helen Boaden, Director of BBC Radio, expressed her pleasure, stating that more people are drawn to the station's unique blend of alternative music and engaging presenters.While Grimshaw's individual numbers fell, Radio 1 as a whole saw an increase, climbing from 9.46 million to 9.87 million weekly listeners in the same period. Including listeners aged 10 to 14, the figure rose to 10.9 million, as the station aims to capture a younger demographic. Ben Cooper, Radio 1's controller, highlighted the significance of these figures alongside the station's digital presence, noting 1.5 million daily views on YouTube and 8.5 million social media users.BBC Radio 4 reported a weekly reach of 11.2 million, its second-highest audience ever. Although its flagship Today programme lost 250,000 listeners, settling at 7.1 million, The World At One achieved a record high of 3.75 million listeners.In the realm of commercial radio, stations like LBC, Heart, and Capital saw an increase in weekly listeners compared to the previous quarter, with Absolute Radio adding over half a million. Classic FM and talkSPORT's breakfast shows expanded their national reach, though some commercial breakfast programmes experienced declines. Kiss's morning show with Rickie, Melvin, and Charlie dropped to 1.83 million from 2.13 million listeners. Meanwhile, Chris Moyles on Radio X lost 36,000 listeners in London but grew his national audience to 703,000.Capital's breakfast show, hosted by Dave Berry, George Shelley, and Lilah Parsons, experienced a slight drop but remains the UK's most popular commercial breakfast show. Overall, Rajar, the official body measuring UK radio audiences, reported that 89% of British adults, equivalent to 48.2 million people, tuned into the radio at least once a week during the quarter, marking an increase of 320,000 from the previous year.For more updates, follow us on Twitter @BBCNewsEnts, on Instagram, or email story suggestions to entertainment.news@bbc.co.uk.

text: It sounds like the screenplay from a heist movie. Burglars have audaciously infiltrated a vault brimming with diamonds, watches, and invaluable family heirlooms, selecting their treasures from hundreds of safe deposit boxes, all while the world outside remained blissfully unaware. The unremarkable row of shops and traders that constitute London's famed jewellery quarter, Hatton Garden, have long been shrouded in tales of clandestine passageways leading to hidden gold reserves and secure workshops where artisans painstakingly craft precious items by hand.This tightly-knit network of family businesses rarely opens its doors to outsiders, making it challenging to discern the truth behind these intriguing stories. Hatton Garden's illustrious reputation for diamond dealing dates back to the late 19th century when De Beers began marketing their South African gems through London.Nestled in Holborn, the Hatton Garden area spans a few streets surrounding its namesake thoroughfare. Within this compact tenth of a square mile, there are 300 shops and companies, including dealers, suppliers, and craftsmen. Joanna Hardy, an independent jewellery expert with over two decades of experience in Hatton Garden, hesitates to confirm any myths or rumors, asserting that doing so contradicts the industry's essence. It's not so much a secret; it's that this is a trade built on trust, she explains. People perceive it as top-secret, but the high value of the goods creates a very closed community. Generations of families have worked here, and an incident like this shocks everyone.The burglars' choice to target the Hatton Garden Safe Deposit company only deepens the enigma. You don't see people holding up banks now; these crimes are done online behind a computer, Ms. Hardy remarks, but this seems all the more shocking because it's so old-school.With an abundance of gold and precious gems housed within these East London buildings, one would expect stringent security measures, such as alarms, double door entry systems, and CCTV at every exit. However, Peter Kirkham, a former detective chief inspector of the Metropolitan Police's specialist Flying Squad, cautions against assumptions. There is a huge amount of difference in the way premises are protected, he notes. From my experience, this trade can be quite complacent, believing it won't happen to them.Kirkham elaborates, It's not unheard of for thieves to trigger the system, wait for the response, and then act when it's assumed to be a false alarm. If there weren't strong security systems and procedures in place, thieves could have had free rein all weekend. Something about it feels very odd.Regardless of how the heist unfolded, Mr. Kirkham is skeptical about recovering the high-value items. Jewellery is notorious for disappearing completely. It's broken up, recut, and sold on the black market because no one wants anything identifiable, he says. In any trade, when it comes to crime, sentimentality is of no concern.

text: Welsh Secretary Stephen Crabb has said the Nato summit in Newport has raised the profile of Wales abroad and would attract investment. “This event has been a tremendous showcase for all that is positive, strong, and admirable about Wales,” remarked Mr. Crabb. This week has indeed demonstrated that.He continued, We have been clear that the NATO summit should leave a lasting economic footprint for Wales. text: Pedro Caixinha insists his Rangers players proved their commitment in the comeback win at Partick Thistle. In a dramatic turn of events at Ibrox, Rangers clinched three crucial Premiership points thanks to Barrie McKay's goal and Joe Garner's stoppage-time header, overturning Kris Doolan's early lead for Partick Thistle. Despite the victory, manager Pedro Caixinha acknowledged that the team's performance was disorientated, yet he praised his players for their determination and unity.If we were not together as a group, I don't think the players would celebrate like that at the end, Caixinha remarked. He expressed admiration for the players' understanding and commitment, noting, There were a lot of moments I really felt the passion from the players.Securing a top-four finish and a spot in European football next season, Rangers were largely outplayed by Alan Archibald's side for much of the match. Caixinha implemented several system and personnel changes, with substitute McKay making a significant impact, but the team struggled to find their rhythm for extended periods.Defending his strategic adjustments following consecutive Old Firm defeats, Caixinha emphasized the importance of showing resilience. Today was really important for us to show a reaction, he added. We showed it in the second half, and I need to be happy with that. We needed to change the course of the game, and we managed it. My passion and dedication to this sport is that I would rather die trying it rather than be alive to see what happens. And that is what the players did.On the other hand, Jags boss Alan Archibald was left to reflect on yet another late-game collapse against Rangers. Recalling a similar scenario in November at Firhill, where a late Joe Dodoo double snatched victory from Thistle, Archibald lamented, It's a sore one. We put a lot into that first-half performance. We created a number of good opportunities - that was the only negative, not adding to our 1-0 lead.He insisted that tactics did not fail them, stating, It's one long ball that outdoes us. You feel guilty about having a go, but we've got to learn from it. We've got to move on. We want to be a top-six side, we want to stay away from the bottom end of the league. You've got to see games out and manage them and learn from it.Archibald highlighted the need for defensive discipline, adding, Once we lost the goal, we didn't react in the right way. We didn't do the basics. With 30 seconds to go, you've got to go and defend your box as if your life depends on it.

text: Donald Trump has said his sons will run his businesses during his presidency but there will be no new deals. Two of my children, Don and Eric, plus executives, will manage them, he tweeted, adding, No new deals will be done during my term(s) in office. text: Governor Scott Walker's campaign for president is premised on more than just his conservative achievements in Wisconsin, of which there are many. The candidate frequently and almost obsessively highlights the challenges he's overcome and the opponents he's vanquished to achieve his goals. Across the United States, conservative audiences seem to adore him for this. Over the past five years, Democratic adversaries in a state known for its progressive policies have battled the governor on every political front. Now, many are questioning if they inadvertently contributed to his emergence as a presidential contender. Is Candidate Walker a creation of their own making?I regard Walker as one of the most destructive forces in American politics today, states Dave Obey, a retired Democratic congressman from Wisconsin. However, he acknowledges that Walker's ascent would not have been possible without the misguided recall efforts that took place in the state.The recall campaign in 2012 aimed to hold a special election to remove Walker from office during his first term as governor. This followed months of protests by over 100,000 demonstrators in Madison, the state capital, who unsuccessfully tried to block a law that significantly reduced the collective bargaining power of the state's public employee unions, including teachers.I don't blame the unions for thinking they should support the recall because he was essentially putting them out of business both economically and politically, Obey adds. But sometimes it helps if you don't think with your spleen.According to Obey, the failed recall efforts turned Walker into a hero among grass-roots conservatives, helped him build a national fundraising network, and provided him with a distinct talking point in the crowded Republican field. Including his 2014 re-election, he has triumphed in three elections over five years in a state that hasn't supported a Republican presidential candidate in over three decades.Another Democratic insider from Wisconsin, speaking anonymously, was more candid about the recall effort. It was something you just couldn't politically oppose because the activists were so angry, he says. I just wanted this to go the [expletive] away. I was hoping they wouldn't gather the signatures, but I couldn't publicly say that.He believes the protests, though well-intentioned, were doomed due to Republican control of the state legislature, and the recall election was a disaster because the Wisconsin public wasn't convinced of its legitimacy. At its core was a sort of purity and innocence that might make you believe in American democracy—but it was tragically flawed, he says. It was not going to work; it was just a children's crusade.During his presidential announcement event on Monday, Walker's political battle scars were repeatedly highlighted. There was talk of agitators being bussed in from out-of-state during the Madison protests and death threats against Walker and his family. Do you remember what it was like to see your governor persecuted for simply putting you back in charge? Wisconsin Lieutenant Governor Rebecca Kleefisch asked the audience of around 300. Like a David to Goliath, Governor Scott Walker had your back. And America, he will again.After Walker spent nearly 40 minutes touting his conservative achievements, audience members echoed similar sentiments. Democrats threw everything at him that they could, and he still won, says Jeff Bishop from Richfield, Wisconsin, who attended the event with his wife. That says a lot.Chris Taylor, who was a Wisconsin lobbyist for Planned Parenthood and among the 2011 protesters at the state capitol, rejects the portrayal of the gathering as an unruly mob. The protests were nonviolent, she says. These were teachers, and kids, and grandmas. They were as Wisconsin as you can get.Taylor argues that progressives shouldn't regret the demonstrations and recall drive, as they represented the people's will, independent of Democratic leaders. Walker, she says, is a tricky guy who has convinced the Wisconsin public he's something he's not. He's very moderate in his speech, he's not bombastic, he's very earnest, he's very Mid-Western, Taylor, now a Wisconsin state representative, explains. He's very appealing in that way, but he governs like an extremist.Joel Rivlin, a Wisconsin-based Democratic political consultant, agrees that the protests and recall efforts gave Walker a significant boost, even though it was apparent from his early days in office that he was positioning himself for a presidential run. Even before the recall, he was receiving a ton of money from outside of Wisconsin, Rivlin notes. People just assumed he was gearing up for something and had bigger ambitions.Now, propelled by liberal opposition, Walker has become a formidable force in national Republican politics. He is the front-runner in neighboring Iowa, the first battleground for the 2016 nomination, and ranks high in national approval polls. While the Republican primary field includes accomplished governors like Florida's Jeb Bush, Texas's Rick Perry, and New Jersey's Chris Christie, Walker stands apart. No other Republican candidate has built a throne of his enemies' skulls, as Rich Cromwell from the Federalist describes, quite like Walker.A famous line by Ralph Waldo Emerson, often cited in the context of coups and revolutions, seems fitting for the leader of this northern dairy state: Never strike a king unless you are sure you shall kill him. Despite all efforts to unseat him, Scott Walker still wears the crown—and now he's setting his sights on a much larger realm.

There was talk of the agitators who came by bus to the protests in Madison, and of threats against Walker and his family. After Walker had spent about forty minutes defending his conservative record, the audience echoed her words. Lt. Governor Rebecca Kleefisch spoke to the audience of about 300 people. “Do you remember when your governor was persecuted just for putting you back in power? The protests were nonviolent, she says, and they were made by teachers, schoolchildren, and grandmothers—they came straight from the heart of the state of Wisconsin. “The Democrats threw everything at him and he still won,” said Jeff Bishop, a Richfield resident who attended the event with his wife. “And America, he will again.” Walker, says Taylor, is a clever man who has made people in Wisconsin believe he was someone he is not. He is moderate in speech, not bombastic, very serious, very moderate, Taylor, who is now a senator, explains, but in action he is a true extremist. Rivlin, a Democratic consultant from Wisconsin, agrees that the protests and recalls were a major boost for Walker, although it was obvious from the very first days of his government that he was preparing a presidential campaign. Now, soaring with the momentum of liberal opposition, Walker has become a formidable force in national Republican politics. He leads in neighboring Iowa, the first electoral battlefield in the race for the Republican presidential nomination in 2016, and is well positioned in national polls. No other Republican candidate has built up as much of a throne of enemies’ skulls, as R. Cromwell writes in The Federalist, as Walker has. text: Los Angeles, known as the homeless capital of the US, has passed a $1.87bn (£1.29bn) plan to help get an estimated 40,000 people off the streets. City authorities in Los Angeles are planning a significant expansion of homeless shelters and the construction of quality housing over the next decade. This initiative is in response to what city official Sachi Hamai described as the most serious humanitarian crisis confronting our county today.Last year, Los Angeles declared a state of public emergency following a dramatic 12.4% increase in the homeless population over two years. Residents and officials attribute this surge to a combination of unemployment, substance abuse, and escalating rents and housing prices.Currently, it is estimated that around 40,000 homeless individuals reside throughout Los Angeles County, with two-thirds living on the streets, in tents, or in their vehicles. To address this crisis, a comprehensive 10-year plan is being proposed. This plan includes investments in both short-term and long-term housing solutions, designated overnight parking areas for those living in cars, and the establishment of a city-wide network of mobile showers and toilets.To fund these measures, officials are set to allocate $150 million over the next two years specifically for housing the homeless. However, some lawmakers have raised concerns about the source of this funding. Mayor Eric Garcetti has suggested that the funds might come from new revenue streams and a reallocation of existing resources. It may include things that have to do with revenue growth or the shifting of priorities of money. We don't have 100 million extra dollars lying around where we can go, 'OK we were going to split this up into other things, let's just put it all into homelessness.' It will require difficult decisions, Garcetti explained.The city council has yet to adopt these plans, as the budget vote is scheduled for April. Annually, Los Angeles already spends approximately $1 billion on medical, psychiatric, and social welfare services for its homeless population.Known as the homeless capital of America, Los Angeles holds a disputed yet persistent title. The heart of this crisis lies in the shadows of downtown's skyscrapers on Skid Row. Amidst the city's glitz and glamour, the forgotten have found refuge. Block after block, the streets are lined with tarpaulins, tents, and shopping carts, sheltering predominantly African-American faces from the relentless sun.Read more here.
