text: Quentin Tarantino's first western, 2013's Django Unchained, was his highest grossing film in the USA - and now the 52-year-old director's latest movie, The Hateful Eight, is also set in the wild west, fulfilling his desire to breathe life into obsolete or dormant genres and make them my own, or even remake them. Set against the rugged backdrop of post-Civil War Wyoming, Quentin Tarantino's film The Hateful Eight assembles a cast of familiar faces, including Tarantino stalwarts Samuel L. Jackson, Kurt Russell, and Reservoir Dogs stars Tim Roth and Michael Madsen. Jennifer Jason Leigh, known for her role in Single White Female, joins as the sole female among the eight, while Tarantino humorously remarks that Channing Tatum is interning for his first part in one of the director's films.Much like Django Unchained, The Hateful Eight has sparked controversy for its racial language and the violence it depicts, particularly towards Leigh's character, at early Hollywood screenings. Despite this, executive producer Harvey Weinstein dismisses claims of misogyny against Tarantino as fishing for stupidity. Both Tarantino and Leigh have received Golden Globe nominations for screenplay and actress, which Tarantino expresses he's thrilled about.Leigh portrays Daisy Domergue, a captured outlaw en route to her execution. Russell, who spent four and a half months handcuffed to Leigh for the film's plot, shares that they meticulously planned the scenes of violence they were to enact. Trust between actors is crucial, Russell explains. I wanted to ensure she felt safe, allowing her to fully immerse in her role.Tarantino defends his script, stating, The violence is designed to shock the audience and evoke sympathy for Daisy. I've trapped my characters in a cabin during a blizzard, creating a pressure cooker scenario. In my films, any outrageous act of violence can occur. So why should the eighth character be off-limits? It defies the entire narrative.On the topic of race, with Jackson playing a former Union soldier carrying a letter from Abraham Lincoln, Tarantino acknowledges that many themes we explore in the film were mirrored on our TV screens, referencing the unrest following the 2014 shooting of Michael Brown in Missouri. After the first draft of The Hateful Eight leaked online in January 2014, Tarantino initially scrapped the project. Now, he appreciates the leak, saying, It's on record that I wasn't writing a script in response to these events.Tarantino believes his scripts carry deeper meanings, stating, I enjoy embedding my messages within a story. Historically, no genre captures modern America better than the western. The 1970s westerns, post-Vietnam and Watergate, were notably cynical. 'Django Unchained' was successful and perhaps reinvented the genre a bit. Now, with 'The Revenant' and this film, we have two major westerns hitting cinemas. I've always said to be known as a western director, you need to make three, so perhaps one more is in my future.Inspired by 1960s TV westerns like Bonanza, The Hateful Eight exudes a nostalgic vibe, complete with a three-hour runtime, a musical overture by Ennio Morricone, and a 12-minute intermission. Filmed in 70mm, the movie utilized the same lenses as the iconic chariot race in Ben Hur (1959), though many theaters will screen a shorter version due to equipment limitations.Last year, Tarantino hinted at retiring after his tenth film, with The Hateful Eight marking his eighth if Kill Bill is counted as one. Russell, who previously worked with Tarantino on 2007's Deathproof, believes it would be a loss if Tarantino retired, claiming the director is in a league of his own. He adds, Within moments of the film's opening, you recognize his signature style. Every few generations, someone like him emerges, and I wish everyone in the industry could experience working with him. It's a wild ride everyone should join.The Hateful Eight is set to debut in the UK on January 8.

text: A motorised wheelchair user has been convicted of ramming a policeman during a loyalist protest in north Belfast. At Belfast Magistrates Court, it was revealed that Samuel Baxter trapped a police officer's leg against a vehicle after being prevented from crossing security lines on Twaddell Avenue. The 53-year-old, from Canmore Close, was also convicted of disorderly conduct during one of the nightly protests in the area. His sentencing is scheduled for next month.Police testimony indicated that a constable sustained a bruised shin due to Baxter repeatedly maneuvering his wheelchair, which weighs up to 28 stone, towards them. Baxter insisted his presence in the area was solely for family matters and denied any involvement in the protests regarding a contentious Orange Order parade. He asserted that he was attempting to pass through the police cordon to transport a friend with a blood clot to the hospital.Baxter claimed the officer he allegedly assaulted instructed him, Sit down, you're not getting through, OK. He argued that the constable's flak jacket inadvertently snagged on his wheelchair's gear stick, causing it to move forward slightly. A police inspector testified that Baxter was using offensive language and behaving abusively. He suggested the incident was part of efforts to provoke a crowd that was recording the scene on their phones.This scenario unfolds nightly and has been ongoing for over 400 nights, the inspector stated. Such actions are orchestrated to agitate the crowd. I learned he emerged with a crowd already filming him.The inspector emphasized the police's attempts to de-escalate the situation. We conduct this protest nightly. If there had been a genuine medical emergency, it would have been evident, and we would have certainly assisted, he explained. When I approached him and offered numerous opportunities to explain the issue, he was just extremely verbally abusive and performing for the crowd.The judge found Baxter guilty of both assaulting police and disorderly behavior, ordering a pre-sentence report to be compiled.

text: The group representing many of Scotland's councils has urged them to reject the Scottish government's funding settlement offer. In a decisive vote, leaders of the Convention of Scottish Local Authorities (Cosla) overwhelmingly rejected the Scottish government's funding deal, with 21 voting against and only 7 in favor. The motion criticized the government's approach as wholly misguided and warned of grievous injury to communities. Finance Secretary John Swinney, however, described the offer as a deal worth taking. Councils have until February 9 to respond to the proposal.All non-SNP councils within Cosla have united in opposition to the deal, with some considering legal action. Additionally, Scotland's four councils outside of Cosla, including Glasgow and Aberdeen, are assessing the legality of the proposed terms. The funding package aims to maintain the council tax freeze, in place since 2007, threatening to cut funding for councils that break it. Despite this, some councils are contemplating tax increases due to budget constraints.Negotiations between Mr. Swinney and council leaders have been ongoing, with the deadline for accepting the deal repeatedly extended. Following a meeting in Edinburgh, Cosla President David O'Neill declared the funding package totally unacceptable, labeling it an assault on their democratic mandate. He stated, The Scottish government is essentially coercing councils into accepting the deal. Unfortunately, due to severe sanctions, many councils may feel compelled to comply with central directives, leaving the most vulnerable to bear the consequences.Cosla's vote, while largely symbolic, underscores the deep dissatisfaction among councils over the budget offer. Of the 28 councils, 21 supported the motion against the funding proposal, with only SNP councils dissenting. This division complicates the ability of local governments to present a united stance. The political tension is heightened as the Holyrood election nears, with councils fearing deeper cuts and struggling with the constraints on raising council tax. For instance, Moray's proposal to increase council tax by 18% now seems unfeasible.SNP councils, while acknowledging the challenges of the funding offer, believe it is the best possible outcome. The government, committed to freezing council tax throughout the parliamentary term, argues this policy has been beneficial for families. It also claims to have shielded councils from the worst of Westminster's spending cuts.The legal exploration by the four non-Cosla councils highlights their serious concerns and illustrates the leverage the Scottish government holds. Realistically, councils have limited options but to accept the government's terms, raising questions about the future of council funding. A recent report, commissioned by both the government and Cosla, proposed various alternatives to council tax. There is ongoing debate about granting councils more autonomy in raising local revenue, with parties expected to present plans ahead of the May Holyrood election.Cosla's motion indicated that the deal would slash council budgets by £350 million, resulting in undeliverable service and staffing cuts. The GMB Scotland trade union warned that 8,785 local authority jobs are at risk due to these budget cuts and plans to hold a rally at the Scottish Parliament next week.Jenny Laing, leader of Aberdeen City Council, which is not part of Cosla, described the relationship with the Scottish government as broken. After a meeting of the Scottish Local Government Partnership (SLGP) in Glasgow, she stated, This is the most significant grant cut ever applied to local government. When we question the settlement on behalf of our residents, we're held to ransom by the government's attempts to control decisions meant for democratically-elected representatives. The group is seeking legal advice on the issue.Scottish Labour and the Liberal Democrats have urged Mr. Swinney to reconsider the deal. Responding to the votes by Cosla and SLGP, John Swinney emphasized, This is a deal worth taking. Our funding proposals offer a robust yet challenging financial settlement for local government, despite UK government cuts. It includes an additional £250 million for social care, supports councils in delivering the Living Wage to 40,000 people, maintains the council tax freeze for a ninth year, and protects the pupil-teacher ratio, aiding in educational attainment. The reduction in local authority budgets is around just 2 percent of total revenue expenditure. While I acknowledge the challenges for councils, some of the language used has been excessive. I hope cooler heads will recognize this is a deal councils can and should accept.

text: Russia's President Vladimir Putin has condemned Turkey's shooting down of a Russian warplane on its border with Syria on 24 November. In a dramatic incident marking the first Russian aircraft crash in Syria since Moscow began airstrikes in September against President Bashar al-Assad's adversaries, Turkey and Russia have confirmed the downing of a Russian Su-24 by Turkish F-16s near the Turkey-Syria border on November 24. President Vladimir Putin stated that the Su-24, an all-weather attack aircraft with two crew members, was at an altitude of 6,000 meters (19,685 feet) when hit by an air-to-air missile. The aircraft crashed in the contested Jabal Turkmen region in Syria's Latakia province, resulting in the deaths of the pilot and a marine involved in a rescue mission.In correspondence to the UN Security Council, Turkey's representative Halit Cevik detailed that two unidentified aircraft approached Turkish airspace near Yayladagi in Hatay province. Despite receiving ten warnings over five minutes to change course, the planes entered Turkish airspace for 17 seconds. Cevik noted, Following the violation, plane 1 left Turkish national airspace. Plane 2 was fired at while in Turkish national airspace by Turkish F-16s performing air combat patrolling in the area. Plane 2 crashed on to the Syria side of the Turkish-Syrian border. The Turkish military released radar data showing the Russian plane's brief incursion into Turkey.However, President Putin contested these claims, asserting the Su-24 was over Syrian territory, 1 km from the Turkish border, when it was shot down, crashing 4 km from the border. The Russian defense ministry supported this, insisting the aircraft never left Syrian airspace and received no warnings. They released a video purportedly showing the Su-24's flight path. Surviving pilot Capt. Konstantin Murakhtin told Russian media he received no warning before being attacked.Putin further accused the US military of complicity, claiming they were informed of the flight details, but the US State Department denied prior notification from Russia. US officials indicated the plane briefly entered Turkish airspace and had been warned.On November 27, Russian air force commander Gen Viktor Bondarev suggested an ambush by Turkish F-16s, which he claimed were in the area for over an hour. He stated the F-16 that fired the missile had briefly entered Syrian airspace. Bondarev added that the Su-24s had just completed a bombing run on rebel positions when one was downed.Video footage from Turkish media depicted the Su-24 crew ejecting as the plane was aflame. Syrian Turkmen rebels reportedly shot at the crew as they descended, killing pilot Lt Col Oleg Peshkov. Capt. Murakhtin was later rescued by Syrian forces. A Russian marine, Aleksandr Pozynich, was also killed during a rescue attempt when their helicopter came under fire.Russia, a key ally of Assad, has been conducting airstrikes in Syria, claiming to target terrorists, primarily IS militants. However, Western analysts argue that Russian strikes have mostly targeted Western-backed rebels. The Su-24s were reportedly targeting terrorists from Russia's North Caucasus, according to Moscow.In retaliation to the downing, Russia deployed S-400 anti-aircraft missiles at its Hmeimim airbase, extending its reach over Syria, Lebanon, Cyprus, and parts of Turkey. Furthermore, Russia suspended its visa-free regime with Turkey, banned charter flights, and advised against travel to Turkey, impacting Turkey's tourism sector. President Putin also decreed economic sanctions against Turkey, including restrictions on imports and Turkish businesses in Russia.Putin has refused communication with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, demanding an apology from Turkey. Turkish PM Ahmet Davutoglu, however, has asserted that Turkey will not apologize for defending its airspace. Putin accused Turkey of facilitating oil trade with IS, which Turkey denies.The incident marks a rare NATO-Russia confrontation, the first since the 1950s. NATO Secretary-General Jens Stoltenberg affirmed support for Turkey's territorial integrity, while President Erdogan defended Turkey's right to protect its borders, citing new engagement rules post-2012 when Syria downed a Turkish jet.

text: For the cynics among us, Valentine's Day is an annual nightmare: everything turns pink and heart-shaped, restaurants slap a premium price on a sub-par special menu, and Hallmark shareholders are laughing all the way to the bank. Beyond the plush toys and bouquets of red roses, Valentine's Day elicits a range of reactions worldwide, from enthusiastic celebrations to outright rejection. Here’s a glimpse into the diverse ways this day of love is embraced or dismissed globally.In parts of Indonesia, authorities have taken a firm stance against Valentine's Day, particularly targeting students. They claim the celebration promotes casual sex. In Makassar, police went so far as to raid shops, dismantling condom displays. The city's mayor informed the BBC that while condoms were removed from public view due to customer complaints, they remain available for discreet purchase. Valentine's Day's origins as a Roman fertility festival, later transforming into a Christian feast, concern conservatives in some predominantly Muslim nations. In Surabaya, Indonesia's second-largest city, students were instructed to reject the holiday, citing it as contrary to cultural norms.Neighboring Malaysia has also seen a backlash against Valentine's Day. The National Muslim Youth Association advised women and girls to avoid using emoticons and excessive perfume in a pre-Valentine's message. Their guidance included suggestions for creating anti-Valentine posters and eschewing themed attire.In stark contrast, Robben Island in South Africa, once notorious for imprisoning Nelson Mandela, has celebrated love en masse since 2000. Initiated by South Africa's Department of Home Affairs and the Robben Island Museum, the event draws couples from around the world. This year, 20 couples plan to wed in the island’s quaint white chapel. For a small fee, the service includes a tour of the island. Organizers noted that 2017's participants were selected for their diversity and compelling love stories.Meanwhile, in Thailand, civil servants are distributing free prenatal vitamins on the streets of Bangkok this Valentine's Day, aiming to counter the country's declining birth rate. The government has invested around 1 million baht ($28,600; £22,900) in these very magical vitamins, which contain folic acid and iron. While Thai couples in 1970 had an average of six children, today the figure has dropped to 1.6.In Pakistan, the High Court in Islamabad has prohibited public Valentine's Day celebrations, asserting that the festival is not part of Muslim culture. Despite its growing popularity, critics label it a decadent Western invention. The court's order restricts media coverage of Valentine's events and bans festivities in public spaces and government offices.Saudi Arabia's religious police remain vigilant against love-themed merchandise, such as flowers and cards, especially red items. Florists have resorted to nighttime deliveries to circumvent the ban, while a black market in roses and wrapping paper allows some to express their affection. For others, it's an opportunity for a romantic getaway to nearby Bahrain or the UAE, where celebrations face fewer restrictions.In Japan, as the 14th of February approached, a group of Marxist protesters, known as the Kakuhido or Revolutionary Alliance of Men that Women find Unattractive, unfurled a massive Smash Valentine's Day banner in Tokyo. They oppose public displays of affection, which they claim hurt their feelings. The group's PR chief, Takayuki Akimoto, stated, Our aim is to crush this love capitalism. People like us, who don't seek value in love, are being oppressed by society. He added, It's a conspiracy by those who think unattractive guys are inferior or losers—public cuddling makes us feel bad. It's unforgivable!These protests coincided with a report from Japan's family planning association, revealing that sexless marriages have reached a record high. Nearly half of married Japanese couples hadn't engaged in sexual activity for over a month and didn't anticipate any change soon.

text: Northern Ireland were beaten by world champions Germany but still advanced to the last 16 of Euro 2016 after the Czech Republic's 2-0 defeat by Turkey. Germany's clash with Northern Ireland in Paris saw the world champions squander multiple opportunities, both before and after Mario Gomez netted the decisive goal. Despite the Czechs' defeat, Northern Ireland secured a place in the last 16 as one of the top four third-placed teams, outperforming Albania and Turkey based on their record. Michael O'Neill's squad is set to face either Wales or the host nation, France, in the knockout stage.Northern Ireland concluded the group phase with three points, identical to Albania and Turkey, but advanced due to a superior goal difference. This marks only the third time in their history that they have progressed to the knockout rounds of a major tournament. Although they lost, Northern Ireland's supporters remained in high spirits, lingering in the Parc des Princes well after the final whistle. The players received an enthusiastic ovation from fans clad in green, who sang passionately throughout the match.Early on, Northern Ireland appeared to be in peril as Germany, who topped Group C over Poland on goal difference, created several prime scoring chances. However, thanks to steadfast defending, exceptional goalkeeping, and a touch of fortune, Northern Ireland's defense was breached only once. Michael O'Neill's squad might have faced a heavier defeat if not for the heroics of goalkeeper Michael McGovern. Out of contract after two years at Hamilton, McGovern delivered a series of remarkable saves, maintaining his record of never conceding more than one goal in any of his 14 national appearances.Although another impressive record—conceding just one first-half goal in their last 22 matches—was broken, Northern Ireland's resistance was undone by Gomez, who scored his 28th international goal, converting Thomas Muller's touch from 10 yards. Germany could have easily extended their lead before halftime, with McGovern making crucial saves and Muller hitting the post and crossbar. The world champions maintained their lead comfortably, and could have increased it early in the second half, but McGovern denied Mario Gotze with another outstanding save, while Gomez missed a close-range opportunity.Out of Germany's 28 attempts, only nine were on target, and McGovern's eight saves preserved Northern Ireland's goal difference, crucial for their qualification. Reflecting on the match, McGovern said, I was busy but it was mentally very hard - I'm immensely proud. We knew every goal was crucial, so we wanted to keep it at one and maybe nick a goal of our own. Germany had a slow start but they were excellent today; we could not get out. I've never had such a busy night and I've never played against such quality opposition.Manager Michael O'Neill expressed pride in his team's performance, stating, Nobody sets up their team to just defend, but you look at the Germany team and you see Bayern, Real Madrid, and so on... it's not in my nature to set the team up to lose 7-0. But we earned the right to be here. I'm immensely proud that we are even playing here against the world champions in Paris. We knew the group would be difficult. What we saw tonight was a team that refused to be beaten by a big margin and did everything possible to stay in the game. Over the three games, we deserve to be in the last 16. What we went through tonight will prepare us for anything in the next round and our players will be ready for whoever.The match concluded with Northern Ireland 0, Germany 1, after a second half marked by missed opportunities and tactical substitutions. Northern Ireland's Kyle Lafferty and Germany's Bastian Schweinsteiger were among those involved in the latter stages, with Lafferty replacing Conor Washington and Schweinsteiger coming on for Sami Khedira. Despite their valiant efforts, Northern Ireland ended the match with a narrow defeat but with their heads held high, ready to face the challenges of the knockout rounds.

text: Comments made by Northern Ireland Health Minister Jim Wells linking child abuse with gay relationships have been rejected by a child protection body set up by his own department. The Safeguarding Board for Northern Ireland (SBNI), established by the Department of Health in 2012, plays a crucial role in advocating for the welfare of children and young people. Glenys Johnston, the independent chair of SBNI, emphasized, There is no evidence that children raised by same-sex couples face any greater risk of abuse compared to those raised by heterosexual couples.Johnston further stated, In many parts of Europe, children who have suffered abuse, whether by a man or woman, often find the best care with same-sex couples of a different gender. I am determined that children with same-sex carers or parents should not worry about being more vulnerable to abuse. Nor should those caring for them face adverse comments or criticism, and the children themselves should not be bullied because their carers share the same gender.The conversation around this topic intensified following remarks by Jim Wells, the DUP South Down candidate for the 7 May election, during a discussion on gay marriage. Wells claimed, You don't bring a child up in a homosexual relationship. That a child is far more likely to be abused and neglected.... However, he later expressed regret, stating, I accept that one line of what I said caused offence and deep concern. I regret having wrongly made that remark about abuse and I'm sorry those words were uttered. The comment did not reflect my view nor that of my party.Johnston refrained from directly addressing Wells' comments, acknowledging his recent personal challenges, I know he's had an extremely difficult personal time for some months. He actually appointed me to my post, and I have no indication at all that he's not committed to safeguarding children in Northern Ireland.Wells' assertions were challenged by Prof Susan Golombok of the University of Cambridge's Centre for Family Research. Speaking on BBC Radio Ulster's Talkback programme, she countered, The minister has got his facts wrong because the evidence points to completely the opposite conclusion. More than 35 years of research on the well-being of children with lesbian mothers, and more recently with gay fathers, have shown that these children do just as well as those with traditional families.In December 2013, Northern Ireland lifted the ban on gay and unmarried couples applying to adopt children. Prior to this, Wells' predecessor, Edwin Poots, had attempted to challenge a court decision extending adoption rights to gay couples. However, the Supreme Court ruled that the Department of Health's argument for appeal did not meet the necessary criteria.

text: The EU has agreed a €1.8bn (£1.3bn; $2bn) loan to Ukraine - described as a landmark deal for a non-EU member. At an EU summit held in Riga, Latvia, an agreement was signed involving leaders from six post-Soviet nations. This agreement includes a loan aimed at aiding Ukraine, which is struggling financially, to implement necessary economic reforms. The ongoing conflict with pro-Russian rebels in the eastern region has severely impacted Ukraine's economy. The EU, along with other international lenders, is exerting pressure on Ukraine to tackle corruption and liberalize its economy.In other developments on Friday, the EU committed €200 million in grants to Ukraine, Georgia, and Moldova, all of which have signed association agreements with the 28-nation bloc. The remaining Eastern Partnership countries are Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Belarus. While Georgia, Moldova, and Ukraine are seeking full integration with the EU, the other three nations are opting for more limited cooperation. Notably, Armenia and Belarus are part of the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union, considered by some analysts as a rival to the EU.The summit's declaration in Riga condemned Russia for the annexation of Ukraine's Crimea peninsula the previous year. It stated, The acts against Ukraine and the events in Georgia since 2014 have shown that the fundamental principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity within internationally recognised borders cannot be taken for granted in the 21st Century on the European continent. The EU reaffirmed its commitment to supporting the territorial integrity, independence, and sovereignty of all its partners. The declaration also acknowledged each partner's sovereign right to determine their level of ambition and goals in their relationship with the EU.During a news conference, European Council President Donald Tusk expressed a desire to be ambitious as possible in granting Georgia and Ukraine a visa-free regime, contingent on meeting key conditions. European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker noted enormous progress on this issue. Although both countries hoped for a positive decision on visa liberalization at the Riga summit, such a decision will not occur until at least next year. Moldova was granted visa-free travel to the EU last year. Tusk emphasized that the partnership process is a long haul, stating, Nobody promised that the Eastern Partnership would be an automatic way to membership of the EU.The crisis in Ukraine began in November 2013 when the previous government withdrew from closer EU ties, sparking mass protests that led to President Viktor Yanukovych's ouster and subsequent conflict in the east. Russian state media remain skeptical about the Eastern Partnership summit. Rossiiskaya Gazeta, a government daily, described the meeting as so lacking in hope and prospects that it can only be compared to fishing without bait. State-controlled Channel One TV criticized the summit for offering nothing, not entry to the EU nor cancellation of visas, but it demands plenty, while Rossiya1 TV claimed the Eastern Partnership scheme has outlived its usefulness.In Ukraine, media reactions to the summit were similarly bleak. The Yevropeyska Pravda website stated, Ukraine itself brought about the Riga summit's failure, blaming Kiev for not implementing a visa liberalization action plan with the EU.According to BBC Monitoring, Ukraine's economy continued to contract in the first quarter of 2015, and Kiev faces substantial debt repayments to international creditors. Since April 2014, more than 6,000 people have died in the conflict in eastern Ukraine, where rebels seized large parts of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions following Russia's annexation of Crimea. The Ukrainian government, Western leaders, and NATO assert that Russia is providing the rebels with heavy weapons and soldiers, a claim supported by independent experts. Moscow, however, denies these allegations, claiming that any Russians fighting with the rebels are volunteers.

text: Jane Haining was a quiet farmer's daughter from the south of Scotland who ended her life as a slave labourer in the most notorious extermination camp the world has ever known. Jane Haining, the only Scot officially recognized for sacrificing her life for Jews during the Holocaust, was far removed from the horrors of Auschwitz in her early years. Born in Dunscore, Dumfriesshire, in 1897, she grew up amidst the serene landscapes of rural Scotland. Her childhood was marked by tragedy when her mother passed away when Jane was just five, leaving her to care for her younger sisters.A bright student with a knack for languages, Jane attended Dumfries Academy before taking a secretarial position at the vast JP Coats weaving factory in Paisley. During her time there, she became an active member of Queen's Park West Church in Glasgow's Crosshill area, where stained glass windows now honor her strong Christian faith.In 1932, Jane responded to an advertisement for a matron's position at the Scottish Mission to the Jews in Budapest. Dr. David Kaufman, director of the Centre for the Study of Modern Conflict at the University of Edinburgh, explains that Budapest was home to a thriving middle-class Jewish community, often referred to as Jewdapest due to the high percentage of Jewish professionals.The Church of Scotland mission school in Budapest, though Christian in its practices, was highly sought after by Jewish parents. Rev. Aaron Stevens, minister at today’s St. Columba's Church of Scotland in Budapest, notes the high quality of education and the acceptance of Jewish girls as equals. Former pupil Katalin Packard recalls Jane as kind, welcoming, and warm, embodying the values of fairness and equality that defined the mission.Jane's arrival in Budapest coincided with a tumultuous period in Europe. Less than a year later, Adolf Hitler rose to power in Germany, initiating widespread anti-Semitic sentiment. Dr. Kaufman notes that Hungary's political elite leaned towards Nazi Germany, despite the Hungarian Jewish community's efforts to assimilate culturally.The outbreak of World War II in 1939 saw Hungary's nationalist government enacting anti-Semitic laws, even as it allied with Germany. Jews in Budapest, despite losing jobs and civil rights, found a semblance of dignity at the Scottish Mission school. Yet, as the Church of Scotland grew concerned for its missionaries' safety, Jane refused to leave, writing, If these children needed me in days of sunshine, how much more do they need me in these days of darkness?Former pupil Annette Lantos reflects on Jane's inability to comprehend the evil surrounding her, living in a world where reason and civility prevailed. This world was shattered in March 1944 when Nazi forces occupied Budapest. Jane, deeply moved, sewed yellow stars onto her students' clothing, an act of defiance that put her in peril.A minor incident soon led to her arrest. After reprimanding the cook's son-in-law for taking food meant for the students, he reported her to the authorities. Arrested for espionage on behalf of England, Jane was initially imprisoned locally before being sent to Auschwitz. There, amidst the peak of the Holocaust, she was forced into labor camps, enduring brutal conditions until her death at 47.Her death certificate cites cachexia following intestinal catarrh, leaving the exact cause of her demise uncertain—whether from illness, starvation, or gas chambers. Recognition of Jane's sacrifice was long in coming. In 1997, following efforts by Queen's Park Church and a decade-long investigation by an Israeli board, she was honored as Righteous Among the Nations at Yad Vashem in Jerusalem. In 2010, she received a Hero of the Holocaust medal from the British government.Though Jane Haining's death was unheralded, her quiet heroism has gained global acknowledgment. Her story is chronicled in the BBC documentary Jane Haining: The Scot Who Died in Auschwitz, available on BBC iPlayer.

text: Reports of child rape to police in England and Wales have risen by 37% over the last five years, figures show. According to Her Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary (HMIC), the number of recorded child rape cases rose from 5,674 in 2009/10 to 7,775 in 2013/14. However, less than one-third of these cases resulted in suspects being charged or summoned. The report also highlighted a 38% increase in recorded adult rapes, which climbed from 9,383 in 2009/10 to 12,952 in 2013/14, with only about 20% of cases leading to charges or summonses.In 2013/14, the Metropolitan Police reported the highest incidence of adult rapes per 100,000 people, totaling 3,056, while Dyfed-Powys reported the lowest with 62. For child rape cases per 100,000 people, North Wales recorded the highest number at 144, whereas Hertfordshire had the lowest at 73. Essex, Kent, and Suffolk were at the bottom of the list for charging or summoning suspects in child rape cases, with only 21% resulting in action. Northumbria topped this list, with 47% of cases leading to charges or summonses.Shadow Home Secretary Yvette Cooper expressed deep concern over these statistics, calling them extremely disturbing and a shocking indictment of the widening justice gap created by this government. She criticized the troubling trend of rising recorded rape incidents coupled with declining prosecutions and convictions over the past four years. Rape and the sexual abuse of a child are some of the most abhorrent and heinous crimes. And victims deserve justice, Cooper stated.Crime Prevention Minister Lynne Featherstone pointed out that both rape sentencing lengths and the total number of rape prosecutions in England and Wales have increased, from 3,819 in 2009/10 to 3,891 in 2013/14. She emphasized the coalition government's stance that every rape report must be taken seriously, victims treated with dignity, and investigations conducted thoroughly. The increase in the number of rapes being reported to police is encouraging as it shows more victims are finding the courage to come forward, she added.Paul Ford, secretary of the Police Federation National Detectives' Forum, highlighted the significant pressure on policing due to budget cuts, which impacts the service provided to victims. In Devon and Cornwall, both adult and child rape rates are among the highest recorded. However, only 15% of adult rape cases and 27% of child rape cases result in charges or summonses. Tony Hogg, the force's Police and Crime Commissioner, stated that police performance on rape is under regular review.Fee Scott from Devon Rape Crisis commented on the situation, saying, We will get a lot better outcomes if we believed people and we don't judge them on what they were wearing, doing, saying or drinking. All of that stops women coming forward because they are fearful of the reaction they will get from the authorities. This report gives a very depressing picture of what the outcome might be.

text: The US government is suing car firm Fiat Chrysler, alleging the firm sold vehicles with defeat devices that helped them pass emissions tests. The Department of Justice (DoJ) has accused Fiat Chrysler of failing to disclose emissions control software to regulators. This software allegedly allowed vehicles to emit lower levels during testing than in regular driving situations. Fiat Chrysler has vowed to defend itself vigorously against these allegations.Eric Mayne, a spokesperson for Fiat Chrysler, stated that the company would specifically counter any claims suggesting it intentionally installed defeat devices to deceive US emissions tests. The DoJ's complaint, filed on behalf of the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), claims this software was installed in approximately 104,000 Dodge Ram 1500 and Jeep Grand Cherokee models from 2014 to 2016 sold in the US.In response, Fiat Chrysler recently announced updates to its emissions software, planning to apply these modifications to both older and new vehicles. The company expressed confidence that these changes would address the agencies' concerns about the vehicles' emissions software calibrations.The situation is reminiscent of the controversy surrounding Volkswagen, which involved devices designed to circumvent emissions tests. The formal complaint, lodged in Detroit on Tuesday, accuses Fiat of equipping some vehicles with defeat devices. This follows the EPA's January notification of its investigation into Fiat Chrysler's adherence to the Clean Air Act. At that time, the agency was examining whether the software could be classified under narrow exclusions sometimes permitted.Other countries, including the UK and France, have also announced investigations into Fiat Chrysler. However, the scale of the issue is not yet comparable to Volkswagen's scandal, despite the DoJ's accusations. The number of affected vehicles is significantly smaller, and the definition of a 'defeat device' remains a point of contention. Volkswagen admitted to deliberately designing software that allowed cars to pass emissions tests while performing well on the road, a move they confessed was cheating.Fiat Chrysler, on the other hand, is accused of using undisclosed software that altered emissions control systems' performance between laboratory and road conditions. Automakers often employ software to manage emissions systems, ensuring they operate correctly under specific conditions, such as temperature, to prevent damage.Fiat Chrysler maintains it did not intentionally cheat the testing process and denies involvement in any deliberate scheme. Nevertheless, the company was alerted to the EPA's concerns earlier this year and asked for clarification. So far, it appears the authorities remain unconvinced by the explanations provided.

text: Rock-bottom Aston Villa avoided defeat for a third successive Premier League match as they held neighbours West Brom in an uninspiring stalemate. Aston Villa was denied what seemed to be a clear first-half penalty when Jordan Ayew was brought down by West Bromwich Albion's Jonas Olsson. Villa's offense was equally uninspiring, with Ashley Westwood's low shot marking their most notable attempt.Often dismissed as certain relegation candidates, Villa has been languishing at the bottom of the Premier League table after a dismal first half of the season. With only eight points from 20 matches, their situation appeared dire. However, recent performances have sparked a glimmer of hope for the team and their long-suffering supporters. A home victory against Crystal Palace, their first since the season's opening day, was followed by consecutive draws against Leicester and Albion. Nonetheless, Villa remains nine points away from safety with 15 matches left to play.Scoring has been Villa's Achilles' heel, with the team netting a mere 18 goals this season. This lack of offensive power was evident again at The Hawthorns. Remi Garde's squad controlled over 60% of possession and fired 15 shots at the Albion goal, yet goalkeeper Ben Foster was seldom tested.Albion, seeking to achieve a league double over Villa for the first time in 51 years after their 1-0 win at Villa Park in September, also struggled offensively. Saido Berahino, the match-winner in their previous encounter, has seen limited impact recently amid uncertainty regarding his future at the club. He was brought on with around 30 minutes remaining in an attempt to inject life into Albion's attack, but he, like the rest of the team, failed to trouble Villa's keeper Mark Bunn.This match mirrored Albion's previous outing at Southampton, where they also did not manage a shot on target. However, the point gained moved Tony Pulis' side, currently 13th, seven points clear of the relegation zone.Aston Villa manager Remi Garde expressed his disappointment: I'm a little bit disappointed because we wanted three points. In another situation, we might be happy with a point, but we need more points than that. We tried, we did our best, especially in the second half, but they defended well. If you see the team playing now, we look more like a team now than we used to. Players have the right attitude, but sometimes we miss talent or quality to score goals. This has been Villa’s weakness this season, they’ve scored only eighteen goals. And this weakness was evident again at The Hawthorns, where they dominated possession, possessed over sixty per cent of the ball and had fifteen shots on goal, but never really troubled Ben Foster. However, Villa is still nine points from safety with fifteen games left. Saido Berahino, who scored the winner in the last meeting between the two teams, has been fading of late as he ponders his future with the club, and although he was sent on with half an hour to go in order to invigorate Albion's attack, he and the rest of the team failed to trouble Mark Bunn in the Villa goal. In a game that resembled the previous visit to Southampton, where Albion also had no shot on goal, Albion collected a point, raising Tony Pulis's side to 13th in the table and seven points clear of the relegation zone. “We tried, especially in the second half, but they defended well. Jordan Ayew had a penalty in the first half. If we had been in a different situation, we might have been satisfied with a draw, but we needed more.” Tony Pulis, West Brom coach, said: “It was a match that had to be won by hard work and perseverance. Yes, perhaps. Our players have the right attitude, but sometimes the talent and quality to score goals. We were the usual derby match: fierce, hard-fought, with a lot of effort and determination. The two teams are now going to turn their attention to the FA Cup, with the Baggies hosting League One Peterborough United on Saturday, and Villa hosting Manchester City the following weekend. We played eight games in four weeks, and however disappointed we are, our effort and determination were top drawer. Even without the penalty, we created many opportunities, and with a bit more accuracy, we could have scored. I do not think it was a penalty for Villa. Jonas Olsson might have pushed him, but the ball was rolling, and the boy went down all too easily. We needed every point to stay in the top division, and we did.

text: The chief executive of tech support firm Zendesk has become the latest high-profile figure to have his Twitter account hacked. The Twitter account of Mikkel Svane was hijacked, with its profile picture replaced by a cartoon image. This incident mirrors recent attacks on accounts belonging to notable figures such as Facebook's Mark Zuckerberg, musicians Keith Richards, Katy Perry, and Bon Iver, as well as model Kylie Jenner. All these breaches have occurred in the past two weeks.Zendesk, the company co-founded by Svane, has downplayed the significance of the breach. This was an isolated incident that affected a personal Twitter account, stated a company spokeswoman. No Zendesk systems or accounts were accessed. We were able to quickly identify and secure the impacted account.Based in San Francisco, Zendesk specializes in providing software for managing customer relations via phone and email. The company asserts that it employs the most stringent security measures. Despite the absence of evidence suggesting that the Twitter hack compromised any other data, the incident is potentially embarrassing for Zendesk. The firm counts the NHS, L'Oreal, and Vodafone among its clients. Notably, Zendesk was also hacked in 2013, resulting in the exposure of some customers' email addresses and other data.The compromised account of Mr. Svane was restored within 30 minutes after the BBC alerted the company to the breach. Meanwhile, Twitter has advised users to enhance their security practices. A spokesman for Twitter remarked, A number of other online services have seen millions of passwords stolen in the past several weeks. We recommend people use a unique, strong password for Twitter. We detail other steps people can take to keep their accounts secure on our help centre.Recent days have seen other prominent accounts fall victim to similar attacks. Some security experts speculate that these breaches may be linked to a recent release of LinkedIn login details from a 2012 breach. Hackers could be cross-referencing these credentials with other social media platforms to find working combinations. Many of us think this shows how infrequently people change their passwords and also the degree of password re-use that goes on, commented Professor Alan Woodward from the University of Surrey.Last year, Twitter introduced two-stage authentication, requiring users to enter a code sent to their phone in addition to their password when logging in. However, many users have been reluctant to adopt this additional security step. There's not much more Twitter can do, said Professor Woodward. This will continue to be an issue until we do away with passwords, which isn't going to happen soon.

text: Nine landless farmers in Paraguay have been charged with murder after six police officers died during clashes in eastern Canindeyu province. On Friday, a tragic clash erupted when six police officers were killed during an attempt to evict around 100 farming families who had occupied land three weeks prior. In the violent confrontation, at least nine farmers also lost their lives. Initially, the police reported seven officer fatalities.In response to the chaos, President Fernando Lugo has deployed the army to the area to restore order. While territorial disputes are not uncommon in Paraguay, this incident marks the most violent in decades. One officer remains in critical condition following the skirmish.Family members of the landless farmers claim to have discovered two additional bodies at the scene, potentially raising the civilian death toll to 11, though this has yet to be officially confirmed.Authorities have arrested nine suspects, including a 15-year-old boy, who are facing charges of murder, attempted murder, and criminal association. Some of the detainees are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained during the eviction attempt.The confrontation began in the early hours of Friday when police attempted to reclaim private land occupied by over 100 farmers. According to police official Walter Gomez, the officers were caught off guard by an ambush in a wooded area. They had anticipated a peaceful eviction and were unprepared for the assault with high-calibre weapons. Tragically, among those killed was Erven Lovera, the chief of the Police Special Operations Force.Jose Rodriguez, a leader of the farmers, stated on Paraguayan radio that the deceased were humble farmers, members of the landless movement, who'd decided to stay and resist. The farmers argue that the land was illegally seized during the 1954-1989 military regime of Gen Alfredo Stroessner and distributed among his allies. The Paraguayan Truth Commission reports that 6.75 million hectares were transferred under irregular circumstances during this period, with nearly 20% of Paraguayan land considered ill-gotten gains.In the aftermath of the incident, Interior Minister Carlos Filizzola and Chief of Police Paulino Rojas have been replaced. The newly appointed Interior Minister, Ruben Candia, has announced that evictions will proceed with the full backing of the law.

text: The SNP won every seat in Tayside on the way to a Scotland-wide landslide in the general election. The Scottish National Party (SNP) achieved a remarkable victory in Dundee, capturing Dundee West from Labour and retaining Dundee East, solidifying their complete control over the city. This triumph extends their hold, as they already commanded both Holyrood seats and the local council. The SNP further cemented its dominance by holding onto Angus and Perth and North Perthshire, while also seizing Ochil and South Perthshire, Falkirk, and Stirling from Labour. The election results marked a disastrous evening for Labour, with Chris Law of the SNP overturning a Labour majority exceeding 7,000 votes in Dundee West. Law secured an impressive 61.9% of the vote, defeating Labour’s Michael Marra by over 17,000 votes. In Dundee East, Stewart Hosie, the SNP's deputy leader, saw his majority skyrocket from 1,800 to more than 19,000 votes, capturing 59.7% of the total votes.In Angus, SNP candidate Mike Weir increased his majority, garnering 54% of the vote and nearly doubling the count of his closest competitor, Conservative Derek Wann. Weir expressed gratitude to the Angus electorate for putting their trust in me and the SNP.Meanwhile, Pete Wishart, previously the SNP's chief whip at Westminster, secured more than half the votes in Perth and North Perthshire, finishing nearly 10,000 votes ahead of Conservative Alexander Stewart. Wishart described the event as a fantastic night, noting he would not be so lonely any more at Westminster.Tasmina Ahmed-Sheikh claimed Ochil and South Perthshire for the SNP, ousting Labour’s Gordon Banks by over 10,000 votes. Similarly, Steven Paterson captured Stirling from Labour, prevailing by a five-figure margin and finishing 10,000 votes ahead of Labour candidate and city council leader Johanna Boyd.The SNP's victory in Falkirk was even more pronounced, with John McNally outpacing Labour's Karen Whitefield by 19,701 votes. This was a significant shift from the previous representative, Eric Joyce, who had secured a majority of 7,843 in 2010.

text: England need to work on how they play spin bowling after their tour of India ended in a crushing Twenty20 defeat, says head coach Trevor Bayliss. In a dramatic collapse, England lost eight wickets for just eight runs in a span of 19 balls, succumbing to a 75-run defeat against India in Bangalore. Spinner Yuzvendra Chahal was the star, claiming six wickets for 25 runs in his four-over spell. This loss resulted in a 2-1 T20 series defeat for England, who also faced setbacks in the Test and one-day series during their tour.We're certainly not world-class players of spin, admitted England coach Trevor Bayliss. He acknowledged the challenge of facing skilled spinners, saying, We're playing against players that are very good players of spin, and they've got very good spinners themselves. When you don't grow up on it, as players here do, it is difficult. It's a learning process.Throughout their tour of India, England lost 86 wickets to spin across all formats, echoing similar struggles they faced during their previous visit to Bangladesh. On Wednesday, while chasing a target of 203, England remained competitive until the halfway mark. However, after Chahal dismissed both captain Eoin Morgan and vice-captain Joe Root, the team crumbled.Reflecting on the series, Bayliss expressed disappointment, stating, It is a little bit disappointing the way we finished our series. It doesn't reflect the type of cricket we have played over here. But it's what can happen in a T20 match when you're chasing a big total.Morgan shared his frustration, saying, Everybody is gutted. Today was a big game for us. There was a series on the line and we wanted to produce a good performance but in fact we have produced one of our worst in a long time. If we can take anything from it, it is that it is the first time it has happened in two and a half years.During the tour, England managed to secure only three wins out of 13 matches, including one ODI, one T20, and a tour match against India A. Despite the disappointing results, they showcased their best cricket in the limited-overs series, consistently scoring over 300 in the ODIs and showing improved bowling in the T20s.Bayliss commented, The results haven't gone the way we'd have liked. We've played some pretty good cricket here at times. We've still got a lot of work to do - the boys have been very honest about where they stand. We've got to put together a batting and a bowling performance in one game - we seem to bat well in some games, and bowl well in others.Morgan noted the narrow margins in the one-day series, saying, There hasn't been a lot between the sides, particularly in the one-day series. There was 15-20 runs between the winning and losing of the series. The improvements we have shown since then have been considerable in our bowling department. When you are going well you have to take advantage of it. But we are really strong at the moment. Home advantage is huge, around the world. We have pushed India right to the cusp in both [limited-overs] series.Following the 4-0 Test series defeat in India, former captain Alastair Cook expressed doubts about his future role, suggesting Joe Root was ready to take over. Australian coach Bayliss mentioned he had not spoken to Cook since his departure but planned to reach out soon. I'm heading home to Australia for a little while in the next day or so, Bayliss said. I'll put the feet up for a little bit and I'm sure I'll speak to him at some stage. I'll give it a couple of days - I'm sure we'll exchange a text message or something. As I said to him when he left, and there was a lot of speculation, it is totally up to him. He will know if it's time to step down. I'm happy either way, whether he stays or goes. There is plenty of time.

text: Nigeria's central bank governor Lamido Sanusi has been suspended by the president for financial recklessness and misconduct. Lamido Sanusi's explosive allegations have sent shockwaves through Nigeria, as he claims that a staggering $20 billion in oil revenue has vanished. This bold assertion has been met with firm denial from Nigeria's state oil firm, which labels the accusation as unsubstantiated. Sanusi, who has been at the helm of Nigeria's central bank since 2009 and was hailed as the central bank governor of the year in 2010 by Banker magazine, is a respected figure, especially for his banking sector reforms.Reporting from Lagos, Will Ross of BBC News suggests that Sanusi's allegations could potentially expose significant fraud within Nigeria's notoriously opaque oil industry. Over a 19-month span, Sanusi claims that more than $1 billion went unaccounted for each month, a revelation that comes as Nigeria braces for upcoming elections. This development has put President Goodluck Jonathan and his administration under intense scrutiny, with some of his senior officials facing uncomfortable questions.Critics of Sanusi speculate about his political motives, questioning whether he is leveraging his position to undermine President Jonathan's 2015 re-election bid. However, to many Nigerians, it appears that the president has chosen to suspend a whistleblower rather than address the underlying fraud.In Nigeria, efforts to combat corruption often stall. A notable example is the 2007 suspension of Nuhu Ribadu, head of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission. As the local pidgin saying goes, To fight corruption. No be easy job o. Sanusi, determined to maintain the central bank's autonomy, has vowed to challenge his suspension.The suspension has caused significant market disruption, halting trading in foreign exchange, bonds, and money markets, according to Reuters. Will Ross notes that Sanusi's allegations strike at the core of vested interests in Nigeria's oil sector, one of the world's largest producers. Sanusi himself acknowledged the risks, telling the BBC's Focus on Africa, The reality is anyone who challenges the oil sector is striking at the heart of the vested interests that control the Nigerian state and one should be ready for the consequences.This controversy unfolds as the ruling party debates whether President Jonathan should run in the next elections. Earlier this month, Sanusi informed a senate committee that $20 billion of the $67 billion in oil sold between January 2012 and July 2013 was unaccounted for. The Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation dismissed these claims, suggesting a lack of understanding of the oil industry's complexities.Currently, Sanusi is in Niger for a meeting with top officials, from which he has now departed. His deputy, Sarah Alade, who accompanied him, will assume his responsibilities until a new governor is appointed. Sources informed the BBC Hausa service that President Jonathan had requested Sanusi's resignation in December, but Sanusi refused. The president lacks the authority to dismiss the central bank governor; only the National Assembly can do so.Although Sanusi's term was set to conclude in June, his suspension is seen as a significant move. The presidential statement regarding his suspension cited investigations into breaches of enabling laws, due process and mandate of the Central Bank of Nigeria, accusing his tenure of financial recklessness and misconduct alongside far-reaching irregularities.While some question Sanusi's intent to damage President Jonathan's re-election prospects, many Nigerians perceive the president's actions as prioritizing the suspension of a whistleblower over tackling corruption, according to our correspondent.

Reporting from Lagos, Will Ross, the BBC correspondent, said that the shocking allegations of Sanusi may open up a significant fraud in the notoriously opaque oil industry. In Nigeria, the war against corruption often stalls. Over a period of 19 months, Sanusi says that every month more than a billion dollars went unaccounted for, which comes just as the country is getting ready for elections, and which has put President Goodluck Jonathan and his administration under intense scrutiny, with some of his senior officials facing uncomfortable questions. Critics of Sanusi, however, suspect his motives and wonder if he is sabotaging the re-election of President Goodluck Jonathan. Sanusi, resolute on retaining the central bank’s autonomy, has vowed to challenge his suspension. The suspension has already caused a significant upheaval in the financial markets, halting trading in the foreign exchange, bond, and money markets, according to Reuters. As the popular pidgin saying goes, “To fight corruption, no be easy job o!” The controversy comes as the ruling party debates whether to run President Jonathan again. Last month, Sanusi told a Senate panel that $20 billion of the $67 billion in oil sales between January 2012 and July 2013 were unaccounted for. Sanusi himself acknowledged the risks: “The reality is that anyone who challenges the oil sector is hitting at the heart of the vested interests that control the state, and one should be ready for the consequences.” Sanusi is presently in Niger for a meeting with top government officials from which he has just left. He will be succeeded by his deputy, Sarah Alade, who accompanied him, until a new governor is appointed. It is reported that President Goodluck Jonathan asked for his resignation in December but he refused. The NNPC, the state-owned oil company, rejected the claim, saying it had no idea what the oil business was all about. Although Sanusi's term was due to expire in June, it is considered a significant move, as a presidential statement cited alleged breaches of enabling laws, due process and mandate of the Central Bank of Nigeria, accusing his reign of financial recklessness and misconduct. According to our correspondent, although the president lacks the power to dismiss the governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria, only the National Assembly has the power to dismiss the governor.

text: Rail passengers have been speaking of their frustration after overrunning engineering works saw services thrown into chaos. Throughout much of the day, train services were disrupted between Paddington in west London and Reading, severely impacting routes to the west country and Wales. At Kings Cross, a major hub for travel to northern and eastern England and Scotland, all services were canceled, leading to long queues at Finsbury Park station as passengers awaited trains heading to Peterborough and beyond.The 12:15 train from Peterborough to Edinburgh, which finally departed at 13:05, was overcrowded. An elderly German couple expressed disbelief at the situation, noting, No chance of getting to the buffet car and when we finally could, it has been closed since Newcastle. They only managed to find seats starting from Doncaster and York, while others remained standing in doorways. The couple lamented the lack of information from seemingly leaderless staff, suggesting that management was absent, perhaps still on holiday. They described waiting an hour in the freezing cold at Peterborough station, where there were insufficient waiting rooms, and noted the train's delay of nearly an hour upon arrival in Edinburgh. Despite the chaos, the atmosphere on the train was friendly, with passengers helping each other with bags and offering seats to those in greater need.A passenger who boarded at Finsbury Park shared that those joining at Peterborough had been misinformed about seat availability. Most of us had been waiting on platforms for more than an hour without adequate information, they said, adding that staff presence was minimal. The passenger had arrived at Finsbury Park at 09:50, only to be informed that no train would depart until 11:00, with no East Coast staff available to provide guidance. The website was outdated, leading to more passengers arriving uninformed. Eventually, they left at around 11:20 without knowing the train's destination.This traveler had planned to visit a friend in Bradford and then continue to Liverpool to see friends after over a year, but the chaos at Finsbury Park thwarted these plans. The station was packed, with passengers struggling to navigate a steep spiral staircase from the Tube platform to the train platforms. At the top, a tunnel was crammed with passengers, including elderly individuals, young children, and crying babies, all with luggage and prams. With no guidance available, the situation grew increasingly chaotic, causing anxiety among travelers.Rail staff pushed through the crowded tunnel, but their responses were often rude and unhelpful. The traveler, standing in the cold, tried to determine if any trains would get them close to Leeds or Bradford. Overhearing that a train to Peterborough was an option, they watched the screen, only for the train never to appear. Exhausted and cold, they decided to abandon their plans and return to Reading. Exiting Finsbury Park, they encountered a massive crowd outside, forcing them to navigate back to the Tube entrance and cross the city to Waterloo to catch a train back to Reading.Reflecting on the experience, the traveler expressed disbelief at having to abandon long-anticipated plans, feeling exhausted and too anxious to consider traveling again the next day.

text: An outspoken member of South Africa's African National Congress (ANC) party has been charged with ill-discipline for speaking out against President Jacob Zuma. MP Makhosi Khoza has been vocal in her calls for President Jacob Zuma to step down, labeling him a disgrace just last week. Her outspoken stance has led to death threats urging her to cease advocating for a secret ballot in the upcoming parliamentary vote on Zuma's leadership. In response, both Parliament and the police have decided to provide her with security.The African National Congress (ANC) has reacted strongly, claiming Khoza has overstepped boundaries and must face disciplinary action for her criticism of the president. The ANC in KwaZulu-Natal, her home province, described her remarks as a blatant betrayal of the core values of the party. Known for her critique of corruption within the ANC, Khoza, 47, continues to challenge the status quo.President Zuma, who has consistently denied numerous corruption allegations, is set to face a no-confidence vote in the National Assembly on August 8. According to Milton Nkosi of BBC News in Johannesburg, charging Khoza with ill-discipline exemplifies the ANC's self-destructive tendencies, especially after its poor showing in last year's local elections. Despite promises to self-correct, the party seems to be exacerbating its issues, potentially harming its prospects for the 2019 general elections.Khoza, a PhD holder and one of the most popular MPs among the over 200 in the National Assembly, is being reprimanded for her willingness to speak truth to power. This scenario echoes Nelson Mandela's warning about the ANC's potential for impunity, urging South Africans to hold the party accountable as they did the apartheid government.The ANC appears to be on a reckless path, risking voter backlash in the upcoming elections. Just last week, Khoza received a death threat, warning her that she had 21 days left to live. She made her critical comments about Zuma during a ceremony on July 18, commemorating Nelson Mandela's birthday, where she addressed civil society groups, unions, and business leaders advocating for Zuma's ouster in the no-confidence vote.There is no evidence linking Zuma to these threats. He has previously survived several no-confidence votes. In June, the constitutional court affirmed Parliament's right to conduct a secret ballot, though the speaker has yet to decide on this matter. As Zuma prepares to step down as ANC president in December, his successor will lead the party into the 2019 elections.

text: A rugby fan was nearly six times over the drink-drive limit after downing a bottle of vodka in the NekNominate craze, a Cardiff inquest has heard. Stephen Brookes, 29, from Rumney, tragically passed away after participating in an online drinking challenge, where a friend filmed him consuming three-quarters of a 75cl vodka bottle. He had been nominated by a friend to complete this dangerous task for Facebook. The coroner concluded that his death was due to acute alcohol poisoning combined with cocaine use.During the inquest, it was revealed that Mr. Brookes had been drinking earlier on Sunday, February 9, after watching the Six Nations rugby match between Wales and Ireland. However, his friends dared him to down the vodka. Before attempting the stunt, laborer Mr. Brookes reassured them that he would be OK. Yet, within minutes, he collapsed and lost consciousness. Though his friends took him home, he was later discovered dead.His cousin, Jodie Cummings, informed South Wales Police, Stephen had been watching a rugby match with friends at a house. He had taken a 75cl bottle of vodka. A few weeks ago, he had been NekNominated. This involves someone nominating a friend to down a drink, like a bottle or a pint. After midnight, while I was in the bathroom, Stephen downed the bottle of vodka. It was filmed, and I saw it on a friend's phone. I watched him neck back the bottle of vodka, holding it in the air. Afterward, he seemed in good spirits and said, 'you know me.' He was dancing around, but 10 minutes later, he lost his balance and started slurring his words—it all happened so quickly.Friends recounted to police that people were urging him to drink the vodka around 1:30 AM, the day after the rugby match. Another friend, Shaun Chivers, described how the vodka disappeared within seconds during the party near Brookes' home. I saw Stephen had three-quarters of the bottle left, and I knew he was going to neck it, Chivers said, advising his friend to stop messing around. He continued, The next thing, he necked the bottle, and it was gone in seconds. Soon after, he was swaying all over the place.Mr. Brookes died within an hour of the NekNominate challenge. Post-mortem results showed he had 458 milliliters of alcohol in his blood, far exceeding the legal drink-drive limit of 80. Additionally, he had consumed a significant amount of cocaine, estimated between 10 and 20 lines. Pathologist Thomas Hockey confirmed that Brookes was well over the fatal range for alcohol.

text: After months of sotto voce claims that some businesses were simply too scared to put their head above the independence parapet, tonight comes the most significant move by anti-independence members of the UK business community ahead of the September vote. A collective of 133 globally-involved businesses has issued a letter warning that the uncertainty surrounding a Yes vote for Scottish independence could be detrimental to business. The signatories represent a diverse range of sectors, including banking, mining, engineering, food, whisky, and technology, with a mix of both familiar and new voices joining the conversation against independence.Notable figures endorsing the letter include Douglas Flint, chairman of HSBC; Andrew Mackenzie, CEO of BHP Billiton; and Sir John Grant, executive vice president of policy at BG Group. Other prominent supporters are Audrey Baxter, executive chairman of Baxters Food Group; Simon Thomson, CEO of Cairn Energy; and Ian Curle, CEO of Edrington, the company behind whisky brands The Macallan and The Famous Grouse. This letter is set to appear in Wednesday's edition of The Scotsman.Keith Cochrane, CEO of Weir Group, orchestrated this initiative, having previously expressed concerns about the substantial risks of Scottish independence. The organizers emphasize that no political groups were involved in compiling the list, which emerged from a shared frustration over the perceived lack of a unified business stance on independence.The signatories are responsible for approximately 50,000 jobs in Scotland, ranging from large entities like Babcock shipbuilding to smaller engineering firms in Glasgow's east end. Meanwhile, advocates for an independent Scotland highlight their own influential supporters from the business and economic sectors.Sir George Mathewson, former chairman of The Royal Bank of Scotland, argues that Scotland's financial services sector would thrive post-independence, drawing parallels with Switzerland and Singapore, both of which host top global financial centers despite their smaller size. Investment is increasingly global, reliant more on talent than borders, he asserts.Economist Sir Donald MacKay, former head of Scottish Enterprise, believes an independent Scotland could possess a stronger fiscal position than the current UK, suggesting that financial advantages should be used to bolster the economy through industrial and manufacturing development.Jim McColl, one of Scotland's wealthiest individuals and head of Clyde Blowers Capital, has expressed such enthusiasm for independence that he would consider relocating from Monaco to Scotland if a Yes vote prevails. Willie Walsh, CEO of IAG, owner of British Airways, also suggests that independence might benefit Scotland.As the debate intensifies, more names may emerge this week. Both sides agree that the ultimate decision lies with the voters. This letter aims to clarify the concerns businesses have about a potential Yes vote, focusing on five main issues: currency, Scotland's EU relationship, potential tax and regulatory changes, pensions, and the impact on exports.The letter emphasizes the stakes: Our economic ties within the United Kingdom are very close and support more than a million Scottish jobs. As job creators, we have carefully evaluated the arguments from both sides. Our conclusion is that the business case for independence has not been made.This initiative is not a new campaign against independence but a standalone statement, coinciding with an upcoming CBI dinner in Glasgow. There, Sir Mike Rake, president of the CBI and chairman of BT Group, is expected to echo similar anti-independence sentiments.In response, Business for Scotland issued a statement highlighting its 2,500 members who believe independence is in Scotland's best business interests. Our stance is based on a thorough analysis of facts and figures, recognizing that independence aligns with our best interests, they assert.Ultimately, it will be up to Scottish voters to weigh the arguments presented by both sides in this pivotal debate.

text: A tipper truck which killed four people when its brakes failed had clocked up almost 450,000 miles (724,000km), the driver's trial has heard. In February 2015, a tragic crash in Bath claimed the lives of four-year-old Mitzi Steady, Robert Parker, 59, Philip Allen, 52, and Stephen Vaughan, 34. Bristol Crown Court was told that the truck involved was essentially an accident waiting to happen.The driver, Phillip Potter, 20, has pled not guilty to charges of causing death by dangerous and careless driving. His employer, Matthew Gordon, faces 14 charges, while Peter Wood, the truck company's mechanic, contests four charges.On February 9, Mr. Potter and Mr. Gordon were transporting 30-tonne loads from a quarry in Wiltshire. Mr. Gordon, leading in his truck, halted on Lansdown Lane in the village of Weston. However, Mr. Potter's brakes failed, forcing him to swerve to avoid a crash, the court was informed.The truck struck several pedestrians, including Mitzi and her grandmother, Margaret Rogers. It also collided with a car carrying Mr. Allen and Mr. Vaughan from Swansea, along with Mr. Parker from Cwmbran, south Wales.Prosecutor Adam Vaitilingam QC described the scene: (Mr Potter's) lorry continued to career down Lansdown Lane out of control. It caused absolute devastation. By the time it finally came to a stop, four people had suffered fatal injuries - a four-year-old girl who had been crossing the road with her grandmother and three men who had been traveling together in the same car.Mr. Vaitilingam characterized Mr. Potter as an inexperienced driver who had only been in the company for a matter of days. He criticized Mr. Gordon's firm, Grittenham Haulage Limited, established in December 2013, as being a shambles from start to finish, lacking a transport manager at the time of the crash.The firm neglected to perform the recommended brake efficiency tests on the vehicle, which Mr. Vaitilingam deemed an accident waiting to happen. Mechanic Peter Wood was tasked with inspecting the trucks, and the last safety check was conducted in January 2015, just weeks before the crash, where he declared the vehicle safe.Mr. Vaitilingam argued, If Mr. Wood did carry out a safety inspection that day, it was wholly inadequate. On the date of the crash, the lorry had serious and longstanding defects with its braking system, meaning that it was and had been for some time in a dangerous condition. This sort of catastrophic brake failure doesn't just happen through bad luck.Mr. Potter, from Dauntsey, Wiltshire, also faces charges of causing serious injuries to Karla Brennan and Margaret Rogers by dangerous driving, denying a total of 10 charges. Mr. Gordon, 30, also from Dauntsey, denies 14 charges, while Mr. Wood, 55, from Brinkworth, Wiltshire, denies four charges. The trial is ongoing.
