text: Great Britain will have a team of 264 athletes competing at the Rio Paralympics in 19 sports. The British Paralympic team has consistently ranked within the top five in the medal table. At the London 2012 Games, they secured 120 medals, including 34 golds, placing third behind China and Russia. Expectations are high for surpassing this achievement in Brazil. Here is the list of athletes selected by the British Paralympic Association.For archery, John Cavanagh and John Stubbs, both previous gold medallists, lead the team. Cavanagh, participating in his fifth Games, clinched gold in Athens, while Stubbs won on his debut in Beijing. Newcomers include Jo Frith, who transitioned from swimming to archery, 16-year-old Jess Stretton, and Invictus Games veteran Mikey Hall. The competition will take place from September 10-17 at the Sambodromo.In athletics, gold medallists David Weir, Richard Whitehead, Aled Davies, and Hannah Cockroft are among 13 track and field athletes selected for Rio. All excelled at the IPC Athletics World Championships in Doha. The team features Libby Clegg, who broke the 200m world record in the T11 class, and Jonnie Peacock, defending his T44 100m title. The events will occur from September 8-18 at the Olympic Stadium.The GB boccia squad, competing from September 10-16 at Carioca Arena 2, includes David Smith, Stephen McGuire, and Nigel Murray. McGuire is the world individual champion in the BC4 classification, while Smith and Murray won team gold in Beijing 2008.Canoeing makes its Paralympic debut in Rio, with Great Britain and Australia fielding full teams. Anne Dickins and Emma Wiggs, both world champions, lead the squad. Wiggs previously played sitting volleyball at London 2012, and Nick Beighton competed in rowing. Jeanette Chippington will participate in her sixth Games after a successful swimming career. Events are scheduled for September 14-15 at Lagoa Rodrigo de Freitas.The British Para-cycling team, successful on track and road, aims to continue their dominance. Dame Sarah Storey, a four-time gold medallist in London, is set for her seventh Games. Medal winners Neil Fachie, Karen Darke, Jody Cundy, Helen Scott, and Jon-Allan Butterworth also join the team, alongside Kadeena Cox, competing in both cycling and athletics. The competitions are from September 8-11 (track) and September 14-17 (road) at the Rio Olympic Velodrome and Pontal.The equestrian team, featuring riders with a combined 30 Paralympic medals, includes Lee Pearson, aiming to add to his 10 golds, and Sophie Christiansen, defending her London titles. Sophie Wells and Natasha Baker return, joined by Anne Dunham, competing in her fifth Games at 67. Events will be held from September 11-16 at the Olympic Equestrian Centre.In football, most of the squad will debut, with Michael Barker and Jonathan Paterson returning for their third Games. Captained by Jack Rutter, the team comprises players from England, Scotland, and Northern Ireland, having competed internationally. Matches are from September 8-16 at Deodoro Stadium.The judo team, the first full GB squad named for Rio, includes London silver medallist Sam Ingram and newcomers Jonathan Drane, Chris Skelley, and Jack Hodgson. Competitions run from September 8-10 at Carioca Arena 3.Ali Jawad leads the powerlifting team, seeking redemption after missing a medal in London. Natalie Blake, Zoe Newson, and newcomer Micky Yule, a former Royal Engineers staff sergeant, complete the team. Events are from September 8-14 at Riocentro Pavilion 2.Rowing sees gold medallists Tom Aggar and Pam Relph head the team. Aggar won in 2008, and Relph returns with new crewmates Dan Brown, Grace Clough, James Fox, and cox Oliver James. Rachel Morris debuts in rowing, while Laurence Whiteley and Lauren Rowles make their first Games appearances. Competitions are from September 9-11 at Lagoa Rodrigo de Freitas.In sailing, defending champion Helena Lucas, the first athlete named for Rio, competes in the 2.4mR category. She joins London bronze medallists Alexandra Rickham and Niki Birrell, with John Robertson, Hannah Stodel, and Stephen Thomas in their fourth Games. Events are from September 12-17 at Marina da Gloria, Guanabara Bay.The shooting team includes Matt Skelhon, a three-time medallist, joined by debutants Issy Bailey, Owen Burke, Lorraine Lambert, and Stewart Nangle. Competitions occur from September 8-14 at the Olympic Shooting Centre.A 30-member swimming team represents GB, including six London gold medallists and 20 with previous Games experience. Abby Kane, turning 13 in August, debuts, while veteran Sascha Kindred attends his sixth Games. Events take place from September 8-17 at the Olympic Aquatics Centre.In table tennis, world number ones Will Bayley and Rob Davies lead the 12-strong team. Sue Gilroy competes in her fifth Games, with Jack Hunter-Spivey making his debut. Matches are from September 8-17 at Riocentro Pavilion 3.The triathlon team, the largest with 11 athletes and two guides, includes reigning world champion Lauren Steadman, Andy Lewis, and Alison Patrick. Events are from September 10-11 at Fort Copacabana.Both the GB men's and women's wheelchair basketball teams compete in Rio. The men's team, three-time European champions, aim to improve on their fourth-place finish from London. Gregg Warburton debuts, while Simon Munn and Terry Bywater bring extensive experience. The women's team, with an average age of 22.5, includes Clare Griffiths in her fifth Games. Matches are from September 8-16 (women) and September 8-17 (men) at the Rio Olympic Arena and Carioca Arena 1.Fencers Dimitri Coutya and Piers Gilliver, silver medallists at the 2015 World Championships, make their Paralympic debuts. Competitions are from September 12-16 at Youth Arena.Finally, the wheelchair rugby squad, including Alan Ash in his fifth Games and Coral Batey, aims for their first medal. Jonathan Coggan, Bulbul Hussain, Mike Kerr, and Mandip Sehmi bring previous experience. Matches are from September 14-17 at Carioca Arena 1.In wheelchair tennis, London medallists Jordanne Whiley, Lucy Shuker, and Andy Lapthorne lead the team. Whiley and Shuker won doubles bronze in London, and Lapthorne won quad doubles silver. Alfie Hewett and Antony Cotterill debut. Matches are from September 9-16 at the Olympic Tennis Centre.

text: California regulators have accepted an offer from farmers to reduce their water usage by 25% in an effort to combat the record four-year drought. In a historic move, hundreds of California farmers have agreed to reduce their water usage after facing threats of water rights cuts from state officials. This decision emerges as California grapples with a severe drought, prompting the state to mandate a 25% water usage reduction in urban areas. Critics, however, argue that Governor Jerry Brown has not adequately addressed the water consumption of influential agricultural water rights holders.The recent agreement between the California Water Resources Control Board and these farmers, who had previously resisted such commitments, underscores the escalating severity of the drought. According to the US Drought Monitor, 94% of California is experiencing severe drought conditions or worse, with agriculture consuming 80% of the state’s water resources.This landmark agreement, the first in over three decades, involves farmers in the Sacramento and San Joaquin river delta. Senior rights holders, including irrigation districts, hydropower utilities, and cities like San Francisco, are also part of this category. Meanwhile, thousands of junior water rights holders—those whose claims date back to 1914 or later—have already faced water use restrictions this year, primarily affecting farmers without federal irrigation deliveries.Under California's water rights system, junior holders must cease diverting water from rivers and streams to ensure that senior rights holders' demands are met. On Thursday, approximately 350 farmers convened to discuss strategies to prevent more severe mandatory cuts to their water allocations.Michael George, the state's water master for the delta, remarked, That doesn't necessarily mean they'll all participate in the voluntary 25% reduction. However, he expressed optimism that many would comply.The farming industry has recently faced criticism from residents who have been forced to reduce their water usage under threat of significant fines. The agreement grants farmers until June 1 to submit plans detailing how they will achieve the proposed reductions.

text: Jacob Boehme remembers when he knew something was seriously wrong. In 1998, Boehme grappled with a persistent cold that wouldn't go away. An Aboriginal elder, in a healing ceremony, sat him between her legs, singing over him. She wiped sweat from his armpits, applying it to his head and neck. Eventually, she advised, “Ahh, you need to go to a Western doctor. Everything is red. I cannot help you.”Boehme was subsequently diagnosed with HIV. At a time when antiretroviral treatments were just emerging, his doctor was delivering such news for the first time. He was choked up and almost crying, Boehme recalls. I had to console him.Now 43, Boehme not only survives but thrives, channeling his journey as a gay, indigenous, HIV-positive man into a solo performance. Blood on the Dance Floor, recently showcased at the Sydney Festival, delves into the multifaceted significance of blood, from ancestry to health.This work blends storytelling with dance, featuring a comedic portrayal of a camp gay elder in drag, discussions on HIV stigma within the gay community, and scenes where Boehme moves against projections of flowing blood and red cells on the wall.Crucially, Boehme aims to reshape the conversation around what it means to live with HIV. Anything shown in the media or entertainment has always been some kind of memorialisation of the AIDS crisis back in the '80s. Everybody dies, he explains. That's not relevant to me and to many other men and women I know living with HIV. There isn't an image of a healthy functioning person with employment and prospects—you don't see that portrayed anywhere.Boehme also stresses the need to expand our understanding of who is affected by the virus. Data from the University of New South Wales reveals that notification rates for indigenous men with HIV have doubled over the past five years, from 6.2 to 12.4 per 100,000. In contrast, rates for non-indigenous individuals fell by 12%, according to the university's Kirby Institute.Despite these statistics, Boehme notes that education campaigns predominantly target white men. Tell me the last time you saw an HIV education campaign with someone from the Aboriginal, Asian, or African identity on those posters? You just see gay white men in their underwear, he observes. It makes quite a lot of people feel completely dismissed, and it's not just the gay male community—it's heterosexual males living with HIV, kids living with HIV too. text: On 15 November 37 police and crime commissioners will be elected in England, along with four in Wales. In an effort to enhance accountability and community involvement, the newly appointed Police and Crime Commissioners (PCCs) will have the authority to oversee their respective police forces. Their responsibilities include hiring and dismissing the chief constable, setting the budget, and empowering local residents to influence crime-fighting strategies in their areas. In South Yorkshire, the nomination period for candidates has officially concluded. As the region prepares for the upcoming elections, BBC News has evaluated the current state of each police force. South Yorkshire, a county characterized by both urban expanses and areas historically dominated by mining, steelworks, and engineering, faces significant challenges.James Vincent, BBC Yorkshire's Political Reporter, highlights the pressing issue of maintaining public safety amidst a shrinking police force. Although crime rates are reportedly declining, the reduction in police personnel is a concern. A recent council tax increase aims to fund an additional 100 officers, partially offsetting the loss of 400 officers in recent years. However, there is apprehension that South Yorkshire is experiencing an erosion of its resources.In a bid to economize, specialized units such as divers, mounted officers, and firearms teams may soon be shared across Yorkshire. The challenge lies in preserving service quality while cutting costs, a common theme in the public sector. Notably, the force has opted to retain its police helicopter while joining the National Police Air Service, set to begin operations in South Yorkshire by April 2013. While the helicopter remains popular, the financial feasibility of maintaining dual services may be an early decision for the newly elected commissioner.Covering an area of 600 square miles (1,554 sq km), South Yorkshire Police serve both urban centers like Sheffield and rural landscapes. Their priorities include boosting public confidence, ensuring community safety, and addressing serious and organized crime, terrorism, and extremism throughout the county.Currently, the force is under the leadership of Chief Constable David Crompton, supported by a deputy, two assistant chief constables, a finance director, and an assistant chief officer for human resources. The force collaborates closely with the county’s police authority and the Police Federation, representing rank and file officers. Additionally, it is part of the Regional Chief Constables' Group (RCCG) and the Joint Police Authorities Committee (JPAC), which set the principles for local policing in Yorkshire and the Humber.For the fiscal year 2012/2013, the South Yorkshire Police Authority has allocated a budget of £251 million. This figure reflects a 3.95% increase in the police authority council tax precept, translating to an additional £5.22 for the average Band D property compared to the previous year. This budget increase aims to prevent a reduction of 110 police officers in 2012/2013 and to fund 22 police and community support officers (PCSOs) for the next three years. The authority has also pledged to mitigate further planned resource reductions in 2013 and 2014. By raising the council tax precept, the police authority hopes to generate approximately £2 million annually, balancing the need for future cuts from 2013 onward.Statistics from 2010/2011 reveal a 9% overall reduction in crime in South Yorkshire, with burglaries down by 5%, criminal damage decreased by 17%, vehicle crime reduced by 17%, and robbery incidents dropping by 14%.

text: We arrive at the Ebola Treatment Centre in the forested town of Gueckedou in South East Guinea to a grim scene. A tiny bundle, wrapped in white plastic sheeting, is carefully placed by stone-faced men loading yellow disinfectant cans into a pick-up truck. We are about to witness a heart-wrenching task. A short drive into the forest brings us to a small, prepared hole—the final resting place of the latest Ebola victim: a four-month-old baby boy named Faya. He contracted the virus from his mother, who passed away weeks earlier. This marks the 20th anonymous grave in this somber clearing.I was there with him just before he died, recounts Adele Millimouno, a nurse with Medicines Sans Frontieres (MSF) from a nearby village. I had been feeding him milk. I stepped away briefly, but when I returned, he was gone. I was utterly devastated. This is a typical day on the front lines of the current Ebola outbreak. Gueckedou, where the first case was reported in March, remains a focal point.Medical charities tackling what is now the deadliest Ebola outbreak in history anticipate the crisis may persist until year's end. Over 670 people in West Africa have succumbed to Ebola. Nigeria recently became the fourth country to confirm a fatality from the virus. Medicines Sans Frontieres and the International Federation of the Red Cross, with nearly 400 international staff fighting the outbreak, report the situation across West Africa remains out of control.At the MSF-run treatment center in Gueckedou, 152 Ebola patients were treated by July 22, with 111 deaths. Yet, Adele draws strength from the survivors. I gather the courage to work here to help save my community. I am proud of our work; we have saved around 40 people.The following morning, we join health officials on a convoy to Kollobengou, a village 12km away. Previous attempts to enter the village resulted in attacks and warnings not to return. Many people died before my eyes. It was especially hard when young children died. Sometimes I went outside and cried, recalls a health worker.Mistrust ran deep; some believed medics brought the virus and harvested organs from the dead. Others, aware of the virus, were too frightened to seek help. After negotiations with community leaders—and another death overnight—medics are finally allowed in. As we enter, fear is palpable. Residents emerge slowly, gathering in the village center.A local health ministry official coordinating the virus fight encourages residents not to fear and to cooperate with health workers assessing potential cases. Soap and chlorine are distributed, as hygiene is key to killing the virus. However, a resident laments, How can we wash all the time if we have no clean water?Eventually, two families bring forward very ill relatives, who are swiftly taken to the treatment center. Health workers knew of four Ebola deaths in the village; now, three more have emerged. Forty-eight people who had close contact with victims will be monitored daily for the three-week incubation period.In Gueckedou, two villages still resist health workers, an improvement from months ago when 28 villages resisted aid. Yet, concern remains. Tarik Jasarevic from the World Health Organization attributes initial resistance to unclear messaging about the virus. People heard there is no vaccine or treatment for Ebola, so they wondered why go to a treatment center. When some who did go died, it seemed like certain death. We didn't emphasize enough that there are survivors and early treatment increases survival chances.Dr. Abdurahman Batchili, the Ebola outbreak coordinator for Gueckedou, notes improved awareness and fewer daily patient registrations. The population is becoming aware of the outbreak's dangers. We hope, with this momentum, to end the outbreak in one or two months. However, we must remain vigilant, especially along our borders with Sierra Leone and Liberia.In the three days up to July 23, there were 71 new cases in Sierra Leone and 25 in Liberia, compared to 12 in Guinea. Thousands cross the extensive borders shared with Sierra Leone and Liberia weekly, yet Guinea has only 13 Ebola screening posts.Medical charities caution against expecting a swift end to the outbreak. Antoine Gauge, head of the MSF emergency response in Guinea, expresses skepticism about resolving the crisis by year's end. Ebola knows no borders. People travel, with family in Sierra Leone and Liberia. While Guinea is more advanced in its response, we can't guarantee no future cases.Back at the treatment center, 13-year-old Alfonz, an Ebola survivor thanks to early treatment, visits his sister Marian. Separated by an orange plastic barrier, he can only watch as a health worker, clad in a biohazard suit, holds her. Initial tests for Marian are negative, but the virus remains cruel and indiscriminate. Their mother is gravely ill and may not survive. As this crisis continues, such heartbreaking stories will persist.Follow @tulipmazumdar on Twitter.

text: One million people who work in crowded places in the UK are to be trained over the next 12 months in how to deal with a possible terrorist attack. The National Police Chiefs Council is set to unveil a new plan aimed at expanding police terror training and advice dissemination across various sectors. This initiative will build on an existing program that currently trains approximately 100,000 workers annually. The police emphasize the need for everyone to play a part in keeping the public alert.Detective Chief Superintendent Scott Wilson, the national counter-terrorism coordinator, will announce the expansion of Project Griffin. This extension will enable current trainers within companies to impart police training and advice to their colleagues. The focus will be on public limited companies located in bustling city centers, as well as those in the entertainment, sports, and retail industries.We need everyone to play a part in keeping the public alert, not alarmed, reiterated Det Ch Supt Wilson. Project Griffin originated in 2004, launched by the City of London and Metropolitan police forces, to provide guidance and training to managers and security personnel of large organizations on handling security and counter-terrorism challenges. It has since been adopted by other police forces across the UK.Police can help explain what the threats and risks to different sectors are, but companies are better placed to explain to staff exactly what action they can take to enhance their security and how to respond if the worst happens, Det Ch Supt Wilson stated. He further noted that individual organizations have vital protective security information such as building layouts, security equipment, and safety procedures. They have the local knowledge that could be vital to keeping staff and the public safe.BBC security correspondent Frank Gardner highlighted that the need to prepare for potential terror attacks has been a concern for police and intelligence agencies since the 2008 Mumbai attacks. In light of the recent attacks in Brussels and Paris, efforts to prepare workers in high-traffic areas will be massively stepped up, with the goal of briefing one million staff over the next year, according to Gardner.The 2008 Mumbai attacks resulted in 174 fatalities, while the November attacks in Paris claimed 130 lives, and the recent bombings in Brussels killed 32 people. The move comes amid an increase in the number of trained police firearms officers to cope with the possibility that criminals inspired by the so-called Islamic State could open fire in a public place using automatic weapons smuggled in from mainland Europe, Gardner added.

text: A mother who took her toddler son to Syria has been jailed for six years for joining the so-called Islamic State. Tareena Shakil, aged 26, has become the first British woman to return from the self-proclaimed caliphate and face conviction for her actions. During her sentencing, Mr. Justice Inman highlighted her lack of remorse and awareness of her son's future as potentially becoming an IS fighter. He reprimanded Shakil, stating, You allowed him to be photographed next to an AK47.Originally from Birmingham and previously residing in Burton-upon-Trent, Staffordshire, Shakil acknowledged her journey to Syria. However, she denied affiliating with IS or promoting terrorism through her Twitter posts. At Birmingham Crown Court, the judge expressed grave concern over her decision to take her young son to Syria, fully aware of the implications. You embraced your role in providing fighters of the future, he remarked.The judge pointed out the disturbing image of her 14-month-old son wearing an IS-branded balaclava, labeling it one of the case's most abhorrent aspects. Mr. Justice Inman further noted that Shakil had embraced Isis, sending messages upon her arrival in Syria, asserting her intent not to return to the UK and expressing a desire to die as a martyr. Her radicalization was evident, he said, following online interactions with influential members of the terrorist group.Convicted on Friday, Shakil maintained that her October 2014 trip to Syria was an attempt to escape an unhappy family life. She departed from East Midlands Airport to Turkey, under the guise of a family beach holiday, before crossing into Syria. Once there, she claimed dissatisfaction and decided to leave, realizing her mistake. She recounted taking a bus and bribing a taxi driver to aid her escape back to Turkey in January 2015.Shakil received a four-year sentence for IS membership, with an additional two years for encouraging acts of terror, to be served consecutively. Mr. Justice Inman noted she would be eligible for release on license after serving half her sentence. As the sentence was announced, Shakil's family voiced their discontent, calling the proceedings a farce.Following the hearing, the children's charity NSPCC commented, This is a deeply disturbing case which could have resulted in tragedy for the toddler involved.

text: Worcester chief executive Jim O'Toole says giving head coach Carl Hogg sole charge of the first team was necessary because players weren't getting the dual-management structure. Following the departure of former director of rugby Dean Ryan on June 30, Carl Hogg and high-performance director Nick Johnston initially shared responsibilities at the Warriors. However, due to a string of disappointing performances, the club decided to revise its management strategy. Entrusting Carl with sole leadership is the right move for us now, O'Toole told BBC Sport.Reflecting on the changes, O'Toole explained, Dean Ryan's exit in the summer left us without his vast experience and rugby intellect, which was a significant loss just before the season began. Under Dean, Carl was in charge of the first team, while Nick focused on athlete preparation.Initially, the club adopted a dual-management approach, a concept championed by England boss Eddie Jones as common in the southern hemisphere. After six months, we evaluated the system, O'Toole continued. My fellow directors and I concluded that the players were not benefiting from it.Although Nick Johnston will maintain his current role, the decision to streamline management by appointing Carl Hogg as the sole leader aims to provide clarity for the players. Ultimately, players need to understand their purpose here, O'Toole emphasized.The Warriors, plagued by injuries, have managed only two wins in 14 matches this season, securing just one victory and two draws in the Premiership. After a 26-12 home defeat by Wasps on Sunday, they sit 11th in the table, six points ahead of bottom-placed Bristol, whom they will face on Boxing Day.Having faced relegation twice since their initial Premiership appearance in 2004, the team’s current struggles, amplified by numerous injuries, have drawn criticism from discontented fans. In response, O'Toole has organized a meeting with 40 of the club's frequent critics, acknowledging that addressing dissatisfied supporters is a crucial aspect of his role.Modern communication channels are accessible to everyone, he remarked. I engage daily with supporters via Twitter, club forums, email, phone, and text. I've even received Facebook Messenger messages from non-friends eager to share their thoughts on improvements.O'Toole clarified, I didn't join the rugby club to socialize with players. For me, the thrill lies in interacting with a passionate group of supporters and the vibrant environment they create. People are eager to voice their opinions, and I'm here to listen. If they approach me respectfully, I consider their feedback. It's the age-old adage: 'the customer is king'.While acknowledging that fans are sometimes mistaken or overly passionate, O'Toole added, People aren't unpleasant without reason; it's only because they care deeply.

text: The SNP will take control of East Dunbartonshire Council. Following local elections earlier this month, a minority administration has been formed by the party after a council meeting. Previously, Labour and the Conservatives shared a minority administration. Despite the SNP emerging as the largest single party, they hold only seven of the 22 council seats, falling short of a majority. The Conservatives and Liberal Democrats each have six councillors, Labour has two, and there is one independent.While most of Scotland's 32 local authorities have established administrations, a few councils are still in the process of making decisions. On Wednesday evening, Stirling Council endorsed an SNP-Labour coalition, appointing Christine Simpson (Labour) as the new provost and Graham Houston (SNP) as depute convener.West Lothian and Edinburgh councils are scheduled to meet on Thursday, having postponed meetings last week. In West Lothian, a proposed Labour-Conservative coalition was blocked by Labour's Scottish Executive Committee, with Labour expressing intentions to govern as a minority. Meanwhile, Edinburgh Council has yet to finalize any agreements. The SNP, as the largest party, and Labour have both stated they will not form formal alliances with the Conservatives in Edinburgh. Inverclyde Council is also set to convene on Thursday.Across Scotland, councils are generally led by minority administrations from the largest local party or coalitions including them, though notable exceptions exist. In Aberdeen, a coalition between Labour and the Conservatives excludes the SNP, leading to the suspension of Labour councillors for defying the party's Scottish Executive Committee. The SNP is similarly excluded from control in Argyll and Bute, Angus, Moray, and North Lanarkshire. In Dumfries and Galloway and East Renfrewshire, the Conservatives are not part of the administration.In Aberdeen, Labour suspended nine councillors after they formed a coalition with the Conservatives. Aberdeenshire is governed by a coalition of Conservative, Liberal Democrats, and independent councillors. Angus sees administration by Conservatives, Independents, and Liberal Democrats. Argyll and Bute is run by an Independent, Lib Dem, and Conservative coalition.Clackmannanshire's council could not agree on an administration in its first meeting and will reconvene on June 1. Dumfries and Galloway is controlled by a Labour-SNP coalition, sidelining the Conservative group with the most seats. Dundee City will have an SNP administration with an Independent. East Ayrshire and East Dunbartonshire councils are under SNP minority administrations, while East Lothian is led by a Labour minority.In East Renfrewshire, despite the Conservatives winning the most seats, the SNP and Labour will run the council. Edinburgh remains without an agreement, delaying the formation of a new administration by at least a week. Falkirk sees an SNP minority taking control, while Fife has joint leadership shared between SNP and Labour. Glasgow witnesses the end of nearly 40 years of Labour dominance with an SNP minority administration.In the Highlands, 28 independents, 10 Lib Dems, and three Labour members form the administration, keeping out the SNP and Tories. Inverclyde's meeting is set for Thursday, May 25, at 16:00. Midlothian will have a Labour minority administration. In Moray, the Conservative group is teaming up with six independent members.North Ayrshire remains under Labour control despite a surge from the Scottish Conservatives, with the SNP holding an equal number of seats as Labour. North Lanarkshire sees Labour forming a minority administration without a formal coalition with the Tories. Perth and Kinross have a Conservative-led coalition with Lib Dems and independents.Renfrewshire will operate under an SNP minority administration. South Ayrshire's council is governed by a coalition of SNP, Labour, and independent councillors. In the Scottish Borders, a new Conservative-independent coalition has taken control, replacing the previous SNP/Lib Dem/independent administration.South Lanarkshire's SNP minority administration takes charge after Labour members abstained from voting on a Conservative alliance. The SNP is seven seats short of a majority, but other parties might collaborate. Stirling sees an SNP-Labour coalition agreement. West Dunbartonshire will have an SNP-independent administration with the 10 SNP councillors joining one of the two independents. West Lothian has no agreement after Scottish Labour's ruling body advised against a Conservative coalition, with another meeting planned for Thursday.In the Western Isles, Orkney, and Shetland, administrations are predominantly led by independents.

In Argyll and Bute, Angus, Moray and North Lanarkshire the SNP is excluded from power. In Aberdeen a coalition between the Conservatives and the Labour Party excluded the SNP and led to the suspension of nine Labour members for joining the Conservatives against the express wish of the Scottish Labour executive. Dumfries and Galloway has been placed under a Labour-SNP administration which excludes the Conservative group which took the most seats; East Ayrshire and East Dunbartonshire are under an SNP minority administration; East Lothian, a Labour minority administration. In Aberdeen the government is a Conservative-Liberal Democrat-Independent coalition; in Angus, a Conservative-Liberal Democrat-Independent administration; in Argyll and Bute, a Conservative-Liberal -Independent administration. In Dundee, the SNP and one independent form a control of the administration. In Falkirk, where the SNP formed a minority administration, Labour’s forty-year rule came to an end and the SNP won by a landslide. In the Highlands, 28 independents, 10 Liberal Democrats and three Labour members form the administration and exclude the SNP and Conservatives. North Ayrshire, despite a swing towards the Conservatives and a parity of seats with the Scottish Nationalists, is to remain under the control of the Labour Party. In Glasgow, which has been under the dominion of the Labour Party for forty years, an SNP minority has just taken office. In Edinburgh, where the new government will not be formed for at least a week, no one can agree. The meeting of the Inverclyde Council has been fixed for 3 p.m. on Thursday, May 25. In Midlothian, Labour will be in a minority. The Conservatives of North Lanarkshire will rule, but not as a formal coalition with the Conservatives. The new SNP government in South Lanarkshire is in charge after the Labourites rejected the Conservative alliance. In South Ayrshire, the Council is governed by a coalition of SNP, Conservatives and Independents. In the Western Isles, Orkney and Shetland, the administrations will be led by independents. In West Dunbartonshire there will be an SNP-Independent administration with the ten SNP councillors joining one of the two independents. In the Scottish Borders, a new Conservative-Independent administration has taken over from the former SNP-Liberal Democrat coalition. Another meeting is scheduled for Thursday. In West Lothian, where the Scottish Labour party's ruling council has recommended against a Conservative-SNP alliance, no decision has yet been reached.

text: Afghanistan's two presidential election candidates have agreed to an audit in an attempt to resolve a dispute over the result of last month's vote, US Secretary of State John Kerry has said. In a significant development, both Abdullah Abdullah and Ashraf Ghani have committed to respecting the outcome of Afghanistan's electoral process. U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry announced that a comprehensive review of all eight million ballots would commence within 24 hours.Preliminary figures indicate a victory for Mr. Ghani, yet both candidates have leveled allegations of electoral fraud against each other. Official results from Afghanistan's election authorities reveal that in the June 14 run-off, Mr. Ghani secured 56.44% of the vote, while Mr. Abdullah received 43.45%. This outcome starkly contrasts with the first round in April, where Mr. Ghani trailed significantly.Outgoing President Hamid Karzai, who assumed office following the U.S.-led removal of the Taliban, has endorsed the audit and agreed to postpone the inauguration of his successor to accommodate the review, anticipated to last several weeks.During a press conference alongside the candidates, Mr. Kerry emphasized the thoroughness of the process, stating, Every single ballot will be audited. He praised the candidates' commitment to restoring legitimacy to Afghan democracy. Initially, ballots in Kabul will be scrutinized, with the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) tasked with transporting the remaining ballots from the provinces.The agreement, reached after two days of intense negotiations, exceeded many expectations, as noted by the BBC's Karen Allen in Kabul. This initiative underscores the international community's vested interest in preventing Afghanistan from descending into chaos.At the press conference, Mr. Ghani described the audit as the most comprehensive in the history of elections, asserting it would dispel any doubts about the results. Mr. Abdullah concurred, highlighting a technical and political agreement and expressing hope for the Afghan people's benefit.Vote counting is slated to begin early Sunday, with ballot boxes transferred under stringent security to designated counting centers, where they will remain under constant surveillance until new results are announced. Although discussions of a unity government framework are underway, specifics regarding the division of power remain unclear.Mr. Kerry's visit, arranged on short notice amid concerns of Mr. Abdullah's alleged plans for a parallel government, underscored the urgency. He cautioned about the difficult road ahead, citing important obligations and tough decisions necessary for moving forward. We hope the coming weeks will yield the authenticity and credibility the Afghan people deserve, he remarked.Analysts warn that both Mr. Ghani and Mr. Abdullah enjoy substantial support, and any governmental or military division could jeopardize the country's stability.

text: New Queens Park Rangers manager Ian Holloway wants the squad to show pride when they are representing the club. Ian Holloway, the 53-year-old former QPR player from the 1990s, is set to begin his second managerial tenure against Norwich on Saturday. Speaking to BBC Radio London, he emphasized the importance of passion and talent, saying, It is all about where you are and what the club means. We need talented boys and for them to be hungry. Reflecting on his playing days, he added, Every time I wore that shirt I was bursting with pride and I want my team to do the same thing.Holloway, who previously managed the Rangers from 2001 to 2006, signed a two-and-a-half-year contract with the club on November 11. He expressed feeling honoured, privileged and proud to return to the Championship side but acknowledged the challenge ahead, noting it will take time to rebuild following the departure of Jimmy Floyd Hasselbaink, who was dismissed after 11 months. Currently, QPR sits 17th in the table, six points away from both the play-off spots and the relegation zone.Holloway questioned, Can I get more out of the lads and make them believe in themselves? He continued, I need to settle down, have a look and orchestrate things. I can't wait to see if my way of doing things makes this side any stronger or whether I will have to adjust it. He assured fans of his genuine intentions, stating, I am not going to change this overnight. I want the fans to understand I am here for the right reasons and I want to help us get back to where I believe we belong.Holloway also reflected on the club's evolution, contrasting the current direction with the excesses under former chairman Flavio Briatore, who sold the club to Tony Fernandes in 2011. Briatore's attempt to rebrand Rangers as a 'boutique club' was documented in 'The Four Year Plan,' which chronicled the Hoops' efforts to reach the top flight between 2007 and 2011. Holloway remarked, I don't want us to be what we turned into. We're not a sparkly circus or 'let's make a film about ourselves'. That is not this club. He praised the current atmosphere, saying, The feeling behind the scenes is fantastic. It is not glitzy or glamorous where other people were trying to take us. The enthusiasm of Tony is immense. Les [Ferdinand, director of football] wants to protect this place and nurture it. I'm tingling with the sense of well-being we have all got about this club.Phil Parry from BBC Radio London noted that as a player, Holloway's industrious nature and positive attitude were well-regarded by both teammates and fans. When he first took the managerial role in 2001, he inherited a club on the brink of dropping to the third tier and facing administration. His character and commitment revitalized Loftus Road through smart recruitment, effective coaching, and excellent man-management. Although his career since leaving Rangers has seen mixed results, it includes two promotions to the Premier League and the implementation of an attacking style of play. Returning to QPR is no easy task, but with the club at a low point, Holloway's proven ability to inject energy and success could be exactly what they need.

text: The number of hours that ambulances spent waiting at A&Es in the North West of England has more than doubled in the past two years, the BBC has found. Recent Freedom of Information (FoI) data reveals a significant surge in ambulance handover times at hospitals, escalating from 17,413 hours in 2013-14 to a staggering 46,160 hours in 2015-16, exceeding the standard 15-minute handover period. The majority of regional trusts have experienced this increase, with the Royal Liverpool Hospital witnessing a six-fold rise in delays.The North West Ambulance Service attributes this to an increasing demand for emergency care. In response, the Royal Liverpool and Broadgreen University Hospitals' Trust has hired several hospital-trained paramedics to its emergency department. This move aims to facilitate the safe handover of patients, enabling ambulances to return to service more quickly.An investigation highlights a national issue: only one out of the UK's 13 ambulance services is currently meeting its target for reaching seriously ill and injured patients. The delays are also linked to a crisis in social care provision, causing bed-blocking due to postponed discharges of elderly patients.During the FoI period, the hours ambulance crews spent waiting to hand over patients at North West A&E units soared by 167%, with some hospitals experiencing even greater increases. Aintree Hospital in Merseyside, for instance, saw a 234% rise. This was highlighted last week when 20 ambulance staff were photographed waiting to hand over patients amid a surge in 999 calls. A paramedic there reported spending more than half their shift standing in corridors.Conversely, Wythenshawe Hospital in Manchester was the only facility where handover times decreased, with a 9% reduction in hours. The prolonged waits at A&E are detrimental not only to patients but also to ambulance crews, as they remain tied up in hospitals instead of responding to other emergencies.Ambulance services typically allocate 15 minutes for patient handovers. The reported figures represent the additional hours spent beyond this timeframe. Last year's total reached 46,160 hours in the North West, a dramatic increase from just under 17,500 hours two years prior.The rising figures can be attributed to a growing A&E attendance as the population ages. Hospital trusts also cite deficiencies in social care, particularly for the elderly. One trust revealed they have the equivalent of three wards occupied by patients who should not be in the hospital, simply because there is no suitable place for them to go. This occupancy reduces bed availability for incoming A&E patients.Nationally, handover delays at hospitals in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland have risen by 52% over the past two years. Lisa Grant, chief nurse at the Royal Liverpool and Broadgreen University Hospitals, stated: Hospitals across the area are collaborating with community and social care partners to safely discharge patients who no longer require hospital care, thus freeing beds for emergency department patients needing ward admission.The North West Ambulance Service commented: We are witnessing a growing number of people requiring our services, particularly for Red incidents involving serious and life-threatening conditions. This increase contributes to heightened activity at hospital emergency departments. During busy periods, this unfortunately results in ambulance crews waiting longer to transfer patients to hospital staff before they can be available for other emergencies.

text: A chronology of key events: In the 9th century, the County of Barcelona was established, alongside other counties, as part of Charlemagne's strategy to create a buffer zone between his Frankish Empire and Muslim-ruled Spain. By 1023-76, under the leadership of Ramon Berenguer I, Barcelona emerged as a dominant power in the region. The 12th century saw the first recorded use of the term Catalonia. During the reign of Ramon Berenguer IV from 1131-1162, his marriage to Queen Petronilla of Aragon led to a dynastic union with the Kingdom of Aragon. Despite becoming part of the Crown of Aragon, Catalonia retained its traditional rights and its own parliament, the Corts catalanes. In the 14th and 15th centuries, Aragon expanded its reach by acquiring the kingdoms of Sardinia, Sicily, and Naples, establishing itself as a prominent Mediterranean maritime empire.The marriage of Ferdinand I of Aragon and Queen Isabella of Castile in 1469 marked a dynastic union that laid the groundwork for the Kingdom of Spain. Christopher Columbus's discovery of the Americas in 1492 initiated Spain's overseas empire, shifting the focus of trade from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic, and diminishing Catalonia's economic and political influence.From 1640 to 1652, Catalonia rebelled against the taxation policies of Philip IV of Spain in the Reapers' War, briefly declaring itself a republic under French protection before Spanish troops reoccupied the region. The War of the Spanish Succession from 1705 to 1714 saw Catalonia support Archduke Charles of Austria against King Philip V. Following Philip's victory, Catalonia's parliament and traditional liberties were suppressed.In 1716, the Nueva Planta decree dismantled Catalonia's separate legal system, bringing it under Madrid's direct rule and abolishing the administrative use of the Catalan language. During 1812-13, Napoleon annexed Catalonia to France, but French troops withdrew from Barcelona after an armistice with the Duke of Wellington. Between 1808 and 1833, Catalonia was a battleground in the First Carlist War, as liberal supporters of Queen Isabella II clashed with absolutists backing her uncle, the Infante Carlos.The 19th century saw Catalonia leading Spain's industrialization and experiencing a cultural renaissance, sparking a movement to revive Catalan culture and language, which fueled the rise of Catalan nationalism. In 1901, the Catalan nationalist Regionalist League was formed. The shadow of General Franco's dictatorship still affects relations between Catalonia and Madrid today.In 1913, limited joint self-government was granted to Catalonia's four provinces under the Commonwealth of Catalonia, led by Enric Prat de la Riba. However, in 1925, the Commonwealth was suppressed during the dictatorship of Spanish Prime Minister Miguel Primo de Rivera. Spain became a republic in 1931, and an autonomous Catalan regional government, the Generalitat, was established under the Revolutionary Left of Catalonia.The Spanish Civil War erupted in 1936 when nationalist troops led by General Francisco Franco revolted. Catalonia remained loyal to the Republic, with both the Generalitat's forces and popular militias fighting on its side. In 1938, George Orwell published Homage to Catalonia, recounting his experiences fighting with Republican forces. By 1939, Franco's forces had overrun Catalonia, leading to the collapse of Republican resistance across Spain.From 1939 to 1975, Franco's dictatorship suppressed political opposition and Catalan autonomy, language, and culture, forcing many Catalan activists into exile or leading to their execution. The 1960s brought economic growth to Catalonia, driven by mass tourism and industrialization, attracting migrants from other Spanish regions. Franco's death in 1975 initiated a democratization process under King Juan Carlos.In 1977, a provisional regional government, once again named the Generalitat, was restored under Josep Tarradellas. The 1978 democratic Spanish Constitution acknowledged distinct national communities within Spain, initiating regionalization. Catalonia was granted a statute of autonomy in 1979, recognized as a nationality, and Catalan became an official language alongside Spanish.In 1980, the Centre-right moderate nationalist party Convergence and Union, led by Jordi Pujol, won the first elections to the new regional parliament, with Pujol becoming the first president of the new regional government. Barcelona hosted the Summer Olympic Games in July-August 1992. Jordi Pujol retired in 2003 after 23 years as president. In November 2003, despite winning the most seats, Convergence and Union was ousted by a coalition of Socialists, the Revolutionary Left, and Greens, with Socialist Pasqual Maragall becoming regional president.In June 2006, Pasqual Maragall stepped down, succeeded by fellow Socialist Jose Montilla. A reformed autonomy statute for Catalonia came into effect in August 2006, granting greater powers and financial autonomy, with its preamble describing Catalonia as a nation. Between December 2009 and April 2011, Catalan nationalists held a series of informal, non-binding votes on independence, including in Barcelona.In July 2010, Spain's Constitutional Court struck down parts of the 2006 autonomy statute, ruling there was no legal basis for recognizing Catalonia as a nation within Spain and that Catalan should not take precedence over Castilian. The decision was criticized by the regional government. Catalonia's parliament voted to ban bullfighting, becoming the first mainland Spanish region to do so. In November 2010, Convergence and Union, led by Artur Mas, returned to power after regional elections.The ban on bullfighting took effect in September 2011. In August 2012, Catalonia requested a 5 billion-euro bailout from the Spanish government. In September, around 1.5 million people participated in Catalonia's annual independence rally in Barcelona, amid growing resentment over financial transfers from the region to the rest of Spain. Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy rejected regional leader Artur Mas's call for greater fiscal independence.In November 2012, snap elections were held to support a referendum on independence. Convergence and Union lost ground to the left-wing Republican Left (ERC) party. Both parties supported independence, but the ERC opposed the Catalan government's spending cuts. In December 2012, Artur Mas was re-elected after Convergence and Union formed a governing pact with the ERC, both supporting a referendum on secession from Spain in 2014.In January 2013, Catalonia's regional parliament approved a declaration of sovereignty, paving the way for a 2014 independence referendum. In March 2014, Spain's constitutional court ruled that the planned November referendum was unconstitutional. In April, the Spanish parliament rejected Catalonia's proposal for a referendum. In September, Regional President Artur Mas signed a decree for a non-binding independence referendum in November. Spain's constitutional court suspended the plans to review the vote's legality.In October 2014, Artur Mas insisted the non-binding referendum would proceed under a different legal framework after the original plan was deemed unconstitutional. In November, more than 80% of participants in the informal vote opted for independence, with about two million of 5.4 million eligible voters casting ballots. In January 2015, Artur Mas called for new regional elections on September 27 to assess support for a possible declaration of independence.

text: A dumped tyre may have caused the sinking of an amphibious vehicle in Liverpool's Albert Dock complex, the attraction's operator has said. On Saturday, a Yellow Duckmarine sank in Salthouse Dock, resulting in 27 individuals receiving hospital treatment. Pearlwild Limited suggested that debris in the water caused severe damage to the hull of the vessel. The incident is currently under investigation by the Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) and coastguard officials. At the time of the sinking, 31 people, including children, were aboard the craft. Fortunately, there were no serious injuries reported. In response, the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) has revoked certification for all vessels of this type. A spokesperson for Pearlwild Limited revealed that photographs of a nearly shredded tire entangled around the propeller have been submitted to the MAIB. We have invested tens of thousands of pounds to enhance the safety of our fleet in recent months to comply with MCA requirements, he stated, adding that the damage was so extensive that the vessel couldn't manage the influx of water. He assured, We will continue to cooperate closely with the MAIB, and we fully anticipate that dock debris will be a significant focus of their investigation. He also noted, This is the first instance in over 35,000 Yellow Duckmarine tours where debris has posed a problem in the dock. I just sat there thinking, this can't be happening to us.Another passenger, Mitul Patni from Leicester, expressed his fear when he couldn't inflate his life jacket in time. text: Rachael Heyhoe Flint, the former England women's cricket captain, has died aged 77. Baroness Heyhoe Flint, a revered figure in sports and vice-president of Wolverhampton Wanderers Football Club, passed away in the early hours of Wednesday following a brief illness. She is survived by her husband Derrick, their son Ben, and stepchildren Rowan, Hazel, and Simon. Expressing the family's sorrow, Ben stated they were deeply saddened.Heyhoe Flint's illustrious cricket career saw her captaining the England women's team from 1966 to 1978. A trailblazer, she played in the inaugural women's match at Lord's against Australia in 1976. Throughout her career, she participated in 22 Test matches and 23 one-day internationals, earning her a place in the ICC Hall of Fame in 2010.Her influence extended beyond the cricket field. She became a successful journalist, after-dinner speaker, and public relations expert, reconnecting with her cherished Wolves by leading the club's community initiatives. Matthew Fleming, MCC president, praised her as a pioneer of women's cricket, acknowledging her as the sport's first global superstar. He emphasized her significant contributions to the MCC, cricket, and sports at large. Clare Connor, director of women's cricket at the ECB, remarked on Heyhoe Flint's lasting impact, saying, She was so special, so ever-present and now she has gone - but her impact can never be forgotten. Rachael was one of our sport's true pioneers and it is no exaggeration to say that she paved the way for the progress enjoyed by recent generations of female cricketers.Tributes poured in for Heyhoe Flint, including from BBC cricket correspondent Jonathan Agnew, who tweeted: Very sad news re Rachael Heyhoe Flint. Great champion of women's cricket, won first World Cup and one of life's real enthusiasts. #RIP.In her honor, flags flew at half-mast at Lord's and Wolves' Molineux stadium. Wolves' players will don black armbands during Saturday's Championship game against Norwich. Laurie Dalrymple, Wolves' managing director, expressed the club's grief, saying, Everyone at Wolves is deeply saddened to hear the news that Rachael has passed away. She was a wonderful lady who meant so much to so many people at the football club, in the city of Wolverhampton, and also much further afield. Rachael's contribution to the world of sport, the local community, and in later years politics, cannot be measured, and neither can her seemingly never-ending kindness and generosity of spirit.The England Cricket Board lauded her immense contributions to the development of cricket. After her playing days, Heyhoe Flint broke new ground as one of the first women admitted to the MCC and, in 2004, became its first female full committee member. Her remarkable achievements were recognized with an MBE in 1972, an OBE in 2008, and she was made a life peer in 2011.

text: As Westminster does from time to time, there is a frothing row this morning over where a memo - which purports to reveal the government's private Brexit woes and is splashed on the front of The Times - actually comes from. Downing Street's anger is palpable, and to say they are merely upset would be a gross understatement. They are seething over a story that not only casts an embarrassing light on the prime minister's leadership style but also claims to be based on a document they argue was crafted by someone lacking true insight. This document, reportedly penned by a consultant from Deloitte, was allegedly part of a business pitch. However, The Times counters this assertion, maintaining that senior civil servants were indeed involved.Regardless of who holds the truth, the document's significance cannot be ignored as it highlights ongoing issues widely reported by various outlets. Five months post-referendum, the cabinet remains entangled in a web of disagreement over the true implications of Brexit means Brexit. Opinions within the cabinet are diverse, and a substantial amount of work has been initiated across different government sectors to forge a unified stance. The Department for Exiting the European Union, or DEXEU—humorously dubbed Dexit—has embarked on 51 separate studies of various economic sectors to aid in this endeavor.Yet, as a senior source candidly remarked this week, they just don't know what course of action to take; the entire situation is described as a frightful mess. Despite an accumulation of information, decision-making remains stagnant. With a slim majority in the Commons, ministers are wary of losing debates and are keen to avoid significant confrontations.The prime minister's placeholder assertion that Brexit means Brexit is now facing intense scrutiny. Downing Street always knew this stance was unsustainable. While there is anticipation that the prime minister might offer more clarity in an upcoming speech at the CBI, there is scant evidence that the government is any closer to reaching definitive conclusions. Until a clearer path is charted, they remain susceptible to criticisms outlined in the memo, irrespective of its authorship, and to accusations of chaos from the opposition.

text: More than 150 people in Wales have been reported to police for meeting children following sexual grooming over the last five years, new figures show. Dyfed-Powys Police recorded the highest number of complaints, totaling 60, while North Wales Police had the fewest, with 26. Nearly 60% of the crimes reported between 2011 and 2015 involved online grooming. NSPCC Cymru is advocating for mandatory online safety lessons to be integrated into the school curriculum. According to figures obtained by the charity through the Freedom of Information Act, 155 complaints were filed against adults accused of meeting a child under 16 following sexual grooming.South Wales Police received 35 complaints, while Gwent Police had 34. Dyfed-Powys Police reported the most crimes involving online grooming, with 37 cases, followed by Gwent Police with 22, North Wales Police with 17, and South Wales Police with 16. NSPCC Cymru is urging for compulsory online safety lessons in schools starting in September, emphasizing the importance of educating students about the dangers of social media and online grooming.Peter Wanless, NSPCC chief executive, stated, Education is the key to teaching children how to use the internet safely so they don't find themselves at risk of serious harm. Online safety is a 21st-century child-protection challenge and it is something that we need to tackle head on.The Welsh Government has highlighted its extensive e-safety education program, which includes online resources and classroom materials designed to help pupils think critically, behave safely, and participate responsibly online. A government spokesman added, We have also created an online one-stop shop, Hwb, providing help for children and young people to stay safe on the web.South Wales Police, Dyfed-Powys, and Gwent Police have collaborated with schools to educate students on issues such as grooming, sexual exploitation, the sharing of inappropriate images, and online safety. Gwent Police Superintendent Leanne Brustad reported that the force delivered 1,874 lessons to nearly 50,000 students in 2014/15. South Wales Assistant Chief Constable Jon Drake mentioned that they worked with agencies to ensure those working with young people recognized the signs of such abuse.Dyfed-Powys Police has increased its resources to address the issue, employing a team of digital detectives and forensic computer and mobile phone investigators. North Wales Police has yet to comment on the matter.

text: A US appeals court has overturned the money laundering conviction of a once-powerful former Republican congressman, citing insufficient evidence. In a dramatic turn of events, the Third Circuit Court of Appeals has overturned the 2010 conviction of Tom DeLay, who was found guilty of illegally channeling corporate funds to Texas Republican candidates. The court, in a 2-1 decision, concluded that the prosecution did not adequately demonstrate that the funds were tainted.Tom DeLay, who first entered Congress in 1984 and ascended to the role of majority leader by 2003, was a formidable figure known as the hammer for his skill in maintaining party discipline during tight votes. However, his career was marred by controversy, leading to his resignation in June 2006 after being indicted on charges of money laundering and conspiracy to commit money laundering.Federal prosecutors had accused DeLay of orchestrating a scheme during the 2002 mid-term elections. They claimed his aides transferred $190,000, contributed by corporate lobbyists to a campaign committee under his control, to a branch of the Republican National Committee. This group then funneled the money to seven state legislative candidates. The success of six of these candidates allowed the Republican Party to seize control of the Texas House of Representatives. This majority subsequently passed a redistricting plan that bolstered Republican representation in Washington in 2004, thereby strengthening DeLay's political influence.DeLay consistently argued that the transaction was lawful and insisted that no corporate funds were directly given to candidates at the state level. He dismissed the charges as a politically motivated attack. Despite his conviction by a Texas jury in November 2010 and a subsequent three-year prison sentence in January, DeLay remained free on appeal.On Thursday, the appeals court delivered its verdict, stating that the prosecution had failed in its burden to prove that the funds that were delivered to the seven candidates were ever tainted. Brian Wice, DeLay's attorney, expressed his client's relief to the Associated Press, saying, He's ecstatic. He's gratified. He's just a little bit numb. I'm hoping with today's victory, he will be able to resume his life as he once knew it.

text: A Taser gun was used three times in less than 30 seconds as police tried to apprehend a man who had killed a woman, an inquest has heard. Matthew Williams was discovered assaulting 22-year-old Cerys Yemm at the Sirhowy Arms Hotel in Argoed on November 6, 2014. The 34-year-old Williams was subdued with a Taser by police, later succumbing to death following his arrest.During proceedings at Gwent Coroner's Court in Newport, it was revealed that Miss Yemm's body bore bite marks and cuts, potentially inflicted by a broken ceramic cereal bowl. Michael Rees, an armourer with South Wales Police, analyzed the Tasers used by officers during the arrest. He testified that only one Taser had been deployed, which was partially stained with blood and discharged four times throughout the incident. The Taser was activated at 01:37:11, followed by three more activations at 01:44:14, 01:44:28, and 01:44:41.Forensic scientist Gillian O'Boyle inspected the crime scene, discovering 15 shards of crockery that reassembled into an almost complete cereal bowl. Most of these fragments were bloodstained, and DNA analysis identified the blood as belonging to both Miss Yemm and Williams. O'Boyle remarked, The pattern of the blood was as if the bowl had been used to hit an individual and had broken as part of this, but she could not determine who had wielded the bowl. Additionally, Miss Yemm's clothing had cuts that could have been made by a sharp-edged object, such as a piece of ceramic, O'Boyle noted.Forensic dentist Romina Carabott concluded that three bite marks on Miss Yemm's abdomen and another on her wrist were likely inflicted by Williams. Released from prison merely two weeks prior to the incident, Williams was in possession of 12.2 grams of class B mephedrone, 9.9 grams of mephedrone mixed with monosodium glutamate, and 1.02 grams of amphetamine sulphate mixed with caffeine.Dr. Richard Jones, a forensic pathologist who conducted Miss Yemm's post-mortem examination, reported 24 injury areas on her body, totaling at least 89 distinct injuries. Half of these injuries were concentrated on her head, and Dr. Jones attributed her death to sharp force trauma to the face and neck. He further clarified that the bite marks and traces of amphetamines and cannabis in her system did not contribute to her death.The inquest is ongoing.

text: All photographs by Olivia Acland During the brutal 11-year civil war in Sierra Leone, the nation gained notoriety for its blood diamonds. Rebel factions and government forces fiercely contested the diamond-rich territories in the north, financing their conflicts by selling these precious stones to international buyers. Fourteen years after the war's conclusion, diamond mining persists in the northern district of Kono.A prominent player in this ongoing industry is Koidu Holdings, a South African company operating a large mine equipped with advanced machinery. This technology allows them to blast through kimberlite, accessing diamond-dense areas deep beneath the earth's surface. Meanwhile, nearby riverbanks are lined with artisanal miners, equipped with only sieves, spades, and buckets.Among these miners is Philo, who has been working in Kono for 23 years. He was forced to flee during the conflict, living as a refugee in Guinea. When the war subsided in December 2000, Philo returned home, resuming diamond mining a year later. Despite the challenges, many artisanal miners, including Philo, admit they haven't found diamonds in months and live in dire poverty. Yet, in a country where youth unemployment is at 70%, mining offers a vital means of survival.Typically, miners work in groups of three. Philo collaborates with two friends: one dives to collect mud and grit from the riverbed, while another holds him steady against the tide. The third man collects the bucket, emptying its contents into a mound for sifting. To combat the cold, they rotate roles frequently. Philo, feeling the chill after emerging from the water, warms himself with a packet of cheap rum, lamenting, This work is tough and physically straining - if I had the qualifications or opportunity to do another job then I would at once.Artisanal miners, scattered across the swampy river area, urgently scoop and sift through the mud. After three hours of labor, Philo is elated to discover a tiny diamond. Some miners have managed to invest in a rocker, a tool that uses a power hose to wash mud through a fine mesh, increasing the chances of spotting a diamond. Unfortunately, Philo lacks this luxury. We are not able to afford this kind of machinery, we have to manage with just a bucket, spade, and shaker [sieve], he explains. On the local market, each shaker costs 25,000 Leones (about £3.50).After finding a diamond, Philo ends his day early and heads into town with his team, satisfied with their success. This was a very good day, we hadn't seen a diamond for nearly a month, he says happily. On his way home, he encounters his elder brother outside a shop, exchanging greetings in the shadow of the rocky kimberlite mountain created by Koidu Holdings' blasts. Philo expresses envy at their machinery and wealth, particularly as diamonds in shallow areas become scarce.Back at home, Philo relaxes in his room with his uncle. text: A US judge in Seattle has issued a temporary nationwide block on President Donald Trump's ban on travellers from seven mainly Muslim nations. In a significant legal setback for the Trump administration, Federal Judge James Robart has dismissed government claims that US states lack the standing to contest President Trump's executive order. This decision follows a turbulent week marked by widespread protests and chaos at airports across the nation. According to the State Department, approximately 60,000 visas have been revoked since the order's implementation.President Trump's executive order includes a 120-day suspension of the US Refugee Admissions Programme and an indefinite ban on Syrian refugees. Additionally, it imposes a 90-day visa suspension for individuals from Iraq, Syria, Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, and Yemen.The initial lawsuit challenging the ban was filed by Washington state, with Minnesota joining the legal battle later. Washington State Attorney General Bob Ferguson has condemned the executive order as both illegal and unconstitutional, citing religious discrimination as its core issue.This ruling represents a significant challenge to Trump's policies, theoretically allowing nationals from the seven affected countries to apply for US visas, as reported by the BBC's David Willis in Washington DC. The administration retains the option to appeal the decision.President Trump has defended the order, asserting it is essential for safeguarding the nation. He stated that visas would be reissued once the most secure policies are established, denying any intent to target Muslims specifically.Numerous state attorneys general have criticized the order as unconstitutional. While several federal judges have temporarily halted the deportation of visa holders, Judge Robart's decision is the first to have nationwide implications. Meanwhile, courts in Virginia, New York, Massachusetts, and Michigan are also hearing cases against the executive order.Earlier on Friday, a Boston judge chose not to extend a temporary ban that prevented the detention or removal of foreigners legally permitted to enter the United States. This Massachusetts-specific ban is set to expire on February 5.

text: This morning on the Today programme, Ed Miliband prayed in aid Sir Nick Macpherson when repeating his view that the big economic mistake of the last Labour government was a failure to regulate the banks properly, rather than to spend too much. Sir Nick Macpherson, the Treasury's permanent secretary and the second most influential civil servant in the UK, serves as George Osborne's chief advisor on fiscal matters and policy implementation. In a review of Bill Keegan's book on austerity, Sir Nick candidly reflected on the 2008 financial crisis, stating: The 2008 crisis was a banking crisis pure and simple. Excessive risk had built up in the system; the regulators failed to appreciate the scale of that risk or to address it. It was 'a failure of the Group of Seven economic policymaking establishment', myself included. Inevitably, countries with bigger banking sectors, notably the UK, were worse affected.In essence, Sir Nick is acknowledging that he and other economic leaders in wealthy nations were blind to the reckless risks banks took in their pursuit of profits and bonuses. He admits that the UK Exchequer overly depended on revenues from a swollen financial services sector. The taxes paid by banks on their inflated profits proved unsustainable, as did the capital gains tax and stamp duty fueled by bubbles in the housing and financial markets, both driven by banks' reckless financing.This context helps explain why the Tories' claims of Labour's overspending and Ed Miliband's assertion that the UK's economic troubles stem from a global banking crisis are not as contradictory as they might seem. As I noted on Friday, Gordon Brown and his economic team—including Nick Macpherson from the civil service and Ed Balls and Ed Miliband from his party—felt confident in increasing spending by four percentage points of GDP from 2000 to 2007. Their optimism was based on the belief that the City's growth and the associated tax revenues would be sustainable.However, they were mistaken. This error now has official recognition: with hindsight, both the IMF and the OECD have determined that the UK's cyclically adjusted deficit—the portion of the gap between spending and revenues that normal growth won't close—was larger than in other major economies. According to the IMF, in 2007, the UK's cyclically adjusted deficit stood at 5.3%, compared to 3.5% in the US and 3.7% in France. A significant factor in this structural deficit was the disproportionate size of the financial services sector within the UK economy compared to the US and other major competitors.This does not absolve the Labour government under Brown, Miliband, and Balls. They must be accountable for making substantial long-term public spending commitments based on revenue from an unreliable banking sector. Notably, just days before Northern Rock's collapse and the end of City euphoria, George Osborne, as shadow chancellor, pledged to match Labour's promises to continue increasing public expenditure. In doing so, Osborne was effectively part of Sir Nick Macpherson's blinkered economic establishment.Nonetheless, Osborne's oversight does not lessen the culpability of Brown, Miliband, and Balls. They were in power, while Osborne was not. Therefore, if Miliband and Balls wish to argue that Cameron and Osborne have failed to restore living standards, they must more convincingly accept responsibility for the initial damage to those standards.

text: Pressure is increasing on world powers and Iran to sew up a deal on Iran's nuclear programme after many months of negotiations. If a deal is reached, the debilitating sanctions that have disrupted daily life in Iran will be lifted. BBC Persian has gathered opinions from everyday Iranians about their expectations for the ongoing talks. These nuclear negotiations have a profound impact on every Iranian, primarily due to the inflation driven by these sanctions. Many families find it increasingly difficult to maintain their previous standard of living.If an agreement isn't reached while President Rouhani is still in office, both parties will likely face significant challenges in the future. Iran's economy has been severely weakened since the imposition of the latest sanctions targeting the oil and banking sectors.I own three factories, one Iranian shared. Eight years ago, they were operating at full capacity, but now all three are shut down. Approximately 400 workers, technicians, and engineers have lost their jobs. Many, like me, who once ran small manufacturing businesses in industrial cities, are in the same predicament. These days, our cemeteries are expanding more rapidly and thriving better than our industrial cities.Reflecting on past negotiations, another Iranian recalled, I followed every moment of the last round. If you remember, you could really see the stress on John Kerry's face. It indicates that Mr. Obama needs to find a way to resolve this issue. Despite the strong opposition lobbies, I believe the US president is committed to making a deal and is capable of achieving it.However, skepticism remains. I'm not optimistic, one individual expressed. As our leader says, we don't trust the US, the UK, or the West in general. Yet, we see some in Iran placing their trust in negotiations, and the [Supreme] leader has agreed to this approach. It's happening, but personally, I believe the process will ultimately fail. It's just a matter of when.Doubts persist about the feasibility of a deal. I don't think a deal is possible, another person commented. There are many entrenched groups in Iran, like the Basij [volunteer paramilitary force], and especially those connected to the Supreme Leader's office. These groups will not allow it, and people will continue to feel the pressure.A farmer lamented, I can't sell the rice I produce. It's unfair to our people. Meanwhile, a teacher expressed mixed feelings, saying, I'm following the negotiations with excitement, but sometimes it feels like they are endlessly dragging on. Regardless, I don't think we'll see any significant changes immediately. Change will require time and won't occur the day after an agreement is reached.

text: Almost half (45%) of young people are checking their mobile phones after they have gone to bed, a poll suggests. A recent survey involving 2,750 young individuals aged 11 to 18 has revealed that one in ten admits to checking their mobile phones for notifications at least ten times during the night. Conducted by Digital Awareness UK in collaboration with the Headmasters' and Headmistresses' Conference, the study highlights a growing concern: students are arriving at school fatigued and struggling to focus due to nighttime mobile usage.The organizations behind the survey suggest a digital detox, advising students to refrain from using mobile devices for 90 minutes before bedtime or to keep them out of the bedroom entirely.Among the 45% of respondents who confess to using their phones when they should be sleeping, a significant 94% are engaged with social media. Alarmingly, 10% express anxiety about missing out if they don't check their devices before sleeping. Within this group, 75% listen to music and over half, 57%, watch films. Additionally, a third of these young people, 32%, admit their parents are unaware of their nighttime phone use.Charlotte Robertson, co-founder of Digital Awareness UK, remarked, Excessive social media consumption and its impact on our physical and emotional wellbeing is a major topic right now. Many children wake up to over 100 notifications from overnight conversations. They feel the need to respond at 1:00 AM to be perceived as cool and not miss out on any jokes, driven by the anxiety of staying informed.Mike Buchanan, chairman of the Headmasters' and Headmistresses' Conference, commented on the findings, stating, The data indicates that those checking their phones are primarily motivated by a fear of missing out. This lack of sleep leads to decreased concentration, affecting their ability to keep up with schoolwork. The desire to remain part of the group is strong.Buchanan added, It's not that technology is inherently bad. Instead, we need to acknowledge this reality and work towards positively influencing technology use.
