text: So Eddie Jones has gone from South Africa's Stormers to England's strugglers, from Cape of Good Hope to capable of good, it is to be hoped. The deal has been finalized swiftly, yet its significance remains undiminished. For the first time in history, the England rugby union team will be guided by a foreign coach. This groundbreaking decision is largely attributed to Eddie Jones' extensive coaching credentials and his availability compared to other ideal candidates.The choice also reflects a familiar pattern in English sports leadership, where decision-makers often opt for the opposite of their predecessor's perceived failings. This approach, perfected by the Football Association, has been adopted across various sports.Historically, these shifts have been evident: the low-profile Roy Hodgson succeeded the costly and authoritarian Fabio Capello; Capello himself had replaced the inexperienced Steve McClaren, who was the vocal contrast to the calm, strategic Sven Goran Eriksson. Eriksson was initially appointed for his tactical acumen, a stark contrast to the passionate yet naive Kevin Keegan, who had taken over from the isolated Glenn Hoddle. Hoddle, a born-again Christian, had succeeded Terry Venables, who stepped down to address off-field controversies. Venables’ international experience and attractive playstyle were a response to Graham Taylor’s straightforward British tactics.This pattern extends beyond football. In cricket, taciturn Duncan Fletcher was replaced by the lively Peter Moores, who was then succeeded by the seasoned Zimbabwean Andy Flower after Moores' lack of international prowess became apparent. When Flower was deemed too stern, Moores returned, only to be replaced by experienced Australian Trevor Bayliss when his previous shortcomings resurfaced.The Rugby Football Union (RFU) has mirrored this strategy since Sir Clive Woodward's departure. Andy Robinson was deemed too dour, leading to the appointment of the attack-minded Brian Ashton. Ashton’s lack of authority prompted the hiring of Martin Johnson, whose inexperience led to Stuart Lancaster, a grassroots coach with minimal public exposure.Enter Eddie Jones. Unlike Lancaster, who had only one season of Premiership experience and had never attended matches at the Millennium Stadium or Stade de France, Jones boasts a global coaching portfolio. He has led two Super Rugby teams in Australia, assisted the South African national team, worked in England with Saracens, and coached Japan leading up to the last World Cup. text: Mexico's Congress has approved sweeping changes to the country's energy industry which will see private oil contracts awarded in the country for the first time since 1938. On Wednesday, a significant shift in Mexico's energy landscape was set in motion as new legislation passed, opening the oil market to foreign companies. This marks the end of the monopoly held by the state-owned Pemex since the industry was nationalized. President Enrique Pena Nieto has championed this energy reform as a pivotal element of his administration, anticipating that it will restore production levels to those seen in 2004 by the year 2025.Mexican oil production has dwindled from 3.6 million barrels per day in 2004 to a mere 2.5 million, hindered by decaying infrastructure, bureaucratic hurdles, and corruption. The dissolution of Pemex's monopoly necessitated constitutional amendments, which were enacted last year. These reforms are poised to draw billions in investment to Mexico, the ninth-largest oil producer globally, and also allow for private electricity production.President Pena Nieto expressed on Twitter, A more competitive and prosperous Mexico. They have laid the foundation for a new era of development and prosperity for Mexican families. Pemex, formally known as Petroleos Mexicanos, will now face competition from international titans like Chevron, Exxon Mobil, and BP. Starting in 2015, these companies are expected to sign contracts with the Mexican government to explore, produce, and refine oil—a privilege previously limited to service contracts with Pemex.This transformation of the oil industry is the culmination of decades-long efforts to liberalize Mexico's economy, a process initiated in the early 1980s. In a related move, legislation passed in July mandated the breakup of Carlos Slim's America Movil, Latin America's largest telecommunications company.A contentious aspect of the energy reforms involves transferring approximately one-third of Pemex's pension liabilities to the federal government's balance sheet. Critics argue this places the burden of the pension fund's historical mismanagement on taxpayers. To underline their opposition, they brought a life-size image of former President Lazaro Cardenas, who nationalized the industry in 1938, into the Senate chamber.

text: The fastest animal on land rarely uses its top speed to capture prey, according to a new analysis. In a groundbreaking study published in Nature, researchers have uncovered that cheetahs rely on astounding acceleration and rapid speed changes to hunt, rather than sheer speed alone. These magnificent animals can exert nearly five times the power of legendary sprinter Usain Bolt during his record-breaking 100m sprint. Prof Alan Wilson from the Royal Veterinary College in Hatfield, UK, who led the study, expressed his astonishment at the findings. They are remarkable athletes—not just for their speed but for their ability to accelerate and maneuver while capturing prey, he shared with BBC News.Traditionally, the cheetah's top speed has been cited as 65 mph (105 km/h), based on a 1965 measurement of a semi-domesticated cheetah running in a straight line on firm ground, published decades later in the Journal of Zoology. However, zoo cheetahs, accustomed to a leisurely life, rarely exceed the speed of a greyhound, about 40 mph (64 km/h).This discrepancy led scientists to speculate whether wild cheetahs could surpass the 65 mph mark when hunting. To investigate, Prof Wilson's team tracked five wild cheetahs over a year using advanced collars equipped with movement detectors and GPS systems. Their research revealed that while cheetahs occasionally reached speeds close to 60 mph, they typically maintained a pace of 30 to 35 mph during hunts. However, their ability to accelerate and change direction was unmatched by any other land animal, with speed increases of nearly 7 mph (10 km/h) in a single stride.They've developed a low gear that allows them to accelerate rapidly to their top speed, Prof Wilson explained. Cheetahs can produce an astounding 120 W/kg of power, dwarfing the 25 W/kg exerted by Usain Bolt in 2009, 30 W/kg by a polo horse, and 60 W/kg by a greyhound.The study also discovered that cheetahs possess an incredibly strong grip, tearing up the ground as they run. Their claws play a crucial role in enabling sharp turns and rapid acceleration or deceleration. These insights were made possible by the innovative collars designed by Prof Wilson specifically for this research. It is challenging for GPS to function accurately on a rapidly moving animal, so the collar itself is a significant innovation, he noted. After 12 years of development, these collars provide positions and speeds five times per second, offering unparalleled accuracy and robustness.Currently, the team is extending their research by using these collars to track lions and African wild dogs, aiming to gather comparative data. text: There may be one positive that comes out of the negative number issued on Wednesday morning by the Scottish government. The Scottish economy's output from October to December saw a slight decline of 0.2%, sparking concern as another quarter of contraction would officially signal a recession. While recessions are a normal part of the economic cycle, typically characterized by slowdowns, they become more perplexing when neighboring economies are not experiencing the same downturn. This disparity with the UK's economic performance is difficult to overlook.As the January to March quarter concludes, there is little that can be done to prevent a recession in Scotland. Recession confirmation, or lack thereof, is expected on July 3. Economic figures often provide more questions than answers, offering insight yet leaving much to be pondered. The final quarter of the year showed stagnant services, which make up three-quarters of the economy, with public sector services showing minimal movement. Financial services and firms in technical, scientific, and administrative support services emerged as the strongest performers.Construction, which had previously helped Scotland avoid recession, has seen a decline in output over the past three years. Within the production sector, manufacturing has dropped by 8% over two years, with textiles falling even more. The metals and machinery sector, vital to the oil and gas supply chain, has plummeted 24% over the same period. The category including computer equipment has decreased 6% since 2013 and 44% since the early 2000s, coinciding with the decline of Silicon Glen. Even the food and drink sector, once a hopeful for production and exports, experienced a slight output fall from 2015 to 2016.Comparing the end of 2016 with the previous year, Scotland's economy has stalled, producing the same amount while the UK economy grew by 1.9%. Over the entire year, Scotland's growth rate was a meager 0.4%, compared to the UK's 1.8%. In contrast, the US economy grew by 2% and the Eurozone by 1.7% during the same period. Developing economies like India and China saw growth rates of 7% and nearly as much, respectively. Closer to home, Ireland and Iceland experienced significant growth, with Ireland at 7.2% and Iceland at 11.3%. Norway, despite the oil and gas downturn, grew by 1.8%, while Sweden and Denmark saw 2.3% growth. Russia, like Scotland, struggled with a growth rate of just 0.3%.The downturn in Scotland is not solely due to the oil and gas slump, as the stagnation and contraction are widespread across various sectors. The expected boost from the pound's depreciation post-referendum has not materialized, with export sectors underperforming and the service sector remaining flat.The Scottish government attributes some of the economic challenges to Brexit uncertainty, noting a drop in consumer sentiment following the referendum. Finance Secretary Derek Mackay suggests that Scots may feel the Brexit impact more acutely due to their pro-European stance. However, other factors are at play, including low business start-up rates, the scarcity of corporate headquarters, and inadequate research and development spending.Some argue that Scotland's reliance on the public sector, especially during spending cuts, could have a disproportionate effect on the economy. Geographic factors, such as being on Europe's periphery, don't seem to hinder countries like Ireland or Iceland. A more subdued property market also limits homeowners' ability to borrow against equity for spending and investment.Political factors, such as the prospect of another independence referendum, add to the uncertainty. When asked if this is beneficial or detrimental to the economy, Mackay asserts that independence could be economically advantageous, even the debate itself.The release of the latest GDP figures revives discussions about the reliability of statistics, which are often based on estimates and seasonal adjustments. The Government Expenditure and Revenue Scotland (GERS) figures, once used to support the economic case for independence, are now less favorable due to shifting oil and gas revenues.Finance Minister Mackay acknowledges GERS as a set of estimates reflecting the current state, not the starting point for an independent Scotland. He believes that with the economic levers of an independent nation, Scotland could achieve better outcomes. The next GERS figures, covering the current financial year, are expected in August.

text: First-time buyers are being warned they could pay tens of thousands of pounds more interest if they sign up for 40-year mortgages. Sales of longer-term mortgages have soared to unprecedented levels, with a significant number of young buyers opting for durations exceeding the traditional 25 years. This shift allows them to secure larger loans with smaller monthly repayments, enabling them to purchase their dream homes. However, a major UK mortgage broker warns that the interest costs can escalate dramatically due to the prolonged payment period.Fifteen years ago, nearly all first-time buyers opted for 25-year mortgages. However, the surge in property prices has compelled people to explore alternative strategies to navigate the market. Currently, 60% of buyers choose extended terms, with the average being 30 years. Many are even opting for 35 or 40-year terms to make larger strides onto the property ladder.Chris Pearson, who recently purchased a house in Cheadle, Manchester, with his partner Katie Baynes, explains, The short-term gain was more beneficial than the long-term pain. After saving diligently for a deposit, they needed a spacious home and secured a 40-year mortgage from Nationwide, borrowing £300,000. Chris acknowledges, I think I'll be 72 when we've just paid it off.The appeal is evident: a typical 25-year mortgage requires monthly payments of £948, whereas extending to 40 years reduces this to £716, saving over £200 monthly. The interest component remains constant, but the capital repayments are spread over a longer period. This is the upside. The downside, however, is the additional interest paid over an extra 15 years, amounting to £60,000 more. Over 25 years, interest totals approximately £84,000, but over 40 years, it balloons to £144,000—a significant burden for borrowers. David Hollingworth from London & Country Mortgages, who calculated these figures, cautions, It's a real danger. They need to understand that they are going to pay thousands more in interest over the life of the mortgage.Katie and Chris are banking on rising house prices to stabilize their finances. We're stuck in a rut really, Katie admits. We're taking a massive risk. Although mortgage regulations have tightened, imposing stricter controls on what people can afford, no rules limit the length of mortgage terms or prevent financially strained families from committing to four decades of payments. Essentially, these borrowers are deferring financial reckoning and depleting future wealth.Hollingworth advises keeping mortgages under review and shortening the repayment period as soon as higher payments become feasible. Such a strategy, he notes, will save them a fortune. However, if interest rates rise or family incomes stagnate, homeowners like Katie and Chris in Cheadle might find themselves tethered to their 40-year deal, turning their mortgage into a burden in later life.

text: Walsall interim head coach Jon Whitney is not certain of his future role at Bescot, despite coming so close to leading the club to promotion. The Saddlers faced a tough defeat in their League One play-off semi-final, losing 6-1 on aggregate to Barnsley. Despite this, Jon Whitney's tenure as manager marked a high point for the team, as they narrowly missed automatic promotion by just a single point.Whitney expressed his desire to remain involved with the club, though he remained uncertain about his future role. I've planned to be part of it. Which role that is then we'll see, he shared with BBC WM. Reflecting on recent events, Whitney added, I need to reflect, sit back, take a breath and see where it takes me.The season had its share of challenges, particularly following the mid-season departure of manager Dean Smith to Brentford. This, combined with a lackluster performance under his successor, Sean O'Driscoll, proved detrimental to Walsall's ambitions. After O'Driscoll's initial success, which saw the team in second place, he remarked to BBC Sport, They are punching above their weight. I think the second half of the season is going to be a little bit more difficult. His prediction rang true as his tenure ended with a home loss to Barnsley in March.Once O'Driscoll left, Walsall's performance improved significantly under Whitney, achieving an impressive win ratio of 2.08 points per game. Had this been sustained throughout the season, the Saddlers would have clinched the League One title with ease.Reflecting on the season's ups and downs, Whitney stated, This has been an incredible shift for me since Dean went, and especially since Sean went. But I need to go where my heart takes me and I'll have to do that over the next few days when all the emotions have settled down.Whitney acknowledged the need for self-assessment, saying, I need to look at myself and look at my staff and see if I could do anything different. But the players have got the taste for it now. He emphasized the club's progress, noting, We are a developing club, who have overachieved this season, but we've got to develop a few more chances like that. This experience can only have been a positive.Looking ahead, Whitney expressed hope for maintaining the squad but recognized the challenges. We are going to try to keep the squad together if we can, but it might be a big ask. We will only be able to judge when we know the players we are keeping and the players we are bringing in.The managerial changes throughout the season are reflected in the team's performance statistics: Under Dean Smith (until November 30), the team played 19 matches, winning 10, drawing six, and losing three, with a total of 36 points, averaging 1.89 points per game. During the interim period with Jon Whitney, John Ward, and Neil Cutler (November 30 to December 18), they played one match, securing a win and three points. Under Sean O'Driscoll (December 18 to March 6), the team played 14 matches, achieving five wins, five draws, and four losses, totaling 20 points, with an average of 1.42 points per game. Finally, from March 6 onwards, excluding play-offs, Whitney led the team through 12 matches, securing eight wins, one draw, and three losses, accumulating 25 points with an average of 2.08 points per game.

text: Technology developed by a professor at Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh could help millions of people exposed to high levels of arsenic in their water supplies. In Bangladesh, a groundbreaking solar-powered, fully autonomous water treatment plant has begun operation, significantly reducing toxic chemical levels. In contrast to the Western world, where water is often taken for granted, many global regions face the peril of contaminated water supplies. Professor Bhaskar Sen Gupta from Heriot-Watt University highlights that over 137 million people in 70 countries are exposed daily to arsenic through their drinking water. This exposure isn't limited to just drinking water; when used for irrigation, arsenic can accumulate in crops.Arsenic, notorious from the golden age of British crime fiction, is not immediately lethal in water but is linked to severe health issues, including cancers, skin conditions, and type 2 diabetes. Prof. Sen Gupta, a water technologist, focuses his research on Bangladesh, where arsenic naturally occurs in the water supply. Originating from the silt of Himalayan rivers, it has been harmlessly present for millions of years until recently, when it began dissolving into shallow aquifers, becoming a hidden threat.The problem, though naturally sourced, has been exacerbated by human intervention. The introduction of high-yielding rice varieties, requiring more water and fertilizer, has disrupted the natural balance. Fertilizer-rich water from the rice fields reaches the sub-surface, explains Prof. Sen Gupta, and in the absence of oxygen, arsenic-bearing minerals become reactive, breaking down into a highly toxic form.Prof. Sen Gupta's innovative solution involves a clever manipulation of natural processes. Water is extracted from a well, slowly oxygenated, and returned. This gradual oxygenation allows bacteria, accustomed to oxygen-free environments, to convert arsenic from a liquid to an inert solid, which adheres to sand grains in the aquifer, all occurring underground without bringing arsenic to the surface. This method, known as subterranean arsenic removal (SAR), is chemical-free and waste-free.After a decade of development, SAR now operates on solar energy and functions autonomously. Once established, the system can be remotely managed. The first plant, located in Comilla district, was funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council with support from the Bangladesh Green Energy Foundation. It currently serves 200 schoolchildren and, as the process extends through the aquifer, will eventually benefit 1,000 people.The World Health Organization's safe arsenic level in water is 10 micrograms per liter. The initial level in the well was 239 micrograms per liter, but within seven weeks, the SAR process reduced it to just two micrograms. In our interconnected world, Prof. Sen Gupta notes, There's an app to run it all. We can manage the plant from anywhere globally with a wifi connection. The NGO operating it, the Bangladesh Green Energy Foundation, runs it from Dhaka, over 300km away.Prof. Sen Gupta aspires to extend this knowledge globally, stating, As a global university, we want to tackle global problems and be part of the solution. He plans to establish a charity to further this work, emphasizing its impact: with £5,000, a thousand lives can be improved.

text: The first victims of the St Petersburg metro explosion have been named, as investigators continue to piece together the identity of the attacker. Monday's devastating blast between two metro stations claimed 14 lives and left nearly 50 injured. Investigators suspect it was a suicide bombing orchestrated by Akbarzhon Jalilov, a man born in Kyrgyzstan. In a tragic turn of events, reports from Russia reveal that Irina Medyantseva, a 50-year-old doll-maker, died while trying to protect her daughter from the explosion. Medyantseva succumbed to her injuries in an ambulance, while her 29-year-old daughter, Yelena, is recovering in the hospital in stable condition.Among the victims was 20-year-old Dilbara Alieva from Azerbaijan, who was hospitalized but later passed away. The oldest victim was Yuri Nalimov, aged 71, and one of the youngest was Ksenia Malyukova, 18, as reported by Russia's investigative committee. Kazakhstan's foreign ministry confirmed the death of one of its citizens, Maksim Aryshev, a 20-year-old student who was mistakenly identified as the bomber on social media.Kyrgyzstan's security service identified the suspect as Akbarzhon Jalilov, born in Osh in 1995, who had acquired Russian citizenship. Russian investigators later confirmed his identity, adding that he had planted a second device that failed to detonate. As of now, no group has claimed responsibility for the attack.In the aftermath, the metro has resumed operations, but passengers at the Sennaya Ploshchad station are greeted by a growing memorial of flowers, notes, and candles. The city, grappling with shock, is trying to return to normalcy. Everyone I know is fine, said Irina, a local resident, but it could have been any one of us. This sentiment echoes throughout the city, which remains on edge following bomb scares that led to temporary closures of several metro stations.The explosion occurred on Monday afternoon shortly after the train departed from Sennaya Ploshchad. Senior investigator Svetlana Petrenko praised the train driver's quick thinking, noting that his decision to proceed to the next station, Tekhnologichesky Institut, likely saved lives by allowing for swift rescue efforts.Train driver Alexander Kaverin recounted the incident, stating, I just followed the procedure. There have been explosions before, and smart people devised smart procedures. I had to take the train to the nearest station, which is what I did. There was a bang and lots of dust, but the train kept moving.The discovery of another explosive device at Ploshchad Vosstaniya station on the same day indicates the attack was coordinated. Metro officials announced that both Kaverin and another employee who discovered the unexploded bomb would be commended for their actions.

text: Chinese central bank governor Zhou Xiaochuan has accused speculative forces of targeting the country's currency, the yuan. In a recent interview with Caixin financial magazine, Mr. Zhou, the governor of the People's Bank of China, asserted that there is no justification for the yuan's continued depreciation and emphasized that China will not allow international speculators to dictate market sentiment. His comments come as Chinese markets are set to resume activity on Monday following a week-long New Year holiday.China's efforts to defend the yuan have significantly reduced its foreign currency reserves. Despite still holding the world's largest reserve at $3.23 trillion (2.84 trillion euros; £2.2 trillion), these reserves have dropped by $420 billion over the past six months, reaching their lowest point since May 2012. In January alone, reserves plummeted by $99.5 billion as the People's Bank of China sold dollars to bolster the yuan's value.In the interview, Mr. Zhou highlighted that international speculative forces have recently focused on shorting China, but he did not provide further specifics. He dismissed concerns about the rapid decline in China's currency reserves, stating, It is normal for foreign reserves to rise and fall as long as the fundamentals face no problems.The Chinese economy experienced a growth rate of 6.9% in 2015, marking its slowest pace since 1990. Concerns over an economic slowdown have prompted some investors to move their capital out of China in search of better returns. Nevertheless, Mr. Zhou clarified that China would not impose stricter capital controls. He explained, Capital outflow and capital flight are two different concepts.Chinese authorities are wary of a rapid currency devaluation, fearing it could destabilize the economy. Many Chinese businesses carry debt in dollars, and a severely weakened yuan could complicate debt management, potentially leading to business failures. Consequently, China has been attempting to orchestrate a controlled devaluation of the yuan, a challenging task.Investors have been withdrawing funds from yuan-denominated investments, while speculators have been betting on further declines in the currency. To stabilize the situation, China has been selling dollars and purchasing yuan. Additionally, the government has employed other strategies, such as curbing currency speculation and instructing offshore banks to maintain their yuan reserves.

The Rovers, who suffered a 50-0 defeat to Leeds in last year's final at Wembley, have struggled this season, with only two wins in the Super League and a recent 40-0 loss to Catalans Dragons. text: Japanese carmaker Toyota has regained its slot as the world's biggest vehicle maker, capping a year of a dramatic turnaround in its fortunes. In 2012, Toyota achieved a remarkable milestone, selling 9.75 million vehicles—a surge of over 22% compared to the previous year. This impressive feat dethroned General Motors, which had been the largest vehicle manufacturer in 2011 with sales of 9.29 million vehicles. Toyota's performance in 2011 had been severely affected by natural disasters in Japan and Thailand, disrupting production at its factories. However, since then, Toyota, along with other Japanese automakers, has been on a steady path to recovery, regaining market share in crucial regions like the United States.The last two years have been very difficult for Toyota, commented Vivek Vaidya, an auto analyst with Frost & Sullivan, in an interview with the BBC. He added, Regaining the top position is certainly encouraging for the company and brings good news for its investors and shareholders.Toyota's competitors also reported impressive sales figures for 2012. Nissan Motor announced global sales of 4.94 million vehicles, marking an almost 6% increase from the previous year. Meanwhile, Honda Motor experienced a 19% rise, selling 3.82 million vehicles.In addition to natural disasters, Japanese carmakers have contended with a strong yen, which has made Japanese goods pricier for foreign buyers and squeezed profits when earnings are repatriated. This has particularly impacted companies like Toyota, which heavily depend on overseas sales. Recently, however, Japanese automakers have benefited from a weakening yen. Since last November, the yen has depreciated nearly 15% against the US dollar, reaching around 90.8 yen per dollar in Asian trading on Monday.Analysts suggest this currency decline could positively influence Toyota's growth. The decline in the yen is a welcome relief for Toyota, stated Mr. Vaidya from Frost & Sullivan. We are likely to see profit margins rise, providing more cash on hand and enabling investment in new technologies, which should support its growth momentum moving forward.In November, Toyota raised its annual profit forecast, projecting a net profit of 780 billion yen ($8.6 billion; £5.4 billion) for the financial year ending March 31, 2013, up from an earlier estimate of 760 billion yen.However, Toyota faces potential challenges, notably from the ongoing territorial dispute between Japan and China. As the world's largest car market, China is critical for the future growth of companies like Toyota. The conflict over a group of islands in the East China Sea, which intensified late last year, has strained relations between the two nations and led to a decline in Japan's exports to China. The dispute remains unresolved, raising concerns that tensions could escalate again, potentially harming trade relations and increasing anti-Japanese sentiment, which could negatively impact sales of Japanese brands in China.Analysts warn that any decline in sales due to these tensions could adversely affect Toyota's growth.

text: History, they say, is written by the victors. Standing beneath the shadow of a towering windmill on what was once a thriving sugar plantation in the West Indies, one can almost envision the commanding presence of Englishmen who once ruled there. While extensive records meticulously document the sugar industry that bolstered the British Empire, scant information exists about the African slaves who were its backbone.In an effort to illuminate this overlooked history, researchers are conducting a significant excavation at the Betty's Hope plantation in Antigua, where they have uncovered an 18th-century slave village. This rare discovery in the Caribbean promises to shed light on a grim chapter of history.Dr. Georgia Fox, who leads the project, recalls the 2013 discovery of the village as a eureka moment after it had evaded archaeologists for decades. By aligning advanced electronic surveying tools with maps from 1710, a student from California State University, Chico, was able to locate the site. It felt like a miracle, Dr. Fox told the BBC. We realized that the dots on the maps indicated the slave village. It was an amazing discovery.Subsequent excavations have unearthed a treasure trove of artifacts, offering unprecedented insights into the daily lives and culture of the plantation's 400 slaves. Dr. Fox explains, We first discovered a specific type of rough pottery known as Afro-Antiguan ware, crafted by slaves using local clay for cooking stews.Delving deeper into the village, the team found cowrie shells from East Africa, used as currency, for games, or as good luck charms. This finding is intriguing, as slaves in Antigua were typically from West Africa. Additionally, they uncovered Dutch delftware, likely bartered or given to slaves, and parts of a limestone wall, unusual since most slave homes were made of wattle and daub.Dr. Fox's team began excavations in 2007 at the plantation's Great House, followed by the Still House, where rum, a crucial by-product of sugar, was produced. Dating back to around 1650, the 700-acre site was a largely self-sustaining community, home to field workers, servants, overseers, tradesmen, a blacksmith, and a doctor. At its peak, each of the plantation's twin windmills could produce 12 tonnes of sugar crystals daily. Yet, less than 5% of the site has been explored.Artifacts from the Great House include children's toys, musket balls, buttons, cutlery, a door knocker, clay tobacco pipes, and a cod liver oil bottle. The organic materials used to construct slave houses, like palm fronds, sticks, and mud, made the village's identification challenging.Local historian and Unesco representative Reg Murphy, overseeing Antigua's archaeology projects, emphasizes the importance of this work in completing the island's history, where most inhabitants are descendants of slaves. Everything we learn focuses on the glory of sugar and the colonial legacy, he says. We rarely hear about the workers' daily lives. This research allows us to see their routine, diet, and lifestyle from their perspective. Over 400 slaves lived at Betty's Hope, and their stories have never been told.For Dr. Fox, the implications are even broader. While sugar plantations existed worldwide, the Caribbean was the gateway to the New World and profoundly influenced America's development. This was the dawn of capitalism, and it all began in the Caribbean. It's crucial to remember how the New World was formed—this is everyone's history.Though slavery was abolished in 1834, sugar production remained Antigua's economic backbone until tourism took over in the 1960s. Dr. Fox concludes, Sugar changed the world. Every time you enjoy a chocolate bar or sweeten your tea or coffee, you connect with a long history and reach into the past.

text: Ulster secured a home quarter-final and condemned Leicester to an away tie as they ended the Tigers' unbeaten home run of 25 matches in the Heineken Cup. In a thrilling match at Welford Road, Leicester and Ulster were deadlocked at 9-9 by halftime, each side benefiting from a trio of penalties, courtesy of Leicester's fly-half Toby Flood and Ulster's scrum-half Ruan Pienaar. The Tigers surged ahead with a Flood penalty and a converted try by Niall Morris, establishing a 19-9 lead. However, Ulster responded with a Pienaar penalty and his own converted try, leveling the score. Pienaar's fifth penalty sealed a dramatic victory for Ulster.With thirty minutes remaining and Leicester leading by ten points, it seemed they were poised to shatter Ulster's unbeaten streak and secure a home quarter-final. Yet, Ulster's relentless defense and strategic play, orchestrated by Pienaar, turned the tide. The Irish province's win at Welford Road ensured their qualification as top seeds.Ulster, champions in 1999 and finalists in 2012, are upgrading their Ravenhill ground to accommodate 18,000 fans, promising a sell-out when they host Saracens in the quarter-finals on April 4-6. Leicester's losing bonus point allowed them to finish as the best runners-up in the group stages, securing Saracens as the eighth qualifier.Initially, Leicester dominated the bruising encounter, with their scrum performing well and full-back Mathew Tait making an impact before leaving injured. Second-row Graham Kitchener almost added a try, showcasing his line-out skills with a 40-meter burst, but Flood's accurate kicking gave the Tigers a 9-3 advantage. Ulster's blend of Irish grit and South African rugby intellect, led by Pienaar, equalized the score by halftime.Post-break, Leicester seemed in control. A penalty from Flood followed by a precise grubber kick set up Morris for a try, which Flood converted, making it 19-9. However, Ulster refused to concede. Five minutes later, Pienaar capitalized on a penalty after Tom Youngs' ruck infringement, then charged down Flood's kick to score and convert his own try, tying the game at 19-19.The match remained open, with Leicester nearly scoring from an attacking line-out, only for Flood to fumble a pass near the try line. Ulster, undeterred, advanced into Leicester territory, where Pienaar's long-range penalty clinched the lead. A late scrum in Ulster's half offered Leicester hope, but Ulster's resilience prevailed, winning the ball and maintaining their perfect record.Ulster captain Johann Muller praised Pienaar's performance: It seems like it's happening every week, when Ruan scores all the points - he was outstanding. text: Auditors have warned MSPs about severe problems faced by three health boards. An Audit Scotland report has revealed that the implementation of a new IT system at NHS24 has exceeded its budget by 50% and has been delayed by two years beyond its original schedule. The report also highlighted financial struggles within NHS Tayside, which has failed to break even for the third consecutive year, necessitating a £14 million loan from the Scottish Government. Concerns were also raised about NHS Highland's finances, with auditors emphasizing the need to reduce reliance on one-off savings. According to the report presented to MSPs, the delay in launching the new computer systems at NHS24 has resulted in substantial additional costs and risks, with the completion date pushed from June 2013 to October 2015. The system's projected cost has now escalated to £117.4 million, marking a 55% increase from the initial estimate of £75.8 million.Auditors attributed NHS Tayside's financial difficulties to overspending on staffing, holiday pay, and primary care prescribing, leading to a dependency on loans for the third year running. In 2014/15, the health board required £14.2 million from the Scottish Government to break even. Additionally, auditors cautioned that the board must achieve savings of £27 million in 2015/16 to stabilize its finances.NHS Highland received a critical review of its 2013/14 accounts, although auditors acknowledged some improvements. They stressed the importance of developing long-term financial strategies and reducing dependency on one-off savings to ensure fiscal health.In response to the report, NHS24's chief executive, Ian Crichton, acknowledged that the report outlines a series of weaknesses dating back to 2011. He stated, Delays in this major IT programme have led to a significant increase in costs. During the last 16 months, an expert team has been working hard to bring the project back on track. The new system will be in place by the end of October.Lesley McLay, chief executive of NHS Tayside, addressed the challenges faced by the board due to increasing service demands. She explained, NHS Tayside's board has been building a programme of improvement and transformation since the beginning of this financial year. This medium-term programme, led by clinical staff in partnership with managers, prioritizes service improvement and benefits for patients, while also supporting sustainable financial balance for NHS Tayside.Garry Coutts, chairman of NHS Highland, welcomed the report, noting the robust measures taken to improve following the 2013/14 audit. He commented, It is heartening to read in this latest report that the auditor has concluded that we have strengthened our financial management arrangements, transparency, and scrutiny of our financial performance. This latest report emphasizes the importance of building on these improvements given the challenges ahead. That is something we are determined to do.

text: The Beast's beastliness falls well short of savage these days, and generates only faux outrage in the stilted setting of green benches. Veteran Labour MP Dennis Skinner, famously known as the Beast of Bolsover, found himself ejected from the chamber after labeling the Prime Minister Dodgy Dave. Though Skinner's anger is undoubtedly sincere, he has become a sort of jester within the establishment, a less dignified component of the political landscape. His remarks pale in comparison to the grievances of some right-wing Labour MPs who feel mistreated by activists, and they certainly don't ignite controversy like tweets glorifying Hitler.Meanwhile, in the United States, a presidential hopeful resorts to calling his critics, especially women, derogatory names such as ugly, dogs, dummies, and clowns—though not all at once. In contrast, Petronella Wyatt's comments about Chancellor George Osborne are far more refined and arguably more cutting. Despite her liking for him, she describes Osborne as having the fish-belly pallor of Vlad the Impaler, with eyes that have a Mongolian slant and a voice resembling a Gypsy's zither.Despite Jeremy Corbyn's advocacy for a new political era, has the discourse become more vulgar and offensive than ever? Perhaps not. Winston Churchill once referred to Ramsey MacDonald as the boneless wonder and Stanley Baldwin as that great turnip. Historical records reveal that James II was insulted directly by a disgruntled subject who called him an ugly lean-jawed, hatchet-faced, Popish dog, while William of Orange was disparaged by someone who labeled him a rogue and a son of a whore.Politicians and public figures need to rise above mere insults. Although I can barely recall the appearance of 18th-century Prime Minister Lord North, Horace Walpole's description is amusing: Two large prominent eyes that rolled about to no purpose (for he was utterly short-sighted), a wide mouth, thick lips and inflated visage, gave him the air of a blind trumpeter, Walpole noted. A deep untunable voice which, instead of modulating, he enforced with unnecessary pomp, a total neglect of his person, and ignorance of every civil attention, disgusted all who judge by appearance.The most enduring insults are those that blend venom with wit and insight. Samuel Taylor Coleridge's critique of Pitt the Younger, while not poetic, cuts to the core of the enigmatic and brilliant man. Coleridge remarked: He has patronised no science, he has raised no man of genius from obscurity; he counts no prime work of God among his friends. He has no attachment to female society, no fondness of children, no perception of beauty in natural scenery; but he is fond of convivial indulgences, of that stimulation which, keeping up the glow of self-importance and the sense of internal power, gives feelings without the mediation of ideas.Perhaps brevity is key. When Lord Sandwich predicted radical MP John Wilkes would die either on the gallows or of the pox, Wilkes retorted, That depends, my Lord, whether I embrace your mistress or your principles. Not only clever but succinct enough for Twitter.This hints at a change. While I resist lamenting technological shifts or claiming the world is spiraling downward, social media has undeniably influenced public sentiment. Twitter's constraints make it perfect for sharing longer articles and blogs, but they discourage thoughtful debate, instead fostering a mob mentality. A fleeting thought becomes text, a momentary irritation over a news story turns into a barrage of arrows aimed at a target. Serious harassment has become so common it has spawned a new vocabulary, from flaming to trolling.On a lighter note, I'm not the only journalist irked by tweets criticizing my work for bias or stupidity without pinpointing the specific offense. Abuse has become the focus, rather than the dramatic flourish of an argument. Engaging only worsens the situation. Twitter's brevity fuels heated exchanges, whereas email or traditional correspondence tends to cool tempers and foster understanding.Social media also promotes the gathering of like-minded individuals who bolster each other's beliefs, shutting out opposing viewpoints. The less they listen, the less they understand, and the more they attribute base motives to their adversaries. There's no consideration of the validity of others' values or viewpoints—they're just sons of whores or hatchet-faced dogs.The virtual mob moves through the digital landscape, and amidst the chaos, only curses and imprecations are discernible. Social media can empower those with a clenched fist mentality. Reactions are immediate—quicker than thought—leaving no time for reflection or debate, and eliminating the need to humanize a loathed meme. While such reactions remain largely online, they undermine the type of politics that seeks to resolve and address complex issues.

text: The cost of a basket of shopping at the same shop in Jersey and the UK can cost up to 10% more. Chris Rayner, BBC Radio Jersey's business reporter, has been delving into the cost of groceries, comparing prices between supermarkets in Jersey and Hampshire. His research involved creating a basic shopping list based on suggestions from Jersey's Consumer Council. The list included essentials such as a litre of milk, a kilo of white potatoes, cat litter, soap, toothpaste, and ketchup.Rayner discovered that certain items, like coffee, were significantly pricier in Jersey, with a noted difference of £1.32 more than the same product in the UK. He remarked, While the quality of life here may be better, many feel we pay more for the privilege, whether it's through higher rents, more expensive food, and travel costs.The BBC's investigation took them to three supermarkets in Jersey: the Co-op in Charing Cross, Waitrose at Rue des Pres, and Marks & Spencer in King Street. For comparison, they also visited three supermarkets in Petersfield, Hampshire: Tesco, Waitrose, and Marks & Spencer.Rayner noted that the cost of doing business in Jersey is notably high. The Channel Islands Co-op, for instance, imports tons of food and other goods from the UK weekly, incurring a hefty monthly expense of £60,000. Colin Mcleod, the Co-op's chief executive, explained, We've got high land costs, we've got high build costs, we've got high labour costs. But we're doing the best we can in that environment for our members.A representative from Waitrose in Jersey stated, We continually monitor our prices to ensure we remain as competitive as possible, and because of this, shoppers may find that many of our products now cost less than when we first opened our shops on the island. We need to reflect the additional costs of getting products to the Channel Islands in our prices but we pass on the savings of UK VAT to our shoppers in Jersey and have hundreds of relevant and meaningful promotions across our branches each week.Tony O'Neill, the chief executive of Sandpiper CI, noted that more than half of the products at Marks & Spencer are sold on promotion.Meanwhile, the Citizens Advice Bureau and the Community Savings Bank have reported an increase in clients. Brian Curtis, executive chairman of the Community Savings Bank, highlighted that it's not only the unemployed seeking help. I know some people on middle incomes who have not had any increase [in wages] for three years. They have still got a job, so that's fine in itself, but adjusting to a different scenario is not easy for some of these people, he said.

text: Charles Green has confirmed that Rangers will apply for Scottish Football League membership. During a pivotal meeting at Hampden on Wednesday, Scottish Premier League clubs decisively voted against the application from Green's Rangers newco. Charles Green expressed his profound disappointment over the rejection, stating, If our application were to be accepted, Rangers will play in whichever division the SFL sees fit and we will move forward from there.Rangers, burdened by debts of up to £134 million to unsecured creditors, entered administration in February. The club is on the path to liquidation, resulting in the termination of its registrations with the Scottish FA and SPL. Green lamented, We regret that our club and our supporters were given false hope.Prior to the vote, a majority of SPL clubs had already signaled their opposition to the newco's application. Despite this, Green voiced his frustration, claiming he had been led to believe there was a chance of success. We are deeply disappointed that our application to rejoin the SPL has been rejected overwhelmingly by the member clubs, Green explained.He continued, Last week, we had accepted that we might not be admitted, largely because of public statements from clubs indicating they would not support our application. However, over the weekend, SPL representatives approached us, suggesting our application might still succeed and encouraged further discussions with clubs. We engaged in these talks in good faith, aware of the challenges ahead.Green revealed that they had inquired whether withdrawing the application would be more appropriate but were advised against it. We presented our proposals to the SPL clubs, including what we considered fair penalties and sanctions for issues preceding our acquisition of the club on 14 June, he noted. Unfortunately, this was rejected, and we regret the false hope given to our club and supporters.Green confirmed that Rangers would now proceed with plans to apply for membership in the SFL, stating, It is entirely a matter for them whether our application will be accepted or rejected, and we will make no representation to any member club prior to that application being considered. He acknowledged the challenging position in which the SPL found itself due to unfolding events.On Tuesday, SFL clubs convened to discuss an SFA proposal that would place Rangers in Division One, with a vote scheduled for 12 July. A simple majority is needed for the decision, but 12 out of 30 clubs have already expressed opposition. Cowdenbeath, whose chairman Donald Findlay QC is a former Rangers vice chairman, indicated support for Rangers joining the SFL, but only if they enter the Third Division.

text: US President-elect Donald Trump will not pursue a further investigation into Hillary Clinton's emails, to help her heal, his spokeswoman has said. During his campaign, Donald Trump had vowed to appoint a special prosecutor to investigate Hillary Clinton, the former Secretary of State. text: The world's highest paid YouTube star, PewDiePie, has defended himself over allegations of anti-Semitism in a new YouTube video. Felix Kjellberg, better known as PewDiePie, has fiercely defended himself against allegations that led Disney to sever ties with him, labeling them as insane and unfair. He claims his words were taken out of context, resulting in a blatant misrepresentation of his intent. Over the past few months, some of his videos have come under scrutiny for containing Nazi references and anti-Semitic imagery.In a YouTube video, Kjellberg expressed remorse, stating, I am sorry for the words I used as I know they offended people. He elaborated, I do strongly believe that you can joke about anything, but I also believe that there is a right way and not the best way to joke about things. Acknowledging his status as a rookie comedian, he admitted to occasionally taking jokes too far.Kjellberg firmly denied any support for right-wing groups that promote hatred and criticized recent media coverage, including articles from the Wall Street Journal, as personal attacks aimed at discrediting him. In 2016, the Swede reportedly earned $15 million through his YouTube ventures. He was previously associated with Disney via Maker Studios, which manages a network of YouTube stars. His channel, attracting billions of views monthly, has generated significant advertising revenue.Disney announced on Tuesday that although Mr. Kjellberg was known for his provocative and irreverent style, some of his content was deemed inappropriate. One particularly controversial video involved Kjellberg paying two individuals in India, via a crowd-sourcing website, to display a sign reading Death to all Jews. He explained this was intended to highlight how people would say anything for $5. Other videos featured swastikas drawn by a fan, the Nazi Party anthem, and a brief Hitler salute, all of which he insists were jokes taken out of context.Kjellberg argued that, contrary to allegations of normalizing hatred through his jokes, it was his media critics who were perpetuating such narratives through their unjust attacks. In response to the controversy, YouTube announced the cancellation of Mr. Kjellberg's new series, Scare PewDiePie 2, and removed him from its Google Preferred program, which promotes advertiser-friendly content creators. Previously, in 2016, PewDiePie faced a temporary suspension from Twitter after making jokes about the so-called Islamic State.

text: Families of some of the 270 people who died in the Lockerbie bombing have welcomed the naming of two new suspects. In a renewed effort to bring justice to those affected by the 1988 Lockerbie bombing, US and Scottish prosecutors are seeking to interview Mohammed Abouajela Masud and Abdullah al-Senussi. These individuals have been identified as new suspects in the catastrophic event that claimed 270 lives when Pan Am Flight 103 exploded over Lockerbie, Scotland, on December 21, 1988. Among the victims were all passengers and crew aboard the flight, as well as 11 residents of the Scottish town. The only person convicted for this atrocity, Abdelbaset al-Megrahi, was sentenced to a minimum of 27 years in prison for mass murder. He was released on compassionate grounds in 2009 due to terminal cancer and passed away in 2012. Stephanie Bernstein, an American whose husband perished in the attack, expressed her mixed emotions upon learning of the new suspects. I am surprised, delighted, and really gratified, she stated, adding, There are many, many people who I hope are not sleeping so well tonight knowing that the Scottish government and the US government are committed to pursuing this case.Despite this development, Frank Duggan, president of Pan Am 103 Relatives, remains skeptical about the possibility of further prosecutions. It's been 26 years. It's too long, people are dead, stories have been forgotten, he lamented. He hopes for closure but is doubtful of achieving the justice they all desire.Dr. Jim Swire, whose daughter died in the bombing, insists that any new prosecution must be supported by stronger evidence than that which convicted Megrahi, whom he believes was innocent.Rana Jawad, North Africa correspondent, reports that Abdullah El Senussi is imprisoned in Al-Hadba, Tripoli, while Masud's location remains uncertain, with claims of him serving a 10-year sentence either in Tripoli or Misrata. The Tripoli general prosecutor's office has been reticent about sharing details after the Crown Office's announcement of the new suspects.The prospect of extraditing the suspects to the US or Scotland seems improbable, given Libya's political chaos. El Senussi, a significant figure as Gaddafi's intelligence chief and brother-in-law, is perceived as holding crucial secrets about Libya's past dealings. There is a suspicion in Libya that the West seeks to capture him for these secrets and would never return him.Interviewing the suspects on Libyan soil might be more feasible, though complicated by the absence of Western diplomatic missions and a recognized government in Tripoli. Both suspects are held by the Islamist-backed administration in Tripoli, not the internationally recognized government in Tobruk.The Crown Office mentioned that the interview request was routed through the British Embassy. Relatives of the bombing victims welcomed the identification of the new suspects, who were also named in a recent American TV documentary. Ken Dornstein, whose brother David died in the bombing, stated on BBC's Today programme that his investigation narrowed down potential suspects from a list originally pulled from thousands of documents.Dornstein highlighted Masud's potential significance, saying, Figuring out simply that he existed would solve many of the unanswered questions to the bombing because he was attached to Megrahi according to the best information there was, including at the airport in Malta on the day that the bomb was said to have been infiltrated into the baggage system and ultimately on to Flight 103.The role of Megrahi in the bombing has been scrutinized in various books and documentaries, keeping the case alive in public discourse.

text: Before February 2015, I'd never heard of the word sepsis. When the doctors informed us about my dad's condition, I was clueless. I turned to Google and discovered it was blood poisoning, a severe response to infection where the body attacks its own organs and tissues. Just weeks later, I realized this condition would lead to my father's death.Alongside my role forecasting weather for Wales Today, I've recently collaborated with BBC Wales' Week In Week Out programme to delve deeper into sepsis. We explored its devastating impact on lives and questioned whether hospitals are equipped to detect and combat it promptly. What I found was startling.Sepsis claims 44,000 lives annually in the UK, surpassing deaths from breast, bowel, and prostate cancer combined—enough to fill a large football stadium. The most terrifying aspect is that sepsis is a silent killer, striking with incredible speed. Regardless of age or fitness, anyone can fall victim.My father, Cliff, was 82, battling health issues including vascular dementia, necessitating care home support. He suffered from various infections leading up to his death. During Christmas 2014, at my sister Kathryn's house, I noticed his frailty and was overwhelmed with sadness, fearing it might be our last Christmas together.A devoted family man, my dad drove a petrol tanker for Esso. I fondly recall joining him in the cab as he made deliveries across south Wales, singing along to Johnny Cash and Kenny Rogers. He was passionate about boxing and football, often taking me and my brother to watch Cardiff City at Ninian Park.As I pursued my dream of becoming a meteorologist, sparked by the heat wave of 1976, my dad was my biggest supporter. He gifted me my first thermometer, took me to the Cardiff weather center, and later drove me to my Met Office interview in Bracknell. He took immense pride in my achievements, and even as his health declined, he watched my TV show Weatherman Walking, tearing up at the mention of my name.I miss my dad dearly, but I find solace in knowing he lived a full life surrounded by love, despite his health struggles. The stories I encountered while creating the documentary are heart-wrenching.Michelle Christopher's 17-year-old daughter, Chloe, passed away just weeks before my dad. Just before Christmas, she had cold and flu symptoms, Michelle recounted. On 30 December 2014, Chloe was at home with a friend while her mother cared for her grandmother nearby. Upon returning, Michelle found Chloe collapsed on the landing.Mam, I'm frightened, I don't feel well, Chloe said. Michelle dialed 999, but Chloe went into cardiac arrest while Michelle was on the call. Chloe's color drained… I had to lie her down and try to do CPR on her, and then she just went before us, she explained. To try to do CPR on your own daughter is unreal.The inquest revealed Chloe had an E. coli urine infection, leading to multi-organ failure and cardiac arrest. Sepsis was the cause of her death. Michelle is tormented by what ifs but insists there were no warning signs. One moment Chloe was planning a New Year's party, the next she was gone.Michelle is now committed to raising awareness of sepsis's rapid onset, emphasizing early detection within an hour of suspicion. Quick administration of antibiotics and intravenous fluids significantly improves survival chances.Despite her grief, Michelle campaigns with the UK Sepsis Trust to save lives. We just need to get the word out there, she said. If only we'd known, maybe Chloe would still be here.For the programme, I revisited the University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff, where my father passed away. Despite the staff's efforts, he was too ill to overcome sepsis. I spoke with medics about their strategies to combat sepsis. Cardiff University research indicates treatment varies across hospitals. I asked Wales' Health Secretary Vaughan Gething if a more coordinated approach is needed. He assured me it's under consideration.Jayne Carpenter, a 49-year-old nurse from Merthyr Tydfil, survived sepsis due to timely treatment, though her life was irrevocably changed. In May, she thought she had a cough, possibly a chest infection. Worsening symptoms led her to the out-of-hours service at Prince Charles Hospital in Merthyr.I went to GP out-of-hours and then woke up two-and-a-half months later, having nearly lost my life, she said. But I did lose my legs, my left arm, and the fingers on my right hand. Unbeknownst to Jayne, pneumonia had triggered sepsis. Surgeons amputated her limbs to halt the infection's spread.I had no real recollection of realizing I didn't have any limbs, she said. One of the nurses said I kept asking 'where's my hand?' Learning how ill she'd been seemed secondary to her survival. Jayne's positive outlook has driven her recovery. With intensive physiotherapy at Cardiff's Rookwood Hospital and support from her husband Rob and dog Harriet, she's rebuilding her life.Her passion for shoes endures as she adapts to prosthetics, and she's relearned to apply her makeup independently. Determined to return to work, she says, I see myself walking my dog on the beach. I want my life back. It was nearly taken away from me so suddenly. I want me back.The experiences of Jayne, Chloe, and their families highlight the critical need for sepsis awareness. It claimed my dad and countless others, leaving a trail of heartache. Though my dad and Chloe are gone, sharing our stories could prevent unnecessary deaths, honoring those we loved and lost, especially during this poignant time of year, Christmas, near their anniversaries.Derek Brockway: Understanding Why My Dad Died airs on BBC One Wales at 20:30 GMT on Monday, 28 November.

I turned to Google and found that it was blood poisoning, a strong reaction to an infection, when the body attacked its own organs and tissues, and I knew that this was going to lead to the death of my father. Along with my weather reporting for Wales Today, I've been working with the BBC Wales programme Week in, Week out, and we've been digging deeper into the subject of sepsis. I found something quite surprising. The worst thing about it is that it attacks suddenly and silently and there’s no time for the body to fight back. Every year, in the UK alone, septicaemia kills 44,000 people—more than breast, bowel, and prostate cancers combined—enough to fill a large stadium. My father, Cliff, was 82, had suffered from a vascular dementia which had put him in a nursing home, and I noticed his wanness during the Christmas season at my sister’s, and I felt saddened and apprehensive, feeling it might be our last Christmas together. During his last weeks he had had a number of infections. He was a boxing and football fan and took my brother and me to Ninian Park to watch the Blues. And when I was finally able to pursue my dream of becoming a meteorologist, which had been triggered by the 1976 heatwave, he was my greatest supporter. He gave me my first thermometer, took me to the weather centre in Cardiff and then drove me to my job interview at the Met Office in Bracknell. I miss my father terribly, but I console myself with the thought that he lived a full life, surrounded by love, despite his illness. I remember with affection joining him in the cab as he made the rounds in South Wales, singing with him to Johnny Cash and Kenny Rogers. The stories I heard during the making of the film were painful. On the 30th of December, Chloe Christopher, weeks before my father, was at home with a friend, while her mother was visiting her grandmother not far off. She died of a cold and a fever, so her mother told me. He was very proud of me and watched the program, The Weatherman Walking, to the end, shedding tears when he heard my name. "Mama, I'm scared, I don't feel good," Chloe said. Michelle, who had just returned, found her lying on the landing. She telephoned the ambulance, but while she was on the phone, Chloe's heart stopped. Chloe's color faded. The post-mortem examination revealed that she had died from a cholera urinaire, a bladder infection, which caused the failure of several organs and caused her to lose consciousness. The cause of death was the sepsis. Michelle was tormented by the “if onlys,” but she insists that there was no warning, that one minute Chloe was organizing a New Year’s Eve party, the next she was gone. I had to put her down and try to revive her, she explained. To revive one’s own daughter is unimaginable. For this programme I revisited the University Hospital of Wales, where my father died of septicaemia, despite the efforts of the staff. Despite her grief, Michelle is now involved in the Sepsis Trust, which saves lives. I spoke to doctors about their strategies against septicemia; I asked the Minister of Health in Wales, Vaughan Gething, if a more concerted action was needed. The University of Cardiff had shown that the treatment varies from hospital to hospital. “If we had known,” she said, “Chloe might still be with us.” In May she thought she had a cough, maybe a chest infection. She went to the out-of-hours doctor, and woke up two and a half months later nearly dead. She went for treatment, and it was a timely one, but her life was forever changed. “I do not remember knowing that I had no limbs,” she said to me. But she had lost her legs, her left arm and the fingers of her right hand. Finally, the pneumonia had given way to septicemia, and the doctors had amputated his limbs. “He assured me that he would investigate.” The fact that she was ill seemed to me secondary to her survival. Jayne and Chloe’s experiences illustrate the importance of raising awareness of septicaemia. Determined to return to work, with her husband Rob, her dog Harriet and the help of physiotherapy at Rookwood Hospital, she is slowly rebuilding her life. Her passion for shoes, adapted to prostheses, hasn’t gone, and she has taught herself to put on her own makeup. The programme is entitled: “Derek Brockway: Understanding Why My Father Died” and will be shown on BBC Wales on Monday, 28 November, at 22:30. I nearly had me for a moment, but I’m back. Chloe and my father are no longer with us. But our stories could prevent needless deaths, and would honor those we have loved and lost, especially at this mournful time of the year, when we celebrate the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ.

text: The Easter Rising was one of the most important, fundamental events in the history of Ireland. During a tumultuous six days in Dublin, republican insurgents launched a rebellion against British rule, resulting in over 450 deaths, thousands of injuries, and vast destruction in the city center from relentless artillery fire. This dramatic event was the story of the century for Ireland's press, yet few could publish it due to chaos, unreliable eyewitness accounts, and stringent restrictions by a British government in wartime mode.In this media blackout, a small weekly newspaper in County Fermanagh, the Impartial Reporter, outpaced larger dailies by delivering the first eyewitness account of the Easter Rising. Owned by William Copeland Trimble in 1916, the paper benefited from his son, William Egbert, being in Dublin when the insurrection erupted on April 24. His presence allowed the Impartial Reporter to publish on-the-ground reports by April 27.The outburst of rebellion in Dublin has astounded the country! the paper reported. It described the carefully-matured plans of the Sinn Feiners executed during a religious festival, with armed Sinn Fein volunteers seizing government buildings and points of vantage, virtually holding control of the chief portions of the city.Dr. Éamon Phoenix, head of history at Stranmillis College, Belfast, noted that William Egbert's firsthand insights provided the Impartial Reporter with a crucial scoop. He quickly tracked down people from Fermanagh caught in the fighting, including British troops, Phoenix explained. He was the only trained reporter on the ground able to send out reliable reports, giving the Impartial Reporter a first.Current editor Sarah Saunderson emphasized William Egbert, known as Bertie, had strong Dublin connections that aided his reporting. He studied law at Trinity College, Dublin, but after a fire at the paper's premises in 1901, he stayed to help with the family business, she said. His Dublin ties placed him perfectly to deliver an impressive scoop for the Impartial Reporter.Amidst the chaos, other newspapers struggled. In Dublin, the Irish Times couldn't distribute, and the Irish Independent's offices were damaged. Belfast papers knew of a serious state of affairs but couldn't publish details due to a lack of firsthand reports and the Defence of the Realm Act, which barred content likely to cause unrest.The Belfast Telegraph's headline on April 25 read Dublin isolated, yet it noted, we are precluded from publishing details. The News Letter reported the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland canceled a Belfast trip to manage the crisis in Dublin, adding, Up till the time of going to press no reports of the happenings in Dublin have come to hand.Dr. Phoenix explained, The first people in Belfast would have heard about the Rising when the viceroy didn't turn up on Easter Monday. A group waiting at the train station learned he was attending to an emergency after calling Dublin.By Thursday, the Belfast Telegraph finally reported on the situation, albeit without firsthand accounts like the Impartial Reporter, and cautiously stated, We hope these reports are correct but it is right to remember the difficulty in maintaining communications.The same day, the Belfast Telegraph attributed its story, Stamping Out Rebellion, to many Belfast people returning from Dublin. It criticized the Rising and its supporters, stating, It is a sad reflection on the Irish race that a very substantial body of ostensibly sane men could be misled by a parcel of frothy ranters.Public sentiment shifted in the days following the Rising, particularly after the execution of 16 leaders. Newspapers then freely covered Ireland's political turmoil. Yet, for one historic week in April, a small paper in Enniskillen led the charge in reporting the events that shook the nation.

text: Some doctors in England are being offered thousands of pounds to cut the number of patients being sent to hospital, an investigation has found. GP practices are receiving financial incentives to help local NHS groups limit patient referrals and cut costs, as revealed by the doctors' magazine Pulse. This initiative impacts appointments for scans and specialist consultations, including those for cancer patients. The British Medical Association criticized the incentives, calling them misguided.Pulse's investigation uncovered that at least nine clinical commissioning groups (CCGs) are offering payments to GP practices for meeting specific targets. For instance, Birmingham South Central CCG is providing over £11,000 to practices that reduce new outpatient attendances, follow-ups, A&E visits, and emergency admissions by 1% compared to 2014/15. These schemes, excluding cancer referrals, aim to incentivize best quality practice and drive improvements in the quality of primary medical care, according to a spokesperson from Birmingham South Central CCG. They emphasized that the priority is ensuring patients access necessary services when needed.Another CCG assured Pulse that it had thoroughly considered the full impact of the incentive scheme and was confident that there is no conflict of interest. Pulse noted that the General Medical Council, which regulates UK medical standards, had already reviewed one scheme after local GP leaders raised concerns. The magazine highlighted that initial hospital referrals for cancer should occur within two weeks of a GP suspecting the condition.Dr. Chand Nagpaul, chairman of the GPs committee of the British Medical Association, expressed on BBC Radio 4's Today programme that these schemes are a financial contaminant to the trust between patients and doctors. He stated, It's short-sighted and misguided of CCGs to introduce such mechanisms, as they may lead patients to question the motives behind GP referrals. We believe CCGs should implement clinical pathways to ensure appropriate patient referrals rather than using crude, salesman-like bonuses for numerical referral reductions.Dr. Peter Melton, a local GP and clinical chief officer for North East Lincolnshire CCG, which offers over £6,000 to practices reducing outpatient referrals to the lowest 25% level (including urgent cancer referrals) from 2014/15, defended the scheme. He explained that the CCG is already among the best in England for referring suspected cancer patients to consultants within two weeks. It's not about avoiding hospital referrals but focusing on better clinical and quality standards for patients, he said. The expectation is that practices will investigate more locally and monitor patients initially rather than automatically referring them to secondary care.BBC's Helen Briggs analyzed that the NHS is under pressure to achieve £22bn in efficiency savings by 2020. NHS leaders aim to reduce inappropriate patient referrals, especially when local care is possible. Clinical Commissioning Groups (CCGs), which plan and design local health services, are offering payments for meeting outpatient referral targets. With over 200 CCGs across England, Pulse found that at least nine are implementing such schemes, though the extent of this practice elsewhere is unclear. Critics argue that patients might miss essential care, while CCGs defend their actions as promoting good practice, not withholding necessary hospital treatment.In November, the NHS advisory board recommended nearly doubling the number of patients referred for cancer tests in England. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence warned that delays in symptom detection could cost thousands of lives annually. NHS England stated, We explicitly want to increase, not deter, appropriate referrals for cancer checks.Dr. Rosie Loftus of Macmillan Cancer Support described Pulse's findings as very worrying, highlighting an overstretched NHS lacking resources and support for GPs. NHS Lambeth Clinical Commissioning Group, which offers payments for practices moving towards the average referral rate, reiterated that the payment related to referral rates is a minor part of funding and not intended to prevent GPs from referring patients with clinical needs, including cancer patients.

text: A villain-turned-leading man of Bollywood, a bohemian at the feet of a hippy guru, a successful politician: Vinod Khanna was a man who lived many lives, writes Sudha G Tilak. Vinod Khanna, who passed away at 70, was a prominent figure in the second wave of Punjabi heroes, often referred to as Partition Punjabis, who dominated Bollywood. His roots traced back to Peshawar, now in Pakistan, from where his family relocated to India during the 1947 partition. The cinematic icons of that era were known for their dashing looks, unique mannerisms, and distinct styles, traits that Khanna embodied with the flair of 1970s cinema.Khanna's journey began in Mumbai, where he completed his college education. However, his passion for films, ignited during his school days, led him to pursue acting full-time. His debut came in 1968 with the film Man ka Meet. Film writer Jai Arjun Singh highlights Khanna's unconventional Bollywood trajectory, noting that he was the first modern hero who began his career with villainous roles. Singh remarks, Khanna's villainy was impressive as it combined his dashing looks with an edgy dangerous menace that made him impressive on screen. He was better at playing villain parts than the conventional Bollywood hero.While Dharmendra was the beefcake of Bollywood in the 1970s, the 1980s saw Amitabh Bachchan emerge as the angry young man. Yet, according to Mr. Singh, there was a period when Khanna was seen as a potential rival to Bachchan's stardom. The two shared the screen in several films, including the blockbuster Amar Akbar Anthony, where a memorable scene had Khanna overpowering Bachchan, leaving fans of the latter in disbelief. Diptakirti Chaudhuri, in his book on Bollywood, writes, It was inconceivable for me to imagine my hero getting beaten. Even by his elder brother in the film.Khanna's combination of dreamy eyes and a muscular physique propelled him to the top, allowing him to excel in action, thrillers, and romances. He reigned over Bollywood with hits like Mera Gaon Mera Desh, Gaddar, Imtihaan, Muqaddar ka Sikander, Inkaar, Amar Akbar Anthony, Qurbani, Kudrat, and Dayavan.However, in the 1980s, despite being a leading star and family man, Khanna chose to leave the film industry to join an ashram led by Rajneesh, a controversial spiritual guru popular among Westerners, in Pune. The tabloids dubbed him the Sexy Sanyasi, a nod to his ascetic lifestyle. In an interview, when asked whether he was a star or a sanyasi, he reflected, I am, I guess, a human being who does what feels right to him at the time, does what he really wants to do. Sure, it is easy to latch onto one thing, to be and do that all your life - but within you is a voice saying there must be something more to life. I look for that something more.After his spiritual retreat, Khanna's marriage ended, and he faded from the public eye. He later remarried and gradually returned to acting. In 1997, he ventured into politics, eventually serving as a member of parliament four times and even as a junior foreign minister.Khanna leaves behind his wife, daughters, and sons. His legacy endures as an actor who charted his own unique path in both Bollywood and life.

text: Fighting has eased in parts of Syria where a Russian-led initiative to halt the country's six-year war took effect from midnight, activists say. On Thursday, Russia unveiled a plan to establish four de-escalation zones in Syria, with the backing of Turkey and Iran. However, the main Syrian opposition group has expressed skepticism about the agreement's effectiveness.Meanwhile, reports from activists indicate that government aircraft have targeted central Hama province, with additional accounts of shelling and gunfire in various regions. The opposition's High Negotiations Committee (HNC) criticized the safe zones proposal on Friday, stating it lacks safeguards and compliance mechanisms. The HNC also rejected Iran as a guarantor of the deal.UN special envoy for Syria, Staffan de Mistura, emphasized to the BBC the significance of the agreement, highlighting that it involves three countries capable of enforcing it.
